profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:41:06.971+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Dìjì Dìyī Shénwǔ Shàng
Qí Gāozǔ Shénwǔ Huángdì,
xìng Gāo míng Huān,
zì Hèlùhún,
Bóhǎi Xiū rén yě.
Liùshìzǔ Yǐn,
Jìn Xuántú Tàishǒu.
Yǐn shēng Qìng,
Qìng shēng Tài,
Tài shēng Hú,
sānshì shì Mùróng shì.
Jí Mùróng Bǎo bài,
guó luàn,
Hú shuài zhòng guī Wèi,
wèi Yòujiāngjūn.
Hú shēng sì zǐ,
dìsān zǐ Mì,
shì Wèi wèizhì Shìyùshǐ,
zuòfǎ xǐjū Huáisuò Zhèn.
Mì shēng Huángkǎo Shù,
xìng tōngshuài,
bù shì jiāyè.
Zhùjū Báidào Nán,
shù yǒu chìguāng zǐqì zhī yì,
línrén yǐwéi guài,
quàn xǐjū yǐ bì zhī.
Huángkǎo yuē:
“Ān zhī fēi jí?”
Jū zhī zìruò.
Jí Shénwǔ shēng ér Huángbǐ Hán shì zū,
yǎng yú tóngchǎn jiěxù Zhènyù Duìwèi Jǐng jiā.
Shénwǔ jì lěishì běibiān,
gù xí qí sú,
suì tóng Xiānbēi.
Zhǎng ér shēncén yǒu dàdù,
qīngcái zhòngshì,
wèi háoxiá suǒ zōng.
Mù yǒu jīngguāng,
chángtóu gāoquán,
chǐ bái rú yù,
shǎo yǒu rénjié biǎo.
Jiā pín,
jí pìn Wǔmíng Huánghòu,
shǐ yǒu mǎ,
dé gěi zhèn wèi Duìzhǔ.
Zhènjiàng Liáoxī Duàn Cháng cháng qí Shénwǔ mào,
wèi yuē:
“Jūn yǒu kāngjì cái,
zhōng bù túrán.”
Biàn yǐ zǐsūn wèi tuō.
Jí guì,
zhuīzèng Cháng Sīkōng,
zhuó qí zǐ Níng yòng zhī.
Shénwǔ zì Duìzhǔ zhuǎn wèi Hánshǐ.
Cháng chéng yì guò Jiànxīng,
yúnwù zhòuhuì,
léishēng suí zhī,
bànhùn nǎi jué,
ruò yǒu shényìng zhě.
Měi xíng dàolù,
wǎnglái wú fēngchén zhī sè.
Yòu cháng mèng lǚ zhòng xīng ér xíng,
jué ér nèixǐ.
Wèi Hánshǐ liù nián,
měi zhì Luòyáng,
gěi Lìngshǐ Má Xiáng shǐ.
Xiáng cháng yǐ ròu dàn Shénwǔ,
Shénwǔ xìng bù lìshí,
zuò ér jìn zhī.
Xiáng yǐwéi màn jǐ,
chī Shénwǔ sìshí.
Jí zì Luòyáng huán,
qīngchǎn yǐ jiékè,
qīn gù guàiwèn zhī.
Dá yuē:
“Wú zhì Luòyáng,
sùwèi yǔlín xiāngshuài fén Lǐngjūn Zhāng Yí zhái,
cháotíng jù qí luàn ér bù wèn,
wèizhèng ruò cǐ,
shì kě zhī yě.
Cáiwù qǐ kě cháng shǒu xié?”
Zì shì nǎi yǒu chéngqīng tiānxià zhī zhì.
Yǔ Huáisuò Shěngshì Yúnzhōng Sīmǎ Zǐrú jí Xiùróng rén Liú Guì, Zhōngshān rén Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì wèi bēnzǒu zhī yǒu,
Huáisuò Hùcáoshǐ Sūn Téng, Wàibīngshǐ Hóu Jǐng yì xiāng yǒujié.
Liú Guì cháng dé yī báiyīng,
yǔ Shénwǔ jí Wèi Jǐng, Cài Jùn, Zǐrú, Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì děng liè yú Wòyě.
Jiàn yī chìtù,
měi bó zhé yì,
suì zhì Huízé.
Zé zhōng yǒu máowū,
jiāng bēnrù,
yǒu gǒu zì wūzhōng chū,
shì zhī,
yīng tù jù sǐ.
Shénwǔ nù,
yǐ míngdí shè zhī,
gǒu bì.
Wūzhōng yǒu èrrén chū,
chí Shénwǔ jīn shèn jí.
Qí mǔ liǎng mù máng,
yè zhàng hē qí èr zǐ yuē:
“Hé gù chù Dàjiā!”
Chū wèng zhōng jiǔ,
pēng yáng yǐ fàn kè.
Yīn zìyán shàn ànxiàng,
biàn mén zhū rén jiē guì,
ér zhǐhuī jù yóu Shénwǔ.
Yòu yuē:
“Zǐrú lìwèi xiǎn,
zhì bù shànzhōng.”
Fàn jìng chū,
xíng shù lǐ huán,
gēng fǎng zhī,
zé běn wú rénjū,
nǎi xiàng fēirén yě.
Yóu shì zhū rén yì jiā jìngyì.
Xiàochāng Yuánnián,
Róuxuán Zhèn rén Dù Luòzhōu fǎn yú Shànggǔ,
Shénwǔ nǎi yǔ tóngzhì cóng zhī.
Chǒu qí xíngshì,
sī yǔ Wèi Jǐng, Duàn Róng, Cài Jùn tú zhī,
bù guǒ ér táo,
wèi qí qí suǒ zhuī.
Wénxiāng jí Wèi Yǒngxī Hòu jiē yòu,
Wǔmíng Hòu yú niú shàng bàofù zhī.
Wénxiāng lǚ luò niú,
Shénwǔ wāngōng jiāng shè zhī yǐ juéqù.
Hòu hū Róng qiújiù,
lài Róng tòuxià qǔ zhī yǐ miǎn.
Suì bēn Gě Róng,
yòu wáng guī Ěrzhū Róng yú Xiùróng.
Xiān shì,
Liú Guì shì Róng,
shèng yán Shénwǔ měi,
zhì shì shǐ dé jiàn,
yǐ qiáocuì gù,
wèi zhī qí yě.
Guì nǎi wèi Shénwǔ gēngyī,
fù qiú jiàn yān.
Yīn suí Róng zhī,
yǒu èmǎ,
Róng mìng jiǎn zhī.
Shénwǔ nǎi bù jiā jībàn ér jiǎn,
jìng bù tí niè,
yǐ ér qǐ yuē:
“Yù èrén yì rúcǐ mǎ yǐ.”
Róng suì zuò Shénwǔ yú chuángxià,
bìng zuǒyòu ér fǎng shíshì.
Shénwǔ yuē:
“Wén gōng yǒu mǎ shí'èr gǔ,
sè bié wèi qún,
jiāng cǐ jìng hé yòng yě?”
Róng yuē:
“Dàn yán ěr yì.”
Shénwǔ yuē:
“Fāng tiānzǐ yúruò,
Tàihòu yínluàn,
nièchǒng shànmìng,
cháozhèng bù xíng,
yǐ Mínggōng xióngwǔ,
chéngshí fènfā,
tǎo Zhèng Yǎn, Xú Hè ér qīng dì cè,
bàyè kě jǔ biān ér chéng.
Cǐ Hèlùhún zhī yì yě.”
Róng dàyuè,
yǔ zì rìzhōng zhì yèbàn,
nǎi chū.
Zì shì měi cāncān jūn móu.
Hòu cóng Róng xǐ jù Bìngzhōu,
dǐ Yángzhōu yìrén Páng Cāngyīng,
zhǐ tuán jiāo zhōng.
Měi cóng wài guī,
zhǔrén yáowén xíng xiǎng dòngdì.
Cāngyīng mǔ shù jiàn tuán jiāo chìqì hèrán shǔ tiān.
Yòu Cāngyīng cháng yè yù rù,
yǒu qīngyī rén bá dāo chì yuē:
“Hé gù chù Wáng!”
Yán qì bù jiàn.
Shǐ yǐwéi yì,
mì zhān zhī,
wéi jiàn chì shé pán chuáng shàng,
nǎi yì jīngyì.
Yīn shā niú fēnròu,
hòu yǐ xiāng fèng.
Cāngyīng mǔ qiú yǐ Shénwǔ wèi yìzǐ.
Jí dézhì,
yǐ qí zhái wèi dì,
hào wèi Nánzhái.
Suī ménxiàng kāiguǎng,
tángyǔ chónglì,
qí běn suǒ zhù tuán jiāo,
yǐ shí è tú zhī,
liú ér bù huǐ,
zhì Wénxuān shí suì wèi gōng.
Jì ér Róng yǐ Shénwǔ wèi Qīnxìn Dūdū.
at that time resented Zhèng Yǎn and Xú Hé, who were pressuring Líng Tàihòu,
but he dared not stop them yet.
He secretly sent Ér Zhū Róng to raise troops and march inward.
Ér Zhū Róng took Shénwǔ as his vanguard.
When they reached Shàngdǎng,
Míngdì again secretly issued an edict to halt them.
When the Emperor suddenly collapsed (died),
Ér Zhū Róng then entered Luòyáng,
and intended to usurp the throne.
Shénwǔ remonstrated,
fearing he would not be listened to,
he requested that they cast a statue to divine the outcome.
The casting failed,
and Ér Zhū Róng stopped (the plan).
When Xiàozhuāng Dì was established,
because of his merit in settling the strategy (of succession),
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Tóngdī.
When Ér Zhū Róng attacked Gě Róng,
he ordered Shénwǔ to persuade seven separate bandit chiefs who had claimed kingship to surrender.
Later, he and the Acting Director Yú Huī defeated Yáng Kǎn at Tài Shān,
and soon after, he and Yuán Tiānmù defeated Xíng Gǎo at Jìnán.
He was repeatedly promoted to Third Garrison Chieftain,
and was always inside Ér Zhū Róng’s camp.
Ér Zhū Róng once asked his attendants,
"If one day I were gone,
who could lead the army?"
They all named Ér Zhū Zhào.
Ér Zhū Róng said:
"He can only command three thousand cavalry or fewer;
the only one capable of replacing me to lead the multitude is Hèlìuhún."
He then warned Ér Zhū Zhào, saying:
"You are no match for him;
you will eventually have your nose pierced by him (be humiliated and controlled)."
Consequently, he appointed Shénwǔ as the Administrator of Jìnzhōu.
Thereupon, Shénwǔ engaged in extensive accumulation of wealth,
and through Liú Guì, he bribed the influential people under Ér Zhū Róng,
thereby obtaining all their true intentions.
At that time, the horn in the provincial treasury spontaneously sounded without cause.
Shénwǔ found this strange.
Not long after, Xiàozhuāng executed Ér Zhū Róng.
When Ér Zhū Zhào prepared to raise troops from Jìnyáng to rush to Luòyáng,
he summoned Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ sent his Chief Clerk Sūn Téng to decline, citing that the Jiàng Shǔ and Fén Hú were planning rebellion,
and he could not abandon his post.
Ér Zhū Zhào resented this.
Sūn Téng returned to report.
Shénwǔ said:
"Zhào is raising troops to offend the sovereign;
he is a great bandit.
I cannot serve him for long."
From then on, he began to scheme against Ér Zhū Zhào.
When Ér Zhū Zhào entered Luòyáng,
he captured Emperor Xiàozhuāng and took him north.
When Shénwǔ heard of this,
he was greatly alarmed.
He again sent Sūn Téng to falsely congratulate Ér Zhū Zhào,
and secretly scouted the location of Emperor Xiàozhuāng,
intending to seize him and raise an army of righteousness,
but did not succeed.
He then used a letter to admonish Ér Zhū Zhào,
saying it was inappropriate to seize the Son of Heaven and thereby incur a bad reputation throughout the land.
Ér Zhū Zhào did not accept the advice,
and killed the Emperor.
He and Ér Zhū Shìlóng and others then established the Prince of Chángguǎng, Yè,
and changed the era name to Jiànmíng.
Shénwǔ was enfeoffed as the Duke of Píngyáng Commandery.
When Fèiyětóu Hédòulíng Bùfān entered Xiùróng,
threatening Jìnyáng,
Ér Zhū Zhào summoned Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ was about to go,
but Hèbá Yānguò'ér requested that he proceed slowly to wear Bùfān down.
Shénwǔ then intentionally delayed his journey repeatedly,
using the excuse that there were no bridges over the river and he could not cross.
Bùfān's army grew strong,
and Ér Zhū Zhào was defeated and fled.
Originally,
when Xiàozhuāng executed Ér Zhū Róng,
he knew that Ér Zhū Róng's faction would certainly harbor rebellious intentions,
so he had secretly commanded Bùfān to attack them from the rear.
After Bùfān defeated Ér Zhū Zhào and his allies,
his military strength grew daily.
Ér Zhū Zhào again requested aid from Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ inwardly schemed against Ér Zhū Zhào,
but also worried that Bùfān would be difficult to eliminate later.
Thus, he combined all forces with Ér Zhū Zhào to defeat Bùfān.
When Bùfān died,
Ér Zhū Zhào deeply appreciated Shénwǔ,
and swore to be his brother.
At that time, Ér Zhū Shìlóng, Ér Zhū Dùlǜ, and Ér Zhū Yànbó jointly controlled the court administration;
Ér Zhū Tiānguāng occupied Guānyòu;
Ér Zhū Zhào occupied Bīngzhōu;
Ér Zhū Zhòngyuǎn occupied Dōngjùn.
Each held military power and committed atrocities.
The world suffered greatly because of them.
The masses of Gě Róng flowed into Bìng and Sì, numbering over 200,000.
They were oppressed by the Qì Hú,
and all found life unendurable.
They rebelled twenty-six times, both large and small.
Half of them had been executed and exterminated,
yet banditry did not cease.
Zhào was troubled by this,
and sought counsel from Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ said:
“The remnants of the Six Garrisons’ rebellion
cannot all be killed.
It is advisable to select one of your Highness’s intimate confidants and secretly put him in charge of them.
If any commit an offense,
only punish their commander;
then the number of those punished will be small.”
Zhào said:
“Excellent.
Who is capable of this?”
Hèbá Yǔn was seated there at the time.
He recommended Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ punched him with his fist,
breaking one of his teeth,
and said:
“When Tiānzhù (Ěrzhū Róng) was alive,
you slaves submitted to orders like hawks and hounds.
Today, the stability of the realm rests with your Highness,
yet Ājūní dares to deceive his superiors by slandering his subordinates,
I request that he be executed.”
Zhào took Shénwǔ’s words as sincere,
and consequently entrusted the task to him.
Shénwǔ, knowing Zhào was drunk,
and fearing that he might become suspicious or change his mind after sobering up,
immediately went out.
He announced that he had been entrusted to command the provincial and garrison troops,
and ordered them to assemble east of the Fén River to receive orders.
He then set up his headquarters in the Yángqǔ River valley,
and arranged his divisions.
There was a man bursting into the military gate,
wearing a purple turban and robe.
He claimed to be Gěngyáng Yìzǐ,
and wished to serve among Shénwǔ’s attendants.
Upon investigation,
he was known for his strength;
he had once killed someone at the Bìngzhou marketplace by slapping them.
Shénwǔ therefore appointed him as a trusted aide.
The soldiers had long disliked Zhào but favored Shénwǔ,
so everyone came.
Not long after,
he again sent Liú Guì to petition Zhào,
stating that Bìng and Sì Provinces had suffered consecutive years of frost and drought,
and the surrendered households were digging up marmots to eat.
All of them had faces lacking the color of sustenance.
They were merely polluting the country's land.
He requested permission to lead them to Shāndōng to seek food,
and only deal with them once they were warm and well-fed.
Zhào followed his proposal.
His Chief Clerk, Mùróng Shàozōng, advised against it, saying:
“This must not be done.
Now the four directions are in turmoil,
and people harbor different ambitions.
Moreover, Gāo Gōng has heroic strategies,
and he commands a great army;
he will become impossible to handle.”
Zhào said:
“We made solemn vows before the incense burner;
what is there to worry about?”
Shàozōng said:
“Even blood brothers are difficult to trust in this manner,
let alone vows made over incense.”
At that time, Zhào’s immediate attendants had already received gold from Shénwǔ.
They consequently slandered Shàozōng, claiming he had an old feud with Shénwǔ.
Zhào then imprisoned Shàozōng and urged Shénwǔ to depart.
Shénwǔ then traveled from Jìnyáng out through Fǔkǒu Pass.
On the road, he encountered Xiāngjùn Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ, Ěrzhū Róng’s wife,
who was coming from Luòyáng.
She had 300 horses.
He seized them all and replaced them [with his own].
When Zhào heard this,
he released Shàozōng and consulted him.
Shàozōng said:
“He is still like an object in the palm of your hand.”
Thereupon, Zhào personally pursued Shénwǔ.
When he reached Xiāngyuán,
it happened that the Zhāng Shuǐ had suddenly flooded,
and the bridge was broken.
Shénwǔ bowed across the water and said:
“The reason I borrowed the Princess’s horses
was for no other purpose
than to prepare against bandits in Shāndōng.
Your Highness, having listened to the Princess’s words,
has personally come to grant me this pursuit.
If I cross the river and die now, I will not refuse,
but these men here will immediately rebel.”
Zhào declared that he had no such intention.
He then crossed the river on a swift horse,
sat with Shénwǔ beneath the tent,
offered his apologies,
and finally offered his knife and bowed his head,
asking Shénwǔ to strike him.
Shénwǔ wept loudly and said:
“Since Tiānzhù passed away,
upon whom else can Hèlùhún rely?
I wish your Highness ten thousand years of life,
so that I may exert my full strength in service.
Now outsiders have created division leading to this,
how can your Highness bear to utter such words again?”
Zhào threw the knife to the ground.
They then sacrificed a white horse and swore an oath,
vowing to be sworn brothers.
They stayed the night drinking.
Wèi Jǐng hid strong men, intending to seize Zhào.
Shénwǔ bit his arm to stop him, saying:
“If we kill him now,
his followers will certainly flee back and regroup.
Our soldiers are hungry and our horses are thin,
and we cannot withstand them.
If heroes should rise up,
the harm would be even greater.
It is better to let him go for now.
Although Zhào is physically robust and swift,
he is savage, cunning, and without strategy;
he is not worth worrying about.”
The next morning,
Zhào returned to his camp.
He summoned Shénwǔ again.
Shénwǔ was about to mount his horse to go to him,
but Sūn Téng grabbed his sleeve,
and he stopped.
Zhào shouted insults across the water,
and galloped back to Jìnyáng.
Niàn Xián, Zhào’s confidant, commanded the surrendered households and their families in a separate camp.
Shénwǔ pretended to befriend him.
He examined Niàn Xián’s scabbard,
then took the knife and killed one of Niàn Xián’s followers.
All the followers immediately dispersed.
Thereupon, all the officers and masses were pleased,
and were doubly willing to join and follow him.
Previously,
during the Wèi Zhēnjūn era, internal scholars presented a memorial stating that Shàngdǎng possessed the ‘Aura of the Son of Heaven,’
located, they said, at Dàwáng Shān in Húguān.
Tàiwǔ Dì therefore made a southern tour to suppress this omen.
He piled up stones into three mounds (fēng),
and severed the Fènghuáng Shān to the north,
thereby destroying its form.
Later, those Shàngdǎng people living in Jìnyáng
called their district the Shàngdǎng Fāng.
Shénwǔ actually lived there.
When undertaking this campaign,
he stopped for sixty days at Dàwáng Shān before advancing.
When preparing to leave Fǔkǒu Pass,
he doubled his restrictions,
not allowing the slightest article
to be taken or violated.
When about to pass through wheat fields,
Shénwǔ always dismounted and led his horse on foot.
When people near and far heard of this,
they all praised Gāo Yítóng for leading his troops with such order and strictness,
and increasingly committed their loyalty to him.
He then advanced,
and encamped at Yè.
He requested provisions from the Inspector of Xiāng Zhōu, Liú Dàn,
but Dàn did not supply them.
There was a grain transport supplying military rations.
Shénwǔ took it himself.
In the second month of the first year of Wèi Pǔtài (531 CE),
Shénwǔ led his army to camp at Xìndū.
Gāo Gān and Fēng Lóngzhī opened the gates to await him,
and consequently, he occupied Jìzhōu.
In this month,
Ěrzhū Dùlǜ deposed Yuán Yè and established Emperor Jiémǐn,
hoping to keep Shénwǔ under control.
In the third month,
he then informed Emperor Jiémǐn,
that Shénwǔ should be enfeoffed as the King of Bóhǎi,
and an envoy was dispatched to summon him for an audience.
Shénwǔ declined.
On the *Guǐsì* day of the fourth month,
he was further granted the titles of Grand Director of the Eastern Circuits (Dōngdào Dà Xíngtái) and Chief Elder of the First Garrison People.
Páng Cāngyīng defected from Tàiyuán and came to him;
Shénwǔ appointed him as an aide (Xíngtái Láng),
and soon thereafter made him the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Ānzhōu.
Shénwǔ himself proceeded toward the region east of the mountains (Shāndōng),
training soldiers and repairing armor,
and prohibiting looting and pillaging.
The common people pledged their loyalty to him.
He then fabricated a letter,
stating that Ěrzhū Zhào was planning to assign the men of the Six Garrisons to the Qìhú tribe to serve as his personal troops (bùqǔ);
the troops were all distressed and resentful.
He also forged a tally/order (fú) from Bìngzhōu,
calling up troops to suppress Bùluòjī.
He mobilized ten thousand men,
and was about to send them off,
when Sūn Téng and Wèi Jǐng requested that they be allowed to stay for five days,
which happened twice.
Shénwǔ personally escorted them to the outskirts (of the city),
wiping away tears as he bade them farewell.
Everyone wailed loudly,
their cries shaking the earth.
Shénwǔ then explained to them, saying:
"We are all guests who have lost our homelands;
by righteous principle, we are one family.
I did not expect those above to summon you thus.
If you go straight West, you will surely die;
if you delay the military deadline, you will also die;
and if you are assigned to the state troops, you will also die.
What should be done!"
The troops replied:
"There is only one option: rebellion."
Shénwǔ said:
"Rebellion is a pressing concern,
but you must select one person to be your leader."
The troops wished to enthrone Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ said:
"Your fellow countrymen are difficult to control.
Did you not see Gě Róng?
Although he had a million men,
because he lacked laws and discipline,
he eventually perished.
If you now take me as your leader,
things must be different from before:
you must not cheat the Hàn people (Hàn’ér);
you must not violate military orders;
if you submit your lives and deaths to my command, then it is acceptable.
Otherwise, I cannot act, lest I become a laughingstock to the world."
The troops all bowed their heads to the ground,
vowing that life and death were his to command.
Shénwǔ said, "Since this is unavoidable,"
the next day,
he slaughtered an ox to feast the soldiers,
and explained the intention to suppress Ěrzhū.
Fēng Lóngzhī stepped forward and said:
"This is a moment that occurs only once in a thousand years,
and the whole world rejoices in this fortune."
Shénwǔ replied:
"To punish the bandits
is a great righteousness;
to save the age
is a great endeavor.
Although I lack military prowess,
I shall pursue this even unto death.
How dare I shirk this responsibility?"
the righteous cause was established at Xìndū,
but they had not yet openly defied the Ěrzhū Shì.
When Lǐ Yuánzhōng and Gāo Gān pacified Yīnzhōu,
they brought the head of Ěrzhū Yǔshēng to report.
Shénwǔ patted his chest,
saying:
"Today, the rebellion is decided!"
Thereupon, he appointed Yuánzhōng as the Inspector of Yīnzhōu (Yīnzhōu Cìshǐ).
At this time, since military might had been established,
he presented a memorial denouncing the crimes of the Ěrzhū Shì.
Shìlóng and others secretly suppressed the memorial and did not submit it.
In the eighth month,
Ěrzhū Zhào attacked and captured Yīnzhōu,
and Lǐ Yuánzhōng came to defect.
Sūn Téng believed that since the imperial court was cut off,
if they did not provisionally establish a Son of Heaven (Emperor),
the hopes of the populace would have nothing to focus upon.
In the tenth month, on the day Rén Yín,
they enthroned Lǎng, the Prefect of Bóhǎi (Bóhǎi Tàishǒu) and son of Zhāngwǔ Wáng Róng, as Emperor.
The era name was Zhōngxīng,
and this was the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì).
At that time, Dùlǜ and Zhòngyuǎn's forces were quartered at Yángpíng,
and Ěrzhū Zhào joined them.
Shénwǔ employed the strategy of Dòu Tài,
spreading counter-espionage,
and Dùlǜ and Zhòngyuǎn retreated without fighting.
Shénwǔ then defeated Zhào at Guǎng'ē.
In the eleventh month,
he attacked Yè.
Liú Dàn, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ), defended the city resolutely.
Shénwǔ raised earthen mounds,
dug tunnels,
and set up large pillars frequently,
burning them all at once,
causing the city wall to sink into the ground.
Má Xiáng was then the Magistrate of Tāngyīn (Tāngyīn Lìng).
Shénwǔ called out to him, saying:
"Má Dū!"
Xiáng fled in shame.
In the first month of the first year of Yǒngxī, on the day Rén Wǔ,
he took Yè city
and occupied it.
The Deposed Emperor promoted Shénwǔ to Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng), Pillar of the State Grand General (Zhùguó Dà Jiāngjūn), and Grand Tutor (Tàishī).
At this time, the righteous cause was established in Qīngzhōu.
The Grand Military Governor (Dà Dūduī) Cuī Língzhēn and the Grand Military Governor (Dà Dūduī) Gěng Xiáng both sent envoys to surrender and submit.
Liú Guì, acting head of Fénzhōu affairs, abandoned the city and came to surrender.
In the intercalary third month,
Ěrzhū Tiānguāng came from Cháng'ān,
Zhào from Bìngzhōu,
Dùlǜ from Luòyáng,
and Zhòngyuǎn from Dōngjùn.
They all converged at Yè.
Their combined forces numbered two hundred thousand.
They camped alongside the Huán Shuǐ.
Jiémǐn appointed Zhǎngsūn Chéngyè as the Grand Director of the Traveling Chancellery (Dà Xíngtái Zǒngdū) to oversee them.
Shénwǔ ordered Fēng Lóngzhī to guard Yè,
while he himself went out and established a camp at Zǐ Mò.
At that time, his cavalry numbered fewer than two thousand,
and his infantry was less than thirty thousand.
The imbalance of forces was great.
So he formed a circular battle array at Hán Líng.
He chained oxen and donkeys together to block the route of retreat,
whereupon all the officers and soldiers became resolved to fight to the death,
attacking them from four sides.
Ěrzhū Zhào reproached Shénwǔ for betraying him.
Shénwǔ said:
"Originally, we exerted ourselves
to jointly assist the imperial house.
Where is the Emperor now?"
Zhào said:
"Yǒng'ān wrongly harmed Tiānzhù;
I am merely taking revenge."
Shénwǔ said:
"I personally heard Tiānzhù's plan in the past.
You were standing right outside the door.
How can you say you were not part of the rebellion?
Moreover, the sovereign killed his minister;
what revenge is there to take?
Today, our ties of righteousness are broken."
They then engaged in battle
and utterly defeated them.
Ěrzhū Zhào beat his chest before Mùróng Shàozōng and said:
"By not following your words,
I have come to this."
He was about to flee with light baggage.
Shàozōng reversed the flags and blew the horns,
gathering the scattered troops,
forming a military formation, and heading west.
Gāo Jìshì pursued the rout with seven horsemen.
Crossing Yěmǎ Gāng,
he encountered Zhào.
Gāo Áng looked for him but could not see him,
and cried, saying:
"My brother is lost!"
Late in the night,
Jìshì returned,
his sleeves covered in blood.
Hú Sīchūn covered twice the distance to preemptively occupy Hé Qiáo (River Bridge).
Originally, in the tenth month of the first year of Pǔtài,
Jupiter (Suì Xīng), Mars (Yíng Huò), Saturn (Zhèn Xīng), and Venus (Tài Bái) gathered in the constellation Zī (Mouth).
The color of the constellation Cān (Orion) was exceptionally bright.
The Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ) divined that
a true king would arise.
At this time,
Shénwǔ rose up at Xìndū,
and now he had defeated Zhào and the others.
In the fourth month,
Hú Sīchūn captured Tiānguāng and Dùlǜ and sent them to Luòyáng.
Zhǎngsūn Chéngyè sent Military Governors (Dūduī) Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì and Zhāng Huān into Luòyáng.
They captured Shìlóng and Yànbó and executed them.
Zhào fled to Bìngzhōu.
Zhòngyuǎn fled to Liángzhōu,
where he subsequently died.
Since the wicked rebels were now eliminated,
the court was joyful.
Previously, in the month before the battle,
Zhāng Shào, a man from Zhāngwǔ, was suddenly taken by several horsemen at night to climb over the city wall.
He was brought before a great general,
who ordered Shào to serve as a guide for the army toward Yè.
The general said he was assisting the one who had received the mandate to eliminate the cruel bandits.
When Shào looked back,
the troops were countless
and moved swiftly and silently.
When they approached Yè,
Shào was released.
On the day of the battle,
the soldiers of the Ěrzhū Shì saw troops and horses merging from all four sides outside the formation.
This was the aid of the gods.
After this, Shénwǔ reached Luòyáng.
He deposed Jiémǐn and the Zhōngxīng ruler and established Xiàowǔ.
After Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,

he granted Shénwǔ the titles of Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng), Pillar of Heaven Grand General (Tiānzhù Dà Jiāngjūn), Grand Tutor (Tàishī), and Hereditary Inspector of Dìngzhōu (Shìxí Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ).
The increased fiefdom, combined with his previous holdings, totaled one hundred fifty thousand households.
Shénwǔ declined the title of Tiānzhù
and reduced the number of households by fifty thousand.
On the day Rén Chén,
he returned to Yè.
The Emperor of Wèi (Wèi Dì) held a farewell banquet for him at Gānfǔ Shān,
and they parted holding hands.
In the seventh month, on the day Rén Yín,
Shénwǔ led his army north to attack Ěrzhū Zhào.
Fēng Lóngzhī said:
"The Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Hú Sīchūn, Hèbá Shèng, Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì, and others formerly served the Ěrzhū clan.
They all universally turned against them.
Now they are in the capital
and greatly favored and trusted.
They will surely cause calamity and strife."
Shénwǔ considered this profoundly true.
He then sent Tiānguāng and Dùlǜ back to the capital
and had them executed.
He then entered through Fǔkǒu.
Ěrzhū Zhào thoroughly plundered Jìnyáng
and fled north to defend Xiùróng.
Bìngzhōu was pacified.
Shénwǔ considered Jìnyáng strategically defensible on four sides,
so he established the Grand Chancellor's Residence (Dà Chéngxiàng Fǔ) there and made it his fixed abode.
After Ěrzhū Zhào reached Xiùróng,
he divided his troops to guard the passes,
constantly raiding and marauding.
Shénwǔ announced his intention to attack him,
mobilizing and halting his army several times,
causing Zhào's vigilance to slacken.
Shénwǔ calculated that Zhào would be hosting a banquet at the start of the year.
He sent Dòu Tài with elite cavalry to speed toward him.
They traveled three hundred *lǐ* in one day and one night.
Shénwǔ followed with the main army.
In the first month of the second year,
Dòu Tài suddenly arrived at Ěrzhū Zhào's camp.
The soldiers were resting idly due to the banquet.
When they suddenly saw Tài's army,
they fled in terror.
The pursuit defeated them at Chìhóng Lǐng.
Zhào hanged himself.
Shénwǔ personally attended and gave him a lavish burial.
Mùróng Shàozōng, taking the wife and children of Ěrzhū Róng and the remaining forces, defended Wūtū Chéng.
He surrendered.
Shénwǔ, based on their former ties of righteousness,
treated him exceedingly well.
Shénwǔ entered Luò,
the Area Commanders (Dūdū) Qiáo Níng and Zhāng Zǐqī, subordinates of Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn, surrendered from Huátái.
Shénwǔ, believing they had aided the rebellion,
and frequently repeated their perfidy,
had them both executed.
Hú Sīchūn consequently felt insecure internally.
He then, along with the Prince of Nányáng, Yuán Bǎojù, and the Martial Guard Generals (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn) Yuán Pí, Wèi Guāng, and Wáng Sīzhèng, denounced Shénwǔ to the Wèi Dì.
The Palace Attendant (Shèrén) Yuán Shìbì also reported that Shénwǔ had shown extreme disrespect when receiving imperial edicts.
Therefore, the Wèi Dì was inwardly disloyal (or divided) toward Hèbá Yuè.
Previously, during the time of Xiàomíng,
in Luò, people said that two 'Bá' were striking each other,
and the popular saying went:
“The Copper Bá strikes the Iron Bá,
the Yuán clan’s lineage will soon end.”
Those fond of omens took the two 'Bá' to mean Tuòbá and Hèbá,
signifying that both were about to decline and fail.
At that time, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Gāo Gān secretly reported to Shénwǔ,
speaking of the Wèi Dì's divided heart.
Shénwǔ sealed the report and presented it (to the Emperor).
The Wèi Dì killed him.
He further sent Pān Shàoyè, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dōng Xúzhōu, with a secret edict instructing the Prefect (Tàishǒu) of Chánglè, Páng Cāngyīng, to kill his younger brother, Āng.
Āng had previously heard that his older brother had died.
He stabbed a pillar with his spear,
and ambushed strong soldiers to seize Shàoyè on the road.
He found the imperial edict inside the collar of his robe,
and came to surrender.
Shénwǔ embraced his head,
and wept, saying:
“The Son of Heaven unjustly murdered the Sīkōng!”
He immediately sent someone with white martial banners to console his family members.
At that time, Gān’s second younger brother, Shèn, was in Guāngzhōu.
His administration was severe and fierce,
and he also allowed his subordinates to extort bribes.
The Wèi Dì ordered him to be replaced.
Shèn, hearing of the calamity,
intended to flee to Liáng.
His attendants said:
“Your Lord’s family has great merit,
surely they will not extend the trouble to the brothers.”
He then put on worn clothes and pushed a deer cart back to Bóhǎi.
Meeting an envoy,
he also came to surrender.
Following this, a rift formed between the Wèi Dì and Shénwǔ.
The Āzhìluó tribe had regularly paid tribute before the Zhèngguāng era.
Since the Wèi court became entangled in many affairs,
they had all rebelled.
Shénwǔ sent envoys to invite them back,
and they immediately attached themselves (to him).
Prior to this,
an edict declared that since the bandits and rebels were pacified,
the Traveling Secretariat (Xíngtái) should be abolished.
Now, at this time,
because of the surrender of the different foreign tribes,
Shénwǔ was again invested as Grand Traveling Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái),
and allowed to handle matters as circumstances required.
Shénwǔ constantly bestowed grain and silks upon them.
Councilors thought this was a useless expenditure of resources,
but Shénwǔ did not heed them,
comforting and placating them as before.
Their chiefs, such as Tǔchén, were grateful,
and all followed his commands.
They rescued Cáo Ní,
captured Mòqí Shòuluògān,
and were greatly utilized by Shénwǔ.
The Fèiyětóu tribesmen west of the river (Héxī), led by Hédòulíng Yīlì, resided in Hé Chí.
Relying on the natural defenses, they gathered their masses.
Shénwǔ sent his Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) Hóu Jǐng repeatedly to invite them, but they refused to comply.
Annals of the Emperor, Second Chapter, Shénwǔ Section II
In the first year of Tiānpíng, the first month, on the Rénchén day,
Shénwǔ marched west against the Fèiyětóu tribesman Hédòulíng Yīlì in Héxī,
and annihilated him.
He relocated his tribe to Hédōng.
In the second month,
the nine-story pagoda (fútú) of Yǒngníng Sì suffered a disaster (a fire).
Subsequently, a man arrived from Dōnglái,
saying that people near the sea had all seen it in the middle of the ocean.
Soon after, mist arose and it vanished.
Interpreters believed that the intention of Heaven was as follows:
Since Yǒngníng suffered a disaster,
Wèi would know no peace (Bù níng).
Flying into the Eastern Sea (Dōnghǎi),
Bóhǎi would respond.
Since the Wèi Dì had already formed a different scheme,
the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Fēng Lóngzhī spoke privately with Sūn Téng.
Lóngzhī had recently lost his wife,
and the Wèi Dì intended to give his sister to him as wife.
Téng did not fully believe this,
and inwardly resented Lóngzhī.
He leaked the conversation to Hú Sīchūn.
Hú Sīchūn reported this to the Wèi Dì.
Furthermore, Sūn Téng had entered the palace bureau bearing arms,
and presumptuously killed a Censor (Yùshǐ).
Both fled and came to surrender.
They claimed that the Wèi Dì had publicly beaten the Palace Attendant (Shèrén) Liáng Xù.
The Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Insignia (Guānglù Shàoqīng), Yuán Zǐgān, bared his arm and struck him (Liáng Xù's abuser),
and said to Téng:
“Tell your King Gāo (Gāo Wáng)
that the punches of the Yuán family children are exactly like this.”
The General Who Leads the Army (Lǐngjūn) Lóu Zhāo pleaded illness and returned to Jìnyáng.
The Wèi Dì then made Hú Sīchūn concurrently Lǐngjūn.
He divided the placement of area commanders (Dūjiàng) and various Governors (Cìshǐ) in Hénán and Guānxī.
Yuán Zhì, the Prince of Huàshān, was in Xúzhōu.
Shénwǔ sent Dǐ Zhēn to seize his seals and tallies (authority).
Hán Xián, the Governor of Jiànzhōu, and Cài Jùn, the Governor of Jìzhōu, were both associates of Shénwǔ.
The Wèi Dì feared them.
Therefore, he abolished Jiànzhōu to remove Xián,
and sent the Palace Deputy Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi) Qí Jùn to investigate Jùn’s crimes,
appointing Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì, who held the Kāifǔ title, to Jìzhōu.
Jùn resisted this,
and the Wèi Dì became extremely angry.
In the fifth month, an imperial decree was issued,
stating that he would campaign against Gōuwú,
mobilizing the troops from the various prefectures in Hénán,
increasing the palace guards,
and guarding the Hé Qiáo (River Bridge).
In the sixth month, on the Dīngsì day,
the Wèi Dì secretly issued an edict to Shénwǔ, saying:
“Since Yǔwén Hēidá pacified and crushed Qín and Lǒng,
he has made many unreasonable demands.
If he makes any treacherous moves,
strategic planning will be necessary.
However, his memorials have not yet shown complete disobedience,
and a direct campaign would be too sudden.
Therefore, I summoned the various ministers
to discuss whether it was permissible.
All agreed that we should falsely claim a southern campaign
and impose martial law inside and outside the capital.
Firstly, to guard against unforeseen trouble from Hēidá,
secondly, to overawe Wú and Chǔ.”
At this time, the Wèi Dì was preparing to attack Shénwǔ,
and Shénwǔ had already deployed his generals and commanders,
fearing suspicion.
Thus, this edict was issued.
Shénwǔ then memorialized, saying:
“Jīngzhōu connects the barbarian tribes (Mán Zuǒ),
and is intimately close to the capital region.
Guānlǒng, relying on its distance,
is about to enact a rebellious scheme.
Your servant has secretly mustered thirty thousand troops,
intending to cross from Hédōng;

I have also sent Shèdí Gān, the Governor of a prefecture, Guō Qióng, the Governor of Yíngzhōu, Húlǜ Jīn, the Governor of Fénzhōu, and the former Martial Guard General (Qián Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn) Péng Lè to command forty thousand troops,
to cross from the Láiwéijīndù Ford;

I have sent the General Who Leads the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn) Lóu Zhāo, Dòu Tài, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Yáo Xióng, the former Governor of Yíngzhōu, and Gāo Lóngzhī, the Governor of Bìngzhōu, to command fifty thousand troops,
to campaign against Jīngzhōu;

I have sent Wèi Jǐng, the Governor of Jìzhōu, Gāo Áocáo, the former Governor of Jìzhōu, Cài Jùn, the Governor of Jìzhōu, and Fēng Lóngzhī, the former Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), to command seventy thousand Shāndōng troops and fifty thousand cavalry,
to campaign against the lower Yángzi region (Jiāng Zuǒ).
All their respective departments have been instructed
to humbly await orders.”
The Wèi Dì realized Shénwǔ’s deception,
and thus revealed Shénwǔ’s memorial,
ordering all officials to discuss it,
intending to halt all of Shénwǔ’s armies.
Shénwǔ then gathered the local subordinates in the prefecture,
ordering them to discuss the matter extensively,
and subsequently sent a memorial back to report their findings.
He then used an oath to affirm his loyalty, saying:
“Your servant has been estranged by sycophants and flatterers.
If Your Majesty should suddenly grant credence to these suspicions,
the crime of madness
will be pursued as it was during Ěrzhū's time.
If your servant does not exert all sincerity and devotion,
daring to betray Your Majesty,
then may I suffer heavenly calamity,
and my descendants be utterly destroyed.
If Your Majesty will put faith in my true heart,
and keep the weapons still,
I wish that one or two of these treacherous officials be weighed and expelled.”
On the Xīnwèi day,
the Emperor again recorded the consensus of the civil and military officials in the capital to reply to Shénwǔ,
ordering the Palace Attendant (Shèrén) Wēn Zǐshēng to draft the edict.
Zǐshēng hesitated and did not dare to compose it immediately.
The Emperor leaned on a camp stool,
drew his sword, and changed color (became angry).
Zǐshēng then drafted the edict, which said: “Previously, I offered my heartfelt thoughts,
sending them far away to show the King (Shénwǔ).
I sincerely hoped that we could both understand and empathize with each other,
yet dishonest people have created internal estrangement.
Recently, Sūn Téng abruptly went
to you.
This caused those who heard of it to suspect a conspiracy,
so I sent the Palace Deputy Censor-in-Chief Qí Jùn to fully explain my intentions.
Now I have received the King’s memorial,
the words of his oath are sincere and poignant.
Thinking it over
repeatedly,
there are still things I do not understand.
Regarding my unworthy self,
I encountered the King's military strategy.
Without the exertion of a single blade,
I sat and became the Son of Heaven.
As the saying goes, ‘Those who gave birth to me are my parents;
those who made me noble are Gāo
Your Highness (Wáng).
Now, if I turn against Your Highness without cause,
planning to attack and suppress you,
then let me and my descendants
suffer the consequences of the oath I swore to Your Highness.
Heaven and Earth (Huángtiān Hòutǔ)
truly hear these words.
Recently, I worried that Yǔwén might cause trouble,
and Hèbá Shèng might respond to him.
Therefore, I prepared strictly,
wishing to act as mutual support (shēngyuán) with Your Highness.
Yǔwén’s envoys today are constantly visible,
but observing
his actions,
there are no unusual signs.
Hèbá is in the south;
he expands the borders
and renders meritorious service to the state.
I believe he cannot be blamed.
If Your Grace wishes to divide and suppress [territories],
what reason
would you use?
The Southeast has been unsubmissive
for a long time.
Since the previous court,
it has been set aside (beyond consideration).
Today, the households (hùkǒu) in the realm are reduced by half;
it is not appropriate to exhaust our military forces and resources.
Since I (Zhèn) am ignorant and dim-witted,
I do not know who these sycophantic people (nìngrén) are.
Please list their names
so that I may know them.
I heard that Kùdí Gān said to Your Highness:
"Originally, we wanted
to take someone weak and pliable as ruler.
Your Highness installed this adult ruler (cháng jūn) without cause,
making him uncontrollable.
Now, just march for fifteen days,
and you can certainly depose him,
and install
someone else."
Such discussions
naturally come from meritorious individuals among Your Highness's ranks;
how could they come from the mouths of sycophantic officials?
Last year Fēng Lóngzhī rebelled,
and this year Sūn Téng fled.
You did not punish
them or send them back.
Who does not blame Your Highness?
Since Téng was the initiator of the trouble,
he showed no shame or fear.
If Your Highness serves the ruler with utter sincerity,
why did you not behead these two and send their heads over?
Although Your Highness reported that you planned to move
west,
yet your four armies are all advancing.
Some intend to cross south toward Luòyáng,
and others intend to reach Jiāngzuǒ in the east.
Even those who speak of this should be surprised at themselves;
how can those who hear it not be suspicious?
If Your Highness maintains sincerity and is unwavering,
dwelling peacefully in the north,
even if I had a million troops here,
I would ultimately have no intention of scheming against you.
Should Your Highness happen to believe evil and abandon righteousness,
raising your banner and pointing
south,
even if I had neither horse nor chariot wheel,
I would still wish to fight to the death with bare fists.
I (Zhèn) am inherently lacking in virtue,
but Your Highness has already installed me.
The common people, being ignorant,
might say this was truly acceptable.
If I were plotted against by others,
it would expose my wickedness.
But suppose I am killed by Your Highness,
imprisoned, disgraced, and shattered,
I would have absolutely no lasting regret.
Why?
Since Your Highness was
supported by virtue
and installed by righteousness,
if you suddenly betray virtue and abandon righteousness,
the fault will then have a definite place to rest.
Originally, I hoped that ruler and subject would be one entity,
like matching tallies (fúqì).
I did not anticipate that today we would become separated
and alienated to this extent.
An ancient saying goes:
"If a Yuè person shoots me,
I laugh and talk about it;
if my older brother shoots me,
I weep and talk about it."
Since I (Zhèn) am close to Your Highness,
our bond is like that of brothers.
Therefore, I throw down my brush, beat my breast,
and cannot help but sigh mournfully.
Initially,
Shénwǔ, when planning to move north from the capital (Jīngshī),
believed that since Luòyáng had long suffered devastation and chaos,
its imperial aura (wángqì) was fully decayed.
Although it had the defenses of mountains and rivers,
its territory was restricted and narrow,
inferior to Yè.
He requested the relocation of the capital.
The Emperor of Wèi said:
"Gāozǔ established the capital (dǐng) on the Hé-Luò [Rivers],
making it the foundation for eternity.
The planning and establishment of its institutions
were completed only by Shìzōng.
Since Your Highness has rendered service to the state and altars (shèjì),
you should adhere to the precedent of Tàihé."
Shénwǔ received the imperial order,
but later schemed again regarding this matter.
He dispatched three thousand cavalry to garrison Jiànxīng,
reinforced the troops in Hédōng and Jìzhōu,
detained boats on the Báigōu river, preventing them from heading toward Luò[yáng],
and directed the various prefectures to purchase and collect grain (sù) to be transported into Yèchéng.
The Emperor of Wèi again commanded Shénwǔ, saying:
"If Your Highness wishes to satisfy public sentiment
and suppress public discussion,
the only way is to recall the troops in Hédōng,
dismiss the garrison at Jiànxīng,
send back the grain from Xiāngzhōu,
recall the army from Jìzhōu,
order Cài Jùn to be relieved of his post,
and make Dǐ Zhēn leave Xú[zhōu].
Stop the fighting and disband the horses,
and let everyone attend to their household affairs.
If grain provisions are needed,
I will separately send provisions.
Then slanderers will be silenced,
and suspicion and regret will not arise.
Let Your Highness rest easy in Tàiyuán,
and I (Zhèn) will rule peacefully in Jīng-Luò.
I will never lift my foot to cross the Yellow River (Hé),
or point weapons at you.
If Your Highness turns your horse’s head south
and questions the weight of the tripod (wèn dǐng) [i.e., challenges imperial authority],
though I (Zhèn) lack military ability,
I will be unable to stop myself;
I will certainly devise a strategy involving ten thousand deaths for the sake of the altars of state (shèjì) and the imperial ancestors (zōngmiào).
The decision rests with Your Highness;
it is not for me (Zhèn) to settle.
To stop building a mountain when only lacking one basket of earth (wèi shān zhǐ kuì)—
I regret this for your sake."
The Emperor of Wèi at that time appointed Rèn Xiáng as Acting Minister of the Left (Jiān Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè),
and granted him the rank of Kāifǔ.
Xiáng abandoned his post and fled to Héběi,
where he occupied a commandery (jùn) awaiting Shénwǔ.
The Emperor of Wèi then ordered that civil and military officials who had come from the north could choose whether to stay or leave.
He issued an edict enumerating Shénwǔ’s crimes
and made preparations for a northern campaign (Běifá).
Shénwǔ also reined in his horse and proclaimed, saying:
"When I (Gū) encountered Ěrzhū seizing power,
I raised the standard of righteousness throughout the realm (sìhǎi),
supported the sovereign,
with loyalty manifest to gods and men (yōumíng).
Unexpectedly, Hú Sī Chūn fabricated slander against me,
treating my sincere integrity as the source of rebellion.
In the past, Zhào Yǎng raised the army of Jìnyáng
to execute the evil men around the ruler.
Now, in marching south,
I merely intend to execute Chūn."
He appointed Gāo Áng as vanguard,
and said:
"If I had followed the words of the Sīkōng,
how could this action today have happened?"
Sīmǎ Zǐrú replied to Shénwǔ, saying:
"The original intention to install a minor ruler
was precisely for this reason."
The Emperor of Wèi mobilized troops in Guānyòu,
summoned Hèbá Shèng to the traveling court (Xíngzàisuǒ),
and dispatched Grand Director of the Secretariat Chángsūn Chéngyè, Grand Commander Yǐngchuān Wáng Bīnzhī, and Hú Sī Chūn jointly to garrison Wǔláo.
Rǔyáng Wáng Xiān garrisoned Shíjì.
Director Chángsūn Zǐyàn led the former Administrator of Agriculture Yuán Hónglüè to garrison Shǎn.
Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì led the Governor of Yùzhōu, Hú Sī Yuánshòu, to attack Cài Jùn.
Shénwǔ ordered Dòu Tài and the Grand Commander of the Left Flank Mòduōlóu Dàiwén to oppose Xiǎnzhì,
and Hán Xián to oppose Xiān.
Yuánshòu's army surrendered.
Tài and Dàiwén met Xiǎnzhì at Chángshòujīn.
Xiǎnzhì secretly agreed to surrender
and retreated his forces.
The Army Administrator Yuán Xuán became aware of this,
rushed back,
and requested reinforcements.
The Emperor of Wèi dispatched Grand Commander Hóu Jǐshào to meet them.
They fought east of Huátái.
Xiǎnzhì surrendered with his army,
and Shào died there.
In the seventh month,
Wèi Dì (魏帝) personally led a large army to encamp at Héqiáo (河橋).
Shénwǔ (神武) arrived within more than ten *lǐ* (里) of the north bank of the river.
He again sent Kǒushēnchéng (口申誠) to relay a message,
but Wèi Dì did not reply.
Shénwǔ then led his army across the river.
Wèi Dì asked his officials for advice.
Some suggested moving south to join Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝),
some suggested moving west to Guānzhōng (關中),
and some suggested holding Luòkǒu (洛口) and fighting to the death.
No decision was made.
Meanwhile, Yuán Bīnzhī (元斌之) and Hú Xīs Chūn (斛斯椿) were contending for power and were not on good terms.
Bīnzhī abandoned Chūn and returned directly,
deceiving the Emperor by saying:
"Shénwǔ's troops have arrived."
That very day,
Wèi Dì withdrew to Cháng'ān (長安).
On the *jǐyǒu* day (己酉),
Shénwǔ entered Luòyáng (洛陽)
and stayed at Yǒngníng Sì (永寧寺).
On the *jiǎyín* day (甲寅) of the eighth month,
he summoned all the officials
and said to them:
"As ministers serving their lord,
you should assist in times of crisis and chaos.
If, while in office, you do not remonstrate,
and when abroad, you do not accompany your lord,
but in times of ease you indulge in favor and contend for glory,
and in times of urgency you flee and hide,
where then is the fidelity of a minister!"

Thereupon, he arrested Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) Chìliè Yánqìng (叱列延慶), concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射) Xīn Xióng (辛雄), concurrently Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Cuī Xiàofēn (崔孝芬), Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書) Liú Xīn (劉廞), concurrently Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書) Yáng Jī (楊機), and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Yuán Shìbì (元士弼), and executed them all,
punishing them for their disloyalty.
Shìbì's family and property were confiscated.
As all affairs of the state could not be neglected,
Shénwǔ discussed with his officials the appointment of Qīnghé Wáng Dǎn (清河王亶) as Dàsīmǎ (大司馬).
He resided in the lower residence of the Shàngshū (尚書) and governed by imperial decree.
The King used imperial escorts (警蹕),
which Shénwǔ disliked.
Shénwǔ soon arrived at Nóng (農),
then captured Tóngguān (潼關) to the west,
and seized Máo Hóngbīn (毛洪賓).
Advancing the army to Chángchéng (長城),
Lóngmén Dūdū (龍門都督) Xuē Chónglǐ (薛崇禮) surrendered.
Shénwǔ withdrew his army to Hédōng (河東),
ordering Xíngtái Shàngshū Zhǎngshǐ (行臺尚書長史) Xuē Yú (薛瑜) to guard Tóngguān (潼關),
and Dàdūdū (大都督) Kùdí Wēn (厙狄溫) to guard Fēnglíng (封陵).
He built a city on the western bank of Pújīn (蒲津),
to guard Huázhōu (華州),
and appointed Xuē Shàozōng (薛紹宗) as Cìshǐ (刺史).
Gāo Áng (高昂) acted as the governor of Yùzhōu (豫州).
From the time Shénwǔ departed from Jìnyáng (晉陽)
until then, there were forty memorials,
but Wèi Dì did not reply to any.
On the *gēngyín* day (庚寅) of the ninth month,
Shénwǔ returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and sent Monk Dàoróng (道榮) to deliver a memorial to Guānzhōng (關中),
which again received no reply.
Thereupon, he gathered all the officials and elders from the four gates
to discuss who should be enthroned.
They believed that since the chaos of Xiàochāng (孝昌),
the imperial succession had been interrupted,
the divine lord had no one to rely on,
and the order of generations was lost.
Yǒng'ān (永安) regarded Xiàowén (孝文) as a paternal elder cousin,
and Yǒngxī (永熙) exiled Xiàomíng (孝明) to a side chamber.
The loss of their enterprise and short reigns
were due to these reasons.
They then deliberated on establishing the heir of Qīnghé Wáng (清河王), Shànjiàn (善見).
After the discussion was settled,
they reported to Qīnghé Wáng.
The King said:
"The Son of Heaven has no father;
if my son is to be enthroned,
I will not begrudge my remaining life."
So he was established,
known as Xiàojìng Dì (孝靜帝).
Wèi (魏) thus began to be divided into two.
As Xiàowǔ (孝武) had gone west,
Shénwǔ feared being pressured at Xiáo (崤) and Shǎn (陝),
and Luòyáng (洛陽) was again outside the river,
close to the territory of Liáng (梁).
If he went towards Jìnyáng (晉陽),
the strategic positions could not connect.
Therefore, he discussed moving the capital to Yè (鄴),
and Hùjūn (護軍) Zǔ Yíng (祖瑩) supported it.
Three days after the imperial edict was issued,
the imperial carriage departed,
and 400,000 households rushed to set out in haste.
Shénwǔ remained in Luòyáng (洛陽) to manage affairs,
and returned to Jìnyáng (晉陽) when they were completed.
From then on, all military and state affairs
belonged to the Prime Minister's residence.
Previously, there was a children's rhyme that said:
"Pity the little green sparrow,
flying to Yèchéng (鄴城) to build its nest.
Its wings are almost fully grown,
and it will transform into a little parrot."
Those who favored omens secretly said
that the sparrow referred to Wèi Dì (魏帝) and the son of Qīnghé Wáng (清河王),
and the parrot referred to Shénwǔ (神武).
Initially, during the Xiàochāng (孝昌) era,
the Shānhú (山胡) Liú Líshēng (劉蠡升) proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
with the era name Shénjiā (神嘉).
He resided in Yúnyáng Gǔ (雲陽谷),
and the western regions were plundered by him every year,
calling it "Hú Wilderness" (胡荒).
In the first month of the second year,
the Western Wèi (西魏) Wèizhōu Cìshǐ (渭州刺史) Kězhūhún Dàoyuán (可朱渾道元) led his followers to defect to them.
Shénwǔ welcomed and accepted him.
On the *rénxū* day (壬戌),
Shénwǔ attacked Liú Líshēng (劉蠡升)
and greatly defeated him.
On the *jǐsì* day (己巳),
Wèi Dì issued an edict of commendation,
appointing Shénwǔ as Xiàngguó (相國),
granting him the *huángyuè* (黃鉞),
permitting him to wear swords and shoes into the palace,
and not requiring him to walk quickly when in court.
Shénwǔ firmly declined.
In the third month,
Shénwǔ wanted to marry his daughter to Líshēng's (蠡升) crown prince.
Waiting for them to be unprepared,
on the *xīnyǒu* day (辛酉),
he secretly led his army to attack them.
Their northern king cut off Líshēng's (蠡升) head and sent it.
His followers then enthroned his son, Nánhǎi Wáng (南海王).
Shénwǔ attacked them again
and captured Nánhǎi Wáng (南海王) and his younger brothers Xīhǎi Wáng (西海王) and Běihǎi Wáng (北海王), as well as the Empress, high officials, and others, totaling over four hundred people,
and fifty thousand households of Hú (胡) and Wèi (魏) people.
On the *rénshēn* day (壬申),
Shénwǔ held court at Yè (鄴).
In the fourth month,
Shénwǔ requested different provisions for the relocated people according to their status.
On the *jiǎyín* day (甲寅) of the ninth month,
Shénwǔ noted that many provincial, commandery, and county officials were acting unlawfully,
and requested to dispatch envoys to inquire about the people's suffering.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day (甲子) of the first month of the third year,
Shénwǔ led Kùdí Gān (厙狄干) and ten thousand cavalry to attack Xi Xī Wèi (西魏) Xiàzhōu (夏州).
He did not cook his food,
arriving in four days.
Binding spears together as ladders,
he entered the city at night,
captured its Cìshǐ (刺史) Fèi Yětóu Húbá Émítū (費也頭斛拔俄彌突),
〔一０〕and subsequently employed him.
He left Dūdū (都督) Zhāng Qióng (張瓊) to garrison it,
and relocated five thousand households of their tribes back.
The Western Wèi (西魏) Língzhōu Cìshǐ (靈州刺史) Cáo Ní (曹泥) and his son-in-law Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (涼州刺史) Liú Fēng (劉豐) sent envoys requesting to defect.
Zhōu Wén (周文) besieged Ní (泥),
flooding the city with water,
leaving four *chǐ* (尺) of it unsubmerged.
Shénwǔ ordered Āzhìluó (阿至羅) to dispatch thirty thousand cavalry to directly cross Língzhōu (靈州),
circling around to the rear of the Western army,
capturing fifty horses,
whereupon the Western army retreated.
Shénwǔ led cavalry to welcome Ní (泥) and Fēng (豐),
relocated five thousand of their remaining households back,
and restored Ní's (泥) official titles.
Wèi Dì issued an edict to bestow the Nine Marks of Distinction (九錫) upon Shénwǔ,
but he firmly declined, and it was halted.
In the second month,
Shénwǔ ordered Āzhìluó (阿至羅) to press the Western Wèi (西魏) Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (秦州刺史) Jiànzhōng Wáng Wànsì Pǔbō (建忠王万俟普撥),
and Shénwǔ supported him with his troops.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day (甲午) of the sixth month,

Pǔbō (普撥), along with his son Tàizǎi Shòuluògān (太宰受洛干), Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ (豳州刺史) Chìgān Bǎolè (叱干寶樂), Right Guard General Pòliùhán Cháng (破六韓常), and over three hundred commanders, surrendered with their tribes.
〔一一〕
On the *dīnghài* day (丁亥) of the eighth month,
Shénwǔ requested that measures and weights be standardized
and promulgated throughout the realm.
On the *xīnhài* day (辛亥) of the ninth month,
the Fénzhōu (汾州) Hú (胡) kings Tiáochù (迢觸) and Cáo Èrlóng (曹貳龍) gathered followers and rebelled,
appointing officials
and establishing the era name Píngdū (平都).
Shénwǔ attacked and pacified them.
On the *dīngchǒu* day (丁丑) of the twelfth month,
Shénwǔ marched west from Jìnyáng (晉陽),
sending concurrently Púyè Xíngtái (僕射行臺) Rǔyáng Wáng Xiān (汝陽王暹) and Sītú (司徒) Gāo Áng (高昂) to head for Shàngluò (上洛),
and Dàdūdū (大都督) Dòu Tài (竇泰) to enter through Tóngguān (潼關).
On the *guǐchǒu* day (癸丑) of the first month of the fourth year,
Dòu Tài's (竇泰) army was defeated, and he committed suicide.
Shénwǔ reached Pújīn (蒲津),
but as the ice was thin, he could not go to rescue them,
so he returned with his army.
Gāo Áng (高昂) attacked and captured Shàngluò (上洛).
On the *yǐyǒu* day (乙酉) of the second month,
Shénwǔ reported that the nine prefectures of Bìng (并), Sì (肆), Fén (汾), Jiàn (建), Jìn (晉), Dōngyōng (東雍), Nánfén (南汾), Tài (泰), and Shǎn (陝) suffered from frost and drought,
the people were starving and scattered,
and requested that granaries be opened in those areas for relief.
〔一二〕
On the *rénshēn* day (壬申) of the sixth month,
Shénwǔ went to Tiānchí (天池),
where he found an auspicious stone,
on which characters subtly rose, reading:
"Liù Wáng Sān Chuān" (六王三川).
Shénwǔ
campaigned in the west.
He crossed the Pújīn ford,
with a host of 200,000. Zhōu Wén
camped at Shāyuàn. Shénwǔ, seeing the terrain was restrictive, slightly retreated.
The Western forces advanced with drums and shouts,
and the army fell into great disorder,
abandoning 180,000 sets of weapons and armor.
Shénwǔ mounted a camel
and waited for a boat to return.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng, the third month, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
Shénwǔ firmly requested to resign the Chéngxiàng (Chancellor) position,
and the Emperor of Wèi permitted it.
In the fourth month, on the *gēngyín* day,
Shénwǔ held court at Yè.
On the *rénchén* day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
He requested the lifting of the ban on alcohol
and also that relief be provided to the military officers of the imperial guard.
In the seventh month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
the Mobile Secretariat Director Hóu Jǐng and Sītú Gāo Áng besieged Dúgū Xìn, a general of Western Wèi, at Jīnyǒng.
The Emperor of Western Wèi and Zhōu Wén both came to their aid.
Grand Commander Kùdí Gān led the various generals as the vanguard,
and Shénwǔ commanded the main force, following up the advance.
In the eighth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
they fought at Héyīn,
severely defeating the Western Wèi army
and capturing tens of thousands.
Sītú Gāo Áng, Grand Commander Lǐ Měng, and Sòng Xiǎn died there.
After the defeat of the Western forces,
Dúgū Xìn first entered the Pass (Guānzhōng).
Zhōu Wén left his Commander Zhǎngsūn Zǐyàn to defend Jīnyǒng,
and then burned his camp and fled.
Shénwǔ dispatched troops to pursue the fugitives,
reaching Xiáo,
but failing to catch them, they returned.
Originally, Shénwǔ, knowing the Western forces were invading,
rushed from Jìnyáng leading his troops,
reaching Mèngjīn.
Before he had crossed,
the army had already achieved victory or defeat.
Subsequently, Shénwǔ crossed the river,
and Zǐyàn also abandoned the city and fled.
Shénwǔ then destroyed Jīnyǒng and returned.
In the eleventh month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
Shénwǔ held court in the capital.
In the twelfth month, on the *rénchén* day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
In the first year of Xīnghé, the seventh month, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Wèi Emperor promoted Shénwǔ to Xiàngguó (Chancellor of State) and Lù Shàngshū Shì (Director of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing).
Only after his firm refusal did the matter cease.
In the eleventh month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Shénwǔ, due to the completion of the new palace,
held court at Yè.
The Wèi Emperor hosted a feast and archery competition with Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ descended the steps to offer congratulations,
and again declined the titles of King of Bóhǎi and Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside.
The imperial edict did not permit it.
In the twelfth month, on the *wùxū* day,
Shénwǔ returned to Jìnyáng.
In the twelfth month of the second year,
a separate division of Āzhìluó sent an envoy to request surrender.
Shénwǔ led his host to meet them,
going out of the Wǔzhōu Pass.
Not finding them,
he held a grand hunt and returned.
In the fifth month of the third year,
Shénwǔ inspected the northern borders,
and sent an envoy to establish peace with the Rúrú.
In the fourth year, the fifth month, on the *xīnsì* day,
Shénwǔ held court at Yè.
He requested that all officials present their administrative affairs face-to-face monthly,
clearly promote the humble and overlooked,
accept counsel and reject wickedness,
personally handle judicial cases and litigation,
and praise or dismiss the diligent and the lazy.
If regional governors and prefects committed transgressions,
they should be held mutually responsible level by level;
within the Jiāoyè (Inner Palace),
consorts should be introduced to the Emperor in sequence;
and the hawks and dogs in the Imperial Garden should all be abandoned.
In the sixth month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
Shénwǔ returned to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month,
Shénwǔ campaigned in the west.
In the tenth month, on the *jǐhài* day,
he besieged Wáng Sīzhèng, I Tóng Sān Sī of Western Wèi, at Yùbì City.
He intended by this to lure the enemy,
but the Western forces dared not leave the city.
In the eleventh month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
Shénwǔ, due to heavy snow
and the high death toll among his soldiers,
consequently withdrew his army.
In the first year of Wǔdìng, the second month, on the *rénshēn* day,
Gāo Shèn, the Prefect of Běiyùzhōu, occupied Wǔláo and rebelled toward the west.
In the third month, on the *rénchén* day,
Zhōu Wén led his host to aid Gāo Shèn,
and besieged the Southern City of Hèqiáo.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Shénwǔ severely defeated them at Mángshān,
capturing over 400 Western Wèi commanders and officers,
with a total count of 60,000 captured and slain.
At that time, a soldier had stolen and killed a donkey.
According to military law, he deserved death,
but Shénwǔ did not execute him,
intending to judge him upon reaching Bìngzhōu.
The next day, when battle resumed,
the soldier fled to the Western army
and reported Shénwǔ's location.
The Western forces launched a full assault.
The troops scattered,
and Shénwǔ lost his horse.
Hèlián Yángshùn dismounted and gave his horse to Shénwǔ.
He and the servant Féng Wénluò helped Shénwǔ mount and fled together,
followed by only six or seven men, both foot soldiers and cavalry.
When the pursuing cavalry arrived,
the trusted Commander Wèi Xīngqìng said:
"Your Highness, go now.
Xīngqìng has a hundred arrows at his waist;
that is enough to kill a hundred men."
Shénwǔ encouraged him, saying:
"If the matter succeeds,
I will appoint you as the Prefect of Huáizhōu.
If you die,
then I will employ your son."
Xīngqìng replied:
"My son is young.
I request you employ my elder brother."
Shénwǔ agreed.
Xīngqìng fought
until his arrows were spent and he died.
Hèbá Shèng, Grand Preceptor (Tàishī) of Western Wèi, pursued Shénwǔ with thirteen horsemen.
Liú Hónghuī, the Prefect of Hézhōu, shot down two of them.
Shèng’s spear was about to strike Shénwǔ,
when Duàn Xiàoxiān shot Shèng’s horse laterally, killing it.
Thus, Shénwǔ escaped.
The two prefectures of Yùzhōu and Luòzhōu were pacified.
Shénwǔ sent Liú Fēng to pursue the fugitives,
expanding the territory up to Hóngnóng before returning.
In the seventh month,
Shénwǔ sent a document to Zhōu Wén,
accusing him of the crime of murdering Xiàowǔ.
In the eighth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
the Wèi Emperor decreed Shénwǔ to be Xiàngguó, Lù Shàngshū Shì, and Dà Xíngtái (Grand Mobile Secretariat Director).
His other positions remained as before.
Only after his firm refusal did the matter cease.
That month,
Shénwǔ ordered the construction of a wall on the northern mountain of Sìzhōu,
running west from Mǎlíng Garrison
eastward to Tǔliú,
and the work ceased after forty days.
In the twelfth month, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
Shénwǔ held court in the capital.
On the *gēngchén* day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
In the second year, the third month, on the *guǐsì* day,
Shénwǔ toured Jìzhōu and Dìngzhōu,
and subsequently held court in the capital.
Because of the severe drought in winter and spring,
he requested the remission of outstanding debts,
relief for the destitute,
and amnesty for those sentenced to death or lesser punishments.
He also requested that elderly men be granted clerical positions, each according to their rank.
In the fourth month, on the *bǐngchén* day,
Shénwǔ returned to Jìnyáng.
In the eleventh month,
Shénwǔ campaigned against the Shānhú,
defeating and pacifying them,
capturing over 10,000 households and persons,
and distributing them among the various prefectures.
In the third year, the first month, on the *jiǎwǔ* day,

Ěrzhū Wénchàng (Kāifǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī), Rèn Zhòu (Kāifǔ Sīmǎ), Zhèng Zhònglǐ (Commander), Lǐ Shìlín (Secretary of the Central Prefecture), Fáng Zǐyuǎn (former Kāifǔ Cānjūn), and others plotted to assassinate Shénwǔ.
Taking advantage of the *dǎcù* ceremony on the night of the fifteenth,
they entered with hidden blades.
Their accomplice Xuē Jìxiào reported them,
and they were all executed.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Shénwǔ requested the establishment of the Jìnyáng Palace in Bìngzhōu
to house the relocated populace.
In the third month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
Shénwǔ held court at Yè.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
In the tenth month, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
Shénwǔ submitted a memorial,
stating that the three prefectures of Yōuzhōu, Ānzhōu, and Dìngzhōu bordered the Xī and the Rúrú to the north,
and requested the construction of fortresses and garrisons in strategic locations to guard against them.
He personally supervised the inspection and construction,
ensuring that all were strictly fortified.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Shénwǔ requested the release of the Mángshān captives from their chains and restraints,
and that they be married to civilian widows.
In the eighth month of the fourth year, on the *Guǐsì* day,
Shénwǔ was about to lead a western expedition.
He gathered troops from Yè at Jìnyáng.
The Palace General Cáo Wèizǔ said:
"This is not advisable.
Now, in the eighth month, the west rules,
and with the energy of death countering the energy of life,
it will be disadvantageous for the guest,
though favorable for the host.
If the army proceeds,
the great general will be harmed."
Shénwǔ did not heed him.
Ever since the Eastern and Western Wèi forces clashed,
there had always been formations of yellow and black ants in Yè.
Diviners considered the yellow ones to be the color of the Eastern Wèi's military uniforms,
and the black ones to be the color of the Western Wèi's military uniforms.
People used this to predict victory or defeat.
At this time,
all the yellow ants died.
In the ninth month,
Shénwǔ besieged Yùbì to provoke the Western army,
but they dared not respond.
Wéi Xiàokuān, the Inspector of Jìnzhōu for Western Wèi, defended Yùbì.
Iron masks were brought out from the city.
Shénwǔ ordered Yuán Dào to shoot at them,
each time hitting their eyes.
Using Lǐ Yèxìng's *gūxū* technique,
he concentrated his forces to the north.
The north
was a natural stronghold.
So, he built earth mounds,
dug ten tunnels,
and also dug twenty-one tunnels on the east side to attack it.
The city had no water,
drawing it from the Fén River.
Shénwǔ ordered the Fén River to be diverted,
which was completed overnight.
Xiàokuān seized and held the earth mounds.
The army was stalled for fifty days;
the city was not taken,
and seventy thousand men died,
piled into a single tomb.
A star fell into Shénwǔ's camp.
All the donkeys brayed together,
and the soldiers were all terrified.
Shénwǔ fell ill.
In the eleventh month, on the *Gēngzǐ* day,
he returned to the capital, carried in a litter due to his illness.
On the *Gēngxū* day,
he dispatched the Duke of Tàiyuán, Yáng, to garrison Yè.
On the *Xīnhài* day,
he summoned the heir apparent, Chéng, to Jìnyáng.
An ominous bird gathered in the pavilion trees.
The heir apparent ordered Húlǜ Guāng to shoot and kill it.
On the *Jǐmǎo* day,
Shénwǔ, having achieved no success,
memorialized to resign from his post as Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs, both within and without.
The Wèi Emperor granted his request with a gracious edict.
At this time, Western Wèi reported that Shénwǔ had been struck by a crossbow bolt.
When Shénwǔ heard this,
he forced himself to sit up and receive the nobles.
He had Húlǜ Jīn lead the *Chìlè* song,
and Shénwǔ joined in,
shedding tears of sorrow.
Hóu Jǐng had always slighted the heir apparent.
He once said to Sīmǎ Zǐrú:
"While the King is alive,
I dare not harbor other intentions.
If the King is gone,
I cannot serve with that Xiānbēi young boy."
Zǐrú covered his mouth.
Now,
the heir apparent wrote a letter to summon Jǐng on behalf of Shénwǔ.
Jǐng had previously agreed with Shénwǔ
that if he received a letter,
and there was a slight dot on the back of the letter,
then he would come.
When the letter arrived,
there was no dot,
so Jǐng did not come.
He also heard of Shénwǔ's illness,
and consequently garrisoned his troops to secure himself.
Shénwǔ said to the heir apparent:
"Although I am ill,
your face shows even more signs of worry.
Why is that?"
The heir apparent did not reply.
He asked again:
"Are you not worried about Hóu Jǐng's rebellion?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Shénwǔ said:
"Jǐng has solely controlled Hénán for fourteen years.
He always has ambitions to be high-flying and overbearing.
I could manage him,
but how could he be controlled by you?
Now, with the four directions still unsettled,
do not immediately show grief.
Kùdí Gān is an old Xiānbēi man,
Húlǜ Jīn is an old Chìlè man.
Both are robust and upright by nature,
and will never betray you.
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán and Liú Fēngshēng traveled a long way to join me;
they will certainly have no disloyal intentions.
Hèbá Yānguò'ér is honest and without fault.
Pān Xiànglè was originally a Buddhist monk,
and is kind and generous at heart;
you brothers will certainly benefit from his help.
Hán Guǐ is somewhat reckless in his youth;
you should be tolerant with him.
Péng Xiànglè is a trusted confidant and hard to replace;
you should protect him.
The only one capable of matching Hóu Jǐng is Mùróng Shàozōng.
I deliberately did not promote him highly,
saving him for you.
You should treat him with profound courtesy
and entrust him with strategic planning."
On the first day of the first month of the fifth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
Shénwǔ said:
"Is this solar eclipse for me?
What regret is there in death?"
On the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
he sent a memorial to the Wèi Emperor.
On that day,
he passed away in Jìnyáng,
at the age of fifty-two.
His death was kept secret and not announced.
In the sixth month, on the *Rénwǔ* day,
the Wèi Emperor held a mourning ceremony in the Eastern Hall.
After three days,
he wore mourning clothes of coarse hemp.
An edict commanded that the funeral rites follow the precedents of the Han Dynasty's Great General Huò Guāng and King Cāng of Dōngpíng.
He was posthumously granted the *jiǎhuángyuè*, *shǐchíjié*, *xiàngguó*, Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs, Prince of Qí, with seals and ribbons,
an armored carriage, a yellow canopy, a left-hand battle standard, front and rear feather banners, drums and wind instruments, light carriages, and armored warriors,
along with the nine extraordinary honors.
His posthumous title was Xiànwǔ Wáng.
In the eighth month, on the *Jiǎshēn* day,
he was buried to the west of the Zhāng River, northwest of Yè.
The Wèi Emperor personally saw him off on the Zǐmò.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was posthumously honored as Xiànwǔ Dì,
with the temple name Tàizǔ,
and his mausoleum was named Yìpíng.
In the first year of the Tiāntǒng era,
his posthumous title was changed to Shénwǔ Huángdì,
and his temple name to Gāozǔ.
Imperial Annals, Volume 3: Wénxiāng.
Shìzōng Wénxiāng Huángdì, personal name Chéng (Gāo Chéng).
Courtesy name Zǐhuì,
the eldest son of Shénwǔ.
His mother was Empress Dowager Lóu.
From birth he was brilliant and discerning;
Shénwǔ regarded him as extraordinary.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng of the Wèi dynasty (531),
he was established as the Heir Apparent of the Prince of Bóhǎi.
He studied under Dù Xún;
his sharp understanding surpassed others,
and Dù Xún greatly admired him.
In the second year (532),
he was granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and married the younger sister of Emperor Xiàojìng, Grand Princess Féngyì.
He was twelve years old at the time.
His spirit and manner were sharp and clear,
as if he were already an adult.
Shénwǔ tested him by asking about the success and failures of current affairs;
his analyses and distinctions never failed to hit the mark.
From then on, he participated in all military and state planning.
In the first year of Tiānpíng (534),
he was granted the titles of Shǐ Chíjié, Shàngshū Lìng, Dà Xíngtái, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Bīngzhōu.
In the third year (536),
he entered to assist in the court administration,
and was additionally appointed Commander of the Guards (Lǐng Zuǒyòu) and Grand Area Commander (Dà Dūdū) of the Capital Region (Jīngjī).
Although people had heard of his capacity and insight,
they still anticipated him performing according to his youth.
However, his strategies were strict and lucid,
and affairs were handled without delay or stagnation.
Thus, the court and the public were awe-struck.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng (538),
he acted as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Since Cuī Liàng in Wèi,
the selection of officials had always been determined by seniority and service tenure.
Wénxiāng thereupon reformed the former system;
selection and promotion focused only on acquiring the right person.
He also purged the Shàngshū Láng (Secretaries of the Departments),
carefully selecting talented individuals to fill the positions.
As for scholars of talent and renown,
all were recommended and promoted.
Even those who had not yet attained high office
were brought to his residence
and treated as honored guests.
Whenever there were excursions or banquets in the mountains or gardens,
they were sure to be invited,
performing archery or composing poetry,
each demonstrating their strengths,
to provide enjoyment and pleasure.
In the second year of Xīnghé (540),
he was promoted to Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
Superintendent of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and continued to act as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Since Zhèngguāng (520–525),
the realm had been troubled by many affairs,
and among the officials in office,
few were honest and clean.
Wénxiāng then nominated Cuī Xiān, a Secretary of the Department of Personnel, to be Grand Chief Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi).
He impeached the powerful and influential
without granting them reprieve or release.
Consequently, customs were renewed,
and the path of private corruption was cut off.
He then posted notices on the streets and avenues,
fully detailing the strategies of governing the state,
and concurrently opened the path for candid speech.
If anyone criticized affairs or presented memorials with earnest and penetrating counsel,
he treated them with great courtesy.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year of Wǔdìng (546),
Shénwǔ campaigned in the west,
but being unwell, he ordered the army to return.
Wénxiāng rushed to the location of the army
and escorted him back to Jìnyáng.
On the day Bǐngwǔ of the first month of the fifth year (547),
Shénwǔ died.
The death was kept secret and not announced.
On the day Xīnhài,
Sītú Hóu Jǐng revolted, basing himself in Hénán.
Sīmǎ Shìyún, the Governor of Yǐngzhōu, responded by yielding the city to him.
Hóu Jǐng lured and captured Gāo Yuánchéng, the Governor of Yùzhōu, Lǐ Mì, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu, and Bào Xiǎn, the Governor of Guǎngzhōu, and others.
He dispatched Sīkōng Hán Guǐ to lead troops to suppress them.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Rénshēn,
Wénxiāng held court in Yè.
In the sixth month, on the day Jǐsì,
Hán Guǐ and others returned from Yǐngzhōu.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Wénxiāng returned to Jìnyáng,
and then announced the death,
informing the civil and military officials,
and explaining the last wishes of Shénwǔ.
In the seventh month, on the day Wùxū,

the Emperor of Wèi issued an edict appointing Wénxiāng as Shǐ Chíjié, Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng), Commander-in-Chief of All Military Forces Domestic and Foreign (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn), Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì), Dà Xíngtái, and Prince of Bóhǎi.
Wénxiāng memorialized declining the offices,
wishing to relinquish the princely rank.
On the day Rén'yín,
the Emperor of Wèi decreed that the Duke of Tàiyuán, Yáng, should temporarily manage military and state affairs,
and dispatched an inner court messenger (zhōngshǐ) to strongly urge Wénxiāng to accept.
In the eighth month, on the day Wùchén,
Wénxiāng memorialized reiterating Shénwǔ's dying instruction,
requesting a reduction of his fief territory to be distributed among the generals and commanders,
according to differing ranks.
On the day Xīnwèi,
he held court in Yè,
and firmly declined the Chancellorship.
The Emperor of Wèi decreed:
“Since the court and the public rely upon you,
and the safety and danger of the state depend on you,
we cannot allow you to fulfill your original intention [of declining].
We must exercise authority [in overruling you].
You are restored to your former rank of Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
the rest remains as before.”
Those who debated the matter all said that Hóu Jǐng still harbored thoughts of turning north,
but his messengers had simply not arrived.
Furthermore, Cài Zūndào, a general under Hóu Jǐng, returned north
and claimed that Hóu Jǐng felt remorse for his transgression.
The Prince (Wáng) believed this to be true,
and thought he could be persuaded to return.
Thereupon, he sent a letter to Hóu Jǐng, which read:
The late King (Shénwǔ) and the Sītú (Hóu Jǐng) shared difficulties and good fortune,
and I, the orphan son, rely upon you.
You were especially cherished as a relative;
our righteousness spanned beginning to end,
and our affection endured the deep cold of the year.
He who is treated as a loyal statesman
establishes the principle of sacrificing one's life (like Qì Shēn);
he who is fed a single meal immediately offers the service of upholding the carriage (fú lún).
How much more is expected in a relationship weightier than this?
The late King, relying on the bond of old acquaintance,
desired to entrust his children and grandchildren
to you,
to be matched like Qín and Jìn [in alliance],
and together form a kinship like Liú and Fàn.
Yet we hear that you abandoned the staff and sang [a marching song],
immediately turning back with the gaze of a wolf, ready to snap and bite.
You failed to walk the path of a loyal subject,
and instead fell into the territory of a rebel.
Your strength is insufficient to empower yourself,
your position is insufficient to protect yourself,
leading a motley crew of followers,
creating a danger as precarious as stacked eggs.
To the west you seek aid from
Yǔwén,
to the south you request support from the Xiāo clan,
possessing the mind of a doubting fox,
committing the deeds of a rat looking back and forth (indecisive and treacherous).
If you enter Qín (Western Wèi), the Qín people will not tolerate you;
if you return to Wú (Liáng), the Wú people will not trust you.
It must be wicked men,
who fabricated groundless rumors,
causing you to harbor the suspicion of a "tiger in the marketplace,"
thereby leading to the bewilderment of "throwing the shuttle."
Your recent actions and bearing
are already visible;
this mutual suspicion and error
is something you must realize yourself.
Everyone in your household, great and small,
is now held by the Sīkòu (Minister of Justice).
They supposed that since the Lǐ clan was not yet destroyed,
they could still talk of your revolt, Shàoqīng.
I, the inept orphan son,
have attracted misfortune
and suffered cruel punishment from Heaven.
But propriety demanded timely action,
and my goal was to forget private feelings.
I reluctantly dispatched subordinate commanders
to serve as vanguards and launch the suppression.
Nányǎnzhōu and Yángzhōu were immediately recovered at that time.
I immediately
desired to seize the opportunity to sweep through Xuànhù,
but owing to the intense heat,
and wishing to make later plans,
I temporarily ordered the army to return
and await the right moment to act again.
Now, the winter ice is about to break,
and the white dew is condensing.
We will rely upon the power of the state
to respectfully execute the Mandate of Heaven.
Our weaponry is refined and new,
our soldiers and horses are powerful and strong.
Those within and without the court are grateful,
and high
and low cooperate fully.
With repeated orders and injunctions, they will go through fire and water.
May the banners and drums be seen one after the other,
and the dust clouds connect one another.
The situation will be like pouring water on snow,
the outcome like quenching a spark.
Truly, the wise
leave danger and pursue security,
and the intelligent transform disaster into blessing.
I would rather others betray me
than I betray others.
You must open the path to follow virtue
