and allow for the opportunity to correct your error.
If you are able
to roll up your armor and come to court,
hanging up your bow case and returning to the capital,
you will immediately be granted Yùzhōu,
and we will surely ensure your career lasts your lifetime.
The civil and military officials under your command will not be pursued or arrested,
and furthermore, they will be able to maintain their.
It was then that unruly individuals,
falsely fabricated groundless rumors,
thereby harboring suspicions like the "city tiger,"
which led to confusion like "throwing the shuttle."
Your recent conduct,
the facts are already evident,
people mutually mistaking each other,
I imagine you yourself are aware.
The entire household, young and old,
are all under the jurisdiction of the Sīkòu,
meaning that the Lǐ family is not yet annihilated,
and that Shǎoqīng can still be reversed.
The orphan, acting improperly,
invited disaster,
and suffered cruel heavenly punishment.
However, ceremony yields to expediency,
and my ambition is to forget private interests.
I merely dispatched auxiliary generals,
to lead the attack,
and Nányān and Yángzhōu were recovered in due course.
I
then wished to seize the opportunity to sweep through Xiànhú,
but due to the intense heat,
I desired to make future plans.
So I ordered the army to return,
and wait for the right moment to act again.
Now the winter glue is about to break,
and white dew is gathering,
I shall rely on the nation's spiritual power,
to execute the heavenly punishment.
Our weapons are refined and new,
our soldiers and horses are strong and vigorous.
Those within and without are grateful,
the
high and low exert themselves,
and after repeated injunctions, they are willing to face fire and water.
So that our flags and drums are within sight of each other,
and our dust clouds connect,
our momentum like melting snow,
our task like extinguishing a lamp.
Indeed, the enlightened
avoid danger and seek security,
the wise turn misfortune into blessing.
Rather let people wrong me,
than I wrong people.
The path of following good should be opened,
allowing a way for those who are lost to change.
If you can
roll up your armor and come to court,
or lower your quiver and return to the capital,
then you shall be granted Yùzhōu,
and your status throughout your life will surely be secured.
Your subordinates, both civil and military, will not be pursued,
they will advance and preserve their
salaries and positions,
and retreat without losing their achievements and fame.
Now Wáng Sīzhèng and others are all isolated forces and partial generals,
who have come deep into our territory from afar.
Their lives are in your grasp,
if you can
assassinate them,
I imagine you will have strength to spare.
Then you will be granted further authority,
and forever secure your borders.
Your family members can be free from harm,
your beloved wife and children will also be sent back to you,
and we shall still be
intermarrying families,
establishing good relations.
You are now unable to seal Hángǔ in the east,
or claim sovereignty as a lone ruler in the south,
but are controlled by others,
your prestige and renown utterly lost.
You gain land but do not wish to hold it,
you gather people but do not consider it
strength.
You merely let yourself bear the name of rebellion,
and your family suffer the calamity of evil defiance,
your clan wiped out and your lineage cut off,
bringing sorrow upon yourself.
Wearing heaven and treading earth,
can you be without shame?
I, the orphan, should not have sent this today,
but I saw Cài Zūndào say,
"The Sītú originally had no intention of returning west,
and deeply regretted his past actions."
I do not know if this statement is
false or true.
The principles of fortune and misfortune,
I imagine you will consider for yourself.
Jǐng's reply stated: I, a humble commoner from the countryside,
was originally unsuited for practical use.
I entered public service for the nation,
and have continuously served for two cycles of twelve years,
facing danger and enduring hardship,
how could I avoid wind and frost?
Thus I obtained wealth
and honor in those years,
and glory in my lifetime.
Why did I suddenly raise banners and flags,
and beat drums and clappers,
and confront you to the north?
It was truly out of fear of peril and destruction,
and apprehension of inviting calamity,
that is all.
In the twilight of last year,
Your Royal Highness fell ill,
the spirits did not bless the good,
and prayers brought no recovery.
This led to favorites usurping power,
and confidantes becoming disloyal.
My wife and children were in
the residence,
and were besieged without cause.
When I returned to Chángshè,
I hoped to state my case personally,
but before the imperial dispatch was sent,
the axes and battle-axes already loomed.
Since our banners and flags faced each other,
not far apart,
I frequently sent letters,
hoping to express my humble feelings.
But the commanders, relying on their might,
disregarded them completely,
and launched their sharp attacks,
intent solely on slaughter and destruction,
digging a siege trench and flooding the area,
leaving only three
slabs of wood.
I looked around,
my life hanging by a thread,
unable to bear death,
I fought outside the city.
To surrender to Qín and yield territory,
how could I do it willingly?
Animals abhor death,
human beings
cherish life.
I am truly innocent,
what crime have Huán and Zhuāng committed?
Moreover, Your Royal Highness usually treated me as an equal,
we exerted ourselves with one heart,
together assisting the imperial house.
Although our power and authority differed
slightly,
and our relationships varied somewhat like hot and cold,
the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng) and the Minister of Education (Sītú)
were merely like geese in a row.
Fortune, emolument, office, and honor
are natural titles,
bestowed after effort;
the principles are not mutually relevant.
To seek
to swallow charcoal,
how preposterous!
However, stealing another's wealth
is still called theft,
but to take emolument from the public treasury
is said not to be taking.
Although the power of Wèi is now in decline,
the Mandate of Heaven has not
changed.
To receive grace in one's private residence,
what is there to dispute?
You mock my inability to seal Hángǔ in the east,
and to be controlled by others,
this is like teaching me to praise Jì Shì while condemning Xián Jìzhòng.
A country without a ruler,
I have not heard of such in the rites.
To act unlawfully,
how can one instruct?
I privately believe that sharing wealth to raise the young
is a matter of achieving a good end,
and giving up one's home to save orphans,
who would say it creates animosity?
You also say that my forces
are insufficient to make myself strong,
and my life is as precarious as stacked eggs.
However, even if a myriad commoners
suddenly overthrow ten tyrants,
and Zhòu achieved a hundred victories,
he ultimately had no successor.
The Battle of Yǐngchuān
is
an example from Yīn.
Weight and lightness depend on people,
the tripod is in virtue, not in power.
If one can be loyal and trustworthy,
though weak, one will surely be strong.
Deep anxiety inspires sages,
what hardship is there in being in danger?
Moreover, the Way of Liáng is now
prosperous and harmonious,
attracting people with rites,
clothing them in tiger patterns,
and tying them with good ranks.
It intends to enclose the Five Sacred Mountains and encompass the Four Seas,
sweeping away impurities and saving the common people.
To be a refugee in the east
Emoluments and high office;
when they retire, they will not lose their meritorious fame.
Now Wáng Sīzhèng and others are all isolated forces and divisional generals,
having traveled far and penetrated deeply.
Yet their lives are in your grasp.
If you can
assassinate them,
I expect you will have strength to spare.
I will immediately grant you corresponding appointments,
ensuring you eternally guard the frontiers.
Your family members can be without worry;
your cherished wife and beloved sons will also be sent back,
and we will still be
connected families,
jointly establishing amity.
Now you cannot seal Hángǔ in the east,
face south and proclaim yourself sovereign,
but instead are controlled by others,
and your imposing reputation is utterly lost.
You acquire territory but do not wish to defend it yourself;
you gather masses but do not deem them
strength.
You merely cause your person to bear the name of betrayal,
and your family to suffer the calamity of wickedness and treason,
destroying your lineage and ending your succession,
bringing this sorrow upon yourself.
Living between Heaven and Earth,
how can you be without shame!
I, the lonely sovereign, should not have sent this today,
but I saw Cài Zūndào report,
“The Sītú fundamentally has no intention of returning west,
and harbors deep regret for his past errors.”
I do not know if this statement is
false or true.
The logic of fortune and misfortune,
I imagine you will determine yourself.
Jǐng replies in his letter: I, your servant, am a commoner from the countryside;
fundamentally lacking applicable talents.
Serving the state since my debut,
I have continuously served for two cycles (24 years).
Enduring danger and treading difficulty,
how could I shun wind and frost?
Consequently, I attained wealth and
rank in those years,
bringing glory to my person and status.
Why, one morning, did I raise the flags and banners,
take up the drum and drumsticks,
and face north to oppose you?
It was truly because I feared danger and ruin,
and worried about incurring calamity and harm,
that I did so.
Late last year,
the honored Prince suffered an illness.
The spirits did not protect the virtuous,
and prayers brought no healing.
Consequently, favorites were allowed to wield power,
and trusted aides became disloyal.
My wife and children, remaining in their
residence,
were besieged without cause.
When I returned to Chángshè,
hoping to personally explain my situation,
the letter of submission had not yet been dispatched,
but the battle-axes of execution had already arrived.
Since banners and flags faced each other,
separated by mere inches,
I frequently sent hasty letters,
hoping to convey my humble sentiments.
But the various commanders relied on their might,
utterly ignoring me,
wielding sharp weapons,
intent solely on slaughter and annihilation.
They dug around the perimeter and dammed up water,
leaving barely three
planks (of dry earth).
Looking around,
my life hung by a thread (like the dropping water in the clepsydra).
Unable to bear death,
I went out to fight beneath the city,
submitting to Qín and surrendering territory.
How could I willingly do this?
Birds and beasts hate death,
and human beings
cherish life.
I am truly not guilty;
what crime did Huán or Zhuāng commit?
Furthermore, the honored Prince usually treated me as his peer,
working together with one heart,
jointly supporting the Imperial House.
Although our power and influence were slightly
uneven,
and the warmth and cold were marginally different,
the Chéngxiàng and the Sītú
were merely aligned like geese in flight.
Fortune, emoluments, office, and glory
are naturally Heaven’s ranks.
They are bestowed after effort;
logically, this matter is unrelated.
To demand that I
swallow charcoal,
how preposterous that is!
Yet, stealing another man’s wealth
is still called thievery,
but when official emoluments depart the public office,
you instead say I should not take them.
Now, although Wèi’s virtue has waned,
Heaven’s mandate has not yet
changed.
Accepting grace in a private residence,
why is this relevant to the discussion?
Your scorn that I cannot seal Hángǔ in the east,
and that I am controlled by others,
is like teaching me to esteem Jì Zhòng while praising Jì Shì.
A state without a lord
has never been
heard of according to the rites.
If one acts without law,
how can one instruct others?
I humbly believe that distributing wealth to support the young
leads to a good outcome;
abandoning one's residence to preserve the isolated,
who would call that a small transgression?
You further stated that my troops
are insufficient to strengthen myself,
and my person is as perilous as stacked eggs.
However, the myriad common people
ultimately submitted to the ten ministers (of King Wǔ).
Though Zhòu had a hundred victories,
he ultimately had no successor.
The Battle of Yǐngchuān,
right
there, serves as a mirror of Yīn.
Importance is determined by people;
the great tripod depends on virtue.
If one can be loyal and trustworthy,
though weak, one will surely become strong.
Deep suffering inspires the sage;
why fear dwelling in danger?
Moreover, now the way of Liáng
is prosperous and magnificent,
attracting allies with propriety.
I am clothed in their tiger-striped uniform,
bound by excellent noble titles.
They are currently aiming to enclose the Five Peaks and form a pool of the Four Seas,
sweeping away defilement and pollution to save the common people.
To the east, they restrain
Ōuyuè;
to the west, they lead armies to Qiānlǒng.
Wúyuè are fierce and tough,
bringing thousands of groups of armored soldiers.
Qín soldiers and Jì horses,
controlling a hundred thousand archers.
When a great wind shakes,
withered branches must be broken;
when solid frost
briefly falls,
autumn foliage naturally perishes.
If this is considered weakness,
who is worthy to be called mighty?
Furthermore, I have been falsely accused of duplicity
and suspected by both states.
Considering human nature and circumstances,
this is exceedingly excessive!
In the past, Chén Píng abandoned Chǔ,
and by returning to Hàn, he became strong.
Bǎilǐ (Xī) departed Yú,
and upon entering Qín, he became dominant.
Truly, wisdom or folly depends on the ruler,
employment or rejection depends on the person.
Acting in accordance with propriety,
how could the spirits
reject me?
Your letter claims your soldiers and horses are elite and fresh,
setting a date to rise together,
exaggerating your power and position,
surely intending mutual annihilation.
I believe that cold glue and white dew
mark the same season.
When the autumn wind
raises dust,
how are the horses' directions different?
You only know of the contest of strength in the North,
but you do not recognize the coalition formed in the Southwest.
If you blindly pursue your ambition on the path ahead,
you will not notice the pit and trap right beside
you.
Abandoning danger and seeking safety,
I now submit to the true dynastic authority.
Turning calamity into fortune,
I have already escaped the snare.
They ought to sneer at my mistake and delusion,
but these also laugh at your confusion and ignorance.
Now leading two states,
raising banners for a northern campaign.
Bears and tigers rise together,
conquering and recovering the Central Plains.
Jīng, Xiāng, Guǎng, and Yǐng already belong to Guānyòu.
Xiàngchéng and Xiànhù also serve the Jiāng (Yangtze River region).
South,
fortunately, I can take it myself.
Why bother seeking assistance?
However, strategy and adaptability are not singular,
and principles have ten thousand paths.
For your Lordship’s consideration,
nothing is better than dividing territory and achieving mutual peace,
with three powers standing like the legs of a tripod
Yān, Wèi, Zhào, and Jìn are enough to provide for mutual stipends,
while Qí, Cáo, Sòng, and Lǔ entirely revert to Dà Liáng.
If I am allowed to exert my strength for the Southern Court,
and strengthen friendly relations in the North,
bolts of silk
will travel by themselves,
and war chariots need not be harnessed.
I will establish a merit for the present age,
and your Lordship will complete the enterprise of your father and ancestors.
Each will secure his borders and ramparts,
and be allowed to enjoy the seasons.
The common people will be governed and peaceful,
and the four classes of people
will live securely.
How is this compared to driving farmers from the fields,
resisting strong enemies on three sides,
avoiding weapons at the front and rear,
and facing arrows and sharp points in the vital center?
Even if Tàigōng were
the general,
he could not ensure survival.
If this is left to men of high repute,
how can they possibly succeed?
The incoming letter said
that my wife, children, old, and young are all held by the Sīkòu,
and by this I am threatened,
hoping that I might return.
This is likely due to suspicious narrow-mindedness,
failing to recognize the greater objective.
Formerly,
Wáng Líng joined the Hàn,
though his mother remained behind and he did not return;
the Tàishàng was imprisoned by Chǔ,
yet he asked for soup with composure.
How much less important are my wife and children,
that they should concern me!
If you believe that executing them would be beneficial,
you will not be able
to stop;
if killing them brings no detriment,
then further massacre them.
The burden of my family rests with your Lordship,
how does it concern me?
What Zūndào has said
is indeed not baseless;
therefore, I reiterate
my words
and further discuss the details.
Previously, with the covenant leader,
our relationship was like the qín and sè (lutes),
but slanderers intervened,
and suddenly we became enemies.
To stroke the bowstring and draw the arrow,
I cannot help but feel heartbroken.
Tearing silk
and returning the letter,
how can I possibly describe the feeling?
Wáng immediately read the letter
and asked who composed it.
Someone said:
“It was the Administrator of the Mobile Secretariat, Wáng Wěi.”
Wáng said:
“Wěi’s talent is like this,
why did you not let me know?”
Wáng wanted to create a rift between Jǐng and Liáng,
so he wrote another letter to Jǐng but falsified the wording,
saying that he originally sent Jǐng Yáng to revolt,
planning to conspire with him for Xī (the West).
When the Xī people learned of this,
Jǐng therefore changed his plans and conspired with Nán (the South) instead.
He allowed this letter to be revealed to Liáng,
but the Liáng people did not believe it either.
On the day Rénshēn,
the Lord of Dōng Wèi hunted with Wáng east of Yè,
galloping and chasing like flying.
The Director-General of the Guards, Wū Nàluó Shòugōngfá, called from behind:
“The Son of Heaven should not run his horse so fast!
The Dà Jiāngjūn (Great General) will be angry.”
Wáng once attended a drinking session,
and raising a large cup, he said:
“I, your subject Chéng, propose a toast to Your Majesty.”
The Lord of Dōng Wèi was displeased and said:
“Since ancient times, there has been no country that did not perish.
Why should I continue to live like this?”
Wáng angrily said:
“Zhèn!
Zhèn!
You dog-legged Zhèn!”
He ordered Cuī Jìshū to hit him three times with his fists,
then he shook his robes and departed.
Soon after, he sent Jìshū in to apologize.
The Lord of Dōng Wèi bestowed silk upon Jìshū.
Jìshū did not immediately dare to accept it,
and petitioned Wáng about it.
Wáng ordered him to take one roll.
The Lord of Dōng Wèi gave him four hundred bolts,
saying:
“That is also just one roll.”
The Lord of Dōng Wèi could not bear the distress and humiliation,
and recited a poem by Xiè Língyùn, saying:
“When Hán perished, Zǐfáng rose up;
when Qín ruled, Lǔ Lián resisted.
Originally people of the rivers and seas,
their loyalty and righteousness move the noble person.”
Thereupon, he wept.
In the third month, on the day Xīnhài,
Wáng went south to Líyáng,
crossed at Hǔláo,
and returned to Jìnyáng from Luòyáng by way of the Tàiháng Mountains.
Along the way, he sent letters to all officials,
to warn and encourage them.
Both court and common society accepted his influence,
and none were not awestruck and sobered.
He further ordered court ministers and regional governors to each select men of virtue, and those brave, martial, and strategically capable of defending border cities,
ensuring that they obtained the truly talented,
regardless of their current official position.
In the sixth month,
Wáng inspected the border cities and garrisons in the north,
and distributed relief and gifts according to rank.
Ōuyùe,
the western route of Qiānlǒng,
Wúyuè is fierce and strong,
with thousands of armored troops.
Qín soldiers and Jì horses,
ten myriad archers.
When a great wind blows,
dry branches must be broken.
When frost
briefly falls,
autumn calyxes naturally wither.
If this is considered weak,
who is fit to be called a hero?
Moreover, to be slandered by both sides,
and suspected by two states,
considering the circumstances,
how truly excessive!
In the past, Chén Píng abandoned Chǔ
and returned to Hàn, becoming strong.
Bǎilǐ Xī left Yú
and entered Qín, becoming dominant.
Indeed, clarity or confusion depends on the ruler;
to be employed or discarded depends on the individual.
If one acts according to propriety,
how could the spirits
spew forth evil?
The letter states that the soldiers and horses are fresh and keen,
and will be mobilized on an appointed day,
exaggerating the situation,
certainly intending to annihilate each other.
I sincerely believe that cold glue and white dew
mark the same season;
when autumn winds
stir up dust,
how can the horses' heads be different?
You only know the北方’s struggle for power,
but have not recognized the Southwest’s alliance.
If you blindly pursue your will on the road ahead,
you will not realize that a pitfall lies at your
side.
To abandon danger and embrace safety,
we now return to the orthodox calendar.
To turn misfortune into fortune,
we have already escaped the net.
They will ridicule my extreme delusion,
while I also laugh at your obscurity.
Now, if you lead these two states,
hoist your banners and march north,
with bears and tigers striving together,
to recover the Central Plains,
then Jīng, Xiāng, Guǎng, and Yǐng will already belong to Guān Yòu,
and Xiàngchéng and Xiànhù will also serve Jiāng
Nán.
You will have fortunately seized it yourself;
why bother with external aid?
However, there is more than one strategy;
reason has myriad paths.
For your sake,
nothing is better than ceding territory for a dual peace,
and a tripartite
standoff.
Yān, Wèi, Zhào, and Jìn would be sufficient for mutual emolument,
while Qí, Cáo, Sòng, and Lǔ would all belong to Dàliáng.
This would allow me to contribute my strength to the Southern Court,
and strengthen good relations with the North.
Bundles of silk
would be sent on their own,
war chariots would not be harnessed.
I would establish a功 for this generation,
and you would complete the enterprise of your father and ancestors.
Each would protect their borders,
and enjoy the seasons in peace.
The populace would be well-governed and tranquil,
and the four peoples
would live in peace.
How could this compare to driving farmers from their fields,
resisting a strong enemy on three fronts,
avoiding weapons at both ends,
and facing blades at the very heart?
Even if Tàigōng were
the general,
he could not survive.
If it is left to an illustrious one,
how can it succeed?
The incoming letter says,
“Your wife, children, old, and young are all in the Sīkòu's custody.
With this, you are constrained,
so you should be able to return.”
This must be due to suspicious and narrow-minded thinking,
not understanding the greater purpose.
In the past,
Wáng Líng adhered to Hàn,
even though his mother was not returned.
Tàishàng was imprisoned by Chǔ,
yet calmly asked for soup.
How much less, then, is one's wife and children,
to be concerned about?
If it is said that killing them is beneficial,
and you
cannot be stopped,
or that killing them causes no harm,
and you further slaughter them by burying them alive,
the burden on the family lies with you,
what concern is it of mine?
What Zūndào said
was not entirely false;
therefore, I reiterate
my words,
and discuss the matter in detail.
In the past, with the sworn ally,
our relationship was like zithers;
slanderers came between us,
and we became enemies.
Plucking strings and nocking arrows,
I cannot but feel sorrow.
Tearing silk
to return the letter,
how can I express it?
The King then read the letter,
and asked who wrote it.
Someone said,
“It is Wáng Wěi, his Xíngtái Láng.”
The King said,
“Wěi's talent is such,
why did I not know of him?”
The King wanted to sow discord between Jǐng and Liáng,
so he sent another letter to Jǐng, distorting its contents,
saying that he had originally instructed Jǐng to rebel,
intending to plot with him against the West.
The Westerners knew of this,
so Jǐng instead plotted with them against the South.
He leaked the letter to Liáng,
but the Liáng people did not believe it either.
On the day Rénshēn,
the Eastern Wèi Emperor hunted with Gāo Yáng in the east of Yè,
racing like flying.
The Jiānwèi Dūdū Wūnàluó Shòugōngfá called from behind,
“Your Majesty, do not run your horse so fast,
the Great General is angry.”
Gāo Yáng once attended a drinking party,
and raising a large goblet, said,
“Your servant Chéng encourages Your Majesty to drink.”
The Eastern Wèi Emperor was displeased and said,
“Since ancient times, no state has not perished.
Why should I live like this!”
Gāo Yáng angrily said,
“Zhèn!
Zhèn!
Dog-foot Zhèn!”
He ordered Cuī Jìshū to hit him three times,
and then Gāo Yáng flung his robes and left.
Soon after, he sent Jìshū to apologize.
The Eastern Wèi Emperor bestowed colored silks upon Jìshū.
Jìshū did not dare to accept them immediately,
and reported it to Gāo Yáng.
Gāo Yáng instructed him to take one piece.
The Eastern Wèi Emperor gave him four hundred bolts,
saying,
“This is also one piece.”
The Eastern Wèi Emperor, unable to bear the anxiety and humiliation,
recited a poem by Xiè Língyùn:
“When Hán perished, Zǐfáng rose.
When Qín reigned, Lǔ Lián disdained to serve.
They were originally men of the rivers and seas,
but loyalty and righteousness moved gentlemen.”
Then he shed tears.
On the Xīnhài day of the third month,
Gāo Yáng went south to Líyáng,
crossed the river at Hǔláo,
and returned to Jìnyáng from Luòyáng via the Tàiháng Mountains.
Along the way, he sent letters to all officials,
to admonish and encourage them.
Both court and common folk were influenced,
and none were not awestruck.
He also ordered court officials, governors, and magistrates to select virtuous and capable individuals, as well as courageous and strategic ones suitable for guarding frontier cities,
ensuring that their talents were secured,
regardless of their previous profession.
In the sixth month,
Gāo Yáng toured the frontier cities and garrisons in the north,
distributing varying amounts of relief and rewards.
In the seventh month,
Wáng returned to Jìnyáng.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Wáng encountered bandits and passed away,
at the age of twenty-nine at the time.
He was buried at Jùnchéng Líng.
When Qí received the abdication,
he was posthumously given the title Wénxiāng Huángdì,
with the temple name Shìzōng.
At that time, there was a nursery rhyme that said:
“A hundred-foot-high pole collapses and breaks,
A lamp lit beneath the water is extinguished.”
Those with foresight believed this to be an omen that Wáng was about to pass away.
A few days earlier,
Cuī Jìshū, without apparent reason, recited the poem of Bāo Míngyuǎn in front of the nobles outside the North Palace Gate, saying:
“Now that the general has passed away,
few of his troops remain.”
His voice was extremely mournful and broken,
and he could not stop his tears.
All who saw him were surprised by this.
Earlier,
Lán Qīn, a general of Liáng, had a son named Jīng who was captured by the Eastern Wèi.
Wáng ordered him to be assigned to the kitchen staff.
Qīn requested to ransom him,
but Wáng refused.
When Jīng sued again,
Wáng ordered Xuē Fēngluò, the head servant supervising the kitchen, to cane him,
saying:
“If you sue again, I will kill you.”
Jīng and six of his associates plotted to rebel.
At that time, Wáng was residing in the Bǎi Táng (Cypress Hall) in the eastern part of the Northern City to manage state affairs.
He did this to favor Princess Lángyé,
desiring that she be able to come and go without hindrance or taboo,
so all his bodyguards
were kept outside.
The Grand Astrologer reported that the star of the chief minister was very dim,
and a crisis would occur within a month.
Wáng said:
“That scoundrel was just newly caned,
so he is merely trying to frighten me.”
When he was about to accept the abdication,
he dismissed those around him and, with Chén Yuánkāng, Cuī Jìshū, and others,
drafted nominations for the hundred officials.
When Jīng was about to present food,
Wáng pushed it away
and said to the others:
“Last night I dreamt this slave chopped me;
he ought to be killed.”
When Jīng heard this,
he placed a knife on the tray
and boldly presented the food.
Wáng angrily said:
“I haven’t asked for food,
why have you rushed in!”
Jīng brandished the knife and said:
“I have come to kill you!”
Wáng threw himself down, injuring his foot,
and hid under the bed.
The gang of bandits pulled the bed away,
and consequently he was killed.
Previously, there was a rumor that said
“Soft hat removed,
panting beneath the bed,”
and the saying was fulfilled.
At that time, the Duke of Tàiyuán, Yáng, was in the Shuāng Táng (Twin Hall) east of the city.
He entered and attacked the bandits,
slicing up Jīng and the others,
and lacquering all their heads.
The death was kept secret,
and he slowly issued a statement saying:
“The slave rebelled,
and the Great General was injured,
but it is not severely painful.”
The Imperial Annals, Fourth Section: Wénxuān
Xiǎnzǔ Wénxuān Huángdì, personal name Yáng,
courtesy name Zǐjìn,
was the second son of Gāozǔ
and the younger brother of Shìzōng by the same mother.
When the empress first became pregnant,
there was a red light illuminating the chamber every night,
and the empress privately found this unusual.
Initially,
when Gāozǔ returned to Ěrzhū Róng,
they went through perilous disorder,
and the household was utterly impoverished.
The empress, facing her relatives,
shared their worry about cold and starvation.
The Emperor could not yet speak at that time,
but he suddenly responded,
“We shall live,”
which greatly astonished the Empress Dowager and those around her, though they dared not speak.
He had skin like scales,
double ankles,
did not enjoy games,
and was deeply reserved with great tolerance.
There was once a Buddhist monk in Jìnyáng,
sometimes foolish, sometimes wise,
whom people of the time could not fathom
and called Ā Tū Shī.
The Emperor once went to see him with the other boys.
The monk asked about the official position and salary of each one in turn.
When he came to the Emperor,
he merely raised his hand and pointed to the sky repeatedly
without speaking a word.
Those who saw it found it extraordinary.
Gāozǔ once tried to observe the awareness of his sons
by having each untangle a bundle of messy silk threads.
The Emperor alone drew a knife and cut through it,
saying:
“What is tangled must be cut.”
Gāozǔ approved of this.
He also distributed soldiers to each of them and sent them out in four directions,
and then had armored cavalry falsely attack them.
Shìzōng and the others were terrified and gave ground,
but the Emperor rallied his troops and engaged Péng Lè.
Even when Lè removed his helmet and confessed the truth,
the Emperor still captured him and presented him.
Later, following Shìzōng and traveling past Mount Liáoyáng,
he alone saw the gates of heaven open;
the others saw nothing.
Although he was inwardly intelligent and astute,
his appearance suggested a lack thereof.
Shìzōng often mocked him,
saying:
“If this person can also attain wealth and nobility,
how can the art of physiognomy possibly be understood?”
Only Gāozǔ considered him extraordinary
and said to Xuē Shū:
“This child’s awareness surpasses mine.”
As a youth, he studied under Lú Jǐngyù of Fànyáng.
His silent memory surpassed others;
Jǐngyù could not fathom him.
In the second year of Tiānpíng (535),
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, and Founding Duke of Tàiyuán Commandery.
In the first year of Wǔdìng (543),
he was given the added title Shìzhōng.
In the second year (544),
he was transferred to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the fifth year (547),
he was appointed Shàngshū Lìng, Zhōngshū Jiān, and Jīngjī Dà Dūdū.
In the eighth month of the seventh year of Wǔdìng (549),
Shìzōng was murdered.
The event happened suddenly,
and the court and people were shaken with alarm.
The Emperor’s expression did not change.
He issued commands and made dispositions,
personally slicing and beheading the group of bandits and lacquering their heads.
He slowly issued a statement saying:
“The slave rebelled,
and the Great General was injured,
but it is not severely painful.”
At that time, everyone inside and outside the court was astonished and impressed.
He then hurried to Jìnyáng,
personally took charge of all political affairs,
and strove for leniency and generosity.
Whatever was inconvenient was abolished and curtailed.
In the tenth month, on the first day, Guǐwèi, in winter,
Tǎn, Prince of Xiányáng, was appointed Tài fù,
and Pān Xiànglè was appointed Sīkōng.
In the eleventh month, on the day Wùwǔ,
the state of Tǔyùhùn sent an envoy to present tribute.
Máo Língbīn, Inspector of Qízhōu for Liáng, Liú Lǐngduì, Inspector of Dézhōu, and Huángfǔ and others, Inspectors of Nán Yùzhōu, all brought their prefectures to defect.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
Péng Lè, Inspector of Bīngzhōu, was appointed Sītú,
and Hèbá Rén, Grand Protector, was appointed Inspector of Bīngzhōu.
In the first month, on the day Gēngshēn, of the eighth year (550) in spring,
Sòng Āngù, Inspector of Chǔzhōu for Liáng, brought his prefecture to defect.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Wèi Emperor held a mourning ceremony for Shìzōng at the Eastern Hall.
Tián Cōngnéng, Inspector of Dìngzhōu for Liáng, Zhāng Xiǎn, Inspector of Hóngzhōu, and others brought their prefectures to defect.
On the day Wùchén,

Wèi issued an edict advancing the Emperor's position to Envoy with Credentials, Chancellor, Area Commander-in-Chief of All Internal and External Military Affairs, Director of the Department of State Affairs, Grand Director of the Traveling Chancellery, and Prince of Qí Commandery,
with an income of ten thousand households.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the state of Dìdòuyú sent an envoy to present tribute.
In the third month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
he was further granted the title Prince of Qí,
with an income drawn from the five commanderies of Bóhǎi, Chánglè, Āndé, Wǔyì in Jìzhōu, and Héjiān in Yīngzhōu,
totaling one hundred thousand households.
Since residing in Jìnyáng,
his sleeping chamber was illuminated at night as bright as day.
After becoming a prince,
he dreamt that someone marked his forehead with a brush.
The next morning, he told his retainer Wáng Tánzhé:
“Should I perhaps retire?”
Tánzhé bowed twice and congratulated him, saying:
“Adding a dot above the character Wáng (王, prince)
forms the character Zhǔ (主, lord),
which means you are about to advance.”
In the summer, fifth month, on the day Xīnhài,
the Emperor went to Yè.
On the day Jiǎyín,
he advanced the Prime Minister (Xiàngguó),
who governed all governmental affairs (Bǎikuí),
and enfeoffed him with ten commanderies: Bóhǎi, Chánglè, Āndé, and Wǔyì of Jìzhōu; Héjiān, Gāoyáng, and Zhāngwǔ of Yíngzhōu; and Zhōngshān, Chángshān, and Bólíng of Dìngzhōu,
totaling two hundred thousand households.
He was granted the Nine Marks of Honor (Jiǔ Xī),
accorded special courtesies (Shū Lǐ),
and the title King of Qí (Qí Wáng) remained as before.

The Emperor of Wèi dispatched Péngchéng Wáng Sháo, who concurrently held the title Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), and Pān Xiānglè, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), to present the formal mandate, which stated: Alas!
Reverently heed Our command!
Indeed, only Heaven is great,
arraying the celestial bodies and stars to display its phenomena;
it is said that Earth is vast,
opening up rivers and mountains to nourish all things.
It is for this reason that
the four seasons proceed in order,
the myriad creatures are closely arrayed,
all species fulfill their nature,
and all forms do not perish prematurely.
Therefore, when enlightened monarchs assume the historical mandate,
they observe profoundly and reside highly,
folding their hands and letting their robes hang (ruling through inaction),
committing their success
to their mentors and ministers.
This is how the Lords of Xià and the Yin Ministers exhausted their strength,
and King Chéng of Zhōu and Emperor Zhāo of Hàn achieved order through non-action.
Recently, the world has faced many difficulties,
the nation's mandate hanging like a banner in the wind (precarious),
and thus the enterprise of
establishing Our state was about to fall to the ground.
Xiànwǔ Wáng of Qí roused himself like wind and clouds,
greatly relieving difficulties and dangers,
and so assisted Our person;
the state was recreated.
He managed all territories
with utmost diligence and care.
When Wénxiāng succeeded to this foundation,
he further expanded the former achievements,
pacifying the state and quelling difficulties;
his Way reached the vast heavens.
Now, the King's virtue responds to the destined time—
emerging once in a thousand years.
In matters of subtle omen
and profound depth,
he is both divine and sagely.
He greatly enhanced the Lord Protector's (Bà) virtue,
and truly broadened the Prime Minister's strategies.
Although his hidden merit and subtle reality
surpass description and imagery,
his renown and manifest traces
must be proclaimed
according to ritual laws.
We now reiterate the previous mandate;
may the King respectfully and humbly accept it.
When the King first soared upon the wind,
raising his banner in the upper lands,
protecting the people and establishing governance,
the seasonal rain poured down.
The lower classes learned integrity and shame;
benevolence extended to land and sea.
He changed customs and transformed habits,
making
Qí transform into Lǔ.
This is an achievement of the King.
He then assumed the management of the Imperial Court (Tiāntái),
and oversaw military regulations.
His strategies emerged as if divine,
his might extending throughout the northern lands.
The archers retreated, concealing their traces;
the pine frontier lacked
smoke (from warfare).
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
Furthermore, he glorified the former succession,
holding the balance and bringing alignment.
The Huá and the Róng were unified;
the world within the four seas was harmonious and peaceful.
The sun and moon shone brightly;
heaven and earth were clear
and tranquil.
Reputations echoed and responses followed;
there was no thought that was not subdued.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
Far away was the southern region (Yánfāng),
which evaded the legitimate calendar (Zhèngshuò).
Holding culture (wén) and displaying might (wǔ),
he assigned strategy and reaffirmed rules.
Huái and Chǔ, with their continuous cities,
crumbled suddenly like falling mulberries.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
Guān and Xiàn are the collar and sash (vital terrain),
crossing over desolate areas,
the land serving as the body's vital organs (chángwèi),
standing high like mountains and squatting like owls.
A small
division had merely approached,
and they melted away like dispersed ice.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
The region of Jìnxī,
where danger lurked along the Jiāng and Léi rivers,
was remotely separated from civilizing influence,
and its deviation remained unchanged.
He ordered generals to gather
troops,
overturning their nests and caves.
His strategic might soared like the wind,
shaking and intimidating the South China Sea.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
The various Mán tribes were rebellious,
having perpetually cut off the southern frontier.
They shook the border regions,
frequently causing disturbance and obstruction.
Cherishing virtue and fearing might,
they turned toward his influence and requested submission.
All their mountain corners were conquered;
those who arrived were numerous as clouds.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
The various branches of Hu people,
extending along
valleys and mountains,
with ten thousand chieftains and clans,
spanning thousands of miles in breadth and length,
relied on rugged terrain and showed no respect,
indulging their cunning and arrogance.
Those who delighted in pure customs
knocked on the gate seeking alliance.
The tribute of grain and silk
filled
the King's storehouse.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
Those sailing the vast sea
were historically rivals to all the Huá.
Moving like the wind and flying like birds,
they came suddenly and went abruptly.
Having drunk the mellow wine,
they adhered like lacquer
and glue.
Pelt garments were piled high in layers;
exotic beasts followed in a line.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
Qín Chuān still maintained its obstruction,
making itself our enemy.
Yet, they presented fragrant offerings (jiāolán),
sending letters requesting peace.
Heaven moved their hearts;
their words were humble and their rites generous.
The whole territory was well-governed and tranquil;
near and far arrived entirely.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
When Jiāngyīn announced calamity,
the people had nowhere to turn.
The descendants of the Xiāo clan
and their younger relatives
still sought refuge under his protection.
They were like birds returning to the mountains,
or streams rushing to the sea.
The ten departments of Jīng and Jiāng
suddenly offered cession.
Taking advantage of this opportunity,
he was about to absorb the Southern
regions.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
Heaven is balanced and Earth is complete;
all the land is prosperous.
Auspicious omens are clearly visible;
the chroniclers cannot stop writing.
Both the connected trees (Lián Bǎimù)
and the nine-tailed
beast were presented.
The white bird surpassed the Qín sparrow;
the dark bird matched the Zhōu crow.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
He sought out and brought forth the stored talents;
the gentry achieved order.
Rituals were observed and music was played;
what had been neglected was entirely restored.
He lightened corvée and abolished taxes;
he was compassionate in legal cases and lenient in punishment.
Great trustworthiness was externally manifested;
profound benevolence extended far and wide.
This, too, is an achievement of the King.
The King possesses the great merit of pacifying the realm (rìxià),
and furthermore
displays magnificent virtue and enlightenment.
He proclaims and assists the grand strategy,
thereby supporting Our words.
In the past, Dàn and Shì were assigned external territories,
while Máo and Bì assisted internally.
The responsibility for both internal and external affairs
is suitable for the King.
In sum,
human and divine counsel,
the two elemental forces cooperating,
the bestowal of the mandate proceeds,
its righteousness establishes public justice.
As the king treads the law and practices propriety,
he brings order to all living beings,
calms the minds of the people,
and guides hearts back to the Way.
Therefore, the king is bestowed one grand carriage (dàlù) and one war chariot (rónglù),
and two teams of black oxen.
The king profoundly values the people as Heaven,
and makes the fundamental his priority;
the provisions of clothing and food,
the source of
honor and disgrace.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with a ceremonial robe (gǔnmiǎn) and
red slippers (chìxì) to accompany it.
The king's profound and extensive benevolence and harmony
easily transform customs and traditions,
the gods and spirits respond,
and his merits and virtues are exemplary.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with the xuānxuán music
and the dance of six lines (liùyì).
The king's fame and prestige vibrate gloriously,
the nine regions are all pacified,
distant people willingly submit,
and hasten to present tribute.
Therefore,
the king is bestowed with a vermilion door (zhūhù) for his residence.
The king seeks the worthy and selects the multitude,
leaving no talent undiscovered,
those who exert their strength take their proper places,
none are unsuitable for their roles.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with an inclined entrance (nàbì) for ascent.
The king's
brilliant plans and fierce determination
elevate and suppress all kinds of things,
his resolute integrity
distinguishes right from wrong and eliminates transgression.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with three hundred Wǔbēn warriors.
The king holds the fate of rise and fall,
controls
the seen and the unseen,
enforces Heaven's punitive expeditions,
and apprehends all offenders.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with one battle-axe (fū) and one hatchet (yuè).
The king soars like a hawk and transforms like a leopard,
truly supporting the world below,
with the gaze of a wolf and the spread of an owl,
none escape his swift arrows.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with one vermilion bow (tónggōng), one hundred vermilion arrows (tóngshǐ), ten black bows (lúgōng), and one thousand black arrows (lúshǐ).
The king's filial piety and fraternal respect reach the utmost,
communicating with the gods,
leading the people to rise
and act,
his influence reaching all corners of the land.
Therefore, the king is bestowed with one jar of black millet wine (jùchàng),
and a jade libation cup (guīzàn) to accompany it.
Go forth with reverence!
Respectfully obey this decree,
assist the imperial house,
to complete
your excellent virtue,
and respond to and glorify the illustrious mandate of Our Great Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
The Wèi Emperor (Wèi Dì), seeing that the hopes of Heaven and man had converged,
on the day of Bǐngchén,
issued an edict saying: "When the Three Powers (sāncái) were first divided and formed,
a hundred kings rose in succession,
governing Heaven and pacifying Earth,
harmonizing spirits and revering ghosts,
protecting the people and creating things.
All these came from auspicious omens;
it is not the great treasure of one person,
but truly the divine instrument of the virtuous.
In the past, Our imperial ancestor (zōngzǔ) answered the call of destiny,
and unified all regions.
Saints succeeded him, bringing renewed glory,
down to the ninth generation.
When virtue was not continued,
the state fell into distress
and ruin.
Those who usurped titles were rampant throughout the nine provinces,
and those who wielded authority were not limited to the Three Dukes (sāngōng).
Rulers were killed, courts were imperiled,
and neither man nor spirit had a guiding principle.
The vastness of the world
was on the verge of
not belonging to Wèi.
Fortunately, Qí Xiànwǔ Wáng (齊獻武王) roused his spiritual military might,
overcame many difficulties,
re-suspended the sun and moon,
and re-arranged the constellations.
The ancestral temple was cleansed,
and the state was rebuilt.
His vast achievements
and immense undertakings
are beyond praise.
Then Wénxiāng (文襄) inherited the foundation,
and the family's enterprise grew even wider.
Those near were pacified, those far submitted,
and the realm was peaceful.
The national destiny was stabilized,
and all living beings found their nature.
Now, Xiàngguó Qí Wáng (相國齊王),
with comprehensive literary and martial skills,
has unified this great undertaking,
exhausted wisdom and delved into subtleties,
studied the profound and measured transformations,
his thoughts follow the mysterious workings of destiny,
his wisdom moves with the gods.
His benevolence is like
springtime,
his majesty like the summer sun.
He lays bare his sincere heart to all beings,
and spreads the Great Way (dàdào) throughout the eight directions.
Thus, all officials are exemplary,
and there is no corrupt governance at court.
The net of law is lenient, but its grace is pervasive,
and the entire land
submits its heart.
Externally, he has pacified the Jiāng-Huái region,
and bent the knee of all who resisted.
He has expanded territory and won over people,
and a hundred cities hasten to him.
Guānlǒng (關隴) admires his righteousness and requests friendship,
Hànmò (瀚漠) looks up to his virtue and expresses sincerity.
This is what is called a destined leader who answers the call of his time,
truly governing for a thousand years.
Auspicious omens are intertwined,
and strange creatures appear together.
Songs of praise fill the land,
and distant lands show a unified resolve.
The signs of the end of a dynasty are
manifest,
and the covenant between man and spirit is sealed.
Heaven's Way is not distant;
I am not the only one who knows.
I inherited the great legacy,
and am to continue the ancestral sacrifices,
relying on the profound support I received,
extending the calculations of the ancestral temple.
Reflecting on the great changes,
I am pleased to yield to the worthy.
Considering the ancient precedents of the abdication of Táng (唐) and
Yú (虞),
and recalling the recent tradition of concession between Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉),
how can I obscure the rites of rise and fall,
and delay the hopes of the gods and spirits?
I shall now retire to a separate palace,
and return
the imperial throne to the state of Qí.
This promotion of the sagacious and capable
perfectly conforms to previous precedents."
The authorities are to announce this throughout the realm
and implement it in due course.
He also sent Pángchéng Wáng Sháo (彭城王韶), acting Tàiwèi (太尉), and Jìng Xiǎnjùn (敬顯儁), acting Sīkōng (司空), to present the imperial edict, saying: "Oh, Xiàngguó Qí Wáng (相國齊王)!
When qi (qì) divides into forms and transforms,
beings are bound to rulers.
Emperors and kings rise in succession,
and mankind is not of a single surname.
In the past, Fàngxūn (放勳) governed the world,
and offered jade to his son (shǔzǐ);
Chónghuá (重華) held the calendar,
and maintained balance and embraced the celestial sphere.
Thus, virtuous and talented individuals, with their flourishing achievements,
have been clearly illuminated through the ages.
How could prosperity and decline not have their cycles,
and rise and fall not be governed by the times?
One who knows the mandate
cannot but bestow it,
and one who fears Heaven cannot but receive it.
Therefore, when the Hàn (漢) of Liú (劉) faced decline,
those who had the right to rule followed the will of the people.
When Cáo's (曹) reign was not long,
the element of Metal yielded the throne.
These are all instances of following established rules
and ancient precedents,
abiding by old customs.
Our ancestors brilliantly settled and
unified the ten thousand realms.
Towards the end of Zhèngguāng (正光),
wicked rebels seized power,
their governance was perverse in many ways,
and the nine regions were in turmoil.
The fate of Yǒng'ān (永安)
was exhausted,
humanity and spirits were in despair,
a multitude of rebels surged to the heavens,
carving up the four seas.
The land and its subjects
were virtually no longer Wèi's.
Qí Xiànwǔ Wáng (齊獻武王) answered the call of the era and lent his hand,
soaring like a phoenix and leaping like a dragon.
Xiāng,
raised up the fallen apex to establish Heaven,
supported the leaning pillar and stabilized the Earth,
cut down and extinguished the toxic masses,
rectified our failing calendar/dynasty,
possessed great virtue toward the Wèi House,
conferred wide benefits upon the common
people.
And when Wénxiāng followed his path,
he greatly illuminated the former achievement.
Internally he suppressed treacherous authorities,
externally he crushed invading rebels,
near and far were tranquil and peaceful,
his merit reached the High Heaven.
Your Majesty, with spiritual presence and corresponding virtue,
served as a boat and bridge for the entire age,
embodied refinement and manifested martial prowess,
pursuing change to the utmost subtleties.
Since rising up in the border regions,
songs of praise have been universally collected;
upon entering to govern the pivotal affairs of state,
your reputation and conduct were grand and far-reaching.
And when you greatly
inherited the hereditary achievement,
supported the state and made the family prosperous,
your virtue as chancellor advanced daily,
and the aura of hegemony became ever more distant.
As soon as your awe-inspiring spiritual power flowed forth, the desolate distances hastened to submit,
and wherever your reputation and strategy spread, neighboring enemies yielded in submission.
Possessing abundant innate ability,
directing extraordinary and superior vitality,
in the space of a single glance,
there was no thought that did not submit.
Prophecies and records secretly stored away,
became clearly manifest after a thousand years;
auspicious signs and hidden portents,
suddenly
piled up in abundance,
thereby indicating the time for the succession of virtue (dynastic change),
and thus commencing the footsteps of founding a state;
the Azure Heaven is above,
watching over and illuminating not far off.
I, the Emperor (Zhèn), being deficient and ignorant,
still have not hesitated,
but contemplating in silence,
I am ashamed of this,
and sit awaiting the dawn.
Moreover, when the time comes and the Mandate moves,
Guī Shùn did not have the luxury to remain facing south;
when the age undergoes revolution and change,
Bó Yǔ did not permit himself to remain facing north;
how much less should one who is meager
and unworthy,
hesitate?
Therefore, looking up, I align with the vast Heaven,
and looking down, I comply with the hundred surnames;
I respectfully transfer the Imperial Throne, as a model, to Your Majesty.
Heaven's emolument has forever ceased,
the Great Mandate has reached its end.
Ah, alas!
May you respectfully receive the calendar and destiny,
sincerely hold fast to the Mean,
and respond with praise to Heaven's benevolence!
May these years number ten thousand times ten thousand!
How glorious this is!
Furthermore, a sealed letter was sent to the Emperor,
dispatching the Acting Grand Tutor, Péngchéng Wáng Sháo, and the Acting Minister of Works, Jìng Xiǎnjùn, to present the Imperial Seal and ribbon.
The rites of abdication and succession followed entirely the precedents of Táng Yú and Hàn Wèi.
Furthermore, the President of the Department of State Affairs, Gāo Lóngzhī, led the numerous officials in urging accession.
On the day Wùwǔ,
he then ascended the Imperial Throne at the Southern Suburb,
mounted the altar, and performed the bonfire sacrifice, announcing to Heaven: "I, Emperor Chén Yáng, dare to use a dark bull
to brightly announce to the August Sovereign and Supreme Thearch: Stagnation and prosperity follow one another,
decline and rise are employed alternately.
The ultimate Way has no partiality,
and assists those who correspond to the Mandate.
Looking up at Táng and Yú,
and down, examining Wèi and Jìn,
none failed to yield the position based on the prior Heaven's decree,
and testing the records, all returned to the destined end.
The Wèi clan suffered many difficulties,
spanning nearly thirty years.
Since Xiàochāng,
both internal and external parties abandoned it.
The way of the world flowed contrary (to order),
and the common people were smeared in mud and charcoal.
Relying on our Xiànwǔ,
he rescued those about to drown,
established the sovereign three times,
and twice re-established the ancestral line.
He swept away and eliminated
the multitude of villains,
cleared out treacherous elements,
his virtue covered the black-haired people,
and his achievements illuminated the universe.
Wénxiāng succeeded his martial (father),
and was able to establish a grand foundation.
His merit permeated the whole world,
and his prestige reached overseas.
Even the distant
barbarian tribes cherished his instruction,
the western bandits offered submission,
Qīngqiū awaited (his command),
and Dānxué came to court.
He assisted and supported the crisis,
and renewed the rectification of the declining Mandate;
this was having a great service done to the Wèi House.
The Wèi Emperor, realizing the calculated lifespan (of his dynasty) had ended,
and that the Supreme Spirits disapproved of his virtue,
respectfully followed Vast Heaven,
sincerely returned the Great Mandate,
and abdicated to me, Chén Yáng.
Now, the four seas are ultimately public,
and All
Under Heaven constitutes one entity;
in uniting the people and governing the age,
a ruler must be established for them.
Since the rivers and mountains revealed the tally (of destiny),
and both men and spirits displayed auspicious signs,
the multitude of dukes, ministers, and gentlemen,
and the countless masses of the eight directions,
all agreed that the Imperial Standard
looked upon me from above,
and the Wèi court advanced me from below,
and the position of Heaven could not be temporarily vacant.
Thus, constrained by the counsel of the many,
I respectfully accepted the great ceremony.
Unworthily, though I am meager and insufficient,
I am placed above the countless
people.
Although the Majesty of Heaven is before my face,
and an inch is not far away,
examining myself and reflecting,
I truly harbor reverence and vigilance.
I respectfully selected an auspicious day,
ascended the altar to receive the abdication,
and now offer this corresponding sacrifice to the Supreme (Thearch)...
Dì,
in response to the aspirations of all nations,
to eternally advance auspiciousness,
and protect and bless Qí,
thereby extending it to an endless reign.
On this day,
the capital obtained a red sparrow,
which was presented at the southern altar.
After the ceremony was complete,
he returned to the palace
and held court in the Tàijí Qiándiàn.
A decree stated:
“Being esteemed without possessing virtue,
replacing punishment with ritual,
being trusted without speaking,
and coming before spring and after autumn.
Thus it is known that the transformation of compassion
is a single principle for Heaven and humanity,
and the way of broad leniency
is the same in ancient and modern times.
I, being of shallow virtue,
have achieved no remarkable deeds.
Formerly, the late Xiànwǔ Wáng encountered a time when Wèi was in decline,
the nine tripods were departing;
he then marshalled the marquises and counts,
and issued a grand proclamation to Yān and Zhào,
rescuing those who had fallen,
and causing the lost to be preserved.
Wénxiāng Wáng outwardly displayed military prowess,
and inwardly possessed brilliant virtue.
He inherited the martial legacy of his predecessors,
expanding territory and subduing distant lands.
Over two decades passed,
and he presided over two capitals;
justice was served in legal cases,
and songs of praise were sung.
Therefore, the Wèi Emperor humbly followed the celestial mandate,
and, recalling the tradition of yielding the throne,
looked to Táng and Yú from afar,
ultimately renouncing his position as if shedding a sandal.
Indeed, my profound worries were unceasing,
my ambition was in Yángchéng;
but the sincerity and loyalty of all the ducal ministers became ever more urgent,
thus the succession was passed to me,
placing me above the people,
like wading through deep water,
with concerns throughout the day.
Upon first departing Jìnyáng,
a nine-tailed fox appeared as an auspicious omen.
At the outer altar, Heaven was invoked,
and a red sparrow demonstrated auspiciousness.
You, my civil and military officials of undivided loyalty,
my generals, my limbs and claws,
who assisted the late kings,
and were able to accomplish great deeds,
may your sincerity and integrity be eternally remembered,
and may you share in this auspiciousness.
I wish to share with the myriad people the beginning of this day;
let there be a great amnesty throughout the realm.
The eighth year of Wǔdìng is hereby changed to the first year of Tiānbǎo.
All officials shall be promoted in rank;
all adult males shall be granted titles of nobility;
widows, orphans, the six infirm, righteous husbands, and chaste wives shall each receive commendations and rewards according to their circumstances.”
On the day Jǐwèi,
a decree enfeoffed the Wèi Emperor as Zhōngshān Wáng,
with a fief of ten thousand households;
when submitting memorials, he was not to address himself as a subject;
responses to him were not to be called decrees;
he was to display the Son of Heaven's banners;
follow the Wèi calendar;
and ride in a vice-chariot of the five seasons.
The king's sons were enfeoffed as Xiàn Gōng,
with a thousand households each;
he was granted ten thousand bolts of silk,
ten million cash,
twenty thousand shí of grain,
two hundred servants,
one watermill,
one hundred qǐng of land,
and one garden.
A decree posthumously honored the Imperial Ancestor Wénmù Wáng as Wénmù Huángdì,
his consort as Wénmù Huánghòu,
the Imperial Father Xiànwǔ Wáng as Xiànwǔ Huángdì,
and the Imperial Brother Wénxiāng Wáng as Wénxiāng Huángdì.
The titles for the ancestors and progenitors
were to be discussed externally and swiftly reported.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Queen Dowager Wáng Tàihòu was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
a decree ordered the reduction of titles and ranks bestowed by the Wèi court, each according to its degree.
However, those from Xìndū who were righteous and loyal, and those who exerted themselves for the hegemonic court,
as well as those who came from the west, and those who came from the south and submitted since the sixth year of Wǔdìng,

On the day Xīnwèi,
grand envoys were dispatched to the four directions,
to observe local customs,
inquire about the people's hardships,
strictly instruct local officials,
urge them to be honest and fair,
promote benefits and eliminate harms,
and strive to ensure peace and tranquility.
If any laws were inconvenient for the times,
or policies were incomplete in their execution,
they were to list the gains and losses in detail
and report back.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the ancestral tablets were moved to the Tàimiào.
On the day Jǐmǎo in the sixth month,
Gāolì sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Xīnsì,
a decree stated:
“Recently, customs have become degenerate,
and superficial competition daily increases.
When families have auspicious or inauspicious events,
they strive for extravagance and novelty.
The expenses of marriages and funerals,
the lavishness of carriages, clothes, food, and drink,
exhaust the annual income
to accumulate daily wealth.
Furthermore, male servants wear gold and jade,
and female servants wear damask and silk.
Initially, novelty was considered remarkable,
then surpassing what came before was deemed beautiful.
Upper and lower, noble and humble,
there is no longer any distinction.
Now that the destiny is to renew,
I wish to eradicate past evils,
return to simplicity and purity,
and guide the people's conduct.
Let regulations be established according to circumstances,
so that frugality may be achieved moderately.”
Another decree enfeoffed Chóngshèng Hóu with one hundred households,
to maintain the sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ,
and ordered Lǔ Jùn to timely repair the temple structures,
striving for the utmost reverence and commendation.
A decree ordered the dispatch of envoys to offer sacrifices at the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers.
The shrines of Yáo and temples of Shùn,
down to Kǒng Fù, Lǎo Jūn, and others recorded in the sacrificial canon,
were all to be honored without omission.
A decree stated:
“The two commanderies of Bóhǎi and Chánglè in Jìzhōu
were the first enfeoffed states of the former Emperor,
and the places where the righteous banner was first raised.

were where the hegemonic enterprise resided,
and the foundation of royal authority.
When a noble man acts,
he values not forgetting his origin.
I wish to extend this benevolence,
and exempt their land taxes.

Chánglè for two years,
and Tàiyuán for three years.”

Yān, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè, as Píngyáng Wáng;
Yóu, Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu, as Péngchéng Wáng;
Yǎn, Yítóng Sānsī, as Chángshān Wáng;
Huàn, Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu, as Shàngdǎng Wáng;
Yù, Yítóng Sānsī, as Xiāngchéng Wáng;
Zhàn, Yítóng Sānsī, as Chángguǎng Wáng;
Jiē as Rènchéng Wáng;
Shí as Gāoyáng Wáng;
Jì as Bólíng Wáng;
Níng as Xīnpíng Wáng;
Rùn as Féngxǔ Wáng;
Qià as Hànyáng Wáng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
an edict was issued to enthrone Prince Yīn 殷 as Crown Prince,
and Queen Lǐ 李 to be Empress.
On the *gēngyín* day,
an edict appointed Grand Tutor Kùdí Gàn 厙狄干 as Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi 太宰),
Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) Péng Lè 彭樂 as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉),
Minister of Education (Sīkōng 司空) Pān Xiānglè 潘相樂 as Minister of Works,
and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* 開府儀同三司 Sīmǎ Zǐrú 司馬子如 as Minister of Education.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the former Grand Commandant and Prince of Qīnghé 清河, Yuè 岳, was appointed as *Shǐchíjié Píqi Dàjiāngjūn Sīzhōumù* 使持節、驃騎大將軍、司州牧.
On the *rénchén* day,
an edict stated:
"From now on,
all memorials and discussions on affairs of state, if they concern vital and confidential matters,
the appropriate officials shall submit them to Us."
On the *jǐhài* day,
to mark the Crown Prince's first entry into the Eastern Palace,
a general amnesty was declared for those sentenced to death or lesser crimes in the imperial domain and Bīngzhōu 並州;
for other prefectures, those sentenced to death were pardoned,
and all those sentenced to penal servitude or banishment or lesser penalties were fully pardoned.
In autumn, on the *xīnhài* day of the seventh month,
an edict honored Concubine Yuán 元, wife of Emperor Wénxiāng 文襄, as Empress Wénxiāng,
and her palace was named Jìngdé 靜德.
Another edict enfeoffed Xiàowǎn 孝琬, son of Emperor Wénxiāng, as Prince of Héjiān 河間,
and Xiàoyú 孝瑜 as Prince of Hénán 河南.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令 and Prince of Píngyuán 平原, Lóngzhī 隆之, was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Shì 尚書事);
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè 尚書左僕射 and Prince of Píngyáng 平陽, Yān 淹, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
Another edict stated:
"The ancients wore deer-skin for clothes
and made tents from book-sacks.
They cherished abundant virtue,
and their elegant style is still imaginable.
The various rare and splendid silks in the Wei imperial treasury that are usually not given to people,
being merely accumulated,
should all be ordered to be taken out
and sent to the rear imperial garden
to be used for the seven-day banquet and bestowals."
In the eighth month,
an edict commanded commanderies and states to establish schools and academies,
widely recruit talented and outstanding individuals,
and promote Confucian customs.
The students of the Guózǐxiàng 國子學亦 should also be selected and appointed according to old regulations,
obediently following their teachers' instructions
and diligently studying the Rites Classics.
The fifty-two stone steles of Cài Yōng 蔡邕's classics, transported earlier by Emperor Wénxiāng,
should immediately be moved to the academic halls
and set up in order.
Another edict stated:
"Those who can speak frankly and offer righteous remonstrance,
without fearing punishment or blame,
forthright like Zhū Yún 朱雲,
and outspoken like Zhōu Shě 周舍,
who can enlighten Our mind
and refresh Our heart,
assisting Us, the sovereign,
and benefiting the common people,
shall certainly be favored with honor and emoluments,
and treated exceptionally."
It also stated:
"All officials who govern the people
should focus intently on agriculture and sericulture,
diligently encouraging and instructing,
to broadly harness the benefits of heaven and earth
to prepare for disasters of flood and drought."
On the *gēngyín* day,
an edict stated:
"Being of limited virtue,
We have succeeded to the great royal enterprise.
We contemplate how to praise great achievements
and broadcast them for ten thousand ages.
Although the court historians wield their brushes,
ensuring that what is heard is not lost,
We still fear that some scattered words of beauty might be overlooked
and occasionally not recorded.
All royal dukes and officials, civil and military, great and small,
down to the common people,
and even Buddhist monks and nuns,
whether they personally heard Our commands
or relayed them through others,
should record anything worthy of being included in historical records
and submit it in a compiled list."
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"The 'Línzhǐ Rules' 麟趾格, settled upon during the Wei dynasty,
became a universal system,
which government offices applied,
but it is still not entirely perfect.
The various officials should be ordered to further discuss and research it.
The methods for appropriate governance
should first fully address critical matters,
guiding the main principles and detailing the articles,
ensuring nothing is omitted."
In the ninth month, on the *guǐchǒu* day,

Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍, Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍, Leader of the Eastern Yi Colonel (Lǐng Dōngyí Xiàowèi 領東夷校尉), Duke of Kāiguó 開國 of Liáodōng Commandery 遼東郡, King of Gāolì 高麗, Chéng 成, was appointed as *Shǐchíjié Shìzhōng Píqi Dàjiāngjūn Lǐnghù Dōngyí Xiàowèi* 使持節、侍中、驃騎大將軍、領護東夷校尉,
with his titles of King and Duke remaining as before.

An edict recognized Liáng 梁 attendant minister (*Shìzhōng* 侍中), *Shǐchíjié* 使持節, *Jiǎhuángyuè* 假黃鉞, Grand General commanding all military affairs inside and outside (*Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì Dàjiāngjūn* 都督中外諸軍事大將軍), acting with Imperial Authority (*Chéngzhì* 承制), Prince of Shàolíng 邵陵 Xiāo Lún 蕭綸, as King of Liáng.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng 晉陽
to pay respects at the imperial mausoleum.
On this day, the Crown Prince entered and resided in the Liángfēng Táng 涼風堂 to supervise all state affairs.
In winter, on the *jǐmǎo* day of the tenth month,
the full imperial equipage was prepared,
the golden chariot was mounted,
and the Emperor entered Jìnyáng Palace
to pay respects to the Empress Dowager in the inner hall.
On the *xīnsì* day,
a partial amnesty was granted to prisoners in the four prisons of Jìnyáng County 晉陽縣, Tàiyuán Commandery 太原郡, Bīngzhōu, and the Grand Chancellor's Office.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
the Rúrú 茹茹 state sent envoys with tribute.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Tèjìn 特進 Yuán Sháo 元韶 was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
and Bīngzhōu Governor Duàn Sháo 段韶 was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè 尚書右僕射.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
the Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾 state sent envoys with tribute.
On the *rénchén* day,
the Grand Chancellor's Office was abolished,
retaining the Cavalry Bureau (*Qíbīng Cáo* 騎兵曹) and Foreign Affairs Bureau (*Wàibīng Cáo* 外兵曹),
each establishing a separate department
to handle confidential matters independently.
In the eleventh month,
Emperor Wén of Zhōu 周 文帝 led his troops to Shǎnchéng 陝城,
divided his cavalry to cross north,
and reached Jiànzhōu 建州.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Xiāo Yì 蕭繹, Prince of Xiāngdōng 湘東 of Liáng, sent envoys with tribute.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
the Emperor personally led the army and encamped east of the city.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu, hearing of the Emperor's imposing military presence,
sighed:
"Gāo Huān 高歡 is not dead!"
And then retreated his army.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
In the twelfth month, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Rúrú and Kùmòxī 庫莫奚 states both sent envoys with tribute.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
In the second year, spring, on the *dīngwèi* day of the first month,
Xiāo Yì 蕭繹, Prince of Xiāngdōng of Liáng, sent envoys with tribute.
On the *xīnhài* day,
rites were performed at the Round Hill (Yuánqiū 圓丘),
with Emperor Shénwǔ 神武 as co-worshipper.
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Emperor personally plowed the sacred field (jítián 籍田) in the eastern suburbs.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
former Imperial Yellow Gate Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎) Yuán Shìbǎo 元世寶 and Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng 通直散騎侍郎) Péng Guìpíng 彭貴平 conspired to rebel;
they were spared death but exiled to the border.
Rites were performed at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Emperor boated east of the city.
In the second month, on the *rénchén* day,
Grand Commandant Péng Lè conspired to rebel
and was executed.
On the *rén'yín* day,
the Rúrú state sent envoys with tribute.
In the third month, on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Yù 淯, Prince of Xiāngchéng 襄城, died.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
an edict recognized Xiāo Yì, Prince of Xiāngdōng of Liáng, acting with Imperial Authority, as *Liáng Shǐchíjié Jiǎhuángyuè Xiàngguó* 梁使持節、假黃鉞、相國,
established the Liáng Platform (Liángtái 梁臺),
to oversee all state affairs,
and act with Imperial Authority.

Li Jǐngshèng 李景盛, Governor of Jiāozhōu 交州; Mǎ Sōngrén 馬嵩仁, Governor of Liángzhōu 梁州; Xiàhóu Zhēnqià 夏侯珍洽, Governor of Yìzhōu 義州; Lǐ Hàn 李漢, Governor of Xīnzhōu 新州, and others, all led their prefectures to submit.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Minister of Education Sīmǎ Zǐrú was dismissed for misconduct.
In summer, on the *rénchén* day of the fourth month,
King of Liáng Xiāo Yì sent envoys with tribute.
In the intercalary month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Shìwěi 室韋 state sent envoys with tribute.
In the fifth month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Húxī Xiǎn 斛斯顯, Governor of Hézhōu 合州, attacked and captured Liáng's Lìyáng 歷陽 garrison.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the Gāolì state sent envoys with tribute.
In this month,
Hóu Jǐng 侯景 deposed Emperor Jiǎnwén 簡文 of Liáng
and enthroned Xiāo Dòng 蕭棟 as ruler.
In the sixth month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the former Minister of Education Sīmǎ Zǐrú was appointed Grand Commandant.
In the seventh month, on the *rénshēn* day,
Rúrú sent envoys with tribute.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Xíng Jǐngyuǎn 邢景遠, a Secretariat official (*Xíngtái Láng* 行臺郎), defeated Liáng's Lóng'ān 龍安 garrison
and captured its town defender Lǐ Luòwén 李洛文.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the Xiǎnyáng Palace 顯陽殿 was renamed Zhāoyáng Palace 昭陽殿.
In the ninth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
an edict exempted all entertainers, laborers, herdsmen, and various miscellaneous service personnel from their servitude, making them commoners (*báihù* 白戶).
On the *guǐsì* day,
the Emperor went to Zhào 趙 and Dìng 定 prefectures,
and then to Jìnyáng.
In winter, on the *wùshēn* day of the tenth month,
the Xuānguāng 宣光, Jiànshǐ 建始, Jiāfú 嘉福, and Rénshòu 仁壽 palaces were constructed.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Xiāo Yì sent envoys with tribute.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the spirit tablet of Emperor Wénxiāng was placed in the ancestral temple.
In the eleventh month,
Hóu Jǐng deposed the lord of Liáng,
and usurped the spurious imperial throne at Jiànyè,
proclaiming himself Hán.
In the twelfth month,
Zhōngshān Wáng passed away.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
the Emperor personally campaigned against the Kùmòxī in Dài Jùn,
and severely defeated them,
capturing over a hundred thousand head of livestock,
which were distributed among the generals and soldiers with varying shares.
The Xī households were sent to Shāndōng to become commoners.
In the second month,
Rúrú lord Ānàguī was defeated by the Türks (lǔ),
and Guī committed suicide;
his crown prince Ānluóchén, and Guī's cousin Dēngzhù Sīlìfā, and Dēngzhù's son Kùtí, all led their multitudes and came to surrender.
The remaining Rúrú established Dēngzhù's second son Tiěfá as their lord.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Qìdān sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the third month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Sīzhōu Mù, Qīnghé Wáng Yuè, was appointed as Shǐchíjié, Nándào Dàdūdū;
Sītú Pān Xiànglè as Shǐchíjié, Dōngnán Dào Dàdūdū;
and Xíngtái Xīn Shù was ordered to lead troops for a southern campaign.
On the day Guǐsì,
an imperial edict promoted Liáng Wáng Xiāo Yì to be the lord of Liáng.
In summer, fourth month, on the day Rénshēn,
Dōngnán Dào Xíngtái Xīn Shù sent the Heirloom Seal of the Realm from Guǎnglíng.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Lìbù Shàngshū Yáng Yīn was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the state of Shìwěi sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the sixth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Qīnghé Wáng Yuè and others returned with their troops.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor traveled from Bìngzhōu to Líshí.
In winter, tenth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
he reached Huánglúlǐng,
and then began constructing the Great Wall,
extending north to Shègānshù, over four hundred *lǐ*,
establishing thirty-six garrisons.
In the eleventh month, on the day Xīnsì,
Liáng Wáng Xiāo Yì ascended the imperial throne in Jiānglíng,
known as Yuán Dì,
and sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the twelfth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
On the day Wùwǔ,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the fourth year, spring, first month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Shānhú besieged Líshí.
On the day Wùyín,
the Emperor campaigned against them,
but before he arrived,
the Hú had already fled,
so he proceeded to inspect the Sānduī garrisons,
and returned after a grand hunt.
On the day Wùyín,
the Kùmòxī sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
new coins were recast,
with the inscription
“Chángpíng Wǔzhū.”
In the second month,
Dēngzhù, father of Rúrú lord Tiěfá, and his son Kùtí, were sent back north.
Tiěfá was soon killed by the Qìdān,
and the people of the state re-established Dēngzhù as their lord,
but he was again killed by his grandee Āfùtí and others,
and the people of the state re-established Kùtí as their lord.
In summer, fourth month, on the day Wùxū,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
On the day Wùwǔ,
there was a great sound like thunder in the southwest.
In the fifth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Emperor held a military hunt at Línlǜ Shān.
On the day Wùzǐ,
he returned to the palace.
In the ninth month,
the Qìdān violated the frontier.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor made a northern inspection of Jì, Dìng, Yōu, and Ān (prefectures),
and then campaigned north against the Qìdān.
In winter, tenth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
the Emperor reached Píngzhōu,
and then proceeded from the western route to Qùchángqiàn.
An edict ordered Sītú Pān Xiànglè to lead five thousand elite cavalry from the eastern route to Qīngshān.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
they reached Báiláng Chéng.
On the day Rényín,
they passed through Chānglí Chéng.
Another edict ordered Āndé Wáng Hán Guǐ to lead four thousand elite cavalry eastward,
to cut off the Qìdān's escape route.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
they reached Yángshī Shuǐ,
traveling double the normal distance day and night,
to surprise and attack the Qìdān.
On the day Jiǎchén,
the Emperor personally crossed mountains and ridges,
leading his soldiers,
directing and inspiring the assault,
severely defeating them,
capturing over a hundred thousand people and hundreds of thousands of head of livestock.
Pān Xiànglè also severely defeated another Qìdān detachment at Qīngshān.
All the captured people were distributed among various prefectures.
During this campaign,
the Emperor went bareheaded and bared his shoulders,
traveling day and night without rest,
covering over a thousand *lǐ*,
subsisting only on meat and water,
his martial spirit ever more fierce.
On the day Dīngwèi,
he reached Yíngzhōu.
On the day Dīngsì,
he ascended Jiéshí Shān,
overlooking the vast sea.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the Emperor traveled from Píngzhōu,
and then went to Jìnyáng.
In the intercalary month, on the day Rényín,
the Liáng Emperor sent envoys to seek an alliance.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the Türks again attacked the Rúrú,
and the Rúrú nation fled south.
On the day Guǐhài,
the Emperor campaigned north from Jìnyáng against the Türks,
and welcomed the Rúrú.
He then deposed their lord Kùtí,
and established Ānàguī's son Ānluóchén as their lord,
settling him in Mǎyì Chuān,
and providing him with provisions, food, silk, and cloth.
He personally pursued the Türks in Shuòzhōu;
the Türks requested to surrender,
which was granted, and he returned.
Thereupon, tributes followed continuously.
In the fifth year, spring, first month, on the day Guǐsì,
the Emperor campaigned against the Shānhú,
taking the Líshí route.
He sent Tàishī, Xiányáng Wáng Húlǜ Jīn, via the Xiǎnzhōu route,
and Chángshān Wáng Yǎn via the Jìnzhōu route,
to attack them from different directions,
severely defeating them,
beheading tens of thousands,
and capturing over a hundred thousand head of livestock,
thereby pacifying Shílóu.
Shílóu was extremely precipitous,
a place unreachable since the time of Wèi.
Consequently, the Shānhú, near and far, were all overawed and submitted.
This month, Zhōu Wén Dì deposed the Western Wèi lord,
and established Qí Wáng Kuò,
who became Gōng Dì.
In the third month,
the Rúrú Ānluóchén rebelled.
The Emperor personally campaigned against him,
and severely defeated him,
and Ānluóchén and his son fled north.
