Tàibǎo Hèbá Rén was dismissed for violating orders.
In summer, fourth month,
the Rúrú raided Sìzhōu.
On the day Dīngsì,
the Emperor campaigned against them from Jìnyáng,
and upon reaching Huángguā Duī in the prefecture,
the barbarian cavalry fled.
At that time, the main army had already returned,
but the Emperor led over a thousand cavalry under his command,
and encountered several tens of thousands of another Rúrú detachment,
who surrounded and pressed in from all sides.
The Emperor remained composed,
directing the tactical situation,
and the barbarian multitude wavered,
whereupon he unleashed his troops, broke through the encirclement, and escaped.
The barbarians then retreated,
and were pursued and attacked,
leaving dead bodies for twenty *lǐ*,
and Ānluóchén's wife and children, and over thirty thousand captives, were seized.
In the fifth month, on the day Dīnghài,
the states of Dìdòugān, Qìdān, and others, all sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Dīngwèi,
he campaigned north against the Rúrú,
and severely defeated them.
In the sixth month,
the Rúrú led their forces eastward,
intending to invade south.
The Emperor led light cavalry to intercept them at the foot of Jīnshān,
and the Rúrú, hearing of this, fled far away.
In autumn, seventh month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Sùshèn sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Rénchén,
pardons were granted to criminals.
On the day Gēngxū,
the Emperor arrived back from the northern campaign.
In the eighth month, on the *dìngsì* day,
the Türks sent envoys to present tribute at court.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé and Governor of Sīzhōu, was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo);
Wèi Càn, Minister of Works (Sīkōng), was appointed Minister over the Masses (Sītú);
〔一○〕Hóumòchén Xiāng, Grand Preceptor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàishī), was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng);
Yān, Prince of Píngyáng and President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), was made Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì);
Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, was appointed President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng);
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), was appointed Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè).
On the *yǐhài* day,
Yuán Xù, with the title of Yítóng Sānsī, was granted death for his crimes.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Emperor visited Jìnyáng.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Gāo Lóngzhī, Prince of Píngyuán, with the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì), passed away.
In this month,

an imperial edict commanded Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, Duàn Sháo, Prince of Píngyuán, and others, to lead their troops to build Fá'è City, Xīn City, Yán City, and Hénán City southwest of Luòyáng.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor personally visited the sites,
intending to lure the Zhōu army out.
As the Zhōu army did not emerge,
he then returned to Jìnyáng.
In winter, the tenth month,
Western Wèi attacked Liáng Yuándì at Jiānglíng.
An imperial edict ordered Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, Pān Xiānglè, Prince of Hédōng, Duàn Sháo, Prince of Píngyuán, and others, to lead their troops to rescue him.
Before they arrived, Jiānglíng fell,
and Liáng Yuándì was killed by Yú Jǐn, a general of Western Wèi.
Liáng general Wáng Sēngbiàn, then in Jiànkāng,
together with others, enthroned Xiāo Fāngzhì, Prince of Jìn'ān, as Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi) and General-in-chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn),
and allowed him to establish all officials by imperial decree.
In the twelfth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor toured north to Dáshù Lǐng,
surveyed the treacherous terrain of the mountains and rivers,
and intended to build the Great Wall.
In the sixth year, spring, the first month, on the *rén'yín* day,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, led a multitude of troops across the river,
and captured Xiàshǒu.
He sent Lù Fǎhé, Inspector of Yǐngzhōu of Liáng.
〔一一〕An imperial edict appointed Xiāo Míng, Gentleman-in-Waiting (Sànqí Chángshì) and Marquis of Zhēnyáng of Liáng, as the ruler of Liáng,
and dispatched Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng and Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), to lead troops to escort him.
In the second month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,

Lù Fǎhé was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Military Governor (Dūdū) of all Military Affairs in the ten prefectures of Jīng, Yōng, Jiāng, Bā, Liáng, Yì, Xiāng, Wàn, Jiāo, and Guǎng,〔一二〕Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Gōng), Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū), and Grand Administrator of the Southwestern Circuit (Xīnán Dào Dà Xíngtái).

Sòng Zhǐ, General Who Guards the North (Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), and Inspector of Jīngzhōu of Liáng, was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), General of Agile Cavalry (Piāoqí Dà Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, captured Qiáojùn.
In the third month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, reached Dōngguān,
beheaded the Liáng general Péi Zhīhéng,
and captured or beheaded several thousand men.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
He enfeoffed Shìzōng’s two sons, Xiào Háng as Prince of Guǎngníng,
and Yánzōng as Prince of Āndé.
On the *wùxū* day,
the Emperor attended to lawsuits and pronounced judgments in Zhaóyáng Hall.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Xiāo Guǐ, with the title of Yítóng, captured Jìnxī City of Liáng,
and made it into Jiāngzhōu.
On the *wùyín* day,
the Türks sent envoys to present tribute at court.
Lǐ Shānhuā, a rebel from Liáng, proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
and pressed upon Lúshān City.
In the fifth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
Lǐ Zhòngkǎn, the city defender, attacked and beheaded him.
On the *gēngyín* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
Xiāo Míng entered Jiànyè.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Rúrú sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In the sixth month, on the *rénzǐ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“The state of Liáng has met with calamity,
its ruler lost, its ministers dispersed;
far in that fiery region,
it is completely overgrown with thorns.
To restore what has fallen and maintain the broken line,
is our righteous duty.
By installing a senior ruler
and rescuing them from their perilous plight,
the ruler of Liáng, whom we escorted,
has already entered Jīnlíng.
Now that the tributary rituals have been performed,
the relationship of loyalty and righteousness should be firm.
The bird of Yuè, in its longing,
does not forget the southern branch.
Therefore, all Liáng people
should be permitted to return to their country,
and be dispatched with due ceremony.”
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
On the *rénshēn* day,
he personally launched a punitive expedition against the Rúrú.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
all armies assembled at Qílián Chǐ.
On the *yǐhài* day,
they exited the frontier pass,
and reached Kùdí Gǔ.
Within a hundred *lǐ* there was no water spring,
and the six armies suffered from thirst.
Shortly after, there was a heavy rain.
On the *wùyín* day,

Xiāo Míng, the ruler of Liáng, sent his son Zhāng, together with Yuán Bì, who held the concurrent post of Palace Attendant (Jiān Shìzhōng), and Yáng Yù, who held the concurrent post of Gentleman-in-Waiting (Jiān Sànqí Chángshì), to present a memorial as tribute.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor stopped at Báidào,
left the baggage train,
and personally led five thousand light cavalry to pursue the Rúrú.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
they caught up with them at Huáishuò Town.
The Emperor personally braved arrows and stones,
repeatedly inflicting great defeats,
and reaching Wòyě.
He captured their Sīlì Āi'yān Lìlóu Ādì and Tùtóufà Yùjiǔlǘ Zhuàngyán,
as well as over twenty thousand people,
and hundreds of thousands of cattle and sheep.
The Rúrú Sīlì Yùjiǔlǘ Lǐ Jiātí, with several hundred of his troops, surrendered.
On the *rénchén* day,
the Emperor returned to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
In winter, the tenth month,
Liáng general Chén Bàxiān attacked Wáng Sēngbiàn,
killed him,
deposed Xiāo Míng,
and re-established Xiāo Fāngzhì as ruler.
On the *xīnhài* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the eleventh month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Gāolì sent envoys to present tribute at court.
Xú Sìhuī, Inspector of Qínzhōu of Liáng, Rèn Yuē, Inspector of Nányùzhōu, and others, attacked and occupied Shítóu City,
and brought their prefectures into allegiance.
On the *rénchén* day,
Grand Commander Xiāo Guǐ led his troops to the river,
and dispatched Commander Liǔ Dámó and others to cross the river and garrison Shítóu.
Zhào Yànshēn, Administrator of the Southeastern Circuit (Dōngnán Dào Xíngtái), captured five cities including Qínjùn,
with over twenty thousand households,
and pacified the local populace.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo) and Governor of Sīzhōu, passed away.
In this month,
Liǔ Dámó was attacked and pressed by Bàxiān,
and surrendered Shítóu.
In the twelfth month, on the *wùshēn* day,
the Kùmòxī sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In this year,
one million eight hundred thousand men were conscripted to build the Great Wall,
from Xiàkǒu north of Yōuzhōu to the capital, over nine hundred *lǐ*.
In the seventh year, spring, the first month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
He held a mounted archery contest west of Yèchéng,
and gathered a large crowd to watch it.
In the second month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict commanded Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, and others, to read memorials and petitions in the Liángfēng Táng,
discuss and determine their merits and demerits,
and the Emperor personally made the final decisions.
In the third month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Grand Commander Xiāo Guǐ and others led their troops across the Jiāng River.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Lóu Ruì, with the title of Yítóng, led troops to suppress the Lúyáng Mán,
and greatly defeated them.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
〔一三〕an imperial edict commanded the construction of Jīnhuá Palace.
In the fifth month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Qià, Prince of Hànyáng, passed away.
In this month,
the Emperor decided to abstain from meat out of compassion,
and never ate it again.
In the sixth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Xiāo Guǐ and others fought with the Liáng army west of Zhōngshān.
Encountering continuous rain,
they suffered a defeat.
Guǐ, and commanders Lǐ Xīguāng, Wáng Jìngbǎo, Dōngfāng Lǎo, and military aide Péi Yīngqǐ, were all lost.
Only two or three tenths of the soldiers scattered and returned.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Lín, Inspector of Xiāngzhōu of Liáng, presented a tamed elephant.
In this year,
the palaces of the Three Platforms were renovated and expanded.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *jǐhài* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the eighth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
the Kùmòxī sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
the Khitan sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In this month,
two thousand six hundred widows from Shāndōng were conscripted to be given to soldiers;
one fifth of those with husbands were unjustly seized.
In this month,
Zhōu Wéndì passed away.
〔一四〕
In the eleventh month, on the day Rénzǐ,
an edict stated: "Kūnshān serves as the central peak,
hence the name Shénzhōu;
the boundless ocean acts as a pond,
thus it is called Chìxiàn.
When the common people prosper,
the herdsmen exist.
The systems of kings
have
evolved and changed successively.
When territorial divisions led to disaster,
they were first divided into twelve,
and once the lands and waters were pacified,
they reverted to nine Zhōus.
While the Dao may be complex or simple,
its essence lies in adapting to the times.
The Yīn dynasty followed the Xià dynasty,
making no fundamental changes.
Yet, the sun and moon revolve through their celestial positions,
and kings and dukes establish states in the earthly realm,
all to align with the profound cosmic order above
and correspond with the rivers and mountains below.
Reaching the Qín
administration,
which scourged the entire realm,
abolished feudal lords and appointed commandery governors,
treating the empire as its private domain.
When the two Hàn dynasties inherited this foundation,
and the Cáo and Mǎ families continued the legacy,
the gains and losses during that period
are too numerous to recount.
Since the late Xiàochāng reign of the Wèi dynasty,
it has repeatedly faced decline and adversity.
Emoluments were removed from the imperial house,
governance came from many factions,
officials lost their integrity,
and the common people suffered greatly.
Followers of the Bronze Horse and Iron Shin
factions,
companions of Black Mountain
and Green Colt,
rose violently in Jìn and Zhào,
and rampaged through Yān and Qín.
From then on, the social order collapsed,
and the established norms became chaotic.
This led to powerful
families and great clans
gathering and leading local communities,
ostensibly to serve the emperor,
but secretly appointing themselves.
Or, imperial princesses from external families,
whose female attendants exerted influence internally,
unscrupulously accepted bribes,
and initiated the establishment of Zhōu
and Jùn.
Dividing large units and combining small ones,
originally followed temporal expediency.
Dividing bamboo tallies and distributing symbols of authority
was done out of necessity.
The number of shepherds, governors, magistrates, and chiefs
was excessively increased,
seeking merit and recording achievements;
this truly
became a burden,
harming both public and private interests,
and its evils have long persisted.
It violated the principles of governance
and only incurred the cost of driving sheep.
Since then, these practices have continued,
without time for reform.
I, having reverently received the precious mandate
and respectfully presided over the eight directions,
in establishing states and managing the land,
strive for simplicity and ease.
I intend to calm the restless and restore tranquility,
to revert from extravagance to simplicity.
If there is a deviation from the
mean,
it should be rectified.
Observing past histories,
and listening to ancient sayings,
the Zhōu dynasty had Chéng and Kāng,
and the Hàn dynasty had Wén and Jǐng,
when the number of registered households was
the highest in ancient and modern times.
Yet,
the population is less than in former days,
while the number of governors and magistrates is double that of olden times.
This is not how to manage customs and regulate traditions,
or to provide guidance to the people.
Moreover, the Wǔlǐng mountains have submitted,
and the Sānjiāng rivers have been pacified,
expanding territory and opening borders,
with benefits reaching the Nánhǎi.
However, in remote and desolate areas,
there was formerly much pretense and falsity.
A town of a hundred households
would arbitrarily be given the name of a Zhōu,
and a population of three households
would be granted the empty title of a Jùn.
This is like a wooden dog,
or a mud dragon,
where seeking reality from the name
results in nothing.
Therefore, the present consolidations and abolitions
shall all follow a separate decree."
Thereupon, three Zhōu, one hundred fifty-three Jùn, five hundred eighty-nine Xiàn, two Zhèn, and twenty-six Shù were consolidated and abolished.
It was also decreed that Cìshǐ must all perform concurrent duties
and would not be provided with additional personnel.
[一五]
In the twelfth month,
Yǔwén Jué, chancellor of Western Wèi, received the Wèi abdication.
Previously,
from Xīhé Zǒngqín Shù eastward to the sea, a Great Wall had been built,
totaling over three thousand lǐ from east to west in successive constructions.
On average, there was one garrison every ten lǐ,
and key strategic points were established as Zhōu-Zhèn,
totaling twenty-five locations.
In the eighth year, in spring, the third month,
there was great heat,
and some people died from sunstroke.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
an edict prohibited the capture of shrimp, crabs, clams, and similar creatures,
permitting only fishing.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
an edict also completely banned private and public ownership of eagles and hawks.
Húli Jīn, Grand Preceptor and Prince of Xiányáng, was appointed Right Chancellor;
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán, former Grand General and Prince of Fúfēng, was appointed Grand Tutor;
Hèbá Rén, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, was appointed Grand Guardian;
Yǎn, Shàngshū Lìng and Prince of Chángshān, was appointed Sīkōng;
Zhàn, Lù Shàngshū Shì and Prince of Chángguǎng, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng;
Yáng Yīn, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè;
Cuī Xiān, who had been consolidated from Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè;
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, was appointed Lù Shàngshū Shì.
In this month,
the emperor practiced archery on horseback east of the capital.
An order was issued for all women in the capital to attend and watch,
with those who did not attend being punished by military law.
This continued for seven days.
In the fifth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Liú Xiàng, a commoner from Jìzhōu, conspired rebellion in the capital,
and his accomplices were all executed.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day Jǐsì,
the Kùmò Xī sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Gēngchén,
an edict stated that for the Qiū, Jiāo, Dì, Xiá, and seasonal sacrifices,
all offerings should be purchased from the market.
The Shàoláo sacrifice must not involve dismemberment.
Officials concerned must supervise
to ensure abundant provisions.
For Nóngshè and Xiāncán,
only wine and meat are sufficient.
For Yú, Méi, wind, rain, Sīmín, Sīlù, Língxīng, and miscellaneous sacrifices,
fruits, cakes, wine, and dried meat are sufficient.
Only utmost sincerity and reverence should be exercised,
with the spirit of the deities being present.
From summer to the ninth month,
there was a great locust plague in six Zhōu north of the Yellow River, twelve Zhōu south of the Yellow River, and eight Jùn within the imperial domain.
In this month,
they flew to the capital,
obscuring the sun,
with a sound like wind and rain.
On the day Jiǎchén,
an edict exempted areas affected by the locusts from taxes for the current year.
In this month,
Yǔwén Hù, chief minister of Zhōu, killed his lord Emperor Mǐn and enthroned the emperor's younger brother Yù,
[一六] who became Emperor Míng.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Chén Bàxiān assassinated his lord Fāng Zhì and enthroned himself,
becoming Emperor Wǔ of Chén.
He sent envoys to declare vassalage and pay tribute.
In this year,
a double wall was built within the Great Wall,
from Kùluòbá eastward to Wǔgē Shù,
totaling over four hundred lǐ.
In the ninth year, in spring, the second month, on the day Dīnghài,
criminals were pardoned.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
an edict limited burning the fields to the month of Zhòngdōng,
prohibiting the use of fire at other times,
to avoid harming insects and plants.
In the third month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
the emperor returned from Jìnyáng.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Xīnsì,
a general amnesty was granted.
This summer,
there was a great drought.
Because prayers for rain were unanswered, the emperor
destroyed the temple of Xīmén Bào and
excavated his tomb.
There was a great locust plague east of the mountains,
and conscripted laborers were dispatched to catch and bury them in pits.
In this month,
Sīmǎ Xiāonàn, the Cìshǐ of Běiyùzhōu, rebelled with his city
and defected to Zhōu.
In the fifth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
Shàngshū Lìng, the Prince of Chángguǎng, Zhàn, recorded the affairs of the Chancellery (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
The Grand General of Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), the Prince of Píngqín, Guīyàn, was made Senior Left Administrator of the Chancellery (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè).
On the day Jiǎchén,
Yáng Yīn, the former Senior Left Administrator of the Chancellery, was made Shàngshū Lìng.
In the sixth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor conducted a northern tour from Jìnyáng.
On the day Jǐsì,
he arrived at Qílián Chí.
On the day Wùyín,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
nine hundred forty-three elderly people in the capital region, including Liú Nú, were granted titles (bǎnzhí), staffs, and caps, each according to their rank.
On the day Wùshēn,

an edict declared that in the five prefectures of Zhào, Yān, Yíng, Dìng, and Nányíng, and the two commanderies of Guǎngpíng and Qīnghé in Sī Zhōu, where fields had been damaged by locusts and floods last year,
combined with little rain during spring and summer,
resulting in thin crops,
their rents and levies for the current year were exempted.
In the eighth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In this month,
Shěn Tài, the Cìshǐ of Jiāng Zhōu for Chén, defected and submitted with three thousand men.
Before this,
over three hundred thousand laborers and artisans were mobilized to construct the Three Terraces (Sān Tái) near Yè,
taking their former foundations and raising and broadening them.
Grand palaces and pleasure gardens were greatly erected.
By this time,
the Three Terraces were completed.
The Bronze Sparrow (Tóngjué) was renamed Golden Phoenix (Jīnfèng),
the Golden Beast (Jīnshòu) was renamed Sacred Response (Shèngyìng),
and the Ice Well (Bīngjǐng) was renamed Exalted Radiance (Chóngguāng).
In the eleventh month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
He ascended the Three Terraces,
held court in the Qiánxiàng Diàn,
and held a banquet for his ministers,
ordering them all to compose poetry.
Because the new palace was completed,
on the day Dīngyǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
All civil and military officials, both internal and external, were universally promoted one rank.
On the day Dīngsì,
Wáng Lín, the Cìshǐ of Xiāng Zhōu for Liáng, sent an envoy requesting the establishment of Xiāo Zhuāng as the ruler of Liáng,
and further submitted Jiāng Zhōu internally (to Northern Qí),
ordering Xiāo Zhuāng to reside there.
In the twelfth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
an edict established Xiāo Zhuāng, Prince of Liáng, as the ruler of Liáng,
and advanced his residence to Jiǔpài.
On the day Wùyín,
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán, the Grand Mentor (Tàifù), was made Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
Wèi Càn, the Minister over the Masses (Sītú), was made Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Duàn Sháo, the Cìshǐ of Jì Zhōu, was made Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Gāo Yǎn, the Prince of Chángshān and recorder of the affairs of the Chancellery, was made Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
Gāo Zhàn, the Prince of Chángguǎng and recorder of the affairs of the Chancellery, was made Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
In this month,
the Dàzhuāngyán Sì temple was constructed.
In this year,
Gāo Jùn, the Prince of Yǒng'ān, and Gāo Huàn, the Prince of Shàngdǎng, were executed.
In the tenth year, spring, first month, on the day Wùxū,
Hóumòchén Xiāng, the Sīkōng, was made Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
On the day Jiǎyín,
the Emperor went to the Gānlù Sì temple in Liáoyáng.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
an edict established Héng Zhōu in Máchéng.
In the second month, on the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor practiced meditation (chánjū shēn guān) at Gānlù Sì,
with only major affairs of state and military being reported to him.
In the third month, on the day Wùxū,
Gāo Dézhèng, the Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng), was made Senior Right Administrator of the Chancellery (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè).
On the day Bǐngchén,
the Emperor arrived from Liáoyáng.
In this month,
Xiāo Zhuāng, the ruler of Liáng, arrived at Yǐng Zhōu,
and sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the intercalary fourth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Gāo Yóu, the Governor (Mù) of Sī Zhōu and Prince of Péngchéng, was made Sīkōng.
Gāo Shí, the Attendant Counselor and Prince of Gāoyáng, was made Senior Right Administrator of the Chancellery.
On the day Yǐsì,
Gāo Yóu, the Sīkōng and Prince of Péngchéng, concurrently served as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
The Imperial son Shàolián was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chánglè Commandery.
In the fifth month, on the day Guǐwèi,
Yuán Shì, the Prince of Shǐpíng, was executed,
along with twenty-five families including Yuán Jǐngshì, the Prince of Dōngpíng.
Nineteen other families, including Yuán Sháo, the Special Advance (Tèjìn), were ordered to be confined.
In the sixth month,
Emperor Wǔ of Chén died.
His elder brother's son, Qiàn, was enthroned,
known as Emperor Wén.
In the autumn, eighth month, on the day Wùxū,
the Imperial son Shàoyì was enfeoffed as the Prince of Guǎngyáng Commandery.
Gāo Xiàowǎn, the Senior Right Administrator of the Chancellery and Prince of Héjiān, was made Senior Left Administrator of the Chancellery.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
an edict was issued that stated: If any military or civilian person had a father or grandfather who changed their surname and falsely claimed membership in the Yuán clan,
or falsely claimed kinship and acknowledgment,
and presumptuously claimed the surname Yuán,
regardless of how many generations had passed,
they were all permitted to revert to their original surname.
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐsì,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In this month,
Lì Huáizé and Lù Rén'huì were sent as envoys to Xiāo Zhuāng.
In the winter, tenth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor suddenly died in the Déyáng Táng of the Jìnyáng Palace.
He was thirty-one years old at the time.
His dying edict stated:
"All funerary affairs shall strictly adhere to frugality.
Although the three-year mourning period
is said to comply with established rites,
Emperor Wén of Hàn instituted a reform,
which has been universally followed since ancient times.
The principle of this exists,
and it may be followed.
The limit for the period of mourning garments is fixed at thirty-six days.
The heir-apparent, the multitude of officials, near and far, within and outside the court, shall observe the decree, restrain their emotions,
and all return to public duties."
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the death was announced,
and the remains were placed in the Xuāndé Diàn.
In the eleventh month, on the day Xīnwèi,
the imperial coffin returned to the capital.
In the twelfth month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
the remains were temporarily interred in the front hall of the Tàijí Diàn.
In the first year of Qiánmíng, second month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
he was buried at Wǔníng Líng.
His posthumous title was Emperor Wénxuān (Wénxuān Huángdì),
with the temple name Wēizōng.
Early in the Wǔpíng era,
the posthumous title was again changed to Wénxuān,
and the temple name to Xiǎnzǔ.
The Emperor possessed great magnanimity in his youth;
his aspirations and judgment were profound and sharp.
He was gentle outwardly but firm inwardly,
decisive and able to make firm resolutions.
He genuinely enjoyed administrative affairs,
could measure the beginning and foresee the end,
managing complex and numerous duties,
without tiring throughout the day.
When he first ascended the throne,
he devoted himself to governing methods,
controlling subordinates through law,
and prioritizing public justice.
If anyone violated the statutes,
even if they were close relatives or former merits,
he would certainly show no leniency.
Inside and outside the court were clean and tranquil,
and none failed to be respectful and solemn.
As for the critical strategies of state and military,
he made decisions solely based on his own judgment.
His scope and pattern were grand and far-reaching,
possessing the great strategies of a sovereign ruler.
Moreover, considering that the Three Regions stood like the legs of a tripod,
and the various barbarian tribes had not yet submitted,
he maintained and repaired armor and weapons,
and selected and trained soldiers.
For the palace guards, he established the Hundred Guard troops (Bǎibǎo Jūnshì).
Whenever he approached the battle line,
he personally faced arrows and stones.
Where blades met,
he only feared that the enemy before him was not numerous enough,
frequently risking difficulty and danger,
but always achieving victories.
Once, while holding a banquet tour on Dōng Shān,
due to Guānlǒng not yet being pacified,
he threw down his cup in shock and anger.
He summoned Wèi Shōu before the imperial presence,
and immediately drafted an imperial edict,
to be proclaimed far and wide,
announcing that he was about to launch a western campaign.
In this year,
Emperor Wén of Zhōu died.
The people in the west were greatly alarmed and terrified,
always making plans to cross the Lǒng mountains.
his might shook the Róng and Xià (barbarians and Chinese states).
Six or seven years later,
he became arrogant regarding his achievements,
and subsequently indulged continuously in pleasure and excess,
recklessly committing acts of debauchery and violence.
Sometimes he personally beat the drum and danced,
singing endlessly,
continuing from dawn through the night,
linking night to day.
Sometimes he exposed his body,
applying cosmetic powders and black paint (for eyebrows),
letting his hair down and wearing Húfú (nomadic clothes),
mixing brocade and colorful silks in his clothing.
Drawing his blade and stringing his bow,
he roamed through the markets,
visiting the mansions of meritorious officials and imperial relatives
morning and evening.
At times he rode camels, oxen, or donkeys,
not using saddle or bridle.
In the intense heat of high summer,
or the cruel cold of deep winter,
sometimes he would expose his body to the midday sun,
discarding his clothes and riding furiously.
While his attendants could not bear it,
the Emperor remained composed and unperturbed.
Imperial relatives, noble ministers,
inner palace officials, and close confidantes
and attendants mingled haphazardly,
with no distinction of rank remaining.
He gathered together loose women,
assigned them to his accompanying officials,
and visited them morning and evening
as entertainment.
Regarding all those he executed,
he often ordered them dismembered;
sometimes they were burned in the fire,
sometimes thrown into the river.
As he continued his profound inebriation for a long time,
he grew increasingly insane and deluded.
By his later years,
he constantly claimed to see various ghosts and spirits,
and also said he heard strange sounds.
If he harbored resentment in his heart,
he certainly executed the person.
All members of the Yuán imperial clan were massacred and suppressed.
The people of Yǒng'ān and Shàngdǎng were subjected to cruel injustice.
Gāo Lóngzhī, Gāo Dézhèng, Dù Bì, Wáng Yuánjǐng, and Lǐ Qiànzhī, among others, were all harmed without committing any crime.
Once in Jìnyáng, he playfully stabbed Military Governor Wèi Ziyào with a spear (shuò),
and the man died instantly upon contact.
Furthermore, when he was atop the Dàguāng Diàn hall in Sāntái,
he used a sword/halberd (jùjù) to wound Military Governor Mù Sōng,
leading to his death.
Another time, he visited the home of Kāifǔ Bào Xiǎn.
A Military Governor named Hán Zhé, who was innocent,
was suddenly called out from the crowd and executed.
The rest of his cruel excesses
are too numerous to recount.
The court and the common people deeply hated him,
each harboring resentment and malice.
Yet, he habitually ruled his subordinates with severe decisiveness,
compounded by his silent recognition (of people) and powerful memory,
causing the multitude of officials to tremble,
daring not to commit misdeeds;
high-ranking civil and military officials worried about surviving the day.
Furthermore, he undertook extensive building projects,
causing countless labor projects to arise,
disturbing the entire state,
and exhausting both public and private resources.
All rewards and gifts
were issued without restraint or limit,
resulting in the national treasuries and reserves
becoming completely empty.
From the Empress Dowager and the various princes to the veteran officials, both inside and outside the court,
all were anxious, fearful, and distressed,
seeing no path forward.
When he reached his final years,
he could not take food,
but only drank wine frequently.
The effects of the alcohol became a sickness,
and he consequently died.
The Commentary states:
Gāozǔ pacified the four barbarian groups (Hú),
and his prestige and authority extended through the generations.
After moving the capital to Yè,
although there was someone (i.e., a nominal ruler) in charge of the state vessel,
all orders issued
and policies enacted came directly from him (Gāozǔ).
Xiǎnzǔ followed the great foundation of the dynasty,
and the internal and external (court and provinces) submitted in unison.
From the court to the countryside,
the hearts of the multitude looked up to him.
Within the territory of Dōng Wèi,
the whole world gladly supported him;
not yet a full year passed
before the Heavenly Mandate gathered upon him.
Initially, he focused his mind on governmental affairs,
and the moral influence was solemn.
Within a few years,
the state achieved unified and sound governance.
Later, he indulged in wine and followed his desires unrestrainedly,
his actions becoming extremely reckless and wild;
his depravity, wickedness, cruelty, and violence
were unprecedented in recent times.
That he did not rule the state for long
was truly due to this sickness,
and the extinction of his heirs
was certainly a remaining evil consequence.
The Encomium states: Tiānbǎo established the position,
and the reception of the Mandate was thereby conferred.
Suddenly dwelling in the central realm (Xià),
he thereupon accepted the Imperial Register.
His authority harmonized with the songs of praise,
but his character ruined the precious tortoise and jade (symbols of legitimacy).
Initially, he preserved the methods of government,
and virtuous words were heard.
He failed to follow restraint and careful thought,
and instead gave free rein to his desires.
He reached the limits of cruelty and tyranny,
and exhausted his nature in debauchery and excess.
Imperial Annals, Chapter Five: The Deposed Emperor (Fèidì)
Fèidì Yīn,
courtesy name Zhèngdào,
was the eldest son of Wénxuān Dì,
whose mother was Empress Lǐ.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (550 CE),
he was established as the Crown Prince,
being six years old at the time.
He was keen and intelligent by nature.
When first learning *fǎnyǔ* (a phonetic spelling method),
he annotated the character
"jì"
by writing "zì fǎn" (self-reversed).
When the attendants at the time did not understand the reason,
the Crown Prince said:
"The character 'jì'
has the 'zú' (foot radical) alongside it also forming 'jì' (footprint/trace),
so is it not 'zì fǎn' (self-reflecting/self-reversed)?"
He often held banquets in the Northern Palace,
but uniquely ordered that the Prince of Héjiān should not enter.
His staff asked him the reason,
and the Crown Prince said:
"This is where Shìzōng met with bandits;
how can the Prince of Héjiān properly be here again?"
Wénxuān Dì often remarked that the Crown Prince possessed the nature of a Hàn person,
and was not like himself;
he wanted to depose him
and establish the Prince of Tàiyuán instead.
Initially, an imperial edict appointed Guózǐ Bóshì Lǐ Bǎodǐng to tutor him;
after Bǎodǐng died,
another edict appointed Guózǐ Bóshì Xíng Zhì to attend and lecture.
Although the Crown Prince was young,
he was warm, generous, and enlightened,
possessing the demeanor of a ruler.
He comprehensively mastered the classics,
and examined current government affairs,
earning a very good reputation.
In the winter of the seventh year (of Tiānbǎo),
Wénxuān summoned court officials, scholars of literature, and ritual specialists for a banquet in the palace,
ordering them to debate the meaning of the classics,
while he personally oversaw and listened.
The Crown Prince personally wrote down questions,
and everyone present expressed admiration.
In the ninth year,
Wénxuān was in Jìnyáng,
and the Crown Prince supervised the state.
He gathered various scholars to lecture on the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety).
He ordered Yáng Yīn to convey his command,
asking Guózǐ Zhùjiào Xǔ Sǎnchóu:
"Sir, how do you sustain yourself in this world?"
He replied:
"Since I, Sǎnchóu, was young,
I have not ascended the couch of a catamite,
nor entered the chamber of a concubine.
I have diligently studied the bamboo slips and texts,
unaware that old age was approaching.
My lifelong aspiration
has merely been this."
The Crown Prince said:
"Yán Zǐ diminished his household structure to show integrity,
and Liǔ Xià Hū embraced a woman without being disordered,
but neither compares to this old gentleman who remains unmarried in old age."
He then bestowed upon him one hundred rolls of silk.
Later, Wénxuān ascended the Jīnfèng Tái terrace
and summoned the Crown Prince, ordering him to personally execute a prisoner with a blade.
The Crown Prince showed sorrowful difficulty
and failed repeatedly to sever the head.
Wénxuān became angry
and personally struck the Crown Prince three times with a horse whip.
Consequently, the Crown Prince suffered from palpitations and stammering,
and his spirit was sometimes confused and troubled.
In the tenth year, tenth month,
Wénxuān passed away.
On the guǐmǎo day,
the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne at the Xuāndé Hall in Jìnyáng,
proclaimed a general amnesty,
and universally promoted all civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court.
Those who had lost their official posts or noble ranks
were permitted to reclaim their former status.
On the gēngxū day,
the Empress Dowager was honored as Grand Empress Dowager,
and the Empress as Empress Dowager.
An imperial edict ordered that all soldiers in the nine provinces aged seventy and above be granted an official position,
and all military officers aged sixty and above, as well as those suffering from chronic illness and unable to serve,
were all discharged.
All construction works involving earth and timber, and all miscellaneous works using gold, copper, and iron,
were completely halted.
In the eleventh month, on the yǐmǎo day,
Húliù Jīn, Right Chancellor and King of Xiányáng, was appointed Left Chancellor.
Yǎn, Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs and King of Chángshān, was appointed Grand Tutor.
Zhàn, Minister of Works and King of Chángguǎng, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Duàn Sháo, Minister of Works, was appointed Minister of Works (Sītú).
Yān, King of Píngyáng, was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Shí, King of Gāoyáng, was appointed Left Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
Xiàowǎn, King of Héjiān, was appointed Governor of Sīzhōu.
Yàn Zǐxiàn, Imperial Attendant, was appointed Right Grand Secretary.
On the wùwǔ day,
envoys were dispatched to tour the four directions,
to inquire into the successes and failures of governance,
to observe the local customs,
and to ask about the people's hardships.
In the twelfth month, on the wùxū day,
Shàorén, King of Shàngdǎng, was re-enfeoffed as King of Yúyáng.
Shàoyì, King of Guǎngyáng, was re-enfeoffed as King of Fányáng.
Shàolián, King of Chánglè, was re-enfeoffed as King of Lǒngxī.
This year
was the first year of Wǔchéng of the Zhōu dynasty.
In the first year of Qiánmíng, gēngchén year,
spring, first month, on the guǐchǒu new moon day,
the reign title was changed.
On the jǐwèi day,
an edict was issued to lighten the corvée and taxes.
On the guǐhài day,
Shí, King of Gāoyáng, passed away.
In this month,
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìnyáng.
In the second month, on the jǐhài day,
Yǎn, Grand Tutor and King of Chángshān, was appointed Grand Preceptor and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Zhàn, Grand Commandant and King of Chángguǎng, was appointed Grand Marshal and concurrently Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Guīyàn, Left Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs and King of Píngqín, was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Ruì, King of Zhàojùn, was appointed Left Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
An edict released
all female relatives of former officials who had been confiscated into the palace or bestowed upon others.
On the jiǎchén day,
the Emperor visited Fānglínyuán Park,
personally reviewed the prisoners,
and those sentenced to death or lesser punishments were pardoned or had their sentences reduced, each according to their circumstances.
On the yǐsì day,
Yǎn, Grand Preceptor and King of Chángshān, fabricated an edict to execute Yáng Yīn, Minister of State Affairs; Yàn Zǐxiàn, Right Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs;
Kězhūhún Tiānhé, General of the Palace Guard; Sòng Qīndào, Imperial Attendant; and Zhèng Zǐmò, Palace Regular Attendant.
On the wùshēn day,
Yǎn, King of Chángshān, was appointed Grand Chancellor, Commander-in-Chief of all military forces inside and outside the court, and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Zhàn, Grand Marshal
and King of Chángguǎng, was appointed Grand Tutor and Grand Commander of the Capital Region.
Duàn Sháo, Minister of Works, was appointed Grand General.
Yān, former Minister of Works and King of Píngyáng, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Guīyàn, Minister of Works and King of Píngqín, was appointed Minister of Works (Sītú).
Yóu, King of Péngchéng, was appointed Minister of State Affairs.
Furthermore, Tāng, Crown Prince of Gāolí, was appointed Envoy with Staff, concurrently Commander of the Eastern Barbarians, Duke of Liáodōng Commandery, and King of Gāolí.
In this month,
Wáng Lín was defeated by Chén,
and Xiāo Zhuāng fled to Hézhōu.
In the third month, on the jiǎyín day,
an edict ordered that all military and state affairs be reported to Jìnyáng
and subject to the calculations and plans of Grand Chancellor Yǎn, King of Chángshān.
On the rénshēn day,
Xiàohéng, the second son of Wénxiāng, was enfeoffed as King of Guǎngníng.
Chánggōng, his third son, was enfeoffed as King of Lánlíng.
Summer, fourth month, on the guǐhài day,
an edict stated that in the nine provinces of Hénán, Dìng, Jì, Zhào, Yíng, Cāng, Nánjiāo, Guāng, and Qīng,
due to a locust plague,
the seasonal crops were quite damaged.
Envoys were dispatched on different routes to provide relief.
In this month,
Emperor Míng of Zhōu passed away.
Fifth month, on the rénzǐ day,
Liú Hónghuī, Open-Commission-Holder with the Rank of Three Grand Ministers, was appointed Right Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
Autumn, eighth month, on the rénwǔ day,
the Grand Empress Dowager ordered the deposed emperor to be made King of Jìnán,
and to be granted one commandery for his sustenance.
Yǎn, Grand Chancellor and King of Chángshān, was to accede to the grand succession.
On that day,
the King resided in a separate palace.
In the ninth month of the second year of Huángjiàn,
he died in Jìnyáng,
aged seventeen.
The Emperor was intelligent and mature from an early age,
generous, benevolent, and wise.
During the Tiānbǎo era, he had an excellent reputation.
When he assumed the great position,
Yáng Yīn, Yàn Zǐxiàn, Sòng Qīndào, and others jointly assisted him.
Because King of Chángshān was a close relative and highly respected,
feared and admired by all,
and moreover, on the day Wénxuān first passed away,
the Empress Dowager had originally intended to establish him [as emperor],
Yīn and others harbored suspicions and jealousy.
The King of Chángshān was worried and displeased,
so he reported to the Empress Dowager to execute their faction.
At that time, Guīyàn, King of Píngqín, was also privy to the plot.
In the autumn of the second year of Huángjiàn,
celestial phenomena indicated a change.
Guīyàn feared future harm,
so he reported to Xiàozhāo [that]
the King would be to blame.
Thus, Guīyàn was dispatched by express courier to the Jìnyáng Palace to kill him.
After the King's death,
Xiàozhāo fell ill,
seeing Wénxuān's ghost tormenting him.
Xiàozhāo deeply detested this,
and despite employing all methods of exorcism, it was to no avail.
Thirty days after his death, Xiàozhāo passed away.
In the second year of Dàníng,
he was buried northwest of Wǔníng,
and was posthumously named King Mǐndào.
Initially, Wénxuān ordered Xíng Shào to devise the Emperor's given name as Yīn and his courtesy name as Zhèngdào.
The Emperor followed up by criticizing him, saying:
"The Yīn dynasty was known for fraternal succession.
The character 'zhèng' (正)
is composed of 'yī' (一) and 'zhǐ' (止).
My children will not succeed me after my death."
Shào was frightened
and requested a change.
Wénxuān did not permit it, saying:
"It is fate."
He then said to Emperor Xiàozhāo:
"You may depose him,
but be careful not to kill him."
Collator's Notes
Annals Six, Xiàozhāo
Emperor Xiàozhāo Yǎn,
courtesy name Yán'ān,
was the sixth son of Emperor Shénwǔ
and the younger brother of Emperor Wénxuān by the same mother.
He was brilliant and extraordinary in his youth,
and early on showed signs of great accomplishments.
Empress Dowager Wǔmíng loved and esteemed him greatly.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng of Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Chángshān Commandery.
When Wénxiāng governed,
he sent Lǐ Tóngguǐ, Central Secretariat Attendant, to the princely residence to be a tutor to his younger brothers.
The Emperor, when perusing texts,
delved into their essence and meaning, rather than focusing on flowery language.
He often sighed, saying:
"Though the masters of Méngjīn,
the left horse shivered but did not flinch."
He considered this to be competence.
He then devoted himself to reading the Hàng Shū,
and upon reaching the biography of Lǐ Líng,
he admired his actions.
He was exceptionally intelligent;
when interacting with others,
once he knew their family taboos,
he never inadvertently violated them throughout his life.
When Tóngguǐ fell ill and died,
Diāo Ròu, who was a Changliu Canjun of the Kaifu, was ordered to replace him.
He was stern and narrow-minded by nature,
unsuitable for gentle guidance and instruction,
and was dismissed midway.
When the Emperor saw him off from his residence,
he looked grim and solemn,
with tears streaming down his face in several lines.
Those around him could not help but sigh in grief.
Such was his respect for his profession and his old acquaintances.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
his rank was elevated to King.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Minister of State Affairs concurrently of Bīng Province.
The Emperor was adept at making decisions
and skilled in managing affairs,
and all within the Department of State Affairs feared and obeyed him.
In the seventh year,
he followed Wénxuān back to Yè.
Wénxuān, finding many discrepancies in the memorials submitted by the Department of State Affairs,
ordered the Emperor to first discuss and settle the merits and demerits with the court officials,
and only then present them.
The Emperor was skilled in political tactics,
and his judgments were always sound and logical.
Wénxuān greatly admired him.
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Grand Marshal,
and still Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, Wénxuān was immersed in feasting and merrymaking,
The Emperor (Dì) showed his worry and indignation in his demeanor.
Wénxuān noticed this,
and said to the Emperor (Dì):
“As long as you are around,
why should I not indulge in pleasure?”
The Emperor (Dì) only wept and bowed low,
ultimately saying nothing.
Wénxuān also grew greatly distressed,
and threw his cup to the ground, saying:
“You resent me for this.
From now on, whoever dares to offer wine,
I shall execute them!”
Consequently, he took all the cups he used and destroyed them.
Later, he became even more deeply addicted,
sometimes entering the homes of various noble relatives to wrestle and grapple,
regardless of rank.
Only when the Prince of Chángshān arrived,
was everyone, inside and out, serious and respectful.
The Emperor (Dì) secretly drafted a list of matters,
intending to remonstrate,
but his friend Wáng Xī thought it was ill-advised.
The Emperor (Dì) did not comply,
and took an opportunity to speak frankly,
which resulted in him incurring great fury.
Empress Shùnchéng was originally a member of the imperial clan of the Wèi dynasty.
Wénxuān wanted the Emperor (Dì) to distance himself from her,
and secretly sought out many virtuous ladies for the Emperor (Dì),
hoping to shift his favor.
Although the Emperor (Dì) complied with the instruction and accepted them,
his affection and bond with the Empress (Shùnchéng) grew deeper.
The Emperor's (Dì) nature was quite severe.
If a Director (lángzhōng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) made an error in judgment or ruling,
he would immediately inflict a beating upon them.
If a clerk (lìngshǐ) committed wickedness or corruption,
they were immediately investigated and executed.
Wénxuān then made the Emperor (Dì) stand before him,
and pointed the ring handle of a sword at his ribs.
He summoned those who had been punished by the Emperor (Dì),
menacing them with a naked blade,
and sought evidence of the Emperor's (Dì) faults.
None of them offered any complaint,
and only then was Wénxuān appeased.
From then on, the Emperor (Dì) was not permitted to cane or whip the Directors (lángzhōng).
Later, Wénxuān bestowed upon the Emperor (Dì) a palace woman from the Wèi period.
When he awoke, he forgot having done so,
and claimed the Emperor (Dì) had taken her without permission.
He immediately used the ring handle of a sword to strike the Emperor (Dì) wildly,
causing him to become critically injured.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) wept day and night.
Wénxuān did not know what to do.
Previously, he had imprisoned the Emperor's (Dì) friend Wáng Xī,
but now he released him,
and ordered him to attend the Emperor (Dì).
After more than a month, the Emperor (Dì) gradually recovered,
and dared not remonstrate again.
When Wénxuān died,
the Emperor (Dì) stayed within the restricted palace area to oversee the funeral rites.
When the young sovereign (yòuzhǔ) ascended the throne,
the Emperor (Dì) took his place in the court ranks.
He was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū).
All state affairs were decided by the Emperor (Dì).
After more than a month,
he moved to his princely residence (fāndǐ).
From then on, imperial edicts and commands mostly did not concern the Emperor (Dì).
A guest spoke to the Emperor (Dì), saying:
“When a bird of prey leaves its nest,
it is bound to face the worry of having its eggs investigated,
and given your current position,
how is it proper to repeatedly go out?”
In the first year of Qiánmíng (560 CE),
he followed the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) to Yè,
and resided in the Lǐngjūn Residence.
At that time, Yáng Yīn, Yān Zǐxiàn, Kězhūhún Tiānhé, Sòng Qīndào, Zhèng Zǐmò, and others, seeing that the Emperor's (Dì) prestige and authority were already great,
privately feared his encroaching power.
They requested that the Emperor (Dì) be appointed Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Governor of Sīzhōu (Sīzhōu Mù), and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì);
and that Chángguǎng Wáng Zhàn be appointed Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) and Director of the Department of State Affairs for Bīng Province (Lù Bīngshěng Shàngshū Shì),
thus removing the office of Grand Area Commander of the Capital Region (Jīngjī Dà Dūdu).
The Emperor (Dì), realizing he was being suspected and marginalized despite his noble kinship,
arranged a hunting trip with the Prince of Chángguǎng,
and plotted with him in the field.
On the *Jiǎxū* day of the third month,
when the Emperor (Dì) first went to the department,
starting from the Lǐngjūn Residence in the morning,
a great storm arose suddenly,
destroying the curtains of his imperial chariot.
The Emperor (Dì) was greatly disturbed by this omen.
When he arrived at the department,
the court officials were all assembled.
After they were seated,
and several rounds of wine had passed,

Yáng Yīn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Yān Zǐxiàn, the Right Vice Director (Yòu Púshè), Kězhūhún Tiānhé, the General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn), and Sòng Qīndào, the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), were arrested at their seats.

The Emperor (Dì), dressed in military attire, along with the Prince of Píngyuán, Duàn Sháo, the Prince of Píngqín, Gāo Guīyàn, and the General of the Palace Guard, Liú Hónghuī, entered through the Yúnlóng Gate.
In front of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng), they encountered Zhèng Zǐmò, the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
and arrested him also.
They were all executed within the Imperial Treasury (Yùfǔ).
When the Emperor (Dì) arrived at the Dōnggé Gate,
Commander Chéng Xiūníng drew his blade and shouted at the Emperor (Dì).
The Emperor (Dì) ordered Gāo Guīyàn to reason with him,
but Xiūníng shouted loudly and refused to comply.
Since Guīyàn was already the General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn),
and was typically respected by the soldiers,
they all laid down their weapons.
Xiūníng sighed and gave up.
The Emperor (Dì) entered and proceeded to the Zhāoyáng Palace.
The young sovereign (yòuzhǔ), the Grand Empress Dowager (Tài Huáng Tàihòu), and the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) all came out and took the imperial seats.
The Emperor (Dì) presented the crimes of Yīn and the others,
requesting that they suffer the penalty for their unauthorized assumption of power.
At that time, more than two thousand imperial guards in the courtyard and under the two corridors were all armored and awaiting orders.
É Yǒnglè, a Guard Commandant (Wǔwèi), possessed unmatched strength.
Moreover, he had been highly regarded by Wénxuān,
and grasped his blade, ready to act.
The Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) was naturally hesitant and slow of speech,
and in the urgency of the moment did not know what to say.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tài Huáng Tàihòu) then swore to the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
saying that the Emperor (Dì) had no rebellious intentions,
but merely wished to remove the oppressors.
Gāo Guīyàn instructed and consoled the guards, ordering them to stand down.
Yǒnglè then sheathed his sword and wept.
The Emperor (Dì) then ordered Guīyàn to lead the imperial bodyguards toward the Huálín Garden,
and had the capital region troops enter to guard the gates and corridors.
É Yǒnglè was executed in the garden.

An edict appointed the Emperor (Dì) as Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng), Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Forces Domestic and Foreign (Dūdu Zhōngwài Zhūjūn), and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
The subordinates in the Chancellor’s (xiàng) establishment were promoted one rank.
The Emperor (Dì) soon went to Jìnyáng,
and there was an imperial command that all major military and state affairs should be consulted with him and decided by him.
Once the Emperor (Dì) held this great position,
he spared no effort in his duties,
selecting excellent regulations,
and examining the correspondence between titles and actual performance.
The Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) adopted a respectful, hands-off approach to governance.
The Grand Empress Dowager (Tài Huáng Tàihòu) soon issued an order to depose the young sovereign (shǎozhǔ),
and commanded the Emperor (Dì) to take charge of the great mandate.
On the *Rénwǔ* day of the eighth month of the first year of Huángjiàn (560 CE),
the Emperor ascended the throne at the Xuāndé Hall in Jìnyáng.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the first year of Qiánmíng was changed to Huángjiàn.
An edict ordered that the Grand Empress Dowager (Tài Huáng Tàihòu) be referred to again as the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
and that the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) be called Empress Wénxuān (Wénxuān Huánghòu).
Her palace was named Zhāoxìn.
On the *Yǐyǒu* day,
an edict stated: Since the founding of the dynasty by Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ),
for all meritorious officials who assisted in the founding, whose descendants have died out and whose hereditary titles have not been passed on,
the relevant officials must search for their nearest relatives,
report their names,
and they shall be appointed successors as appropriate.
Elders in all commanderies and states were each granted official titles,
and given yellow hats and dove staffs.
Another edict stated: Those who are outspoken and upright scholars are all permitted to be granted audience to present matters.
Military personnel who died in battle or perished in royal service
must be reported promptly,
and shall be granted posthumous honors.
Area commanders and court officials whose reputations have long been high,
whose positions were prestigious and prominent,
but who have not yet received posthumous honors since the Tiānbǎo era,
must also all be recorded and presented to the throne.
Furthermore, regarding the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi) and the Palace Deputy Director (Zhōngchéng),
whose offices enforce the law,
they must investigate offenses and determine crimes;
they are not permitted to manipulate texts or abuse the law.
All state slaves, male and female, aged sixty and above, were exempted and made commoners.
On the *Wùzǐ* day,
Zhàn, Prince of Chángguǎng and Grand Tutor (Tàifù), was appointed Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng).
Yān, Prince of Píngyáng and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
Yóu, Prince of Péngchéng and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), was appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
On the *Rénchén* day,
an edict ordered the dispersal of great envoys to inspect the four directions,
to observe customs,
inquire about the hardships of the people,
investigate successes and failures,
and search for virtuous and worthy men.
On the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
“In the past, when King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he first enfeoffed the rulers of the previous two dynasties.
The Hàn, the Wèi, and the two Jìn dynasties
never abolished this custom.
However, when the Yuán clan ruled,
they did not adhere to the old principles.
We have inherited the great mandate,
and intend to revive this ancient custom.
Regarding the matter of ‘Two Kings and Three Reverences’ (Èr Wáng Sān Kè),
the historical explanations differ.
Let officials deliberate on what is right and wrong,
and present a detailed memorial with names listed.
The forms and rituals pertaining to this should also be deliberated upon.”
Another edict ordered the Guózǐ Temple to establish its official staff,
appoint students as before,
lecture and study the Classics,
and conduct examinations seasonally.
The Stone Classics transported by Emperor Wénxiāng (Wénxiāng Dì)
should immediately be displayed in the academy.
The administrators of the Grand Colleges (Dàxué) in the outer provinces are also required to diligently supervise the teaching.
On the *Bǐngshēn* day,
an edict stated that meritorious persons in the nine provinces who hold multiple enfeoffments
are permitted to divide and bestow them upon their sons and younger brothers,
in order to extend kindness toward family members.
On the *Rénshēn* day of the ninth month,
an edict ordered deliberation and finalization of the music for the Three Ancestors.
In the winter, the eleventh month, on the *Xīnhài* day,
Consort Yuán Shì was established as Empress.
The Heir Apparent, Bǎinián, was made Crown Prince.
A grade of nobility was granted throughout the realm to those who had succeeded their fathers.
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
the officials concerned memorialized that the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ Xiànwǔ Huángdì should appropriately play the Music of Martial Virtue (*Wǔdé*)
and dance the Dance of Brilliant Merit (*Zhāoliè*);
the ancestral temple of Shìzōng Wénxiāng Huángdì should appropriately play the Music of Civil Virtue (*Wéndé*)
and dance the Dance of Proclaimed Governance (*Xuānzhèng*);
the ancestral temple of Xiǎnzǔ Wénxuān Huángdì should appropriately play the Music of Civil Rectitude (*Wénzhèng*)
and dance the Dance of Grand Radiance (*Guāngdà*).
An imperial edict stated: "Approved."
On the *Gēngshēn* day,

an edict decreed that thirteen men—the late Grand Tutor Wèi Jǐng, the late Grand Tutor Dòu Tài, the late Grand Tutor, Prince of Tàiyuán, Lóu Zhāo, the late Grand Minister Qùdí Gān, Prince of Zhāngwǔ, the late Grand Commandant Duàn Róng, the late Grand Tutor Mòqí Pǔ, the late Minister of Works Cài Jùn, the late Grand Tutor Gāo Gān, the late Minister of Works Mòduōlóu Dàiwén, the late Grand Guardian Liú Guì, the late Grand Guardian Fēng Zǔyì, and the late Governor of Guǎngzhōu Wáng Huái—should be inducted to enjoy sacrificial offerings at the temple court of Tàizǔ.

Seven men—the late Grand Tutor, Prince of Qīnghé, Yuè, the late Grand Minister, Prince of Āndé, Hán Guǐ, the late Grand Minister, Prince of Fúfēng, Kězhūhún Dàoyuán, the late Grand Tutor Gāo Áng, the late Grand Marshal Liú Fēng, the late Grand Tutor Mòqí Shòuluògān, and the late Grand Commandant Mùróng Shàozōng—should be inducted to enjoy sacrificial offerings at the temple court of Shìzōng.

Three men—the late Grand Commandant, Prince of Hédōng, Pān Xiānglè, the late Minister of Works Xuē Xiūyì, and the late Grand Tutor Pòliùhán Cháng—should be inducted to enjoy sacrificial offerings at the temple court of Xiǎnzǔ.
In this month,
the Emperor personally led the army north to attack the Kùmò Xī.
He passed outside the Great Wall.
The captives fled and scattered.
He divided his forces to pursue and attack,
gaining a great haul of oxen and horses,
which were collected and brought into the Jìnyáng Palace.
The twelfth month, on the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Jìnyáng.
The second year, in spring, the first month, on the *Xīnhài* day,
sacrifices were offered at the Round Mound (*Yuánqiū*).
On the *Rénzǐ* day,
the *dì* sacrifice was performed at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
an edict decreed that punishments for criminals be reduced, each according to degree.
The second month, on the *Dīngchǒu* day,

an edict instructed that all officials, both inside and outside the court, holding rank five or higher, as well as Chief Clerks, Recorders of the Three Departments (*Sānfǔ*), Erudites of the various princes, Palace Censors, the three offices of the Grand Judge, Department Heads of the Ministry of Personnel (*Shàngshū*), and Attendants at the Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shèrén*),
must each recommend one person within a period of two years.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
Wèi Yǒu, Prince of Péngchéng and Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Lìng*), was made Grand Guardian (*Tàibǎo*).
Wèi Càn, Prince of Chánglè, was made Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*).
On the *Jǐyǒu* day,
a wild pheasant roosted in the court of the Front Palace.
The eleventh month, on the *Jiǎchén* day,
an edict stated:
"I have been afflicted by this sudden illness,
and suddenly I am beyond recovery.
Now, the successor is young and inexperienced,
not yet practiced in the methods of governance.
The undertaking of the state and the ancestral altars is weighty,
and authority logically belongs to the loftiest virtue.
Zhàn, the Right Chancellor and Prince of Chángguǎng, investigates principles and measures transformations,
embodies the Way and holds the lineage;
he is the hope of heroes among men,
looked up to by all within the seas.
Sharing the same womb and spirit,
he is the reliance of both family and state.
Jì Ruì, the Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs and Prince of Zhàojùn, should be dispatched to convey this instruction,
summoning the Prince to assume this Great Treasure (the throne).
The rituals for mourning should entirely follow those of Hàn Wén[dì].
After thirty-six days, all should revert to normalcy (public affairs resume).
The goods and materials used for the imperial tomb (*shānlíng*)
must strictly adhere to frugality."
Previously, although the Emperor was ill, he did not fail to attend to state affairs and readings.
In this month,
he passed away at Jìnyáng Palace,
aged twenty-seven.
In the first year of Dàníng, the intercalary twelfth month, on the *Guǐmǎo* day,
the coffin returned to Yè.
He was granted the posthumous title Xiàozhāo Huángdì.
On the *Gēngwǔ* day,
he was interred at Wénjìng Líng.
The Emperor was intelligent, discerning, and possessed insight and breadth of mind.
He was profound, steady, and capable of decision-making,
impossible to gauge or predict.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
his waist measured ten spans,
his demeanor and appearance were striking,
outstandingly unique.
Since holding positions in the ministries and departments (*táishěng*),
he dedicated his mind to methods of governance.
He was skilled and knowledgeable in official documents and systems,
surpassing what his subordinates could achieve.
When he formally ascended to the imperial seat,
he applied himself even harder.
He lightened corvée and lowered taxes,
diligently showing compassion for the hidden sufferings of the people.
Inside the court, there were no private favorites;
outside, he recruited talented individuals.
Although the Empress’s father held the position of Grandee of the Special Progression (*Tèjìn*), there was no favoritism shown.
He held court until late afternoon,
striving to know the good and bad qualities of men.
He frequently questioned his close attendants,
hoping to obtain straightforward critiques.
Once, he asked Palace Attendant Péi Zé about the general discussions outside regarding gains and losses.
Zé replied casually:
"Your Majesty is intelligent and perfectly impartial,
and naturally can match the ancients,
but thoughtful scholars
all say you are excessively meticulous,
and the proper measure of an emperor
is somewhat insufficiently broad."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Indeed, as you say.
When I first supervised the myriad affairs,
my considerations were not fully comprehensive,
thus leading to that result.
How can this practice be maintained for long?
I fear later there will be complaints of laxity."
Zé was consequently favored and treated well.
This shows how much he enjoyed hearing about his faults.
Jì Ruì, Prince of Zhàojùn, and Qùdí Xiǎn'ān were in attendance.
The Emperor said:
"Xūbá is my paternal cousin, and Xiǎn'ān is my maternal cousin.
Today, we observe the rites of family members,
setting aside the respect due between ruler and subject.
You may speak of my shortcomings."
Xiǎn'ān said:
"Your Majesty frequently speaks falsehoods."
He asked:
"In what way?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty formerly saw Wénxuān beat people with a horsewhip
and always deemed it wrong,
yet now you do the same.
Is this not speaking falsehoods?"
The Emperor clasped his hand and thanked him.
He then told him to speak plainly again.
He replied:
"Your Majesty is too meticulous;
the Son of Heaven resembles a clerk instead."
The Emperor said:
"I am well aware of this.
However, the state has been without laws for a long time,
and I intend to straighten things out until we reach a state of non-action (*wúwéi*)."
He also questioned Wáng Xī.
Xī's reply was the same as Xiǎn'ān’s,
and he calmly accepted all their criticisms.
He was naturally extremely filial.
When the Empress Dowager was ill,
she moved out to reside in the Southern Palace.
The Emperor did not walk properly or adjust his shoes;
his expression was depressed and miserable.
He did not loosen his garments (sleep fully dressed)
for nearly forty days.
The distance from his palace to the Southern Palace was more than five hundred paces.
He left at cock-crow
and only returned around *chén* time (7–9 AM).
He walked back and forth on foot,
without using an imperial carriage or palanquin.
If the Empress Dowager's suffering increased slightly,
he would immediately sleep lying down outside her apartments.
He personally attended to all her food, drink, and medicine.
When the Empress Dowager frequently suffered from heart pain that she could not bear,
the Emperor stood attending before the curtain,
pinching his own palm with his fingernails,
until the blood flowed down his sleeve.
He was affectionate toward his younger brothers,
without the barrier of ruler and subject.
He was resolute and strategic.
At that time, the state was rich and the army strong.
He intended to avenge the long-standing grievance of Shénwǔ,
planning to station his forces at Píngyáng,
as a strategy for advancement and conquest.
That his grand strategy was not fulfilled,
is indeed a pity!
Initially, the Emperor (Dì) and Jǐnán (Zhái) had agreed not to harm each other.
When the imperial carriage was in Jìnyáng,
Wǔchéng was stationed at Yè,
and those who observed the cosmic atmosphere claimed that Yèchéng (the city of Yè) possessed the aura of the Son of Heaven.
The Emperor constantly feared Jǐnán’s potential resurgence,
so he secretly administered poisonous zhen wine (zhèndú).
Jǐnán refused to drink it,
so he strangled and killed him.
Afterward, he felt considerable shame and remorse.
He initially suffered from internal heat,
and frequently took medicinal decoctions (tāng) and powders (sǎn).
At that time, there was a secretarial clerk (lìshǐ) of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) whose surname was Zhào,
who saw Wénxuān (Dì) traveling west from Yè, accompanied by Yáng Yīn, Yān Zǐxiàn, and others,
saying they intended to seek revenge together.
The Emperor, while in Jìnyáng Palace (Jìnyáng Gōng),
and his consort Máo Fūrén, also saw them.
Consequently, he gradually became critically ill.
He prepared ceremonies for exorcism and suppression.
Sometimes oil was sprinkled everywhere;
sometimes torches were held to burn and drive them away.
The various malevolent spirits (lì) emerged from the hall rafters,
riding upon the roof ridge,
singing and shouting naturally,
showing no sign of fear whatsoever.
At one time, a celestial dog (Tiāngǒu) descended,
so he conducted military maneuvers (jiǎngwǔ) at that location to suppress it.
A rabbit startled his horse,
and the Emperor fell, breaking his ribs.
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) visited him during his illness,
asking three times where Jǐnán was,
but the Emperor did not reply.
The Empress Dowager angrily said:
"Did you kill him?
You did not heed my words,
it is fitting that you should die!"
At the time of his death,
he merely leaned upon the bed and pillow,
kowtowing and begging for mercy.
He dispatched an envoy with an imperial edict summoning the Prince of Chángguǎng (Chángguǎng Wáng) to enter and succeed to the great lineage,
and wrote a personal letter saying:
"You should place my wife and children in a good situation,
do not imitate those who came before."
A commentary states:
Shénwǔ stabilized the four directions,
holding authority and power himself.
After moving the capital to Yè,
although there was a designated successor (zhǔqì),
all edicts issued
and policies enacted originated from him.
Wénxuān followed the great enterprise.
The interior and exterior harmoniously obeyed.
From the court to the countryside,
the hearts of the populace looked toward him with hope.
In the territory of Dōng Wèi,
the whole nation happily supported his ascension.
In less than a full month,
he ascended to the imperial throne (Chénjí).
Initially, he devoted his heart to governance,
and social customs (fēnghuà) were solemn and orderly.
Within several years,
both court and populace were secure and stable.
Afterward, he indulged in wine and unrestrained desire,
his actions reaching the extreme of madness.
His depravity, wickedness, cruelty, and violence
were unprecedented in recent times.
That his reign was not long-lasting
was truly due to this ailment.
Jǐnán succeeded to the inheritance,
greatly reforming its deficiencies.
Educational influence (fēngjiào) was brilliant and clear,
and the officials (jìnshēn) hailed it as fortunate.
His trusted ministers (gǔgōng fǔbì),
though harboring sincerity,
were neither able to assist in propagating virtue and morality,
nor harmonize close relatives,
nor were they able to plan ahead to protect themselves,
or deeply scheme to safeguard their sovereign.
Failing to execute what needed execution,
they brought disaster upon themselves.
When the ministers were executed,
the sovereign was soon deposed and disgraced.
This was all caused by employing people who were not suited to their positions.
Xiàozhāo had resided early in the high government offices (Táigé),
was perfectly familiar with past affairs,
and among the populace and officials,
there was nothing he was not entrusted with.
After Wénxuān’s death,
he greatly reformed previous abuses.
When he approached the highest dignity (zūnjí),
his attentiveness deepened even further.
People of the time admired his brilliance but criticized his focus on minutiae.
He loved investigating antiquity
and generally followed ritual standards.
He intended to grant feudal titles to the descendants of previous dynasties,
and moreover, emphasized the customs of schools and academies.
He summoned outstanding talents,
and civil and military officials all gathered.
At that time, the court governance of the Zhōu clan was shifting towards the chief ministers,
and the lords and generals suspected each other,
thus creating no small danger.
He looked upon Guānyòu (the region west of the passes),
truly cherishing the ambition of annexing it.
His planning was grand and far-reaching;
he was indeed an enlightened sovereign of his time.
But why was his life not prolonged?
What was the reason for this?
Could it be that between the seen and the unseen realms
there was truly retribution?
Or that the foundation of Qí (Zhāi) was destined to end here,
and though the Emperor wished to expand it,
Heaven did not permit it?
Imperial Annals VII: Wǔchéng
Shìzǔ Wǔchéng Huángdì, personal name Zhàn,
was the ninth son of Shénwǔ Huángdì,
and the younger brother by the same mother as Xiàozhāo Huángdì.
His demeanor and appearance were remarkable,
and Shénwǔ especially loved him.
When Shénwǔ was pacifying and attracting distant tribes,
he arranged a marriage for the Emperor (Dì) with the daughter of the Rúrú crown prince Ānluóchén,
who was titled
"Princes Línhé" (Línhé Gōngzhǔ).
The Emperor was eight years old at the time;
his cap and robes were dignified and formal,
and his expression was calm and detached.
Both the Chinese (Huá) and the non-Chinese (Róng) marveled at his distinction.
During the Yuánxiàng period,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chángguǎng Commandery (Chángguǎng Jùngōng).
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo period,
his rank was advanced to Prince (Wáng).
He was appointed Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
soon after concurrently serving as Minister of Education (Sītú),
and then transferred to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
At the beginning of the Qiánmíng period,
Yáng Yīn and others secretly alienated and feared him,
so they made the Emperor (Dì) Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ),
and concurrent Governor of Bīngzhōu (Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
After the Emperor (Dì) and Xiàozhāo plotted to execute the various governing officials,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tài Fù), Director of Affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì), and concurrent Grand Governor of the Capital Region (Jīngjī Dà Dūdū).
At the beginning of the Huángjiàn period,
his rank was advanced to Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng).
When Xiàozhāo visited Jìnyáng,
the Emperor (Dì), as a close relative, remained to guard Yè,
and all governmental affairs were entrusted to him.
In the second year,
Xiàozhāo died.
His dying edict summoned the Emperor (Dì) to enter and assume the great throne.
When he arrived at Jìnyáng Palace,
the mourning rites were initiated at Chóngdé Hall (Chóngdé Diàn).
The Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) ordered the relevant offices to proclaim the dying edict.
The Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng), Húlǜ Jīn, led all the officials in earnestly urging him (to accept),
and after presenting three petitions,
he agreed.
In the winter, the eleventh month, Guǐchǒu day, of the first year of Dàníng,
the Emperor (Huángdì) was enthroned in the Southern Palace (Nángōng).
A general amnesty was granted,
and the second year of Huángjiàn was changed to Dàníng.
On Yǐmǎo day,
Sītú and Prince Píngqín, Guī Yàn, was made Grand Tutor (Tài Fù).
Shàngshū Right Assistant Director (Yòu Púshè) and Prince of Zhàojùn, Ruì, was made Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
Tàiwèi Wèi Càn was made Grand Guardian (Tài Bǎo).
Shàngshū Lìng Duàn Sháo was made Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
Governor (Cìshǐ) of Fēngzhōu, Lóu Ruì, was made Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Tài Fù and Prince Píngyáng, Yān, was made Grand Minister (Tài Zǎi).
Tài Bǎo and Prince Péngchéng, Yóu, was made Grand Preceptor (Tài Shī) and Director of Affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu and Prince Bólíng, Jì, was made Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Jiān) and Prince Rènchéng, Jiē, was made Shàngshū Left Assistant Director (Zuǒ Púshè).
Cìshǐ of Bīngzhōu, Húlǜ Guāng, was made Right Assistant Director (Yòu Púshè).
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) of Xiàozhāo Huángdì, Bǎinián, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lèlíng Commandery (Lèlíng Jùnwáng).
On Gēngshēn day,
an edict was issued for grand envoys (dàshǐ) to travel throughout the land,
to investigate the good and bad aspects of governance,
inquire about the suffering of the people,
and promote worthy and talented individuals.
In this year,
it was the first year of Bǎodìng of Zhōu Wǔ Dì.
In the spring, the first month, Yǐhài day, of the first year of Héqīng,
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìnyáng.
On Xīnsì day,
sacrifices were offered at the Southern Suburb (Nánjiāo).
On Rénwǔ day,
sacrifices were offered at the Grand Ancestral Temple (Tài Miào).
On Bǐngxū day,
Consort Hú Shì was established as Empress (Huánghòu),
and his son Wěi was established as Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
A general amnesty was granted.
All civil and military officials were universally advanced one grade,
and those who succeeded their fathers were granted one rank of nobility.
On Jǐhài day,
the former Governor of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ) and Prince Féngyì, Rùn, was made Shàngshū Left Assistant Director (Zuǒ Púshè).
An edict forbade slaughtering to accord with the spring ordinances.
In the second month, on Dīngwèi day,
Tài Zǎi and Prince Píngyáng, Yān, was made Governor of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ), Grand Tutor (Tài Fù), and concurrent Minister of Education (Sītú).
Commander-in-Chief of the Guards (Lǐng Jūn Dà Jiàngjūn), Zōngshī, and Prince Píngqín, Guī Yàn, was made Grand Minister (Tài Zǎi) and Governor of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu Cìshǐ).
On Yǐmǎo day,
the concurrent Shàngshū Lìng and Prince Rènchéng, Jiē, was made Minister of Education (Sītú).
An edict commissioned the Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) Cuī Zhān to go on a diplomatic mission to Chén.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day *Xīnchǒu* (48th of the cycle),
Empress Dowager Lóu Shì died.
On the day *Yǐsì* (6th of the cycle),
the Regional Inspector (*Cìshǐ*) of Qīngzhōu reported,
that this month, on the day *Gēngyín* (27th of the cycle), the Hé (Yellow River) and the Jǐ were clear.
Because the Hé and Jǐ were clear,
the name of the second year of *Dàníng* was changed to *Héqīng*,
and convicts were demoted by varying degrees.
Fifth month, on the day *Jiǎshēn* (21st of the cycle),
Empress Wǔmíng was interred beside the Emperor at Yìpíng Líng.
On the day *Jǐchǒu* (26th of the cycle),
Húlǜ Guāng, the Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Yòupúyè*), was made Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Lìng*).
In the autumn, seventh month,
Guī Yàn, the Grand Tutor (*Tàizǎi*), Regional Inspector of Jìzhōu, and Prince of Píngqín, seized the prefecture and rebelled.
An imperial edict ordered Duàn Sháo, the Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*), and Lóu Ruì, the Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*), to suppress and capture him.
On the day *Yǐwèi* (32nd of the cycle),
