Guī Yàn, along with his three sons and twenty associates, were executed in the marketplace of the capital.
On the day *Dīngyǒu* (34th of the cycle),
Duàn Sháo, the Grand Marshal, was made Grand Preceptor (*Tàifù*).
Lóu Ruì, the Minister of Works, was made Minister over the Masses (*Sītú*).
Yān, the Grand Preceptor and Prince of Píngyáng, was made Grand Tutor.
Húlǜ Guāng, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, was made Minister of Works.
Ruì, the Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Tàifù*) and Prince of Zhàojùn, was made Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Xiàowǎn, the Director of the Palace Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Jiān*) and Prince of Héjiān, was made Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè*).
On the day *Guǐhài* (60th of the cycle),
the Emperor traveled to Jìnyáng.
Envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
Winter, eleventh month, on the day *Dīngchǒu* (14th of the cycle),
an imperial edict appointed Fēng Xiàoyǎn, Acting Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (*Jiān Sǎnqí Chángshì*), as envoy to Chén.
Twelfth month, on the day *Bǐngchén* (53rd of the cycle),
the Imperial carriage arrived back from Jìnyáng.
This year,
Shàodé, the Prince of Tàiyuán, was executed.
Year 2, spring, first month, on the day *Yǐhài* (12th of the cycle),
the Emperor issued an edict to personally supervise the examination of the *Xiùcái* (Flourishing Talents) candidates in the court hall.
Wèi Shōu, the Junior Preceptor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Shàofù*), was made Acting Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the day *Jǐmǎo* (16th of the cycle),
Wèi Shōu, the Acting Right Assistant Director, was stripped of his rank for laxity and excessive leniency.
On the day *Dīngchǒu* (14th of the cycle),
Empress Wǔmíng was sacrificed to alongside the Emperor in the northern suburban ritual.
On the day *Xīnmǎo* (28th of the cycle),
the Emperor visited the Imperial Pavilion (*Dūtíng*) to review the prisoners,
and reduced the sentences of criminals in the capital by varying degrees.
Third month, on the day *Yǐchǒu* (2nd of the cycle).
An edict ordered Húlǜ Guāng, the Minister of Works, to supervise the five corps of soldiers building a defensive rampart at Zhǐguān.
On the day *Rénshēn* (9th of the cycle),
The state of Shìwéi sent envoys to court with tribute.
On the day *Bǐngxū* (23rd of the cycle),
Zhào Yànshēn, Acting Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was made Left Assistant Director.
Summer, fourth month,
the five prefectures of Bìngzhōu, Fénzhōu, Jìnzhōu, Dōngyōng, and Nánfén suffered crop damage due to insects and drought.
Envoys were dispatched to distribute relief.
On the day *Wùwǔ* (55th of the cycle),
Envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
Fifth month, on the day *Rénwǔ* (19th of the cycle),
an edict repurposed the park containing the Shuāngtáng (Twin Halls) and Rùnwèi (Intercalary Seat) palaces south of the city,
to construct the Dàzǒngchí Temple.
Sixth month, on the day *Yǐsì* (6th of the cycle),
Qízhōu reported that eight dragons were seen ascending to heaven at the junction of the Jǐ and Hé (Yellow River) rivers.
On the day *Yǐmǎo* (52nd of the cycle),
an edict appointed Cuī Zǐwǔ, Acting Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, as envoy to Chén.
On the day *Gēngshēn* (57th of the cycle),
Xiàoyú, the Governor of Sīzhōu and Prince of Hénán, died.
Autumn, eighth month, on the day *Xīnchǒu* (8th of the cycle),
an edict repurposed the Sāntái Palace as the Dàxīngshèng Temple.
Winter, twelfth month, on the day *Guǐsì* (30th of the cycle),
Envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
On the day *Jǐyǒu* (46th of the cycle),
Yáng Zhōng, a general of Zhōu, leading the Turkic (*Tūjué*) forces under Āshǐnà Mùhàn and over 200,000 men, divided them into three routes from [unspecified] Zhōu,
killing and plundering officials and common people.
At this time,
heavy snow fell continuously for months.
The snow reached several feet deep on flat ground for over a thousand *lǐ* north to south.
Frost fell during the day,
and blood rained in Tàiyuán.
On the day *Wùwǔ* (55th of the cycle),
the Emperor arrived at Jìnyáng.
On the day *Jǐwèi* (56th of the cycle),
the Zhōu army threatened Bìngzhōu.
They also sent the Grand General (*Dà Jiāngjūn*) Dáxī Wǔ leading tens of thousands of troops to Dōngyōng and Jìnzhōu,
to link up with the Turkic forces.
This year,
Shìwéi, Kùmò Xī, Mòjié, and Qìdān all sent envoys to court with tribute.
Year 3, spring, first month, on the day *Gēngshēn* (57th of the cycle), the new moon,
the Zhōu army reached the base of the city wall and lined up their formation.
They fought west of the city.
The Zhōu army and the Turkic forces were utterly routed.
The dead, both men and livestock, lay piled upon each other,
stretching continuously for hundreds of *lǐ*.
An edict ordered Duàn Sháo, the Prince of Píngyuán, to pursue them beyond the border and then return.
Third month, on the day *Xīnyǒu* (58th of the cycle),
the codes and statutes (*Lǜlìng*) were promulgated.
A general amnesty was granted.
On the day *Jǐsì* (6th of the cycle),
Yóu, the Grand Preceptor (*Tàishī*) and Prince of Péngchéng, was assassinated by a bandit.
On the day *Gēngchén* (17th of the cycle),
Húlǜ Guāng, the Minister of Works, was made Minister over the Masses (*Sītú*).
Pǔ, the Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*) and Prince of Wǔxīng, was made Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the day *Jiǎshēn* (21st of the cycle),
Rùn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs and Prince of Féngxǔ, was made Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*).
Summer, fourth month, on the day *Xīnmǎo* (28th of the cycle),
an edict appointed Huángpǔ Liàng, Acting Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, as envoy to Chén.
Fifth month, on the day *Jiǎzǐ* (1st of the cycle),
the Emperor arrived back from Jìnyáng.
On the day *Rénwǔ* (19th of the cycle),
Ruì, the Director of the Department of State Affairs and Prince of Zhàojùn, was made Recorder of the Department of State Affairs (*Lù Shàngshū Shì*).
Lóu Ruì, the former Minister over the Masses, was made Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*).
On the day *Jiǎshēn* (21st of the cycle),
Duàn Sháo, the Grand Preceptor, was made Grand Tutor (*Tàishī*).
On the day *Dīnghài* (24th of the cycle),
Jiē, the Grand Commandant and Prince of Rènchéng, was made Grand General (*Dà Jiāngjūn*).
On the day *Rénchén* (29th of the cycle),
the Emperor traveled to Jìnyáng.
Sixth month, on the day *Gēngzǐ* (37th of the cycle),
heavy rain fell day and night without stopping,
and only ceased on the day *Jiǎchén* (41st of the cycle).
This month,
a rumor spread in Jìnyáng that there were ghost soldiers.
The populace competed to strike copper and iron objects to ward them off.
Bǎinián, the Prince of Lèlǐng, was executed.
Old Lady Yǔwén was returned to Zhōu.
Autumn, ninth month, on the day *Yǐchǒu* (2nd of the cycle),
Chāo, the imperial son, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nányáng.
Yǎn was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōngpíng.
This month,
Old Lady Yán was returned to Zhōu.
Envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
The Turkic forces raided Yōuzhōu,
entered the Great Wall,
plundered, and returned.
Intercalary month, on the day *Yǐwèi* (32nd of the cycle),
an edict dispatched twelve envoys to tour the prefectures suffering from flooding,
and exempted them from rents and levies.
On the day *Yǐsì* (42nd of the cycle),
The Turkic forces raided Yōuzhōu.
The Zhōu army advanced simultaneously along three routes,
sending their general Yùchí Jiǒng to raid Luòyáng,
Yáng Jí to enter Zhǐguān,
and Quán Jǐngxuān to hasten toward Xuánhù.
Winter, eleventh month, on the day *Jiǎwǔ* (31st of the cycle),
Jiǒng and his troops besieged Luòyáng.
On the day *Wùxū* (35th of the cycle),
an edict appointed Liú Tì, Acting Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, as envoy to Chén.
On the day *Jiǎchén* (41st of the cycle),
Lóu Ruì, the Grand Commandant, severely defeated the Zhōu army at Zhǐguān,
capturing Yáng Jí.
Twelfth month, on the day *Yǐmǎo* (52nd of the cycle),
Wáng Shìliáng, the Regional Inspector of Yùzhōu, surrendered the city to the Zhōu general Quán Jǐngxuān.
On the day *Dīngsì* (54th of the cycle),
the Emperor personally led a campaign south from Jìnyáng.
On the day *Jǐwèi* (56th of the cycle),
Yān, the Grand Tutor and Prince of Píngyáng, died.
On the day *Rénxū* (59th of the cycle),
Duàn Sháo, the Grand Tutor, severely defeated Yùchí Jiǒng and his forces,
lifting the siege of Luòyáng.
On the day *Dīngmǎo* (4th of the cycle),
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng.
The region of Luòzhōu that had been traversed by the Zhōu army was exempted from taxes and levies for one year,
and prisoners guilty of capital crimes and lesser offenses within the prefecture city were pardoned.
On the day *Jǐsì* (6th of the cycle),
Duàn Sháo, the Grand Tutor, was made Grand Tutor (*Tàizǎi*).
Húlǜ Guāng, the Minister over the Masses, was made Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*).
Chánggōng, the Regional Inspector of Bìngzhōu and Prince of Lánlíng, was made Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the day *Rénshēn* (9th of the cycle),
the Emperor arrived at Wǔláo,
passed through Huátái,
and halted at Líyáng.
In the places he passed through, sentences for criminals were reduced.
On the day *Bǐngzǐ* (13th of the cycle),
the Imperial carriage arrived back from Luòyáng.
This year,
Gāolì, Mòjié, and Xīnluó all sent envoys to court with tribute.
There were massive floods in Shāndōng.
The number of people who starved to death was countless.
An edict ordered the distribution of relief provisions,
but the measure was ultimately not carried out.
Year 4, spring, first month, on the day *Guǐmǎo* (40th of the cycle),
Jiē, the Grand General and Prince of Rènchéng, was made Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*).
On the day *Xīnwèi* (8th of the cycle),
The Emperor visited Jìnyáng.
Second month, on the day *Jiǎyín* (51st of the cycle),

an edict appointed Kim Jīnhīng, the King of Xīnluó, as Bearer of Credentials (*Shǐ Chíjíe*), Colonel Protector of the Eastern Barbarians (*Dōngyí Xiàowèi*), Duke of Lèlàng Commandery, and King of Xīnluó.
On the day *Rénshēn* (9th of the cycle),
as the year's harvest was poor,
the sale of alcohol was prohibited.
On the day *Jǐmǎo* (16th of the cycle),
an edict reduced the stipends and allowances of all officials by varying degrees.
In the third month, on the day Wùzǐ,
an edict was issued granting grain to the impoverished households in Xīyǎn, Liáng, Cāng, and Zhào Prefectures,
as well as the commanderies of Dōngjùn, Yángpíng, Qīnghé, and Wǔdū in Sī Prefecture,
and Chánglè and Bóhǎi in Jì Prefecture, which had suffered from floods and torrential rains.
The amounts varied.
However, the amount granted per household was only a dòu or a shěng,
and in many cases, it was not even delivered.
In this month,
a comet was seen;
an object fell onto the palace courtyard,
resembling a red lacquered drum with a small bell attached;
stones on the palace platform spontaneously rose up,
standing in pairs facing each other.
Furthermore, a deity was seen in a cave on the mountain in front of the Wànshòu Hall in the imperial garden.
Its physique was massive;
its face was indistinguishable,
but its two teeth were extremely white
and protruded long past its lips.
Seven hundred people, including the Emperor's personal attendants and concubines, saw it.
The Emperor also dreamed of it.
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day Wùwǔ,
Grand General, Prince of Dōng'ān, Lóu Ruì, was dismissed due to an incident.
On the day Yǐhài,
envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
The Grand Astrologer reported a celestial anomaly,
the omen of which indicated an imminent change of king.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Grand Tutor, Duàn Sháo, was therefore ordered to concurrently hold the position of Grand Commandant.
He held the staff of authority and presented the Emperor’s seals and ribbons, abdicating the throne to the Crown Prince.
A general amnesty was granted,
the reign title was changed to Tiāntǒng First Year,
and civil and military officials received advancements in rank or reductions in punishment, each varying accordingly.
An edict also proclaimed the Crown Prince's consort, Húlǜ Shì, as Empress.
Thereupon, the high officials offered the honorary title of Tài Shàng Huángdì (Retired Emperor),
and all major military and state affairs were still to be reported to him.
When the transfer of power was about to commence,
the internal Palace Attendant and Horseman Zishàng was sent by post-horse to deliver the imperial edict to Yè.
As Zishàng left Jìnyáng City,
he saw a rider following him,
who suddenly vanished.
Before he reached Yè, the news had already spread.
In Tiāntǒng Fourth Year, the twelfth month, on the day Xīnwèi,
the Retired Emperor died in the Qiánshòu Hall of the Yè Palace
at the age of thirty-two.
His posthumous title was Wǔchéng Huángdì,
and his temple name was Shìzǔ.
In the fifth year, the second month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
he was buried at Yǒngpíng Ling.
Imperial Annals 8: The Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) and the Young Ruler (Yòuzhǔ)
The given name of the Later Ruler was Wěi,
and his courtesy name was Rén'gāng.
He was the eldest son of Emperor Wǔchéng.
His mother was Empress Hú,
who dreamed that she was sitting on a jade basin upon the sea,
and the sun entered beneath her skirt.
She subsequently became pregnant.
On the fifth day of the fifth month of Tiānbǎo Seventh Year,
the Emperor was born at the residence in Bìng Prefecture.
The Emperor was handsome in appearance since he was young,
and Wǔchéng especially loved and favored him,
appointing him as the Heir Apparent.
When Wǔchéng assumed the great inheritance,
in Dàníng Second Year, the first month, on the day Bǐngxū,
he was established as the Crown Prince.
In Héqīng Fourth Year,
Wǔchéng abdicated the throne to the Emperor.
In Tiāntǒng First Year, the summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Emperor ascended the throne at the Jìnyáng Palace.
A general amnesty was granted,
and Héqīng Fourth Year was changed to Tiāntǒng.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Grand Protector Hèbá Rén was made Grand Tutor,
Grand Commandant Hóumòchén Xiàng was made Grand Protector,
Minister of Works, Prince Rùn of Féngxǔ, was made Minister of the Masses,
Director of Affairs of the Department of State, Prince Ruì of Zhàojùn, was made Minister of Works,
and Left Assistant Director of the Department of State, Prince Xiàowǎn of Héjiān, was made Director of the Department of State.
On the day Wùyín,
Wèi Càn, the Inspector of Yíng Prefecture, was made
Grand Commandant Húlǜ Guāng was made Grand General,
Prince Lóu Ruì of Dōng'ān was made Grand Commandant,
and Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Zhào Yànshēn was made Left Assistant Director.
In the sixth month, on the day Rénxū,
a comet appeared northeast of Wénchāng.
It was as large as a hand,
then gradually grew longer,
reaching over a zhàng (ten feet),
and disappeared after a hundred days.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict commissioning Wang Jìgāo, acting as Palace Gentleman for Attendant Counsel, as envoy to Chén.
In the autumn, the seventh month, on the day Yǐwèi,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict to increase the number of Administrators of Waterways by one.
In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day Kuǐwèi,
the Retired Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict changing
“Tàizǔ Xiànwǔ Huángdì”
to
“Shénwǔ Huángdì,”
and the temple name
“Gāozǔ.”
“Xiànmíng Empress”
was changed to
“Wǔmíng Empress.”
The
posthumous title
“Wénxuān” was entrusted to the relevant authorities for deliberation and determination.
In the twelfth month, on the day Gēngxū,
the Retired Emperor held a hunt in the Northern Suburbs.
On the day Rénzǐ,
he hunted in the Southern Suburbs.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
he hunted in the Western Suburbs.
On the day Rénxū,
the Retired Emperor proceeded to Jìnyáng.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
the authorities reported a motion to change
“Gāozǔ Wénxuān Huángdì”
to
“Wēizōng Jǐngliè Huángdì.”
In this year,
Gāolì, Qìdān, and Mòhé all sent envoys to offer tribute.
There was a great plague in Hénán.
In the second year, the year Bǐngxū, spring, the first month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
sacrifices were offered at the Round Mound.
On the day Guǐsì,
the joint sacrifice was offered at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and an edict was issued to reduce the sentences of convicted criminals, each varying accordingly.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Wèi Jǐn, Minister of the Civil Service, was made Right Assistant Director of the Department of State.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor journeyed to Jìnyáng.
In the second month, on the day Gēngxū,
the Retired Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Rénzǐ,
envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
In the third month, on the day Yǐsì,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict to move the Sān Tái (Three Terraces) structure to Xīngshèng Temple.
Due to the drought,
sentences for prisoners were reduced.
In the summer, the fourth month,
Emperor Wén of Chén died.
In the fifth month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
Pǔ, Prince of Wǔxīng and acting Left Assistant Director of the Department of State, was made Director of the Department of State.
On the day Jǐhài,
the Retired Emperor's sons Yǎn was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng,
Rénhóng as Prince of Qí'ān,
Rénjiān as Prince of Běipíng,
Rényīng as Prince of Gāopíng,
and Rénguāng as Prince of Huáinán.
In the sixth month,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict commissioning Wéi Dàorú, acting as Palace Gentleman for Attendant Counsel, as envoy to Chén.
In the autumn, the eighth month,
the Retired Emperor proceeded to Jìnyáng.
In the winter, the tenth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Grand Protector Hóumòchén Xiàng was made Grand Mentor,
Grand Marshal, Prince Jiē of Rènchéng, was made Grand Protector,
Grand Commandant Lóu Ruì was made Grand Marshal,
Prince Rùn of Féngyì was transferred and made Grand Commandant,
and Hán Zǔniàn, who held the rank of Starter of the Mansion with the Same Rights as the Three Dukes, was made Minister of the Masses.
In the eleventh month,
there was heavy snowfall.
Imperial robes were stolen from the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
In the twelfth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
envoys from Chén came to offer tribute.
In this year,
Prince Xiàowǎn of Héjiān was executed.
The states of Tūjué and Mòhé both sent envoys to offer tribute.
This was the first year of Tiānhé in Zhōu.
In the third year, spring, the first month, on the day Rénchén,
the Retired Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Yǐwèi,
there was a heavy snowfall,
reaching two feet on level ground.
On the day Wùxū,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict that officials serving in the capital and officials without specific duties holding Grade Three rank and above should each recommend three persons;
those holding Grade Five rank and above should each recommend two persons;

those designated for service holding Grade Seven rank and above, along with Palace Attendant Censors, Department of State All-Circuit Inspectors, Verification Censors, Chief Clerks, and Recorders of the Secretariat, should each recommend one person.
Fire broke out at the Jiǔlóng Hall of the Yè Palace,
spreading to and burning the West Corridor.
In the second month, on the first day Rén'yín,
the Emperor underwent the capping ceremony,
a general amnesty was granted,
all functionaries in the nine provinces were advanced four ranks,
and all internal and external officials were generally advanced two ranks.
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict commissioning Sīmǎ Yòuzhī, acting as Palace Gentleman for Attendant Counsel, as envoy to Chén.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict making Yǎn, Grand General of the Palace Guard and Prince of Dōngpíng, Director of the Department of State.
On the day Yǐwèi,
there was a great wind that darkened the sky during the day,
unroofing houses and uprooting trees.
In the sixth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded that Imperial Prince Rénjī be enfeoffed as the King of Xīhé;
Rén Yuē as the King of Lèlàng;
Rén Jiǎn as the King of Yǐngchuān;
Rén Yǎ as the King of Ānlè;
Rén Tǒng as the King of Dānyáng;
Rén Qiān as the King of Dōnghǎi.
In the intercalary sixth month, on the day Xīnsì,
the Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng), Húlǜ Jīn, passed away.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded that Yǎn, the Shàngshū Lìng and King of Dōngpíng, manage the affairs of the Shàngshū (Lù Shàngshū Shì);
Zhào Yànshēn, the Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng;
Lóu Dìngyuǎn, the Bǐngshěng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè;
Xú Zhīcái, the Zhōngshū Jiān, was appointed Yòu Púshè.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day Xīnwèi,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded that Jiē, the Tài Bǎo and King of Rènchéng, be appointed Tài Shī;
Rùn, the Tài Wèi and King of Féngyì, be appointed Dà Sīmǎ;
Duàn Sháo, the Tài Zǎi, be appointed Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng);
Hèbá Rén, the Tài Shī, be appointed Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng);
Hóumòchén Xiàng, the Tài Fù, be appointed Tài Zǎi;
Lóu Ruì, the Dà Sīmǎ, be appointed Tài Fù;
Húlǜ Guāng, the Dà Jiāngjūn, be appointed Tài Bǎo;
Hán Zǔniàn, the Sī Tú, be appointed Dà Jiāngjūn;
Ruì, the Sī Kōng and King of Zhàojùn, be appointed Tài Wèi;
Yǎn, the Shàngshū Lìng and King of Dōngpíng, be appointed Sī Tú.
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded:
"Regarding the miscellaneous protection households (zá bǎohù) surnamed Gāo who are attached to various temples and offices,
although preferential decrees were issued at the start of Tiānbǎo [era],
there are still those temporarily conscripted for labor who have not yet been exempted.
Now, all these miscellaneous households (záhù) may be exempted,
allowing them to be administered by the associated commanderies and counties,
treated uniformly as commoners."
On the day Dīngsì,
the Tàishàng Huángdì visited Jìnyáng.
This autumn,
there was a great flood east of the mountains (Shāndōng);
people starved,
and corpses filled the roads.
In winter, the tenth month,
the states of Tūjué, Dà Mòlóu, Shìwéi, Bǎijì, Mòhé, and others each sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the eleventh month, on the day Bǐngwǔ,
because the Dàmíng Hall in Jìnyáng was completed,
a general amnesty was declared.
All civil and military officials were promoted two ranks,
and the residents within the walls of Bīngzhōu and the entire commandery of Tàiyuán were exempted from rent and taxes for the coming year.
On the day Guǐwèi,
the Tàishàng Huángdì arrived back from Jìnyáng.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐsì,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded that the late Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng), Chēn, King of Zhàojùn, be enshrined in the Shénwǔ Temple courtyard.
In the first month of the fourth year,
a command was issued that Yuè, the late King of Qīnghé, Pān Xiānglè, the King of Hédōng, and ten others all be enshrined in the Shénwǔ Temple courtyard.
On the day Guǐhài,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded Zhèng Dàhù, acting as Sànqí Chángshì, to be an envoy to Chén.
In the third month, on the day Yǐsì,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded that Yǎn, the Sī Tú and King of Dōngpíng, be appointed Dà Jiāngjūn;
Chuò, the King of Nányáng, be appointed Sī Tú;
Xú Xiǎnxiù, the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, be appointed Sī Kōng;
Xiàohéng, the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and King of Guǎngníng, be appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Xīnwèi,
the Zhāoyáng Hall in the Yè Palace caught fire,
as did the Xuānguāng and Yáohuá Halls.
On the day Xīnsì,
the Tàishàng Huángdì visited Jìnyáng.
In the fifth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Hú Chángrén, the Shàngshū Yòu Púshè, was appointed Zuǒ Púshè;
Hé Shìkāi, the Zhōngshū Jiān, was appointed Yòu Púshè.
On the day Rénxū,
the Tàishàng Huángdì arrived back from Jìnyáng.
It had not rained since the first month until this month.
In the sixth month, on the first day Jiǎzǐ,
there was heavy rain.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
there was a great wind,
uprooting trees and snapping branches.
In this month,
a comet was seen in Dōngjǐng (Eastern Well mansion).
In autumn, the ninth month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
the Zhōu people came to establish peace.
The Tàishàng Huángdì commanded Hú Sīwénlüè, the Shìzhōng, to return the mission to Zhōu.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Xīnsì,
Xiàohéng, the Shàngshū Lìng and King of Guǎngníng, was appointed Manager of the Shàngshū (Lù Shàngshū);
Hú Chángrén, the Zuǒ Púshè, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng;
Hé Shìkāi, the Yòu Púshè, was appointed Zuǒ Púshè;
Táng Yōng, the Zhōngshū Jiān, was appointed Yòu Púshè.
In the eleventh month, on the day Rénchén,
the Tàishàng Huángdì commanded Lǐ Zhù, acting as Sànqí Chángshì, to be an envoy to Chén.
In this month,
Xū, the King of Ānchéng of Chén, deposed his lord, Bózōng, and established himself [as Emperor].
In the twelfth month, on the day Xīnwèi,
the Tàishàng Huángdì passed away (bēng).
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
a general amnesty was declared.
Officials across the Nine Provinces were universally promoted four ranks,
and all civil and military officials, internal and external, were promoted two ranks.
On the day Wùyín,
the esteemed title Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager) was conferred upon the Tàishàng Huánghòu (Empress of the Retired Emperor).
On the day Jiǎshēn,
a command was issued to halt all minor construction projects (xì zuò) and dismiss all various artisans (bǎi gōng) in their respective locations.

Furthermore, a command was issued that regarding the palace women in Yètíng, Jìnyáng, and Zhōngshān, and the official workers (guān kǒu) of the Imperial Kitchens (Tàiguān) in Yè and Bīngzhōu (two locations),
those aged sixty and above or suffering from chronic illness
should be reviewed and released by the responsible authorities.
On the day Gēngyín,
a command was issued that all families who had been implicated and exiled since the seventh year of Tiānbǎo [era]
be ordered to return to their homes.
In this year, the states of Qìdān and Mòhé both sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the fifth year, spring, the first month, on the day Xīnhài,
a command was issued that the three terraces (tái), including Jīnfèng, which had not yet been converted into temples, be donated to the Xīngshèng Temple (Dà Xīngshèng Sì).
In this month,
Jì, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dìngzhōu and King of Bólíng, was executed.
In the second month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
a command was issued that all those subject to castration (gōng xíng) be universally exempted from the punishment and designated as official workers (guān kǒu).
Another command prohibited netting and catching falcons and hawks, and the keeping and caging of birds and animals.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
the state of Dà Mòlóu sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Yǎn, the King of Dōngpíng, was renamed King of Lángyá.
A command was issued for Chìliè Chángchā, the Shìzhōng, to be an envoy to Zhōu.
In this month,
Ruì, the Tài Wèi and King of Zhàojùn, was executed.
In the third month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Xú Xiǎnxiù, the Sī Kōng, was appointed Tài Wèi.
Lóu Dìngyuǎn, the Bǐngshěng Shàngshū Lìng, was appointed Sī Kōng.
In this month,
the Emperor proceeded to Jìnyáng.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
a command was issued that the Bīngzhōu Shàngshū Province be converted into the Dà Jīshèng Temple,
and the Jìn Ancestral Shrine (Jìn Cí) be converted into the Dà Chónghuáng Temple.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
the Imperial carriage arrived back from Jìnyáng.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
a command was issued to reduce the sentences of criminals, each case according to degree.
On the day Wùshēn,
a command was issued to send envoys to inspect the regions in Héběi that had received no rain.
Those areas within the borders suffering from localized drought were granted preferential exemption from rent and tax levies.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Rénxū,
a command was issued prohibiting the production of alcohol.
In the eleventh month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
a command was issued that Húlǜ Guāng, the Tài Bǎo, be appointed Tài Fù.
Rùn, the Dà Sīmǎ and King of Féngyì, be appointed Tài Bǎo.
Yǎn, the Dà Jiāngjūn and King of Lángyá, be appointed Dà Sīmǎ.
In the twelfth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
Chánggōng, the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and King of Lánlíng, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
On the day Gēngchén,
Wèi Shōu, the Zhōngshū Jiān, was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púshè.
In the first year of Wǔpíng, spring, the first month, on the first day Yǐyǒu,
the era name was changed.
Lóu Ruì, the Tài Shī, Governor of Bīngzhōu, and King of Dōng'ān, passed away.
On the day Wùshēn,
a command was issued for Péi Xiànzhī, acting as Sànqí Chángshì, to conduct the marriage formalities with Chén.
In the second month, on the day Guǐhài,
Yú Chāng, the King of Bǎijì, was appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjí), Shìzhōng, General-in-Chief of Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn), and Duke of Dàifāng Commandery.
His title as King remained as before.
On the day Jǐsì,
Húlǜ Guāng, the Tài Fù and King of Xiányáng, was appointed Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng).
Hèbá Rén, the Governor of Bīngzhōu, Right Chancellor, and King of Āndìng, was appointed Manager of Affairs of the Shàngshū (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
Jiē, the Governor of Jìzhōu and King of Rènchéng, was appointed Tài Shī.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
sentences for prisoners condemned to death and below were reduced.
In the intercalary month, on the day Wùxū,
Hèbá Rén, the Manager of Affairs of the Shàngshū and King of Āndìng, passed away.
In the third month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Xú Zhīcái, the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè.
In summer, the sixth month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
Xiàohéng, the King of Guǎngníng, was appointed Sī Kōng.
On the day Jiǎchén,
because an Imperial Prince was born,
a general amnesty was declared.
All internal and external civil and military officials were universally promoted two ranks,
and officials across the Nine Provinces were universally promoted four ranks.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
a command was issued that Táng Yōng, the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, be appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púshè.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
Yànjī, son of Emperor Xiàozhāo, was enfeoffed as the King of Chéngyáng;
Yànkāng as the King of Dìnglíng;
Yànzhōng as the King of Liángjùn.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Chánggōng, the Shàngshū Lìng and King of Lánlíng, was appointed Manager of Affairs of the Shàngshū (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
Hé Shìkāi, the Zhōng Lǐngjūn, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
On the day Guǐhài,
the state of Mòhé sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Níng, the King of Huàshān, was appointed Tài Fù.
In the eighth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor proceeded to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the day Yǐsì,
the Imperial Prince was established as the Heir Apparent (Huáng Tàizǐ).
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Xīnsì,
Xiàohéng, the Sī Kōng and King of Guǎngníng, was appointed Sī Tú.
Sīzōng, the King of Shàngluò, was appointed Sī Kōng.
Xiāo Zhuāng was enfeoffed as the King of Liáng.
On the day Wùzǐ,
sentences for prisoners in Bīngzhōu condemned to death and below were partially reduced.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the posthumous title of Emperor Wēizōng Jǐngliè was restored and changed to
"Emperor Xiǎnzǔ Wénxuān."
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìn Yáng.
An imperial edict ordered Right Chancellor Hú Lǜ Guāng to proceed along the Jìn Zhōu road
to repair the city defenses.
In the second year, spring, first month, on the day Dīngsì,
an edict ordered Concurrent Mounted Regular Attendant Liú Huán Jùn to serve as an envoy to Chén.
On the day Wùyín,
Yú Chāng, the King of Bǎijì, was appointed as Authorized with Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief, and Governor of Dōngqīng Zhōu.
Second month, on the day Rényín,
Cháng Gōng, the Prince of Lánlíng, holding the post of Director of the Affairs of the Department of State, was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi);
Zhào Yàn Shēn, who concurrently held the post of Director of the Affairs of the Department of State, was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng);
Hé Shì Kāi, Prefect of the Department of State, was appointed Director of the Affairs of the Department of State;
Xú Zhī Cái, Left Assistant Director of the Department of State, was appointed Prefect of the Department of State;
Táng Yōng, Right Assistant Director of the Department of State, was appointed Left Assistant Director of the Department of State;
Féng Zǐ Cóng, Minister of Personnel, was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Department of State.
Summer, fourth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Yǎn, the Prince of Lángyá, holding the post of Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ), was appointed Grand Guardian (Tài Bǎo).
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Chén dispatched an envoy to propose an alliance
and plan an attack on Zhōu,
but the court conference did not approve.
Sixth month,
Duàn Sháo attacked Zhōu's Fén Zhōu,
conquered it,
and captured Governor Yáng Fū.
Autumn, seventh month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
Yǎn, the Prince of Lángyá and Grand Guardian, falsely issued an edict and executed Hé Shì Kāi, Director of the Affairs of the Department of State, in the Southern Terrace (Nántái).
On the same day, Grand General of the Palace Guard Kù Dí Fú Lián and Palace Aide to the Censorate Wáng Zǐ Xuān, among others, were executed;
Féng Zǐ Cóng, Right Assistant Director of the Department of State, was granted death inside the palace.
Eighth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the imperial procession journeyed to Jìn Yáng.
Ninth month, on the day Xīnhài,
Jiē, the Prince of Rènchéng and Grand Tutor (Tài Shī), was appointed Grand Minister (Tài Zǎi);
Rùn, the Prince of Féngyì, was appointed Grand Tutor.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Duàn Sháo, the Prince of Píngyuán and Left Chancellor, died.
On the day Wùwǔ,
a partial commutation of capital crimes and lesser offenses was granted within the borders of Bìng Zhōu, varying according to severity.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Yǎn, the Prince of Lángyá and Grand Guardian, was executed.
On the day Rénshēn,
envoys from Chén arrived to offer congratulations.
Winter, tenth month,
the Jīng Jī Fǔ was abolished and incorporated into the Lǐng Jūn Fǔ.
On the day Jǐhài,
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìn Yáng.
Eleventh month, on the day Gēngxū,
an edict ordered Attendant-in-Ordinary Hè Lián Zǐ Yuè to serve as an envoy to Zhōu.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Xiào Héng, the Prince of Guǎngníng and Director of Xú Zhōu Regional Affairs, was appointed Director of the Affairs of the Department of State.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Xiào Héng, the Prince of Guǎngníng and Director of the Affairs of the Department of State, was appointed Minister of Instruction (Sītú).
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Hú Lǜ Guāng, the Right Chancellor, was appointed Left Chancellor.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the day Jǐsì,
sacrifices were offered in the Southern Suburbs.
On the day Xīnhài,
the deceased Yǎn, Prince of Lángyá, was posthumously granted the title Emperor of Chǔ.
Second month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
Wèi Pú Sà was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
On the day Xīnsì,
Gāo Yuán Hǎi, who concurrently held the post of Minister of Personnel, was appointed Right Assistant Director of the Department of State.
On the day Gēngyín,
Táng Yōng, Left Assistant Director, was appointed Prefect of the Department of State;
Zǔ Tǐng, Attendant-in-Ordinary, was appointed Left Assistant Director.
In this month,
an imperial order commanded the compilation of the *Xuán Zhōu Yuàn Yù Lǎn*,
which was later renamed the *Shèng Shòu Táng Yù Lǎn*.
Third month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
an imperial edict ordered all civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above to nominate one person each.
In this month,
Zhōu executed the Chief Minister, Yǔwén Hù.
Summer, fourth month,
envoys from Zhōu arrived to offer congratulations.
Autumn, seventh month, on the day Wùchén,
Hú Lǜ Guāng, the Left Chancellor and Prince of Xiányáng, was executed, along with his younger brother Fēng Lè, the Duke of Jīngshān and Director of Yōu Zhōu Regional Affairs.
Eighth month, on the day Gēngyín,
Empress Hú Lǜ Shì was deposed and reduced to commoner status.
Jiē, the Prince of Rènchéng and Grand Minister, was appointed Right Chancellor;
Rùn, the Prince of Féngyì and Grand Tutor, was appointed Grand Commandant;
Cháng Gōng, the Prince of Lánlíng, was appointed Grand Marshal;
Xiào Héng, the Prince of Guǎngníng, was appointed Grand General;
Yán Zōng, the Prince of Āndé, was appointed Minister of Instruction.
Fēng Fǔ Xiàng, Director of the Palace Guard, was sent as an envoy to Zhōu.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Consort Hú Shì (Right Zhāoyí) was appointed Empress.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Rén Jiān, the Prince of Běipíng and Prefect of Sī Zhōu, was appointed Prefect of the Department of State;
Xǔ Jì Liáng, Special Advanced Official, was appointed Left Assistant Director;
Bǎo Dé, the Prince of Péngchéng, was appointed Right Assistant Director.
On the day Guǐsì,
the imperial procession journeyed to Jìn Yáng.
In this month,
the *Shèng Shòu Táng Yù Lǎn* was completed;
an imperial order commanded it be deposited in the Archives Hall,
and it was later renamed the *Xiū Wén Diàn Yù Lǎn*.
Ninth month,
envoys from Chén arrived to offer congratulations.
Winter, tenth month,
those imprisoned for capital crimes and lesser offenses were reduced in penalty.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Consort Mù Shì (Hóngdé Fūrén) was appointed Left Empress,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Twelfth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
Empress Hú Shì was deposed and reduced to commoner status.
In this year,
Xīnluó, Bǎijì, Wùjí, and Tújué all dispatched envoys to pay tribute.
In Zhōu, this was the first year of Jiàndé.
In the fourth year, spring, first month, on the day Wùyín,
Gāo Ā Nà Gōng, who concurrently held the post of Prefect of the Department of State, was appointed Director of the Affairs of the Department of State.
On the day Gēngchén,
an edict ordered Concurrent Mounted Regular Attendant Cuī Xiàng to serve as an envoy to Chén.
In this month,
fox spirits appeared in Yè Dū and Bìng Zhōu,
frequently cutting people’s hair.
Second month, on the day Yǐsì,
Mù Shì, the Left Empress, was appointed Empress.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Wén Lín Guǎn was established.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Rén Jiān, the Prince of Běipíng and Prefect of the Department of State, was appointed Director of the Affairs of the Department of State.
On the day Dīngsì,
the imperial procession journeyed to Jìn Yáng.
In this month,
envoys from Zhōu arrived to offer congratulations.
Third month, on the day Xīnwèi,
bandits entered Xìn Zhōu
and killed Governor Hé Shì Xiū.
Xiān Yú Shì Róng, Governor of Nányǎn Zhōu, suppressed and pacified them.
On the day Gēngchén,
the imperial carriage arrived at Jìn Yáng.
Summer, fourth month, on the day Wùwǔ,
Cháng Gōng, the Prince of Lánlíng and Grand Marshal, was appointed Grand Guardian;
Chuò, the Prince of Nányáng, Grand General, and Governor of Dìng Zhōu, was appointed Grand Marshal;
Wèi Pú Sà, Grand Commandant, was appointed Grand General;
Yán Zōng, the Prince of Āndé and Minister of Instruction, was appointed Grand Commandant;
Pǔ, the Prince of Wǔxīng and Minister of Works, was appointed Minister of Instruction;
Zhào Yàn Shēn, the Prince of Yíyáng and Official with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes, was appointed Minister of Works.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
within the boundary fences of the altar for the Imperial Ancestor sacrifices, wheel tracks suddenly appeared;
upon investigation, there were no human footprints nearby,
and the origin of the carriage was unknown.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
an imperial edict proclaimed this a great felicitation
and announced it to the realm.
On the day Jǐwèi,
envoys from Zhōu arrived to offer congratulations.
Fifth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
an edict ordered the historical officials to recompile the *Wèi Shū*.
On the day Guǐsì,
Mù Tí Pó, Director of the Palace Guard, was appointed Left Assistant Director of the Department of State;
Duàn Xiào Yán, Attendant-in-Ordinary and Prefect of the Central Secretariat, was appointed Right Assistant Director.
In this month,
Wèi Pò Hú, Cháng Sūn Hóng Lüè, and others, Officials with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes, fought against the Chén general Wú Míng Chè south of Lǚ Liáng;
they suffered a great defeat;
Pò Hú escaped by fleeing,
but Hóng Lüè perished in battle,
and consequently Qín and Jīng Zhōu were captured.
Míng Chè advanced and captured Hé and Gé Zhōu.
In this month,
Cháng Gōng, the Prince of Lánlíng and Grand Guardian, was executed.
Sixth month,
Míng Chè advanced his forces and besieged Shòuyáng.
On the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor toured the Southern Park;
sixty accompanying officials died of sunstroke.
Gāo Ā Nà Gōng, Director of the Affairs of the Department of State, was appointed Minister of Instruction.
On the day Bǐngchén,
an edict ordered Wáng Shī Luó, Official with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes, to serve as an envoy to Zhōu.
Ninth month,
a hunting expedition was held east of Yè.
Winter, tenth month,
the Chén general Wú Míng Chè captured Shòuyáng.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Attendants-in-Ordinary Cuī Jì Shū and Zhāng Diāo Hǔ were executed,
along with Mounted Regular Attendants Liú Tì and Fēng Xiào Yǎn,
and Palace Gate Gentlemen Péi Zé and Guō Zūn.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the imperial procession journeyed to Jìn Yáng.
Twelfth month, on the day Wùyín,
Gāo Ā Nà Gōng, Minister of Instruction, was appointed Right Chancellor.
In this year,
Gāolì and Mòhé both dispatched envoys to pay tribute;
an envoy from Tújué arrived to request a marriage alliance.
In the fifth year, spring, first month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
one Left É Yīng and one Right É Yīng were established.
Second month, on the day Yǐwèi,
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìn Yáng.
Sī Hǎo, the Prince of Nán'ān and Director of Shuò Zhōu Regional Affairs, rebelled.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
the imperial procession journeyed to Jìn Yáng.
Táng Yōng, Prefect of the Department of State, and others utterly defeated Sī Hǎo;
Sī Hǎo drowned himself,
and his corpse was burned,
along with his wife, Lady Lǐ.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìn Yáng.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Táng Yōng, Prefect of the Department of State, was appointed Director of the Affairs of the Department of State.
In summer, the fifth month,
there was a great drought.
In Jìnyáng, a dead *bá* (drought demon) was obtained,
two *chǐ* long,
having two eyes on its face and two on the crown of its head.
The Emperor heard of this,
and commanded a wooden likeness of its form to be carved and presented.
On *Gēngwǔ* day,
there was a general amnesty.
On *Dīnghài* day,
the Chén people raided Huáiběi.
In autumn, the eighth month, on *Guǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor toured Jìnyáng.
On *Jiǎchén* day,
Gāo Mài was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púshè.
In this year,
Zhuō, Prince of Nányáng, was executed.
In the sixth year, spring, the third month, on *Yǐhài* day,
the Imperial carriage arrived from Jìnyáng.
On *Dīngchǒu* day,
the wicked bandit Zhèng Zǐráo was boiled in the marketplace.
In this month,
people from Zhōu came to pay a formal visit.
In summer, the fourth month, on *Gēngzǐ* day,
Yáng Xiūzhī, the Zhōngshū Jiān, was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púshè.
On *Guǐmǎo* day,
the Mòhé sent envoys to pay tribute.
In autumn, the seventh month, on *Jiǎxū* day,
the Emperor toured Jìnyáng.
In the eighth month, on *Dīngyǒu* day,
the six provinces of Jì, Dìng, Zhào, Yōu, Cāng, and Yíng suffered massive flooding.
In this month,
the Zhōu army entered Luòchuān,
stationed troops at Mángshān,
attacked and pressed the city of Luòchéng,
launched fire boats to burn the pontoon bridge,
and the River Bridge was destroyed.
In the intercalary month, on *Jǐchǒu* day,
Right Chancellor Gāo Ānàgōng was dispatched from Jìnyáng to defend against them.
When his forces reached Héyáng,
the Zhōu army fled during the night.
On *Gēngchén* day,
Zhào Yànshēn, the Sīkōng, was made Sītú,
and Húlǜ Ālièluó was made Sīkōng.
On *Xīnsì* day,
because military and state funds were insufficient,
taxes were levied on customs and markets, boats and carriages, mountains and marshes, salt and iron, and shops;
the severity of the tax varied,
and the prohibition on alcohol was lifted.
In the seventh year, spring, the first month, on *Rénchén*
day, an edict commanded that, for those suffering from floods and famine
since the previous autumn who could not sustain themselves,
they should be handed over to major monasteries and various wealthy households in their localities to save their lives.
On *Jiǎyín* day,
there was a general amnesty.
On *Yǐmǎo* day,
the Imperial carriage arrived from Jìnyáng.
In the second month, on *Xīnyǒu* day,
unmarried women from miscellaneous households aged under twenty but above fourteen were all registered and gathered for inspection.
Household heads who concealed them were sentenced to death.
In the second month, on *Bǐngyín* day,
a wind arose from the northwest,
destroying houses and uprooting trees.
It ceased only after five days.
In summer, the sixth month, on *Wùshēn*, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On *Gēngshēn* day,
Sītú Zhào Yànshēn died.
In autumn, the seventh month, on *Dīngchǒu* day,
there was heavy and prolonged rain.
In this month,
due to the flooding, envoys were dispatched to tour and comfort the migrating households.
In the eighth month, on *Dīngmǎo* day,
the Emperor toured Jìnyáng.
Pheasants gathered near the imperial seat;
they were captured,
but the officials concerned dared not report it.
An edict ordered the construction of the Hándān Palace.
In winter, the tenth month, on *Bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor held a great hunt at Qílián Chí.
The Zhōu army attacked Jìnzhōu.
On *Guǐhài* day,
the Emperor returned to Jìnyáng.
On *Jiǎzǐ* day,
troops were mobilized,
gathering massively at Jìncí.
On *Gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor departed Jìnyáng.
On *Guǐyǒu* day,
the Emperor marched in battle formation
and ascended Jīqī Yuán,
where he faced Xiàn, Prince of Qí of Zhōu.
There was no fighting until night,
when the Zhōu army gathered its ranks and retreated.
In the eleventh month,
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu retreated back to Cháng'ān,
leaving a detached force to guard Jìnzhōu.
Gāo Ānàgōng and others besieged the city of Jìnzhōu.
On *Wùyín* day,
the Emperor arrived at the siege site.
In the twelfth month, on *Wùshēn* day,
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu came to relieve Jìnzhōu.
On *Gēngxū* day,
a battle was fought south of the city,
and our army suffered a great defeat.
The Emperor abandoned his army and returned first.
On *Guǐchǒu* day,
he entered Jìnyáng,
anxious and fearful, not knowing where to go.
On *Jiǎyín* day,
there was a general amnesty.
The Emperor said to his court officials:
“The Zhōu army is very strong,
what is to be done?”
All the officials replied:
“Heaven’s Mandate has not yet changed;
one moment of gain and one of loss
has always been so since ancient times.
We should halt all taxes,
reassure the court and the populace,
rally the remaining troops,
fight to the death with our backs to the city,
in order to preserve the state.”
The Emperor hesitated,
wishing to head toward Běishuòzhōu.
He then left Yánzōng, Prince of Āndé, and Xiàohéng, Prince of Guǎngníng, and others to guard Jìnyáng.
If Jìnyáng could not be held,
he intended to flee to the Tūjué.
All the officials said this was unacceptable,
but the Emperor did not heed their words.
Hèbá Fú'ēn (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), Fēng Fǔxiāng, Mùróng Zhōngkuí, and over thirty other close attendants of the palace guard fled west to the Zhōu army.
On *Yǐmǎo* day,
an edict ordered the mobilization of troops,
appointing Yánzōng, Prince of Āndé, as the Left Commander,
and Xiàohéng, Prince of Guǎngníng, as the Right Commander.
Yánzōng entered for an audience,
and the Emperor informed him of his intention to go to Běishuòzhōu.
Yánzōng tearfully remonstrated,
but the Emperor did not comply.
The Emperor secretly dispatched Wáng Kāngdé, along with the attendant Qí Shào and others, to escort the Empress Dowager and the Crown Prince to Běishuòzhōu.
On *Bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor visited the troops south of the city
and comforted the officers and soldiers.
That night he wished to flee,
but the generals refused to follow.
On *Dīngsì* day,
there was a general amnesty,
and the seventh year of Wǔpíng was changed to the first year of Lónghuà.
On that day,
Mù Típó surrendered to Zhōu.
An edict appointed Yánzōng, Prince of Āndé, as Xiàngguó,
entrusting him with defense.
Yánzōng wept as he received the order.
The Emperor then chopped down the Wǔlóng Mén (gate) at night and left,
intending to flee to the Tūjué.
Many of his accompanying officials dispersed.
The Lǐngjūn, Méi Shèngláng, stopped his horse to remonstrate,
whereupon he turned back toward Yè.
At that time, only Gāo Ānàgōng and a little over ten horsemen remained.
Xiàohéng, Prince of Guǎngníng, and Yàndào, Prince of Xiāngchéng, arrived subsequently,
enabling several dozen people to travel together.
On *Wùwǔ* day,
Yánzōng followed the public decision and immediately ascended the throne as Emperor in Jìnyáng,
changing Lónghuà to the first year of Déchāng.
On *Gēngshēn*,
the Emperor entered Yè.
On *Xīnyǒu*,
Yánzōng fought the Zhōu army at Jìnyáng,
suffered a great defeat,
and was captured by the Zhōu army.
The Emperor sent people to recruit soldiers,
heavily increasing official ranks and rewards,
but though these words were spoken,
no material goods were actually distributed.
Gǔangníng Wáng Xiàohéng submitted a memorial requesting the release of palace women and treasures to be distributed among the generals and soldiers,
but the Emperor was displeased.
Húlǜ Xiàoqīng resided in the palace center and was entrusted with duties;
wearing armor, he administered the affairs.
He requested the Emperor personally address and comfort the troops,
and he drafted a speech for the Emperor,
adding that he should be emotional and shed tears
to inspire gratitude in people's hearts.
When the Emperor came out before the masses
and was about to speak,
he forgot the words he had been taught.
He then burst into loud laughter,
and his attendants also guffawed together.
The generals and soldiers were completely demoralized.

Thereupon, officials from Great Chancellor (*Dà Chéngxiàng*) down to Grand Tutor (*Tàizǎi*), the Three Masters (*Sān Shī*), Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*), Grand General (*Dà Jiāngjūn*), and the Three Dukes (*Sān Gōng*) were all granted to increasing numbers of appointees,
sometimes three or four people receiving the same post,
making the number uncountable.
On *Jiǎzǐ*,
the Empress Dowager arrived from the northern route.
The civil and military officials of the first rank and above were admitted into the Zhūhuá Gate,
given wine and food,
provided with paper and brushes,
and asked for strategies to defend against Zhōu.
The officials offered various differing opinions,
and the Emperor did not know which to follow.
He also summoned Gāo Yuánhǎi, Sòng Shìsù, Lú Sīdào, Lǐ Délín, and others,
intending to discuss abdicating the throne to the Crown Prince.
Previously, observers of astronomical portents had said
that a change was imminent.
Consequently, following the precedent of the Tiāntǒng era,
the position was bestowed upon the Young Lord.
The Young Lord's name was
and he was the Emperor's eldest son.
His mother was Empress Mù,
and he was born in Yè in the sixth month of the first year of Wǔpíng (570 CE).
In the tenth month of that year,
he was established as the Crown Prince.
In the spring, the first month, on *Yǐhài* of the second year of Lónghuà (573 CE),
he ascended the imperial throne,
at the age of eight.
The era name was changed to Chéngguāng first year.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
The Empress Dowager was honored as the Grand Empress Dowager (*Tài Huáng Tàihòu*),
the Emperor was honored as the Retired Emperor (*Tài Shàng Huángdì*),
and the Empress was honored as the Retired Empress (*Tài Shàng Huánghòu*).
Thereupon, Yellow Gate Attendant Yán Zhītuī, Palace Attendant Lǐ Délín, and Chamberlain Chén Déxìn urged the Retired Emperor to travel outside the Hé region to recruit soldiers
and formulate new strategies.
If that failed,
he should defect south to the Chén state.
He agreed to this.
On *Dīngchǒu*,
the Grand Empress Dowager and the Retired Empress first proceeded from Yè toward Jìzhōu.
The Zhōu army gradually approached.
On *Guǐwèi*,
the Young Lord also fled east from Yè.
On *Jǐchǒu*,
the Zhōu army reached Zǐmò Bridge.
On *Guǐsì*,
they burned the western gate of the city.
The Retired Emperor, with over a hundred riders, fled eastward.
On *Yǐhài*,
he crossed the river and entered Jìzhōu.
On that same day,
the Young Lord abdicated the throne to the Great Chancellor, Rénchéng Wáng Jiē.
He ordered the Chamberlain Húlǜ Xiàoqīng to send the abdication documents and the imperial seals and ribbons to Yíngzhōu.
Xiàoqīng, however, took them and defected to Zhōu.
A decree was also issued in the name of Rénchéng Wáng,
honoring the Retired Emperor as the Supreme Retired Emperor (*Wú Shàng Huáng*),
and the Young Lord as the Heavenly King, Defender of the State (*Shǒuguó Tiānwáng*).
The Grand Empress Dowager was left behind in Jìzhōu,
and Gāo Ānàgōng was sent to stay there as the guardian.
The Supreme Retired Emperor, along with the Empress, took the Young Lord and fled to Qīngzhōu.
Hán Chángluán, Dèng Yǒng, and several tens of others followed him.
Once the Supreme Retired Emperor arrived at Qīngzhōu,
he immediately planned to enter Chén.
But Gāo Ānàgōng summoned the Zhōu army,
promising to deliver the Qí ruler alive,
and repeatedly sent messengers reporting
that the enemy forces were far away
and that he had ordered the bridges and roads to be burned and cut off.
This is why the Supreme Retired Emperor delayed.
The Zhōu army suddenly arrived at Qīngzhōu.
The Supreme Retired Emperor was distressed and anxious,
intending to surrender to Chén.
He placed a bag of gold behind his saddle,
and with Chángluán, Consort Shūfēi, and about ten other riders, he reached Dèngcūn, south of Qīngzhōu,
where he was captured by the Zhōu general Yùchí Gāng.
He was sent to Yè,
and Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu treated him with the courtesy accorded to a guest-ruler.
He, along with the Empress Dowager, the Young Lord, and all the princes, were sent to Cháng'ān.
The Emperor was enfeoffed as the Duke of Wēn State (*Wēn Guó Gōng*).
In the seventh year of Jiàndé (578 CE),
he was falsely accused of conspiring rebellion with Mù Típó, the Inspector of Yízhōu,
and he and Yánzōng, along with several tens of others, regardless of age, were all granted death.
Only one or two descendants of Shénwǔ survived.
Towards the end of Dàxiàng (581 CE),
Yáng Xiūzhī and Chén Déxìn petitioned the Great Chancellor, the Duke of Suí,
requesting permission to collect and bury the remains.
It was granted.
He was buried in Hóngdúchuān on the North Plain of Cháng'ān.
When the Emperor was young, he was intelligent and benevolent.
When he grew older,
he studied literature quite a bit,
established the Wénlín Hall,
and invited various literary scholars there.
However, his speech was halting
and he lacked ambition or demeanor,
and he did not enjoy meeting court officials.
Unless they were favored confidants or intimate companions,
he never spoke to them.
He was naturally weak and intolerable.
If someone looked at him,
he would become angry and scold them.
Those who submitted memorials,
even if they were the Three Dukes, Chief Ministers, or Palace Secretariats, were not allowed to look up at him.
They all briefly presented the main gist
and fled out in haste.
Whenever there were natural disasters, anomalies, banditry, floods, or droughts,
he would not reduce his expenditures.
He only set up vegetarian fasts in various places,
taking this as cultivating virtue.
He was highly trusting of shamans and sorcerers,
and practiced countless methods of supplication.
Initially, when the Prince of Lángxié raised troops,
someone mistakenly reported that Kùdí Fúlián had rebelled.
The Emperor said:
"This must be Rénwēi."
Furthermore, after Húlǜ Gūang died,
various military officials nominated Gāo Sīhǎo as capable of being Grand General.
The Emperor said:
"Sīhǎo likes to rebel."
Everything turned out as he had predicted.
He thus came to believe that his strategies were flawless,
and he became even more arrogant and reckless.
He frequently composed the tune "Wúchóu" (No Sorrow).
The Emperor played the Hu *Pípá* himself and sang it,
and the number of attendants harmonizing with him was in the hundreds.
People in the world called him the "Son of Heaven of No Sorrow."
He once went out and saw a group of lepers.
He killed them all.
Sometimes, he would peel off a person's face skin just to look at it.
He allowed Lù Lìngxūan, Hé Shìkāi, Gāo Ānàgōng, Mù Típó, Hán Chángluán, and others to control the empire.
Chén Déxìn, Dèng Chángyǒng, and Hé Hóngzhēn participated in confidential power.
Each drew in relatives and associates,
placing them in positions far exceeding their rank.
Offices were obtained through wealth,
and legal judgments were settled by bribes.
The ways in which they corrupted governance and harmed people
are difficult to fully record.
The number of palace servants, bondservants, eunuchs, merchants, Hu households, mixed households, dancers, and ghost-seers who improperly gained wealth and high status was nearly ten thousand.
The common surnames enfeoffed as princes numbered in the hundreds,
too many to record.
There were over a thousand recipients of the *Kāifǔ* title,
and countless *Yítóu*.
At one time, there were twenty Chief Controllers (*Lǐngjūn*).
When jointly signing documents,
they each wrote the character *Yī* (accordingly)
without filling in their full names,
so nobody knew who they were.
The ancestors of the highly favored received posthumous official titles.
They were promoted once a year
until they reached the highest position, and then they stopped.
The maids of the inner palace were all enfeoffed as
More than five hundred palace women wore luxurious silks and ate delicacies.
A single skirt was worth ten thousand bolts (of cloth),
and a dressing table was worth a thousand gold pieces.
They competed in creating novel designs;
clothes worn in the morning were discarded by evening.

they believed this was natural for emperors.

At night, work was lit by torches;

All the artisans were exhausted and impoverished,

Ten thousand basins of oil were burned in a single night,

Pushing the limits of craftsmanship,
transporting stones and filling springs,
the labor and expenditure amounted to hundreds of millions,
and the deaths of men and oxen could not be counted.
Imperial horses were covered with embroidered blankets
and their food consisted of more than ten varieties.
When they were to breed,
a blue tent (qīnglú) was erected,
sacrificial feasts were prepared, and the Emperor personally observed the event.
Dogs were fed fine grain and meat.

Dogs, horses, chickens, and hawks often consumed the tribute provided by the counties.
Hawks brought in to be raised
were gradually fed by cutting up dog meat,

where the Emperor himself wore tattered clothes and acted as a begging child.
He also set up a market for poor children,

He had several cities rebuilt to resemble those on the western frontier,
and ordered men dressed in black clothes to act as
They would shout and challenge the cities,
while the Emperor personally led the inner attendants to resist them.
Sometimes he actually drew his bow and shot people.
When touring eastward from
he would gallop alone on a single horse,
returning with his clothes untied and his hair disheveled.
He also enjoyed engaging in non-urgent affairs.
Once, he spent a night hunting for scorpions,
and by dawn had collected three *shēng*.
He especially prized things that were out of season,
demanding them urgently.
Everything had to be requested in the morning and provided by evening.
Those in power took advantage of this,
lending one unit and demanding ten back.
Taxes grew heavier daily,
and forced labor grew more frequent daily.
When the people's strength was exhausted,
the national treasury became empty.
Consequently, he granted the sycophants licenses to sell official posts.
Some acquired two or three commanderies (jùn);
others acquired six or seven counties (xiàn).
They divided the prefectures and commanderies among themselves.
Even down to the village officials (xiāng guān), many were appointed via Imperial Decree (zhōng zhǐ).
Therefore, there were appointments decreed by edict for Prefectural Clerks (zhōu zhǔbù),
and appointments decreed by edict for
As a result, many prefectural and county positions were filled by wealthy merchants and great traders,
who competed in greed and tyranny,
making it impossible for the common people to live in peace.

taxes were levied everywhere,
with a hundred kinds of levies arising simultaneously.
All these services and levies
had gradually started under
but were greatly amplified by the current Emperor.
However, there was never any corruption or sexual depravity (in the inner chambers);
in this regard alone, he was said to be superior to
Earlier, at the end of the
Wǔchéng dreamed that large hedgehogs (wèi) attacked and breached the city of Yèchéng.
He thus demanded hedgehog fat (wèi gāo) throughout the territory to ward off the evil.
Those who understood the omen believed that the reputation of the
portending the downfall of
Furthermore, all women had their hair cut short and wore false hairpieces,
which were styled precariously and askew like flying birds.
When facing south,
the center of the hairpiece pointed directly west.
This fashion started in the palace
and spread everywhere.
The implication of Heaven seemed to be that the Head of State (yuánshǒu) would be cut down (or fall),
and that in peril, he ought to flee to the west.
Also, for those who made small knives (dāozǐ), the blades were narrow and fine,
named "Jìn Shì" (Exhausting Power).
Roaming children who played preferred holding a rope with both hands,
sweeping the ground and jumping backward,
leaping and singing,
"Gāo mò!" (Gāo's end!).
The phrase
likely referred to the end of the dynasty and fortune of the
Thus, the pattern of chaos and downfall must have had omens.
Commentary says:
his strategic planning was grand and far-reaching.
His civil and military officials
all exerted their utmost strength.
He certainly possessed the capacity of an emperor.
However, he loved and associated closely with worthless servants,
entrusting them with court authority.
In the inner chambers,
his indulgence and extravagance were excessive.
Were the omens of destruction
not rooted in this?
When the heavenly omens signaled change,
he passed the throne to his eldest son (yuánzǐ).
Although the titles (Emperor and Ex-Emperor) were different,
the governance still originated from him.
The actions were empty pretense,
and the events violated constitutional norms.
With such clarity (in his son) overseeing the lower ranks,
how easily could deceit be practiced?
Furthermore, the various princes, such as the Prince of
some due to political suspicions of the time,
others due to jealousy and distrust,
all perished without committing a crime.
This is not the meaning of knowing fate and resigning to the way of Heaven.
The
and easily corrupted nature,
considered the everlasting warnings of his predecessors,
but his instruction lacked righteous guidance.
From infancy
until the transmission of the throne,
he was shielded from upright persons,
blocking the path to goodness.
The moral cultivation he underwent
differed from the readings in spring and the musical practice in summer;
what he heard when passing the court
was nothing but rebellious and improper conduct.
He was assisted by maids and wet nurses of the central palace,
introduced to beautiful women and seductive music,
indulging in the pleasure of hawks and dogs,
and giving free rein to his preference for debauched companions.
The saying goes,
"Following evil is like a collapse,"
meaning how easy it is.
During the
the ruin became increasingly evident.
He rarely received court officials
and did not personally attend to government affairs.
The ten thousand affairs of the day
were entrusted to wicked relatives.
Inner attendants controlled the court,
dispensing imperial orders externally.
Their authority was harsh like wind and frost,
and their will could reverse Heaven and the Sun.
They tyrannized the people and harmed creatures,
preying without satiety.
They sold judgments and trafficked in offices;
their rapacity was harder to fill than canyons and ravines.
Compounding this, famous generals caused trouble,
and loyal ministers were executed publicly.
Then began the symptoms of gradual weakening,
swiftly followed by the spectacle of total collapse.
Zhōu Wǔ (Emperor Wu of Zhou) seized the opportunity
and unified the central domain (China).
Alas!
Indeed, Jié and Zhòu were criminals,
and their demise was swift—
this is the natural order of things.
began the foundation of hegemony;
Wénxiāng, with wise and brilliant strategies,
attacked rebels and pacified distant regions.
At that time, those who had lost their lord found a new one,
and armies marched out disciplined.
In the Battle of Héyīn,
he crushed Yǔwén as easily as turning his palm;
in the Battle of Wōyáng,
he swept away Hóu Jǐng as easily as pulling up withered weeds.
Thus, he was able to intimidate the western neighbors,
and extend his authority over the southern subordinates.
The royal house relied on him,
and the people of the Eastern Xià submitted their hearts.
Wénxuān, utilizing the resources accumulated over generations,
received the mandate by popular will.
His position was centered, dominating the empire,
and consequently, he transferred the Wèi Dǐng (the throne).
He harbored extraordinary and cunning talent,
and wielded strange and unpredictable wisdom.
He recruited talented and virtuous men,
exercised keen judgment over his subordinates,
and famous civil and military ministers
exhausted their efforts and utility.
He personally led armies out beyond the frontiers,
and ordered generals to approach the river.
He stabilized the Chányú at Lóngchéng,
and took in the eldest sovereign from Liáng Guó.
Internally and externally, the state was prosperous,
and the borders were free from alarms.
Barbarian cavalry ceased their southward invasions,
and the Qín people (Western powers) dared not look eastward.
Subsequently, however, he became dissolute and ruined his virtue,
abandoning reflection and acting wildly.
Though his virtuous deeds could not save him,
the remaining calamity was sufficient to be passed down to his descendants.
That he attained a natural end to his life
was fortunate;
that his successors did not last long
was fitting indeed.
Xiàozhāo, constrained by his geographical location and facing personal danger,
gained power through unusual means but maintained it correctly.
Externally, he spread civilizing influence,
internally, he harbored grand ambitions.
He intended to encompass the entire territory,
and unify the whole of Huáxià.
His lifespan was not long,
and his accomplishments remained unfinished.
Had Heaven granted him more years,
it would surely have caused Qín and Wú to delay their meals in anxiety.
When Wǔchéng ascended the throne,
the virtuous path declined,
the customs established by Xiàozhāo and Wénxiāng
had miserably fallen away.
When it reached the Hòuzhǔ (Later Lord),
the state disintegrated internally and externally.
The populace scattered at Píngyáng,
and his person was captured at Qīngtǔ.
The Way of Heaven is profound and distant,
and perhaps not easy to discuss;
but fortune and misfortune stem from man,
and thus can still be generally assessed.
Consider the peak prosperity of the Northern Qí state:
it controlled vast and strategic regions.
To the west, it embraced Fén and Jìn;
to the south, it reached the Jiāng and Huái;
to the east, it stretched to the ocean edge;
to the north, it extended into the deserts.
Of the lands of the Six States,
we secured five;
of the territories of the Nine Provinces,
the rival divided four.
Estimating the strength of the armed forces,
and comparing the fullness or emptiness of the treasuries,
along with generals who could prevail over enemies a thousand miles away,
and strategists with supreme tactical brilliance,
when comparing the superiority and inferiority of the two sides,
there was no degree of comparison worth mentioning.
Yet, the defenses of Tàiháng and Chángchéng remained intact;
the strategic strongholds of Jiāng, Huái, Fén, and Jìn were unchanged;
the revenue from taxes filling the treasuries had not diminished;
and the populace, scholars, and armed forces were not lacking.
Nevertheless, the former lords used these resources and had a surplus,
while the Later Lord guarded them and found them insufficient.
What was the reason for this?
When the former lords governed,
they bathed in the rain and combed their hair in the wind (working tirelessly);
they rescued those drowning and saved those being burned;
they reliably rewarded and certainly punished;
they pacified and benefited the people.
Since they shared existence and non-existence (fate) with the people,
they were able to share life and death with them.
The Later Lord was not like this:
he made others submit to his desires,
harming others to benefit himself.
Carved walls and lofty palaces,
sweet wines and craving for music,
were indulged everywhere in the palaces and gardens;
lust and debauchery were rampant inside and outside.
He caused day to become night,
and used boats where there was no water.
What he desired was sure to be accomplished,
what he sought was sure to be obtained.
He was both lawless and inhuman,
and also blind in listening and accepting advice.
Loyal and honest counsel went unheard,
while slander and fabrication always gained entry.
He viewed people as mere grass and weeds,
following evil as if going downstream.
Flattering eunuchs occupied the pivotal positions of power,
and maidservants and old women usurped the power to alter destiny.
They sold offices and trafficked in judgments,
disrupting governance and committing excessive punishments.
Mutilation and slashing were inflicted upon the loyal and good,
while stipends and rank were bestowed upon dogs and horses.
Slanderous and wicked people advanced together,
and laws and statutes were frequently changed.
Those holding gourds (beggars/sycophants) were not limited to a hundred men,
and those shaking the tree (instigators of trouble) were not merely one hand.
Consequently, the state disintegrated entirely,
the populace rebelled and relatives deserted him.
Looking toward the Zhōu state (Western Zhōu),
everyone harbored the intention to return west.
At that very time, he further embellished his palaces and temples,
reaching the extreme of debauchery and excess.
He considered the black-haired people (commoners) easy to deceive,
and pointed to the white sun (swearing by Heaven) to ensure his own safety.
He sent forth armies who turned their spears,
and mobilized forces who sang of the enemy.
The foundation built up over five generations,
was destroyed in one action.
Was this not because engraving metal and stone is hard work,
while destroying withered and rotten wood requires little effort?
Moreover, I have heard: August Heaven shows no partiality,
it only assists the virtuous.
The timing of Heaven is inferior to the advantages of the Earth,
and the advantages of the Earth are inferior to the harmony of men.
In Qí, since the time after Héqīng (reign title),
up until the end of Wǔpíng (reign title),
construction projects never ceased,
and the selection of concubines never ended.
Taxes were exhausted,
manpower was depleted.
Material resources could not supply his demands,
and all the rivers and seas could not satisfy his desires.
It is like saying, when the fire is already blazing fiercely,
one adds firewood to fuel it further,
and when fate is already at its limit,
one commits further evil to hasten it.
To wish for a great mansion not to burn down,
and to prolong its duration beyond its destined span,
is this not difficult indeed!
Judging from this,
the defeat and downfall of the Qí clan
was presumably caused by man,
and not solely by the Way of Heaven.
Biographies 1: Empress Lóu of Shénwǔ, Empress Yuán of Wénxiāng, Empress Lǐ of Wénxuān, Empress Yuán of Xiàozhāo, Empress Hú of Wǔchéng, Empress Hú Lǜ of Hòuzhǔ, Empress Hú, Empress Mù.
Shénwǔ Míng Huánghòu, of the Lóu Shì,
personal name Zhāojūn,
was the daughter of the posthumously designated Sītú Nèigān.
When young, she was intelligent and insightful.
Many powerful clans sought her hand in marriage,
but she refused them all.
When she saw Shénwǔ working on the city wall,
she exclaimed in astonishment:
"This truly is my husband!"
She then sent a maidservant to convey her intent,
and repeatedly sent private wealth,
instructing him to use it to propose marriage to her.
Her parents, having no choice, agreed.
Shénwǔ already harbored the ambition to bring order to the chaos,
and spent his entire wealth to gather heroes.
In secret plots and concealed strategies,
the Empress participated.
When she was invested as the Bóhǎi Wáng Fēi (Princess of Bóhǎi),
all matters of the inner court were decided by her.
The Empress was insightful, decisive, and strict,
gracefully adhering to frugality and restraint.
When traveling to her outside residence,
her entourage did not exceed ten people.
Her nature was tolerant and generous,
and she was not jealous.
She treated all of Shénwǔ’s
concubines and attendants with kindness.
Shénwǔ was once leading an army out for a western campaign.
That night, the Empress gave birth to twins, a boy and a girl.
Her attendants considered this an emergency
and requested to send a courier to recall Shénwǔ.
The Empress refused to listen, saying:
"The King is out commanding a great army;
how can he easily leave the military camp on my account?
Life and death are destiny.
What purpose would his return serve!"
When Shénwǔ heard this,
he sighed in admiration for a long time.
After the defeat at Shāyuàn,
Hóu Jǐng repeatedly suggested requesting twenty thousand elite cavalry,
asserting that he could surely capture the enemy.
Shénwǔ was pleased
and told the Empress.
The Empress said:
"If he is as effective as he claims,
how could he ever return?
To gain an otter and lose Jǐng
would be of what benefit?"
(Shénwǔ) therefore stopped the plan.
Shénwǔ, pressured by the Rúru,
wished to marry their daughter but had not yet decided.
The Empress said:
"This is a great national plan;
may Your Majesty not be hesitant."
When the Rúru Princess arrived,
the Empress yielded the main residence to her.
Shénwǔ felt ashamed and bowed in thanks,
saying:
"She might realize [the situation];
please cease and do not worry about it."
She loved all the princes and
treated them no differently from her own children.
She personally spun and wove,
granting each person one gown and one pair of trousers.
She hand-stitched military uniforms
to present to the officers around her.
Her younger brother, Zhāo,
achieved prominence through his own merit and reputation.
For her remaining relatives,
she never requested titles or ranks on their behalf.
She often said that those with talent should be employed,
and it was unjust to let private concerns corrupt public affairs.
When Wénxiāng succeeded to the throne,
she was elevated to Tàifēi.
When Wénxuān was about to accept the abdication of Wèi,
the Empress adamantly refused to permit it,
which is why the Emperor stopped the plan.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
she was honored as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager),
and her palace was named Xuānxùn.
When Jìnán ascended the throne,
she was honored as Tài Huáng Tàihòu (Grand Empress Dowager).
Yáng Yīn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, and others received the imperial edict to assist in government,
and they grew wary of the various princes.
The Tài Huáng Tàihòu secretly planned with Xiàozhāo and the various great generals to execute them,
and issued an order for deposition and installation.
When Xiàozhāo ascended the throne,
she was again honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
When Emperor Xiàozhāo died,
the Empress Dowager again issued an edict to establish Emperor Wǔchéng.
In the spring of the second year of Dàníng (563 CE),
the Empress Dowager fell ill.
Her clothes suddenly rose up by themselves,
and following the words of a shamaness, she changed her surname to Shí Shì.
On the Xīnchǒu day of the fourth month,
she died in the Běigōng (Northern Palace),
at the age of sixty-two.
On the Jiăshēn day of the fifth month,
she was interred together at Yìpíng Líng.
The Empress Dowager had been pregnant with six sons and two daughters in total,
and all pregnancies involved auspicious dreams: when pregnant with Wénxiāng, she dreamt of a segmented dragon;
when pregnant with Wénxuān, she dreamt of a great dragon
whose head and tail spanned heaven and earth,
opening its mouth and moving its eyes,
its appearance shockingly impressive;
when pregnant with Xiàozhāo, she dreamt of a dragon wriggling on the ground;
when pregnant with Wǔchéng, she dreamt of a dragon bathing in the sea;
when pregnant with the two Wèi Empresses, she dreamt of the moon entering her bosom;
when pregnant with the two Princes of Xiāngchéng and Bólíng, she dreamt of rats entering beneath her clothes.
Before the Empress Dowager died,
there was a children’s rhyme saying,
"The mother of the Nine Dragons dies, but filial piety is not shown."
When the Empress Dowager died,
Wǔchéng did not change his attire,
wearing his scarlet robe as before.
Soon after,
he ascended the Sāntái (Three Terraces)
and held a drinking party with music.
The Emperor's daughter presented a white robe,
but the Emperor was enraged
and threw it down from the terrace.
Hé Shìkāi requested that the music be stopped,
and the Emperor grew furious
and lashed him.
The Emperor was actually the ninth among his brothers;
this was likely the verification of the prophecy.
Empress Jìng of Wénxiāng, née Yuán,
was the elder sister of Emperor Xiàojìng of Wèi.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
she was titled Princess of Féngyì and married to Wénxiāng.
She was beautiful in appearance and virtue,
showing utmost harmony and respect.
When she first gave birth to Prince Xiàowăn of Héjiān,
Wénxiāng was then the Shìzǐ (Heir Apparent).
Three days later, Emperor Xiàojìng visited the Shìzǐ’s residence
and presented ten thousand bolts of silk and cloth.
The Shìzǐ declined,
requesting instead to receive gifts generally presented by the nobles,
and consequently, ten rooms were filled.
Next, she gave birth to two princesses.
When Wénxuān received the abdication,
she was honored as Empress of Wénxiāng
and resided in Jìngdé Gōng.
In the sixth year of Tiānbǎo (555 CE),
Wénxuān gradually became deranged and reckless.
He then moved her residence to the Gāoyáng estate,
took possession of her treasury,
and said:
"My elder brother previously seduced my wife;
I must now seek revenge."
He then raped the Empress.
Regardless of whether the women of the Gāo clan were close or distant relatives,
he ordered his attendants to violate them publicly before him.
He made a rope out of kudzu vine,
ordered the Princess Āndé of Wèi to ride on it,
and had men push and pull her.
He also commanded a Hú (non-Han) man to severely humiliate her.
The Emperor also exposed himself
to display to his subordinates.
During the Wǔpíng era,
the Empress died
and was buried alongside (Wénxiāng) at Yìpíng Líng.
Empress Lǐ of Wénxuān,
whose taboo name was Zǔ'é,
was the daughter of Lǐ Xīzōng of Zhàojùn.
She was extremely beautiful in appearance and virtue.
Initially, she was the wife of the Duke of Tàiyuán.
When the Emperor was about to establish the central palace (Empress),
Gāo Lóngzhī and Gāo Dézhèng argued that a Hàn woman could not serve as the mother of the empire
and that a beautiful consort should be chosen instead.
Yáng Yīn firmly requested that the Emperor follow the precedents of Hàn and Wèi
and not change the principal consort.
However, Gāo Dézhèng still adamantly requested that the Empress be deposed and Duàn Zhāoyí be established,
hoping to secure the support of the honored nobles.
The Emperor ultimately did not follow him and established Lǐ Shì as Empress.
