The Emperor enjoyed flogging and beating his consorts and ladies-in-waiting,
even resulting in some being killed,
but only the Empress received respectful treatment.
In the tenth year of Tiānbǎo (559 CE),
her title was changed to Kèhèdūn Huánghòu.
When Xiàozhāo ascended the throne,
she was moved to Zhāoxìn Gōng,
and titled Empress Zhāoxìn.
When Wǔchéng took the throne,
he coerced the Empress into sexual relations,
saying:
"If you do not agree,
I will kill your son."
The Empress was afraid
and complied.
Later, she became pregnant.
Prince Shàodé of Tàiyuán arrived at her chamber
but was refused entry.
He said angrily:
"Does the child not know?
Elder Sister’s belly is big,
so she won’t see the child."
When the Empress heard this,
she was greatly ashamed,
and consequently, when she gave birth to a daughter, she did not raise her.
The Emperor wielded a sword and cursed her, saying:
"You killed my daughter!
Why should I not kill your son!"
He then had Shàodé beaten to death right in front of the Empress.
The Empress wept loudly.
The Emperor became even angrier,
stripped the Empress naked, and mercilessly flogged and beat her,
crying out to Heaven incessantly.
He put her in a silk sack,
streaming with blood,
and threw her into a ditch of water.
After a long time, she revived,
and was transported by a calf-drawn cart to the Miàoshèng Nísì (nunnery).
The Empress naturally loved the Buddhist Dharma,
and thus became a nun.
When Qí fell, she moved into the Guān region.
During the Suí dynasty, she was able to return to Zhàojùn.
Empress Xiàozhāo, Mǔ Yuánshì,
was the daughter of Kāifǔ Yuán Mán.
Initially, she was the consort of the Prince of Chángshān.
At the end of Tiānbǎo,
she was granted the surname Bùliùgū.
When Xiàozhāo ascended the throne,
she was established as Empress.
When the Emperor died,
the imperial coffin was taken to Yè.
When they first crossed the Fénqiáo Bridge,
Wǔchéng heard that the Empress possessed a strange medicine,
sought it out, but failed to obtain it,
and had eunuchs subject her to public humiliation near her carriage.
She was demoted and resided in the Shùnchénggōng Palace.
After Wǔchéng killed the Prince of Lèlíng,
Yuán was confined and isolated,
unable to communicate with her family.
Suddenly, rumors circulated within the palace chambers.
The Emperor ordered an investigation,
and letters from the Empress’s father and elder brother were discovered.
Yuán Mán was consequently relieved of his office for this offense.
When Qí fell, the Empress entered the palace of the Zhōu clan.
When Emperor Wéndì of Suí became Chancellor,
she was released back to Shāndōng.
Empress Wǔchéng, Mǔ Húshì,
was the daughter of Hú Yánzhī of Āndìng.
Her mother was the daughter of Lú Dàoyūe of Fànyáng.
When she was first pregnant,
a Buddhist monk from the Western Regions came to the door and said,
“In the gourd of this house, there is the moon.”
Soon thereafter, the Empress was born.
In the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
she was selected to be the consort of the Prince of Chángguǎng.
On the day after she gave birth to the later Emperor,
an owl hooted atop the birthing tent.
When Wǔchéng died,
she was honored as the Empress Dowager.
Lù Ǎo and Hé Shìkāi secretly plotted to kill Zhàojùnwáng Ruì,
and sent Lóu Dìngyuǎn and Gāo Wényáo out to serve as governors (cìshǐ).
Hé and Lù flattered and served the Empress Dowager,
stopping at nothing.
Previously, during Wǔchéng’s reign,
the Empress had engaged in indecent familiarity with several eunuchs.
Wǔchéng favored Hé Shìkāi,
who frequently played *wòshuò* (a board game) with the Empress,
and thus committed adultery with her.
After Wǔchéng died,
she frequently went out to Buddhist temples,
and also engaged in sexual relations with the *shāmén* (monk) Tán Xiàn.
She scattered gold coins beneath Xiàn’s mat,
and hung an ornate Hu chair on the wall of Xiàn’s room,
which had been used by Wǔchéng throughout his life.
She then placed a hundred monks in the inner palace hall,
under the pretext of listening to lectures,
and slept with Tán Xiàn day and night.
She made Xiàn the Zhāoxuántǒng (Director of Monks).
The monks would point from afar at the Empress Dowager to tease Tán Xiàn,
even referring to him as the Tàishàng (Supreme Emperor).
The Emperor heard that the Empress Dowager was indiscreet but did not yet believe it.
Later, when he visited the Empress Dowager,
he saw two young nuns,
was pleased, and summoned them,
but they turned out to be men.
Thereupon, the affair involving Tán Xiàn was also revealed,
and they were all executed according to the law,
along with the three Commandery Ladies (Jùnjūn)—Yuán, Shān, and Wáng—
who were all intimates of the Empress Dowager.
The Emperor escorted the Empress Dowager from Jìnyáng back to Yè.
Upon reaching Zǐmò,
they suddenly encountered a great storm.
The Palace Attendant Wèi Sēngjiā, skilled in meteorological predictions (*fēngjiǎo*),
reported that a violent rebellion was imminent.
The Emperor falsely claimed that there was an emergency in Yè,
drew his bow and raised his spear,
and galloped into the Southern City.
He ordered Dèng Chángyóng to confine the Empress Dowager in the Northern Palace,
and subsequently issued an edict forbidding all relatives, internal or external, from meeting the Empress Dowager.
After a long time,
the Emperor welcomed the Empress Dowager back.
When the Empress Dowager first heard that the messenger had arrived,
she was greatly alarmed,
fearing the worst.
Whenever the Empress Dowager prepared food,
the Emperor dared not taste it.
When the Zhōu envoy Yuán Wěi came to make a marriage proposal,
he composed the *Fù* on Travel,
which alluded to Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng defeating Duàn and moving Lady Jiāng.
Although the text was not skillful,
at the time, (Qí officials) felt deeply ashamed by it.
When Qí perished, she entered Zhōu,
indulging in illicit filth.
She died during the Kāihuáng era of Suí.
The Empress of the Latter Lord, Mǔ Húlǜshì,
was the daughter of the Left Chancellor Húlǜ Guāng.
Initially, she was the Crown Prince’s consort.
When the Latter Lord received the abdication,
she was established as Empress.
In the first month of the third year of Wǔpíng, she gave birth to a daughter.
The Emperor, wishing to please Guāng,
falsely claimed it was a son,
and granted a great amnesty for the occasion.
When Guāng was executed,
the Empress was deposed and kept in a separate palace.
Later, she was ordered to become a nun.
When Qí was destroyed,
she married Kāifǔ Yuán Rén.
The Empress of the Latter Lord, Mǔ Húshì,
was the daughter of Lǒngdōngwáng Hú Chángrén.
Empress Dowager Hú regretted having failed in the proper conduct of a mother figure,
and felt deep shame about it.
Wishing to please the Latter Lord,
she therefore adorned the Empress (Húshì) within the palace
and ensured the Emperor saw her.
The Emperor was indeed pleased,
and established her as Hóngdé Fūrén,
then promoted her to Zuǒzhāoyí,
and she was greatly favored and loved.
When Empress Húlǜ was deposed,
Lù Ǎo wanted to replace her with Lady Mù Fūrén,
but the Empress Dowager did not permit it.
Zǔ Xiàozhēng requested that Consort Hú Zhāoyí be established,
and she subsequently ascended to the position of Empress.
Since Lù Ǎo had not advised her establishment,
and since her intention was focused on Lady Mù Fūrén,
she later spoke angrily before the Empress Dowager, saying:
“How dare this niece of yours utter such words!”
The Empress Dowager asked what words she had uttered.
She replied:
“They cannot be spoken.”
When pressed,
she finally said:
“She told everyone that
the Empress Dowager’s conduct is often improper
and cannot serve as an instruction.”
The Empress Dowager was greatly enraged,
called the Empress out,
immediately shaved her hair,
and sent her home.
The Emperor missed her,
and frequently sent gifts to communicate his feelings.
Later, she and the deposed Empress Húlǜ were both summoned back inside the palace.
A few days later, Yè could not be defended.
She also remarried.
Hòuzhǔ’s Empress Mùshì,
whose personal name was Yélì,
was originally a maidservant following Empress Húlǜ.
Her mother’s name was Qīngxiāo,
who was originally the maidservant of Mù Zǐlún,
but was transferred into the household of the Attendant-in-ordinary Sòng Qīndào.
She became intimate with him and gave birth to the Empress.
Her lineage was unknown,
and some said the Empress was Sòng Qīndào’s daughter.
Her childhood name was Huánghuā,
and later she was named Shèlì.
Sòng Qīndào’s wife was jealous,
and tattooed Qīngxiāo’s face with the
character
“Sòng.”
When Sòng Qīndào was executed,
Huánghuā consequently entered the palace
and received the favor of Hòuzhǔ.
She was called Attendant Shèlì within the palace.
The female Attendant-in-ordinary Lù Tàijī, knowing of her favor,
adopted her as her daughter
and recommended her to be named Lady Hóngdé.
In the sixth month of the first year of Wǔpíng (570 CE),
she gave birth to an Imperial Prince.
At that time, Hòuzhǔ had no heir apparent.
Lù Tàijī secretly gained favor and,
seeing that the responsibility of guardianship could not be without a master,
and as the current Empress Húlǜshì
was the daughter of the Chancellor Húlǜ Guāng,
she feared Húlǜ Guāng might harbor resentment,
so she first allowed the mother to raise the child
and had him established as the Crown Prince.
Lù Tàijī, considering the importance of the imperial surname
and the corresponding relationship between Mù and Lù,
also memorialized to bestow the surname Mùshì upon her.
When the Commoner Hú was deposed,
Lù Tàijī assisted in the matter.
Therefore, she was eventually established as Empress,
and a general amnesty was declared.
Originally,
a Colonel of the Impetuous Advance, Yuán Zhèngliè, obtained a seal from the water east of Yèchéng and presented it.
The inscription read:
“Seal of the Queen of Heaven.”
It was probably made by the Shí family.
An imperial decree announced it
and considered it an auspicious omen for Empress Mù.
During Wǔchéng’s reign,
a pearl skirt and trousers were made for Empress Hú,
the cost of which was immeasurable,
but they were destroyed by fire.
After Hòuzhǔ established Empress Mù,
he again set about constructing them.
It happened that Zhōu Wǔ was observing mourning for the Empress Dowager,
and an edict commissioned the Attendants-in-ordinary Xuē Gū and Kāng Mǎi to be envoys of condolence.
He also dispatched merchants carrying 30,000 bolts of brocade and silk to travel with the envoys of condolence,
intending to buy pearls to make a carriage of seven treasures for the Empress.
The Zhōu people refused to trade,
but the carriage was ultimately constructed nonetheless.
Previously, there was a children’s rhyme that said:
“The power of Huánghuā is about to fall,
the clear wine cup is filled to the brim.”
It meant that Huánghuā would not last long.
After Hòuzhǔ established Empress Mù,
he indulged in excessive drinking,
which is why it said, “the clear wine cup is filled to the brim.”
Lù Tàijī’s daughter’s husband, Luò Típó, was renamed Mù by imperial decree,
and Lù
Tàijī
herself, all because of the Empress.
Since the Empress took Lù Tàijī as her mother
and Luò Típó as her family,
she no longer favored Qīngxiāo.
Qīngxiāo later treated her own face
and sought an audience,
but the Empress Dowager and the old woman Lù ordered her to be detained and guarded,
and she ultimately was not allowed to see the Empress.

Biographies, Volume Two: Eleven Kings of Gāozǔ: Prince Jiǎnpíng of Yǒng'ān, Jùn; Prince Jìngyì of Píngyáng, Yān; Prince Jǐngsī of Péngchéng, Yóu; Prince Gāngsù of Shàngdǎng, Huàn; Prince Jǐng of Xiāngchéng, Yù; Prince of Rènchéng, Jiē; Prince Kāngmù of Gāoyáng, Shí; Prince Wénjiǎn of Bólíng, Jì; Prince of Huàshān, ; Prince of Fēngyì, Rùn; Prince Jìnghuái of Hànyáng, Qià.
Shénwǔ Huángdì had fifteen sons: Empress Wǔmíng Lóu gave birth to Emperor Wénxiāng, Emperor Wénxuān, Emperor Xiàozhāo, Prince Jǐng of Xiāngchéng Yù, Emperor Wǔchéng, and Prince Wénjiǎn of Bólíng Jì.
Wángshì gave birth to Prince Jiǎnpíng of Yǒng'ān Jùn.
Mùshì gave birth to Prince Jìngyì of Píngyáng Yān.
The elder Ěrzhūshì gave birth to Prince Jǐngsī of Péngchéng Yóu, and the Prince of Huàshān.
Hánshì gave birth to Prince Gāngsù of Shàngdǎng Huàn.
The younger Ěrzhūshì gave birth to Prince of Rènchéng Jiē.
Yóushì gave birth to Prince Kāngmù of Gāoyáng Shí.
Zhèngshì gave birth to Prince of Fēngyì Rùn.
Féngshì gave birth to Prince Jìnghuái of Hànyáng Qià.
Yǒng'ān Jiǎnpíng Wáng Jùn,
courtesy name Dìnglè,
was Shénwǔ’s third son.
When Shénwǔ first took Jùn’s mother,
she conceived that very month.
When Jùn was born,
Shénwǔ suspected he was not his own flesh
and did not greatly favor him.
However, Jùn was intelligent from an early age,
and later received more affection.
When he was eight years old,
he asked the Erudite Lú Jǐngyù:
“ ‘When sacrificing to the spirits, treat them as if the spirits are present.’
Are there spirits,
or are there no spirits?”
He replied:
“There are.”
Jùn said:
“If there are spirits, it should say, ‘When sacrificing to the spirits, the spirits are present.’
Why bother with the word
‘as if’?”
Lú Jǐngyù was unable to answer.
When he grew up,
his playful indulgence was unrestrained.
He once made a request to receive an inner chamber attendant,
and was severely beaten with a rod
and confined in the governmental prison,
but later he was pardoned.
Afterward, he gradually curbed his behavior
and somewhat devoted himself to reading.
In the Yuánxiàng era,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yǒng'ān Jùn.
He was bold, straightforward, and physically strong;
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
he was loved by Wénxiāng.
Wénxuān's nature was timid and weak;
whenever he met Wénxiāng,
sometimes tears would flow.
Jùn often criticized the Emperor’s attendants,
asking why they did not wipe the nose of his Second Elder Brother (Wénxuān).
Because of this, he incurred resentment.
He was successively promoted to Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Jiān) and concurrently Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
He was sent out to serve as the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Qīngzhōu.
He was quite fond of hunting.
He was intelligent, dignified, and forgiving,
and those above and below him both feared and admired him.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
his peerage was advanced to King.
In Wénxuān's later years, he drank heavily.
Jùn said to his close associates:
"My Second Elder Brother was not very discerning in the past,
but since ascending the throne,
his understanding and insight have greatly advanced.
Now, due to wine, he ruins his virtue,
and no court official dares to admonish him.
The great enemy has not yet been eliminated.
I am deeply concerned about this.
I wish to travel by express messenger to Yè and admonish him face-to-face,
but I do not know if he will heed me."
Someone learned of this,
and secretly reported it to the Emperor,
causing him to incur further resentment.
In the eighth year (of Tiānbǎo), he came to the capital for an audience,
and followed the Emperor on a tour to Dōngshān.
The Emperor enjoyed stripping naked,
mixing freely with women,
and performing the "fox wagging its tail" game.
Jùn advanced to speak, saying,
"This is not proper behavior for a ruler of men."
The Emperor was extremely displeased.
Jùn also summoned Yáng Zūnyàn to a secluded place,
criticizing him for not offering remonstrance.
The Emperor at that time did not wish for high officials to communicate privately with the various kings.
Zūnyàn, fearful, reported this in a memorial.
The Emperor became greatly enraged and said:
"Petty men are inherently difficult to tolerate!"
Thereupon he ceased drinking and returned to the palace.
Jùn soon returned to his province,
and again submitted a strongly worded memorial of remonstrance.
An imperial edict ordered Jùn to be summoned.
Jùn, fearing disaster,
excused himself on the grounds of illness and did not go.
The Emperor was furious,
and dispatched couriers to arrest Jùn.
Thousands of people, old and young, wept as they saw him off.
When he arrived,
he was placed in an iron cage,
and together with the King of Shàngdǎng, Huàn, he was thrown into the underground dungeon of the Northern Wall (Běichéng).
Food, drink, urine, and filth were all kept in the same place.
The following year,
the Emperor personally brought his attendants to the edge of the pit and began singing,
ordering Jùn to harmonize.
Jùn and the others were terrified and sorrowful,
and their voices trembled uncontrollably.
The Emperor became saddened by this,
and wept,
intending to pardon them.
Zhǎngguǎng Wáng Zhàn had previously been on bad terms with Jùn.
He stepped forward and said:
"How can ferocious beasts be allowed out of the pit?"
The Emperor remained silent.
Jùn and the others heard this,
and called Zhǎngguǎng by his infant name, saying:
"Bùluòjī,
May August Heaven witness you!"
All the attendants who heard this
were mournful.
Jùn and Huàn both possessed heroic strategies
and were admired and respected by the various kings.
The Emperor feared they would cause trouble,
so he personally stabbed Huàn,
and then ordered the strongman Liú Táozhī to randomly stab into the cage.
Each time the spear struck,
Jùn and Huàn would grab it with their hands and break it,
wailing loudly and calling out to Heaven.
Thereupon, firewood and torches were wildly thrown in,
burning them to death,
and the pit was filled with stones and earth.
When they were later taken out,
their skin and hair were completely destroyed,
and the color of their corpses was like charcoal.
All under Heaven grieved deeply for this.
Afterwards, the Emperor married his consort, Lady Lù, to Aid-to-the-Court Administrator (Yítóng) Liú Yùjié,
who had formerly been the Emperor's personal slave.
He was employed due to military merit,
and had been ordered at the time to harm Jùn,
which is why the Emperor married the Lady to him.
A few days later,
the Emperor, noting that Lady Lù had previously received no favor from Jùn,
ordered the marriage to be broken off.
In the first year of Qiánmíng,
he was posthumously granted the title Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Having no son,
an edict ordered Zhǔn, the second son of Péngchéng Wáng Yóu, to inherit his title.
Yān, the Jìngyì King of Píngyáng,
courtesy name Zǐsuì,
was the fourth son of Shénwǔ.
In the Yuánxiàng era,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Píngyáng Jùn,
and was successively promoted to Left Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè).
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
his peerage was advanced to King,

and he successively held the positions of Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Administrator with the Status of Three Grand Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), Minister of Works (Sīkōng), and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
In the beginning of Huángjiàn,
he became the Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
and together with the Kings of Péngchéng and Héjiān, he was granted personal guards
and one hundred Yǔlín guards.
In the first year of Dàníng,
he was promoted to Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi).
His nature was reserved and cautious,
and he was renowned for his magnanimity.
In the third year of Héqīng,
he died in Jìnyáng.
Some say he died by poisoning.
His body was returned to Yè for burial.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Acting Yellow Axe Holder (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi), and Director of Affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
His son, Désù, inherited the title.
Yóu, the Jǐngsī King of Péngchéng,
courtesy name Zǐshēn,
was the fifth son of Shénwǔ.
In the second year of Yuánxiàng,
he was appointed Palace Attendant in Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Chánglè Jùn.
Erudite (Bóshì) Hán Yì taught Yóu calligraphy.
Seeing that Yóu's handwriting was not yet skillful,
he jokingly said to Yóu:
"The Fifth Young Master's writing and drawing are like this,
yet he suddenly becomes a Palace Attendant and the founder of a state (Kāiguó).
From now on, you should apply yourself more diligently."
Yóu, with a serious expression, replied:
"In the past, Gān Luó was young when he became the Chancellor of Qín,
yet I have not heard that he was skilled in calligraphy.
People are judged only on their talents and capacity;
why must one always boast of handwriting?
The Erudite is a capable person in the present day,
why does he not become one of the Three Dukes (Sāngōng)?"
At that time, he was probably eight years old.
Yì was greatly ashamed.
In the sixth year of Wǔdìng,
he was sent out to serve as the Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor).
His governance was strict and observant,
and the region was orderly.
Prefects (Shǒulìng) and their aides (Cānzuǒ),
down to the lowest clerks (Xūlì),
when traveling or visiting,
all brought their own provisions.
Yǒu subtly knew of all human affairs.
Zhāng Dá, the Registrar (Zhǔbù) of Shīwò County, once visited the capital,
stayed overnight in someone’s house,
and ate chicken broth.
Yǒu observed and knew about this.
When the Prefects had all assembled,
Yǒu addressed the crowd, saying:
"Why did you eat chicken broth and not repay its price?"
Dá immediately confessed the offense.
The entire region called him a divine administrator (Shénmíng).
Furthermore, there was a man who came from Yōuzhōu,
whose donkey carried dried venison (lùpǔ).
When he reached the border of Cāngzhōu,
his feet hurt and he walked slowly.
He happened to meet a man who traveled with him,
who subsequently stole the donkey and the venison and left.
The next morning,
he reported to the prefecture (Zhōu).
Yǒu then ordered his attendants and the officials of the administration to buy dried venison widely,
without setting a price limit.
The owner saw the venison and recognized it,
leading to the apprehension of the thief.
He was transferred to be Dūdū (Area Commander) and Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor).
At that time, someone had a black ox stolen,
which had white hair on its back.
The Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) Wéi Dàojiàn said to the Central Attendant (Zhōng Cóngshì) Wèi Dàoshèng:
"When the Governor (Shǐjūn) was in Cāngzhōu,
he captured villains like a spirit;
if he catches this thief,
he will truly be divine."
Yǒu then pretended to purchase ox hides for the upper administration,
paying double the price,
and allowed the ox owner to identify them,
thereby capturing the thief.
Jiàn and others praised and submitted to him.
Furthermore, there was an old woman whose surname was Wáng,
who was lonely and solitary.
She planted three *mǔ* of vegetables,
but they were frequently stolen.
Yǒu secretly ordered a person to go and write characters on the vegetable leaves.
The next day, someone saw vegetable leaves with characters written on them in the marketplace,
and the thief was captured.
After that, there were no thefts within the territory,
and his governing influence (Zhènghuà) was considered the foremost of that era.
Early in Tiānbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Péngchéng.
In the fourth year,
he was summoned to serve as Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
The people and officials cried mournfully while seeing him off.
Several hundred elders gathered together and prepared a meal, saying:
"Since Your Highness arrived five years ago,
the people do not recognize the officials (as oppressors),
and the officials do not deceive the people.
Since the common folk attained consciousness,
they have only now encountered such governance.
Your Highness has only drunk the water of this region,
but has not yet eaten the food of this region.
We humbly offer this small, simple gift."
Yǒu respected their intention,
and ate one mouthful.
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to Sīzhōu Mù (Governor of Sīzhōu).
He selected his subordinates (Cóngshì) solely from scholarly men who were bright and skilled at judicial judgment.
This was called an excellent selection at the time.
There were over five hundred old cases in the prefecture (Zhōu).
Yǒu settled all of them completely within less than a year.
The Assistant Governor (Biéjià) Yáng Xiū and others feared infringing upon powerful relatives (Quánqī),
and therefore went to the residence (Gě) to consult and present their concerns.
Yǒu sent a message saying:
"I act justly on a straight path.
Why should I fear powerful relatives?
You should be helping to complete a worthy deed,
but instead you speak of powerful relatives."
Xiū and the others withdrew, ashamed and alarmed.
Later, he was promoted to Tèjìn (Special Advanced Rank),
concurrently serving as Sīkōng (Minister of Works) and Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant),
retaining his position as Zhōu Mù (Governor) as before.
When the Grand Consort (Tàifēi) died,
he resigned his post.
Soon after, an imperial edict restored him to his original office.
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed Sīkōng,
concurrently Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs).
When Jìnán succeeded to the throne,

he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Residence with Ceremonial Privileges Equal to the Three Dukes), Shàngshū Lìng, and concurrently Dàzōngzhèng Qīng (Minister of the Imperial Clan Court).
Early in Huángjiàn,
he was appointed Dà Sīmǎ (Grand Marshal),
concurrently Shàngshū Lìng,
and later transferred to Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian).
When Wǔchéng entered to inherit the great enterprise,
he was promoted to Tàishī (Grand Preceptor) and Lù Shàngshū Shì (Manager of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs).
Yǒu was insightful regarding governmental affairs,
decisive in judgment,
and whether matters were great or small,
he settled them all with fairness.
Lǐ Gōngtǒng of Zhàojùn was involved in the rebellion of Gāo Guīyàn.
His mother, Lady Cuī, was the cousin of the Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) Cuī Áng,
and also the wife's sister of the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púyè) Wèi Shōu.
According to regulation,
if one was over sixty years old,
they were exempt from being imprisoned or confiscated as property.
Lady Cuī falsely claimed advanced age and appealed.
The relevant authorities, due to Áng and Shōu,
consequently allowed Lady Cuī to be exempted.
Yǒu exposed this affair,
and Áng and the others were stripped of their ranks due to their offense.
Whenever the Imperial carriage traveled on inspection tours,
Yǒu always remained in Yè.
In the third month of Héqīng Third Year,
dozens of bandits, including Tián Zǐlǐ, plotted to seize Yǒu and make him their leader.
They falsely claimed to be imperial envoys,
went straight to Yǒu’s residence,
reached the inner chamber,
claimed to have an imperial edict, pulled Yǒu onto a horse,
threatened him with drawn blades,
and attempted to lead him toward the Southern Palace.
Yǒu shouted loudly and refused to comply,
and was subsequently murdered.
He was thirty-two years old at the time.
The court and the common people deeply regretted his loss.
Before Yǒu was first kidnapped,
his Consort, Lady Zhèng, dreamed that someone cut off Yǒu’s head and carried it away.
She considered it an ill omen,
and several days later Yǒu was killed.
He was posthumously granted the titles Jiǎ Huángyuè (Bearing the Honorary Yellow Battle-Axe), Tàishī, Tàiwèi, and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and provided with a Wēnliáng carriage (a heated carriage).
His son, Bǎodé, succeeded him,
reaching the rank of Kāifǔ,
concurrently serving as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (Left Director of the Department of State Affairs).
Huàn, Prince Gāngsù of Shàngdǎng,
courtesy name Jìngshòu,
was the seventh son of Shénwǔ.
His natural disposition was heroic and outstanding,
unconventional and unique.
Even in childhood,
he prided himself on his military strategy.
Shénwǔ admired and loved his strength,
saying:
"This boy resembles me."
When he grew up,
his strength was such that he could lift a tripod (Dǐng),
and his talent in military matters was unparalleled.
He often said to his attendants:
"A person must not be uneducated,
but they must strive not to become a mere scholar (Bóshì)."
Therefore, when reading books, he knew the general outline,
but did not indulge much in study.
During the Yuánxiàng period,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Píngyuán Commandery.
When Wénxiāng encountered rebels,
Huàn was still young.
He was in the Western Study.
Hearing the commotion in the palace,
he was alarmed and said:
"The Eldest Brother must have met with disaster!"
He drew his bow and went out.
Late in Wǔdìng,
he was appointed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jìzhōu).
He had excellent governance in the prefecture.
Early in Tiānbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shàngdǎng,
and subsequently served as Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat) and Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
He built various cities, including Fá'è, with Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, and others.
Subsequently, he gathered frivolous people from Yè,
who infringed upon commanderies and counties,
and he was reprimanded by the judicial authorities (Fǎsī).
Wénxuān executed several of his attendants,
and Huàn was also censured.
In the sixth year,
he led troops to escort Xiāo Míng, Prince of Liáng, back to Jiāngnán.
He then defeated Dōngguān,
beheading Péi Zhīhéng, Tèjìn of Liáng, and others.
His prestige and reputation were extremely great.
In the eighth year,
he served as Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Initially,
sorcerers said that the one who would destroy Gāo (高) would wear black clothing.
Because of this, since Shénwǔ (神武) [Di],
whenever [the emperor] traveled,
he did not wish to see Buddhist monks,
because of the black robes.
At that time, Wénxuān (文宣) traveled to Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and asked his attendants about the thing he dreaded, saying:
“What substance is the blackest?”
They replied:
“Nothing surpasses lacquer.”
The Emperor considered Huàn (渙), the seventh son, to be the one referred to,
so he ordered Kùzhēn Dūdu (庫真都督) Pa-liù-hán Bóshēng (破六韓伯昇) to Yè (鄴) to summon Huàn.
When Huàn reached Zǐmò Qiáo (紫陌橋),
he killed Bóshēng and fled.
He crossed relying on the river (Hé),
but the local people seized him and sent him to the Emperor.
He was placed in an iron cage
and put into an underground dungeon along with the Prince of Yǒng'ān (永安), Jùn (浚).
After more than a year,
he was killed along with Jùn.
He was twenty-six years old at the time.
His consort, Lady Lǐ (李), was given in marriage to Féng Wénluò (馮文洛).
Wénluò was an old slave of the imperial household,
who through accumulating merit had reached the rank of Cìshǐ (刺史).
The Emperor had ordered Wénluò and others to kill Huàn,
thus he gave Huàn's wife to him as a wife.
In the first year of Qiánmíng (乾明),
the remaining bones of the two princes were collected and buried.
He was posthumously granted the rank of Sīkōng (司空),
and given the posthumous title Gāngsù (剛肅).
An imperial edict ordered Lady Lǐ to return to her residence.
However, Wénluò, still holding to his previous intention,
smartened himself up and went to see Lady Lǐ.
Lady Lǐ had her attendants form a strict array
and summoned Wénluò to stand below the steps,
rebuking him, saying:
“I encountered disaster and displacement,
leading to this great disgrace.
My resolve and integrity were too weak
to take my own life.
Fortunately, I received the gracious imperial edict,
and was able to return to the princely residence.
You are merely some family’s slave—
yet you still wish to insult me!”
Thereupon, she had him beaten with one hundred strokes of the staff,
and the flowing blood spattered the ground.
Huàn had no legitimate son.
His eldest concubine-born son, Bǎoyán (寶嚴), succeeded to the peerage in the second year of Héqīng (河清).
His rank was Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
Yù (淯), the Prince Jǐng (景王) of Xiāngchéng (襄城),
was the eighth son of Shénwǔ [Di].
His appearance was very handsome,
and in his youth he possessed talent and high aspirations.
During the Yuánxiàng (元象) era,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhāngwǔ (章武) Commandery.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo (天保) era,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiāngchéng Commandery.
In the spring of the second year,
he passed away.
When the various princes of the Qí (齊) clan selected officials for their states and aides for their households,
they often chose wealthy merchants, petty men, and young hawk-and-hound enthusiasts.
Only the Princes of Xiāngchéng, Guǎngníng (廣寧), and Lánlíng (蘭陵), etc., tended to appoint refined scholars and men of clear judgment.
They were praised for this at the time.
In the second month of the first year of Qiánmíng,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Jiǎ Huángyuè (假黃鉞), Tàishī (太師), Tàiwèi (太尉), and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事).
He had no son.
An imperial edict designated Liàng (亮), the second son of Yǎn (演), Prince of Chángshān (常山), as his heir.
Liàng’s courtesy name was Yàndào (彥道).
He was inherently respectful and filial,
had a fine demeanor,
and loved literature.
He served as the Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu (徐州),
but was dismissed from office for seizing property from merchants.
When the Later Lord (Hòu Zhǔ) was defeated and fled to Yè,
Liàng followed him.
He was promoted to Adjunct Tàiwèi and Tàifù (太傅).
When the Zhōu (周) army entered Yè,
Liàng resisted and defended Qǐxià Mén (啟夏門).
All the other armies were defeated without a fight,
and the Zhōu army entered through all the city gates;
only Liàng’s army retreated.
Liàng entered the precinct rails of the Great Ancestral Temple,
wept bitterly, and bowed in farewell,
and then he was captured by the Zhōu army.
Upon entering the Pass (Guān),
he was granted the title Yítóng (儀同) according to custom,
assigned to a distant border region,
and died in Lóngzhōu (龍州).
Jiē (湝), the Prince of Rènchéng (任城),
was the tenth son of Shénwǔ [Di].
As a youth, he was bright and intelligent.
He was enfeoffed at the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era.
Since the time of Xiàozhāo (孝昭) and Wǔchéng (武成),
when the imperial carriage returned to Yè,
Jiē was always ordered to garrison Jìnyáng,
managing the affairs of the Bīng (幷) Province.
He successively held the posts of Sītú (司徒), Tàiwèi, and Lù Shàngshū Shì for Bīng Province.
In the third year of Tiāntǒng (天統),
he was appointed Tàibǎo (太保) and Cìshǐ of Bīngzhōu,
and separately enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhèngpíng (正平) Commandery.
At that time, there was a woman washing clothes by the Fén River (Fén Shuǐ).
A man on horseback exchanged her new boots for his old ones and galloped away.
The woman took the old boots
and went to the provincial government to report the incident.
Jiē summoned all the old women from outside the city,
showed them the boots,
and deceived them, saying:
“A rider was robbed and murdered on the road,
leaving these boots behind.
Might he be related to any of you?”
One old woman struck her chest and wept, saying:
“My son wore these boots yesterday when going to his wife’s family.”
Acting on her words,
they captured the criminal.
At the time, he was praised for his perceptiveness.
At the beginning of Wǔpíng (武平),
he was promoted to Tàishī and Shepherd of Sīzhōu (司州).
He was sent out to serve as Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu (冀州),
was given the additional title Tàizǎi (太宰),
and was promoted to Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng), Grand Commandant (Dūdu), and Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu (青州).
Jiē repeatedly governed large provinces.
Although he was not entirely upright himself,
his generosity and clemency won the affection of the officials and people.
In the fifth year,
Cuī Wèibō (崔蔚波) of Qīngzhōu and others launched a night attack on the provincial capital.
Jiē organized his forces during the sudden crisis,
and everything was well-ordered.
He attacked the rebels
and thoroughly defeated them.
He was appointed Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng),
and transferred to Cìshǐ of Yíngzhōu (瀛州).
When the Later Lord fled to Yè,
Jiē was given the additional title of Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng).
When the Prince of Āndé (安德) claimed the exalted title in Jìnyáng,
he sent Liú Zǐ’áng (劉子昂) to present a memorial to Jiē [which said]:
“Since the Supreme Lord (Zhì Zūn) has fled,
and the Ancestral Temple is endangered,
the officials urged and pressured me
to temporarily take charge of the command.
When affairs are settled, rule will ultimately revert to you, my uncle.”
Jiē said:
“I am a subject;
how can I receive such a memorial?”
He arrested Zǐ’áng and sent him to Yè.
When the Emperor reached Jìzhōu (濟州),
he abdicated the throne in favor of Jiē,
but the imperial proclamation never reached him.
Jiē and Gāo Xiàohéng (孝珩), the Prince of Guǎngníng, recruited more than forty thousand men in Jìzhōu
to resist the Zhōu army.
Xiàn (憲), the Prince of Qí (齊) of Zhōu, came to attack.
He first sent letters and an amnesty decree,
but Jiē threw both into a well.
They were defeated in battle,
and Jiē and Xiàohéng were both captured.
Xiàn said:
“Why did the Prince of Rènchéng suffer to come to this?”
Jiē replied:
“Your humble servant is a son of Emperor Shénwǔ.
Among fifteen brothers,
I was fortunate to be the only one remaining.
Now that the dynastic altars have collapsed,
to die today
is to have no shame before my ancestral tomb.”
Xiàn admired his spirit
and returned his wife and children to him.
As he approached Yè City,
Jiē wept loudly while on horseback,
threw himself to the ground,
and had blood streaming down his face.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān (長安),
he soon died along with the Later Lord.
His consort, Lady Lú (盧), was bestowed upon Húxī Zhēng (斛斯徵).
She wore messy hair and a dirty face,
maintained a perpetual vegetarian fast, and did not speak or smile.
Zhēng released her,
and she became a Buddhist nun.
In the third year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
she submitted a memorial requesting Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) to bury Jiē and his five sons on the northern plain of Cháng'ān.
Gāoyáng Kāngmù Wáng Shí,
was the eleventh son of Shénwǔ.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of Tiānbǎo (550 CE).
In the tenth year (559 CE),
he was gradually promoted to Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
Because of his wit and flattery (or expediency),
he was favored by Wénxuān,
and was constantly at the Emperor’s side,
wielding the rod to strike the various princes.
The Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) deeply resented him.
Zhāng Yànzhī, Military Protector Grand Clerk (Hùjūn Zhǎngshǐ) and father of Wáng Shí’s consort, once requested permission to perform a major bow (bài) to Shí,
but Shí treated him discourteously.
The Emperor asked the reason,
and he replied:
“He is a Hàn (Chinese) man without official rank;
why should he be given courtesy?”
The Emperor thereupon promoted Yànzhī to be Governor of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ).
When Wénxuān died,
Shí was additionally appointed Minister of Education (Sītú),
and led the funeral procession of the Emperor’s coffin (Zǐgōng).
He played the flute,
and said,
“Does His Supremacy still know me or not?”
He also beat a barbarian drum (hú gǔ) for entertainment.
The Empress Dowager struck Shí more than a hundred times with a rod,
and shortly thereafter he died.
The Empress Dowager wept bitterly for him,
saying:
“I feared he would not achieve maturity,
so I administered the rod;
how could I have expected him to die from those wounds?”
In the beginning of Qiánmíng (560 CE),

he was posthumously granted the titles of Acting Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Minister of Education (Sītú), and Director of Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
His son Shìyì succeeded to the title.
Bólíng Wénjiǎn Wáng Jǐ,
was the twelfth son of Shénwǔ.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of Tiānbǎo.
Jǐ once followed Wénxuān on an imperial tour,
and while en route suddenly missed the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
so he ran away and returned home.
The Emperor was enraged,
and approached him with a drawn weapon (bái rèn),
causing him to become mentally disturbed.
He successively held the position of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
In the beginning of Héqīng (562 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Governor of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the fifth year of Tiāntǒng (569 CE),
while in the province he said to people:
“Considering the sequence, it should be my turn now.”
The Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ) heard this,
and secretly sent someone to murder him.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Acting Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), and Director of Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
His son Zhì succeeded to the title.
Huàshān Wáng Cáo,
was the thirteenth son of Shénwǔ.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīnpíng Commandery;
in the ninth year (558 CE),
his title was changed to Āndìng;
in the tenth year (559 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Huàshān.
He successively held the positions of Minister of the Palace Library (Zhōngshū Lìng) and Governor of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Cìshǐ),
and was concurrently granted the title of Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
He died in the province,
and was posthumously granted the titles of Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng), Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), and Director of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū).
Among the princes, he was the weakest and most incompetent.
His consort, Lady Wáng,
was the daughter of Wáng Qià, Groom to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
She committed adultery with a common servant (cāngtóu).
Cáo knew about it but was unable to prohibit her.
Later, when the matter was revealed,
Lady Wáng was granted death (cì sǐ),
and Cáo was sentenced by imperial decree to receive one hundred strokes of the rod.
His foolishness was thus extreme.
Féngyì Wáng Rùn,
courtesy name Zǐzé,
was the fourteenth son of Shénwǔ.
When he was young,
Shénwǔ remarked, saying:
“This is the ‘colt that runs a thousand *lǐ*’ of our family.”
He was enfeoffed at the beginning of Tiānbǎo.
He successively held the positions of Grand Controller of the Northeast Circuit (Dà Xíngtái), Right Executive Assistant (Yòu Púshè), Area Commander (Dūdū), and Governor of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Rùn had handsome features and bearing.
When he was fourteen or fifteen years old,
his mother, Consort Zhèng, slept with him,
and there were sounds of impropriety.
When he grew up,
he was honest, cautious, upright, and refined.
He was skilled in administrative affairs,
even to the point of exposing hidden deceit,
and corrupt officials had no way to conceal their true intentions.
Wáng Huíluò, who established a manor (Kāifǔ), and Dúgū Zhī, Grand Area Commander of Six Provinces (Liù Zhōu Dà Dūdū), encroached upon and stole public fields,
and accepted bribes.
Rùn investigated and reported their actions.
The two men submitted a memorial stating that,
when the Prince went out to send off the Controller's Envoy (Táishǐ),
he ascended the old altar of Wèi Wén,
looked south, and sighed deeply,
the meaning of which was unfathomable.
Wǔchéng ordered Yuán Wényáo to proceed to the province and declare an imperial edict, saying:
“Féngyì Wáng has been cautious since childhood,
and has committed no unlawful acts while in the province.
We trust him thoroughly.
Ascending a height and gazing into the distance
is a normal human sentiment.
These rat-like creatures want to lightly slander and frame him,
creating trouble where there is none (qū shēng méimù).”
Thereupon, Huíluò was sentenced to two hundred strokes of the whip,
and Dúgū Zhī was sentenced to one hundred strokes of the rod.
Soon after, he became Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
and concurrently held the position of Junior Preceptor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàoshī).

He successively held the positions of Minister of Education (Sītú), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ), Provincial Governor of Sīzhōu (Sīzhōu Mù), Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo), Controller of the Hénán Circuit (Hénán Dào Xíngtái), and Director of State Affairs (Lǐng Lù Shàngshū).
He was separately enfeoffed as Duke of Wénchéng Commandery (Wénchéng Jùn Gōng),
and held the titles of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī) and Grand Minister (Tàizǎi).
He later served again as Governor of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ).
He died,
and was posthumously granted the titles of Acting Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè) and Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng).
His son Màodé succeeded him.
Hànyáng Jìnghuái Wáng Qià,
courtesy name Jìngyán,
was the fifteenth son of Shénwǔ.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of Tiānbǎo.
In the fifth year (554 CE),
he died,
aged thirteen.
In the first year of Qiánmíng (560 CE),
he was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
He had no son;
therefore, Jiàndé, the second son of Rènchéng Wáng, was made his heir.
Biographies, Chapter 3: The Six Princes of Wénxiāng: Hénán Kāngshū Wáng Xiàoyú, Guǎngníng Wáng Xiàohéng, Héjiān Wáng Xiàowǎn, Lánlíng Wǔ Wáng Xiàoguàn, Āndé Wáng Yánzōng, Yúyáng Wáng Shàoxìn.
Wénxiāng had six sons: Héjiān Wáng Xiàowǎn was born of Empress Wénjìng Yuán;
Hénán Wáng Xiàoyú was born of Lady Sòng;
Guǎngníng Wáng Xiàohéng was born of Lady Wáng;
Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng (Xiàoguàn) did not record the name of his mother;
Āndé Wáng Yánzōng was born of Lady Chén;
Yúyáng Wáng Shàoxìn was born of Lady Yàn.
Hénán Kāngshū Wáng Xiàoyú,
courtesy name Zhèngdé,
was the eldest son of Wénxiāng.
He was initially enfeoffed as Duke of Hénán Commandery (Hénán Jùn Gōng).
When Qí accepted the abdication (of Eastern Wèi),
his peerage was elevated to Prince (Wáng).
He successively held the positions of Minister of the Palace Library (Zhōngshū Lìng) and Provincial Governor of Sīzhōu (Sīzhōu Mù).
Originally,
Xiàoyú was raised in Shénwǔ’s palace,
and being of the same age as Wǔchéng, they loved each other.
When they planned to execute Yáng Yīn and others,
Xiàoyú participated in the plot.
When Wǔchéng ascended the throne,
he was treated with exceptional courtesy.
When the Emperor was in Jìnyáng,
he personally issued an edict to Xiàoyú, saying:
“I have drunk two cups of Fénqīng wine;
I urge you to pour yourself two cups in Yè.”
Their intimacy and affection was thus deep.
Xiàoyú’s appearance was imposing and grand;
his spirit was vigorous and resolute.
He was humble, cautious, generous, and tolerant,
and also loved literature.
He read books quickly and alertly,
reading ten lines at once.
When reviewing, he never missed a single element.
Initially,
Wénxiāng had constructed a park with mountains and ponds east of Yè for recreational viewing,
and the customs of the time were dazzled by it.
Xiàoyú thereupon built a water pavilion and a dragon boat in his residence,
erecting banners and spears on the boat,
and frequently gathered the various princes for banquets and archery games.
Wǔchéng visited his residence,
saw it, and was pleased.
Therefore, the Emperor greatly increased the magnificence of the recreation in the Imperial Rear Garden.
Consequently, both the noble and the humble admired and imitated this,
building such structures everywhere.
*Wǔchéng* often made *Hé Shìkāi* and Empress *Hú* sit opposite each other and play *shuò* (a board game).
*Xiàoyú* remonstrated, saying:
"The Empress is the mother of the realm;
she should not touch hands with subjects."
The Emperor deeply accepted this.
Later, he also said that the father of the Prince of *Zhàojùn* had died unnaturally,
and should not be trusted.
Because of this, both *Ruì* and *Shìkāi* viewed him with hostility.
*Shìkāi* secretly reported his extravagance and presumption.
*Ruì* also said that east of the mountains, they only heard of the Prince of *Hénán*,
and did not hear of Your Majesty.
The Emperor consequently grew jealous of him.
*Ěrzhū* the royal consort, named *Mónǚ*,
had previously served the Empress Dowager.
*Xiàoyú* had previously had relations with her.
Later, during the night of the Crown Prince's wedding,
*Xiàoyú* secretly spoke with her.
*Wǔchéng* became furious,
and immediately made him drink thirty-seven cups of wine.
His body was extremely large and fat;
his belt measured ten *wéi* (fathoms/circumferences).
He ordered *Lóu Zǐyàn* to take him out in a carriage,
and poisoned him in the carriage.
When they reached *Xīhuámén* (West Glorious Gate),
he was distressed by heat and agitation,
and he threw himself into the water and died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of *Tàiwèi* (Grand Commandant) and *Lù Shàngshūshì* (Director of Affairs of the Secretariat).
His son, *Hóngjié*, succeeded him.
*Xiàoyú*'s mother,
was the granddaughter of *Wèi* Minister of Personnel *Sòng Biàn*.
Originally, she was the concubine of *Wèi* Prince of *Yǐngchuān*, *Bīn*,
but was taken by *Wénxiāng*,
and gave birth to *Xiàoyú*.
When *Xiàoyú* returned to his residence,
she became the Grand Consort (*Tàifēi*).
*Xiàoyú*'s Consort,
was the daughter of *Lú Zhèngshān*,
and was the elder maternal cousin of *Wǔchéng*'s Empress *Hú*.
After *Xiàoyú* died,
Grand Consort *Sòng* was slandered and accused by Consort *Lú*.
*Wǔchéng* killed her.
*Guǎngníng* Prince *Xiàohéng*,
was the second son of *Wénxiāng*.

He successively held the positions of Governor of *Sīzhōu*, Director of the Secretariat (*Shàngshūlìng*), Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*), Minister over the Masses (*Sītú*), Director of the Secretariat Affairs (*Lù Shàngshū*), Grand General (*Dà Jiāngjūn*), and Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*).
*Xiàohéng* appreciated and admired talented people,
studied widely in the Classics and Histories,
enjoyed composing literature,
and possessed artistic skills.
He once painted a goshawk himself on the wall of the main hall;
everyone who saw it thought it was real.
He also painted a portrait of court officials,
which was also considered the finest masterpiece of the time.
When the Later Ruler fled to *Yè* after his defeat at *Jìnzhōu*,
he summoned the princes and dukes to discuss matters in the *Hánguāng* Palace.
*Xiàohéng* argued that since the great enemy had advanced deeply,
the situation required swift adaptation (strategic changes).
It was fitting to order the Prince of *Rènchéng* to lead the troops from the *Yōuzhōu* circuit and enter *Tǔmén*,
making a loud display heading toward *Bìngzhōu*.
*Dúgū Yǒngyè* should lead the *Luòzhōu* troops toward *Tóngguān*,
making a loud display heading toward *Cháng'ān*.
"I request permission to lead the capital troops out of *Fǔkǒu*,
advancing with drums beating to meet and fight the enemy.
When the enemy hears that there are forces north and south,
they will naturally scatter and disperse."
He also requested that court ladies and treasures be distributed to the officers and soldiers.
The Emperor could not adopt these plans.
When *Chéngguāng* ascended the throne,
he appointed *Xiàohéng* as *Tàizǎi* (Grand Tutor).
He conspired with *Hūyán Zú*, *Mòduōlóu Jìngxiǎn*, and *Wèi Xiāngyuàn*,
setting the fifth day of the first lunar month as the date.
*Xiàohéng* was to execute *Gāo Ānàgōng* at the *Qiānqiū* Gate;
*Xiāngyuàn*, being inside, would respond with the palace guards;
and *Zú* and *Jìngxiǎn* would lead their forces out from the *Yóuyù* Park.
Soon afterward, however, *Ānàgōng* took a shortcut from his separate residence and entered the palace,
and the plan failed.
*Xiàohéng* then requested permission to go out and resist the Western army.
He said to *Ānàgōng*, *Hán Chángluán*, *Chén Déxìn*, and others:
"If the court does not graciously send me to strike the bandits,
aren't they afraid that *Xiàohéng* will rebel?
If *Xiàohéng* defeats *Yǔwén Yōng*,
and then reaches *Cháng'ān*,
how would rebellion then relate to the affairs of the state?
Given the urgency of today,
they are still harboring such suspicion."
*Gāo* and *Hán* feared that he might revolt,
and sent *Xiàohéng* out as the Prefect of *Cāngzhōu*.
Upon arriving at the prefecture,
he gathered five thousand men and met the Prince of *Rènchéng* at *Xìndū*,
where they jointly planned the restoration.
When the *Zhōu* Prince of *Qí*, *Xiàn*, came to attack,
their forces were too weak to resist.
*Xiàohéng* angrily said:
"Because of that petty man, *Gāo Ānàgōng*,
my path is blocked!"
*Qí* turncoat subject *Qǐfú Lìnglìnghé* stabbed *Xiàohéng* with a spear, causing him to fall from his horse.
His servant *Báizé* shielded him with his body,
but *Xiàohéng* was still wounded in several places,
and was subsequently captured.
Prince of *Qí*, *Xiàn*, asked *Xiàohéng* the reason for *Qí*'s fall.
*Xiàohéng* recounted the national crisis,
his words and tears flowing together,
with dignified bearing.
*Xiàn* changed his expression for him,
personally washed his wounds and applied medicine,
and treated him with great courtesy.
*Xiàohéng* sighed privately, saying:
"*Lǐ Mùshú* said the *Qí* clan would last twenty-eight years;
now it has turned out to be true.
Apart from Emperor *Shénwǔ*,
none of my uncles or brothers have lived to forty;
this is fate.
The reigning monarch lacked unique foresight,
and the chancellors were not entrusted with pillar-like responsibility.
I only regret that I could not hold the military tally,
receive the strategy decided in the ancestral temple,
and fully exert my utmost strength."
Upon arriving at *Cháng'ān*,
he was granted the titles of *Kāifǔ* and County Marquis, according to standard practice.
Later, when Emperor *Wǔ* of *Zhōu* was at *Yúnyáng*,
he hosted a banquet for the former *Qí* ruler and officials.
He personally played the *Hú* *pípá* (lute),
and ordered *Xiàohéng* to play the flute.
*Xiàohéng* declined, saying:
"The music of a ruined state
is not worth listening to."
The Emperor insisted that he play.
As he lifted the flute barely to his mouth,
tears streamed down and he choked with sobs.
Emperor *Wǔ* then stopped (insisting).
In the tenth month of that year,
his illness worsened.
He requested permission to be buried back in *Shāndōng*.
This was granted.
He died soon after.
An order was issued for him to be returned and buried in *Yè*.
*Héjiān* Prince *Xiàowǎn*,
was the third son of *Wénxiāng*.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of *Tiānbǎo* (550 CE).
During the *Tiāntǒng* era,
he was repeatedly promoted to Director of the Secretariat (*Shàngshūlìng*).
Previously,
when the *Tūjué* and *Zhōu* armies invaded *Tàiyuán*,
*Wǔchéng* intended to evade them and flee east.
*Xiàowǎn* struck his horse and remonstrated,
requesting that the matter be entrusted to the Prince of *Zhàojùn* for deployment,
assuring that the arrangements would be orderly.
The Emperor accepted his suggestion.
*Xiàowǎn* removed his helmet and prepared to leave (to execute the command).
The Emperor sent someone to call him back.
When the *Zhōu* army retreated,
he was appointed Prefect of *Bìngzhōu*.
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬), being the legitimate eldest son of Wénxiāng (文襄),
was arrogant and conceited.
When the King of Hénán (河南王) died,
none of the princes in the palace dared to speak out,
only Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) cried loudly and exited.
He also resented the powerful officials,
making a straw man and shooting arrows at it.
Hé Shìkāi (和士開) and Zǔ Tǐng (祖珽) slandered him,
saying:
"The straw man represents Your Sacred Person.
Also, earlier when the Tujue (突厥) arrived at the prefecture,
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) took off his helmet and threw it to the ground,
saying 'Am I an old woman
who needs to wear this?'
These words referred to the empress dowager."
Initially,
there was a rumor in the Wèi (魏) era:
"Grain planted in Hénán (河南) grows in Héběi (河北),
a golden rooster crows on a white poplar tree."
Zǔ Tǐng (祖珽) explained it thus:
"Hénán (河南) and Héběi (河北)
refer to Héjiān (河間).
The golden rooster crowing means
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) will establish the golden rooster and grant a general amnesty."
The Emperor was somewhat misled by this.
At that time, Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) obtained a Buddha tooth,
which he placed in his residence,
and at night it emitted divine light.
Zhāoxuán Dū Fǎshùn (昭玄都法順) requested to report this to the throne,
but Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) did not agree.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he ordered a search,
and hundreds of spears and banners for guarding the treasury were found.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he considered it an act of rebellion.
He interrogated Gāo Xiàowǎn's (孝琬) concubines;
one named Chén (陳), who was out of favor,
falsely replied
"Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) drew a likeness of Your Majesty and cried over it,"
but in reality, it was an image of Wénxiāng (文襄),
and Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) often wept before it.
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered Wǔwèi Hèlián Fǔxuán (武衞赫連輔玄) to flog him with a reverse whip.
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) called out "Uncle,"
the Emperor angrily said:
"Who is your uncle?
How dare you call me uncle!"
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) said:
"As the legitimate grandson of Shénwǔ Huángdì (神武皇帝),
the legitimate son of Wénxiāng Huángdì (文襄皇帝),
and the maternal nephew of Wèi Xiàojìng Huángdì (魏孝靜皇帝),
why can I not call you uncle?"
The Emperor became even more furious,
broke both his shins, and he died.
He was buried in the Western Hills;
after the Emperor's demise,
he was reburied.
His son Zhèng Lǐ (正禮) succeeded him;
he was intelligent and bright in his youth,
and could recite the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋).
When Qí (齊) fell,
he was moved to Miánzhōu (綿州) where he died.
Lánlíng Wǔ Wáng Gāo Chánggōng (蘭陵武王長恭),
also named Gāo Xiàoguàn (孝瓘),
was the fourth son of Wénxiāng (文襄).
He successively served as Píngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史).
When the Tujue (突厥) invaded Jìnyáng (晉陽),
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) fought with all his might against them.
During the defeat at Mángshān (芒山),
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) led the central army,
and with five hundred cavalry, he re-entered the Zhōu (周) army's lines,
then reached below Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Being severely besieged,
the people on the city wall did not recognize him,
so Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) removed his helmet to show his face,
and then crossbowmen were sent down to rescue him,
resulting in a great victory.
The warriors together sang a song about him,
which is the "Lánlíng Wáng Rùzhèn Qǔ" (蘭陵王入陣曲).
He successively held posts as Sīzhōu Mù (司州牧) and governor of Qīng (青) and Yíng (瀛) prefectures,
and accepted quite a lot of wealth.
Later he became Tàiwèi (太尉),
and with Duàn Sháo (段韶) he attacked Bǎigǔ (栢谷),
and also assaulted Dìngyáng (定陽).
When Duàn Sháo (韶) fell ill,
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) took command of his troops.
For his military achievements, he was successively enfeoffed as Duke of Jùlù (鉅鹿), Chánglè (長樂), Lèpíng (樂平), and Gāoyáng (高陽) commanderies.
After the victory at Mángshān (芒山),
the Later Emperor said to Gāo Chánggōng (長恭):
"You entered the lines too deeply;
if you had suffered a defeat, you would have regretted it too late."
He replied:
"It was a family matter and urgent,
so I didn't realize it."
The Emperor disliked his referring to it as a "family matter,"
and thus grew wary of him.
When he was in Dìngyáng (定陽),
his subordinate Wèi Xiāngyuàn (尉相願) said to him:
"Since Your Highness has received the court's trust,
how can you be so greedy and cruel?"
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) did not answer.
Wèi Xiāngyuàn (相願) said:
"Is it not because of the great victory at Mángshān (芒山),
that you fear being envied for your prestige and might,
and wish to defile yourself?"
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) said:
"Indeed."
Wèi Xiāngyuàn (相願) said:
"If the court truly envies Your Highness,
committing this offense will certainly incur punishment;
seeking fortune will instead hasten disaster."
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) wept,
knelt forward and asked for a method to ensure his safety.
Wèi Xiāngyuàn (相願) said:
"Your Highness already has achievements from before,
and now you have reported another victory;
your prestige and renown are too great.
You should feign illness and stay at home,
not getting involved in affairs."
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) thought his words were right,
but was unable to retire.
When Jianghuai (江淮) was plagued by bandits,
he feared being made a general again,
and sighed:
"My face was swollen last year;
why does it not flare up now?"
From then on, he suffered from illness but did not seek treatment.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Wǔpíng (武平)
the Emperor sent Xú Zhīfàn (徐之範) to give him poisoned wine.
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) said to his consort, Lady Zhèng (鄭氏):
"I served my sovereign loyally;
what sin have I committed against Heaven
to suffer poisoning?"
His consort said:
"Why not request an audience with His Majesty?"
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) said:
"How can I gain an audience with His Majesty?"
He then drank the poison and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi (太尉).
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) had a gentle appearance but a strong heart,
and possessed both a beautiful voice and countenance.
As a general, he was diligent in minor matters,
and whenever he received delicacies,
even a single melon or a few fruits,
he would certainly share them with his officers and soldiers.
When he was first in Yíngzhōu (瀛州),
his staff officer Yáng Shìshēn (陽士深) impeached him for corruption,
and he was dismissed from office.
Later, when attacking Dìngyáng (定陽),
Yáng Shìshēn (士深) was in the army,
and feared that misfortune would befall him.
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) heard of this and said:
"I never had such an intention."
He then sought a minor fault,
and had Yáng Shìshēn (士深) flogged twenty times with a rod to reassure him.
Once, he went to court, and his retainers all dispersed,
with only one remaining;
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) returned alone,
without scolding or punishing anyone.
Wǔchéng (武成) rewarded his merits,
ordering Jiǎ Hù (賈護) to buy twenty concubines for him,
but he only accepted one.
He had a debt bond for a thousand pieces of gold;
on the day of his death,
he burned them all.
Ān Dé Wáng Yánzōng
was the fifth son of Wénxiāng.
His mother, Lady Chén,
was a courtesan of Guǎngyáng Wáng.
Yánzōng was raised by Wénxuān from a young age.
When he was twelve,
Wénxuān still had him ride on his belly,
letting him urinate into his navel,
and hugging him, said:
“It is pitiful that I only have this one.”
He asked what king he wanted to be,
and Yánzōng replied:
“I wish to be Chōngtiān Wáng.”
Wénxuān asked Yáng Yīn,
who said:
“There is no such commandery name in the world.
I wish for him to be at peace with virtue (ān yú dé).”
Thereupon, he was enfeoffed as Ān Dé Wáng.
When he was the Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu,
he defecated from an upper story,
making people below open their mouths to receive it.
He mixed steamed pork with human feces to feed his attendants,
and those who showed reluctance were whipped.
When Xiàozhāo Dì heard of this,
he sent Zhào Dàodé to the prefecture to whip him one hundred times.
Dàodé, seeing that Yánzōng did not receive the flogging with proper respect,
added thirty more blows.
He also used prisoners to test swords,
to examine their sharpness or dullness.
He was arrogant, indulgent, and committed many unlawful acts.
Wǔchéng had him flogged,
and killed nine of his close attendants.
From then on, he deeply reformed himself.
When Lánlíng Wáng achieved victory at Mángshān,
he boasted of his military might,
and all his brothers admired him.
Yánzōng alone said:
“The fourth brother is no true hero.
Why did he not press on with the victory and directly enter?
If Yánzōng were in that position,
how could Guānxī possibly still exist?”
When Lánlíng died,
his consort, Lady Zhèng, donated her pearl necklace to the Buddha.
Guǎngníng Wáng tried to redeem it.
Yánzōng wrote a letter to remonstrate,
and his tears filled the paper.
When Héjiān died,
Yánzōng also cried many tears.
He also made a straw figure in the likeness of Wǔchéng,
whipped it, and questioned it, saying:
“Why did you kill my brother!”
His servant reported this,
and Wǔchéng pinned Yánzōng to the ground,
flogged him two hundred times with a horsewhip,
nearly killing him.
Later, he successively held the posts of Sītú and Tàiwèi.
During the campaign of Píngyáng,
the Hòuzhǔ personally commanded,
ordering Yánzōng to lead the right army to fight first,
capturing Zhōu Kāifǔ Zōngtǐng outside the city.
During the great battle,
Yánzōng, with his subordinates, entered the Zhōu army twice,
and none failed to be scattered.
While all other armies were defeated,
Yánzōng alone preserved his entire army.
When the Hòuzhǔ was about to flee to Jìnyáng,
Yánzōng said:
“Your Majesty, just stay in the camp and do not move.
Entrust the troops to your servant,
and your servant can defeat them.”
The Emperor did not accept this.
When he arrived at Bīngzhōu,
and further heard that the Zhōu army had already entered Quèshǔ Gǔ,
he then appointed Yánzōng as Xiàngguó and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
to take overall command of the military affairs of Shānxī.
He said:
“Bīngzhōu, brother, you take it for yourself.
I am leaving now.”
Yánzōng said:
“Your Majesty, for the sake of the altars of soil and grain, do not move.
Your servant will fight with all his might for Your Majesty.”
Luò Típó said:
“The Supreme One’s plan is already decided,
Your Highness must not obstruct it.”
The Hòuzhǔ ultimately fled to Yè.
The generals and officers in Bīngzhōu all pleaded, saying:
“If Your Highness does not become the Son of Heaven,
we truly cannot fight with all our might.”
Yánzōng, having no choice,
ascended the imperial throne,
and issued an edict saying:
“Wǔpíng is weak,
the government is controlled by eunuchs,
strife is within the inner court,
and bandits rise on the frontiers.
Breaking through the passes and fleeing by night,
his whereabouts unknown,
the enterprise of our High Ancestor will fall to the ground.
The princes, dukes, ministers, and officials
have earnestly urged and compelled me;
I now respectfully assume the revered position.
Let there be a great amnesty throughout the realm,
and change the seventh year of Wǔpíng to the first year of Déchāng.”
He appointed Jìnchāng Wáng Táng Yōng as prime minister,
Qíchāng Wáng Mòduōlóu Jìngxiǎn, Shùyáng Wáng Hé'ā Yúzǐ,
the Right Protector-General Duàn Chàng, Wǔwèi General Xiānglǐ Sēngjiā, Kāifǔ Hán Gǔhú, and Hóumòchén Luòzhōu as his close aides.
When the people heard of this,
those who came without being summoned
followed one after another.
Yánzōng was physically robust;
when sitting, he leaned back,
when lying down, he lay prostrate.
People laughed at him,
but then he would rise up with a roar.
His strength was extraordinary,
and he galloped through battle formations,
swift and agile as if flying.
He emptied the treasuries and the beautiful women of the imperial harem,
distributing them to his generals and soldiers,
and confiscated over a thousand households of inner attendants.
The Hòuzhǔ said to his close ministers:
“I would rather the Zhōu obtain Bīngzhōu
than Ān Dé obtain it.”
His attendants said:
“That is reasonable.”
When Yánzōng saw the soldiers,
he personally held their hands,
stated his name and expressed his resolve,
weeping and sobbing.
Everyone vied to die for him;
even children and women climbed onto roofs, bared their arms,
and threw bricks and stones to resist the Zhōu army.
The Tèjìn and Kāifǔ, Nàlú Ānshēng, who was defending Tàigǔ,
rebelled with ten thousand troops.
The Zhōu army besieged Jìnyáng,
appearing like black clouds gathering from all four directions.
Yánzōng ordered Mòduōlóu Jìngxiǎn and Hán Gǔhú to defend the south of the city,
and Hé'ā Yúzǐ and Duàn Chàng to defend the east of the city.
Yánzōng personally confronted Zhōu Qí Wáng north of the city,
wielding a great spear,
going back and forth supervising the battle,
sweeping away all in his path.
The Shàngshū Lìshǐ Jǔshān was also large and strong,
and followed on foot, wielding a long saber,
killing and wounding many.
Wǔwèi Lán Fúróng and Qílián Yáncháng both died in battle.
Ā Yú Zǐ and Duàn Chàng defected to Zhōu with a thousand cavalry.
The Zhōu army attacked the eastern gate.
As dusk fell,
they managed to enter.
They advanced their troops and burned the gatehouse of the Buddhist temple;
the flying flames illuminated Heaven and Earth.
Yán Zōng and Jìng Xiǎn entered through the gate
and struck them from both sides.
The Zhōu army fell into great disorder,
struggling for the gate, crushing each other.
The Qí people hacked and stabbed from the rear,
and over two thousand men died.
Almost all of Zhōu Wǔ Dì's attendants were gone.
He had no path to extricate himself.
The Palace Attendant, Senior Officer Zhāng Shòu Zhé, managed to pull the horse's head,
while Hèbá Fó'ēn used his whip to clear the way behind him.
With great difficulty, he barely managed to get out.
The Qí people fought fiercely,
nearly striking him.
The area east of the city was narrow and winding;
Fó'ēn and the surrenderer Pí Zǐxìn guided him,
and he narrowly escaped.
It was the fourth watch of the night.
Yán Zōng believed Zhōu Wǔ Dì had been killed by the disordered soldiers,
and sent men to search among the piled corpses for the one with the long beard,
but they did not find him.
At that time, since the Qí people had won,
they entered the residential wards and drank wine,
all lying down completely drunk.
Yán Zōng was no longer able to organize them.
Zhōu Wǔ Dì exited the city,
feeling extremely hungry,
and planned for escape and concealment.
The Prince of Qí, Yǔwén Xiàn, and the Pillar of the State Wáng Yì remonstrated,
believing that if he left, he certainly would not survive.
Yán Zōng's defecting general, Duàn Chàng, also strongly asserted that the city interior was empty.
Zhōu Wǔ Dì then halted his horse,
sounded the horn to gather his troops,
and shortly thereafter, the army rallied again.
The following morning,
he returned to attack the eastern gate
and subdued it,
and also entered the southern gate.
Yán Zōng fought
until his strength was exhausted,
fled to the north of the city,
and was captured in a private house.
Zhōu Wǔ Dì immediately dismounted,
and held his hand.
Yán Zōng declined, saying:
"How dare the hand of a dead man approach the Most Honored One?"
The Emperor said:
"We are both Sons of Heaven of two states;
what resentment or hatred is there?
I came simply for the sake of the common people.
Do not be afraid;
I will certainly not harm you."
He ordered him to put his official robes and cap back on,
and treated him with respect.
Previously,
there was a mountain in Gāodū Jùn,
whose sheer cliff overlooked the water,
where suddenly a black inscription appeared,
saying:
"Qí perishes, Yán Zōng."
When washed, the writing became even clearer.
The Emperor sent someone to copy it,
but the messenger changed 亡 (wáng, perish) to 上 (shàng, ascend/superior).
The events now corresponded to the original omen.
Before Yán Zōng's defeat,
while in the administration hall in Yè,
he saw two suns placed side by side.
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, at the hour of *bū*, he received the imperial mandate to defend Bīng Zhōu.
The following day he established his honorable title [as emperor].
Without skipping a day, he was surrounded,
and after one night,
he was defeated by mealtime.
His era name was Déchāng.
Enthusiasts (of omens) said this was because he had obtained "two suns."
Afterwards, Zhōu Wǔ Dì asked Yán Zōng for a plan to capture Yè.
He refused, saying:
"A high official of a ruined state cannot plan for survival;
this is not something your servant can address."
When strongly pressed,
he then said:
"If the Prince of Rènchéng goes to reinforce Yè,
your servant cannot know [the result].
But if the current ruler (Gāo Wěi) defends himself,
Your Majesty’s soldiers will not need to stain their blades with blood."
When they arrived at Cháng'ān,
Zhōu Wǔ drank wine with the Qí ruler and his officials.
He ordered the Hòu Zhǔ to rise and dance.
Yán Zōng was overwhelmed by grief and could not control himself.
He repeatedly tried to take poison and kill himself,
but his attending maidservant desperately restrained him and stopped him.
Not long after,
Zhōu Wǔ falsely accused the Hòu Zhǔ and Yán Zōng, among others,
claiming they had secretly supported Mù Típó's rebellion,
and ordered them all to be granted death.
They all declared themselves innocent.
Yán Zōng merely rolled up his sleeve,
wept, but remained silent.
They all died with peppercorns stuffed in their mouths.
The following year,
Consort Lǐ collected and buried them.
When the Hòu Zhǔ abdicated in favor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
Sūn Zhèngyán secretly told someone:
"During the Wǔdìng period, I served as the Personnel Officer in Guǎng Zhōu,
and heard Cáo Pǔyǎn of Xiāngchéng say:
'Among the sons of King Gāo (Gāo Huān),
Ā Bǎo shall be the Son of Heaven,
and until Gāo Dé zhī Chéng zhī, [the dynasty] will perish.'
'Ā Bǎo' refers to Tiānbǎo,
'Dé zhī' refers to Déchāng,
and 'Chéng zhī' refers to the Hòu Zhǔ's era name Chéngguāng.
These words finally proved true."
Shào Xìn, the Prince of Yúyáng,
was the sixth son of Wén Xiāng.

He successively held the posts of Special Advanced Official (Tè Jìn), Governor-General (Kāi Fǔ), Central Commander (Zhōng Lǐng Jūn), Protector General (Hù Jūn), and Governor of Qīng Zhōu (Qīng Zhōu Cì Shǐ).
When he traveled through Yúyáng,
he sat on the same couch with the greatly wealthy man Zhōng Chángmìng.
When the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) Zhèng Dàogài came for an audience,
Chángmìng wanted to rise,
but Shào Xìn would not allow it,
saying:
"What kind of small man is this,
that the master should rise for him?"
He then swore brotherhood with Chángmìng,
and his consort became sworn sisters with Chángmìng’s wife.
He demanded that the entire Zhōng household, young and old, provide gifts and bribes.
Consequently, the Zhōng family became poor.
When Qí was destroyed,
he died in Cháng'ān.

Memoir Four: The Four Princes of Wén Xuān: Shào Dé, Prince of Tàiyuán; Shào Yì, Prince of Fànyáng; Shào Rén, Prince of Xīhé; Shào Lián, Prince of Lǒngxī. The Six Princes of Xiào Zhāo: Bǎinián, Prince of Lèlíng; Yàndé, Prince of Shǐpíng; Yànjī, Prince of Chéngyáng; Yànkāng, Prince of Dìngyáng; Yànzhōng, Prince of Rǔyáng; Yànlǐ, Prince of Rǔnán. The Twelve Princes of Wǔ Chéng: Chuò, Prince of Nányáng; Yǎn, Prince of Lángyé; Kuò, Prince of Qí'ān; Zhēn, Prince of Běipíng; Rén Yīng, Prince of Gāopíng; Rén Guāng, Prince of Huáinán; Rén Jǐ, Prince of Xīhé; Rén Yōng, Prince of Lèpíng; Rén Jiǎn, Prince of Yǐngchuān; Rén Yǎ, Prince of Ānyáng; Rén Zhí, Prince of Dānyáng; Rén Qiān, Prince of Dōnghǎi.
The five sons of Wén Xuān: Empress Lǐ Hòu gave birth to the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì) and Shào Dé, Prince of Tàiyuán.
Consort Fèng Shì Fù gave birth to Shào Yì, Prince of Fànyáng.
Consort Péi Pín gave birth to Shào Rén, Prince of Xīhé.
Consort Yán Pín gave birth to Shào Lián, Prince of Lǒngxī.
Shào Dé, Prince of Tàiyuán,
was the second son of Wén Xuān.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was appointed Governor-General with the Honors of the Three Dukes (Kāi Fǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī).
Wǔ Chéng, enraged at Empress Lǐ Hòu,
cursed Shào Dé, saying:
"When your father beat me,
you didn't even come to save me!"
He bludgeoned him to death with the ring of a sword,
and personally buried him with earth in the Yóuyù Yuán garden.
In the first year of Wǔpíng,
an imperial edict made Biàn Cái, the son of the Prince of Fànyáng, his successor,
inheriting the title of Prince of Tàiyuán.
Fànyáng Wáng Shàoyì
was the third son of Wénxuān.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as Guăngyáng,
later as Fànyáng.
He successively held the positions of Shìzhōng and Qīngdū Yĭn.
He enjoyed drinking with petty officials,
arbitrarily appointed Neicān (palace attendants),
and beat to death the scholar Rèn Fāngróng.
Wŭchéng once beat him two hundred strokes with a staff,
then sent him to Zhāoxìn Hòu,
who then beat him another hundred strokes.
When the Latter Lord (Hòuzhŭ) fled to Yè,
Shàoyì was made Shàngshū Lìng and Dìngzhōu Cìshĭ.
When Zhōu Wŭdì conquered Bīngzhōu,
he appointed Fēng Fŭxiàng as the Commander-in-Chief (Zŏngguăn) of Běishuòzhōu.
This place was a critical garrison of Qí,
where many brave warriors gathered.
The former Chief Clerk Zhào Mù
and the Marshal Wáng Dāngwàn, among others, plotted to seize Fŭxiàng
and welcome the Prince of Rènchéng from Yíngzhōu.
When the plan failed,
they welcomed Shàoyì instead.
Shàoyì arrived at Măyì.
Fŭxiàng and his subordinates, such as Hán Āgè'nú, numbering several dozen people, were all rebellious officials of Qí.
More than two hundred and eighty garrisons north of Sìzhōu had followed Fŭxiàng.
When Shàoyì arrived,
they all revolted.
Shàoyì and the Inspector of Língzhōu, Yuán Hóngmĕng, led troops south,
intending to capture Bīngzhōu.
They reached Xīnxīng, but Sìzhōu had already been secured by Zhōu.
The two Yítóng (Attendants) of the vanguard surrendered to Zhōu with their respective units.
Zhōu troops attacked Xiănzhōu,
captured the Inspector Lù Qióng,
and subsequently attacked and breached several other cities.
Shàoyì returned to secure Běishuò.
The Zhōu general Yŭwén Shénjŭ marched upon Măyì.
Shàoyì dispatched Dù Míngdá to resist him,
but the troops were utterly defeated.
Shàoyì said:
"There is only death;
I cannot surrender to others."
Thereupon, he fled to the Tūjué (Turks).
His followers numbered three thousand households.
He ordered them, saying:
"Those who wish to return may do so freely."
Consequently, more than half wept, bowed, and departed.
Tūjué Khagan Tābō Kèhán considered Wénxuān an emperor of heroic caliber.
Seeing that Shàoyì resembled him due to his heavily boned ankles,
he cherished and respected him greatly.
All Qí people who were in the north
were placed under Shàoyì's command.
Gāo Băoníng, being in Yíngzhōu,
submitted a memorial proclaiming his exalted title.
Shàoyì then ascended the imperial throne,
proclaiming the first year of Wŭpíng.
He made Zhào Mù the Prince of Tiānshuĭ.
Tābō, hearing that Băoníng had secured Píngzhōu,
also summoned various tribes.
They each raised troops heading south,
claiming they would jointly establish the Prince of Fànyáng as the Qí Emperor
and avenge him.
Zhōu Wŭdì gathered a large army at Yúnyáng,
intending to personally lead the northern campaign,
but he was struck by illness and suddenly collapsed (died).
Shàoyì heard of this
and believed that Heaven was assisting him.
Lú Chāngqī, who occupied Fànyáng,
also submitted a memorial welcoming Shàoyì.
Soon after, the Zhōu general Yŭwén Shénjŭ attacked and eliminated Chāngqī.
On that day,
Shàoyì happened to arrive at Yōuzhōu.
Hearing that the Zhōu Commander-in-Chief had sent troops out,
he intended to seize Jìchéng while it was undefended.
He displayed the emperor's banners and flags,
ascended the tomb of King Zhāo of Yān,
and, taking advantage of the height to gaze far,
divided his forces.
Shénjŭ dispatched the General-in-Chief Yŭwén Ēn with four thousand men to rush to the aid of Yōuzhōu.
Half of them were killed by the Qí army.
Shàoyì heard that Fànyáng city had fallen.
He donned mourning clothes and expressed his grief,
then turned his army back into Tūjué territory.
The people of Zhōu offered a bounty for him from Tābō,
and also sent Hèruò Yì to persuade him.
Tābō still felt reluctant,
so he pretended to hunt with Shàoyì in the southern border region
and had Yì capture him.
He was exiled to Shŭ.
Shàoyì’s consort, the daughter of Fēng Xiàowăn of Bóhăi,
escaped from the Tūjué and returned.
While Shàoyì was in Shŭ,
he sent a letter to his consort saying:
"The barbarians are faithless;
they sent me here."
He eventually died in Shŭ.
Xīhé Wáng Shàorén
was the fourth son of Wénxuān.
At the end of Tiānbăo
he served as Kāifŭ Yítóng Sānsī.
He died soon after.
Lŏngxī Wáng Shàolián
was the fifth son of Wénxuān.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as Chánglè,
but this was later changed.
His nature was crude and violent.
He once drew a knife and chased Shàoyì.
Shàoyì fled into the palace,
closed the door, and resisted him.
When Shàoyì was first appointed Qīngdū Yĭn,
before he could take office,
Shàolián went there first,
called out all the prisoners,
and released them according to his own whims.
He was able to drink heavily,
several *shēng* in one sitting,
and eventually died because of this.
Xiàozhāo had seven sons: The Principal Empress (Yuánhòu) gave birth to Lèlíng Wáng Bǎinián;
Madam Sāng (Sāng Shì) gave birth to Xiāngchéng Wáng Liàng,
who was subsequently adopted as heir to Xiāngchéng Jĭngwáng;
and various concubines gave birth to Rŭnán Wáng Yànlĭ, Shĭpíng Wáng Yàndé, Chéngyáng Wáng Yànjī, Dìngyáng Wáng Yànkāng, and Rŭyáng Wáng Yànzhōng.
Lèlíng Wáng Bǎinián
was the second son of Xiàozhāo.
When Xiàozhāo first ascended the throne
in Jìnyáng,
the officials requested the establishment of the Empress and the Crown Prince.
The Emperor, being modest, had not yet permitted it.
The numerous officials in the capital again made the request,
and so, citing the order of the Empress Dowager, he was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizĭ).
When the Emperor was about to collapse (die),
he left an imperial decree transferring the throne to Wŭchéng,
along with a handwritten note,
the end of which read:
"Bǎinián is innocent.
You may place him happily somewhere;
