do not imitate former people."
During the Dàníng reign period,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lèlíng.
In the fifth month of the third year of Héqīng,
a white rainbow encircled the sun in a double ring,
and also passed horizontally through it but did not reach across.
A red star appeared.
The Emperor caught the star's reflection in a basin of water and covered it.
Overnight, the basin broke by itself.
He wished to suppress the omen using Bǎinián.
At that time, Jiă Dézhòu of Bólíng was teaching Bǎinián calligraphy.
Bǎinián once wrote several
"chì"
characters (imperial orders).
Dézhòu sealed them and presented them in a memorial.
The Emperor then flew into a rage
and ordered Bǎinián to be summoned.
When Bǎinián was summoned,
knowing he could not escape,
he cut off a jade arch from his belt and left it for his consort, the Húlǜ Shì.
He was brought before the Emperor in the Liángfēng Táng (Cool Breeze Hall) of the Xuándū Yuàn.
The Emperor made Bǎinián write the
"chì"
character,
and confirmed that it was similar to the one Dézhòu had submitted.
He ordered attendants to beat and strike him severely.
He also commanded men to drag Bǎinián around the hall, running and beating him simultaneously.
The blood stained the ground wherever they passed.
When his breath was almost gone,
he said:
"I beg for my life!
I wish to be a slave to Uncle Ā."
He was then decapitated
and thrown into a pond.
The pond water became entirely red.
The Emperor personally oversaw his burial in the rear garden.
His consort grasped the jade arch, weeping mournfully,
and refused to eat.
After more than a month, she also died.
The jade arch was still clutched in her hand,
her fist unable to be opened.
She was fourteen years old at the time.
Her father, Guāng, personally prized her hand open,
and only then did it open.
During the time of the Latter Lord (Hòuzhŭ),
when the Nine Courts were reorganized into Twenty-Seven Courts,
a small corpse was unearthed,
dressed in a scarlet robe with a gold belt,
with one hair tuft tied up and one loosened,
and one foot wearing a boot.
The various Neicān secretly remarked
that it was Crown Prince Bǎinián,
or perhaps Tàiyuán Wáng Shàodé.
An imperial edict commanded that Bái Zé, the son of the Prince of Xiāngchéng, succeed to the title of Lèlíng Wáng.
When Qí fell,
he entered the Pass,
was exiled to Shŭ, and died there
Rǔnán Wáng Yànlǐ,
in the early Wǔpíng period, was enfeoffed as a Prince (Wáng),
holding the positions of Kāifǔ and Qīngdū Yǐn.
When Qí perished,
he entered the Pass (Guān),
and, following the standard precedent, was granted the title Yítóng Dà Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as a County Viscount (Xiànzǐ).
Since his daughter had entered the Crown Prince's Palace,
he was therefore spared execution.
In the middle of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
he died while serving as Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Shǐpíng Wáng Yàndé, Chéngyáng Wáng Yànjī, Dìngyáng Wáng Yànkāng, and Rǔyáng Wáng Yànzhōng were enfeoffed at the same time as Rǔnán [Wáng Yànlǐ],
and all were additionally granted Yítóng Sānsī.
Their subsequent history is missing.
Emperor Wǔchéng had thirteen sons: Empress Hú bore the Hòuzhǔ and Lángyé Wáng Yǎn.
Consort Lǐ bore Nányáng Wáng Chuò.

The other palace women bore Qí'ān Wáng Kuò, Běipíng Wáng Zhēn, Gāopíng Wáng Rényīng, Huáinán Wáng Rénguāng, Xīhé Wáng Rénjǐ, Lèpíng Wáng Rénwēng, Yǐngchuān Wáng Rénjiǎn, Ānlè Wáng Rényǎ, Dānyáng Wáng Rénzhí, and Dōnghǎi Wáng Rénqiān.
Nányáng Wáng Chuò,
courtesy name Rèntōng,
was the eldest son of Emperor Wǔchéng.
He was born on the fifth day of the fifth month, during the *chén* hour (7-9 AM).
By the time of the *wǔ* hour (11 AM - 1 PM),
the Hòuzhǔ was born.
Because Consort Lǐ, Chuò's mother, was not the official primary wife, Emperor Wǔchéng
therefore demoted him to second son.
His original given name was Róng,
courtesy name Jūnmíng,
and he was adopted out as heir to the former Hànyáng Wáng.
In the third year of Héqīng,
he was re-enfeoffed as Nányáng [Wáng],
and a separate heir was established for Hànyáng.
When Chuò was just over ten years old,
he was left to guard Jìnyáng.
He loved Persian dogs.
When the guard Wèi Pòhú remonstrated with him about this,
Chuò suddenly chopped several dogs to death,
leaving them scattered on the ground.
Pòhú fled in shock,
not daring to speak again.
Later he served as Sītú and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
He enjoyed stripping people naked,
making them squat like beasts,
and setting dogs upon them to bite and eat them.
He was later transferred to Dìngzhōu.
He drew well water to create a back pond,
and shot pellets at people from the tower above.
He liked to travel incognito,
hunting excessively.
His temperament was fierce and violent.
He claimed he was emulating Wénxuān Bó in his conduct.
There was a woman carrying a child on the road;
she ran into the grass to avoid him.
Chuò seized her child and fed it to his Persian dogs.
The woman wailed and wept.
Chuò grew angry
and again ordered the dogs to eat her.
The dogs refused to eat,
so he smeared them with the child's blood,
and then they ate her.
The Hòuzhǔ heard of this
and issued an edict ordering Chuò to be shackled and brought to the imperial temporary residence (xíngzài suǒ).
Upon arrival, he pardoned him.
He asked, "What did you find most enjoyable while you were in the province?"
He replied:
"Gathering many scorpions and mixing them with maggots,
watching that is the greatest pleasure."
That very night, the Hòuzhǔ ordered a *dǒu* (peck) of scorpions to be sought.
By dawn, three or two *shēng* (pints) were procured.
He placed them in a bathtub
and ordered a naked man to lie inside the tub,
screaming and writhing.
The Emperor and Chuò watched over him,
laughing ceaselessly with joy.
The Emperor said to Chuò:
"Such a delightful activity!
Why didn't you quickly dispatch a messenger to report it?"
Because of this, Chuò was greatly favored by the Hòuzhǔ.
He was appointed Dà Jiāngjūn,
and they played together morning and night.
Hán Chángluán became jealous and caused trouble between them,
and Chuò was dismissed to serve as Qízhōu Cìshǐ.
As he was about to depart,
Chángluán instructed Chuò's trusted attendants to falsely accuse him of rebellion,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"This man has violated national law
and cannot be pardoned."
The Hòuzhǔ could not bear to execute him publicly,
so he ordered his favored Hu (non-Han foreigner), Hé Wěisà, to wrestle with Chuò in the rear garden,
and strangle him to death.
He was buried at Xīngshèng Fósì.
After more than four hundred days, he was given a proper re-embalming.
His complexion and hair were still like those of a living person.
It was popularly said that those born on the fifth day of the fifth month do not suffer brain decay.
Chuò and his brothers all called their father *xiōngxiōng* (elder brother),
their primary mother *jiājiā* (house person),
their wet nurse *jiějiě* (elder sister),
and their wife *mèimei* (younger sister).
When Qí perished,
his consort, Zhèng Shì, was favored by Emperor Wǔdì of Zhōu,
and she requested permission to bury Chuò.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to inter him north of Yǒngpíng Líng.
Lángyé Wáng Yǎn,
courtesy name Rénwēi,
was the third son of Emperor Wǔchéng.
He was initially enfeoffed as Dōngpíng Wáng.
He was appointed Kāifǔ, Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Jiān, Jīngjī Dà Dūdū, Lǐngjūn Dà Jiāngjūn, and concurrently Lǐng Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He was promoted to Sītú,
Shàngshū Lìng, Dà Jiāngjūn, Lù Shàngshū Shì, and Dà Sīmǎ.
According to the old regulations of the Wèi dynasty,
when the Zhōngchéng went out,
the path was cleared.
He traveled on a separate road from the Crown Prince.
All princes (Wáng) and high officials (Gōng) had to stop their carriages from afar,
detach their oxen,
and lay the yoke on the ground,
waiting for the Zhōngchéng to pass.
If anyone delayed or disobeyed,
they would be beaten with red rods.
Since moving the capital to Yè,
this ceremony had gradually ceased.
Emperor Wǔchéng, wanting to greatly favor and glorify Yǎn,
ordered that everything should follow the old system.
When he first left the Northern Palace
to ascend to the position of Zhōngchéng,
all the infantry and cavalry of the capital region (Jīngjī),
the subordinates of the Lǐngjūn [Dà Jiāngjūn],
the ceremonial guards of the Zhōngchéng,
and the imperial procession (lǔbù) of the Sītú,
were fully assembled.
The Emperor and Empress Hú set up a tent outside the east gate of Huálín Yuán
and observed the scene from behind a blue gauze screen.
He sent a palace official (zhōngguì) who rode quickly toward the ranks.
When the official was prevented from entering,
he loudly claimed to be carrying an imperial edict.
The red rods instantly smashed his saddle,
and his horse bolted, causing the man to fall.
The Emperor laughed heartily,
believing this was good.
He then issued another edict ordering the procession to stop,
and instructions were conveyed for a long time.
Spectators flooded the entire capital.
While Yǎn was in the palace,
he sat in Hánguāng Diàn to conduct official business,
and all his uncles paid obeisance to him.
When the Emperor visited Bīngzhōu,
Yǎn always remained behind to guard the capital.
Whenever he escorted the imperial carriage,
he would return either halfway
or only after reaching Jìnyáng.
Wang Shīluó, who usually followed the imperial carriage,
arrived late.
Emperor Wǔchéng intended to punish him.
He apologized, saying:
"I was bidding farewell to the third son,
and lingered without realizing the hour."
Emperor Wǔchéng missed Yǎn
and wept for him,
pardoning Shīluó without question.
Yǎn's utensils, clothes, ornaments, and decorations
were all identical to those of the Hòuzhǔ.
Everything he required was provided by the government.
He once saw newly harvested ice and early plums at the Southern Palace.
When he returned,
he angrily said:
"Since my honored elder brother already has them,
why am I lacking them?"
From that time on,
if the Hòuzhǔ obtained anything new or rare first,
the relevant officials and artisans would certainly be punished.
The Tàishàng [Emperor Wǔchéng] and Empress Hú still felt this was insufficient favor.
Yǎn often suffered from throat ailments.
When he instructed a doctor to use acupuncture,
he stared wide-eyed without blinking.
He also said to the Emperor:
"My elder brother (Hòuzhǔ) is weak;
how can he manage his retainers?"
The Emperor often praised him, saying:
"This is a clever boy;
he is destined for great things."
He considered the Hòuzhǔ inferior
and had intentions of dethroning him and setting up Yǎn.
When Emperor Wǔchéng died,
Yǎn's title was changed to Lángyé [Wáng].
Yǎn greatly resented the extravagant and unrestrained behavior of Hé Shìkāi, Luò Típó, and others,
who were lavishly constructing mansions.
He felt deeply indignant,
and once said to them:
"When will the mansions you gentlemen are building finally be completed?
Why is it taking so long?"
The two men said to each other:
"Lángyé Wáng's eyes are dazzling and brilliant,
piercing people even from several paces away.
Just now, facing him briefly,
we broke out in a sweat without realizing it.
It is not even like this when we report to the Son of Heaven."
Because of this, they became wary of him.
Yǎn was moved out to reside in the Northern Palace (Běigōng)
. He attended court once every five days
and could no longer see the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) daily
. In the fourth month
, an imperial decree relieved him of the title of Grand Protector (Tàibǎo)
. All other offices were stripped
, though he was allowed to retain the post of Palace Assistant Censor (Zhōngchéng)
, supervising the Capital Region (Jīngjī)
. Since there was an arsenal (Wǔkù) in the northern city
, they planned to relocate Yǎn outside
, and subsequently seize his military authority

. The Palace Recorder (Zhìshū Shì Yùshǐ), Wáng Zǐyí, together with Yǎn’s aides, the Left and Right Governors (Kāifǔ) Gāo Shèluò, and the Palace Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì) Liú Pìjiāng, advised Yǎn, saying
: "Your Highness is being alienated
precisely because of the machinations of Shìkāi
. How can you leave the Běigōng and move among the common populace?"
Yǎn said to the Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng), Féng Zǐcóng
: "Shìkāi’s crime is severe
; I wish to kill him."
Zǐcóng secretly wished to depose the Emperor (Dì) and install Yǎn
, so he agreed to support the plan
. Yǎn therefore ordered Zǐyí to submit a memorial impeaching Shìkāi for his crimes
, requesting that he be handed over for investigation
. Zǐcóng mixed this document with other memorials when presenting it
, and the Latter Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) approved it without careful review
. Yǎn falsely told the General of the Army (Lǐngjūn), Kùdì Fúlián
: "I have received an imperial order (chì) commanding the General to arrest Shìkāi."
Fúlián consulted Zǐcóng about this
, and further requested permission to report back to the throne
. Zǐcóng said
: "The Prince of Lángyé (Lángyé Wáng) received the imperial order (chì)
; why is a repeated report necessary?"
Fúlián believed him
, and ambushed fifty men outside the Shénshòumén Gate
. At dawn
, he seized Shìkāi and delivered him to the Censorate (Yùshǐ)
. Yǎn sent Féng Yǒngluò to the Censorate headquarters to execute him
. Yǎn’s followers originally intended only to kill Shìkāi
, but upon reaching this point
, they forced Yǎn, saying
: "Since the deed is done
, we cannot stop now."
Yǎn subsequently led more than three thousand soldiers from the Capital Region (Jīngjī) forces to encamp at the Qiānqiūmén Gate
. The Emperor (Dì) ordered Liú Táozhī to lead eighty Imperial Guards to summon Yǎn
. Táozhī bowed from a distance
, but Yǎn ordered him to be bound and executed
, causing the Imperial Guards to flee
. The Emperor again sent Féng Zǐcóng to summon Yǎn
. Yǎn declined, saying
: "Shìkāi deserved ten thousand deaths
for plotting to depose the Supreme Sovereign (Zhìzūn)
and shaving *Jiājiā's* head to make her a nun (Āní)
. Therefore, I rallied my troops to encamp on the residence of Sūn Fèngzhēn
, and as your subject, I issued a false edict to execute him
. If the Honored Elder Brother (Zūn Xiōng) wishes to kill me
, I dare not evade the crime
. If you pardon me
, I wish you would send *Zǐzǐ* (Elder Sister) to escort me
, and I will immediately come in for an audience."
*Zǐzǐ* was Lù Lìngxuān
. Yǎn intended to lure her out and kill her
. Lìngxuān, holding a knife behind the Emperor
, trembled upon hearing this
. The Emperor again sent Hán Chángluán to summon Yǎn
. As Yǎn was about to enter
, Liú Pìjiāng pulled his clothes and advised him, saying
: "If you do not execute Típó (Lù Lìngxuān) and her son
, Your Highness will have no means of safely entering."
The two princes, Guǎngníng and Āndé, happened to arrive from the west
, hoping to help bring the matter to fruition
. They said
: "Why don’t you go in?"
Pìjiāng replied
: "We have too few men."
The Prince of Āndé (Āndé Wáng) looked around at the crowd and said
: "When Emperor Xiàozhāo (Xiàozhāo Dì) killed Yáng Zūnyàn
, he had only eighty men
. Now we have several thousand
, how can you say the men are few?"
The Latter Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) tearfully informed the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu), saying
: "If we have fate, we will see *Jiājiā* again
; otherwise, this is eternal separation."
He immediately summoned Húlǜ Guāng
. Yǎn also summoned him
. Guāng, upon hearing that Shìkāi had been killed
, clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying
: "When the Dragon Son (Lóngzǐ) takes action
, he is truly unlike ordinary men!"
He entered to see the Latter Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) in the Yǒngxiàng Palace
. The Emperor (Dì) led four hundred guards, both foot soldiers and cavalry
, who donned their armor and prepared to fight
. Guāng said
: "These youngsters are playing with weapons
; if you engage them, they will immediately fall into disorder
. The vulgar proverb says, 'When a slave sees the master (*Dàjiā*), his heart dies.'
The Supreme Sovereign (Zhìzūn) should personally go to the Qiānqiūmén Gate
, and Lángyé (Yǎn) certainly will not dare to move."
Pí Jǐnghé also agreed
. The Latter Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) followed this advice
. Guāng walked ahead
, and sent men out shouting
: "The Master (*Dàjiā*) is coming!"
Yǎn’s followers scattered in panic
. The Emperor (Dì) halted his horse on the bridge
and called out to him from a distance
, but Yǎn stood still and did not advance
. Guāng went up to him and said
: "The Emperor's younger brother kills one man (Hàn)
, what harm is there in that?"
He seized Yǎn's hand
and forcibly led him forward
. He petitioned the Emperor (Dì)
: "The Prince of Lángyé (Lángyé Wáng) is young
, with fatty guts and a full brain (i.e., ignorant and reckless)
, and he acts rashly
. When he grows up, he will certainly no longer be like this
. I beg you to pardon his crime."
The Emperor (Dì) drew the dagger from Yǎn’s belt, wildly hammered him with the ring on its handle
, and braided his hair
. After a long time, he finally released him
. Fúlián, along with Gāo Shèluò, Wáng Zǐyí, Liú Pìjiāng, and the Area Commander (Dū Dū) Zhái Xiǎnguì, were arrested and taken to the rear garden
. The Emperor (Dì) personally shot them with arrows before beheading them
. All were dismembered
and their bodies exposed beneath the main street of the capital
. The Emperor wanted to kill all the civil and military officials implicated
. Guāng argued that since they were all sons of meritorious and noble families
, he feared general unrest
. Zhào Yànshēn also cited the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chūnqiū), which places blame primarily on the leader (*shuài*)
. Consequently, the punishments were graded
. Before Yǎn incurred guilt
, there was the White Horse Pagoda (Báimǎ Fótǎ) in the northern city of Yè
, originally built by Shí Jìlóng for Duke Chéng (Chéng Gōng)
. Yǎn intended to renovate it
. A shaman said
: "If this stupa is moved
, the northern city (Běichéng) will lose its master."
He did not heed the warning
. When they tore it down to the second tier
, they found a white snake several *zhàng* long
. It circled and disappeared
, and a few decades later, Yǎn failed
. Thereafter, the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu) kept Yǎn within the palace
, and personally tasted all his food
. Lù Lìngxuān persuaded the Emperor (Dì), saying
: "People say the Prince of Lángyé (Lángyé Wáng) is intelligent, valiant, and courageous
, without equal today
. Judging by his appearance and demeanor
, he is surely no subject of a ruler
. Since he acted on his own to kill (Shìkāi)
, he has constantly harbored fear
. We should plan quickly."
Hé Hóngzhēn, who had long been friends with Hé Shìkāi
, also requested that Yǎn be killed
. Since the Emperor was undecided
, he secretly sent a food palanquin to fetch Zǔ Tǐng for consultation
. Tǐng cited the precedents of Duke Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) punishing Guǎn Shū
and Jì Yǒu poisoning Qìng Fù
. The Emperor accepted his advice
. They planned to send Yǎn to Jìnyáng
, and ordered the General-in-Chief of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn), Zhào Yuánkǎn, to lure and seize Yǎn
. Yuánkǎn said
: "When I formerly served the Previous Emperor (Xiāndì)
, I saw daily how the Previous Emperor loved the Prince
. I would rather face death today
than carry this out."
The Emperor (Dì) sent Yuánkǎn out to become the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu
. In the last third of the ninth month
, the Emperor (Dì) informed the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu), saying
: "Tomorrow morning, I intend to go hunting with Rénwēi
, so we must leave early and return early."
That night, at the fourth watch
, the Emperor (Dì) summoned Yǎn
. Yǎn was suspicious
. Lù Lìngxuān said
: "Your Elder Brother (*Xiōngxiōng*) calls for you
, why would you not go, my son?"
Yǎn went out to the Yǒngxiàng Palace
. Liú Táozhī bound his hands behind his back
. Yǎn cried out
: "I beg to see *Jiājiā* (Empress Dowager) and the Honored Elder Brother (Zūn Xiōng)!"
Táozhī stuffed his mouth with his sleeve
, used his inverted robe to cover his head, and carried him out on his back
. Upon reaching Dàmíng Gōng
, Yǎn's face was covered in blood from his nose
. He was immediately killed
, aged fourteen at the time
. They did not remove his boots
, wrapped him in a mat
, and buried him inside the chamber
. The Emperor (Dì) sent a message to the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu)
. She approached his body and wept ten or more times
, then was forcibly escorted into the palace hall
. In the third month of the following year
, he was buried west of Yè
, and posthumously honored with the title Emperor Gōng'āi of Chǔ (Chǔ Gōng'āi Dì)
, in order to comfort the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu)
. He left behind four sons, born posthumously
. All died in confinement a few months after birth
. Gāo Shìjùn, the grandson of the Prince of Píngyáng, Gāo Yān (Píngyáng Wáng Yān), was appointed as his successor
, the daughter of Lǐ Zǔqīn
, was promoted to become the Empress of Chǔ Dì
, residing in Xuānzé Gōng
. When Qí perished
, she was married
. Qí'ān Wáng Kuò
, courtesy name Rén Hóng
, was the fourth son of Wǔchéng
. His character was that of an elder
, and he had no transgressions
. His position was Tèjìn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Prefect of Dìng Zhōu
. Běipíng Wáng Zhēn
, courtesy name Rénjiān
, was the fifth son of Wǔchéng
. He was deep, careful, lenient, and forgiving
. The Emperor often said
: "This child has attained the phoenix feathers (excellence) of mine
." His position was Governor of Sī Zhōu, Grand Military Governor of the Capital Region
, concurrently Shàngshū Lìng and Lù Shàngshū Shì
. When the Emperor went on tours
, he managed all affairs of the Lúi Tái (Stay-behind Administration)
. After accumulating years
, Hòuzhǔ (the Latter Lord)
, because Zhēn had grown up
, gradually grew jealous of him. Ānà Gōng, receiving the imperial decree
, ordered Féng Shìgàn to impeach and imprison Zhēn
, stripping him of his power to act as the stay-behind authority
. Gāopíng Wáng Rényīng
was the sixth son of Wǔchéng
. His demeanor was lofty and spirited
, and his disposition lacked restraint
. His position was Prefect of Dìng Zhōu
. Huáinán Wáng Rénguāng
was the seventh son of Wǔchéng
. His nature was restless and violent
. His position was Qīngdū Yǐn
. Next was Xīhé Wáng Rénjǐ
. He was born without bones
and could not support himself
. Next was Lèpíng Wáng Rénwēng
; next was Yǐngchuān Wáng Rénjiǎn
; next was Ānlè Wáng Rén Yǎ
, who suffered from muteness since childhood
. Next was Dānyáng Wáng Rénzhí
; next was Dōnghǎi Wáng Rénqiān
. All were raised in the Northern Palace
. After the death of Lángyá Wáng
, the restrictions imposed upon the various princes became even stricter
. In the final years of Wǔpíng
, Rénwēng and those younger
were finally allowed to go out. Their supplies were meager
, just enough to get by
. Soon thereafter, when Hòuzhǔ was distressed and struggling
, he appointed Kuò as Prefect of Guāng Zhōu
, Zhēn as Prefect of Qīng Zhōu
, Rényīng as Prefect of Jì Zhōu
, Rénjiǎn as Prefect of Jiāo Zhōu
, and Rénzhí as Prefect of Jǐ Zhōu
. From Kuò downwards
, most died with Hòuzhǔ in Cháng'ān
. Rényīng, due to his apparent eccentricity (Qīngkuáng)
, and Rén Yǎ, due to his muteness
, were spared
and were both exiled to Shǔ
. During the Kāihuáng period of the Suí dynasty
, Rényīng was summoned
and was ordered by imperial decree, along with Xiāo Cóng and Chén Shúbǎo, to maintain the ancestral sacrifices of his original lineage
. He died shortly thereafter
Hòuzhǔ
had five sons: Mù Huánghòu gave birth to Yòuzhǔ (the Young Lord)
; the various concubines gave birth to Dōngpíng Wáng Kè
, next Shàndé
, next Mǎidé
, and next Zhìqián
. Hú Tàihòu had Kè succeed Lángyá Wáng
, but he died young soon after
. When Qí was extinguished
, Zhōu Wǔdì brought thirty princes, both major and minor, starting from Rènchéng Wáng downwards, back to Cháng'ān
, and all were granted titles and fiefdoms
. Those who were later not executed were scattered and distributed to the western lands
, and all died on the border
. An appraisal states
all possessed dignity and integrity (fēnggǔ)
. Although in the ways of literary refinement and elegance
they yielded to Jiàn and Píng
, their military skills and heroic bearing
were mostly capable of resisting insult and attack
. Even if the sword granted at Xiányáng
showed a sign of subsequent defeat and ruin
, had Lánlíng been allowed to survive
, the outcome could not have been measured
. Yet they were ultimately executed
, leading to total collapse (tǔbēng)
. This is truly lamentable
. Āndé
, concealed his presence and hid his brilliance
. But during the battle of Píngyáng
, he displayed his loyalty and courage
. This was because when facing peril and difficulty
, his loyalty to his family and state ran deep
. Dèchāng launched a great movement
, and the matter pressured the sentiments of the populace
, inevitably leading to ruin and demise
, leaving nowhere to turn for life
. Guǎngníng requested permission for the Empress Dowager to leave the palace
, but ultimately did not succeed
. It was not that Xiàohéng’s wording and rhetoric
were inferior to that of Lǐ Tóng
; rather, it was because Hòuzhǔ had already lost his consciousness and judgment
. Píngyuán had passed long ago
. The circumstances of survival and death were different
. How can they be discussed together in the same light
? Wǔchéng was cruel, brutal, and engaged in depraved misconduct
, reaching the extreme limits of human relations
. Tàiyuán’s actions were peculiar and aroused suspicion
, but his intentions were not rebellious or seditious
. The disaster began with Zhāoxìn
and ultimately involved cruel punishment
. Alas
, such a thing was not possible
. Considering Xiàozhāo’s virtuous reputation
, it might have been hoped that his blessings would flow to his descendants
. Yet the century of cruelty
originated with Jìnán
. His words
saying
, "Do not follow the example of previous people"
, are a cause for sorrowful sighing
. Did they truly love their sons
? How could that be
? Although Lángyá
lacked the qualities of a mentor or instructor
, he had an early reputation for spirit and demeanor
. Shìkāi’s debauchery and chaos
lasted for many years
. When he was finally eradicated in one morning
, celebration gathered among the court and the populace
. To die because of this
is profoundly regrettable
. However, the crime of arbitrary execution
was not avoided
. To posthumously bestow upon him the imperial title of Gōng
was to overcorrect an error
. Judging virtue by observing error
, is this not different from that principle
Biography 5: Zhào Jùn Wáng Chēn (Son Ruì); Qīnghé Wáng Yuè (Son Mài). Zhào Jùn Wáng Chēn
, courtesy name Yǒngbǎo
, was the younger brother of Gāo Zǔ
. When young, he was skilled in archery and horsemanship
and possessed ambition and spirit
. After Gāo Zǔ had restored order to the empire
, at the beginning of Zhōngxīng
, Chēn was appointed Sànqí Chángshì, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn, and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū
. Once he was stationed in the Imperial Guard
, he was respectful, diligent, and careful
, taking the lead among those around the emperor
. At the beginning of Tàichāng
, he was made Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū
, and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Nán Zhào Jùn
, receiving a fiefdom of five thousand households
. Soon after, he was appointed Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn, Tèjìn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Sànqí Chángshì
. In the second year of Yǒngxī (533 CE)
, he was made Envoy Holding Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Grand Military Governor overseeing Dìng Zhōu Prefect, and Grand Military Governor of Six Zhōu
. Chēn showed sincerity in pacifying and incorporating people
, and promoted capable individuals
. He had an excellent reputation
. When Hú Sīchūn and others formed alliances that led to conflict
, Gāo Zǔ intended to launch an internal punitive campaign
. Considering Jìnyáng to be the foundation
, he summoned Chēn to stay behind and manage affairs
, making him the Grand Director (Dà Xíngtái Púshè) of Bīng, Sì, and Fén Zhōu
, leading the Grand Military Governorship of six zhōu and nine tribal chiefs
. Chēn decided all governmental affairs in the Chancellor's residence (Xiàngfǔ)
. During the Tiānpíng era
, he was appointed Imperial Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi)
. He maintained a stern demeanor while investigating and impeaching
, avoiding no one
. All near and far were awestruck
. Shortly after, he caused disorder in Gāo Zǔ’s inner court
. Gāo Zǔ reprimanded and punished him
, and he died under the beating of the staff
, at the age of twenty-three

. He was posthumously granted the titles of Envoy Holding Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Attendant at the Palace (Shìzhōng), Grand Military Governor overseeing all military affairs of the ten zhōu: Jì, Dìng, Cāng, Yíng, Yōu, Yīn, Bīng, Sì, Yún, and Shuò
, Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn, Prefect of Jì Zhōu, Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), and Shàngshū Lìng
. His posthumous name was Zhēngpíng. In the third year of Tiāntǒng
, he was again posthumously granted the titles of Substitute for the Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng), Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Lù Shàngshū Shì, and Prefect of Jì Zhōu
. His noble rank was elevated to Prince (Wáng)
, and he was accorded sacrifice alongside Gāo Zǔ in the ancestral temple
. His son Ruì succeeded him
nickname was Xūbá.
He was orphaned thirty days after birth.
He was intelligent and precociously accomplished,
he was particularly loved by Gāozǔ,
who raised him within the palace.
He ordered Madame Yóu to mother him,
and the favor shown was the same as that granted to Gāozǔ's other sons.
During the Xīnghé era of the Wèi,
he inherited the title of Nánzhàojùn Gōng.
Until he was four years old,
he had never known his birth mother.
His mother was Princess Huáyáng of Wèi.
There was a woman of the Zhèng clan,
who was the daughter of his mother's maternal cousin,
who playfully spoke to Ruì, saying:
"You are the son of my maternal aunt,
why have you inverted this relationship and taken the Yóu clan as kin?"
Ruì then made inquiries,
and his spirit consequently became distressed.
Gāozǔ found this extremely strange,
suspected he was afflicted by illness,
and intended to command a physician to examine him.
Ruì replied:
"Your son has no suffering,
but having heard of the one who gave me birth,
I wish to see her temporarily."
Gāozǔ exclaimed in surprise:
"Who spoke to you about this?"
Ruì fully explained the circumstances.
Gāozǔ commanded Madam Yuán to let her meet Ruì at the palace.
Ruì stepped forward and knelt in obeisance,
and then embraced his head and wept bitterly.
Gāozǔ was deeply sorrowful.
He spoke to the Prince of Píngqín, saying:
"This child possesses innate, profound filial piety.
None of my sons can equal him."
Consequently, he suspended his official duties for one day.
When Ruì first read the *Xiàojīng*,
reaching
the line "drawing upon resources to serve one's father,"
he would invariably shed tears and sob.
At the age of ten, he lost his mother.
Gāozǔ personally escorted Ruì to the Lǐngjūnfǔ,
where he formally announced the mourning period for Ruì.
(Ruì) cried out and collapsed,
and his sorrow moved those on his left and right.
For three days, no water or liquid passed his lips.
Gāozǔ and Empress Wǔmíng Lóu earnestly and repeatedly admonished him,
only then did he gradually comply.
He fulfilled all prescribed rituals during the mourning period,
maintaining a strict vegetarian fast before the image of the Buddha.
He became emaciated, practically standing only by bone,
and could only rise afterward with a staff.
Gāozǔ ordered the Prince of Chángshān to sleep and rise with him,
advising and comforting him day and night.
Moreover, he commanded attendants not to allow him water.
Although he was denied rinsing liquids,
he still invariably refused to eat after midday.
Because of this, Gāozǔ always summoned Ruì to share the same table when he ate.
His compassion and cherishing were like this.
When Gāozǔ passed away,
he wept and cried until he vomited blood.
When he grew up,
preparations were made for his wedding,
but his face bore an expression of distress.
Shìzōng said to him:
"I am arranging your marriage to the daughter of Zhèng Shùzǔ,
whose lineage is very high.
What is it that you dislike that makes your spirit unhappy?"
Ruì replied:
"Since grieving my state as an orphan,
I have always profoundly yearned for the affection of parents (beneath the knees).
Now that I am proceeding toward marriage and capping (adulthood),
this feeling is acutely intense."
Before he finished speaking,
he sobbed uncontrollably.
Shìzōng was moved to pity and kept silent.
He exerted himself and studied diligently,
often stopping only late at night.
At the end of the Wǔdìng era,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shùzǐ.
When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication,
his peerage was advanced to Zhàojùn Wáng,
with an enfeoffment of 1,200 households,
and he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
Ruì was seven *chǐ* tall,
his appearance and bearing were magnificent.
He was experienced in official duties,
and possessed the discernment to judge men.
In the second year,
he was appointed Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and given the concurrent titles of Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn and Grand Area Commander of Six Prefectures.
He was seventeen years old at the time.
Ruì paid close attention to administrative affairs,
investigated and exposed corruption,
and encouraged farming and sericulture.
He welcomed and treated local talent with respect,
and the area under his jurisdiction was greatly well-governed,
earning him the name of "worthy shepherd."
In the third year,
he was granted the honorific Yítóng Sānsī.
In the sixth year,
an imperial edict commanded Ruì to lead tens of thousands of soldiers from Shāndōng to supervise the construction of the Great Wall.
At that time, it was the height of summer, the sixth month.
While Ruì was on the road,
he cast aside his canopy and fan,
personally sharing the labor and suffering with the soldiers.
Dìngzhōu already had an ice cellar,
where ice was stored every year.
The Chief Clerk Sòng Qīndào, realizing Ruì was enduring the oppressive summer heat,
immediately dispatched ice by cart,
doubling the distance traveled daily to catch up and deliver it.
It arrived exactly when the army halted at midday,
when the scorching heat was particularly intense,
and everyone found it unbearable.
When the ice delivery arrived,
everyone believed that receiving the ice was the most essential necessity of the moment.
Ruì then faced the ice and sighed, saying:
"The men of the entire army
are all drinking warm water.
By what righteousness
should I alone partake of cold ice?
I am not seeking the fame of ancient generals;
it is truly something my heart cannot bear."
He allowed it to melt completely,
and ultimately did not taste it once.
The soldiers were moved and delighted,
and people near and far spoke of him admiringly.
Previously,
when the conscripted laborers finished their work,
they were allowed to return on their own.
The strong and able-bodied
returned home first by themselves;
the frail and weak
were abandoned north of the mountains.
Coupled with hunger and illness,
many resulted in death and collapse.
Ruì therefore personally led his command,
returning alongside them.
He matched them to their prefectures and villages,
divided them into camps and ranks,
and commanded officers to supervise and lead them.
The strong supported the weak.
Whenever they encountered good water and pasture,
they immediately paused.
They shared what was abundant
to sustain the needy,
and those who were saved because of this totaled three or four out of ten.
In the seventh year,

an edict appointed him, maintaining his current office, as Area Commander of military affairs in the six prefectures of Cāngzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Yōuzhōu, Ānzhōu, Píngzhōu, and Dōngyànzhōu, and Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eighth year,
Ruì was summoned to Yè,
and subsequently appointed Běishuòzhōu Cìshǐ,
Area Commander of Běiyànzhōu, Běiwèizhōu, and the three Běizhōu prefectures,
as well as military affairs of all garrisons along the Great Wall west of Kùtuī and east of the Yellow River.
Ruì comforted and pacified the newly settled population,
strategically established beacon towers and garrisons,
managing internal defense and external resistance,
and preparing comprehensive regulations.
He was greatly reassuring to both soldiers and civilians.
In places where there was no water,
he prayed and dug wells.
As soon as the spades and shovels went down,
springs of water gushed forth.
To this day, these are called the Zhàojùn Wáng Quán.
In the ninth year,
the imperial carriage visited Lóufán.
Ruì paid homage at the temporary palace,
and subsequently followed the entourage back to Jìnyáng.
At this time, Jǐnán was serving as regent for the Crown Prince,
and consequently established the Dà Dūdu Fǔ,
which managed various affairs in coordination with the Shàngshū Shěng,
and also established an administration (Kāi Fǔ) and appointed aides.
Xiǎnzǔ specifically elevated the criteria for selection.
He then appointed Ruì as Shìzhōng and acting Chief Clerk of the Dà Dūdu Fǔ.
Later, Ruì was attending a banquet.
Xiǎnzǔ casually looked upon the Prince of Chángshān Yǎn and others, saying:
"Has there ever been a Chief Clerk like this before?
How do you regard my employment of this Chief Clerk?"
Yǎn replied:
"Your Majesty devotes his mind to administrative affairs,
treating the worthy with favor and respect.
Xūbá is promoted to the glory symbolized by the *chán ěr* (high office),
and when he retires, he holds a position of crucial trust.
Since antiquity,
truly such a selection and appointment has never been heard of."
The Emperor said:
"I, too, regard this as a suitable arrangement."
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to Yítóng Sānsī,
while his positions as Shìzhōng, Jiāngjūn, Chángshǐ, and Wáng remained as before.
Soon afterward, he was granted the concurrent titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn, and Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
he managed the affairs of Bìngzhōu.
When Xiàozhāo was approaching his death,
he received the pre-arranged entrustment.
He respectfully welcomed Shìzǔ at Yè,
and due to his merit, he was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
Separately, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Fúyáng Jùn,
Superintendent of the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ),
Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù),
and deliberator on the statutes and ordinances (Lǜlìng).
Furthermore, for the merit of suppressing the Northern Dí,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yǐngchuān Jùn.
He was again appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
and provisionally managed the affairs of Dàzōngzhèng Qīng.
During the Tiāntǒng era,
Rùi's father Chēn was posthumously granted the title Jiǎ Huángyuè (False Imperial Axe),
and his mother, Lady Yuán, was posthumously granted the title of Princess Consort of Zhàojùn,
with the posthumous name Zhēnzhāo.
Huáyáng Chánggōngzhǔ retained her previous status.
The responsible officials prepared the rites and ceremonies and conferred the titles at the tomb.
At the time, it was deep winter and bitterly cold,
Rùi walked barefoot and wailed loudly,
his face was completely lacerated,
and he vomited several pints of blood.
When he returned,
he was too weak to attend court and offer thanks.
The Emperor personally went to his residence to visit and inquire after him.
He was appointed Sīkōng,
and provisionally managed the affairs of the Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
The Tūjué once invaded and raided as far as Bìngzhōu.
The Emperor personally took charge of the military operation,
and commanded that all advances and retreats of the Six Armies must follow Rùi’s direction.
For this merit, he was again enfeoffed as the Duke of Xuānchéng Jùn.
He provisionally managed the Zōngzhèng Qīng,
and was promoted to Tàiwèi,
overseeing the deliberation on the Five Rites (Wǔ Lǐ).
Rùi had long managed court affairs,
remaining pure and holding fast to integrity.
His reputation and prestige grew daily,
and gradually he became alienated and feared [by others].
He thus compiled a work about loyal officials and righteous scholars of antiquity,
calling it *Yàoyán* (Essential Words),
in order to express his underlying concerns.
When Shìzǔ died,
several days after the burial,
Rùi, along with Fèngyì Wáng Rùn, Āndé Wáng Yánzōng, and Yuán Wényáo, memorialized Hòuzhǔ (the Later Lord), saying:
“Hé Shìkāi should not remain in his internal post.”
They also went in to report this to the Empress Dowager (Tàihòu),
consequently forcing Shìkāi out to be the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu.
The Empress Dowager said:
“Shìkāi has served me formerly,
I want him to stay for more than one hundred days.”
Rùi spoke severely and refused her request.
Within several days,
the Empress Dowager repeatedly brought this matter up.
An influential palace eunuch (Zhōngguān), knowing the Empress Dowager’s private intention,
said to Rùi:
“Since the Empress Dowager’s intention is thus,
why must Your Highness oppose it so bitterly?”
Rùi said:
“The affairs of our state are grave,
and I will not shrink even from death.
If I cling to life and seek temporary safety,
causing the state to become chaotic,
that is not my intention.
Moreover, I received the last decree of the former Emperor,
and the trust placed in me is heavy.
Now the Successor Lord is young and immature;
how can I allow a treacherous official to remain by his side?
If I fail to protect him with righteousness,
how can I look up to Heaven?”
He then memorialized again,
using urgent and sincere reasoning.
The Empress Dowager ordered wine to be poured and offered to Rùi.
Rùi, speaking sternly, said:
“Today we are discussing vital state affairs;
this is no time for wine!”
Having spoken, he immediately departed.
That night,
while Rùi was sleeping,
he saw a person about fifteen feet tall,
whose arms were over ten feet long,
standing at the door facing the bed.
It used its arm to press down on Rùi.
After a long while,
it suddenly vanished.
Rùi felt extremely disturbed by this,
and he immediately rose, sat up, and sighed to himself, saying:
“A great man’s destiny has suddenly reached this point!”
Fearing he would be killed by the Empress Dowager,
when dawn broke and he intended to go to court,
his wife and children all tried to dissuade him.
Rùi said:
“Loyal officials since antiquity
all disregard their personal lives.
The matter of the state is serious;
I must serve it even unto death.
How can I allow one woman to endanger the dynastic temple?
Moreover, what kind of mere boy is Hé Shìkāi,
acting so recklessly?
I would rather die serving the Former Emperor
than bear to see the court overthrown.”
When he reached the palace gate,
another person said:
“I beg Your Highness not to enter,
fearing there may be danger and upheaval.”
Rùi said:
“I have not failed Heaven above;
even dying, I will have no regrets.”
He entered and saw the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager again brought up the matter,
but Rùi held his position even more firmly.
Coming out to Yǒngxiàng (the Long Alley),
he encountered soldiers and was seized.
He was sent to Huálín Yuán,
where, in the Quèlí Buddhist Temple, Liú Táozhī was ordered to strangle and kill him.
He was thirty-six years old at the time.
A great fog lasted for three days,
and the court and the populace mourned his unjust fate.
A year later,
an imperial edict permitted him to be buried with the rites of a prince (wáng lǐ),
but ultimately, no posthumous honors or title were granted.
His son, Zhěngxìn, succeeded him.
He served successively as Sànqí Chángshì and Yítóng Sānsī.
He loved learning and had excellent conduct.
In his youth, he fell from his horse while hunting,
injuring his waist and legs.
He was subsequently unable to walk or stand,
and he died in Cháng'ān.
Chēn’s younger brother by the same mother, Huìbǎo, died young.
In the beginning of Yuánxiàng,
he was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Lìng, Military Governor of the Armies of Four Circuits (Dūdū Sìzhōu Zhūjūn Shì), and Governor of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the third year of Tiāntǒng,
he was again posthumously granted Military Governor of Ten Circuits (Shízhōu Dūdū),
enfeoffed as the Prince of Chénliú (Chénliú Wáng),
with the posthumous title Wéngōng.
Qīnghé Wáng Yuè’s tenth son, Jìngwén, was appointed to succeed him.
Qīnghé Wáng Yuè,
courtesy name Hóngluè,
was a younger paternal cousin of Gāozǔ.
His father, Fān,
courtesy name Fēiquè,
was posthumously granted Tàiwèi by the Wèi court,
with the posthumous title Xiàoxuān Gōng.
When Yuè was young, he was orphaned and poor,
and people did not yet know him.
As an adult, he was honest and upright,
his appearance was outstanding,
and he was profound and capable.
Initially, Yuè lived in Luòyì (Luò City).
Whenever Gāozǔ was sent on a mission to Luò,
he would definitely stay at Yuè’s residence.
Yuè’s mother, Lady Shān,
once rose at night
and saw a light inside Gāozǔ’s room.
She secretly went to observe,
but there was no lamp.
She immediately moved Gāozǔ to another room,
and the light appeared just as she had seen before.
Thinking this divine and miraculous,
she went to a diviner to cast lots.
The hexagram obtained was *Qián Zhī Dàyǒu* (The Creative, leading to Great Possessing).
The interpretation was:
“Auspicious!
The *Yì* [Classic of Changes] says, ‘The flying dragon is in the sky;
the great man acts.’
The hexagram of the flying dragon in the ninth position is that of a great man;
his nobility cannot be measured.”
Lady Shān returned and reported this to Gāozǔ.
Later, when Gāozǔ raised an army in Xìndū,
Lady Shān heard about it
and was overjoyed.
She said to Yuè:
“The auspicious sign of the red light
must now be proven true.
You should secretly travel and follow him,
and together plan the great undertaking.”
Yuè then traveled to Xìndū.
When Gāozǔ saw him,
he was greatly pleased.
Zhōngxīng era,
he was appointed Sǎnjì Chángshì, Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn, and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently commanding the Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn.
Gāo Zǔ fought the Sī Hú (Four Barbarians) at Hánlíng.
Gāo Zǔ commanded the central army,
Gāo Áng commanded the left army,
and Yuè commanded the right army.
The central army was defeated.
The bandits pressed the attack.
Yuè raised his banner and shouted loudly,
charging straight across the enemy formation.
Only then was Gāo Zǔ able to turn his forces around,
join the spirited counterattack,
and consequently deliver a great defeat to the bandits.
For this merit, he was appointed Wèi Jiāngjūn and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū,
retaining command of the Wǔwèi.
In the beginning of the Tàichāng era,
he was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
commanding the Zuǒyòu Wèi,
and was enfeoffed as Qīnghé Jùngōng,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
His mother, Shān Shì,
was enfeoffed as Jùn Jūn,
and granted the title Nǚ Shìzhōng,
entering the palace to serve the Empress.
At that time, Ěrzhū Zhào still occupied Bīngzhōu.
Gāo Zǔ was preparing to suppress him
and ordered Yuè to remain and guard the capital.
Yuè was promoted to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
In the second year of Tiānpíng,
he was appointed Shìzhōng and Dūdū of Military Affairs of Six Prefectures,
and soon thereafter was given the added title of Kāifǔ.
Yuè recruited and invited the capable men of the time
to be his subordinates.
Commentators considered this admirable.
Soon he was appointed Dūjiān Diǎnshū (Superintendent of Records),
and returned to the position of Shìxué (Palace Academician).
He was appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Grand Dūdū of Six Prefectures, and Jìzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed Grand Dūdū of the Capital Region (Jīngjī).
All matters concerning the six prefectures were transferred to the Capital Region administration.
At that time, Gāo Zǔ governed affairs from Jìnyáng.
Yuè, along with Shìzhōng Sūn Téng and others, remained in the capital assisting with governance.
In the second year of Yuánxiàng,
he suffered the mourning period for his mother and left office.
Yuè was naturally extremely filial,
dedicating his strength to caring for her.
If his mother became ill,
he would not untie his belt.
When the period of mourning arrived,
his sorrow and emaciation reduced him to skin and bones.
Gāo Zǔ was deeply concerned for him,
sending people daily to console and encourage him.
Soon he was recalled to his original post.
Two years later,
he was appointed concurrent Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the beginning of the Xīnghé era,
Shì Zōng entered to assume control of court affairs.
Yuè was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Dūdū, and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
His titles of Shìzhōng, Piàojì, and Kāifǔ Yítóng remained as before.
In the third year,
he was transferred to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yuè had held power for a long time
and was traditionally held in awe and respect by the court and the populace.
When he served in these two peripheral positions,
the common people were terrified merely at the mention of his reputation.
In the first year of Wǔdìng,
he was appointed Jìnzhōu Cìshǐ and Grand Dūdū of the Southwest Route,
and gained the reputation for pacifying the border.
At that time, Yuè fell ill.
Gāo Zǔ ordered him to return to Bīngzhōu for treatment.
When he recovered from his illness,
he was ordered to return to his post.
When Gāo Zǔ died,
Hóu Jǐng rebelled.
Shì Zōng summoned Yuè back to Bīngzhōu
to jointly plan the strategy for capturing Hóu Jǐng.
Meanwhile, Liáng Wǔdì took advantage of the situation and sent his Zhēnyáng Hóu Míng to lead troops at Hánshān,
damming the Sìshuǐ River to flood Péngchéng,
acting in concert with Hóu Jǐng as a supportive flank.
Yuè commanded all the armies for the southern campaign,
and together with the Xíngtái Mùróng Shàozōng and others, attacked Míng.
They completely routed them,
capturing Míng and his general Hú Guìsūn on the battlefield.
The remaining captives and slaughtered numbered in the tens of thousands.
Hóu Jǐng then massed his troops at Wōyáng,
engaging in a standoff with the Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Liú Fēng and others.
Yuè turned his army and pursued the rebels,
defeating them again.
Hóu Jǐng fled alone on horseback.
In the sixth year,
for his merit, he was appointed Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi.
His other titles remained unchanged,
and he was additionally enfeoffed as Xīnchāng Xiànzǐ.
He was also appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Hénán Zǒngguǎn, and Grand Dūdū,
commanding Mùróng Shàozōng, Liú Fēng, and others to suppress Wáng Sīzhèng at Chángshè.
Sīzhèng fortified the city and held fast.
Yuè and the others diverted the Wěishuǐ River to flood the city.
Mùróng Shàozōng and Liú Fēng were captured by Sīzhèng.
Troops from Guānxī (West of the Pass) mobilized to reinforce Sīzhèng.
Yuè managed the defenses both internally and externally
with considerable foresight and planning.
Only three planks high of the city wall remained above the water.
Coincidentally, Shì Zōng personally arrived,
and the city fell several days later,
capturing Sīzhèng and others.
For this merit, he was separately enfeoffed as Zhēndìng Xiànnán.
Shì Zōng claimed the accomplishment for himself,
thus the award was not generous.
When Shì Zōng died,
Xiǎnzǔ went out to pacify Jìnyáng.
He ordered Yuè, retaining his original position, to concurrently serve as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè,
remaining to guard the capital.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was promoted and enfeoffed as Qīnghé Jùnwáng.
Soon after, he was appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Zōngshī, and Sīzhōu Mù.
In the fifth year,
he was granted the title Tàibǎo.
Liáng Xiāo Yì was hard pressed by the Zhōu army,
and sent an envoy reporting the emergency
and requesting assistance.
In the winter,
an edict appointed Yuè as Grand Xíngtái of the Southwest Route,
to command Sītú Pān Xiānglè and others to relieve Jiānglíng.
In the first month of the sixth year,
his army reached Yìyáng.
He learned that Jīngzhōu had fallen.
Consequently, he seized territory, heading south to Yǐngzhōu,
capturing the Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Sītú Lù Fǎhé,
and then conquering Yǐngzhōu.
Yuè first sent Lù Fǎhé to the capital,
and dispatched Yítóng Mùróng Yǎn to garrison Yǐngchéng.
The court, knowing that Jiānglíng had fallen,
ordered Yuè to withdraw his forces.
Since Yuè had campaigned at Hánshān and Chángshè, and had been successful in the campaigns against the Súi and Lù families,
he possessed outstanding merit,
and his prestige grew even greater.
However, his nature was extravagant and luxurious,
and he especially delighted in wine and women.
With singing girls and dancing women,
arranging tripods and striking bells,
none of the other princes could compare.
Previously,
when Gāo Guīyàn was young and orphaned,
Gāo Zǔ ordered Yuè to raise him.
Yuè slighted him due to his youth,
treating him with very little affection or courtesy.
Gāo Guīyàn secretly resented this but never spoke of it.
When Gāo Guīyàn became Lǐngjūn
and received great imperial favor,
Yuè believed Gāo Guīyàn was indebted to him
and consequently relied upon him.
Gāo Guīyàn secretly reported Yuè’s faults.
Yuè built a residence in Chéngnán,
constructing a lane behind the main administrative hall.
Gāo Guīyàn memorialized the Emperor, saying:
“Qīnghé (Yuè) built his residence
presumptuously mimicking the imperial palace,
constructing a Yǒngxiàng (private corridor);
the only thing lacking is a watchtower.”
Xiǎnzǔ heard this and was displeased,
gradually alienating Yuè.
At that time, Xiǎnzǔ summoned a woman named Xuē Shì from Yèxià into the palace.
Yuè had previously summoned her to his residence
through her elder sister.
The Emperor hung Xuē Shì's sister up and sawed her to death,
reprimanding Yuè for involving the daughter of a traitorous citizen.
Yuè said:
“I originally intended to take her,
but disliked her frivolous nature and did not use her;
this was not treason.”
The Emperor became even angrier.
In the eleventh month of the sixth year,
he sent Gāo Guīyàn to Yuè’s residence to sternly reprimand him.
Yuè was so terrified and anxious he did not know what to do,
and died a few days later.
Therefore, opinions at the time were confused,
believing he had been granted poisoned wine.
The court and the populace sighed and lamented him.
He was forty-four years old at the time.
An edict ordered the Dà Hónglú to supervise the funeral rites.
He was posthumously granted Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Dūdū of All Military Affairs of the Seven Prefectures of Jì, Dìng, Cāng, Yíng, Zhào, Yōu, and Jì, Tàizǎi, Tàifù, and Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
given the honorary designation of Huángyuè (Yellow Axe),
provided with a Wēnliáng carriage (hearse),
and two thousand rolls of burial cloth.
His posthumous title was Zhāowǔ.
Initially, Gāo Yuè, along with Gāo Zǔ, managed the affairs of the realm.
His household maintained private troops,
and furthermore stored military equipment,
accumulating over a thousand suits of armor.
Towards the end of Shì Zōng’s reign,
Gāo Yuè, believing the four seas to be peaceful,
memorialized requesting to surrender them.
Shì Zōng emphasized the importance of their close kinship,
trusted him fully,
saying:
“You, my uncle (Shū), belong to my inner circle,
your duty is to guard the state.
The armor you possess
is fundamentally available for state use.
Why do you, uncle, doubt and wish to surrender it?”
During the reign of Wénxuān,
he repeatedly requested to surrender them again,
but again, it was firmly disallowed.
When he was about to die,
he left a memorial expressing gratitude for Imperial favor,
and requested to turn over the armor to the military arsenal.
It was not until his burial was complete
that the surrender was finally permitted.
During the Huángjiàn era,
he was ritually enshrined alongside Shì Zōng in the ancestral temple.
Later, when Hú Guīyàn rebelled,
Shì Zǔ learned of his previous slander
and said:
“Qīnghé was loyal and valorous,
he exerted all his strength for the Imperial house,
yet Hú Guīyàn destroyed him
and alienated my flesh and blood.”
Hú Guīyàn’s assets were confiscated,
and a hundred mouths, both free and enslaved, were bestowed upon Gāo Yuè’s family.
Later, reflecting further on Gāo Yuè’s merits,
he was additionally granted the posthumous titles of Tàishī and Tàibǎo;
other provisions remained as before.
His son, Gāo Mài, succeeded him.
Gāo Mài,
courtesy name Jìngdé,
was intelligent and mature from an early age,
and was beloved by Xiǎn Zǔ.
At the age of seven,
he was sent to attend the Crown Prince.
Later he was appointed Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
On the day of his appointment,
Xiǎn Zǔ cautioned him, saying:
“Your late uncle previously governed Qīngzhōu
and left behind great kindness.
Therefore, I send you to comfort those common people.
You ought to govern diligently,
and do not let his good reputation and achievements fall.”
Gāo Mài wept and replied:
“I am young and naive,
and have been wrongly advanced.
Although I will exhaust my mediocre abilities,
I fear I will disgrace the previous administration.”
The Emperor said:
“Since you are capable of saying this,
I have no worries.”
Soon after, he was successively appointed Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn, Lǐngjūn, Cíbù Shàngshū, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Because Qīnghé was located within the capital region,
his title was changed to Prince of Lè'ān (Lè'ān Wáng).
He was transferred to Shìzhōng and Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
then sent out to serve as Xíngtái Púshè of Shuòzhōu.
After the Hòu Zhǔ was defeated at Jìnzhōu,
the Empress Dowager returned to the capital via the Tǔmén Dào.
Gāo Mài was ordered to command the troops
and escort the Empress Dowager.
At that time, the fawning favorites and eunuchs
were still committing atrocities,
all the common people's chickens and pigs
were seized by setting hunting falcons and dogs upon them to fight and consume them.
Gāo Mài arrested Gǒu Zǐyì, who held the title Yítóng Sānsī, and exposed him publicly to the army,
intending to execute him severely.
The Empress Dowager issued an order,
and only then was he released.
Liú Wénshū secretly said to Gāo Mài:
“Gǒu Zǐyì and his ilk
can manipulate speech to cause disaster or prosperity.
How can you act like this?
Are you not worried about the slanders that will arise later?”
Gāo Mài rolled up his sleeves and addressed Liú Wénshū:
“Since the time of Emperor Xiànwǔ,
the troops and soldiers were fostered and maintained,
and the government was entrusted to relatives and the worthy.
When using military force and deploying armies,
there was never a defeat.
Now the Western invaders have reached Bīngzhōu,
and most high officials have surrendered and betrayed us.
This is precisely because this group monopolizes power and manipulates authority,
which is why people internally and externally have become alienated,
and the court structure has collapsed.
If I could execute this scoundrel today,
and even if I were executed tomorrow,
I would have no regrets.
You are a relative by marriage to the Imperial house;
you should share the hatred of evil.
To retort with such words,
is this what is expected of you!”
When the Empress Dowager reached Yè,
the Zhōu army arrived immediately after.
Everyone was terrified,
lacking the will to fight.
Court officials went out to surrender,
one after another, day and night.
Gāo Mài then memorialized the Hòu Zhǔ, saying:
“Those who have now betrayed and rebelled
are mostly nobles,
while the rank-and-file soldiers
have not yet deserted.
I request that the family members of all officials of the fifth rank and above be summoned
and placed on the Sāntái.
Then threaten the officials, saying: ‘If the battle is not victorious,
we will retreat and burn the Sāntái.’
These men, mindful of their wives and children,
will certainly fight to the death.
Furthermore, our Imperial army has frequently been defeated,
so the rebels underestimate us.
If we now fight decisively with our backs to the city,
we will logically defeat them.
This is the best plan.”
The Hòu Zhǔ ultimately could not utilize this plan.
When Qí fell, he entered Zhōu,
and was granted the title Kāifǔ according to standard practice.
Under the Suí Dynasty, he successively served as Cìshǐ of Yáng, Chǔ, Guāng, and Táo four prefectures.
He died during the Kāihuáng era.
The Historian comments: The *Yì Jīng* says:
“Heaven and Earth wax and wane,
decreasing and increasing with the times,
how much more so for humans.”
This is because success and obstruction have their seasons,
and decline and prosperity align with the Way.
When the entire world yearns for order,
the benevolent manifest themselves to respond;
when the Way of the petty man flourishes,
one must hide virtue and withdraw to avoid them.
As for those who bear the designs of a Bólù,
occupying the position of a feudal bulwark,
how can they wish to confuse the state and avoid danger?
How can that be achieved?
Zhàojùn, by virtue of his close kinship,
bore the heavy responsibility of assisting the dying emperor.
If he had withdrawn, the dynasty would easily have been endangered,
but by eliminating the evil, both men and spirits were at peace.
Therefore, he stabilized the unified virtue
and shared this steadfast heart,
treading the fearful path without hesitation,
and facing crisis without fear.
By this loyalty and righteousness,
he was killed by the villainous.
Was it that his Way illuminated the four seas,
yet he did not encounter the wisdom of Zhōu Chéng;
or that the court expelled the Sānrén,
ultimately leading to the disaster of the Yīn Ruins?
If not, why did the state decay and weaken,
and why were the consequences so swift?
Qīnghé (Gāo Mài) was part of the era when order was established,
and achieved high position by his own efforts.
Going out as a general and coming in as a minister,
he aided in achieving great accomplishments.
Even Liú Jiǎ of the Hàn Dynasty
and Cáo Hóng of the Wèi house
are insufficient comparisons to discuss his merits.
The Tiānbǎo era was unlucky,
easily leading to remorse and failure.
Although his heroic spirit cannot be concealed,
it serves to reveal the lack of virtue in Xiǎn Zǔ.
The Eulogy says: Zhàojùn (Gāo Yuè) was heroic and outstanding,
his manner composed and upright.
Heaven’s Way shows no favoritism;
such a person met such a fate.
Glorious was Qīnghé (Gāo Mài),
by whom the state was managed.
His later career had minor flaws,
but these did not constitute moral failure.

Biography Six: Duke of Guǎngpíng, Gāo Shèng; Duke of Yángzhōu, Gāo Yǒnglè (Younger brother Gāo Chángbì); Prince of Xiānglè, Gāo Xiǎnguó; Prince of Shàngluò, Gāo Sīzōng (Son Gāo Yuánhǎi; Younger brother Gāo Sīhǎo); Prince of Píngqín, Gāo Guīyàn; Prince of Wǔxīng, Gāo Pǔ; Administrator of Chánglè, Gāo Língshān (Successor Gāo Fúhù).
Gāo Shèng, Duke of Guǎngpíng,
was a paternal grand-uncle of Emperor Shénwǔ.
He was tolerant and generous, possessing the manner of a venerable elder.
When Shénwǔ raised troops at Xìndū,
he appointed Gāo Shèng as Zhōngjūn Dàdūdū,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Guǎngpíng Jùn.
He successively held the positions of Sītú and Tàiwèi.
In the third year of Tiānpíng,
he died while in office.
He was posthumously granted the titles Jiǎ Huáng Yuè,
Tàiwèi, Tàishī, and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
He had no son,
so his elder brother’s son, Gāo Zǐyuàn, succeeded him.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
his title was changed to Prince of Píngchāng.
He died while serving as Wèiyǐn.
Yángzhōu Gōng Yǒnglè,
was the son of Shénwǔ's paternal cousin (from his grandfather's generation).
At the beginning of Tàichāng,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Yángzhōu County,
and later advanced in rank to Duke (Gōng).
He was successively promoted to serve as the Cìshǐ of Běiyù Zhōu.
During the Battle of Héyīn,
Sītú Gāo Áng suffered a defeat and retreated.
Yǒnglè defended the southern city of Héyáng.
Áng fled towards the city.
As the pursuing Western Army was about to arrive,
Yǒnglè did not open the gates.
Consequently, Áng was captured by the Western Army.
Shénwǔ was greatly angered
and had him beaten with 200 strokes of the rod.
Later, he was dismissed from Yù Zhōu,
and his household wealth did not accumulate.
Shénwǔ asked the reason why,
and he replied:
"Péi Jiān serves as the Zhǎngshǐ,
and Xīn Gōngzhèng serves as the Biéjià.
They received the King's commission,
and not a measure of wine or a single chicken has entered (my household)."
Shénwǔ then appointed Yǒnglè to Jì Zhōu,
retaining Jiān and Gōngzhèng as the Zhǎngshǐ and Biéjià, respectively.
He instructed Yǒnglè, saying:
"You must not be overtly greedy,
but do not fear taking small gains justly."
When Yǒnglè arrived at the province,
Jiān and Gōngzhèng remonstrated with him but were not heeded.
They reported the situation to Shénwǔ.
Shénwǔ sealed the memorial and showed it to Yǒnglè.
Only then did (Yǒnglè) realize the two men were honest and upright,
and he promoted and employed them both.
Yǒnglè died while in the province.
He was posthumously granted the titles Tàishī, Tàiwèi, and Lù Shàngshūshì.
His posthumous title (Shì) was Wǔzhāo.
Having no son,
his cousin Sīzōng used his second son, Xiàoxù, as heir,
who inherited the rank.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiūchéng Commandery.
Yǒnglè’s younger brother, Chángbì,
whose nickname was Āgē.
His temperament was coarse and aggressive.
Whenever he entered or exited the city,
he liked to beat up passersby.
People at the time all called him the Young Master Āgē (Āgē Lángjūn).
Being a member of the imperial clan (Zōngshì), he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Guǎngwǔ.
At that time, there was a Daoist called Tiān'ēn Dàorén,
who was extremely violent,
and rampaged through the villages and markets.
Later, he joined Chángbì’s faction,
specializing in fighting.
Wénxuān had them both arrested and imprisoned.
Tiān'ēn and over ten members of his faction were all executed publicly in the marketplace,
while Chángbì received one hundred lashes.
Soon after, he became the Cìshǐ of Nányíng Zhōu.
While in the province, he suddenly fled in panic without cause,
defecting and escaping to the Tūjué (Turks).
Ultimately, the place of his death remains unknown.
Xiānglè Wáng Xiǎnguó,
was Shénwǔ's paternal cousin (from his grandfather's generation).
He possessed no talent or skill,
but solely because he was a cautious and sincere member of the imperial clan (Zōngshì),
in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiānglè,
and held the position of General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
He died.
Shàngluò Wáng Sīzōng,
was Shénwǔ's cousin.
His temperament was lenient and mild,
and he possessed considerable military competence.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shàngluò Commandery.
He successively held the posts of Sīkōng and Tàifù.
He died while in office (hōng).
His son Yuánhǎi
was successively promoted to Sanqí Chángshì.
He desired to live in the mountains and forests
and practice Buddhist doctrines (Shìdiǎn).
Wénxuān permitted this.
He then entered Línlǜ Shān.
After two years,
he abandoned worldly affairs.
However, his resolve could not be maintained,
so he submitted a memorial requesting to return.
He was summoned back to his original post,
whereupon he indulged in drinking and unrestrained passion,
widely taking on concubines and attendants (Jīshì).
He was also appointed Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn).
Though he had limited capacity, his ambition was great,
and he regarded himself highly for his strategic planning.
At the end of the Huángjiàn era,
Xiàozhāo traveled to Jìnyáng,
Wǔchéng remained in charge of the capital,
Yuánhǎi, as the Sànqí Chángshì, was kept behind to manage confidential affairs.
Previously, when Xiàozhāo executed Yáng Yīn and others,
he had told Wǔchéng,
"If the matter succeeds, I will establish you as the Huáng Tàidì."
When he ascended the throne,
he instead made Wǔchéng oversee the military in Yè,
and established his son, Bǎinián, as the Huáng Tàizǐ.
Wǔchéng was very unhappy.
Earlier,
Jǐnán Wáng was kept in Yè,
the Língjūn Shèdí Fúlián was removed and made the Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu,
and Húlǜ Fēnglè was made Língjūn,
in order to divide Wǔchéng’s authority.
Wǔchéng detained Fúlián and did not permit Fēnglè to attend to business.
Thereupon, he pretended to hunt with Hénán Wáng Xiàoyú,
plotted in the field,
and returned only when it was dark.
Previously, a children’s rhyme said:
"Inside the Zhōngxīng Sì is a white Fúwēng,
the four directions listen carefully to the resonant sound,
the Dàorén hears it and strikes the bell at night."
At that time, the Chéngxiàng’s residence was within the Northern City,
which was formerly the Zhōngxīng Sì.
Fúwēng,
referred to a rooster,
presumably pointing to Wǔchéng's childhood name, Bùluòjī.
Dàorén,
was the childhood name of Jǐnán Wáng.
Dǎ Zhōng (striking the bell),
meant that he was about to be struck.
Soon afterward, the Tàishǐ reported that the Northern City had the aura of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ Qì).
Emperor Zhāo believed Jǐnán was the corresponding person,
so he sent Píngqín Wáng Guī Yàn to Yè,
to welcome Jǐnán to Bīngzhōu.
Wǔchéng first consulted Yuánhǎi,
and asked about a plan for his own security.
Yuánhǎi said:
"The Huáng Tàihòu is in excellent health,
His Majesty's filial nature is extraordinary,
Your Highness does not need to harbor separate anxieties."
Wǔchéng said:
"Are those my true feelings of sincerity?"
Yuánhǎi requested to return to his chamber to deliberate overnight.
Wǔchéng immediately detained Yuánhǎi in the rear hall.
Yuánhǎi did not sleep until dawn,
only pacing slowly around the bed.
Before the night watches indicated dawn,
Wǔchéng hurried out,
saying:
"What is your brilliant strategy?"
He replied:
"I devised three plans during the night,
but I fear they may not be worth using."
He then spoke of the affair where Liáng Xiàowáng, fearing execution, entered the pass,
and requested Wǔchéng to take a few riders to Jìnyáng,
first to see the Tàihòu and plead for compassion,
then to see the Zhǔshàng,
requesting to relinquish military authority,
taking death as the boundary [of his commitment],
seeking not to interfere in court governance,
which would certainly ensure the safety of Mount Tài.
This is the Shàngcè.
If not,
he should submit a detailed memorial,
stating:
" 'My authority and power have greatly flourished,
I fear attracting censure from the populace,'
request the governorships of Qīngzhōu and Qízhōu.
Residing there quietly,
you will certainly not attract public criticism.
This is the Zhōngcè."
Wǔchéng further asked about the worst plan (Xiàcè).
Yuánhǎi replied:
"If I speak, I fear extermination of my clan."
Wǔchéng then pressed him,
and he replied:
"Jǐnán is the designated heir (Shìdí);
the Zhǔshàng uses the Tàihòu's decree as a pretense to strip him of his status.
Now, assemble the civil and military officials,
show them this imperial mandate,
seize Fēnglè,
execute Guī Yàn,
honor Jǐnán,
issue orders to the realm,
and use righteousness to punish treason.
This is a unique opportunity in ten thousand generations."
Wǔchéng was delighted,
but he was suspicious and hesitant,
and ultimately could not adopt it.
He then had Zhèng Dàoqiān divine the matter,
and all replied:
"It is unfavorable to start an undertaking;
stillness brings good fortune."
He also summoned Cáo Wèizǔ,
and asked him about state affairs.
He replied:
"There is bound to be great misfortune."
Furthermore, at that time there was a certain Pān, the Magistrate of Línlǜ,
who was skilled in divination,
and who secretly told Wǔchéng:
"The palace carriage is about to pass away,
and Your Highness will become the master of the realm."
Wǔchéng detained him within the inner quarters to await confirmation.
He also ordered shamans to divine the future,
most of whom said there was no need to raise troops,
as great celebration would come naturally.
Wǔchéng then accepted the imperial decree,
ordering several hundred cavalry to escort Jǐnán to Jìnyáng.
When Xiàozhāo died,
Wǔchéng ascended the throne,
and appointed Yuánhǎi as Shìzhōng, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
In the second year of Héqīng,
Yuánhǎi was slandered by Hé Shìkāi,
and was beaten sixty times with a horse whip.
He was reproached, saying:
"When you were in Yèchéng,
you counseled me, the younger brother, to rebel against the elder brother—
how unrighteous!
Using Yèchéng's troops to resist Bīngzhōu—
how foolish!
Unrighteous and foolish—
how can you be employed?"
He was exiled to become the Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu.
Yuánhǎi’s later wife
was the niece of Lù Tàijī,
so he was quickly recalled and reinstated.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he managed court affairs together with Zǔ Tǐng.
Yuánhǎi often told Tǐng secrets he learned from Tàijī.
Tǐng requested the post of Língjūn,
but Yuánhǎi disallowed it.
Tǐng then reported what Yuánhǎi had confided to Tàijī.
Tàijī was enraged,
and expelled Yuánhǎi to become the Cìshǐ of Zhèngzhōu.
When Yèchéng was on the verge of defeat,
he was summoned back as Shàngshū Lìng.
In the seventh year of Zhōu Jiàndé,
he plotted treason in Yèchéng,
and was put to death.
Yuánhǎi delighted in chaos and rejoiced in misfortune,
yet he falsely feigned benevolence and compassion,
neither drinking wine nor eating meat.
In the late Tiānbǎo years of Wénxuān, the Emperor revered and believed in Buddhist law,
going so far as forbidding blood sacrifices in the Zōngmiào.
This was all devised by Yuánhǎi.
When he became Yòu Púshè,
he also persuaded the Hòu Zhǔ to prohibit slaughter [of animals],
and ban the sale of alcohol.
However, his fundamental disposition was not peaceful,
thus he eventually brought about ruin.
Sīzōng’s younger brother was Sīhǎo.
Sīhǎo was originally the son of the Hào clan,
but Sīzōng adopted him as a younger brother,
treating him very poorly.
When young, he served Wénxiāng with his mounted archery skills.
When Wénxuān received the mandate,
he was made Zuǒ Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn.
His original name was Sīxiào.
In the fifth year of Tiānbǎo,
when attacking the Rúrú,
Wénxuān was delighted by his valor,
and said to him:
"When you strike the enemy, you are like a falcon entering a flock of crows;
you should think of good things (Yì Sī Hǎo Shì)."
Therefore, his name was changed.
He successively rose to Shàngshū Lìng, Shuòzhōu Dào Xíngtái, Cìshǐ of Shuòzhōu, Kāifǔ, and Nán'ān Wáng,
and was highly successful in winning the support of the people in the border region of Shuò.
During the reign of Hòuzhǔ,
Zhuóxū Guāngbiàn served as an envoy arriving at the province.
Sīhǎo welcomed him with great caution.
Guāngbiàn was arrogant,
and Sīhǎo subsequently harbored deep resentment.
In the fifth year of Wǔpíng,
he therefore raised troops and rebelled.
He wrote a letter to the various nobles of Bìngzhōu, saying:
"The Sovereign grew up in the deep palace from youth,
unable to distinguish between genuine and false characters.
He drew close to the fierce and cunning,
and alienated the loyal and good.
Consequently, those maimed by knives and saws
gained status exceeding the palace steps;
merchant and barbarian rabble
usurped authority in the inner court.
They exploited the populace
and plundered the court and markets.
He was dim in hearing counsel,
and acted solely through cruelty and harm.
Imprisoning his mother in the deep palace,
he lacked the courtesy due from a son.
His two brothers were mutilated and slaughtered,
completely severing the righteousness of fraternal affection.
Furthermore, he indulged Zǐlì in seizing horses at the East Gate,
and Guāngbiàn in holding hawks at the West Market.
Bólóng obtained the title of Yítóng,
and Xiāoyáo received the name of Jùnjūn.
Dogs and horses held ranks,
their glory crowning the officials' caps and carriages.
The people cannot endure their burdens,
and thoughts of fostering chaos are growing.
Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì is truly the hero of the clan,
the one upon whom the state relies.
The Left Chancellor Húlǜ Míngyuè,
whose family served as chief ministers for generations,
his might was renowned among neighboring states.
Without crime or fault,
they were suddenly executed and exterminated.
I am part of the imperial lineage,
and have truly received special commendations.
Now I shall lead the righteous army,
aiming to eliminate the evildoers near the ruler.
I hope you fully understand this intention,
and do not give rise to doubt."
This was the composition of Wáng Xíngsī, Administrator of the Xíngtái.
Sīhǎo arrived at Yángqǔ,
proclaiming himself Great Chancellor,
and established all officials.
He appointed Wáng Shàngzhī, the Left Administrator of the Xíngtái, as Chief Clerk.
The Grand Commandant Zhào Hǎi, who was in Jìnyáng commanding troops,
was pressed by time and did not have leisure to submit a report.
He forged an imperial edict and deployed troops to resist Sīhǎo.
The troops all said:
"When Nán'ān Wáng comes,
we only need to shout 'Wànsuì!' and respectfully welcome him."
The Emperor heard of the change,
and sent Táng Yōng, Mòduōlóu Jìngxiǎn, Liú Táozhī, and the General of the Central Guards Qùdì Shìwén racing to Jìnyáng.
The Emperor mustered troops and followed continuously.
Sīhǎo's army was defeated,
and he and Xíngsī plunged into the water and died.
As for the two thousand men under his command,
Táozhī surrounded them,
killing and attempting to recruit them simultaneously,
but they ultimately did not surrender until they were all annihilated.
While the Emperor was on the road,
Chìnú Shì'ān was sending the victory report from Jìnyáng to Píngdū,
where he encountered Húsī Xiàoqīng.
Xiàoqīng tricked him into eating,
and then rode quickly to the temporary imperial residence,
shouting that the matter was settled.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and his attendants shouted Wànsuì.
After a long time,
Shì'ān then presented his report in person.
The Emperor said:
"What kind of affair was in your report
that allowed you to sit and eat?"
Thereupon, he rewarded Xiàoqīng and pardoned Shì'ān’s crime.
Sīhǎo’s corpse was exposed for seven days,
then it was butchered, flayed, and burned.
Shàngzhī was boiled in the market of Yè.
The Emperor ordered the inner chamberlains to shoot Sīhǎo’s consort in the palace,
and then burn her to death.
Fifty days before Sīhǎo rebelled,
someone reported his conspiracy.
Hán Chángluán's daughter was married to Sīhǎo's son.
Therefore, he reported that someone was falsely accusing the various nobles,
causing public unrest.
[He claimed] that if this person was not killed, future trouble could not be stopped,
so he had him executed.
After Sīhǎo was executed,
the executed man's younger brother knelt beneath the palace gate, appealing for a posthumous honor for his brother,
but Chángluán would not relay [the request].
Píngqín Wáng Guīyàn,
courtesy name Rén'īng,
was a cousin of Shénwǔ.
His father, Huī,
at the end of the Wèi dynasty, was due to be banished to Liángzhōu for an offense.
When traveling to the area between the Hé and Wèi Rivers,
he encountered bandits,
and by military merit was spared banishment.
Consequently, he lived in Hézhōu for many years.
Because he understood barbarian languages,
he was made Grand Envoy to the Western Regions.
He managed to acquire and present a barbarian lion as tribute,
and for this achievement obtained the post of Governor of Hédōng.
He soon died there.
Huī’s old bond of favor with Shénwǔ was very deep.
When Shénwǔ pacified Jīngluò,
he welcomed the corpse and buried him in the same ground as Mù.
He was posthumously granted Sītú,
with the posthumous appellation Wénxuān.
Initially, Huī had once passed through Cháng'ān market,
had a private affair with a woman named Wáng Shì, and fathered Guīyàn.
By this time, Guīyàn was already nine years old.
Shénwǔ sought him out and met him,
embracing him with mixed feelings of sorrow and joy.
[Guīyàn] was gradually promoted to Governor of Xúzhōu.
Guīyàn was simple in his youth,
but later changed his ways,
becoming dissolute, fond of music and women,
singing and drinking day and night.
His wife was the daughter of Yuán Tiānmù, Prince of Shàngdǎng of Wèi.
She was not beautiful but extremely spoiled and jealous.
They frequently quarreled.
He secretly petitioned Wénxuān seeking separation,
but the matter stalled and was not acted upon.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as Píngqín Wáng.
His formal consort Kāng and his birth mother Wáng Shì were both made Tàifēi.
He was good at serving both mothers
and was famous for his filial piety.
He was summoned to serve as Acting Attendant Gentleman
and gradually gained intimacy and favor.
For his merit in suppressing Hóu Jǐng,
