he was separately enfeoffed as Duke of Chánglè Commandery.
He was appointed General-in-Chief of the Guards.
The practice of adding the character Dà to the Lǐngjūn title
began with Guīyàn.
When Wénxuān executed Gāo Dézhèng,
all the gold, jewels, property, and goods were bestowed upon him.
At the beginning of Qiánmíng,
he was appointed Sītú,
and continued to oversee the Imperial Guards.
When Jìnán first traveled from Jìnyáng to Yè,
Yáng Yīn issued an edict
to keep five thousand escort troops in the western sector,
secretly preparing for the unexpected.
Several days after arriving at Yè,
Guīyàn finally learned of this.
Because of this, he secretly resented Yáng Yīn and Yàn.
Yáng Yīn and Yàn wanted to eliminate the two princes,
and sought Guīyàn's advice.
Guīyàn feigned delight,
and requested to discuss the plan with Yuánhǎi.
Yuánhǎi also agreed verbally but disagreed internally,
and rushed to inform Chángguǎng.
Chángguǎng thereupon executed Yáng Yīn, Yàn, and the others.
When Xiàozhāo was about to enter the Yúnlóng Gate,
the Grand Commandant Chéng Xiūníng arrayed his guards and refused him entry.
Guīyàn persuaded him,
and only then was he able to enter.
The situation was similar when he advanced toward the Bǎigé and Yǒngxiàng.
When Xiàozhāo ascended the throne,
he was especially favored and respected for this reason.
Whenever he entered the court, he was always ranked above Píngyuán Wáng Duàn Sháo.
He was appointed Sīkōng,
and concurrently Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
According to the Qí regulations,
only the Son of Heaven wore a gauze cap within the palace;
ministers all wore military caps.
Guīyàn was specially bestowed a gauze cap to honor him.
Emperor Xiàozhāo died,
Guī Yàn followed Wǔchéng from Jìnyáng and welcomed him to Yè.
When Wǔchéng ascended the throne,
Guī Yàn was promoted to the rank of Tàifù,
and concurrently held the post of Sītú,
and was habitually allowed to have three men of his private retinue bearing knives enter the imperial guards.
Following Wǔchéng back to the capital,
all the imperial relatives and powerful officials vied to invite him;
wherever he went,
everyone present utterly admired him.
Since Guī Yàn held the high position of general and minister,
his ambition was overly full,
his speech was insulting and overbearing,
behaving as if there was no one else around.
Those who discussed the matter believed that his prestige and authority shook the sovereign,
and would certainly lead to disaster and chaos.
The Emperor also recalled his previous acts of treachery,
and gradually grew suspicious of him.
Gāo Yuánhǎi, Bì Yìyún, Gāo Gānhé, and others frequently spoke of his faults.
The Emperor visited Guī Yàn’s house,
summoned Wèi Shōu to draft an imperial edict before him,
intending to bestow upon him the title of Yòu Chéngxiàng.
Wèi Shōu said to Yuánhǎi:
“His Majesty ascended the throne using the title of Yòu Chéngxiàng.
Now, because Guī Yàn’s prestige is too excessive,
he is being sent out.
How can this title be bestowed upon him again?”
Thereupon, he was appointed Tàizǎi and Prefect of Jìzhōu.
Gānhé immediately copied out the document.
During the day,
an order was also given to the gate officers forbidding anyone to enter the interior without authorization.
At that time, Guī Yàn was indulging in wine at home,
and did not know (about the appointment) until the night passed.
The next morning, when he wished to attend court,
he reached the gate and learned of it,
and was greatly alarmed and withdrew.
When he announced his name and expressed thanks,
an imperial order commanded him to depart quickly,
and separately bestowed money, silk, ceremonial music (gǔ chuī), and medicine;
everything was complete and thoughtful.
Furthermore, military officials and supervising generals were ordered to escort him all the way to Qīngyáng Gōng.
They bowed and withdrew,
none daring to speak with him.
Only with Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì did he speak for a long time,
but no one heard what was said at the time.
Upon reaching the prefecture,
he felt uneasy,
and plotted rebellion.
He intended to wait until the receipt of rations was finished,
distribute rewards to the soldiers,
watch for the imperial carriage to go to Jìnyáng,
and then take advantage of the emptiness to enter Yè.
He was reported by his Lángzhōng Lìng, Lǚ Sīlǐ.
An imperial edict ordered Píngyuán Wáng Duàn Sháo to attack him.
Guī Yàn had previously established private relay stations in the southern borders.
When he heard that the army was approaching,
he was informed,
and immediately encircled the city and defended it.
Before this,
the Jìzhōu Chief Clerk Yǔwén Zhòngluán, Commandant Lǐ Zǔyì, Adjutant Chén Jìqú, Senior Staff Officer Fáng Zǐbì, and Chánglè Commandery Prefect Wèi Pǔxīng suspected Guī Yàn of having ill intent,
and had jointly signed a secret memorial.
Guī Yàn pursued and captured them,
and thereupon arrested and imprisoned these five men including Zhòngluán.
As they all still refused to submit,
he killed them all.
When the army had already pressed against the city,
Guī Yàn ascended the wall and shouted loudly, saying:
“When Emperor Xiàozhāo first died,
the million men of the Six Armies were all in the hands of your subject.
I committed myself to Yè to welcome Your Majesty.
If I did not rebel at that time,
how could I have a rebellious heart today?
I only hate that Gāo Yuánhǎi, Bì Yìyún, and Gāo Gānhé have misled the Emperor,
and envied and hated loyal and good men.
If only these three men are killed for my sake,
I will immediately approach the city wall and cut my own throat.”
Afterwards, the city was breached,
and he fled north alone on horseback.
He was captured upon reaching Jiāojīn,
chained and sent to Yè.
The Emperor ordered Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì to privately ask him the reason.
Guī Yàn said:
“If immature youths are allowed to manipulate me,
how can I not rebel?”
Ruì asked:
“Who are they?”
Guī Yàn said:
“How can Yuánhǎi and Gānhé be veteran officials of the court?
If it were the time of the old man of the Zhào family,
how could I harbor resentment?”
Thereupon, the Emperor again sent someone to censure him.
He replied:
“Gāo Yuánhǎi received Bì Yìyún’s residence,
and used it to become the Prefect of his home prefecture,
and was granted the ceremonial music of the rear division.
I am a Fān Wáng and a Tàizǎi,
yet I did not receive ceremonial music.
Just kill Yuánhǎi and Yìyún, and that will be all.”
The Emperor ordered Area Commander Liú Táozhī to drag him in.
Guī Yàn still repeated his previous words, hoping to live.
The Emperor commanded discussion regarding his crime,
and all said that he could not be pardoned.
Thereupon, he was loaded onto an open cart,
gagged and with his hands tied behind his back.
Liú Táozhī approached him with a blade,
and followed him with drumming.
He, along with fifteen of his sons and grandsons, were all executed publicly.
He was posthumously bestowed the title of Prefect of Rénzhōu.
During the Wèi era, a mountain collapsed,
and two stone horns were found,
and stored in the military arsenal (Wǔkù).
Emperor Wénxuān entered the arsenal,
bestowed weapons upon his attendants,
and specifically gave the two stone horns to Guī Yàn.
He said:
“When you served Chángshān, you must not rebel;
when you serve Chángguǎng, you are permitted to rebel.
When you rebel,
take these horns to frighten the Hàn (officials).”
Guī Yàn had three ridges on his forehead bone,
which made wearing a turban uneasy.
Emperor Wénxuān once saw this,
and, angered,
ordered him to be struck on the forehead with a horse whip,
so that blood covered his face.
He said:
“When you rebel, you should use this bone to frighten the Hàn (officials).”
It is said that his words about rebellion were finally verified.
Pǔ, Prince of Wǔxīng,
courtesy name Déguǎng,
was the son of Guī Yàn’s elder brother, Guī Yì.
His nature was gentle, temperate, and he was magnanimous.
When he was nine years old,
Guī Yàn came with him from Hézhōu to Luòyáng,
and Emperor Shénwǔ ordered him to study and reside with his own sons.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Wǔxīng Commandery.
In the second year of Wǔpíng,
he was successively promoted to Sīkōng.
In the sixth year,
he served as the Director of the Mobile Secretariat of Yùzhōu Circuit and Shàngshū Lìng.
When the Later Emperor fled to Yè,
he was immediately promoted to Tàizǎi.
When the Zhōu army approached,
he surrendered.
He died in Cháng'ān.
He was posthumously bestowed the titles of Shàng Kāifǔ and Prefect of Yùzhōu.
Língshān, Grand Administrator of Chánglè,
courtesy name Jǐngsōng,
was a kinsman of Emperor Shénwǔ.
He followed Emperor Shénwǔ when he raised troops in Xìndū,
and died in office as Grand Administrator of Chánglè.
He was posthumously bestowed the titles of Dà Jiāngjūn and Sīkōng,
with the posthumous name Wénxuān.
His son, Yì,
died as Garrison Commander of Wǔpíng,
and had no son.
Emperor Wénxuān installed Fúhù, the son of Língshān’s cousin Jiànguó, Prefect of Qízhōu, as Língshān’s heir.
Fúhù,
courtesy name Chényuán,
had rough clerical ability.
At the beginning of the Tiāntǒng era,
he was successively promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
Fúhù served across several reigns,
participating in vital affairs,
but he loved wine by nature.
He frequently made mistakes while drunk,
and this became even more severe in his later years,
to the point where he did not eat for consecutive days,
dedicated solely to excessive drinking.
His spirit and consciousness became confused,
and thus he died.
He was posthumously bestowed the title of Prefect of Yǎnzhōu.
His grandson Yì, Marquis of Jiànguó, inherited the title.
Yì was cautious in his youth.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was a Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
During the Suí Kāihuáng era,
he served as Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Shǎoqīng),
and died due to a legal incident.
Biographies Chapter Seven: Dòu Tài, Wèi Jǐng, Lóu Zhāo (Son of elder brother Ruì), Shèdí Gān (Son Shìwén), Hán Guǐ, Pān Lè.
Dòu Tài,
courtesy name Shìníng,
was a man of Dà'ān Hànshū.
His ancestry originally descended from Qīnghé Guānjīn.
His grandfather, Lúo,
was the Wèi Tǒngwàn Zhènjiàng,
and therefore resided in the northern frontier.
His father, Yuè,
when Pòliùhán Bá líng created chaos at the end of the Wèi dynasty,
stood firm and defended the area with Zhènjiàng Yáng Jūn,
and was killed.
When Tài became eminent,
he was posthumously granted the title Sītú.
Initially,
Tài's mother dreamt that wind and thunder suddenly arose,
appearing as if there would be rain.
She went out to the courtyard to observe,
saw lightning that dazzled the eyes,
and driving rain that soaked and splashed her.
She woke up startled and sweating,
and subsequently became pregnant.
The term was reached but she did not give birth,
causing great fear.
A shaman said:
"Cross the river and rinse your skirt,
and giving birth to the child will certainly be easy."
She immediately went toward the water,
and suddenly saw a person,
who said:
"You are about to give birth to a noble son;
you should move south."
Tài's mother followed this advice.
Soon after, she gave birth to Tài.
When he grew up,
he excelled at mounted archery,
and possessed courage and strategy.
Tài's father and brothers died in battle at the garrison,
and Tài personally carried their remains back to Ěrzhū Róng.
For his meritorious service in accompanying the punitive expedition against Xíng Gǎo,
he was granted the title Guǎng'ā Zǐ.
When Shénwǔ was stationed at Jìnzhōu,
he requested Tài to serve as the Zhènchéng Dūdū,
and participate in military planning.
He was successively promoted to Shìzhōng and Jīngjī Dà Dūdū,
and shortly thereafter served as Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi.
Tài held a position in the Censorate based on his merit and status as a relative of the imperial family;
although he did not make many investigations or arrests,
the officials were all fearful of him.
In the third year of Tiānpíng (Heavenly Peace),
Shénwǔ led an expedition to the west,
ordering Tài to enter through Tóngguān.
In the fourth year,
Tài reached Xiǎoguān,
where he was ambushed by Emperor Wén of Zhōu,
his entire army was lost,
and Tài committed suicide.
When Tài was about to depart from Yè,
there was a rumor among the Buddhist nuns of Huìhuà temple in Yè saying:
"Dòu Xíngtái,
goes but does not return."
Before he left,
in the third watch of the night,
suddenly several thousand people in red robes, wearing caps and headbands, entered the Censorate,
saying
"Arrest Dòu Zhōngwèi."
The soldiers and clerks on duty were all startled.
These figures entered several rooms,
and quickly departed.
In the morning, they checked the locks and keys, finding nothing amiss,
and then realized they were not human.
Everyone knew he was certain to be defeated.
He was posthumously granted Dà Sīmǎ, Tàiwèi, and Lù Shàngshūshì,
and his posthumous name was Wǔzhēn.
Tài's wife
was the younger sister of Empress Lóu Wǔmíng.
Although Tài was treated favorably due to his relation,
his accomplishments and reputation were self-established.
When Qí accepted the abdication,
a sacrificial announcement was made at his tomb.
At the beginning of Huángjiàn,
he was inducted to share sacrificial rites in the temple courtyard of Shénwǔ.
His son Xiàojìng succeeded him.
His position was Yítóng Sānsī.
Wèi Jǐng,
courtesy name Shìzhēn,
was a man of Shànwú.
The Qín and Hàn dynasties established the Wèihòu Guān;
his ancestors held this position,
and thus took this as their clan name.
Jǐng's nature was gentle and sincere,
and he possessed considerable chivalrous spirit.
During the Wèi Xiàochāng period,
when the Northern Garrisons revolted,
Jǐng and Shénwǔ joined Dù Luòzhōu's ranks,
and later both submitted to Ěrzhū Róng.
For his military merit, he was enfeoffed as Bóyě Xiàn Bó.
Later, he followed Shénwǔ when he raised troops at Xìndū.
In the Battle of Hánlíng,
only the forces commanded by Jǐng suffered a loss.
When Shénwǔ entered Lùo,
he left Jǐng to garrison Yè.
Shortly thereafter, he was promoted in rank to Gōng (Duke).
Jǐng's wife, Chángshān Jūn,
was Shénwǔ's elder sister.
Because of his meritorious service and status as a relative of the imperial family,
whenever there were military affairs,
he and Shèdí Gān were always heavily entrusted,
but he could not abandon his passion for seeking profit,
and Shénwǔ often criticized and blamed him for it.
He was transferred to be Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
where he again accepted large bribes,
and mobilized laborers for hunting,
resulting in three hundred deaths.
Shèdí Gān and Jǐng were seated with Shénwǔ,
and [Shèdí Gān] requested to serve as Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi.
Shénwǔ said:
"Why would you stoop to request such a humble office?"
Gān replied:
"To arrest Wèi Jǐng."
Shénwǔ laughed heartily,
and ordered the actor Shí Dǒngtǒng to ridicule him.
Dǒngtǒng stripped Jǐng's clothes,
and said:
"Your Grace strips the common people;
why shouldn't Dǒngtǒng strip Your Grace?"
Shénwǔ admonished Jǐng, saying:
"You should be without greed."
Jǐng replied:
"Let's calculate whose livelihood is greater:
I only take from those above me,
while you cut the Imperial levies."
Shénwǔ laughed and did not reply.
He was renamed Chánglè Jùngōng.
He successively held the positions of Tàibǎo and Tàifù,
but was subsequently placed under restriction for harboring fugitives.
He sent Cuī Xiān to tell Wénxiāng:
"Tell Ahuì'ér,
is wealth and prominence trying to kill me?"
Shénwǔ wept upon hearing this,
and went to the palace gate, saying:
"Had it not been for Wèi Jǐng,
I would not have reached today."
He requested three times,
and the Emperor finally permitted it.
Jǐng was consequently demoted to Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Shénwǔ visited him,
Jǐng lay down stiffly in anger,
crying out:
"Is this the time you choose to kill me?"
Chángshān Jūn said to Shénwǔ:
"The old man is close to death;
how can you bear to oppress him to this extent?"
She also said:
"I bore calluses drawing water for you."
She then showed her palm.
Shénwǔ stroked Jǐng
and knelt before him.
Previously,
Jǐng possessed a Guǒxiàmǎ.
Wénxiāng asked for it,
but Jǐng refused to give it,
saying:
"Earth supporting each other becomes a wall;
men supporting each other become a king.
Should I not even be allowed to keep a single horse that you ask for?"
Shénwǔ confronted Wénxiāng in front of Jǐng and Chángshān Jūn, criticized him, and beat him with a rod.
Chángshān Jūn wept and pleaded for him.
Jǐng said:
"The boy is used to such things.
Let him be used as a trusted subordinate;
why must you cry dry tears and weep wet tears, preventing him from being beaten?"
Soon after, he was granted the position of Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and his conduct was considerably reformed;
the common people were settled because of him.
He was summoned and appointed Dà Sīmǎ.
He fell ill,
and died in the province.
He was posthumously granted Tàishī and Shàngshūlìng.
When Qí accepted the abdication,
because Jǐng was a founding meritorious official,
an edict was issued for a sacrificial announcement at his tomb.
At the beginning of Huángjiàn,
he was inducted to share sacrificial rites in the temple courtyard of Shénwǔ,
and posthumously enfeoffed as Chánglè Wáng.
Zǐ Càn,
while young, held prominent posts.
His nature was rough and martial.
In the early Tiānbǎo
period, Gēdì Gān and others were enfeoffed as princes (wáng).
Càn was greatly angered and resentful
that his father was not included in the princely ranks.
For more than ten days, he shut his gate and did not attend court.
The Emperor found this strange
and sent an envoy to his residence to inquire about it.
Speaking to the envoy through the gate,
he said: "Since the Son of Heaven has not enfeoffed Càn's father as a prince,
Càn might as well die."
The envoy said:
"You must open the gate to receive the imperial edict."
Càn then drew his bow and shot the envoy through the gate.
The envoy reported the situation.
Wénxuān sent Duàn Sháo to convey the imperial command.
Càn met Sháo,
only beating his chest and weeping loudly,
without answering a single word.
Wénxuān personally visited his residence to comfort him,
and only then did he resume attending court.
Soon after, Jǐng was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince Chánglè.
Càn succeeded to the title.
He reached the positions of Sītú and Tàifù before he died.
His son, Shìbiàn, succeeded him.
When the Zhōu army was about to enter Yè,
Biàn was ordered to lead over a thousand cavalry to scout.
He exited through Fǔkǒu,
ascended a high mound and looked west.
He saw a flock of crows flying up in the distance,
and thought they were the banners and standards of the Western Army.
He immediately rode back.
By the time he reached Zǐmò Qiáo,
he dared not look back.
During the Kàihuáng period of the Suí dynasty,
he died while serving as the Administrator (Cìshǐ) of Xīzhōu.
Lóu Zhāo,
courtesy name Púsà,
was a man from Píngchéng, Dàijùn Commandery,
and the younger maternal brother of Empress Wǔmíng.
His grandfather, Tí,
was heroic, outstanding, and discerning.
His household servants numbered in the thousands,
and his cattle and horses were measured by volume of grain.
His nature was generous and helpful,
and many gentlemen flocked to him.
During the time of Emperor Tàiwǔ
of the Wèi dynasty, he was enfeoffed as Marquis Zhēndìng for his achievements.
His father, Nèigān,
possessed martial strength,
but died before entering official service.
Because of Zhāo's eminence,
the Wèi court posthumously granted him the title Sītú.
When Qí received the abdication,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince Tàiyuán.
Zhāo was principled, refined, and upright.
He possessed great tolerance and deep strategy.
His belt was eight *chǐ* long,
and his archery and horsemanship surpassed the age.
Shénwǔ esteemed and relied heavily upon him since his youth.
Zhāo also recognized Shénwǔ early
and showed him the utmost reverence and respect.
He often accompanied Shénwǔ on hunts
and frequently advised that he should not ride into danger or traverse perilous terrain.
When Shénwǔ was about to leave Xìndū,
Zhāo supported his grand plan
and was immediately made Grand Military Governor of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Dà Dūdū).
He followed in defeating Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ē,
and was enfeoffed as Earl of Ānxǐ County.
This was changed to Duke of Jǐběi,
and later transferred to Duke of Púyáng Commandery.
He was appointed General Director of the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
When Emperor Xiàowǔ of Wèi was preparing to oppose Shénwǔ,
Zhāo resigned due to illness and returned to Jìnyáng.
He followed Shénwǔ in entering Luòyáng.
When Fán Zǐhú, the Administrator of Yǎnzhōu,
rebelled, Zhāo was made Grand Military Governor of the Eastern Route (Dōngdào Dà Dūdū) to suppress him.
After Zǐhú was killed,
the generals urged Zhāo to arrest and execute all his followers.
Zhāo said:
"The state of this province
is due to improper conduct, subjecting people to cruel harm.
The fault lies with their lord;
what crime have the people committed?"
He subsequently released them all.
Later, he was transferred to Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ),
still holding the post of Director of the Army.
He was promoted to Sītú,
and then went out to serve as the Administrator of Dìngzhōu.
Zhāo was fond of wine.
Later in life, he suffered from partial paralysis (piānfēng).
Although he recovered,
he was still unable to handle arduous duties.
While in the province, he delegated matters to his subordinates.
Zhāo only managed the general principles.
He died in the province.
He was posthumously granted the title of Acting Imperial Ax, Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
His posthumous name was Wǔ.
When Qí received the abdication,
an imperial edict was issued announcing sacrifices at his tomb,
and he was enfeoffed as Prince Tàiyuán.
In the early Huángjiàn
period, he was accorded the right to be enshrined in the ancestral temple of Shénwǔ.
His eldest son, Zhòngdá, succeeded him.
He was re-enfeoffed as Prince Púyáng.
His second son, Dìngyuǎn,
held prominent posts while young.
Among the maternal relatives, he was particularly favored and intimate with Wǔchéng.
He was separately enfeoffed as Prince of Línhuái Commandery.
When Wǔchéng was critically ill,
he, along with the Prince of Zhàojùn and others, received the dying instructions.
His position was Sīkōng.
When the Prince of Zhàojùn impeached and dismissed Hé Shìkāi,
Dìngyuǎn conspired with him,
but then accepted bribes from Shìkāi,
leading to the downfall of the Prince of Zhàojùn.
His avarice and baseness were like this.
He was soon appointed Administrator of Yíngzhōu.
Originally, Dìngyuǎn's younger brother, Jìlüè,
was asked by Mù Típó for his singing girl concubine,
but Dìngyuǎn refused.
When Gāo Sīhǎo rebelled,
Típó ordered the Gentleman of the Palace (Lángzhōnglìng) of the State of Línhuái to accuse Dìngyuǎn of secretly communicating with Sīhǎo.
The Later Lord ordered the Kaifǔ, Duàn Chàng, to lead three thousand cavalry to surround him,
and ordered the Palace Supervising Censor (Shì Yùshǐ), Zhào Xiùtōng, to arrive at the province
and impeach Dìngyuǎn on charges of accepting illicit goods and bribes.
Dìngyuǎn suspected a coup
and consequently hanged himself.
Zhāo’s elder brother's son was Ruì.
Ruì's courtesy name was Fórén.
His father, Bá,
was the Minister (Shàngshū) of the Southern Department during the Wèi dynasty.
Ruì was orphaned young
and raised by his uncle, Zhāo.
He served as Commandant (Dūdū) within Shénwǔ's tent,
was enfeoffed as Viscount (Zǐ) of Yè County,
and was successively promoted to Administrator of Guāngzhōu.
While in office,
he was greedy and unrestrained, and was severely reprimanded by Wénxiāng.
Later, his title was changed to Duke of Jiǔmén County.
When Qí received the abdication,
he was appointed General Director of the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn),
and separately enfeoffed as Marquis of Āndìng.
Ruì had no other talents or abilities;
he was honored and favored due to being a maternal relative,
and indulged in wealth and lust.
While serving as Administrator of Yíngzhōu,
he accumulated wealth without satiety.
In the early Huángjiàn
period, he was enfeoffed as Prince Dōng'ān.
In the first year of Dàníng,
he was promoted to Sīkōng.
He pacified Gāo Guīyàn in Jìzhōu,
and upon returning, was appointed Sītú.
In the third year of Héqīng,
he wrongly killed people.
He was impeached by the Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng), Sòng Zhòngxiàn.
He was pardoned only after a general amnesty.
Soon after, he became Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
and was promoted to Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) for his military merits.
When Wǔchéng reached Héyáng,
he was still ordered to lead a detached force to Xuánhù.
Ruì remained in the Yù region for over a hundred days,
exclusively engaging in illegal activities.
An edict dismissed him from office,
and he returned to his residence as a prince.
Soon after, he was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi)
and died.
He was posthumously granted Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
His son, Zǐyàn, succeeded him.
His position was Kaifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Gēdì Gān,
was a man from Shànwú.
His great-grandfather, Yuèdòujuàn,
during the time of Emperor Dàowǔ of Wèi, was granted an area of a hundred *lǐ* square encompassing Xīlàwū Shān, west of Shànwú, for his achievements, where he settled.
Later, he led his tribe to relocate north
and made his home in Shuòfāng.
Gān was straightforward and spoke little,
possessing martial skills.
In the early Zhèngguāng
period of Wèi, he cleared out the rebellious faction,
was appointed General (Jiāngjūn),
and served as an imperial guard inside the palace.
Because his family lived in a cold region
and was not suited to the severe heat,
in winter he was allowed to enter the capital,
and in summer, he returned to his hometown.
In the first year of Xiàochāng,
the northern frontier became troubled.
He fled to Yúnzhōng,
and was subsequently sent by the Administrator (Cìshǐ) Fèi Mù to Ěrzhū Róng.
As a Military Commander (Jūnzhǔ), he followed Róng into Luòyáng.
Afterwards, [he] followed Shénwǔ [Gāo Huān] in raising troops.
He defeated the Sīhú (Four Hu tribes) at Hánlíng,
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Guǎngpíng County.
Soon after, [he] was advanced to the status of Commandery Duke.
During the Campaign of Héyīn,
while the various generals achieved great victories,
only Gān’s troops retreated.
Shénwǔ, valuing his former merits,
ultimately did not criticize or dismiss him.
Soon after, [he] was transferred to Grand Protector (Tàibǎo) and Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
When Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled using Wǔláo,
Shénwǔ campaigned against him,
appointing Gān as the Grand Military Governor (Dà Dūdū) leading the vanguard.
Gān, upon setting out, did not even pass by his home.
When meeting Hóu Jǐng, [he] did not have time to eat.
Jǐng sent cavalry to chase after him and present the meal.
At that time, Emperor Wén [Yuán Bǎo jù] personally led troops to Luòyáng.
The military presence was very imposing.
The various generals were hesitant to cross southwards,
but Gān decisively planned to cross the Hé (Yellow River).
Shénwǔ's main army followed immediately and arrived,
and consequently they achieved a great victory over them.
Returning, [he] became the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dìngzhōu.
[He] was not skilled in administrative affairs,
and matters were often chaotic and troublesome.
However, [he] lived plainly and abstemiously,
and was not resented by the officials and common people.
[He] was promoted to Grand Master (Tàishī).
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
recognizing his primary merits from the Tiānpíng era in assisting the mandate,
[he] was enfeoffed as the Prince of Zhāngwǔ Commandery,
and transferred to Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi).
Gān married Shénwǔ’s younger sister, the Eldest Princess of Lèlíng.
[He] was treated with respect due to this familial relationship.
Since participating in the loyal service to the throne,
[he] always commanded the large armies.
His heavy prestige and reputation
caused the various generals to submit to him.
Furthermore, [he] was extremely severe and fierce.
Once, when [he] visited the capital,
Yuán Xiàoyǒu, the Prince of Qiáo of Wèi, spoke jestingly and excessively at the Duke's gate.
None of the other Dukes dared to openly rebuke him.
Gān sternly reproached him.
Xiàoyǒu was greatly ashamed.
People at the time praised this as excellent.
[He] died.
[He] was posthumously granted the honorific Ax of Authority (Jiǎ Huángyuè),
Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi),
and provided with a covered carriage (Wēnliáng Chē).
His posthumous name (shì) was Jǐngliè.
Gān was illiterate.
When signing his name, [he] wrote the character
“Gān”
character,
but drew the top stroke backward (starting from the right).
People at the time called this "Piercing Awl" (Chuānzhuī).
There was also a military general, Wáng Zhōu,
whose signature first formed the character
“Jí”
before completing its outer strokes.
It was only by the time of the descendants of these two men that they both became literate.
Gān,
in the beginning of the Huángjiàn era, was enshrined alongside Shénwǔ in the ancestral temple courtyard.
[His] son, Jìngfú,
held the rank of Integrator of the Three Ducal Ministries (Yítóng Sānsī),
and died.
[Jìngfú's] son, Shìwén, succeeded him.
Shìwén was solitary and upright by nature.
Even neighbors and closest relatives
did not communicate intimately with him.
While in Qí [Northern Qí],
[he] inherited the title Prince of Zhāngwǔ Commandery.
[He] held the position of General Who Leads the Army (Lǐng Jūn Jiāngjūn).
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu pacified Qí,
many gentry and officials east of the mountains (Shāndōng) came out to welcome him.
Only Shìwén kept his gate closed and maintained his solitude.
The Emperor admired him for this.
[He] granted him the titles Founding Officeholder (Kāifǔ) and Integrator of the Three Ducal Ministries (Yítóng Sānsī),
and Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Suízhōu.
When Emperor Wén of Suí received the imperial mandate,
[he] was additionally granted the rank of Founding Officeholder (Kāifǔ),
and enfeoffed as the Viscount of Húpō County.
Soon after, [he] was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Bèizhōu.
His nature was clean and austere.
[He] refused public provisions.
His family had no surplus wealth.
His son once secretly ate a pastry from the official kitchen.
Shìwén put him in the stocks in prison for several days,
beat him two hundred strokes with a staff,
and sent him back to the capital on foot.
Servants and bondmen dared not leave the house.
The salt and vegetables purchased
had to be bought outside the commandery borders.
Whenever [he] went out or came in,
[he] sealed and locked his gate.
Relatives and old friends ceased visiting.
Congratulations and condolences were not exchanged.
Laws and decrees were strict and severe.
Officials and common people obeyed submissively.
Nothing was picked up from the road.
Whenever there was a minor offense,
Shìwén would surely implicate and punish them harshly.
Once, when [he] attended court,
the Emperor happened to grant permission for the Dukes and Ministers to enter the Zǔocáng (Left Repository),
allowing them to take as much as they wished.
Everyone loaded themselves heavily.
Shìwén alone held one bolt of silk in his mouth,
and carried one bolt in each hand.
The Emperor asked him why.
Shìwén replied:
"My mouth and hands are all sufficient [for carrying],
I need nothing more."
The Emperor found this remarkable,
and presented him with additional gifts separately.
When Shìwén arrived at the Prefecture,
[he] exposed corrupt officials.
For graft amounting to a foot of cloth or a bushel of grain,
[he] showed no leniency.
[He] reported having caught a thousand people,
all of whom were assigned to garrison duty in Lǐngnán (South of the Ridge).
Relatives saw them off.
Cries of lamentation spread throughout the prefecture borders.
Upon reaching Lǐngnán,
eighteen or nineteen out of twenty died due to the infectious diseases and pestilence.
Consequently, the parents, wives, and children only wept curses upon Shìwén.
Shìwén heard of this,
and ordered men to arrest them.
Though flogging and beating were abundant before them,
the weeping intensified further.
The Aide-de-camp (Sīmǎ) Wéi Kūn of Jīngzhào, and the Magistrate (Lìng) Zhào Dá of Hédōng of Qīnghé, were both harsh and demanding.
Only the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) administered benevolent governance.
People at the time had a saying:
"The Prefect [rules] with Ràchà (Rakshasa/Demon) governance,
the Aide-de-camp glares like a viper (Fùshé),
the Chief Clerk judges with a gentle smile,
and Qīnghé eats people alive."
The Emperor heard this,
and sighed, saying:
"Shìwén’s tyranny exceeds that of fierce beasts."
Ultimately, [he] was dismissed from his post due to these charges.
Before long, [he] became the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Yōngzhōu.
[He] said to others:
"I adhere deeply to the law,
and cannot spy out or attend upon powerful nobles.
I fear I shall surely die in this office."
When [he] took up the office,
[he] enforced the law strictly and justly.
[He] did not spare powerful relatives of the imperial house.
Guests dared not come to his gate.
Many people held grudges and resentments.
Shìwén's cousin (paternal younger cousin) became a consort of the Qí imperial family.
She was beautiful.
After Qí was destroyed,
she was bestowed upon Chángsūn Lǎn, the Duke of Xuē.
Lǎn's wife, Madame Zhèng, was jealous.
[She] defamed the cousin to Empress Wénxiàn.
The Empress ordered Lǎn to divorce her.
Shìwén was ashamed of this,
and refused to meet with his cousin.
Later, Táng Jūnmíng, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yìngzhōu, while observing mourning for his mother,
engaged her as his wife.
Because of this, Jūnmíng and Shìwén were both impeached by the Censorate (Yùshǐ).
Shìwén was of a rigid nature.
After several days in prison,
[he] died of anger and indignation.
His family had no surplus wealth.
[He] had three sons.
Their daily necessities were lacking.
No relatives or friends were willing to support them.
Hán Guǐ,
courtesy name Bǎinián,
was a native of Dínà in Tài'ān.
When young, he possessed integrity and ambition.
His nature was profound and reserved;
happiness or anger did not show on his face.
When Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) guarded Jìnzhōu,
he appointed him as the Commandant of the Garrison City.
When he raised troops in Xìndū,
Guǐ supported the grand plan.
He followed in defeating Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā,
and again followed in the battle at Hán Líng.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngchāng County.
He subsequently supervised the Central Army,
and followed in defeating Ěrzhū Zhào at Chìhóng Lǐng.
He was promoted again to be the Governor of Tàizhōu,
where he greatly achieved peace on the border.
When Shénwǔ toured Tàizhōu,
he wished to bring Guǐ back (to the capital),
and subsequently bestowed upon the residents of the city, per household, two bolts of silk and cloth.
The seven thousand households of the prefecture, led by Tián Zhāo, all declined the gifts,
requesting only that Guǐ be retained.
Shénwǔ praised this highly,
and therefore allowed him to remain.
Repeatedly for military merits,
he was advanced in title to Duke of Āndé Commandery.
He was transferred to be the Governor of Yíngzhōu.
While in the prefecture, he engaged in excessive accumulation (of wealth),
and was impeached by the Censorate,
resulting in the removal of his office and title.
Not long after,
he was restored as Duke of Āndé Commandery.
He successively held the positions of Prefect of the Central Secretariat and Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
When Qí received the abdication (mandate),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Āndé Commandery.
Guǐ's sister had been taken into Shénwǔ's harem
and bore Shàngdǎng Prince Huàn (Gāo Huàn).
Moreover, due to his achievements,
he successively ascended to high positions of authority.
He always conducted himself with humility and reverence,
and did not use his wealth and high rank to lord over others.
Later, he was appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
He followed Wénxuān in campaigning against the Rúrú
and died suddenly of illness while in the army.
He was posthumously granted the title of Proxy with the Yellow Axe,
Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi), and Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
His posthumous title was Sùwǔ.
In the beginning of the Huángjiàn era,
he was accorded the right to be enshrined in the temple of Wénxiāng.
His son Jìnmíng succeeded him.
During the Tiāntǒng era,
he was restyled as the Prince of Dōnglái.
Jìnmíng possessed the spirit of a chivalrous knight.
Among the descendants of the honored and noble families, he was the most devoted to learning.
He loved wine and was unrestrainedly lavish.
He frequently entertained guests.
The cost of a single banquet
often reached ten thousand cash,
yet he still regretted that it was meager.
Whenever the court placed him in a high and important position,
he invariably resigned due to illness.
He told people:
"A useless person like me drinks fine wine and enjoys beautiful scenery.
How can I act as a petty clerk, turning over old papers?"
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè).
After barely a hundred days, he resigned the office due to illness.
Pān Lè,
courtesy name Xiāngguì,
was a native of Shímén in Guǎngníng.
Originally a prominent clan in Guǎngzōng,
during the Wèi dynasty, they were sent to garrison the northern frontier,
and settled there.
His father, Yǒng,
possessed technical skills,
and inherited the noble title of Viscount of Guǎngzōng.
When Lè was first born,
a sparrow landed on his mother's left shoulder.
The fortune-tellers all said it was an omen of wealth and nobility,
so he was named Xiāngguì,
which later became his courtesy name.
When he grew up,
he was magnanimous and courageous.
He first submitted to Gě Róng,
who appointed him Prince of Jīngzhào.
He was nineteen years old at the time.
When Róng was defeated,
he followed Ěrzhū Róng.
He served as a detached general to campaign against Yuán Hào,
and for his merit, he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Fūchéng County.
When Qí Shénwǔ went out to govern Jìnzhōu,
he appointed Lè as the Garrison City Commander.
He followed in defeating Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā,
and his noble rank was advanced to Earl of Guǎngzōng County.
For accumulated military merits, he was appointed Governor of Dōngyōngzhōu.
Shénwǔ once discussed abolishing the prefecture.
Lè argued that Dōngyōng was bordered by mountains and rivers,
and its territory linked the Hú and the Shǔ (barbarians),
making it a strategic and formidable location
that could not be abandoned.
Consequently, it remained as before.
Later, after defeating the Zhōu army at Héyīn,
a discussion was held about pursuing them.
It was ordered that those who wished to pursue should stand on the west,
and those who did not should stand on the east.
Only Lè and Liú Fēng stood on the west.
Shénwǔ thought this good,
but stopped the pursuit because the general consensus was different.
He was restyled as the Duke of Jīnmén Commandery.
When Wénxuān succeeded to the throne,
Lè was stationed at Héyáng,
where he defeated the Western general Yáng Jí and others.
At that time, the Emperor considered abandoning the fortress that Píng Jiàn, the Governor of Huáizhōu, and others had constructed,
because it was too deep within enemy territory.
Lè argued that Zhǐ Guān was a strategic pass
and had to be strongly defended.
So, he refurbished it,
increased the placement of troops and generals,
and then returned to garrison Héyáng.
He was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
When Qí received the abdication,
Lè presented the imperial seal and ribbon.
He was advanced in title to Prince of Hédōng Commandery,
and promoted to Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
When Zhōu Wén (Yǔwén Tà) advanced east to Xiáo and Shǎn,
he dispatched his Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs Hóumòchén Chóng from Qízǐ Lǐng to head toward Zhǐ Guān.
Yítóng Yáng Jí traveled via Gǔzhōng Dào and emerged at Jiànzhōu,
capturing Gūgōng Garrison.
An imperial edict commanded Lè to take overall command of the main army to resist them.
Lè marched day and night,
reaching Chángzǐ.
He dispatched Yítóng Hán Yǒngxīng to proceed west from Jiànzhōu toward Chóng.
Chóng subsequently retreated.
He was also made Grand Commander of the Southern Route (Nán Dào Dà Dūdū),
to suppress Hóu Jǐng.
Lè set out from Shíbiē,
advancing south for over a hundred *lǐ*,
reaching Liáng's Jīngzhōu.
Jīngzhōu had formerly been at Shíliáng,
but Hóu Jǐng had changed it to Huáizhōu.
Lè recovered this territory
and re-established Jīngzhōu there.
He also captured Ānzhōu.
He was appointed Governor of Yíngzhōu
and subsequently raided the Huái and Hàn regions.
In the sixth year of Tiānbǎo,
he died at Xuánhù.
He was posthumously granted the title of Proxy with the Yellow Axe,
Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ), and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
His son Zǐhuàng succeeded him.
While the sons and younger brothers of the generals
were generally arrogant and unrestrained,
Zǐhuàng was reserved, meticulous, and cautious,
keeping himself pure and detached.
He married a princess
and was appointed Commandant-in-chief of the Imperial Son-in-law (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he served as the Right Vice Director of the Acting Department of State Affairs for the Yōuzhōu Circuit, and Governor of Yōuzhōu.
When the Zhōu army was about to enter Yè,
Zǐhuàng led tens of thousands of light cavalry to rush to its aid.
Upon reaching Bólíng,
knowing that Yè City could not be defended,
he went to Jìzhōu and surrendered.
Zhōu granted him the title Superior Founding Establishment (Shàng Kāifǔ).
He died at the beginning of the Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty.
Biographies, Section 8: Róng (Zǐsháo, Zǐxiàoyán)
Duàn Róng,
courtesy name Zǐmào,
was a man from Gūzāng in Wǔwēi.
His grandfather, Xìn,
served the Jǔqú clan.
Later, he entered Wèi,
and as a prominent family, was relocated to the northern frontier,
subsequently settling his family in Wǔyuán Jùn.
His father, Lián,
was the Sīmǎ of the Ānběi Prefecture.
Róng enjoyed calendrical science in his youth,
and focused particularly on astronomy.
Early in the Zhèngguāng era,
he spoke to people, saying:
“The *Yì* states, ‘Observe the patterns of Heaven to discern the changes of the times,’
and also says, ‘Heaven displays signs
to show fortune and misfortune.’
Now observing the dark patterns [of the sky]
and examining human affairs,
in less than ten years,
there will surely be chaos.”
Someone asked:
“Where will it arise,
and can it be avoided?”
Róng replied:
“The source of the disturbance
will begin in this very region.
I fear that the world will consequently be overwhelmed by chaos,
and there will be nowhere to hide.”
Not long after,
events transpired just as he had said.
Róng encountered the chaos,
and taking his wife and children with his old neighbors,
fled south toward Píngchéng.
When Dù Luòzhōu created disturbances,
Róng conspired with Gāozǔ to execute him.
The plot failed,
and they both fled to Ěrzhū Róng.
Later, when Gāozǔ raised the standard of righteousness east of the mountains,
Róng supported the great strategy.
He served as the Right Assistant of the Traveling Department of State Affairs,
and the Grand Envoy for Consolation and Pacification of the Northwest Circuit.
He toured the region, clarifying and persuading,
and the various localities submitted to him.
When Gāozǔ campaigned south to attack Yè,
he left Róng to garrison Xìndū,
and also conferred upon him the title of General Pacifying the North,
and Governor of Dìngzhōu.
At that time, Yè had not yet been overcome,
but Róng ensured that the military supplies needed
were transferred without fail.
When Gāozǔ entered Luò,
based on his merits, Róng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gūzāng County,
with eight hundred households in his domain.
He was subsequently appointed Governor of Yíngzhōu.
Róng's wife
was the Empress's elder sister.
Fearing Gāozǔ would incur criticism for favoring private relatives,
Róng strongly recommended other generals,
and ultimately did not go to the prefecture.
Soon after, he was acting governor of Xiāngzhōu,
and later became Governor of Jìzhōu.
In the third year of Tiānpíng,
he was transferred to be acting governor of Tàizhōu.
Róng was gentle and amiable by nature;
in every post he held, he promoted benevolence and clemency,
and the people and officials loved him.
Initially, when Gāozǔ planned to seize Guānyòu,
he discussed the matter secretly with Róng.
Róng emphatically stated it was not yet feasible.
When they suffered the defeat at Wèiqū,
Gāozǔ regretted it,
saying:
“I did not follow Duàn Róng's advice,
which is why we have come to this.”
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Grand Supervisor of the Traveling Department of State Affairs for Shāndōng and Grand Commander.
He greatly won the hearts of the people.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng,
he was appointed Honorary Minister Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers.
He died in the fifth month of the second year,
at the age of sixty-two.

He was posthumously granted the titles of Envoy Holding Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of the four prefectures of Dìng, Jì, Cāng, and Yíng, Governor of Dìngzhōu, Grand Commandant, and Left Chief Administrator of the Department of State Affairs.
His posthumous name was Zhāojǐng.
At the beginning of the Huángjiàn era,
he was granted the honor of sacrifice within Gāozǔ's ancestral temple courtyard.
In the second year,
he was further posthumously granted the titles of Grand Marshal, Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and Prince of Wǔwēi.
His eldest son, Sháo, inherited the title.
Sháo,
courtesy name Xiàoxiān,
had the nickname Tiěfá.
In his youth, he was skilled at horsemanship and archery,
and possessed the talents and strategies of a general.
Because Gāozǔ regarded him as the son of Empress Wǔmíng’s sister,
he valued and loved him even more,
always keeping him close by his side,
treating him as a trusted intimate.
At the beginning of the Jiànyì era,
he served as Commander of the Trusted Guards.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng,
he followed Gāozǔ to resist Ěrzhū Zhào,
fighting at Guǎng'ā.
Gāozǔ said to Sháo:
“They are numerous while we are few;
what should be done about this?”
Sháo replied:
“Those who are called numerous
only succeed in securing the death of the masses;
those who are strong
are those who hold the hearts of the world.
Ěrzhū is reckless and cunning.
As everyone saw on the road,
he shattered the crown and destroyed the regal robes,
uprooting the foundation and blocking the source.
At the assembly at Mángshān,
what crime did the scholarly elite commit?
Moreover, he murdered his sovereign and established a new ruler,
all within ten days to a month.
Nine out of ten families [in the world]
desire rebellion.
Your Royal Highness personally manifests virtue and righteousness,
eliminating evil from the ruler’s side.
Where could you go and not succeed!”
Gāozǔ said:
“Although I am using the orthodox to attack the rebellious,
carrying out the mandate and punishing the wicked,
we are but the weak and small caught between the powerful and great.
I fear we lack the Mandate of Heaven.
Have you not heard this?”
He replied:
“Sháo has heard that the small can overcome the great,
and the small Way triumphs over the great excess.
Heaven has no favorites;
it assists only the virtuous.
The Ěrzhū externally plunder the world
and internally lose the good people.
The wise refuse to strategize for them,
and the brave refuse to fight for them.
The unworthy lose their positions,
and the worthy will seize them.
What need is there for doubt?”
Thereupon, they fought Zhào,
and Zhào’s army scattered.
They then attacked Liú Dàn at Yè.
During the Battle of Hán Líng,
Sháo commanded his divisions
and served as the vanguard, breaking the enemy lines.
Soon after, he followed Gāozǔ out of Jìnyáng
to pursue Ěrzhū Zhào at Chìhóng Lǐng,
and subjugated him.
For his military service, he was enfeoffed as the Baron of Xiàluò County.
He further followed the raid and seizure of Xiàzhōu,
capturing Húlǜ Mí'étū.
He was given the additional titles of General Who Soars Like a Dragon and Grand Master of Remonstrance,
and was repeatedly promoted to General of the Martial Guard.
Later, he retroactively received his father's title, Marquis of Gūzāng County.
He requested that his own title, Baron of Xiàluò County, be yielded to his younger half-brother, Níng'ān.
In the fourth year of Xīnghé,
he followed Gāozǔ to resist Emperor Wén of Zhōu at Mángshān.
Gāozǔ was personally in the ranks
when he was recognized by the Western Wèi General Hèbá Shèng,
who led his elite troops to press forward.
Sháo rode his horse forward from the side, drawing his bow and shooting backward.
One arrow killed their vanguard,
causing the pursuing cavalry to become fearful and apprehensive;
none dared to advance.
The Western army retreated.
He was rewarded with horses and gold,
and his noble rank was advanced to Duke.
In the fourth year of Wǔdìng,
he followed the campaign against Yùbì.
At that time, Gāozǔ was unwell.
The siege had not yet succeeded.
He summoned all the generals
to jointly discuss the advisability of advancing or halting.
He said to Grand Marshal Húlǜ Jīn, Minister over the Masses Hán Guǐ, General of the Left Guard Liú Fēng, and others:
"Whenever I discuss military matters with Duàn Xiàoxiān,
he shows exceptional strategic brilliance.
If we had employed his counsel recently,
we would not have the toil of today.
My illness is critically dangerous,
and I fear the unexpected.
I wish to entrust Xiàoxiān with the affairs of Yè,
what do you think? "
Jīn and the others replied:
"No one knows a minister better than his sovereign.
Truly, no one surpasses Xiàoxiān."
Then he said to Sháo:
"In the past, I and your father braved dangers and difficulties,
jointly assisting the royal house,
and established these great accomplishments.
Now my illness is such,
that I am perhaps beyond recovery.
You should ably assist each other
to bear this responsibility."
He immediately ordered Sháo to follow Xiǎnzǔ to garrison Yè,
and summoned Shìzōng to come to the army.
Gāozǔ’s illness became severe.
He gave his dying instructions to Shìzōng, saying:
"Duàn Xiàoxiān is loyal, honest, benevolent, and generous.
He possesses both wisdom and courage.
Among my relatives,
only this son is worthy.
Regarding important military matters,
you should plan them together."
In the spring of the fifth year,
Gāozǔ died in Jìnyáng,
and the mourning was secretly withheld.
Soon after, Hóu Jǐng incited rebellion.
Shìzōng returned to Yè,
and Sháo remained to guard Jìnyáng.
When Shìzōng returned,
he bestowed female musicians numbering ten or more people,
ten catties of gold,
silks and cloth matching that amount,
and enfeoffed him as the Duke of Chánglè Commandery.
When Shìzōng campaigned against Yǐngchuān,
Sháo remained to garrison Jìnyáng.
He was separately enfeoffed as the Baron of Zhēndìng County,
and served provisionally as the Inspector of Bīngzhōu.
When Xiǎnzǔ accepted the abdication,
he was separately enfeoffed with Cháolíng County,
and further enfeoffed with Bàchéng County,
and given the added rank of Special Advance (Tèjìn).
He memorialized requesting to return the title of Duke of Cháolíng,
and begged that his stepmother, Lady Liáng, be enfeoffed as a Commandery Mistress (Jùnjūn).
Xiǎnzǔ commended him for this,
and separately appointed Lady Liáng as the Commandery Mistress of Āndìng.
He also yielded the Marquis of Bàchéng County title to his stepmother's younger brother, Xiàoyán.
Commentators praised him for this.
In the third year of Tiānbǎo,
he became the Inspector of Jìzhōu and Grand Military Governor of Six Zhōu.
He governed with benevolence,
and won the hearts of the officials and the people.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year,
the Liáng general Dōngfāng Bái'é secretly arrived at Sùyù,
recruited border people,
and killed the chief administrators.
The Huái and Sì regions were greatly disturbed.
In the second month of the fifth year,
an imperial edict summoned Sháo to suppress him.
When he arrived,
it happened that the Liáng general Yán Chāodá and others were pressing Jīngzhōu with their armies;
furthermore, Emperor Wǔ of Chén was leading troops to attack Guǎnglíng,
and the Inspector Wáng Jìngbǎo had dispatched an envoy to report the emergency;
there was also Yǐn Sīlìng,
whose followers numbered over ten thousand men,
planning to raid Xūyí.
All three armies were alarmed.
Sháo said to his generals:
"Since the disorder following the downfall of the Liáng clan,
the state has lacked a stable ruler.
People harbor intentions of departure or submission,
following whoever is strong.
Bàxiān and his peers have little wisdom but great ambitions.
Their governmental decrees are not unified.
Externally they profess shared virtue,
but internally they are disunited.
Gentlemen, you need not worry,
I have calculated this thoroughly."
He then left Protocol Official Jìng Xiǎnjùn, Yáo Nánzōng, and others to surround and guard Sùyù,
while he personally led several thousand infantry and cavalry, traveling at double speed toward Jīngzhōu.
On his route, he passed Xūyí.
Sīlìng did not anticipate the sudden arrival of the main army,
and upon seeing their banners, fled north.
He advanced and joined battle with Chāodá,
thoroughly defeating him,
and capturing all his ships, vessels, and equipment.
He said to the assembled generals and soldiers:
"The people of Wú are fickle and rash.
They fundamentally lack grand strategy.
Now that Chāodá is defeated,
Bàxiān will certainly flee."
He immediately turned and hastened toward Guǎnglíng.
Emperor Wǔ of Chén indeed absconded.
He pursued them as far as Yángzǐ Barrier,
sighted Yángzhōu city, and then returned,
having captured a great quantity of their military supplies and equipment.
He led his army back to Sùyù.
In the sixth month,
Sháo sent an eloquent speaker to explain misfortune and fortune to Bái'é.
Bái'é subsequently opened the gates and requested a treaty.
Sháo discussed this with the Mobile Chancellery Administrator Xīn Shù and others,
and temporarily accepted the alliance.
After the treaty was concluded,
calculating that Bái'é would ultimately not serve them,
he seized and executed him.
He sent the heads of Bái'é and his younger brothers to the capital.
The Jiāng and Huái regions were completely settled,
and the people were all pacified.
Xiǎnzǔ commended his accomplishment,
issuing an edict rewarding him with seventy captive Wú people,
and enfeoffing him as the King of Píngyuán Commandery.
When the Prince of Qīnghé, Yuè, conquered Yǐngzhōu
and captured Minister over the Masses Lù Fǎhé,
Sháo also participated in the campaign.
He built Lǔchéng
and established the Guō Mò Garrison at Xīncài before returning.
In the first year of Huángjiàn,
he assumed the office of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
In the second year of Dàníng,
he was appointed Inspector of Bīngzhōu.
When Gāo Guīyàn raised a rebellion in Jìzhōu,
an imperial edict ordered him and the Prince of Dōng'ān, Lóu Ruì, to lead troops and suppress him.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
and bestowed ten female musicians
and one thousand *mǔ* of Guīyàn’s fruit orchards.
He continued to govern Bīngzhōu.
In his administration, he grasped the broad principles
and did not dwell on minor details,
greatly achieving harmony among the people.
In the twelfth month,
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu dispatched generals leading Qiāng and Yí tribesmen, who combined forces with the Tujue (Tūjué) to threaten Jìnyáng.
Shìzǔ traveled at double speed and continuously from Yè to rush to the rescue.
The Tūjué formed ranks and advanced from the north,
extending eastward to the Fén River,
and westward covering the Fēng Valley.
As the situation was sudden and urgent,
and the troops were not yet organized,
Shìzǔ, seeing this state of affairs,
also wished to avoid battle and retreat eastward.
He eventually accepted the request of the Prince of Héjiān, Xiàowǎn,
and ordered the Prince of Zhàojùn to take overall command of all the generals.
It was after a heavy snowfall.
The Zhōu forces used infantry as their vanguard,
descending from the Western Mountains,
two *lǐ* away from the city.
All the generals wanted to meet them with a counterattack.
Sháo said:
"The momentum of the infantry is inherently limited.
Since the accumulated snow is deep,
engaging in a counterattack is not advantageous.
It is better to form ranks and wait for them.
When they are weary and we are rested,
victory is assured."
Subsequently, when they engaged in battle,
they utterly defeated them.
The enemy vanguard was completely wiped out;
none were left remaining.
The rest fled throughout the night.
Sháo was then ordered to lead cavalry in pursuit,
but he returned after failing to catch them beyond the pass.
Shìzǔ commended his achievement,
separately enfeoffing him as the Duke of Wǔdé Commandery of Huáizhōu,
and promoting his rank to Grand Preceptor (Tàishī).
Zhōu Zhǒngzǎi Yǔwén Hù's mother, Lady Yán (Yán Shì), was previously assigned to the Zhōngshān Palace.
Hù heard that Yán was still alive,
and therefore, using the border region, sent a letter,
requesting the return of his mother,
and simultaneously opening up neighborly relations.
At that time, the Tūjué repeatedly invaded the border,
and Sháo was stationed below the fortifications.
Shìzǔ (Emperor) sent the Huángmén Xú Shìróng, traveling by relay post, carrying a Zhōu letter to ask Sháo [for his opinion].
Sháo believed that the Zhōu people were treacherous,
and fundamentally lacked sincerity and righteousness;
citing the battle at Jìnyáng,
their actions were evident.
Hù outwardly claimed the position of Prime Minister (Xiàng),
but in reality, he was a king (Wáng).
Since he requested peace for the sake of his mother,
yet did not send a single personal envoy to express his feelings and reasoning,
but merely relied on the official letter,
if we immediately send his mother,
I fear it will show weakness.
According to your servant's humble view,
we should provisionally agree outwardly,
and wait to release her later; it would not be too late.
The Emperor did not listen.
Consequently, an envoy was sent to escort her with proper ceremony.
Once Hù had obtained his mother,
he nevertheless sent General Yǔchí Jiǒng and others to attack Luòyáng.
An imperial edict was issued, sending Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng and Great General Húlǜ Guāng to lead troops and strike them,
and they camped below Máng Shān,
lingering and not advancing.
Shìzǔ summoned [Sháo] and addressed him, saying:
"Now I wish to send the Prince to relieve the siege of Luòyáng,
but the Tūjué are here,
and we still need to defend and govern [the area].
What does the Prince think of this?"
Sháo replied:
"The Northern Barbarians (Běi Lǔ) invading the border,
is a matter comparable to a mere skin rash.
Now the Western Qiāng are spying and pressing [us],
which is the sickness unto death.
I request permission to obey the edict and march south."
Shìzǔ said:
"My intention is also thus."
He then ordered Sháo to command one thousand elite cavalry,
setting out from Jìnyáng.
After five days, they crossed the river,
and consulted with the Great General regarding advance and halt.
That morning, Sháo led two hundred cavalry from his personal command and ascended the Máng Bǎn (Máng Slope) together with the various armies,
merely to observe the Zhōu army's disposition.
Upon reaching the Dàhé Gǔ (Dàhé Valley),
they immediately encountered the Zhōu army.
Sháo immediately dispatched riders to report to all the camps,
gathering the soldiers and horses.
He then formed a battle array with the various generals to await them.
Sháo served as the Left Army,
Lánlíng Wáng served as the Center Army,
Húlǜ Guāng served as the Right Army,
facing the Zhōu people.
Sháo addressed the Zhōu people from afar, saying:
"You, Yǔwén Hù, fortunately received his mother,
yet you cannot harbor gratitude and repay the kindness.
What is the intention
behind coming today?"
The Zhōu people replied:
"Heaven sent us here.
What is there to ask?"
Sháo said:
"The Way of Heaven (Tiāndào) rewards good and punishes evil.
It must have sent you here merely to die."
The Zhōu army then put their infantry in front,
ascending the hill to fight against them.
Sháo, knowing they were infantry and his were cavalry,
alternately withdrew and drew them in,
waiting until their strength was exhausted.
He then ordered [his troops] to dismount and attack them.
As soon as the short weapons met,
the Zhōu people suffered a massive defeat.
Those facing the Center Army (Zhōngjūn)
also dissolved instantly,
and those who threw themselves into or fell into the streams and valleys and died were very numerous.
The besiegers of Luò Chéng (Luò City)
immediately fled,
abandoning all their camps and tents.
From Máng Shān to the Gǔ Shuǐ (Gǔ River), a distance of thirty *lǐ*,
military provisions and equipment filled the rivers and marshes.
The Imperial Carriage (Chējià) visited Luòyáng,
personally commending the officers and soldiers.
A great banquet with wine was set up at Héyīn,
meritorious service was evaluated, and rewards were conferred.
Sháo was appointed Tài Zǎi (Grand Chancellor),
and enfeoffed as Língwǔ Xiàn Gōng (Duke of Língwǔ County).
In the third year of Tiāntǒng (Tiāntǒng Sān Nián),
he was appointed Zuǒ Chéngxiàng (Left Chancellor),
Yǒngchāng Jùn Gōng (Duke of Yǒngchāng Commandery),
and given the income of Cāngzhōu Gàn.
In the first month of the second year of Wǔpíng (Wǔpíng Èr Nián),
he traveled out via the Jìnzhōu Road,
reached Dìnglǒng,
built the two cities of Wēidí and Píngkòu, and returned.
In the second month,
the Zhōu forces came to raid.
The Emperor sent Sháo, together with Yòu Chéngxiàng Húlǜ Guāng and Tàiwèi Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng, to go and defend against them.
By the end of the third month, they traveled and reached the western border.
There was a city called Bǎigǔ Chéng,
which was an extremely strategic stronghold of the enemy.
The stone city was a thousand *rèn* high,
and none of the generals were willing to attack or besiege it.
Sháo said:
"The area north of the Fén River (Fén Běi) and east of the [Yellow] River (Hédōng),
is strategically held by our state (Guójiā).
If Bǎigǔ is not removed,
the matter will be like a chronic illness.
I estimate that their reinforcing troops
will gather on the southern road.
If we now cut off their vital path,
their relief forces will be unable to arrive.
Moreover, although the city walls are high,
the interior is extremely narrow.
If we shoot fire arrows and bolts at it,
we can wipe them out in one morning."
The generals praised his plan,
and consequently beat the drums and attacked it.
The city fell,
and they captured Yítóng Xuē Jìnglǐ,
heavily defeating and capturing enemy heads and captives.
They then fortified Huágǔ,
stationed a garrison, and returned.
Sháo was enfeoffed as Guǎngpíng Jùn Gōng (Duke of Guǎngpíng Commandery).
In this same month,
Zhōu again sent a general to raid the border.
Yòu Chéngxiàng Húlǜ Guāng first led his army out to campaign,
and Sháo also requested to go.
In the fifth month,
they attacked and subdued Qín Chéng.
The Zhōu people had newly constructed a fortified town south of Yáo Xiāng Chéng,
connecting eastward to Dìngyáng,
and also dug a deep moat,
cutting off the thoroughfare.
Sháo then secretly withdrew elite warriors,
and attacked the town from the north.
He also sent men to secretly cross the river,
informing those inside Yáo Xiāng Chéng,
to coordinate the effort internally and externally.
There were over a thousand people who crossed,
only then did the Zhōu people realize [what was happening].
Thereupon, they engaged in battle,
utterly defeating them,
and capturing their Yítóng Ruògān Xiǎnbǎo and others.
All the generals wanted to attack their new city.
Sháo said:
"This city has one side blocked by the river,
and three sides featuring dangerous terrain.
It cannot be attacked.
Even if we manage to take it,
it is only the land of one city.
It is better to build another city to block its path,
defeat Fú Qín,
and combine our strength to plan the taking of Dìngyáng.
This is the superior strategy."
The officers and soldiers all agreed.
In the sixth month,
they shifted and besieged Dìngyáng.
The city's master, Kāifǔ Yítóng Yáng Fàn, held firm and did not surrender.
Sháo ascended a mountain to observe the city's defenses,
and then unleashed his troops in a fierce assault.
In the seventh month,
they captured the outer city,
and executed a great number of enemy heads.
At that time, Sháo was ill in the army camp.
Since the inner city (Zǐ Chéng) had not yet been subdued,
he said to Lánlíng Wáng Chánggōng:
"Three sides of this city are steep gorges and difficult terrain,
providing no escape route.
I only fear the single location to the southeast.
If the bandits break the siege,
they must exit this way.
Just select elite soldiers and concentrate on guarding it,
and they will certainly be captured."
Chánggōng then ordered over a thousand brave warriors to set up an ambush at the entrance of the southeastern gorge.
That night, it happened just as planned.
The bandits immediately left the city.
The hidden troops attacked them,
routing them completely.
Fàn and others tied their hands behind their backs,
and all their forces were captured.
Sháo's illness worsened severely,
and he returned ahead of the army.
For his merit, he was separately enfeoffed as Lèlíng Jùn Gōng (Duke of Lèlíng Commandery).
He eventually died due to his illness.
The Emperor expressed deep mourning in the Eastern Hall,
granted him a thousand rolls of silk, *wēnmíng* secret funerary items, and a *wēnliáng* carriage.
Officers and soldiers of the army lined up as guards to escort [the coffin] to the burial site in Píng'ēn,
and troops were mobilized to construct the tomb.

He was posthumously granted the titles of Jiǎ Huángyuè (Wielding the Ceremonial Battle Axe), Shǐ Chíjié (Holding the Credential), Dū Dū (Area Commander) of the military affairs of the twelve prefectures of Shuò, Bīng, Dìng, Zhào, Jì, Cāng, Qí, Yǎn, Liáng, Luò, Jìn, and Jiàn;
Xiàngguó (Chancellor), Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant), Lù Shàngshū Shì (Director of the Affairs of the Department of State), and Cìshǐ (Governor) of Shuòzhōu.
His posthumous title (Shì) was Zhōngwǔ.
went out commanding the military forces,
and indoors participating in the inner council.
His achievements already ranked highly,
compounded by matrimonial alliances,
his prestige swayed both the court and the countryside.
He excelled at strategy,
was skilled at controlling the masses,
won the hearts of his officers and soldiers,
and on the day he faced the enemy,
everyone strove vigorously.
Furthermore, his natural disposition was gentle and cautious,
possessing the demeanor of a prime minister (zǎixiàng).
In educating his sons and younger relatives,
his household (guīmén) was harmonious and solemn.
He was famous for his filial piety in serving his stepmother;
few among the families of merit and nobility during the Qí era could equal him.
However, he had a weakness for lust,
and although he held important posts,
he traveled privately in disguise (wēifú).
There was a woman of the Huángpǔ lineage,
the wife of Yuán Yǔ, Attendant at the Yellow Gates (Huángmén Láng) of Wèi.
(Her husband's) younger brother Jǐn plotted rebellion,
and consequently, Lady Huángpǔ was confiscated by the government (mòguān).
Sháo admired her beauty and quality,
and memorialized the throne, urgently requesting her.
Shìzōng was reluctant to deny his wishes,
and therefore bestowed her upon him.
He was especially frugal (sè) with wealth;
even to relatives and old friends, he gave almost nothing.
When his son Shēn married a princess (shàng gōngzhǔ),
the Censors (chéng láng) from the various departments (bìng shěng) assisted in the household duties for over ten days.
When the affair concluded and they took leave to return,
each person was merely presented with one cup of wine.
His eldest son, Yì, succeeded him.
Yì,
courtesy name Déyóu,
had a fine appearance and demeanor,
understood music somewhat,
and was also skilled at archery and riding.
Early in the Tiānbǎo era,
he married the Eldest Princess of Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ).
Successively promoted to Right Vice Director (Yòu Púshè) of the Traveling Chancellery (Xíngtái),
concurrently Minister of the Palace Affairs (Diànzhōng Shàngshū),
he was sent out to become the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu.
He died.
His son, Bǎodǐng, succeeded him.
He married the Eldest Princess of Zhōngshān (Zhōngshān Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ).
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was bestowed the title Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
During the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
he held the posts of Establishing a Residence Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) and General of the Swift Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn).
Early in the Dàyè era,
he died while serving as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Ráozhōu.
Sháo’s second son was Shēn,
courtesy name Déshēn.
He had a handsome appearance,
and was tolerant and cautious, possessing his father's style.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he received the title Duke of Gūzāng County (Gūzāng Xiàn Gōng) from his father’s enfeoffment.
Early in the Dàníng era,
he was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Shìláng).
In the second year (of Dàníng),
an imperial edict commanded him to marry Princess Yǒngchāng.
Before the marriage,
the princess died.
In the third year of Héqīng,
he was again commanded by edict to marry Princess Dōng'ān.
Because his father had frequently established great merit,
he was successively promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), General (Jiāngjūn), Grand Director of Centrality (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Yuánzhōu,
and held the stipend-producing area of Zhàojùn.
When Sháo was critically ill,
an edict enfeoffed Shēn as the Prince of Jìběi (Jǐběi Wáng),
to comfort (Sháo’s) mind.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was Left Vice Director (Zuǒ Púshè) of the Xúzhōu Traveling Chancellery (Xúzhōu Xíngtái) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu.
Upon entering Zhōu (the Northern Zhōu dynasty),
he was appointed Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
and Commander of a Commandery (Jùn Gōng).
He was executed for an offense.
Sháo’s third son was Dégǔ.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
In the seventh year of Jiàndé of Zhōu,
while in Yèchéng, he plotted rebellion with Gāo Yuánhǎi and others,
and was executed.
Sháo’s fourth son was Déhéng.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was Establishing a Residence Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
During the Lónghuà era,
he was Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu.
Upon entering Zhōu,
he was appointed General Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn).
Sháo’s seventh son was Dékān.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he was Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
Early in the Dàyè era of Suí,
he was Governor (Cìshǐ) of Biànzhōu,
and died while serving as the Administrator (Jùn Shǒu) of Rǔnán.
Dùan Róng’s second son was Xiàoyán.
In his youth, he was alert, intelligent, and had a fine demeanor.
At the end of the Wǔdìng era of Wèi,
he began his career as Military Advisor (Cānjūn Shì) to the Minister of Education (Sītú).
When Qí accepted the abdication (received the mandate),
his elder brother Sháo gave him the separate enfeoffment of Marquis of Bàchéng County (Bàchéng Xiàn Hóu).
Successively promoted to Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī), Minister of Finance (Dùzhī Shàngshū), and Metropolitan Magistrate of Qīngdū (Qīngdū Yǐn).
Xiàoyán originally achieved his prominent status
due to the remnants of his family's merit and imperial relationship.
Upon reaching this point, he became arrogant, extravagant, and licentious,
fearing nothing.
Once, when traveling at night,
he stayed overnight at the home of his retainer Sòng Xiàowáng.
He summoned the neighborhood citizens to provide defense and support.
When they did not respond promptly,
he flogged and killed them.
Furthermore, he secretly associated with various adulterous women.
When discovered by their husbands,
he again relied on his official power
to flog them until they died.
At that time, when the Imperial Park (yuàn nèi) needed fruit trees,
he requisitioned them from commoners and Buddhist monasteries for delivery.
He then distributed all of them to be planted at his private residence.
Also, when the palace and gardens needed stones,
he organized carts and oxen to transport them from the Zhāng Hé river.
He then diverted some of the carts to acquire items for himself.
When all these incidents became known,
he was sent out to become the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Hǎizhōu.
Shortly after, due to his elder brother’s connections (gù),
he was summoned and appointed Minister of the Revenue (Dūguān Shàngshū),
held the stipend-producing area of Yángchéng Commandery,
and was additionally granted Establishing a Residence (Kāifǔ).
He was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng),
then appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qízhōu.
He was impeached by the Censor (Yùshǐ) for corruption and bribery.
It happened that Shìzǔ died,
and he was pardoned during the general amnesty.
He was appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng),
transferred to receive the stipend from Hénán Commandery,
and promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
When Zǔ Tǐng was in power,
intending to dismiss Zhào Yànshēn,
he enlisted Xiàoyán as an accomplice.
He was appointed Acting Palace Attendant (Jiān Shìzhōng),
entered the Imperial Secretariat (Nèi Shěng),
and managed secret affairs.
Soon after, he became the Principal Palace Attendant (zhèng),
retaining his post as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Xiàoyán lacked deep insight,
and also treated people unfairly.
Those he promoted
were either bribers or old acquaintances.
Cuī Chéng, Assistant Prefect of the Palace Buildings (Jiāngzuò Chéng),
suddenly spoke up publicly, declaring:
"A Minister (Shàngshū) is the Minister of the whole realm!
How can he be merely the Minister of the Duàn family?"
Xiàoyán had no words to reply,
and merely changed his expression to severe and dismissed (Cuī Chéng).
Soon after, he was appointed Prefect of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and elevated to Special Advanced Rank (Tèjìn).
He also relied upon Hán Chángluán
to jointly frame Zǔ Tǐng's flaws.
After Zǔ (Tǐng) was dismissed,
Xiàoyán was appointed Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè).
He retained control over selections,
exercising his power of employment and dismissal willfully.
Solicitations and requests were rampant.
An imperial order commanded the dredging of the northern moat of the capital city.
Xiàoyán supervised the work.

Cuī Shìshùn (Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers), Yuán Shìjiāng (Grand Master of Works, Jiāngzuò Dàjiāng), Lì Xiàoyù (Vice Minister of the Grand Treasury, Tàifǔ Shǎoqīng), Xuē Shūzhāo (Left Director of Populace Affairs, Shàngshū Zuǒ Mín Lángzhōng), Cuī Lóngzǐ (Magistrate of the Capital Province, Sīzhōu Zhìzhōng), Lǐ Dàolóng (Assistant Metropolitan Magistrate of Qīngdū, Qīngdū Yǐn Chéng), Wèi Chángqīng (Prefect of Yè County), Cuī Xiàng (Prefect of Línzhāng), and Gāo Zǐchè (Prefect of Chéng'ān), among others, were all under Xiàoyán's command.
On the days of supervision,
he separately hosted banquets with grand gatherings.
The various officials crawled forward on their knees and prostrated themselves,
raising their cups to offer longevity blessings.
Some presented their complaints about being held back
and requested promotion again.
Xiàoyán appeared elated in manner and color,
taking it upon himself (to grant these wishes).
He replied to all requests according to the circumstances
and promised additional appointments.
Many wealthy merchants and great traders were selected and promoted.
Even when he did bring forward scholars for employment,
they were all coarse, treacherous, and licentious individuals.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè).
The titles Special Advanced Rank (Tèjìn) and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) remained as before.
Xiàoyán was rich, noble, extravagant, and luxurious;
he especially loved women.
Later, he married Dǒng Shì, the concubine of Lóu Dìngyuǎn,
and indulged greatly in affection for her.
Because of this, there was disharmony between his inner and outer circles.
They repeatedly accused and listed each other's faults.
Due to these disputes, he was dismissed from office and exiled to Guāngzhōu.
After the Lónghuà defeat,
there was an imperial order for his recall.
Although Xiàoyán was insatiably greedy for wealth
and indulged freely in wine and women,
his demeanor was nonetheless graceful,
and he attracted renowned scholars.
Beautiful scenery and good times,
he never wasted them in vain.
They composed poetry and performed music,
enjoying complete delight and harmony.
Even scholars who resided in obscurity (cǎolái zhī shì),
if they were slightly skilled in literature and arts,
were frequently brought into his guest quarters,
where they shared excitement and enjoyment.
To those who were poor and struggling, he often provided gifts upon request.
Public opinion, in turn, frequently praised him for this.
When Qí fell, he entered Zhōu (service).
He was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Dà Jiāngjūn.
Later, he was promoted to Kāifǔ.
The historian states: Duàn Róng relied on the importance of his marriage relationship
and met a timely opportunity.
The extent of his achievements and campaigns
is indeed worth mentioning.
Sháo Guāng assisted seven rulers,
and was able to expand his family’s enterprise.
Whenever he went out, he was tasked with military command (kǔnwài),
or entrusted with managing the Rear Administration (Liú Tái).
In a court filled with suspicion and jealousy,
he completed his full lifespan.
As the border posts (Tíng Hòu) were prone to alarms,
how could he serve as a Supreme General of Qí?
How could this be so?
It must be because his ambition declined to boast of achievements,
his reputation did not exceed his reality,
he did not govern things through prestige and power,
and he did not leverage shrewd calculations to meet the moment.
If he wished to overturn the tripod (suffer disgrace),
how could he achieve it?
The saying goes,
"Following one's inherent nature is called the Way (Dào)."
Is this not its consequence?
The Eulogy says: Róng initiated the source,
Sháo magnified the house.
Their position was manifest through achievements,
their reputation honored through virtue.
Biographies, Chapter Nine: Hú Lǜ Jīn (Sons: Guāng, Xiàn)
Hú Lǜ Jīn,
courtesy name Ā Liù Dūn,
was a man of the Chì Lè tribe in Shuòzhōu.
His high ancestor, Bèi Hóu Lì,
was renowned beyond the frontier for his strength and courage.
During the time of Emperor Dào Wǔ, he led his household to submit internally (to the Northern Wèi court),
and was granted the title Duke of Mèngdū.
His grandfather, Fān Dì Jīn,
was the Director of the Palace Secretariat (Diànzhōng Shàngshū).
His father, Dà Nà Guī,
was Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū) and Chief of the First Division of Leading People.
During the Tiānpíng era,
since Jīn was honored,
his father was posthumously granted the title Duke Sīkōng.
Jīn was honest and straightforward by nature,
and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
When campaigning, he used the methods of the Xiōngnú:
by observing the dust, he could tell the number of mounted and foot soldiers,
and by smelling the ground, he could know the distance of the army's movement.
Initially, he served as Army Commander.
He accompanied Yáng Jūn, the Garrison Commander of Huáishuò, in escorting Ā Nà Guī, the ruler of the Rúru, back north.
Guī saw Jīn hunting and shooting,
and deeply praised his skill.
Later, Guī invaded and attacked Gāolù.
Jīn repelled the attack and defeated him.
At the end of the Zhèngguāng era,
when Pò Liùhán Bá Líng raised a rebellion,
Jīn gathered his followers and joined him.
Líng bestowed the title of King upon Jīn.
Jīn realized that Líng would ultimately be defeated and perish,
