so he led his affiliated ten thousand households to Yúnzhōu to request surrender,
and was immediately appointed Chief of the Second Division of Leading People.
He was gradually led south out of Huángguā Duī,
but was defeated by Dù Luòzhōu.
His troops scattered.
Jīn and his elder brother Píng escaped and returned to Ěrzhū Róng.
Róng recommended Jīn as a Deputy General.
He was repeatedly promoted to Area Commander.
When Emperor Xiàozhuāng ascended the throne,
he was granted the title Viscount of Fùchéng County,
and additionally named General Who Pacifies the North and Colonel of the Garrison Cavalry.
He followed the campaign to defeat Gě Róng and Yuán Hào,
frequently achieving military merit.
He was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Guards the South.
When Ěrzhū Zhào and others rebelled,
Gāozǔ (Gāo Huān) secretly planned the restoration,
and Jīn, along with Lóu Zhāo and Kùdí Gān, supported the great plan.
He subsequently joined the uprising.
When Gāozǔ attacked Yè in the south,
he left Jīn to guard Xìndū,
serving as the Grand Area Commander for the six provinces of [unnamed province], Yún, Yàn, Shuò, Xiǎn, and Wèi,
entrusting him with affairs in the rear.
He separately campaigned against Lǐ Xiū,
and defeated him.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Right.
He met Gāozǔ at Yè,
and subsequently followed him to pacify Jìnyáng
and pursue and destroy Ěrzhū Zhào.
At the beginning of the Tàichāng era,
Jīn was appointed Governor of Fénzhōu and Grand Area Commander of that province,
and promoted in rank to Marquis.
He followed Gāozǔ to defeat Hé Dòu Líng west of the river.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
the capital moved to Yè.
Jīn was ordered to lead 30,000 infantry and cavalry to garrison Fēnglíng to guard against western invaders.
When the campaign ended,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
He followed Gāozǔ to fight at Shā Yuàn.
As the situation was unfavorable, the army was recalled.
Consequently, various cities in Dōngyōng were again seized by the Western army.
Jīn was dispatched along with Wèi Jǐng and Kùdí Gān to suppress them and retake the cities.
During the Yuánxiàng era,
Emperor Wén of Zhōu again launched a major expedition toward Héyáng.
Gāozǔ led his troops to attack them,
and ordered Jīn to proceed directly to Tàizhōu
to form a pincer attack.
When Jīn arrived at Jìnzhōu,
he ceased further movement because the enemy army had retreated.
He then jointly besieged the bandits of Qiáoshān with the Traveling Secretariat, Xūe Xiūyì.
Soon after, Gāozǔ arrived,
and they jointly attacked and pacified the area.
Subsequently, he followed Gāozǔ to attack and conquer several cities including Nánjiàng and Shàojùn.
At the beginning of the Wǔdìng era,
Gāo Zhòngmì, the Governor of Běiyùzhōu, seized the city and rebelled toward the west.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu invaded and attacked Luòyáng.
Gāozǔ ordered Jīn to command Liú Fēng, Bù Dàhán Sà, and tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to defend Héyángchéng and resist them.
When Gāozǔ arrived,
he subsequently followed to defeat Mì.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Grand Marshal,
his title was changed to Duke of Shíchéng Commandery,
with an income of one thousand households.
He was transferred to be Chief of the First Division of Leading People.
In the third year,
Gāozǔ mobilized the army to attack the Shānhú,
dividing the forces into two routes.
Jīn was made Army Administrator of the Southern Route,
departing via Huánglú Ridge.
Gāozǔ himself took the Northern Route,
crossing Chìhóng Ridge.
They met Jīn at Wūtū Outpost,
and combined their attack to defeat the enemy.
When the army returned,
he was sent out to serve as the Governor of Jìzhōu.
In the fourth year,
an imperial edict ordered Jīn to lead his troops along the Wūsū Route to meet Gāozǔ at Jìnzhōu.
He then followed the attack on Yùbì.
When the army returned,
Gāozǔ made Jīn the General Supervisor of the main force,
to escort them back to Jìnyáng.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
Hóu Jǐng used Yǐngchuān as a base and surrendered to the Western Wèi.
An imperial edict ordered Jīn to command Pān Lè, Xuē Gūyán, and others to firmly defend Héyáng in preparation.
The Western Wèi sent their Grand Area Commanders Lǐ Jǐnghé and Ruògān Bǎo to lead tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry,
intending to proceed from Xīnchéng to reinforce Hóu Jǐng.
Jīn led his troops and stationed them at Guǎngwǔ to intercept them.
Jǐnghé and the others heard this and retreated.
He returned to become the Governor of Sìzhōu.
He subsequently led his subordinates to construct three outposts at Yíyáng—Yáng Zhì, Bǎijiā, and Hūyán—
established defenses, and then returned.
When Hóu Jǐng fled to Nányù,
Wáng Sīzhèng, having the rank Yítóng Sānsī from the Western Wèi, entered and occupied Yǐngchuān.
Shìzōng sent Gāo Yuè, Mùróng Shàozōng, Liú Fēng, and others to lead troops to surround it.
An edict was again issued ordering Jīn to supervise Péng Lè, Kě Zhūhún Dàoyuán, and others to move out and garrison Héyáng,
to cut off the enemy's escape and reinforcement routes.
Jīn was also ordered to lead his forces to join the attack on Yǐngchuān.
When the affair was settled,
Jīn was again instructed to lead troops from È Ridge to transport rice to Yíyáng.
Mǎ Shàolóng, the outpost commander of Jiǔ Qū of the Western Wèi, occupied a strategic height and fought.
Jīn defeated him.
For his merit, he was separately enfeoffed as Viscount of Ānpíng County.
Xiǎn Zǔ 顯祖 received the abdication,
and [Jīn] 金 was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiányáng Jùn 咸陽郡,
and his post as Regional Inspector remained as before.
In the winter of that year,
he presented himself at the Jìnyáng Gōng 晉陽宮 (Jìnyáng Palace).
When Jīn was ill,
the Emperor visited his residence to see him,
bestowed upon him medicine and treatments,
and imperial envoys were constant.
When his illness was cured, he returned to his prefecture.
In the third year,
he was appointed Grand Preceptor (Tài Shī 太師) in place of his previous post.
When the Emperor campaigned against the Xī 奚 rebels,
Jīn accompanied the Emperor on the campaign.
When the army returned,
the Emperor visited Sì Zhōu 肆州,
and held a banquet and archery contest with Jīn before departing.
In the fourth year,
he was relieved of his post as Regional Inspector
and returned to Jìnyáng 晉陽 as Grand Preceptor.
The imperial carriage again visited his residence,
and the Six Palaces (Harem) and all the princes followed,
where wine was set out and music played,
only ending late into the night.
The Emperor was extremely delighted,
and ordered Jīn’s second son, Fēng Lè 豐樂, to be appointed General-in-Chief of the Palace Guard (Wǔ Wèi Dà Jiāng Jūn 武衞大將軍),
and then said to Jīn:
“Sir, with your great merit and assistance in establishing the dynasty,
and the loyalty of father and son,
I ought to form a bond of marriage with you,
to perpetually serve as a protective barrier.”
He subsequently ordered Jīn’s grandson, Wǔ Dū 武都, to marry Princess Yìníng 義寧 Gōng Zhǔ.
On the day the marriage ceremony was completed,
the Emperor, accompanied by the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tài Hòu 皇太后), visited Jīn’s residence;
the Empress (Huáng Hòu 皇后), the Crown Prince (Tài Zǐ 太子), and all the princes followed.
His closeness and favor were thus.
Later, because the Rúru 茹茹 were defeated by the Tūjué 突厥,
their tribes were dispersed.
Fearing that they might violate the border wall
and cause distress to the border people,
he issued an edict for Jīn to lead twenty thousand cavalry to garrison Bái Dào 白道 to guard against them.
The captive chieftain Dòu Pó Tǔ Jiǔ Bèi 豆婆吐久備, leading over three thousand households, secretly intended to pass westward.
When the reconnaissance cavalry returned and reported,
Jīn commanded his troops to pursue and attack,
capturing all their people.
When Rúru’s Dàn Bō 但鉢 was preparing to move his entire nation westward,
Jīn captured his reconnaissance cavalry and sent them back,
and also submitted a memorial setting forth the strategy for attacking and taking the captives.
Xiǎn Zǔ 顯祖 thereupon led the troops to attack them together with Jīn at Tuō Lài 吐賴,
and returned with over twenty thousand households captured.
He was promoted to Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéng Xiàng 右丞相),
given Qí Zhōu 齊州 as a maintenance area (gàn 幹),
and then transferred to Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéng Xiàng 左丞相).
When Sù Zōng 肅宗 ascended the throne,
he accepted Jīn’s granddaughter as the Crown Prince’s Consort (Huáng Tài Zǐ Fēi 皇太子妃).
He also ordered Jīn to attend court,
allowing him to be drawn in a cart by foot to the steps.
When Shì Zǔ 世祖 ascended the throne,
his courteous treatment became even greater;
he also accepted Jīn’s granddaughter as the Crown Prince’s Consort.
Jīn’s eldest son, Guāng 光, was General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāng Jūn 大將軍);
his second son, Xiàn 羨, and his grandson, Wǔ Dū, were all granted the rank of Opening the Residence with the Honored Triple Guards (Kāi Fǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī 開府儀同三司)
and sent out to govern the regional military commands (fāng yuè 方岳).
His other sons and grandsons were all enfeoffed as marquises and achieved high status.
One Empress,
two Crown Prince Consorts,
and three princesses came from his single family.
The grandeur of his honor and favor
was unmatched at the time.
Jīn once said to Guāng:
“Although I have not studied,
I have heard that historically, the maternal relatives like Liáng Jì 梁冀 and others were all overthrown and destroyed.
If a daughter is favored,
the other nobles are jealous of her family;
if a daughter is not favored,
the Son of Heaven suspects her family.
Our family attained wealth and high status purely by establishing merit and embracing loyalty;
how could we rely on our daughters?”
He declined, but was unable to be excused,
and often worried about this.
He died in the third year of Tiān Tǒng 天統,
at the age of eighty.
Shì Zǔ 世祖 mourned in the Western Hall,
and the Later Ruler (Hòu Zhǔ 後主) also mourned in the Jìnyáng Gōng 晉陽宮.

He was posthumously granted the title of Acting Yellow Ax (Jiǎ Huáng Yuè 假黃鉞), Bearing the Credentials of Imperial Envoys (Shǐ Chí Jié 使持節), Grand Commandant of the Twelve Military Affairs of Shuò, Dìng, Jì, Bīng, Yīng, Qīng, Qí, Cāng, Yōu, Sì, Jìn, and Fén Prefectures (Dū Dū Shuò Dìng Jì Bīng Yīng Qīng Qí Cāng Yōu Sì Jìn Fén Shí Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūn Shì 都督朔定冀幷瀛青齊滄幽肆晉汾十二州諸軍事),
Chancellor (Xiàng Guó 相國), Grand Commandant (Tài Wèi Gōng 太尉公), Director of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàng Shū 錄尚書), and Regional Inspector of Shuò Zhōu 朔州.
His titles of Chieftain (Qíu Zhǎng 酋長) and Prince (Wáng 王) remained as before.
One million coins were granted,
and his posthumous name was Wǔ 武.
His son, Guāng 光, succeeded him.
Guāng,
courtesy name Míng Yuè 明月,
was skilled at riding and archery in his youth,
and was known for his military prowess.
In the late Wèi 魏 dynasty,
he followed Jīn on the western campaign.
Mò Zhě Huī 莫者暉, the Chief Clerk of Emperor Wén of Zhōu (Zhōu Wén Dì 周文帝), was then among the ranks.
Guāng rode his horse and shot him,
subsequently capturing him on the battlefield.
Guāng was seventeen years old at the time.
Gāo Zǔ 高祖 praised this
and immediately promoted him to Commandant (Dū Dū 都督).
When Shì Zōng 世宗 was the heir apparent,
he appointed Guāng as his trusted Commandant,
and he was gradually promoted to General Who Campaigns Against the Captives (Zhēng Lǔ Jiāng Jūn 征虜將軍),
and repeatedly advanced to General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāng Jūn 衞將軍).
In the fifth year of Wǔ Dìng 武定,
he was enfeoffed as the Sub-Marquis of Yǒnglè Xiàn 永樂縣.
He once accompanied Shì Zōng in a hunt at Huán Qiáo 洹橋.
Seeing a large bird,
flying high in the clouds,
Guāng drew his bow and shot it,
hitting it directly in the neck.
This bird was shaped like a carriage wheel,
spinning as it descended,
and when it reached the ground, it was a great eagle (dà diāo 大鵰).
Shì Zōng took it and examined it,
and greatly admired its strangeness.
Xíng Zǐ Gāo 邢子高, an aide to the Chancellor, saw this and sighed:
“This is an eagle-shooting hand!”
He was then commonly referred to as the Eagle-Dropping Commandant (Luò Diāo Dū Dū 落鵰都督).
Soon after, he concurrently held the post of General of the Left Guards (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāng Jūn 左衞將軍)
and was advanced in rank to Count (Bó 伯).
When Qí received the abdication (of the former dynasty),
he was granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Separately, he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Xī'ān County.
In Tiānbǎo 3rd year (552),
he followed the campaign out of the border passes.
Guāng spearheaded the effort, defeating the enemy.
He captured many, beheading and taking prisoners,
and captured various livestock.
Upon return,
he was appointed Jìnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jìnzhōu).
To the east were three garrisons: Zhōu Tiānzhù, Xīn'ān, and Niútóu.
They attracted fugitives and rebels,
and frequently acted as bandits and thieves.
In the 7th year (556),
Guāng led five thousand infantry and cavalry to attack and destroy them.
He also greatly defeated Zhōu Yítóng Wáng Jìngjùn and others,
capturing over five hundred people,
and over a thousand heads of livestock before returning.
In the 9th year (558),
he again led his forces to take the four Zhōu garrisons of Jiàngchuān, Báimǎ, Huìjiāo, and Yìchéng.
He was appointed Shuòzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the 10th year (559),
he was appointed Tèjìn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the second month,
he led ten thousand cavalry to suppress the Zhōu Kāifǔ Cáo Huígōng,
and beheaded him.
Xuē Yǔshēng, the Yítóng and commander of Bǎigǔ City, abandoned the city and fled.
(Guāng) then took Wénhóu Garrison,
established a post, set up fences, and returned.
In Qiánmíng 1st year (560),
he was appointed Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In Huángjiàn 1st year (560),
his noble rank was advanced to Duke of Jùlù Commandery.
At that time, Prince of Lèlíng, Bǎinián, was the Crown Prince.
Sùzōng (Emperor Xiào Zhāo) considered Guāng's family lineage to be pure and careful,
and also noted his distinguished service to the Imperial House.
He therefore accepted Guāng's eldest daughter as the Crown Princess (Tàizǐ Fēi).
In Dàníng 1st year (562),
he was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púshè (Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs),
and received the revenues of Zhōngshān Commandery.
In the 2nd year (563),
he was appointed Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince).
In Héqīng 2nd year, 4th month (563),
Guāng led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to build Xūnzhǎng City west of Zhǐ Pass.
Following this, he built a Great Wall two hundred *lǐ* long,
and established thirteen garrisons.
In the 3rd year, 1st month (564),
Zhōu dispatched generals Dáxī Chéngxīng and others to invade Píngyáng.
An edict ordered Guāng to lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to defend against them.
Chéngxīng and his allies heard this and retreated.
Guāng pursued them,
and subsequently entered their territory,
capturing over two thousand people before returning.
In the 3rd month of that year,
he was promoted to Sītú (Minister of Education).
In the 4th month,
he led cavalry north to attack the Tūjué,
and captured over a thousand horses.
In the winter of this year,
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu dispatched his Pillars of State (Zhùguó) and Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ), Yùchí Jiǒng; Duke of Qí State, Yǔwén Xiàn; Pillar of State and Duke of Yōng State, Kěchì Xióng; and others.
Their forces numbered a hundred thousand,
and they invaded Luòyáng.
Guāng led fifty thousand cavalry, racing to meet and attack them.
They fought at Mángshān.
Jiǒng and the others were greatly defeated.
Guāng personally shot Xióng,
killing him.
Over three thousand enemy heads and prisoners were captured,
while Jiǒng and Xiàn barely managed to escape.
(Guāng's forces) seized all their armor, weapons, and baggage train,
and furthermore, piled up the corpses of the fallen to form a Jīngguān (trophy mound).
Shìzǔ (Emperor Wǔ Chéng) visited Luòyáng,
recorded merits and distributed rewards.
(Guāng) was promoted to Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant),
and separately enfeoffed as the Duke of Guānjūn County.
Earlier, Shìzǔ had commanded that Guāng’s second daughter be accepted as the Crown Princess.
In Tiāntǒng 1st year (565),
she was established as Empress.
In that same year,
Guāng was transferred to Dà Jiāngjūn (Grand General).
In the 3rd year, 6th month (567),
he left office due to the mourning rites for his father.
In the same month,
an edict ordered Guāng and his younger brother Xiàn to both rise (from mourning) and resume their former posts.
In the autumn,
he was appointed Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian),
inherited the rank of Prince of Xiányáng,
and inherited the position of Dìyī Lǐngmín Qiúzhǎng (First Chieftain Governing the People).
Separately, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Wǔdé Commandery,
and transferred his revenue stipend to Zhàozhōu.
He was promoted to Tàifù (Grand Tutor).
In the 12th month,
Zhōu dispatched generals to besiege Luòyáng,
blocking and cutting off the supply routes.
In Wǔpíng 1st year, 1st month (570),
an edict ordered Guāng to lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to suppress them.
When the army reached Dìnglǒng,
the Zhōu generals—Duke of Zhāngyè Yǔwén Jié, Governor of Zhōngzhōu Liáng Shìyàn, and Kāifǔ Sīshuǐ Dàfū Liáng Jǐngxīng—had also camped at Lùlú Jiāodào.
Guāng donned armor and grasped sharp weapons,
personally leading the charge.
As soon as the blades met,
Jié’s forces suffered a massive rout,
with over two thousand enemy heads taken.
He proceeded directly to Yíyáng,
where he confronted the Zhōu Duke of Qí State Yǔwén Xiàn and Duke of Shēn State Bá Xiǎnjìng for ten *xún* (100 days).
Guāng constructed the two cities of Tǒngguān and Fēnghuà,
thereby opening the road to Yíyáng.
When the army returned,
marching to Ānyè,
Xiàn and his forces, numbering fifty thousand,
followed closely behind.
Guāng unleashed his cavalry to strike them,
and Xiàn’s forces were utterly routed.
He captured their Kāifǔ Yǔwén Yīng, Dūdū Yuèqín Shìliáng, Hán Yán, and others,
and further beheaded over three hundred.

Xiàn then ordered Jié, his Grand General and Duke of Zhōngbù Liáng Luòdū, along with Jǐngxīng, Shìyàn, and others, totaling thirty thousand infantry and cavalry, to block the main road at Lùlú Jiāo Sài.
Guāng, together with Hán Guìsūn, Hūyán Zú, Wáng Xiǎn, and others, launched a combined attack,
greatly defeating them.
Jǐngxīng was beheaded,
and a thousand horses were captured.
An edict bestowed upon him the title Yòu Chéngxiàng (Chancellor of the Right),
and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
That winter,
Guāng again led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to Yùbì and constructed the two cities of Huágǔ and Lóngmén.
He held his position against Xiàn, Xiǎnjìng, and the others.
Xiàn and his allies dared not move.
Guāng then advanced and besieged Dìngyáng,
and furthermore built Nánfén City,
establishing a *zhōu* (prefecture) to press the attack.
Over ten thousand households, both barbarian and Chinese, came to defect and submit.
In the 2nd year (571),
he led his forces to build thirteen garrisons and posts, including Pínglǒng, Wèibì, and Tǒngróng.
Zhōu Pillars of State—Duke of Báohǎn Pǔtún Wēi, Pillar of State Wéi Xiàokuān, and others,
totaling over ten thousand infantry and cavalry—
came to pressure Pínglǒng.
They fought Guāng north of the Fén River.
Guāng greatly defeated them,
taking thousands of captives and beheaded enemies.
He was again enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhōngshān Commandery,
and his stipend increased by one thousand households.
When the army returned,
an edict again ordered him to lead fifty thousand infantry and cavalry out via the Píngyáng route,
attacking the garrisons of Yáoxiāng and Báitíng City.
He captured them all,
taking nine prisoners, including the city commander Yítóng and the Grand Area Commander (Dà Dūdū),
and capturing several thousand prisoners.
Separately, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chánglè Commandery.
In this month,
Zhōu dispatched its Pillar of State Gēgān Guǎnglüè to besiege Yíyáng.
Guāng led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to rush to its aid,
and fought a great battle beneath the city walls.
He then took the four Zhōu garrisons of Jiàn'ān and others,
capturing over a thousand prisoners before returning.
Before the army reached Yè (the capital),
an imperial decree ordered the immediate dispersal of the troops.
Guāng believed that many soldiers had rendered meritorious service,
but had not yet received commendation or rewards.
If they were immediately dispersed,
imperial benevolence would not be properly bestowed.
He secretly submitted a memorial requesting an envoy to convey the imperial instructions,
while the army continued to advance temporarily.
The court was slow in sending the envoy.
When the army returned,
and was approaching Zìmò,
Guāng still halted the camp to await the envoy.
The Emperor heard that Guāng’s military camp was already too close,
and felt great displeasure in his heart.
He urgently ordered an attendant (Shèrén) to pursue Guāng and summon him for an audience,
and only then were the commendations announced and the troops dispersed.
(Guāng) was appointed Zuǒ Chéngxiàng (Chancellor of the Left),
and separately enfeoffed as the Duke of Qīnghé Commandery.
Hú Lǜ Guāng entered,
and often sat behind a screen in the imperial court.
Zǔ Tǐng did not know this,
and rode his horse past the front of the screen.
Guāng was angered,
and said to people:
"This person dares to act like this!"
Later, Tǐng was in the inner chamber (Nèishěng),
speaking in a loud and arrogant voice.
Guāng happened to pass by,
heard it,
and was again angered.
Tǐng knew that Guāng was indignant,
and bribed Guāng's attendant slave and asked him:
"Is the King-Chancellor (Xiàngwáng) angry at Xiàozhēng (Zǔ Tǐng)?"
He replied:
"Since you (Gōng) took charge of affairs,
the King-Chancellor sighs every night, hugging his knees, saying: 'The blind man (mángrén) has entered,
the state is certainly going to be ruined!'"
Mù Tí-pó sought to marry Guāng's illegitimate daughter,
but was refused.
The Emperor (Dì) granted Tí-pó land in Jìnyáng,
and Guāng said in court:
"This land,
since the time of Emperor Shénwǔ, has always been planted with grain,
to feed several thousand horses,
in preparation for foreign invasion and difficulties.
Now that it is granted to Tí-pó,
will it not hinder military affairs?"
Because of this, Zǔ (Tǐng) and Mù (Tí-pó) accumulated resentment.
The Zhōu General Wéi Xiàokuān was apprehensive of Guāng's heroism,
so he created a rumor,
and ordered a spy to leak its words in Yè.
The rumor said:
"A hundred liters (bǎishēng) flies up to the sky;
the bright moon (míngyuè) shines upon Cháng'ān."
It also said:
"The high mountain (gāoshān) collapses without being pushed;
the oak tree (húshù) stands up without being supported."
Zǔ Tǐng then added to it, saying:
"The blind old man (mángyǎn lǎogōng) has a great axe on his back;
the talkative old mother (ráoshé lǎomǔ) cannot speak."
He had small children sing this on the roads.
Tí-pó heard of it,
and told his mother Lìng Xuān.
Xuān believed that the talkative old mother (ráoshé)
referred to herself,
and the blind old man (máng lǎogōng)
referred to Tǐng.
Thus, they conspired together,
and used the rumor to inform the Emperor:
"Hú Lǜ has been a great general for generations;
Míngyuè's (Hú Lǜ Guāng's courtesy name) fame shakes Guānxī;
Fēnglè's (Hú Lǜ Xiàn's courtesy name) authority extends to the Tujue (Tūjué);
his daughter is the Empress;
his son is married to a Princess.
The rumor is very dreadful."
The Emperor asked Hán Chángluán about this,
and Luán thought it was unacceptable,
so the matter was shelved.
Zǔ Tǐng again saw the Emperor and asked for a private audience,
with only Hé Hóngzhēn beside them.
The Emperor said:
"When I received your memorial (gōng qǐ) earlier,
I immediately wanted to implement it,
but Chángluán thought there was no such reason."
Before Tǐng could reply,
Hóngzhēn stepped forward and said:
"If you originally had no intention, then that would be fine.
But since you had this intention and did not decisively act,
what if the matter is leaked?"
The Emperor said:
"Hóngzhēn speaks correctly."
He was still hesitating and could not decide.
It happened that Fēng Shìràng, an aide in the Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng) Office, sent a secret memorial saying:
"When Guāng returned from the western campaign earlier,
an imperial decree ordered him to dismiss and disband his troops,
but Guāng ordered his army to press towards the imperial capital,
intending to commit rebellion.
The matter did not succeed and was stopped.
He keeps crossbows and armor hidden in his house,
and has thousands of slaves and attendants.
He frequently sends envoys to Fēnglè and Wǔdū's residences,
plotting secretly back and forth.
If we do not plan against him early,
we fear the consequences will be unpredictable."
The memorial stated that
"the army pressed towards the imperial capital,"
which concurred with the Emperor's previous suspicions.
He said to Hé Hóngzhēn:
"The human heart is also greatly sagacious!
I suspected earlier that he wanted to rebel,
and it turned out to be true."
The Emperor was naturally extremely fearful and cowardly.
Fearing that a revolt would immediately break out,
he ordered Hóngzhēn to rush and summon Zǔ Tǐng and tell him.
He was also afraid that summoning Guāng would result in his refusal to obey the command.
Tǐng then said:
"If you just summon him like that,
he might suspect something and refuse to enter.
You should send an envoy to bestow upon him a swift horse,
and say: 'Tomorrow, I intend to go to Dōngshān for sightseeing.
The King (Wáng) may ride this horse and accompany me.'
Guāng will surely come to offer thanks,
and we can lead him in and seize him."
The Emperor followed his words.
A moment later,
Guāng arrived.
He was led into the Liángfēng Táng,
and Liú Táozhī strangled and killed him from behind.
He was fifty-eight years old at the time.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, stating that Guāng had plotted rebellion
and had now faced the law,
and that the rest of his family members did not need to be investigated.
Soon after, another edict was issued,
exterminating his entire clan.
Guāng was naturally taciturn, stern, and impatient.
He was strict in his command of subordinates,
and in managing troops and overseeing the masses,
he relied only on prestige and punishment.
During corvée labor for earthworks (bǎnzhù zhī yì),
he flogged scholars and commoners,
and his tyranny was widely spoken of.
Since donning the hair-net and joining the military,
he had never violated military discipline,
and was deeply feared and dreaded by neighboring enemies.
As his crime was not clearly proven,
his sudden massacre shocked
the court and the countryside who mourned him deeply.
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu heard of Guāng's death,
he was greatly pleased,
and granted a general amnesty throughout his domain.
Later, when he entered Yè,
he posthumously appointed Guāng as Supreme Pillar of State (Shàng Zhùguó) and Duke of Chóngguó.
He pointed to the imperial decree and said:
"If this man were alive,
how could We have reached Yè?"
Guāng had four sons.
The eldest son, Wǔdū,

held positions successively as Special Advancement (Tèjìn), Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo), Founding Prefect with the Same Authority as the Three Grand Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Administrator of Liáng and Yǎn Prefectures (Cìshǐ).
Wherever he served, he had no governing achievements,
and only focused on accumulating wealth,
preying upon the common people.
When Guāng died,
an envoy was sent to his prefecture to execute him.
The next son, Xūdá,
was Middle Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn) and Founding Prefect with the Same Authority as the Three Grand Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
and died before Guāng.
The next son, Shìxióng,
was Founding Prefect with the Same Authority as the Three Grand Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
The next son, Gā,
was Acting Founding Prefect with the Same Authority as the Three Grand Ministers (Jiǎ Yítóng Sānsī).
They were all granted death.
Guāng's youngest son, Zhōng,
was only a few years old,
and was spared.
In the Zhōu Dynasty, he inherited the title of Duke of Chóngguó.
He died during the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí Dynasty while serving as General of Swift Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
Hú Lǜ Xiàn,
courtesy name Fēnglè,
was quick-witted in his youth,
and especially skilled in archery.
Gāozǔ saw him and praised him.
Shìzōng promoted him to Military Advisor to the Founding Prefect (Kāifǔ Cānjūnshì).
He was transferred to General Who Punishes the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Middle Grand Master (Zhōng Sàndàfū),
given the additional title of General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn),
promoted to Hereditary Viscount of Dàxià County,
and appointed Administrator of Tōng Prefecture (Cìshǐ).
When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication,
he was promoted to the title General Who Campaigns in the West (Zhēngxī),
and separately enfeoffed as Count of Xiǎnqīn County.
, he was transferred to be Shǐchíjié
, Grand Supervisor of Military Affairs of the six zhōu—Yōu, Ān, Píng, Nán Yíng, Běi Yíng, and Dōng Yàn
, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yōuzhōu
. That autumn
, the Tūjué masses, numbering over 100,000, came to invade the borders of the zhōu
. Xiàn led all the generals to defend against them
. The Tūjué, seeing that the military power was extremely well organized
, subsequently dared not fight
, and immediately dispatched an envoy to seek a truce
. Fearing they were engaging in deceit
, he then instructed them, saying
: “This journey by your multitude
was fundamentally not for paying tribute
. You only changed your minds upon seeing the opportunity
, which was not your long-held intention
. If you truly possess sincerity
, you should quickly return to your lairs
and send a separate envoy to come
.” Thereupon, they retreated and fled
. In the fifth month of summer of the first year of Tiāntǒng
, Mùhán of the Tūjué sent an envoy requesting to pay tribute
. Xiàn first reported this
. From then on, annual tribute continued uninterrupted
, and Xiàn had played a vital part in this
. An imperial decree promoted him to Xíngtái Púshè
. Because the northern barbarians frequently violated the border
, Xiàn determined that preparations must be made against unforeseen trouble
. Starting from Kùduī Shù
, extending east to the sea
, winding through the mountains for over two thousand lǐ
, wherever there were strategic passes within that two-hundred-lǐ stretch
, he either cut through mountains to build cities
or blocked valleys to erect barriers
, establishing over fifty garrisons and watchtowers in total
to join Yìjīng in the north
, and meet Lù in the east
, thereby using it to irrigate the fields
. Border supplies accumulated annually
, transportation costs were reduced
. In the sixth month of that year
, he resigned from office due to mourning his father
. Along with his elder brother Guāng
, he was reinstated to his post, returning to govern Yānjì
. In the third year
, his rank was increased to Tèjìn
. In the fourth year
, he was promoted to Xíngtái Shàngshū Lìng
, and separately enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gāochéng County
. In the first year of Wǔpíng
, he was given the title of Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn
. At that time, Guāng’s son, Wǔdū
, was the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu
, and was respected for his diligence and uprightness
. Although he achieved extreme glory and favor
, he did not boast
. By this time, seeing his entire family was prominent and powerful
, he was deeply concerned
. He therefore submitted a memorial declining the honors
, requesting to be relieved of his duties
. A gracious imperial decree did not permit it
. That autumn
, his noble title was advanced to Prince (Wáng) of Jīngshān Commandery
In the seventh month of the third year
, Guāng was executed
. An imperial edict commissioned Zhōnglǐngjūn Hèbá Fú'ēn and over ten others to pursue and arrest Xiàn by courier
. He sent Lǐngjūn Dàjiàngjūn Xiānyú Táozhī and Luòzhōu Xíngtái Púshè Dúgū Yǒngyè to immediately mobilize the cavalry from Dìngzhōu to follow up
, and Yǒngyè was appointed to replace Xiàn
. When Fú'ēn and his party arrived
, the gatekeeper reported that the envoys were wearing armor under their clothes and their horses were sweating
, suggesting the city gates should be closed
. Xiàn said
: "How can an imperial envoy be suspected and refused? "
He went out to meet them
. Fú'ēn took his hand
and subsequently seized him
. He died in the hall of the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ Tīngshì)
. As he faced death, he sighed, saying
: "With such wealth and prominence
, my daughter is Empress
, princesses fill the household
, yet I only kept three hundred soldiers
. How could I avoid ruin?"
As for his five sons—Shìdá, Shìqiān, Shìbiàn, Shìqiú, and Fúhù
—those under the age of fifteen were pardoned
. Before Xiàn was executed
, he suddenly ordered five or six of his sons who were in the zhōu, starting with Fúhù
, to put collars on their necks, ride donkeys, and leave the city
. The entire family cried while escorting them to the gate
. They returned late in the day
. All the officials and commoners were astonished
. The acting Administrator of Yàn Commandery (Xíng Yàn Jùnshǒu), Mǎ Sìmíng, who was skilled in medicine
and admired and favored by Xiàn
, secretly questioned him
. [Xiàn] replied
: "I must perform an exorcism."
A few days later, this catastrophe occurred
. Both Xiàn and Guāng were skilled in riding and archery when young
. Their father daily ordered them to go hunting
. Upon return, he would compare the birds and beasts they had acquired
. If Guāng's catch was sometimes small
, the vital organs were always struck
. Although Xiàn's catch was abundant
, he rarely hit the vital spots
. Guāng always received rewards
, while Xiàn was sometimes beaten
. When people asked the reason
, Jīn replied
: "Míngyuè
always strikes the arrow to the back
shoots wherever he can strike
, he is far inferior to his elder brother
." Those who heard him were all convinced by his words
. Jīn’s elder brother, Píng
, was proficient in archery and riding
, and capable in administration
. During the Wèi Jǐngmíng period
, he received his first official post as Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn
, and was promoted to Xiāngwēi Jiāngjūn
. At the end of Zhèngguāng
, the Six Garrisons were in turmoil
. He was subordinate to Dàjiàngjūn Wèi Bīn during the northern campaign
. The army was defeated
, and he was captured by the rebels
. Later, he fled to his younger brother Jīn in Yúnzhōu
, and was given the honorary title Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn
. He and Jīn led their forces south
. Upon reaching Huángguā Duī
, they were defeated by Dù Luòzhōu
, and their tribes dispersed
. When he submitted to Ěrzhū Róng
, he was treated very generously
. Píng inherited his father’s title as Dìyī Lǐngmín Qiúzhǎng
When Gāozǔ
raised his righteous banner, Píng followed him as a Dūdū
. Gradually, he was promoted to Píngběi Jiāngjūn and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiǎnzhōu
, and given the additional title of Zhènnán Jiāngjūn
, enfeoffed as the Earl (Bó) of Gù'ān County
. Soon after, he was advanced to Marquis (Hóu)
, and acted as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sìzhōu
. Zhōu Wéndì sent his Right General Lǐ Xiǎoguāng to occupy Liángzhōu
. Píng, with a detached force, attacked and captured him
. He was sent out to serve as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yànzhōu
. He returned to serve concurrently as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn
, leading a force of ten thousand to campaign against the rebels of Běi Xú
. He defeated them
, and was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu
. When Hóu Jǐng crossed the Yangzi River
, an imperial decree appointed Píng as Dà Dūdū
, leading Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Jìng Xiǎnjùn, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Kùdí Fúlián, and others to campaign and settle over thirty cities, including Shòuyáng and Sùyù
. After the mission was completed, he returned to his zhōu
, was granted Kāifǔ
, promoted to the rank of Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn
, and advanced in noble title to Duke (Gōng)
. When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication
, Píng was separately enfeoffed as Xiànyáng Hóu
. He acted as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu
, but was stripped of his title for excessive corruption
. Later, he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī
. When Fèidì ascended the throne
, he was appointed Tèjìn
, and granted the revenues of Lèlíng Commandery in Cāngzhōu
. In the beginning of Huángjiàn
, he was enfeoffed as Duke (Gōng) of Dìngyáng Commandery
, and appointed Hùjūn
. Later, he served as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qīngzhōu
, and died
. He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi
Húlǜ Jīn, starting when Gāozǔ began restoring order,
helped establish the imperial foundation,
with the utmost loyalty and fervor,
achieved this great merit.
Therefore, he was able to enjoy a long life until the end,
with a rank exceeding all officials.
Observing the warnings regarding overabundance,
his actions were subtle.
However, the calamity only reached his descendant,
leading subsequently to execution and destruction.
Although this was due to the weight of his power and authority,
it generally accords with what Dàojiā cautioned against.
Guāng, as the son of a Supreme General,
possessed a reserved and resolute nature.
His battle tactics and military authority
secretly matched the arts of war;
facing the enemy, he achieved victory,
changing his methods endlessly.
Since the separation of the Guān and Hé (Guānzhōng and Hénán),
nearly four *jì* (forty-eight years) have passed.
During Gāozǔ’s time of hegemony and kingship,
coinciding with Yǔwén’s initial struggles,
he launched armies for punitive expeditions,
frequently blunting the enemy's military edge.
However, since Dàníng,
the eastern neighbor gradually weakened.
Guānxī had previously conquered Bāshǔ,
and also destroyed Jiānglíng.
Following the strategy of pouring water from a house-top, they employed military force,
forming the great ambition of unification.
Húlǜ managed his troops and marshaled his forces,
restraining the border regions.
When he fought, no formation before him remained intact;
when he attacked, few cities remained whole.
The Qí clan required his troops to hold Yuán (the capital);
the Qín people had no policy to reopen the passes (to attack Qí).
But the age was chaotic and slander prevailed,
falsehoods used the gravity of the sovereign’s displeasure;
the sovereign was unenlightened and the times were difficult,
thus destroying the strength of their own bulwark.
In the past, when Lǐ Mù was a general for Zhào,
he crushed the Hú bandits in the north,
and repelled the Qín army in the west.
Guō Kāi slandered him,
and Mù died, leading to Zhào's destruction.
Those who plotted to execute Guāng—
were they perhaps the counter-agents of Qín?
Why were their methods the same, leading to the same ruin?
Internally, they caused all the generals to lose cohesion;
externally, they avenged the powerful neighbor.
Alas!
Later gentlemen should take this as a profound warning.
The Eulogy says: Towering Xiányáng,
the glory of the state and family.
Míngyuè, loyal and valiant,
served as general and chancellor for generations.
His fame shook Guānyòu,
his influence rose beyond temporal expectations.
Pressured by this prestige and fame,
slander easily arose.
It began with skillful words,
and ended in mutual destruction.
Biography Chapter Ten: Sūn Téng, Gāo Lóngzhī, Sīmǎ Zǐrú
Sūn Téng,
courtesy name Lóngquè,
was a man of Shí'ān in Xiányáng.
His grandfather, Tōng,
served the Jǔqú clan as *Zhōngshū Shèrén*.
When Jǔqú was destroyed,
he entered Wèi,
and consequently settled in the northern border region.
When Téng achieved prominence,

the Wèi court posthumously bestowed upon Tōng the titles of *Shǐchíjié*, *Shìzhōng*, *Dūdū Yōng Huà Qí Bīn Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnjì*, *Piàojì Dàjiàngjūn*, *Sītú Gōng*, *Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè*, and *Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ*.
His father, Jī, was posthumously bestowed with *Shǐchíjié*, *Shìzhōng*, *Dūdū Jì Dìng Cāng Yíng Yīn Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnjì*, *Tàiwèi Gōng*, *Shàngshū Lìng*, and *Jìzhōu Cìshǐ*.
When Téng was young, he was sincere and upright,
and clearly understood official affairs.
During the Zhèngguāng reign of Wèi,
the northern regions were in turmoil.
Téng traveled through dangerous and difficult paths,
and managed to reach Xiùróng.
When Ěrzhū Róng established his righteous cause,
Téng followed Róng into Luòyáng,
and was appointed *Rǒngcóng Púshè* by general selection.
Soon after, he became Gāozǔ’s *Dūdūfǔ Zhǎngshǐ*,
and followed Gāozǔ on the eastern campaign against Xíng Gǎo.
When the army halted at Qíchéng,
some soldiers from the Fǔyí garrison plotted rebellion,
intending to harm the commanders.
Téng became aware of this,
and secretly reported it to Gāozǔ.
Shortly thereafter, the incident occurred,
but because Gāozǔ was prepared,
they captured and crushed the rebels.
When Gāozǔ was posted to Jìnzhōu,
Téng served as *Zhǎngshǐ*,
was given the title *Hòujiàngjūn*,
and enfeoffed as the Count of Shí'ān County.
Gāozǔ departed Jìnyáng and exited through Fǔkǒu.
Traveling until they reached Xiāngyuán,
Ěrzhū Zhào led his forces in pursuit.
Gāozǔ and Zhào dined and drank by the waterside,
swearing to be brothers,
and then each returned to their own camp.
The next morning,
Zhào again invited Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ wished to appease him,
and was about to go.
As he was mounting his horse,
Téng tugged at his robe and stopped him.
Zhào then shouted insults across the water,
and galloped back to Jìnyáng.
Gāozǔ then headed east.
When he raised the banner of righteousness in Xìndū,
Téng, with sincerity and fervor,
always participated in planning strategies.
Téng felt that the imperial court was cut off,
and commands had nowhere to settle.
If they did not expediently establish a sovereign,
the multitudes would become discouraged and disperse.
He earnestly pleaded with Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ agreed with him,
and consequently established the Sovereign of Restoration.
He was appointed *Shìzhōng*,
and soon after was granted *Shǐchíjié*, *Liùzhōu Liúmín Dàdūdū*, and *Běidào Dàxíngtái*.
When Gāozǔ advanced his army to Yè,
he initially left Duàn Róng to guard Xìndū.
Soon after, he sent Róng to garrison Zhōngshān,
and subsequently ordered Téng to remain there in charge of the defense.
When Yè was pacified,
he was appointed *Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ*,
his title was changed to Duke of Xiányáng Commandery,
and his stipend increased to a total of one thousand three hundred households.
He was brought in to serve as *Shìzhōng*.
At that time, Princess Píngyuán, the daughter of Wèi’s King Jīngzhào, Yú, was widowed.
Téng wished to marry her,
but the Princess did not consent.
The *Shìzhōng* Fēng Lóngzhī was wifeless,
and the Princess desired him.
Téng was jealous of Lóngzhī,
and consequently sowed discord between them.
Gāozǔ requested Téng be relieved of office,
and asked that he be transferred to an outer post.
Soon after, he was restored.
Téng, as Gāozǔ’s trusted confidant,
entered and resided in the *Ménxià*,
managing classified matters alongside Húsī Chūn.
Since Chūn subsequently developed unorthodox ideas,
he contradicted established norms everywhere he went.
Téng felt profound suspicion and jealousy,
fearing the calamity would reach him.
He therefore secretly took more than ten riders and galloped to Jìnyáng.
Gāozǔ entered to suppress Húsī Chūn,
leaving Téng to manage the affairs of Bìngzhōu.
He also appointed Téng as *Xíngtái Púshè* for eight provinces—Jì, Xiāng, Yīn, Dìng, Cāng, Yíng, Yōu, and Ān—and acting Governor of Jìzhōu,
and later acting Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
In the early Tiānpíng reign,
Téng entered as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
Of all matters, internal and external,
Téng was thoroughly aware.
He also held the concurrent titles of Sīkōng and Shàngshū Lìng.
At that time, the Western Wèi dispatched generals to raid Nányān Commandery.
An imperial edict appointed Téng as Nándào Xíngtái,
leading various generals to suppress them.
Téng was by nature timid
and lacked strategic prowess,
suffering a defeat and returning.
He was then appointed Sītú.
Initially, when the northern frontier was in chaos,
he lost a daughter.
After he became prominent,
he made extensive inquiries from afar,
but ultimately failed to find her,
suspecting she had become a lowly maidservant.
When he became Sītú,
regarding those who sued for their freedom from servitude,
he did not investigate the truth,
but generally freed them.
He wished to free a thousand people,
hoping to find his daughter among them.
At that time, Gāozǔ entered the court,
and some attendants spoke of this.
Gāozǔ was greatly enraged
and dismissed him from his position as Sītú.
During the Wǔdìng reign,
he was sent to Qīngzhōu
to investigate and register fugitive households.
He was then promoted to Tàibǎo.
Initially, Cuī Xiàofēn of Bólíng adopted a poor family's daughter named Jiǎ as his foster daughter.
After Xiàofēn died,
his wife Yuán remarried Zhèng Bóyóu
and brought Jiǎ with her to the Zhèng family.
Jiǎ possessed beauty,
and Téng took her in.
Initially, she was his concubine.
When his wife, Lady Yuán, died,
Téng, because Jiǎ had a son,
formally made her his wife.
An imperial edict enfeoffed her as Dānyáng Jùnjūn.
He further requested that the title of Lady Yuán be transferred to his daughter.
Such disregard for rites and indulgence of personal desires
were common for him.
Téng had early on attached himself to Gāozǔ.
Through hardship and peril,
he diligently and respectfully served,
earning deep trust and favor.
When Gāozǔ established him in the Wèi court,
entrusting him as a confidant,
his ambition and arrogance swelled.
He had the power to grant and seize as he pleased.
He sought and accepted bribes
without limit.
Appointments in life and posthumous honors in death
did not pass without payment.
He concealed silver vessels,
stealing them for his own household.
He befriended petty men
and specialized in extortion.
In Yè,
he, Gāo Yuè, Gāo Lóngzhī, and Sīmǎ Zǐrú were known as the Four Nobles.
They wantonly abused their power,
and Téng was the worst of them.
Gāozǔ repeatedly censured him,
but he never repented.
The court and public deeply scorned him.
In the fourth month of Wǔdìng 6, he passed away
at the age of sixty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Jì Dìng děng Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Jìzhōu Cìshǐ, Tàishī, Kāifǔ, and Lùshàngshūshì.
His posthumous name was Wén.
In the early Tiānbǎo reign,
due to Téng's assistance in establishing the dynasty,
an imperial edict ordered a sacrifice at his tomb.
During the Huángjiàn reign,
he was enshrined in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son Fèngzhēn inherited his title.
Fèngzhēn was mediocre and dull.
During the Wǔpíng reign,
he died holding the rank of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Gāo Lóngzhī,
courtesy name Yánxīng,
originally bore the surname Xú.
He claimed descent from Gāopíng Jīnxiāng.
His father Gàn,
Wèi Bái Shuǐ Jùnshǒu,
was adopted by his paternal aunt's husband, the Gāo family,
and thus adopted their surname.
When Lóngzhī became prominent,
the Wèi court posthumously granted Gàn the titles of Sītú Gōng and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Later, Lóngzhī contributed to policy discussions,
and Gāozǔ ordered him to be considered a younger cousin,
stating he was from Bóhǎi Xiū.
Lóngzhī was eight feet tall,
had a handsome beard,
and was profound and ambitious.
When Yuè, Prince of Rúnán, was Sīzhōu Mù,
he appointed Lóngzhī as Hùcáo Cóngshì.
In the early Jiànyì reign,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì without formal examination.
He went out with Xíngtái Yú Huī to suppress Yáng Kǎn in Tàishān.
Huī appointed Lóngzhī as Xíngtái Lángzhōng,
and he was also appointed Gěishìzhōng.
He formed a deep bond with Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ took charge of Jìnzhōu,
he appointed Lóngzhī as Zhìzhōng,
acting as Píngyáng Jùnshì.
He followed Gāozǔ in his uprising in Shāndōng,
and was appointed Dàxíngtái Yòuchéng.
In the early Wèi Zhōngxīng reign,
he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi,
also holding the post of Shàngshí Diǎnyù.
He followed Gāozǔ in pacifying Yè,
acting as Xiāngzhōu Shì.
He followed in defeating the Four Hú at Hánlíng.
In the early Tàichāng reign,
he was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
Emperor Wén of Western Wèi once had a heated argument with Lóngzhī due to wine.
Emperor Wén was subsequently dismissed and demoted.
Gāozǔ criticized Lóngzhī for his inability to maintain harmony,
and then proposed that he be sent out as Běidào Xíngtái.
He was then transferred to be Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
enfeoffed as Píngyuán Jùngōng,
with a stipend of one thousand seven hundred households.
Lóngzhī requested a reduction of seven hundred households
and also asked to be demoted by four ranks to yield to his elder brother Téng.
An imperial edict graciously permitted this,
and Téng was then made Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Húxī Chūn,
he appointed Lóngzhī as Dàxíngtái Shàngshū.
When Dàsīmǎ and Qīnghé Wáng Dǎn held power,
Lóngzhī was appointed Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
and concurrently Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi.
He extensively employed laborers
to construct grand temples and pagodas,
for which he was reprimanded by Gāozǔ.
In the early Tiānpíng reign,
he resigned due to his mother's mourning.
Soon, an imperial edict appointed him Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and he later entered as Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
At that time, when land was first distributed to the people,
the powerful and influential all occupied the fertile and beautiful fields,
while the poor and weak received only barren plots.
Lóngzhī memorialized Gāozǔ,
requesting a complete reversal and redistribution,
and thus fairness was achieved.
He also concurrently served as Yínggòu Dàjiàng.
All construction in the capital city
was overseen by him.
He extended the southern city wall to a circumference of twenty-five *lǐ*.
Because the Zhāng River was close to the imperial city,
he built a long dike to prevent the danger of flooding.
He also dug canals to divert the Zhāng River to flow around the city,
and constructed water mills,
all of which were beneficial at the time.
From the Xiàochāng reign onwards,
the Wèi dynasty faced many difficulties.
Cìshǐ and Tàishǒu all became Dūdū of their respective departments.
Even without military affairs,
they all appointed assistant officials,
which caused considerable vexation in various localities.
Lóngzhī memorialized, requesting that,
unless they were truly in border vital areas
and had existing troops,
all such appointments should be abolished.
Furthermore, many court nobles falsely assumed the title of Chángshì to obtain the adornments of mink and cicada.
Lóngzhī himself submitted a memorial to resign as Shìzhōng,
and also stated that all those who falsely wore the attire of Chángshì
should also be dismissed.
The imperial edict granted all his requests.
Since the state had many military and governmental affairs,
those who falsely claimed titles and usurped offices were countless.
Lóngzhī memorialized to investigate them,
finding over fifty thousand people.
However, the crowd of petty individuals clamored,
and Lóngzhī, fearing them, stopped.
An imperial edict appointed him Jiānjǐqíjūshì
and promoted him to Sītú Gōng.
During the Wǔdìng reign,
he served as Héběi Kuòhù Dàshǐ.
He was recalled
and appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn and Lùshàngshūshì,
soon also holding the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
He then served as acting Qīngzhōu Shì.
He was recalled
and appointed Tàizǐ Tàishī, concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè, and Lìbù Shàngshū.
He was then promoted to Tàibǎo.
At that time, Shìzōng was in charge of governance,
and customs were strictly purified.
Lóngzhī sometimes accepted bribes,
for which Shìzōng severely reprimanded and humiliated him in the Shàngshū Shěng.
When Qí received the abdication,
he was promoted in rank to King.
Soon after, he was appointed to his original post as Commissioner of the Secretariat,
Great Superintendent of the Imperial Clan,
and Supervisor of National History.
Lóngzhī's nature was somewhat petty and fond of novelty.
As for the imperial regalia, various entertainments, and dress codes for the government, he often made changes,
not following established precedents.
Contemporary opinion criticized him for this.
On the archery target mound, he erected three human statues in a posture of valor and strength.
Xiǎnzǔ once visited Dōngshān,
and while shooting, he said to Lóngzhī:
"On the archery target mound, fierce beasts should be depicted
to preserve the ancient meaning.
Why place human figures?
Shooting at humans all day
is something I do not approve of."
Lóngzhī had no reply.
Initially, Shìzōng had entrusted affairs to Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat Cuī Xiān and Imperial Household Attendant Cuī Jìshū, among others.
When Shìzōng passed away,
Lóngzhī petitioned Xiǎnzǔ, wishing to harm them all,
but was not permitted.
Xiǎnzǔ, considering Lóngzhī an old acquaintance,
entrusted him with government affairs.
Jìshū and others, holding onto previous grievances,
then slandered him, saying:
"Whenever Lóngzhī sees a litigant,
he invariably shows pity and compassion,
to indicate that he is not capable of arbitrating."
Xiǎnzǔ thought that since he had been entrusted with such heavy responsibilities,
and knew of the injustice,
he should have rectified it appropriately.
How could he shirk responsibility and seek fame?
This was not the duty of a great minister.
In the fifth year of Tiānbǎo (554),
he was prohibited from the Department of the Imperial Secretariat.
Lóngzhī once feasted and drank with Yuán Chǎng.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he said to Chǎng:
"When befriending a king,
one should not betray him in life or death."
Someone secretly reported this.
Furthermore, before the Emperor ascended the throne,
Lóngzhī often harbored contempt for him.
When the Emperor was about to receive the abdication from Wèi,
all the great ministers said it was not yet time,
The Emperor held a deep grudge against him.
Because of this,
he then erupted in great anger,
ordering strongmen to beat him over a hundred times.
When he was released,
thirsty, he was about to drink water,
but someone stopped him.
Lóngzhī said:
"What does today matter!"
and then drank.
Subsequently, he followed the imperial carriage
and died on the road,
at the age of sixty-one.

He was posthumously granted the titles of Commander of Military Affairs for the Five Prefectures of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Cāng, and Yōu; Grand General; Grand Commandant; Grand Protector; and Governor of Jì Prefecture;
and Prince of Yángxià.
He ultimately did not receive a posthumous title.
Although Lóngzhī was not well-versed in scholarship,
he admired and esteemed literary elegance.
He always treated gentry and literati
with proper courtesy.
His widowed elder sister was a nun,
and he served her as he would his mother.
In instructing and supervising his sons,
he always prioritized literature and righteousness.
The world greatly praised him for this.
In Xiǎnzǔ's later years,
as he became increasingly suspicious and cruel,
he remembered his resentment towards Lóngzhī,
and executed more than ten of his sons, including Déshū,
and threw them all into the Zhāng River.
He also desecrated Lóngzhī's tomb,
exhumed his corpse –
which had been buried for many years,
but its appearance had not changed –
hacked and cut his bones,
and also cast them into the Zhāng River,
thus ending his lineage.
During the Qiánmíng era (560),
an imperial edict appointed his elder brother's son, Zǐyuǎn, as Lóngzhī's successor,
to inherit the title of Prince of Yángxià,
and returned his property.
Initially,
Lóngzhī, trusting Gāozǔ,
was inherently insidious and malicious.
He never failed to retaliate
for even the smallest grievance.
When Grandee Secretary Cuī Xiàofēn failed to secure a marriage alliance with him,
and Grand Minister of the Imperial Treasury Rèn Jí, while jointly supervising construction,
had some disagreements with him,
and Governor of Yíng Prefecture Yuán Yàn's solicitations were not successful,
he subsequently fabricated charges against them,
and had them all executed.
In the end, his own family was annihilated.
Commentators said that this was retribution.
Sīmǎ Zǐrú,
courtesy name Zūnyè,
was a native of Wēn, Hénèi.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Mó,
was Grand Commandant and Prince of Nányáng in the Jìn dynasty.
Mó's heir, Bǎo,
fled to Liángzhōu during the Jìn disturbances
and settled there.
When Wèi pacified Gūzāng,
they moved to Yúnzhōng,
as his autobiography states.
His father, Xīnglóng,
was Administrator of Lǔyáng for Wèi.
Zǐrú was astute and quick-witted in his youth,
eloquent,
and enjoyed befriending heroes.
He formed a deep bond
of righteousness with Gāozǔ.
During the Xiàochāng era (525-528),
when the northern provinces fell,
Zǐrú took his family south to Sìzhōu,
where he was treated with courtesy by Ěrzhū Róng,
who granted him command of the Central Army.
When Róng marched towards Luò,
he appointed Zǐrú as Sīmǎ,
with credentials, acting General Who Pacifies the South,
and Supervisor of the Vanguard.
Upon reaching Gāodū,
Róng, fearing that Jiànxīng's treacherous terrain
and crucial location for passage
would pose a threat to his rear,
appointed Zǐrú as acting Administrator of Jiànxīng and Area Commander of that commandery.
In the early Yǒng'ān era (528),
he was enfeoffed as a County Baron of Píngyáo,
with three hundred households,
and remained as a Supervising Secretary of the Grand Imperial Secretariat.
Róng, recognizing Zǐrú's eloquence
and ability to explain current affairs,
frequently dispatched him as an envoy to the court.
He often pleased the emperor,
and Xiàozhuāng also received him courteously.
During Gě Róng's rebellion,
Xiāngzhōu was isolated and precarious.
Róng sent Zǐrú through enemy lines to Yè,
to assist in its defense.
After Gě Róng was pacified,
he was promoted in rank to Marquis.
When Yuán Hào entered Luò,
people's hearts were divided.
Knowing that Zǐrú had once defended Yè City
and had considerable prestige,
he appointed him to act as Governor of Xiāng Prefecture.
After Hào was pacified,
he was summoned to be Grand Master of Radiance with Golden Seals and Purple Ribbons.
When Ěrzhū Róng was executed,
Zǐrú, knowing of the coup,
rushed out of the palace,
went to Róng's residence,
abandoned his family, and fled the capital with Róng's wife and Ěrzhū Shìlóng, among others.
Shìlóng immediately wished to return north.
Zǐrú said:
"In affairs, it is crucial to respond to opportunity.
In warfare, deceit is not disdained.
The world is in turmoil,
and only the strong are observed.
At this critical juncture,
we cannot show weakness.
If we must flee north,
I fear that unforeseen changes will arise.
It is better to divide our troops to guard the river bridge,
turn our army back towards the capital,
and take them by surprise.
Perhaps they will collapse.
Even if it doesn't go as we wish,
it will still be enough to show that we have remaining strength,
and make the world observe and listen,
fearing our might."
Thereupon, Shìlóng returned and pressed upon the capital.
Wèi appointed Prince of Chángguǎng and Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
The former deposed emperor appointed him as Attendant at Court, General of Agile Cavalry, Grandee Secretary,
and advanced his peerage to Duke of Yángpíng Commandery,
with one thousand seven hundred households.
He firmly declined the title of Grandee Secretary.
When Gāozǔ raised an army in Xìndū,
Shìlóng and others, knowing Zǐrú's old ties with Gāozǔ,
became suspicious
and sent him out as Governor of Nánqí Prefecture.
Zǐrú was indignant,
wept and pleaded his case,
but was not spared.
. Zǐrú sent an envoy to present congratulations
, relying still on their lifelong former favor
. He was soon summoned to the capital
, and made Dà Xíngtái Shàngshū
. He was by the sovereign's side day and night
, participating in the affairs of the military and the state
. At the beginning of Tiānpíng
, he was appointed Zuǒ Púshè
. Together with Shìzhōng Gāo Yuè, Shìzhōng Sūn Téng, Yòu Púshè Gāo Lóngzhī, and others, he administered the court affairs
. He was greatly trusted and esteemed
. When Gāozǔ was garrisoned at Jìnyáng
, Zǐrú often went to pay respects and seek audience
. He was treated extremely well
; they sat together and shared meals
. From dawn until dusk
, and when he was due to return
, Gāozǔ and the Empress Wǔmíng both presented him with gifts
. This was generally the custom
. Zǐrú’s nature was already bold and forthright
, and he also relied upon former favors
. In matters of administration and control
, his grants and seizures were based solely on his own inclination
. He openly accepted bribes
, without any fear or hesitation
. In the middle of Xīnghé
, he was appointed Běidào Xíngtái
, to tour and inspect the various prefectures
. He was entrusted with the power to dismiss or promote all those from the prefects and magistrates downward [29, 30]. When Zǐrú arrived at Dìngzhōu
, he executed the magistrate of Shēnzé County
. When he arrived at Jìzhōu
, he executed the magistrate of Dōngguāng County
. All of them were accused of delay and dereliction of duty
, and he subjected them to the severest punishment
. If anyone’s statement contained equivocation
, or failed slightly to meet his approval
, he immediately ordered the armed guards to throw them down and drag them
, with bright blades held at their necks
. Officials and common people were terrified
, not knowing what to do
. He was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng
. At the beginning of the righteous uprising
, Zǐrú himself had not participated
. It was simply because he was an old acquaintance of Gāozǔ
, that he was entrusted with such weighty responsibilities
. His spirit and pride were extremely high
, and his accumulation of wealth never ceased
. At that time, Shìzōng entered to assist in governing the court
. He harbored some internal resentment towards Zǐrú
. Soon after, Zǐrú was impeached for corruption and bribery by Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Cuī Xiān
, and confined to the Shàngshū Shěng
. An imperial decree pardoned his capital offense
, but stripped him of his official rank and noble titles
. Not long after
, he was appointed to manage the affairs of Jìzhōu
. Zǐrú was able to exert himself and reform
, and gained much renown
. He exposed treachery and corruption
, and the officials and subordinates feared and submitted to him
. He was transferred to manage the affairs of Bìngzhōu
. An imperial decree restored his official rank and noble titles
, and he was separately enfeoffed as the Earl of Yěwáng County
, with two hundred households
. When Qí received the abdication
, on account of his services in assisting and supporting the throne
, he was separately enfeoffed as the Duke of Xūchāng County
. Soon after, he was appointed Sīkōng
. Zǐrú's nature was jocular
; he did not adhere to restraint and discipline
. His joking words were coarse and vulgar
, and those who were discerning disapproved of him
. However, he served his elder sister with respect
, and treated his nephews with loving kindness
. The famous scholars of the time all admired and loved him
. The world praised him for these reasons
. Nevertheless, he fundamentally lacked integrity and uprightness
, and could not handle matters with impartiality
. During the time of Shìzōng
, Zhōngwèi Cuī Xiān and Huángmén Láng Cuī Jìshū were both employed
. When Shìzōng died
, Xiān and the others proceeded to Jìnyáng
. Zǐrú then memorialized Xiǎnzǔ
, speaking of their crimes and evil deeds
, and urged that they be executed
. Afterward, Zǐrú allowed horses to pass through the barrier
, and was impeached by the appropriate authorities
. Xiǎnzǔ summoned Zǐrú and repeatedly reprimanded him, saying
: “Cuī Xiān and Jìshū served my predecessors
. What great crime did they commit
, that you commanded me to kill them?”
Consequently, he was dismissed from office
. After a long time
, still valuing him as an old official of the late emperor
, he was appointed Tàiwèi
. Soon after, he died of illness
, at the age of sixty-four
. He was posthumously granted the titles Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of the five prefectures of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Cāng, and Huái, Tàishī, Tàiwèi, and Huáizhōu Cìshǐ
. One thousand bolts of silk were granted posthumously
. His posthumous name was Wénmíng
. His son, Xiāonán, succeeded him
. He married a daughter of Gāozǔ
. As the Princess's husband and a noble young man
, he repeatedly held positions as Zhōngshū Láng and Huángmén Láng
, and Guānglù Shàoqīng
. He was posted out as Běiyùzhōu Cìshǐ
, garrisoning Wǔláo
. Xiāonán extensively studied historical records and commentaries
. He had a refined demeanor
, but he was unable to be honest and clean
. While in the prefecture, he was impeached by the Yùshǐ
. Furthermore, his relationship with the Princess was strained
. The Princess spoke ill of him to the court
. Fearing punishment
, he consequently sought out neighboring enemies
, and fled to Guānxī
. Zǐrú’s elder brother, Zuǎn
, had died earlier
. When Zǐrú became eminent
, Zuǎn was posthumously granted Yuèzhōu Cìshǐ
. Zuǎn’s eldest son, Shìyún
, was frivolous, deceitful, and lacked moral conduct
. He was successively promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ
. Shìyún originally had no meritorious achievements
; it was simply because of Zǐrú
, that he repeatedly served in prefectures and commanderies
. Relying on his uncle’s influence
, wherever he served, he accumulated wealth through extortion
, and indulged in corrupt and vile deeds
. When he was about to be investigated and prosecuted
, he harbored internal alarm and fear
. When Hóu Jǐng rebelled
, he consequently led the entire prefecture to follow Hóu Jǐng
. At that time, Shìyún’s full brother was in Yè
, and promptly devoted himself to attaching to Hóu Jǐng
, having no further concern for consequences
. When the various generals besieged Jǐng at Yǐngchuān
, Shìyún stood on the city wall and verbally confronted the generals from afar
. His words were extremely insolent
. Shìzōng, nevertheless, considered the former favors shown to Zǐrú
, and pardoned his younger brothers from the death penalty
. They were exiled to the northern frontier
. After Hóu Jǐng was defeated at Guōyáng
, Shìyún again entertained rebellious intentions
, and was killed by Jǐng
. Shìyún’s younger brother, Yīngzhī
, courtesy name Zhòngqìng
. He was fond of learning in his youth
, and had a handsome and dignified presence
. In the middle of Tiānpíng
, when Zǐrú was powerful and eminent
, Yīngzhī progressed from Shàngshū Láng through Zhōngshū Láng and Huángmén Láng
. The title of Duke of Xūchāng County, separately granted to Zǐrú
, was subsequently transferred to Yīngzhī
. Yīngzhī’s family was rich in wealth
, and he greatly increased his holdings
. Wáng Yuánjǐng, Xíng Zǐcái, and their ilk respected him for his fundamental character
. Because he was careless, simplistic, and arrogant toward others
, throughout the era of Tiānbǎo
, he remained neglected and unranked
. In the middle of Qiánmíng
, Wáng Xī advised Sùzōng
, and Yīngzhī was appointed Wèi Wèi Shàoqīng
. At the end of Héqīng
, he became Guānglù Dàfū
. He suffered from chronic diarrhea
, and was bedridden for years
. Reaching the middle of Wǔpíng
, he was still unable to attend court audiences
. He was granted the title Yítóng Sānsī at his home
. He enjoyed reading the Tàixuán Jīng
, and annotated Yáng Xióng’s Shǔ Dū Fù
. He often said
: “I wish to associate with Yáng Zǐyún.”
In the year Qí fell
, he died of his chronic diarrhea
, at the age of seventy-one
. Yīngzhī’s nephew, Zǐruì
, served as Dìngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ during the Tiānbǎo era
. He was promoted to Lìbù Lángzhōng
. He was praised for being honest, diligent, fair, and frugal
. He was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ
, concurrently serving as Tíng Wèi Qīng
. He was renowned for his fairness and uprightness
. At the beginning of Qiánmíng
, he was appointed acting Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng
. He maintained a stern expression during his inspections and investigations
, and was praised by the court
. He resigned due to illness
. He was subsequently appointed Cíbù Shàngshū
. He died
. He was posthumously granted Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ
. His posthumous name was Wénjié
*Zǐruì*'s younger brother, *Yòuzhī*,
was pure, upright, and possessed integrity.
Early in life, he held prominent positions.
During the *Kāihuáng* era of the *Suí* Dynasty,
he died while serving as the Prefect of *Méizhōu*.
*Zǐruì*'s wife
was *Lìngxuān*'s younger sister.
When *Lìngxuān* gained favor with the Later Lord (*Hòuzhǔ*),
*Zǐruì* was posthumously granted the title of Prefect of *Huáizhōu* (*Huáizhōu Cìshǐ*),
and all his sons also occupied prominent offices.
*Tóngyóu*
was Attendant Gentleman of the Palace Gate (*Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng*) at the end of the *Wǔpíng* era.
*Tónghuí*
was Minister of the Imperial Treasury (*Tàifǔ Qīng*).
*Tóngxiàn*
was Palace Attendant (*Tōngzhí Chángshì*).
However, *Tóngyóu* ultimately proved to be an excellent official;
during the *Kāihuáng* era of the *Suí*, he was Secretariat Director of the Ministry of Civil Affairs (*Shàngshū Mínbù Shìláng*),
and died while serving as the Prefect of *Suìzhōu*.
The Historian comments: The High Ancestor (*Gāozǔ*) utilized *Jìnyáng*, a strategic military region,
where the design for hegemony rested,
managed the troops and trained the armies,
remotely controlling the authority of the court.
Regarding the crucial affairs of the Imperial Palace,
his reliance and trust were deep and far-reaching.
*Sūnténg* and the others were all unable to remain pure, upright, and uphold the Dao;
they did not concern themselves with bringing order out of chaos,
but heavily amassed wealth and goods,
filling up those streams and ravines [with their greed].
Formerly, when *Xiāo Hé* governed *Guānzhōng*,
and when *Xún Yù* resided in *Xǔxià*,
were they not utterly different from this!
Fortunately, when Emperor *Shìzōng* entered to assist,
he censured them for their arrogance and self-indulgence,
highly regarding *Cuī Xiān*
who wielded his severe authority.
Otherwise, gentlemen would have become weary,
and how could such practices have been easily checked?
*Sūnténg*'s sincerity in pulling the robe [to remonstrate]
is worth praising.
*Lóngzhī* exhausted his mental and physical strength,
planning and initiating the construction of the Capital *Yè*.
Moreover, they all possessed hidden virtue as officials and peers,
and were early granted trust and favor.
Their fame and positions were exalted,
and the court order was not lost.
*Zǐrú* merely because of their mutual familiarity and trust in youth,
had deep affection and intimacy.
His significance was not foundational [to the state],
but favor was established through private indulgence.
No meritorious achievements or virtue were known,
yet he simply obtained high ministerial office.
The love shown to his nephew
was based on instruction in righteous principles.
*Yīng*'s integrity and manner were worthy of respect,
and *Yòu*'s purity, simplicity, and independence
are worth praising.
The Eulogy says: *Hóng* and *Sǎn* relied on each other;
*Xiāo* and *Cáo* lent their assistance.
When the destiny of *Qí* vigorously arose,
*Sūn* and *Gāo* exerted their strength.
Defiled by greed and never satisfied,
they brought great shame upon their high offices.
*Sīmǎ* was a jester,
with skillful talk and a flattering appearance.

Collected Biographies 11: *Hèbá Yǔn*, *Cài Jùn*, *Hán Xián*, *Wèi Chángmìng*, *Wáng Huái*, *Liú Guì*, *Rèn Yánjìng*, *Mòduōlóu Dàiwén*, *Gāo Shìguì*, *Shèdí Huíluò*, *Shèdí Shèng*, *Xuēgū Yán*, *Zhāng Bǎoluò*, *Hóumòchén Xiàng*.
*Hèbá Yǔn*,
courtesy name *Kění*,
was a man from *Jiānshān* in *Shénwǔ*.
His grandfather was *Ěrtóu*,
his father was *Dùbá*.
Both are mentioned in the *Wèi Shǐ* (History of the *Wèi*).
*Yǔn* was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and possessed considerable courage and strategy.
He and his younger brother *Yuè* killed the bandit leader *Wèi Kěgōng*,
and subsequently fled to the *Wèi* [Dynasty].
Yuán Shēn, Prince of *Guǎngyáng*, appointed *Yǔn* as General of Accumulated Arrows (*Jīshè Jiāngjūn*),
holding the Imperial credentials to defend *Fǔkǒu*.
When *Shēn* was defeated,
he submitted to *Ěrzhū Róng*.
*Yǔn*'s father, son, and brothers were all famous for their martial skills,
and *Róng* had long heard of them.
When he met *Yǔn*,
he treated him very generously.
At the beginning of the *Jiànyì* era,
he was appointed General Who Conquers the East (*Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn*) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (*Guānglù Dàfū*),
enfeoffed as the Marquis of *Shòuyáng* County (*Shòuyáng Xiàn Hóu*),
with a stipend of seven hundred households.
During the *Yǒng'ān* era,
he was appointed General Who Conquers the North (*Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn*) and Prefect of *Yùzhōu* (*Yùzhōu Cìshǐ*),
and his title was advanced to Duke.
When Prince *Chángguǎng* of *Wèi* was enthroned,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Duke of *Yànjùn* (*Yànjùn Gōng*),
and concurrently served as Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*).
He was sent as an envoy to the *Rúru*,
and upon returning, he reached *Jìnyáng*.
He happened upon the High Ancestor (*Gāozǔ*) who was about to move out to *Shāndōng*.
*Yǔn* had long known that the High Ancestor was no ordinary man,
and had established ties with him early on.
The High Ancestor, because *Yǔn* was a figure of renown among the Northern gentry,
treated him with especial intimacy and respect.
He thereupon went with *Yǔn* to *Xìndū*,
participating in settling the great strategy.
At the beginning of the *Zhōngxīng* era of the *Wèi*,
he was transferred to Minister of Education (*Sītú*),
and supervised the Director of the Secretariat (*Shàngshū Lìng*).
When the High Ancestor entered *Luò*,
he was advanced in rank to Prince,
transferred to Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*),
and conferred the title of Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*).
When Emperor *Wǔ* of *Wèi* grew suspicious and fearful of the High Ancestor,
he deeply relied upon *Yǔn*'s brother, *Yuè*,
and secretly sent him back and forth.
At that time, everyone worried that *Yǔn* would cause trouble.
When *Yuè* died,
Emperor *Wǔ* again entrusted the crucial responsibility of a trusted confidant to *Yuè*'s brother, *Shèng*.
The High Ancestor valued their old connection
and protected him completely for a long time.
In the first year of the *Tiānpíng* era, he was finally granted death [ordered to commit suicide].
He was forty-eight years old.
The High Ancestor personally attended the mourning.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Prefect of *Dìngzhōu* (*Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ*) and Military Commander of Five Prefectures (*Wǔzhōu Jūnsì*).
*Yǔn* had three sons:
the eldest son *Shìwén*,
the second *Shìlè*,
and the third *Nántuó*.
At the end of the *Xīnghé* era,
the High Ancestor summoned them all to study alongside his own sons.
During the *Wǔdìng* era,
an imperial decree ordered them to reside in *Dìngzhōu*,
and granted them fields and dwellings.
*Cài Jùn*,
courtesy name *Jǐngyàn*,
was a man from *Shímén* in *Guǎngníng*.
His father, *Pǔ*,
when the North was turbulent,
hastened to *Wǔyuán*,
and gained merit through defensive fighting.
He was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (*Níngshuò Jiāngjūn*),
enfeoffed as Baron of *Ānshàng* County (*Ānshàng Xiàn Nán*),
with a stipend of two hundred households.
He soon died,
and was posthumously granted the titles of General Who Assists the State (*Fǔguó Jiāngjūn*) and Prefect of *Yānzhōu* (*Yānzhōu Cìshǐ*).
*Jùn* was bold, straightforward, and courageous.
When the High Ancestor was still obscure,
he was deeply attached to him.
He and *Duàn Cháng* of *Liáoxī* and *Páng Cāngyīng* of *Tàiyuán* all possessed the perception of foresight.
*Cháng* was the Defense Commander of *Huáishuò* for the *Wèi*.
He once met the High Ancestor
and greatly admired him,
and said to the High Ancestor:
“You possess the talent to bring peace to the world.
You will certainly not remain insignificant.
I beg to entrust my descendants to you.”
During the *Xīnghé* era,
he was memorialized for the posthumous grant of Duke of Works (*Sīkōng Gōng*).
His son, *Níng*,
was a Staff Officer (*Cóngshì Zhōngláng*) in the Prime Minister's office.
At the beginning of the *Tiānbǎo* era,
he concurrently served as General of the Southern Gentlemen (*Nán Zhōngláng Jiāng*).
*Cāngyīng* associated with heroic and chivalrous people,
treated guests and travelers generously,
and lived in the prefectural city.
The High Ancestor stayed as a guest at his house,
initially residing in a small dwelling.
*Cāngyīng*'s mother frequently saw a crimson aura rising above the hut and reaching the sky.
*Cāngyīng* also knew that the High Ancestor had the potential of a hegemon,
and always secretly increased his respect.
He dedicated half of his residence to the High Ancestor,
and consequently received his intimacy and recognition.
When the High Ancestor governed *Jìnzhōu*,
he brought *Cāngyīng* in as acting Administrator (*Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Shǐ*),
and tasked him with managing the affairs of *Yìníng* Commandery.
When the banner of righteousness was raised,
*Cāngyīng* abandoned his family, traveled secretly, and returned to the High Ancestor.
The High Ancestor appointed him as acting Director of the Bureau of Granaries (*Cāngbù Lángzhōng*) in the Traveling Chancellery (*Xíngtái*).
He died while serving as Prefect of *Ānzhōu* (*Ānzhōu Cìshǐ*).
Jùn was initially captured by Dù Luòzhōu.
At that time, Gāozǔ was also in Luòzhōu's army.
Gāozǔ planned to execute Luòzhōu,
and Jùn was involved in the scheme.
The matter was exposed,
so he fled to Gě Róng,
and subsequently abandoned Gě Róng and submitted to Ěrzhū Róng.
When Róng entered Luò,
he was made Píngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Zhàngnèi Biéjiàng.
Following the defeat of Gě Róng,
he was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū.
He further followed in pacifying Yuán Hào,
and was enfeoffed as the Nán of Wūluò Xiàn.
He followed Gāozǔ in raising the standard of righteousness,
and served as a Dūdu.
When Gāozǔ pacified Yè,
and defeated the Four Hú at Hánlíng,
Jùn was instrumental in both battles.
During the Tàichāng era,
he was sent out to serve as the Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu.
His governance was harsh and violent,
and he also accepted many bribes.
However, he was also clear-headed and organized,
so the officials and common people feared and obeyed him.
He enjoyed entertaining guests
and was known for his generosity.
Later, Hú Qiān and others occupied Yǎnzhōu and rebelled.
Jùn, along with Wèi Jǐng, the Cìshǐ of Qízhōu, suppressed them.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi harbored doubts about Gāozǔ,
and considering Jìzhōu strategically important,
wished to have a trusted confidant occupy it.
He secretly ordered the Yùshǐ to fabricate charges against Jùn,
intending to replace Jùn with the King of Rǔyáng.
Consequently, Jùn was transferred to manage the affairs of Yǎnzhōu.
Gāozǔ believed Jùn was innocent
and petitioned for his reinstatement.
Emperor Wǔ did not permit it.
He appointed Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì as Cìshǐ
and ordered him to lead troops to the prefecture.
Jùn's defenses were strict and prepared.
Xiǎnzhì feared him,
and upon reaching Dōngjùn,
dared not advance.
During the Tiānpíng era,
he served as a Dūdu,
and followed the Commander Lóu Zhāo in attacking Fán Zihú in Yǎnzhōu.
He also joined the Xíngtái Yuán Zisī in suppressing Yuán Qìnghé,
and together they pacified him.
When Hóu Shēn rebelled,
Jùn was again appointed Dà Dūdū,
leading troops to suppress him.
Shēn was defeated and fled.
He was then transferred to be the Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
In the autumn of the third year of Tiānpíng (536),
he died while in the prefecture,
at the age of forty-two.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Chíjié, Shìzhōng, Dūdu, Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu, Shàngshū Lìng, and Sīkōng Gōng,
and given the posthumous name Wēiwǔ.
When Qí received the abdication,
an imperial edict mandated offerings and announcements at his tomb.
In the beginning of the Huángjiàn era,
he was enshrined in the ancestral temple of Gāozǔ.
Hán Xián,
courtesy name Pǔxián,
was a native of Shímén in Guǎngníng.
He was strong, robust, and militarily capable.
He initially followed Gě Róng in rebellion.
When Róng was defeated,
he went to Bìngzhōu following the standard procedure,
and Ěrzhū Róng promoted him to serve among his attendants.
When Róng's wife and children fled north,
Shìlóng and others established Yè, the Prince of Chángguǎng of Wèi, as their leader.
Xián was appointed Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Túntú Qí Xiàowèi.
Before this,
when Shìlóng and others attacked Jiànzhōu and Shíchéng,
Xián demonstrated military merit in both actions.
