Ěrzhū Dùlǜ employed him as Zhàngnèi Dūdu,
enfeoffing him as the Bó of Fényáng Xiàn,
with four hundred taxable households.
In the beginning of Pǔtài,
he was appointed Qián Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu.
As Gāozǔ was raising the standard of righteousness,
Dùlǜ, knowing that Xián was well-known to Gāozǔ,
feared he might defect,
and sent an envoy to summon him.
Xián was unwilling to answer the summons,
so he secretly dispatched groups of barbarians
to raise many signal fires,
simulating an imminent attack or disaster.
The envoy thus reported this,
and Xián was permitted to remain.
Xián subsequently sent a messenger secretly to convey his loyalty to Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ entered Luò,
all Ěrzhū appointments and titles were generally stripped.
Because Xián had sent a message of loyalty from afar,
he was ordered to retain his former position.
In the beginning of Tàichāng,
he was successively promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Guānglù Dàfū,
and sent out as Cìshǐ of Jiànzhōu.
When Emperor Wǔ fled west,
he was transferred to manage the affairs of Jīngzhōu.
In the beginning of Tiānpíng,
he became Cìshǐ of Luòzhōu.
The commoner Hán Mùlán and others led local people in rebellion.
Xián attacked and defeated them.
He personally inspected the site
intending to collect the armor and weapons.
One rebel, in desperation,
hid among the corpses.
Seeing Xián approaching,
he suddenly jumped up and hacked at him,
severing his shin bone, resulting in his death.
Although Xián was a military commander,
his nature was mild and upright,
and he was not excessively greedy or brutal.
Although he did not establish good governance in the places he served,
he did not cause suffering for the officials and common people.
Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
the Western Regions brought Buddhist scriptures carried by a white horse to Luò.
Consequently, the Báimǎ Sì was established.
The scripture casket was passed down in this temple;
its form was simple and ancient,
and people considered it an antique,
cherished as a treasure through the generations.
Xián needlessly chopped and broke it.
Not long after, he died.
Commentators sometimes suggested that Xián brought this disaster upon himself due to this action.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Chíjié, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Dìngzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Ānzhōu, and Píngzhōu, Dà Jiāngjūn, Shàngshū Lìng, Sīkōng Gōng, and Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu.
His son Yì succeeded him.
Wèi Chángmìng,
was a native of Dínà in Tài'ān.
His father, Xiǎn,
was Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Dàijùn during the Wèi dynasty.
Chángmìng was mild and sincere by nature,
possessing talent and discernment.
During the chaos of Fúyáng,
he took refuge in Tàiyuán.
When Gāozǔ was about to initiate his great righteous undertaking,
Chángmìng participated in the planning.
He followed Gāozǔ in defeating the Four Hú at Hánlíng,
and was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn.
When Fán Zihú occupied Yǎnzhōu and rebelled,
he was appointed Dà Dūdū of the Southeast Route
and pacified him alongside the various armies.
He was transferred to defend Fànyáng Chéng,
and thereupon appointed Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu,
supervising the affairs of Ānzhōu and Píngzhōu.
The prefecture was located on the northern frontier;
the land was desolate and the population dispersed.
Although Chángmìng engaged in much collection,
he governed the people with kindness,
and they were somewhat stabilized and settled.
Soon after, he left office due to illness.
Not long afterwards,
he was again summoned and appointed Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Xīyàn, Yōuzhōu, Cāngzhōu, and Yíngzhōu, and Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu.
He died while in the prefecture.
He was posthumously granted his original titles,
additionally Sīkōng,
and given the posthumous name Wǔzhuàng.
His son Xīngjìng
was skilled in archery and horsemanship
and possessed martial arts skills.
Gāozǔ brought him in as Zhàngnèi Dūdu.
He was appointed Cānjūn Shì of the Chángshān Gōng's administration,
and granted the title of Bó of Jízhōng Xiàn.
The commoner Lǐ Xiǎoxīng of Jìnzhōu gathered a gang and became a bandit.
Xīngjìng followed Sīkōng Hán Guǐ in suppressing and pacifying them.
His noble rank was advanced to Hóu.
When Gāozǔ attacked Emperor Wén of Zhōu at Mángshān,
Xīngjìng was struck by a stray arrow during the battle
and died.
He was posthumously granted the Military Affairs of Jīngzhōu, Qízhōu, and Bīnzhōu,
his noble rank raised to Gōng,
and given the posthumous name Mǐnzhuāng.
Gāozǔ deeply mourned him,
personally offered condolences,
and granted his wife and children emoluments as though Xīngjìng were still alive.
His son Shìlín succeeded him.
Wáng Huái,
courtesy name Huáizhōu,
his native place is unknown.
From youth he loved archery and horsemanship
and possessed notable spirit and ambition.
Encountering the chaos and turmoil on the northern frontier,
he joined the army early.
Hán Lóu rebelled in Yōuzhōu.
Huái knew that his cause would fail.
He secretly gathered his confidants,
and in the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era, defected from Lóu and submitted to Wèi.
He was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, First Lǐngmín Qiúzhǎng, and Hóu of Wǔzhōu Xiàn.
When Gāozǔ moved east,
Huái led his tribal people, more than three thousand households,
and followed Gāozǔ to Jìzhōu.
When the Banner of Righteousness was raised,
Gāozǔ appointed him Grand Commandant (Dà Dūdū).
He followed in the campaign against Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā,
and defeated him.
He was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn)
and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu.
He subsequently followed Gāozǔ in attacking Yè.
It was conquered.
He participated in defeating the Four Hú tribes at Hánlíng,
and his noble rank was advanced to Marquis (Hóu).
He then followed him into Luò[yáng],
was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn),
and his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Lúxiāng County (Lúxiāng Xiàn Hóu).
During the Tiānpíng reign [period],
he was appointed Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié) and Military Administrator of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Jūnshì).
When the Liáng dynasty sent generals Zhàn Sēngzhēn and Yáng Jiǎn to raid [the borders],
Huái and the Deputy Administrator (Xíngtái) Yuán Yàn attacked Xiàngchéng,
captured it,
and seized Jiǎn.
He again followed Gāozǔ in surprising and capturing Xī Xiàzhōu.
Returning,
he was made Grand Commandant (Dà Dūdū),
defending Xiàguǎn,
and was appointed Companion to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
At the beginning of the Yuánxiàng reign [period],
he was made Grand Commandant (Dà Dūdū),
and campaigned west with the various generals.
He fell ill and died in Jiànzhōu.

He was posthumously granted Military Administrator over Dìng, Yōu, Sì, and four other prefectures (Dìng Yōu Sì Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), Governor (Cìshǐ), Duke Grand Minister over the Masses (Sītú Gōng), and Palace Grand Secretary (Shàngshū Púshè).
Huái was recognized by Gāozǔ for his martial skill, merit, and sincerity.
His ambitions and strength were not yet fully realized,
and commentators regretted that his success was incomplete.
At the beginning of the Huángjiàn reign [period],
he was sacrificed to alongside Gāozǔ in the ancestral temple courtyard.
Liú Guì
was a man of Yángqǔ, Xiùróng.
His father, Gān,
was posthumously granted General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sìzhōu during the Wèi era.
Guì was stern, principled, and decisively spirited.
He served as Cavalry Staff Officer in Ěrzhū Róng’s establishment.
At the beginning of the Jiànyì reign [period],
for his merit in participating in setting the strategic plan,
he was enfeoffed as Earl of Fūchéng County (Fūchéng Xiàn Bó),
with five hundred households.
He was appointed General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn) and Grand Master of the Middle (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
and shortly thereafter was advanced to Duke (Gōng).
Róng was fierce and impatient,
and Guì was particularly severe and strict.
Whenever he was appointed to a task,
he often satisfied Róng’s wishes,
and thus received trust and favor.
His position and prestige daily increased,
and he was promoted to General Who Calms the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the third year of Yǒng'ān,
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Liángzhōu.
At the beginning of the Jiànmíng reign [period],
Ěrzhū Shìlóng monopolized power.

He appointed Guì General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn), Golden and Purple Chief Controller (Jīnzǐ Guānglù), concurrently Palace Grand Secretary of the Left (Zuǒ Púshè), and Deputy Administrator of the Western Circuit (Xīdào Xíngtái),
sending him to oppose Emperor Xiàozhuāng’s Deputy Administrator (Xíngtái) Yuán Xiǎngōng at Zhèngpíng.
Guì defeated Xiǎngōng
and captured him,
along with Grand Commandant (Dà Dūdū) Péi Jùn and others.
He was subsequently appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìnzhōu.
At the beginning of the Pǔtài reign [period],
he was transferred to administer the affairs of Fénzhōu.
When Gāozǔ raised the righteous revolt,
Guì abandoned the city and defected to Gāozǔ at Yè.
At the beginning of the Tàichāng reign [period],
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sìzhōu based on his previous office,
and was then transferred to administer the affairs of Jiànzhōu.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng reign [period],
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Shǎnzhōu.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Palace Vice Marshal (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi) and Grand Controller of Sìzhōu (Sìzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
In the same year,
he was promoted to Deputy Administrator Palace Grand Secretary (Xíngtái Púshè),
and, along with Hóu Jǐng, Gāo Áng, and others, campaigned against Dúgū Rúyuàn at Luòyáng.
In every place Guì served,
he never failed to unleash his harsh severity.
When building city walls,
his supervision and demands were extremely severe.
He unjustly killed people,
treating his subordinates like weeds.
However, by using strict decisions to manage affairs,
he benefited prompt execution.
His nature was harsh and upright,
and he denounced wrongdoing without evasion;
therefore, he was appreciated at the time.
Although he was not among the chief founding meritorious officials,
since he was an old commoner friend of Gāozǔ,
he was especially regarded as close and important.
He died in the eleventh month of the first year of Xīnghé.

He was posthumously granted Military Administrator over Jì, Dìng, Bīng, Yīn, and Yíng five prefectures (Jì Dìng Bīng Yīn Yíng Wǔzhōu Jūnshì), Grand Protector (Tàibǎo), Duke Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi Gōng), Director of the Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū Shì), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu.
His posthumous name was Zhōngwǔ.
When the Qí accepted the abdication,
an imperial decree was issued to make sacrifices and reports at his tomb.
During the Huángjiàn reign [period],
he was sacrificed to alongside Gāozǔ in the ancestral temple courtyard.
His eldest son, Yuánsūn,
was a Court Gentleman (Yuánwàiláng) and Controller (Zhōngzhèng) of Sìzhōu,
but died young.
He was posthumously granted Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sìzhōu.
His second son, Hónghuī, inherited [the title].
At the end of the Wǔpíng reign [period],
he was provisionally made Companion to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī),
and memorialized on affairs for the Secretariat.
Rèn Yánjìng
was a man from Guǎngníng.
His paternal uncle, Táo,
became a military officer in Yúnzhōng at the beginning of the Tàihé reign [period].
Yánjìng followed him
and consequently settled there.
In his youth, Yánjìng was harmonious and generous,
and possessed great capacity.
He initially followed Gě Róng as a rebel.
Róng appointed him Prince (Wáng)
and trusted him greatly.
When Róng was defeated,
Yánjìng gathered his subordinates and was the first to surrender.
He was appointed General Who Guards the Distant (Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Guǎngníng (Guǎngníng Tàishǒu),
and was granted the noble rank of Duke of Xīhé County (Xīhé Xiàn Gōng).
Later, he followed Gāozǔ in raising the righteous revolt.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng reign [period],
he was successively promoted to Grand Master of the Imperial Clan (Guānglù Dàfū).
At the beginning of the Tàichāng reign [period],
he was successively transferred to Palace Grand Secretary of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè),
and his position was advanced to Establishment of a Palace and Companion to the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
As Yánjìng’s position and prestige were now high,
he was able to treat others with leniency and harmony,
and scholars praised him.
When the trouble caused by Hú Sīchūn erupted,
Yánjìng abandoned his family and fled north.
He reached Héběi Commandery
and consequently led the local people to occupy it,
waiting for Gāozǔ.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi entered the Pass (Rù Guān),
the Jīngmán barbarians were disobedient.
Yánjìng was appointed Commissioner with Credentials and Grand Commandant of the Southern Circuit (Chíjié Nándào Dà Dūdū),
and he campaigned to pacify them.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng reign [period],
he was again appointed Attendant in Ordinary (Shìzhōng).
At that time, Lú Zhòngyán of Fànyáng led refugees from Héběi in rebellion at Yángxià.
Tián Lóng, a citizen of Xī Yǎnzhōu, gathered a crowd to support him.
Yánjìng was appointed Grand Commandant (Dà Dūdū) and Military Supervisor of the Eastern Circuit (Dōngdào Jūnsī),
and he led Commandants (Dūdū) Yuán Zhěng, Chìliè Tuó, and others to campaign against them.
He was soon made Deputy Administrator Palace Grand Secretary (Xíngtái Púshè),
and appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu.
At that time, the Liáng dynasty sent Yuán Qìnghé and its various generals to raid the border.
Yánjìng defeated Huáng Dàoshǐ, the Liáng Governor (Cìshǐ) of Rénzhōu, at Běi Jìyīn,
and then defeated Liáng Jùn at Shànfù,
capturing and executing ten thousand men.
He was again appointed Attendant in Ordinary (Shìzhōng).
While serving in the prefecture, he accepted large amounts [of bribes or gifts],
but his administration was not cruel.
He treated scholars with courtesy and respect,
and was not a source of suffering or hardship for the common people.
Hèrě Huī, the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu, seized the Governor (Cìshǐ) Tián Xùn, occupied the city, and surrendered to the Western Wèi (Xī Wèi).
Yánjìng was again ordered to lead Yáo Xióng, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu, and others to campaign against them.
The Western Wèi (Xī Wèi) sent its general Yí Fēng to lead troops in support.
Yánjìng and the others were defeated in battle
and retreated to Běi Yù[zhōu].
He then met with Deputy Administrator (Xíngtái) Hóu Jǐng and Minister over the Masses (Sītú) Gāo Áng,
and together they attacked Yǐngchuān,
capturing it.
In the autumn of the first year of Yuánxiàng,
he died in Yè,
aged forty-five.

He was posthumously granted Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Grand Protector (Tàibǎo), Duke Grand Marshal (Tàiwèi Gōng), Director of the Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū Shì), Grand Military Administrator over Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Yōu, and Ān five prefectures (Dūdū Jì Dìng Yíng Yōu Ān Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu.
His son, Zhòu, inherited [the title].
Zhòu was reckless and chivalrous,
quite quick-witted and kind.
While young, he was near Gāo Zǔ,
and during the Tiānpíng era,
he was promoted to be the Administrator of Dōngjùn.
His family was originally wealthy,
and he also accumulated much wealth;
his actions were utterly extravagant.
When guests came and went,
the welcoming and sending off were extremely generous.
Soon after, he was impeached by the officials for corruption and embezzlement,
but Gāo Zǔ forgave him.
When he finished his term as Administrator,
Gāo Zǔ appointed him as Dūdū (Area Commander).
At the end of the Xīnghé era,
Gāo Zǔ returned after attacking Yùbì.
Considering the southwestern region of Jìnzhōu to be strategically important,
he left Qīnghé Gōng Yuè as Xíngtái (Mobile Secretariat) to defend it,
and sent Zhòu to assist him.
Zhòu indulged in drinking and unrestrained wandering,
neglecting defense.
Gāo Zǔ reprimanded him.
Zhòu became fearful
and secretly sent an envoy to send (a pledge) to Zhōu.
He was exposed by others,
but an exhaustive investigation did not reveal the full truth.
Gāo Zǔ specifically spared him,
saying to Zhòu:
"I treat all people with sincerity,
and I believed you certainly would not do such a thing.
Furthermore, the defectors from Hēità [Yǔwén Tà]
follow one after another.
Your true situation,
how can I worry about not knowing it later?"
Zhòu was inwardly ill at ease.
At this time,
Yítóng Ěrzhū Wénchàng and the Staff Officers Fáng Zǐyuǎn and Zhèng Zhònglǐ, all of whom were treacherous, vile, and lawless,
Zhòu heavily befriended them,
and then secretly plotted assassination and rebellion.
On the fifteenth day of the first month of the third year of Wǔdìng,
taking advantage of Gāo Zǔ watching an evening performance,
they planned to secretly launch the attack.
Someone informed against them,
orders were given to arrest and thoroughly investigate,
and the facts were all confirmed.
Zhòu, along with his sons and younger brothers, were all executed.
Mòduōlóu Dàiwén
was a native of Dínà, Tàiyán.
He was brave, decisive, and possessed courage.
He followed Gāo Zǔ when he raised the banner of righteousness.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
he was appointed General Fúbō, Lieutenant-General Wǔbèn, and Grand Area Commander Yúhòu.
He followed in the attack on Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā,
distinguished himself with merit,
was promoted to General Qián,
enfeoffed as Viscount of Shíchéng County,
with an income of three hundred households.
He also followed in defeating the Four Hú at Hánlíng,
and his noble rank was advanced to Marquis.
He followed in subduing Ěrzhū Zhào at Chìhóng Lǐng.
Zhào, hard-pressed and desperate, hanged himself;
Dàiwén captured his corpse.
He was transferred to Grand Area Commander of the Left Flank.
When the conflict involving Húsī Chūn arose,
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi sent Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì to hold and defend Shíjì.
Gāo Zǔ ordered Dàiwén to lead thirty thousand elite troops,
meet with Dòu Tài and others at Dìngzhōu,
proceed together to Shíjì,
and defeat Xiǎnzhì.
During the Tiānpíng era,
he was appointed Governor of Jìnzhōu.
When the Hú bandits of Fénzhōu caused disturbances and theft,
Gāo Zǔ personally campaigned against them,
using Dàiwén as the vanguard,
and he frequently achieved battle merits.
Upon returning,
he was rewarded with thirty slaves, fifty head of cattle and horses each, and one thousand bolts of cloth.
He was subsequently made Grand Area Commander of the five prefectures: Fén, Shǎn, Dōngyōng, Jìn, and Tài.
Later, he attacked the two prefectures of Dōngyōng and Nánfén with Tàibǎo Wèi Jǐng,
and conquered them.
At the beginning of the Yuánxiàng era,
he was appointed Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yítóng (Equivalent to Three Dukes), and Grand Area Commander of the Southern Route.
He attacked Dúgū Rúyuàn at Jīnyǒngchéng with Xíngtái Hóu Jǐng.
When Emperor Wén of Zhōu’s army marched out of Hángǔ,
Jǐng and Gāo Áng discussed organizing the ranks and training the soldiers
to await their arrival.
Dàiwén requested to lead his division
to attack the vanguard,
but Jǐng and the others resolutely refused.
Dàiwén was by nature brave but headstrong,
and refused to accept the order.
Leading one thousand light cavalry ahead of the main army for scouting,
he passed west of Chánjiàn,
encountered the Zhōu army,
and died in battle.

He was posthumously granted commandership of the forces of the five prefectures of Bīng, Sì, Yún, and Shuò, Governor of Bīngzhōu, Shàngshū Yòu Púshè (Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs), and Sītú Gōng (Duke of the Minister of Education).
His son, Jìngxiǎn,
was resolute, upright, and industrious;
he became known for his military prowess when young.
Following Húlǜ Guāng on campaigns,
he frequently gained military merit.
Guāng always ordered Jìngxiǎn to be the advance guard,
establish camps and fortresses,
and patrol throughout the night,
sometimes remaining sleepless until dawn.
When facing the enemy and arranging formations,
he also ordered Jìngxiǎn to divide the generals and soldiers;
in the short time available,
the ranks would be orderly and disciplined.
He was deeply valued by Guāng.
His position reached General Lǐngjūn,
supervising Yúhòu affairs.
During the Wǔpíng era,
when the imperial carriage went to Jìnyáng,
Jìngxiǎn was always ordered to supervise the troops remaining at the Secretariat,
investigate and arrest bandits,
and the capital remained peaceful.
In the seventh year,
he followed the Latter Ruler to Píngyáng,
and after the defeat, returned to Bīngzhōu.
There, he and Táng Yōng and others urged the enthronement of the Prince of Āndé to assume the imperial title.
When Āndé was defeated,
all the civil and military officials surrendered to the Zhōu army;
only Jìngxiǎn fled back to Yè.
He was given the position of Sītú (Minister of Education).
The day after Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu pacified Yèchéng,
he arrested Jìngxiǎn and executed him outside the Chānghé Gate,
blaming him for not remaining in Jìnyáng.
Gāo Shìguì
was a native of Shànwú.
When young, he possessed military talent.
At the beginning of Xiàochāng,
the Cílè within the prefecture, such as Liú Lún, gathered masses and rebelled.
Shìguì served as Dūdū,
led his troops to suppress Lún,
and defeated them in a single battle.
He was repeatedly promoted to General Fǔjūn and Grand Master Jiànyì.
When Ěrzhū Róng enthroned Emperor Zhuāng of Wèi,
Shìguì participated in the merit of supporting the enthronement.
He was promoted to General Wèi, Guānglù Dàfū, Grand Area Commander of Xiùróng, and First Chieftain Leading the People.
He was granted the title of Earl of Shàngluò County.
When Ěrzhū Róng attacked Gé Róng at Fǔkǒu,
he appointed Shìguì as Vanguard Dūdū.
After Róng was pacified,
he was appointed bearer of credentials and Governor of Fénzhōu,
and soon after, Governor of Jìnzhōu.
When Hédòulíng Bùfān invaded and caused chaos in Bīngzhōu,
Gāo Zǔ defeated him.
Shìguì also participated in the campaign and achieved merit,
for which he was appointed Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yítóng Sānsī (Equivalent to the Three Dukes),
enfeoffed as Duke of Chángshān Commandery,
with an income of one thousand five hundred households.
When Gāo Zǔ raised the righteous banner,
Shìguì was involved in the planning.
When Fán Zihú occupied the prefecture and rebelled,
he followed Grand Area Commander Lóu Zhāo to suppress him.
After Zihú was pacified,
he was appointed Governor of Xīyǎnzhōu,
but he did not proceed to the prefecture.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
he was again appointed Governor of Jìnzhōu.
Gāo Zǔ soon considered Hóngdòng to be a strategically crucial and dangerous spot,
and sent Shìguì to garrison it.
When Gāo Zǔ suffered a defeat at Shāyuàn,
the acting official of Jìnzhōu, Fēng Zǔyè, abandoned the city and returned.
The people of the prefecture, led by Chái Lǎn, gathered a following and revolted.
Gāo Zǔ ordered Shìguì to suppress Lǎn.
Lǎn fled to Cháibì,
and Shìguì defeated and beheaded him.
At this time,
the border regions of the two prefectures, Dōngyōng and Nánfén, were infested with many groups of bandits,
gathered together as robbers.
Due to Shìguì's pacification of Lǎn,
they all dispersed, returning to their former occupations.
Later, five thousand households of Xiùróng people rebelled and responded to the Shānhú.
Shìguì was again appointed Xíngtái,
to command all armies and suppress them.
During the Yuánxiàng era,
he followed Gāo Zǔ in defeating Emperor Wén of Zhōu at Mángshān.
He was again appointed Governor of Jìnzhōu and Military Commander of the Western Route,
leading troops to attack the rebel Pān Jí of Huáizhōu.
Before arriving,
he succumbed to illness on the road.
He was posthumously granted commandership of the forces of the five prefectures of Bīng, Fén, Huái, Jiàn, and Dōngyōng, Grand Commandant Gōng (Duke), and Governor of Bīngzhōu.
His son Ānàgōng was highly favored and honored,
and was enfeoffed as Prince of Chénggāo.
An imperial decree ordered his second son, Kǒngquè, to inherit the title.
Shèdí Huíluò,
was a person of Dài.
In his youth, he possessed martial strength,
and his bearing and appearance were grand and imposing.
He initially served Ěrzhū Róng as a Commander (tǒngjūn).
He participated in establishing Emperor Zhuāng,
and was promoted to Separate General (biéjiàng),
and was granted the peerage Lord (Bó) of Wújí.
He followed (Ěrzhū Róng) in defeating Gě Róng,
and was promoted to Area Commander (dūdū).
When Róng died,
he belonged to Ěrzhū Zhào.
When Gāozǔ raised troops in Xìndū,
Huíluò gathered his followers and pledged allegiance.
He followed in defeating the Four Hú Tribes at Hánlíng.
For his military merit, he was appointed Area Commander (dūdū),
and granted the titles General of the Rear (Hòujiāngjūn) and Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
He was enfeoffed as Viscount (Zǐ) of Shùnyáng County, receiving four hundred households in his stipend.
He was transferred to Area Commander of the Right Wing (Yòuxiāng Dūdū).
He followed in campaigning against the Shānhú tribes.
As vanguard, he beheaded (the enemy),
and was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Shuò Prefecture.
He defeated Zhōu Wén at Héyáng,
and was transferred and appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xià Prefecture.
During the Battle of Máng Shān,
he fought vigorously and achieved merit,
increasing his stipend to seven hundred households, including the previous grant.
When Shìzōng succeeded to authority,
he followed in pacifying Yǐngchuān.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiàn Prefecture.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Prince (Wáng) of Shùnyáng Commandery.
At the beginning of Dàníng,
he was transferred to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Shuò Prefecture,
and received the revenues (gàn) of Bólíng Commandery.
He was transferred to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàishī).
He encountered sickness and died.

He was posthumously granted Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Military Governor (Dūdū) of the armies of five prefectures (Dìng, Yíng, Shuò, Yún), Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Gōng),
and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dìng Prefecture.
He was posthumously granted one thousand bolts of material.
Shèdí Shèng,
was a person of Huáishuò.
His nature was gentle and yielding,
and in his youth, he had military prowess.
He initially served Gāozǔ as his trusted Area Commander (qīnxìn dūdū),
and was appointed General Quelling Waves (Fúbō Jiāngjūn).
He followed in every campaign and punitive expedition.
For his merit, he was enfeoffed as Lord (Bó) of Xíngtáng County.
Furthermore, he was successively promoted to General Pacifying the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn),
Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yōu Prefecture,
granted the additional title General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn),
and served as Garrison Commander (Zhènchéng Dūdū) of Yù Prefecture.
For his meritorious seniority, his peerage was advanced to Duke (Gōng).
Shìzōng reduced the fiefs (of others) by two hundred households
to increase his stipend.

He was appointed General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn), Director of the Secretariat with the Rights of the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Shuò Prefecture.
When Qí received the abdication (Shàn),
his enfeoffment was changed to Duke (Gōng) of Huáyáng County.
He was also appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Běishuò Prefecture.
Since the enfeoffment of Huáyáng was distant,
following established precedent, several tens of households were carved out from Shíài County in Bīng Prefecture, Píngkòu County in Sì Prefecture, and Mǎyì County in Yuánpíng,
totaling two hundred households, to serve as his revenue fief.
Not long after,
(this practice) was abolished by precedent.
He was appointed Grand Master of Court (Tèjìn),
and then died.

He was posthumously granted Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Military Governor (Dūdū) of the military affairs of five prefectures (Shuò, Yíng, Zhào, Yōu, Ān), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Gōng), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Shuò Prefecture.
Xuēgū Yán,
was a person of Dài.
In his youth, he was fierce and resolute,
and possessed martial strength.
When Hán Lóu rebelled,
Yán followed the masses and joined him.
Later, he secretly planned with Wáng Huái and others to attack Lóu,
but was discovered by Lóu's military commander (wèishuài), Yǐfú Chǒu.
He fought vigorously and defeated Chǒu,
and subsequently led his followers to submit (to the legitimate authority).
Liú Guì, the Mobile Secretariat (Xíngtái), recommended him as Area Commander (dūdū),
granted him the additional title General Who Conquers the Captives (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and bestowed upon him the peerage Marquis (Hóu) of Yǒnggù County.
Later, he belonged to Gāozǔ as Area Commander (dūdū),
and thereupon followed in raising the banner of righteousness.
He defeated Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā,
and consequently followed in pacifying Yè.
For his merit, his peerage was advanced to Duke (Gōng),
and he was promoted to Grand Area Commander (Dà Dūdū).
He followed in defeating the Four Hú Tribes at Hánlíng,
and was granted the additional title Grand Master of Radiant Merit with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
He followed in pursuing Ěrzhū Zhào at Chìhóng Lǐng,
and was appointed First Chieftain Leading the Populace (Dìyī Lǐngmín Qiúzhǎng).
When Xiàojìng was established,
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiǎn Prefecture,
and successively granted the additional title General of Cavalry and Chariots (Jūqí Jiāngjūn).
In the fourth year of Tiānpíng (537 CE),
he followed Gāozǔ in campaigning westward.
When they reached Pújīn,
Dòu Tài suffered a defeat south of the Yellow River.
Gāozǔ withdrew the army,
and Yán guarded the rear,
fighting and marching simultaneously.
In one day, he broke fifteen blades by chopping (at the enemy).
Upon returning,
he was transferred to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Liáng Prefecture.
He followed in campaigning against Yùbì,
and was again transferred to a Provincial Governor (Zhōu Cìshǐ).
He followed in defeating Emperor Zhōu Wén at Máng Shān,
his peerage was advanced to County Duke (Xiàn Gōng),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Gāozǔ once reviewed horses at Běimù.
On the road, they encountered a downpour,
and a loud thunder shook the ground.
Ahead was a single Buddhist stupa (fútú).
Gāozǔ ordered Yán to inspect it.
Yán then galloped his horse, holding his spear straight forward.
Before reaching thirty paces,
the thunder fire scorched his face.
Yán shouted "Kill!"
and raced around the stupa,
and the fire subsequently extinguished.
When Yán returned,
his eyebrows, temples, and the mane and tail of his horse were all scorched.
Gāozǔ sighed and said:
"Xuēgū Yán is truly capable of fighting the thunderbolt!"
His bravery and decisiveness were like this.
He also repeatedly followed Gāozǔ in attacking and defeating the Shānhú tribes,
and campaigning westward against Yùbì.
Returning (to the capital), he became General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn),
and his enfeoffment was changed to Duke (Gōng) of Píngqín Commandery.
He served as Grand Area Commander of the Left Wing (Zuǒxiāng Dà Dūdū),
and campaigned with various generals to attack Yǐng Prefecture.
Yán was solely responsible for overseeing the construction of the earth mound (tǔshān).
Due to his drunkenness, the mound was attacked and seized by the enemy.
When Yǐng Prefecture was pacified,
the generals returned to the capital,
and were feasted in Huálínyuán Park.
Shìzōng petitioned the Wèi Emperor
to seat Yán below the steps to humiliate him.
Later, he concurrently held the position of General Director of the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
He was sent out to serve as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Cāng Prefecture,
and separately enfeoffed as Baron (Nán) of Wēn County,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
When Qí received the abdication,
he was separately granted the peerage Duke (Gōng) of Dūchāng County.
His nature was fond of alcohol,
and he was usually muddled and drunk.
However, because of his bravery, decisiveness, and skill in fighting,
whenever the main army campaigned,
he was always the vanguard.
Therefore, he was ranked alongside Péng, Liú, Hán, and Pān.
In the second year of Tiānbǎo (551 CE),
he was appointed Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo),
and promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
In the eighth year (557 CE),
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sì Prefecture,
granted the additional title Director of the Secretariat with the Rights of the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
received the revenues (gàn) of Luòyáng Commandery,
and soon after, this revenue was changed to Héjiān Commandery.
Zhāng Bǎoluò,
was a person of Dài,
claiming his ancestry originated from Xī'è in Nányáng.
His family generations were fond of guests,
valuing chivalry and spiritedness,
and he was quite well known in the Northern lands.
Bǎoluò was vigorous in his youth,
and skilled in archery and horsemanship.
During the Xiàochāng reign of Wèi (525–528 CE),
the Northern Garrisons were in turmoil,
and Bǎoluò also followed the masses southward.
When Gě Róng usurped authority and rebelled,
he made Bǎoluò Commander of the Retainers (Lǐng Zuǒyòu).
When Róng was defeated,
he continued serving Ěrzhū Róng as a Commander (tǒngjūn),
and was successively promoted to General Manifesting Ardor (Yángliè Jiāngjūn) and Commandant of Escort (Fèngchē Dūwèi).
Later, he belonged to Gāozǔ as Area Commander (dūdū),
and followed in campaigning against Bù Fān.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness,
Bǎoluò served as an Inner Tent Attendant (zhàngnèi),
and followed in defeating Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā.
Soon after, he was transferred to General of the Right (Yòujiāngjūn) and Grand Master of the Center (Zhōngsàn Dàfū).
Still as an Inner Tent Attendant, he followed Gāozǔ in besieging Yèchéng.
After it was taken,
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) and Grand Master of Radiant Merit (Guānglù Dàfū).
He followed in defeating Ěrzhū Zhào and others at Hánlíng, and subsequently followed Gāozǔ into Luò.
He was granted the additional title General Pacifying the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn).
Later, Gāozǔ requested to reduce the Imperial domain's fiefs
and distribute them among the officers and soldiers.
Bǎoluò, following precedent, was enfeoffed as Baron (Nán) of Bójiāchéng Township in Chāngpíng County, with one hundred households.
When Wèi Emperor Chū was in disagreement with Gāozǔ,
he ordered the Director of the Secretariat (Yítóng), Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì, to lead Hú Sīshòu, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yù Prefecture, eastward toward Jì Prefecture.
Gāozǔ dispatched Grand Area Commander Dòu Tài to cross (the river) from Huátái and resist Xiǎnzhì.
Bǎoluò belonged to Tài's vanguard.
When the matter was settled,
he was promoted to Area Commander (dūdū).
to attack Xiàzhōu,
and conquered it.
When Mòqí Shòuluògān surrendered,
Gāozǔ sent Bǎoluò and various generals to meet and reinforce him along the road.
In the beginning of the Yuánxiàng era,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Xīxiàzhōu and Grand Area Commander (Dà Dūdū) of that province.
Furthermore, for his merits both early and late,
he was enfeoffed as the Count (Bó) of Ānwǔ County,
with four hundred taxable households.
He was then transferred to serve temporarily as Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu.
He followed Gāozǔ to attack Emperor Wén of Zhōu at Mángshān,
besieged Yùbì,
and attacked Lóngmén.
Upon returning,
he was stationed in Jìnzhōu.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
Bǎoluò was made Grand Area Commander (Dà Dūdū) of the Left Flank (Zuǒxiāng).
Later, when he left Jìnzhōu,
he was promoted to General Who Conquers the West (Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn).
When Wáng Sīzhèng reinforced Yǐngzhōu,
the siege was ongoing but unsuccessful.
Shìzōng then ordered Bǎoluò to garrison Yángzhìwù,
forming a pincer movement (jǐjiǎo zhī shì) with Yángzhōu.
When Yǐngchuān was pacified,
he was soon appointed Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication (shòuchán),
he remained as Cìshǐ.
His focus was accumulating wealth wherever he was stationed,
causing resentment among the common people and officials.
In the beginning of the Jǐnán era,
he was sent out as Cìshǐ of Cāngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as the Prince (Wáng) of Fūchéng Commandery.
Because he accumulated wealth while in the province,
he was dismissed from office,
and stripped of his princely rank.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted his former official titles,
and his original enfeoffment was retroactively restored.
His son Mòyán succeeded him.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn).
Those who followed Gāozǔ out to Shāndōng as attendants (zhàngnèi)
included Qū Zhēn, Duàn Chēn, Dié Shělè, Wèi Biāo, Qǐfú Guìhé, and his younger brother Lìnghé, and Wáng Kāngdé,
all of whom reached high office through military merit.
Qū Zhēn, courtesy name Shělè, was a man from Jiǔquán in Xīpíng.
He was robust, courageous, and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
As an attendant, he followed Gāozǔ to Jìnzhōu,
and participated in the uprising (qǐyì),
engaging in campaigns wherever he went.
At the end of the Wǔdìng era,
he was enfeoffed as the Count (Bó) of Fùpíng County.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was given the income supervisor position (gàn) for Líyáng Commandery,
and appointed Cìshǐ of Jìnzhōu.
In the beginning of the Wǔpíng era,
he was promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Travelling Imperial Secretariat (Xíngtái) for the Yùzhōu Circuit, and Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Duàn Chēn, courtesy name Huáibǎo,
was a man from Dài.
From a young age, he showed military prowess.
He followed Gāozǔ in the uprising at Xìndū.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he was Cìshǐ of Guāngzhōu.
Dié Shělè,
during the Wǔchéng era, was granted the title of Grandee with Privilege of Establishing a Mansion (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
Cìshǐ of Yíngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as the Duke (Gōng) of Hànzhōng Commandery.
He died in battle in Guānzhōng.
Wèi Biāo,
was a man from Dài.
In the beginning of the Dàníng era,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince (Wáng) of Hǎichāng.
His son Xiāngguì succeeded him.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púshè) for the Jìnzhōu Circuit Travelling Imperial Secretariat (Xíngtái) and Cìshǐ of Jìnzhōu.
His Assistant Director of the Travelling Imperial Secretariat (Xíngtái Zuǒchéng), Hóu Zǐqīn, and others secretly petitioned Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu to request an army,
with Zǐqīn and the others acting as internal contacts.
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu personally led his troops to the base of the city wall.
Zǐqīn and the others opened the city gates at night to let the army in,
chained Xiāngguì and sent him to Cháng'ān.
He soon died.
His younger brother Xiāngyuàn
was strong, capable, and courageous.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was General-in-Chief of the Palace Guard (Lǐng Jūn Dà Jiāngjūn).
From Píngyáng to Bīngzhōu,
and when he reached Yè,
he repeatedly planned to kill Gāo Ānàgōng,
depose the Last Ruler (Hòuzhǔ),
and install the Prince of Guǎngníng.
The matter ultimately failed to materialize.
When the Prince of Guǎngníng was taken out,
Xiāngyuàn drew his belt knife, struck a pillar, and sighed, saying:
"The great cause is lost!
What else is there to say?"
Guìhé and his brother Lìnghé,
at the end of the Wǔpíng era,
were both granted the title Grandee with Privilege of Establishing a Mansion (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
Lìnghé
was General of the Palace Guard (Lǐng Jūn Jiāngjūn).
Before Bīngzhōu fell,

he defected successively to the Zhōu army, along with General-in-Chief of the Palace Guard (Lǐng Jūn Dà Jiāngjūn) Hán Jiànyè and General-in-Chief of the Martial Guard (Wǔ Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn) Fēng Fǔxiāng.
Lìnghé was granted the title Pillar of the State (Zhùguó),
and enfeoffed as the Duke (Gōng) of Xīhé Commandery.
In the beginning of the Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty,
he died while serving as Governor-General (Zǒngguǎn) of Qínzhōu.
The origins of both Jiànyè and Fǔxiāng
are unknown.
Jiànyè was granted the title Superior Pillar of the State (Shàng Zhùguó),
enfeoffed as the Duke (Gōng) of Xún State,
and died during the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty.
Fǔxiāng
was Superior Pillar of the State (Shàng Zhùguó),
and enfeoffed as a Commandery Duke (Jùngōng).
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu pacified Bīngzhōu,
he immediately made him Governor-General (Zǒngguǎn) of Shuòzhōu.
Kāngdé
was a man from Dài.
He successively served as Cìshǐ of several provinces and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) in Bīng Province,
and was enfeoffed as the Prince (Wáng) of Xīncài Commandery.
Hóumòchén Xiāng
was a man from Dài.
His grandfather Fútúi
was the paramount chieftain (lǐng mín qiúzhǎng) of the Wèi dynasty.
His father Húgǔtí
was Cìshǐ of Shuòzhōu and the Duke (Gōng) of Báishuǐ Commandery.
Soon he was appointed Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu,
and also Grand Travelling Imperial Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái),
commanding all military affairs of the Western Circuit.
Later he was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chē Qí Jiāngjūn),
and Cìshǐ of Xiǎnzhōu.
He returned to the capital and was appointed Minister Steward of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Qīng).
After a while,
he was sent out to serve as Cìshǐ of Fénzhōu.
Separately he was enfeoffed as the Baron (Nán) of Āncì County,
and also separately enfeoffed as the Duke (Gōng) of Shǐpíng County.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was appointed Grand Mentor (Tàishī),
transferred to Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōng),
and his title was advanced to Prince (Wáng) of Báishuǐ,
with 1,100 taxable households.
He was repeatedly granted the position of Grand Preceptor (Tàifù),
advanced to receive income supervision (gàn) from Jiànzhōu,
and separately enfeoffed as the Duke (Gōng) of Yìníng Commandery.
In the fourth month of the second year of Wǔpíng,
he died in the province,
aged eighty-three.

He was posthumously granted the titles of Acting Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Ten Provinces—Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Cāng, Jì, Zhào, Yōu, Bīng, and Shuò (Dū Jì Dìng Yíng Cāng Jì Zhào Yōu Bīng Shuò Shí Zhōu Jūnshì), Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng), Grand Minister (Tàizǎi), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Gōng), and Cìshǐ of Shuòzhōu.
He had two sons.
The eldest son, Guìlè,
married a princess,
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
The second son, Jìn'guì,
was General of the Martial Guard (Wǔ Wèi Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
During the Lónghuà era,
when Bīngzhōu fell,
Jìn'guì sent an envoy to surrender to Zhōu,
and was granted the title Superior Grand General (Shàng Dà Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed as the Duke (Gōng) of Xìn'ān County.
The Imperial Historian states: Gāozǔ lived for generations in Yún and Dài,
and was recognized for his heroic qualities.
Later, encountering Ěrzhū,
his military achievements gradually grew,
and his fellow villagers and old acquaintances
increasingly held him in high regard.
Hèbá Yǔn, due to the estrangement of his brothers,
found himself in a position of suspicion and distrust.
Initially, he was respected and protected due to his long-standing reputation,
but ultimately failed to achieve a peaceful end.
Compared with Ān Jǐn and Liàng of Wú and Shǔ,
one recognizes the depth or shallowness of their capacity and insight.
Liú Guì and Cài Jùn possessed foresight.
When the foundation of the hegemonic enterprise began,
their loyalty in assisting and supporting it was profound.
That they are celebrated in the ancestral temple
is surely not unwarranted!
When Hán Xián and the others heard of the righteous uprising,
they rushed competitively to join the military ranks.
Relying on the subsequent brilliance (of Gāozǔ),
they realized their ambitions and strength,
transforming into dukes and marquises (gōnghóu).
This was certainly appropriate.
The Eulogy says: In the home
of the Emperor's relatives,
such men appear throughout the ages. Spiritual potency descended upon Yún and Shuò,
producing worthy ministers.
The fields of achievement and fame,
look upon the ancients as neighbors.
Zhāng Qióng, Húlǜ Qiāngjǔ, Yáo Xióng, Sòng Xiǎn, Wáng Zé, Mùróng Shàozōng,
Xuē Xiūyì, Chìliè Píng, Bùdàhánsà, Mùróng Yǎn.
Zhāng Qióng,
courtesy name Liándé,
was a man from Dài.
When young, he was robust
and skilled in military matters.
During the Wèi dynasty, he served as a Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn,
and later as an Wàibīng Cānjūn in the Shuòzhōu Zhēnglǔ Fǔ.
He followed Gě Róng in rebellion.
When Gě Róng was defeated,
Ěrzhū Róng appointed him as Dūdū.
He rendered meritorious service in subjugating Yuán Hào,
and was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Jǐjùn.
In the early Jiànmíng period,
he served as the Eastern Circuit Wèiláo Dàshǐ (Grand Emissary of Consolation and Pacification),
and was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Xíngtáng County,
with an estate of three hundred households.
He was transferred to Taìwèi Zhǎngshǐ,
then went out to serve as the Grand Administrator of Hènéi,
and was appointed as the Regional Inspector of Jìzhōu.
When Ěrzhū Zhào was defeated,
he submitted to Gāozǔ (Gāo Huān),
and was promoted to Regional Inspector of Fénzhōu.
During the Tiānpíng period,
Gāozǔ attacked and captured Xiàzhōu,
appointing him as Wèiláo Dàshǐ,
and subsequently leaving him to garrison it.
He was soon captured by Zhōu Wéndì (Yǔwén Tà),
and died.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shǐchíjié Yān Yún Shuò Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Dà Jiāngjūn, Sītú Gōng, and Zhōu Cìshǐ.
He had two sons.
The elder was Xīn,
the younger was Zūnyè.
Xīn,
during the Pǔtaì period, served as Dūdū,
and followed Ěrzhū Shìlóng.
For his merit, he married the Wèi Princess Píngyáng,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi, Dà Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Regional Inspector of Jiànzhōu, and Earl of Nánzhèng County.
Zhāng Qióng often worried about his excessive success,
and frequently said to his close acquaintances:
“For all men in official positions and ranks,
it is best to remain in the middle.
Xīn's rank and position are too high;
I am deeply concerned about this.”
Xīn, however, was arrogant, reckless, and unrestrained,
and consequently his relationship with the princess became discordant.
He was soon killed by Wǔdì (Yuán Xiū).
People at the time praised Zhāng Qióng’s foresight.
Zūnyè,
rendered meritorious service in subjugating Yuán Hào,
and was enfeoffed as the Founding Son of Gù'ān County.
He was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Grand Director of Yúnzhōu.
During the Tiānpíng period,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Qīnghé,
and soon after was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn and Regional Inspector of Jiànzhōu.
During the Wǔdìng period,
he followed Yítóng Liú Fēng in subjugating Hóu Jǐng,
but was captured by Hóu Jǐng.
When Hóu Jǐng was defeated,
Zūnyè was killed at Wōyáng.
When his remains returned,
Shìzōng (Gāo Chéng) personally attended the mourning ceremony.
He was posthumously granted the titles Bīng Sì Yōu Ān Sìzhōu Jūnjì, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Regional Inspector of Bīngzhōu.
Húlǜ Qiāngjǔ,
was a man from Tà'ān.
His family served as tribal chiefs for generations.
His father, Jǐn,
was Wèi Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn and Wǔchuān Zhènjiāng.
Qiāngjǔ was brave and fierce when young,
possessing courage and strength.
During the Yǒng'ān period,
he followed Ěrzhū Zhào into Luò,
and achieved military merit.
He was highly favored and appreciated by Ěrzhū Zhào,
and followed him on campaigns.
When Gāozǔ defeated Ěrzhū Zhào,
he finally submitted his loyalty.
Gāozǔ, because of his loyalty to his previous master,
also praised and admired him.
During the Tiānpíng period,
he was appointed Grand Dūdū,
and was ordered to lead three thousand infantry and cavalry to guide the combined forces in a western attack on Xiàzhōu,
which they captured.
Later, he followed Gāozǔ on a western campaign.
When the great army crossed the Yellow River,
the generals gathered to discuss the plan for advancement.
Qiāngjǔ said:
“The Black Badger (Yǔwén Tà) has gathered a wicked faction;
their strength and weakness are evident.
If they intend to hold fast,
they have no supplies or reinforcements to rely on.
Now, evaluating their situation,
they are already like cornered beasts.
If we do not engage them in battle,
but proceed directly toward Xiányáng,
Xiányáng is empty
and can be captured without a fight.
Once their foundation is pulled out,
they will have nowhere to turn,
and the Black Badger’s head will hang from the gate of our camp.”
The generals’ opinions varied,
and consequently, a battle was fought at Wèiqū,
where the main army suffered a defeat.
At the end of the Tiānpíng period,
Zhāng Jiǎn from Yǐngchuān gathered a multitude and rebelled,
making contact with Guān Yòu in the west.
Qiāngjǔ followed Dūdū Hóu Jǐng, Gāo Áng, and others in attacking and defeating them.
During the Yuánxiàng period,
he was appointed Regional Inspector of Qīngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Mì County.
In the beginning of the Xīnghé period,
Gāozǔ appointed him Zhōngjūn Dà Dūdū,
and he was soon transferred to Regional Inspector of Dōngxiàzhōu.
At the time, Gāozǔ wished to attract and pacify distant barbarians,
and ordered Qiāngjǔ to act as emissary to Āzhìluó,
to proclaim the imperial might and virtue.
His reports consistently met the Emperor’s satisfaction,
and he was greatly acknowledged and rewarded.
He died in the province
at the age of thirty-six.
Gāozǔ deeply mourned and regretted his loss.
He was posthumously granted the titles Bīng Èrzhōu Jūnjì and Zhōu Cìshǐ.
His son, Xiàoqīng,
was clever, quick-witted, and perceptive when young,
and possessed propriety and self-restraint.
He frequently held prominent positions.
At the end of the Wǔpíng period,
he was Shìzhōng, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
enfeoffed as the Prince of Yìníng,
and managed the affairs of the Nèishěng (Inner Province),
overseeing military secrets concerning the Wàibīng and Qíbīng (External and Cavalry Forces).
At this time,
the court administration grew increasingly chaotic,
with governance resting in the hands of various eunuchs and petty officials.
Since the death of Zhào Yànshēn,
among the nobility who held court secrets,
only Xiàoqīng maintained a degree of refined conduct,
avoiding greed and corruption.
When the Later Emperor reached Qízhōu,
he made Xiàoqīng Shàngshū Lìng.
He also made Xuē Dàohéng, Zhongshū Shìláng, Shìzhōng,
and enfeoffed him as the Prince of Běihǎi.
The two men advised the Later Emperor to issue the Chéngguāng Zhǔ Zhào,
ceding the throne to the Prince of Rènchéng,
and ordered Xiàoqīng to carry the imperial decree, the edict, and the Heirloom Seal of the Realm to Yíngzhōu.
Xiàoqīng immediately proceeded to Yèchéng,
and submitted to Zhōu Wǔdì (Yǔwén Yǒng).
He then followed him into Cháng'ān,
and was granted the position Nàyán Shàngshì.
During the Kāihuáng period of the Suí dynasty,
he held the position of Tàifǔ Qīng,
and died while serving as Mínbù Shàngshū.
Liú Shìqīng, a man from Dài,
whose grandfather Báo
was Wèi Regional Inspector of Yānzhōu;
his father, Wēi,
was Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Shìqīng,
at the end of the Wǔpíng period,
was Shìzhōng and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His appointment and treatment were equal to Xiàoqīng’s.
His disposition was very orderly,
and he was more meticulous, cautious, and reserved
than Xiàoqīng.
He was able to understand the languages of the Four Barbarians,
and was considered the foremost expert of his time.
The Later Emperor ordered Shìqīng to translate the Nirvana Sūtra into the Turkic language
to present to the Turkic Khagan,
and commanded Zhōngshū Shìláng Lǐ Délín to write a preface for it.
Shìqīng,
during the Kāihuáng period of the Suí dynasty,
died while serving as Kāifǔ and Qīnwèi Piàoqí Jiāngjūn.
Yáo Xióng,
courtesy name Xiūwǔ,
was a man from Zhǎngzǐ in Shàngdǎng.
His grandfather, Xuān,
was Wèi Sīnóng Qīng.
His father, Róng,
was Yuánwài Shìláng.
Yáo Xióng was brave and fierce when young,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
valued character over wealth,
and was respected by his peers.
During the Yǒng'ān period,
he was appointed Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn, Jǐshì Zhōng, and Shǐchíjié Wèiláo Yān Shuò Sānzhōu Dàshǐ.
He was subsequently appointed Dūdū,
and followed Chìliè Yán to subdue Liú Língzhù.
After pacifying him,
he was appointed Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn and Regional Inspector of Yānzhōu,
enfeoffed as the Earl of Chéngpíng County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
When the banner of righteousness was first raised,
Xióng followed Ěr Zhū Zhào and was defeated at Guǎng'ā.
He subsequently led his subordinates to occupy Dìngzhōu and submitted to Gāo Zǔ.
At that time, Xióng's cousin, Jié,
was employed by Ěr Zhū Zhào as the Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Cāngzhōu).
When he reached Yíngzhōu,
knowing that Zhào was defeated,
he also sent an envoy to surrender.
Gāo Zǔ, seeing that both brothers possessed sincerity
allowed Jié to provisionally manage the affairs of Yíngzhōu.
Soon after, Xióng was made Chējì Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of Cavalry) and Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ, replacing Jié.
He was promoted in rank to Gōng (Duke),
and his stipend was increased by five hundred households.
At that time, legal restrictions were lax,
and officials generally engaged in accumulation and extortion.
Only Xióng took what was righteous before accepting anything;
furthermore, he treated his subordinates with generous kindness.
He was greatly cherished and supported by the officials and the populace.
When Wèi Wǔdì (Emperor Wǔ of Wèi) entered the pass,
Xióng served as Dà Dūdū (Grand Area Commander).
He followed Gāo Áng and defeated Hèbá Shèng at Rángchéng.
He participated in various campaigns to conquer Sān Jīng (the three Jīng regions).
He was subsequently appointed Dūdū (Area Commander) of the four prefectures: Èr Yù (the two Yù), Yáng, and Yǐng,
and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Yùzhōu).
Yuán Hóngwēi occupied Yǐngzhōu and rebelled.
The commoner Zhào Jìzōng killed Shào Zhāo, the Tàishǒu (Administrator) of Yǐngchuān,
occupied Yuèkǒu,
proclaimed himself Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and aligned with Hóngwēi in the north.
Xióng led his troops to attack him,
and Jìzōng was defeated and fled.
When the commoners learned that Xióng had left,
they subsequently nominated Wáng Cháng, a native of the city, as Cìshǐ,
occupied the prefecture, and invited Xī Wèi (Western Wèi).
Xióng again joined Xíngtái (Mobile Department Director) Hóu Jǐng in attacking and pacifying them.
The Liáng generals Lǐ Hóngzhī and Wáng Dāngbó unexpectedly attacked and captured Píngxiāngchéng (Píngxiāng City),
and harassed the prefectural borders.
Xióng set up an ambush and intercepted them,
capturing Hóngzhī and Dāngbó alive,
and taking many prisoners.
Chén Qìngzhī, the Sízhōu Cìshǐ of Liáng, again led troops to pressure the prefectural seat.
Xióng went out and engaged him in battle.
Wherever he advanced, the enemy scattered.
Although he sustained two wounds himself,
his heroic spirit grew stronger.
Qìngzhī was defeated,
abandoned his baggage train, and fled.
Later, Qìngzhī again besieged Nán Jīngzhōu.
Xióng said:
"Báigǒuduī,
is an important northern garrison for Liáng.
Taking advantage of its emptiness,
if we attack it, we will surely conquer it.
If they hear of the difficulty there,
the siege of Jīng will naturally lift.
This is what is meant by 'the opportune moment must not be lost.'"
He subsequently led his troops to attack it.
Qìngzhī indeed abandoned Jīngzhōu and came.
Before he arrived,
Xióng had already captured the city,
and captured Gǒu Yuánguǎng, the Liáng Garrison General,
and two thousand soldiers.
Liáng made Yuán Qìnghé the Wèi Wáng (Prince of Wèi),
and he harassed the southern borders.
Xióng led his troops to attack him,
and severely defeated Qìnghé at Nándùn.
Soon after, he joined Xíngtái Hóu Jǐng in defeating Liáng at Chǔchéng.
The people of Yùzhōu submitted a memorial,
again requesting Xióng to be their Cìshǐ,
and he was reinstated to provisionally manage the affairs of Yùzhōu.
Hèruò Huī, the Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk) of Yǐngzhōu, seized Tián Xùn, the Cìshǐ, occupied the prefecture, and surrendered to Xī Wèi.
An imperial edict ordered Xióng, along with Zhào Yù, the Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ, and Shì Yúnbǎo, the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, to each command the soldiers and horses of their respective prefectures,
to join Xíngtái Rèn Yánjìng and combine forces to attack them.
Xī Wèi sent its general Yí Fēng to lead troops in support of them.
Yánjìng and the others were defeated in battle.
Yù
and Bǎo each returned to their original prefectures,
occupied their cities, and surrendered to the enemy.
Xióng gathered the scattered soldiers
and held Dàliáng.
Zhōu Wéndì (Emperor Wén of Zhōu), capitalizing on Yánjìng's defeat,
sent his Right Vice Director Wéi Xiàokuān and others to attack Yùzhōu.
Xióng's Dūdū Guō Chéngbó and Chéng Duōbǎo, among others, offered up Yùzhōu and surrendered to the enemy,
seizing Fèng Yōng, the Cìshǐ, along with his family and the wives and children of his subordinates, totaling several thousand individuals.
They intended to send them to Cháng'ān.
When they reached Yuèkǒu,
Wáng Qié, Xióng's Wàibīng Cānjūn (Adjutant for External Military Affairs), and Hèlián Jùn, a Dūdū, along with several dozen cavalrymen from Dàliáng, intercepted them.
They executed Duōbǎo,
and rescued Xióng's and others' family members, returning them to Dàliáng.
Xī Wèi appointed Chéngbó as the Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
Xióng subsequently joined Xíngtái Hóu Jǐng in attacking him.
Xióng separately attacked and captured Yuèkǒu,
and captured Chéngbó.
He advanced to attack Xuánhù,
and chased away Zhào Jìzōng, Wéi Xiàokuān, and others, the Cìshǐs of Xī Wèi.
Xióng was again reinstated to provisionally manage the affairs of Yùzhōu.
Xī Wèi appointed Shì Yúnbǎo as the Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
who occupied Xiàngchéng;
Hán Xiǎn, the Yìzhōu Cìshǐ, occupied Nándùn.
Xióng again led his troops to attack them,
capturing both cities in a single day.
He captured Xiǎn and his Zhǎngshǐ, Qiū Yuè.
Bǎo fled,
and Xióng captured his wives, concubines, generals, and officials, totaling two thousand people.
All were escorted and sent to the capital.
He was granted the title Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of Cavalry).
He subsequently followed Hóu Jǐng to pacify Lǔyáng,
and was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Although Xióng was a military general,
his nature was generous and benevolent.
In governing the people, he was quite sincere and trustworthy.
His administration removed excessive complexity,
addressing only the major policies.
He cared for and nurtured the soldiers and the populace,
and utilized their strength effectively.
Having been on the border for ten years,
he repeatedly achieved merit.
The people of Yù still cherish him to this day.
Furthermore, he valued people and things,
and gave generously.
When guests visited,
his gifts and formalities were exceedingly lavish.
He was also praised for this.
In the third year of Xīnghé,
he was summoned back to the capital.
Soon after, he was placed in command of one hundred thousand soldiers and officers from the ten prefectures of Sī, Jì, Yíng, Dìng, Qí, Qīng, Jiāo, Yǎn, Yīn, and Cāng.
He toured the southwest,
and distributed them to guard strategic points.
In the fourth year,
he died at Yè,
at the age of forty-four.

He was posthumously granted Shǐ Chíjié (Bearer of the Credentials), Dūdū Jūnshì (Area Commander of Military Affairs) of the three prefectures of Qīng, Xú, and Jiāo, Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General), Sītú Gōng (Minister of Works Duke), and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
His posthumous name was Wǔgōng.
His son, Shī, succeeded him.
Xióng's younger brother, Fèn,
courtesy name Yànjǔ.
He began his career as Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe) and Jǐshìzhōng (Attendant Official).
He was transferred to Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn (General of the Steadfast Center) and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Radiance with Gold and Purple).
He was granted the rank of Ānyí Xiàn Zǐ (Viscount of Ānyí County).
He followed Gāo Zǔ to pacify Yè,
and defeat Ěr Zhū Zhào and others.
He was promoted in rank to Bó (Earl).
He was sent out as Nánfénzhōu Cìshǐ.
The Hu and Yí feared and respected him.
Xuē Chónglǐ, Xī Wèi's Xíngtái, led his forces to attack Fèn.
Fèn engaged them in battle
and severely defeated them.
Chónglǐ and his brother begged for surrender,
and were delivered to the Chancellor's residence (Xiàngfǔ).
Fèn was transferred to Piàojì Jiāngjūn (General of Cavalry), Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Radiance of the Left), and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and then died.
He was posthumously granted Zhū Jūnshì (Commander of Military Affairs) of the three prefectures of Yǎn, Yù, and Liáng, Sīkōng (Minister of Works), and Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xióng's cousin, Jié,
courtesy name Shòu.
His nature was frivolous and careless,
and he was fond of drinking,
but he possessed considerable military capability.
He successively held Jǐshìzhōng and Yǔlín Jiān (Supervisor of the Feathered Forest Guard).
He followed Gāo Zǔ and achieved merit in defeating Gědòulíng Bùfān.
He was appointed Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the East),
and enfeoffed as the Luòchéng Xiàn Bó (Earl of Luòchéng County),
with one hundred households.
He was sent out as Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When the righteous army rose,
he submitted to Gāo Zǔ.
He followed in the pacification of Yè and the defeat of Ěr Zhū Zhào.
He was promoted in rank to Hóu (Marquis).
Later, he became Dūdū,
leading troops to follow Fán Zǐhú in attacking Yuán Shù at Qiáochéng.
They pacified him.
He was subsequently appointed Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
He often engaged in taking and accepting (ill-gotten gains).
However, his nature was resolute and decisive,
and the officials and people feared him.
Soon after, he was granted the provisional management of Yǎnzhōu affairs.
At the beginning of Yuánxiàng,
he was appointed Chējì Dàjiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī (Treated the Same as the Three Dukes),
and promoted in rank to Gōng (Duke).
He was sent out as the Dà Dūdū of Móchéng Zhèn (Móchéng Garrison).
He was transferred to Ānzhōu Cìshǐ,
and died in office.
He was posthumously granted Shǐ Chíjié, Zhū Jūnshì (Commander of Military Affairs) of the two prefectures of Cāng and Yíng, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè (Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His posthumous name was (Missing).
Sòng Xiǎn,
courtesy name Zhònghuá,
was a man from Xiàogǔ, Dùnhuáng.
His nature was resolute and courageous,
and he was capable and useful.
He initially served Ěrzhū Róng as an Army Commander (Jūnzhu),
and was promoted to Aide-de-camp (Cānjūn) of the Changliu.
During the Yǒng'ān reign (528–530),
he was appointed General of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xiāngyuán,
then transferred to Aide-de-camp and Secretary (Jìshì Cānjūn) in Róng's establishment.
He followed Ěrzhū Róng in suppressing Yuán Hào,
and was given the title General Who Pacifies the East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn).
When Róng died,
Shìlóng and others advanced toward Luò,
and Xiǎn was again made Grand Administrator of Xiāngyuán.
At the beginning of Pǔtài (531),
he was promoted to Imperial Commissioner (Shǐ Chíjíe), General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jìnzhōu.
Later, he submitted to Gāozǔ,
who made him Assistant Director of the Right of the Moving Chancellery (Xíngtái Yòuchéng).
When Fán Zǐhú occupied Yǎnzhōu and rebelled,
the former Governor of Xī Yǎnzhōu, Yǐ Yuàn, and the Grand Administrator of Qiáojùn, Xīn Jǐngwēi, garrisoned and occupied Wǔliáng,
in response to Zǐhú.
Gāozǔ ordered Xiǎn to administer the affairs of Xī Yǎnzhōu,
and he led his troops to attack and defeat them,
beheading Yuàn,
while Jǐngwēi fled.
He was appointed Governor of Xī Yǎnzhōu.
At that time, the Governor of Liángzhōu, Lù Yǒngjí, occupied the province and rebelled externally,
and Xī Wèi (Western Wèi) sent the Prince of Bólíng, Yuán Yuē, and the Prince of Zhàojùn, Yuán Jǐngshén, leading troops to receive him.
Xiǎn assembled the officers and horses of the province and ambushed and defeated them,
beheading Yuē and the others,
and subsequently met up with the General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn), Húlǜ Píng, at Dàliáng.
He was appointed Companion, of the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóu Sānsī).
While serving as governor, he accepted many bribes and goods,
yet he was courageous, resolute, and spiritedly capable.
He maintained control over his subordinates;
all were able to exert their utmost effort for him.
During the Battle of Héyīn,
he plunged deep into the enemy lines,
and consequently perished in the battle array.
He was posthumously granted the title Duke of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōng).
Xiǎn's cousin, Huì (Sòng Huì),
was diligent in study in his youth,
read widely,
and loved to write.
During the Wèi period,
Zhāng Miǎn's *Jìn Shū* had not yet entered the country.
Huì, relying on and following the style of Péi Sōngzhī’s commentary on the *Guó Zhì*,
annotated the works of Wáng Yǐn and the *Zhōngxīng Shū*.
He also compiled ten volumes of the *Zhōngcháo Duōshì Zhuàn* (Biographies of Many Scholars of the Central Court),
and fifty fascicles of the *Xìngxì Pǔlù* (Genealogical Records).
Because the chronological records of various houses differed
and contained many errors,
he set out to examine and correct the discrepancies
and compile a *Niánpǔ Lù* (Record of Chronologies),
but it was incomplete.
In the fifth year of Héqīng (566), all these works were lost due to flooding.
Although Huì was broadly knowledgeable and possessed a strong memory,
his nature was vague and distractible,
and later in life he suffered from a wind ailment,
making his speech slow and hesitant.
When he lost the books he had compiled,
he pounded his chest and wailed, saying:
"It can truly be said that Heaven has destroyed me!"
He died during the Tiāntǒng period (565–569).
Wáng Zé,
courtesy name Yuán Guǐ,
claimed to be a man from Tàiyuán.
He was brave and valiant in his youth,
and skilled in martial arts.
He initially followed his uncle, Lǎoshēng, the Internal Historian (Nèishǐ) of Guǎngpíng in Wèi, on campaigns,
and always achieved military merit.
Lǎoshēng became known to the court,
and Zé played a considerable part in this.
He was first appointed Attendant in the Palace (Jǐshì Zhōng) for his military achievements,
and bestowed the title Viscount (Zǐ) of Báishuǐ.
Later, he followed Yuán Tiānmù to campaign against Xíng Gǎo,
and, riding lightly equipped, plunged deep into the enemy lines,
He was captured by Gǎo.
When Yuán Hào entered Luò,
Zé and Lǎoshēng both surrendered to Hào;
Hào, however, suspected Lǎoshēng,
and subsequently killed him.
Zé fled to the Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Zhèng Xiānhù,
and together they resisted Hào.
After Hào was defeated,
Zé was promoted to General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and went out to serve as Garrison Commander (Fángchéng Dūdū) of Dōng Xúzhōu.
When Ěrzhū Róng died,
the Governor of Dōng Xúzhōu, Húsī Chūn, was one of Róng's faction,
and harbored internal anxiety and fear.
At that time, the state of Liáng installed Yuán Yuè, the Prince of Rǔnán of Wèi, as the Lord of Wèi,
provided him with troops and horses,
and sent him to the border.
Chūn subsequently overturned the city and surrendered to Yuè.
Zé and the Grand Administrator of Lánlíng, Lǐ Yì, attacked Yuè's detached force
and defeated it.
Wèi (Northern Wèi) subsequently ordered Zé to administer the affairs of Běi Xúzhōu.
Later, he was subordinated to Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn.
When Zhòngyuǎn was defeated,
he finally submitted to Gāozǔ.
He was then further appointed General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn) and Grand Master of the Palace with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
He first followed the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Hèbá Shèng,
and later followed the Moving Chancellery, Hóu Jǐng,
engaging in campaigns and expeditions
and repeatedly achieving merit.
At the beginning of Tiānpíng (534),
he took charge of the affairs of Jīngzhōu,
served as Area Commander (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the six provinces (Sānjīng, Èrxiāng, and Nányōng),
and was the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Zé possessed great authority and martial presence,
and the border people feared and respected him.
During the Campaign of Wèiqǔ (Battle of Xiǎoguān),
Zé was surrounded and pressured by the Western forces,
and consequently abandoned the city and fled to Liáng.
Liáng soon sent him back,
and Gāozǔ forgave him and did not punish him.
At the beginning of Yuánxiàng (538),
he was appointed Governor of Luòzhōu.
Zé was greedy by nature;
while in the province, his acceptance of bribes was illegal.
He took the statues from the old capital
and melted them down to cast coins.
At that time, these were commonly called 'Héyáng coins',
and they all originated from his household.
During the Wǔdìng period (543–550),
he again followed Hóu Jǐng in campaigning to the west.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled at Yǐngchuān,
Zé was stationed at Bǎiyá Shù.
Shìzōng (Emperor Xiǎojìng) valued Zé's military prowess
and summoned him to be the Governor of Xúzhōu.
After Hóu Jǐng fled south to Liáng,
Liáng dispatched Xiāo Míng, the Marquis of Zhēnyáng, leading a large army toward Xúzhōu,
to act as a strategic support.
They dammed the Qīngshuǐ River to flood the provincial city.
Zé held fast to the defense for a prolonged period,
but his acceptance of bribes became scandalous.
He was chained and sent to Jìnyáng,
but Shìzōng pardoned his crime.
In the spring of the seventh year of Wǔdìng (549),
he died,
at the age of forty-eight.
He was posthumously granted Area Commander of Qīng and Qí Provinces, Minister of Works (Sīkōng), and Governor of Qīngzhōu.
His posthumous title was Lièyì.
Zé's younger brother, Jìngbǎo (Wáng Jìngbǎo),
held prominent positions in his youth.
Later, he became Governor of Dōng Guǎngzhōu,
and participated with Xiāo Guǐ and others in attacking Jiànyè.
They failed,
and perished there.
Mùróng Shàozōng
was a descendant of Mùróng Huǎng's fourth son, Kè (Mùróng Kè), the Prince of Tàiyuán.
His great-grandfather, Téng,
submitted to Wèi,
and subsequently settled in Dài.
His grandfather, Dū,
was the Governor of Qízhōu.
His father, Yuǎn,
was a Provincial Governor.
Shàozōng had a magnanimous and resolute appearance,
spoke little,
was profound, reserved, and had strategic bravery.
Ěrzhū Róng was his maternal cousin.
When the northern frontier was thrown into turmoil,
Shàozōng led his household to Jìnyáng to submit to Róng,
and Róng treated him with great respect.
When Róng proclaimed his army and entered Luò,
he privately informed Shàozōng, saying:
"The officials and gentry in Luò are numerous and flourishing,
and arrogance and extravagance have become the custom.
If they are not purged,
I fear they will be difficult to control.
I intend to seize the opportunity when the multitude of officials comes out to greet me
and execute them all.
Do you think this is acceptable?"
Shàozōng replied:
"The Empress Dowager usurped the court,
was lustful, tyrannical, and without the Way.
The people of the realm were resentful
and wished to abandon her.
Now, you yourself command the divine troops
and hold faithfulness and righteousness in your heart.
To suddenly plan to annihilate the multitude of gentry
is, I believe, not a sound long-term strategy,
and I sincerely urge you to reflect upon it."
Róng did not heed him.
Later, for his military achievements, Shàozōng was enfeoffed as Viscount (Zǐ) of Suǒlú County,
and shortly thereafter his rank was advanced to Marquis (Hóu).
He followed Gāozǔ in defeating Yáng Kǎn,
and further assisted Yuán Tiānmù in suppressing Xíng Gǎo.
He was repeatedly promoted, reaching the position of Governor of Bìngzhōu.
besieged Jìnyáng.
Ěrzhū Zhào attacked him,
and was repeatedly defeated by Bùfān.
(Zhào) wished to summon Gāozǔ with Jìnzhōu
to jointly plan against Bùfān.
Shàozōng remonstrated, saying:
"Currently, the world is in chaos;
people harbor ambitions and covetousness.
This is precisely the time for wise scholars to employ strategies.
Gāo Jìnzhōu (Gāo of Jìnzhōu) is immensely talented and fiercely spirited,
his heroic strategy surpasses the age.
If likened to a *jiāolóng* (flood dragon),
how can you lend him the clouds and rain (power)?"
Zhào was angry and said:
"I treat Jìnzhōu (Gāo) with utmost sincerity;
why do you suddenly suspect and obstruct him,
arbitrarily uttering these words!"
He immediately confined Shàozōng,
releasing him only after several days.
Thereupon, he assigned the Xianbei (troops) to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ jointly attacked Bùfān,
and destroyed him.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness in Xìndū,
Zhào appointed Shàozōng as Chief Clerk (*Zhǎngshǐ*),
and further ordered him to serve as Temporary Inspector (*Xíngtái*).
He led troops to Húguān
to resist Gāozǔ.
After the defeats at Guǎng'ā and Hánlíng,
Zhào then beat his chest and blamed himself,
saying to Shàozōng:
"Had I followed your words earlier,
how could things have come to this now?"
When Zhào was defeated at Hánlíng,
most of the soldiers fled.
Zhào was afraid
and intended to secretly abscond.
Shàozōng raised the banners and sounded the horns,
gathering the loyal followers.
Once the military morale was restored,
he and Zhào slowly mounted their horses.
Later, Gāozǔ proceeded from Yè to attack Zhào at Jìnyáng.
Zhào was distressed and cornered;
he fled to Chìhóng Lǐng
and hanged himself to death.
Shàozōng marched until he reached Wūtū Chéng.
Seeing Gāozǔ arriving in pursuit,
he took his wife and children, along with Zhào's remaining troops, and surrendered.
Gāozǔ still showed him favor and courtesy;
all his official posts and titles remained as before.
In military planning and strategy,
he often participated.
In the beginning of Tiānpíng (era),
the capital was moved to Yè.
As various governmental affairs were not yet complete,
Shàozōng was ordered, along with Gāo Lóngzhī, to oversee all matters concerning the governmental treasury, archives, and registers.
In the second year (of Tiānpíng),
the commoner Lǐ Yánsūn of Yíyáng gathered a crowd and rebelled.
Shàozōng was thus appointed Military Commander (*Jūnsī*) of the Southwestern Route,
leading commanders like Kùdí Ānshèng to attack and defeat the rebels.
When the army returned,
he acted as the Governor (*Cìshǐ*) of Yángzhōu,
and shortly thereafter acted as the Governor of Qīngzhōu.
Sūn Qiān, the Secretariat Recorder (*Jìshì*) of the Chancellor's Office, requested Shàozōng to appoint his elder brother as a Prefecture Clerk (*Zhǔbù*).
Shàozōng refused.
Qiān slandered him to Gāozǔ,
saying:
"Mùróng Shàozōng once ascended Guǎnggù Chéng and sighed deeply,
saying to his confidantes, 'Is there any reason for a great man to restore the former industry (dynasty)?'"
Because of this, he was recalled.
In the beginning of Yuánxiàng (era),
Dúgū Rúyuàn, a general of Western Wèi, occupied Luòzhōu.
Between Liáng and Yǐng (Prefectures),
robbers and bandits rose up sharply.
Gāozǔ ordered Shàozōng to lead troops to Wǔláo,
and together with the Temporary Inspector Liú Guì, they pacified the area.
He was promoted in peerage to Duke (*Gōng*),
and appointed Minister of the Revenue (*Dùzhī Shàngshū*).
Later, he served as Governor of Jìnzhōu and Grand Temporary Inspector (*Dà Xíngtái*) of the Western Route.
Upon returning to court,
he was transferred to Commissioner of the Palace Guard (*Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi*).
At that time, Liú Wūhēi of Liáng invaded Xúfāng (the Xú region).
Shàozōng was ordered to lead troops to attack and suppress him,
severely defeating him.
He was then appointed Governor of Xúzhōu.
Wūhēi gathered his scattered followers
and resumed raiding and plundering.
Shàozōng secretly lured Wūhēi’s followers,
and within a few months,
he captured Wūhēi and killed him.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Shàozōng was appointed Temporary Inspector of the Southeast Route,
given the title *Kāifǔ*,
and transferred his feudal title to Duke of Yànjùn.
He proceeded to Xiáqiū with Hán Guǐ and others,
planning to advance.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng dispatched his elder brother's son, Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng, and others, leading a host of 100,000,
to encamp at Hánshān,
forming a pincer movement with Hóu Jǐng,
damming the Sì Shuǐ (River) to flood Péngchéng.
An imperial edict then appointed Shàozōng as Temporary Inspector,
regulating the military affairs of the three Xú and two Yǎn Prefectures.
He went out to attack, accompanied by the Grand Commander Gāo Yuè and others,
severely defeating the enemy.
They captured Yuānmíng and his commanders,
taking many prisoners.
They then turned the army around to attack Hóu Jǐng at Wōyáng.
At that time, Jǐng's army was very numerous,
and all previous generals who went forth had been looked down upon by him.
But when he heard that Shàozōng and Yuè were about to arrive,
he showed deep fear,
saying to his subordinates:
"Yuè commands elite troops,
and Shàozōng is an experienced general.
We must be extremely cautious of them."
Thereupon, they engaged Jǐng in battle.
The various generals hesitated,
none willing to lead the charge.
Shàozōng waved his troops straight forward,
and the other generals followed him,
achieving a great victory.
Jǐng subsequently fled.
Upon returning the army,
he was separately enfeoffed as Viscount (*Zi*) of Yǒnglè County.
Initially, Gāozǔ, in his last command to Shìzōng, had said:
"If Hóu Jǐng rebels,
Mùróng Shàozōng should deal with him."
By this time,
he finally established merit and achievement.
Western Wèi dispatched its great general Wáng Sīzhèng to occupy Yǐngzhōu.
Shàozōng was again appointed Temporary Inspector of the Southern Route.
Along with the Grand Commandant Gāo Yuè and Administrator Liú Fēng, he led troops to surround and attack (Wáng Sīzhèng),
damming the Wěi Shuǐ (River) to flood the city.
At this time, Shàozōng frequently had ill omens in his dreams;
he was always troubled by them.
He secretly told his attendants:
"Since I turned twenty,
I have had a 'garlic hair' (a specific mark/hair).
Recently, this garlic hair suddenly disappeared.
Reasoning this out,
*suàn* (garlic) is a homophone for *suàn* (calculation/fate).
Is my fate about to run out?"
Not long after,
while inspecting the dam with Fēng,
they saw dust rising from the north.
They boarded a boat to sit together.
A fierce storm came from the northeast;
everything far and near grew dark.
The boat cable snapped,
and the boat drifted directly toward the enemy city.
Shàozōng judged that he could not escape,
and consequently threw himself into the water and died.
He was forty-nine years old at the time.
The officers and soldiers of the three armies were all grieved and mournful;
the court sighed in sorrow.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Envoy with Credentials (*Shǐ Chíjié*), Military Affairs Regulator of Qīng, Jǐ, Guāng, the two Qīng, and the two Yǎn Prefectures (seven prefectures in total),
Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Lìng*),
Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*),
and Governor of Qīngzhōu,
with the posthumous name Jǐnghuì.
His eldest son, Shìsù, was appointed Gentleman of the Household (*Sànqí Chángshì*).
He was shortly executed for plotting rebellion.
He was punished.
Due to Shàozōng's merits, the court decreed
that the crime should stop with Shìsù's person.
In the beginning of Huángjiàn (era),
he was inducted into Shìzōng’s ancestral temple court for worship.
Shìsù’s younger brother, Jiànzhōng,
inherited Shàozōng’s noble title.
Late in Wǔpíng (era),
he was Administrator, Equal in Rank to the Three Dukes (*Yítóu Sānsī*).
During the Kāihuáng (era) of Suí,
he was Grand General and Governor-General (*Zǒngguǎn*) of Diézhōu.
Xuē Xiūyì,
courtesy name Gōngràng,
was a native of Fényīn in Hédōng.
His great-grandfather, Shào,
was Minister of the Seven Military Ministries (*Qībīng Shàngshū*) and Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Tàibǎo*) in Wèi.
His grandfather, Shòurén,
served as Administrator of the two Commanderies of Hédōng and Héběi, Governor of Qínzhōu, and Duke of Fényīn.
His father, Bǎojí,
was Administrator of Dìngyáng.
Xiū Yì was treacherous and gallant in his youth;
he valued righteousness over wealth,
and gathered heroic ruffians.
Whenever people faced pressing difficulties and fled to him,
he was generally able to hide and protect them.
When Wèi Xiányáng Wáng served as Sī Zhōu Mù,
he employed him as Fǎ Cáo Cóngshì.
When Wèi Běihǎi Wáng Hào garrisoned Xú Zhōu,
