he invited him to serve as Mò Cáo Cānjūn.
At the end of the Zhèngguāng era,
soldiers rose up across the land.
Hào became Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn,
Dū Dū of the military affairs of Huá, Bīn, and Dōng Qín,
concurrently Zuǒ Púyè and Xī Dào Xíngtái.
He appointed Xiū Yì as Tǒng Jūn.
At that time there was an imperial edict
stating that anyone who could recruit three thousand men would be appointed Biéjiàng.
Thereupon, Xiū Yì returned to Hédōng,
and proceeded through the various commanderies of Píngyáng and Hóngnóng,
assembling more than seven thousand men.
He was immediately granted the temporary titles Ān Běi Jiāngjūn and Xī Dào Biéjiàng.
Soon after, the Dōng Xī Èr Xià, Nán Běi Liǎng Huá, and Bīn Zhōu rebelled.
Hào advanced to suppress them.
Xiū Yì led his department
and achieved considerable merit.
When the Jiàng Shǔ bandits, led by Chén Shuāngchì, gathered at Fén Qǔ,
an edict appointed Xiū Yì as Dà Dū Dū
to jointly suppress them with Xíngtái Zhǎngsūn Zhì.
Because Xiū Yì knew Shuāngchì was his fellow townsman,
he lightly ventured to the foot of their encampment,
instructing them on the benefits and dangers.
Shuāngchì and his followers subsequently surrendered.
Xiū Yì was appointed Lóngmén Zhènjiàng.
Later, Xiū Yì’s kinsman Fèng Xián and others caused unrest,
besieging the garrison city.
Xiū Yì, also seeing the realm in chaos,
planned to act independently and arbitrarily.
Thus, he joined Fèng Xián, gathering a multitude to commit rebellion,
and proclaimed himself Huáng Yuè Dà Jiāngjūn.
An edict commanded Dū Dū Zōngzhèng Zhēnsūn to suppress them.
Before the army arrived,
Xiū Yì felt shame and regret,
and dispatched his subordinate Sūn Huáiyàn to present a memorial detailing his situation,
begging for a high-ranking general to come and reassure him.
Wèi Xiàomíng sent Xīběi Dào Dà Xíngtái Hú Yuánjí with an imperial decree to instruct and console him,
and Xiū Yì surrendered.
Fèng Xián and the others still occupied strategic positions and formed garrisons.
Zhǎngsūn Zhì’s army was stationed at Hóngnóng,
and Zhēnsūn’s army was at Língqiáo,
unable to advance.
Xiū Yì, along with his paternal cousin Shàn Lè and younger paternal cousin Jiā Zú, each led righteous volunteers, creating a posture of attack and capture.
He wrote a letter to Fèng Xián showing him the misfortunes and blessings.
Fèng Xián surrendered.
Fèng Xián was appointed Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn, granted Jiǎ Jié, Jìshān Zhènjiàng,
and the title Xiàyáng Xiàn Zǐ, with an assigned income of three hundred households.
Xiū Yì was enfeoffed as Fényīn Xiàn Hóu,
with an assigned income of eight hundred households.
Ěrzhū Róng considered Xiū Yì to be gallant, cunning, and fickle,
and had him registered and sent to Jìnyáng,
where he was detained and guarded along with Gāo Áng and others.
When Róng went to Luò,
he took Xiū Yì and the others with him
and placed them in the Tuóniú Shǔ.
When Róng died,
Wèi Xiàozhuāng appointed Xiū Yì as Dà Dū Dū of the four commanderies: Hóngnóng, Héběi, Hédōng, and Zhèngpíng.
At that time, Gāozǔ was Jìn Zhōu Cìshǐ.
He met Xiū Yì
and treated him extremely well.
When Ěrzhū Zhào installed Wèi Chángguǎng Wáng as the ruler,
Xiū Yì was appointed Yòu Jiāngjūn and Shǎn Zhōu Cìshǐ,
and granted the temporary title Ān Nán Jiāngjūn.
In the beginning of the reign of Wèi Qián Fèidì,
Xiū Yì was made Chí Jié, Hòu Jiāngjūn, and Nánfén Zhōu Cìshǐ.
When Gāozǔ raised the army of righteousness at Xìndū
and defeated the four Hú tribes at Hán Líng,
he sent for Xiū Yì.
Xiū Yì followed him to Jìnyáng,
where Gāozǔ appointed him to manage the affairs of Bīng Zhōu.
He then followed Gāozǔ in suppressing Ěrzhū Zhào.
When Wǔdì entered the Passes,
Gāozǔ went to receive him at Líntóng Guān,
and appointed Xiū Yì as Guān Yòu Xíngtái.
He crossed the Yellow River from Lóngmén.
Xuē Chónglǐ, the Xī Wèi Běihuá Zhōu Cìshǐ, was garrisoned at Yángshì Bì.
Xiū Yì used a letter to persuade him to surrender,
and Chónglǐ led more than ten thousand men to defect.
When Fán Zǐhú occupied Yǎn Zhōu,
Xiū Yì followed Dà Sīmǎ Lóu Zhāo to defeat and pacify him.
During the Tiānpíng era,
he was appointed Wèi Jiāngjūn and Nán Zhōngláng Jiàng,
concurrently serving as Jí Jùn Tàishǒu,
and Dū Dū of five commanderies: Dùnqiū, Huáiyáng, Dōngjùn, and Líyáng.
He was promoted to Dōngxú Zhōu.
In the beginning of the Yuánxiàng era,
he was appointed Yítóng.
During the Battle of Shā Yuàn,
he retreated with the various armies.
Upon his return,
Fēng Zǔyè, who was managing the affairs of Jìn Zhōu, abandoned the city and fled.
Xiū Yì pursued him as far as Hóngdòng
and persuaded Zǔyè to return and defend the area,
but Zǔyè did not comply.
Xiū Yì returned and occupied Jìn Zhōu,
pacifying the people and holding firm defense.
Zhǎngsūn Ziyàn, Yítóng of Xī Wèi, besieged and pressed the city gates.
Xiū Yì opened the gates and concealed armed men to wait for him.
Ziyàn could not determine the truth or falsehood of the situation,
and thus fled.
Gāozǔ praised this greatly.
He was then appointed Jìn Zhōu Cìshǐ and Xíngtái over the four prefectures of Nánfén, Dōngyōng, and Shǎn,
and rewarded with one thousand bolts of silk.
While Xiū Yì was in the prefecture,
he captured Duàn Róngxiǎn, the Zhèngpíng Tàishǒu appointed by Xī Wèi.
He induced the surrender of several thousand people from the tribes led by the Hú chieftain Hú Chuílí,
and memorialized to establish Wǔchéng Jùn in order to settle them peacefully.
When Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled,
Xiū Yì was appointed Xīnán Dào Xíngtái,
to serve as a supportive military presence,
but he did not proceed.
Soon thereafter, he was appointed Qí Zhōu Cìshǐ,
but was dismissed from his post due to his avarice.
In consideration of his previous meritorious service defending Jìn Zhōu,
his official rank and title were restored,
and he was subsequently appointed Wèi Wèi Qīng.
At that time, the Shān Hú invaded and caused chaos in Jìn Zhōu.
Xiū Yì was dispatched to pursue and suppress them,
and he defeated them.
His noble title was promoted to Zhèngpíng Jùn Gōng,
and he was granted Kāifǔ status.
Shìzōng, following Gāozǔ’s dying wish,
reduced his allotted households by two hundred,
and additionally enfeoffed Xiū Yì as Píngxiāng Nán.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was appointed Hù Jūn,
additionally enfeoffed as Lántián Xiàn Gōng,
and furthermore appointed Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
In the seventh month of the fifth year (of Tiānbǎo), he died,
aged seventy-seven.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Sīkōng, Jìn Zhōu Cìshǐ, and overseer of military affairs of Jìn and Tàihuà Sān Zhōu.
He was presented with three hundred bolts of funeral silk.
His son, Wénshū, succeeded him.
Xiū Yì’s younger paternal cousin, Jiā Zú,
was also heroic and forthright by nature.
He first served as Yuánwài Sànjí Shìláng,
and was gradually promoted to Zhèngpíng Tàishǒu.
When Gāozǔ was at Xìndū,
Jiā Zú heard this and rushed to join the righteous cause.
He followed Gāozǔ in pacifying the four Hú tribes at Hán Líng,
and was appointed Huá Zhōu Cìshǐ.
When Hèbá Yuè resisted the command,
Jiā Zú was ordered to station cavalry along the river
to resist the main army.
Jiā Zú subsequently abandoned his riding horse,
floated across the river,
and returned to Gāozǔ.
Because of this, he was appointed Yáng Zhōu Cìshǐ,
and died while in office.
His son was Zhèn,
courtesy name Wénxióng.
In the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
he received orders to garrison and defend Lóngmén,
but he was captured by Xī Wèi.
In the Yuánxiàng era,
he finally managed to escape and return.
Gāozǔ praised his utmost loyalty
and appointed him Guǎng Zhōu Cìshǐ.
Later, he followed Mùróng Shàozōng in suppressing Hóu Jǐng,
and due to his achievements, he was additionally enfeoffed as Fūshī Xiàn Nán.
In the fourth year of Tiānbǎo,
he followed in the campaign against the Shān Hú
and defeated the Rúrǔ.
He achieved merits in both campaigns,
and was repeatedly promoted to Qiáo Zhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiū Yì’s paternal cousin’s son, Yuán Yǐng,
whose father was Guāngchì,
served as Dōngyōng Zhōu Cìshǐ and Tàicháng Qīng.
Yuán Yǐng was upright, cautious, trustworthy, and principled.
He started his career as Yǒng'ān Wáng Cānjūn.
He managed the affairs of Xiùróng Xiàn
and gained a reputation for integrity.
He was repeatedly transferred and promoted to Dìng Zhōu Biéjià.
He was cited as upright, fair, diligent, and capable,
and was appointed Yúyáng Tàishǒu.
Chìliè Píng,
courtesy name Shāguǐ,
was a man of the western part of Dàijùn.
His family had been tribal chiefs for generations.
Píng had a fine appearance,
a handsome beard and whiskers,
and was skilled in archery from horseback.
He succeeded to the position of the First Chieftain Leading the People,
and the title of Earl of Línjiāng.
At the end of the Xiàochāng era,
when Bálíng rebelled,
and the remnants of the Rúrú invaded Mǎyì,
Píng served as Tǒngjūn (Overall Commander) subordinate.
Having military achievements,
he was appointed Biejàng (Deputy General).
Later, when the Mùzi caused trouble,
and Liú Húlún and Húlǜ Kěnàlǜ simultaneously instigated rebellion,
Píng was made Dūdū (Area Commander),
and suppressed and pacified Húlún and his associates.
At the beginning of Emperor Wèi Xiàozhuāng's reign,
he was appointed Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Martial Guard).
He followed Ěrzhū Róng in defeating Gě Róng
and pacifying Yuán Hào.
He was promoted to Zhōngjūn Dūdū (Commander of the Central Army) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard),
enfeoffed as the Earl of Yǐngtáo County,
with an income of seven hundred households.
When Róng died,
Píng fled north with Róng’s wife and Ěrzhū Shìlóng and others.
When the Prince of Chángguǎng, Yè, was enthroned,
Píng was awarded the title of Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and given the additional title of Grand Area Commander of the Capital Region (Jīngjī Dàdūdū).
As the Ěrzhū clan was arrogant and oppressive at that time,
Píng constantly feared disaster.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness,
Píng submitted sincerely.
He followed in the pacification of Yè,
and defeated the Sì Hú (Four Barbarians) at Hánlíng.
When Zhòngyuǎn fled,
Píng was made Dàxíngtái (Grand Mobile Secretariat) of Dōngjùn.
When the army returned,
he followed Gāozǔ in pacifying Ěrzhū Zhào.
He again followed Lǐngjūn Lóu Zhāo in attacking and pacifying Fán Zǐhú.
He was appointed Envoy Holding Credentials, Administrator of Huàzhōu.
When Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled,
Píng followed Gāozǔ in defeating Emperor Zhōu Wéndì at Mángshān.
At the beginning of the Wǔdìng era,
he was appointed Administrator of Kuòzhōu.
In the fifth year,
he was given the additional rank of Yítóu Sānsī (Worthy of the Three High Offices),
and garrisoned Héyáng.
In the eighth year,
his noble rank was advanced to Marquis.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was awarded the post of Administrator of Yǎnzhōu.
Shortly after, he was given the additional title of Kāifǔ (Establishment of a Mansion),
and separately enfeoffed as Viscount of Líntáo County.
In the third year,
he followed the generals south to attack the Jiānghuái region,
and captured Yángpíng Commandery.
When the Chén people besieged Guǎnglíng,
an imperial decree ordered Píng to command the various Hénán armies to assist.
The Chén people retreated,
and he subsequently returned.
In the summer of the fifth year,
he died while in his post in the province,
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted Military Governor of the three provinces of Yíng, Cāng, and Yōu, Administrator of Yíngzhōu, and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
His posthumous name was Zhuānghuì.
His son, Xiàozhōng, succeeded him.
His younger brother was Chángchā.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he held the titles Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Kāifǔ Yítóu Sānsī,
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīnníng.
During the Suí Kāihuáng era,
he was Shàng Zhùguó (Pillar of the State),
and died while serving as Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu.
Although he had no other specialized skills,
he was previously renowned in office for his purity and capability.
Bù Dàhán Sà
was a man of Tàiān Dínà.
His great-grandfather, Róng,
served the Wèi dynasty, successively holding the position of Grand Administrator of the two commanderies, Jīnmén and Huàzhèng.
His father, Jū,
was Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (General Resembling a Dragon) and Deputy General Leading the People.
At the end of the Zhèngguāng era,
when the Six Garrisons rebelled,
Sà led his family south to escape the danger,
fleeing to Ěrzhū Róng in Xiùróng.
Later, he followed Róng into Luòyáng,
and based on his military achievements, he was appointed Tǒngjūn (Overall Commander) within the staff of the Yángwǔ Army,
and was granted the noble rank of Viscount of Jiāngxià.
He followed in the pacification of Gě Róng.
Accumulating previous and subsequent merit,
he was given the additional title of Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the South).
After Róng died,
he followed Ěrzhū Zhào into Luòyáng,
and was appointed Grand Area Commander of the staff.
He followed Zhào in resisting battle at Hánlíng.
When Zhào was defeated,
Sà surrendered with his unit.
Gāozǔ appointed him the Third Chieftain Leading the People.
He was successively promoted to Fortress Commander of Qínzhōu, and Administrator of Běiyōngzhōu.
During the Tiānpíng era,
he was transferred to Area Commander of Dōng Shòuyáng and Sānquán.
During the Yuánxiàng era,
he served as acting Administrator of Yānzhōu,
and was successively promoted to Grand Area Commander Leading the People of Línchuān,
and granted the noble rank of Earl of Chángguǎng.
At that time, the Rúrú engaged in raiding and pillaging,
frequently causing border disturbances.
Gāozǔ sought to conciliate them
and sent Sà to carry out the mission.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Yítóu Sānsī.
He was sent out to serve as Grand Area Commander of Wǔchéng,
garrisoning Héyáng.
He was further given the additional titles of Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry) and Kāifǔ,
and promoted to Duke of Xíngtáng County.
Three hundred households were reduced from Bóhǎi to increase his enfeoffment.
He was subsequently awarded the position of Administrator of Jìnzhōu,
and separately enfeoffed as Baron of Ānlíng County,
with an income of two hundred households,
and given the additional title of Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of Agile Cavalry).
When Qí received the abdication,
his title was changed to Duke of Yìyáng Commandery.
Mùróng Yǎn,
courtesy name Shìdé,
was a man of Qīngdū Chéng'ān,
and a descendant of Mùróng Guī.
His father, Chìtóu,
was the Wèi Grand Administrator of Nándùn.
He was ten *zhàng* tall,
and his belt was nine *chǐ* long.
At the beginning of the Wǔpíng era,

he was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóu Sānsī, Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), Envoy Holding Credentials, Military Governor of the two provinces of Cāng, and Provincial Administrator.
Yǎn's appearance surpassed the ordinary,
and his dress and demeanor were imposing.
He did not like reading,
but he was somewhat versed in military strategy,
and skilled in archery from horseback.
During the Zhèngguāng era,
when the Wèi Prince of Héjiān, Yuán Chēn, led troops to relieve Shòuchūn,
Yǎn was recruited as Commander of the Left Flank.
For his military achievements, he was rewarded with fifty rolls of silk.
The army reached Xīxiáshí
and consequently lifted the siege of Guōyáng,
and pacified Cānglíng City and Jīngshān Garrison.
Liáng sent General Zhèng Sēng and others to intercept and fight.
Yǎn attacked them,
beheading their general Xiāo Qiáo,
and the Liáng forces fled.
He also raided and defeated the forces of Wáng Shénniàn and others,
capturing over two hundred men.
Shénniàn barely escaped with his life.
In the third year,
Liáng sent a general to attack Dōng Yùzhōu,
and Grand Area Commander Yuán Bǎozhǎng was sent to suppress them.
Yǎn served as a Deputy General.
He fought Zhèng Hǎizhēn,
beheading his army commander Zhū Sēngzhēn and the deputy commander Qín Tài.
He also attacked the bandit Wáng Gǒu at Yángxià
and pacified the region.
During the Xiàochāng era,
when Ěrzhū Róng entered Luòyáng,
Yǎn was appointed Area Commander of the Southern Sector of the Capital Region.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
Xī Jīngzhōu was besieged by the Liáng general Cáo Yìzōng.
Yǎn responded to the recruitment call and went to its aid.
At that time, the Grand Administrator of Běiyù, Sòng Dàijiàn, was plotting rebellion.
Yǎn took light cavalry and, catching him unexpectedly,
went straight to the foot of the city wall,
and called out:
"The main army has arrived!
Why does the Grand Administrator not come out to welcome us?"
Dàijiàn, flustered and terrified, did not know what to do,
so he came out to welcome him.
Yǎn immediately captured him,
and the commandery was thus secured.
He also defeated the Liáng generals Mǎ Yuándá, Cài Tiānqǐ, Liǔ Báijiā, and others,
accumulating achievements.
He was appointed Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Powerful Crossbows).
He fought against the Liáng generals Wáng Xuánzhēn, Dǒng Dāngmén, and others,
and defeated them all,
relieving the siege of Rángchéng,
and recapturing Nányáng and Xīnxiāng.
He was transferred to Jīshè Jiāngjūn (General of Massed Archers),
Envoy Holding Credentials, and Grand Area Commander Guarding the City of Yùzhōu.
Ěrzhū (爾朱) was defeated.
Yǔ (與) and Yùzhōu (豫州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Lǐ Ēn (李恩) returned to Gāozǔ (高祖).
For his merits, he was repeatedly promoted to Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍) and Gāoliáng Tàishǒu (高梁太守).
[二二] He was transferred to Wǔchéng Tàishǒu (五城太守) and Dōngyōngzhōu Cìshǐ (東雍州刺史).
At the defeat of Shāyuàn (沙苑),
the Western Wèi (西魏) Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Guō Luán (郭鸞) led his troops to attack Yǎn (儼).
He resisted the siege for over two hundred days,
fighting day and night with all his might,
and severely defeated Luán’s (鸞) army.
He pursued and decapitated over three hundred enemy soldiers,
and also captured the Western Wèi (西魏) Cìshǐ (刺史) Guō Tā (郭他).
At that time, many prefectures had defected or fallen,
but only Yǎn (儼) remained intact.
He was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍).
In the third year of Wǔdìng (武定) [545 CE],
he led an army to relieve the siege of Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
He frequently served as an envoy to Rúróu (茹茹).
He also participated in the attack on Yùbì (玉壁),
and was bestowed with seven hundred bolts of silk, along with clothing and hats.
In the fifth year [547 CE],
he garrisoned Héquiáo (河橋) and Wǔchéng (五城).
When Hóu Jǐng (侯景) rebelled,
Yǎn (儼) attacked the bandits of Chénjùn (陳郡),

capturing Qùdí Hélài (厙狄曷賴) from Jǐng’s (景) command, as well as the falsely appointed Tàishǒu (太守) Zhèng Dàohé (鄭道合), Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史) Wáng Yànxià (王彥夏), and Xíngtái (行臺) Dí Chàng (狄暢), among others.
He captured and killed over a hundred enemy soldiers.
When he returned to Xiàngchéng (項城),
he again captured Jǐng’s (景) falsely appointed Cìshǐ (刺史) Xīn Guāng (辛光) and Cài Zūn (蔡遵),
along with two thousand of their subordinates.
In the sixth year [548 CE],
he was appointed Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ (譙州刺史).
He frequently achieved military successes,
and many surrendered and submitted to him.
In the seventh year [549 CE],
he was again appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (膠州刺史).
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo (天保) [550 CE],
he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
In the sixth year [555 CE],
Liáng (梁) Sītú (司徒) Lù Fǎhé (陸法和) and Yítóng (儀同) Sòng Chǎi (宋茝), among others, led their subordinates and offered the city of Yǐngzhōu (郢州) in surrender.
[二三] At that time, Qīnghé Wáng Yuè (清河王岳) led his army along the river.
He then gathered all the generals and deliberated, saying:
“The city is outside the Jiāng (江),
and the people’s morale is still resistant.
We must have someone with both talent and strategy,
and outstanding loyalty and courage,
to be entrusted with this responsibility.”
All unanimously recommended Yǎn (儼).
Yuè (岳) agreed,
and so sent him to garrison Yǐngchéng (郢城).
As soon as he entered,
Hóu Tián (侯瑱) and Rèn Yuē (任約), Grand Commanders of Liáng (梁), immediately led their land and naval forces to the city gates.
Yǎn (儼) deployed defenses in every direction,
and Tián (瑱) and the others could not overcome him.
He also built an extensive pontoon bridge of reeds, several *lǐ* (里) long, upstream at Yīngwǔzhōu (鸚鵡洲),
to block the ship passage.
Communication was cut off,
and the city was isolated and suspended.
The morale of the multitude was fearful.
Yǎn (儼) guided them with loyalty and righteousness,
and also pleased them to calm them.
There was previously a shrine in the city,
popularly known as the Chénghuáng Shén (城隍神) (City God).
Both public and private individuals would pray there.
Therefore, in accordance with the wishes of his officers and soldiers,
he led them to pray,
hoping for divine assistance.
After a short while,
a strong wind suddenly arose,
and surging waves violently stirred,
breaking the reed pontoon bridge.
Yuē (約) again repaired it by linking iron chains,
making the defenses even tighter.
Yǎn (儼) again led the collective prayers,
and a storm arose in the night,
again breaking it apart.
This happened two or three times.
The people in the city were overjoyed,
believing it to be divine assistance.
Tián (瑱) moved his army to the north of the city,
built stockades and set up camps,
and burned down the residential areas outside the city,
destroying all property.
Yuē (約) led over ten thousand warriors,
each carrying siege equipment,
and set up camps and fortifications to the south of the city,
forming a combined force from north and south.
Yǎn (儼) then led his cavalry and infantry out of the city and fiercely attacked,
greatly defeating them,
and capturing over five hundred people.
Previously, Yǐngchéng (郢城) was low-lying,
and its earthen walls were loose and dilapidated.
Yǎn (儼) repaired the city walls and battlements,
and built many tall towers.
He also constructed ships and vessels,
equipping both land and water forces,
with no temporary shortage of workers.
Xiāo Xún (蕭循) also led fifty thousand troops,
and joined forces with Tián (瑱) and Yuē (約),
attacking at night.
Yǎn (儼) and his generals and soldiers fought fiercely all night.
By dawn,
Yuē (約) and the others retreated.
They pursued and decapitated Zhāng Báishí (張白石), a valiant general of Tián (瑱).
Tián (瑱) offered a thousand gold pieces to ransom it,
but Yǎn (儼) refused.
In the fifth month of summer,
Tián (瑱), Yuē (約), and others again combined their forces,
and attacked the city with all their troops.
Food in the city was scarce,
and grain transport was cut off.
There was no plan to remedy this,
and they only ate the leaves of huái (槐) and chǔ (楮) trees, mulberry leaves, jute roots, duckweed, kudzu, mugwort, and other grasses, as well as boots, leather belts, and horn pieces.
When someone died,
their flesh was immediately taken,
divided and eaten by fire,
leaving only the bones.
Yǎn (儼) still issued orders to his generals and soldiers,
ensuring rewards and punishments,
sharing sweet and bitter,
and dedicating their lives to it.
From the first month to the sixth month,
no one harbored dissenting thoughts.
Later, Xiāo Fāngzhì (蕭方智) was enthroned,
and sent an envoy to request peace.
Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖), considering that the city was located south of the Jiāng (江) and inconvenient to hold,
issued an imperial edict to return it.
Yǎn (儼) gazed at the Emperor,
and was overcome with sorrow.
The Emperor called him forward,
held his hand,
touched Yǎn’s (儼) beard and temples,
took off his hat to look at his hair,
and sighed for a long time.
He said to Yǎn (儼):
“Looking at your appearance,
I no longer recognize you.
From ancient times, has any loyal and valiant person
surpassed this!”
Yǎn (儼) replied:
“I relied on Your Majesty’s divine might
to express my foolish integrity,
not bending to the young upstarts,
and again beholding the sacred countenance.
Even if I die tonight,
I will have no regrets in death.”
The Emperor ceaselessly praised him.
He was appointed Zhàozhōu Cìshǐ (趙州刺史),
promoted from Bo (伯) to Gōng (公),
and bestowed with one thousand bolts of silk and one hundred thousand cash.
In the ninth year [558 CE],
he again achieved merit in suppressing bandits,
and was bestowed with one hundred bolts of silk and one hundred thousand cash.
In the tenth year [559 CE],
an imperial edict appointed him Yángzhōu Xíngtái (揚州行臺).
He and Wáng Guìxiǎn (王貴顯) and Hóu Zǐjiān (侯子監) led troops to escort Xiāo Zhuāng (蕭莊).
They built the two cities of Guōmò (郭默) and Ruòxié (若邪).
He fought against Chén (陳) Xīncài Tàishǒu (新蔡太守) Lǔ Xīdá (魯悉達) at Dàshédòng (大蛇洞),
defeating and routing him.
He also supervised Xiāo Zhuāng’s (蕭莊) and Wáng Lín’s (王琳) armies,
and fought against Chén (陳) generals Hóu Tián (侯瑱) and Hóu Āndū (侯安都) at Wúhú (蕪湖),
suffering a defeat.
At the beginning of Huángjiàn (皇建) [560 CE],
he was separately enfeoffed as Chéngyáng Jùngōng (成陽郡公).
In the second year of Tiāntǒng (天統) [566 CE],
he was appointed Tèjìn (特進).
In the tenth month of the fourth year [568 CE],
he was again separately enfeoffed as Yīshì Xiàn Gōng (猗氏縣公),
and also bestowed with one gold and one silver wine cup, and one Hu (胡) horse.
In the fourth month of the fifth year [569 CE],
his noble rank was advanced to Yì'ān Wáng (義安王).
In the first year of Wǔpíng (武平) [570 CE],
he was sent out as Guāngzhōu Cìshǐ (光州刺史).
Yǎn (儼) was a chivalrous youth,
associated with frivolous people,
and roamed between Jīng (京) and Luò (洛).
When he participated in campaigns,
he always achieved merits.
Although strategy and planning were not his strong points,
he possessed the qualities of a commander.
In all the prefectures he governed,
though he could not maintain perfect integrity,
he was also not greedy or cruel.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the titles of Sītú (司徒) and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
His son, Zǐyóng (子顒),
was Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎).
Among the generals of Ěrzhū (尒朱),
those who submitted and achieved merits after the establishment of the righteous banner,
such as Wǔwēi Dié Shèlè (武威牒舍樂) and Dàijùn Fàn Shèlè (代郡范舍樂),
also attained prominence.
Dié Shèlè,
while young, followed Ěrzhū Róng, serving as Jūnzhǔ and Tǒngjūn.
Later, he became Lǐngmín Dūdū of Xīhé.
When Ěrzhū Zhào was defeated,
he led his troops to submit to Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāozǔ).
He was appointed Zhènxī Jiāngjūn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
As a Dūdū, he was assigned under Hóu Jǐng,
and defeated Hèbá Shèng at Rángchéng.
He then joined various generals in suppressing and pacifying Qīng, Yǎn, and Jīng three prefectures (Zhōu).
He was appointed Zhènxī Jiāngjūn and Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Hànzhōng Commandery (Jùn Gōng).
Later, due to a battle,
he perished in Guānzhōng.
Fàn Shèlè,
possessed martial skills,
and his physical strength surpassed others.
In the late Wèi dynasty,
he followed Cuī Xiān and Lǐ Chóng in campaigns and achieved merit,
and was granted the title of Tǒngjūn.
Later, he entered the army of Ěrzhū Róng,
frequently achieved military successes,
and was granted the title of Dūdū.
Subsequently, he followed Ěrzhū Zhào and defeated Bù Fān in Liángjùn.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness,
he abandoned Zhào and submitted to Xìndū.
He followed Gāozǔ in defeating Zhào at Guǎng'ā and Hánlíng,
and achieved merit in both instances,
receiving the conferred title of Baron of Píngshū (Píngshū Nán).
Whenever he joined campaigns,
he often achieved victories.
He was appointed the Grand Military Governor of the Left Wing of the Chancellery (Xiàng Fǔ Zuǒxiāng Dà Dūdū).
Soon after, he was sent out to serve as the Cìshǐ of Dōngyōngzhōu.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the affairs of government,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngshū County (Píngshū Xiàn Hóu),
and was appointed Yítóng.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
his rank was advanced to Kāifǔ.
There was also Qùdí Fúlián, a native of Dài,
courtesy name Zhòngshān.
While young, he served Ěrzhū Róng due to his military competence,
rising to Zhíhé Jiāngjūn.
Later, he followed Gāozǔ when he raised the banner of righteousness,
and was granted the title of Baron of Shéqiū (Shéqiū Nán).
When Shìzōng administered the government,
he was promoted to Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he became Yítóng Sānsī.
In the fourth year [of Tiānbǎo],
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Zhèngzhōu,
and soon thereafter was promoted to Kāifǔ.
Fúlián was simple and unadorned,
and diligent in official duties.
Serving as an immediate guard at the palace (Guān Quē),
he remained near the Emperor day and night,
and was noted for this.
However, he was mean-spirited, ignorant, and ruthless,
lacking in the policies and methods needed to govern the populace.
When he held the post in the prefecture,
he focused entirely on extortion and hoarding.
His temperament was also harsh and cruel,
and he held no regard for the scholarly elite.
Most of the advisors (Cānjūn) in his Kāifǔ office were esteemed gentry families (Yīguān Shìzú),
but Fúlián beat them,
forcing them to build walls.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yídū Commandery (Yídū Jùn Wáng),
and appointed Lǐngjūn Dà Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he and the Prince of Lángyá, Yǎn, assassinated Hé Shìkāi,
and he was executed.
Fúlián's household consisted of hundreds of people.
During the height of summer,
they were allotted two sheng (liters) of coarse grain from the granary,
and were not provided with salt or vegetables,
always showing signs of hunger.
On the day of the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì),
when relatives came to offer congratulations,
his wife prepared bean cakes for them.
Fúlián asked where the beans came from.
His wife replied that she had skimmed them from the beans meant to feed the horses.
Fúlián was furious,
and both the stablemaster and the person in charge of food were beaten and punished.
The items bestowed upon him over the years,
were stored in a separate treasury,
and he sent a single maidservant to specialize in guarding the keys.
Whenever he entered the treasury to inspect them,
he would surely tell his wife and children:
"These are official goods (Guān Wù);
you must not use them arbitrarily."
When the confiscation occurred (upon his execution),
they all reverted to the Imperial Treasury (Tiān Fǔ).
The historian comments: When Gāozǔ first established the foundation of his hegemonic undertaking (Bà Yè),
he gathered heroes and brave men.
Although Zhāng Qióng and the others were not known for prescience,
they were fortunate that the time had come for their destiny.
They campaigned vigorously in the armies,
occupied day and night.
Their righteous declaration of resistance against insult,
coincided with the great plan,
and their ability to face the enemy and secure victory,
is certainly worthy of praise.
Mùróng Shàozōng’s military strategy and martial competence,
were recognized by his contemporaries.
When he formerly served Ěrzhū,
he firmly adhered to loyalty and righteousness.
Not using the advice of Fàn Zēng [referencing Hóu Jǐng],
ultimately led to the disaster at Wūjiāng [a reference to Hóu Jǐng's eventual failure].
Hóu Jǐng was savage and cruel (láng lì),
and certainly not a suitable subject for the Later Ruler.
His final testament and last words,
truly revealed his insight into men.
At Hánshān and Guōshuǐ,
the advance was like destroying dry rot.
His planning exhausted, and his luck failed him,
causing him to meet this misfortune.
Alas!
Eulogy says: The hegemonic plan was established at the beginning,
and the royal enterprise was founded upon it.
How magnificent were these generals,
truly called meritorious subjects (Gōng Chén).
Ever mindful of Gěng and Jiǎ [ancient loyal ministers],
they did not stain their pure reputation.
Chapter 13, Biographies: Gāo Gān (younger brother Shèn, younger brother Áng, younger brother Jìshì); Fēng Lóngzhī (son Zǐhuì, paternal cousin's son Xiàowǎn, Xiàoyǎn)
Gāo Gān,
courtesy name Gānyōng,
was a native of Tiáo in Bóhǎi.
His father, Yì,
courtesy name Cìtóng,
was chivalrous and possessed a fine demeanor,
and was respected by his prefecture and village.
In the late Xiàochāng era,
Gě Róng raised a rebellion in Yān and Zhào.
The court, knowing Yì was a wealthy and powerful figure east of the mountains (Shāndōng Háoyòu),
immediately appointed him Bóhǎi Tàishǒu from his home.
Not long after arriving at the commandery,
the rebel forces grew increasingly strong.
Yì led his entire jurisdiction,
and migrated to the region between the Hé (Yellow River) and Jǐ (Jǐ River).
The Wèi (dynasty) consequently established Dōngjìzhōu,
making Yì the Cìshǐ,
and adding the titles Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn and Marquis of Lèchéng County (Lèchéng Xiàn Hóu).
When Ěrzhū Zhào assassinated Emperor Zhuāngdì,
Yì guarded his borders and maintained his position.
He told his sons:
"When the ruler is anxious, the subject is disgraced;
when the ruler is disgraced, the subject dies.
Now the state (Shèjì) is in peril,
and both men and spirits are enraged.
Sacrificing one's family to repay the nation,
this is the time for it.
The Ěrzhū brothers,
are extremely suspicious by nature.
Suspicion leads to much harm.
You should plan against them early.
One must strike before others do (lit. The early person possesses the heart to seize others' opportunities),
the moment must not be lost."
He died before the matter was concluded.
In the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,

he was posthumously granted the titles Shǐ Chíjié, Shìzhōng, Tàibǎo, Lù Shàngshū Shì, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for the six prefectures of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Xiāng, Yīn, and Yōu (Jì Dìng Yíng Xiāng Yīn Yōu Liù Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu.
His posthumous name (Shì) was Wénxuān.
Gān was bright and perceptive by nature,
heroic, great, and possessed knowledge and strategy.
He had a beautiful voice and appearance,
and his movements were refined and elegant.
When young, he was restless and chivalrous,
frequently violating public laws.
When he grew up, he reformed his conduct,
valued righteousness above wealth,
and formed many associations.
Yuán Chā, the Wèi Lǐngjūn,
whose power was significant at the time,
enjoyed Gān's spirit and character,
and treated Gān very favorably.
Starting his official career, he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng,
and concurrently held the post of Zhíhòu.
He was transferred to Tàiwèi Shìcáo, Sītú Zhōngbīng, and promoted to Yuánwài [Sànqí Shìláng].
Wèi Xiàozhuāng lived in the provinces (as a prince),
Gān secretly attached himself to him. When Ěrzhū Róng
entered Luò, Gān fled east to Yì.
When Emperor Zhuāng
was established, he was appointed remotely as General of the Soaring Dragon (Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn) and Palace Attendant and Regular Mounted Guard (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
Gān and his brother originally harbored ambitions of strategic maneuver,
and seeing Róng murdering scholars and officials,
they believed that the realm would inevitably fall into chaos.
They therefore led
refugees from Héběi in rebellion between the Hé and Jì rivers, accepting official titles from Gě Róng,
and repeatedly defeating the troops and cavalry of Qízhōu.
Emperor Zhuāng soon sent the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púyè), Yuán Luó, to tour and pacify the region of Sān Qí.
Gān and his brother led their followers out and surrendered.
The court appointed Gān as Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
Ěrzhū Róng, citing Gān's previous offenses,
argued he should not hold a crucial position again.
Emperor Zhuāng permitted Gān
to resign his office and return to his hometown. Thereupon, he recruited brave and fierce men,
entertaining himself with archery and hunting.
When Róng died,
Gān galloped to Luòyáng.
Emperor Zhuāng, seeing him,
was greatly pleased.
At that time, Ěrzhū's followers maintained armies outside the capital,
and Emperor Zhuāng appointed Gān as Grand Master of the Palace with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū) and Envoy to Héběi (Hébĕi Dàshǐ),
instructing him to gather his fellow villagers to serve as external support and protection for the court.
Gān received the decree with tears,
and his younger brother, Áng, drew his sword and began to dance,
requesting permission to dedicate himself unto death.
Soon after, Ěrzhū Zhào entered Luò.
He quickly sent his Military Supervisor (Jiānjūn), Sūn Báiyào, with over a hundred cavalry to Jìzhōu,
pretending to levy horses from the general populace,
intending to wait until Gān and his brother delivered their horses,
and then arrest them.
Gān already harbored a long-standing desire for revenge,
and when Báiyào suddenly arrived,
he knew he was about to be targeted.
He therefore preemptively settled his strategy,
secretly organized strong men,
attacked and seized the prefecture seat,
issued manifestos to the prefectures and commanderies,
killed Báiyào,
and captured the Inspector (Cìshǐ), Yuán Zhòngzōng.
He supported Fēng Lóngzhī to temporarily manage the affairs of the prefecture,
held mourning rites for Emperor Zhuāng,
and the entire army dressed in white mourning clothes.
Gān ascended the altar and addressed the masses,
his words and demeanor spirited and stirring,
tears flowing freely.
None among the officers and soldiers were not sorrowful and indignant.
He submitted to the command of Liú Língzhù, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
in the north, and together they formed a coordinated strategy.
Shortly thereafter, Língzhù was killed.
It happened that Gāozǔ emerged from Shāndōng,
announcing his intention to attack and punish.
Everyone felt alarmed and fearful.
Gān said to his followers:
"I have heard that Gāo Jìnzhōu's
heroic strategy surpasses the age, and his ambition is not to serve beneath others.
Moreover, the Ěrzhū clan is lawless,
murdering their sovereign and oppressing the people.
This is precisely the occasion for heroes to demonstrate loyalty and righteousness.
His arrival today
must involve a profound strategy.
I must ride lightly to welcome him,
and secretly confer with him regarding his intentions.
You gentlemen must not worry or fear,
just wait for me to go."
Gān then took a dozen riders to the pass entrance to meet and pay respects.
As Gān was already perceptive regarding the times and opportunities,
and skilled in worldly affairs,
his words were spirited and sincere,
perfectly aligning with Gāozǔ's profound intentions.
Gāozǔ greatly appreciated and honored him,
and even shared a tent with him for sleeping.
Although Gāozǔ privately harbored long-term plans at this time,
they were not yet apparent externally.
Ěrzhū Yǔshēng was the Inspector of Yīnzhōu.
Gāozǔ secretly sent Lǐ Yuánzhōng to raise troops and pressure the city,
instructing Gān to lead his forces in a feigned attempt to rescue it.
Gān then rode lightly into the city to see Yǔshēng,
and discussed military strategy with him.
Yǔshēng and Gān went out together,
whereupon Gān captured him,
thus pacifying Yīnzhōu.
They also jointly decided on the strategy to nominate and enthrone the Restorer of the Dynasty,
and Gān was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Previously, when Xìndū was first established (in their military uprising),
and the affairs of the army and state were just beginning,
Gān had been prevented by mourning for a parent from completing the standard mourning period.
When Emperor
Wǔ was established, and the realm was newly stabilized,
Gān submitted a memorial requesting to resign his posts
to observe the three-year mourning rite.
An imperial edict permitted him to resign as Shìzhōng,
but he retained the post of Sīkōng,
and he was enfeoffed as Duke of Chánglè Commandery (Chánglè Jùngōng),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Although Gān had requested retirement,
he did not expect to be immediately granted permission.
Having left his position as Palace Attendant,
he rarely became involved in court affairs,
and he was constantly discontented.
Emperor Wǔ planned to betray Gāozǔ.
Hoping Gān would serve him,
once, after a banquet in the Huálín Garden (Huálínyuán),
he detained Gān alone,
and said to him:
"Minister of Works (Sīkōng), your family has been loyal and virtuous for generations,
and today you have again achieved extraordinary merit.
Although we relate as sovereign and subject,
in righteousness, we are truly like brothers.
We should establish a covenant together to solidify our relationship."
He pressed him earnestly.
Gān replied:
"Your servant has served the court for generations,
and received extraordinary favor.
Having pledged my life to the state,
how dare I harbor a second loyalty?"
Although Gān gave this reply,
it was not his true intention.
The event occurred suddenly,
and he did not believe Emperor Wǔ had immediate divergent plans.
Consequently, he did not firmly refuse,
nor did he inform Gāozǔ.
When Emperor Wǔ established his personal military units (*bùqǔ*),
Gān privately told his close associates:
"The Sovereign does not favor meritorious officials,
but instead gathers minor officials.
He frequently sends Yuán Shìbì and Wáng Sīzhèng to travel back and forth to Guānxī (west of the pass),
to scheme with Hèbá Yuè.
Furthermore, he sent Hèbá Shèng out to be the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
outwardly pretending to distance himself and be wary of him,
but actually intending to establish a faction,
allowing the brothers (Hèbá Yuè and Hèbá Shèng) to be close,
hoping to occupy the West.
Disaster is about to strike,
and it will surely reach us."
He then secretly informed Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ summoned Gān to Bīngzhōu.
They discussed current affairs face-to-face,
and Gān subsequently urged Gāozǔ to accept the abdication of Wèi.
Gāozǔ covered his mouth with his sleeve and said:
"Do not speak carelessly.
I shall now memorialize the Emperor for the Sīkōng
to be reinstated as Shìzhōng, and the affairs of the Palace Gate (the Chancellery)
shall all be entrusted to you."
Gāozǔ memorialized the throne repeatedly,
but the imperial edict was ultimately not issued.
Gān, seeing that his frequent requests were not granted,
knew that turmoil was about to arise.
He secretly appealed to Gāozǔ,
requesting to be assigned to Xúzhōu.
Consequently, he was appointed Shǐ Chíjīe, Dūdū Sānxú Zhūjūnshì, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
When the designated departure date approached,
the Emperor (Wǔdì) realized that Gān had leaked previous affairs,
and thus issued an edict to Gāozǔ saying:
“I previously had a private covenant with Gān Yōng,
but now he is duplicitous and unreliable.”
Gāozǔ immediately gathered the several memorials Gān had previously submitted discussing current affairs,
sealed them, and sent them via envoy to Emperor Wǔdì.
The Emperor summoned Gān Yōng and showed them to him,
confined him in the Ménxiàshěng,
and confronted him before Gāozǔ’s envoy,
criticizing Gān for his previous errors.
Gān said:
“I serve the country with my life,
having fulfilled my loyalty and sincerity.
Since Your Majesty has established an alternate plan,
you now accuse me of being unreliable.
Even if such an accusation were leveled against a commoner,
they might still find it difficult to avoid;
how much more so when the sovereign promotes evil?
How can I escape death?
When one desires to inflict a crime,
is there ever a lack of excuse?
Great merit leads to personal danger;
this has been true since ancient times.
If I have knowledge after death,
I hope that I shall not have failed Emperor Zhuāngdì.”
He was subsequently granted death,
at the age of thirty-seven.
When Gān faced death,
his expression did not change;
all who witnessed it sighed in admiration and pity.
At that time, Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Yuán Zhěng supervised the execution,
and asked Gān:
“Have you written anything to your family members?”
Gān replied:
“My brothers have been separated
and are each in different places.
Given the events of today,
I presume none will be spared.
My sons are young
and have no understanding yet,
but I also fear that the nest will be overturned and the eggs broken.
What more could I say?”
Later, when Gāozǔ was campaigning against Hú Sīchūn and others,
and arrived at Méng Jīn,
he said to Gān’s younger brother, Áng:
“If I had used the Sīkōng’s strategy earlier,
how could this current campaign have been necessary?”
In the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
Gān was posthumously granted the titles Zèng Shǐ Chíjīe, Dūdū Jì Dìng Cāng Yíng Yōu Qí Xú Qīng Guāng Yǎn Shízhōu Jūnshì, Tàishī, Lù Shàngshū Shì, and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and given the posthumous name Wénzhāo.
His eldest son, Jìshū, inherited the ancestral title Lèchéng Xiànhóu,
and his second younger brother's son, Lǚ'ér, inherited Gān's peerage.
Gān’s younger brother, Shèn,
courtesy name Zhòngmì,
was widely read in literature and history.
His ambitions and disposition differed from his brothers,
and he was particularly loved by his father.
In the beginning of Wèi Zhōngxīng,
he was appointed Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ and Dōngnán Dào Xíngtái Shàngshū.
In the beginning of Tàichāng,
he was promoted to Guāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and given the additional titles Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
As the empire had just been settled,
Shèn was allowed to keep several thousand troops from his home district with him.
Shèn was cruel and harsh in his governance,
and also indulged his staff,
causing suffering among the officials and the populace.
When his elder brother Gān died,
Shèn secretly abandoned the governorship and returned to Gāozǔ.
Emperor Wǔdì ordered Qīngzhōu to cut off his route of return.
Shèn traveled secretly and reached Jìnyáng.
Gāozǔ appointed him Dà Xíngtái Zuǒchéng,
then transferred him to Shàngshū.
While in office, he avoided nothing,
and everyone at the time feared and respected him.
Since the raising of the righteous standard,
the people of Ānzhōu relied on the ruggedness of their frontier
and refused to submit to the imperial transforming influence.
Soon after, Shèn was appointed Xíngtái Púyè,
and he led troops to attack and pacify them.
At the end of the Tiānpíng era,
he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and received the additional title Kāifǔ.
In the beginning of Yuánxiàng,
he was sent out as Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was recalled to serve as Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi.
When selecting Censors (Yùshǐ),
he favored his relatives and fellow villagers,
failing to meet court expectations.
Shìzōng submitted a memorial asking for him to change his selection.
Shèn's former wife was the younger sister of Lìbù Lángzhōng Cuī Xiān,
but she had been discarded by Shèn.
Cuī Xiān was at that time trusted by Shìzōng.
Shèn believed Cuī Xiān was plotting against him.
As his nature was impatient and hasty,
he accumulated resentment.
Because of this, he rarely impeached anyone
and showed much leniency.
Gāozǔ suspected and criticized him,
making Shèn feel increasingly insecure.
He was sent out as Běiyùzhōu Cìshǐ,
whereupon he seized Wǔláo and surrendered to Xī Wèi.
Shèn entered the Pass first.
When Zhōu Wéndì led troops eastward,
Gāozǔ defeated them at Máng Shān.
Shèn’s wife and children were traveling west to cross the border,
and they were all captured en route.
Because of Shèn's family's military merit,
Gāozǔ memorialized that only Shèn's immediate household be confiscated and enslaved.
Áng,
courtesy name Áocáo,
was Gān’s third younger brother.
In his youth,
he already possessed heroic spirit.
As he grew, he was unconventional and unrestrained,
his courage and strength surpassing others.
With dragon eyebrows and a leopard neck,
his appearance and physique were remarkably imposing.
His father sought a strict teacher for him,
allowing the teacher to use corporeal punishment.
Áng did not follow the teacher's instructions,
focusing instead on riding and hunting.
He often said that a man should sweep across the world,
seizing wealth and honor for himself.
Who could sit upright and study
to become an old scholar?
He and his brother Gān frequently committed acts of robbery,
which the provinces and counties were unable to fully investigate or punish.
He gathered swordsmen,
spending all his family wealth.
The villagers feared him
and dared not oppose him.
His father, Yì, often said to people:
“If this child does not destroy my clan,
he will certainly bring greatness to my house;
he will not merely be a local provincial magnate.”
In the beginning of Jiànyì,
the brothers jointly raised troops.
Afterward, they dispersed the troops following an imperial order,
and Áng was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng,
enfeoffed as the Earl of Wǔchéng County (Wǔchéng Xiànbó),
with an income of five hundred households.
When Gān resigned his office and returned home,
he and Áng were both in the countryside,
secretly gathering brave men.
Ěrzhū Róng heard of this and disliked it.
He secretly ordered the Cìshǐ Yuán Zhòngzōng to lure and arrest Áng,
and send him to Jìnyáng.
At the end of Yǒng'ān,
when Róng entered Luò,
he took Áng with him
and confined him at the Tuóniúshǔ.
After Róng died,
Emperor Wèi Zhuāngdì immediately summoned and encouraged him.
At that time, Ěrzhū Shìlóng was pressing upon the palace gates again.
The Emperor personally ascended the Dàxiàmén to direct and organize the defenses.
Áng, having just been released from chains,
donned armor and grasped a spear horizontally,
determined to overcome the powerful enemy.
He advanced directly with his nephew Chángmìng and others, leading the charge.
Wherever they went, the enemy scattered.
The Emperor and the onlookers were all moved by his valor.
He was immediately appointed Zhíhé Jiāngjūn,
and awarded one thousand bolts of silk.
Āng, believing the bandit troubles were still numerous,
and could not be remedied by a single man,
requested to return to his native village,
to gather and mobilize his troops.
He was subsequently appointed Tōngzhí Chángshì,
and given the title Píngběi Jiāngjūn.
Valiant volunteers from all locations,
rushed to join him competitively.
Soon after, when the capital fell,
he and his father and elder brothers seized Xìndū and raised an army.
Yīnzhōu Cìshǐ Ěrzhū Yǔshēng stealthily brought his army to attack,
and suddenly arrived below the city walls.
Āng did not have time to don his armor,
but led more than ten riders to charge them.
Yǔshēng retreated,
and public morale was thus stabilized.
Afterwards, when the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Jìzhōu Cìshǐ for the rest of his life.
He also served as Dà Dūdū,
leading troops to follow Gāozǔ and defeat Ěrzhū Zhào at Guǎng'ā.
When Yè was pacified,
he separately led his assigned division to command Líyáng.
He then followed Gāozǔ to campaign against Ěrzhū Zhào at Hánlíng.
Āng personally commanded three thousand of his fellow villagers and troops, including Wáng Táotāng, Dōngfāng Lǎo, and Hūyán Zú.
Gāozǔ said:
"Gāo Dūdū is commanding pure Hàn troops.
I fear this may not succeed.
I should now allocate more than a thousand Xiānbēi soldiers to mix in.
What is your opinion on this?"
Āng replied:
"The troops that Áocáo commands,
have been trained for a long time.
In previous battles,
they are no less capable than the Xiānbēi.
If we mix them now,
their sentiments will not harmonize.
If we win, they will fight over credit;
if we retreat, they will shift blame.
I wish to lead the Hàn army myself,
without the trouble of further assignments."
Gāozǔ agreed with him.
When they fought,
Gāozǔ suffered a disadvantage.
The army slightly retreated.
Zhào and his forces then pressed their advantage.
Gāo Yuè and Hán Xiōngnú, leading five hundred cavalry, charged their front.
Húlǜ Dūn gathered the scattered soldiers and tracked their rear.
Āng and Cài Jùn, leading a thousand cavalry, emerged from Lìyuán,
and struck Zhào's army laterally.
Zhào’s forces were consequently greatly defeated.
On that day, without Āng and the others,
Gāozǔ would have been almost fatally endangered.
At the beginning of Tàichāng,
he first went to Jìzhōu.
Soon after, he was granted the titles Shìzhōng and Kāifǔ,
and advanced in rank to Marquis (Hóu),
with a fief of seven hundred households.
When his elder brother Gān was killed,
he led more than ten riders to flee to Jìnyáng,
and submitted to Gāozǔ.
When Húsī Chūn initiated trouble,
Gāozǔ campaigned in the south,
ordering Āng to serve as the vanguard.
When Wǔdì fled west,
Āng led five hundred cavalry, traveling doubled distances day and night,
reaching Xiáoshǎn.
He failed to overtake him and returned.
Soon after, he provisionally served as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
He then campaigned against those who refused to submit in the various states of Sānjīng,
and pacified them all.
At the beginning of Tiānpíng,
he was appointed Shìzhōng and Sīkōng Gōng.
Since his elder brother Gān had died while holding this position,
Āng firmly declined the appointment.
He was transferred to Sītú Gōng.
At that time, Gāozǔ was planning a military campaign against Guānlǒng.
He appointed Āng as Xīnán Dào Dà Dūdū,
to proceed directly toward Shāngluò.
The mountain paths were steep and narrow,
and already defended by bandits who held the strategic points.
Āng fought continuously as he advanced,
and none dared to meet his spearhead.
He subsequently attacked and captured Shàngluò,
capturing Quán Qǐ, the Luòzhōu Cìshǐ of Western Wèi,
along with several dozen commanders.
Coincidentally, Dòu Tài suffered a defeat,
and Āng was recalled to cease operations and return.
At that time, Āng was struck by a stray arrow.
His wound was severe.
He looked back at his attendants and said:
"I have offered my body to the state,
and I have no regrets in dying.
What I truly sigh about,
is not seeing Jìshì become a Cìshǐ."
Gāozǔ heard this,
and immediately dispatched a swift courier to request that Jìshì be made Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Āng returned,
he was again appointed Jūnsī Dà Dūdū,
commanding seventy-six dūdū,
and trained troops with Xíngtái Hóu Jǐng at Wǔláo.
Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Liú Guì was also leading troops in Běi Yùzhōu at that time.
He had a minor dispute with Āng.
Āng became angry,
beat the drums to assemble his soldiers, and attacked him.
Hóu Jǐng and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Mòqí Shòuluògān intervened to mediate and stop the fighting.
His heroic spirit and audacity toward others were like this.
At that time,
the Xiānbēi generally looked down upon the Hàn Chinese court officials.
Only Āng commanded their awe and submission.
Whenever Gāozǔ issued orders to the three armies,
he usually used the Xiānbēi language.
If Āng was among the ranks,
he would speak the Huá (Chinese) language instead.
Āng once went to the Prime Minister’s residence.
The gatekeeper refused him entry.
Āng grew angry,
drew his bow and shot him.
Gāozǔ knew about it but did not reprimand him.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng,
he was advanced in peerage to Jīngzhào Jùn Gōng,
with a fief of one thousand households.
He and Hóu Jǐng and others jointly attacked Dúgū Rúyuàn at Jīnyǒng Chéng.
Zhōu Wéndì led troops to rescue him.
They fought at Mángyīn.
The division commanded by Āng suffered a defeat.
His attendants scattered.
He rode alone eastward,
intending to reach Héliáng Nánchéng.
The gates were closed and he could not enter.
He was subsequently killed by the Western Army.
He was forty-eight years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shǐchíjié, Shìzhōng, Dūdū Jì Dìng Cāng Yíng Yīn Wǔzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Tàishī, Dàsīmǎ, Tàiwèi Gōng, Lù Shàngshū Shì, and Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
His posthumous title was Zhōngwǔ.
His son Tūqí succeeded him,
but died early.
Shìzōng subsequently summoned all of Āng's sons,
and personally selected his third son, Dàohuō, to succeed.
At the beginning of Huángjiàn,
Āng was posthumously enfeoffed as Yǒngchāng Wáng.
Dàohuō inherited the title.
At the end of Wǔpíng,
he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Upon entering Zhōu,
he was granted Yítóng Dà Jiāngjūn.
During the Kāihuáng era,
he died while serving as Huángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jìshì,
courtesy name Zǐtōng,
was Gān’s fourth younger brother.
He also possessed courage.
At the beginning of Zhōngxīng,
he was appointed Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Zhèngyuán Láng,
then promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Soon after, he was granted Sànqí Chángshì,
and commanded the Zhǔyī Dūtǒng.
At the beginning of Tàichāng,
he was appointed Shàngshí Diǎnyù.
he was sent out to serve as the Prefect of Jìzhōu.
Old bandits in Shāndōng, such as Liú Pántuó and Shǐ Míngyào, attacked and robbed travelers on the roads,
plundering villages and towns.
The four provinces of Qí, Yǎn, Qīng, and Xú suffered greatly from them,
and successive governments were unable to suppress them.
When Jì Shì arrived,
he completely defeated and destroyed them.
Soon after, the people of Púyáng, Dù Língchūn and others, attacked cities and plundered the countryside,
gathering a host of nearly ten thousand men.
Jì Shì sent three hundred cavalry,
and captured them in a single battle.
Furthermore, the followers of Lù Wén from Yángpíng, such as Xù Xiǎn, erected camps and stockades to create disorder.
Jì Shì suppressed and pacified them.
There was also a group of bandits who broke into Nánhé Jùn.
Jì Shì dispatched troops to confront them,
executing them immediately.
From this time onward,
peace and tranquility reigned far and near.
Jì Shì and his brothers were highly distinguished and prosperous,
all having rendered meritorious service at the time.
He personally led over a thousand personal retainers and troops,
with eight hundred horses,
and all their spears, armor, and weapons were fully equipped.
Therefore, whenever he pursued and supervised the pursuit of bandits and thieves,
he often achieved victory.
A guest once said to Jì Shì:
"Púyáng and Yángpíng are within the capital region.
Since the bandits did not refuse orders,
nor did they infringe upon your border,
what was the urgency
that required you to send private troops to fight far away?
If by any chance they failed,
wouldn't that invite punishment?"
Jì Shì replied:
"How extremely disloyal your words are!
By duty, I share the country's safety and danger.
How could there be a reason to see bandits and not suppress them?
Moreover, the bandits knew that the court armies could not come suddenly,
and they did not suspect that help would come from an outside province.
While they were unprepared,
defeating them was certain.
Warfare values divine speed;
how can one fall behind the opportunity?
If I am to incur punishment for this,
I have no regrets."
During the Yuánxiàng era,
the western invaders arrived in great force.
Gāo Zǔ personally led the three armies to resist them,
arraying the formation at Máng Běi.
His forces suffered a great defeat,
floating corpses in the river followed one after another,
and retreating soldiers stretched ceaselessly from front to back.
People's morale was disturbed,
saying that the state of affairs was dire.
His close retainers pleaded with Jì Shì, saying:
"The current situation
means the great cause is lost.
You should take two hundred of your trusted cavalry and flee to Liáng.
Not only will you avoid disaster,
you will not lose wealth and high rank.
Why should you sit here and await death?"
Jì Shì said:
"My brothers and I have received profound kindness from the state.
We helped Prince Gāo establish control over the realm.
To flee when danger suddenly appears
would be unrighteous.
If the state is overthrown,
I ought to fight to the death with my back to the city walls.
How could I merely be concerned with cowardly snatching a moment of life?"
In this campaign,
the Sītú perished.
He entered the capital to serve as Sànqí Chángshì.
During the Xīnghé era,
he acted in the capacity of the Jìnzhōu governorship.
After being relieved of Xièzhōu,
he continued to guard Yǒng'ān Shù.
Gāo Shèn rebelled at Wǔláo,
and sent a messenger to inform Jì Shì.
Jì Shì was startled and afraid upon receiving the letter,
and immediately rushed in panic to report to Gāo Zǔ.
Gāo Zǔ recognized his utter sincerity,
and treated him as before.
During the Wǔdìng era,
he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and soon was additionally made Dà Zhōngzhèng of Jìzhōu.
At that time, Shìzōng had previously held this post,
and memorialized to transfer it back.
He served as a Dūdū,
and followed Qīnghé Gōng Yuè in defeating Xiāo Míng at Hánshān,
and routing Hóu Jǐng at Wōyáng.
Returning,
he was appointed Wèiwèi Qīng.
He again served as a Dūdū,
following Qīnghé Gōng to attack Wáng Sīzhèng at Yǐngchuān,
and captured the city.
Due to these accumulated merits, he was granted the title Yítóng Sānsī.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Chéngshì County,
and continued to serve as Dūdū,
following Sītú Pān Yuè on punitive expeditions between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
He privately directed musicians to trade along the borderlands.
Upon returning to the capital,
he was implicated and banned from office,
but was soon pardoned.
In the summer of the fourth year,
he died of carbuncles
at the age of thirty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng, Envoy with Credentials, Military Commander (Dūdū) of Cāng and Jìzhōu, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Prefect of Jìzhōu.
His posthumous name was Gōngmù.
Jì Shì was bold, unconventional, and fond of wine.
Furthermore, relying on the merits of his entire family,
he disregarded rules and self-discipline.
He had a lifelong close friendship with Lǐ Yuánzhōng, the Prefect of Guāngzhōu.
One night while drinking in Jìzhōu,
he remembered Yuánzhōng,
opened the city gate,
and ordered his attendants to take a relay horse carrying a pot of wine to Guāngzhōu to encourage Yuánzhōng.
The court knew about this and tolerated it.
A short time after his brother Shèn rebelled,
Jì Shì was dismissed from his post.
Sīmǎ Xiāonàn, the Huángmén Láng,
was the son of Zuǒ Púyè Zǐrú,
and was also the son-in-law of Gāo Zǔ,
making his influence great at the time.
Taking advantage of time off after finishing his meal,
he sought out Jì Shì and drank heavily with him.
After staying overnight until the next day,
all the inner gates were shut,
and the locks and bars were impenetrable.
Xiāonàn earnestly pleaded, saying:
"I am a Huángmén Láng,
a close minister to the Son of Heaven.
How can there be a reason for me not to attend court?
Moreover, having not returned home for one night already,
my father must be greatly worried.
If you keep me here again to drink recklessly,
I will have no excuse for my offense,
and I fear you will not escape reprimand either."
Jì Shì said:
"You claim to be a Huángmén Láng,
and you speak of fearing your father's worry.
Do you intend to coerce me with your status?
Gāo Jì Shì has his own way of dying;
he certainly does not fear this."
Xiāonàn bowed and requested to leave,
but was ultimately not permitted.
When the wine arrived,
he refused to drink.
Jì Shì said:
"I kept you here to fully enjoy yourself.
What kind of man are you
that you will not drink heartily for me?"
He ordered his attendants to fetch a carriage wheel and place it around Xiāonàn's neck,
and then fetched another wheel and placed it around his own neck.
He then ordered wine, filling the cups to the brim, and urged Xiāonàn to drink with him.
Having no choice, Xiāonàn
smiled happily and complied.
Only then did they both remove the carriage wheels,
and he stayed for another night.
At that time, Xiāonàn had been missing for two nights,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
The court and the public were greatly alarmed.
When Xiāonàn finally emerged,
he fully recounted the events.
Shìzōng, who was assisting in governing the capital,
reported to Wèi Dì, who bestowed upon Xiāonàn several *shi* of fine wine
and ten cartloads of rare delicacies,
and furthermore ordered court officials who were close to Jì Shì
to gather for a banquet at Jì Shì's residence.
His favored treatment was of this nature.
Yì's eldest brother's son, Yǒnglè, and second brother's son, Yánbó,
were both harmonious and generous, praised as noble persons.
They both followed Yì in raising the righteous banner.
Yǒnglè served as General of the Guard, Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, and Grand Central Judge of Jìzhōu.
He was sent out to be the Administrator of Bólíng.
Because the people's affairs were not thriving,
he committed suicide.
He was posthumously granted Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Cāng and Jì Two Prefectures, Initiator of Same Rank, and Governor of Jìzhōu.
His son, Chángmìng,
originally came from a humble background,
and was only recognized and raised when he was over twenty years old.
He was fierce and fond of killing,
but also resolute in combat.
He first repelled Ěrzhū Shìlóng at the Dàxiàmén (Great Summer Gate),
and was successively promoted to Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness for his merit.
Gāozǔ remotely appointed Chángmìng as Governor of Yōngzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Baron of Jǔyáng Township,
with one hundred households.
Soon after, he was advanced in peerage to Earl of Yānlíng County,
with an increase of two hundred households.
During the Wǔdìng reign,
he followed Initiator of Same Rank Liú Fēng to suppress Hóu Jǐng,
and was killed by Jǐng.
He was posthumously granted Governor of Jìzhōu.
Yánbó successively held the posts of Grand Master for Consultation, and Governor of Ānzhōu,
and was enfeoffed as Baron of Wànnián County,
with an estate of two hundred households.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was given the title General Who Conquers the West,
and his noble rank was advanced to Viscount.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted Vice Minister of the Grand Treasury.
Since Āng first established his name through heroism and chivalry,
those who acted as his wings were
Hūyán Zú, Liú Guìzhēn, Liú Chángdí, Dōngfāng Lǎo, Liú Shìróng, Chéng Wǔ,
Hán Yuànshēng, and Liú Táobàng.
Those who followed him in establishing the righteousness were
Lǐ Xīguāng, Liú Shūzōng, and Liú Mènghé.
They all attained prominence in officialdom.
Mènghé's personal name was Xié,
and he was a native of Ráo'ān, Fúyáng.
Mènghé was fond of archery and horsemanship in his youth,
and was naturally heroic and chivalrous.
When Liú Língzhù, the Governor of Yōuzhōu, raised troops,
Mènghé also gathered followers and attached himself to the Āng brothers.
Āng responded to him remotely.
When Língzhù was defeated,
Āng then occupied Jìzhōu,
and Mènghé exerted himself on his behalf.
When Gāozǔ raised the righteous banner in Jìzhōu,
he appointed Mènghé as Area Commander.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
he was appointed Grand Master of Transmission.
In the second year,
he was made General Who Pacifies the East,
and soon after was promoted to General Who Conquers the East and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple.
For his merit in establishing the righteousness,
he was granted the title Earl of Chángguǎng County.
During the Tiānpíng era,
he was General of the Guard and Administrator of Shàngdǎng.
When he was relieved of the commandery,
he was made Chief Clerk to the Grand Chancellor.
In the first year of Wǔdìng,
he died due to an incident.
Shūzōng, courtesy name Yuáncuàn,
was a native of Píngchāng, Lèlíng.
He was moderate and cautious,
and possessed considerable scholarship.
He was recommended as a Cultivated Talent.
He gradually rose to be Chief Administrator of Cāngzhōu.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
he was promoted to General Who Guards the Distant and Grand Master Remonstrant.
His elder brother, Hǎibǎo,
was a light-mannered cavalier in his youth,
but was loved by the prefecture and his community.
When Āng raised the righteous banner,
Hǎibǎo led the villagers to attack Cāngzhōu in response to Āng.
Āng appointed Hǎibǎo to provisionally manage the affairs of Cāngzhōu.
Diāo Zhěng, the former Administrator of Fànyáng, secretly supported Ěrzhū,
and sent his nephew Ānshòu to attack and kill Hǎibǎo.
Shūzōng then returned to Āng.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
Gāozǔ appointed him General of the Vanguard and Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
At the beginning of the Tàichāng era,
he was promoted to General Who Guards the Army and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
he was made General of Chariots and Cavalry and Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
He died in the second year.
He was posthumously granted Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Initiator of Same Rank, and Governor of Dìngzhōu.
Lǎo was a native of Gé, Āndé.
His family lineage was poor and humble.
He was seven *chǐ* tall,
with strength surpassing ordinary men.
In his youth, he was coarse, unruly, and unreliable.
He gathered light-minded and dangerous people to commit robbery,
and the local community was troubled by him.
When the wars arose at the end of the Wèi dynasty,
he then became a subordinate to Āng.
When the righteous banner was established,
he followed in the campaigns and expeditions.
For his military merits, he was made Palace General.
He was successively promoted to General Who Pacifies the Distant,
and made Administrator of Lǔyáng.
Later, he was made Governor of Southern Yìzhōu,
and concurrently held the post of Administrator of Yíyáng,
and was granted the title Viscount of Chánglè.
Lǎo served in the two commanderies frequently,
entering and leaving over several years.
His borders neighbored various Mán tribes,
and also the western enemies.
Regarding attacking cities or fighting in the field,
he led the officers and soldiers first,
and often controlled the many with the few.
The western people feared him.
When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication,
he was separately enfeoffed as Earl of Yángpíng County,
and promoted to Governor of Southern Yǎnzhōu.
Later, he crossed the Yangtze River with Xiāo Guǐ and others,
and died in battle.
Xīguāng was a native of Tiáo, Bóhǎi.
His father, Shào,
was the Wèi Administrator of Chángguǎng.
Xīguāng followed Gāo Gān in raising the righteous banner in Xìndū.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
he was made General Who Pacifies the South and Administrator of Āndé Commandery.
Later, he served as Chief Clerk of the Established Prefecture for Shìzǔ.
At the end of the Wǔdìng era,
he followed Gāo Yuè in pacifying Yǐngchuān,
was enfeoffed as Founding Marquis of Yìníng County,
and successively served as Governors of Yǐng, Liáng, and Southern Yǎn three prefectures.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he was Governor of Yángzhōu.
He crossed the Yangtze River with Xiāo Guǐ and others,
and died in battle.
He was posthumously granted Initiator of Same Rank of the Established Prefecture and Governor of Western Yǎnzhōu.
His son, Zǐlìng,
was Director in the Bureau of External Military Affairs in the Department of State Affairs.
At the end of Wǔpíng,
he was Grand Master of Transmission.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he died while serving as Governor of Yìzhōu.
Xīguāng's kinsman's son, Zǐgòng,
for his merit with the righteous banner,
rose to the office of Director of the Bureau of Civil Office,
and later became Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
He was killed by Shìzōng for corruption and violence.
Xiǎnzǔ held Chén Wǔ responsible for overthrowing Xiāo Míng,
and ordered Initiator of Same Rank Xiāo Guǐ to lead Xīguāng, Dōngfāng Lǎo, Péi Yīngqǐ, and Wáng Jìngbǎo with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to attack him.
They crossed the Yangtze River in the third month of the seventh year
and successfully launched a surprise attack on Shítóu City.
The five generals held comparable rank.
Yīngqǐ, as Attendant-in-Chief, served as the Army Adjutant.
Xiāo Guǐ and Xīguāng were both Area Commanders.
They treated each other with equal ceremony in the army,
and would not submit to or command one another.
They competed to present strategies and plans,
and every action inevitably became discordant.
They encamped below Dānyáng City,
where they encountered fifty-odd days of continuous rain.
When they engaged in battle,
their weapons were all unfit for use,
which led to their defeat and destruction.
The commanders and generals all died.
Only twelve or thirteen percent of the officers and soldiers managed to return.
The lost weapons, equipment, and military supplies were countless.
The accounts of Xiāo Guǐ and Wáng Jìngbǎo are missing in the histories.
Péi Yīngqǐ was a native of Hédōng.
His ancestors crossed the Huái River at the end of the Jìn dynasty
and settled temporarily in Shòuyáng County, Huáinán.
His grandfather, Yànxiān,
followed Xuē Āndū into Wèi,
and his office reached Administrator of Zhàojùn.
His father, Yuē,
was Chancellor of Bóhǎi.
Yīngqǐ was intelligent and humorous,
fond of theatrical talk,
and unrestrained by ritual standards.
He served in Wèi until he reached Chief Clerk of Dìngzhōu.
Shìzōng appointed him Assistant Left Affairs Manager of the Traveling Chancellery.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he was Minister of the Department of Justice,
and concurrently Attendant-in-Chief.
When he died in battle,
he was posthumously granted Initiator of the Established Prefecture and Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Fēng Lóngzhī,
courtesy name Zǔyì,
childhood name Pí,
was a native of Tiáo, Bóhǎi.
His father, Huí,
was the Sīkōng of Wèi.
Lóngzhī was broad-minded and gentle by nature,
and possessed great tolerance.
When he came of age (at twenty),
he served as Zhǔbù for the commandery and province.
He started his official career as Fèng Cháoqǐng,
and oversaw the Zhíhòu.
When Yuè, Prince of Rǔnán, established his administration (kāifǔ),
Lóngzhī served as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Earlier,
during the Yánchāng era,
the Daoist Fǎqìng incited rebellion in Jìfāng (Jì Province area).
He called himself
"Dàshèng" (Great Vehicle),
and had over fifty thousand followers.
Dà Dūdū Yuán Yáo and Lóngzhī were dispatched to capture Fǎqìng,
and he was bestowed the noble title of Wǔchéng Zǐ.
Soon after, he concurrently held the posts of Sītú Zhǔbù and Hénán Yǐn Chéng.
At that time, the gentry and populace of Qīng and Qí Provinces rebelled.
Lóngzhī was sent on a mission to comfort and persuade them,
and they all immediately submitted.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
he was appointed Fǔjūn Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ.
Ěrzhū Zhào and others garrisoned Jìnyáng.
The Wèi court, considering Hénèi a crucial pass,
appointed Lóngzhī as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Hénèi Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was granted the Staff of Authority (Chíjié), promoted to Hòu Jiāngjūn, made acting Píng Běi Jiāngjūn, and Dūdu of the commandery.
Before he could reach the commandery,
Ěrzhū Zhào entered Luòyáng,
and Emperor Zhuāng died in confinement.
Since Lóngzhī's father had been murdered,
he always harbored the desire for vengeance.
Therefore, he retained the Staff of Authority and returned east,
planning a righteous uprising.
At that time, Gāo Gān informed Lóngzhī, saying:
"The Ěrzhū rebels are violent and treacherous;
disaster has befallen the Emperor (Zhìzūn).
You and I both owe extraordinary gratitude to the late Emperor.
How can we not step forward for the Sovereign
to avenge this shame and enmity?"
Lóngzhī replied:
"The national shame and personal grievance
pain me to the bone marrow.
To seize the opportunity and act,
now is truly the time."
They then settled their plans with Gān and the others,
attacked the provincial capital by night,
and conquered it.
Gān and the others, knowing Lóngzhī was highly trusted by his local community,
then nominated him as Cìshǐ.
Lóngzhī devoted himself fully to comforting and pacifying the people,
and everyone felt joy.
Soon after, Gāozǔ came out of Jìnyáng heading east.
Lóngzhī sent his son Zǐhuì to respectfully welcome him at Fǔkǒu,
and Gāozǔ greatly commended this.
Upon arriving at Xìndū,
he gathered the chief military officers and civil officials from the various provinces and commanderies and discussed, saying:
"The treacherous barbarian Ěrzhū Zhào is utterly vicious and tyrannical,
unacceptable to Heaven and Earth,
and cast aside by gods and men.
Now, uprisings are spreading everywhere;
this is the time for Heaven to destroy them.
I wish to eliminate these fierce Jié with you gentlemen.
Wherein lies the strategy?"
Lóngzhī replied:
"The Ěrzhū are brutal and tyrannical;
their destruction by Heaven is imminent.
With angered spirits and resentful people,
their followers defect and relatives abandon them.
Although they command heavy troops,
their strength is easily transformed into weakness.
Furthermore, Your Highness is devoted to the imperial house,
and has been the first to raise the righteous banner.
Among the people of the world,
who would not rally and look up to you?
I urge Your Highness not to hesitate."
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
he was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Lìbù Shàngshū.
Ěrzhū Zhào and others encamped at Guǎng'ē.
In the tenth month,
Gāozǔ engaged them in battle
and utterly routed them.
Lóngzhī was then sent with the Staff of Authority as Běidào Dàshǐ (Grand Envoy of the Northern Circuit).
When Gāozǔ was about to attack Ěrzhū Zhào and the others at Hán Líng,
he left Lóngzhī to guard Yèchéng.
When Ěrzhū Zhào and the others fled,
Lóngzhī was made acting governor of Jì Zhōu,
and subsequently took charge of over thirty thousand surrendered captives,
distributing them among the various provinces.
Soon after, he was summoned to serve as Shìzhōng.
At this time, Gāozǔ led his army back from Luòyáng to Yè.
When Lóngzhī was about to proceed to the capital,
he took the opportunity to pay his respects and
addressed Gāozǔ, saying:
"Húxī Chūn, Hèbá Shèng, Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì, and others formerly served the Ěrzhū clan.
In the middle of the chaos, they became estranged,
but when you attacked Zhòngyuǎn,
they allied with him again.
These suspicious and ruthless people
have boundless ambitions.
Moreover, Chìliè Yánqìng
and Hóu Niànxián are both in the capital.
If Your Highness grants them status and rank,
these men will certainly sow the seeds of disaster."
Gāozǔ pondered overnight and then said to Lóngzhī:
"The words the Shìzhōng spoke yesterday truly show profound foresight."
Soon after, he was enfeoffed as Āndé Jùn Gōng,
with a stipend of two thousand households,
and promoted to the rank of Yítóng Sānsī.
At that time, the court discussed that since Ěrzhū Róng had aided the previous dynasty in establishing itself,
he should be enshrined and worshipped in the ancestral temple of Emperor Míng.
Lóngzhī argued:
"Róng, as a minister,
personally carried out murder and rebellion.
How can one who harmed the mother of the man
be worshipped alongside the son?
Searching ancient records and inquiring today,
I have not seen the righteousness of this."
His opinion was adopted.
An edict commanded Lóngzhī to participate in discussions at Línzhǐ Gé
to establish new regulations.
His wife, née Zǔ, was posthumously granted the title of Fànyáng Jùn Jūn.
Lóngzhī submitted a memorial requesting that his previous noble titles, Fùchéng Zǐ and Wǔchéng Zǐ, be transferred to his nephew Xiàowǎn and others.
The court praised his action and complied.
Later, he was framed by Húxī Chūn and others before the Emperor of Wèi,
and he fled back to his hometown.
Gāozǔ, knowing he had been falsely accused,
summoned him to Jìnyáng.
The Emperor of Wèi subsequently summoned him back to his original post,
but Lóngzhī firmly declined to go.
He was then made acting Cìshǐ of Bīng Zhōu.
Dǎn, Prince of Qīnghé of Wèi, was Dà Sīmǎ.
Lóngzhī was his Zhǎngshǐ.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
he returned to serve as Shìzhōng,
and participated in the discussion concerning moving the capital.
Emperor Jìng of Wèi issued an edict making him Shìjiǎng (Imperial Lecturer).
He was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū,
given the additional post of Shìzhōng,
and used his current rank to govern Jì Zhōu (Jì Province).
Lù Shàozūn of Yángpíng gathered a crowd and rebelled.
He called himself Xíngtái.
He broke through Bólíng Commandery in Dìng Zhōu,
captured the Tàishǒu Gāo Yǒnglè,
and invaded Jì Zhōu from the south.
Lóngzhī ordered his subordinates, including Chánglè Tàishǒu Gāo Jǐng, to attack and defeat the rebels,
capturing Shàozūn alive
and sending him to Jìnyáng.
At the beginning of the Yuánxiàng era,
he was appointed Jì Zhōu Cìshǐ,
and soon received the title of Kāifǔ.
At that time, when brave men were first being recruited,
the Dūdū Bèi Bā, Gāo Fǎxióng, Fēng Zǐyuán, and others, unwilling to serve on distant garrisons,
gathered followers and caused trouble.
Lóngzhī led the provincial army and defeated and pacified them.
In the first year of Xīnghé (539 CE),
he was again summoned to serve as Shìzhōng.
Lóngzhī had always won the hearts of his local community.
Having frequently governed his native province,
he focused carefully on comforting and nurturing the people.
Officials and citizens remembered him fondly
and erected a stele praising his virtues.
