He was transferred to govern Liáng Zhōu,
and later governed Jì Zhōu.
He was then summoned and appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
At the beginning of the Wǔdìng era,
Gāo Zhòngmì, the Cìshǐ of Běiyù Zhōu, was planning rebellion.
He secretly sent envoys to communicate with the powerful families in Jì Zhōu,
asking them to act as internal support.
The frivolous element
was considerably agitated.
An edict commanded Lóngzhī to travel rapidly by post-horse to comfort and pacify them,
and stability was achieved.
Shìzōng sent a secret letter to Lóngzhī, saying:
"Those factions associated with Zhòngmì who have sided with the evil ones in the West
should have their entire families arrested
to serve as a warning for the future."
Lóngzhī believed that since the merciful decree had already been implemented,
it was unreasonable to revoke it later.
If arrests were made now,
it would show the people a lack of trust.
Should this cause disturbance or panic,
the resulting damage would be substantial.
He therefore memorialized Gāozǔ,
and the matter was consequently suspended.
Fēng Lóngzhī, since the initial establishment of the banner of righteousness,
first participated in the strategic planning.
His brilliant schemes and clever calculations,
were secretly reported (to the emperor),
written by hand and destroyed after drafting,
were rarely known to outsiders.
Gāozǔ praised his loyalty and meticulousness,
and often followed his advice.
He was subsequently appointed to manage the affairs of Jìzhōu while retaining his original office,
then transferred to Qízhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third year of Wǔdìng (545 CE), he died in office,
aged sixty-one.
An imperial edict ordered the dispatch of the Secretariat Director, Shén Guì, to offer condolences,
and bestowed 500 lengths of cloth (as funeral aid).

He was posthumously granted the titles of Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Cāng Yíng Èrzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Area Commander-in-chief of Cāng and Yíng prefectures), Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn (General of Cavalry), Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yíngzhōu), and Sītú Gōng (Minister of Education).
Gāozǔ, considering that Lóngzhī's merits and long service
were not fully reflected by the posthumous honors,

petitioned again, requesting that he be posthumously granted Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Jì Yíng Cāng Qí Jì Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Area Commander-in-chief of Jì, Yíng, Cāng, Qí, and Jì prefectures), Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jìzhōu), and Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian).
The rest [of the honors] remained as before.
His posthumous title was Xuānyì.
Later, when Gāozǔ arrived at the border of Jìzhōu,
and stopped at Jiāojīn,
remembering Lóngzhī,
he looked and spoke to the Acting Governor of Jìzhōu, Sīmǎ Zǐrú, saying:
"The Duke (Fēng Lóngzhī) accumulated virtue and practiced benevolence,
his physique was robust, and his nature was perceptive.
Since taking charge of military and state affairs,
it has been nearly twenty years.
Through separation, hardship, and anxiety,
he remained constant from beginning to end.
Because his loyalty and trustworthiness could be relied upon,
I intended to entrust him with future affairs.
How could I have expected that the reward for goodness would be unproven,
and that he would suddenly pass away?
Whenever I speak of this loyal and worthy man,
it is truly painful and regrettable."
He wept for him.
He ordered the Military Advisor Sòng Zhòngxiàn to offer a grand sacrifice (tàiláo) at his resting place.
His eldest son died early.
His second son, Zǐhuì, succeeded him.
Zǐhuì,
courtesy name Zhòngzǎo,
his childhood name was Sāo.
His nature was harmonious and orderly,
and he possessed administrative capacity.
He started his career as Mìshū Lángzhōng.
When Ěrzhū Zhào murdered Emperor Zhuāng of Wèi,
he and his father Lóngzhī raised the banner of righteousness in Xìndū,
and were dispatched as envoys to Gāozǔ.
Upon arriving at Xìndū,
he was summoned and appointed as the Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) under the Kāifǔ,
and also managed the secretarial duties.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng (531 CE),
he was transferred to be the Chief Clerk to the Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù),
and was given the title Fúbō Jiāngjūn.
He followed Gāozǔ in the campaign against Ěrzhū Zhào.
When Zhōngshān was pacified,
and the army returned,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Chángshì and Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
concurrently leading the Zhōngshū Shèrén office.
He left office due to mourning for his mother,
but soon resumed his original post.
During the Tàichāng period,
he followed Gāozǔ in stabilizing the prefectures of Bīng, Fén, and Sì,
and pacifying Ěrzhū Zhào and the Shānhú (Mountain Barbarians), among others.
He was promoted to Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
At the end of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's reign,
when Húsī Chūn and other flattering favorites held power,
his father Lóngzhī, due to suspicion and jealousy,
feared trouble and secretly returned to his hometown.
Zǐhuì also abandoned his office and returned with him.
At the beginning of Xiàojìng's reign,
he was concurrently appointed Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and, alongside Tàicháng Qīng Lǐ Yuánzhōng and others, carried the credentials (chíjié) on an official mission,
to observe and inspect local customs,
and inquire about the people's sufferings.
Upon returning,
he proceeded to Jìnyáng,
and followed Gāozǔ on the campaign against Xiàzhōu.
In the second year (of Wǔdìng),
he was appointed Wèi Jiāngjūn and Píngyáng Tàishǒu,
and soon after was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
Huòtài Shān, located on the northern border of Jìnzhōu,
was traditionally known as the Thousand Li Path.
Its slopes and ridges were high and steep,
and whenever large armies traveled along it,
the soldiers and horses suffered greatly.
Zǐhuì petitioned Gāozǔ,
requesting that a new road be opened in the valley east of the old path.
Gāozǔ agreed,
and ordered Zǐhuì to supervise the laborers from Fén and Jìn prefectures in the construction.
It was completed within ten days.
Gāozǔ personally commanded the six armies,
and when he passed along the new road,
he praised its convenience and relief (from hardship).
He bestowed two hundred *hú* of grain upon Zǐhuì.
Later, the great army campaigned to retake Dōngyōng,
and pacified Cháibì, as well as Qiáoshān,
Zǐgǔ, and Jiàngshǔ, among others.
Zǐhuì, acting as Administrator, served as the vanguard to comfort the troops,
raise soldiers, and transport provisions,
so the soldiers lacked nothing.
At the beginning of Xīnghé,
he was summoned from his prefecture and appointed as the Lìbù Lángzhōng for the Dà Xíngtái.
In the first year of Wǔdìng (543 CE),
when Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled in Wǔláo and went west,
Emperor Wén of Zhōu (Yǔwén Tàijù) led his forces in an invasion eastward.
Gāozǔ defeated him at Máng Shān,
and, capitalizing on the victory, drove straight onward,
and consequently reached Tóngguān.
Some advised against continuing the advance (exhausting the troops and displaying excessive military power).
Gāozǔ summoned all the officials to discuss whether to proceed or stop.
Zǐhuì spoke, saying:
"The enemy commander's talent is not that of a human hero.
He merely stole his title,
and thus dared to lead fugitives and rebels,
sending them to their deaths between the Yī and Chán rivers.
The Way of Heaven brings calamity upon wickedness,
and they scattered in a single morning.
Although he barely escaped with his life,
his spirit and courage are completely lost.
The unification of chariots and writing (i.e., the realm),
is precisely achievable today.
If Heaven grants it and we do not take it,
we will instead incur blame.
Opportunities are hard to come by and easy to lose.
In the past, when Wèi Zǔ (Cáo Cāo) pacified Hànzhōng,
he failed to capitalize on the victory to take Bāshǔ (Sichuan).
The mistake lay in his hesitation,
and the regret was insurmountable.
I earnestly hope that Your Highness will not harbor doubts."
Gāozǔ highly agreed with this.
However, because it was the height of summer,
he decided to plan for a later campaign,
and subsequently ordered the army to return.
In the third year (545 CE),
he left office due to the mourning for his father.
In the fourth year (546 CE),
when Gāozǔ campaigned in the west,
he was raised [from mourning] to serve as Dà Dūdū,
leading the Jìzhōu troops to Yè,
and followed Gāozǔ from Fǔkǒu westward toward Jìnzhōu,
joining the main army at Yùbì.
Zǐhuì was again appointed Lìbù Lángzhōng of the Dà Xíngtái.
When Gāozǔ became gravely ill,
the army returned to Jìnyáng.
Zǐhuì was led into the inner chamber,
where he personally received secret instructions,
and was entrusted with the mission to Shāndōng (east of the mountains),
to soothe and stabilize the prefectures.
When Gāozǔ died,
the mourning was kept secret and not yet announced.
Shìzōng appointed Zǐhuì as Bóhǎi Tàishǒu,
and ordered him to hasten to his post by courier relay.
Shìzōng personally took his hand and said:
"I truly know that this prefecture does not match your merit or prestige,
but the current situation is unstable,
and requires you to pacify and stabilize it.
Moreover, 'to wear embroidered robes and travel by day,'
is something valued by the ancients.
Plan well,
and pacify the coastal region.
There is no need to trouble yourself with learning the protocols of ordinary Administrators who report to the provincial capital."
He was further permitted to gather a personal military contingent of one thousand men.
Later, his rank was advanced by one grade,
and he was promoted to Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Tiānbǎo (551 CE),
he was appointed Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ.
In the third year (552 CE),
he repeatedly managed the affairs of Nán Qīngzhōu twice while retaining his original office.
In the fourth year (553 CE),
he was dismissed due to an incident.
In the sixth year (555 CE),
he managed the affairs of Nán Yǎnzhōu,
and was subsequently appointed Chíjié Hǎizhōu Cìshǐ,
but did not take up the post.
In the seventh year,
he was transferred and appointed Cìshǐ of Hézhōu.
Not long after arriving at the prefecture,
he happened upon Xiāo Guǐ (蕭軌), Péi Yīngqǐ (裴英起), and others being defeated and destroyed east of the river (Jiāngdōng).
Xíngtái Sīmǎ Gōng (司馬恭) mobilized Lìyáng,
and returned directly to Shòuchūn.
The border regions were greatly alarmed.
Furthermore, the weapons and equipment in the prefecture
had nearly all been taken by the army,
and much of the city walls, moats, and watchtowers
were damaged or ruined.
Zǐhuì (子繪) therefore repaired and constructed the city walls, moats, and watchtowers,
mended the military equipment,
and prepared all necessities for defense,
and the populace gradually felt secure.
Soon after, an imperial edict commanded the construction of ships and vessels in the prefecture.
Zǐhuì (子繪) served as the Grand Envoy,
overseeing the whole project.
Emperor Wǔ of Chén (Chén Wǔdì) had once dispatched his General of the Palace Guard, Xú Dù (徐度), and others to lead light boats from Shàkǒu, pass through Dōngguān, and enter Cháohú,
directly attacking Héféi,
planning to burn the ships and vessels.
During the first watch of the night, they secretly raided the area beneath the city walls.
Zǐhuì (子繪) led his officers and soldiers in close combat,
and the Chén (陳) forces fled.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to be Cìshǐ of Zhèngzhōu.
Zǐhuì (子繪) was insightful in governance,
excelled at conciliation and pacification,
and wherever he governed, be it a prefecture or a commandery,
the area achieved stability.
He was summoned to serve as Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ of the Sītú,
acting as the Prefect of Wèi (Wèiyǐn).
At the beginning of Qiánmíng (乾明),
he was transferred to Dà Sīnóng,
and soon after officially appointed as Wèiyǐn.
During Huángjiàn (皇建),
he was granted the title General-in-Chief of Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn).
In the second year of Dàníng (大寧),
he was promoted to Minister of the Department of the Capital (Dūguān Shàngshū).
When Gāo Guīyàn (高歸彥) rebelled,
Zǐhuì (子繪) was summoned to an audience in the Zhāoyáng Diàn.
The Emperor personally issued an edict to Zǐhuì (子繪), saying:
"Jìzhōu (冀州) is very close to the capital region,
and Gāo Guīyàn (歸彥) dares to indulge in vicious defiance.
I have already commanded the Grand Marshal, Prince of Píngyuán, Duàn Xiàoxiān (段孝先), to command the main forces,
moving swiftly when the opportunity arises;
and the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Prince of Dōng'ān, Lóu Ruì (婁叡), to lead the various armies,
following closely in succession.
You, Sir, come from a distinguished lineage for generations,
and your kindness is widespread in that prefecture.
Therefore, I send you to participate and advise in military affairs,
offering comfort and pacification as appropriate.
You should implement good strategies
to fulfill the trust placed in you."
On that very day, he was rushed by relay post to the army.
Zǐhuì’s (子繪) grandfather had served in that native prefecture for generations,
and the common people had always attached themselves to the family.
Once he arrived,
he toured the city, explaining the consequences of rebellion and loyalty.
The commoners and officials surrendered and submitted,
succeeding one another day and night.
The movements of the rebels,
both minor and major, were inevitably known.
After the rebellion was suppressed,
an edict instructed Zǐhuì (子繪) to temporarily manage the affairs of the prefecture.
Soon after, he was summoned back
and commanded to deliberate with the high officials on fixing the legal code.
He was granted the title Yítóng Sānsī.
Later, when the Tujue (Tūjué) entered and pressed Jìnyáng (晉陽),
an imperial decree ordered Zǐhuì (子繪) to act as Prefect of Huáizhōu (懷州),
traveling by relay carriage to take up the post.
Returning, he served as Minister of the Department of the Seven Military Affairs (Qībīng Shàngshū),
and was transferred to Minister of the Department of Sacrifices (Cíbù Shàngshū).
In the third year of Héqīng (河清), he died suddenly of illness,
aged fifty.
Shìzǔ (世祖) deeply lamented his passing.

He was posthumously granted the titles Commissioner with Imperial Authority (Shǐchíjié), Military Supervisor of Yíngzhōu and Jìzhōu, Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu, Kàifǔ Yítóng, and Right Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè),
with the posthumous name Jiǎn (簡).
His son, Bǎogài (寶蓋), inherited the title.
At the end of Wǔpíng (武平),
he was Tōngzhí Chángshì.
Zǐhuì’s (子繪) younger brother, Zǐxiù (子繡),
served during Wǔpíng (武平) as
Grand Administrator of Bóhǎi and Cìshǐ of Huòzhōu.
When the Chén (陳) general Wú Míngchè (吳明徹) invaded Huáinán,
Zǐxiù’s (子繡) city fell,
and he was sent to Yángzhōu.
After Qí (齊) fell,
he escaped and returned.
At the beginning of Kāihuáng (開皇) under the Suí (隋) dynasty,
he died while serving as Cìshǐ of Tōngzhōu.
Zǐxiù (子繡) had a refined and scholarly appearance,
but his chivalrous nature was easily provoked.
The Minister of Works, Lóu Dìngyuǎn (婁定遠),
who was the son-in-law of Zǐxiù’s (子繡) older brother,
served as Cìshǐ of Yíngzhōu.
When Zǐxiù (子繡) was in Bóhǎi,
Lóu Dìngyuǎn (定遠) visited him.
While feasting with his wife and various daughters,
their conversation and banter showed a slight disrespect.
Zǐxiù (子繡) became enraged,
beat the drum to gather the troops, intending to attack Lóu Dìngyuǎn (之).
In a short time,
several thousand soldiers arrived,
along with nearly a thousand horses.
Lóu Dìngyuǎn (定遠) removed his cap, bowed, and offered an apology.
Only after a long time did Zǐxiù (之) release him.
Lóngzhī’s (隆之) younger brother, Yánzhī (延之),
courtesy name Zǔyè (祖業).
Since youth, he was perceptive and discerning,
and useful to the state.
He started his career as Yuánwài Láng.
At the beginning of Zhōngxīng (中興),
he was appointed General of Loyal Steadfastness.
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed him Grand Master of the Left of the Court of Imperial Insignia in the Department of the Grand Secretariat,
enfeoffed him as Viscount of Jiáchéng County,
and put him in charge of Bóhǎi Commandery affairs.
As a military supervisor he followed Lóu Zhāo (婁昭) in attacking Fán Zihú (樊子鵠).
When the matter was settled,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
Yánzhī (延之) loved wealth and profit,
and while in the prefecture, he accepted and collected many gifts.
Later, he was put in charge of Jìnzhōu affairs.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) returned after being defeated at Shāyuàn (沙苑),
Yánzhī (延之) abandoned the prefecture and fled north.
Gāozǔ (高祖) was furious.
All others guilty of the same crime were executed,
but for the sake of Lóngzhī (隆之),
he alone was spared.
He died in the second year of Xīnghé (興和),
aged fifty-four.

He was posthumously granted the titles Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Military Supervisor of the Forces of the Three Prefectures of Jìzhōu, Yīnzhōu, and Yíngzhōu, General-in-Chief of Cavalry, Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), Minister of the Masses (Sītú), and Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu,
with the posthumous name Wéngōng (文恭).
His son, Xiàozuǎn (孝纂), inherited the title.
Lóngzhī’s (隆之) nephew, Xiàowǎn (孝琬),
courtesy name Zǐqiàn (子蒨).
His father, Zǔ Cáo (祖曹),
was Chief Clerk of the General Who Pacifies the North in Jìzhōu under the Wèi (魏).
Due to Lóngzhī’s (隆之) merit in aiding the establishment of the dynasty,
he was posthumously granted Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu and Minister of the Palace Affairs.
Xiàowǎn (孝琬) was orphaned at the age of seven,
and was solely raised and nurtured by Lóngzhī (隆之),
who had extremely deep parental love for him.
At age sixteen,
he was appointed Chief Clerk by his native prefecture.
In the second year of Yǒngxī (永熙) of the Wèi (魏),
Lóngzhī (隆之) petitioned for him to be granted his father's noble rank, Viscount of Fùchéng.
In the third year,
he was formally appointed as Counsellor to the Minister in the Kàifǔ establishment.
During Tiānpíng (天平),
he served as General of Light Chariots and Chief Clerk to the Sītú.
During Wǔdìng (武定),
he became Chief Clerk in the Kàifǔ establishment of Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖),
and was promoted to Gentleman-General,
concurrently leading the Crown Prince’s Equerry.
He died in the second year of Tiānbǎo (天保),
being thirty-six years old at the time.
The Emperor heard of it and sighed with regret.
He was posthumously granted General of the Left and Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Shǎoqīng).
Xiàowǎn (孝琬) was placid by nature
and quite fond of literature and poetry.
The Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince, Xíng Shào (邢卲), and the Minister of the Department of the Seven Military Affairs, Wáng Xīn (王昕), were both eminent and talented predecessors.
Although there was a great difference in age and rank between them and Xiàowǎn (孝琬),
they met later in life,
and their friendship became very deep.
When Xiàowǎn’s (孝琬) coffin was taken home,
the two men escorted it outside the suburbs,
weeping mournfully and heartbrokenly,
moving passersby.
Xiàowǎn’s (孝琬) younger brother, Xiàoyǎn (孝琰),
courtesy name Shìguāng (士光).
In his youth, he was refined in appearance and aspired to scholarship,
possessing a noble demeanor.
At age sixteen,
he was appointed Chief Clerk of the prefecture,
and formally appointed Secretary.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (天保),
he became a Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Crown Prince.
He moved in and out of the Eastern Palace,
and held a high reputation.
When his mother died,
he resigned his post.
He was appointed Judicial Counsellor of Jìnzhōu.
Soon after, he was summoned back
and reappointed Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Crown Prince.
At the beginning of Qiánmíng (乾明),
he became Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
At the beginning of Huángjiàn (皇建),
he served as Aide to the Minister of Works and Vice Director of the Imperial Library.
He served as Palace Attendant Consultant
and headed the mission to Chén (陳).
After he had already departed,
he was remotely granted the title Vice Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
Upon returning,
he was stripped of his title due to an offense.
In the third year of Tiāntǒng (天統),
he was appointed Director of the Personnel Department of Bīngshěng and Companion to the Prince of Nányáng.
He proceeded to Jìnyáng (晉陽) to manage confidential affairs.
Hé Shìkāi’s mother died.
All those who relied on him went to mourn and weep.
Among the wealthy merchants in Yèzhōng, Dīng Zōu and Yán Xīng, etc., all acted as dutiful sons,
and there was one scholar
who also wept within the prescribed bounds.
Xiàoyǎn entered to offer condolences,
and upon exiting, he said to someone:
“South of Yán Xīng
and north of Dīng Zōu,
there is a court official
wailing most sorrowfully.”
Those who heard it spread the word.
Shìkāi knew of it and was greatly enraged.
Later, when the Huángmén Láng Lǐ Huái impeached Nányáng Wáng Chuò for being self-indulgent and arbitrary,
Shìkāi took the opportunity to slander him, saying:
“Xiàoyǎn went out with Chuò,
riding his secondary horse,
leaving his ranks,
and chatting idly elsewhere.”
At that time, Xiàoyǎn’s daughter was the Fànyáng Wángfēi,
and because of a ritual matter, she took leave to bid farewell.
The emperor then had him flogged with a horsewhip over a hundred times,
and expelled him.
He also sent Gāo Ānàgōng to flog him another fifty times,
almost to the point of death.
Upon returning to the capital,
he was in the Jíshū Shěng, both above and below (meaning, involved in its affairs),
and from then on, he fell into obscurity.
After Shìkāi’s death,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
Later, when diplomatic relations were established with the Zhōu dynasty,
Zhào Yànshēn recommended him,
and an imperial edict appointed him deputy envoy to Zhōu.
Zǔ Tǐng, assisting in government,
again recommended that he enter the Wénlín Guǎn
to compile the Yùlǎn.
Xiàoyǎn’s literary style was not outstanding,
but he established himself through his elegant demeanor,
his skill in witty conversation,
his calm and graceful bearing,
and his dignified movements and conduct.
Everyone admired him.
He once said to Zǔ Tǐng:
“You are a chancellor of official attire,
different from others.”
Those close to the emperor heard this
and greatly resented it.
Soon after, he was appointed concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng with his original office.
Many of his impeachments
were in accordance with imperial wishes.
At that time, there was a Buddhist monk, Tánxiàn,
who was favored by the Huángtàihòu.
His rewards and grants were lavish,
and his carriages and attire were excessive.
He also requested to be Shāmén Tǒng.
The Hòuzhǔ did not intend to permit it,
but the empress dowager desired it,
so he obtained the position.
However, the Hòuzhǔ always resented him.
Because there were monks and nuns who sued each other over other matters,
their testimonies implicated Tánxiàn.
The emperor ordered the relevant officials to investigate.
Xiàoyǎn investigated his acceptance of bribes
and brought him to extreme justice.
Consequently, his home was searched,
and many rare treasures were found,
all of which were confiscated by the state.
Because of this, he was formally appointed Zuǒchéng
and was ordered to report on matters of the Ménxià.
His nature was quite arrogant and aloof,
and he did not conform to current customs.
As imperial favor gradually increased,
he became even more conceited and boastful.
His actions were slow and deliberate,
and he yielded to no one.
Those who knew him disdained him.
He died along with Cuī Jìshū and others for righteous remonstrance,
at the age of fifty-one.
His two sons, Kāifǔ Xíngcānjūn Jūnquè and Jūnjìng, were exiled to the northern frontier.
His younger sons, Jūnyán and Jūnzàn, were castrated in the cánsì.
During the defeat of Nán'ān,
Jūnquè and the other were both executed.
The historiographer says: Gāo and Fēng, the two gentlemen,
without an inch of land or a single resource,
rose with upraised arms in Héshuò,
intending to perform loyal service to the emperor
to avenge the murder of Zhuāngdì.
Was this not grand!
After conquering their native province,
they completed their act of yielding virtue,
unlike Hán Fù who was intimidated by Yuán Shào’s might.
However, their strength was inferior to the heroes of the time,
and their talents were not for a fated age.
Therefore, they welcomed the imperial banners
to fulfill their original plan.
Gāozǔ, relying on this,
then achieved hegemony.
Furthermore, with Āng’s courage and strength,
his spirit surmounted all things,
at Hánlíng,
he was like wind flying and lightning striking.
Thus, the original meritorious achievement of the Qí clan
was by this one family alone.
But because they were not from Yǐngchuān,
nor old acquaintances from Fēngpèi,
their trusted position
was not fully accepted.
Their memorials were exposed,
and heavenly punishment was carried out through others.
The extent of wrongful injustice
could not exceed this.
His son Huì’s talent and ability
could be said to uphold the family legacy,
passing down virtue for generations.
This is indeed commendable.
Eulogy says: How glorious Wénzhāo,
whose heroic plans were fulfilled.
How brilliant Zhōngwǔ,
whose heroic talents surpassed the world.
The cruelty of the Ménxià,
advance or retreat, all were in peril.
By the banks of the Yellow River,
they trod righteousness and lost their lives.
Lord Fēng, how lofty,
together they weathered the difficult times.
Compared to inheriting shining virtue,
their brilliance daily renewed.

Biographies Chapter 14: Lǐ Yuánzhōng (Cousin Mì, Kinsman Mǐn, Uncle Jǐngyí) Lú Wénwěi (Grandson Xúnzǔ, Kinsman Yǒng) Lǐ Yìshēn
Lǐ Yuánzhōng
was a native of Bǎirén, Zhàojùn.
His great-grandfather, Líng,
was the Wèi Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ and Jùlù Gōng.
His grandfather, Huī,
was Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn.
His father, Xiǎnfǔ,
was Ānzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yuánzhōng, from a young age, cultivated his aspirations and conduct.
He was known for his filial piety during his mother’s mourning.
He inherited the title Píngjí Zǐ.
When Wèi Qīnghé Wáng Yì was Sīkōng,
he appointed him Shìcáo Cānjūn;
when Yì was promoted to Tàiwèi,
he again recommended him as Chángliú Cānjūn.
Later, Yì became Tàifù,
and soon received an imperial edict appointing him Dà Dūdū for the construction of the Míngtáng.
He again invited Yuánzhōng to be his Zhǔbù.
Yuánzhōng had a rough understanding of historical books and yin-yang numerology.
He could play the gǔzhēng,
and also enjoyed archery and pellet shooting.
He was skilled in ingenuity.
He encountered his mother’s mourning,
and left his post.
Not long after,
the Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Ānlè Wáng Jiàn, invited him to be his Fǔ Sīmǎ,
but Yuánzhōng, due to his grief and difficulties,
firmly declined the appointment.
Initially, Yuánzhōng’s mother was old and frequently ill,
so he devoted himself to medicine,
studying for many years,
and thus became skilled in medical techniques.
His nature was benevolent and forgiving.
When he saw sick people,
regardless of their status,
he would treat them.
His family was originally wealthy,
and his family members in his hometown
often lent money for profit.
Yuánzhōng often burned the contracts to waive their debts.
The villagers greatly respected him.
During the reign of Wèi Xiàomíng,
bandits rose up everywhere.
Five hundred men from Qīnghé were garrisoned in the west.
Upon their return, they passed through Nánzhàojùn,
and because the road was blocked, they jointly sought refuge with Yuánzhōng.
They offered a thousand bolts of silk.
Yuánzhōng only accepted one bolt,
slaughtered five sheep to feed them,
and sent a servant as a guide,
saying:
“If you encounter bandits,
just say that Lǐ Yuánzhōng sent you.”
The servant did as he was told, and the bandits all moved aside.
Early in the Yǒng'ān [period],
he was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Nánzhàojùn,
but because he was fond of wine, he had no administrative achievements.
When Luòyáng was overthrown,
and Emperor Zhuāng died in confinement,
Yuán Zhōng abandoned his post and returned home,
secretly planning a righteous uprising.
Meeting Gāozǔ as he led his troops eastward,
he immediately went personally to pay respects and welcome him.
Riding an open carriage,
carrying an unpainted zither and cloudy wine to meet Gāozǔ,
he then presented stratagems of maneuvering,
fully expressing his sincerity,
and was deeply welcomed and accepted.
At that time, the Inspector Ěrzhū Yǔshēng blocked the military route and occupied the prefecture.
Yuán Zhōng first gathered followers at Xīshān,
then joined with the main army,
and captured and executed Yǔshēng.
He was immediately ordered to act as the governor of Yīnzhōu.
Early in the Zhōngxīng [period],
he was appointed as General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn) and Minister of the Palace Guard (Wèiwèi Qīng).
In the second year,
he was transferred to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng) and Grand Arbiter of Yīnzhōu (Yīnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
Later, seeing that his cousin Jǐn was older,
he yielded the position of Arbiter (Zhōngzhèng) to him.
Soon after, he was granted the title General Who Attacks the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn).
When Emperor Wǔ was about to take a consort,
who was Gāozǔ's eldest daughter,
an imperial decree ordered Yuán Zhōng and the Director of the Department of State Affairs Yuán Luó to offer the betrothal gifts in Jìnyáng.
Whenever Gāozǔ discussed old affairs during banquets,
he would clap his hands and laugh happily, saying:
"This man forced me to raise troops."
He was bestowed one white horse.
Yuán Zhōng jestingly said to Gāozǔ:
"If you do not grant me the position of Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng),
I should look for another place to establish righteousness."
Gāozǔ replied:
"I am not worried about there being no place to establish righteousness;
I am only afraid that such an old man [like you] cannot be encountered."
Yuán Zhōng said:
"It is only because this old man is difficult to encounter
that I have not left."
He then stroked Gāozǔ's beard and laughed heartily.
Gāozǔ fully understood his refined intent
and deeply valued and esteemed him.
Later, when Gāozǔ escorted the Empress
and hunted in Jìnzé,
Yuán Zhōng's horse fell, and he was injured.
At that moment, he collapsed and lost consciousness,
and only revived after a long time.
Gāozǔ personally attended to him.
That year, he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Jìnyáng County (Jìnyáng Xiàn Bó),
with an estate of five hundred households.
Later, due to a minor offense, he lost his post.
At that time, the court was divided and estranged,
and the righteous standard was often met with suspicion and obstruction.
Hú Sīchūn and others believed that Yuán Zhōng cared little for fame and profit,
and furthermore, did not dwell on worldly affairs,
therefore he was not in a position to be suspected or envied.
Soon after, he concurrently held the position of Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
Early in the Tiānpíng [period],
he returned to Tàicháng.
Later, he was granted the title General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
In the fourth year,
he was appointed as an Imperial Commissioner (Shǐ Chíjié) and Inspector of Guāngzhōu (Guāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
At that time, the prefecture suffered from disaster and famine,
and the people all had the look of starvation.
Yuán Zhōng memorialized, requesting relief and loans,
to be collected when autumn came.
He received a reply,
permitting the use of ten thousand *dàn* [of grain].
Yuán Zhōng believed that distributing ten thousand *dàn* to the people,
calculated per family, would be no more than a *shēng* or a *dǒu*,
resulting in only an empty reputation
and not solving their distress.
He therefore issued one hundred fifty thousand *dàn* for relief.
After the matter was concluded, he memorialized the facts,
and the court commended him and did not reprimand him.
Late in the Xīnghé [period],
he was appointed Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng).
Although Yuán Zhōng held an important post,
he never allowed material affairs to trouble his mind;
he only entertained himself with music and wine,
and was mostly always drunk.
He was completely unconcerned
with matters, great or small, of the family.
Within his garden court,
he systematically grew fruits and herbs.
When friends and relatives came to visit,
he would inevitably delay them for feasting and enjoyment.
He often carried a slingshot and a wine gourd,
wandering freely through the neighborhoods.
Whenever he met an assembly for drinking,
he would be perfectly content.
He often openly stated to those in charge:
"My years are gradually growing late,
my ambition and strength have already declined.
I have long disgraced these named offices,
obstructing the path of the worthy.
If the court, through its great benevolence,
is not willing to immediately dismiss me,
I beg to be placed in an idle and superfluous position,
so that I may nurture my remaining years."
In the first year of Wǔdìng,
he was appointed Inspector of Dōngxúzhōu (Dōngxúzhōu Cìshǐ),
but he firmly declined the appointment.
Instead, he was appointed General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn) and Regulator of the Three Dukes (Yítóng Sānsī).
He once presented Emperor Shìzōng with a plate of grapes.
Emperor Shìzōng rewarded him with one hundred bolts of white silk
and sent him a letter saying:
"The Regulator (Yítóng)'s rank is second only to the highest ministers [Tái Xuàn],
his understanding is pure and honest,
serving abroad and entering to attend,
he has experienced all key responsibilities.
Yet his family still possesses neither *dàn* nor *shí* [of grain],
and his rooms are as bare as a hanging chime stone.
Is this not because he values righteousness over wealth
and follows the times while cherishing himself?
I have long esteemed and admired you,
and my praises and sighs are boundless.
I have wished to mark my appreciation,
but though I had the intention, I lacked the means.
Suddenly having received the favor of grapes,
I am truly deeply grateful.
I tentatively use one hundred bolts of silk
to repay your pure virtue."
This shows how much he was valued.
Sūn Téng and Sīmǎ Zǐrú once visited Yuán Zhōng together.
They saw him sitting under a tree,
wrapped in a quilt facing a wine pot,
the courtyard and rooms overgrown and empty.
He said to the two Dukes:
"I did not expect to be pushing aside weeds and vines today."
He then called his wife out,
whose robes did not drag the ground.
The two Dukes looked at each other, sighed, and departed,
lavishly gifting him rice, silk, and clothing.
Yuán Zhōng accepted it and then distributed it.
In the third year,
he again concurrently held the post of Minister of the Palace Guard (Wèiwèi Qīng) with his existing titles.
That year he died in office,
aged sixty.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him five hundred bolts of fine silk,

Imperial Commissioner (Shǐ Chíjié), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Dìng, Jì, Yīn, and Yōu Prefectures (Dū Dìng Jì Yīn Yōu Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnfù), Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn), Minister over the Masses (Sītú), and Inspector of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His posthumous name (shì) was Jìnghuì.
When Yuán Zhōng was first about to take office,
he dreamed that he held a torch and entered his father's tomb.
He awoke in terror in the middle of the night
and considered it extremely ill-omened.
In the morning, he told his teacher
who divined, saying:
"This is greatly auspicious.
This means illuminating your ancestors;
you will ultimately achieve high rank and distinction."
His son Sāo succeeded him.
Sāo,
courtesy name Dékuàng,

possessing talent and skill.
He mastered
various subjects, including musicology and games.
He once collected various sounds
and separately constructed a musical instrument,
which he named the Bāxián (Eight Strings).
People of the time praised his ingenuity.
He started his career as Aide-de-camp to the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Xíng Cānjūn).
Through successive promotions, he became the Grand Administrator of Hénèi,

Upon returning to the capital, he became the Director of the Bureau of Rituals (Yí Cáo Láng) in the Department of State Affairs.

Yuánzhōng’s clan younger brother Mì,
courtesy name Xīyōng,
was a man of Píngjí.
His grandfather Bóyīng,

His father Huàn,
was the Palace Subordinate Censor (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ) and Grand Administrator of Hènnèi,

Mì, in his youth, possessed integrity and moral fiber.
When Ěrzhū Zhào carried out his murderous rebellion,
Mì secretly allied himself with local powerful figures,
and planned countermeasures with Gāo Áng of Bóhǎi.
When Gāozǔ led his forces out to Shāndōng,
Mì joined the righteous uprising with his troops.
He was granted the title of Inspector of Bīngzhōu remotely,
ennobled as the Marquis of Róngchéng County,
with an estate of four hundred households.
When Ěrzhū Zhào reached Guǎng'ā,
Gāozǔ ordered Mì to recruit five thousand soldiers from Yīn and Dìng prefectures to garrison the two passes of Huángshā and Jǐngxíng.
When Zhào was defeated at Hánlíng and returned to Jìnyáng,
Mì followed the army to suppress Zhào.
Gāozǔ subsequently appointed Xuē Xiūyì to manage the affairs of Bīngzhōu,

He was later appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
He served in the prefecture for over ten years,
and was very skilled in methods for securing the frontier,
his prestige and credibility being known even in foreign territories.
Gāozǔ frequently sent personal letters expressing commendation and inquiry,

When Hóu Jǐng rebelled externally,

When Jǐng was defeated and Mì returned to court,

In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,

He died.
He was posthumously granted the titles of President of the Board of Palace Affairs (Diànzhōng Shàngshū) and Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Mì’s nature was upright and honest,
and he possessed good conduct.
Because his mother had been ill for years,
though she received treatment from famous physicians,
she did not recover.
Consequently, he thoroughly studied medical classics,
gained complete understanding of acupuncture and medicines,
and his mother's illness was cured.
Everyone at the time admired his brilliant understanding,
and because of this, he also became famous for his medical skills.
(Missing name/text) served as the Acting Marshal of the Guard (Xíng Hùjūn Sīmǎ) at the end of the Wèi dynasty,
and Grand Administrator of Wǔyì.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was the Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ).
During the Dàníng and Wǔpíng eras,
he was the Grand Administrator of Qīnghé and Guǎngpíng Commanderies,

His son Dàoqiān,

Dàoqiān’s younger brother Dàozhēn,

Yuánzhōng’s clan member Mǐn,
courtesy name Mólián,
was imposing and outstanding in appearance,
and was regarded as extraordinary by his contemporaries.
In his youth, he had great ambitions,
but even at forty years of age,
he still did not serve in the prefectures or commanderies,
only attracting cunning and chivalrous men,

At the end of the Xiàochāng era,
when armies rose throughout the land,

When the bandit leaders Xiānyú Xiūlǐ and Máo Pǔxián rebelled,

Zhì had long heard of Mǐn’s reputation,
and summoned him to concurrently serve as Commander of the Tent Guard (Zhàngnèi Tǒngjūn).
When the army reached Hūtuó,
the bandits came to meet them in battle,
and Zhì’s army was defeated by the bandits.
Mǐn consequently returned home.
The Prince of Ānlè, Yuán Jiàn, served as the Grand Director of the Northern Circuit (Běidào Dà Xíngtái).
When he reached Yè,
because the bandit forces were flourishing and strong,

He sent an envoy to summon Mǐn,
and memorialized to appoint him to Cavalry Attendant (Wǔqí Chángshì), Acting Imperial Envoy (Jiǎ Jié), and Separate General (Bié Jiàng),
to garrison the eastern outer wall of Yèchéng.
When Gě Róng besieged Xìndū,
the remaining partisans plundered southward,
and the area north of Yángpíng
was entirely controlled by the bandits.
Jiàn ordered Mǐn to serve as the vanguard,
to suppress them separately,
and he achieved considerable kills and captures.
When Jiàn plotted rebellion,
Mǐn pretended to be afflicted by a sudden wind disease,
Jiàn believed him,
and thus Mǐn managed to escape.
Not long after,
the Grand Commander Yuán Zǐyōng was stationed at Ānyáng,
and the Grand Commander Péi Yǎn was stationed at Yèchéng,
marching west to suppress Jiàn.
Mǐn abandoned his family and household and fled to Zǐyōng.
Subsequently, he was summoned to Luò,
appointed Commandant of Cavalry (Fèngchē Dūwèi),
given the staff of authority to garrison Zhīhé,
and served as a Separate General.
Zhīhé was located northwest of Yè,
amidst massive mountains,
at the intersection of Bīng and Xiāng prefectures.
Because Gě Róng was pressing southward,
Mǐn was appointed to garrison the area.
Róng dispatched his uncle, the Prince of Lèlíng, Gě Cháng, leading ten thousand elite cavalry to attack Mǐn.
Mǐn held the strategic vantage point and resisted the battle,
and Cháng was unable to advance.
When Ěrzhū Róng arrived at Dōngguān,
Mǐn went to see Róng.
Róng intended to divide the bandit strength,
and dispatched Mǐn by a separate route toward Xiāngguó,
to assault the army of Tián Hù, whom the bandits had appointed as Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Before Mǐn reached Xiāngguó,
Gě Róng had already been captured.
Róng immediately memorialized to appoint Mǐn as General Who Establishes Loyalty (Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn);
He separated the three counties of Yìyáng from Guǎngpíng, Xiāngguó,
and Zhōngqiū from Nánzhàojùn to form Yìyáng Commandery,
and made Mǐn the Grand Administrator;
He was granted the noble title Marquis of Xiāngguó.
At the end of the Yǒng'ān era,
he was appointed Acting General Who Pacifies the North (Jiǎ Píngběi Jiāngjūn), received the staff of authority, and served as Grand Commander of the Commandery.
He was transferred to Grand Administrator of Lèpíng.
Before he reached the commandery,
Luòjīng (Luò Capital) was overthrown.
Mǐn led his department west to secure Shímén Mountain,
and secretly conspired with Liú Língzhù, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Gāo Áng and his brothers, and Lú Cáo, the Inspector of Ānzhōu, to launch a righteous uprising.
When Zhù was defeated,
Mǐn consequently entered Shímén.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness,
he sent a letter inviting Mǐn.
Mǐn received the letter,
and gathered several thousand troops to join Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ personally went out to welcome him.
He was appointed Imperial Envoy with Staff (Shǐ Chí Jié), General Who Attacks the South (Zhēng Nán Jiāngjūn), Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs in Xiāngzhōu, and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
concurrently serving as Director of the Department of State Affairs for the Southwest Circuit (Shàngshū Xīnán Dào Xíngtái) and Area Commander-in-Chief.
Mǐn was ordered to lead his original forces west back to his old garrison,
and Gāozǔ personally saw him off.
When Mǐn arrived in his native area,
he occupied Mǎ'ān Mountain,
building fortifications based on the terrain's dangers,
collecting provisions and assembling troops,
to create an imposing military presence.
Ěrzhū Zhào marched out of Jǐngxíng,
and Gāozǔ defeated Zhào at Guǎng'ā.
Mǐn commanded his original forces,
and garrisoned Gùchéng to guard against Ěrzhū Zhào.
Once Xiāngzhōu was pacified,
Mǐn was ordered to return to Yè,
appointed President of the Board of Works (Dūguān Shàngshū) for the Southwest Circuit Directorate (Xīnán Dào Xíngtái),
and again garrisoned Gùchéng.
When Ěrzhū Zhào and others were about to arrive,
Gāozǔ summoned Mǐn to assist in guarding Yèchéng.
In the beginning of the Tàichāng era,
he was appointed Minister of the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu Qīng).
Later, he was sent out to be Inspector of Nánjīngzhōu and Grand Commander of that prefecture.
Since the Xiàochāng era,
the old road to this prefecture had been cut off.
Previous inspectors all had to use unofficial routes to reach the prefecture.
Mǐn commanded several thousand troops,
marching directly toward Xuánhù,
and restored the old route starting from Bǐyáng.
Fighting while advancing for over three hundred *lǐ*,
wherever he passed,
he immediately established postal relay stations.
The Mán tribes and others were greatly impressed.
The Liáng dynasty dispatched Rèn Sīzǔ, their Inspector of Nánsīzhōu, and Huán Hé, the Grand Administrator of Suíjùn, leading thirty thousand cavalry and infantry,
and also mobilizing border Mán tribes,
to besiege and press Xiàzhà Garrison.
Mǐn personally attacked and suppressed them,
and defeated them.
An edict was issued promoting him to General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn).
Mǐn opened and established reservoirs and canals within the prefecture,
irrigating over a thousand *qǐng* of rice paddies,
which benefited both the state and private citizens.
He was transferred to the duties of Inspector of Dōngjīngzhōu,
and subsequently appointed General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), Inspector of Dōngjīngzhōu, and Grand Commander of that prefecture,
with the added title of Palace Aide to the Emperor (Sànqí Chángshì).
In the second year of Tiānpíng,
he died.

He was posthumously granted the titles Imperial Envoy with Staff, Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Dìng and Yīn Prefectures, Honorary Third Rank Official (Yítóng), and Inspector of Dìngzhōu.
Jǐng Yí, a paternal cousin of Yuán Zhōng,
was heroic and martial in his youth,
possessed courage and strength,
liked gathering fugitives,
and together they engaged in robbery.
The local community constantly suffered from this.
At the end of the Yǒng'ān period,
his elder brother, Wú Wéi, the Grand Administrator of Nán Jùlù, was impeached by the Censorate for embezzlement
and confined in the provincial prison.
Jǐng Yí led a dozen or so cavalrymen,
falsely claiming to be an envoy from the Court,
entered the provincial city directly,
and forcibly released Wú Wéi.
The provincial forces pursued them,
but ultimately could not capture them.
Because of this, he became known as a gallant hero.
When Gāozǔ raised the standard of righteousness in Xìndū,
Jǐng Yí presented himself at the camp gates.
Gāozǔ had long heard of his reputation
and received him very well.
He ordered him and Yuán Zhōng to raise troops in Xīshān,
and then joined the main army,
capturing the Regional Inspector, Ěrzhū Yǔshēng.
For his service, he was appointed Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn,
Duke of Chāngpíng County,
with an estate of 800 households.
When Ěrzhū Zhào came to attack,
he again fought hard and achieved merit,
and was appointed Shǐ Chíjié, Dà Dūdu, and Zuǒ Jiāngjūn.
In the early Tàichāng period,
he was promoted in rank to Duke of Chāngpíng Commandery,
his estate was increased by 300 households,
and he was additionally appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
In the early Tiānpíng period,
he was sent out to serve as the Regional Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
Not long after,
he was ambushed and killed by Yuán Hóngwēi, the former Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Military Administrator of Yīn and Cāng provinces, Dà Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ, and Regional Inspector of Yīnzhōu.
His son Jiālín inherited the title.
Lú Wénwěi,
courtesy name Xiūzú,
was a native of Zhuō in Fànyáng.
He was a premier clan of the Northern Provinces.
His father, Chǎng,
was transferred to succeed his uncle Jiǎ.
Wénwěi was orphaned young,
had high aspirations,
was quite versed in the classics and histories,
and was devoted to his friendships.
In his youth, he was respected by the villagers.
The province appointed him Zhǔbù.
At thirty-eight years old,
he was first nominated as a Xiùcái candidate.
He was appointed Chángliú Cānjūn in the Píng Běifǔ of his home province.
He persuaded the Regional Inspector, Péi Jùn, to restore the Dūkàng embankment according to the old plans,
irrigating over ten thousand qǐng of farmland.
The people relied on this benefit,
and the work of construction and repair
was largely entrusted to Wénwěi.
Since Wénwěi was skilled in management
and also applied his private resources,
his family, which had always been poor and frugal,
became wealthy as a result.
During the middle of the Xiàochāng period,
an imperial edict appointed him concurrently as Shàngshū Lángzhōng.
At that time, Cháng Jǐng, the Xíngtái, memorialized that he be kept on as Xíngtái Lángzhōng.
When the northern region was approaching chaos,
Wénwěi accumulated grain and rice in Fànyáng city.
As the area experienced famine and scarcity,
he provided extensive relief and sustenance,
and was all the more supported by the local community.
Soon after, he was captured by Dù Luòzhōu.
When Luòzhōu was defeated,
he subsequently joined Gě Róng.
When Róng was defeated,
he returned home.
At that time, Hán Lóu occupied Jìchéng.
Wénwěi led the local community to garrison Fànyáng,
and resisted Lóu.
Consequently, Wénwěi was appointed to manage the affairs of Fànyáng Commandery.
He defended the area for two years,
sharing hardships with the soldiers and officers,
distributing his family wealth,
and rescuing the poor and needy.
Everyone spoke of him gratefully.
Ěrzhū Róng sent the general Hóu Shēn to suppress Lóu
and pacified the area.
Wénwěi was enfeoffed for his merit as Viscount of Dàxià County,
with an estate of 200 households,
and appointed Grand Administrator of Fànyáng.
Shēn then remained to garrison Fànyáng.
When Róng was executed,
Wénwěi knew Shēn was untrustworthy,
so he lured him out hunting,
closed the gates, and barred him entry.
Shēn lost his position
and consequently fled to Zhōngshān.
When Emperor Zhuāng died,
Wénwěi and Liú Língzhù, the Regional Inspector of Yōuzhōu, conspired to raise an army of righteousness.
Língzhù conquered Yíngzhōu,
leaving Wénwěi in charge of administration.
He personally led troops toward Dìngzhōu,
but was defeated by Hóu Shēn, a general of Ěrzhū Róng.
Wénwěi abandoned the province,
fled back to his home commandery,
and then coordinated with the Gāo Gānyōng brothers.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Xìndū,
Wénwěi sent his son Huáidào to present a memorial expressing his sincerity.
Gāozǔ praised and accepted it.
In the early Zhōngxīng period,
he was appointed Āndōng Jiāngjūn and Regional Inspector of Ānzhōu.
As Ānzhōu had not yet submitted at that time,
he remained in his command post,
administering the affairs of Yōuzhōu,
and was additionally appointed Zhènjūn and official Regional Inspector.
At that time, Lú Cáo, the Regional Inspector of Ānzhōu, had also raised troops with Língzhù.
When Língzhù was defeated,
he consequently occupied Yōuzhōu and surrendered to Ěrzhū Zhào.
Zhào continued to employ him as Regional Inspector,
and he held the city, refusing to submit.
Wénwěi could not enter the provincial seat,
so he established the provincial government at the commandery seat.
In the early Tàichāng period,
he was transferred to Regional Inspector of Ānzhōu,
and repeatedly promoted to Sǎnjì Chángshì.
At the end of the Tiānpíng period,
Gāozǔ appointed Wénwěi to administer the affairs of Dōng Yōngzhōu,
and subsequently transferred him to administer the affairs of Qīngzhōu.
Wénwěi was by nature generous with wealth,
loved guests,
was skilled in governing and engaging with people,
and enjoyed giving minor favors.
Therefore, wherever he was stationed, he gained significant popular support.
Although he accepted goods,
the officials and people did not particularly suffer because of it.
His management of his resources
always seemed insufficient (for personal needs),
yet he managed to accumulate wealth
to curry favor with important figures,
and his presentation of gifts was constant.
He died in the province in the third year of Xīnghé,
at the age of sixty.
He was posthumously granted Shǐ Chíjié, Shìzhōng, Military Administrator of the three provinces of Dìng, Yíng, and Yīn, Sītú, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè, and Regional Inspector of Dìngzhōu.
His posthumous name was Xiàowēi.
His son Gōngdào,
was gentle and good-natured
and quite literary.
The province appointed him Zhǔbù.
When Lǐ Chóng campaigned in the north,
he appointed him Mòcáo Cānjūn in his Kāifǔ.
Since Wénwěi occupied Fànyáng,
and frequently endured banditry and disaster,
Gōngdào constantly assisted his father in defense.
Guō Xiù, the Qī Bīng Shàngshū, had long been friendly with Gōngdào.
When he took office,
he repeatedly praised and recommended him,
and Gāozǔ also heard of his reputation.
In the early Tiānpíng period,
he was specially appointed Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Fànyáng.
While in the commandery, he was benevolent.
He died before Wénwěi.
He was posthumously granted Shǐ Chíjié, Military Administrator of the two provinces of Yōu and Píng, Regional Inspector of Yōuzhōu, and Dùzhī Shàngshū.
His posthumous name was Dìng.
His son Xúnzǔ
inherited his grandfather’s title, Viscount of Dàxià.
He possessed specialized knowledge,
and his literary compositions were florid and sumptuous,
making him a talent among the younger generation.
He was nominated as a Xiùcái and entered the capital.
Lǐ Zǔxūn once hosted a banquet for scholars.
Xiǎnzǔ sent a junior court attendant to command Zǔxūn’s mother, saying:
“Since the Rúrú have been defeated,
why is there no congratulatory memorial?”
The messenger stood waiting for it.
All the guests composed memorials,
but Xúnzǔ completed his in an instant.
Later, when the court performed large-scale transfers and appointments,
they were ordered to present themselves (for appointment) on the same day.
Xúnzǔ stood outside the eastern gate of the army headquarters,
writing memorials for over twenty people.
His writing required no correction,
and the rhetoric and reasoning were remarkable.
Xúnzǔ first inherited the noble title and was enfeoffed as the Baron of Dàxià.
An elderly and virtuous court official said to him:
"Dàxià has just been established."
He immediately responded:
"It merely means that swallows and sparrows can congratulate each other."
Late in the Tiānbǎo period,
due to his official capacity, he was sent out to serve as the Superintendent for Constructing the Great Wall (Zhú Chángchéng Zǐ Shǐ).
Vainly proud of his talent,
he harbored frustration and resentment internally.
Consequently, he disfigured his appearance and dressed like a humble laborer to go see Yáng Yīn.
Yīn said:
"All old acquaintances have been appointed,
only Dàxià has not yet received an assignment."
Xúnzǔ said in a sharp voice:
"Whose fault is that!"
Once he arrived at the worksite,
he composed the *Fù* on Constructing the Great Wall (*Zhú Chángchéng Fù*).
An excerpt reads:
"The planks are made of purple cypress,
the pestles are made of quince.
Why are such materials used in such a manner?
The grasses are scattered and drooping,
planted along the ridges.
If only there were one fragrant thing every ten steps,
why would I refuse to stand among the thorns and brambles?"
Xíng Shào once joked, saying:
"In your youth, your talent and learning are flourishing and abundant.
But those that wear horns do not have upper teeth,
I fear you may not live long."
He replied:
"When Xúnzǔ first heard this statement,
I was truly fearful.
However, seeing that your respected self has graying hair at the temples,
I am slightly reassured."
Shào greatly valued his quickness and resourcefulness.
Since he possessed verbal eloquence,
he liked to criticize and evaluate people.
He once told someone:
"Yesterday, before dawn in the east,
I passed the gate of the Hé family,
and already saw the two Lù and the two Yuán,
standing straight and tall alongside the locust trees and willows."
This referred generally to Yànshī and Rénbè, and Wénzōng and Nuóyán.
Xíng Shào highly praised Lú Sīdào,
judging Xúnzǔ to be inferior to him.
Xúnzǔ said:
"Seeing those who cannot fly high, he lends them his feathers;
knowing those whose soaring power reaches the sky, he clips their wings."
Slander and destruction came daily,
and those who were always objective generally thought poorly of his character.
Xíng Ziguǎng, the Administrator of Chángguăng, evaluated the two Lú (Lú Xúnzǔ and Lú Sīdào), saying:
"Xúnzǔ possesses the decorum and restraint of Mǐ Héng,
Sīdào lacks the icy sharpness of Kǒng Wénjǔ."
Afterwards, he somewhat curbed his arrogance.
He served successively as Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén) and Recorder for the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Jìshì).
He died in office.
He had a collected works in ten *juǎn* (scrolls),
all of which are mostly lost.
He once composed a dirge for the consort of the Prince of Zhàojùn, Madam Zhèng.
One piece goes:
"The lord's grace flourishes within the seas,
his consort's virtue fills the realm.
Her feminine demeanor eclipses Zhèngguó,
her beauty as a consort shines in the Zhàogōng Palace.
Spring’s glamour is like peach blossom water,
autumn passes like cassia branch wind.
Thenceforth, at the Terrace of Cóng,
the bright moon fills the empty bed."
Huáidào was the younger brother of Gōngdào.
His nature was frivolous and fond of wine,
and he held somewhat elevated aspirations.
For his service in defending Fànyáng,
he started his career as a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sănqí Shìláng).
Wénwěi sent him to present a memorial to Gāozǔ.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng period,
he was granted the titles General Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Guānglù Dàfū).
At the beginning of the Yuánxiàng period,
Commissioner Xuē Shú recommended him to act as Administrator of Píngzhōu.
He was summoned to the Supreme Commander’s headquarters (Bàfǔ).
During the Xīnghé period,
he acted as Administrator of Fénzhōu.
Huáidào's family participated in the righteous uprising,
and Gāozǔ treated him personally and favorably.
He was sent out to become the Regional Commander of the Garrison City of Wūsū.
He died in office.
Huáidào’s younger brother was Zōngdào.
His nature was crude and impulsive,
and he valued knight-errantry (rènxiá).
He served successively as Secretary of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Láng) and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary with the Right to Memorialize (Tōngzhí Sănqí Chángshì).
Later, he acted as the Governor of Nányíngzhōu.
He once hosted a banquet in Jìnyáng,
filling the seats with guests and friends.
Mă Shìdá, a Palace Writer (Zhōngshū Shèrén), looked at the female musician playing the konghou and said:
"Her hands are extremely delicate and white."
Zōngdào immediately gave this serving girl to Shìdá.
Shìdá firmly declined.
Zōngdào ordered his attendants to pretend to cut off her wrist.
Shìdá had no choice but to accept her.
When he was about to proceed to Yíngzhōu,
he gathered a large number of local people at Dūkàng Pō,
slaughtered oxen, and held a gathering.
An old student of his, drunk with wine,
during the course of his speech,
made a minor mistake.
Zōngdào immediately ordered him drowned in the water.
Later, he was stripped of his status due to extreme cruelty and abuse of power.
Yǒng, a relative of Wénwěi,
had the courtesy name Jìlǐ.
His father, Bì,
was the Administrator of Xiàpī for the Wèi dynasty.
When Yǒng was young, he and his older cousin Jǐngyù studied together.
Their uncle collectively praised them, saying:
"Báitóu (Jǐngyù) will surely succeed through literary means,
Jìlǐ (Yǒng) will reach prominence through military means.
The rise of our family rests with these two sons."
Púgŭ Nuó, the rebel in Yōuzhōu, made Yǒng the Prince of Fànyáng of his home commandery.
He was then eighteen years old.
Later, when Gě Róng rebelled,
he again made Yǒng the Prince of Yàn.
When the banner of righteousness was raised,
Lú Wénwěi summoned him,
but he did not respond.
After the destruction of the Ěrzhū clan,
he then went to Jìnyáng.
Gāozǔ appointed Yǒng as Secretary to the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Zhǔbù).
At that time, because of frost and famine west of the mountains (Shānxī),
rural taxes and tribute from east of the mountains (Shāndōng) were being transported.
It was ordered that all loads must be genuinely full,
and offenders would be punished.
Yǒng was ordered to oversee this matter.
The Princess of Lángyé fraudulently rented over a thousand carts.
Yǒng investigated and impeached her.
The princess complained to Gāozǔ,
but Yǒng adhered to the law and refused to yield.
Gāozǔ said to Guō Xiù:
"Lú Yǒng has an inviolable bearing;
he is truly an honest and upright man.
We should entrust him with great affairs,
not just the collecting of rent."
He was promoted to Administrator of Rǔběi,
acted as Administrator of Shănzhōu,
and was transferred to act as Administrator of Luòzhōu.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng,
the imperial army besieged Guăngzhōu,
but failed to capture it after several weeks.
Commissioner Hóu Jǐng heard that the rescue troops of the Western Wèi (Xī Wèi) were about to arrive,
and gathered the generals to discuss the situation.
Yǒng stepped forward to observe the situation.
Thereupon, he led a hundred cavalrymen,
each leading an extra horse.
Upon reaching Dàkuí Shān,
he learned that the Wèi general Lǐ Jǐnghé was about to arrive with his troops.
Yǒng set up numerous banners and flags on the treetops,
divided his cavalry into ten squadrons,
sounded the horns, and charged straight ahead.
He captured Chéng Huá, an Auxiliary Commissioner (Yítóng) of the Xī Wèi,
and beheaded the Auxiliary Commissioner Wáng Zhēngmán.
He drove away three hundred horses,
and returned that same night.
Luò Chāo, the defending general of Guăngzhōu, surrendered the city.
Gāozǔ ordered Yǒng to act as Administrator of Guăngzhōu.
For this merit, he was appointed Auxiliary Commissioner of the Three Bureaus (Yítóng Sānsī) and Governor of Yángzhōu,
garrisoning Yíyáng.
Rebellious commoners like Hán Mùlán and Chén Xīn constantly caused border troubles.
Yǒng completely defeated them.
He memorialized asking to enter the court for an audience.
Gāozǔ bestowed a letter upon Yǒng, saying:
"I entrust you with Yángzhōu;
I can merely rest my head easily and sleep soundly,
having no worries about the southwest.
You should just rely on the commission given by the court,
and memorials requesting an audience should cease.
Your wife and children may live in the prefecture;
among the Hàn youths, there must be none who surpass you."
He died in the second year of Wǔdìng (544),
at the age of thirty-two.
Yǒng possessed five hundred horses,
and had prepared six cartloads of armor and weapons.
In his final memorial, he offered all of them to the imperial court.
In addition to the funeral gifts,
he was separately granted four thousand bolts of cloth and silk.
He was posthumously appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Governor of Jìzhōu,
and granted the posthumous title Wǔzhēn Hóu (Martial and Upright Marquis).
Lǐ Yìshēn,
was a man from Gāoyì, Zhàojùn.
His grandfather, Zhēn,
was a Zhōngshū Shìláng of Wèi.
His father, Shàozōng,
was the Biéjià of Yīnzhōu.
Yìshēn studied widely in the Classics and Histories,
and possessed talent and utility fitting the age.
He began his career as the Gōngcáo Cānjūn in the Zhēngdōng Fǔ of Jìzhōu,
and was successively promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
At the beginning of the righteous banner (uprising),
he defected to Gāozǔ at Xìndū,
who made him a Dàxíngtái Lángzhōng.
At the beginning of the restoration,
he was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn and Hónglú Shǎoqīng.
Yìshēn, seeing that the forces of Ěrzhū Zhào were flourishing,
subsequently betrayed Gāozǔ and fled to him.
When Zhào was suppressed,
Gāozǔ forgave his crime,
and made him the Jìshì Cānjūn of the Dà Chéngxiàng Fǔ.
He was successively promoted to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Sīmǎ of the Prime Ministerial Residence (Xiàng Fǔ);
in the posts he held, he was praised as competent.
He was transferred to Bīngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ.
At that time, the Cìshǐ Kězhūhún Dàoyuán did not personally handle minor affairs,
and entrusted most civilian matters to Yìshēn,
which greatly helped with efficiency and speed.
He again served as Dà Chéngxiàng Sīmǎ.
During the Wǔdìng era,
he was appointed Qízhōu Cìshǐ,
where he loved financial gain
and accepted much in bribes.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he acted in the affairs of Zhèngzhōu,
and was transferred to act in the affairs of Liángzhōu.
Soon after, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
and served as the Tàishǒu of Yángxià.
Duàn Yè accused him of excessive taxation while in the prefecture.
He was detained
and sent to Liángzhōu for thorough investigation,
which was not yet complete.
In the third year,
he fell ill and died while imprisoned,
at the age of fifty-seven.
His son, Tǎotú,
had talent and eloquence,
and was a Shàngshū Láng and Magistrate of Yè County (Yè Xiànlìng).
At the beginning of the Wǔpíng era,
he served concurrently as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and was sent on an embassy to Chén.
He was praised by the people of Chén.
Later he became the Zuǒchéng of the Shòuyáng Circuit Xíngtái,
and was captured along with Wáng Lín and others.
He escaped and returned during the end of the Zhōu Dynasty.
At the beginning of the Kāihuáng era,
he was the Tàishǒu of Yǒng'ān.
He died while serving as the Zhǎngshǐ of Jiàngzhōu.
His son, Zhèngzǎo,
was intelligent, quick-witted, and capable.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was an Yítóng Kāifǔ Xíng Cānjūn, and concurrently oversaw the affairs of the Jíshū Shěng (Pàn Jíshū Shěng Shì).
Because his father Tǎotú had perished in Chén,
Zhèngzǎo resigned from office citing illness.
He was worn out and emaciated from worry and grief.
His living habits and diet adhered to the rites of mourning,
and he was praised by scholars.
During the Suí Kāihuáng era,
he successively served as Shàngshū Gōngbù Yuánwàiláng and Magistrate of Zhì County (Zhì Xiànlìng).
He died while serving as the Zhǎngshǐ of Yízhōu.
Tǎotú’s younger brother, Wénshī,
was a Zhōngshū Shèrén and Tàishǒu of Qíjùn.
Yìshēn had seven brothers,
many of whom were renowned for their learning.
His second younger brother, Tóngguǐ, was famous for his Confucian studies.
His sixth younger brother, Zhìlián, has a separate biography.
Shénwēi was a cousin of Yìshēn.
His great-grandfather, Róng,
was a Zhōngshū Shìláng of Wèi.
Shénwēi had dignified bearing in his youth,
inherited his family's scholarship,
and was generally versed in the principles and teachings of ritual studies.
He also loved music,
and compiled and collected books on music,
totaling nearly one hundred scrolls.
At the end of Wèi Wǔ's reign,
he was Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Cìshǐ of Xìnzhōu.
The court historian comments: Yuánzhōng originally came from an unadorned family line,
and had a reputation for adherence to proper teachings and righteous principles,
and respect for human relations;
he was not generally known for his political manipulation.
When Emperor Zhuāng Dì was secretly deposed and died,
the various barbarian groups became manipulative and dominant.
All scholars who had ambition and vigor hoped for an army to serve the Emperor.
When Gāozǔ headed east,
the event met their deepest aspirations.
Once they encountered his heroic bearing,
they devoted their hearts and souls.
Casting a stone into the water (i.e., immediate response),
how could it have been otherwise?
After enjoying achievement and fame,
he eventually knew when to stop and be content.
The way in which he advanced and withdrew,
is worthy of observation.
Wénwěi was highly regarded in an illustrious land,
and had ambitions from an early age.
Amidst difficulties and dangers,
he eventually met a heroic lord.
Although his ritual rank was not extensive,
he was still one of those who helped establish the reign.
Xúnzǔ’s rhetoric was brilliant and eloquent,
and he achieved fame early.
Relying on his talent and background,
he indulged in arrogance and exaggeration.
Among the scholars in the capital,
none failed to fear the tip of his tongue.
His appointments and treatment are not widely known,
and he died young.
If he had been able to live out a full lifespan,
whether he would have succeeded or failed cannot be measured.
Eulogy says: Jìnyáng and Dàxià,
held integrity and possessed refinement.
Treading in benevolence and walking in righteousness,
they were stirred by the changing times.
Lú Yīng amassed wealth;
Lǐ was weary of the tumultuous atmosphere.
By the integrity of their beginnings and ends,
the clear and the turbid are thus distinguished.
Yìshēn served in counsel;
he fell short of complete loyalty and diligence.
Biography Fifteen: Wèi Lángēn, Cuī Gěng, (Zizhān)
Wèi Lángēn,
was a man from Xiàqǔyáng, Jùlù.
His father, Bóchéng,
was Tàishān Tàishǒu of Wèi.
Lángēn was eight feet tall,
with an imposing and magnificent appearance.
He extensively read various books,
and recited the Zuǒshì Zhuàn and the Zhōu Yì.
He was perceptive and insightful.
He began his career as Shìláng in the Kingdom of Běihǎi,
and subsequently served as Chángliú Cānjūn of Dìngzhōu.
When his mother died,
he earned a reputation for filiality while observing mourning.
When he was about to bury her within the borders of Chángshān Commandery,
there was previously a shrine dedicated to Dǒng Zhuó,
and the shrine had cypress trees.
Lángēn believed that Dǒng Zhuó was ruthless, rebellious, and lacked the Way,
and that his shrine should not remain until the present day.
Therefore, he cut down the cypress trees to use as coffin wood.
Some people advised him not to cut them down,
but Lángēn took them all,
completely without doubt or fear.
When he suffered his father's death,
he built a hut beside the tomb,
carried earth to form the grave mound,
and his grief and emaciation nearly destroyed his life force.
Later he served as Jìshì Cānjūn in the residences of the Sīkōng and Sītú,
and was transferred to Píngběi Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ of Xiàzhōu.
He returned to the capital to serve as a Sītú Yuàn,
and then went out to serve as Tàishǒu of his native commandery.
In all positions, he displayed competence.
At the end of the Zhèngguāng period,
Lǐ Chóng, the Shàngshū Lìng, was the Dūdū of his home commandery.
He led troops to suppress the Rú Rú,
and appointed Lán Gēn as Zhǎngshǐ.
He then advised Chóng, saying:
“The various garrisons along the border
control territories that are vast and far-reaching.
When they were first established in the past,
the land was wide and the population sparse.
They either conscripted the strong clan members and youths from the Zhōngyuán,
or individuals who were the vital organs of the state,
entrusting them to be the protectors.
Since the middle period,
the officials have deviated from the original intent,
calling them fǔhù,
their service being no different from servants and slaves.
Their official marriages, ranking, and seniority
have caused them to lose their status among the pure lineage (qīngliú).
Meanwhile, their original clan members and old associates
are all flourishing and prominent.
Looking at the difference between them,
it is reasonable that they feel anger and resentment.
To enact a great reform,
now is the time.
Pacifying the territory and securing the border
is the greatest of tasks.
It is advisable to change the garrisons into zhōu,
and divide them to establish commanderies and xiàn.
All those who are fǔhù
should be entirely pardoned and made commoners.
Their ranking for entering officialdom
should wholly conform to their former status.
Both civil and military talents should be used,
and both authority and kindness applied.
If this plan is carried out,
the state will mostly have no worries about the north.”
Chóng presented this to the throne,
but the matter lapsed and was not acted upon.
When the army returned,
he was appointed Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
then transferred to Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ,
granted the Jiǎ Jié,
and managed the affairs of Yùzhōu.
At the beginning of the Xiàochāng period,
he was transferred to be the Cìshǐ of Qízhōu.
He followed Xíngtái Xiāo Bǎoyín in attacking and defeating Wǎnchuān.
The local populace was captured as slaves and bondservants,
and ten beautiful women were awarded to Lán Gēn.
Lán Gēn declined, saying:
“This district bordered strong barbarians,
and Imperial prestige had not yet reached them.
They had nowhere to turn,
and thus they became rebels.
Now we should clothe those who are cold
and feed those who are hungry.
How can we make them into bondservants?”
He returned all of them to their fathers and brothers.
The wheat within his district often bore five heads,
and while neighboring zhōu suffered damage from field mice,
the disaster did not cross into Qízhōu territory.
At the time of the Qín and Lǒng rebellion,
Xiāo Bǎoyín was defeated at Jīngzhōu.
The barbarian bandits of Gāopíng pressed upon Qízhōu.
The city dwellers of the zhōu forced Lán Gēn to be imprisoned and surrender to the bandits.
Bǎoyín reached Yōngzhōu,
collected the scattered and missing troops,
and his military might was restored.
The city dwellers then killed the bandit Cìshǐ Hóumòchén Zhònghé
and supported Lán Gēn in resuming his post.
Since the court realized Lán Gēn had won the hearts of the people in the Western lands,
they granted him Chí Jié, Jiǎ Píngxī Jiāngjūn, and Dūdū of the military affairs of the four zhōu: Jīngzhōu, Qízhōu, Dōng Qín, and Nán Qí.
He concurrently served as Xíngtái Shàngshū of the four zhōu.
Soon after, he entered the capital and was appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
At the end of the Xiàochāng period,
as refugees from Héběi crossed south,
Lán Gēn was made concurrent Shàngshū,
serving as Pacification Commissioner for the four zhōu: Qízhōu, Jìzhōu, and the two Yǎnzhōu,
and establishing commanderies and xiàn there.
Xíng Gǎo of Héjiān rebelled between Qīngzhōu and Yǎnzhōu.
Gǎo
was Lán Gēn's nephew.
An edict again commanded Lán Gēn to convey the Imperial message of consolation,
but Gǎo did not surrender.
He then followed Yuán Tiānmù to suppress him.
Upon returning,
he was appointed Tàifǔ Qīng,
but declined the post.
He was transferred to Āndōng Jiāngjūn and Zhōngshū Lìng.
When Emperor Zhuāng was about to execute Ěrzhū Róng,
Lán Gēn heard of the plan
and secretly informed Ěrzhū Shìlóng.
After Róng died,
Lán Gēn feared that Emperor Zhuāng would discover this,
and was worried and frightened, not knowing how to proceed.
At that time, Wáng Dàoxí, the Yìng Zhào, was trusted by Emperor Zhuāng.
Lán Gēn thus attached himself to him,
seeking permission to gain merit outside the capital.
Dàoxí memorialized on his behalf,
and Lán Gēn was appointed Héběi Xíngtái, leading the recruitment of local men in Dìngzhōu,
intending to guard Jǐngxíng.
At this time, Hóu Shēn, a general under Ěrzhū Róng, advanced from Fànyáng toward Zhōngshān.
Lán Gēn engaged in battle,
suffered a crushing defeat,
and fled to seek refuge with Gāo Gān of Bóhǎi.
As Gān and his brothers raised a righteous revolt,
he was consequently among them.
When Gāozǔ arrived,
due to Lán Gēn’s long-standing reputation,
he treated him with profound courtesy.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng period,
he was granted Chējì Dàjiāngjūn and Shàngshū Yòu Púshè.
When Gāozǔ was about to enter Luòyáng,
he sent Lán Gēn ahead to the capital.
At that time, the matter of succession (deposing and establishing an emperor) was undecided.
He ordered Lán Gēn to observe the Former Deposed Emperor of Wèi.
The Emperor’s bearing was lofty and bright,
and Lán Gēn feared that he would be unpredictable in the future.
He consequently, along with Gāo Gān’s brothers and the Huángmén Cuī Rǔ, wholeheartedly and strongly requested of Gāozǔ,
stating that the Deposed Emperor had originally been installed by barbarian bandits.
If he were still allowed to reign now,
it would not be appropriate according to principle.
Gāozǔ had no choice,
and consequently enthroned Emperor Wǔ.
The Deposed Emperor originally possessed virtue and achievements,
but was maliciously slandered by Lán Gēn and others.
This was deeply criticized by contemporary opinion.
At the beginning of the Tàichāng period,
he was appointed Yítóng Sānsī.
Soon after, he was granted Kāifǔ
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jùlù Xiàn,
with an income of seven hundred households.
He requested that the title be granted to his elder brother’s son, Tóng Dá.
Since Lán Gēn had already participated in the meritorious revolt,
and held a position in the high administration,
at this time his merit from Qízhōu was finally recognized,
and he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yǒngxīng Xiàn,
with an income of one thousand households.
Upon the death of Gāo Gān,
Lán Gēn was fearful,
left his residence,
and sought refuge in a temple.
Emperor Wǔ severely reprimanded him.
Lán Gēn was worried and terrified,
so he claimed illness and resigned as Púshè.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng period,
claiming his illness was severe, he submitted a memorial requesting permission to return to his hometown.
The Wèi Emperor sent the Shèrén Shí Chángxuān to his home to convey comfort and inquiry.
Still holding the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng,
and being granted the privilege of having horses pass through his gate,
he returned to his native district.
He died the following year,
aged sixty-one.
He was posthumously granted Dūdū of the military affairs of three zhōu: Jìzhōu, Dìngzhōu, and Yīnzhōu, Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu, Sītú Gōng, and Shìzhōng.
His posthumous title was Wénxuān.
Although Lán Gēn established himself through merit and fame,
he was skilled at joining factions.
At crucial moments in his career,
he often prioritized calculation and strategy,
and therefore was not approved by orthodox criticism.
His eldest son, Xiāngrú,
was a Bìshū Lángzhōng.
Due to merit in the righteous revolt,
he was soon granted the title of Jiāngjūn.
He inherited his father’s noble rank,
and was promoted to Āndōng Jiāngjūn and Biéjià of Yīnzhōu,
and later served in the capital as Shì Yùshǐ.
He died in the third year of the Wǔdìng period.
His second son was Jìngzhòng.
During the reign of Sù Zōng,
ministers who assisted in the founding of the dynasty received sacrificial honors,
but Lán Gēn was not among them.
Jìngzhòng submitted a memorial petitioning this omission.
The Emperor stated that since the Imperial command had already been executed,
it was difficult to retroactively amend it,
but promoted Jìngzhòng to Cíbù Lángzhōng.
He died while serving as Tàishǒu of Zhāngwǔ.
Lángēn’s clansman younger brother, Mínglǎng,
was considerably versed in the classics and history,
and roughly possessed literary talent.
He was repeatedly promoted, becoming Staff Officer of the Legal Section in the Grand Marshal’s (Dà Sīmǎ) establishment,
concurrently holding the post of Director (Lángzhōng) of the Treasury Bureau (Jīnbù) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
When Yuán Hào entered Luòyáng,
Mínglǎng served as Director (Lángzhōng) in the Southern Route Mobile Secretariat (Nándào Xíngtái),
and was captured by Hào.
Later, he abandoned Hào and fled back.
He was appointed General Who Rises Like a Dragon (Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Zhōngsàn Dàfū),
and was granted the noble title Marquis of Jùlù.
At the end of the Yǒng’ān era,
Lángēn served as the Hébĕi Mobile Secretariat (Hébĕi Xíngtái),
and brought Mínglǎng in as Left Assistant (Zuǒ Chéng).
When Lángēn suffered defeat at Zhōngshān,
they both returned to Gāozǔ.
At the beginning of the Zhōngxīng era,
he was appointed General Who Soothes the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
and was sent out to be the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Āndé.
Later he was transferred to General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn), Right Grand Master of Radiant Honor (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū), and Great Moderator (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Dìngzhōu.
At the beginning of the Wǔdìng era,
he became Advisory Staff Officer (Zīyì Cānjūn) to Xiǎnzǔ.
He was sent out as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Píngyáng,
but was impeached by a Censor (Yùshǐ),
and was subsequently barred from office.
He died of illness.
Mínglǎng’s paternal cousin, Kǎi,
was assertive, straightforward, talented, and articulate in his youth.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty,
he was appointed Staff Officer of an Opening the Palace establishment (Kāifǔ Xíng Cānjūn),
and gradually rose to Director (Láng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) and Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Qízhōu.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he served as the deputy envoy sent to Chén.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Qīngzhōu,
but firmly declined the post and did not accept it.
Yáng Yīn reported this to the Emperor.
Xiǎnzǔ was furious,
and said to Yīn:
“What kind of Hàn fellow is this?
I grant him office,
but he refuses to accept it!
Tomorrow, I will summon him,
and I will speak with him myself.”
At this time, Xiǎnzǔ had already lost moral authority,
and everyone in court feared him,
but Kǎi appeared completely calm and composed.
Xiǎnzǔ severely reprimanded him,
and then said:
“Which is better, death or the Chief Clerkship (Zhǎngshǐ)?
I permit you, sir, to choose one.”
Kǎi replied:
“The one who can kill your subject is Your Majesty;
