the one who refuses the Chief Clerkship (Zhǎngshǐ) is your foolish subject.
I humbly await your enlightened decree.”
Xiǎnzǔ said to Yīn:
“Why worry that there will be no one to serve in office?
Why should we insist on employing this Hàn fellow?
Send him home,
and never again shall he be recommended or employed.”
Consequently, he remained disgraced and unemployed for many years.
Later, he encountered Yáng Yīn on the road
and subtly presented his grievances.
Yáng replied:
“Issuing edicts and granting offices
are entirely matters of the Sacred Will,
not something known by the Selection Bureau.
Sir, you do not need to trouble yourself by complaining to me.”
Kǎi responded immediately, saying:
“Although light rain may fall from the heavens,
it still awaits the rising clouds from the Four Great Peaks (Sì Yuè).
How can you, sir, claim not to know?”
Yáng was delighted and said:
“This statement is extremely concise and to the point.
There is no need for further words.”
A few days later,
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Huòzhōu.
While in office, he governed effectively,
and the border populace respected and submitted to him.
During the Dàníng era,
he died while serving as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāozhōu.
Kǎi’s nephew, Yànqīng,
was the son of Jìjǐng, the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng) of Wèi.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he concurrently held the position of Palace Attendant in Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
serving as the deputy envoy sent to Chén.
Yànqīng’s younger brother, Tàn,
was learned and possessed literary talent.
In the early Wǔpíng era,
he was Palace Censor (Diànzhōng Yùshǐ),
and was promoted to Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
awaiting imperial summons in the Wénlín Hall.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he served as Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén) and Gentleman of Literary Composition (Zhùzuò Láng).
He compiled the *History of the Later Wèi* (Hòu Wèi Shū) in ninety-two scrolls,
which adhered closely to the standard historical form.
People of the time praised its excellence.
Cuī Mào,
courtesy name Chángrǔ,
was a native of Dōngwǔchéng in Qīnghé.
His father, Xiū,
was Minister of Military Supplies (Qī Bīng Shàngshū) in the Wèi dynasty,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Supervisor (Púyè).
Mào had a magnificent and handsome appearance,
was skilled in deportment,
had a famous reputation in his youth,
and was well-known at the time.
Initially, he served as a bier attendant for Emperor Shìzōng of Wèi,
and later shed his civilian clothes to become Erudite of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì).
During the Yǒng’ān era,
he was dismissed due to an incident and returned to his hometown.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness at Xìndū,
Mào joined him.
Gāozǔ met him,
was greatly pleased,
and appointed him Advisory Staff Officer (Zīyì Cānjūn).
Soon after, he was appointed Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
and promoted to General (Jiāngjūn)
and Right Grand Master of Radiant Honor (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
When Gāozǔ entered Luò,
a discussion was held to determine the deposition and establishment [of the emperor].
Qí Jùn, the Grand Coachman (Tàipú), highly praised the ruler Pǔtài as virtuous and enlightened,
suitable to be the lord of the state.
Mào said:
“If he were truly enlightened and sagely,
he could wait for our King Gāo,
and gradually ascend to the throne.
Since he was established by a rebellious barbarian (hú),
how can he still be considered the Son of Heaven?
If we follow Jùn’s words,
what justification does the Royal Army (Wáng Shī) have for its righteous action?”
Because of this, both Zhōngxīng and Pǔtài were deposed,
and the Prince of Píngyáng was established as emperor instead.
Due to his merit in establishing the righteous cause,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Wǔchéng County,
with an estate of 1,400 households,
and advanced to the rank of General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn) and Left Grand Master of Radiant Honor (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū),
while continuing to oversee the Palace Attendants (Huángmén Láng).
Mào, residing in the Secretariat (Ménxià),
relied on his participation in the righteous uprising,
and was quite arrogant and unrestrained.
Soon after, he was impeached by a Censor (Yùshǐ) for corruption,
and consequently fled back to his home village,
only emerging when an amnesty was granted.
Because Mào had originally participated in the righteous uprising,
Gāozǔ restored his position as Palace Attendant (Huángmén).
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
he served as Attendant Reader (Shì Dú),
overseeing the Imperial Archives (Diǎn Shū).
Soon after, he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu,
and was provided with 300 soldiers from Guǎngzōng and 1,000 soldiers from Qīnghé.
Mào was naturally extravagant and insolent.
He favored his concubine, Lady Féng,
who borrowed his authority to administer punishment,
and indulged in seizing bribes freely,
so his governance failed to take hold.
When Mào first served as a Chángshì (Attendant-in-Ordinary),
he sought someone to compile the *Diaries of Activity and Repose* (Qǐjū Zhù).
Someone suggested:
“Wèi Shōu would be suitable.”
Mào said:
“Shōu is merely a frivolous person.”
Instead, he nominated Zǔ Hóngxūn for the task.
Once Mào held a key position,
he also had Lú Yuánmíng replace Shōu as Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng).
Consequently, Shōu bore a grudge against him.
When Shōu was sent as an envoy to Liáng,
he passed through Xúzhōu.
Mào prepared the Governor’s (Cìshǐ) official equipage to see him off,
and sent someone to tell Wèi:
“Do not be surprised by the large escort;
it is due to the power of studying antiquity.”
Shōu replied:
“Tell Governor Cuī of Xúzhōu,
this is the merit of participating in the righteous cause.
What does it have to do with studying antiquity?”
Mào, believing his family lineage was traditionally high,
was particularly offended by this remark.
Shōu acted on his long-held resentment,
thus frustrating Mào.
After being relieved of the governorship,
Mào was appointed Minister of Military Supplies (Qī Bīng Shàngshū) and Moderator (Zhōngzhèng) of Qīnghé Commandery.
Lǐ Hún of Zhàojùn once held a banquet gathering famous scholars.
When they were joyfully bustling with poetry and wine,
Mào arrived later,
and immediately no one in the assembly dared to speak again.
Zhèng Bóyóu sighed and said:
“He stands eight feet tall,
his face is like a carved portrait,
his slightest cough sounds like a great bell,
and his chest holds a thousand scrolls of books.
How can one not stand in awe of him?”
Cuī Xiè often boasted of his ancestral prominence,
saying to Lú Yuánmíng:
“Among the great houses of the realm,
there are only I and you.
As for the Bó Cuī and Zhào Lǐ,
what account are they?”
Cuī Siān heard this and resented it.
After Gāozǔ’s funeral,
Cuī Xiè also privately remarked:
“Can a yellow-chinned, small-bodied person bear heavy responsibility?”
Siān’s maternal cousin, Lǐ Shèn, reported Cuī Xiè’s words to Siān.
Siān petitioned Shìzōng,
and Cuī Xiè was forbidden from court audience.
Cuī Xiè insisted on bowing by the side of the road.
Shìzōng erupted in anger, saying:
“A yellow-chinned little child!
Why should he be worthy of a bow?”
Thereupon, Cuī Xiè was shackled and sent to Jìnyáng for interrogation,
but Cuī Xiè did not submit.
Siān introduced Xíng Zǐcái as a witness,
but Zǐcái maintained that no such words were spoken.
While in detention,
Cuī Xiè said to Zǐcái:
“Do you know that my intention is directed toward Tàiqiū?”
Zǐcái went out and told Cuī Xiè’s son, Zhān, saying:
“Your respected father’s intent is truly to seek a marriage alliance with Chén Yuánkāng.”
Zhān had a daughter,
so he promised her in marriage to Yuánkāng’s son,
and appealed to Yuánkāng for help.
Yuánkāng spoke about the matter to Shìzōng, saying:
“Cuī Xiè’s reputation and standing have always been significant;
it is improper to execute him based merely on words spoken in private.”
Shìzōng said:
“If his life is spared,
he should still be banished to distant regions.”
Yuánkāng replied:
“If Cuī Xiè is placed on the frontier,
he might defect externally;
it is inappropriate
to provide an eminent and worthy man as aid to the enemy.”
Shìzōng said:
“Since he has the crime of Jìguī,
would it be acceptable to instead order him to perform penal labor?”
Yuánkāng replied:
“I once read the biography of Cuī Yǎn
and regretted that Wèi Wǔ was not magnanimous.
If Cuī Xiè were to perish while performing labor,
would later generations really say that Your Excellency did not kill him?”
Shìzōng said:
“In that case, what should be done?”
Yuánkāng replied:
“That Cuī Xiè deserves death
is known to everyone in court and country.
If Your Excellency could truly temper severity with leniency,
and specifically lighten his punishment,
then your benevolence and virtue would be profoundly manifested,
and the hearts of the world would return to you.”
Thereupon, he was pardoned.
Cuī Xiè proceeded to court to offer thanks.
Shìzōng was still angry and said:
“Although I am inadequate,
I bear the heavy responsibility of office.
You publicly called me a ‘yellow-chinned little child.’
Metal and stone can be dissolved,
but these words are hard to erase!”
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was appointed Shìzhōng
and Supervising Diarist of the Court (Jiān Qǐjū).
During the period of abdication and transition,
he participated in managing rituals and ceremonies.
He was separately enfeoffed as the male (Nán) of Xīnfēng County,
with two hundred taxable households,
which he subsequently transferred to his ninth younger brother, Yuē.
The marriages of Cuī Xiè’s family
were all exemplary of the highest official standards;
his funeral and wedding rites
were praised by contemporaries.
Empress Dowager Lóu arranged for the Prince of Bólíng to take Cuī Xiè’s younger sister as consort.
She ordered the palace messenger, saying:
“Ensure the preparations follow proper precedent,
lest the Cuī family laugh at us.”
On the wedding night,
Xiǎnzǔ raised his cup and offered a toast, saying:
“May the new bride bear sons,
be filial, obedient, wealthy, and noble.”
Cuī Xiè presented a memorial, saying:
“Filial piety and obedience originate from my family,
but wealth and nobility are gifts derived from Your Majesty’s grace.”
In the fifth year [of Tiānbǎo],
he was sent out to serve as the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dōngyǎn Prefecture,
and once again brought along his concubine, Féng Shì.
Cuī Xiè soon suffered a stroke (paralysis),
and Féng Shì became arrogant and reckless,
accepting bribes wantonly.
She was impeached by the Censor (Yùshǐ),
and both she and Cuī Xiè were summoned to the Court of the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
Soon after, there was a separate imperial decree
to execute Féng Shì in the marketplace.
Cuī Xiè died of illness in prison,
aged sixty-one.
Cuī Xiè extensively reviewed various writings
and possessed literary talent.
From the establishment of the restoration
until the time of Wǔdì,
many of the imperial edicts, proclamations, memorials, and declarations were written by Cuī Xiè.
However, by nature, he was extravagant and unrestrained,
addicted to wealth and women.
Among his brothers,
he could not fully maintain harmonious and respectful relations,
and public opinion criticized him for this.
Cuī Xiè had always been on poor terms with Wèi Shōu.
Since Wèi Shōu was solely in charge of compiling the National History,
Cuī Xiè feared being maligned.
He therefore sought to please him, saying:
“In the past there was Bān Gù,
now there is Master Wèi.”
Shōu laughed, but his resentment was not dispelled.
His son, Zhān, succeeded him.
Zhān,
courtesy name Yàntōng,
was intelligent, brilliant, and hardworking in study.
He possessed literary sentiment,
had excellent demeanor,
and a distinguished, impressive spirit;
he never spoke rashly.
At age fifteen,
Prefect Gāo Áng summoned and appointed him Clerk (Zhǔbù).
The Duke of Qīnghé, Yuè, invited him to serve as Libationer of the Western Gate of the Kaifǔ establishment.
When Cuī Siān was Grand Marshal (Zhōngwèi),
he memorialized for Zhān to be appointed Censor (Yùshǐ).
His talent and reputation were recognized,
but this was not his preferred post.
When Gāozǔ returned to court
and went back to Jìnyáng,
Zhān was summoned to accompany him alongside Běihǎi Wáng Xī,
both serving as guests and friends to Gāozǔ’s sons.
He then became the Central Military Consultant (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn) in the Chancellor’s establishment,
and was later promoted to Clerk (Zhǔbù).
When Shìzōng died,
the mourning was secretly withheld.
Xiǎnzǔ ordered Zhān to concurrently serve as Commandant (Sīmǎ) of the Chancellor’s establishment and proceed to Yè.
When Emperor Xiàojìng of Wèi ascended the Yúnlóng Gate on the Rénrì festival,
his father, Cuī Xiè, was in attendance at the banquet.
Zhān was also ordered to sit near the Imperial Seat.
He also presented a poem in response to the imperial request.
He asked Xíng Shào and others:
“How does this poem compare to his father’s work?”
They all replied:
“Cuī Xiè is erudite, refined, and grand;
Zhān’s style is fresh and clean.
Both are the finest among poets.”
When the banquet concluded,
they all sighed in admiration,
saying
“Today’s banquet belongs entirely to the father and son, Cuī Zhān.”
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he concurrently served as Director (Lángzhōng) of the Personnel Department of the combined Ministries.
Soon after, he entered mourning.
He was subsequently recalled to serve as Staff Officer (Shǔ) to the Minister of Education (Sītú).
Yáng Yīn wanted to bring Zhān in as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
At that time, Lú Sīdào was serving in the Central Secretariat.
Yáng Yīn therefore asked Sīdào:
“I have many duties these days,
and I haven't been able to see Cuī Zhān’s literary refinement.
Since you are personally close to him,
you should naturally be familiar with him.”
Sīdào replied:
“The excellence of Cuī Zhān’s writing
is truly commendable,
but the whole world values his refinement and charisma,
which is why his talent is obscured.”
Yīn said:
“That statement makes sense.”
He immediately memorialized for his appointment.
After the measure was carried out,
Yīn further remarked:
“In the past, Péi Zàn served as Central Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Láng) during the Jìn dynasty.
His spirit and manner were lofty and transcendent,
and whenever he passed through the palace gates,
the guards were awestruck.
Master Cuī’s dignified appearance
must surely rival Master Péi.”
first year,
he was appointed to *Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng* (Attendant Gentlemen of the Yellow Gates).
He became an intimate friend of Lǐ Gài [Lǐ Gài] of Zhàojùn.
When Gài was about to return east,
Zhān sent him a letter saying:
"Reliance on spirit and indulgence in wine
are my constant flaws,
but in railing against and sharply criticizing others,
you, Sir, are especially severe.
Now that you, Your Excellency, have requested retirement,
how shall I hear of my faults?"
Zhān suffered from a respiratory ailment,
and his nature was slow and reserved;
although he held positions in the Two Departments,
he was ultimately incapable of drafting formal memorials.
He was granted the title *Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn* (General Who Attacks the Captives),
and appointed *Zhōngzhèng* (Impartial Judge) of Qīnghé yì.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
the Crown Prince went to his tutor to receive instruction.
An imperial edict appointed him *Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ* (Central Attendant of the Crown Prince),
and summoned him to Jìnyáng.
The imperial command stipulated that he focus entirely on the Eastern Palace,
managing and protecting the lectures and studies,
as well as matters of conduct and propriety,
all of which were entrusted to him.
When the Crown Prince married his consort, the Húlǜ clan member,
an imperial order commanded Zhān, together with the *Hónglú* (Court of State Ceremonial) official Cuī Jié [Cuī Jié], to compile and establish the marital rites and regulations.
He also personally received a separate imperial instruction, which stated:
"Although there are precedents,
I fear they are not fully perfect.
You must establish these rites properly,
so that they may serve as a future model."
In the first year of Dàníng,
he was appointed *Wèiwèi Shǎoqīng* (Vice Minister of the Court of the Guard),
soon thereafter also serving as *Sànqí Chángshì* (Palace Attendant),
and served as the chief envoy sent to Chén.
Zhān’s language and demeanor were gentle and elegant,
and the Southern people greatly admired and respected him.
They then said:
"During the days when previous dynasties maintained friendly relations,
why did you not intend to come then?"
This shows the high regard in which he was held.
Upon his return, he was appointed *Tàicháng Shǎoqīng* (Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices),
granted the title *Guànjūn Jiāngjūn* (General Who Campaigns Vigorously),
and transferred to *Shàngshū Lìbù Lángzhōng* (Director in the Ministry of Civil Office).
Due to illness, he took emergency leave for more than ten days.
According to the old regulation,
if one did not attend to office for one hundred days, one was relieved of duty.
Wèi Jǐn [Wèi Jǐn], the Minister of Civil Office (*Lìbù Shàngshū*), was irritable and impatient by nature.
Seeing that Zhān’s movements and gestures were slow and relaxed,
and that his departmental duties were numerous and heavy,
he immediately submitted a memorial via courier,
and Zhān was consequently replaced.
Zhān was then released from duty and returned to his home village.
Late in the Tiāntǒng era,
he was granted the title *Piàoqí Dà Jiāngjūn* (General of Cavalry),
and concurrently appointed *Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū* (Grand Master of the Palace with Silver and Blue Seal).
He died in the third year of Wǔpíng,
at the age of fifty-four.
He was posthumously granted *Shǐ Chíjìe*, *Dūdū Jìzhōu Jūnshì*, *Dàlǐ Qīng*, and *Cìshǐ* (Governor),
with the posthumous name Wén.
Zhān’s nature was aloof and arrogant;
he prided himself on his talent and standing.
Those with whom he associated
were all famous figures of the time.
While serving in the Censorate (*Yùshǐ Tái*),
food was sent to his residence,
prepared with every delicacy.
He ate alone in a separate room,
treating the situation with composure.
There was a man from Hédōng named Péi,
who was also a Censor.
He watched for when Zhān was eating,
and went over to visit him.
Zhān did not exchange words with him,
nor did he offer him chopsticks or a spoon.
Péi sat and watched until Zhān finished eating, then withdrew.
The next day,
Péi brought his own chopsticks and spoon,
and freely ate and drank to his heart’s content.
Zhān then said to Péi:
"I did not initially invite you to eat,
nor did I speak with you.
Yet, you were able to disregard minor etiquette.
In the past, Liú Yì [Liú Yì] was in Jīngkǒu,
and presumptuously requested roasted goose.
Are you indeed different from him in this regard?
You are truly a distinguished scholar."
Thereafter, he always ate with him.
Zhān's younger brother, Zhòngwén [Zhòngwén],
possessed academic excellence.
He was *Gāoyáng Tàishǒu* (Prefect of Gāoyáng) and *Qīnghé Nèishǐ* (Administrator of Qīnghé) under the Wèi.
During the Xīnghé era,
he served as Aide to the Chancellor (*Chéngxiàng Yuàn*).
During the defeat at Shāyuàn,
Zhòngwén held onto a horse’s tail to cross the river.
He was alternately submerged and resurfacing in the waves.
Gāozǔ saw him from afar and said:
"That is Aide Cuī [Cuī Yuàn]!"
He immediately sent a boat to rush forward and rescue him.
After he crossed,
Gāozǔ comforted him and said:
"You act for your parents and for your sovereign,
disregarding the myriad perils of death.
You can be called a filial son of the family,
and a loyal official of the state."
He was granted the title *Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn* (General of the Central Army).
Early in the Tiānbǎo era,
he was appointed *Sànqí Chángshì* and *Guānglù Dàfū* (Grand Master of the Palace).
He died in the seventh year,
at the age of sixty.
His son, Yǎn [Yǎn],
during the Wǔpíng era,
served successively as *Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ* (Attendant to the Crown Prince) and *Shàngshū Láng* (Director).
Yǎn’s younger brother, Biāo [Biāo],
possessed learning and literary talent,
and his temperament was very noble.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he was *Zhōngbīng Cānjūn* (Military Adjutant) to the Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*), the Prince of Lángyá.
He participated in determining the Five Rites,
and was Waiting Attendant in the Wénlín Guǎn (Hall of Literary Scholars).
During the Rénshòu era of the Suí dynasty,
he died while serving as *Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì* (Palace Attendant and General Attendant).
His uncle, Rén [Rén],
was *Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ* (Governor of Yǐngzhōu) under the Wèi.
His son, Yànwǔ [Yànwǔ],
was insightful and capable.
He was *Cháogē Lìng* (Magistrate of Cháogē).
Early in the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he was *Wèizhōu Cìshǐ* (Governor of Wèizhōu).
His son, Kǎn [Kǎn],
late in the Wèi dynasty, also served as *Tōngzhí Chángshì* (General Attendant),
and was an envoy sent to Liáng.
His son, Jí [Jí],
early in Wǔpíng, was *Tàizǐ Pú* (Palace Steward of the Crown Prince),
and died while serving as *Wǔdé Jùnshǒu* (Prefect of Wǔdé Commandery).
His son, Yù [Yù],
was *Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu* (Prefect of Dōngguǎn) under the Wèi.
His son, Yuē [Yuē],
was *Sīkōng Jìjiǔ* (Libationer to the Minister of Works).
Zhān’s cousin-uncle, Jǐngfèng [Jǐngfèng],
courtesy name Luánshū,
was the great-great-great-grandson of Zhān’s fifth-generation ancestor Chěng [Chěng].
Jǐngfèng studied widely,
and was famous for his medical skills.
He was *Shàngyào Diǎnyù* (Director of Palace Physicians) under the Wèi,
and *Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ* (Governor of Qiáozhōu) during the Tiānbǎo era.
Jǐngfèng’s elder brother, Jǐngzhé [Jǐngzhé],
was *Tàizhōng Dàfū* (Grand Master of the Palace) and *Sītú Zhǎngshǐ* (Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses) under the Wèi.
His son, Guó [Guó],
courtesy name Fǎjùn,
loved learning since childhood,
read extensively in the classics and commentaries,
possessed many skills,
and was especially skilled in physiognomy.
Early in Tiānbǎo, he was *Shàngyào Diǎnyù*.
During Qiánmíng, he was appointed *Gāoyáng Jùn Tàishǒu* (Prefect of Gāoyáng Commandery) and *Tàizǐ Jiālìng* (Prefect of the Crown Prince’s Household),
during Wǔpíng, he was granted *Yítóng Sānsī* (Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers),
and died while serving as *Hónglú Qīng* (Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial).
In the sixth year of Wǔpíng, Fǎjùn accompanied the emperor to Jìnyáng.
He once said to Lǐ Délín [Lǐ Délín], the *Zhōngshū Shìláng* (Gentleman Attendant at the Secretariat):
"Today, observing the physiognomy of the civil and military officials, from Prime Minister Gāo [Gāo Xiàng] and Prince Wáng [Wáng] downward,
all their affairs are doomed to end;
I cannot bear to speak of it.
Only you, younger brother,
are destined for further wealth and high position.
This will occur in another state,
not in this present court.
I, however, shall not live to see it."
His precision and subtlety were like this.
Cuī Zúzi Zhàoshī,
was the grandson of Wèi Shàngshū Púyè Liàng.
His father, Shìtài,
was a Jiànyì Dàfū.
When Zhàoshī was young, he was unrestrained and unconventional,
but upon growing up, he completely changed his character,
and became careful and sincere.
He widely read the Classics and Histories,
and possessed considerable literary talent.
He inherited his father's noble title, the Viscount (Nán) of Lèlíng.
Upon beginning his official career,
he served as the Kāifǔ Dōnggé Jìjiǔ,
and was transferred to Sīkōng Wàibīng Cānjūn,
and promoted to Dà Sīmǎ Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn.
In the beginning of Tiānpíng [era],
he was transferred to Tōngzhí Shìláng,
and appointed as the envoy to comfort and console Qīngzhōu.
When he reached the borders of Qízhōu,
he was captured by local bandits led by Cuī Jiāyè and others,
who tried to force him to join their cause.
Zhàoshī held firm to his integrity and did not yield,
explaining to them the consequences (misfortune and blessing).
The bandits subsequently released him.
He then completed his tour of consolation of the Qīng region and returned.
During the Yuánxiàng [era],
he repeatedly used the position of Zhōng Shèrén to receive envoys from Liáng.
During the Wǔdìng [era],
he concurrently resumed the office of Zhōng Zhèngyuán Láng,
escorting the Liáng envoy to Xúzhōu.
Upon his return,
he was commanded to compile the Diary of the Emperor’s Activity (Qǐjū Zhù).
Soon after, he concurrently served as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
as Vice Envoy (Fùshǐ) to Liáng.
He was transferred to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In the beginning of Tiānbǎo [era],
he participated in determining the rites and protocols for the abdication,
and was enfeoffed as the Viscount (Nán) of Xiāngchéng County,
while continuing to concurrently hold the position of Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He died in the second year [of Tiānbǎo],
at the age of forty-nine.
The Court Historian says: Lán'gēn early established a reputation for conduct,
and was praised by the contemporary discourse;
Chángrú, with his excellence in talent and prestige,
was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
Both rendered meritorious service in the establishment of hegemony,
and achieved prominent official positions and favored treatment.
Were they not perhaps figures of the righteous banner, along with Lǐ Yuánzhōng and Lú Wénwěi?
Wèi, by relying on powerful favor, formed attachments;
Cuī, because of his family status, was arrogant and stubborn.
Even if they possessed the excellence of Zhōu Gōng,
these aspects would still be considered blemishes upon their virtue,
let alone their inability to even compare in stature.
Zhān's diction and rhythm were warm and elegant,
his spirit and bearing were refined and outstanding,
and he was also a leader of his time.
The Eulogy says: Cuī and Wèi, for their talent and prestige,
were highly regarded at the beginning of the hegemony.
However, their adherence to the principles of virtue,
was still flawed.
Yàntōng valued ambition,
the legacy of his family was abundant.
Biography Sixteen: Sūn Qiān, Chén Yuánkāng, Dù Bì
Sūn Qiān,
courtesy name Yànjǔ,
was a native of Lè'ān.
In his youth, he disciplined his ambition and studied diligently.
Starting from Jiǎnjiào Yùshǐ, he was twice promoted, reaching Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
Tàibǎo Cuī Guāng appointed him to compile the National History,
and he frequently served as Xíngtái Láng,
becoming famous for his literary talent.
When Cuī Zǔchī rebelled,
Qiān was involved.
He fled and hid in the house of Wáng Yuánjǐng,
and only came out after a general amnesty.
Sūn Téng recommended him based on kinship,
but he was not yet appointed.
Coincidentally, when Gāozǔ campaigned in the west,
and ascended Fēnglíng,
he ordered Lǐ Yìshēn, Sīmǎ of the Central and Outer Bureaus, and Lǐ Shìlüè, Chéngjú of the Prime Ministerial Establishment, to jointly draft an urgent proclamation.
Both men declined,
requesting that Qiān replace them.
Gāozǔ summoned Qiān into his tent,
personally fanning the lamp,
and urged him on.
Qiān took up the brush and completed it immediately;
the composition was extremely beautiful.
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased,
and immediately appointed him as Zhǔbù of the Prime Ministerial Establishment,
placing him entirely in charge of literary duties.
Furthermore, he understood the Xiānbēi language,
and concurrently announced and transmitted orders.
He held strenuous and critical responsibilities,
and was greatly appreciated and valued.
He was granted Wéi Shì as his wife;
she was the daughter of a gentry member,
and possessed both beauty and appearance.
People of the time considered this an honor.
Soon after, he was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
while constantly retaining the position of Zhǔbù.
When Shìzōng first wished to go to Yè,
and oversee all court affairs,
Gāozǔ thought he was too young,
and did not grant permission.
Qiān spoke on his behalf,
and thus the trip was finally made.
Relying on this service, he personally requested the rank of Tèjìn,
but Shìzōng only added Sànqí Chángshì.
At that time, there was also a mass conscription of the populace from Yān, Yù, Yún, Shuò, Xiǎn, Wèi, the two Xiàzhōu, Gāopíng, and Píngliáng to serve as soldiers.
Those who hid or absconded, along with their hosts, the Sānzhǎng, and the local officials, were punishable by execution,
and their families were confiscated.
Consequently, the number of recruits obtained was very large;
this was Qiān's strategy.
Qiān's scholarship was shallow and his conduct was slight.
Xíng Shào once said to him:
"You still need to read more books."
Qiān replied:
"My three thousand elite cavalrymen
are enough to defeat your several tens of thousands of weak soldiers."
He once took a medicine known as the 'Tribulus terrestris pill'.
Lǐ Xié and others teased him, saying:
"Your thorny nature should be sufficient on its own,
why do you need to seek it externally?"
Everyone sitting there laughed.
Sīmǎ Zǐrú and Gāo Jìshì summoned Qiān to drink alcohol,
and he died from extreme drunkenness,
at the age of fifty-two.
Gāozǔ personally attended the mourning.
Zǐrú knocked his head on the ground and begged for forgiveness.
Gāozǔ said:
"You have broken off my right arm.
Look up and find me a good replacement."
Zǐrú nominated Wèi Shōu, and Jìshì nominated Chén Yuánkāng,
to succeed Qiān.
He was posthumously granted Yítóng Sānsī, Lìbù Shàngshū, and Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
Chén Yuánkāng,
courtesy name Chángyóu,
was a native of Guǎngzōng.
His father, Zhōngdé,
was the Nèishǐ of Jìyīn during the Wèi dynasty,
and ultimately served as Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
When Yuánkāng achieved prominence,
Zhōngdé was posthumously granted the title of Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu,
with the posthumous name Zhēn.
Yuánkāng had extensive knowledge of literature and history,
and was quick-witted and capable in administration.
In the fifth year of Zhèngguāng of Wèi,
he followed Shàngshū Lìng Lǐ Chóng on the northern expedition,
and was granted the noble title Viscount (Nán) of Línqīng County for military merit.
During the Pǔtài [era],
he was appointed Zhǔshū,
and given the title Wēiliè Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Tiānpíng,
he compiled the Diary of the Emperor’s Activity.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Sītú Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn,
and was especially trusted and relied upon by Gāo Áng, the duke of the establishment.
He left to serve as Kāifǔ Sīmǎ of Yíngzhōu,
and was given the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
In every post he held, he was deemed competent.
Gāozǔ heard of this and summoned him.
He was gradually entrusted with assignments,
and appointed Gōngcáo Cānjūn of the Prime Ministerial Establishment,
internally managing secret affairs.
Gāozǔ managed the great enterprise,
military affairs were numerous and extensive.
Yuánkāng received and carried out instructions,
which greatly helped efficiency.
His nature was also gentle and cautious,
and he understood worldly affairs thoroughly.
Gāozǔ once grew angry at Shìzōng,
personally beating and kicking him in the interior apartments,
and cursing him fiercely.
He came out and told Yuánkāng about it.
Yuánkāng remonstrated, saying:
"When Your Highness instructs the heir,
there are proper rites and laws.
He is an example to be looked upon;
how can it be appropriate to go to such an extreme?"
His words were earnest and sincere,
even to the point of tears.
From then on, Gāozǔ restrained his anger because of him.
Sometimes, when he was enraged and about to strike,
he would immediately say:
"Do not let Yuánkāng know about this."
His reverence and apprehension were like this.
When Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled,
Gāozǔ knew it was because of Cuī Xiān,
and intended to kill Xiān.
Shìzōng hid him and pleaded on his behalf.
Gāozǔ said:
"I will spare his life,
but he must receive a heavy beating."
Shìzōng then produced Xiān and said to Yuánkāng:
"If you let Cuī receive the beating,
then we shall not see each other again."
Xiān was in the courtyard,
taking off his clothes, about to receive punishment.
Yuánkāng hurried in,
ascended the steps,
and spoke, saying:
"Your Highness is about to entrust the empire to the Grand General;
can you not tolerate one Cuī Xiān?"
Gāozǔ subsequently pardoned him.
When Shìzōng entered to assist the capital court,
Cuī Xiān, Cuī Jìshū, Cuī Áng, and others were all appointed and employed.
Zhāng Liàng and Zhāng Huīzuǎn were both well-treated by Gāozǔ,
yet the trust placed in them was all below that given to Yuánkāng.
People at the time had a saying:
"The three Cuī's and two Zhāng's,
are not worth one Kāng."
The daughter of Lú Dàoqián of Fànyáng, the Wèi Shàngshū Púyè, was the wife of the son of Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Guō Qióng.
Qióng was condemned to death and his property confiscated by the government.
Gāozǔ memorialized the court to grant her to Yuánkāng as his wife.
Yuánkāng thereupon abandoned his former wife, née Lǐ,
which those who understood propriety criticized.
Yuánkāng was obsequious and skillful at serving others,
observing faces and anticipating intentions.
He often received promotions,
but he could not manage affairs impartially.
He was consumed by avarice for wealth and profit.
The gold and silks he accepted
were too numerous to count.
His practice of issuing loans and demanding repayments,
spread throughout the prefectures and commanderies,
and he was mocked by the righteous critics.
He followed Gāozǔ in defeating Zhōu Wén Dì at Máng Shān.
All the generals gathered for a great meeting,
to discuss strategy for advancing or retreating.
Everyone agreed that since there was no green grass in the fields,
the men and horses were thin and exhausted,
and they should not pursue far.
Yuánkāng said:
"The two powers have been fighting
for many years.
Now that we have achieved a great victory,
this is a gift from Heaven.
The opportunity must not be missed;
we must take advantage of the victory and pursue them."
Gāozǔ said:
"If we encounter an ambush,
how can I manage?"
Yuánkāng said:
"When Your Highness returned from Shāyuàn before,
they still had no ambush set up.
Now that they are fleeing and defeated like this,
how could they plan far ahead?
If we abandon the pursuit,
it will surely become a future calamity."
Gāozǔ ultimately did not follow him.
For his merit, he was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Ānpíng Xiànzǐ,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
Soon after, he was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn and Tōngzhí Chángshì,
then transferred to Dà Xíngtái Lángzhōng,
and later moved to Yòuchéng.
When Gāozǔ was gravely ill,
he said to Shìzōng:
"In the Battle of Máng Shān,
I did not use Yuánkāng's words,
which will certainly bring you trouble later.
I regret this deeply,
and when I die, I shall not close my eyes."
When Gāozǔ died,
the mourning was kept secret and not announced.
Only Yuánkāng knew about it.
Shìzōng succeeded to the authority,
and was again trusted and relied upon.
He was appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and separately enfeoffed as Duke of Chāngguó Xiàngōng,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Shìzōng was pressured by the generals,
and intended to kill Cuī Xiān in order to placate them.
He secretly told Yuánkāng.
Yuánkāng remonstrated, saying:
"Currently, the four seas are not yet settled,
but the governmental regulations are already established.
If, because a few generals are outside,
you blindly seek to please them,
wrongfully killing the innocent,
and thus violate the penal code,
how can this simply be failing the gods above?
How can you use this to bring peace to the common people below?
Consider the previous case of Cháo Cuò;
I wish Your Grace to be mindful of this."
Shìzōng then ceased the plan.
Gāo Yuè attacked Hóu Jǐng but had not yet defeated him.
Shìzōng wanted to send Pān Xiānglè to assist him.
Yuánkāng said:
"Xiānglè is slow in responding to changing circumstances.
He is not as good as Mùróng Shàozōng.
Moreover, the late King [Gāozǔ] issued an order,
stating that he was capable of fighting Hóu Jǐng.
Your Grace need only show your sincere loyalty to this man,
and then Hóu Jǐng will not be a worry."
At this time, Shàozōng was far away,
and Shìzōng wished to summon him,
but feared he might be alarmed and rebel.
Yuánkāng said:
"Shàozōng knows that Yuánkāng is especially favored and relied upon.
He recently sent someone to bring gold as a gift,
thereby showing his sincerity and devotion.
Yuánkāng wished to reassure him,
so I accepted it and replied to his letter generously.
I guarantee there will be no trouble."
Shìzōng then appointed Shàozōng,
and subsequently defeated Hóu Jǐng.
Yuánkāng was rewarded with fifty catties of gold.
Wáng Sīzhèng entered Yǐng Chéng.
The various generals attacked it,
but could not breach it.
Yuánkāng offered a plan to Shìzōng, saying:
"Your Grace supports the imperial government,
but has not yet achieved extraordinary merit.
Although Hóu Jǐng was defeated,
he was fundamentally not an external enemy.
Now Yǐng Chéng is about to fall;
I wish Your Grace to take advantage of this opportunity
which will be sufficient to establish your prestige and secure your foundation."
Shìzōng ordered Yuánkāng to ride by post relay to observe the situation.
He returned and reported, saying:
"It can definitely be breached."
Shìzōng consequently led a personal campaign,
and upon arrival, conquered it.
Yuánkāng was rewarded with one hundred ingots of gold.
Previously, the Wèi court granted Shìzōng the titles of Xiàngguó and Qí Wáng.
Shìzōng repeatedly declined them.
He then summoned the generals and Yuánkāng to discuss the matter in secret.
All the generals urged Shìzōng to respectfully accept the imperial command.
Yuánkāng thought it was not yet appropriate.
He also said to Wèi Shōu:
"Looking at what these men say, they are entirely intent on misleading the King.
I have already advised the King that,
when he accepts the imperial command,
and establishes an official bureaucracy,
Yuánkāng, unworthy as he is, might receive the position of Huángmén Láng,
but the time is simply not right yet."
Cuī Xiān seized this opportunity to sow discord,
recommending Lù Yuánguī for Dà Xíngtái Láng,
intending thereby to divide Yuánkāng's power.
Since Yuánkāng was greedy for wealth and bribes,
Shìzōng gradually grew suspicious of him internally.
Yuánkāng himself was somewhat fearful.
Shìzōng also wanted to appoint him Zhōngshū Lìng,
placing him in an inactive post,
but the matter had not yet been carried out.
It happened that Shìzōng was about to receive the abdication of Wèi.
Yuánkāng, Yáng Yīn, and Cuī Jìshū were all seated with Shìzōng.
(Shìzōng) was preparing to make large-scale removals and appointments among the court officials,
and they were discussing and evaluating them together.
Lán Gùchéng, a slave of Shìzōng's household (a 'blue-headed slave'), previously managed the kitchen and meals,
and was greatly favored and trusted.
Previously,
Shìzōng had beaten him several dozen strokes.
Wú Rén (Gùchéng's nature) was irritable,
and he also relied upon his past favor.
Consequently, he became deeply resentful and angry,
and conspired with his colleague Āgǎi to murder Shìzōng.
Āgǎi currently served Xiǎnzǔ,
and always carried a knife while following him.
(He) said
"If I hear shouting from the East Chamber,"
"I will immediately use the blade against Xiǎnzǔ."
On that day,
it happened that the Wèi Emperor was first establishing the Eastern Palace,
and all the officials were submitting memorials.
When the affair concluded,
Xiǎnzǔ left through the East Zhǐchē Gate,
having gone elsewhere (for a separate matter).
Before he had returned, the disaster occurred.
Gùchéng took advantage of serving the meal,
placed a knife beneath the tray, and murdered Shìzōng.
Yuánkāng used his body to shield (Shìzōng),
was severely wounded by the stab,
and died by nightfall,
at the age of forty-three.
Yáng Yīn frantically fled,
Jìshū hid himself in the privy,
and Kùzhēn Hēxī Shèlè died defending against the rebel.
At this time, the news of Shìzōng's death was kept secret,
therefore Yuánkāng was entombed within the palace,
and it was falsely announced that he had been dispatched on a mission to the southern borders,
and the position of Zhōngshū Lìng was formally vacated.
The following year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Yuánkāng's understanding surpassed past sages,
and his talent matched the era's heroes.
He was impossible to gauge like a thousand-fathom cliff,
and difficult to measure like ten thousand acres (of water).
He thoroughly controlled military administration,
and perfected the hegemonic Way.
He planned the initial strategies at Shàolíng,
and assisted the assembly at Héyáng.
He managed schemes and set policy,
devoting all his strength and heart,
offering loyal advice and correcting errors,
sacrificing his family for the nation.
He swept clean and pacified the remnant bandits,
and cleared the Jīng-Chǔ region.
Shēn and Fǔ during the flourishing Zhōu dynasty,
or Zǐfáng during the great Hàn dynasty—
separated by generations, they shared the same model,
lauded together despite different times.
But before the great work was complete,
the mountain fell upon him suddenly.
Our grief and sorrow are profound,
and it is fitting to elevate the solemn ceremony."
He was posthumously granted Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié),

Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of the Five Prefectures of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Yīn, and Cāng (Dū Dū Jì Dìng Yíng Yīn Cāng Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiàngjūn), Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōng), and Governor of Jì Prefecture (Jìzhōu Cìshǐ).
He was posthumously enfeoffed with Wǔyì County, receiving one thousand households,
and his former enfeoffment remained as before.
His posthumous title was Wénmù.
Twelve hundred rolls of funeral gifts were provided.
The Grand Herald (Dà Hónglú) supervised the funeral rites.
Whatever was required for the tragic ceremony,
was to be supplied by the state. "
Yuánkāng’s mother, Lady Lǐ,
after Yuánkāng's death,
fell ill from sorrow and grief, and passed away.
She was posthumously granted the title of Grand Lady of Guǎngzōng Commandery (Guǎngzōng Jùn Jūn),
with the posthumous title Zhēnzhāo.
Yuánkāng’s son, Shàncáng,
was gentle, refined, and possessed good judgment.
At the end of Wǔpíng, he was temporarily appointed Integrator of the Three Dukedoms (Yí Tóng Sān Sī) and Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
During the Kāihuáng reign of Suí,
he was Secretary of the Ministry of Rites (Shàngshū Lǐbù Shìláng).
At the beginning of Dàyè,
he died while serving as Attendant to the Administrator of Péngchéng Commandery (Péngchéng Jùn Zànzhì).
Yuánkāng’s younger brother, Chén,
reached the office of Grand Herald (Dà Hónglú).
His youngest brother, Jìqú,
was the Administrator of Jùlù,
and was then transferred to Deputy Governor of Jì Prefecture (Jìzhōu Biéjià).
When the Prince of Píngqín, Guīyàn, rebelled,
Jìqú maintained his integrity and refused to follow him,
and was consequently murdered.
He was posthumously granted Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng) and Governor of Zhào Prefecture (Zhàozhōu Cìshǐ).
Dù Bì,
courtesy name Fǔxuán,
was a native of Qǔyáng in Zhōngshān.
His informal name was Fǔguó.
According to his own preface,
he was originally from Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
His ninth generation ancestor, Ào,
was a Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) during the Jìn dynasty.
On a diplomatic mission, he was stranded in Zhào,
and consequently settled there.
His grandfather, Yànhéng,
was the Administrator of Huáinán.
His father, Cídù,
was the Magistrate of Fánzhì.
Bì was intelligent and quick-witted in youth.
His family was poor and possessed no books.
At the age of twelve,
he enrolled at the commandery school to receive instruction.
During the lectures and teaching,
his teacher always regarded him as extraordinary.
Zhēn Chēn, from the same commandery, was Chief Clerk of Dìng Prefecture (Dìngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ).
He examined and tested various students.
Upon seeing (Bì), he questioned him on policy.
Bì's analysis of the meaning was fluent and clear,
and his answers were like an echo.
Chēn greatly praised him as exceptional.
Chēn's son, Kuān, became friends with Bì.
Chéng, the Prince of Rènchéng and Governor of the Prefecture (Zhōu Mù), heard of him and summoned him for questioning.
He deeply admired and praised him,
recognizing his talent as fit for assisting a king.
When Chéng and Chēn returned to Luò,
they spoke highly of him at court.
The Chancellor, the Prince of Gāoyáng, and many others frequently invited him to serve.
During the Yánchāng period,
he established his career through military merit.
He was appointed General of Guǎngwǔ (Guǎngwǔ Jiàngjūn) and Secretary of the Administrative Section (Mòcāo Cānjūn) in the Prefecture's Zēnglǔ Headquarters,
overseeing documentation.
Bì excelled at writing documents,
and was constantly recommended by his peers.
Early in Xiàochāng,
he was appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì).
He concurrently held the position of Acting Secretary of the Judicial Section (Făcāo Xíng Cānjūn) in the Headquarters of the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Fǔ) under the Prince of Guǎngyáng,
and Director of Finance (Dùzhī Lángzhōng) in the Mobile Department (Xíngtái).
Upon returning,
he was appointed Magistrate of Qǔchéng in Guāng Prefecture.
His governance was clear and peaceful,
striving completely for kindness and leniency.
Litigation ceased,
and he was praised by those near and far.
At that time, the world was fraught with trouble,
and bandits filled the land.
When soldiers were levied and summoned,
many fled along the route.
The court was concerned by this.
Therefore, an order was issued that the military gear carried by the soldiers,
should be transported separately in carts along the way;
and further, that the county magistrates must personally escort them to the military headquarters.
When Guāng Prefecture dispatched troops,
Bì escorted his detachment until they reached Běihǎi Commandery.
All the prefectural troops scattered and deserted simultaneously,
only those Bì escorted did not move.
Rebel soldiers from other areas,
all came to attack and loot,
wishing them to join the defection.
Bì led the trusted soldiers under his command to fight back,
and they ultimately refused to comply.
Thus, they were able to reach the military headquarters together.
The Army Administrator (Jūnsī), Cuī Zhōng, reported the situation to the throne.
This is how he won the hearts of the people.
During Pǔtài,
the Ministry of Personnel (Lìcáo) sought out especially distinguished administrators and magistrates.
Bì had already been replaced and returned.
Wáng Xīn, the Administrator of Dōnglái, recommended Bì in response to the inquiry.
When Bì's father was in their home village,
he was killed by bandits.
Bì observed mourning for six years.
By regular appointment, he was made Censor (Yùshǐ),
promoted to General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiàngjūn) and Grand Master of the Center (Tài Zhōng Dàfū),
and was concurrently in charge of Correcting Characters within the Palace (Nèi Zhèngzì).
All impeachment memorials submitted by the Censorate,
were written by Bì.
The documents and reports submitted by the Censors on their official missions,
were entrusted to Bì for review and inspection,
before they were implemented.
He was promoted to General of the Central Army (Zhōng Jūn Jiàngjūn) and Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) in the Headquarters of the General of Agile Cavalry of Běi Yù Prefecture.
Before he took up this post,
Dòu Tài, the Integrator (Yítóng), commanded the troops on a western expedition.
An edict ordered Bì to be the Army Supervisor (Jiānjūn) for Tài.
When Tài suffered defeat and committed suicide,
Bì, along with six of his followers, fled back to Shǎn Prefecture.
The Governor, Liú Guì, locked them up and sent them to Jìnyáng.
Gāozǔ questioned him, saying:
"For Zhōngwèi Dòu's expedition,
I had already provided methods for action.
Yet he violated my instructions,
and brought about his own defeat and death.
How is it that you did not offer a single word of remonstrance?"
Bì replied:
"I am but a minor functionary, skilled in drafting documents.
I possess only the humble skill of writing.
Matters of military expediency,
are beyond my scope to discuss."
Gāozǔ became even angrier.
Fortunately, Fáng Mó advised (Gāozǔ), and Bì was spared.
He was demoted and transferred to Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) of the Xiàguàn Garrison.
Yuánxiàng
era, Gāozǔ summoned Bì to serve as the Acting Adjutant of the Legal Registrar in the Office of the Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng Fǔ Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn),
and appointed him to manage the affairs of the Records Secretary (Jìshì).
He was transferred to be a Director (Lángzhōng) of the Grand Mobile Secretariat (Dàxíngtái),
and soon thereafter was granted the title General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn).
Gāozǔ again appointed Bì to manage confidential affairs,
and Bì was greatly trusted and favored.
Sometimes, when matters were urgent and there was no time to write instructions,
[Gāozǔ] would directly hand over blank paper,
and immediately order him to promulgate [the decree].
Bì once took the opportunity to secretly advise Gāozǔ to accept the abdication of Wèi (Wèi Chán),
but Gāozǔ raised his staff and struck him, driving him away.
Xīn Zǐyán, the Legal Registrar (Fǎcáo) of the Chancellor's Office (Xiàngfǔ), consulted on a matter,
saying that he must obtain a signature (shǔ).
Zǐyán read
the character “署” (shǔ)
as
“樹” (shù).
Gāozǔ grew furious and said:
“This common fellow does not know how to avoid my personal taboo name!”
He had him caned in front of him.
Bì stepped forward and said:
“According to the Rites (Lǐ),
in the case of a two-character name, one does not partially avoid [both characters simultaneously].
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) when speaking of ‘Zhēng’
did not speak of ‘Zài,’
and when speaking of ‘Zài’
did not speak of ‘Zhēng.’
The offense of Zǐyán
can perhaps be forgiven on principle.”
Gāozǔ cursed him, saying:
“You see I am angry,
yet you still dare to drag in the classics and cite the Rites (Lǐ)!”
He shouted, ordering him to leave.
Bì walked about ten paces,
when [Gāozǔ] called him back,
and Zǐyán was also pardoned and released.
The Heir Apparent (Shìzǐ), who was in the capital, heard of this
and said to Yáng Yīn:
“The Prince (Wáng) relies on having this upright man by his side,
so that all under Heaven may receive benefit from him;
how could this benefit be limited solely to our family?”
Bì, believing that few civil and military officials currently in office
possessed integrity and honesty,
spoke of this to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ said:
“Come here, Bì,
I will tell you.
The world is mired in chaos and disorder,
and these customs have been long established.
Currently, the families of my commanders (Dūjiāng) are mostly in Guānxī,
and the Black Otter (Hēidá) constantly tries to lure them away;
the loyalty of the people, whether they stay or go, is yet unsettled.
Furthermore, in Jiāngdōng, there is that old man, Xiāo Yǎn of Wú,
who is entirely devoted to proper dress, Rites, and Music (Yīguān Lǐyuè).
The scholars and officials of the Central Plain (Zhōngyuán) look toward him, believing that the legitimate mandate (Zhèngshuò) resides with him.
If I hastily impose strict laws
and show no leniency,
I fear that all the commanders will defect entirely to the Black Otter (Hēidá),
and the gentry will all flee to Xiāo Yǎn.
If the population and resources scatter,
how can I maintain the state?
You should wait a little while;
I will not forget this.”
When the Battle of Shāyuàn (Shāyuàn zhī Yì) was about to take place,
Bì again requested that they first eliminate the internal enemies,
and then proceed to attack the external invaders.
Gāozǔ asked who the internal enemies were.
Bì replied:
“They are all the honored nobles (Xūnguì) who plunder the common people.”
Gāozǔ did not reply.
Instead, he ordered all the soldiers to draw their bows and fit arrows,
raise their swords, and press down their lances (shuò), lining the road,
and made Bì pass dangerously through their ranks,
saying:
“There will certainly be no injury.”
Bì trembled and sweated profusely.
Gāozǔ then explained to him, saying:
“Though the arrows were aimed,
they did not shoot;
though the swords were raised,
they did not strike;
though the lances were pressed down,
they did not stab.
Yet you immediately lost your courage.
All the meritorious men faced sharp blades with their own bodies,
surviving only one in a hundred deaths.
Even if they are greedy and vulgar,
the risks they undertook were enormous,
and they cannot be treated according to ordinary regulations.”
Bì was greatly terrified at that moment,
and immediately knocked his forehead on the ground and apologized, saying:
“I was foolish and lacked wisdom,
failing to recognize the highest principle.
Now that I have been enlightened,
I finally see the sagely mind of true understanding.”
Afterward, he followed Gāozǔ in defeating the Western Wèi (Xī Wèi) at Mángshān.
He was ordered to compose the proclamation of victory (Lùbù),
which Bì immediately wrote by hand onto silk,
never having prepared a draft.
For this merit, he was granted the noble title Male of Dìngyáng County (Dìngyáng Xiàn Nán),
with a fief of two hundred households,
and appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary, Cavalry-Retainer (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì) and General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn).
He received orders to serve as an envoy to the Imperial Palace (Què).
The Wèi Emperor (Wèi Dì) received him in the Hall of Nine Dragons (Jiǔlóng Diàn),
and said:
“I have just begun reading the Zhuāngzǐ,
and happened upon the name Qín (referring to Qín Bì).
You must truly embody the Dào and grasp the truth,
achieving mysterious unity and the equalization of all things (Xuántóng Qíwù).
I hear that you excel in your studies,
so I have a brief question for you.
In the scriptures, are the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) and the Dharma Nature (Fǎxìng) one or different?”
Bì replied:
“The Buddha Nature and the Dharma Nature
are merely a single principle.”
The Emperor further asked:
“Since the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is distinct from the Dharma Nature (Fǎxìng),
how can they be one?”
[Bì] replied:
“Nature (Xìng) is nowhere absent;
therefore, we do not speak of two.”
The Emperor further asked:
“Exponents all say that the Dharma Nature (Fǎxìng) is wide,
and the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is narrow.
Since wide and narrow are different,
how can they not be two?”
Bì replied again:
“Residing in the wide, it becomes wide;
residing in the narrow, it becomes narrow.
But if we discuss the fundamental essence of Nature (Xìngtǐ),
it is neither wide nor narrow.”
The Emperor asked:
“Since you say it becomes wide and becomes narrow,
how can it be neither wide nor narrow?
If it were definitely narrow,
it also could not become wide.”
[Bì] replied:
“Because it is neither wide nor narrow,
it is able to become both wide and narrow.
Although that which is formed (the wide and the narrow) is different,
the fundamental capacity that forms them is one.”
The Emperor was pleased and praised the answer as excellent.
He then led Bì into the Scripture Treasury (Jīngshūkù),
bestowed upon him one volume of the Dìchí Jīng,
and one hundred bolts of silk.
When Yān, Duke of Píngyáng (Píngyáng Gōng Yān), became the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Bīngzhōu,
Gāozǔ again commanded Bì to concurrently hold the position of Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of the Cavalry General’s Command (Piàojífǔ) in Bīngzhōu.
Bì's nature loved discussions of principle (mínglǐ),
exploring the flavor of the profound essence (Xuánzōng).
While serving in the military,
he carried classics with him throughout his service.
He annotated the two scrolls of the Lǎozǐ Dàodé Jīng,
and presented a memorial saying:
“Your servant has heard that by riding the wind and arranging the arrows,
one pursues the escaped plumage among the high clouds;
by facing the waves and ordering the hook,
one draws the submerged scales from the great ravines.
If one truly grasps its Way (Dào),
one excels in the task.
Since this is true concerning things,
the principle (lǐ) is also certainly so.
I humbly consider that the two classics, the Dào and the Dé,
elucidate the hidden ultimate,
their purport harmonizing movement and stillness,
and their utility encompassing the ordinary and the sagely.
When discussing conduct,
it focuses on clarity, purity, gentleness, and yieldingness;
when speaking of achievements (jì),
it covers accomplishing works and achieving good governance (zhì).
It is truly the river and sea for all streams,
and the root and foundation of all arts.
Your servant, having read the classics since youth,
was particularly and earnestly fond of them.
Although serving in the military administration (jūnfǔ),
I never abandoned my intellectual recreation (yóuxī).
Having pondered and savored them for a long time,
I felt faintly as if I had some insight.
Compared to previous annotations,
I humbly submit that it differs slightly from the old explanations.
As feelings are generated within and revealed externally,
I rashly used a pipe to peep (guǎnkuī),
and thereby committed over-scrutiny (chuānzáo).
It does not reach the skill of 'gliding the blade' (yóurèn),
and I am ashamed regarding the 'wielding of the axe' (yùnjīn).
It is insufficient to break open the arguments concerning autumn down (qiūháo),
how then can it untangle the knots of connected rings (liánhuán)?
Originally intending to keep it within my own gate,
to bequeath it to my young and inexperienced,
and additionally, to serve as a recent resource for my foolishness and crudeness,
privately preparing it for the sake of noting what I might forget.
I did not realize that the concentrated spirit of Gūyè,
and the radiating brilliance of Fényáng,
can indeed hear the low,
and that common speech is subject to examination.
At the end of spring, having received the Imperial order (zhǐ),
I was humbly favored by your instruction,
commanding me to present my annotation of the Lǎozǐ.
I reverently dare to seal and present it,
along with the separate preface.”
The Imperial edict (zhào) replied, saying:
“Lǐ Jūn's spirit wanders in the deep obscurity (míngyǎo),
and he singularly observes the vague and indistinct (huǎnghū).
Profoundly aligning with Creation (Zàohuà),
his essence reaches the ultimate of all existence.
From within, it spreads outside,
and its pervasive responses can establish completion.
From oneself, it extends to all things,
and its operation can be utilized for benefit.
To elevate the family and pacify the state,
the meaning lies in this literature (sīwén).
Your talent and thought are excellent and thorough,
your studies honor what is comprehensive and far-reaching.
You rest and dwell in the Ru school (Rúmén),
yet gallop freely in the realm of the profound (Xuánsì).
You have not only inaugurated the learning of the specialized school,
but also clarified the words of Shì (Buddhism) and Lǎo (Daoism).
The doors are opened and the gates are spread wide,
the paths and routes are clear and accessible.
Principle (lǐ) and affairs (shì) are both expounded,
capacity and utility are both manifested.
These are things that previous worthies did not realize,
and that surviving elders have not heard.
The purport is ultimately subtle and minute,
the words exhaust the deep mysteries.
We have savored these two classics,
but grew weary of the old explanations.
Having examined your new annotation,
our gain has been substantial.
This praise and appreciation,
is truly not a matter of a single utterance.
We have already commanded that it be edited onto bamboo slips (shāqīng biān),
and stored in the Yángé.”
He also presented one copy to Gāozǔ,
and one copy to Shìzōng.
During the Wǔdìng period,
he was promoted to Minister of the Imperial Guard (Wèiwèi Qīng).
At that time, Liáng dispatched Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng and others to invade Péngchéng. Grand Commander Gāo Yuè and Administrator Mùróng Shàozōng led various armies to suppress them.
An edict (zhào) appointed Bì as Army Supervisor (Jūnsī),
acting as Left Assistant (Zuǒ Chéng) of the Traveling Chancellery (Xíngtái).
Before departing,
Shìzōng bestowed upon him a Hu horse,
and spoke to Bì, saying:
“This is the second best horse I possess;
I ride it myself.
Now that we are parting for a long time,
I offer it as a gift.”
He also commanded him to state the essentials of governance that could serve as lessons and warnings,
and record one or two points.
Bì requested to explain orally, saying:
“The great affairs of the realm (Tiānxià),
are none other than the two principles of reward and punishment (shǎng fá).
Reward one person and make everyone in the realm rejoice;
punish one person and make everyone in the realm submit.
If only these two matters can be achieved moderately (dézhōng),
then naturally everything will be perfect.”
Shìzōng was greatly pleased and said:
“Although your words are few,
they are crucial to the principle (lǐ).”
They clasped hands and parted.
He defeated Xiāo Míng at Hánshān,
and separately joined Commander Pān Lè in attacking and capturing Tóngzhōu, which belonged to Liáng.
He then joined Yuè and others in consoling the troops and comforting the populace,
and the entire region relied upon them heavily.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of the sixth year,
the Wèi Emperor gathered famous monks at the Xiǎnyáng Hall to lecture and discuss Buddhist principles (fólǐ).
Bì, along with Minister of Personnel Yáng Yīn, Director of the Central Secretariat Xíng Shào,
and Palace Secretary Wèi Shōu, all attended the Dharma assembly (fǎyán).
The Emperor ordered Bì to ascend the lion throne (shīzǐ zuò),
and expound before the assembly.
Zhāoxuándū Monks Sēng Dá and Sēng Dàoshùn, who were both outstanding figures in the black robes (zìlín),
raised pointed questions and challenges.
After dozens of exchanges,
no one was able to subdue him.
The Emperor said:
“If this worthy had been born during the time of the School of Kǒng (Confucius),
what would he have been like?”
Guānzhōng sent Administrator Wáng Sīzhèng to occupy Yǐngzhōu,
and Grand Commandant Gāo Yuè and others attacked it.
Bì managed the affairs of Yǐngzhōu,
acting as Left Assistant of the Traveling Chancellery.
At that time, the main army was within the borders,
and provisioning involved great expense.
Bì balanced the hardships and comforts (jūn qí kǔ lè),
managing both public and private matters.
He was greatly praised by the people of the prefecture.
When Yǐngzhōu was pacified,
Shìzōng said: "Qīng, try to discuss why Wáng Sīzhèng was captured.”
Bì said:
“Sīzhèng did not examine the principle of rebellion and compliance (nìshùn zhī lǐ),
did not recognize the configuration of size (dà xiǎo zhī xíng),
nor estimate the momentum of strength and weakness (qiáng ruò zhī shì).
Having these three blind spots (sān bì),
it was appropriate that he was captured.”
Shìzōng said:
“In antiquity, there was 'gaining through rebellion and holding through compliance' (nì qǔ shùn shǒu).
Great Wú was constrained by small Yuè.
Weak Yān was able to defeat strong Qí.
How can your three principles, Qīng,
sustain themselves?”
Bì said:
“If the king is compliant but not great,
great but not strong,
or strong but not compliant,
the meaning might indeed be partial,
as indicated by Your Sacred Intent (Shèngzhǐ).
However, since [our side] now possesses all these superior advantages simultaneously,
my humble words can still be maintained.”
Shìzōng said:
“Whenever one wishes to maintain an argument,
it ought to have a definite point.
How can you widely encompass all principles,
seeking to secure yourself through multiplicity?"
Bì said:
“Your Majesty's (Dàwáng) majestic virtue,
involves all merits combined.
Because the meaning is broad, the words are broad;
it is not that the words are applied externally to the meaning.”
Shìzōng said:
“If so,
why was it not taken for a full year,
yet when We (gū) arrived, it was immediately captured?”
Bì said:
“This was surely the will of Heaven (Tiānyì), desiring to manifest Your Majesty's achievement.”
Xiǎnzǔ appointed him Acting Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ),
and added the title of General of the Guard (Wèijiāngjūn).
He was transferred to Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
retaining the position of Chief Clerk.
His noble rank was advanced to Marquis of Dìngyáng County (Dìngyáng Xiàn Hóu),
and the size of his stipend territory (yì) was increased to five hundred households in total.
Bì's ambition was to assist and support,
doing everything he knew how to do.
When Xiǎnzǔ was about to receive the abdication from Wèi,
traveling from Jìnyáng to Píngchéng Dū,
he commanded Bì and Minister of Works Sīmǎ Zǐrú to rush ahead by post-relay carriage,
to observe the public sentiment.
After ascending the throne (jiàn zuò zhī hòu),
he ordered that [Bì's writings] be placed in boxes on the left and right and moved into the Bǎigé (Cypress Pavilion).
Due to his merit in assisting the formulation of the plan,
he was promoted to General of Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) and Minister of the Imperial Guard (Wèiwèi Qīng),
and separately enfeoffed as Earl of Cháng'ān County (Cháng'ān Xiàn Bó).
(I/He) once attended Xíng Shào while accompanying the sovereign/prince to Dōngshān,
where they jointly discussed profound principles.
Xíng Shào believed that arguing for
a dead person to return to life risked being like drawing feet on a snake (a superfluous action).
Bì replied:
"Generally speaking, when a person dies,
they return to nothingness (wú), and do not possess the power to be reborn.
However, before a thing is born,
it is fundamentally also nothingness.
If nothingness can become existence,
this is not considered doubtful.
If the succeeding arises from the preceding,
why should this alone cause surprise?"
Xíng Shào said:
"The Sages established their teachings
primarily for encouragement and reward.
Therefore, they instilled fear regarding the future
hoping that all would properly fulfill their nature."
Bì said:
"The Sages unite their virtue with Heaven and Earth,
and align their trustworthiness with the four seasons.
What they say becomes canon;
what they do becomes law.
To say they use falsehoods to instruct creatures,
and use deceit to exhort the people,
would be equivalent to the writing in the fish's belly (a deceptive omen),
or diverging from the announcement carved into the pillar (a genuine decree).
How, then, could they make the Northern Dipper shed its light,
or the Dragon Palace store the writings?
Even granting what you argue,
if the rewards of good fortune can mold and refine human nature and spirit,
thereby greatly encouraging morality and teaching,
the magnitude of the benefit
could not be surpassed.
This, then, is true teaching.
How can it be called unreal?"
Xíng Shào said:
"The word for 'death' (sǐ) means 'to dissipate' (sī),
meaning the vital spirit is exhausted."
Bì replied:
"The dissipation you speak of
is like the arrows running out,
having run out from the hand (i.e., temporary exhaustion in one locus).
The Xiǎoyǎ says: 'No plant does not die,'
and the Yuèlìng also states: 'The creeping grasses die.'
Although moving creatures and plants are different,
they are also of this category.
If soulless vegetation
can still return to life,
why should creatures possessing spirit
be prevented from being remade?
If you say that when grass dies, the seed remains,
then similarly, when a person dies, consciousness remains.
If the seed of consciousness is not seen,
one calls it non-existent.
The spirit (shén) dwelling in the form (xíng)
is also not inherently visible.
Even the keen sight of Lí Zhū cannot perceive it.
Although Jiǎng Jì observes the eyes,
and the wise and foolish can be discerned;
and Zhōng Shēng listens to music,
causing mountains and rivers to appear in form.
These are the functions of the spirit,
not the substance of the spirit itself.
It is like how jade and silk are not the rites themselves,
and bells and drums are not the music itself.
If we extrapolate from this,
the meaning becomes clear."
Xíng Shào said:
"Jì Zhá spoke of going everywhere (wú bù zhī),
which also implies complete dispersion.
If it were to reassemble and become a new thing,
one could not speak of its going everywhere."
Bì replied:
"The bones and flesh return below to the earth;
the spiritual breath (hún qì) goes everywhere.
This is the form falling and the spirit wandering—
it moves on but is not exhausted.
It is like a bird leaving its nest,
or a snake leaving its hole.
Because it still exists,
it can go everywhere.
If it truly ceased to exist,
where would it go?
Yánlíng (Jì Zhá) had the knowledge to perceive the subtle,
knowing that the spirit does not follow the form;
Zhòngní expressed the admiration for practiced rites (funeral rites),
praising how the spirit separates from the form.
If you allow the spirit to be utterly dispersed,
then everyone would be Jì Zǐ.
I would not call that a high theory,
to insist on this being nothingness."
Xíng Shào said:
"The spirit in a person
is like the light in a candle.
When the candle is exhausted, the light is extinguished;
when a person dies, the spirit perishes."
Bì replied:
"Old scholars and former Confucians
often use this phrase,
and all doubts and confusions
arise from it.
This is because those who argue it are not precise,
and those who contemplate it are not sincere.
I humbly have a small insight
that can examine this comparison.
The candle produces light because of its substance;
if the substance is large, the light is also large.
In a person, however, the spirit is not bound to the form;
if the form is small, the spirit is not small.
Thus, the wisdom of Zhòngní
must not have been shorter than that of the Cháng Dí (giants);
and the heroism of Mèngdé
was far more extraordinary than that of Cuī Yǎn (who was very tall).
The spirit relative to the form
is also like a ruler possessing a state.
The state is indeed governed by the ruler,
but the ruler is not produced by the state.
If they did not arise together,
who can say they perish together?"
Xíng Shào said:
"To abandon this and go to that,
continuous generation exists.
Zhōu and Kǒng should naturally emulate Zhuāng Zhōu beating the earthen basin
and harmonizing with Sānghù's singing (i.e., accepting death cheerfully)?"
Bì replied:
"If one rests together under the same shade,
there is still sorrow upon imminent separation.
If one travels in a narrow rut,
one also gives rise to sighs of distress midway.
How much more so when speaking of joining bodies and sharing breath,
transforming into different beings!
Mourning that expresses genuine emotion
does not harm the nature of the Sage."
Xíng Shào said:
"The hawk transforms into a dove,
the rat changes into a quail.
The 'yellow mother' becomes a soft-shelled turtle.
All these are types of birth.
Classification transforms and mutually produces life,
just as light leaves this candle
and ignites that candle."
Bì replied:
"Before the hawk transforms into a dove,
the dove is not yet in existence.
(The same goes for the) rat
Since neither is a dual existence,
how can both exist simultaneously?
If the light leaves this candle
and can ignite that candle,
then the spirit leaving this form
must also be able to inhabit that form.
Why be confused by this?"
Xíng Shào said:
"If one wishes the soil to transform into a person,
or wood to grow eyes and a nose,
the spiritual intelligence of Creation
should not behave in this manner."
Bì replied:
"Decaying grass turns into fireflies;
old wood turns into scorpions.
If Creation could not do this,
who made it so?"
Afterwards, Bì wrote a separate letter to Xíng Shào, saying:
"In proposing words and clarifying principles,
one should cite sources for evidence.
If one violates Kǒng (Confucius) and goes against Shì (Buddhism),
one remains alone as a superior person (jūnzǐ).
If one does not take the Sages as teachers,
every creature will have its own mind.
If every horse's head desires to go east,
who can stop them?
What is gained by fitting one's inner thoughts,
and why value attaining unity?
Although your untrammeled style is lofty,
my narrow view has not been enlightened."
They exchanged letters back and forth repeatedly,
until Xíng Shào's reasoning failed, and he stopped.
The text is voluminous and is not recorded here.
before he had departed,
a household retainer accused Bì of plotting rebellion.
He was arrested and imprisoned.
The investigation found no proof
and after a long time, he was pardoned.
Consequently, he ceased attending court audiences.
He was again punished because his second son, Táiqīng, the Tíngwèi Jiān (Director of the Court of Judicial Review), delayed verdicts,
and together with the court officials, he was impeached by Lángzhōng Fēng Jìngzhé.
Once the matter reached the emperor's ears,
Xiǎnzǔ became enraged,
and consequently exiled Bì to Línhǎi Zhèn.
At that time, Dōngfāng Bái'é, a native of Chǔzhōu, rebelled,
with people responding in both the north and south.
Línhǎi Zhèn was attacked by the bandit leaders Zhāng Chuò, Pān Tiānhé, and others.
Bì led the men of Lìchéng,
and ultimately managed to hold the area intact and secure.
Xiǎnzǔ praised him
and ordered him to act in the affairs of Hǎizhōu,
which was the very prefecture to which he had been exiled.
While in the prefecture, he memorialized to open up the Língdào road and the former route of Hán Xìn.
Furthermore, east of the prefecture, along the coast, he erected a long embankment,
to block the salty tides externally
and draw in fresh water internally.
An imperial edict ordered both proposals to be implemented.
He was transferred to be the Cìshǐ (Governor) of Xúzhōu,
but before he took office,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu.
Bì was refined, cultured, generous, and forgiving.
He was especially knowledgeable about administrative duties.
Wherever he served, he maintained integrity
and was cherished by the officials and the people.
He indulged in and loved profound principles (Xuánlǐ),
and his devotion deepened with age.
He also annotated the "Huì Shī Piān" chapter of the *Zhuāngzǐ* and the upper and lower *Xì* (Appendices) of the *Yì*,
naming his new commentary the *Yìyuàn*,
and both circulated throughout the world.
Bì was fundamentally straightforward.
Earlier, when serving the hegemon court (Bàcháo),
he often offered correction and rectification.
When Xiǎnzǔ became chancellor,
and Bì reached the position of head of the staff,
when he first heard the discussion of abdication (yīràng),
he still offered words of remonstrance.
Xiǎnzǔ once asked Bì,
"Who should be employed to govern the state?"
He replied:
"The Xiānbēi (Chē Mǎ Kè) riders and cavalry,
will eventually need to employ people from Zhōngguó (the Central Plains)."
Xiǎnzǔ believed this statement mocked him.
Gāo Dézhèng held a crucial position,
and Bì was unable to defer to him.
Thus, he publicly rebuked him in front of the assembled officials, saying:
"The Huángmén (Palace Attendant), being near the sovereign,
how can he hear of good things and not be startled,
only liking to cut down, suppress, and thwart others!"
Dézhèng deeply resented this
and repeatedly spoke ill of him.
Dézhèng also ordered the scribe Dù Yǒngzhēn to secretly memorialize that when Bì was Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk),
he accepted favors and recommendations from people
and extensively managed weddings and marriages.
Xiǎnzǔ held this grudge internally.
Bì relied on their past acquaintance and still submitted petitions concerning public affairs.
In the summer of the tenth year (of the reign),
the sovereign, while drinking,
enumerated Bì's mistakes and faults
and immediately sent an order to have him executed in the prefecture.
He was sixty-nine years old at the time.
Afterwards, the sovereign regretted it,
but the courier dispatched to stop the execution arrived too late.
His eldest son, Ruí, and his fourth son, Guāng,
were exiled far away to Línhǎi Zhèn.
His second son, Táiqīng,
had previously been banished to Dōng Yùzhōu.
In the beginning of Qiánmíng,
they were all permitted to return to Yè.
In the fifth year of Tiāntǒng (569),
Bì was posthumously granted the titles of Shǐ Chíjié, Military Governor of Yáng and Yǐng Prefectures, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, and Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
His posthumous name (shì) was Wénsù.
Ruí and Táiqīng
both possessed scholarly achievements.
Táiqīng was especially skilled in writing and calligraphy,
and was highly praised by his contemporaries.
Ruí,
courtesy name Zǐměi.
During the Wǔpíng era, he served as Dàlǐ Shàoqīng (Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review),
concurrently Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant),
and led the mission to the Chén dynasty.
In his later years,
he was Lìbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Ministry of Personnel).
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he died while holding the post of Cìshǐ of Kāizhōu.
Táiqīng, courtesy name Shǎoshān,
served successively as Zhōngshū Shìláng (Secretariat Gentleman) and Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Gate Gentleman),
concurrently Dà Zhùzuò (Great Editor) and Compiler of the National History.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the Directorate of Education),
overseeing the Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng (Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs).
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu conquered Qí,
he ordered Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Yáng Xiūzhī and seventeen other well-known court scholars to follow his carriage into the Pass (Guān),
but the brothers Ruí and Táiqīng were not included in this list.
Although Táiqīng was summoned later,
he was sent home due to his deafness.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he was summoned to serve as Zhùzuò Láng (Editor),
but after slightly more than a year, he retired due to old age.
An imperial decree granted his request.
His treatment was exceptionally generous;
he was granted salary for the rest of his life.
He died shortly thereafter.
The official historian says: Sūn Qiān served closely around the Imperial Domain (Biànfān),
holding literary positions.
Having entered the staff not long before,
his emotional loyalty was already profound.
When he met his sudden demise,
Gāozǔ said, "I have broken my right arm."
Although the military banners had not yet been furled (the war was ongoing),
he cherished talented men.
Otherwise, how could he have accomplished the work of a Hegemon King (Bàwáng)?
The Grand Historian (Tàishǐ Gōng) said:
"It is not the one who dies who finds it difficult;
it is the one who faces death who finds it difficult."
"Some deaths are weightier than Tài Shān,
while others are lighter than a swan's feather."
This is the meaning of it.
Yuánkāng, relying on his wisdom, intelligence, and ability,
dedicated himself to the hegemon court (Bàcháo),
intimately serving in the inner counsels,
where the trust placed in him was heavy.
When danger struck, he did not seek temporary escape,
but sacrificed his life for righteousness.
He can be said to have met his proper end.
Yáng Yīn considered himself to possess extraordinary conduct and rare talent,
far surpassing ordinary men.
Yet, during the time of regicide and rebellion,
he ran away and avoided it.
Thus, it is not only difficult for the one who faces death,
but for the one who dies, it is also difficult.
In his youth, Xiǎnzǔ concealed his abilities,
and was not yet recognized by the court officials.
When the disaster of the Northern Palace occurred,
he was elevated according to seniority,
therefore, the proposal for the transfer of the mandate (shòuzhōng)
was not entirely accepted at the time.
Dù Bì's learning and knowledge were discriminating and clear.
His words were sincere and upright.
At the time of the abdication and dynastic change,
he was the first to conceive a differing plan.
The Emperor's wrath did not subside,
and he finally suffered public execution.
There have been many cases of straightforward speech,
but could any have avoided such an outcome?
Eulogy says: Yànjǔ strove tirelessly;
his talent was high, but his conduct was flawed.
Yuánkāng was loyal and brave,
abandoning life to preserve righteousness.
Áng'áng (Bì) proudly assisted Xuán (Emperor Xuānwǔ),
his thoughts extended to discussing Heaven (Tántiān).
When the Way perished and the time was obscured,
he died, but his reputation remained whole.
