Chapter 17: Biographies of Zhāng Zuǎn, Zhāng Liàng, Zhāng Yào, Zhào Qǐ, Xú Yuǎn, Wáng Jùn, Wáng Hóng
Zhāng Zuǎn,
courtesy name Huīzuǎn,
was a native of Píngchéng, Dàijùn.
His father, Liè,
was the Tàishǒu (Administrator) of Sānggān.
Zuǎn first served Ěrzhū Róng,
and later served as Dū Dū Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Area Commander) for Ěrzhū Zhào.
He was sent by Zhào as an envoy to Gāozǔ
and was consequently recognized and favored by him.
When Gāozǔ raised the righteous army east of the mountains (Shāndōng),
Liú Dàn occupied Xiāngzhōu and resisted.
Zuǎn was among those besieged.
Gāozǔ attacked and took the city,
and employed Zuǎn to participate in the Chancellor's military affairs.
Zuǎn's nature was accommodating and skillful.
In going in and out (of the palace/camp),
he gradually became favored and trusted.
Consequently, he was appointed Xíngtái Lángzhōng (Director in the Traveling Chancellery).
Gāozǔ requested the reduction of his own fiefdom
to distribute rewards to civil and military officials.
Zuǎn was granted the title of Earl (Bó) of Shòuzhāng in accordance with the standard procedure.
At the end of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's reign,
Gāozǔ went to Luò(yáng).
He appointed Chēn, Duke of Zhàojùn, as Xíngtái (Traveling Chancellor),
to guard Jìnyáng,
and made Zuǎn the Yòu Chéng (Vice Director of the Right).
He was transferred to be Gōngcáo Cānjūnshì (Adjutant in charge of Meritorious Services) in the Chancellor's Department,
and appointed Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Right with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon).
He was sent as an envoy to the Rúru,
and performed his mission in a manner that pleased the court.
He successively held the post of Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Gentleman-in-Attendance) in both the central and outer departments and the Chancellor's Department.
During the Battle of Máng Shān,
a great number of captives were seized.
Gāozǔ ordered Zuǎn to lead the escort of these captives to the capital (Jīngshī).
The Emperor of Wèi bestowed upon him five hundred bolts of silk
and enfeoffed him as the Earl of Wǔ'ān County.
and followed the campaign against Yùbì.
When the main army was about to return to Shāndōng,
they marched until they reached Jìnzhōu.
Suddenly, they encountered cold rain.
The soldiers were starving and freezing,
to the point where some died.
Due to border security regulations, the prefecture did not permit them entry into the city.
At that time, Zuăn was a Special Envoy.
Upon meeting them,
he immediately ordered the gates opened and let them in,
divided them up and billeted them in civilian homes,
supplying them with cooked food,
thereby saving many lives.
Gāozǔ heard of this and praised him.
Zuăn served Gāozǔ for over twenty years,
transmitting orders and mandates,
and was greatly cherished and rewarded.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
Hóu Jǐng started a rebellion in Yǐngchuān,
inviting the aid of the Western Wèi.
Zuăn was appointed Traveling Chancellery Administrator for the Southern Circuit,
and was put in charge of suppressing them with various generals.
Upon returning,
he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yíngzhōu.
He met Shìzōng.
He entered the capital and became Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
Later, he and Duàn Xiàoxiān, Prince of Píngyuán, Xīn Shù, Administrator of the Traveling Chancellery, and others besieged Dōngchǔ,
subsequently capturing several cities, including Guǎnglíng and Jīngzhōu,
and beheading the bandit leader Dōngfāng Bái'é.
He was granted the title of Attendant Official, Third Rank (Yítóng Sānsī),
and the post of Grand Commissioner Supervising the Construction of the Great Wall (Jiān Zhù Chángchéng Dàshǐ).
Leading several thousand infantry and cavalry, he garrisoned and defended the northern frontier.
Upon returning,
he was promoted to General Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
and died shortly thereafter.
Zhāng Liàng,
courtesy name Bódé,
was a man from Xíchéng, Xīhé.
In his youth, he possessed competence and utility.
He first served Ěrzhū Zhào,
and was appointed General Who Pacifies the Distant (Píngyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
Due to his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Earl of Xíchéng County (Xíchéng Xiàn Bó),
with five hundred taxable households.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Zhào at Jìnyáng,
Zhào fled to Xiùróng.
All of Zhào’s immediate followers secretly communicated surrender terms,
but only Liàng did not send any message.
When Zhào was defeated,
he hid in a remote mountain
and ordered Liàng and the servant Chén Shāntí to behead him and surrender.
Both could not bear to do it.
Zhào then hanged himself from a tree.
Bódé threw himself upon the corpse and wept.
Gāozǔ praised and admired him.
He was appointed Administrative Assistant in the Chancellery of the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng Fǔ Cānjūnshì),
and gradually received close favor and trust,
being entrusted with secretarial duties.
During the Tiānpíng reign period (534-537),
he served as Director (Lángzhōng) of Shìzōng’s Traveling Chancellery,
presiding over military affairs (Seven Arms).
Although he was a Director in the Chancellery,
he was constantly at Gāozǔ’s side.
He was promoted to Right Assistant of the Traveling Chancellery.
When Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled,
Liàng defended Héyáng with Grand Marshal Húlǜ Jīn.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu floated fire ships downstream to burn the river bridge.
Liàng prepared more than a hundred small boats,
all carrying long chains,
with spikes attached to the chain ends.
When the fire ships approached,
they immediately sped out in the small boats,
hooked them with the spikes,
and pulled the chains toward the bank.
Thus, the fire ships were unable to reach the bridge.
The bridge was saved;
this was Liàng’s strategy.
Early in the Wǔdìng reign period (543),
he was appointed Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
Xuē Shú once dreamed that Liàng was hanging silk thread on a mountain.
He told Liàng,
and interpreted it the next morning, saying:
"Silk thread on a mountain
forms the character *Yōu* (幽).
Are you perhaps to become the Governor of Yōuzhōu?"
A few months later,
Liàng was posted out as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yōuzhōu.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Liángzhōu.
Soon after, he was granted the added title of Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs across eleven prefectures, including Yáng and Yǐng,
and concurrently served as Director of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Diànzhōng Shàngshū) in the Traveling Chancellery.

He was then transferred to Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs across eight prefectures, including the two Yùzhōu, Yáng, and Yǐng, Grand General Who Campaigns in the West (Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn), Governor of Yùzhōu, Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè), and Traveling Chancellery Administrator for the Southwestern Circuit.
He attacked and captured seven cities belonging to the Southern Liáng dynasty, including Jiāngxià and Yǐngyáng.
Liàng was naturally straightforward
and worked diligently and vigorously to succeed.
He was deeply trusted by Gāozǔ and Shìzōng,
and entrusted with confidential responsibilities.
However, he lacked high moral standards
and was fond of wealth.
Although he served at the side of his superiors for a long time,
he was unable to maintain integrity.
When he held various gubernatorial posts,
there were always reports of his corrupt dealings.
At the end of the Wǔdìng reign period (c. 550),
he was summoned to court and appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Grand Administrator (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Fénzhōu.
Early in the Tiānbǎo reign period (c. 550),
he was appointed Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù Xūn),
with the added titles of Grand General of Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn) and Attendant Official, Third Rank (Yítóng Sānsī).
He was separately enfeoffed as Baron of Āndìng County (Āndìng Xiàn Nán).
He was transferred to General Commander of the Guards (Zhōng Lǐngjūn),
and soon died in office.
He was posthumously granted the title Duke of Works (Sīkōng Gōng).
Zhāng Yào,
courtesy name Língguāng,
was a man from Chāngpíng, Shànggǔ.
His father, Fèng,
was the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Jìnzhōu.
Yào was chaste and cautious in his youth,
and quite knowledgeable about official duties.
After leaving his initial post, he became a Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng),
and was transferred to Provisional Administrative Assistant in charge of Waterways in the Department of the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Shuǐcáo Xíng Cānjūn).
When the Righteous Banner was raised (i.e., Gāozǔ started his campaign),
Gāozǔ promoted him to Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) in the headquarters of Hán Guǐ, Commander-in-Chief of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Dà Dūdū).
When Guǐ was appointed Governor of Yíngzhōu and Jìzhōu,
Yào was again made Advisory Administrative Assistant (Zīyì Cānjūn) for Guǐ.
Later, he was impeached by a Censor.
Over a hundred officials and assistants in the prefecture administration, as well as Guǐ’s personal staff, were caught in the net for bribery and theft.
Only Yào was spared due to his integrity.
He was summoned to court and became Registrar of Granaries (Cāngcáo) in the Chancellery of the Prime Minister.
When Xiǎnzǔ succeeded to power,
Yào was promoted to Clerk (Yuàn) in the Chancellery.
Early in the Tiānbǎo reign period,
he was granted the title Baron of Dūtíng Township (Dūtíng Xiāng Nán).
He oversaw the affairs of both the Granary and Treasury Registries,
and all distributions and grants
were typically entrusted to Yào.
He was transferred to Assistant Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng),
and promoted to Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Chéng).
Xiǎnzǔ once went out nearby
and ordered Yào to remain and guard the capital.
The Emperor returned at night.
Yào did not immediately open the gates,
but commanded his soldiers to remain on strict guard.
The Emperor waited outside the gate for a long time,
urging and pressing urgently.
Yào reasoned that since the night was deep,
the genuine identity was difficult to discern,
and the gate could only be opened after a torch arrived and the person was recognized face-to-face.
Thereupon, he went out alone to meet the Emperor.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"You intend to emulate Zhì Jūnzhāng!"
He then ordered Yào to proceed and open the gate,
and then entered.
He deeply commended and praised him,
and bestowed silk and brocade upon him.
He was posted out as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nánqīngzhōu,
but did not yet take up the post.
When Sùzōng assisted in government,
Yào was repeatedly promoted to Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
Yào served successive generations,
performing his duties faithfully and diligently,
and was always closely favored and trusted.
He never committed a fault.
Whenever he received emoluments or rewards,
he distributed them among his relatives.
He was naturally frugal and plain,
taking only what was necessary
for his carriage, clothes, and food.
He enjoyed reading the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
reading it through once a month.
People of the time compared him to Jiǎ Liángdào.
Zhào Yànshēn once said to Yào:
"Since you study the *Zuǒ Shì* (Commentary),
are you looking for the errors of Fú Qián and Dù Yù?"
Yào replied:
"Why would that be the case?
The book of the *Zuǒ Shì*,
fully discusses events.
The wicked (examples) can serve as self-warning,
and the virtuous (examples) can serve as models to strive for.
Therefore, I diligently review it
not intending to criticize the successes and failures of the ancients."
In the first year of the Tiāntǒng reign period (565),
when Shìzǔ presided over court,
Yào was presenting a memorial
when he suddenly fell ill
and collapsed before the imperial presence.
The Emperor left his seat to look upon him,
calling his name several times, but receiving no response.
The Emperor wept and said:
"How can I lose my good minister!"
He died ten days later,
at the age of sixty-three.
An imperial decree stated that Yào was loyal, faithful, fair, and straightforward,
gentle, respectful, honest, and cautious.

He was posthumously granted the titles Attendant Official, Third Rank (Fǔ Yítóng Sānsī), Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yānzhōu.
His posthumous name was Zhēnjiǎn.
Zhào Qǐ,
courtesy name Xīngluò,
was a native of Guǎngpíng.
His father, Dá,
was the Lùshì Cānjūn of Yōuzhōu.
Qǐ was by nature prudent and capable.
When the banner of righteousness was raised,
Gāozǔ appointed Duàn Róng as the Cǐshǐ of Dìngzhōu,
and appointed Qǐ as Róng's Diǎnqiān,
then made him Fèngchē Dūwèi.
During the Tiānpíng era,
he was summoned to serve as the Qícáo of the Xiangfǔ,
and was successively promoted to Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he was sent out as the Cìshǐ of Jiànzhōu,
and was successively promoted to Shìzhōng.
Qǐ,
during Gāozǔ's reign, frequently served in the two cavalry bureaus of the Xiangfǔ,
managing military horses for over ten years.
After Xiǎnzǔ ascended the throne,
Qǐ was dismissed from his provincial post and returned to the capital.
Although he held positions such as Jiǔqīng and Shìzhōng,
he constantly oversaw military horses in his original capacity,
directing them in and out,
holding a crucial and confidential responsibility,
on par with the two Zhāngs.
He was sent out as the Cìshǐ of Xīyǎanzhōu,
where he investigated, impeached, and prohibited (wrongdoings).
After more than a year,
he was acquitted due to lack of evidence.
In the second year of Héqīng,
he was summoned back to Jìnyáng.
In the third year,
he was further promoted to Cíbù Shàngshū and Kāifǔ.
At the beginning of the Tiāntǒng era,
he was transferred to Tàicháng Qīng,
and granted the income of Lángyá Commandery.
In the second year,
he was appointed Cāngzhōu Cǐshǐ,
and given the additional title of Liùzhōu Dūdū.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he died in office.
Xú Yuǎn,
courtesy name Yànxiá,
was a native of Shímén, Guǎngníng.
His ancestors originated from Guǎngpíng.
His great-grandfather, Dìng,
served as a Jūnjiàng of Yúnzhōng and the Shùzhǔ of Píngshuò,
and thus settled his family in Shuò.
Yuǎn was skilled in official affairs from a young age,
and was appointed Gōngcáo by the commandery.
Soon after,
he and the Tàishǒu led households to join the banner of righteousness,
and he was appointed Fángchéng Dūdū,
then made the Xiànlìng of Yǐngtáo.
Gāozǔ, recognizing Yuǎn's proficiency in writing and accounting,
appointed him as Céngxiàng Qíbīng Cānjūnshì.
He often participated in military campaigns and successfully managed military affairs,
and was highly regarded by Gāozǔ.
He successively served as Tàishǒu of Jùlù and Chénliú Commanderies.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was impeached by the Yùshǐ,
but was pardoned and acquitted.
He remained inactive for two years.
Xiǎnzǔ, considering Yuǎn's old merits,
specifically appointed him as Lǐngjūnfǔ Zhǎngshǐ,
and he was successively promoted to Dōngxúzhōu Cìshǐ,
then entered (the capital) to serve as Tàizhōng Dàfū.
At the beginning of the Héqīng era,
he was given the additional title of Wèijiāngjūn.
In the second year,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Dōngchǔzhōu Zhūjūnshì, and Dōngchǔzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year of Tiāntǒng,
he was granted Yítóng Sānsī and Wèiwèi.
In the fourth year,
he was further promoted to Kāifǔ and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū.
He died at the beginning of the Wǔpíng era.
Yuǎn's governance aimed for leniency and harmony,
and he showed kindness.
Upon arriving in Dōngchǔ,
in the winter of that year,
a great fire broke out in the city,
and the city dwellers lost their property.
Yuǎn personally went to rescue them,
weeping as he faced them.
He then worked to assist them,
and all were able to settle down.
His eldest son, Shìróng,
was Zhōngshū Shèrén and Huángmén Shìláng.
Wáng Jùn,
courtesy name Luánsōng,
was a native of Língqiū.
He was intelligent and had strategic abilities.
Gāozǔ appointed him as Céngxiàngfǔ Mòcáo Cānjūn,
but he lost his official position due to an incident.
After a long time,
Xiǎnzǔ, as Yítóng Kāifǔ,
brought him in as Chéngjú Cānjūn.
He was successively promoted to Zhōu Dàzhōngzhèng,
and Shìzōng Xiàngfǔ Wàibīng Cānjūn.
He followed the various armies in pacifying Huái yīn,
and was bestowed the noble title of Běipíng Xiànnán.
He was appointed Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yíngzhōu bordered frontier cities,
and bandits frequently troubled the people.
When Jùn arrived at the province,
he set up distant scouts
and widely deployed decoy troops.
Whenever bandits appeared,
he would often launch unexpected surprise attacks,
so the bandits dared not make raids,
and the entire region gained peace.
Previously, Cìshǐ Lù Shìmào had treacherously killed over eight hundred Shīwéi people,
which caused the tribute to cease thereafter.
At this time,
Jùn dispatched his generals and soldiers
to intercept them on their travel routes.
The Shīwéi indeed arrived,
and were greatly defeated.
Their chief leader, Yùjiǔlǘ Dòubátí, and others were captured and returned.
He then treated them with great kindness and courtesy,
and released them.
The Shīwéi then offered sincere allegiance,
and tribute never ceased,
for which Jùn was instrumental.
Initially, the Rúrú lord Ānluóchén led his remaining followers to migrate east.
Jùn anticipated their arrival
and made preparations in advance.
Soon after,
Ānluóchén arrived
and encamped his army west of the city.
Jùn then set up cunning ambushes and greatly defeated them,
capturing dozens of their renowned kings, including Yùjiǔlǘ Dòubátí,
and sent them to the capital.
Ānluóchén then fled.
The emperor greatly praised him.
He was promoted to Mìshūjiān.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Luòzhōu Cìshǐ and Héyángdào Xíngtái Zuǒchéng.
During the Huángjiàn era,
an imperial edict ordered the digging of a three hundred *lǐ* long trench on the western border of Luòzhōu
and the establishment of cities and garrisons to prevent espionage.
In the first year of Héqīng,
he was summoned to serve as Cíbù Shàngshū.
An edict ordered him to go to Jìnyáng to inspect military horses,
and soon after he returned to Yè,
and was transferred to Tàipú Qīng.
When the imperial carriage made tours,
he, along with Lìbù Shàngshū Wèi Jǐn, often assisted the Crown Prince and various princes in managing affairs behind the scenes.
He was also granted the income of Liángjùn,
promoted to Shìzhōng,
and appointed Dūguān Shàngshū.
When the Zhōu army invaded,
an edict ordered Jùn, in his original capacity, along with Dōngān Wáng Lóu Ruì and Wǔxīng Wáng Pǔ, to lead troops from Yè to Héyáng to resist them.
The imperial carriage then went to Luòyáng.
As Xuánhù was occupied by the Zhōu people,
an edict again appointed Jùn as Nándào Xíngtái,
to lead troops with Lóu Ruì on a southern expedition.
Before they arrived,
the Zhōu army abandoned the city and fled.
They then were ordered to comfort and stabilize Yǒng and Yǐng prefectures.
In the spring of the fourth year,
he returned to the capital.
For violating regulations by privately transferring prohibited goods and illegally intercepting military provisions,
the authorities sentenced him to decapitation according to regulations,
and his family members were confiscated.
A special edict ordered him to be flogged one hundred times,
his name removed from the official register, and assigned to the armor workshops,
and his family members were exempted.
He then received a pardon,
and remained inactive in private.
In the second year of Tiāntǒng,
he was granted Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī,
and soon after was promoted to Kāifǔ.
At the beginning of Wǔpíng,
he was appointed Shìzhōng.
He died in the fourth year.
He was posthumously granted Sīkōng Gōng.
Wáng Hóng,
courtesy name Shīluó,
was a native of Dínà in Tàian.
He served as the chieftain of a small tribe.
His father, Jī,
read quite a few books
and possessed wisdom and strategy.
He initially rebelled by following Gě Róng.
Gě Róng appointed Jī as the King of Jìběi and Inspector of Níngzhōu.
Later, when Gě Róng was defeated,
Jī held his city and refused to surrender.
Ěrzhū Róng sent an envoy to persuade him,
and only then did he submit.
Ěrzhū Róng later made him a Chief Clerk (Cóngshì Zhōngláng Lìng) of his administration,
leading his forces to garrison Mòchuān.
When Ěrzhū Róng died,
Hédòulíng Bùfān captured Jī and took him back to Hexī.
He later escaped and returned to Ěrzhū Zhào.
When Gāozǔ (Emperor Xiǎojìng) defeated Ěrzhū Zhào,
he made Jī a Grand Military Governor (Dūdū)
and appointed him as the Administrator of Yìníng.
Jī had previously befriended Zhōu Wéndì (Yǔwén Tài) in Gě Róng's army.
When Zhōu Wéndì secured Guānzhōng,
Gāozǔ sent Jī, along with the Chief Clerk Hóu Jǐng, as envoys to Zhōu Wéndì.
Zhōu Wéndì detained Jī and did not send him back.
Jī later escaped and returned.
He was appointed Chief Clerk of Jìzhōu,
and later acted as the Administrator of Sìzhōu.
At the beginning of Yuánxiàng era (532 CE),
he was successively promoted to Inspector of Nán Yìzhōu and Inspector of Běi Yùzhōu.
In all the places he governed, he was fond of accumulating wealth,
but his nature was honest and straightforward,
so the officials and people did not suffer greatly because of him.
In the winter of Xīnghé 4th year (542 CE), he was murdered by his slave,
at the age of sixty-five.
He was posthumously granted the titles of General Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn), Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), and Inspector of Dìngzhōu.
Hóng was fond of archery and horsemanship in his youth,
was skilled in riding and shooting,
and greatly loved literature.
His nature was quick-witted,
and his responses were prompt and sharp.
At the age of thirteen,
he met Guō Yuánzhēn of Tàiyuán, the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Guō Yuánzhēn patted his back and said:
“What book are you reading?”
He replied:
“I recite the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety).”
Guō Yuánzhēn asked:
“What does the *Xiàojīng* say?”
He answered:
“When in high position, be not arrogant;
when in low position, be not rebellious.”
Guō Yuánzhēn said:
“I serve as an Inspector;
how could I be arrogant?”
Hóng replied:
“Although you are not arrogant,
a gentleman guards against things before they sprout,
and I hope you will still pay attention.”
Guō Yuánzhēn praised him.
At the age of fifteen,
he was with his father in Běi Yùzhōu.
The Field Marshal (Xíngtái), Hóu Jǐng, was debating with others whether the method of fastening the lapel (yǎn yī fǎ) should be on the left
or on the right.
The Minister (Shàngshū), Jìng Xiǎnjùn, said:
“Confucius said: ‘But for Guǎn Zhòng,
we should now be wearing our hair unbound, with our garments folded to the left.’
Judging by this statement,
folding the garment to the right (yòurèn) is correct.”
Hóng stepped forward and said:
“When our state rose gloriously in the northern wilds,
and strode mightily across the Central Plain,
the Five Emperors had different rituals,
and the Three Kings had different systems.
Whether the lapel is fastened left or right
is not worth debating as right or wrong.”
Hóu Jǐng was amazed by his early intelligence
and bestowed upon him a famous horse.
During the Xīnghé era,
Shìzōng (Emperor Wénxuān) summoned him to serve as a Palace Guard (Kùzhí),
and he was appointed Gentleman for Attendance (Fèng Cháoqǐng).
When Shìzōng died suddenly,
Hóng braved the blades to defend and guard (the body).
For his loyalty and integrity, he was granted the noble title of Male of Píngchūn County,
and rewarded with seven hundred bolts of silk, fifty rolls of fine silk damask, thirty thousand cash, along with a gold belt and a swift horse.
He was then appointed Magistrate of Jìnyáng.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era (550 CE),
he was promoted to General Quelling the Distant (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn),
and was quite favored and esteemed by Xiǎnzǔ (Emperor Wénxuān).
The Emperor once drank wine with his attendants
and said:
“What great joy!”
Hóng replied:
“There is great joy,
and there is also great suffering.”
The Emperor said:
“What is great suffering?”
Hóng said:
“Spending endless nights recklessly drinking without realizing it,
leading to the ruin of the state and the destruction of the family,
where the body dies and the name vanishes—
that is what is called great suffering.”
The Emperor fell silent.
Later, the Emperor reprimanded Hóng, saying:
“You and Hēxī Shèlè served my brother together;
Shèlè died,
why didn't you die?”
Hóng replied:
“When a ruler perishes, his subject dies;
this is indeed the common standard of integrity.
However, the weak villain's attack was light,
which is why your subject did not die.”
The Emperor ordered Yān Zixuàn to tie Hóng up backwards,
the Prince of Chángguǎng held his head,
and the Emperor personally brought the blade down.
Hóng cried out:
“Yáng Zūnyàn and Cuī Jìshū fled and avoided calamity,
yet reached the high posts of Minister (Púshè) and Minister (Shàngshū).
But officials who risked death to perform their duty
are instead being slaughtered—
such a thing has never happened throughout history!”
The Emperor threw the blade to the ground and said:
“Wáng Shīluó must not be killed.”
He then spared him.
In Qiánmíng 1st year (560 CE),
when Zhāo Dì (Emperor Xiào Zhāo) acted as Chancellor,
Hóng was appointed Military Advisor and Registrar (Gōngcáo Cānjūn Shì) in the Central and Outer Palace Administration.
In Huángjiàn 1st year (560 CE),
he was promoted to the noble title of Viscount of Yìyáng County.
In Héqīng 3rd year (564 CE),
he campaigned against the Turks (Tūjué) with various generals,
and was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn).
In Tiāntǒng 1st year (565 CE),
he was appointed Palace Attendant Yellow Gate Regular Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
promoted to Colonel of Elite Archers (Shèshēng Xiàowèi),
and then promoted four times to Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
At the beginning of Wǔpíng era (570 CE),
he was granted the Open Office with the Rank of the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
Hóng submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Tūjué are exchanging sons and daughters with the Yǔwén (Northern Zhōu),
and they will surely collaborate and influence each other,
and raid our northern and western borders.
It is appropriate to select the strongest and bravest crossbowmen from the Nine Provinces
and occupy more crucial strategic locations.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty takes pity on the loyal and remembers the old,
cherishes the orphaned and cares for the widowed,
is sympathetic to the foolish and praises the good,
overlooks transgressions and records merits,
strengthens the bonds of kin,
widens the path of broad benevolence,
reflects upon the customs of Yáo and Shùn,
emulates the virtue of Yǔ and Tāng,
subdues oneself and returns to propriety,
to bring about beautiful transformation.
The empire would be exceedingly fortunate.”
In the 5th year (574 CE),
the Chén people raided Huáinán.
An imperial decree ordered all officials to discuss the defense measures.
Fēng Fǔxiàng requested permission to lead an expedition to attack.
Hóng said:
“The government armies have suffered continuous losses,
and popular sentiment is agitated.
If we once again mobilize a great force
and station troops along the Jiāng and Huái (rivers),
I fear that the Northern Di and Western raiders
will take advantage of our exhaustion
and come with the whole nation,
in which case, the state affairs will be gone.
It is better to lighten the taxes and reduce the corvée,
allow the people to rest and nurture the soldiers,
ensure harmony in the court,
and ensure that those far and near submit wholeheartedly.
We should conquer them with benevolence and righteousness,
and encourage them with morality and virtue.
Then the whole world will naturally be pacified;
why only the false Chén?”
Gāo Ānàhóng said to the assembled people:
“Those who follow Wáng Wǔwèi (Wáng Hóng) sit on the southern side.”
Everyone agreed.
Soon after, he was concurrently appointed Attendant Consultant (Shìzhōng)
and went on an embassy to Zhōu (Northern Zhōu).
Upon returning from the mission, he officially held the post,
but died shortly thereafter.
Hóng was fond of writing
and authored *Jiàn Jiè* (Admonitions and Warnings) in twenty-four chapters,
which contained considerable literary quality and meaning.
The Court Historian says: Zhāng Zuǎn and the others all served in the dominant court
and exerted their utility;
they were all excellent ministers of Qí.
The lamentation of Bódé (Xǔ Yuǎn), weeping over the dead,
and Língguāng's (Wáng Hóng) blocking the pass to halt the imperial procession,
have the spirit of the ancients.
Eulogy: Zuǎn, Liàng, Yào, Qǐ, Xǔ Yuǎn, Hóng, Jùn,
Ascended high beneath the sun,
Their fame extended far on the wind.
Xu [Yuǎn] died resisting the pass,
Eventually demonstrating integrity and obedience.
Biographies, Chapter 18: Xuē Shú, Jìng Xiǎnjùn, Píng Jiàn
Xuē Shú,
courtesy name Tánzhēn,
was a native of Hénán.
His ancestors were Dài people,
originally bearing the surname Chìgān shì.
His father, Bàozǐ,
was the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu during the Wèi dynasty.
Shú's physique and appearance were grand and imposing,
and when young, he was known for his administrative ability.
He served as the Director of Guests (Diǎnkèlìng).
Whenever he introduced guests for audience,
his bearing and demeanor were extremely fine.
The Wèi Emperor summoned him and said:
"Your bearing and manner are dignified and correct,
and your appearance is outstanding and unusual.
When you are promoted later,
how will you conduct your official duties?"
Shú replied:
"Regarding the rites of the ancestral temple (Zōngmiào),
I dare not be disrespectful.
Regarding the affairs of the court,
I dare not be disloyal.
Beyond this,
it is not what a mediocre official (yōng chén) can achieve."
During the Zhèngguāng period,
he acted as the Magistrate of Luòyáng (Luòyánglìng).
Order prevailed throughout the jurisdiction.
When there were those who violated the law,
before applying torture or flogging,
he merely used reasoning and cross-examination to thoroughly investigate,
and often uncovered the truth of the matter.
Consequently, the powerful and cunning feared his authority,
and official affairs were simple and quiet.
At that time, due to a long drought,
all prisoners in the capital were summoned to Huálín
to investigate injustices and delays.
In the Luòyáng prison,
there remained only three people incarcerated.
Emperor Xiàomíng of Wèi praised this,
and bestowed upon him one hundred bolts of silk.
He was promoted to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
Cūi Liàng, the Minister (Shàngshū), proposed establishing a rule based on seniority (tíngnián zhī gé),
not selecting talent,
but specializing in examining those with long service.
Shú submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The lives of the common people (lí yuán)
depend upon the chief officials (zhǎnglì).
If the right person is obtained,
they will have a place to recover and rest.
If the appointment does not match the capacity,
the resulting suffering will be even deeper.
If the selecting department (xuǎncáo) only takes age and seniority,
without distinguishing between the worthy and the unworthy,
then the principle is simply like geese flying in a line,
or sequence like fish strung together.
Holding the register and calling out names,
a single clerk would suffice.
Why employ several people
if the goal is merely weighted selection (quánhéng)?
I request that this not be followed."
The memorial was submitted but received no reply.
Later, during an imperial audience,
he again offered remonstrance, saying:
"The responsibility for governing the realm together
fundamentally belongs to the officials (bǎiguān).

Therefore, the Hàn court regularly ordered the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) and great ministers to recommend those who were worthy, upright (xiánliáng fāngzhèng), and capable of offering frank criticism (yǒudào zhíyán zhī shì),
to serve as chief officials (zhǎnglì),
overseeing and pacifying the common people.
Since the end of the Jìn dynasty,
this tradition has ceased.
Now that the four directions are newly settled,
the priority must be nurturing the populace.
Your subject requests that we reestablish the Four Categories (Sìkē) according to the Hàn system,
and order the Sāngōng and noble ministers to each recommend worthy individuals of the time,
to fill posts in the commanderies and districts (jùnxiàn),
clearly setting up regulations
to prevent favoritism and factionalism."
The edict was sent down for the Dukes (Gōng) and Ministers (Qīng) to deliberate,
but the matter was ultimately dropped.
When Yuán Tiānmù campaigned against Xíng Gǎo,
he appointed Shú as Acting Minister (Xíngtái Shàngshū).
At that time, Yuán Hào had already occupied Cuóchéng.
Tiānmù gathered civil and military officials to discuss which enemy to target first.
The conferees all thought that Gǎo's forces were very large,
and that it was appropriate to plan for dealing with them first.
Shú believed that Xíng Gǎo's gathering of troops lacked legitimacy,
and although strong, they were still bandits.
Yuán Hào, being a close relative of the imperial house,
came claiming a righteous cause (yì jǔ).
This was perhaps difficult to predict (or deal with).
Gǎo was merely a petty thief (like a rat and a dog),
and did not possess high ambitions.
It was proper to campaign against Hào first.
Tiānmù, influenced by the general consensus,
consequently campaigned against Gǎo first.
Gǎo surrendered. When the army returned,
Hào had entered Luòyáng.
Tiānmù said to Shú:
"If I had not disregarded your words,
this would not have happened."
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
Gāozǔ brought him in to serve as the Chief Clerk to the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Zhǎngshǐ).
Shú had a long-established reputation for competence,
and was treated with great courtesy.
Concerning military and state affairs,
he was privy to much information.
Shú also acted with complete sincerity and devotion,
frequently offering loyal and candid advice.
When Gāozǔ launched a major western campaign,
he planned to cross the Pújīn ford.
Shú remonstrated, saying:
"The Western bandits have suffered famines for successive years,
and have nothing to eat.
Therefore, they risked death to enter Shǎnzhōu,
wanting to seize the grain from the storehouses.
Now Sītú Gāo has already surrounded Shǎnchéng,
and the grain cannot be brought out.
Simply station troops along various routes,
and do not engage them in open battle.
By the time the wheat harvest arrives next year,
the people will all starve to death,
and Bǎojù and Hēità [Yuán Bǎojù and Yǔwén Tà]
will naturally surrender.
I urge Your Highness not to cross the river."
Hóu Jǐng also said:
"This current campaign,
with the troops being extremely large,
if by chance we fail to achieve victory,
it will be difficult to regroup quickly.
It would be better to divide the forces into two armies,
advancing one after the other.
If the vanguard wins,
the rear army can join forces.
If the vanguard is defeated,
the rear army can support it."
Gāozǔ accepted neither suggestion,
and consequently suffered the defeat at Shāyuàn.
He was promoted repeatedly, reaching the rank of Assistant Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè),
and then died.
Approaching death,
he ordered his sons to dress the body in ordinary clothes,
and bury him after a month,
not allowing them to lobby for posthumous official titles.
He personally designed his funeral cart,
without adding carvings or decorations,
using only hemp for the tassels,
and rope for the netting, nothing more.
He did not permit the placement of burial items (míngqì) or similar objects.
Shú spent a long time in the ministries (shěngtǎ),
being proficient and clear in administrative matters,
and when solving legal cases in office,
he was quick and smooth as flowing water.
However, his nature was treacherous and jealous,
his feelings and loyalty were not earnest.
Externally he appeared upright,
but internally he was volatile and unstable.
He accepted bribes,
bent the law,
was deeply unkind and harsh (kèbó),
and harmed many people.
Officials and commoners feared and detested him.
Zhāng shì, the concubine of Yuán Kuāng, the Prince of Dōngpíng of Wèi, was dissolute and reckless.
Shú initially engaged in illicit relations with her,
and later took her as his wife.
Seduced by her slander,
he drove away his former wife, Yú shì,
and refused to acknowledge his son.
Resentment arose within the family,
and they competed to report the matter to the authorities,
earning him deep scorn and ridicule from the world.
He was posthumously granted the title of Governor of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Jìng Xiǎnjùn,
courtesy name Xiàoyīng,
was a native of Píngyáng.
In his youth, he was heroic and chivalrous with moral integrity,
and associated with prominent figures.
He served as the Superintendent of the Feathered Forest Guard (Yǔlínjiān).
When Gāozǔ arrived at Jìnzhōu,
Jùn seized the opportunity to request an audience.
Gāozǔ was pleased after conversing with him,
and subsequently appointed him as an Assistant Governor (Biéjià).
When the righteous uprising (yì jǔ) occurred,
Jùn was made Director of the Granary Department (Cāngbù Lángzhōng) in the Mobile Secretariat (Xíngtái).
He followed in the attack on Yè,
and Jùn was ordered to supervise the construction of the siege mounds.
When the city was captured,
he again followed in pacifying the Western Hú.
He was transferred to be Minister of the Department of Justice (Dūguān Shàngshū).
He campaigned with various generals,
accumulating merit repeatedly.
He also followed Gāozǔ in quelling rebellions and disturbances,
and defeated Emperor Wén of Zhōu [Yǔwén Tà].
He defeated Hóu Jǐng,
pacified Shòuchūn,
and stabilized the Huáinán region.
He also seized territory at Sānjiāngkǒu,
and constructed many fortifications and garrisons.
He was repeatedly appointed Governor of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ),
and then died.
Píng Jiàn,
courtesy name Míngdá,
was a man from Jì in Yān Jùn.
His father, Shèng,
was the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Ān Zhōu.
Jiàn was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and possessed considerable ambition and strength of will.
He studied under Xú Zūnmíng,
but did not stick to rigid textual analysis.
Although he honored Confucian studies,
he possessed the spirit of a chivalrous hero (háoxiá).
At the end of the Xiàochāng period,
bandits rose up like swarming bees.
Seeing that the world was about to fall into chaos,
he went to Luòyáng
and befriended Mùróng Yǎn, traveling with him on horseback.
Jiàn was naturally skillful.
At night, he would paint Hu-style pictures
to provide for his clothes and food.
He said to his relatives:
“Fortune experiences decline and prosperity.
When chaos reaches its extreme, order will return.
Bīng Zhōu is a land of military horses,
and Ěrzhū Róng is a hero destined by fate to rule the world.
Wielding righteousness and raising the banner,
he carries out the decree to punish the guilty.
This is the time
to exert loyalty and dedicate strength.”
Thereupon, they led each other to join Ěrzhū Róng at Jìnyáng,
and subsequently presented strategies for quelling the chaos and pacifying the people.
Róng was greatly impressed by him,
and immediately appointed him as Military Advisor (Cānjūn).
He served as a vanguard in the campaigns to pacify Gǒng and Mì,
and was always the first to ascend the ramparts in every battle.
He was appointed Commander Who Maintains the Army (Fǔjūn) and Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Xiāng Zhōu.
When Gāozǔ (Emperor Xiǎowǔ) raised the banner of righteousness at Xìndū,
Jiàn submitted himself.
Gāozǔ said to Jiàn:
“Previously, when the Imperial order was loosening,
you had already exhausted your loyalty and sincerity early on.
Now, Ěrzhū is running rampant,
but you were still able to abandon rebellion and follow the good.
Only in the time of wilting and decay
can one recognize the pine and the bamboo.”
He was immediately nominated to be appointed General Who Attacks the West (Zhēngxī),
and Prefect of Huái Zhōu.
Jiàn submitted a memorial requesting permission to build a city west of the prefecture, at the old Zhǐdào, to defend against the western invaders.
The court consented.
Soon after, the Western Wèi came to attack.
At that time, the newly built city
had not yet gathered provisions or arms.
Traditionally, it lacked water,
and the hearts of the people were greatly fearful.
Inside the south gate, there was a well,
but it dried up immediately upon drawing water.
Jiàn therefore put on his ceremonial robes and hat, bent over the well, and prayed.
By dawn, spring water had overflowed the well,
and the whole city drew from it.
The Wèi army was defeated and retreated.
For his merit, he was promoted to Governor-General (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
At that time, Hé Shìkāi held great power in the court due to his flattering favor,
and sent someone to request Jiàn’s beloved concubine, Lady Liú.
Jiàn immediately sent her over.
He then said to others:
“For this old man to lose Āliú,
how is it different from death?
But I must make plans for myself;
I had no choice but to do this.”
Because of this, he was appointed Prefect of Qí Zhōu.
Jiàn governed eight prefectures successively
and served twice as the administrator of Huái Zhōu.
Wherever he served, he was remembered fondly by the officials,
and stelae were erected praising his virtues.
Upon entering the capital, he became the Director of the Department of Justice (Dūguān Shàngshū Lìng).
Biographies, Chapter 19: Wànqí Pǔ (Son Luò), Kězhūhún Yuán, Liú Fēng, Pòliùhán Cháng Jīnzuò, Wéi Zǐcàn.
Wànqí Pǔ,
courtesy name Pǔbō,
was a man from Tàipíng.
His ancestors were a separate branch of the Xiōngnú.
He was courageous, decisive, and militarily capable.
During the Zhèngguāng period,
Pòliùhán Bálíng plotted rebellion
and appointed Pǔ as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
He led his division and surrendered to Wèi,
and was appointed General of the Rear (Hòu Jiāngjūn),
and Second Chieftain Who Governs the People (Lǐngmín Qiúzhǎng).
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness,
Pǔ communicated his sincerity from afar.
Gāozǔ greatly praised him.
Húsī Chūn forced the Emperor to move west,
and appointed Pǔ as Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Prefect of Qín Zhōu,
stationed at Fùmò Chéng.
When Gāozǔ pacified Xià Zhōu,
Pǔ then led his tribe to defect.
Gāozǔ personally welcomed him
and appointed Pǔ as Duke of Héxī.
He was repeatedly promoted to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Prefect of Shuò Zhōu,
and then died.
His son, Luò,
courtesy name Shòuluògān.
He was brave, imposing, and skilled in martial arts;
his equestrian archery surpassed others,
and he was respected by his local community.
When Bálíng rebelled,
he followed his father and submitted.
He was appointed General Who Displays Martial Might (Xiǎnwǔ Jiāngjūn).
He followed Ěrzhū Róng and achieved military merits repeatedly.
He was successively promoted to Prefect of Fén Zhōu and General of the Swift Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness at Xìndū,
he sent assurances of sincerity from afar.
Gāozǔ praised the fact that both father and son had come
and treated them with exceptionally high courtesy.
He was appointed Commander Who Maintains the Army (Fǔjūn),
concurrently serving as Prefect of Líng Zhōu.
When Wǔdì entered the passes (Rù Guān),
he was appointed Left Assistant Director (Zuǒ Púyè).
During the Tiānpíng period,
he followed his father and returned east.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiànchāng Jùn,
and was then promoted again to General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
He participated with the other generals in besieging Dúgū Rúyuàn at Jīnyǒng,
and in the Battle of Héyīn;
in both, he achieved merit.
Because Gāozǔ respected his father Pǔ’s age,
he treated him with particularly high honor,
once personally helping him mount his horse.
Luò removed his hat, bowed low, and said:
“I am willing to dedicate my life’s strength to repay this profound kindness.”
During this campaign,
while all the armies crossed the bridge to the north,
Luò kept one division stationary.
He said to the western men:
“Wànqí Shòuluògān is here!
If you are able to come, then come!”
The western men grew afraid and left.
Because Gāozǔ saw his imposing bravery,
he named the area where Luò had established his camp Huíluò Chéng.
Luò was spirited and held firm principles (qìjié),
and his courage and sharp spirit were unmatched at the time.
He was praised by his contemporaries as a famous general.
He died early in the Xīnghé period.
Kězhūhún Yuán,
courtesy name Dàoyuán.
He claimed to be a native of Liáodōng.
His family were hereditary chieftains.
During the Wèi period, they led their followers and submitted internally.
His great-grandfather, Hùyěgōng, died while serving as the Garrison Commander (Zhènjiàng) of Huáishuò.
They subsequently settled their family there.
Yuán was generous, benevolent, and possessed military strategies.
In his youth, he was well acquainted with Gāozǔ.
When the northern frontier was in turmoil,
he led his family and followers to Dìng Zhōu.
He happened upon Xiānyú Xiūlǐ, who was rising in rebellion,
and Yuán brought his followers and joined him.
Gě Róng absorbed Xiūlǐ’s forces,
and subsequently appointed Yuán as the Prince of Liáng.
He then fled to Ěrzhū Róng,
who made him a detached general.
He served under Tiānguāng in the campaign to conquer Guānzhōng,
and for his merit was appointed Prefect of Wèi Zhōu.
Hóumòchén Yuè killed Hèbá Yuè,
Emperor Wén of Zhōu led Yuè's remaining forces back to jointly plot against Yuè.
At that time, Yuán assisted Yuè.
Yuè fled,
Yuán gathered his multitude,
entered and occupied Qínzhōu.
He was attacked and besieged by Zhōu,
fought bitterly,
and an alliance was concluded, and they withdrew.
Since Yuán had long been recognized and befriended by Gāozǔ,
and moreover, his mother and elder brother were in the East,
he frequently harbored the intention of returning,
sending memorials and petitions to Gāozǔ, communicating secretly.
Zhōu Wén was wary of Yuán's intelligence and courage,
and knowing Yuán harbored duplicity,
he dispatched troops to attack him.
Yuán then led his forces,
departing from Wèizhōu,
and crossed the Wūlánjīn Ford to the northwest.
Zhōu Wén frequently sent troops to intercept him,
but Yuán invariably crushed them in battle.
He led his army through the borders of Hézhōu and Yuánzhōu,
and thus was able to emerge to the east.
Liú Fēng, the son-in-law of Cáo Fēng, the Inspector of Língzhōu, was deeply connected with Yuán.
Yuán then persuaded Fēng that Gāozǔ was extraordinarily heroic and martial,
and capable of completing the great enterprise.
From this point, Fēng conceived the intention of dedicating himself,
and subsequently provided Yuán with resources for his departure.
Yuán traveled northeast from Língzhōu and entered Yúnzhōu.
When Gāozǔ heard of his arrival,
he sent Gāo Sōng, the Prefect of Píngyáng, holding a single golden ring, to bestow upon Yuán,
and also transported supplies and provisions,
dispatching greeters far ahead.
When Yuán arrived at Jìnyáng,
he was granted an audience, and they clasped hands.
He was bestowed a thousand bolts of silk, along with slaves, maidservants, fields, and residences.
His four brothers who were already in Bìngzhōu,
were promoted in office and rank.
The supervising generals under Yuán's command,
were all rewarded with noble ranks and fiefs.
Yuán was enfeoffed as a County Duke,
and appointed as General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry.
He campaigned against the Yítóng Jīn Zuò and Huángfǔ Zhìdá of the Western Wèi at Dōngyōng,
capturing them.
He was transferred to become the Inspector of Bìngzhōu.
He also campaigned with various generals,
repeatedly achieving victories and securing surrenders.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo period,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Fúfēng.
He frequently followed Xiǎnzǔ to suppress the Shānhú and the Rúrú,
accumulating military achievements.
He was promoted to Grand Preceptor,
and passed away.
He was posthumously granted the titles Authority to use the Yellow Axe, Grand Chancellor, and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Yuán was skilled at managing troops;
in marching armies and employing forces,
he prioritized maintaining stability and caution.
In all his campaigns, before and after,
he never suffered defeat.
When he passed away,
the imperial court deeply mourned him.
In the beginning of the Huángjiàn period,
he was accorded the honor of being enshrined alongside Shìzōng in the ancestral temple.
Liú Fēng,
courtesy name Fēngshēng,
was a man from Pǔlè.
He possessed a heroic bearing and magnificent spirit,
was resolute and decisive beyond others,
was eloquent in speech,
and enjoyed discussing military matters.
During the rebellion of Pòliùhán Báling,
Fēng, based on his merit in defending the city,
was appointed Prefect of Pǔlè.
In the beginning of the Yǒng'ān period of Wèi,
he was appointed Grand Commander of the Língzhōu Garrison City.
Zhōu Wén offered him the title of Grand General of the Guards,
but Fēng did not accept it.
Consequently, (Zhōu Wén) sent forces to attack and besiege him,
but failed to overcome him.
Fēng admired the prestige and virtue of Gāozǔ from afar,
and subsequently led tens of thousands of households to defect.
Gāozǔ recommended Fēng for the titles General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Nánfénzhōu.
He then campaigned with various generals,
stabilizing banditry and rebellions.
He also followed Gāozǔ to defeat Zhōu Wén at Héyīn,
and Fēng's contribution was substantial.
Gāozǔ clasped his hands and praised him admiringly.
Upon entering court, he was appointed Left Guard General,
and when he went out, he was appointed Governor of Yīnzhōu.
When Wáng Sīzhèng occupied Chángshè,
Shìzōng ordered Fēng and Yuè, the Prince of Qīnghé, to attack him.
Fēng proposed the strategy of hydraulic siege,
and consequently dammed the Wěishuǐ River to inundate the city.
The water rose high;
fish and turtles all swam there.
From the ninth month until the fourth month,
the city was about to fall.
Fēng and the Acting Director Mùróng Shàozōng saw white vapor to the north,
and both entered a boat.
Suddenly, a violent gale came from the northeast,
turning midday dark.
Sand flew and pebbles raced,
and the boat cable suddenly snapped.
They drifted right to the base of the city wall.
Fēng swam toward the earth mound,
but was battered by the waves,
and could not reach it in time.
The Westerners hooked him.
He, along with others, was killed by the enemy.
Fēng was brave, courageous, and skilled in warfare,
and was highly regarded by all the generals.
On the day of his death,
the court and the populace were shocked and grieved.
He was posthumously granted Grand Marshal, Duke Minister of the Masses, and Director of the Department of State Affairs.
His posthumous title was Zhōng.
His son Yè succeeded him.
Pòliùhán Cháng,
courtesy name Bǎonián,
was a man from Fùhuà,
a descendant of the Xiōngnú Chányú.
Pānliùxī, the Right Gǔlí King, was absorbed by the Wèi dynasty.
His descendants adopted Pānliùxī as their surname.
Later generations, due to error,
believed it to be Pòliùhán.
The family had led the tribe for generations.
His father, Kǒngquè,
inherited the position of chieftain for generations.
Kǒngquè was brave and fierce in his youth.
At that time, his kinsman Báling caused a rebellion,
and appointed Kǒngquè as Grand Commander, Minister of the Masses, and Prince Who Pacifies the South.
Kǒngquè led ten thousand subordinates to surrender to Ěrzhū Róng.
An imperial decree added the titles General Who Pacifies the North and First Chieftain Leading the People.
He died.
Cháng was reserved, astute, and possessed courage and strategy;
he was skilled at horsemanship and archery.
He was repeatedly promoted, reaching General Who Pacifies the West.
When Gāozǔ raised his army for justice,
Cháng was defending Fùhuà.
He returned east with Mòqí Shòuluògān.
Gāozǔ praised him,
and recommended him for Protector of the Army.
He campaigned with various generals,
and again followed Gāozǔ to attack various bandits.
He was repeatedly promoted, reaching General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry, honored with the establishment of a mansion,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Píngyáng.
He was appointed Inspector of Luòzhōu.
Cháng memorialized Shìzōng, saying:
“Since I have been stationed in Héyáng,
I have frequently gone out through the passes
and the two routes of Tàigǔ.
The area north of Běijīng
and south of Luòzhōu—
all the strategic choke points there,
I know them quite well.
The southern entrance of Tàigǔ is over one hundred *lǐ* from the Jīng road.
It passes through Chìgōng Bǎn.
This is the great east-west road used by the bandits for travel and return.
In the middle, there is an open, undefended stretch of one hundred and fifty *lǐ*.
The bandits' provisions
only pass through this road.
I humbly suggest selecting a strategically superior location there,
building fortifications and garrisons,
stationing soldiers and horses,
to cut off their ability to return from afar.
Naturally, they will no longer be able to travel or transport supplies.”
Shìzōng adopted his plan,
and sent Grand Marshal Húlǜ Jīn and others to construct the three garrisons of Yángzhì, Bǎijiā, and Hūyán.
When Cháng's term of office expired,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
He was appointed Grand Protector and Inspector of Cāngzhōu,
and died.
He was posthumously granted Director of the Department of State Affairs, Duke Minister of the Masses, Grand Tutor, and First Chieftain Leading the People,
and given the pretense of a Prince.
His posthumous title was Zhōngwǔ.
Jīn Zuò,
courtesy name Shénjìng,
was a man from Āndìng.
His nature was valiant and heroic;
he valued spirit and acted as a knight-errant.
During the Zhèngguāng reign period of the Wèi dynasty,
bandits arose in Lǒngyòu.
An imperial edict commanded Yuán Měng, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, to suppress them.
He recruited "wolf families" (lángjiā)
to serve as military guides,
and Zuò answered the selection call.
Based on his military achievements, he was successively promoted to General of the Rushing Dragon (Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Língzhōu.
When Gāozǔ raised the banner of righteousness,
Ěrzhū Tiānguāng led the masses of Guānyòu to resist the righteous army in the north, along with Zhòngdá and others.
Tiānguāng left Zuò in Dōngqín,
giving him overall command of three prefectures,
and pacifying two prefectures.
When Tiānguāng was defeated,
[Zuò] returned to Gāozǔ,
and was appointed Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dàjiāngjūn).
In the Battle of Mángshān,
serving as Grand Military Governor (Dà Dūdū), he participated in defeating the Western Army.
Zuò was appointed Inspector of Huázhōu,
given the additional title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
separately enfeoffed as Viscount of Línjì County,
and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Wéi Zǐcàn,
courtesy name Huīmào,
was a man from Jīngzhào.
His great-grandfather, Lǎng,
was the Administrator (shǒu) of Xiányáng during the Wèi dynasty.
His father, Jùn,
was the Commissioner of Canals and Irrigation (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě).
Zǐcàn served as the Merits Supervisor (Gōngcáoshǐ) of the commandery,
and was successively promoted to Secretary (Lángzhōng) of the Grand Central Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái).
He followed Ěrzhū Tiānguāng to pacify Guānyòu.
When Xiàowǔ entered the Pass,
he appointed him Inspector of Nánfénzhōu.
Shénwǔ ordered a general to go out and suppress him.
The city fell,
and his sons and younger brothers were all captured and defeated,
and sent to Jìnyáng.
They were granted release and pardon.
Zǐcàn was made Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Bīngzhōu,
and was successively promoted to Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and died.
Originally, Zǐcàn had thirteen brothers.
His sons, nephews, and relatives,
amounting to one hundred family members, were all in the Western Wèi.
Because Zǐcàn failed to die in the crisis when the city fell,
many [of his relatives] were condemned and exterminated.
Among those who returned to the state and survived,
there were only him and his younger brother, Dàoxié.
Xié and Càn both entered the state.
After Càn became wealthy and noble,
he deliberately abandoned Dàoxié,
ordering him to live separately.
The emoluments he received
were virtually never shared with him.
His disregard for kindness and righteousness was like this.
Biographies Chapter 20: Yuán Tǎn, Yuán Bīn, Yuán Xiàoyǒu, Yuán Huīyè, Yuán Bì, Yuán Sháo
Yuán Tǎn:
His grandfather was Emperor Xiànwén of the Wèi.
He was the seventh son of Xǐ, the Prince of Xiányáng.
After Xǐ was executed,
five of his elder brothers, including Yì and Shù, successively fled south.
Therefore, Tǎn was able to inherit the title,
and was renamed Prince of Fūchéng.
At the beginning of the Yǒng'ān reign period,
he was restored to his original title, Prince of Xiányáng Commandery,
and was successively promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Emperor Zhuāng casually said to him:
"Your talent, O Prince, is not comparable to Xún or Cài.
That you have been repeatedly promoted in middle age
must be because you grew up in My household,
which is why you received extraordinary appointments."
Originally, after Xǐ died,
his sons were impoverished.
Tǎn and his brothers were taken in and raised by Xié, the Prince of Chéng.
Hence, this statement was made.
At the beginning of the Xiàowǔ reign period,
his elder brother, Shù, was captured.
Tǎn saw that Shù was both senior and worthy,
and worried that he might replace him.
He secretly advised the imperial court to eliminate him according to the law.
Shù knew of this
and wept, saying to Tǎn:
"Because of the difficulty faced by our family in the past,
I could not die,
but had to rely on others for food in the wilderness,
and accepted their noble titles and mandates.
My return now
was not motivated by righteousness,
but merely by seeking to survive.
How could I hope for glory and splendor?
Why do you indulge in such jealousy and suspicion,
forgetting the duty of kinship?
Though your physique is grand,
there is no virtue worth praising."
Tǎn changed countenance and left.
When Shù died,
[Tǎn] ultimately did not attend the funeral to weep.
Tǎn successively held the posts of Minister of the Masses (Sītú), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), and Grand Tutor (Tàifù),

with the added titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Director of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing (Lù Shàngshūshì), Director of the Imperial Clan Court (Zōngzhèng), and Governor of Sìzhōu.
Although his salary was generous and his position esteemed,
his greed and demands became increasingly excessive.
He sold judicial verdicts and peddled offices,
without limit or restraint.
He was impeached by the Censor (Yùshǐ) and dismissed from office,
returning to his residence as a Prince.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Grand Master of Court Discussion (Tèjìn).
He was dispatched as Inspector of Jìzhōu,
where he specialized again in amassing wealth.
Whenever the common people paid their taxes,
besides the regular levy,
he would first separately demand five bolts of silk,
before accepting the tax payment.
He was fond of hunting and fishing,
and never failed to go out daily.
In autumn and winter, he hunted pheasants and rabbits;
in spring and summer, he caught fish and crabs.
He constantly kept several hundred eagles and dogs.
He himself said that he would rather go without food for three days
than go without hunting for a single day.
He returned [to the capital] to serve as Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo reign of Qí, his noble rank was lowered according to regulation.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Xīnfēng County,
and appointed Grand Master of Court Discussion (Tèjìn) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
He was implicated because his son, Shìbǎo, along with Péng Guìpíng, the Attendant-in-Ordinary with Special Access (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng), made slanderous remarks while drunk,
and wildly discussed prognostic charts (túchèn).
The relevant authorities memorialized that they should be put to death,
but an imperial edict pardoned them all.
Tǎn was exiled to Běiyíngzhōu,
and died at the place of exile.
Yuán Bīn,
courtesy name Shànjí,
had Emperor Xiànwén of the Wèi as his grandfather.
His father, Yōng, the Prince of Gāoyáng,
was murdered at Héyīn along with Xiàozhuāng.
Bīn inherited his grandfather's title while young,
and successively held the posts of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè).
Bīn had handsome features and demeanor;
his nature was generous and gentle.
In office, he was serious and cautious,
and was highly admired by Wénxiāng of Qí.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo reign of Qí,
his noble rank was lowered according to regulation.
He was made Duke of Gāoyáng County,
and appointed Right Grand Master of Remonstrance (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
In the second year [of Tiānbǎo],
while returning with Wénxuān after suppressing the Qìdān,
upon reaching the Báiláng River,
he was executed by order due to an offense.
Yuán Xiàoyǒu:
His grandfather was Emperor Tàiwǔ of the Wèi.
His elder brother, Yù, the Prince of Línhuái, had no son,
and ordered Xiàoyǒu to inherit the title.
He was successively promoted to Inspector of Cāngzhōu.
His governance was gentle and moderate,
and he liked to perform small acts of kindness.
Although he could not maintain strict integrity,
he committed no infringements,
and the common people found this acceptable.
Emperor Jìng of the Wèi hosted Wénxiāng at Huálín.
Xiàoyǒu, while drunk, praised himself,
and further said:
"Your Majesty promised to grant me ability."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"I heard that the Prince himself claimed to be clean."
Wénxiāng said:
"The Prince of Línhuái, receiving the imperial decree, abandons his offense."
Thus, the ruler and his ministers all laughed,
and did not punish him.
Xiàoyǒu was knowledgeable regarding political administration.
He once submitted a memorial that stated: According to the established system: one hundred households form a Dǎngzú (Tribe),
twenty households form a Lǘ (Neighborhood),
and five households form a Bǐlín (Vicinity).
Within one hundred households,
there are twenty-five leaders (shuài).
Their conscripted duties
are all exempted,
leading to unequal burdens of hardship and ease.
The sheep are few and the wolves are many,
leading to further encroachment and erosion.
This malpractice has persisted for a long time.
In the various wards of the capital city,
perhaps seven or eight hundred households have only one Lǐzhèng (Ward Chief)
and two clerks (shǐ),
and yet public affairs suffer no neglect.
How much more so in the outer prefectures?
I request that the established system of having Three Chiefs (Sānzhèng) remain unchanged in name.
However, one hundred households should form a Zú (Tribe),
four Lǘ,
and two Lǘ...
According to calculations,
each *zú* (clan/household) is short twelve *dīng* (able-bodied men),
which amounts to twelve *pǐ* of commutation silk (*zī juàn*).
Roughly calculating the households currently under management, they should number more than twenty thousand *zú*,
yielding twenty-four
hundred thousand *pǐ* of commutation silk annually.
Fifteen *dīng* constitute one rotation of soldiers,
calculated to produce sixteen thousand troops.
This is the way to enrich the state and bring peace to the people.
In antiquity, the feudal lords (*zhūhóu*) married nine women;
the scholars (*shì*) had one wife and one concubine (*qiè*).
The Jìn decree stipulated: All princes (*zhū wáng*) could keep eight concubines;
commandery lords (*jùnjūn*) and marquises (*hóu*),
six concubines.
The official ranks decree stipulated:
The first and second ranks (*pǐn*) have four concubines,
the third and fourth ranks have three concubines,
the fifth and sixth ranks have two concubines,
and the seventh and eighth ranks have one concubine.
This is how the feminine virtues (*yīnjiào*)
can be fostered,
and the line of succession (*jìsì*) expanded.
Expanding the line of succession is Filial Piety (*xiào*);
fostering feminine virtues is Propriety (*lǐ*).
Yet the sagely court has suddenly abandoned these rules,
and this situation has gradually persisted for a long time.
Generals (*jiàng*) and chancellors (*xiàng*) often marry
imperial princesses (*gōngzhǔ*),
and princes and marquises marry into the Empress's clan (*hòuzú*).
Thus they do not keep concubines (*qièyìng*),
having grown accustomed to this practice.
Unfortunately for women,
those born in the present age,
since the entire court is without concubines,
the entire
realm is consequently mostly limited to one wife.
Even if a person forcefully decides to marry many women,
then the domestic affairs become fractured and strained,
personal matters meet with difficulty,
and relatives and acquaintances, both inside and outside the household,
mutually ridicule and criticize him.
Generally, the people
of today
do not adhere to any standards or regulations.
When parents marry off their daughter,
they instruct her in jealousy (*dù*);
aunts and sisters, when meeting her,
invariably encourage her in envy (*jì*).
Controlling one's husband is considered a woman's virtue (*fùdé*);
being skilled in jealousy
is considered a woman's accomplishment (*nǚgōng*).
They claim that they will not be bullied by others,
and fear others will laugh at them.
Since princes and dukes keep only one mind,
how dare those below them have a second intention.
If the heart of envy and jealousy arises,
then the rites between wife and concubine are discarded;
if the rites between wife and concubine are discarded,
then the omens of illicit sexual conduct arise.
This is what your servant deeply resents.
I request that princes and dukes of the first rank
marry eight [concubines],
making nine women in total, including the wife;
those commensurate with the second rank should have seven [women in total];
the third and fourth ranks should have five [women in total];
the fifth and sixth ranks should have one wife and two concubines.
Set a time limit of one
cycle,
and require all to fulfill these numbers.
If one does not fulfill the numbers,
or if one treats a concubine impolitely,
causing the wife, out of jealousy, to strike or beat her,
he should be removed from his current official post.
If a man’s wife is barren and he does not take
a concubine,
this is self-termination [of the line],
leaving no one to provide ritual sacrifices to his ancestors.
I request that he be charged with the crime of Unfilial Conduct (*bùxiào zhī zuì*),
and his wife divorced and sent away.
Your servant’s earnest heart,
is solely devoted to duty regarding family and state.
I wish to ensure that auspicious and inauspicious events all accord with Propriety,
and that the noble and the humble each have their appropriate customs.
Supervise the leaders of men in order to muster able-bodied soldiers,
establish granary
stores to enrich grain supplies,
institute reward systems to capture criminals and thieves,
and implement standardized regulations to display court rules.
In this way, may there be sufficient food and sufficient military strength,
and the people will have faith.
Furthermore, I venture to restate the required numbers of wives and
concubines,
precisely because I wish for the sons and younger brothers of princes, marquises, generals, chancellors, and meritorious officials,
whose descendants (*miáoyìn*) fill the court,
to transmit their lineage endlessly.
This is your servant’s ambition.
The edict was transmitted to the relevant authorities (*yǒusī*),
but the resulting memorial presented differing opinions.
Hèlián Xiàoyǒu further stated:
“Nowadays, people who live as humble servants,
are buried in a style comparable to princes and marquises.
The paths of the living and the deceased are disparate,
and there are no longer any regulations governing limits.
They grandly elevate the grave mounds (*qiūlǒng*),
elaborately decorate the sacrificial rites,
neighbors honor each other [for doing so],
and call this Ultimate Filial Piety (*zhìxiào*).
Furthermore, regarding the commencement of marriage,
which is prioritized by Royal Transformation (*wánghuà*),
sharing food from a divided gourd (*hépáo*) is
sufficient to complete the rites.
Yet the rich today are increasingly extravagant.
The arrangement of the shared meal (*tóngláo*)
is far greater than the sacrificial trays.
They stack fish to form mountains,
where the mountains have images of forests and trees,
and phoenixes and mythical birds reside.
This only causes unnecessary trouble and toil,
and eventually all is discarded.
Reflecting upon Heaven’s Will (*tiānyì*),
this is probably not correct.
I request that from this point forward,
anyone whose weddings or funerals exceed the proper rites,
be charged with defying the imperial decree.
If the officials fail to investigate and impeach them,
then they should be charged with the same crime.”
Hèlián Xiàoyǒu served as the administrator (*yǐn*) for many years,
and maintained himself according to the law.
He established a great reputation,
but his nature lacked rigidity and integrity,
and he was skilled at serving those in power,
which caused him to be ridiculed by the upright.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era of Qí,
in accordance with precedent, his rank was lowered,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Línhuái Xiàn,
and appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (*Guānglù Dàfū*).
In the winter of the second year, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the Jìnyáng Palace,
and upon leaving, he and Yuán Huīyè were both killed.
Yuán Huīyè,
courtesy name Shàoyuǎn,
was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Jǐngmù of Wèi.
In his youth, he was treacherous and shallow,
and often associated with bandits and robbers.
Upon reaching adulthood, he changed his conduct,
studied the philosophers and histories (*zǐ shǐ*),
and was also quite literary,
being generous and possessing ambition and integrity.
He successively held the posts of Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*) and Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*),
was given the title Grand Officer of Distinguished Merit (*Tèjìn*),
served concurrently as Director of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Jiān*),
and recorded the affairs of the Department of State Affairs (*Lù Shàngshū Shì*).
Wénxiāng once asked him:
“Recently, what have you been reading?”
He replied:
“I frequently study the biographies of Yī [Yǐn] and Huò [Guāng],
but I do not read the writings of Cáo [Cāo] or Mǎ [Téng].”
Huīyè, believing the age was gradually declining,
no longer sought to preserve his life intact.
He only devoted himself to drinking and eating—
one sheep per day,
and one calf every three days.
He also once composed a poem saying:
“In the past, residing where the Royal Way was peaceful,
many illustrious heroes flourished;
now encountering obstructed world paths,
foxes and rabbits roam freely and unchecked.”
At the beginning of Qí,
his title was lowered to Duke of Měiyáng Xiàn,
and he was appointed Administrator with Authority Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers (*Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*) and Grand Officer of Distinguished Merit (*Tèjìn*).
When Huīyè was in Jìnyáng,
he had no external interactions.
He was constantly at leisure,
and therefore compiled the lineage of the Princely Houses of Wèi,
entitled *Biànzōng Lù* (Records Clarifying the Clans), in forty volumes, which circulated in the world.
Although his position and reputation were profoundly esteemed,
because his temperament was unconventional,
he was constantly suspected and envied.
, he followed the imperial carriage to Jìnyáng
, and outside the palace gate, he cursed Yuán Sháo, saying
: "You are not worth even an old woman
. You carried the imperial seal on your back and handed it over to others
. Why did you not smash it
? When I speak these words
, I already know I will die
, but how much time do you have left either
!" Wénxuān (Emperor Wénxuān) heard this and executed him
, and also executed Xiàoyǒu, the Duke of Línhuái
. When Xiàoyǒu faced execution
, he was terrified and distraught
, but Huīyè's expression remained composed
. Their corpses were then sunk after breaking through the ice
. Huīyè's younger brother, Zhāoyè
, was quite scholarly
, and held the position of Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū)
. When Emperor Zhuāng (Zhuāng Dì) traveled south of Luò
, Zhāoyè stood outside the Chānghé Gate, striking his horse in remonstrance
. The Emperor avoided him and passed by
, but later offered him comfort and encouragement
. He held the positions of Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng), General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn), and Grand Master of the Right Shining Brightness (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū)
, and then died
. His posthumous title was Wén Hóu
. Yuán Bì
, courtesy name Fǔzōng
, was the son of Huī, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) of the Wèi
. ((His nature was firm and upright
, and he possessed literary talent
. He held the position of Grand Master of the Central Scattered Ranks (Zhōng Sàn Dàfū)
. As the hereditary legitimate heir, he should have inherited his ancestor's title
. However, his uncle, Lì, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púshè), relied on the favor of the Yú clan
, and thus seized Bì's princely title
, wrongly granting it to Dàn, the son of his older brother by the same mother
. Thereupon, Bì completely abandoned worldly affairs
, feigned illness, and returned to his private residence
. Xuānwǔ (Emperor Xuānwǔ) summoned him to be an Attendant in Ordinary (Shìzhōng)
. Bì submitted a memorial firmly declining
, entered Sōng Shān
, used a cave as his dwelling
, wore simple clothes, ate vegetarian food
, and died
. In the first year of Jiànyì
, his son Huīyè petitioned for the restoration of the princely title
. In the third year of Yǒng'ān, he was posthumously granted the titles of Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) and Minister over the Masses (Sītú Gōng)
, with the posthumous title Wénxiàn
. Previously, Bì had once dreamed that someone told him
: "You yourself will not receive the inherited fief
. The one who will continue the ancestral title
is your eldest son, Shàoyuǎn
." Bì woke up
, immediately told Huīyè
, and ultimately it was as the words foretold
Yuán Sháo
, courtesy name Shìzhòu
, was the nephew of Emperor Xiàozhuāng of Wèi
. Avoiding the troubles caused by Ěrzhū
, he hid in Sōng Shān
, and possessed a beautiful appearance and bearing
. Originally, when Ěrzhū Róng was about to enter Luò
, his father Shào was fearful
, and entrusted Sháo to his relative, Zhèng Zhòngmíng, the Administrator of Xíngyáng
. Zhòngmíng was soon killed by the city residents
, and Sháo, due to the chaos, became separated from his wet nurse
. He then fled the trouble with Sēngfù, the nephew of Zhòngmíng's older brother
. While on the road, they were pressured by bandits
, and Sēngfù feared they would not escape
. He therefore ordered Sháo to dismount
. Sēngfù said to the strangers
: "A desperate bird seeking refuge with people
may still be pitied
; how can we abandon a prince
?" Sēngfù raised his blade to pressure them
, and the strangers then withdrew
. Sháo met an old woman whose surname was Chéng
. She pitied him
and concealed him in her private home for over ten days
. Emperor Zhuāng searched for and found him
, and he succeeded to the title of Prince of Péngchéng
. The Divine Martial Emperor (Shénwǔ Dì) of Qí married him to the Empress of Emperor Xiàowǔ
. Many rare treasures of the Wèi imperial house
followed the Empress into Sháo’s household
. There were two jade bowls nested together
, which could be rotated but not separated
; and an agate wine cup holding three *shēng*
, which was stitched together with jade
. All were said to be crafted by ghosts from the Western Regions (Xīyù)
. He successively held the positions of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Attendant in Ordinary (Shìzhōng), Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū), and Governor of Sī Zhōu (Sī Zhōu Mù)
, and was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàifù)
. In the first year of Tiānbǎo of Qí
, his title was demoted to County Duke (Xiàn Gōng)
. Sháo's character and conduct were mild and generous
. As the son-in-law of the Gāo clan
, he enjoyed considerable contemporary favor
. He was capable of humility and withdrawal
, and when governing people, he implemented benevolent policies
. He loved Confucian studies
, courteously invited talented scholars
, loved forests and springs
, and repaired residences
which were splendid but not extravagant
. Emperor Wénxuān shaved Sháo’s beard and mustache
, applied powder and cosmetics
, dressed him in women's clothing to keep him in attendance
, saying
: "I regard the Prince of Péngchéng (Péngchéng) as my concubine
." This was to ridicule the Yuán clan as weak
, comparing them to women
. In the tenth year
, the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ) reported
: "This year, the old must be removed and the new established
." Wénxuān said to Sháo
: "Why did Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn restore the dynasty
?" Sháo replied
: "Because he failed to completely execute all members of the Liú clan
." Thereupon, he executed the members of the Yuán clan to satisfy the prophecy
. Consequently, in the fifth month, he executed Yuán Shìzhé, Jǐngshì, and twenty-five other households
. The remaining nineteen households were all placed under restriction
. Sháo was imprisoned in a dungeon near the capital
, stopped eating
, chewed on his clothes and sleeves, and died
. By the seventh month
, there was a major execution of the Yuán clan
. None who descended from Zhāochéng were spared
. Those whose fathers or grandfathers were princes
, or who had themselves been constantly high-ranking and prominent
, or whose brothers were vigorous and strong
, were all beheaded in the eastern market
. Their infants were tossed into the air
and caught on spears
. A total of seven hundred and twenty-one people died during this time
. All their bodies were thrown into the Zhāng River
. When fish were cut open, many nails and claws were found
, and because of this, the residents of the capital long ceased eating fish
. Eulogy says: The Yuán clan flourished luxuriantly
, relying on blessed spiritual powers
. But their Way followed the ending of their fortune
, and their destiny met with excessive punishment
. Biographies, Chapter Twenty-one: Lǐ Hún (Hún’s brother, Huì), Lǐ Yú, Zhèng Shùzǔ
Lǐ Hún
, courtesy name Jìchū
, was a native of Bǎirén, Zhào Jùn
. His great-grandfather, Líng
, was the Duke of Jùlù of Wèi
. His father, Zūn
, was the Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) in the Governor-General’s Office of Jì Zhōu for Wèi
. Yú, the Prince of Jīngzhào, started a rebellion in Jì Zhōu
and harmed Zūn
. Because Hún’s father died serving the Prince
, Hún was appointed Gentleman of the Household (Jǐshì Zhōng)
. As there were many troubles throughout the land at that time
, he declined, citing illness
, and requested to be Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) in the Governor-General’s Office of Qīng Zhōu
. Together with Xíng Shào of Héjiān and Wáng Xīn of Běihǎi, he took his elderly mother and wife and proceeded together to Qīng and Qí
. Not long after, Ěrzhū Róng entered Luò
, and all the officials were exterminated
. Commentators considered him to have known the opportune moment
. Early in Yǒng'ān
, he was appointed Regular Mounted Attendant (Sǎnjì Chángshì)
. During the Pǔtài period
, Cuī Shèkè rebelled in Hǎidài
and attacked and besieged Qīng Zhōu
. An imperial edict appointed Hún as General Who Attacks the East (Zhēng Dōng Jiāngjūn)
, Minister of the Department of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū), and Mobile Department Director (Xíng Tái) to go aid the area
. Shèkè's veteran generals were resourceful
. The various cities held fast to their defenses
, strengthening their walls and clearing the countryside
. Opinions were divided at the time
. Hún said
: "Shèkè is the root of the bandits
, and the siege of the city has already lasted more than a month
. This ragtag collection of troops
can easily be broken and dispersed
. If we select brave and strong men
, muzzle their mouths, and launch a night attack
, heading straight toward their camp
and catching them unaware
, in the short span of a moment
, we can capture and exterminate them
