. If Shèkè is captured
, then the various districts can be pacified simply by circulating a written proclamation
. Why would we risk the heat to assault the city
and exhaust our soldiers
?" The various generals hesitated
, but Hún decided to proceed
. Before dawn
, they reached the city wall
. The bandit troops scattered in panic
. He captured Shèkè alive
, cut off his head, and sent it to Luò
. The coastal region was thus cleared and pacified
Later, he was appointed Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently holding Chángshì,
and was dispatched as an envoy to Liáng.
Liáng Wǔ addressed him, saying:
"The descendants of Bóyáng,
after long ages, only become more prominent.
Among the talented people of Zhào Lǐ,
you are truly numerous today.
The Chángshì previously served as a commander,
and now again serves as an envoy.
Civil and military accomplishments have not declined;
truly such a person belongs here."
When the mission returned,
he was made Dōng Jùn Tàishǒu.
He was recalled due to corruption.
Shìzōng ordered Wǔ Shìtí to bring him in.
Hún defiantly said:
"Does the General still show courtesy to the worthy today?"
Shìzōng laughed and released him.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shàobǎo.
Xíng Shào was Shàoshī,
and Yáng Yīn was Shàofù.
Commentators considered this an honor.
For participating in compiling the rituals for the abdication ceremony,
he was granted the title Jīngyáng Xiàn Nán.
He revised and fixed the Línzhǐ Gé.
Soon after, he was appointed Hǎizhōu Cìshǐ.
The local people revolted,
and jointly attacked the prefectural city.
The city contained many stones,
but no wells,
so they usually drank seawater.
The rebels cut off their route.
Inside the city there had previously been a pool,
but due to the drought, it had long been dry.
One morning, it rained,
and a spring gushed forth, overflowing.
The rebels took this as a divine sign,
and scattered in astonishment immediately.
Hún supervised and encouraged his officers and soldiers,
capturing and executing the main leader.
Hún's concubine, Lady Guō, interfered in governance and accepted bribes in the prefecture,
for which he was dismissed from office.
He died.
His son, Zhàn,
courtesy name Chǔyuán.
He briefly studied literature and history,
possessing the family tradition.
He served as Tàizǐ Shèrén,
concurrently holding Chángshì,
and was Deputy Envoy on a mission to Chén.
He inherited the title Jīngyáng Xiàn Nán.
Hún, along with his younger brothers Huì and Wěi, had all been chief envoys to Liáng,
and Zhàn was again a deputy envoy.
Because of this, the people of Zhào Jùn,
referred to their house as "The Gate of Four Envoys."
Huì,
courtesy name Jìngwén.
At the age of six,
he personally desired to enter school,
but his family happened to forbid it due to seasonal taboos,
promising later but not allowing it now.
He watched the writing materials of his elder sister,
and secretly used them constantly.
Before long, he mastered the Jíjiù Zhāng.
Everyone, both within and outside the family, regarded him as extraordinary,
believing him to be an unusual child.
When he grew up,
his appearance and demeanor were upright and impressive,
his spirit and expression bright and outstanding.
Xíng Yàn of Héjiān,
was Huì's maternal uncle.
He had pure conversations with Huì,
and praised his loftiness and depth.
He often remarked:
"It is like parting the clouds and mist,
or being confronted by pearls and jade.
The responsibility for the Prime Minister's residence,
truly rests with this nephew."
Qí Wáng Xiāo Bǎoyín engaged him as Zhǔbù Jìshì,
specifically managing memorials and official dispatches,
treating him with the courtesy due to a guest and friend.
Sītú Gāo Yōng invited him to serve as Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
summoning him to Luò.
At that time, an imperial edict commanded Shìzhōng, Prince of Xīhé, and Mìshūjiān Cháng Jǐng to select ten Confucian scholars to compile the Wǔ Lǐ.
Huì and Wáng Yì of Tàiyuán jointly oversaw the Military Rites.
Wèi Jìng Dì, lecturing on the Xiàojīng and the Lǐjì in the Xiǎnyáng Diàn,
had Huì, along with his cousin Qiān, Péi Bómào,
Wèi Shōu, Lú Yuánmíng, and others, all serve as recorders of the discussion.
He was naturally skilled at writing,
especially capable in receiving and transmitting information.
He structured and pieced together words and arguments,
offering concise and noteworthy summaries.
At the beginning of the Tiānpíng era,
Shìzōng employed him as Chéngxiàng Sīmǎ.
Whenever the court adjourned,
all civil and military officials gathered,
speaking before the royal court.
Huì was regularly ordered to initiate the discussions,
serving as the head of all the officials.
His voice and delivery were eloquent and precise,
his manner was elegant and refined,
causing listeners to feel deeply respectful.
At the beginning of the Wǔdìng era,
concurrently holding Chángshì,
he became the chief envoy on a mission to Liáng.
Liáng Wǔ Dì asked Huì:
"Where is Chancellor Gāo now?"
Huì replied:
"He is currently in Jìnyáng,
solemnly checking the border bandits."
Liáng Wǔ said:
"How would you describe Hēidá?
What strategies is Chancellor Gāo employing?"
Huì replied:
"Hēidá is like a wandering ghost west of the pass,
hated by both men and gods.
Disasters and calamities have occurred for consecutive years,
and the common people yearn for their homeland.
The Chéngxiàng's extraordinary strategies are unmatched,
storing strength and observing opportunity,
attacking the ignorant to hasten their downfall.
The realization of this prospect is certainly not far off."
Liáng Wǔ said:
"What you say is excellent."
He then casually discussed clans and lineages with the people of Liáng.
Yuán Xiá said:
"It is not as good as my origin, which stems from Huáng Dì,
my surname being among the Fourteen Categories."
Huì replied:
"Though your origin, Sir, is distant,
you must share one character with Chē Qiānqiū."
Everyone present burst into laughter.
Previous envoys,
all presented petitions seeking trade,
but Huì alone maintained a pure and lofty standard.
The people of Liáng respected his integrity.
When the mission returned,
he was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Gāoyáng Nèishǐ.
Fierce beasts previously existed in the commandery territory,
which the people constantly feared.
Huì planned to repair the enclosures,
and they consequently died from fighting amongst themselves.
Everyone believed this was caused by his transforming influence,
and all requested that this be reported to the throne.
Huì did not allow it.
When Gāozǔ toured the commanderies and states in the East,
he halted his horse west of the Yíngzhōu city wall and stood there for a long time,
and sent someone to comfort him, saying:
"When I was in Jìn,
I knew that among the governors East of the Mountains, only you focused on your duties.
Upon entering your border and observing the customs,
it is truly as I heard.
If you maintain a good beginning and ensure a good conclusion,
your position will reach extraordinary heights."
Cuī Móu, the Prefect of Héjiān, relying on the influence of his younger brother Xiān,
requested elk antlers and wagtail feathers from Huì.
Huì replied in a letter:
"The wagtail has six wings;
when it flies, it soars to the sky.
The elk has four legs;
when it runs, it rushes into the sea.
This humble official is physically slow and lazy,
my hands and feet are sluggish,
unable to chase down things that fly or pursue things that run,
nor can I attend upon fawning men from afar."
At that time, Shìzōng ordered Xiān to select the Sītú Zhǎngshǐ.
Xiān recommended Huì,
but eventually, it was not realized.
Everyone believed this was due to that letter.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he became Sītú Yòuzhǎngshǐ.
Huì's essential character was upright and serious,
he never submitted to power and influence,
and for this reason, he was suppressed and kept low for a long time.
He died.
Gōngxù,
courtesy name Mùshū,
was the son of Hún's paternal cousin, Jiè.
His nature was intelligent and sensitive,
widely understanding the classics and commentaries.
At the end of Wèi, he was Jìzhōu Sīmǎ,
but left office due to illness.
Later, he was summoned to serve as Shìyùshǐ,
but he did not arrive.
He died.
Gōngxù was profound and focused on the Way,
not involving himself in worldly affairs,
therefore, he vowed not to serve in office.
He was especially skilled in the studies of Yīnyáng and the Túwěi (Apocryphal Texts).
He once told people:
"Whenever I observe the celestial divisions of Qí,
its fortune and virtue are not abundant,
the hereditary rule of the state
will end in twenty-eight (four times seven)."
When the year of Qí's demise came,
it had been twenty-eight years since the first year of Tiānbǎo.
Gōngxù lived in seclusion, awaiting [his fate],
he was fond of writing books.
He compiled *Diǎnyán* (典言) in ten volumes,
and also compiled *Zhìyí* (質疑) in five volumes,
*Sāngfú Zhāngjù* (喪服章句) in one volume,
*Gǔjīn Lüèjì* (古今略記) in twenty volumes,
*Xuánzǐ* (玄子) in five volumes,
*Zhàoyǔ* (趙語) in thirteen volumes,
all circulated throughout the world.
Lǐ Yú,
courtesy name Dàofán,
was a man from Lǒngxī Chéngjì.
He was the fifth-generation descendant of Liáng Wǔzhāowáng Gǎo.
His father, Sháo,
both held great reputations during the Wèi dynasty.
Yú was gentle, elegant, knowledgeable, and measured.
He began his career as Acting Staff Officer to the Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant),
and was successively promoted to Right Chief Clerk to the Sītú (Minister of Education).
When the capital was moved to Yè,
he remained behind,
supervising and managing the official treasury,
and overseeing the dismantling and transport of materials from the palaces and ancestral temples.
He was praised for his clear competence.
He was successively promoted to General-in-Chief of Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dōngxúzhōu.
When he retired from the governorship and returned,
he then claimed old age and illness,
and did not seek office.
When Qí received the abdication,
Yú was summoned to serve concurrently as General of the Vanguard (Qiánjiāngjūn),
to escort [the emperor] during the ritual at the Yuánqiū (Round Mound).
Yú did not wish to have his name recorded in service under two dynasties.
Although he was summoned due to his seniority,
as soon as the ceremony was over, he immediately ceased attending court requests.
He died in the fourth year of Tiānbǎo.
His sons were Quán and Yùn.
Sòng and Yùn lacked moral conduct.
Sòng married his daughter to Húaiwěi, the son of Mù Típó,
and was rapidly promoted to Magistrate (Lìng) of Línzhāng and Commissioner Bearing Insignia (Yítóu Sānsī).
Yùn engaged in an illicit affair with Lù Lìngxuān’s younger sister.
Lìngxuān memorialized to have him appointed to Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
His younger brother was Jǐn,
courtesy name Dàoyú.
His name is recorded in the *Wèi Shū*.
His talent and knowledge
were praised by his contemporaries.
Jǐn had six sons:
Chǎnzhī,
Qiànzhī, Shòuzhī, Lǐzhī, Xíngzhī, and Níngzhī.
All possessed ability and reputation.
Xíngzhī had a profound fraternal affection for his brothers,
and his manner was calm, simple, and modest.
He was praised by scholars and friends.
Lú Sīdào of Fànyáng was his cousin (son of his maternal uncle).
He once presented him with a poem saying:
"The Director of the Treasury calls him a recluse,
Pān and Yáng have familial ties extending generations,
his physical form participates in officialdom,
but his mind transcends the earthly dust."
Contemporaries regarded this as a true description.
Yú’s paternal cousin was Xiǎo,
courtesy name Rénlüè.
He was the son of Wèi’s Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant), Qián.
He was widely educated and possessed deep reasoning.
He started his career as an Expectant Vice Director (Yuánwài Shìláng).
When Ěrzhū Róng was about to harm the court officials,
and Xiǎo was preparing to set out,
Xiǎo's court robe and cap were chewed by a rat.
Consequently, he failed to make the journey,
and thus escaped the disaster of Héyīn.
When the capital was moved to Yè,
Xiǎo then settled temporarily in Qīnghé,
staying at the residence of his maternal cousin, Cuī Yá.
He was provided with thirty *qǐng* of good farmland.
Xiǎo consequently built a house and lived peacefully,
teaching and encouraging his sons and nephews,
without any further desire for official career.
In the late Wǔdìng period,
believing that the world was becoming peaceful,
he entered the capital to serve in office.
He was appointed Administrator (Shǒu) of Dùnqiū,
and died [in office].
Zhèng Shùzǔ,
courtesy name Gōngwén,
was a man from Kāifēng, Xíngyáng.
His grandfather, Xī,
was Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng) for Wèi.
His father, Dàozhāo,
was Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān) for Wèi.
Shùzǔ was clever and perceptive in his youth,
fond of literary composition,
and possessed good conduct and discipline,
praised by respected elders.
He started his career as Acting Staff Officer to the Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
In the early Tiānbǎo period,
he was successively promoted to Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàoshī), Commissioner Bearing Insignia (Yítóu Sānsī), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu.
At that time, Mù Zǐróng served as the Circuit Inspector,
and sighed, saying:
"The ancients said: 'Hearing the reputation of Bóyí,
the greedy become pure,
and the timid acquire resolve.'
Now I see this in Governor Zhèng of Yǎnzhōu."
Previously, when Shùzǔ’s father was [Governor of] Guāngzhōu,
he built a study pavilion on a small hill south of the city wall,
and carved an inscription in stone to commemorate it.
Shùzǔ was nine years old at the time.
When he became Governor,
he went to seek out the old traces,
and found a broken stone.
The inscription read:
"The Hall of White Clouds (Báiyúntáng) belonging to the Master of the Central Marchmount, Zhèng Dàozhāo."
Shùzǔ sobbed facing it,
and his grief moved all his subordinates.
A man entered the marketplace and stole cloth.
His father angrily said:
"How dare you deceive the people's ruler!"
He arrested the thief and brought him back [to Shùzǔ] to confess.
Shùzǔ specifically pardoned him.
After this,
there were no more thieves within the borders.
People sang a song about them:
"The great Lord Zhèng,
the lesser Lord Zhèng,
separated by fifty years,
their moral influence is still the same."
Shùzǔ was skilled at playing the *qín* (zither).
He personally composed the *Lóngyín Shínòng* (Ten Melodies of the Dragon's Roar).
He said he once dreamt that someone was playing the *qín*.
When he awoke, he was able to write down the music.
Contemporaries considered them to be exquisitely wonderful.
Wherever he went, he liked to construct artificial hills and ponds,
planting pines and bamboos together,
preparing sumptuous feasts to host guests,
receiving and welcoming them tirelessly.
Before he became noble,
he was traveling alone on horseback in the countryside.
Suddenly, there were several hundred riders.
Upon seeing Shùzǔ, they all dismounted,
and said,
"The Lord is here,"
and bowed in ranks.
Shùzǔ consulted his attendant,
but the attendant saw nothing.
He found this very strange in his heart.
Not long after, he was summoned [to court],
and eventually attained prominent positions.
When his illness became critical,
he finally spoke of this incident himself.
And he said:
"I am now old.
The wealth and nobility of my life are enough.
Leaving a reputation for integrity to my descendants,
I have no regrets upon death."
He subsequently died in his province.
Shùzǔ’s daughter became the consort (Fēi) of Zhàojùnwáng Ruì.
Shùzǔ habitually remained seated when receiving the Prince’s bow,
and only when he commanded him to sit,
did the Prince sit.
After the consort died,
the Prince married the daughter of Zhèng Dàoyìn instead.
The Prince remained seated when receiving Dàoyìn’s bow.
When the Prince commanded him to sit,
he then dared to sit.
The Prince said to Dàoyìn:
"Minister Zhèng (Zhèng Shàngshū) had such moral character,
and was highly respected as a senior statesman.
You cannot compare yourself to him."
His son, Yuándé,
was skilled in many arts.
His highest office was Administrator (Shǒu) of Lángyá.
Yuándé’s paternal cousin was Yuánlǐ,
courtesy name Wénguī.
In youth, he loved learning,
cherished literary elegance,
and possessed renown.
Shìzōng invited him to be a guest at his residence.
He successively served as Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
The wife of Cuī Áng
was Yuánlǐ’s elder sister,
and Wèi Shōu was Cuī Áng’s brother-in-law (husband of his younger sister).
Áng once showed several poems by Yuánlǐ to Lú Sīdào,
and said to Sīdào:
"Looking at Yuánlǐ's recent poetry,
surely he is no less than Wèi Shōu?"
Sīdào replied:
"I do not yet perceive Yuánlǐ to be superior to Wèi Shōu,
I only know that a sister's husband is less familiar than a wife's brother."
Yuánlǐ entered Zhōu [service],
and died while serving as Assistant Administrator (Biéjià) of Shǐzhōu.
Biography Twenty-two: Cuī Xiān, Gāo Dézhèng, Cuī Áng
Cuī Xiān,
courtesy name Jìlún,
was a native of Ānpíng, Bólíng.
He was a descendant of Shàngshū Shí of the Hàn dynasty,
and his family had been a prominent clan in the Northern Provinces for generations.
His father, Mù,
was a Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk) of the Prefecture.
When Xiān was young, he was a scholar (shūshēng).
He fled to Bóhǎi
and relied upon Gāo Gān,
giving his younger sister in marriage to Gān's younger brother, Shèn.
When Shèn later governed Guāngzhōu,
he memorialized for Xiān to become his Chángshǐ (Chief Administrator).
When Zhàojùn Gōng Chēn was stationed at Dìngzhōu,
he was appointed Kāifǔ Zīyì (Consultant to the Governor).
He followed Chēn to Jìnyáng.
Gāozǔ (Gāo Huān) spoke with him and was pleased,
appointing him concurrently as Chéngxiàng Chángshǐ (Chief Administrator to the Chancellor).
When Gāozǔ raised troops and was about to enter Luò,
he left Xiān behind to assist Chēn in managing affairs in the rear.
He said to him:
“How men trust one another
is not dependent on how long they have known each other.
Military matters are grave,
and the responsibility of staying behind is crucial.
My younger brother is young
and not yet familiar with necessary procedures.
All post-war affairs,
I entrust entirely to you.”
He grasped his hand earnestly,
doing so three or four times.
Later, he was promoted to Zuǒchéng (Assistant Director of the Secretariat) and Lìbù Láng (Director of the Bureau of Personnel),
and was put in charge of deliberating the Línzhǐ Statutes (Línzhǐ Gé).
Xiān's personal favor grew daily.
He was fond of recommending talented people.
He said that Xíng Shào was suitable to serve as a high official (fǔliáo)
and concurrently handle confidential matters.
Shìzōng (Gāo Chéng) consequently summoned Shào,
and treated him with great intimacy and respect.
During their conversations,
Shào proceeded to malign Xiān.
Shìzōng was displeased
and said to Xiān:
“You speak of Zǐcái’s (Xíng Shào’s courtesy name) strengths,
but Zǐcái speaks only of your shortcomings.
This man is foolish.”
Xiān said:
“Zǐcái speaks of Xiān’s shortcomings,
and Xiān speaks of Zǐcái’s strengths—
both are factual,
and should not cause resentment.”
When Gāo Shèn rebelled,
he had a feud with Xiān.
Gāozǔ wished to execute Xiān,
but Shìzōng interceded and saved him from execution.
At the beginning of the Wǔdìng era,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi (Palace Censor-in-Chief).
He selected Bì Yìyún, Lú Qián, Sòng Qīndào, Lǐ Yīn, Cuī Zhān, Dù Ruí, Jī Yè, Lì Bówěi, Cuī Zǐwǔ, and Lǐ Guǎng, all to be Censors (Yùshǐ).
The people of the time praised him for his judgment of character.
Shìzōng wished to lend Xiān prestige and power.
While all the high officials were seated,
he instructed Xiān to enter walking slowly and looking straight ahead,
with two men holding his robe (to indicate his importance).
Shìzōng stood in the courtyard and bowed to him in return,
but Xiān took his seat without deference.
When the wine had circulated twice,
he immediately took his leave.
Shìzōng said:
“Your humble servant has a simple meal prepared;
I hope you, Sir, will stay a little longer.”
Xiān replied:
“I have just received an imperial order to inspect matters at the Censorate.”
He then left without waiting for the meal.
Shìzōng stepped down from the dais to see him off.
A few days later,
Shìzōng and the high officials went out to Dōngshān.
They encountered Xiān on the road.
Xiān’s vanguard struck Shìzōng’s forward guard with red staffs (as a warning to clear the path).
Shìzōng turned his horse aside to avoid him.

Xiān successively submitted memorials impeaching Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs) Sīmǎ Zǐrú, along with Shàngshū (Minister) Yuán Xiàn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōngzhōu) Mùróng Xiàn.
He also impeached Tàishī (Grand Tutor) Xiányáng Wáng Tǎn and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ Kězhūhún Dàoyuán.
He detailed their crimes fully in writing,
and they were all dismissed from office.
Many others were subsequently executed or degraded.
Gāozǔ wrote a letter to the various nobles in Yè:
“In the past, Cuī Xiān served my younger brother as Dìngzhōu Chángshǐ.
Later, he served my son as Kāifǔ Zīyì.
When he was promoted to Zuǒchéng and Lìbù Láng,
I did not know his true abilities.
Only when he began residing in the Censorate (Xiàntái)
did he carry out impeachments like these.
Xiányáng Wáng and Sīmǎ Lìng were both old commoner friends from my neighborhood.
In terms of prestige, closeness, and affection,
no one surpassed those two.
They were convicted simultaneously,
and I was unable to save them.
All of you gentlemen must be cautious.”
When Gāozǔ arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
the assembled officials welcomed him at Zǐmò.
Gāozǔ grasped Xiān’s hand and praised him, saying:
“In the past, the court certainly had judicial officials,
but the entire realm was greedy,
and no one was willing to prosecute.
The Zhōngwèi (Cuī Xiān) has served the state devotedly,
without avoiding the powerful and influential.
Consequently, places near and far have been purified,
and all the high officials adhere to the law.
There are many men
who charge the enemy and breach defenses.
But one who handles official duties with integrity
is only now seen.
The glory, splendor, wealth, and status you now enjoy
were entirely gained by the Zhōngwèi himself.
Gāo Huān and his son
have nothing to offer in return.”
He bestowed a fine horse upon Xiān,
and made him ride it as he followed,
talking as they proceeded.
When Xiān dismounted to bow,
the horse panicked and bolted.
Gāozǔ secured it and handed him the reins.
The Wèi Emperor (Wèi Dì) held a banquet at Huálín Yuán,
and said to Gāozǔ:
“Recently, many of the court nobles, governors, magistrates, and numerous officials everywhere have been greedy and cruel,
encroaching upon and exploiting the common people.
Among those at court, if there is anyone who acts with fairness,
speaks truthfully in impeachments,
and does not spare relatives,
the Prince may offer him wine.”
Gāozǔ stepped down from the dais,
knelt, and said:
“That is none other than Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Cuī Xiān alone.
I respectfully follow your clear decree,
and dare to offer him wine,
and I beg that the thousand pieces of silk cloth previously granted to your servant for archery
be transferred and bestowed upon him.”
The Emperor said:
“Because of Zhōngwèi Cuī’s enforcement of the law,
monastics and laymen alike are orderly.”
Xiān bowed and replied:
“This is due to the transforming influence of Your Majesty,
and the encouragement and support of the Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn), your servant Chéng.”
Shìzōng withdrew and said to Xiān:
“Even I stand in awe and admiration;
how much more must others feel.”
From this point on, his prestige grew daily,
and everyone inside and outside the court feared and obeyed him.
When Gāozǔ died,
before the mourning period had begun,
Shìzōng appointed Xiān Dùzhī Shàngshū (Minister of Finance),
concurrently Púshè (Director of the Department of State Affairs),
entrusting him with confidential and crucial responsibilities.
Xiān worried about the state as if it were his own family,
and took the welfare of the realm upon himself.
When Shìzōng’s carriages and attire were extravagant,
when his executions were unusual,
or when his manner of speech and conduct
contained improprieties,
Xiān always spoke sternly and remonstrated strongly,
and Shìzōng would cease the behavior.
There were several hundred prisoners
whom Shìzōng wanted to execute entirely.
He constantly pressed for the documents (concerning their crimes).
Xiān deliberately slowed the process
and did not submit the documents in a timely manner.
Shìzōng’s mood subsequently eased,
and the prisoners were eventually spared.
Since entering official life,
he usually returned home late in the day.
At dawn, he would ask his brothers about their mother’s well-being.
In the evening, he would taste her food and supervise her bedding,
and only then would he go to the outer study (Wàizhāi) to meet with close guests.
He never concerned himself with household affairs throughout his life.
When Wèi and Liáng established peaceful relations,
all the high nobles sent people to follow the envoys to engage in trade.
Xiān alone sent a request for Buddhist scriptures.
Liáng Wǔdì (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) heard of this,
had the scriptures copied,
and sent them to the residence (guǎn) accompanied by banners, flowers, and chants (zànbài).
However, he was fond of exaggeration
and indulged in excessive teasing.
He secretly ordered the monk Míngzàng to write the *Fóxìng Lùn* (Treatise on Buddha Nature) but signed his own name to it,
and circulated it south of the Yangtze River (Jiāngbiǎo).
His son, Dáná, was thirteen years old.
Xiān commanded the scholar Quán Huì to teach him how to pronounce the two characters *Zhōu Yì* (Classic of Changes).
He then gathered court nobles and famous scholars,
and made Dáná ascend a high platform to lecture.
Suī Zhòngràng of Zhàojùn pretended to be convinced and deferred to him.
Xiān was pleased
and promoted him to Sītú Zhōngláng (Central Administrator to the Minister of Education).
The people of Yè (Yèxià) created a saying about this:
“He earned the position of Zhōngláng (Central Administrator) by lecturing on two lines of text.”
These were all Xiān’s shortcomings.
Xiǎnzǔ initially succeeded to the hegemonic enterprise.
Sīmǎ Zǐrú and others harbored old grudges.
They claimed that Xiān's crimes were severe,
saying he ought to be punished.
Gāo Lóngzhī also said that the net of governance should be loosened,
the strict investigative magistrates should be removed,
and Cuī Xiān should be dismissed,
which would win the approval of people near and far.
Xiǎnzǔ followed this advice.
When he ascended the throne,
those who slandered and ruined him still did not stop.
The Emperor then ordered the Regional Inspector Chén Shāntí and others to search Xiān's house.
It was extremely poor and destitute;
they only found over a thousand sheets of correspondence between Gāozǔ, Shìzōng, and Xiān,
most of which discussed major military and national affairs.
The Emperor sighed in admiration.
However, he still could not escape public criticism,
so he banished Xiān to Mǎchéng.
By day, he carried earth to serve his labor duties;
by night, he was placed in an underground prison.
After more than a year,
a slave accused Xiān of planning rebellion.
He was chained and sent to Jìnyáng.
The accusation was baseless,
so he was released and rewarded.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
The Emperor said to his ministers:
“Minister Cuī Tàicháng is pure and upright;
none in the world can match him.
None of you equals him.”
Initially, Shìzōng intended to marry his sister to Xiān's son,
but as it happened, Shìzōng died,
and the plan was abandoned.
Now, at this time,
the ministers were feasting in the Xuānguāng Diàn (Palace Hall).
Many sons of noble relatives were present.
Xiǎnzǔ spoke with them one by one.
While sitting, he personally wrote a letter to Xiān, saying:
“Your worthy son, Dáná,
possesses great talent and learning.
My deceased elder brother's daughter, the Princess Lè'ān Zhǔ,
is the maternal niece of the Wèi Emperor.
She is treated with respect both inside and outside the court,
surpassing all my sisters.
I wish to fulfill the longstanding wish of my elder brother.”
He then gave the Princess in marriage to Dáná.
Toward the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
he became Minister of the Right (Yòu Púshè).
The Emperor said to his attendants:
“Cuī Xiān advises me against excessive drinking,
but how does my drinking hinder anything?”
The Prince of Chángshān privately said to Xiān:
“When the Supreme One is often drunk,
even the Empress Dowager cannot offer advice,
and we, his brothers, keep silent.
Only the Púshè (Minister) is able to brave his wrath.
Those inside and outside the court are deeply moved and ashamed [that they cannot do the same].”
In the tenth year,
Xiān died of illness.
The Emperor stroked his coffin and wept.
He was posthumously granted the title of Opener of the Palace (Kāifǔ).
Dáná was gentle, good, pure, and cautious,
and had profound knowledge and learning.
In his youth, he held various positions, serving as Minister of the Court of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng).
After entering Zhōu,
he plotted rebellion and was executed.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Xiǎnzǔ once asked Princess Lè'ān Zhǔ:
“What do you think of Dáná?”
She replied:
“We greatly respect each other,
but his mother hates me.”
Xiǎnzǔ summoned Dáná’s mother into the palace,
killed her,
and threw the corpse into the Zhāng River.
When Qí was destroyed,
Dáná killed the Princess to take revenge.
Gāo Dézhèng,
courtesy name Shìzhēn,
was a person from Bóhǎi Xiū.
His father, Hào,
was the Inspector of Cāngzhōu for Wèi.
Dézhèng was quick-witted and intelligent in his youth,
possessing a dignified bearing and appearance.
Xiǎnzǔ invited him to be an Administrator (Cānjūn) in the Office of the Opener of the Palace (Kāifǔ),
and entrusted him with handling records and documentation.
They were extremely close and intimate.
Gāozǔ later promoted him to Clerk (Yuàn) in the Chancellor's Office,
entrusting him as a confidant.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Huángmén Shìláng).
When Shìzōng succeeded to the enterprise
and went to Jìnyáng,
Xiǎnzǔ remained in the capital city to oversee the defense,
and ordered Dézhèng to assist in managing secret affairs.
He was seen as even more intimate and important.
Shìzōng died suddenly.
The event occurred abruptly,
and the hearts of the officials were distraught.
The meritorious generals considered the inheritance of the military enterprise to be grave,
and urged the Emperor to proceed quickly to Jìnyáng.
The Emperor was also hesitant and unable to decide for himself.
In the middle of the night, he summoned Yáng Yīn, Dù Bì, Cuī Jìshū, and Dézhèng, among others,
and only then settled on a plan.
He appointed Yáng Yīn to remain and oversee the capital.
Dézhèng had long been intimate and beloved by the Emperor,
and held nothing back in his speech.
Xú Zhīcái, Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), and Sòng Jǐngyè, Palace Guest (Guǎn Kè), who were skilled in astronomy, diagrams, and prognostications,
and Yáng Zǐshù, a retainer of Chén Shāntí, whom he had introduced,
all utilized Dézhèng,
to urge Xiǎnzǔ to carry out the affair of abdication and succession.
Dézhèng also opened his heart and firmly pleaded for it.
The Emperor then personally wrote a letter to Yáng Yīn,
fully discussing the intention of the various people who urged him to assume the throne.
Dézhèng feared that Yīn might hesitate and be indecisive,
so he requested permission to rush by post-horse to the capital,
ostensibly for other business.
He spoke only with Yáng Yīn,
and Yīn then agreed and complied.
Before Dézhèng returned,
the Emperor immediately departed Jìnyáng.
Upon arriving at Píngdūchéng,
he summoned the meritorious generals to enter,
and informed them of the matter of abdication and concession.
When the generals suddenly heard this,
they were all astonished,
and none dared to reply.
At that time, Dù Bì was the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ).
He secretly reported to Xiǎnzǔ, saying:
“Guānxī (the West) is a strong enemy of the state.
If we now accept the abdication of Wèi,
we fear they will claim a righteous army, seize the Son of Heaven, and advance eastward.
How will Your Highness receive them?”
Xiǎnzǔ entered (the inner chamber),
summoned Bì to enter, and informed Xú Zhīcái [of Bì's concern].
Zhīcái said:
“As for those who now contend with Your Highness for the world,
their intention is also to become Emperor.
It is like chasing a rabbit through a crowded market;
when one person catches it,
the hearts of the multitude are settled.
If we accept Wèi's abdication first now,
Guānxī will naturally set aside their ambition.
Even if they wish to remain defiant,
they will only be chasing after me, claiming the title of Emperor.
It is essential to understand the opportunity and act first,
and not allow yourself to learn from others later.”
Bì had no reply.
The Emperor had already sent couriers speeding by post to Yè,

writing to Grand Commandant Gāo Yuè, President of the Department of State Affairs Gāo Lóngzhī, General of the Army Lóu Ruì, Attendant Counselor Zhāng Liàng, Gentleman of the Yellow Gates Zhào Yànshēn, Yáng Yīn, and others.
Gāo Yuè and the others rushed by carriage to the Gāoyáng Post Station.
The Emperor sent a message saying:
“I know the intentions of all you nobles,
but you do not need to come.”
Only Yáng Yīn was received;
Gāo Yuè and the others returned.
Since the Emperor felt that the sentiments of the populace were not yet harmonious,
and had previously received the Empress Dowager’s decree saying:
“Your father was like a dragon,
your brother was like a tiger,
yet they both ended their lives as ministers to others.
How dare you wish to carry out the affairs of Shùn and Yǔ (i.e., peaceful abdication)?
This is not even your own intention;
it is precisely Gāo Dézhèng instructing you.”
Furthermore, someone argued that in the past, King Wǔ of Zhōu rode twice to Méngjīn (before revolutionizing the government).
Only then did he change the mandate.
Consequently, he returned to Jìnyáng.
From then on, he was frequently unhappy.
Xú Zhīcái, Sòng Jǐngyè, and others repeatedly invoked divination, miscellaneous prognostications, and theories of Yin-Yang and cosmic measurement,
insisting that the time was surely the fifth month, corresponding to Heaven and according with the people.
Dézhèng also urged him ceaselessly.
The Emperor then reported that Wèi Shōu should be recalled.
When Shōu arrived,

he was ordered to compose the imperial edicts and documents regarding the abdication and concession, the Nine Awards (Jiǔ Xī), the establishment of the administrative court (jiàntái), and the memorial urging assumption of the throne.
the Emperor departed Jìnyáng.
Gāo Dézhèng again recorded various affairs and items that were in Yè and submitted them to the Emperor.
The Emperor ordered Chén Shāntí to ride post-haste, carrying the items concerning affairs along with a secret letter to Yáng Yīn.
The general instruction was to compose the ceremonial regulations (yízhù),
and to guard against and observe the various princes of the Wèi house.
Shāntí arrived in Yè in the fifth month.

Yáng Yīn immediately summoned the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng) Xíng Shào, Minister of the Army (Qībīng Shàngshū) Cuī Jì, Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū) Lù Cāo, Chief Steward (Zhānshì) Wáng Xīn, Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng) Yáng Xiūzhī, Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng) Péi Ràngzhī, and others to discuss and compose the ceremonial regulations.
On the sixth day,
they summoned the Grand Tutor of Wèi (Wèi Tàifù), Prince Tǎn of Xiányáng, and others to assemble generally.
They were ushered into the Northern Palace,
and detained in the East Retreat.
After the abdication was received,
they were then allowed to return to their residences.
When the Emperor first departed and reached a pavilion,
the horse he was riding suddenly stumbled and fell.
He considered this highly inauspicious,
and greatly hesitated.
Upon reaching the city of Píngchéng,
he subsequently refused to advance further.
Gāo Dézhèng and Xú Zhīcái urgently pleaded with the Emperor, saying:
"Shāntí went ahead first.
If news of this situation [is reported],
we fear it might leak out and prevent the outcome."
He immediately commanded Sīmǎ Zǐrú and Dù Bì to ride post-haste and enter subsequently,
to observe the general sentiment.
On the seventh day,
Zǐrú and the others arrived in Yè.
Since everyone felt the general situation was already decided,
no one dared to voice dissent.
On the eighth day,
Yáng Yīn wrote down the central instruction,
instructing Prince Xù of Xiāngchéng of Wèi
along with Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōng) Pān Xiànglè, Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Zhāng Liàng, and Palace Attendant (Huángmén) Zhào Yàn, to enter deeply and report on the affair.
Emperor Xiàojìng of Wèi was in the Zhāoyáng Hall,
and granted them an audience.
Xù said:
"The Five Phases follow their cycles,
having a beginning and an end.
The Prince of Qí possesses sagely virtue, respected and enlightened;
all directions submit and look up to him.
Your servants, risking death, present this to you,
wishing Your Majesty would emulate Yáo ceding power to Shùn."
The Emperor of Wèi immediately composed his face and said:
"This matter of ceding power has been promoted for a long time.
I will respectfully yield and step aside."
He continued:
"If so,
an Imperial Edict must be composed."
Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng) Cuī Jié reported:
"The edict has already been completed."
It was immediately handed to Yáng Yīn to present to Emperor Jìng of Wèi.
There were altogether more than ten clauses,
all written down.
Emperor Jìng of Wèi said:
"Where will I be settled,
and how shall I depart?"
Yáng Yīn replied:
"There is a separate residence within the Northern City.
The imperial chariot will be prepared again,
and you shall leave escorted by the usual guards."
Emperor Jìng of Wèi then descended from his throne,
went to the East Corridor,
and recited from memory the encomium in Fàn Wèizōng's Book of the Later Hàn (Hòuhàn Shū), saying:
"Xiàn was born at an unfortunate time;
his person was scattered amid the nation's distress.
Ending our four hundred years,
forever to be a noble guest of Yú."
The responsible officials promptly requested permission for his departure.
Emperor Jìng of Wèi said:
"Men think of their discarded hairpins and worn shoes.
I wish to bid farewell to the Six Palaces [my consorts].
Is that permitted?"
He then entered and took a final leave of the Empress, consorts, and subordinates.
None of them failed to weep and wipe away tears.
His consort, Madam Lǐ of Zhàoguó, recited from the poem of the Prince of Chénsī, saying:
"May the Prince cherish his noble body,
and both of us enjoy the time of yellowing hair [old age]."
Emperor Jìng of Wèi ascended the carriage and exited the Wànchūn Gate.
The Court Attendant (Zhícháng) Zhào Dàodé accompanied and served him inside the carriage.
All the officials bowed their farewells outside the gate.
He subsequently entered the Northern City and was lodged in Sīmǎ Zǐrú's southern residence.
The [new] Emperor arrived at the encampment south of the city.
On the day the abdication was received,
Gāo Dézhèng was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Soon after, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lántián.
In the seventh year [of the reign],
he was promoted to Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúyè),
concurrently holding the post of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
receiving the revenues of Bóhǎi Commandery.
Gāo Dézhèng and the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) Yáng Yīn managed the government affairs,
achieving many great benefits.
In the later years of Emperor Xiǎnzǔ’s reign,
he indulged in alcohol and heavy drinking,
acting unlawfully.
Gāo Dézhèng repeatedly offered loyal advice.
Later, the Emperor summoned Gāo Dézhèng to drink.
Dézhèng refused.
He again presented words before the Emperor,
remonstrating:
"Your Majesty claims you will soon stop,
yet now it is worse than before.
What will become of the altars of the soil and grain [the state],
and what of the Empress Dowager!"
The Emperor was displeased,
and told his attendants:
"Gāo Dézhèng oppresses people with his spirit."
Gāo Dézhèng was greatly afraid,
so he claimed illness and confined himself to a Buddhist temple,
also studying meditation (zuòchán),
making a plan for retirement.
The Emperor said to Yáng Yīn:
"I am greatly worried about Gāo Dézhèng.
How is his sickness?"
Yīn, noting that during the period of abdication
Gāo Dézhèng’s words had been profoundly sincere,
and had expressed full loyalty,
had always secretly resented him.
Therefore, he replied:
"If Your Majesty appoints him as the Governor of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu Cìshǐ),
his sickness will immediately cure itself."
The Emperor agreed to this.
Gāo Dézhèng saw the letter of appointment and rose [from his supposed sickbed].
The Emperor became greatly enraged,
summoned Gāo Dézhèng, and said to him:
"Hearing you are sick,
I will acupuncture you."
He personally used a knife to stab him;
blood flowed and drenched the ground.
He then ordered that he be dragged down,
and his toes be chopped off.
Liú Táozhī, holding the knife, dared not strike.
The Emperor stood up, approached the steps,
and severely reprimanded Táozhī, saying:
"Your head will drop to the ground right now!"
He then demanded a large sword and put it on himself,
intending to go down the steps.
Táozhī then chopped off three toes from Dézhèng's feet.
The Emperor's anger was not appeased.
He imprisoned Gāo Dézhèng outside the palace gate.
That night, the city gate was opened,
and he was sent back home by palanquin.
The next morning,
Gāo Dézhèng's wife brought out valuables filling four couches [mats],
intending to entrust them to someone.
The Emperor suddenly arrived at the residence,
saw this, and angrily said:
"My imperial treasury still does not possess these items!"
When questioned where they came from,
they were all bribes given by the various Yuán princes.
He was then dragged out and executed.
At that time, his wife came out to bow;
she was also executed,
along with his son, Libationer (Jìjiǔ) Bójīan.
After Gāo Dézhèng died,
Emperor Xiǎnzǔ said to his officials:
"Gāo Dézhèng always said that Hàn people should be employed
and Xiānbēi people dismissed.
This alone merits death.
Furthermore, he taught me to execute the various Yuán princes.
Now that I have killed him,
I am avenging the Yuán princes."
The Emperor later regretted the act,
and granted him the posthumous title of Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo).
His legitimate grandson Wángchén succeeded to the title.
Cuī Áng,
courtesy name Huáiyuǎn,
was a man from Ānpíng, Bólíng.
His grandfather was Tǐng,
the Governor of Yōuzhōu (Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ) during the Wèi dynasty.
Áng became an orphan at the age of seven.
His paternal uncle, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) Xiàofēn, once said to his confidants:
"This child will certainly achieve eminence;
he is the thousand-li colt of our family."
Áng was upright and honest by nature, lacking flamboyance,
profound, with strategic ambition,
and firm and difficult to sway.
In his youth, he enjoyed textual studies
and was quite adept at literary composition.
When Shìzōng broadly established his staff headquarters,
he introduced him as Secretary (Jìshì Cānjūn),
entrusting him with duties of close confidence.
When Shìzōng entered to assist in court affairs,
he summoned Áng to be the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of his establishment.
At that time, the relatives and clients of meritorious generals who were in the capital
were reckless and often acted improperly.
This was particularly severe in the households of Sūn Téng and Sīmǎ Zǐrú.
Áng received a secret order from Shìzōng
to control them strictly according to the law.
Before long,
the inner and outer administrations were orderly and solemn.
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng).
That same year,
he concurrently held the post of Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū).
A Vice Director concurrently holding the post of Minister (Shàngshū)
had not occurred in recent times.
Only Áng alone held the foremost position,
and the court and public honored him for it.
In the sixth year of Wǔdìng,
sweet dew (Gānlù) descended upon the palace,
and the civil and military officials together offered congratulations at Xiǎnyáng Diàn.
Wèi Dì asked the Excellency of the Affairs of the Secretariat (Púshè), Cuī Xiān, and the Minister (Shàngshū), Yáng Yīn, and others, saying:
"Regarding the auspicious sign of Gānlù since ancient times,
how often did it occur during the Hàn and Wèi Dynasties?
Let each of you speak about the locations where it previously descended
and the reasons (the moral transformation) that caused it to be manifested."
Next, he asked Áng.
Áng said:
"According to the Illustrated Records of Auspicious Signs (Fúruì Tú),
when a king's virtue reaches Heaven,
then Gānlù descends.
The gates of fortune and misfortune
are not governed solely by auspicious signs.
For example, when the mulberry tree transformed and the pheasant warned,
it truly initiated a restoration;
(when) a small bird carried a large one,
no blessings were heard to have resulted.
I only wish that Your Majesty, although successful, does not rest on success."
The Emperor lowered his gaze and said:
"Since I lack virtue,
how can I deserve this?"
When Qí accepted the abdication (Shòuchán),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Sǎnqí Chángshì),
concurrently serving as Minister of the Palace Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng) and Minister of the Great Granary (Dàsīnóng Qīng).
The responsibilities of these two ministries (sì)
were widely known to be complex and heavy,
but Áng managed and regulated them skillfully,
so that subordinates committed no fraud or deceit.
Whatever passed through his hands and eyes,
he ensured everything was done properly;
the court praised his utmost fairness.
He further presented a memorial listing three hundred and fourteen instances of unwarranted expenditure in the illicit markets.
An imperial edict was issued,
ordering that the matter be swiftly discussed and reported, based on his memorial.
That same year,
he discussed and established the founding rituals of the state with the Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàoshī), Xíng Shào,
and was consequently enfeoffed as the Baron (Nán) of Huáyáng.
Another edict commanded the revision of the statutes and ordinances,
and the modification of the rites and music.

Forty-three men, including the Excellency of the Affairs of the Secretariat of the Right (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè), Xuē Shú, were ordered to deliberate and finalize them in the Headquarters of the Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn Fǔ).
Furthermore, an imperial mandate (chì) was given to Áng, saying:
"If the officials do not comply and accept the revisions,
you may report the matter to me based on the facts."
Áng, upon receiving the mandate, smiled and said:
"This perfectly matches my lifelong wish."
Áng was always diligent and cautious.
After receiving the mandate,
he redoubled his self-exhortation and alertness.
He organized the statutes and sections,
correcting and comparing the additions and deletions between the present and the past, amounting to seven or eight tenths (seventy or eighty percent).
He was transferred to be Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng).
Áng’s inherent nature was pure and stern.
Whenever he saw those who defiled themselves with bribes,
he detested them as if they were enemies.
Because of this, his legal rulings were stringent and severe,
and public opinion did not concede that he was lenient or forgiving.
Xiǎnzǔ visited Dōngshān,
and all the officials attended the banquet
and ascended the Archery Hall (Shètáng).
The Emperor summoned Áng before the imperial seat
and addressed him, saying:
"Many of the old officials are leaving to serve in provinces (zhōu).
I wish to entrust you with central government positions.
I plan to appoint you as President (Lìng) or Excellency of the Affairs of the Secretariat (Púshè);
do not expect to be a Governor (Cìshǐ).
After you turn sixty, I will grant you your native province.
In the interim,
a governorship cannot be obtained."
Later, the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) and higher officials gathered at the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng).
The Emperor pointed to Áng, Wèi Jǐn, and Sīmǎ Zǐruì and said to the Heir Apparent:
"These are the pillars and rocks of the state.
You should remember them."
Not long after,
he again attended a banquet at Jīnfèng Tái.
The Emperor reviewed the various officials,
all of whom had committed faults or crimes.
When he came to Áng, he said:
"Cuī Áng is an upright minister,
Wèi Shōu is a talented scholar.
They are linked as wife’s brother and sister’s husband,
and both have refrained from offenses."
In the tenth year of Tiānbǎo,
when the Imperial Mandate (Cè) appointed Yí Tóng Yān Zǐxiàn,
all the hundred departments attended in rank.
Áng was among the assembled lines.
The Emperor specially summoned Áng to his presence
and said:
"After reflecting on all the officials capable of handling the governmental affairs of the Secretariat (shěngtà),
I look only to you."
That very day, he was appointed concurrently as the Excellency of the Affairs of the Secretariat of the Right (Yòu Púshè).
A few days later,
when Áng entered to report on affairs,
the Emperor said to the President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Yáng Yīn:
"The reason I did not appoint Cuī Áng to the full position yesterday
was that I said it was too soon,
and I wanted to make the appointment permanent (zhēn) next year.
Since he will be appointed to the full position eventually,
what difference does a slight delay make?
He can be appointed as the permanent Púshè now."
The next day,
he was officially appointed.
Yáng Yīn had long been resentful of Áng.
After Xiǎnzǔ died,
he consequently dismissed Áng from the position of Púshè
and made him Yí Tóng Sān Sī.
Later, he was stripped of his rank due to an offense
and died while holding the title of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Cíbù Shàngshū).
Áng possessed graceful bearing, talent, and insight,
and had long established a reputation for being firm, upright, and rigorously honest.
However, he liked to divine and gauge the superior's intentions,
inspiring the current ruler.
Sometimes he listed hidden personal failings and faults [of others],
and was deeply appreciated and rewarded by Xiǎnzǔ.
When the Emperor spoke in his favor and protected him,
no one was able to slander him.
Discussions on statutes and ordinances,
the secret prisons in the capital region,
and major affairs of the court were often entrusted to him.
He favored severity and fierceness,
and liked to administer whipping and flogging.
Even when the suffering was extreme in myriad ways,
he faced it calmly.
Formerly, Cuī Xiān and Jìshū had supported him closely,
and later Gāo Dézhèng became his maternal relative (or relative through his mother’s family).
He constantly relied on this backing,
and his demeanor was arrogant and self-important.
Because of this, he was not respected by the renowned scholars of the time.
His son, Yè, succeeded him.
Biography Twenty-three: Wáng Xīn (younger brother Xī).
Wáng Xīn,
courtesy name Yuánjǐng,
was a man from Jù in Běihǎi.
His sixth generation ancestor, Měng,
was Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) under Fú Jiān of Qín,
and settled his family in Fūchéng near Huàshān.
His father, Yún,
held a famous reputation while serving the Wèi court.
Xīn was devoted to learning and reading in his youth.
The Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Yuè, Prince of Rǔnán, appointed him as Cavalry Aide (Qìbīng Cānjūn).
According to old custom,
when the Prince went out to shoot,
attendants accompanied him, wearing military dress and carrying swords.
Xīn never followed the ranks.
Yuè enjoyed leisurely excursions,
sometimes riding swiftly for days (stopping overnight once or more).
Xīn would often abandon him and return.
Yuè then ordered him to ride his horse ahead
and personally whipped the horse on.
Xīn released the reins, bowed his hands high,
and allowed the horse to go where it willed.
Those around him remarked that he was arrogant and disrespectful.
Yuè said:
"The reputation of this Princely establishment depends only on this worthy man,
he must not be reproached."
Yuè often scattered copper coins on the ground,
ordering the aides to compete in picking them up,
but Xīn alone did not pick any up.
Yuè then scattered silver coins and signaled to Xīn with his eyes.
Xīn then took just one.
When Yuè was drinking with his aides,
he rose to move his own couch.
Everyone rushed forward to help,
but Xīn alone stood back, holding his court tablet (bǎn).
Yuè then changed his expression and said:
"I am the Emperor’s grandson, the Emperor’s son, the Emperor’s brother, and the Emperor’s uncle.
Now, during this joyous banquet,
I personally rise to move my seat.
Who are you,
that you alone stand stiffly aloof!"
Xīn replied:
"Yuánjǐng’s position and reputation are insignificant,
insufficient to cause Your Highness to look to him as a model of proper deportment.
How dare I, a high official of an Imperial Prince,
undertake the duties of a servant."
Yuè apologized to him.
Everyone seated there drank their fill cheerfully.
Xīn was the first to rise,
and went to sleep in a quiet room.
He was frequently summoned but did not return.
Yuè then personally went to him and called out, saying:
"To possess talent and yet disregard your superior
— can this be called benevolence (rén)?"
Xīn said:
"Shāng Xīn indulged in deep drunkenness,
and his downfall came suddenly.
Since the master of the residence disregards himself,
how dare this humble official bear the blame for it?"
Yuè laughed loudly and left.
He was repeatedly promoted until he became the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Dōnglái.
Later, Lǐ Shénjùn, the President of the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Shàngshū), submitted a memorial stating:
"Recently, due to many troubles,
the regular attendants (Chángshì) have had no set limit on personnel.
Now, we designate Wáng Yuánjǐng and others as Chángshì,
setting the limit at eight officials."
He was further granted the title of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
Emperor Wǔdì sometimes exposed his body,
and joked casually with his close ministers.
Whenever he saw Xīn,
he would immediately straighten his cap and adopt a serious expression.
Xīn was naturally very stout,
but after experiencing mourning,
he remained thin and emaciated for the rest of his life.
Yáng Yīn valued his virtue and achievements,
considering him a model teacher for others.
He was promoted to Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
When Xīn was young, he and Xíng Shào were both retainers of Yuán Luó.
When he governed Dōnglái,
Shào moved his entire household to join him there.
The people of the commandery, knowing Shào was the cousin of Xíng Gǎo,
gathered soldiers intending to arrest him.
Xīn shielded and concealed him with his own body,
shouting:
"If you want to seize Xíng Zǐcái,
you must kill me first."
Shào was thus spared.
Xīn habitually enjoyed refined conversation (qīngyán),
and his words were never shallow or vulgar.
While in Dōnglái,
he captured a man who had murdered his travel companion.
The accused was questioned but did not confess.
Xīn said to him:
"He died and did not return,
but you came back unharmed.
How do you explain yourself?"
Later, Xíng Shào saw Emperor Shìzōng,
and recounted this saying for amusement.
When Xīn heard of it,
he intentionally visited Shào and said:
"You do not understand the principles of creation (zàohuà)."
Returning home, he said to others:
"Zǐcái deserves to die.
My rebuke of him was profoundly harsh."
Xiǎnzǔ considered Xīn negligent and unconventional,
not the type required for administering the world.
He scolded him, saying:
"Good family background (Mén-hù),
bad person."
Furthermore, someone slandered him, saying:
"Wáng Yuánjǐng often laments that the Water Cycle (Shuǐyùn) should not have been utterly broken off."
The Emperor grew even angrier,
and issued an edict banishing him to Yōuzhōu.
Later he was recalled,
appointed Grand Master of Silver and Green Splendor (Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū),
and concurrently administered the affairs of the Board of Rites (Cíbù Shàngshū).
The Emperor was angry at Jī Yè, the Magistrate of Línzhāng, and Lǐ Wénshī, the Palace Gentleman (Shèrén).
He gave Yè as a slave to Xuē Fēngluò,
and Wénshī as a slave to Cuī Shìshùn.
Zhèng Zǐmò privately said to Xīn:
"Since ancient times, no court official has ever been made a slave."
Xīn replied:
"Jīzǐ became a slave for him (King Zhòu of Yīn).
Why do you say there are none?"
Zǐmò subsequently reported Xīn’s words to Xiǎnzǔ,
and added:
"Wáng Yuánjǐng compares Your Majesty to Yīn Zhòu."
Yáng Yīn subtly attempted to defend him.
The Emperor said to Yīn:
"Wáng Yuánjǐng is your teacher (bóshì).
All your words are taught by Yuánjǐng."
Later, the Emperor was heavily drinking with his court officials.
Xīn claimed illness and did not attend.
The Emperor sent cavalry to seize him.
When captured, he was found swaying his knees and reciting poetry.
He was then executed in the Emperor's presence,
and his body was thrown into the Zhāng River.
This was the tenth year of Tiānbǎo (559 CE).
He left a collection of twenty scrolls of writings.
His son was Wáng Yǐ.
Xīn's mother, Lady Cuī of Qīnghé,
possessed scholarship, knowledge, refinement, and instruction.
She bore nine sons,
all of whom were elegant and refined.
They were known collectively as the Nine Dragons of the Wáng Clan.
His younger brother was Wáng Xī,
courtesy name Shǔlǎng,
childhood name Shāmí.
As a child, he was filial and respectful.
He was broad, refined, and had great capacity (qìdù).
He loved learning tirelessly,
possessed a beautiful appearance,
and was principled.
Late in the Wèi dynasty,
he followed his mother and elder brothers eastward to the seashore,
where he associated with Xíng Zǐliáng.
Zǐliáng admired his purity and clarity,
and wrote to his two elder brothers, who were in Luò:
"Your virtuous younger brother, Míláng,
has profound and far-reaching consciousness,
is liberal and unrestrained,
avoids trivial details,
and his words always reach the core of reason.
His recitation of emotions and nature (qíngxìng)
is often exquisitely beautiful.
I fear you will soon find it difficult to maintain the role of elder brother,
so there is no need to worry about his lack of advancement."
Early in Wèi Yǒng'ān period,
his second elder brother, Wáng Huī, was sent as an envoy to Liáng.
Huī petitioned that Xī be released from common status and appointed Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary (Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng).
He was summoned and appointed Recorder (Gōngcáoshǐ) in the Residence of the Prince of Guǎngpíng who had established a secretariat (Kāifǔ).
Xī wished to care for his mother,
and ultimately did not accept the appointment.
After his mother passed away,
circumstances required him to move to Yè.
He traveled freely between Gǒng and Luò,
delighted by the mountains and waters.
He formed a fellowship and shared vows with Lú Yuánmíng of Fànyáng and Wèi Jìjǐng of Jùlù,
heading to Tiānlíng Mountain,
harboring a lofty ambition to spend the rest of his life there.
When Dúgū Xìn, a general of Western Wèi, entered Luò,
Xī was appointed Secretary (Jìshì) in Dúgū Xìn's Residence (Kāifǔ).
Xī claimed that he had previously been bitten by a dog,
and was severely ill and unable to rise.
An old acquaintance doubted that the injury was caused by rabies (zhì),
and wrote urging him to recover.
Xī replied by letter, saying:
"I am honored by your message of concern,
advising me to overcome my sickness.
Reviewing your kind words,
it seems you doubt that my injury was necessarily caused by rabies.
How could I wish for it to definitely be rabies?
It is simply that based on the principles, there is no room for doubt.
Even if you doubt it,
your argument is flawed.
Since you doubt it is rabies,
you should equally suspect that it *is* rabies.
The uncertainty is halved.
If one suspects it is rabies and treats it diligently,
even if it is not rabies, no harm is done;
if one suspects it is not rabies and does not treat it,
should it actually be rabies, it will be hard to save the person.
Therefore, excessive treatment leads to complete safety,
while excessive non-treatment may lead to death.
If Wáng Xī is not worth preserving,
then he is not worth appointing.
Since he has been appointed,
he must be worth preserving.
How can you deny him complete safety,
and allow him to possibly die?
Moreover, the General's (Dúgū Xìn's) prestige and virtue extend everywhere;
they surge like gales and settle like mist,
about to cover the entire world.
Why should he be concerned about just one humble official?
If he must start by following the example of Wěi (the story of appointing an inferior man first),
he should first save the lives of his people.
Why don't you gently speak on my behalf to the General?"
Only then was he granted reprieve.
Shortly thereafter, Xìn returned (to Western Wèi territory),
and Xī consequently returned to Yè.
Shénwǔ of Qí sought out loyal, filial, cautious, and secretive young men among the court families,
ordering them to associate with his sons.
Xī, along with Cuī Zhān of Qīnghé, Lǐ Dù of Dùnqīu, and Lú Zhèngtōng of Fànyáng, were the first selected for this purpose.
Wénxiāng was then General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn).
He held the hands of Xī and the others and said:
"My younger brothers are approaching adulthood,
their ambitions and knowledge are not yet settled.
Proximity to the good or familiarity with the wicked,
inevitably leads to change.
If my brothers are established (in virtue),
and do not betray righteous principles,
your rank and position shall always be second only to my brothers.
However, if you cause them to turn toward wickedness,
leading them into confusion and error,
the guilt will extend to your whole clan,
not just your own person."
Xī followed Shénwǔ to Jìnyáng,
and was appointed Recorder (Gōngcáo Cānjūn) in the Central and Outer Secretariat (Zhōngwàifǔ), concurrently serving as the Aide to the Administrator (Gōngyǒuhu) of Chángshān.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo [period] of Qí,
he acted as Prefect of Tàiyuán Commandery.
When Wénxuān became dissolute and negligent,
the Prince of Chángshān frequently remonstrated,
and the Emperor suspected that the Prince was borrowing words from Xī
and wished to impose a heavy penalty.
The Prince privately said to Xī:
“Doctor [Bóshì],
tomorrow I must contrive a matter;
this is intended to save your life,
and also to secure my own survival.
You must understand this deeply and not be surprised.”
Thereupon, in the presence of the crowd, he had Xī beaten twenty strokes with the rod.
The Emperor soon erupted in anger,
but hearing that Xī had been beaten,
he therefore did not kill him,
but had him shaved, shackled, and assigned to Jiǎfāng [the armorers’ workshop].
After residing there for three years,
the Prince again vehemently remonstrated and argued,
and was severely driven away and flogged,
closing his mouth and refusing to eat.
The Empress Dowager was extremely worried about this.
The Emperor said to his attendants:
“If the little child dies,
what shall I do about my old mother?”
Therefore, every time he asked about the Prince’s illness,
he would say:
“Exert yourself and force yourself to eat;
I will restore Wáng Xī to you.”
Thereupon, he released Xī and ordered him to go.
The Prince embraced Xī and said:
“My vital energy is failing,
I fear we will never see each other again.”
Xī wept and said:
“The Way of Heaven is divine and bright;
how could it let Your Highness perish in this chamber?
The Supreme Sovereign is personally a brother to man,
and honored as a Lord of men;
how can one contend and calculate with him?
If Your Highness does not eat,
the Empress Dowager also will not eat.
Even if Your Highness does not value himself,
does he not value the Empress Dowager?”
Before his words were finished,
the Prince forced himself to sit up and eat.
Xī was thus able to escape penal servitude [tú],
and returned to be the Prince’s Friend [Wáng Yǒu].
The Prince again administered the affairs of the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Shì].
New officials who had been appointed necessarily visited the Prince to express gratitude for their positions,
and would take leave when departing.
Xī spoke to the Prince, saying:
“Receiving rank at the Heavenly Court,
but performing rites of gratitude at a private residence,
has been regarded since ancient times as transgressing the fundamental principles.
The civil and military officials of the court,
coming and going to express thanks and take leave,
should all be curtailed and stopped.
The Sovereign looks forward eagerly,
relying on Your Highness’s assistance and support.”
The Prince accepted this.
He often spoke casually to Xī, saying:
“The Sovereign’s daily life is not proper.
You have everything in your ears and eyes.
How can I, merely because I previously encountered one fit of anger,
remain tongue-tied like that?
You should draft a remonstrance for me,
and I shall watch for an opportunity to remonstrate fully.”
Xī then listed more than ten items and presented them.
He spoke with urgent remonstrance to the Prince, saying:
“If the court is like this now,
and you wish to emulate Jiè Zǐ, a mere commoner who lightly regarded the commands of the court,
the mad drug makes people lose self-awareness,
and how could knives and arrows recognize kinship or distance?
If disaster suddenly strikes contrary to reason,
what will become of Your Highness’s family inheritance,
and what will become of the Empress Dowager?
I beg you to comply temporarily,
and be more cautious day by day.”
The Prince sighed and could not control himself,
saying:
“Has it come to this?”
The next day, he saw Xī and said:
“I have contemplated deeply all night long.
I will stop this intention now.”
He immediately ordered a fire and burned the draft in front of Xī.
Later, the Prince took advantage of an interval to remonstrate bitterly,
and consequently offended the imperial intention.
The Emperor ordered strongmen to pinion his arms behind his back,
pulled out a bright blade and pointed it at his neck,
and cursed, saying:
“What does a young child know?
You try to criticize me with the talent of a mere official.
Who taught you this?”
The Prince said:
“The whole world is keeping silent;
besides your servant, who dares to speak?”
The Emperor hurried them to apply the rod and the whip,
and he was lashed dozens of times with disorderly strokes.
It happened that the Emperor then fell into a drunken sleep, and the Prince was able to be released.
Thereafter, the familiarity and debauchery [of the Emperor]
extended throughout the imperial clan,
and wherever he went, he would linger,
turning day into night.
Only the residence of Chángshān mostly avoided his presence.
When the Emperor died,
Jìnán succeeded to the throne.
The Prince said to Xī:
“With one person ruling by folding his arms,
we too can preserve our ease and leisure.”
He then spoke of the court being lenient, benevolent, compassionate, and forgiving—
truly a good ruler who maintains tradition.
Xī said:
“During the Tiānbǎo [reign],
the Eastern Palace entrusted everything to a single Hú person.
Now he has suddenly taken charge of ten thousand affairs [of state],
managing the valiant and outstanding figures.
If the sacred virtue is still young,
and not yet capable of handling many difficulties,
and he allows people of other surnames to issue and receive edicts,
power must inevitably converge somewhere.
Even if Your Highness wishes to maintain his princely post,
can he succeed?
Supposing he is allowed to achieve tranquility and withdrawal,
does he think his family fortune can be preserved forever?”
The Prince pondered in silence,
and after a long time said:
“What should I do?”
Xī said:
“The Duke of Zhōu embraced King Chéng and ruled over the feudal lords,
acting as regent for seven years,
and then restored the clear ruler [King Chéng].
Fortunately, there is a historical precedent.
Your Highness should consider it.”
The Prince said:
“How dare I compare myself to the Duke of Zhōu?”
Xī said:
“Given Your Highness’s current status and reputation,
can you avoid the comparison to the Duke of Zhōu?”
The Prince did not reply.
When the Emperor was about to set out,
he commanded the Prince to follow the imperial carriage,
and appointed Xī as Administrator [Zhǎngshǐ] of Bīngzhōu.
Yè,
he executed Yáng, Yān, and others.
An edict appointed the Prince as Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng) and Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì),
supervising both civil and military officials. When he returned to
Bīng,
he invited Xī and said:
"Had I not adopted your counsel earlier,
allowing lesser men to manipulate power,
I would have almost reached utter ruin.
Although the area around the ruler is now temporarily purified,
how ultimately should I be situated?"
Xī replied:
"If His Highness held the position he had previously,
it would still be possible to determine his situation according to moral teachings (míngjiào).
Given the current state of affairs and momentum,
it now hinges upon heavenly timing,
and is no longer something achievable by human effort."
A short time later,
he memorialized that Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì should be made Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ),
and Xī should be made Sīmǎ (Military Advisor/Marshal).
Every night, he would take Xī in his carriage,
but during the day, he would not speak with him.
This was because Xī was known for his scholarly deliberation (rúhuǎn),
and he feared that this would not please the military generals.
Later, he brought Xī into a private room and said:
"Lately, the various princes, marquises, and nobles have repeatedly pressured me,
claiming that I have violated Heaven and brought ill fortune.
I fear that a change or revolt might suddenly arise,
and I truly wish to restrain them with the law."
Xī replied:
"The Imperial Court has recently distanced itself from relatives;
it should instead consider the importance of blood ties.
The actions taken by His Highness in haste,
are no longer those of a subject.
With prickles on the back,
spears crossed at the neck,
and suspicion between the high and the low,
how can this possibly last long?
Moreover, the Way of Heaven is not fixed;
decline and fulfillment alternate.
The subtle workings of the spirits change,
and omens naturally assemble.
Although you maintain humility and self-restraint,
treating the sacred implements of power as chaff,
this is precisely violating the will of the Highest Heaven,
and destroying the foundation laid by the former Emperor."
The Prince said:
"How dare you utter inappropriate words?
I must subject you to the law."
Xī replied:
"I humbly believe that heavenly timing and human affairs
should be one, without differing plans.
Therefore, I risked offending your thunderous majesty,
and did not fear the executioner's axes.
That I am able today to lay bare my heart,
is also because the spirits have favored it."
The Prince said:
"To relieve difficulty and restore assistance,
one should await the sage and the wise.
How dare I discuss this privately?
Please do not speak further."
Shortly thereafter, an edict stated that since the Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng's) responsibilities were heavy,
all officials in the Chancellor's staff would universally be promoted one rank.
Xī, as Sīmǎ, was appointed to serve concurrently as Director of the Personnel Bureau (Lìbù Lángzhōng).
Lù Yǎo, the Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng's) Attendant Official (Cóngshì Zhōngláng), was about to depart on a mission.
Grasping Xī's hand upon departure, he said:
"The accomplishments of the Chancellor Prince (Xiàng Wáng) have reached every corner of the realm,
and the world gladly supports him.
Songs and ballads fill the roads,
and no one entertains dissenting wishes.
Yǎo and others wished to reveal their true hearts, but suddenly received an external mission;
thus, there is no way to fully present my humble sincerity in person.
I reverently submit this small thought."
Xī soon reported Yǎo's words.
The Prince said:
"If everyone, both internal and external, shares this differing expectation,
Zhào Yànshēn is by my side morning and evening,
why has he made no mention of it at all?
You should try to speak with him secretly according to your own view."
Xī asked Yànshēn when there was a break in official duties.
Yànshēn said:
"I, too, have recently been alarmed by these songs and rumors.
Every time I wanted to present the matter,
my mouth would freeze and my heart would tremble.
Since you have raised the discussion,
I, too, shall risk death to lay bare my heart."
Thus, he joined in the persuasion.
At this time, all the princes, dukes, generals, military commanders, and regional governors memorialized, presenting signs of divine mandate (fú mìng).
In the eighth month of the first year of Qiánmíng,
Emperor Zhāo ascended the throne.
An edict addressed Xī, saying:
"Why do you treat yourself like an outside visitor,
and rarely make yourself seen?
From now on, even if it is not related to your bureau's duties,
if you have anything on your mind,
write a memorandum as appropriate,
and submit it directly whenever there is a small opportunity."
Consequently, he commanded the Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū) Yáng Xiūzhī, the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Qīng) Cuī Jié, and one other person,
that every day, after finishing their primary duties,
they should all enter the East Corridor,

and together record and deliberate upon the ritual and music that previous dynasties had abolished or abandoned, the establishment or dissolution of official posts, similarities and differences in court banquets, and increases or decreases in carriages and clothing.
Or, regarding those whose virtue and excellence were superior,
but who had long remained in obscurity;
or those who used clever words to deceive the populace,
and whose wicked influence harmed governance;

as well as matters concerning fields, markets, boats, and carriages, the flow and obstruction of taxes and levies, the prescribed forms for marriage and burial rituals, and the mourning grades (zīcuī) for nobles and commoners;
or matters inconvenient for the current time but which have been continuously practiced from antiquity;
or matters that have been beneficial since antiquity but are currently discarded: all these should be thoroughly considered,
and memorialized gradually in sequence.
Do not wait until all is fully prepared;
whenever something is recalled, continue to report it.
They were provided with imperial meals morning and evening,
and were permitted to return after sunset.
At that time, the various officials requested the establishment of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng, i.e., the Heir Apparent).
An imperial command had not yet granted this.
He constantly ordered Xī to go to the Eastern Hall (Dōng Táng) to supervise the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ's) caps and robes,
guiding him in mannerisms and salutations.
Xī was made Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tài Fù).
Xī, through his bureau's duties, presented the seals and ribbons.
When the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) performed the Shìdiàn ceremony,
Xī also concurrently served as Palace Gentleman (Zhōng Shùzǐ).
The Emperor said to him:
"Now that you occupy such crucial posts,
you cannot treat things with casual ease."
When the Emperor was about to launch a northern campaign,
he commanded Xī to ask what rumors had been heard outside recently.
Xī replied:
"Word is circulating on the roads
that the Imperial Carriage is about to depart."
The Emperor said:
"The Kùmò Xī have invaded the south.
I have not yet personally led an army,
so I merely wish to practice military skills through this."
Xī said:
"If the Imperial Carriage is making a tour of inspection,
that would perhaps be permissible.
But if you readily deploy it for minor tasks,
I fear the people will be disappointed."
The Emperor said:
"This is the usual concern of the fainthearted.
I will certainly deliberate on the matter when the time comes."
The Emperor employed Guard Commander Péi Zé and Chief Scribe Cài Huī to observe and investigate all subordinates.
They were fond of falsely accusing others,
and the court officials referred to them as Péi and Cài.
At that time, the two reported that after the Imperial Carriage set out for the northern campaign,
people were saying that Yáng Xiūzhī and Wáng Xī frequently joined others for entertainment and banquets,
and did not hold public affairs to heart.
The Emperor had Xiūzhī and Xī beaten forty times on the shins.
The Emperor executed a man in his presence,
and asked Xī,
saying: "Does this man deserve death?"
Xī replied:
"His crime truly deserves death,
but I regret that he did not die in the proper place.
Your servant has heard that punishments should be executed in the marketplace,
and that the body should be abandoned for the populace to see.
The palace hall is not the location for killing."
The Emperor changed his expression and said:
"From now on, I shall change this practice for the sake of the princes and dukes."
The Emperor wished to make Xī (晞) a Shìzhōng (侍中),
but he desperately declined and did not accept.
Some advised Xī (晞) not to distance himself.
Xī (晞) said:
“Since I was young,
I have observed many important people.
Those who bent and straightened for a short time
rarely avoided defeat.
Moreover, my nature is genuinely relaxed and slow-paced;
I am incapable of handling the demands of the time.
How can the private favor of the ruler
be guaranteed?
If it were one day to be exposed or spread widely,
I would have nowhere to retreat to.
It is not that I do not love holding a 'hot official position,'
but I have thought it through completely.”
The officials were once awarded a feast where archery was practiced.
Xī (晞) hit the target,
and should have received silk,
but because he failed to mark his arrow,
the official in charge did not grant it.
Xī (晞) said jovially:
“Now I can truly be called sufficient in military skill (wǔ, 武) but lacking in refinement (wén, 文).”
Xī (晞) had no son.
The Emperor intended to bestow a concubine upon him
and sent a minor court attendant (xiǎohuángmén, 小黃門) to his residence to announce the decree.
The Empress (Hòugōng, 皇后) also sent a message to Xī (晞)'s wife.
Xī (晞) instructed his wife to reply,
but his wife absolutely refused to speak.
Xī (晞) struck his chest with his hand and withdrew.
When the Emperor heard this, he laughed.
When Xiàozhāo (孝昭) died,
Xī (晞)'s mourning and sorrow almost overcame him,
and he subsequently became thin and weak.
Wǔchéng (武成) originally resented his Confucian slowness,
and due to this, he disliked him even more.
He was once severely reproached and scolded during a presentation of reports,
yet his dignified demeanor remained calm and peaceful.
He successively served as Cìshǐ (刺史) of Dōngxú Zhōu (東徐州) and Mìshū Jiān (祕書監).
In the beginning of Wǔpíng (武平) era,
he was promoted to Dàhónglú (大鴻臚),
awarded the rank of Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司),
supervised the compilation of the records of court life (Qǐjū Zhù, 起居注),
and was retained as a scholar (dài zhào, 待詔) in the Wénlín Guǎn (文林館).
His nature was tranquil, indifferent, and moderate in desires.
Although royal affairs kept him extremely busy,
his dignified conduct never shifted.
When he was in Bīng Zhōu (幷州),
even when warhorses filled the lanes,
he never considered worldly matters to be a burden.
During pleasant seasons and beautiful scenery,
he would whistle, recite poetry, and roam,
climbing mountains and overlooking waters,
making conversation and feasting his main business.
Scholars called him “The Sīmǎ (司馬) Beyond the World.”
He once visited Jìn Cí (晉祠)
and composed a poem, saying:
“The sun sets, and I ought to return,
