but the fish and birds seem to keep me lingering.”
Suddenly, an envoy from the Prince of Xiāng (相王) arrived,
summoning Xī (晞), but he did not arrive immediately.
The next day, Lú Sīdào (盧思道), the Jìjiǔ (祭酒) of the Chancellor's Western Pavilion (Chéngxiàng Xī Gé, 丞相西閤), said to Xī (晞):
“Yesterday you were summoned when you were already flushed with drink;
were you not faulted because of the fish and birds?”
Xī (晞) smiled slowly and said:
“Last night I was indeed jovial
and was slightly chastised because of the wine.
You gentlemen are also among the things that keep me lingering;
why limit it merely to the fish and birds?”
When Jìnyáng (晉陽) was conquered and defeated,
he fled northeast with his companions, avoiding the Zhōu (周) forces.
The mountain road was perilous and remote,
and they feared encountering local bandits.
Yet Xī (晞) warmed wine and took tonics
without ever pausing even once.
He was constantly unwilling to leave,
which his traveling companions found fault with.
Xī (晞) said:
“Do not find fault with me.
If I had not regretted the way I handled affairs,
I would have long ago become one of the Three Dukes (Sāgōng, 三公).”
When Qí (齊) fell,
Emperor Wǔ (武) of Zhōu (周) appointed Xī (晞) as Yítóng Dàjiàngjūn (儀同大將軍) and Tàizǐ Jiànyì Dàfū (太子諫議大夫).
In the first year of the Kāihuáng (開皇) era of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
he died in Luòyáng (洛陽),
at the age of seventy-one.
He was posthumously granted Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) and Cáo Zhōu Cìshǐ (曹州刺史).
Biographies, Chapter 24: Lù Făhé (陸法和), Wáng Lín (王琳)
Lù Făhé (陸法和),
it is unknown where he was from.
He lived in seclusion on Bǎilǐ Zhōu (百里洲) in Jiānglíng (江陵).
His clothing, food, and dwelling
were exactly the same as those of an ascetic Śramaṇa (shāmén, 沙門).
The elders who had seen him since their youth
said his appearance was always changing,
and people were unable to fathom him.
Some said he came from Sōnggāo (嵩高)
and had traveled widely across near and far lands.
When he entered Zǐshí Shān (紫石山) in Gāo'ān Xiàn (高安縣), Wènyáng Jùn (汶陽郡) of Jīng Zhōu (荊州),
he inexplicably abandoned the mountain dwelling where he lived.
Shortly after, there was the turmoil caused by the barbarian bandit Wén Dàoqī (文道期).
People at the time believed he had foreseen the emerging signs.
When Hóu Jǐng (侯景) first announced his surrender to Liáng (梁),
Făhé (法和) said to Zhū Yuányīng (朱元英) of Nán Jùn (南郡):
“The poor Daoist (píndào, 貧道) will go with you, benefactor (tán yuè, 檀越), to strike Hóu Jǐng (侯景).”
Yuányīng (元英) said:
“Hóu Jǐng (侯景) is rendering service to the state.
Why does the master (shī, 師) say we should strike him?”
Făhé (法和) replied:
“It is simply so.”
When Jǐng (景) crossed the Yangzi River,
Făhé (法和) was then in Qīngxī Shān (青谿山).
Yuányīng (元英) went and asked him:
“Jǐng (景) is now besieging the capital city.
What is the outcome of this affair?”
Făhé (法和) said:
“When ordinary men gather fruit,
they should wait until it is ripe.
It will fall without being plucked.
Benefactor, just wait for Hóu Jǐng (侯景) to ripen,
why bother asking?”
When pressed to ask further,
he then said:
“He will both conquer and not conquer.”
Jǐng (景) sent his general Rèn Yuē (任約) to attack the Prince of Xiāngdōng (湘東王) of Liáng (梁) at Jiānglíng (江陵).
Făhé (法和) then went to Xiāngdōng (湘東) to request permission to march against Yuē (約).
He summoned eight hundred Mán (蠻) disciples to the riverside at Jiāng Jīn (江津).
They departed two days later.
Xiāngdōng (湘東) sent the monk Hú Sēngyòu (胡僧祐) leading over a thousand men to travel with them.
Făhé (法和) boarded the ship and laughed loudly, saying:
“Innumerable soldiers!”
Jiānglíng (江陵) had many spirit shrines
where the populace prayed.
But since Făhé (法和)’s army marched out,
not one prayer was made anymore,
which people believed was because all the spirits had followed him.
They reached Chìshā Hú (赤沙湖)
and faced Yuē (約).
Făhé (法和) rode a light boat,
unarmored,
and drifted down the current.
He turned back only when he was about one *lǐ* (里) away from Yuē (約)’s army.
He said to his officers and soldiers:
“I merely observed that their dragon is asleep and immobile.
The dragon of our army is extremely vibrant and leaping.
Attack them immediately.
If we could wait until tomorrow,
we would defeat the bandits without losing a single person from either side,
but there is a negative aspect to that.”
Thereupon, he released fire rafts ahead of them,
but the unfavorable headwind made it difficult.
Făhé (法和) held a white feather fan and waved it towards the wind,
and the direction of the wind immediately reversed.
Yuē (約)’s troops all saw the Liáng (梁) soldiers walking upon the water.
Thereupon, they suffered a great collapse
and all threw themselves into the water and drowned.
Yuē (約) fled and hid, and his whereabouts were unknown.
Făhé (法和) said:
“We will catch him tomorrow at noon.”
When the appointed time came, he was still not caught.
People asked him,
and Făhé (法和) said:
“Before, when the water of this islet was dry, I erected a stūpa (chà, 剎) here.
I told you benefactors
that although this is a stūpa,
it is actually a marker for the bandit.
Why are you not searching for the bandit beneath the marker?”
Following his words,
they indeed saw Yuē (約) in the water, clinging to the stūpa,
with his head tilted back so only his nose was above the surface.
They captured him immediately.
Yuē (約) requested to die right before the master (shī, 師).
Făhé (法和) said:
“Benefactor, you have the physiognomy of a leader;
you will certainly not die by military means.
Furthermore, you have a connection with the Prince (Wáng, 王).
There is absolutely no need for other worries.
The Prince will later rely on your strength.”
Xiāngdōng (湘東) did indeed release and employ him as a Jùnshǒu (郡守).
When Wèi (魏) besieged Jiānglíng (江陵),
Yuē (約) led troops to reinforce the defense
and fought bravely.
Fǎhé, having already arranged the truce,
went to present himself before Wáng Sēngbiàn at Bālíng,
and said:
“This humble monk has already severed Hóu Jǐng’s arm;
what more can he accomplish?
Patron (Tányuè), you should proceed and seize him immediately.”
He then requested permission to return,
and said to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng):
“Hóu Jǐng will naturally be pacified,
there is nothing to worry about.
The Shǔ bandits are about to arrive,
Fǎhé requests permission to guard Wū Xiá (Wū Gorge) and await them.”
He then gathered all the armies and went there,
personally carrying stones to fill the river.
After three days,
the water subsequently divided its flow,
and he barred it with iron chains.
Prince Jì of Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng Wáng Jì) indeed sent Shǔ soldiers to cross,
but the force at the mouth of the gorge was constricted,
making advance or retreat impossible.
Wáng Lín and Fǎhé planned the operation,
and annihilated them in a single battle.
The army arrived at Báidì,
and he said to the people:
“Zhūgě Kǒngmíng can truly be called a famous general,
I see evidence of it myself.
Near this city, he buried about a *hú* (bushel) of crossbow bolts and arrowheads.”
He then planted a marker and ordered them to dig,
and it was as he had said.
He also once went to a large tree north of the city wall of Xiāngyáng,
drew a square area two *chǐ* (feet) in size on the ground,
and ordered his disciples to dig it up.
They found a turtle,
a foot and a half long.
He tapped it with his staff and said:
“You wished to emerge but could not,
having been here for hundreds of years.
If you had not met me,
how could you ever have seen the light of day?”
He administered the Three Refuges to it,
and the turtle then entered the grass.
Originally, Bādié Shān (Bādié Mountain) had many people suffering from severe illnesses.
Fǎhé gathered herbs and treated them;
they were all cured in no more than three doses,
and immediately sought to become his disciples.
As for the poisonous insects and fierce beasts of the mountain,
Fǎhé taught them precepts of restraint,
and they no longer bit or stung people.
Wherever he stayed near rivers or lakes,
he would always erect a marker on the side of a peak,
saying,
“Release life here.”
Fishermen would catch nothing;
if they did manage a small catch,
a great storm and thunder would immediately arise.
The boatmen, fearing this, would release the catch,
and the wind and rain would then subside.
Even later, when he commanded troops,
he still forbade the armies from fishing or hunting.
If anyone secretly violated this,
a fierce beast would inevitably come in the middle of the night attempting to devour them,
or their boat cables would be lost.
There was a young disciple who playfully cut off a snake’s head,
and came to Fǎhé.
Fǎhé said:
“Why did you intend to kill the snake?”
He then pointed it out and showed him,
and the disciple saw the snake's head still hanging from his trousers’ crotch without falling off.
Fǎhé made him repent,
and perform meritorious deeds for the snake.
Furthermore, there was a man who tested a knife on an ox,
and its head was severed in one blow.
He came to Fǎhé.
Fǎhé said:
“A decapitated ox
is urgently demanding your life;
if you do not perform meritorious deeds for it,
retribution will arrive within one month.”
The man did not believe it,
and indeed died shortly thereafter.
Fǎhé also planned residences and plotted tombs for people,
in order to avoid disaster and seek fortune.
He once said to a man:
“Do not tie your horse to a mortar (for pounding grain).”
That man was traveling through a village area,
and there was a mortar next to the gate.
He thus tied his horse to its post.
Having entered the gate,
he remembered Fǎhé’s warning,
and ran out intending to untie it,
but the horse was already dead.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng (Liáng Yuándì) appointed Fǎhé as Grand Commander (Dūdu) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐng Province (Yǐngzhōu),
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Jiāngchéng County (Jiāngchéng Xiàn Gōng).
Fǎhé did not refer to himself as a subject;
in his formal memorials, where his name was stamped with the vermillion seal,
he referred to himself as Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
Emperor Yuán of Liáng said to his Minister Wáng Bāo:
“I never intended to appoint Lù (Fǎhé's secular surname) as one of the Three Dukes,
so why does he name himself so?”
Wáng Bāo replied:
“Since he attributes his life to spiritual arts,
it is possible this is premonition.”
As Fǎhé’s achievements and merit gradually became weighty,
Emperor Yuán of Liáng subsequently promoted him to Sītú,
while his positions as Dūdu and Cìshǐ remained unchanged.
His subordinate troops numbered several thousand men,
who were universally referred to as his disciples.
He governed purely through spiritual arts and moral transformation,
and did not subject people to the law and prisons.
Furthermore, within the markets,
he did not establish the system of market administrators or auxiliary officials.
There was no one to collect fees;
only an empty box with a lock was placed on the road,
with a single hole opened at the top to receive money.
Merchants and shopkeepers, based on the quantity of their goods,
calculated the assessed limit (tax rate),
and voluntarily deposited it inside the box.
The officials in charge of circulation
would only open and collect it in the evening,
itemize the contents of the holes (accounts),
and submit them to the treasury.
Furthermore, Fǎhé usually spoke little,
but when he did discuss something,
his eloquence was unmatched,
though he retained a southern accent.
He was skilled at constructing siege weapons and instruments of war.
When he was in Jiāngxià,
he amassed large numbers of troops and ships,
intending to attack Xiāngyáng and enter Wǔguān.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng sent a messenger to stop him.
Fǎhé said:
“Fǎhé is a seeker of the Buddha;
I do not even yearn for the seat of Śakra or Brahmā Devarāja,
how could I scheme for the royal throne?
It is only that I have a spiritual bond of incense and fire (karma) with the Emperor from the time of the Buddha Kōngwáng,
and I saw that retribution was due to reach the Emperor,
which is why I sought to intervene.
Now that I have been suspected,
this determined karma cannot be altered.”
Thereupon he prepared a ceremonial meal,
including large *shǎn* (meat offerings) and flatbreads.
When Wèi raised troops,
Fǎhé moved from Yǐng to Hànkǒu,
intending to rush to Jiānglíng.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng sent someone to intercept him, saying:
“I can break the rebels myself.
Just defend Yǐngzhōu,
there is no need to move.”
Fǎhé then returned to the province,
whitewashed the city gates,
put on a rough white cotton shirt, cotton trousers, and a coarse turban,
bound his waist with a thick rope,
and sat upon a rush mat.
He did not take these clothes off until the end of the day.
When he heard of the defeat and destruction of Emperor Yuán of Liáng,
he again donned the aforementioned mourning attire,
wept, and received condolences.
People from Liáng who entered Wèi territory
later indeed saw the *shǎn* (meat) and flatbreads.
Fǎhé first constructed Shòuwáng Sì (Shòuwáng Temple) on Bǎilǐ Zhōu (Bǎilǐ Isle).
After erecting the main Buddha hall,
he intentionally shortened the pillars and beams,
saying:
“In about forty years, the Buddhist faith will encounter disaster by thunder and lightning (persecution).
This temple is secluded and remote,
so it can escape the calamity.”
When Wèi pacified Jīngzhōu (Jīng Province),
and the palaces and homes were burned to ashes,
the Governor-General (Zǒngguǎn) wished to dismantle and take the materials of the Shòuwáng Buddha Hall,
but disliked its short timbers,
and therefore stopped.
Later, when the Zhōu regime (Zhōu Shì) suppressed the Buddhist faith,
this temple was isolated within Chén territory (Chén Jìng),
and thus did not suffer the calamity.
In the spring of the sixth year of Tiānbǎo,
the Prince of Qīnghé, Yuè, advanced his forces to Línjiāng.
Fǎhé surrendered the entire prefecture to Qí.

Wénxuān appointed Fǎhé as Grand Commander of Military Affairs in Ten Prefectures (Dà Dūdū Shí Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Gōng), and Grand Administrator of the Southwest Circuit (Xīnán Dào Dà Xíngtái).

Sòng Lì, who was Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū), Military Affairs in Five Prefectures (Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), Governor of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ), and Duke of Ānxiāng Commandery (Ānxiāng Jùn Gōng), was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu (Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Their official ranks and titles remained as before.

Lì’s younger brother, Zào, was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì), Acting of the Third Rank (Yí Tóng Sānsī), Governor of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ), and Duke of Yìxīng County (Yìxīng Xiàn Gōng).
The Liáng general Hóu Tiàn came and pressed upon Jiāngxià.
The Qí army abandoned the city and retreated.
Fǎhé and the Sòng Lì brothers entered court.
Wénxuān, hearing of his strange arts,
received him with an open mind.
He prepared the official escort paraphernalia (lǔbù) of the Three Dukes (Sāngōng),
setting up tents twelve *lǐ* south of the capital city to await him.
Fǎhé, seeing Yèchéng from afar,
dismounted and performed the Yǔ Pace (Yǔ Bù).
Xīn Shù said to him:
“Since you, Sir, have come from ten thousand *lǐ* to show your sincerity,
and the sovereign awaits you with an open mind, why do you perform this art?”
Fǎhé, holding an incense burner in hand,
walked behind the state carriage (lùchē)
until they reached the residence.
The next day he was granted an audience.
He was given a netted carriage with covered sides (tōng xiǎn yóu luò wǎng chē)
and a retinue of one hundred guards.
When approaching the palace gate (què), he announced his name,
but did not state his official rank,
nor did he call himself a subject.
He merely said he was the Recluse of Jīngshān (Jīngshān Jūshì).
Wénxuān feasted Fǎhé and his followers in the Zhāoyáng Hall.
Fǎhé was gifted a million coins, a thousand lengths of silk goods, a first-class mansion, a hundred *qǐng* of land, two hundred slaves, and living assets and household goods to match this.
Sòng Lì received a thousand lengths of silk goods.
The rest, from those with Acting of the Third Rank down to the Governors, received gifts according to their respective ranks.
The slaves Fǎhé received,
he freed them all,
saying:
“Each of you may follow your karma (yuán) and go.”
The money and silks he distributed as charity,
and they were gone in a single day.
He used the residence bestowed by the court to build a Buddhist temple.
He himself lived in a single room,
no different from an ordinary person.
Within three years he was twice appointed Grand Commandant,
but people of the time still referred to him as the Recluse.
Without being ill, he announced his date of death to his disciples.
When the time arrived,
he burned incense and paid respect to the Buddha,
and died seated on a rope bed.
After bathing, when they were about to shroud the body,
the corpse was small,
having shrunk to only about three *chǐ*.
Wénxuān ordered the coffin opened to inspect it.
It was empty.
Fǎhé had written on the wall of his residence and covered it up.
When the plaster peeled off,
there was an inscription which read:
“A Son of Heaven for ten years is still acceptable;
A Son of Heaven for a hundred days is quick like fire;
Sons of Heaven for a full year succeed each other in sitting [on the throne].”
It also said:
“One mother gives birth to three heavens;
two heavens together total five years.”
Commentators believe this refers to Empress Dowager Lóu giving birth to three Sons of Heaven.
From the enthronement of Emperor Xiàozhāo,
until Emperor Wǔchéng passed the throne to the Later Lord,
it totaled five years.
When Fǎhé was in Jīng and Yǐng,
he had a young concubine,
aged about twenty,
who called herself Yuè Mǔ.
She wore monastic robes,
did not marry,
and followed Fǎhé everywhere.
It was rumored that he had secretly been intimate with her for more than ten years.
Now she was dismissed (by imperial order),
and went on to have other illicit affairs.
The relevant authorities investigated and verified all these facts.
Yuè Mǔ subsequently remarried
and bore several children.
Wáng Lín,
courtesy name Zǐháng,
was a native of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
His father, Xiǎnsì,
was an Attendant-in-Ordinary in the kingdom of the Prince of Xiāngdōng of Liáng.
Lín was originally from a military family.
When Emperor Yuán resided in his fief,
Lín’s sisters all entered the inner court and were favored.
Lín consequently gained the position of close attendant before reaching the age of twenty.
In his youth, he loved martial pursuits,
and consequently became a military commander.
In Tàiqīng second year,
Hóu Jǐng crossed the Yangzi River.
He sent Lín to deliver ten thousand *dàn* of rice.
Before arriving,
the capital fell.
He therefore sank the rice in the middle of the river
and returned to Jīngzhōu in a fast boat.
He was gradually promoted to Administrator of Yuèyáng,
and due to his military accomplishments, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiànníng County.
When Hóu Jǐng sent the general Sòng Zǐxiān to occupy Yǐngzhōu,
Lín attacked and conquered it,
capturing Zǐxiān.
He later followed Wáng Sēngbiàn in defeating Jǐng.
Afterward, he was appointed Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Lín was exceptionally resolute and vigorous,
and moreover, he was able to humble himself before scholars.
The rewards he received
he did not take home for his family.
He commanded ten thousand men,
many of whom were bandits from the Jiāng and Huái regions.
His merit in pacifying Jǐng
was ranked first, along with Dù Kān.
Relying on the emperor's favor, he acted wildly and brutally in Jiànyè.
Wáng Sēngbiàn tried to restrain him but could not,
fearing that he would soon cause trouble.
He memorialized requesting his execution.
Lín also suspected disaster.
He ordered his Chief Clerk Lù Nà to lead his personal troops ahead to Xiāngzhōu.
He himself proceeded directly upriver to Jiānglíng.
As he was about to leave,
he said to Nà and the others:
“If I do not return,
what will you do?”
They all said:
“We beg to die in order to repay you.”
They wept and parted.
When he arrived,
the Emperor ordered him handed over to the legal officials.
Huáng Luóhàn, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, and Zhāng Zài, Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, were dispatched to announce the order to Lín’s army.
Lù Nà and the soldiers all wept when confronting the envoys,
and none were willing to accept the command.
They consequently seized Huáng Luóhàn
and killed Zhāng Zài.
Zài was harsh and unforgiving by nature,
and trusted by the Emperor.
Jīngzhōu hated him like an enemy.
Therefore, Nà and the others, capitalizing on the people's desire,
pulled out his intestines and tied them to a horse's leg,
making the horse circle and run.
When his intestines were fully pulled out, he expired.
Then they butchered him, subjected him to the five punishments, and finally executed him by beheading.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng sent Wáng Sēngbiàn to suppress Nà.
Nà and his cohorts were defeated and fled to Chángshā.
At that time, Xiāngzhōu had not yet been pacified,
and the forces of the Prince of Wǔlíng were also very powerful.
Both the government and the populace of Jiānglíng were terrified,
and people harbored intentions of revolt.
Nà memorialized, asserting Lín’s innocence,
and requested that Lín be restored to his original rank,
while Nà and his group would forever be slaves.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng then shackled Lín and sent him to Chángshā.
At that time, Nà’s troops had advanced and were fighting.
When Lín arrived,
Sēngbiàn had him ascend a turreted carriage to display him to the troops.
Nà and his cohorts threw down their spears and bowed together.
The entire army wept,
saying:
“If Lord Wáng is allowed into the city,
we will immediately surrender.”
When Lín was released and entered,
Nà and his cohorts surrendered,
and Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
He was consequently restored to his original rank,
and was ordered to resist Xiāo Jì.
After Jì was pacified,
he was appointed Governor of Héngzhōu.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng was prone to suspicion.
Since Lín’s subordinates were very numerous
and he also possessed the hearts of the people,
he consequently sent him outside the mountains (Lǐng Wài).
Lín also received the titles of Grand Commander and Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
His friend, the Official Clerk Lǐ Yīng,
was trusted and favored by the Emperor.
Lín informed him, saying:
“I, Lín, having received promotion,
have always wished to dedicate my life to repaying the state’s grace.
Now the realm is still not pacified,
yet I am moved outside the mountains.
If, by some remote chance, an unexpected event occurs,
how can they obtain Lín’s strength?
I estimate that the court merely suspects me.
My station and ambitions are limited;
how could I contend with the court to become Emperor?
Why not appoint Lín as Governor of Yōngzhōu,
and have him guard Wǔníng?
Lín will dismiss his troops and engage in farming himself,
acting as the nation’s defense.
If there is an alert or an emergency,
we can stay informed of the situation.
How can this compare to being cast away far in Lǐngnán,
ten thousand *lǐ* away?
If a disturbance occurs one day,
what will be done?
I, Lín, do not wish to remain permanently in Jīngnán;
I speak only for the sake of the state’s plans.”
Yīng affirmed his statement
but dared not report it [to the Emperor].
Therefore, [Lín] subsequently led his forces to garrison Lǐngnán.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng was surrounded and pressured by Wèi,
so he summoned Wáng Lín to rush to the rescue,
and appointed him Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiāngzhōu.
Wáng Lín's army reached Chángshā,
when he learned that Wèi had subjugated Jiānglíng,
and had already enthroned Xiāo Chá as the King of Liáng.
He therefore held mourning rites for Emperor Yuán of Liáng,
and the three armies donned white mourning clothes.
He dispatched the separate general Hóu Píng to lead the naval forces and attack Liáng.
Wáng Lín garrisoned troops at Chángshā,
sent manifestos to all sides,
making plans for moving forward.
At that time, the vassal king of Chángshā, Xiāo Sháo, and the various generals upriver supported Wáng Lín as the leader of the alliance.
Although Hóu Píng could not cross the river,
he repeatedly defeated the Liáng army.
Yet, since Wáng Lín's military authority did not reach him,
he subsequently refused to follow orders.
Wáng Lín sent a general to suppress him,
but was unsuccessful.
Furthermore, his army was worn out and exhausted, unable to advance.
So he dispatched envoys bearing a memorial to Qí,
and also presented trained elephants;
he also sent an envoy to offer tribute to Wèi,
requesting the return of his wife and children;
and likewise declared himself a subject to Liáng.
After Chén Bàxiān killed Wáng Sēngbiàn,
and enthroned Emperor Jìng,
Wáng Lín was summoned with the titles of Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Wáng Lín did not obey the command,
but instead heavily constructed tower ships,
intending to launch a righteous campaign.
Wáng Lín's generals and commanders each rode a massive ship.
Whenever they mobilized,
the warships numbered in the thousands,
and used
"Wild Boar"
as the designation.
Emperor Wǔ of Chén dispatched generals Hóu Āndū, Zhōu Wényù, and others to execute Wáng Lín,
and subsequently received the abdication from Liáng.
Hóu Āndū sighed, saying:
"I am likely to be defeated,
since our campaign lacks justification."
They engaged in battle at Dùnkǒu.
Wáng Lín rode a flat sedan chair,
holding a battle-axe and directing his forces,
capturing Hóu Āndū and Zhōu Wényù.
None of the others escaped.
Since only Zhōu Tiěhǔ alone had betrayed his trust,
he executed him.
He chained Hóu Āndū and Zhōu Wényù and placed them aboard the flagship where Wáng Lín was seated,
ordering a eunuch to monitor and guard them.
Wáng Lín then moved the military headquarters of Xiāngzhōu to Yǐngchéng,
leading a hundred thousand armored troops,
and drilled his forces at Báishuǐ Pǔ.
Wáng Lín inspected his army and said:
"This force is certainly capable of serving the legitimate sovereign.
Who was Wēn Tàizhēn anyway!"
The regional leaders of Jiāngnán, Xióng Tánlǎng and Zhōu Dí, harbored double intentions.
Wáng Lín sent Lǐ Xiàoqīn and Fán Měng to suppress them jointly with Yú Xiàoqǐng.
The three generals were defeated,
and were all imprisoned by the enemy.
Hóu Āndū, Zhōu Wényù, and the others all escaped back to Jiànyè.
Initially, when Wèi captured Jiānglíng,
Xiāo Zhuāng, the King of Yǒngjiā, was barely seven years old,
and fled and hid in a civilian home.
Later, Wáng Lín welcomed him back to Xiāngzhōng,
and escorted him eastward downriver.
When Emperor Jìng was established,
Wáng Lín sent a hostage to Qí,
requesting the installation of Xiāo Zhuāng as the ruler of Liáng.
Emperor Wénxuān dispatched troops to assist and escort him,

and also sent the concurrently serving Prefect of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), Lǐ Táotú, to formally invest Wáng Lín as Chancellor of Liáng (Liáng Chéngxiàng), Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūn), and Director of the Affairs of the Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì).
Palace Attendants (Shèrén) Xīn Hú, Yóu Quánzhī, and others carried imperial edicts sealed with the imperial seal across the Yangtze to acknowledge their service,
and gifts were distributed to everyone from Wáng Lín downwards.
Wáng Lín then sent his elder brother's son, Wáng Shúbǎo, leading the sons and younger brothers of the governors of his ten controlled provinces, to proceed to Yè,
and supported Xiāo Zhuāng to continue the Liáng succession in Yǐngzhōu.
Xiāo Zhuāng conferred upon Wáng Lín the titles of Attendant (Shìzhōng), Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Great General (Dà Jiāngjūn), and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and changed his enfeoffment title to Duke of Ānchéng Commandery,
the rest of the appointments followed the previous mandates of the Qí court.
When Chén Bàxiān ascended the throne,
Wáng Lín assisted Xiāo Zhuāng and encamped at Rúxūkǒu.
Qí dispatched Mùróng Yǎn, the Touring Secretariat Director for Yángzhōu Circuit, leading troops to the river bank,
to provide them with vocal support.
Chén sent Wú Míngchè, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Ānzhōu, to advance upriver during the night,
planning to raid Pénchéng.
Wáng Lín sent Rèn Zhōng, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Bālíng, who heavily defeated him,
Wú Míngchè barely escaped with his life.
Wáng Lín's army subsequently moved eastward downriver.
Chén sent Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Hóu Āndū and others to resist him.
Hóu Tián and the others considered Wáng Lín's army to be currently powerful,
and led their armies into Wúhú to avoid him.
At that moment, a southwest wind suddenly arrived.
Wáng Lín believed he had received the aid of Heaven,
and intended to proceed directly to seize Yángzhōu.
Hóu Tián and the others slowly emerged from Wúhú,
and followed closely behind him.
By the time the armies engaged,
the southwest wind had reversed and was utilized by Hóu Tián.
Those of Wáng Lín’s troops who released fire tubes and threw them onto the ships,
all had their own ships burned back at them.
Wáng Lín’s fleet scattered in disorder,
twelve or thirteen parts of his soldiers jumped into the water and perished,
the remainder all abandoned their ships and went ashore,
and were nearly all killed by the Chén army.
Wáng Lín had initially ordered Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) Yuán Bì and Palace Deputy Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) Liú Zhòngwēi to jointly command the troops guarding Xiāo Zhuāng.
When the army was defeated,
Yuán Bì subsequently surrendered to Chén,
while Liú Zhòngwēi took Xiāo Zhuāng and defected to Lìyáng.
Wáng Lín soon surrendered to Yè Dū along with Xiāo Zhuāng.
Emperor Xiàozhāo dispatched Wáng Lín to Héféi,
to rally his former loyal subordinates,
and plan for further advances.
Wáng Lín then repaired his ships,
and sent out separate forces for recruitment.
The Cāng Chǔ peoples of Huáinán,
all wished to exert their strength.
Péi Jǐnghuī, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Hézhōu under Chén,
who was the son-in-law of Wáng Mín, Wáng Lín’s elder brother,
requested to use his private retinues to guide the Qí army.
Emperor Xiàozhāo entrusted Wáng Lín and Assistant Director of the Touring Secretariat (Xíngtái Zuǒ Chéng) Lú Qián to lead troops to respond,
but he hesitated and remained undecided.
Péi Jǐnghuī feared the matter would be leaked,
and fled alone to Qí.
Emperor Xiàozhāo bestowed upon Wáng Lín an imperial edict sealed with the imperial seal,
ordering him to guard Shòuyáng,
and permitted all of his subordinate generals and commanders to accompany him.
Wáng Lín was thus appointed General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn), Administrator Vested with the Privileges of the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yángzhōu,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Kuàijī Commandery.
His military rank was further increased,
and he was granted the use of drums and wind instruments.
Wáng Lín made solemn preparations by land and water,
intending to observe the vulnerability before acting.
However, the Chén house established friendly relations with Qí,
causing Wáng Lín to await further planning.
While Wáng Lín was at Shòuyáng,
he was in disagreement with Lú Qián, the Director (Shàngshū) of the Touring Secretariat,
and they criticized each other.
He was summoned back to Yè,
but Emperor Wǔchéng was lenient and did not investigate the matter.
He was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Cāngzhōu.
Later, Wáng Lín was appointed Special Advanced (Tè Jìn) and Attendant (Shìzhōng).
The ridge of the roof where he resided inexplicably peeled and cracked,
and several pints of red maggots emerged,
turning into blood upon falling to the ground,
and squirmed.
Furthermore, a dragon emerged from the ground outside his gate,
clouds and fog arose,
making the day dark.
Soon after, the Chén general Wú Míngchè came to invade.
The Emperor commanded the General Commandant (Lǐng Jūn Jiāngjūn) Wèi Pòhú and others to march out and reinforce Qínzhōu,
and ordered Wáng Lín to join them in developing the strategy.
Wáng Lín said to his close associates:
"Currently, the Grand Duke Jupiter (Tàisuì) is in the southeast,
and Jupiter (Suì Xīng) resides in the Dǒu and Niú regions of the sky,
Venus (Tàibái) is already high,
all favorable to the attacking side.
I am about to face disaster."
He also said to Wèi Pòhú:
"The Wú troops are very sharp,
it is advisable to use a prolonged strategy to control them,
be cautious not to engage in light fighting."
Wèi Pòhú did not comply,
and consequently fought.
The army was greatly defeated.
Wáng Lín broke through the encirclement alone on horseback,
and barely managed to escape.
Returning to Péngchéng,
the Emperor ordered him to immediately proceed to Shòuyáng,
and permitted him to recruit forces.
He was further enfeoffed as the Prince of Bālíng Commandery.
The Chén general Wú Míngchè advanced his troops and besieged him,
damming the Féi River to flood the city.
Yet Pí Jǐnghé and others were garrisoned west of the Huái River,
and ultimately did not come to the rescue.
Wú Míngchè attacked day and night.
The moisture inside the city gradually intensified,
everyone suffered from swelling,
the dead and the sick lay piled together.
From the seventh month to the tenth month,
the city fell and he was captured.
The common people wept and followed him.
Wú Míngchè feared that this would cause an upheaval,
and killed him twenty ěrlǐ northeast of the city.
He was forty-eight years old at the time,
the sound of those weeping was like thunder.
An old man brought wine and dried meat to pour a libation,
grieving profoundly.
He collected his blood,
concealed it, and departed.
His head was sent to Jiànkāng,
and hung in the marketplace.

Zhū Yáng, Wáng Lín’s former official serving as Commandant for Supply Registers (Cāngcáo Cānjūn) in the General of Agile Cavalry's (Piàojì Fǔ) establishment under Liáng, sent a letter to Xú Líng, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè) under Chén, requesting Wáng Lín’s head, saying: "I humbly believe that courts and marketplaces shift and change,
the tradition of courage and integrity is transmitted;
and as historical eras transition,
the mark of loyalty and devotion is revealed.
Therefore, when the Diǎn Wǔ was about to perish,
Xú Guǎng became the heir of the Jìn house—
Old;
Dāngtú had already failed,
Mǎ Fú was known as a loyal minister of the Wèi house.
Thus he was able to spread his good reputation in earlier records,
and hand down his name to later generations.
Xiāo Lín (琳), the former Duke of Jiànníng of the Liáng,
was a descendant of the Lúobīn
lineage,
and an old clan of Yíchuān.
He established merit in the Palace of the Heir Apparent (Dàidǐ),
and proved his achievements in the Imperial Court (Zhōngcháo);
when it was a time of chaos and separation,
he assumed the responsibility of regional governor (fāngbó).
Thereupon he lightly sacrificed himself for his lord,
dedicated his body to the state,
truly following in the steps of past worthies,
faithfully treading the path of former paragons.
But Heaven grew weary of the virtue of Liáng,
and the sovereign desired to right the succession,
he merely harbored the thought of Bāo Xū,
and eventually
encountered the misfortune of Cháng Hóng.
When the royal cause was gloriously initiated,
and the dynastic destiny found its rightful place,
he then distanced himself to Shāndōng,
entrusting his life to Héběi.
Although he lightly sighed over the fate of a traveling minister,
he still cherished
the courtesy of a guest official (kèqīng),
moved by this appreciation,
he forgot the sacrifice of his own body.
This led to his body resting in the Nine Springs (death),
and his head traveling ten thousand *lǐ*.
Truly, to have his corpse wrapped in horse hide,
fulfilled his lifelong
ambition;
his bones exposed in the wilderness,
met the standard of a loyal subject.
However, the separation of head and body,
is something truly lamentable;
lacking a settled grave site,
is indeed heartbreaking.
Yáng (瑒) early occupied a low position,
receiving the consideration of Lord Xuē,
and benefiting from the appreciation of the Duke of Wèi.
Therefore, my handkerchief is wet and my sleeves are rainy (I weep),
mourning the face I knew;
my intestines twist and I grieve over his
head,
keenly missing his face as if he were still alive.
I humbly reflect that the Divine Grace is broad and generous,
the enlightened edicts are issued,
pardoning Wáng Jīng’s cry,
and permitting Tián Héng’s burial.
Although I, Yáng, am humble and worthless,
I secretly
have the same desire.
Lín previously governed Shòuyáng,
where he left behind considerable affection;
he once traveled to Jiāngyòu,
and was not without remaining virtue.
Alongside the officials of the Eastern Chamber (Dōnggě),
and following the guests of the Western Garden (Xīyuán),
we desire to return him to that region,
and properly conduct the burial.
Hopefully, when the isolated tomb is built,
perhaps swallows carrying earth will fly there;
when a grand stele is erected,
people who shed 'falling tears' will linger there.
Recently,
former acquaintances such as Wáng Wǎn and others have already presented memorials,
yet having received the imperial deliberation,
their requests were not granted.
Formerly, when Duke Lián passed away,
he was buried near the Féichuān River and a burial ground was established;
when Sūn Shū’yún
died,
catalpa and thorn trees were planted around the Quèpí Reservoir.
Judging by this,
there are precedents for this.
Let it not be that beneath the walls of Shòuchūn city,
only the tale of the one who reported on Gě is circulated;
and on the island of Cāngzhōu,
there is only the solitary guest who grieves for Tián.
I present this plea, risking death,
awaiting your punitive decision.
Líng (the emperor) praised his ambition and integrity.
Furthermore, Wú Míngchè also repeatedly dreamed that Lín requested his head,
so he jointly reported this to the Lord of Chén and was granted permission.
He then took Lín’s head back to Huáinán, along with the Chief Clerk Liú Sháohuì of the Rank of Open-Palace Attendant and others,
and temporarily buried it beside Mount Bāgōng.
Several thousand loyal friends attended the funeral.
Yáng and the others then took a hidden route northward,
and separately discussed receiving (the body).
Soon after, five people from Yángzhōu, including Máo Zhīshèng, secretly delivered the coffin to Yè.

He was posthumously granted the titles General Military Governor of Fifteen Provinces, Governor of Yángzhōu, Palace Attendant, Special Advance, Open-Palace Attendant, and Director of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing.
His posthumous title was Zhōngwǔ Wáng (Loyal and Martial King),
and he was provided with an official warm carriage for the funeral.
Lín’s appearance was relaxed and elegant,
his standing hair reached the ground,
and his joy and anger were not shown on his face.
Although he lacked formal scholarship,
he had a strong memory and internal shrewdness,
and among the thousands of officers and clerks in his command,
he recognized all their names.
Punishments were not excessive,
he valued wealth lightly and loved scholars,
thus winning the hearts of his officers and soldiers.
He served as a military commander from a young age,
repeatedly experienced loss and chaos,
and inherently possessed the virtue of loyalty and integrity.
Although his original plan was not realized,
the people of Yè also respected him for this,
and treated him very generously.
When he was defeated,
he was captured by the Chén army.
Wú Míngchè wished to spare him,
but many of the generals under him were Lín's former subordinates,
who eagerly came to plead for him,
and also supplied him with resources.
Míngchè consequently grew suspicious of him,
which led to his execution.
At that time, field laborers and old villagers,
those who knew him and those who did not,
all sighed and wept for him.
Observing how his sincerity and trustworthiness moved others,
even the earnest and skillful encouragement of General Lǐ,
could scarcely surpass it.
Lín had seventeen sons.
His eldest son, Jìng,
succeeded to the ducal title in Qí,
and at the end of Wǔpíng,
served as Administrator of the Palace Gentlemen.
His ninth son, Yǎn,
served as Open-Palace Attendant with the Same Authority as the Three Ducal Ministers during the Kāihuáng era of the Suí,
and in the early Dàyè era,
died while serving as Governor of Yúzhōu.
Biographies Twenty-Five: Xiāo Míng, Xiāo Zhī, Xiāo Tuì, Xiāo Fàng, Xú Zhīcái.
Xiāo Míng,
a native of Lánlíng,
was the son of Xiāo Yì, Prince of Chángshā and elder brother of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
In his native court,
he was greatly loved and favored by Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
While young, he held prominent offices,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhēnyáng.
During the Tàiqīng era,
he was appointed Governor of Yùzhōu.
After the Lord of Liáng had accepted Hóu Jǐng,
he commanded Míng to lead all the land and water forces toward Péngchéng,
with the major objective of advancing and conquering.
He also ordered Xiāo Huìlǐ, the Hereditary Prince of Nánkāng and Governor of Yǎnzhōu, to assume command over the various generals,
and instruct them on strategy.
Not long after Míng crossed the Huái River,
the government forces defeated him,
capturing all his troops.
The Wèi Emperor ascended the gate tower,
personally received Míng and the other generals,
released them from confinement,
and sent them to Jìnyáng.
Shìzōng treated Míng with great respect,
saying to him:
"The former king maintained friendly relations with the Lord of Liáng for more than ten years.
I heard that in their Buddhist liturgies,
they always said they performed them for the Lord of Wèi,
including the former king.
This truly showed the profound goodwill of the Lord of Liáng.
I did not expect that one morning trust would be lost,
causing this turmoil.
Since our forces were sent out for a minor punitive campaign,
there has been no battle we haven't won,
and no city we haven't captured.
We now desire peace voluntarily,
not because our strength is exhausted.
The matters on the border,
I know are not the original intention of the Lord of Liáng;
it must be Hóu Jǐng disobeying orders and instigating trouble.
You may send an envoy to discuss this.
If he still preserves the integrity and righteousness established by the former king,
and wishes to renew the alliance,
I dare not violate the intent of the former king,
and you and the others shall all be released immediately and sent back."
Thereupon, he sent someone to inform the Lord of Liáng with Míng’s letter,
and the Lord of Liáng then wrote a letter to appease Shìzōng.
In the sixth year of Tiānbǎo (555 CE),
Liáng Yuán (Emperor Yuán of Liáng) was destroyed by the Xī Wèi (Western Wei).
Xiǎnzǔ issued an edict establishing Míng as the Lord of Liáng.
The former Liáng generals who had been captured, Zhàn Hǎizhēn and others, were all permitted to follow Míng back.
He ordered Shàngdǎng Wáng Huàn to lead troops to escort them.
At this time, the Liáng Grand Commandant Wáng Sēngbiàn and Minister of Works Chén Bàxiān were in Jiànyè.
They supported Jìn'ān Wáng Fāngzhì as Chancellor.
Xiǎnzǔ bestowed Wáng Sēngbiàn and Chén Bàxiān with sealed letters (imperial decrees).
Sēngbiàn had not yet accepted the edict.
The Prince of Shàngdǎng advanced his army.
Míng again wrote to Sēngbiàn,
repeating the exchange several times,
explaining the impending disaster and fortune (consequences).
Sēngbiàn initially refused to accept (the proposal).
Soon after, the Prince of Shàngdǎng defeated Dōngguān
and beheaded Péi Zhīhéng.
The region south of the river (Jiāngbiǎo) became alarmed and fearful.
Sēngbiàn then reported to Shàngdǎng, requesting to accept Míng,
and dispatched ships and vessels to welcome him.
The Prince hosted a banquet for the officers and soldiers of the Liáng court,
and together with Míng, slaughtered a sacrifice and smeared blood,
recording the event in writing and swearing an alliance.
Consequently, the Liáng carriages proceeded eastward,
and the Qí army returned north.
The Palace Attendant Péi Yīngqǐ escorted Míng into Jiànyè.
Míng then assumed the revered title (Emperor),
changed the fourth year of Chéngshèng to the first year of Tiānchéng (557 CE),
and issued a general amnesty upon the land.
Yǔwén Hēidà and the bandit Chá were not included in the scope of the amnesty.
He appointed Fāngzhì as Crown Prince
and conferred the title of Grand Marshal upon Wáng Sēngbiàn.
Míng submitted a memorial and sent his second son, Zhāng, galloping to the capital
to express thanks to the imperial palace.
In winter,
Bàxiān attacked and killed Sēngbiàn,
and re-established Fāngzhì (as the nominal ruler),
appointing Míng as Grand Tutor and Prince of Jiàn'ān.
Bàxiān submitted a memorial to the Imperial Court
claiming that Sēngbiàn had secretly plotted usurpation and rebellion,
and was therefore executed.
Fāngzhì requested to declare himself a subject
and forever remain a vassal state.
Qí sent the Acting Director of the Department of State Affairs, Sīmǎ Gōng, to form an alliance with the Liáng people at Lìyáng.
The following year,
an imperial edict summoned Míng.
Bàxiān still declared himself a vassal,
intending to dispatch an envoy to send Míng (north).
Coincidentally, Míng died from a carbuncle that erupted on his back.
The Liáng general Wáng Lín resisted Bàxiān along the Yangtze River.
Xiǎnzǔ sent troops to install the Liáng Prince of Yǒngjiā, Xiāo Zhuāng, to preside over the Liáng sacrifices.
In the second month of the ninth year (558 CE),
(Xiāo Zhuāng) crossed the river from Pénchéng.
In the third month,
he ascended the imperial throne at Yǐngzhōu,
adopting the reign title Tiānqǐ.
Wáng Lín commanded his military and state affairs.
Míng was posthumously honored as Emperor Mǐn.
The following year, Zhuāng was defeated by the Chén people
and subsequently entered the court (of Qí).
He was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
The Imperial Court promised to restore him,
but ultimately failed to do so.
On the day the Last Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) perished,
Zhuāng died of sorrow (or stifled rage) in Yè.
Xiāo Zhī,
courtesy name Jìngshì,
was the son of Wěi, Prince Nánpíng, Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's younger brother.
In his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted,
possessing a fine countenance.
While in Liáng,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dìngxiāng
and held the post of Governor of Dōngyángzhōu.
At that time, the area south of the Yangtze River (Jiāngzuǒ) was enjoying peace;
governance was lenient and the people were slack.
Zhī alone governed with strictness and severity,
which pleased Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
He was promoted to Governor of Běiyǎnzhōu.
In the second year of Tàiqīng (548 CE),
Hóu Jǐng besieged Jiànyè.
Hearing that Táichéng (the capital city) had fallen,
Zhī immediately defected (to the North).
He arrived in Yè in the seventh year of Wǔdìng (549 CE).
Wénxiāng ordered Wèi Shōu and Xíng Shào to meet and converse with him.
He successively held the posts of Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince
and concurrently served as Tutor to the Prince of Píngyáng,
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Qīnghé Commandery.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo (550 CE) of Qí,
he was granted the title Grand Master of the Right of Brilliant Merit
and concurrently served as Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
At that time, Emperor Yuán of Liáng pacified Hóu Jǐng
and resumed friendly relations with Qí.
Wénxuān wished to release Zhī and others to return south.
Soon afterwards, Xī Wèi captured Jiānglíng,
so he remained in the capital Yè
and died there.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat, General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry,
and Governor of Yángzhōu.
Xiāo Tuì
was the son of Huī, Prince Póyáng and Minister of Works, who was the younger brother of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
While Tuì was in Liáng,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xiāngtán
and held the post of Governor of Qīngzhōu.
When Jiànyè fell,
he entered Dōng Wèi (Eastern Wei) along with his cousin Zhī.
During the Tiānbǎo era of Qí,
he held the post of Grand Master of Brilliant Merit with Gold and Purple
and died.
His son, Kǎi,
was profound and courteous,
enjoyed virtue and loved learning,
and practiced the cursive (Cǎo) and clerical (Lì) scripts.
Among the Southern literati, he was known as a noble gentleman (Zhǎngzhě).
He successively served as Auxiliary Gentleman of the Imperial Archives,
Attendant in the Hall of Literary Arts (Wénlín Guǎn),
and died while holding the post of Internal Attendant of the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
Xiāo Fàng,
courtesy name Xīyì,
followed his father Zhī to Yè.
After Zhī died,
Fàng became known for his filial piety while observing mourning rites.
In front of the mourning hut where he lived, two benevolent crows (Cíwū) came and gathered,
each claiming a tree for a nest.
Before noon,
they would tame the courtyard, drinking and pecking.
After noon, they would no longer descend from the trees.
Every time (Fàng performed a rite),
they would spread their wings and cry sadly,
exactly like weeping in sorrow.
His family members observed this
and noted that it was never once amiss.
People at the time believed it was a reaction to his utmost filial piety.
When the period of mourning concluded,
he inherited the noble title.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he served as an Attendant in the Hall of Literary Arts (Wénlín Guǎn).
Fàng was fond of literature and poetry,
and was quite skilled in painting (Dānqīng).
Because of this, while in the palace, he reviewed historical books and modern poetry and prose,
and supervised the painting of screens and various other items, which brought him recognition.
He was subsequently favored and treated kindly.
He was successively promoted to Palace Deputy Director to the Crown Prince and Cavalry Attendant in Ordinary.
Xú Zhīcái
was a native of Dānyáng.
His father, Xióng,
served the Nán Qí (Southern Qí).
He held the post of Administrator of Lánlíng
and was renowned in Jiāngzuǒ (south of the river) for his medical skills.
Zhīcái was brilliant and quick-witted in his youth.
At five, he recited the *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiàojīng*).
By eight, he had a rough understanding of its meaning.
He once accompanied his cousin Kāng to the house of Zhōu Shě of Rǔnán, the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince of Liáng, to listen to *Lǎozǐ* (Lao Tzu).
Shě provided a meal for them
and then jokingly said to him:
"Young Master Xú, why do you not concentrate on the meaning,
but only concern yourself with eating?"
Zhīcái replied:
"I have heard that the Sage empties his mind but fills his belly."
Shě sighed in appreciation.
At the age of thirteen,
he was summoned to be a student at the Imperial Academy (Tàixuéshēng).
He had a basic understanding of the *Rites* (*Lǐ*) and the *Changes* (*Yì*).
Liú Xiào-chuò of Péngchéng, Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng, Zhāng Shěng of Wúzhùn, and others would often discuss the *Changes of Zhōu* (*Zhōu Yì*) and the rites for mourning garments (Sāngfú Yí).
His responses were like an echo.
They all sighed and exclaimed:
"This is a divine child!"
Xiào-chuò also said:
"Young Master Xú has a swallow's jaw (Yànhàn),
possessing the physiognomy of Bān Dìngyuǎn (Bān Chāo)."
Yuán Áng of Chénjùn served as the Prefect of Dānyáng.
He appointed Zhīcái as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
Whenever there were public duties and appropriate matters,
he always sought Zhīcái's consultation.
The administrative office of the Commandery suffered a fire.
Zhīcái rose to look;
during the night, he was not fully clothed,
but wrapped a red cloth cover (or garment) around himself and exited his room.
Reflected by the light, he was seen by Áng.
The Attendant Official (Gōngcáo) requested that Zhīcái be dismissed.
Áng valued his talent and skill,
and therefore granted him special pardon.
When Zōng, Prince of Yùzhāng, was sent out to govern Jiāngdū,
Zhīcái was again appointed Left Attendant of the Yùzhāng Princedom,
and was later transferred to be Chief Clerk for Zōng as the General Guarding the North (Zhèn Běi Zhǔbù).
When Zōng entered Wèi,
his three armies scattered and fled.
Zhīcái retreated to Lǚliáng.
As the bridge was broken and the road cut off,
he was stopped by the Wèi Tǒngjūn, Shí Màosūn.
Zōng was in Wèi for ten days or a month,
and rose in rank to Sīkōng.
Wèi allowed Zōng to gather his subordinates.
He then inquired where Zhīcái was in Péngsì,
and reported to the Wèi Dì, saying:
“Zhīcái is exceptionally skilled in medical arts,
and also possesses strategic eloquence.”
An imperial edict summoned Zhīcái.
In the second year of Xiàochāng
he arrived in Luò.
He was ordered to reside in the Southern Hostel,
where he was treated with extreme courtesy.
His cousin’s son, Jiǎn Zǐjiàn, petitioned for Zhīcái to return to his home.
Zhīcái’s medicines and stones were often effective;
moreover, he had studied the classics and histories.
His speech was quick and clever.
The court officials competed to invite him,
and they praised him widely.
During the reign of Wǔ Dì,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chāng'ān County (Chāng'ān Xiàn Hóu).
During the Tiānpíng era,
Qí Shénwǔ summoned him to Jìnyáng.
He frequently resided in the Inner Hostel,
and his courteous treatment gradually increased.
In the fourth year of Wǔdìng,
he was transferred from Sànqí Chángshì to Mìshū Jiān.
When Wénxuān became prime minister,
he broadly demoted and promoted officials.
Yáng Yīn believed that because Zhīcái was a man from the southern lands,
he was unsuitable to manage the archives.
He was instead given the title Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and Wèi Shōu was appointed to replace him temporarily.
Zhīcái was greatly resentful and displeased.
Zhīcái had studied astronomy since youth,
along with the learning of prognostication and prophecy.
He consulted with the guest Sòng Jǐngyè on auspicious and inauspicious matters,
and knew that the year Wǔ (Horse) would certainly bring about change.
He consequently informed the emperor through Gāo Dézhèng.
Wénxuān heard this and was greatly pleased.
At that time, from Empress Dowager Lóu Tàihòu down to the meritorious nobles,
all said that since Guānxī (the region west of the pass) was a formidable enemy,
they feared that the enemy might use the rhetoric of "holding the Son of Heaven hostage to command the feudal lords,"
and therefore the matter of abdication should not proceed first.
Zhīcái alone said:
“If a thousand men chase a rabbit,
and one man obtains it,
all the others cease their effort.
You must establish the great task (of usurpation);
how can you turn around and wish to learn from others?”
He further cited evidence,
providing detailed arguments,
and the Emperor followed his advice.
After ascending the throne,
Zhīcái was seen as increasingly intimate.
Zhīcái did not merely advance through his medical skill;
he was also the first to advocate for the abdication.
Furthermore, he was humorous and witty,
and his words lacked no edge,
so he was greatly befriended and cherished.
Soon after, he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and enfeoffed as the Count of Chíyáng County (Chíyáng Xiàn Bó).
Seeing that Wénxuān’s governance was becoming stricter,
he requested to leave the capital,
and was appointed Cìshǐ of Zhàozhōu.
Ultimately, he was unable to take up his post,
still serving as a court jester.
In the second year of Huángjiàn,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Xī Yǎnzhōu.
Before he went to his post,
Empress Dowager Wǔmíng Huáng Tàihòu became indisposed.
Zhīcái treated her,
and she recovered immediately upon his application of medicine.
Xiàozhāo awarded him a thousand bolts of colored silk and four hundred bolts of brocade.
Since Zhīcái was skilled in medical arts,
although he received external appointments,
he was soon recalled.
Since he was widely learned and well-informed,
he was especially adept in divination and occult arts.
In the spring of the second year of Dàníng,
Empress Dowager Wǔmíng Tàihòu fell ill again.
Zhīcái's younger brother, Zhīfàn, who was Shàngyào Diǎnyù,
was ordered to examine her condition.
All the court historians were ordered to refer to the Empress Dowager as "Stone Woman" (Shí Pó).
This was likely due to a popular taboo,
so her name was changed to suppress it.
Zhīfàn came out and told Zhīcái:
“The children’s rhyme says: ‘In Zhōulǐ, Qǐqiújiā,
married Shí Pó in the leopard shrine.
A severed tomb serves as the matchmaker,
yielding only one measure of purple silk boots (zǐyán xuē).’
Now the Empress Dowager has suddenly changed her name,
which I privately find strange.”
Zhīcái said:
“Qǐqiújiā
is a Hu term meaning ‘gone forever.’
A leopard shrine marrying Shí Pó,
how can that be a good thing?
A severed tomb acting as a matchmaker
simply indicates that a joint burial will sever the tomb.
As for obtaining the purple silk boots,
she will last until the fourth month.
Why?
The character for ‘purple’ (zǐ) is composed of
‘this’ (cǐ) above, and ‘cord’ (xì) below.
The character ‘silk’ (yán)
means ripe (shú),
and this must occur in the middle of the fourth month.”
Zhīfàn asked what the significance of the boots (xuē) was.
Zhīcái said:
“A boot is ‘leather’ (gé) beside ‘change’ (huà).
How can it be something lasting?”
On the first day of the fourth month,
she consequently died.
There was a person suffering from swelling and pain in the heel,
which all doctors failed to diagnose.
Zhīcái said:
“This is the disease of the clam spirit,
caused by riding a boat into the sea
and dangling the feet in the water.”
The patient said:
“Indeed, I did this.”
Zhīcái operated and extracted two clam embryos
the size of elm seeds.
There was also someone who used bone for a knife handle,
which was multicolored and mottled.
Zhīcái said:
“This is human osteoma (tumor).”
When asked where he got it,
he said he had seen a skull in an ancient tomb with a forehead bone several inches long.
He tested it by whittling it,
and it had patterned grain,
so he used it.
His penetrating understanding was comprehensive like this.
In the fourth year of Tiāntǒng,
he was repeatedly promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
Soon after, he was appointed Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu,
and specially granted a full set of ceremonial drums and horns.
Zhīcái’s medical skill was the greatest,
and he was frequently summoned by imperial command.
Wǔchéng indulged excessively in wine and women,
and became delirious and unbalanced.
He once suffered an episode
and said he first saw a multicolored object in the air.
As it drew closer,
it transformed into a beautiful woman,
standing gracefully
several dozens of feet above the ground.
After the time it takes for a meal,
it transformed into Guānshìyīn (Avalokiteśvara).
Zhīcái said:
“This is caused by excessive lust
and severe depletion (great vacuity).”
He immediately prescribed a decoction.
After taking one dose,
the Emperor felt the vision move slightly further away.
After another dose,
it returned to being the multicolored object.
After several doses of the decoction,
the illness was finally cured.
Whenever the Emperor had an episode,
riders would be immediately dispatched to pursue Zhīcái.
The acupuncture and medicine he applied
were always effective instantly.
Thus, he was frequently appointed to high office.
Entering autumn,
Wǔchéng stabilized slightly
and had no further episodes.
Hé Shìkāi wished to advance in rank based on sequence.
Since Zhīcái was registered in Yǎnzhōu,
which was his original jurisdiction,
Shìkāi therefore memorialized to have him appointed Cìshǐ there,
appointing Hú Chángrén as Zuǒ Púyè,
and Shìkāi himself as Yòu Púyè.
When the tenth month arrived,
the Emperor had another episode of illness.
He said to Shìkāi:
“I regret assigning Zhīcái to an outer post;
it has caused me distress.”
On the eighth day of that month,
an imperial edict was sent via post horse to recall Zhīcái.
The Emperor died on the tenth day.
Zhīcái only arrived on the eleventh day,
and since he was too late,
he returned to his post in the province.
While in office, he committed no acts of invasion or cruelty,
but he was not very familiar with legal principles.
He was quite casual and negligent,
acting according to his own preference regarding appointments and dismissals.
In the winter of the fifth year,
the Hòuzhǔ summoned Zhīcái.
Soon, the position of Zuǒ Púshè became vacant.
Zhīcái said:
“I can naturally restore Yǔ’s accomplishments.”
In the first year of Wǔpíng,
he was again appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè.
Zhīcái utterly humbled himself before the mother and son, Hé Shìkāi and Lù Lìngxūan.
When the two families suffered distress,
he offered hundreds of ways to assist and protect them.
Because of this, he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīyáng Commandery.
When Zǔ Tǐng held power,
he dismissed Zhīcái and made him Shìzhōng, Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Zhīcái resentfully said:
“Zǐyě is weeding me out.”
Tǐng had an eye disease,
so he compared him to Shī Kuàng.
Zhīcái was intelligent, eloquent, and had a powerful memory.
He had quick wits surpassing others.
He particularly enjoyed intense discussions and witty exchanges.
In both public and private gatherings,
they often mocked and joked with each other.
Zhèng Dàoyù often jokingly called Zhīcái Shī Gōng.
Zhīcái said:
“Since I am your master,
and also your duke,
of the three essential relationships,
I immediately occupy two of them.”
He also mocked Wáng Xīn’s surname, saying:
“If you add speech, it becomes [⿱雨金].
Near a dog, it becomes ‘mad.’
Add a neck and feet, and it becomes a horse.
Apply horns and a tail, and it becomes a sheep.”
Lú Yuánmíng therefore joked to Zhīcái, saying:
“Your surname has not yet become a person.
Your personal name is a mistake in character composition;
‘Zhī’
should actually be ‘Fá’.”
He immediately replied, saying:
“Your surname placed near ‘death’ becomes cruel.
Placed on a mound, it becomes ‘empty.’
If you give birth to a man, it becomes a captive.
If you raise a horse, it becomes a donkey.”
He once,
when he went out traveling with court officials,
looked far off and saw a pack of dogs racing.
The others challenged him to describe them.
Zhīcái immediately replied verbally:
“Are these Sòng Què,
or Hán Lú?
Are they chasing Lǐ Sī running eastward,
or carrying the Emperor’s daughter fleeing south?”
Lǐ Xié, in a large assembly,
referred to his father’s personal name
and asked:
“Are you fond of raw bear paw fat (xióng bái)?”
Zhīcái said:
“It is passable.”
Lǐ Xié asked again:
“Is your comment morally acceptable?”
Xié hastily left to avoid him,
and on the road encountered his nephew, Gāo Dézhèng.
Dézhèng asked:
“Uncle, why are you looking unhappy?”
Xié told him the reason.
Dézhèng immediately went to the assembly seat
and repeatedly asked for bear paw fat.
Zhīcái said to those seated:
“What name does this person taboo?”
No one present knew.
Zhīcái said:
“If living, he is not known by people.
If dead, his name is not tabooed by people.
Why is this worth asking?”
Táng Yōng and Bái Jiàn were currently influential.
People at the time said:
“In Bīngzhōu, the glorious are Táng and Bái.”
Zhīcái held them in contempt.
On New Year’s Day,
in front of Yōng, he toasted the various clerks, saying:
“I hope your positions will reach Táng and Bái.”
Also, because a young clerk liked to chew on his brush,
he once held a writing brush and went close to Yuán Wényáo’s mouth, saying:
“Lend me your teeth.”
His lack of deference was like this.
He served successive emperors,
and gained favor through jesting and familiar conduct.
When Wǔchéng grew overlapping teeth,
he asked various doctors.
The Director of Imperial Medicine, Dèng Xuānwén, answered truthfully,
and Wǔchéng was angered and flogged him.
Afterwards, he asked Zhīcái.
Zhīcái bowed and offered congratulations, saying:
“These are wisdom teeth.
Those who grow wisdom teeth are intelligent and long-lived.”
Wǔchéng was delighted and rewarded him.
When he was Púshè,
he said to people:
“When I was in Jiāngdōng,
I saw Xú Miǎn serving as Púshè.
There was no court official who did not flatter him.
Now I am also ‘Púshè Xú,’
yet not a single person flatters me.
How can I survive?”
Zhīcái’s wife was the younger sister of the Prince of Guǎngyáng of Wèi.
Zhīcái obtained her as his wife by requesting her from Wénxiāng.
Hé Shìkāi knew this,
and committed adultery with his wife.
Zhīcái encountered them but avoided them.
Retreating, he said:
“I am disturbing the young people’s sport and laughter.”
His tolerance was like this.
At the age of eighty,
he died.
He was posthumously granted the titles Sītú Gōng and Supervisor of Shàngshū Affairs,
with the posthumous name Wénmíng.
His eldest son was Lín,
courtesy name Shàoqīng,
serving as Tháiwèi Sīmǎ.
His second son was Tóngqīng,
serving as Tàizǐ Shùzǐ.
Zhīcái considered that they lacked scholarly discipline,
and often lamented, saying:
“I fear they will eventually be like the melody Guǎnglíng Sǎn (lost to posterity).”
His younger brother, Zhīfàn,
was also known for his medical skills.
He reached the position of Tàicháng Qīng,
and was specially allowed to inherit Zhīcái’s title, Prince of Xīyáng.
Upon entering Zhōu,
he was granted the title Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn.
He died during the Kāihuáng era.
Biographies Twenty-six: Yáng Yīn (Yān Zǐxiàn, Sòng Qīndào, Zhèng Yí)
Yáng Yīn,
courtesy name Zūnyàn,
nickname Qín Wáng,
was a native of Huàyīn, Hóngnóng.
His father, Jīn,
during the Wèi period, repeatedly served as Sīkōng and Shìzhōng.
When Yīn was a child,
his mouth seemed unable to speak,
but his demeanor was profound and sharp.
When entering or leaving the house,
he never engaged in games or mischief.
At six, he studied history books.
At eleven, he received instruction in the Shī and the Yì.
He loved the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū.
When young, his mother died.
He once went to visit his maternal uncle, Yuán Zǐgōng.
Zǐgōng drank with him.
He asked what book he was reading.
Yīn replied:
“I am reciting the Shī.”
Zǐgōng asked:
“Have you recited up to ‘Wèiyáng’ yet?”
Yīn immediately cried out, moved and choked up.
Zǐgōng also sighed and wept in response,
and consequently stopped the drinking session for his sake.
Zǐgōng later said to Jīn:
“I always thought Qín Wáng was not particularly discerning and smart.
From now on,
I will watch him with fresh eyes.”
Yīn’s family lived together for four generations under one roof.
The family was very prosperous.
More than thirty cousins and younger brothers studied together.
In front of the study hall there was a crabapple tree.
When the fruit fell to the ground,
the group of children all scrambled for them.
Yīn alone sat slumped in a composed manner.
His youngest uncle, Wěi, happened to enter the school hall.
Seeing this, he was greatly surprised and praised him.
He looked around and said to the guests:
“This boy is peaceful and self-possessed.
He possesses the temperament of our family.”
Inside the residence there was lush bamboo.
Consequently, he built a separate room for Yīn beside the grove,
ordering him to stay there alone,
and regularly fed him by placing sumptuous meals on a bronze platter.
He then used this to urge and encourage his other sons, saying:
“If you all are as cautious and careful as Zūnyàn,
you will naturally receive the food of the separate room by the bamboo grove and the heavily loaded bronze platter.”
Yīn’s cousin, the Huángmén Shìláng Yù, especially valued him.
He once said to others:
“This child still has his foal teeth,
but he is already the Dragon Pattern of our family.
After another ten years,
we will have to seek him out a thousand *lǐ* away.”
Yù once composed poetry with more than ten other people.
Yīn read it once and could recite it,
without missing anything.
When he grew up,
he excelled at pure conversation,
had a beautiful voice and manner,
his spirit and demeanor were brilliant and perceptive,
and his appearance and mannerisms were remarkable.
When scholars and officials saw him,
none failed to respect him and find him unusual.
Those with foresight often predicted a great future for him.
During the Zhèngguāng period,
he followed his father to Bǐngzhōu.
His nature was tranquil and silent,
and he loved mountains and waters.
He consequently entered Xuánwèng Shān, west of Jìnyáng, to study.
At the beginning of the Xiàochāng era,
Jīn became the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dìngzhōu,
and Yīn also followed his father to the post.
For military merit, he was appointed Supervisor of the Yǔlín Guards (Yǔlín Jiān),
and was granted the title Viscount (Nán) of Wèichāng,
but he did not accept the appointment.
When Zhōngshān was captured by Dù Luòzhōu,
his entire family was imprisoned and bound.
Not long after,
Luòzhōu was defeated,
and the family fell captive to Gě Róng.
Róng wished to give him his daughter as a wife,
and also forced him to accept a false official position.
Yīn then feigned illness,
secretly held several measures (gě) of ox blood in his mouth,
and spat it out in front of the crowd,
then pretended to be mute and unable to speak.
Róng believed it to be true,
and ceased his attempts.
In the beginning of the Yǒng'ān era,
he returned to Luò(yáng),
and was appointed Attendant Gentleman of the Palace (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng).
He was eighteen years old at the time.
When Yuán Hào entered Luò(yáng),
Yīn’s cousin Kǎn, who was the General of the Northern Palace (Běi Zhōngláng Jiāng),
was stationed at Héliáng.
Yīn happened to arrive at Kǎn’s location
just as the Emperor (Chéngyú) lost control of the capital,
and arrived at the river at night.
Although Kǎn escorted the imperial carriage (Chējià) across the river northward,
he secretly wished to flee south.
Yīn strongly advised him against it.
They consequently escorted the entourage together, reaching Jiànzhōu.
He was appointed Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
Yīn believed that the troubles of the world had not yet ceased,
and his intention was to retire and conceal himself.
Thus, he pleaded illness,
and went into seclusion on Sōngshān with his friend, the Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngzhí Shìláng) Xíng Shào of Héjiān.
When Emperor Zhuāng executed Ěrzhū Róng,
his cousin Kǎn participated and assisted in the councils (Wéiwò).
The imperial court appointed his father Jīn as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Bǐngzhōu and Grand Administrator of the Northern Circuit (Běidào Dà Xíngtái).
Yīn followed him to the post.
There was a man from Hándān named Yáng Kuān,
who requested to join the righteous followers (Yìcóng) serving outside the court.
Yīn requested Jīn to accept him.
Soon after, Emperor Xiàozhuāng died in captivity (Yōubēng).
Yīn, intending to return to the capital at that time,
traveled until he reached Hándān.
Passing by Yáng Kuān’s house,
he was captured by Kuān.
Arriving at Xiāngzhōu,
he met the Governor (Cìshǐ) Líu Dàn.
Considering Yīn's renowned family and great virtue,
(Líu Dàn) felt profound sympathy for him.
He handed him over to the Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) Mùróng Báizé for restricted detention.
He dispatched the company commander Gǒng Róngguì to guard him under restriction and send him to the capital.
When they reached Ānyáng Pavilion,
Yīn said to Róngguì:
"My family has been loyal officials for generations,
dedicating sincerity to the Wèi court.
Our family is ruined and the state is broken,
resulting in this situation.
Although I am called a captive,
what face do I have left to see the enemies of my sovereign and father?
To be allowed to hang myself with a single rope,
and then have my head sent away,
that would be your great kindness."
Róngguì felt deeply sympathetic and moved,
and consequently fled together with him.
Yīn then sought refuge with the Gāo Áng brothers.
After hiding in concealment for several years,
when Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) arrived at Xìndū,
(Yīn) presented his calling card at the outer gate (Yuánmén).
He was immediately granted an audience.
He praised the rise of the new destiny,
and recounted the disasters that had befallen his family.
His words were sorrowful yet spirited,
tears and mucus flowed copiously,
and Shénwǔ changed his demeanor because of him.
He was immediately appointed Gentleman of the Secretariat of the Grand Administrator (Xíngtái Lángzhōng).
When the main army marched south to attack Yè,
they passed through Yáng Kuān’s village.
Kuān kowtowed before Yīn’s horse, begging for forgiveness.
Yīn said to him:
"For a person not to recognize kindness and righteousness
is also probably a common occurrence.
I do not resent you,
there is no need to be alarmed."
At that time Yè had not yet fallen.
Shénwǔ commanded Yīn to compose a text for the sacrifice to Heaven.
As soon as the offering was burned, the city fell.
Following this, he was promoted to Vice Director of the Right of the Grand Administrator (Dà Xíngtái Yòuchéng).
At that time, the foundation of the hegemonic enterprise was being laid,
and military and state affairs were extensive.
All official documents, proclamations, and orders
originated from Yīn and Cuī Xiǎo.
Having suffered the misfortune of his family,
he followed the rituals of mourning,
eating only salt and rice,
grieving and emaciated to the bone.
Shénwǔ pitied him
and tried to comfort him.
During the Battle of Hánlíng,
Yīn was always the first to charge the enemy line.
His colleagues all marveled and sighed, saying:
"Yáng, the scholar,
has now become a warrior!
The benevolent must be brave;
this is certainly not an empty theory."
After a period,
he submitted a memorial requesting release from his post to return and bury his family.
Within his immediate family,
two persons were posthumously granted the titles Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Grand Tutor (Tàifù), Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), and Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn);
three persons were granted Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū), and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng);
five persons were granted Grand Minister (Púyè) and Minister (Shàngshū);
and more than twenty persons were Governors (Cìshǐ) and Grand Administrators (Tàishǒu).
The lavishness of these posthumous honors
was unprecedented in history.
When the funeral procession set out,
the auspicious and inauspicious ritual guards stretched for more than twenty *lǐ*.
Nearly ten thousand people attended the funeral.
That day was deep winter with bitter cold,
and the wind and snow were severe and heavy.
Yīn walked barefoot, wailing loudly.
All who saw him grieved for him.
Soon after, he was summoned to Jìnyáng,
and remained in his original post.
Yīn’s cousin Yòuqīng, who was the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qízhōu,
was executed for straight talk that offended the Emperor's intent.
Yīn was sad and terrified upon hearing this.
Due to grief and distress, he fell ill.
Later, he urgently traveled to the warm springs of Yànmén to treat his sickness.
Guō Xiù, who had always resented Yīn's ability,
consequently sent him a letter to frighten him, saying:
"King Gāo (Gāo Huān) intends to send you to the Emperor."
He then advised Yīn to flee.
Yīn then abandoned his clothes and hat by the riverside as if he had drowned himself,
changed his name and surname,
called himself Líu Shì'ān,
entered Sōngshān,
and lived in seclusion with the Śramaṇa Tánmú Zhǐ and others, erasing his traces.
He also secretly traveled to Guāngzhōu,
and then went east to Tián Héngdǎo.
He made teaching and recitation his occupation.
The scholars along the coast
called him Mr. Líu (Líu Xiānshēng).
The Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) Wáng Yuánjǐng secretly protected him.
Shénwǔ learned that Yīn was still alive.
He dispatched Yīn’s cousin Bǎo Yī carrying a letter to console him,
and also sent Xī Sīyè, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guāngzhōu, to search for him,
and send him forth with propriety.
Shénwǔ was pleased to see him.
He was appointed Administrator (Sīmǎ) in the establishment of the Duke of Tàiyuán (Tàiyuán Gōng Kāifǔ).
He was promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ).
He was again appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Grand Administrator (Dà Xíngtái Yòuchéng).
He was enfeoffed as Marquis (Hóu) of Huàyīn County.
He was promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Palace Gate (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
Shénwǔ married him to his concubine-born daughter.
He also held the concurrent post of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
and served as the chief envoy to court Liáng.
When he reached Què'áo Garrison,
there was an old Buddhist temple belonging to Yīn’s family within the prefecture.
He entered the monastery to pay his respects.
Seeing the portrait (róngxiàng) of the Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
he was so overcome with grief that he wailed loudly,
vomiting several *shēng* of blood.
Consequently, he became ill and could not continue the journey.
He was carried, sick, back to Yè.
After a long time,
he concurrently held the position of Gentleman (Lángzhōng) of the Personnel Department (Lìbù) of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū) while retaining his original post.
At the end of the Wǔdìng era,
because of his excellent reputation and merit,
he was promoted directly to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
He was granted the additional titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn),
retaining his roles related to imperial studies and personnel selection (Diǎn Xuǎn) as before.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he held the position of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince concurrently with his original office,
and was separately enfeoffed as the Baron of Yángxià County.
He was further ordered to supervise the Grand Astrologer,
and was promoted to Right Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He married the Grand Princess Tàiyuán,
who was the former Empress of Wèi Xiàojìng.
When a pheasant gathered at his dwelling,
he was again appointed Administrator with the Rights of the Three Dukes and Left Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and his title was changed to Duke of Huàshān Commandery.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to be Prefect of the Department of State Affairs,
and was again appointed Grandee Consultant and General of the Cavalry.
In the tenth year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Kāifēng Wáng.
When Emperor Wénxuān died,
none of the officials shed tears,
but Yīn was overcome by grief.
When the heir of Jǐnán took power,
his position and trust grew even greater;
court regulations and state commands
were decided by him alone.
He practiced sincerity and embodied the Way;
at that time, there were no dissenting opinions.
In the second month of the first year of the Gānmíng era,
he was executed by Emperor Xiàozhāo.
He was fifty years old at the time.
At the end of the Tiāntǒng era,
he was posthumously granted the title Minister of Works.
Yīn was a son of a noble house,
and earned early renown.
His demeanor, appearance, and critical judgment
were praised by both the court and the public.
When his family met disaster,
only two younger brothers, one younger sister, and several granddaughters of his older brother remained.
He raised the orphans and infants,
his compassionate intent and gentle expression
far surpassed others.
He valued righteousness and slighted wealth.
The gifts and awards he received throughout his career
were mostly distributed among his relatives.
More than ten cousins, younger brothers, and nephews
depended on him to provide their meals.
He frequently encountered misfortune and difficulty,
daringly facing hardship and danger.
For even the smallest kindness,
he repaid it heavily;
but enemies who threatened his life,
he dismissed without question.
He managed official selection for over twenty years,
regarding the commendation and promotion of worthy men
as his personal responsibility.
However, in selecting officials, he often focused on their speech and appearance,
which sometimes attracted criticism.
People said that Yīn's appointment of personnel
was like a poor scholar buying melons,
always choosing the biggest ones.
When Yīn heard this,
he dismissed it.
He had keen hearing and a powerful memory;
half a face (a brief sight) he did not forget.
Whenever he summoned someone for an interview,
sometimes he would call out only the surname,
or sometimes only the given name,
and there was never a mistake.
Later, an official candidate named Lǔ Mànhàn
claimed he was too lowly and insignificant
to be recognized personally.
Yīn said:
"Previously, when you were in Yuánzǐsī Fāng,
riding a scraggly donkey with a docked tail,
you passed by me without dismounting.
