You covered your face with a block of yeast.
How could I not recognize you?"
Mànhàn was astonished and submitted.
Yīn further teased him, saying:
"The name defines the substance;
Mànhàn truly lives up to his name."
Once, he ordered a clerk to announce a person's name,
and the clerk mistakenly called Lú Shìshēn as Shìchēn.
Shìshēn identified himself.
Yīn said:
"Master Lú (Lú Láng) is as glossy as jade;
therefore, his name ought to follow the character for jade."
After marrying the Princess,
he wore a purple silk robe
and a large belt woven with gold thread.
When he met Lǐ Shù,
he felt somewhat ashamed,
and said:
"These clothes of mine
were all tailored within the palace.
Now that I have seen Zǐjiāng,
I cannot help but feel embarrassed."
When he held the position of Chief Minister,
he controlled the critical affairs of state,
and though there were countless threads and myriad beginnings,
his spirit never stalled in their application.
From the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era onward,
when the sovereign lost virtue,
maintaining order and correcting errors
truly depended upon him.
Whenever the Son of Heaven appeared on the balcony,
and Dukes and Ministers knelt to receive appointments,
issuing decrees and commands,
and proclaiming imperial edicts,
Yīn's language was gentle and articulate,
his divine demeanor impressive and outstanding.
When the hundreds of officials watched and listened,
none failed to be moved with awe.
From the time he occupied high office,
private interactions ceased at his gate.
He slighted goods and wealth,
and valued benevolence and righteousness.
The accumulated rewards and gifts he received throughout his career,
which amounted to vast sums,
were scattered among his extended family.
In his personal cabinet,
there were only several thousand scrolls of books.
The Grand Guardian, Píngyuán Wáng Lóngzhī, was Yīn's neighbor.
Yīn once saw several wealthy Hu men outside Lóngzhī's gate,
and said to his attendants:
"Fortunately, I do not have such things outside my gate."
His nature was thorough, cautious, and circumspect,
as if he lacked sufficiency.
Whenever he heard a post-imperial decree,
his complexion would instantly change to severe.
When Emperor Wénxuān was critically ill,
seeing that the positions of the two princes, Chángshān and Chángguǎng, brought them close to the center of power,
he deeply worried about the succession.
Yīn, along with the Left Director of the Department of State Affairs Píngqín Wáng Guīyàn,
Court Attendant Yān Zǐxiàn, and Palace Gate Attendant Zhèng Zǐmò, received the final edict to assist in governance.
They all realized that the prestige and reputation of the two princes were already immense and harbored suspicious and fearful intentions toward them.
Initially, when in Jìnyáng,
since the great sovereign was lying in the funeral hall,
and the Son of Heaven was in mourning,
they proposed that the Prince of Chángshān should reside in the Eastern Residence,
and that all matters they wished to memorialize
should first be referred to him for consultation and decision.
This lasted for twenty days and then stopped.
They subsequently wanted the Prince of Chángshān to follow the imperial coffin to Yè,
and leave the Prince of Chángguǎng to guard Jìnyáng.
The administrators again conceived doubts and misgivings,
so both princes followed the procession all the way to Yè.
Zǐxiàn established a plan
to place the Grand Empress Dowager in the Běi Gōng,
transferring authority to the Empress Dowager.
Furthermore, since the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
titles and rewards had been excessively conferred.
At this point,
Yīn first memorialized to relinquish his title of Administrator and Prince,
and all those who had illicitly received favors and honors were subsequently dismissed and stripped of rank.
Because of this, those courtiers and favorites who had lost their positions
all turned their allegiance to the two uncles.
Although Gāo Guīyàn initially shared the same intent,
he soon turned against them,
revealing all the details of the plots for exclusion and suspicion to the two princes.
Kězhūhún Tiānhé also frequently said:
"If the two princes are not executed,
the young sovereign will never be secure."
Sòng Qīndào reported directly to the Emperor,
claiming that since the prestige and power of the two uncles were immense,
it was advisable to quickly eliminate them.
The Emperor did not permit this, saying:
"You may discuss the details of this matter thoroughly with the Prefect (Yīn)."
Yīn and the others discussed appointing the two princes as Regional Governors.
Believing the Emperor to be compassionate,
and fearing he might not approve their memorial,
they instead sent a joint report to the Empress Dowager,
detailing the risks and security issues.
There was a palace woman named Lǐ Chāngyí,
who was the wife of Gāo Zhòngmì, the Regional Governor of Běi Yùzhōu.
She had entered the palace due to Gāo Zhòngmì's incident.
The Empress Dowager treated Chāngyí with familiarity, recognizing her as kin,
and loved her dearly.
The Empress Dowager showed the report to her,
and Chāngyí secretly informed the Grand Empress Dowager.
Yīn and the others then discussed that it would not be suitable for both princes to leave together.
They memorialized that the Prince of Chángguǎng should be made Grand Marshal and Regional Governor of Bìngzhōu,
and the Prince of Chángshān should be made Grand Tutor and Director of the Affairs of the Department of State.
When the Èr Wáng (Two Kings) accepted their posts,
they held a great assembly of all officials at the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs).
Yáng Yīn and his associates were all preparing to attend together.
Zǐmò stopped them,
saying:
"The situation is unpredictable,
and we must not act carelessly."
Yīn said:
"We are wholly sincere in serving the state.
How can Chángshān Wáng take up his post,
and we refuse to attend?
Why do you suddenly have this concern?"
Chángguǎng Wáng had already concealed several tens of household servants in the rear chambers of the Lù Shàngshū's (Director of the Department of State Affairs) office,
and he had connections with several esteemed nobles present at the banquet.
He also made an agreement with these powerful aristocratic families:
when serving wine reached Yīn and his group,
"We will each urge them to drink double cups,
and they will certainly make a formal refusal.
On my first call,
'Seize the wine!'
the second call,
'Seize the wine!'
the third call,
'Why don't you seize them?'
you fellows immediately seize them."
When the banquet took place, everything proceeded accordingly.
Yīn declared loudly:
"Are the various kings forming a rebellion,
intending to kill loyal and upright men?
Honoring the Son of Heaven,
reducing the power of the feudal lords,
and sincerely serving the nation
should not lead to this outcome!"
Chángshān Wáng wanted to delay,
but Chángguǎng Wáng said:
"We cannot."
Thereupon, Yīn, Tiānhé, and Qīndào were all violently beaten with fists and clubs,
blood streaming from their heads and faces,
each held down by ten men.
Xuēgū Yán and Kāng Mǎi were sent to seize Zǐmò at the Shàngyào Jú (Imperial Medical Office).
Zǐmò said:
"Not listening to the words of the wise
has led to this situation.
Is this not fate?"
The two paternal uncles led Gāo Guīyàn, Hèbá Rén, and Húlǜ Jīn, surrounding Yīn and his associates, and violently burst into the Yúnlóng Mén (Gate).
They saw the Commander-in-Chief Chìlì Sāo;
they beckoned him but he did not advance,
so they ordered the cavalry to kill him.
The Kāifǔ (Founder of a Prefecture), Chéng Xiūníng, blocked the gate,
but Guīyàn explained the situation to him,
and then they were able to enter.
They brought Yīn and his associates before the Emperor.
Chángguǎng Wáng and Guīyàn remained outside the Zhūhuá Mén (Gate).
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu (Grand Empress Dowager) oversaw the proceedings from the Zhāoyáng Diàn (Hall),
while the Tàihòu (Empress Dowager) and the Dì (Emperor) stood nearby.
Chángshān Wáng knocked his head on the ground [using a tile],
stepped forward and said:
"Your subject and Your Majesty are connected by blood.
Yáng Zūnyàn and his group wished to usurp imperial authority,
monopolizing power and benefits for themselves.
From the Wáng (Princes) and Gōng (Dukes) downward,
everyone has been standing still and holding their breath in fear.
They acted as interdependent conspirators,
creating the foundation for rebellion.
If we did not plan quickly,
they would certainly become a calamity for the Imperial Ancestral Temple and the State.
Your subject and Zhàn and the others, valuing the affairs of the nation,
and Hèbá Rén, Húlǜ Jīn, and others, regretting the foundation established by Xiàn Huángdì (the Late Emperor),
jointly seized Zūnyàn and his associates and brought them into the palace.
We dared not execute them yet.
For this mistake of acting without permission,
our crime warrants ten thousand deaths."
The Emperor remained silent at the time.
The Lǐngjūn (Commander) Liú Táozhī and his attendants guarding the steps
knocked their swords and looked up,
but the Emperor did not glance at them.
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu ordered them to withdraw their arms,
but they refused.
She then sternly shouted:
"If you wretches do not obey now, your heads will fall immediately!"
Then they withdrew.
She then asked where Yáng Láng (Sir Yáng) was.
Hèbá Rén replied:
"One eye has already popped out."
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu sadly exclaimed:
"What crime has Yáng Láng committed?
Wouldn't it have been better to let him live?"
She then reproached the Emperor, saying:
"These people harbored rebellion,
intending to kill my two sons,
and then me.
Why did you allow them freedom?"
The Emperor still could not speak.
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu was both angry and mournful,
and the Wáng and Gōng all wept.
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu said:
"How can I allow my mother and son to be controlled by an old Hàn woman?"
The Tàihòu bowed in thanks.
Chángshān Wáng continued knocking his head without stopping.
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu said to the Emperor:
"Why don't you comfort your uncle?"
The Emperor then said:
"Even the Son of Heaven dare not treat his uncles sparingly;
how dare I spare these Hàn fellows?
I only beg for my own life;
I will descend from the hall myself,
and these people may be dealt with by my uncle as he sees fit."
Consequently, they were all executed.
Because Zǐmò had previously slandered him,
Chángguǎng Wáng fabricated an imperial edict
and therefore first ripped out his tongue
and cut off his hands.
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu went to Yīn's funeral,
weeping and saying:
"Yáng Láng was loyal but suffered punishment."
She used imperial gold to fashion an eye for him,
personally inserting it,
saying:
"To show my sentiment."
Chángshān Wáng also regretted having killed him.
Previously, a children's rhyme said:
"The white sheep is bald head and tail,
the male goat sprouts horns."
It also said:
"Sheep, sheep, eat wild grass;
if you don't eat wild grass, stay away from my path;
if you don't stay away, I will beat your brains."
It also said:
"Ādī Gū is in danger,
Dàorén Gūfū is dead."
The character for "sheep" refers to Yīn;
the component "horn"
refers to the use of a knife (or blade).
"Dàorén"
refers to the deposed Emperor's childhood name.
Tàiyuán Gōngzhǔ (Princess) once became a nun,
hence she was called
"Ādī Gū."
Yīn, Zǐxiàn, and Tiānhé were all maternal uncles-by-marriage to the Emperor.
Thereupon, by the command of the Son of Heaven, an edict was issued condemning them,
confining the crime to their persons alone,
and not prosecuting their family members.
Shortly afterward, the assets of the five families were still confiscated.
Wáng Xī firmly remonstrated,
and consequently, only one branch of each family was stripped of assets,
and the younger children and brothers were simply stripped of their official titles.
After Zūnyàn died,
Zhào Yànshēn, the Zhōngshū Lìng (Prefect of the Imperial Secretariat), replaced him to oversee all governmental affairs.
Yáng Xiūzhī, the Hónglú Shàoqīng (Vice Director of the Court of Dependencies), privately said to someone:
"To travel a thousand *lǐ*,
yet kill the finest steed and drive a lame donkey,
is truly deeply regrettable."
The poems, *fù*, memorials, and treatises written by Yīn were numerous,
but scattered and lost after his execution.
His disciples collected what they could find, amounting to over ten thousand words.
Yàn Zǐxiàn,
courtesy name Jìzé,
was a man from Xiàluò in Guǎnghàn.
When he was young, a physiognomist told him:
"Your service will be in the Hú (Northern Barbarian) dynasty,
but your wealth and honor will be in Qí and Zhào."
Later,
when the Yǔwén clan established supremacy in Guānzhōng,
he was employed as a Diǎnqiān (document clerk),
and was assigned to travel on a mission to the Rúrú.
Zǐxiàn wished to verify the physiognomist's words,
and returned home.
Gāozǔ (Emperor) was greatly pleased upon seeing him,
gave him Huáiyáng Gōngzhǔ (Princess) in marriage,
and treated him exceptionally well.
During Xiǎnzǔ's reign,
his office reached Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Kāifǔ.
After Jǐnán ascended the throne,
the trust placed in him became even greater,
and he was appointed Yòu Púshè (Right Director of the Department of State Affairs).
Zǐxiàn was naturally very strong,
and also had little hair on his head.
During the moment of distress,
he pushed through the crowd and ran out of the Department gates,
but Húlǜ Guāng pursued and captured him.
Zǐxiàn sighed, saying:
"A man's planning was too slow,
and thus I have come to this end."
Kězhūhún Tiānhé
was the youngest brother of Dàoyuán.
Because Dàoyuán's merits were great,
he was given Dōngpíng Gōngzhǔ (Princess) in marriage.
He was repeatedly promoted to Lǐngjūn Dà Jiāngjūn (Commander-in-Chief of the Guards),
and Kāifǔ.
When Jǐnán Wáng ascended the throne,
he was granted the position of Tèjìn (Special Advance),
renamed Bólíng Gōng (Duke),
and killed together with Yáng Yīn.
Sòng Qīndào,
a native of Guǎngpíng,
was the grandson of Biàn, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of the Wèi dynasty.
He first served as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) to the General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn),
managing the documents and records.
Later, he became a Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng).
He was also ordered to reside in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) to teach the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ) state affairs.
Zhèng Zǐmò became known for his literary talent,
and was also favored by the ruler.
Qīndào was originally a legal official,
not very knowledgeable about ancient and modern matters.
Whenever there was a doubtful issue,
he invariably consulted Zǐmò.
The two men were favored in both palaces (the imperial palace and the crown prince’s palace),
and even the princes and high-ranking officials treated them with reverence and awe.
Qīndào was further promoted to Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
He and Yáng Yīn were jointly commissioned to bestow posthumous titles upon the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) and Prefect of Zhàozhōu.
Zhèng Yí,
styled Zǐmò,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His great-grandfather, Jù,
served as the Administrator of Péngchéng during the Wèi dynasty,
having moved there from Xíngyáng.
Yí was intelligent and astute,
and fairly well-versed in literary studies.
He initially served as Wine Libationer (Jìjiǔ) of the Eastern Gallery (Dōnggé) for the Duke of Tàiyuán.
He had a particularly close and friendly relationship with Sòng Qīndào,
and Qīndào always treated him as a mentor.
Yáng Yīn initially slighted Sòng and Zhèng,
and did not treat them with due respect.
Soon, however, Yīn formed a bond with the sovereign
and participated in handling the ruler’s final decree (Gùmìng).
Qīndào resumed his old intimacy with [Fà] of Jìnán,
and they mutually promoted each other,
sharing everything without reservation.
In the early period of the Qiánmíng era,
Qīndào was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
The power and influence of the two men
was equal to that of Yīn.
When Yīn was about to be executed,
Xíng Zǐcái wept and said:
“Although Lord Yáng is dying today,
it is regrettable that he does not have a good companion (to die with).”
Yí was later commissioned together with Yīn to bestow posthumous titles upon the Minister of the Palace (Diànzhōng Shàngshū) and Prefect of Guǎngzhōu.
Yí’s younger brother, Kàng,
styled Zǐxìn,
had considerable literary talent.
In the late period of the Wǔpíng era,
he concurrently served as a Junior Secretary of the Left and Right (Zuǒyòu Lángzhōng),
and was commissioned as an attending scholar at the Wénlín Guǎn.
Biographies, Chapter 27: Péi Ràngzhī (Younger brothers: Zhōu Zhī, Yàn Zhī) - Huángfǔ Hé - Lǐ Gòu - Zhāng Yànzhī - Lù Áng - Wáng Sōngnián - Liú Yī
Péi Ràngzhī,
styled Shìlǐ.
When he was sixteen, he lost his father,
and was almost unable to bear the grief.
His mother, Lady Xīn, tearfully patted him and said:
“If you abandon me and destroy your nature,
can you be considered a filial son?”
From then on, he exerted himself.
Lady Xīn
was an exemplary woman of high integrity
and was also familiar with rites and regulations.
After her husband's death,
since most of her sons were young and weak,
she broadly invited teachers and friends,
or personally taught them.
For all the auspicious and inauspicious rituals and ceremonies of her inner and outer relatives,
many took her as a model.
Ràngzhī was fond of learning in his youth,
possessed literary talent and sharp debating skills,
and quickly gained renown.
During the Tiānpíng era of the Wèi dynasty, he was recommended as an Outstanding Talent (Xiùcái),
and achieved the highest rank in the policy examination.
He was successively promoted to Administrator (Lángzhōng) of Military Farms (Túntián) and Guests (Zhǔkè).
A saying circulated in the Provincial Department (Shěngzhōng):
“The one who can compose poetry
is Péi Ràngzhī.”
He became the Recording Secretary (Jìshì) for the Duke of Tàiyuán's Establishment (Kāifǔ).
He was friendly with Yáng Yīn,
and when they met, they engaged in pure conversation (qīngtán) all day long.
Yīn often said:
“This man is elegant and prominent,
Péi Wénjì has not perished!”
When an envoy from Liáng arrived,
the Emperor ordered Ràngzhī to act concurrently as Administrator of Guests (Zhǔkè Láng).
His second younger brother, Zhōu Zhī, fled to Guān Yòu (the area west of the pass),
and all five of Ràngzhī’s brothers were arrested and imprisoned.
Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) asked:
“Where is Zhōu Zhī?”
Ràngzhī replied:
“In the past, regarding the two states of Wú and Shǔ,
the Zhūgě brothers were each able to achieve their ambitions.
Moreover, Ràngzhī’s aged mother is still alive,
and the division between ruler and subject is settled.
Losing loyalty and filial piety
is something a common fool would not do.
I sincerely wish for Your Excellency to treat others with sincerity and trustworthiness.
If you deal with people without trustworthiness,
how can people trust you in turn?
To establish supremacy based on this
is like seeking the Way by walking backward.”
Shénwǔ praised his words,
and his brothers were all released.
He successively served as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) to the General-in-Chief Wénxiāng,
and concurrently as Draftsman (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
Later, he concurrently served as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and was sent as an envoy to Liáng.
Wénxiāng once entered the court,
and Ràngzhī served as his guide and usher.
His deportment was refined and reserved.
Wénxiāng looked at him and said:
“Shìlǐ is a fine Draftsman.”
He was promoted to Supervising Vice Director (Cháng Jiān Zhōngshū Shìláng),
and took charge of the Draftsmen.
When Qí received the abdication,
Emperor Jìng ceded his throne and resided in a separate palace.
When bidding farewell to his ministers,
Ràngzhī wept and sighed mournfully.
For his participation in managing the ritual procedures,
he was enfeoffed as a male of Níngdū County (Níngdū Xiàn Nán).
The Emperor wanted to appoint him Palace Attendant (Huángmén Láng),
but some argued that he was physically heavy
and unsuitable for quick service (qūshì).
He was then appointed Administrator of Qīnghé (Qīnghé Tàishǒu).
Not long after arriving in the commandery,
Yáng Yīn said to Ràngzhī’s younger brothers:
“I have a close relationship with your esteemed elder brother.
I was looking forward to hearing about his good governance.
Just now, someone came from Qīnghé
and reported that corrupt officials have retracted their activities,
and bandits and thieves have ceased their disturbances.
The predicted achievement within a year
has arrived even sooner.”
In Qīnghé, there were two influential officials, Tián Zhuǎn Guì and Sūn Shě Xīng, who, as longtime officials, were deceitful and cunning.
They engaged in much encroachment and extortion.
They used various pretexts to threaten people and seize their wealth.
Based on the law, the value of their illicit gains was not sufficient for the death penalty.
Ràngzhī, viewing their actions as disrupting the law,
executed them.
At that time, Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, was the Area Commander (Cīzhōu Mù).
He sent his subordinate official (Bù Cóngshì) to investigate the case.
Gāo Dézhèng, the Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng), who had a previous disagreement with Ràngzhī,
submitted a memorial stating:
“At the moment Your Majesty received the abdication,
Ràngzhī was attached to and cherished the Wèi court,
weeping and sighing.
Compared to being an inner official,
this appointment (as Prefect) was not what he truly desired.”
Subsequently, Yáng Yīn pleaded for him,
saying:
“His crime does not warrant death.”
Wénxuān (Emperor) was greatly angered
and said to Yīn:
“Do you wish to share a grave with Péi Ràngzhī?”
After this, no one dared to speak up.
The memorial was presented,
and he was eventually granted death at his home.
Ràngzhī’s second younger brother was Zhōu Zhī.
Zhōu Zhī,
styled Shìzhèng,
was fond of Confucian studies in his youth.
He started his career as a Doctor (Bóshì) of the Imperial University (Tàixué).
He once borrowed a hundred scrolls of books from Cháng Jǐng,
and returned them after about ten days.
Jǐng doubted that he could have read them,
so he questioned him on each scroll.
Zhōu Zhī answered every question without fail.
Jǐng exclaimed with admiration:
“Yīng Fèng read five lines at a glance,
Ní Héng memorized upon a single reading.
Now I see this again in Master Péi!”
When Yáng Yīn closed his gates to rebury his family members,
he entrusted Zhōu Zhī to write over ten tomb inscriptions (mùzhì) at once,
and all the writings were commendable.
Ràngzhī, Zhōu Zhī, and Huángfǔ Hé’s younger brother Liàng, were all famous in Luòxià (Luòyáng).
People at the time had a saying:
“Zhōu is superior to Ràng,
and Hé is inferior to Liàng.”
Gāo Gān, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), sent a letter saying:
“I invite you to serve as Staff Officer (Cānjūn) of the Household Department (Hù Cáo).”
Zhōu Zhī wrote back refusing the appointment.
When the Prince of Pèi established the Grand Marshal’s (Dà Sīmǎ) headquarters,
Zhōu Zhī was summoned to be the Recording Secretary (Jìshì).
After the capital was moved to Yè,
Zhōu Zhī remained in Hénán.
Dúgū Xìn, the Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn) of Western Wèi, entered and occupied Jīnyǒng.
He appointed Zhōu Zhī as an Aide (Shǔ) in his Establishment (Kāifǔ),
and referred to him as
the “Lost Talent of Luòyáng.”
When Xìn was defeated,
Zhōu Zhī lived on Mount Nánshān.
Wáng Yuánguǐ, the Prefect of Luòzhōu, summoned him to be an Inner Attendant Official (Zhōng Cóngshì).
Suddenly, the Western army arrived,
but soon retreated.
Zhōu Zhī then followed the Western army into the pass (Guān).
Emperor Wén of Zhōu appointed him as Administrator (Lángzhōng) of the Granary Department (Cāng Cáo) of the Grand Central Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái).
He died in office.
He was posthumously granted the title of Prefect of Xúzhōu.
Yàn Zhī,
courtesy name Shìpíng,
began diligent study at seven years old,
and was known early.
He was successively promoted to Registrar to the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Zhǔbù).
Yáng Yīn often praised him, saying:
“Among the gentry families of Hédōng,
there are quite a few capital officials,
but only the brothers of this family
have completely lost their provincial accent.”
Although Yàn Zhī was young,
he did not make frivolous friendships.
He only formed close friendships, despite the age difference, with Xīn Shù of Lǒngxī, Lǐ Huì of Zhàojùn, Lǐ Gòu of Dùnqiū, and Cuī Zhān of Qīnghé.
When Emperor Zhāo Dì’s casket was about to return to Yè,
he was transferred to be a Gentleman of the Bureau of Rites (Yícáo Láng).
He was especially versed in the historical precedents and ceremonial records of past dynasties,
and was able to standardize and rectify all funeral rites.
He served as the Administrator of Yǒngchāng Commandery (Tàishǒu).
When travelers passed through the commandery,
he provided supplies from his private funds,
something unprecedented among officials,
often paying expenses on behalf of the populace,
and he was cherished by the clerks and people.
When Qí perished, he served Zhōu,
and died while serving as the Administrator of Yīchuān (Yīchuān Tàishǒu).
Huángpǔ Hé,
courtesy name Chángxié,
was a native of Cháonà in Āndìng.
His ancestors moved to reside in Hànzhōng due to official posts.
His grandfather, Chéng,
was the Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Qín and Liáng prefectures during the Southern Qí.
His father, Huī,
courtesy name Zǐxuán,
was the Administrator (Jùnshǒu) of Āndìng and Lüèyáng commanderies under the Liáng dynasty.
In the second year of Zhèngshǐ of Wèi (505 CE),
he followed his father-in-law, Xiàhóu Dàoqiān, into Wèi territory.
Dàoqiān separately submitted a record of merit,
wishing to list Huī as the chief conspirator.
Huī said:
“At the inception of the planning,
I was fundamentally not involved.
Although I covet honor and reward,
I would be inwardly ashamed.”
He thus refused and did not consent.
Yáng Língyòu, the Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Liángzhōu, respected his sincerity and integrity,
and memorialized to have him appointed as Commandant of the General Who Subdues the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Fǔ Sīmǎ).
He died later.
Hé became fatherless at eleven,
and his mother, Lady Xiàhóu Shì,
was talented, intelligent, and upheld ritual principles.
She personally taught him the Classics.
When he grew up,
he was deep and composed, possessing refined tolerance,
and was especially knowledgeable about rites and ceremony.
Family relatives often
consulted him regarding auspicious and inauspicious events.
He died while serving as the Administrator of Jìyīn (Jìyīn Tàishǒu).
Lǐ Gòu,
courtesy name Zǔjī,
was a native of Líyáng.
His grandfather, Píng,
was the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè) under the Wèi dynasty.
When Gòu was young, he was praised for his integrity and uprightness.
He began his career as a Staff Officer to an Open-Palace (Kāifǔ Cānjūn),
and was successively promoted to Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Qiáozhōu,
where he died.
Gòu's younger paternal cousin, Shù,
was the son of Xié, the Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng) under the Wèi dynasty.
He was upright, refined, and fond of learning.
His demeanor and principles
were strongly characteristic of his family style.
He was gradually promoted to Magistrate of Línzhāng (Línzhāng Lìng).
When the *Wèi Shū* (History of the Wèi) was released,
Shù, along with Lú Fěi, Wáng Sōngnián, and others, complained about its unfairness,
and were all imprisoned.
Wèi Shōu’s book stated that Wáng Huìlóng claimed to be a native of Tàiyuán,
and also said that Wáng Qióng did not manage affairs well;
it appended Lú Tóng to the biography of Lú Xuán;
it recorded that Lǐ Píng was from Chénliú,
and claimed his family was poor and humble.
Therefore, Fěi and the others initiated the lawsuit,
telling Yáng Yīn:
“Wèi Shōu deserves execution.”
Yīn sided with and assisted Wèi Shōu,
and consequently reported Fěi and the others to Emperor Xiǎnzǔ as criminals,
resulting in them all having their heads shaved and receiving two hundred lashes.
Shù died in the Línzhāng prison.
Shù’s elder brother, Yuè, grieved over this,
and for the rest of his life never passed through the gates of Línzhāng County (Línzhāng Xiàn).
Zhāng Yànzhī,
courtesy name Xīdé.
He was orphaned young but possessed true filial nature.
Taught and guided by his mother, Lady Zhèng Shì,
his conduct always followed ritual precedents.
He followed Ěrzhū Róng in suppressing Yuán Hào,
and was granted the title Viscount of Wǔchéng (Wǔchéng Zǐ).
He was successively promoted to Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lángzhōng) with a salary of two thousand measures.
When Gāo Yuè campaigned against Yǐngchuān,
he was again appointed as Staff Officer of the Central Army and Concurrent Recorder (Dūdū Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Jiān Jìshì).
Yànzhī was a literary scholar,
but also possessed military ability.
He often participated in Gāo Yuè’s strategy sessions,
and frequently engaged in close combat,
personally capturing heads.
He was deeply admired and praised by Yuè.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era (550 CE),
Emperor Wénxuān arranged for the Prince of Gāoyáng (Gāoyáng Wáng) to marry Yànzhī’s daughter as his consort,
and ordered him to go to Jìnyáng to complete the ceremony.
Yànzhī attended a banquet in the rear garden,
and all the seated guests composed poems.
Yànzhī’s poem said:
“When the world possesses the Way,
the sovereign is enlightened, and the ministers are upright.
Though blessed, do not rest in blessing,
that principles may forever be bequeathed to posterity.”
Emperor Wénxuān laughed and said:
“To receive your counsel and admonition
is deeply reassuring to my heart.”
Later, he was acting Regional Inspector of Běixúzhōu,
and soon afterward was appointed formally.
He was beloved by the officials and the people.
The Censor, Cuī Zǐwǔ, inspected the prefectures and commanderies.
When he reached Běixúzhōu,
he found nothing to report or impeach,
but only received several odes praising his clean governance composed by the common people.
He sighed and said:
“I originally sought evidence of wrongdoing,
but instead heard songs of praise.”
He was promoted to Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu,
but died
before taking the post.
He was posthumously granted the title of Regional Inspector of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Cìshǐ).
Lù Áng,
courtesy name Yúnjū.
In his youth, he was quick-witted and astute,
with excellent demeanor and spirit.
He loved studying tirelessly,
read widely in various texts,
and was well-versed in the greater meaning of most of the Five Classics (Wǔjīng).
He was skilled at composition,
and greatly admired by Xíng Shào of Héjiān.
Shào also associated with Áng's father, Zǐzhāng,
and once said to Zǐzhāng:
“You are like an old clam that has produced a bright pearl.
I intend to chronicle his receiving appointments among the masses, would that be acceptable?”
Because of this, his reputation grew daily,
and the refined scholars and officials
especially recommended and approved of him.
He started his career as a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng),
and successively served as Registrar to the Generalissimo Wénxiāng (Wénxiāng Dàjiāngjūn Zhǔbù),
Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
Concurrent Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
and held his main post concurrently with Equerry to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
Since the normalization of relations between Liáng and Wèi,
there were yearly diplomatic missions.
Áng always held concurrent posts for reception banquets.
When poems were composed at the emperor's table,
Áng would always finish first.
Although his skill might not be perfect,
he was praised for his quickness.
He was appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
and oversaw the compilation of the National History.
He resigned due to mourning for his father.
He observed the mourning rites perfectly,
wasting away from grief until only bones remained.
An imperial edict ordered him to resume his original post.
Wénxiāng, who was then garrisoned at Yè,
commended his extreme filial piety,
and personally visited his home to comfort and encourage him.
Áng’s mother was Princess Shàngyōng (Shàngyōng Gōngzhǔ) of Wèi,
initially enfeoffed as Lántián.
She was a noble and discerning woman
and possessed great strength of character.
Áng had five brothers (six siblings total),
all born by the Princess.
Thus, Xíng Shào often said to people:
“That Lántián produces jade
is certainly no empty saying.”
The Princess educated her sons,
and they all followed righteous principles.
Although their overwhelming grief
sprang from their nature,
their actions were nonetheless based on ritual propriety,
which was also due to the instruction of their mother.
Áng and his brothers led one another to build huts beside the grave,
carrying earth to build the mound.
The imperial court deeply admired and respected this,
issuing an edict to praise them,
and renaming the neighborhood where they lived Xiàozhōng Lǐ (The Hamlet of Completed Filial Piety).
When the mourning period was finished and he was due to inherit,
he could not bear to succeed the marquisate.
era,
the Prince of Chángshān recommended Áng for his ability.
Wénxuān personally appointed him Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
and he was later promoted to Department Director of the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Lángzhōng).
Sīzōng, the Prince of Shàngluò, served as the Magistrate of Qīngdū,
and he hired [Áng] as the Town Validator (Yì Zhōngzhèng),
allowing him to draw income (gàn) from Bèiqiū County.
When he suffered the loss of his mother,
his sorrow and mourning caused him to waste away and become haggard,
almost unable to bear the grief.
He became gravely ill,
falling into a stupor, confined to his pillow.
He also contracted a wind illness (fēng jí).
His fifth younger brother Bó fell ill and was nearing death.
He instructed his brothers, saying:
"The eldest brother’s illness is severe,
and his nature is extremely loving and compassionate.
On the day Bó dies,
you must not let the eldest brother know of it,
and the sounds of weeping must absolutely not reach him,
lest it cause him deep emotional distress."
His family did not inform him until the ritual departure (zǔ zài).
Only then was he told.
Áng heard the news and was overcome with sorrow.
He cried out once and died,
at the age of forty-eight.
Throughout Áng’s time at court,
he was profoundly cautious, reserved, and discreet.
He did not speak ill of others’ shortcomings,
nor did he boast of his own merits.
His discourse was pure and far-reaching,
and he possessed insight into human character and judgment.
Both the court and the populace deeply mourned his loss.
He was posthumously granted the titles General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His posthumous name (shì) was Wén.
The writings he authored comprised fourteen volumes
circulated throughout the world.
Many of the songs for the suburban altars and ancestral temples
of Qí were composed by Áng.
His son Yì succeeded him,
inheriting the title Marquis of Shǐpíng.
Wáng Sōngnián
was well-known in his youth.
When Wénxiāng governed Bìngzhōu,
he was appointed Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
He was repeatedly promoted to Regular Mounted Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
and assisted Lǐ Wěi as deputy envoy to Liáng.
Upon his return,
he held successive positions as Department Director in the Board of Ministries (Shàngshū Lángzhōng).
When Wèi Shōu completed the compilation of the *Book of Wèi* (*Wèi Shū*),
Sōngnián made slanderous remarks.
Wénxuān became angry,
prohibited him from office,
and administered a beating with a staff.
After more than a year he was pardoned,
appointed Magistrate of Línzhāng,
and then promoted to Grand Marshal (Sīmǎ), Adjutant (Biéjià), and Grand Validator (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of his home province.
Xiàozhāo promoted and appointed him Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
The Emperor frequently granted him a seat,
discussing governmental affairs with him,
and held him in high regard.
When Xiàozhāo died,
Sōngnián rode post haste to Yèdū to proclaim the imperial will (yí zhào).
Though tears flowed profusely as he spoke,
until the announcement was concluded,
his countenance remained unchanged,
and his speech was harmonious and rhythmic.
Once the proclamation was finished,
he wept uncontrollably, losing consciousness on the ground.
All the officials were deeply moved by his grief.
Returning to Jìnyáng,
he concurrently held the position of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and escorted the Imperial Coffin (Zǐ Gōng) back to Yè.
All the former officials avoided drawing attention to themselves,
and none dared to express their sorrow fully.
Only Sōngnián wept deeply, shedding copious tears,
which alarmed the court officials.
Although Wǔchéng resented Sōngnián's intense lingering affection for the departed ruler,
he also greatly respected him.
Sōngnián was granted the additional title of Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) while retaining his original office,
allowed to draw income (gàn) from Gāoyì County,
and participated in fixing the laws and ordinances.
He was entrusted with many important matters, both before and after this period.
He concurrently served as Vice President of the Censorate (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
Traveling from Jìnyáng to Yè,
he contracted an illness on the road and died.
He was posthumously granted the titles Minister of the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Shàngshū) and Governor of Bìngzhōu (Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His posthumous name (shì) was Píng.
His third son, Shào,
was the most renowned.
Liú Yī,
courtesy name Yànyīng,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His father, Shìmíng,
was the Wèi Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Yī’s nature was broad and generous;
he possessed dignity and seriousness.
His demeanor was admirable.
Even his close friends and intimate associates,
who spent mornings and evenings with him,
treated him with increased respect.
He loved learning,
was skilled in the Three Rites (Sān Lǐ),
and paid particular attention
to the ceremonial regulations for auspicious and inauspicious occasions.
During the Wèi Xiàochāng era,
he set aside his scholarly cap and became an Erudite of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì).
He was repeatedly promoted to Governor of Jūzhōu (Jūzhōu Cìshǐ).
The people of the border regions submitted to his authority and trustworthiness,
and he successfully maintained peace on the frontier.
When Shìzōng governed as regent,
he sent down a letter praising and commending him,
saying:
"Because your family has been loyal and pure for generations,
holding high offices (guān miǎn) through successive eras.
Your worthy younger brothers and worthy sons
all work alongside me,
entrusting their hearts to one another,
and this trust remains steadfast.
You should exert your utmost effort
to live up to the responsibilities entrusted to you,
and have no worries about wealth or high status."
When his term of office ended,
he went straight back to his hometown to attend to his father's illness,
and ultimately did not return to court.
Upon his father's death,
he became gravely ill for several years,
unable to rise without a staff.
Shìzōng summoned him to office,
but Yī pleaded illness and did not move.
His five sons,
Xuán, , Pú, Yuàn, and Zàn,
all possessed integrity and ambition
and were praised by the world.
Biography Twenty-Eight: Xíng Shào
Xíng Shào,
courtesy name Zǐcái,
was a native of Mào in Héjiān,
and a descendant of Zhēn, the Wèi Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
His father, Qiú,
was the Wèi Minister of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Guānglù Qīng).
Shào’s childhood name (xiǎo zì) was Jí.
Due to a taboo (bì) in his youth,
he never used his formal given name.
When he was five years old,
Cuī Liàng of Qīnghé, Department Director of the Wèi Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Láng), saw him and found him remarkable,
saying:
"This child will achieve great things later,
rising to prominence in status and reputation."
By the age of ten,
he was already able to write,
possessing elegant talent and insight.
He was intelligent and had a powerful memory,
reciting more than ten thousand characters daily.
His cousin Luán
had insight into human character.
He told his juniors, saying:
"To have this child among our clan members
means he is no ordinary person."
While young in Luòyáng,
as the world was peaceful,
he devoted himself, along with the renowned figures of the time, entirely to excursions in the mountains and rivers for pleasure and feasting,
neglecting diligent study.
Once, during continuous rain,
he began reading the *Book of Hàn* (*Hàn Shū*).
In five days,
he was able to generally recall the whole text.
Later, tiring of drinking and jesting,
he extensively sought out the Classics and Histories.
He could read five lines at once;
he memorized what he saw at a single glance,
forgetting nothing.
His prose was elegant and ornate,
being both comprehensive and rapid.
Before the age of twenty,
his fame was known among the high officials (yī guān).
Once, he, along with Yáng Gù of Yòuběipíng, Péi Bómào of Hédōng, his cousin Fú, Lù Dàohuī of Hénán, and others, visited the residence of Xīn, the Prince of Běihǎi, to stay overnight and drink.
They composed several dozen poems together,
all of which were left with the host's servant.
The next morning, the servant left,
and the others could not retrieve their poems.
Shào recited all of them for them.
When some gentlemen doubted the accuracy of the recitation,
the servant returned with the originals,
which proved Shào had not erred by a single character.
Everyone compared him to Wáng Càn.
Lǐ Shénjùn of Lǒngxī, Minister of the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Shàngshū), greatly admired and respected him,
establishing a relationship of friendship despite the difference in their ages (wàng nián zhī jiāo).
Removing the headcloth (from mourning) to serve as a pallbearer (wănláng) for Wèi Xuānwǔ,
he was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng,
and later promoted to Zhùzuò Zuǒláng.
He was deeply honored by the Commander (Lǐngjūn), Yuán Chā.
When Chā was newly appointed President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
Shénjùn and Yuán Fān of Chénjùn were at the banquet.
Chā ordered Shào to compose a memorial of thanks (xièbiǎo).
It was completed instantly,
and shown to all the guests.
Shénjùn said:
“Xíng Shào’s memorial,
is enough to make Lord Yuán (Yuán Gōng) change countenance.”
At the beginning of Xiàochāng,
he managed court rites alongside the Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Huángmén Shìláng), Lǐ Yǎnzhī.
Since the time of Xiàomíng,
literary refinement greatly flourished.
The beauty of Shào's literary craftsmanship ("carving insects"),
was unparalleled at the time.
Whenever a new piece of his literature was released,
paper became expensive in the capital for its sake,
and it was read and recited widely, near and far.
At that time, Yuán Fān and Zǔ Yíng of Fànyáng, whose positions and reputations were prominent,
and the excellence of whose writings,
were praised by their predecessors,
found Shào’s ornate thoughts and rich ornamentation outstanding,
and deeply envied him.
Whenever a noble person in Luòyáng received an appointment,
they mostly relied on Shào to write the memorial of thanks.
Once, a certain high-ranking noble first received office,
and gathered many guests for a banquet.
Fān and Shào were both sitting there.
Fān expected the host would entrust the writing of the memorial of declining the honor (ràngbiǎo) to him.
Instead, he commanded Shào to write it.
Fān was extremely displeased,
and often told people:
“That little boy of the Xíng family often works as a hack writer for memorials,
buys his own yellow paper,
writes them, and then sends them off.”
Shào feared he would be harmed by Fān,
and thus resigned, citing illness.
Coincidentally, when the President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Yuán Luó, went out to govern Qīngzhōu,
he petitioned for Shào to be appointed Chief Clerk of the Administration (Fǔ Sīmǎ).
Consequently, he stayed in the territory of Qīngzhōu,
spending the entire day enjoying drink and scenery,
making the most of the charm of the mountains and springs.
At the beginning of Yǒng'ān,
he was repeatedly promoted to Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
The imperial edicts and pronouncements he composed,
possessed a grand and beautiful literary style.
When Ěrzhū Róng entered Luòyáng,
the capital was thrown into chaos.
Shào and Yáng Yīn of Hóngnóng fled to Sōnggāoshān (Mount Sōnggāo).
During Pǔtài,
he additionally served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
and shortly thereafter became Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì).
At the beginning of Tàichāng,
an imperial decree ordered him to directly attend the inner palace offices (nèishěng),
and he was provided with imperial food.
He was ordered to review and verify matters of the Departments of State Affairs (Shàngshū) and the Chancellery (Ménxià),
and whenever a high official was appointed,
his opinion on the suitability of the candidate was sought first,
before the appointment was carried out.
He was appointed General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) and Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
Due to the old age of his parents, he returned to his hometown.
An edict ordered that he be specially provided with five guards wherever he resided,
and also commanded him to come to court once a year,
to be available for consultation.
Upon the death of his mother,
his sorrow and physical deterioration exceeded the prescribed rites.
Afterwards, Yáng Yīn, Wèi Shōu, and Shào jointly requested the establishment of schools.
((Their memorial said: The Ancestral Temple (Shìshì) and the Bright Hall (Míngtáng),
were prominent during Zhōu and Xià;
the establishment of one central college and two schools,
flourished since Yú and Yīn.
The reason for matching the Ancestor to the Supreme Deity (Shàngdì),
is to display the utmost solemnity;
the reason for promulgating principles throughout the land,
is to demonstrate the heavenly mandate.
Fostering the yellow-haired (the elderly) to consult their wise words,
cultivating the blue-collared (the students) to spread teaching statutes—
it is by these means that a state can enjoy long life,
and its glorious reputation last for ten thousand years.
When the Qín state perished,
it altered
and reformed this Way.
It buried the Confucians alive and destroyed the schools,
thereby obscuring the common people.
Consequently, the Nine Domains (Jiǔfú) fragmented,
and the dynasty ended after two generations.
The Glorious Hàn suddenly arose,
and renewed Confucian methods.
Thus, the Western Capital (Xījīng) had the principle of Six Schools,
and the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū) had the flourishing Three Foundations.
Subsequently, during Wèi and Jìn,
correcting disorder followed one after another,
yet amidst the conflicts of war,
schools were not discontinued.
Reflecting upon the fact that Emperor Gāozǔ Xiàowén received sagacity from Heaven,
his Dao mirrored
the present and the past,
he established schools and colleges in villages and townships,
and encouraged the Odes and Documents (Shī Shū) throughout the commanderies and states.
However, as the initial planning was still intense,
and military chariots were frequently driven,
he lacked the leisure to achieve much,
and was pursued by the bow and sword (died prematurely).
When Shìzōng governed the calendar,
he then
followed the preceding tradition.
During Yǒngpíng,
great construction works using boards and earth were undertaken.
Subsequently, due to floods and droughts,
and military horses breeding in the suburbs (warfare),
although we were close to forming a mountain,
work halted with just one basketful (of earth left).
Consequently, the foundation of the rites and music of the Bright Hall,
is instead overgrown with a forest of brambles
and thorns;
the foundation for virtue and righteousness in the schools (jiāoxù),
is only filled with the traces of cowherds;
the importance of firm and solemn city walls (chénghuáng),
lacks the construction of bricks and stones;
the necessity of prominent and magnificent structures (yōnggòu),
lacks the ornamentation of towers and pavilions.
Furthermore, as the wind and rain gradually encroach,
they are progressively causing damage and collapse.
This is not what is meant by highly advancing the foundation,
or serving as a model for ten thousand states.
We humbly hear that the court deliberates that since Gāozǔ greatly created and governed the land,
and his Way was comparable to Jī
Wén (King Wén of Zhōu),
it is fitting to sacrifice to him in the Bright Hall,
ritually matching him with the Supreme Deity.
If the foundations and site are not repaired now,
they will resemble mere mounds and ditches.
Even if the spirit of the August Founder (Gāohuáng) is worshiped,
if it is lacking in the central place of the state (guóyáng),
the ritual concerning ancestral affairs,
will have reputation but no
substance.
This is why your subjects are uneasy,
and why the billions of people look forward with expectation.
Your subjects have also heard that official positions are granted to the capable,
in order to employ them in service.
Once they are employed in service,
they are rewarded with emoluments.
If this is so, then superiors will have no criticism of neglected offices,
and subordinates will avoid the slander of being useless placeholders.
Today,
although the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ) has the name of a school office,
it lacks the substance of teaching and instruction.
How is this different from Dodder and Wild Oats?
Or the Southern Sieve and the Northern Dipper?
Formerly, Liú Xiàng had a saying:
“A true sovereign should establish the Pìyōng, display rites and music, thereby setting a moral example for the world.”
Rites and music are the means by which people are cultivated;
penal laws are the means by which people are killed.
Yet the authorities diligently
and earnestly,
request the establishment of penal codes.
When it comes to rites and music,
they say they dare not proceed.
This means they dare to kill people,
but dare not cultivate people.
Your subjects believe that now the Four Seas are peaceful and clear,
and the Nine Domains are tranquil and settled.
The essential importance of governing the state,
logically requires construction to begin first.
If construction is again delayed,
then Liú Xiàng’s words will be proven true.
However, affairs cannot flourish simultaneously;
there must be priority given and withheld.
According to your subjects’ humble judgment,
it is appropriate to cease the extravagant
carving and ornamentation work in the Imperial Workshops (Shàngfāng),
significantly reduce the earth and wood labor at Yǒngníng,
and reduce the material and tile resources used at Yáoguāng,
and also divert labor from carving and chiseling the stone caves,
as well as other non-urgent public works.
During the agricultural slack periods
of the three seasons,
these few items should be repaired.
This will allow the rites of the Pìyōng,
to prosperously revive;
the sounds of recitation,
to brilliantly resume.
Beautiful pavilions and high walls will be solemn and magnificent on the outside,
and the Huái Palace and Jí
Temple will be prominently splendid within.
Then, the differences between ancient and modern times can be further illuminated,
the village drinking ritual (xiāngyǐn) can be properly followed again,
the commandery schools can be enthusiastically advanced,
and the study of the classics meticulously evaluated.
If this is done, then Yuán and Kǎi (exemplary ministers) can be acquired among the highest ranks,
and Yóu and Xià (exemplary disciples of Confucius) can be brought
to the lesser states,
how could this not be excellent!
Empress Dowager Líng (Líng Tàihòu) issued an order saying:
"The great ritual of associate sacrifice [to the imperial ancestors]
is the foundation of the state.
Recently, due to military activities outside the capital,
there was no time to undertake repairs.
Now the four borders are peaceful and calm.
The officials concerned must be instructed
to discuss and
initiate this separately."
[He] was repeatedly promoted to Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) and
Zhōngshū Jiān (Director of the Central Secretariat),
acting concurrently as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the Directorate of Education).
At that time, most court officials held a single post,
and few concurrently held two offices.
Shào Dùn held three offices simultaneously,
all being leading positions in literary affairs,
which was considered an honor in that generation.
When Emperor Wénxuān (Wénxuān) visited Jìnyáng,
auspicious sweet dew frequently appeared on the road.
All court officials composed encomiums on the sweet dew,
and the Department of State Affairs ordered Shào to write the preface for them.
When Emperor Wénxuān (Wénxuān Huángdì) died,
he was frequently consulted regarding funeral rites,
and was ordered to draft the elegiac text.
Later, he was granted the position of Tèjìn (Special Advance),
and then he died.
Shào was naturally simple and plain,
and his private conduct was meticulous and cautious.
Among his brothers and relatives by marriage,
he was praised for being harmonious and cordial.
He widely read ancient texts and classics,
mastering them all.
In his later years, he focused particularly on the textual interpretation of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng),
exhausting their essential meaning.
Regarding auspicious and inauspicious rituals,
people consulted him both publicly and privately.
He clarified doubts and removed confusion,
acting as a guide for the world.
Whenever high officials held a conference,
and the matter concerned precedents or classical usages,
Shào would immediately take up his brush and finish the text.
His supporting citations were thorough and apt.
Imperial decrees and court regulations
were finalized in a short time based on his drafts.
His writing style was grand and profound,
unmatched at the time.
He and Wēn Zǐshēng of Jìnyīn were considered the foremost literary figures,
and contemporary opinion referred to them as Wēn and Xíng.
Wèi Shōu of Jùlù,
although his talent shone brightly,
was younger than the two men.
Therefore, only after Zǐshēng died
did people start speaking of Xíng and Wèi.
Although his reputation and substance were equally high,
he did not treat others with arrogance due to his talent or position.
He was free-spirited and simple,
paying no attention to dignified deportment.
His carriages, robes, and utensils
were just sufficient for the purpose.
He had studies but did not live in them;
he sat and slept in a small hut.
Fruits and pastries
were sometimes placed on the rafters.
When guests arrived,
he took them down to eat together.
His natural disposition was genuine and simple,
and he was especially comfortable with differences [in opinion or custom].
Whether scholars were talented or foolish,
he was able to pay attention to and interact with them.
While facing guests, he sometimes took off his clothes to look for lice,
yet continued chatting vigorously with them.
He owned many books,
but rarely proofread them.
When he saw others proofreading,
he would often laugh and say:
"How utterly foolish!
The books in the world cannot be read completely even by the time of death,
so how can one start trying to proofread them?
Moreover, contemplating a mistake in the text,
that is another kind of pleasure."
His wife's younger brother, Lǐ Jìjié,
an educated man of talent,
said to Zǐcái:
"Most people in the world are not intelligent;
how could they possibly figure out the mistaken text by contemplation?"
Zǐcái replied:
"If one cannot figure it out by contemplation,
then there is no point in reading books."
He was very distant from his wife,
never spending the night in her chamber.
He once said he entered the inner quarters during the day
and was barked at by a dog,
and finished speaking by slapping his hands and laughing loudly.
He enjoyed talking and appreciating things,
and could not bear to be alone.
When he returned home from public duty to rest,
he required guests to keep him company.
He served his widowed sister-in-law very respectfully
and raised the orphaned son Shù,
showing him profound compassion and love.
While he was in Yǎnzhōu,
a message came saying that Shù was ill.
He immediately worried about him,
neglecting sleep and food,
and his complexion deteriorated.
When [Shù] died,
scholars were heartbroken for him.
Although his grief was intense,
he ultimately did not cry again.
When guests offered condolences,
he merely wiped away his tears.
His noble sentiment and broad understanding,
enabling him to dispel persistent sorrow,
were unmatched since Dōngmén Wú.
This had not been seen before.
He has a collection of thirty scrolls
currently circulated in the world.
His son, Dàbǎo,
possessed literary sentiment.
His illegitimate sons, Dàdé and Dàdào,
were virtually illiterate.
[Biographies, Chapter 29] Wèi Shōu
Wèi Shōu,
courtesy name Bóqǐ,
nickname Fózhù,
was a man from Xiàqǔyáng, Jùlù.
His great-grandfather was Jī,
his grandfather Sháo.
His father, Zǐjiàn,
courtesy name Jìngzhōng,
was posthumously granted the titles of Yítóng and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dìngzhōu.
When Shōu was fifteen,
he was already quite capable of writing prose.
When he accompanied his father to the frontier,
he enjoyed practicing archery and horsemanship,
hoping to make his mark through military skills.
Zhèng Bó of Xíngyáng ridiculed him, saying:
"How much spear-play has Young Master Wèi done?"
Shōu felt ashamed,
and consequently changed his behavior and dedicated himself to studying.
In the summer months,
he sat on a wooden plank bed,
reciting classics while following the shade of the trees.
After years of this,
the wooden plank bed was visibly worn down,
but his diligent effort did not cease.
He became prominent through his literary brilliance.
He was first appointed Erudite (Bóshì) of the Imperial University (Tàixué).
When Ěrzhū Róng indiscriminately killed court officials at Héyīn,
Shōu was also among those surrounded,
but escaped because the day was late.
The Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), Lǐ Shénjùn, valued Shōu’s talent and learning,
and recommended him for appointment as Staff Administrator (Jìshì Cānjūn) of the Minister of Education (Sītú).
In the third year of Yǒng'ān,
he was appointed Director (Lángzhōng) of the Bureau of Northern Foreign Relations (Běi Zhǔkè).
When Emperor Jiémǐn (Jiémǐn Dì) ascended the throne,
he carefully selected close attendants.
He commanded Shōu to write an essay on the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices as a test.
Shōu immediately completed it upon putting brush to paper,
without needing a rough draft.
The text was nearly a thousand characters long,
with hardly anything needing correction.
At that time, the Palace Attendant (Huángmén Láng), Jiǎ Sītóng, stood nearby.
He was deeply impressed,
and reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Even the talent of the seven-step poet
could not surpass this."
[He] was promoted to Cavalry Attendant-in-ordinary (Sànqí Shìláng).
Soon after, he was ordered to manage the Diaries of Activity and Repose (Qǐjū Zhù),
and concurrently compile the National History,
while also serving as Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
At that time, he was twenty-six years old.
an edict again commanded Wèi Shōu to resume his original post.
The official documents and pronouncements piled up,
and his performance consistently satisfied the emperor's wishes.
Cuī Xià, the Palace Attendant (Huángmén Láng), followed Qí Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) when he entered court,
and wielded great influence in the world.
Wèi Shōu initially did not call upon his gate.
When Cuī Xià drafted the imperial amnesty for the emperor’s ascension,
it said,
"I [Zhèn] model myself upon Xiàowén,"
and Wèi Shōu scoffed at its clumsy straightforwardness.
Lǐ Shèn, a Regular Gentleman (Zhèngyuán Láng), informed Cuī Xià of this,
and Cuī Xià became deeply resentful and jealous.
At that time, Emperor Jiémǐn passed away,
and Wèi Shōu was ordered to draft the edict.
Cuī Xià then openly declared: "Wèi Shōu served in the innermost chambers during the Pǔtài era,
and now, in a single day, he drafts this edict,
producing superior phrasing and intent.
If this is true, then all the men of the righteous banner are rebels;
furthermore, Wèi Shōu’s father is elderly,
and he should resign his post and return home to serve him."
The Southern Bureau (Nántái) was about to impeach him,
but fortunately, Xīn Xióng, a Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū), spoke on his behalf to Qí Jùn, the Commandant of the Metropolitan Area (Zhōngwèi),
and the matter was dropped.
Wèi Shōu had a younger half-brother, Zhòngtóng,
who previously had not been officially recorded,
and because of this incident, Wèi Shōu was frightened.
He registered [Zhòngtóng],
and sent him back to their hometown to assist in attending their father.
Xiàowǔ once mobilized a large number of soldiers,
conducting a hunt south of Mount Sōng and Mount Shào for sixteen days.
The weather was cold then,
and both the court and the common people lamented and complained.
The emperor, his retinue, and various imperial consorts and princesses
engaged in strange displays of skill and wore bizarre adornments,
much of which violated proper propriety.
Wèi Shōu wanted to speak but was afraid;
he wanted to remain silent but could not stop himself.
Thus, he presented the "Rhapsody on the Southern Hunt" (Nán Shòu Fù) to subtly criticize the matter.
He was twenty-seven years old at the time;
although the language was extravagant and ornate,
it ultimately returned to elegance and correctness.
The emperor replied with an edict written by his own hand,
praising and commending him greatly.
Zhèng Bó said to him,
"If you had not encountered this old man,
you would still be chasing rabbits."
Initially, Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) firmly declined the title of Grand General Supporting Heaven (Tiānzhù Dàjiāngjūn).
The Wèi Emperor commanded Wèi Shōu to draft an edict,
allowing him to proceed with his request.
When the emperor wished to bestow upon Wèi Shōu the title Minister of State (Xiàngguó),
he asked about his rank.
Wèi Shōu replied truthfully,
and the emperor consequently stopped [the promotion].
Wèi Shōu, being unsure of the intentions of the ruler and the prime minister,
and feeling uneasy about the previous events,
requested to resign.
An edict granted his request.
After a long time,
he was appointed Central Clerk to the Established Administration of Zàn, the Prince of Guǎngpíng and nephew of the emperor.
Wèi Shōu dared not refuse,
so he composed the "Rhapsody on the Court Bamboo" (Tíng Zhú Fù) to express his feelings.
Soon after, he concurrently held the post of Drafting Clerk (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
He was equally famous alongside Wēn Zǐshēng of Jìyīn and Xíng Zǐcái of Héjiān,
and the world called them the Three Talents (Sāncái).
At that time, Xiàowǔ was suspicious and jealous of Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān),
and there was internal discord.
Wèi Shōu consequently firmly resigned on the grounds of illness and was relieved [of his duties].
His maternal uncle, Cuī Xiàofēn, found this strange and asked him why.
Wèi Shōu replied,
"I fear the armor of Jìnyáng."
Soon after, Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) marched south,
and the emperor moved west into the Passes (Guān).
Wèi Shōu concurrently served as Internunciary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
He served as the deputy to Wáng Xīn on a mission to Liáng [Dynasty].
Wáng Xīn possessed elegance and literary eloquence,
while Wèi Shōu's literary language was rich and unrestrained.
The Liáng ruler and his ministers all treated them with reverence and distinction.
Prior to this, when the North and South first achieved harmony,
Lǐ Xié and Lú Yuánmíng were the first to be sent on missions.
The talents and capabilities of those two men
were highly valued by the neighboring state.
Upon this occasion,
the Liáng ruler remarked,
"Lú and Lǐ were born for their age;
Wáng and Wèi mark a revitalization.
I wonder what later envoys will be like?"
While Wèi Shōu was staying at the residence,
he proceeded to buy a maid from Wú and brought her into the residence.
When someone in his staff bought a maid,
Wèi Shōu also summoned her and took her.
He engaged in illicit and vulgar behavior throughout the area,
and the officials in charge of the residence for the Liáng court were all penalized because of him.
People praised his talent but despised his conduct.
On the journey, he composed the "Rhapsody on the Mission Journey" (Pìnyóu Fù),
the language of which was extremely beautiful and grand.
When he returned from the mission,
Gāo Lóngzhī, the Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè), requested Southern goods from Wáng Xīn and Wèi Shōu.
Because they could not satisfy his desire,
he consequently hinted to Gāo Zhòngmì, the Commandant of the Censors (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi), to detain Wáng Xīn and Wèi Shōu at his office,
and after a long time, they were released.
When Sūn Qiān died,
Sīmǎ Zǐrú recommended Wèi Shōu.
Wèi Shōu was summoned to Jìnyáng,
and appointed Clerk (Zhǔbù) of the Central and External Headquarters.
Because he executed orders improperly or failed to comply,
he was repeatedly criticized and reproved,
and even subjected to flogging.
For a long time, he could not achieve his ambitions.
Coincidentally, Sīmǎ Zǐrú was serving on a mission to the court of the Hegemon (Bàcháo),
and Wèi Shōu benefited from his reflected glory.
During a banquet, Sīmǎ Zǐrú jokingly said to Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān),
"Wèi Shōu was the Emperor's Drafting Clerk (Zhōngshū Láng),
a great talent in the entire state.
I wish Your Highness would show him some favor."
Following this, he was transferred to a staff position in the headquarters,
though he was not yet treated with great courtesy.
Wèi Shōu's paternal cousin, Jìjǐng,
possessed talent and learning,
and was famous in all the offices he held.
He always ranked higher than Wèi Shōu,
yet Wèi Shōu regularly slighted and overlooked him.
When Jìjǐng and Wèi Shōu first went to Bìng [Province],
Lǐ Shù of Dùnqiū,
who was the son of Lǐ Xié, the former Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sī nóng),
was praised for his flowery rhetoric.
He once said to Wèi Shōu,
"The court of the Hegemon immediately has two Wèis."
Wèi Shōu replied rashly,
"To be compared with my cousin [Jìjǐng]
is like Yēshū being compared to you."
Yēshū
was the son of Jì Bó, the Duke of Chénliú and former Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
He was famous for his foolishness and stupidity,
liked to enter markets,
and buy things at high prices.
Merchants and traders all mocked and ridiculed him.
Wèi Shōu slighted Jìjǐng,
and therefore compared him [to Yēshū].
His instances of impertinence were often like this.
originally relied on his literary talent,
certainly hoping to stand out and become recognized.
Since his official position was not fulfilled,
he requested to compile the National History (Guóshǐ).
Cuī Xiān spoke on his behalf to Wénxiāng, saying:
"The matter of the National History is weighty.
The hegemonic accomplishments of your father and son, the Duke,
must all be fully recorded.
It must be Shōu."
Wénxiāng memorialized that Shōu be appointed concurrently as Sǎnqí Chángshì,
to compile the National History.
In the second year of Wǔdìng (544 CE),
he was appointed Regular Chángshì,
additionally leading the concurrent post of Zhōngshū Shìláng,
continuing the historical compilation.
The Emperor of Wèi hosted a banquet for the officials,
and asked why the seventh day of the first lunar month was called Rénrì (Human Day).
No one was able to answer.
Shōu replied, saying:
"Dǒng Xūn, the Counselor (Yìláng) of Jìn, in his reply concerning ritual customs, said: 'The first day of the first month is for the chicken,
the second day is for the dog,
the third day is for the pig,
the fourth day is for the sheep,
the fifth day is for the ox,
the sixth day is for the horse,
and the seventh day is for humanity.'"
Xíng Shào was also nearby at the time,
and felt very ashamed.
Since Wèi and Liáng established peace,
the official documents always included the phrase:
"We imagine that territory is peaceful and tranquil,
and this land is secure and harmonious."
Later, when the Liáng court sent an envoy,
their letter actually removed
the character *bǐ* (彼, "that/their"),
and in their self-address, they still retained
the character *cǐ* (此, "this/our"),
intending to show
the meaning of "no outside (foreign territory)."
Shōu drafted the reply letter, saying:
"We imagine your territory is clear and peaceful,
and now all nations (wànguó) are secure and harmonious."
The Liáng people replied,
adopting this phrasing as their standard.
Later, when Shénwǔ returned to the capital,
Emperor Jìng offered him the position of Prime Minister (Xiàngguó).
He firmly declined,
and ordered Shōu to draft the memorial.
After the memorial was completed and presented,
Wénxiāng was attending nearby.
Shénwǔ pointed at Shōu and said:
"This man will likely become another Cuī Guāng."
In the fourth year [of Wǔdìng],
Shénwǔ held a banquet at the temple of Xī Mén Bào.
He said to Sīmǎ Zǐrú:
"Wèi Shōu is the official historian,
recording our good and bad deeds.
I heard that during the Northern Campaigns,
the various nobles often provided food and drink to the official historians.
Sīmǎ Púyè (Director Sīmǎ), have you ever provided provisions?"
Everyone burst into laughter.
He then turned to Shōu and said:
"You must not see Yuán Kāng and the others running around under my eye,
and assume I value their diligence.
My name and reputation for posterity rest in your hands.
Do not think I am unaware of this."
Soon after, he was granted the concurrent post of Zuòzuò Láng (Compiler).
Shōu, when he was previously in Luòjīng (Luòyáng capital),
was extremely frivolous and shallow.
People nicknamed him, saying,
"Wèi Shōu, the Startled Butterfly (Jīng Jiádié)."
Wénxiāng once visited Dōngshān (East Mountain),
and ordered Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate) Hào and others to hold a banquet.
Wénxiāng said:
"Wèi Shōu relies on his talent and is inappropriate everywhere (lacks restraint).
Someone must expose his shortcomings."
After several rounds of discussion back and forth,
Shōu suddenly shouted loudly:
"Yáng Zūnyàn is logically defeated and has fallen!"
Yīn calmly replied:
"I have plenty of composure and leisure time,
standing still like a mountain, immovable.
But if one encounters the Roadside Flower (dāngtú),
I fear they will flutter away immediately."
*Dāngtú* (Roadside Flower) was
Wèi (referring to Wèi Shōu),
and "fluttering away" (piānpiān) meant
the butterfly.
Wénxiāng already knew this context,
and laughed heartily, praising the remark.
Wénxiāng further said:
"The previous words were too subtle.
You should point it out more explicitly."
Yīn immediately responded:
"Wèi Shōu composed a poem in Bīngzhōu,
and after reading it to the assembly,
he said: 'Even if I demanded six hundred *hú* of rice from my younger uncle, Jìjǐng,
he still wouldn't understand this poem.'
This is known far and wide,
I dare not speak falsely."
Wénxiāng was delighted and said:
"I also heard this previously."
Everyone laughed.
Although Shōu defended himself,
he could not refute them further,
and was bothered by this matter for the rest of his life.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled and defected to Liáng,
attacking the southern border,
Wénxiāng was in Jìnyáng at the time.
He ordered Shōu to write a manifesto (xí) of over fifty pages,
which was completed in less than a day.
He also wrote a manifesto to the Liáng court,
ordering them to send Hóu Jǐng back.
He took up the brush at dusk,
and finished by the third watch (around midnight).
The text exceeded seven pages.
Wénxiāng commended him.
The Emperor of Wèi once held a grand archery contest in late autumn,
ordering all attendees to compose poems.
Shōu's poem concluded with the lines:
"A single letter summons Jiànyè,
a simple note summons Cháng'ān."
Wénxiāng was impressed by this,
and looked around at the other officials, saying:
"Having Wèi Shōu in court today,
is truly the glory of the state.
In refined and common literary matters,
he is comprehensively brilliant and fluent.
Although I also have Zǐcái and Zǐshēng occasionally write something,
regarding rhetoric and literary spirit,
they both cannot compare to him.
Sometimes, I have an idea I cherish,
but forget to mention it,
or mention it but not exhaustively,
or the intention is incomplete.
When Shōu presents a draft, it is always comprehensive and thorough.
This quality is also rare."
He was also commanded to concurrently serve as Zhǔkè Láng (Director of Guests) to receive the Liáng envoys Xiè Tǐng and Xú Líng.
After Hóu Jǐng captured Liáng,
Fàn, Prince of Póyáng in Liáng, was serving as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Hézhōu.
Wénxiāng commanded Shōu to write a letter persuading him.
Fàn received the letter,
and subsequently led his troops westward.
Governor Cuī Shèngniàn subsequently entered and occupied his city.
Wénxiāng said to Shōu:
"Now we have secured a prefecture.
You contributed to this effort.
I only regret that 'A single letter summons Jiànyè'
has not yet been realized."
When Wénxiāng died,
Wénxuān went to Jìnyáng.
He ordered Shōu, along with Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate) Cuī Jìshū and Gāo Dézhèng,
and Lìbù Lángzhōng (Vice Director of the Personnel Bureau) Wèi Jǐn, to manage confidential matters at the Northern Residence (Běi Dì).
Shōu was transferred to Mìshū Jiān (Palace Library Director),
concurrently serving as Zuòzuò Láng (Compiler).
He was also appointed Dà Zhōngzhèng of Dìngzhōu.
At this time, Qí was about to receive the abdication.
Yáng Yīn memorialized that Shōu be placed in a separate residence,
ordering him to compose the imperial edicts and documents for the abdication and succession.
Xú Zhīcái was sent to guard the gate and prevent him from leaving.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (550 CE),
he was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat),
retaining the concurrent post of Zuòzuò Láng,
and was enfeoffed as the Viscount (zǐ) of Fùpíng County.
In the second year,
an imperial edict commanded the compilation of the history of the Wèi (Wèi Shǐ).
In the fourth year,
he was dismissed as Wèi Yǐn (Governor of Wèi).
Therefore, he was amply provided with salary and manpower,
and focused solely on the historical archives (Shǐ Gé),
without involvement in prefectural affairs.
When the Emperor first ordered his ministers to each state their aspirations,
Shōu said:
“Your servant wishes to wield a frank brush in the Eastern Archives (Dōng Guān),
and quickly complete the Book of Wèi (Wèi Shū).”
Therefore, the Emperor tasked Shōu to preside over this duty.
He also issued an edict appointing the Prince of Píngyuán, Gāo Lóngzhī, to generally oversee it,
but merely to affix his name.
The Emperor instructed Shōu, saying:
“Wield a good and frank brush.
I will certainly not act like Emperor Tàiwǔ of Wèi (Wèi Tàiwǔ), who executed the historians.”
In the beginning of the Wèi dynasty, Dèng Yànhǎi compiled more than ten scrolls of the Records of Dài (Dài Jì).
Subsequently, Cuī Hào managed the history (Diǎn Shǐ).
Yóu Yǎ, Gāo Yǔn,
Chéng Jùn, Lǐ Biāo, Cuī Guāng, Lǐ Yǎnzhī, and others inherited and carried on this work generation after generation.
Hào compiled it in annalistic style (biānniántǐ).
Biāo first began dividing it into Annals (Jì), Tables (Biǎo), Treatises (Zhì), and Biographies (Zhuàn).
The book was still unpublished.
During the time of Xuānwǔ [Di],
Xíng Luán was commanded to retrospectively compile the Diary of Activity and Rest (Qǐjūzhù) for [Emperor] Xiàowén.
The compilation covered up to the fourteenth year of Tàihé.
Cuī Hóng and Wáng Zūnyè were subsequently commanded to supplement and continue it.
It concluded with [Emperor] Xiàomíng,
and the events were extremely detailed and thorough.
The Prince of Jìyīn, Huīyè, compiled thirty scrolls of the Records Clarifying the Imperial Clan (Biàn Zōngshì Lù).

Shōu then placed the Grand Masters of Remonstrance Fáng Yányòu, the Sikong Sīmǎ Xīn Yuánzhí, the National University Scholars (Guózǐ Bóshì) Diāo Róu and Péi Ángzhī, and the Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Láng) Gāo Xiàogàn in charge of deliberating and coordinating [the materials],
in order to complete the Wèi Shū.
They clarified and determined nomenclature,
selected and cataloged entries according to category,
and also searched and collected materials that had been lost or missed,
and appended subsequent events.
Upon completing the historical records for that dynasty,
they presented them in a memorial to the throne.
They compiled the great canon for the dynasty: there were twelve Annals (Jì),
ninety-two Biographies (Lièzhuàn),
totaling one hundred and ten scrolls.
They presented it to the throne in the third month of the fifth year.
In autumn,
he was appointed Governor of Liángzhōu (Liángzhōu Cìshǐ).
Since Shōu had not yet finished the Treatises (Zhì),
he memorialized requesting to complete the work,
which was permitted.
In the eleventh month,
he again presented the Ten Treatises (Shí Zhì): Astronomy (Tiānxiàng) in four scrolls,
Geography (Dìxíng) in three scrolls,
Harmonics and Calendar (Lǜlì) in two scrolls,
Rites and Music (Lǐyuè) in four scrolls,
Food and Money (Shíhuò) in one scroll,
Penal Law (Xíngfá) in one scroll,
Auspicious Omens (Língzhēng) in two scrolls,
Officialdom (Guānshì) in two scrolls,
Buddhism and Daoism (Shìlǎo) in one scroll,
totaling twenty scrolls.
These were appended to the Annals and Biographies,
making a total of one hundred and thirty scrolls,
divided into twelve bundles (zhì).
The history contained thirty-five editorial rules (lì),
twenty-five prefaces (xù),
ninety-four historical judgments (lùn),
and two memorials (biǎo) and one report (qǐ) presented before and after.
Regarding the historians he brought in,
fearing they might be too overbearing,
he only selected those scholars who had previously attached themselves to him.
Fáng Yányòu, Xīn Yuánzhí, and Suī Zhòngràng,
although they had long held court positions,
were none of them talented historians.
Diāo Róu and Péi Ángzhī were known for their Confucian learning,
but were utterly unsuited for editing and compilation.
Gāo Xiàogàn sought advancement through unorthodox means (zuǒ dào).
The ancestors, relatives, and in-laws of the various people involved in compiling the history were frequently included in the records,
embellished with laudatory language.
Shōu was rather impetuous by nature
and was not very impartial.
For those with whom he previously had grievances,
he often suppressed their good deeds.
He often said:
“What young brats
dare show hostility toward Wèi Shōu?
If I raise them up, I can make them ascend to heaven;
if I press them down, I ought to make them sink into the earth.”
When Shōu was first serving as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shǎoqīng) and compiling the national history during the time of Shénwǔ,
he received assistance from Yáng Xiūzhī.
Consequently, he thanked Xiūzhī, saying:
“I have nothing to repay your kindness with,
but I shall compose a fine biography for you.”
Xiūzhī’s father, Gù,
had served as the Administrator of Běipíng (Běipíng Tàishǒu) during the Wèi era.
Due to his greed and cruelty, he was impeached by the Central Inspector (Zhōngwèi) Lǐ Píng and incurred guilt,
which was recorded in the Wèi Qǐjūzhù.
Shōu’s history recorded:
“Gù, while in Běipíng,
implemented extremely benevolent governance,
and was dismissed from office due to official business.”
It also said:
“Lǐ Píng deeply respected him.”
Ěrzhū Róng was a rebel against Wèi.
Since the Gāo clan originated from Ěrzhū [by marriage],
and furthermore accepted Róng’s son, Jīn,
Shōu therefore diminished Róng’s faults and exaggerated his virtues.
The historical judgment (lùn) stated:
“If he had cultivated the character of virtue and righteousness,
then Wéi, Péng, Yī, and Huò would not be worth mentioning.”
