As contemporary opinion already stated that Shōu’s historical writing was unfair,
Wénxuān [Di] ordered Shōu to debate and discuss the matter with the descendants of various families at the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng).
More than one hundred people lodged complaints both before and after,
stating
that he had “omitted the hereditary offices of their families,”
or stating
that “their families were not recorded,”
or stating
that he had “maliciously slandered them.”
Shōu answered each case according to the circumstance.
Lú Fěi of Fànyáng complained that his father, Tóng, was merely appended to the biography of his clan ancestor, Xuán;
Lǐ Shù of Dùnqīu complained that his family biography claimed their origin was from Méng in Liángguó.
Fěi and Shù criticized and commented, saying:
“The history book is unfair.”
Shōu was impatient by nature,
unable to bear this indignation,
and memorialized falsely accusing them of plotting murder and harm.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and personally interrogated and reprimanded them.
Fěi said:
“My father served Wèi,
achieving the rank of Yítóng (Equivalent in Status),
and his meritorious achievements were outstanding
and famous throughout the land.
Because he had no kinship with Shōu,
no biography was written for him.
Cuī Chuò of Bólíng,
whose rank only reached Gōngcāo (Merit Examiner) in his home commandery
and had no other accomplishments,
is Shōu’s relative by marriage,
and yet was given the foremost biography.”
Shōu said:
“Although Chuò held no high position,
his reputation and virtue were commendable,
which is why he deserved a biography.”
The Emperor said:
“How do you know that he was a good man?”
Shōu said:
“Gāo Yǔn once composed a eulogy (zàn) for Chuò,
praising his virtue and morals.”
The Emperor said:
“A talented scholar like the Sikong,
when composing a eulogy for someone,
is naturally expected to praise them.
Just like when you write an essay for someone,
can all the good things you mention about them necessarily be true?”
Shōu had nothing to reply,
and merely trembled.
However, the Emperor had previously esteemed Shōu’s talent
and did not wish to punish him.
At that time, Wáng Sōngnián of Tàiyuán also slandered the history.
Sōngnián, Fěi, and Shù all incurred guilt,
and were each whipped and assigned to the military workshops (jiǎ fāng),
some subsequently dying from this,
and Lú Sīdào also incurred punishment.
Nevertheless, because the common people were in an uproar,
an imperial command ordered that the Wèi Shǐ temporarily not be implemented [published/circulated],
and instructed all officials to widely discuss it.
Those with family matters [not recorded] were permitted to enter the department,
and those who believed the history was untrue were to submit petitions.
Consequently, there was a public uproar,
and the history was labeled
“The Tainted History” (Huì Shǐ).
Petitioners arrived one after another,
and Shōu had no means to oppose them.

At that time, the Left Director of the Department of State Affairs (Zuǒ Púshè) Yáng Yīn and the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè) Gāo Dézhèng were extremely influential across the government and populace.
Both were close to Shōu,
and Shōu consequently wrote biographies for their families.
The two men did not wish to declare the history untrue,
so they suppressed the petitions and statements.
Throughout the rest of Emperor Wénxuān’s (Wénxuān Di) reign, the matter was never discussed again.
Furthermore, the Secretariat Director (Shàngshū) Lù Cāo once said to Yīn:
“Wèi Shōu’s Wèi Shū can be called vastly learned and immensely talented,
and it has rendered a great service to the Wèi court.”
Yīn said to Shōu:
“This can be called an unchangeable book (bù kān zhī shū),
to be transmitted for ten thousand generations.
I only regret that when discussing the collateral branches and relatives of various families,
it is excessively detailed and fragmented,
which differs from the structural style of previous histories.”
Shōu said:
“Previously, due to the chaos and turmoil in the Central Plains,
the genealogical records (pǔdié) of scholars
were almost entirely lost.
It is for this reason that I recorded the collateral branches in detail.
I hope, Sir, that by observing this flaw, you will recognize my benevolent intent,
and thus spare me further criticism.”
In the summer of the eighth year,
he was appointed Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎofù) and Supervisor of the National History (Jiān Guóshǐ).
He also participated in deliberating on the laws and ordinances (Lǜlìng).
When the three towers were completed,
Wénxuān said:
"Since the towers are finished, there must be a rhapsody (fù)."
Yáng Yīn (Yīn) had informed Shōu beforehand.
Shōu then presented the Rhapsody on the Emperor's New Palace Towers (Huángjū Xīndiàn Tái Fù).
Its composition was magnificent and beautiful.
Among those writing at the time,
all below Xíng Shào were unable to match it.
Shōu only informed Shào a few days before submitting the rhapsody.
Shào later told people:
"Shōu is a very wicked person;
he didn't tell me earlier."
The Emperor once toured Dōngshān (East Mountain),
ordering Shōu to compose an imperial edict [zhào],
proclaiming his might and virtue,
and using analogies referencing Guānxī (the region west of the Hangu Pass).
It was completed in a short time,
and the language and reasoning were grand and vigorous.
The Emperor greatly praised and admired it before the multitude of officials.
He was subsequently concurrently appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
Shōu married his maternal cousin,
the younger sister of Cuī Áng.
She bore one daughter,
but no son.
The granddaughter of the Wèi Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng) Liú Fāng,
and the daughter of the Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Láng) Cuī Zhàoshī—
their husband's families were implicated in a case.
The Emperor bestowed both upon Shōu as wives.
People at the time compared this to Jiǎ Chōng establishing his left and right ladies (fūrén).
Nevertheless, he had no son.
Later, when he was gravely ill,
fearing discord between his principal wife (dí) and concubines (yìng) after his death,
he dismissed the two secondary ladies (jī).
When he recovered from his illness, he recalled them with longing,
and composed the Rhapsody on the Sorrow of Separation (Huáilí Fù) to express his feelings.
Whenever Wénxuān was deeply immersed in feasting,
he would say:
"The Crown Prince's nature is weak,
and the affairs of the imperial ancestral shrine (Zōngshè) are weighty;
eventually I must pass the throne to Chángshān."
Shōu said to Yáng Yīn:
"The ancients said,
the Crown Prince is the root of the state,
and must not be shaken.
After the Supreme One (Zhìzūn) has had three cups of wine,
he always speaks of transmitting the throne to Chángshān,
causing suspicion and disloyalty among the officials.
If this is true,
then it must be carried out decisively.
These words are not a joke.
Since Wèi Shōu is unworthy to hold the post of Tutor,
he should simply defend it until death.
I am only concerned that the state will be unstable."
Yīn reported Shōu's words to the Emperor,
and from then on, the Emperor stopped saying it.
The Emperor often held joyful feasts,
and Shōu always participated in attendance.
When the Crown Prince received the lady Zhèng Liángdì,
the responsible officials prepared grand sacrificial feast dishes (láo zhuàn).
The Emperor, being deep in his cups,
stood up and personally destroyed and overturned them.
He then ordered Shōu, saying:
"Do you know my intention?"
Shōu replied:
"This humble subject foolishly believes that since the Liángdì is merely a concubine of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
logically, sacrificial dishes are not required.
Reflecting on Your Sacred Heart,
this is the reason they were destroyed."
The Emperor laughed heartily,
clasped Shōu's hand, and said:
"You know my intention."
Yánzōng, Prince of Āndé, married the daughter of Lǐ Zǔshōu of Zhàojùn as his consort (fēi).
Afterwards, the Emperor visited the Lǐ residence for a banquet.
The consort's mother, Lady Sòng, presented two pomegranates before the Emperor.
When he asked the others, no one knew the meaning,
so the Emperor threw them down.
Shōu said:
"The pomegranate's chambers contain many seeds,
and the Prince has recently married.
The consort's mother desires numerous descendants."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and ordered Shōu,
"You, Sir, retrieve them,"
and subsequently bestowed upon Shōu two bolts of fine brocade.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Minister Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
While the Emperor was at a banquet,
he verbally decreed that Shōu should be appointed Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
He ordered the Secretariat Director Lǐ Yīn to draft the edict beneath a tree.
Yīn considered Shōu a great talent of his generation,
difficult to appoint casually,
and was slow to finish.
By the time it was completed,
the Emperor had sobered up,
and consequently did not mention it again.
Yīn therefore did not present it,
and the matter eventually lapsed.
When the Emperor died at Jìnyáng,
a relay dispatched messengers to summon Shōu and the Administrator of Zhōngshān, Yáng Xiūzhī, to participate in discussions regarding auspicious and inauspicious rites (jílì),
and to jointly oversee the imperial edicts and pronouncements (zhào gào).
He was subsequently appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
Wénxuān's posthumous name (shì), temple name (miàohào), and tomb name (língmíng)
were all matters decided upon by Shōu.
When Emperor Xiàozhāo took up residence within the palace to govern affairs,
he ordered Shōu to compose various imperial edicts inside the forbidden palace (jìnzhōng).
Shōu did not emerge for many days.
He was transferred to Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
In the first year of Huángjiàn,
he was concurrently appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Grand Master of Remonstrance and Scrutiny of the Right (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū),
retaining his titles of Yítóng and Supervisor of History (Jiān Shǐ).
Shōu had previously served as a deputy envoy to Liáng under Wáng Xīn,
and they had not been in harmony.
At this time, Xīn’s younger brother, Wáng Xī, was close to the Emperor.
Furthermore, Xiàozhāo separately ordered Yáng Xiūzhī to concurrently serve in the Central Secretariat,
managing the imperial edicts and pronouncements in Jìnyáng,
while Shōu was kept in Yè.
This was likely Wáng Xī’s doing.
Shōu was greatly displeased
and said to the Crown Prince’s Palace Gentleman (Tàizǐ Shèrén), Lú Xúnzǔ:
"If they had appointed you to write the edicts and pronouncements,
I would not have complained."
Furthermore, Zǔ Tǐng was appointed Director of the Imperial Library (Zhùzuò Láng),
intending to replace Shōu.
Lǐ Zhù, Clerk to the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Zhǔbù),
who was a man of letters,
heard this and told people:
"All the edicts and pronouncements have gone to Yáng Zǐliè [Yáng Xiūzhī],
and the literary works are being entrusted to Zǔ Xiàozhēng [Zǔ Tǐng].
If the literary history is suddenly lost,
I fear Duke Wèi [Wèi Shōu] will develop a severe back carbuncle."
At that time, there was an imperial debate on the two kings (Èr Wáng) and three honors (Sān Kè).
Shōu adhered to the interpretation of Wáng Sù and Dù Yù,
holding that the Yuán and Sīmǎ clans should be treated as the two kings,
and including the Cáo clan to fulfill the three honors.
The Emperor ordered all officials specializing in ritual studies
to adhere to Zhèng Xuán's proposal of five generations.
Since Empress Xiàozhāo's surname was Yuán,
the discussion about the honors did not want to include too many ancestors.
Therefore, the deliberation followed Shōu's opinion.
He was again concurrently appointed Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shǎofù),
and relieved of the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) post.
Because the History of Wèi (Wèi Shǐ) had not yet been formally distributed,
the Emperor ordered Shōu to further research and scrutinize it.
Shōu received the edict
and made several corrections.
When the imperial edict authorized the distribution of the Wèi Shǐ,
Shōu believed that if it were simply stored in the Imperial Library (Bìgé),
outsiders would have no means of seeing it.
He therefore ordered one copy to be sent to the Bīngshěng (Bīng Province Headquarters),
and one copy to be sent to Yè,
allowing people to copy it freely.
In the first year of Dàníng,
he was granted the title Opening a Mansion (Kāifǔ).
In the second year of Héqīng,
he was concurrently appointed Right Grand Secretary (Yòu Púshè).
At that time, Emperor Wǔchéng spent the entire day heavily drinking,
and governmental affairs were entirely entrusted to the Palace Attendant Gāo Yuánhǎi.
Yuánhǎi was mediocre
and incapable of handling major responsibilities.
Because Shōu's talent and reputation were renowned throughout society,
and Bì Yìyún, Minister of the Department of Civil Affairs (Dūguān Shàngshū), was skilled in arbitration and decision-making,
Yuánhǎi sincerely relied upon them.
Shōu, however, was fearful and evasive, unable to offer correction or assistance,
and was criticized by commentators.
The Emperor established the Xuánzhōu Park (Xuánzhōu Yuàn) separately in the Huálín (Magnificent Woods),
featuring the beauty of mountains, water, towers, and observation decks.
He ordered Shōu's portrait to be painted on the viewing pavilion;
his esteemed status was thus evident.
Shǐ Shōu compared Wēn Zǐshēng and Xíng Shào as slightly junior contemporaries.
After Xíng Shào was dismissed and sent away,
and Zǐshēng died tragically due to a crime,
Shōu was subsequently greatly employed,
monopolizing the era.
Their opinions and discussions mutually slandered and disparaged each other,
each having their own factions.
Shōu always spoke ill of Xíng Shào’s writings.
Shào, in turn, said:
“Rèn Fǎng of Jiāngnán,
his literary style is inherently simple,
Wèi Shōu does not merely imitate,
but also heavily plagiarizes.”
Shōu heard this and replied:
“He (Xíng Shào) often acted as a thief within Shěn Yuē’s collected works,
why does he claim that I stole from Rèn Fǎng?”
Rèn and Shěn both held great reputations,
and Xíng and Wèi each had their own preferences.
During the Wǔpíng period,
the Huángmén Láng Yán Zhītuī asked the Púshè Zǔ Tǐng about the views of the two gentlemen,
Tǐng replied:
“Observing the merit or flaw in Xíng and Wèi’s work,
is exactly the superiority or inferiority of Rèn and Shěn.”
Shōu noted that Wēn Zǐshēng never wrote any fù (rhapsodies),
and although Xíng had one or two pieces,
they were not his forte,
and he often said:
“One must be able to compose fù;
only then can one be considered a great scholar.
To limit oneself to memorials, petitions, and tomb inscriptions,
everything outside of that is like child’s play.”
Since the second year of Wǔdìng,
imperial edicts concerning major state affairs,
and military and governmental literary compositions,
were all composed by Shōu.
Whenever there was an emergency,
upon receiving an edict, he would complete it instantly;
sometimes when a court messenger pressed him,
Shōu’s writing appeared as if it had been prepared beforehand,
this efficiency and speed,
was unmatched by Xíng or Wēn,
while his involvement in discussing rites and ceremonies was equal to Xíng.
Subsequently, in Zhàojùn.
Gōng.
Zēng Nián was granted immunity (from execution),
Shōu knew about it and overlooked his fault,
and when the matter came to light, he was stripped of his position.
That same year, he again entrusted items to the Chén envoy Fēng Xiàoyǎn,
instructing his retainer to travel with the envoy,
and encountering a Kūnlún ship arriving,
he obtained dozens of rare goods, including fur rugs (guǒrán rùbiǎo), beautiful jade measuring more than a foot, and other items.
His crime warranted exile,
but he was allowed to commute the sentence.
Three years later,
he was reinstated and appointed Qīngdū Yǐn.
Soon after, he dispatched the Huángmén Láng Yuán Wényáo to issue an imperial decree to Shōu, saying:
“You are an old official,
having served My house for the longest time.
Regarding your previous crime,
the circumstances are pardonable.
Recently, in appointing you as Yǐn,
I did not intend it as a fine conferment,
but since it was your initial reinstatement,
this was the appropriate consideration.
How could We use your talent and yet neglect your person?
Wait until the tenth month,
and I shall restore you to the rank of Kài fǔ.”
In the first year of Tiāntǒng,
he was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
In the second year,
he served provisionally as Qízhōu Cìshǐ,
and soon became the substantive appointee.
Because his sons and nephews were young, Shōu,
extended warnings and encouragement to them,
composing the *Zhěn Zhōng Piān* (Pillow Scroll Essay).
The text says: I once examined the writings of Guǎn Zǐ,
whose words state:
“Of heavy responsibilities, none is like the self;
of fearful paths, none is like the mouth;
of distant goals, none is like the span of years.
To carry a heavy burden, walk a fearful path,
and reach the distant goal,
only the Jūnzǐ is capable of achieving it.”
Reflecting upon these words and contemplating their meaning,
I sighed profoundly.
As for mountains standing high, being immense burdens,
some carry them secretly
without tilting;
a mountain cavern is called secure,
yet one may rush toward it, bearing burdens, without pause;
Lǚ Liáng is uniquely profound,
yet one may pass through singing without alarm;
Jiāo Yuán is deemed perilous,
yet some hasten
through without fear;
The Nine Heavens are now assembled,
thus one soars swiftly and indistinctly;
The Five Standards are to be fixed,
imagining the deep void and ascending the journey.
If the heavy burden has measure,
then taking it on makes one increasingly
secure;
if navigating peril has a method,
then surely one can traverse it without anxiety.
If that distant goal can be achieved,
the outcome will correspond, and it can be counted upon.
How could the principle of the divine be alone in this?
Human affairs are also exactly the same.
Alas!
Living between Heaven and Earth,
toiling in the domain of life and death,
one is assailed by appetites and desires,
pulled by fame and profit.
Fine grain and meat arrive
unexpectedly,
pearls and jade are amassed without effort;
consequently, arrogance and extravagance continually arise,
and peril and ruin swiftly follow.
Yet, the greatly virtuous of superior wisdom,
those who are perceptive and wise,
sometimes
emerge, sometimes withdraw,
their integrity is not fixed.
When they are at ease, they save the age and accomplish tasks;
when they are withdrawn, their fame dissolves and their traces vanish.
Jade, silks, sons, and daughters,
pepper, orchids, and musical melodies,
flattery has no
precedence;
judging appearance and physique,
oiling the lips and inciting the tongue,
resentment and malice do not come before them.
Their merit and fame endure as long as mountains and rivers,
their aspirations and achievements are as firm as metal and stone.
This is surely like a sturdy
pillar that does not yield,
and the moving knife blade makes a swift, clean cut.
It extends to those whose virtue is inconstant,
who lose their inherent purity.
Rushing recklessly through the mortal world,
stirring up popular trends.
They hug the boiling sun yet claim it is cold,
they encompass deep valleys yet still feel dissatisfied.
If the source is unclear, the stream is muddy,
if the surface is not straight, the shadow is crooked.
Alas!
How can their bonds (like glue and lacquer) be firm?
The seasons are extremely fleeting.
They turn
benefit into harm,
and transform glory into humiliation.
Joy and sorrow alternate,
and gain and loss follow continuously.
It comes to the point where their bodies are haunted by malevolent spirits,
and their souls sink into the prison of the underworld.
Is this not because their inherent
strength is weak,
and they are lost within the current circumstances?
Who can say that a cart warns against tipping forward,
or that people follow the example of those who are first to realize truth?
I have heard of true gentlemen,
scholars of refined principles,
who delve into the classical arts,
sated by literature and history.
Their brushes possess extraordinary keenness,
their discussions contain superior reasoning.
When filial piety and fraternity reach their ultimate height,
their spiritual
understanding is penetrating.
They scrutinize the Way and proceed,
they gauge the road and know when to halt.
They extend themselves to others,
putting others before themselves.
Their emotions are not bound by glory or decline,
their minds are not fixated on resentment or joy.
They do not cultivate reputation in the mountains and valleys,
nor wait for their value to be sought in the cities and towns.
Their words and actions are mutually consistent,
they are as cautious at the end as at the beginning.
If one possesses even one of these qualities,
they flourish as a lofty model.
They reside diligently and carry out
their tasks,
knowing everything they must do.
Whether serving left or right,
this is appropriate for the outstanding scholar;
having no regret and no distress,
thus they are high-ranking yet not imperiled.
They are unlike those who bravely advance and forget retreat,
who hastily seek gain
and worry about loss,
aiming for assets worth a thousand gold pieces,
seeking official rank with ten thousand measures of stipend,
casting themselves into the gate of fierce winds,
and hurrying toward the chamber of blazing fire.
They trip repeatedly and lose the pleasant things they acquired,
or crouch down and then lose
Its constancy brings good fortune.
How can one not be fearful!
How can one not be cautious!
If calamity leans against the door,
affairs must necessarily be kept secret;
If hidden bandits lie behind the wall,
words must not be spoken carelessly.
One should examine one's words carefully,
one should straighten one's actions.
If words are not
good,
and actions are not upright,
Ghosts will seize the strong and violent,
men will imprison them in the courts.
In darkness, their soul is taken,
in daylight, their life is cut short.
Do not submit to the unlawful,
do not walk the wrong path.
Let the public
tripod be one’s faith,
private jade is not a personal treasure.
Exceeding black pigment makes deep purple,
surpassing indigo makes blue.
Hold the line to check straightness,
place water to observe levelness.
Only take when the time is right,
but it is not
equal to having no desires.
To know when to stop and know contentment,
is likely to spare one from disgrace.
Therefore, one must observe the subtle movements,
and every action must be careful regarding the minute details.
If one knows the subtle movements and considers the minute details,
then destruction will be rare.
Once observing and being careful,
fortune and emolument will accumulate.
In the past,
Qú Yuàn recognized forty-nine faults,
and Yán Zǐ was nearly three months without deviation.
If one ceaselessly takes small steps,
one reaches a thousand *lǐ*.
If one continues to overturn a single basket (of soil),
one reaches ten thousand *rèn*.
Therefore, it is said: traveling far begins nearby,
ascending heights starts from below.
One can be great and enduring,
moving along with the world's changes.
When the moon is full like a circle,
it wanes the next night.
The hibiscus flourishes on the branch,
but looking toward
dusk, it withers.
What profit is there that does not lead to loss?
What loss is there that does not lead to harm?
Profit should not be sought in excess,
gain should not be desired greatly.
Only those who dwell in virtue fear excess,
those who embody
the genuine dread magnitude.
When the Way is honored, a multitude of slanders gather;
when the responsibility is heavy, public resentment assembles.
When seeking prominence, Nífù was distressed and wandering;
when demonstrating loyalty, Zhōu Gōng was in a state of desperation
and difficulty.
Do not say that others restrict me;
it is because I myself am deficient and cannot cover (everything).
Do not say that others favor me;
it is because I myself am flawed and cannot avoid blame.
Like the greatness of a mountain,
there is nothing it does
not contain;
Like the emptiness of a valley,
there is nothing it does not receive;
If one can be strong and can be yielding,
heavy burdens can be borne;
If one can be trustworthy and can be compliant,
dangers can be overcome;
If one can be wise and can be foolish,
the mandate can be
long-lasting.
The man of the Zhōu temple,
kept his mouth thrice sealed.
The leaky goblet was placed in front,
the tipping vessel was kept behind.
This was intended for all later generations,
to be passed down as a constant reminder.
Afterward, the assembled officials often said the Wèi history was inaccurate,
so Wǔchéng again commanded a review and re-examination,
and Shōu (Wèi Shōu) once more altered and replaced sections.
Consequently, a biography was compiled for Lú Tóng,
and Cuī Chuò's was inserted separately.
Yáng Yīn's family biography
originally said,
"Since the establishment of Wèi, there has been only one family,"
but by this time, these eight characters were changed;
it had also previously stated
"a native of Huáyīn, Hóngnóng,"
but this was changed to
"who claimed to be from Hóngnóng,"
to match Wáng Huìlóng who claimed to be from Tàiyuán.
These were his faults.
Soon after, he was appointed Kāifǔ and Zhōngshū Jiān.
When Wǔchéng died,
the mourning period had not yet been announced.
The assembled lords inside the court doubted whether a general amnesty should be issued, as the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) had already been on the throne for several years.
The lords summoned Shōu to inquire about this.
Shōu firmly maintained that grace and favor should be granted,
so they followed his advice.
He was put in charge of imperial edicts,
appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
and oversaw the discussions and supervision of the Five Rites;
his rank was Tèjìn.
Shōu submitted a memorial requesting that Zhào Yànshēn, Hé Shìkāi, and Xú Zhīcái supervise the rites together.
He first informed Shìkāi,
who was astonished and declined, citing a lack of learning.
Shōu said:
"All affairs in the realm depend on Your Highness;
the Five Rites cannot be resolved without Your Highness."
Shìkāi thanked him and agreed.
He frequently invited literati to hold the writing brushes,
but the scholars Mǎ Jìngdé, Xióng Ānshēng, and Quán Huì were the actual chief authorities.
He died in the third year of Wǔpíng (572 CE).
He was posthumously granted the titles Sīkōng and Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
with the posthumous name Wénzhēn.
He left a collection of seventy volumes.
Shōu was a man of great scholarship and talent,
but his nature was narrow,
and he could not comprehend destiny or embody the Way.
When meeting influential nobles and grandees,
he always pleased them with his words and demeanor.
However, in promoting younger generations,
he prioritized integrity and conduct;
he did not value
those who were flashy, frivolous, and dangerous,
even if they possessed talent.
Initially, Xíng Zǐcái of Héjiān and Jìjǐng (Wēn Zǐshēng) were prominent alongside Shōu due to their literary talent.
The public called them Great Xíng and Little Wèi,
meaning they were especially outstanding.
Shōu was ten years younger than Zǐcái.
Zǐcái often said:
"The Buddha aids the greatness of my colleague."
Later, Shōu gradually competed with Zǐcái for reputation.
Wénxuān demoted Zǐcái, saying:
"Your talent does not equal Wèi Shōu."
Shōu increasingly felt satisfied.
He wrote in his own preface:
"First, they spoke of Wēn and Xíng,
later they said Xíng and Wèi."
However, Shōu inwardly slighted Xíng [Shǎo],
and mentally refused to concede the comparison.
Shōu was also flippant and hasty,
fond of music,
and skilled at Hú dance.
Towards the end of Wénxuān's reign,
he frequently performed monkey-and-dog fights with various entertainers on Dōngshān;
the Emperor favored and treated him intimately.
Shōu's cousin, Cuī Yán of Bólíng, once mocked Shōu using alliteration (shuāngshēng), saying:
"Yú Wèi Shuāi Shōu (Foolish Wèi, Waning Shōu)."
Shōu replied:
"Yán Yán Xīng Shòu (Swarthy Yán, Smelly and Lean),
by whom were you born?
You have a sheep's jaw and a dog's cheek,
a round head and a flat nose,
you occupy the rice shed like a basket,
and wear armor that jingles through the holes."
His verbal quickness and lack of restraint were thus demonstrated.
Because of his historical writings,
he caused great offense to many people.
In the year Qí perished (577 CE),
Shōu's grave was opened,
and his bones were discarded outside.
He had adopted his younger brother’s son, Rénbiǎo, as his heir,
who reached the position of Shàngshū Shànbù Lángzhōng.
During the Kāihuáng period of Suí, he died while serving as Wēn Xiàn Lìng.
Biographies, Chapter Thirty: Xīn Shù, Yuán Wényáo, Zhào Yànshēn
Xīn Shù,
courtesy name Huáizhē,
was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and possessed discernment and breadth of mind.
He entered officialdom as Sīkōng Zhòucáo Cānjūn.
He jointly supervised the construction of the Yè Dū palaces with Púyè Gāo Lóngzhī.
Shù had a well-organized mind,
and all the craftsmen successfully completed their tasks.
He was twice promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
He was sent out to serve as Qīnghé Tàishǒu,
and gained a reputation for competent governance.
He was subsequently appointed Bīngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ,
but resigned due to mourning his father.
Several hundred elders from Qīnghé went to the palace gates to request a stele be erected to commemorate his virtue.
When Wénxiāng succeeded to power,
Shù, along with Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Sòng Yóudào and Zhōngshū Shìláng Lǐ Huì, were summoned to Jìnyáng,
and all were treated as honored guests.
He was successively promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
, Hóu Jǐng rebelled
. (He) was appointed Minister of the Mobile Secretariat of the Southeast Circuit
and enfeoffed as Viscount of Jiāngxià County
. He and Gāo Yuè, among others, defeated Hóu Jǐng
and captured Xiāo Míng
. He was promoted to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dōngxú Prefecture
and served as Commissioner for Pacifying Huáinán
. In the first year of Tiānbǎo of Qí
, Hóu Jǐng levied taxes and grain from Jiāngxī
. Shù led various armies across the Huái River to intercept this
and burned several million *shí* of their rice
. He returned to garrison Xiàpī
. Over three thousand families followed Shù north across the Huái River
. Guō Zhì, the Governor of Dōngxú Prefecture, killed the Prefect
. Wénxuān, hearing of this
, commanded Shù that henceforth, regarding all lawbreakers in the ten-plus prefectures under his jurisdiction
, the governors (cìshǐ) must first submit a request and await approval
; those below the rank of governor should be judged first and then reported
. During the Qí dynasty, the Mobile Secretariats concurrently supervised all personnel matters
, beginning with Shù
. The Governor of Ān Prefecture, the Administrator of Línqīng Commandery, and the two garrison commanders of Xūyí and Qíchéng committed crimes
. Shù investigated, memorialized, and executed them all
. The Governor of Suī Prefecture and the Commandery Administrator under his jurisdiction both committed capital crimes
. The court bestowed their hundred-odd slaves and all their property upon Shù
. He declined three times but was not permitted to refuse
, so Shù then sent them to the relevant authorities
, reporting nothing further about them
. Xíng Shào heard of this
and sent a letter to Shù, saying
: “In the past, Zhōnglí Yì said, 'Confucius, though thirsty, endured not drinking from the Spring of the Thieves (Dàoquán)'
; therefore, he cast pearls and jades onto the ground
. That Your Excellency can now act in this manner
is truly exceptional in this age, compared to all past ages.”
When Wáng Sēngbiàn defeated Hóu Jǐng
, Shù sought out, welcomed, and pacified the populace
. Fortified cities and towns successively came over and submitted
, totaling more than twenty prefectures
. Thereupon, he moved his garrison to Guǎnglíng
. He obtained the Imperial Seal of State Transmission (Chuánguó Xǐ) and sent it to Yè
. Wénxuān reported the seal's acquisition to the Imperial Ancestral Temple
. This seal was originally manufactured by Qín
. It was four *cun* square
, with interlocking coiling dragons as the knob handle on top
, and its inscription read
: "Received Mandate from Heaven
, May Longevity and Eternal Prosperity be achieved."
The Two Hàn dynasties passed it down
, and it was subsequently passed to Wèi and Jìn
. When Emperor Huái was defeated
, it was lost to Liú Cōng
. When Cōng was defeated
, it was lost to the Shí family
. When the Shí family was defeated
, during the Yǒnghé reign of Emperor Mù of Jìn
, Dài Sēngshī, the Administrator of Púyáng, obtained it
and dispatched Supervisor Hé Róng to deliver it to Jiànyè
. It passed through Sòng, Qí, and Liáng
. When Liáng was defeated
, Hóu Jǐng obtained it
. When Jǐng was defeated
, Palace Attendant Zhào Sīxián handed the seal to Guō Yuánjiàn, Jǐng’s Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture
, who sent it to Shù
. Thus, Shù presented it
. Soon after, he was summoned to serve as Minister of the Palace Affairs (Diànzhōng Shàngshū)
, concurrently holding the post of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng)
, and continuing to deliberate on laws and statutes with court dignitaries
. He was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū)
and drew a salary from Liáng Commandery in Nányǎn Prefecture
. After the capital moved to Yè
, in the office of Grand Selection (dàxuǎn)
, several famous individuals served consecutively
. They all had successes and failures
, and none managed perfection
. Emperor Wénxiāng was young and outspoken
, his failing was being overly lax
. Yuán Shūdé was reserved, meticulous, and sincere
, his flaw was focusing too much on minor details
. Yáng Yīn was cultured, eloquent, and quick-witted
, but in selecting officials, he erred toward superficial glamour
. Only Shù’s nature prized integrity and clarity
. He selected officials based on talent and ability
, matched titles to actual performance
, recommended both new and old (officials)
, was certain to promote even minor officials
, and did not overlook established noble families
. Comparing him to earlier and later heads of personnel
, Shù was the most balanced and equitable
, and was highly praised by his contemporaries
. At the end of Tiānbǎo
, Wénxuān once ordered Shù to select a hundred officials
from two or three thousand candidates
. Shù designated and named the scholarly candidates
without anyone casting aspersions
. Those whom he recognized and promoted
later all achieved high prominence
. Shù was clean and frugal
, with few desires
. He was diligent in his duties
and never slacked off
. When commanding troops, he was stern and imposing
; when governing the people, he exercised benevolent policies
. In his youth, he loved literature and history
; in his later years, he furthered his studies
. Even while on campaign
, he never let go of a book
. When he pacified Huáinán
, he did not touch a single item of ordinary wealth or goods
. He only collected a great number of classics and records
, mostly fine editions from the Sòng, Qí, and Liáng periods
. He gathered over ten thousand volumes
, along with famous paintings by the likes of Gù and Lù
, and a considerable number of calligraphy works by the Two Wángs and others
. None of these were sent to the Royal Treasury
; they only entered his private household
. When he returned to court
, he frequently gave these items as gifts to influential figures
. Public opinion criticized him somewhat for this
. In the tenth year (of Tiānbǎo) he died
, aged sixty
. In the second year of Huángjiàn
, he was posthumously granted Excellency Who Opens a Residence with the Same Honors as the Three Ministers, Director of the Central Secretariat, and Governor of Qīng Prefecture
. His son, Géqīng
, was a Gentleman of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng)
. Géqīng’s younger brother, Héngqīng
, was knowledgeable and scholarly
, and served as an Administrator in the Excellency’s Residence
. At the beginning of the Dàyè reign of Suí
, he died while serving as Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices
. Yuán Wén-yáo
, courtesy name Déyuǎn
, was a native of Luòyáng, Hénán
, and a sixth-generation descendant of Emperor Zhāochéng of Wèi
. His fifth-generation ancestor was Zūn, Prince of Chángshān
. His father, Xī
, was known for his filial conduct
. When his own father died
, he lived in a mourning hut beside the tomb until his own death
. When Wén-yáo became eminent
, Xī was posthumously granted Special Advancement, Excellency Who Opens a Residence with the Same Honors as the Three Ministers, and Director of the Central Secretariat
, with the posthumous title Xiào (Filial)
. Wén-yáo was intelligent and wise, achieving maturity early
. Huīyè, Prince of Jìyīn, always said
: "This child possesses the talent to assist a king."
Huīyè once hosted a great gathering of guests
. Someone brought the collected works of Hé Xùn, which had just arrived in Luòyáng
, and all the dignitaries praised them
. Xíng Shào of Héjiān tested Wén-yáo
, asking after how many readings he could recite it
? Wén-yáo recited it after a single glance
. He was only a little over ten years old at the time
. The Prince of Jìyīn said
: "What do you now think of my spirited colt, capable of a thousand *lǐ* (qiānlǐ jū)?"
Xíng said
: "This has scarcely been seen throughout history."
He started his career as an Unattached Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary
. Upon suffering the loss of his father
, after the mourning period ended
, he was appointed Libationer in the Eastern Gallery of the Grand Commandant
. Given that the realm was in chaos
, he consequently resigned his post to attend to his mother
, and retired to Mount Línglǜ
. During the Wǔdìng reign
, Wénxiāng summoned him to be the Registrar of the Grand General’s Residence
. When Qí received the abdication (Shòuchán)
, he was appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat at the altar where the ceremony took place
, responsible for proclaiming military and civil decrees
. Yáng Zūnyàn often said
: "The one capable of holding the seal of Marquis Ráng
must be this man."
Later, he was suddenly imprisoned and detained by imperial decree
, though the reason was entirely unknown
. This lasted for several years
. Later, Wénxuān personally visited the prison
, held his hand, and apologized shamefacedly
. He personally removed the golden belt he was wearing and the imperial robes and bestowed them upon him
. Effective immediately, he was appointed Gentleman of the Bureau of Sacrifices (Cíbù Lángzhōng) in the Secretariat
. When Xiàozhāo assumed regency
, Wén-yáo was appointed Administrator and Staff Officer in the Residence of the Grand Chancellor
, managing confidential matters
. When Xiàozhāo ascended the throne
, Wén-yáo was appointed Palace Aide to the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng)
, enfeoffed as the Earl of Yǒnglè County
, and participated in major military and state affairs
. When the Emperor became gravely ill
, he, along with Guī Yàn, Prince of Píngqín, and Wáng Ruì, Prince of Zhàojùn, among others, received the dying entrustment
, and welcomed and enthroned Wǔchéng
. Upon his (Wǔchéng's) enthronement
, Wén-yáo's employment and treatment became increasingly lavish
. He successively held the posts of Palace Aide to the Gentlemen-at-the-Gate, Unattached Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), and Director of the Central Secretariat
. In the second year of Tiāntǒng
, an imperial edict specifically bestowed upon him the surname Gāo
, registered him in the Imperial Clan Court
, and allowed his sons and younger brothers to attend court annually according to the prescribed rules
. He was again promoted to Minister of the Left of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè)
, further enfeoffed as Duke of Níngdū Commandery
, and served as Palace Attendant
Wén Yáo served successively under three lords,
being perceptive regarding worldly affairs.
Whenever he attended court,
he often received orders to proclaim edicts,
issuing commands to both civil and military officials.
His voice was high and clear,
and his delivery fluent and unimpeded.
However, when probing the intentions of his superiors,
he sometimes uttered vulgar or coarse language,
hence he was not highly regarded by those who truly understood taste.
Because Qí inherited the practices of the Wèi dynasty,
county magistrates were often appointed from amongst the vulgar and incompetent,
to the extent that members of the gentry class considered serving as a county official shameful.
Wén Yáo believed that the county magistrate was crucial for governing the people,
and thus requested a reform of the selection process.
Thereupon, he secretly ordered the search and promotion of the sons of noble families and high officials,
and issued edicts appointing them.
Still fearing they might object,
he gathered them all together at Shénwǔ Mén (Divine Might Gate),
and ordered Zhào Jùnwáng Ruì to proclaim the imperial decree and announce their names,
adding lavish words of comfort and persuasion.
The practice of gentlemen serving as county officials
began from this point.
Since he received appointments and favorable treatment alongside Zhào Yànshēn and Hé Shìkāi,
although he was not as pure, steadfast, and faithful to the Dao as Yànshēn,
nor did he engage in the greed, immorality, and misrule of Shìkāi,
he stood somewhere between Jì and Mèng (second and third place).
However, his nature was gentle and generous,
and he competed with no one,
thus the popular opinion of the time did not place him below Yànshēn.
When Wén Yáo first moved from Luò to Yè,
he only possessed ten *qǐng* of land,
his family was poor,
and his means were only sufficient for clothing and food.
When the Wèi dynasty was nearing its end,
members of the imperial clan were often insulted.
Someone presumed to encroach upon and seize his property,
and Wén Yáo immediately yielded it to him.
When Wén Yáo later achieved high rank,
this man was still residing there,
and subsequently fled with his family.
Wén Yáo was greatly surprised,
and pursued him to offer comfort and reassurance,
returning the property to him.
That man was ashamed and refused to accept it;
both sides yielded the land,
and it eventually became unused land.
When the Latter Lord succeeded to the throne,
Zhào Jùnwáng Ruì, Lóu Dìngyuǎn, and others planned the removal of Hé Shìkāi,
and Wén Yáo also participated in the discussion.
When Ruì was killed,
Wén Yáo was consequently sent out to serve as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xī Yǎnzhōu.
He went to bid farewell to Shìkāi.
Shìkāi said:
"Having such a post,
allowing the Yuán family child (meaning himself, implying low status) to become the Director (Lìngpú),
deeply shames the court."
Having spoken, he regretted it,
and grasped Wén Yáo's hand to comfort and encourage him.
Still worried that Wén Yáo might be suspicious,
he appointed his son Xínggōng as a Director (Shàngshū Láng),
in order to soothe his heart.
When Shìkāi died,
Wén Yáo was summoned back to court from his post as Governor of Dōng Xúzhōu,
but ultimately was not utilized,
and he died.
Xínggōng had fine features,
possessed his father's demeanor,
and was also a brilliant talent.
He held the position of Palace Writer (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
and was retained for service at the Wénlín Guǎn.
When Qí fell,
Yáng Xiūzhī and eighteen others entered the Pass (Guān) together.
He gradually advanced to Sīxūn Xià Dàfū.
During the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
he held the position of Director (Shàngshū Láng),
but for an offense he was banished to Guāzhōu and died there.
When Xínggōng was young, he was rather arrogant and unruly.
Wén Yáo instructed him to associate with Fànyáng Lú Sīdào.
Wén Yáo once said to Sīdào:
"My son has recently gained a little knowledge,
which is thanks to the efforts of my younger brother (referring to Lú Sīdào himself).
However, his excessive drinking and dice playing,
greatly resembles the master's style."
Sīdào replied:
"The young master's manner of speech and spirit are brilliant and outstanding;
naturally, he is capable of continuing your great family lineage.
As for the excessive drinking and dice playing,
that is also a gift of his natural disposition."
Xínggōng's younger brother, Xíngrú,
was also clever and matured early.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he served as Aide to the Director of the Imperial Library (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng).
Zhào Yànshēn,
originally from Nányáng Wǎn in the South,
was a descendant of Hàn Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Xǐ.
His great-great-grandfather, Nàn,
served as the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Qīnghé,
governed kindly,
and consequently settled his family there.
Qīnghé was later changed to Píngyuán,
hence he was considered a person of Píngyuán.
His original name was Yǐn;
to avoid the Qí dynastic taboo name (miàohuì),
he changed to using his courtesy name (zì).
His father, Fèngbó,
served in Wèi in the position of Palace Writer (Zhōngshū Shèrén) and Acting Magistrate of Luòyáng.
When Yànshēn achieved prominence,
Fèngbó was posthumously given the title Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Yànshēn was orphaned and poor in his youth,
and served his mother with great filial piety.
At the age of ten,
he once paid a visit to Minister over the Masses (Sītú) Cuī Guāng.
Cuī Guāng said to his guests:
"The ancients judged a man by observing the pupils of his eyes;
this person will surely achieve great distinction."
His nature was intelligent and quick-witted,
he was skilled at writing and calculating,
he was tranquil and content with the Way,
and he did not engage in mixed social circles.
He was respected and admired by refined scholars.
At the break of dawn,
he would always sweep outside his gate himself,
without letting anyone see him,
making it his routine practice.
Initially, he served as a humble retainer of the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Sīmǎ Zǐrú,
assisting in copying documents.
Zǐrú praised his lack of errors
and wished to bring him into the government offices.
Yǐn had no boots,
and his clothes and cap were worn and tattered.
Zǐrú provided them.
He was employed as a Clerk (Shū Lìngshǐ).
After more than a month,
he was promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhèng Lìngshǐ).
When Shénwǔ was in Jìnyáng,
he requested two clerks,
and Zǐrú recommended Yànshēn.
Later, he was appointed Adviser to Zǐrú's Establishment (Kāifǔ Cānjūn),
and subsequently promoted exceptionally to Director of Waterways (Shuǐbù Láng).
When Wénxiāng served as Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) and oversaw selections,
he carried out a purge of the Directors of various Bureaus.
Yǐn, due to his humble background, was dismissed and appointed Vice Governor of Cāngzhōu (Cāngzhōu Biéjià),
but he refused the post.
Zǐrú spoke on his behalf to Shénwǔ,
and he was summoned and appointed Recorder and Adviser to the Grand Chancellor (Dà Chéngxiàng Gōngcāo Cānjūn).
He was solely in charge of military secrets and confidential matters,
and many important documents came from his hand;
he was known for being prompt and resourceful.
Shénwǔ once sat facing him,
sent him to draft military orders,
and touched his forehead, saying:
"If Heaven grants you longevity,
you will surely achieve great things."
He often said to Minister over the Masses (Sītú) Sūn Téng:
"Yànshēn's meticulousness, respectfulness, and prudence
are unmatched throughout the ages."
When Shénwǔ died,
the news of the mourning was kept secret.
Wénxiāng feared instability south of the Yellow River (Hénán),
and went personally to pacify the region.
He entrusted Yànshēn with the subsequent affairs,
who was transferred to Director of the Bureau of Judicial Affairs for the Central Mobile Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái Dūguān Lángzhōng).
Before departing,
he grasped Yànshēn's hand and wept, saying:
"I entrust you with matters concerning my younger brother (the heir),
and am fortunate to have such a reliable heart (in you)."
Afterward, stability prevailed both inside and outside the court,
which was due to Yànshēn's efforts.
When Wénxiāng returned and officially announced the mourning,
he praised Yànshēn highly,
and by going through the county records, he selected and enfeoffed him as the Earl of Ānguó County (Ānguó Xiàn Bó).
He followed in the campaign against Yǐngchuān.
At that time, they diverted water to flood the city,
and the battlements were on the verge of collapsing,
yet Wáng Sīzhèng, the general of Xī Wèi, still wished to fight to the death.
Wénxiāng ordered Yànshēn to enter the city alone to persuade them.
On that very day, the city surrendered,
and Yànshēn personally led Sīzhèng out of the city by the hand.
Previously,
Wénxiāng had said to Yànshēn:
"Last night I dreamed I was hunting,
and encountered a herd of swine.
I shot and captured all of them,
but one large boar could not be caught.
You said you would capture it for me,
and shortly thereafter, you captured the swine and presented it."
When this event (the surrender) occurred,
Wénxiāng laughed and said:
"The dream has been verified."
He immediately removed Sīzhèng’s scabbard knife and gave it to Yànshēn, saying:
"May you always achieve such success."
When Wénxuān succeeded to the throne,
he still managed confidential affairs,
and was advanced in rank to Marquis.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was successively promoted to Secretariat Director (Mìshū Jiān).
Because he was deemed loyal and careful,
whenever there were sacrifices at the suburban altars or imperial temples,
he was certainly ordered to concurrently serve as Grand Coachman (Tài Pú Qīng),
holding the reins and accompanying the Emperor in the carriage.
He was then transferred to Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sī Nóng).
When the Emperor occasionally toured or traveled,
he would assist and advise the Crown Prince
and oversee affairs of state.
He was posted out as Department Director of the Mobile Secretariat of the Southeast Circuit (Dōngnán Dào Xíngtái Shàngshū) and Prefect of Xúzhōu.
In governance, he prioritized kindness and trustworthiness,
and was cherished by the officials and common people.
He managed to appease many who had surrendered.
The location where he established military camps
was commemorated by the soldiers and commoners
and named Zhào Xíngtái Dùn (Campsite of Director Zhào).
Wénxuān sent an imperial seal letter to commend and encourage him,
and summoned him back to serve as Attendant Consultant (Shì Zhōng),
where he again handled confidential affairs.
In the first year of Héqīng (562 CE),
he was advanced in rank to Duke of Ānlè.

He was successively promoted to Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè), Chief Central Regulator of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng), and Supervisor of State History.
He was promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
served as Minister without Portfolio (Tè Jìn),
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yíyáng.
In the second year of Wǔpíng (571 CE), he was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Due to the slander of Zǔ Tǐng,
he was sent out to serve as Prefect of Xīyǎnzhōu.
Four years later,
he was summoned back as Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and then transferred to Minister of Education (Sītú).
He mourned the death of his mother,
but was soon recalled to his original post.
In the sixth month of the seventh year (576 CE), he died suddenly from illness,
at the age of seventy.
Yànshēn served through several reigns,
always participating in close confidential matters.
He was gentle and cautious,
and his joy or anger never showed on his face.
Since the Huángjiàn era (560-561 CE),
the rites shown toward him grew heavier.
Whenever he was granted an audience,
he was sometimes allowed to ascend the imperial couch,
and the Emperor always referred to him by his official title and never by his personal name.
For all selections and appointments,
he was first ordered to evaluate and decide.
When recommending and advancing personnel,
he always prioritized their conduct and profession,
and the frivolous and shallow sort
were never considered by him.
After Xiàozhāo seized power over the court,
many ministers secretly urged him to ascend the throne,
but Yànshēn alone did not make such a statement.
Xiàozhāo once said to Wáng Xī:
“If you say that the public heart believes that the realm has found its rightful master,
why have I not heard Yànshēn speak?”
Xī relayed this to him,
and Yànshēn had no choice
but to present his plea [for the ascension].
Such was the esteem in which he was held at the time.
He was always humble in speech and respectful of himself,
never treating others with arrogance or self-importance.
This is why he was sometimes sent out and sometimes stayed in court,
and when he left, he always returned.
His mother, Fù Shì,
was refined and possessed moral integrity.
When Yànshēn was three years old,
Fù Shì became a widow.
Her family wanted her to remarry,
but she swore to remain a widow until death.
When Yànshēn was five,
Fù Shì said to him:
“The family is poor and the child is young.
How can we manage?”
Yànshēn wept and replied:
“If Heaven pities us,
when this child grows up, I will certainly repay your kindness.”
Fù Shì was moved by his intention,
and wept with him.
When Yànshēn was appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tài Cháng Qīng)
and returned home,
he did not remove his court robes,
but first went in to see his mother,
kneeling to explain how, as a young and vulnerable orphan,
he had been able to reach his present position through her instruction.
Mother and son wept together for a long time,
and only then did he change his clothes.
Later, she became the Grand Consort of the Princedom of Yíyáng.
Yànshēn had seven sons;
Zhòngjiāng was the most famous.
Zhòngjiāng
was composed, sharp-witted, and possessed his father’s demeanor.
He was gentle, virtuous, respectful, and frugal.
Even when facing his wife and children,
he was never careless or neglectful,
and maintained a solemn composure all day long.
He studied a variety of texts
and was skilled in *cǎo* (cursive) and *lì* (clerical) scripts.
Even when writing a letter to his younger brother,
his characters were neat and standard,
saying that although one should understand *cǎo* script,
if it were used toward others,
it would seem like treating them lightly;
and if used toward juniors in the household,
he feared they might suspect that this was appropriate for the circumstances;
therefore, he insisted on using *lì* script.
Yànshēn requested that the hereditary position of Viscount of Wànnián County be transferred and conferred upon him.
He held the positions of Palace Attendant (Jǐ Shì Huángmén Shìláng) and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sàn Qí Chángshì).
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he served as Bureau Director of Personnel (Lìbù Láng),
and finally died while holding the post of Prefect of Ānzhōu.
Among the chancellors of the Qí dynasty,
Yànshēn was the only one who began well and ended well.
However, he implicitly requested the court to appoint his son, Shūjiān, as Secretariat Drafting Official (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
which attracted considerable public criticism.
At that time, the son of Féng Zǐcóng, Címíng, and the son of Zǔ Tǐng, Jūnxìn, were also successively serving in the Secretariat,
thus the saying at the time was:
“Féng, Zǔ, and Zhào
have defiled our Phoenix Pool [Secretariat].”
However, Shūjiān was the least capable in appearance and talent.
Biography Thirty-One: Cuī Jìshū, Zǔ Tǐng
Cuī Jìshū,
courtesy name Shūzhèng,
was a native of Ānpíng, Bólíng.
His father, Yúzhī,
was Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Qīng) of the Wèi dynasty.
Jìshū lost his father when young.
He was intelligent and sharp-witted by nature,
studied widely in the Classics and Histories,
was skilled in correspondence,
and possessed the talents necessary for his time.
At the age of seventeen,
he became Clerk of the Prefecture (Zhōu Zhǔbù).
He was highly valued by the Grand General, Duke Chēn of Zhàojùn,
who mentioned him to Shénwǔ [Gāo Huān].
Shénwǔ personally inspected the chief and subordinate officials
and appointed Jìshū as Section Chief of the Board of Justice of the Mobile Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái Dūguān Lángzhōng).
When Wénxiāng [Gāo Chéng] was assisting in government,
he was transferred to Central Military Counselor to the Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn),
and was greatly favored and trusted.
Since reliable men were needed close to the Wèi Emperor,
and trusted confidants had to be placed there,
Jìshū was promoted and appointed Secretariat Drafting Official (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
Wénxiāng became Supervisor of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and transferred all confidential matters from the Department of the Palace Gate (Ménxià) to the Secretariat.
Moreover, Jìshū was skilled in music,
so the imperial entertainers were also placed under his jurisdiction.
The subordination of the imperial entertainers to the Secretariat
began with Jìshū.
Whenever Wénxiāng submitted memorials to the Wèi Emperor,
offering advice or requests,
the wording might sometimes be overly complicated.
Jìshū would invariably revise and clarify the text,
ensuring that the advice or warnings could be expressed successfully.
When Emperor Jìng Dì replied to the court of the Hegemon (Bà Cháo),
he discussed the reply with Jìshū,
saying:
“Secretariat Official Cuī is my wet nurse.”
He was transferred to Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng)
and concurrently served as Commander-in-Chief of the Wardrobe (Zhǔ Yī Dūtǒng).
Although his office was in the Wèi court,
his heart belonged to the Hegemon’s Residence (Bà Fǔ),
and he was allowed to participate
in all secret schemes and grand strategies.
Consequently, guests flocked to him,
and he received them wholeheartedly with proper ceremony,
thus gaining great renown,
and his power overshadowed that of Cuī Xiān.
Xiān once bowed to him privately in the court hall, saying:
“If Xiān can become an Assistant Director (Púshè),
it will all be due to your kindness, Shūzhèng.”
His influence was that immense.
At that time, many meritorious nobles acted unlawfully,
and Wénxiāng spared none of them.
Public opinion wrongly attributed these acts to Jìshū and Cuī Xiān,
and they were greatly resented and hated.
When Wénxiāng met with disaster [i.e., was assassinated],
Wénxuān was preparing to depart for Jìnyáng.
Palace Attendant Yáng Xiūzhī urged Jìshū to accompany the journey,
saying:
“If one is absent from court for a day,
a blade can be placed in that interval.”
Jìshū loved music and women [sights and sounds],
and preferred a life of ease and indulgence,
so he did not ask to go,
wishing to indulge his pleasures.
Sīmǎ Zǐrú, because of a long-standing grudge,
together with the Director of Imperial Meals (Shàng Shí Diǎnyù), Chén Shāntí, et al., compiled a list of his transgressions.
As a result, Jìshū and Xiān were each flogged two hundred times
and exiled to the northern border.
In the early Tiānbǎo period,
Wénxuān knew he was innocent,
and posthumously appointed him Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng.
He was twice promoted to Shìzhōng.
Soon after, he concurrently held the positions of Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè and Yítóng Sānsī,
and was greatly favored.
In the early Gānmíng period,
Yáng Yīn, following Wénxuān's dying wishes,
suspended his position as Púyè.
He resigned due to his mother's mourning.
After resuming office,
he was appointed Guānglùxūn,
and concurrently Zhōngbīng Shàngshū.
He was sent out as Qízhōu Cìshǐ.
He was impeached for sending people across the Huái River for mutual trade,
and also for graft and bribery.
He was impeached by the Yùshǐ,
but a general amnesty meant the matter was not pursued.
When Wǔchéng was a prince,
he once fell ill.
Wénxuān ordered Jìshū to treat his illness,
and he put forth his utmost effort.
In the early Dàníng period,
he was recalled,
brought in, and comforted and encouraged.
He was repeatedly appointed Dùzhī Shàngshū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When the Zhāoyáng Hall was being constructed,
he was ordered to supervise its building.
Because Hú Chángrén secretly spoke ill of his style of judging cases,
he was sent out as Xīyǎnlüzhōu Cìshǐ.
For recommending a Diǎnqiān to the Lìbù,
he was reprimanded and dismissed from office.
He was also ordered to go to Guǎngníngwáng's residence
and receive dozens of horsewhip strokes.
When Wǔchéng died,
he was not allowed to participate in the mourning.
After a long time,
he was appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ,
then promoted to Shìzhōng and Kāifǔ,
and received income from the two commanderies of Xīn'ān and Héyīn.
He was granted the title Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
attended the Wénlín Guǎn by imperial decree,
and supervised the compilation of the Yùlǎn.
He was granted the title Tèjìn and supervised the national history.
Jìshū was always fond of books and documents.
In his later years, he became even more diligent.
He also recommended talented individuals
and encouraged literature.
The discussions of the time were universally positive,
and he was praised far and wide.
Zǔ Tǐng, having been entrusted with power,
recommended Jìshū to oversee all internal works.
When Tǐng was dismissed,
Hán Chángluán considered him a partisan of Tǐng's,
and also wanted to dismiss him.
It happened that the emperor was about to go to Jìnyáng.
Jìshū discussed with Zhāng Diāo,
believing that with Shòuchūn under siege
and a large army deployed to resist,
messengers traveling back and forth would need instructions.
Moreover, ordinary people on the roads
might be alarmed,
saying that the emperor was heading to Bīng
to evade southern invaders.
If they did not admonish,
it would certainly stir up public sentiment.
Thus, he, along with the accompanying civil officials, jointly submitted an admonition.
At that time, the high officials Zhào Yànshēn, Táng Yōng, Duàn Xiàoyán, and others were initially in agreement,
but at the crucial moment, they wavered.
Jìshū argued with them, but no decision was reached.
Chángluán then reported,
"The Han civil officials have jointly signed a memorial,
claiming to advise against going to Bīng.
In reality, they may well be plotting rebellion,
and should be executed."
The emperor immediately summoned the officials who had signed the memorial to the Hánzhāng Hall,
and, with Jìshū, Zhāng Diāo, Liú Tì, Fēng Xiàoyǎn, Péi Zé, and Guō Zūn as the leaders,
had them all beheaded in the palace courtyard.
Chángluán ordered their bodies to be thrown into the Zhāng River.
As for the others who had signed,
they were about to be flogged,
but Zhào Yànshēn remonstrated and they were spared.
The male and female family members of Jìshū and the others were exiled to the northern frontier.
Their wives and daughters-in-law were assigned to the Xī Guān (slave bureau),
their young sons were sent to the Cán Shì (silkworm chamber for castration),
and their property was confiscated.
Jìshū was very fond of medicine.
During the Tiānbǎo period,
he had nothing to do at his place of exile,
so he devoted himself to intensive study,
and thus became a renowned practitioner,
saving many lives.
Although his position and prestige grew,
he never slackened.
Even for the poor and lowly servants,
he would treat them.
His illegitimate son, Chángjūn,
was Shàngshū Yòuwàibīng Lángzhōng.
His second son, Jìngxuán,
was Zuòzuò Zuǒláng.
Both were exiled to distant, desolate places.
Not long after,
the wives of Jìshū and the other six men were released due to old age.
Later, Nán'ān Wáng Sīhǎo further denounced the court's transgressions,
using the wrongful killing of Jìshū and the others as justification.
He summoned all the brothers, sons, and nephews of the six men to join his army and head to Jìnyáng.
When the plot failed,
Chángjūn and the others were all executed.
The wives of the six men were again recalled to government service.
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu conquered Qí,
an imperial edict stated that Húlǜ Guāng and the six men including Jìshū would all receive posthumous honors.
Jìshū was posthumously granted the titles Kāifǔ Yítóng Dàjiàngjūn and Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zǔ Tǐng,
courtesy name Xiàozhēng,
was a native of Qiú, Fányáng.
His father, Yíng,
was Wèi Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Tǐng was quick-witted and alert in spirit,
and his literary style was vigorous and refined.
He gained an excellent reputation at a young age,
and was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng.
His policy responses ranked highly,
and he became Shàngshū Yí Cáo Lángzhōng,
in charge of ceremonial records.
He once composed the "Qīngdé Sòng" (Eulogy of Pure Virtue) for Wànsì Shòuluò, the Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Its text was elegant and beautiful,
and because of this, Shénwǔ heard of him.
At that time, Wénxuān was Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and appointed Tǐng as Kāifǔ Cāocáo Cānjūn.
Shénwǔ orally dictated thirty-six matters to Tǐng,
and when he wrote them down,
not a single one was missed.
He was greatly admired by his colleagues.
At that time, Shénwǔ sent Wèi Lánlíng Gōngzhǔ out of the frontier to marry the Rúrú.
Wèi Shōu composed two poems, "Chūsài" and "Gōngzhǔ Yuǎnjià,"
and Tǐng harmonized with both of them,
which were widely circulated and recited by people of the time.
Tǐng’s nature was negligent and unrestrained,
unable to be honest, cautious, or adhere to principles.
Although the Cāngcáo (Granary Registrar) was nominally a local office,
it received taxes and tribute from Shāndōng;
because of this, he gained large receipts,
and became rich in property.
He also taught himself how to play the pípá (lute),
and could compose new tunes.
He invited young men from the city to sing for entertainment,
and often gathered at various entertainers' homes.
He engaged in revelry involving music and women with Chén Yuánkāng, Mù Zǐróng, Rèn Zhòu, Yuán Shìliàng, and others.
These men once stayed overnight at Tǐng’s place.
He brought out over a hundred bolts of finely patterned silk from Shāndōng, including “linked-pearl peacock damask,”
and ordered the female servants to play chūpú (a dice game) and gamble with them,
taking pleasure in the spectacle.
The Staff Officer Yuán Jǐngxiàn
was the son of the former Grand Secretary Yuán Shìjùn.
His wife was the daughter of Sīmǎ Qìngyún,
and was born to Wèi Xiàojìng Dì’s paternal aunt, Bólíng Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ.
Tǐng suddenly welcomed Jǐngxiàn’s wife to the banquet,
where she slept with the various men in rotation,
this also being achieved through the use of goods and money.
His extravagance, license, and dissipation were like this.
He often said:
“A true man must never cheat himself in this lifetime.”
When Wénxuān left his post as Governor,
Tǐng should have, by precedent, accompanied the commandery.
He sought to stay within the granary office,
and appealed to Chén Yuánkāng.
Yuánkāng reported on his behalf,
and consequently, Tǐng returned to his post as Cāngcáo.
Tǐng subsequently entrusted himself completely to the Staff Officer acting as Diǎnqiān (Palace Usher), Lù Zǐxiān,
and they plotted together.
When requesting rations,
he ordered Zǐxiān to issue an edict
to take ten carts of grain from the granary
and deliver them to the colleagues.
Shénwǔ personally questioned him.
Tǐng claimed that he had not issued the order,
shifting the blame to Zǐxiān.
Shénwǔ believed him and released him.
Tǐng left and said:
“This was due to the Chancellor’s (Shénwǔ’s) natural insight,
but it was actually Xiàozhēng who did it.”
His nature was unrestrained and permissive.
Once, when he went drinking at the home of the Jiāozhōu Governor Sīmǎ Shìyún,
he secretly hid two bronze mirrors.
Someone requested that all the guests be searched,
and indeed, they found them inside Tǐng’s robes.
Those who witnessed it considered it a deep disgrace.
The old horse he rode
he always called a red colt (liú jū).
Furthermore, he had an illicit affair with the widow Wáng Shì,
and they often communicated back and forth openly in front of others.
Péi Ràngzhī and Tǐng were close early on.
In front of the crowd, he ridiculed Tǐng, saying:
“How can you be so strange and perverse?
Your old horse is ten years old,
yet you still call it a red colt;
your wife is sixty years old,
yet you still call her ‘young lady’ (niángzǐ).”
At that time, this story was noisily circulated.
Later, he became the Gōngcáo (Merit Officer) for Shénwǔ's central and outer headquarters.
Shénwǔ held a banquet for his subordinates.
A gold drinking cup (pǐluó) was lost during the seating.
Dòu Tài ordered everyone who had been drinking to remove their caps.
It was found on top of Tǐng’s hairknot.
Shénwǔ was unable to punish him.
Later, he served as Mìshū Chéng (Secretary-General),
overseeing the Shèrén (Secretaries),
and serving Wénxiāng.
When a guest from the province arrived,
he asked to sell the *Huálín Biànlüè*.
Wénxiāng gathered many scribes
and had it copied entirely within one day and one night.
He returned the original text, saying:
“I don’t need it.”
Tǐng used several scrolls of the *Biànlüè* as collateral for money to play chūpú.
Wénxiāng beat him forty times with a rod.
He also worked with Clerk Lǐ Shuāng and Granary Supervisor Chéng Zǔ, among others, to forge a petition to Jìnzhōu,
requesting three thousand *shí* (measures) of grain,
claiming to substitute for the Gōngcáo Staff Officer Zhào Yànshēn in transmitting Shénwǔ's order for the allocation.
The Staff Officer of the City Bureau, Gāo Jǐnglüè, who was acting as Diǎnqiān,
doubted that the order was genuine,
and secretly questioned Yànshēn.
Yànshēn replied that no such event had occurred.
Tǐng was subsequently interrogated and investigated,
and immediately confessed.
Shénwǔ was furious,
ordering two hundred lashes,
assignment to the armor workshops,
and the application of a collar (cangue).
The grain had to be repaid twofold.
Before the punishment could be carried out,
it happened that the Dìngguó Sì in Bìngzhōu was newly completed.
Shénwǔ said to Chén Yuánkāng and Wēn Zǐshēng:
“In the past, when we commissioned the inscription for the Mángshān Sì stele,
it was praised as supremely wonderful.
Now, for the Dìngguó Sì stele, whom should we ask to compose the text?”
Yuánkāng took the opportunity to recommend Tǐng for his talent and learning,
adding that he also understood the Xiānbēi language.
Tǐng was then provided with writing materials at his place of confinement to draft the text.
He finished it within two days,
and the composition was very beautiful.
Shénwǔ, seeing that it was both skillful and fast,
specially pardoned him and did not pursue the matter further,
though he was still stripped of his official post and served as an unofficial Staff Member at the Xiàngfǔ (Chancellor’s Residence).
When Wénxiāng succeeded (to authority),
he appointed Tǐng as Gōngcáo Cānjūn (Merit Officer Staff Member).
When Wénxiāng was assassinated,
Yuánkāng was heavily wounded.
He asked Tǐng to write a letter arranging his family affairs,
and also said:
“I have a few small items with Zǔ Xǐ;
you should retrieve them quickly.”
Tǐng did not deliver this letter.
Instead, he summoned Zǔ Xǐ and questioned him privately.
He obtained twenty-five gold ingots.
He only gave Xǐ two ingots,
keeping the rest for himself.
He also stole several thousand scrolls of Yuánkāng's family writings.
Zǔ Xǐ harbored resentment,
and consequently informed Yuánkāng’s two younger brothers, Shūchén and Jìqú.
Shūchén told Yáng Yīn,
who frowned and replied:
“I fear this will not benefit the deceased.”
Thus, the investigation was halted.
When Wénxuān became Chancellor,
Tǐng nominated over ten clerks for appointments,
all involving bribery.
According to the law, this warranted execution by strangulation,
but the Emperor soon pardoned him.
He also stole an official copy of the *Biànlüè*.
When the matter was discovered,
Wénxuān handed the case to the Executive Director Wáng Shǐyǎ for investigation,
and also wrote a letter to Píngyáng Gōng Yān,
ordering him to seize Tǐng and commit him to prison,
and not allow him to escape.
Yān dispatched the Agricultural Registrar Staff Officer Sūn Zǐkuān to summon him.
Tǐng received the order,
and immediately fled secretly.
The Court Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Gāo Dézhèng, who was assisting in the retention of the secretariat matters,
schemed, saying:
“Tǐng knows he committed a crime,
so fleeing in panic is expected.
We should only issue one order to the Secretariat,
stating
that ‘in accordance with the Bìngzhōu regulations, three sets of the Five Classics are required,
and the Secretary-General must personally verify and dispatch them.’
If we do this, Tǐng will feel safe,
and he will surely return home at night,
whereupon we can seize him.”
Tǐng indeed acted according to Dézhèng’s plan,
and returned home.
In the early evening,
they surrounded his house and captured him,
binding Tǐng and sending him to the Tíngwèi (Commander of Justice).
Based on the crime of bending the law for personal gain, he was sentenced to execution by strangulation.
Wénxuān, considering that Tǐng had served his predecessors,
subtly directed the department concerned to grant him special leniency in his punishment.
Consequently, a memorial was submitted recommending commutation of the death penalty and removal from office.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (550 CE),
he was again summoned to accompany the Emperor.
Following the precedent for those pardoned and dismissed,
he served in Jìnyáng.
Tǐng was naturally intelligent;
there was nothing difficult for him to learn.
He paid attention to all kinds of arts and skills.
None failed to occupy his interest.
Aside from literature,
he was also skilled in music,
understood the languages of the four surrounding tribes, as well as cosmology and divination,
and medical techniques were particularly his forte.
Although Emperor Wénxuān Dì disliked his frequent violations of the law,
he cherished his talent and skills.
He ordered Tǐng to serve in the Zhōngshū Shěng (Palace Secretariat),
in charge of edicts and pronouncements.
Tǐng submitted a confidential report,
implicating Zhōngshū Shìláng (Palace Attendant Secretary) Lù Yuánguī.
An imperial edict ordered Péi Yīng to interrogate him.
Yuánguī, because his responses displeased the Emperor,
was assigned to the armor workshops.
Tǐng was appointed Shàngyào Chéng (Assistant Administrator of the Imperial Pharmacy),
and soon after was promoted to Diǎnyù (Palace Manager).
He also proposed the manufacture of walnut oil.
He was again dismissed from office for embezzlement/cutting costs.
Whenever Wénxuān saw him,
he always called him a “thief.”
When Wénxuān died,
veteran officials were broadly selected (for promotion).
Tǐng was appointed Zhāngwǔ Tàishǒu (Governor of Zhāngwǔ Commandery).
At the time of the execution of Yáng Yīn and others,
he did not take up the post,
but was appointed Zhùzuò Láng (Compiler).
He repeatedly submitted confidential memorials,
which angered Xiàozhāo.
An imperial edict was issued to the Zhōngshū and Ménxià (Palace Secretariat and Palace Chancellery) Ministries, ordering them to refuse Tǐng's memorials.
Tǐng was skilled at making walnut oil for painting,
and he presented it to the Prince of Chángguǎng,
consequently saying:
"Your Highness possesses an extraordinary physique and demeanor.
Xiàozhēng dreamed Your Highness rode a dragon up to heaven."
The Prince said to him:
"If this is so,
I shall ensure that my elder brother achieves great wealth and nobility."
When he ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Wǔchéng,
he promoted Tǐng to be a Zhōngshū Shìláng.
In the rear garden, the Emperor had Tǐng play the pípá,
and Hé Shìkāi performed a Hu dance,
each receiving a reward of a hundred pieces of fabric.
Shìkāi envied him,
and Tǐng was sent out to become the Administrator of Āndé,
then transferred to be the Administrator of Qíjùn.
Citing his mother's old age, he requested to return home to serve and care for her,
which the imperial decree permitted.
At that time, an envoy from Jiāngnán came to seek an alliance,
and Tǐng served as the Zhōngláo Shǐ.
Soon after, he became Tàicháng Shàoqīng, Sànqí Chángshì, and Jiǎ Yítóng Sānsī,
overseeing imperial decrees and edicts.
Earlier, during the Qiánmíng and Huángjiàn eras,
Tǐng knew Wǔchéng secretly harbored great ambitions,
and thus deeply sought to ally himself with Wǔchéng,
bowing to respectfully serve him.
Wǔchéng had frequently been reprimanded during the Tiānbǎo period,
and his heart always resented this.
Tǐng, seeing this opportunity to anticipate the Emperor's wishes,
submitted a memorial requesting that the ancestral title Tàizǔ Xiànwǔ Huángdì be posthumously honored as Shénwǔ,
and that the ancestral title Gāozǔ Wénxuān Huángdì be changed to Wēizōng Jǐngliè Huángdì,
in order to please Wǔchéng.
The request was granted.
At that time, the Empress loved her youngest son, Prince Yǎn of Dōngpíng,
and wished to make him heir.
However, since the Later Lord was legitimate and the eldest, Wǔchéng
found it difficult to change the succession.
Tǐng spoke privately to Shìkāi:
"Your favor and fortune
are unparalleled throughout history.
If the imperial carriage departs late one day (i.e., the Emperor dies),
how will you manage to bring your career to a successful conclusion?"
Shìkāi then requested a plan.
Tǐng said:
"You should persuade the Emperor,
saying that the sons of Emperors Xiāng, Xuān, and Zhāo Dì all failed to maintain the throne.
It is fitting now to order the Crown Prince to assume the great position early,
thereby establishing the relationship between sovereign and minister firmly.
If this succeeds,
the Empress and the young Prince will both be grateful to you.
This is the most secure plan.
You should subtly mention this,
so that the Emperor gains a rough understanding,
and I shall then submit a memorial from the outside to argue the case."
Shìkāi agreed.
Coincidentally, a comet appeared,
and the Grand Astrologer reported that it was a sign of 'removing the old and establishing the new.'
Tǐng then submitted a letter,
stating:
"Although Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven,
this is not the ultimate nobility.
According to the Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo, it says: 'The year of Yǐyǒu
removes the old and changes the government.'
This year's Grand Cycle is Yǐyǒu;
it is fitting to pass the throne to the Eastern Palace (Crown Prince),
allowing the division between sovereign and minister to be settled early,
and moreover, to accord with the Mandate of Heaven."
He also presented the historical precedent of Emperor Xiànwén of Wèi abdicating to his son.
The Emperor followed the advice.
Consequently, Tǐng was appointed Bìshū Jiān,
given the honorary title Yítóng Sānsī,
and received great personal favor.
Having gained importance in both palaces,
he set his sights on the chancellorship.
Previously, he was good friends with the Huángmén Shìláng, Liú Tì.
Tǐng therefore listed the crimes of the Shìzhōng Shàngshū Lìng Zhào Yànshēn, the Shìzhōng Zuǒ Púyè Yuán Wényáo, and the Shìzhōng Hé Shìkāi,
instructing Tì to present the list.
Tì was afraid and dared not convey it.
The matter was somewhat leaked,
and Yànshēn and the others went first to the Emperor to present their own case.
The Emperor was furious,
seized Tǐng, and interrogated him, saying:
"Why did you defame my Shìkāi?"
Tǐng then said in a stern voice:
"I gained promotion through Shìkāi,
and originally had no intention of defaming him.
Since Your Majesty now questions me,
I dare not fail to reply with the truth.
Shìkāi, Wényáo, Yànshēn, and the others monopolize power and authority,
controlling the imperial court.
They collaborate internally and externally with the Lìbù Shàngshū Wèi Jǐn,
jointly engaging in conspiracy,
selling offices and trading judicial outcomes.
Governance is achieved through bribery,
leading to popular songs and ballads (of complaint).
If this were known to those who are discerning,
how could it possibly be heard by the four frontiers!
If Your Majesty pays no attention to this,
I fear the achievements of Dà Qí will be ruined."
The Emperor said:
"Then you are slandering me!"
Tǐng said:
"I dare not slander you,
