but Your Majesty took a certain man's daughter."
The Emperor said:
"I saw she was poor and starving,
so I took her in and cared for her."
Tǐng said:
"Why did you not open the granaries to provide relief,
but instead bought her and brought her into the imperial harem?"
The Emperor grew increasingly enraged,
struck Tǐng in the mouth with the ring end of a saber,
and ordered whips and staffs to rain down randomly,
intending to beat him to death.
Tǐng shouted loudly, saying:
"If you do not kill me,
Your Majesty will gain fame.
If you kill me,
I will gain fame.
If you wish to gain fame,
do not kill me.
I will synthesize immortal elixirs for Your Majesty."
Consequently, he was granted a small reprieve.
Tǐng also said:
"Your Majesty has a Fàn Zēng whom you cannot utilize;
do you know what the consequences will be?"
The Emperor angrily replied:
"You are making yourself Fàn Zēng,
and taking me for Xiàng Yǔ!"
Tǐng said:
"How could one possibly reach the level of Xiàng Yǔ himself,
were it not that the Mandate of Heaven did not reach him?
Xiàng Yǔ, a commoner,
led a haphazard crowd,
and in five years established the hegemony of a king.
Your Majesty relies on the resources of your father and brother
to have reached this point.
I do not think Xiàng Yǔ can be easily dismissed.
Why should I stop at comparing myself to Fàn Zēng?
Even Zhāng (Liáng) cannot surpass me.
Zhāng Liáng, though he was the tutor to the Crown Prince,
still had to rely on the Four White-Headed Ones
to finally secure the succession of the Hàn dynasty.
I hold no advisory or auxiliary position;
I am an outsider.
Yet I exhausted my strength and loyalty
to urge Your Majesty to abdicate the throne,
so that Your Majesty might be honored as the Tàishàng Emperor,
and your son might occupy the throne.
This allows both yourself and your son
to preserve your blessings.
The paltry Zhāng Liáng
is not even worth mentioning."
The Emperor became even more furious
and ordered earth to be stuffed into Tǐng's mouth.
Tǐng spat out the dirt and continued speaking,
refusing to yield or submit.
He was then given two hundred lashes,
assigned to the Jiǎfāng barracks,
and soon after, was exiled to Guāng Zhōu.
The Cìshǐ, Lǐ Zǔxūn, treated him very kindly.
The Biéjià, Zhāng Fènglǐ, wishing to curry favor with the powerful ministers,
submitted a report, saying:
"Although Tǐng is a banished prisoner,
he constantly sits opposite the Cìshǐ."
The imperial reply stated:
"Imprison him."
Fènglǐ stated:
"Láo (prison)
means an underground dungeon."
He then dug a deep pit,
placed Tǐng inside,
severely enforced restrictions and prohibitions,
kept shackles constantly on him,
and prevented family and relatives from visiting.
At night, he used candles made of turnip seeds to smoke Tǐng's eyes,
When Wǔchéng died,
the Hòuzhǔ remembered him,
and forthwith appointed him Cìshǐ of Hǎizhōu.
At that time, Lù Língxuān meddled externally in court politics,
and her son, Mù Típó, was favored and trusted.
Tǐng then sent a letter to Lù Ǎo's brother, Xīdá, saying:
"Zhào Yànshēn is a deep and profound schemer;
he wishes to enact the deeds of Yī and Huò.
How can the Yítóng and his sister enjoy peace?
Why not employ wise gentlemen early?"
Hé Shìkāi also believed that Tǐng was capable of deciding great affairs,
and wished to make him his chief strategist.
Therefore, he abandoned their former enmity,
and treated him with an open mind.
He spoke with Lù Ǎo to the Emperor, saying:
"The three emperors, Xiāng, Xuān, and Zhāo,
none of their sons were permitted to ascend the throne.
That the Zhìzūn is still on the imperial seat today
is truly due to Zǔ Xiàozhēng.
This man has rendered great service,
and he should be repaid with heavy favor.
Although Xiàozhēng's integrity might be thin,
his unique strategies surpass others,
and he can truly be relied upon in emergencies.
Furthermore, since he is blind in both eyes,
he surely harbors no rebellious intentions.
Please summon him and ask for his plans and schemes."
He agreed.
[Zǔ Tǐng] entered to become Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū and Mìshū Jiān,
and was granted the rank of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
After Hé Shìkāi died,
[Zǔ Tǐng] still persuaded Lù Ǎo to remove Yànshēn,
and made Tǐng himself Shìzhōng.
While in Jìnyáng,
he submitted a secret memorial requesting the execution of the Prince of Lángyé.
Once his plan was executed,
he was gradually appointed and favored.
Furthermore, when the Tàihòu was confined,
Tǐng wished to make Lù Ǎo the Tàihòu.
He compiled precedents concerning the Empress Dowagers of the Wèi Dynasty
and spoke of them to the Tàijī.
He said to people:
"Although the Tàijī is said to be a woman,
she is truly a heroine and outstanding figure;
none like her have appeared since Nǚwā."
The Tàijī also called Tǐng the Guóshī and Guóbǎo.
Because of this, he was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
Supervisor of the Guóshǐ,
granted the rank of Tèjìn,
entered the Wénlín Guǎn,
supervised the overall compilation of documents,
was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yānjùn Gōng,
received the revenues of Tàiyuán Jùn,
and was supplied with seventy soldiers.
His residence was located in Yìjǐng Fāng.
He expanded it, encroaching upon neighboring houses,
carrying out massive construction.
Lù Ǎo personally went to inspect the works.
His influence overshadowed the court and countryside.
Húlǜ Guāng greatly disliked him.
Seeing him from afar, he secretly cursed, saying:
"That busy, begging, petty man,
what scheming is he planning to carry out now!"
He often said to his generals:
"News from the borders,
troop movements and assignments—
Zhào Lìng used to discuss them with us.
Since that blind man took charge of military secrets,
he doesn't speak with us at all.
I am merely afraid he will ruin the affairs of the state."
Tǐng, having heard of these remarks,
used the fact that Húlǜ Guāng's daughter, the Empress, had fallen out of favor,
and presented a rumor to the Emperor, saying:
"A hundred measures fly up to the sky,
the bright moon shines on Cháng'ān."
He ordered his wife's elder brother, Zhèng Dàogài, to memorialize it.
The Emperor questioned Tǐng,
and Tǐng confirmed the story.
He also related a different rumor, saying:
"The high mountain collapses,
the oak tree rises,
the blind old man carries a large axe on his back,
the busy old mother cannot speak."
Tǐng added that
"the blind old man is your servant,"
meaning he shared the country's sorrow and trouble.
He advised the Emperor to carry out the necessary action,
saying
"That busy old mother
seems to refer to the female Shìzhōng, Lady Lù."
The Emperor inquired about this to Hán Chángluán and Mù Típó,
and also commanded Gāo Yuánhǎi and Duàn Shìliáng to discuss it secretly.
The group did not immediately agree.
Subsequently, Fēng Shìràng, an aide in Húlǜ Guāng's commandery, memorialized claiming Guāng was rebellious,
and consequently, his entire clan was exterminated.
Tǐng again attached himself to Lù Ǎo,
and sought the position of Lǐngjūn.
The Hòuzhǔ granted it.
The edict required review,
necessitating the signature of the Shìzhōng, Húlǜ Xiàoqīng.
Xiàoqīng secretly informed Gāo Yuánhǎi.
Yuánhǎi told Hóu Lǚfēn and Mù Típó:
"Xiàozhēng is a Hàn man,
and moreover, he cannot see with both eyes.
How can he possibly serve as Lǐngjūn?"
The next morning, they memorialized in person,
fully stating why Tǐng was unsuitable,
and also wrote that Tǐng was associating with the Prince of Guǎngníng, Xiàohéng,
thus lacking the demeanor of a high minister.
Tǐng also requested a personal audience.
The Emperor ordered him brought in.
Tǐng defended himself,
and stated that he and Yuánhǎi had always been mutually suspicious,
and that Yuánhǎi must have slandered him.
The Emperor was embarrassed and could not deny it,
saying:
"Yes, that is so."
Tǐng then listed Yuánhǎi's formation of cliques and parties with Yǐn Zǐhuá, the Sīnóng Qīng, Lǐ Shūyuán, the Tàifǔ Shǎoqīng, and Zhāng Shūlüè, the Píngzhǔn Lìng.
Consequently, Zǐhuá was removed to become Cìshǐ of Rénzhōu,
Shūyuán became Tàishǒu of Xiāngchéng Jùn,
and Shūlüè became Lùshì Cānjūn of Nányíng Zhōu.
Lù Ǎo then joined the chorus,
and Yuánhǎi was again removed to become Cìshǐ of Zhèngzhōu.
From then on, Tǐng solely controlled the pivotal government affairs,
overseeing all matters of the cavalry and external military forces.
His relatives, both immediate and extended,
all attained prominent positions.
The Hòuzhǔ also ordered several key eunuchs to support and attend him when entering and exiting.
Wearing his gauze cap, he went directly to the Yǒngxiàng,
passed through Wànchūn Mén toward the Shèngshòu Táng.
He frequently discussed and decided political matters while sitting beside the Emperor on the imperial couch.
The trust placed in him was so great
that no minister could compare.
Since Hé Shìkāi took charge of affairs,
the structure of governance had crumbled.
Tǐng promoted men of high reputation,
and officials performed their duties competently,
earning praise both within and outside the court.
He also intended to improve and rationalize government affairs,
and sift out unfit personnel.
He first memorialized requesting the abolition of the Jīngjī Fǔ,
merging its duties into the Lǐngjūn [office].
Matters concerning the common people
were all relegated back to the commanderies and counties.
Titles and ranks for the Imperial Guards and Dūdū, etc., reverted to their former official names,
and the formal attire for civil and military officials all followed established precedents.
He also intended to dismiss all eunuchs and petty individuals,
to foster sincerity in the court,
and make this the path to good governance.
Lù Ǎo and Mù Típó held somewhat differing opinions on this matter.
Tǐng thus prompted Lì Bóshì, the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, to impeach the zhǔshū Wáng Zǐchōng for taking bribes.
Knowing that the case involved Mù Típó,
he hoped that the crime of corruption would implicate him,
and expected that, through this indictment,
Lù Ǎo would also be affected.
Still fearing that the Hòuzhǔ was infatuated with his close attendants,
he sought to use the Empress's faction for support.
He requested that the Empress's elder brother, Hú Jūnyú, be made Shìzhōng and Zhōng Lǐngjūn,
and also summoned Jūnyú's older brother, Jūnbì, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu,
intending to make him Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Lù Ǎo heard of this and harbored anger,
devising a hundred ways to oppose and destroy Tǐng.
She immediately dismissed Jūnyú, making him Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
relieving him of the Zhōng Lǐngjūn post,
and Jūnbì was sent back to govern Liángzhōu.
The deposition of the Empress
was also partly due to this.
Wáng Zǐchōng was released and not questioned further.
Tǐng became increasingly estranged,
and the various eunuchs, in turn, slandered and ruined him,
going to every extreme.
The Hòuzhǔ questioned the Tàijī about him.
She lowered her head and remained silent, not replying.
After being asked three times,
she finally stepped down from the couch, bowed, and said:
"This old servant deserves death.
Originally, I saw Hé Shìkāi say that Xiàozhēng was highly talented and learned,
declaring him a good man,
so I recommended him.
Judging from recent events,
he is extremely guilty.
Men are truly difficult to know.
This old servant deserves death."
The Hòuzhǔ ordered Hán Chángluán to investigate the case,
and discovered more than ten instances where Tǐng had fraudulently issued imperial decrees or accepted bribes.
Since the Emperor had previously made a solemn vow not to kill him,
Tǐng was stripped of his Shìzhōng and Púyè titles
and sent out to be Cìshǐ of Běixú Zhōu.
Tǐng sought an audience with the Hòuzhǔ.
Hán Chángluán, having long resented Tǐng,
sent men to push him out of the Bǎigé.
Tǐng stubbornly insisted on a personal audience,
and sat down, refusing to move.
Chángluán then ordered soldiers to drag him out,
stood Tǐng in the court hall,
and severely reprimanded him.
After he had set off on the road,
the Emperor ordered him recalled,
stripped him of his Kāifǔ Yítóng and Duke titles,
and left him simply as a Cìshǐ.
When he arrived at the zhōu,
it happened that there were invaders from Chén,
and many common people rebelled.
Tǐng did not close the city gates.
He ordered all guards posted on the earthen ramparts to come down from the wall and sit quietly.
Pedestrians were forbidden from the streets and alleys.
Chickens and dogs were not allowed to crow or bark.
The bandits heard and saw nothing,
and could not fathom the reason why.
They suspected that the inhabitants had fled and the city was empty,
and thus did not set up guards or preparations.
Tǐng suddenly ordered a great shout,
beating drums and shouting loudly enough to shake the heavens.
The bandits were greatly startled,
and immediately scattered and fled.
Later, they reformed their ranks and approached the city.
Tǐng rode out personally on horseback,
ordering the Lùshì Cānjūn Wáng Jūnzhí to lead the troops and horses.
He then personally oversaw the battle.
The bandits had previously heard he was blind,
and thought he would be unable to resist.
Suddenly, they saw him personally among the fighting ranks,
bending his bow and shooting arrows.
They were mutually astonished and amazed,
and feared him, consequently withdrawing.
At that time, Mù Típó resented him incessantly,
wishing for the city to fall and be lost to the bandits.
Although he knew the critical danger,
he did not send aid.
Tǐng fought and defended for more than ten days,
and the bandits finally fled,
and the city was ultimately preserved intact.
He died in the zhōu.
His son, Jūn​xìn,
casually studied books and history,
and excelled in various minor arts.
His post included Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
Deputy Envoy when sent to Chén,
and Zhōngshū Láng.
When Tǐng was dismissed,
he was also removed from office.
Jūn​xìn's younger brother, Jūn​yàn,
was short in appearance,
and his speech was stuttering and slow.
In his youth, he possessed talent and learning.
During the Dàyè period of the Suí dynasty,
his post reached Dōngpíng Jùn Shūzuǒ.
When the commandery fell to Zhái Ràng,
he was consequently captured by Lǐ Mì.
Mì treated him with great courtesy,
and appointed him Jìshì.
Military documents and urgent war reports were all completed by his hand.
When Mì was defeated,
he was killed by Wáng Chōng.
Tǐng's younger brother, Xiàoyǐn,
also had literary talent,
and was famous early on.
Although his literary compositions did not reach the level of his elder brother,
he was also quick-witted, eloquent,
and understood music theory.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty, he served as Sànqí Chángshì,
and welcomed the Liáng envoy.
At that time, Xú Jūnfáng and Yǔ Xìn came on their mission.
Their fame and reputation were very high.
The Wèi court heard of them and held them in high regard.
Those selected to receive them were mostly the outstanding talents of the time.
Lú Yuánjǐng and his associates all lowered their ranks and took on temporary duties,
taking turns managing the guests.
Xiàoyǐn, though young, was placed among them,
and public opinion praised him.
Xiàoyǐn's cousin, Mào,
had considerable literary feeling,
but loved wine and had an unruly nature,
and was not respected by his contemporaries.
During the Dàníng period,
he was recommended by his hometown for his mastery of the Classics,
and appointed Gěishì.
He declined due to illness,
and never served again.
Tǐng, having received an important appointment,
therefore sent for Mào.
Mào, having no choice,
came to him temporarily.
Tǐng wanted to recommend him for an official post,
but Mào then fled.
Tǐng's cousin of the same clan, Chóngrú,
was learned and skilled in rhetoric,
and was famous in his youth for his capable bearing.
At the end of Wǔpíng,
he held the posts of Sīzhōu Biéjià and Tōngyí Chángshì.
Upon entering Zhōu,
he became the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Róngchāng Jùn.
Early in the Kāihuáng period of the Suí dynasty,
he died in office as Dàngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ.
(Compiler's Note)
Biographies XXXII: Wèi Jǐn, Féng Zǐcóng, Hè Yùn Zǐyuè, Táng Yōng, Bái Jiàn.
Wèi Jǐn,
courtesy name Ānrén.
His father, Qìngbīn,
was the Cìshǐ of Sìzhōu in Wèi.
Jǐn was quick-witted and intelligent in his youth,
fond of learning and aspiring to virtue.
He was gradually promoted to Zhíhòu.
When Sīmǎ Zǐrú held power,
Jǐn married his sister's daughter, a woman of the Pí clan.
Because of this, he was promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Since he was Sīmǎ Zǐrú's relative by marriage,
he frequently visited him,
and consequently became slightly intimate with esteemed contemporaries who were already established.
When Shìzōng entered court,
he ordered Jǐn, along with Gāo Dézhèng, to manage confidential matters in the Northern Palace in Yè.
When Sùzōng assisted in government,
he was repeatedly promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Zhào Yànshēn was originally Sīmǎ Zǐrú's subordinate,
and Yuán Wényáo and Hé Shìkāi were both old acquaintances from the Emperor's hometown.
They jointly recommended him for promotion,
and his appointment and treatment became increasingly important.
Furthermore, since the Lìbù controlled appointments,
many matters were confidential.
Consequently, he was
considerably informed about the sensitive affairs of the court.
Soon after, he concurrently held Yòu Púshè,
managing selections (elections).
Not long after, he received the full title.
He died of illness.
Shìzǔ was then drinking wine on the Sāntái Terrace.
Wényáo reported the news,
and the Emperor immediately ordered the music stopped and the drinking ceased.
Although Jǐn was outwardly successful and prominent,
internally he lacked moral instruction.
His domestic affairs were filthy and disorderly,
for which he was scorned by society.
Nevertheless, he was able to humble himself before gentlemen,
intending to welcome famous scholars,
but he failed to distinguish them.
When his office became high and his responsibility heavy,
he became extremely irritable and impatient.
He would preemptively scold and curse any Lángzhōng in the Department who intended to discuss matters,
making it impossible to consult with him.
Once he held the crucial selection post,
he became even more arrogant and cruel.
His son, Dézài, succeeded him.
Féng Zǐcóng
was a native of Xìndū,
and a descendant of Féng Bá, the ruler of Běi Yàn.
His father, Língshào,
was Dùzhī Lángzhōng.
Zǐcóng was naturally astute and clever,
and studied various books and histories.
He served.
Sùzōng appointed him Fǎcáo in the Lǐngjūn Fu,
where he managed confidential matters
and oversaw the Treasury Department temporarily.
Sùzōng once reviewed the ledgers
and tested him by ordering him to recite the contents orally.
Zǐcóng answered from memory
without any omission or error.
Zǐcóng's wife
was the younger sister of Empress Hú.
He was promoted to Diànzhōng Láng,
and given the additional title of Guǎnjì of the Eastern Palace.
He also received a special decree
ordering him to assist Hú Chángcàn in tutoring the Crown Prince,
and was transferred to Shùzǐ.
In the first year of Tiāntǒng,
Shìzǔ abdicated the throne to the Latter Lord.
Shìzǔ presided in the main hall
and said to Zǐcóng:
"The staff around the Young Sovereign should be upright individuals.
Since your heart is truly honest and upright,
I now entrust you with future matters."
He was appointed Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
and simultaneously held Zhǔyī Dūtǒng.
Shìzǔ was in Jìnyáng.
Since he resided in the old palace,
and the Young Emperor did not yet have a separate residence,
an edict ordered Zǐcóng to supervise the construction of the Dàmíng Palace.
When the palace was finished,
Shìzǔ personally toured it,
and was surprised that it was not grand or splendid enough.
Zǐcóng replied:
"His Supreme Majesty is young,
having succeeded to the great enterprise.
I wished to make him practice frugality earnestly
to serve as an example to all nations.
Moreover, since this structure is connected north to the gates of Heaven,
it is not fitting for it to be excessively lofty and imposing."
Shìzǔ praised his advice.
the Director of the Department of State Affairs, Hé Shìkāi,
who had previously attended the illness, kept the death secret for three days without announcing it.
Zǐcóng asked Shìkāi why he had not announced the mourning.
Shìkāi cited the precedent that Shénwǔ and Wénxiāng had both kept their deaths secret and unannounced when they first passed away,
saying that since Zhìzūn (His Majesty) was young,
he feared the princely lords might harbor dissenting intentions.
He intended to summon everyone to the Liángfēng Táng (Hall of Cool Breezes),
and then deliberate in detail with the dukes.
At that time, Zhào Jùn Wáng Ruì, the Grand Marshal and Director of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs, was already residing inside the palace
participating in the strategy within the screens.
Zǐcóng knew that Shìkāi inherently resented Ruì and Lóu Dìngyuǎn, the Commander of the Guards and Prince of Línhuái.
He feared that Shìkāi might forge the late Emperor’s will to send Ruì out to an external post
and seize Dìngyuǎn's authority over the imperial guards.
He therefore replied:
"The Great Departed (Dàxíng, the late Emperor)
was the son of Shénwǔ.
Furthermore, the present Emperor received the throne by the prior Emperor's transmission.
All those among the officials who are wealthy and noble owe their positions to the grace of His Majesty and his father.
Provided that the noble officials inside the palace are not altered in the slightest,
the princely lords and those below them certainly won't harbor differing hopes.
Times have changed and circumstances are different;
we cannot compare this to the era of the Hegemon (Bà Cháo).
Moreover, it has been several days since the Duke left the palace gates.
The matter of the ascension,
is already being rumored by people on the road.
If it is delayed and not announced,
I fear there might be other trouble."
Thereupon, the mourning was announced.
Yuán Wényáo considered Zǐcóng to be the husband of the Empress Dowager's sister.
Fearing that he would assist the Empress Dowager in interfering with government,
he persuaded the Prince of Zhàojùn and Shìkāi to send him away.
Zǐcóng was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Zhèngzhōu
and immediately ordered to proceed to his post.
Zǐcóng's appointment as Governor
was not the Hòuzhǔ's (Later Emperor's) original intention.
The imperial decree (Zhōngzhǐ) was exceptionally gracious;
he was specifically granted the Hòubù Gǔchuī (rear section military band)
and an additional fifty soldiers,
and permitted to take his property past the passes to his prefecture.
Not long after,
the Empress Dowager arranged for Qí'ān Wáng (Prince of Qi'an) to marry Zǐcóng's eldest daughter as his Consort (Fēi).
Zǐcóng subsequently requested leave to travel to Yè,
and was then appointed Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
His wife, relying on her connection to the Empress Dowager, acted recklessly.
Requests and recommendations were openly conducted,
bribes and goods piled up.
For the appointment of regional governors and magistrates,
the amount of money and silk was first determined,
and only then was the matter reported to the throne.
Whatever she facilitated
was invariably approved.
Zǐcóng also failed to restrain her.
Soon after, he was promoted to Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè),
and concurrently oversaw personnel selection.
Hé Shìkāi had held a critical position for a long time.
Zǐcóng had previously depended on him,
using humble speech and bowing deeply,
consulting him on every matter.
When Shìkāi's younger brother, Xiū, married into the Lú clan,
Zǐcóng oversaw the arrangements and errands,
acting no differently from Shìkāi's personal staff.
At this time, the appointments of internal palace officials were mostly nominated by Shìkāi.
Since Zǐcóng relied on his connection as an imperial relative
and concurrently managed personnel selection,
he monopolized power and favor,
thus gradually creating a rift.
Lángyé Wáng Yǎn assassinated Shìkāi,
and Zǐcóng was involved in the affair.
Shìkāi was strangled to death within the inner palace department.
Zǐcóng originally possessed some degree of discernment.
However, as his position and reputation grew more eminent,
his former character completely changed.
He promoted and patronized unsuitable people,
treating them as close confidants.
He indulged his sons and younger brothers,
whose official positions did not follow proper seniority.
Furthermore, he specialized in arranging marriages,
actively seeking out high-ranking families.
As a rule, he promised them official positions and titles,
which were confirmed within ten days.
His son was Cízhèng.
Hèlián Zǐyuè,
courtesy name Shìxīn,
was a descendant of Bóbó.
Early in the Wèi Yǒng'ān era,
due to his military merit, he was made Assistant to the Governor (Biéjià) of Jìzhōu.
When Gāozǔ raised his righteous army,
Hóu Jǐng was the Governor.
Jǐng was originally a close associate of Ěrzhū.
Zǐyuè urged Jǐng to join the cause,
and Jǐng followed his advice.
Zǐyuè was appointed Administrator (Shǒu) of Línlǜ.
When Shìzōng traveled to Jìnyáng,
his route passed through this commandery.
He asked about anything inconvenient (in the administration).
Yuè replied:
"The two counties of Línsǔi and Wǔ'ān are far from the commandery
and the mountains are layered thickly.
Travel by cart and foot is arduous.
If they were moved eastward and belonged to Wèijùn,
the land would be flat and the road short."
Shìzōng laughed and said:
"You only know how to benefit the people,
but you don't realize you are reducing the territory of the main commandery."
Zǐyuè replied:
"What I speak of stems from the distress of the people;
I dare not betray my conscience for private gain."
Shìzōng said:
"That you can behave like this
is very good,
very good."
An order was immediately issued to implement the matter as suggested.
When his term in the commandery was completed,
he was recalled and appointed Magistrate (Lìng) of Línzhāng.
Later, he was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Zhèngzhōu.
At that time, the area had recently suffered severe flooding from the Hé Qīng (Yellow River clearing event),
and many people had fled and dispersed.
Zǐyuè personally provided relief and care,
and the registered households increased.
His administration was the best in the realm.
He entered the capital to become Minister of the Department of Revenue (Dūguān Shàngshū).
Over eight hundred people from Zhèngzhōu requested that a stele be erected to praise his virtue,
and an imperial decree permitted it.
Later, he concurrently held the post of Minister of Personnel (Lìbù) alongside his original position.
While in office, Zǐyuè
maintained only honesty and diligence.
However, since he lacked academic skill
and was deficient in dignified demeanor,
assessment of character
was far removed from him.
When he suddenly held the head position in personnel selection (Quánhéng),
it caused great public criticism.
Because of this, he was appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng),
and died thereafter.
Táng Yōng,
courtesy name Dàohé,
was a native of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
His ancestors had moved there from Jìnchāng.
His father, Língzhī,
was the Magistrate (Lìng) of Shòuyáng during the Wèi dynasty.
Yōng was intelligent and astute in his youth,
and possessed the talent for governing the world.
Early in the Tàichāng era,
someone recommended him to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ ordered him to serve as an Attendant (Zhí) in the External Military Bureau (Wài Bīngcáo),
where he handled military records and accounts.
Táng Yōng was skilled in calligraphy and calculation.
He had a powerful memory and remembered things implicitly.
He became recognized for his efficiency and capability,
and was promoted to Aide to the Grand General's Residence under Shìzōng.
When Shìzōng died
and events occurred suddenly,
Xiǎnzǔ deployed officers and soldiers
to suppress the four directions (the realm).
He summoned Yōng at night to manage the distribution and deployment,
which he completed quickly and effectively.
Xiǎnzǔ valued him greatly.
Xiǎnzǔ frequently went outside the frontier in successive years,
and Yōng invariably accompanied him,
exclusively managing military affairs.
His understanding and insight were sharp and clear,
and his reception of orders was swift and quick.
From the supervising generals downward,
and military clerks upward,
regarding the sequence of their merits and achievements,
there was nothing he was not intimately familiar with.
Whenever he was consulted,
his answers and replies were immediate, like an echo.
Sometimes he would inspect troops before the Emperor.
Even if there were three or five thousand men,
Yōng usually did not hold the written register,
but recited the official positions and names from memory,
and never made a mistake.
In the seventh year (of Tiānbǎo),
military training was conducted at the Yángfén Embankment.
Yōng was ordered to take overall charge of the discipline and command of all the armies.
When the affairs were concluded,
he also supervised the ceremony of the banquet and archery.
On that day,
Xiǎnzǔ personally grasped Yōng's hand,
led him before the Empress Dowager,
and seated him above the Chancellor Hú Lǜ Jīn.
He then addressed the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Táng Yōng is capable and efficient;
one man is worth a thousand."
Following this, he was specially granted silks, cash, and cloth.
Yōng was not only capable, efficient, and discerning,
but he was also skilled at gauging the Emperor's intention,
and had many ways of advancing his career.
For this reason, imperial favor grew daily,
and the burdens of his office became heavier.
Xiǎnzǔ also once spoke to the Empress Dowager about Yōng, saying:
"Táng Yōng is clear-minded and possesses a strong memory.
Whenever there are major military affairs,
his hands are writing documents,
his mouth is giving orders,
and his ears are simultaneously listening and receiving information.
He is truly an extraordinary person."
Within a single day,
he was granted gifts six times.
The Emperor also once took off the blue squirrel fur coat he was wearing and bestowed it upon Yōng,
saying:
"My intention is that the carriages, horses, clothing, and furs should be worn out jointly by you and me."
In the tenth year,
he accompanied the Emperor on a visit to Jìnyáng,
and was appointed concurrently Attendant-in-ordinary and Palace Gate Retainer,
and concurrently Head of the Palace Writers.
Xiǎnzǔ once ascended the Tóngzǐ Buddhist Temple,
and looked upon the city of Bīngzhōu, saying:
"What kind of city is this?"
Someone replied:
"This is a metal-walled, boiling-moated city,
a land of heavenly storehouses."
The Emperor said:
"I consider Táng Yōng to be the metal city;
this is not the metal city."
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
Afterward, the Emperor spoke to Yōng, saying:
"Since you have worked assiduously for a long time,
I wished to appoint you as a prefectural governor.
I repeatedly ordered Yáng Zūnyàn to seek out another person who could replace you,
but Zūnyàn reported that after extensive inquiries among civil and military officials,
someone of your caliber is truly unobtainable.
Therefore, I halted this intention.
You should strive hard."
Xiǎnzǔ sometimes severely reprimanded attendants who failed to satisfy him, saying:
"Looking at your conduct and actions,
you are unfit even to be Táng Yōng's slave."
The recognition and favorable treatment he received were often of this nature.
When Sùzōng became Chancellor,
Yōng was appointed Palace Gate Retainer.
During an archery event in the Huálín Garden,
he was specially granted a golden belt, precious vessels, clothing, playthings, and five hundred other kinds of miscellaneous items.
At the beginning of the Tiāntǒng era,
he was appointed Palace Attendant and Grand Arbitrator of Bīngzhōu.
He was also appointed Protector-General,
with his other posts remaining as before.
Since the military and the common people were habitually practicing hunting,
according to the regulation, in the twelfth month,
they held three hunts per month.
Yōng considered that this exhausted the men and horses,
and petitioned to reduce it to two hunts per month.
Shìzǔ agreed.
Later he was sent out to serve as the Prefect of Zhàozhōu,
with his other official posts remaining as before.
Shìzǔ said to Yōng:
"No court official has yet held the posts of Palace Attendant, Protector-General, and Arbitrator while serving as a prefectural governor.
This measure is being taken because of you.
I am letting you rest for over a hundred days,
and I will recall you immediately in the autumn."
He was promoted to Right Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and later promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìnchāng,
and granted the authority to record the affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Subsequently, when the Zhōu army came to invade,
Chancellor Gāo Ānàgōng led troops to provide reinforcement.
Yōng's allocation of resources and deployment was not entirely compliant or satisfactory,
which created a rift between them.
Gōng slandered him,
and the Emperor sent Palace Attendant Hú Lǜ Xiàoqīng to declare an edict of censure and blame.
Yōng was temporarily detained and forbidden from service,
but was soon released.
When the Emperor was about to visit Jìnyáng,
he ordered Xiàoqīng to take overall charge of the cavalry and financial expenditure.
Xiàoqīng often made decisions independently,
without consulting or reporting to Yōng.
Yōng relied on the fact that he had always managed crucial governmental affairs since the beginning of the hegemonic court,
having served six emperors,
and had enjoyed very great favor.
When he was suddenly slighted by Xiàoqīng,
he felt resentful and depressed,
which showed in his speech and expression.
After the Emperor was defeated at Píngyáng,
he fled back desperately to Yèdū.
Yōng, fearing Gāo Ānàgōng's slander
and resenting Hú Lǜ Xiàoqīng for slighting him,
therefore remained in Jìnyáng,
and, together with Mò Duō Lóu Jìngxiǎn and others, supported and established the Prince of Āndé as Emperor.
Two nights later, the city fell.
Yōng subsequently surrendered to Zhōu,
and was granted the title of Grand General, Equivalent in Rank to the Three Dukes, according to standard practice.
He died while serving as the Prefect of Fèngzhōu.
Yōng was by nature discerning and quick-witted,
and understood contemporary affairs completely.
Throughout the entire generation of the Qí clan,
he controlled military affairs.
Regarding all the soldiers in the nine provinces, and the brave recruits from the four directions—
their strength, weakness, and numbers,
their rotation and movement,
as well as the quality of weapons and tools, and the real or assumed status of grain reserves—
he meticulously devoted himself to his work
and knew everything intimately.
Since the Dàníng era,
extravagance and wastefulness had prevailed,
and by the end of the Wǔpíng era,
the imperial treasuries had gradually become empty.
Yōng's management of expenditure and decisions regarding income and outlay
brought great benefit.
However, having been placed in such high office,
his disposition gradually became arrogant.
The instances where he bypassed the proper bureaus and courts to address petitions,
and exceeded his authority in reviewing documents and memorials,
were numerous.
All these incidents were impeached and censured by the Judicial Censorate and the Left Vice-Director,
but he was repeatedly pardoned by imperial decree.

Fēng Chángyè, Attendant Central Administrator in the Ministry of Works, and Píng Tāo, Registrar in the Grand Commandant's Office and Aide to the Army, were both found to have collected official funds past the deadline.
Yōng gave each of them twenty strokes with the rod on the back.
In the time of Qí, no chancellor had ever beaten court officials,
and this incident greatly shocked public opinion.
Yōng had three sons.
The eldest son, Jūnmíng,
held the title of Establishing a Residence, Equivalent in Rank to the Three Dukes.
At the beginning of the Kāihuáng era,
he died while serving as the Prefect of Yìngzhōu.
The second son, Jūnchè,
was a Palace Writer.
During the Suí dynasty, he served as the Prefect of Shùnzhōu and Róngzhōu.
During the Dàyè era,
he died while serving as Commandant of the Martial Vanguards.
The youngest son, Jūndé,
was executed due to Yōng's surrender to Zhōu.
During the Qí dynasty, following Gāozǔ becoming Chancellor,
the External Military Affairs Office and the Cavalry Office within the Chancellor's Residence separately managed military affairs.
When Tiānbǎo received the abdication,
all bureaus and offices were placed under the Department of State Affairs,
but only these two offices were not abolished.
Táng Yōng and Bái Jiàn were ordered to take charge of their administration,
and they were referred to as the External Military Secretariat and the Cavalry Secretariat.
Later, the status and reputation of Yōng and Jiàn grew even higher,
and they each became the head of a Secretariat.
Palace Writers were ordered to divide and adjudicate the affairs of the two Secretariats.
Thus, the world referred to them as Táng and Bái.
, courtesy name Yǎnjǔ
, was a man from Yángyì [Yángyì]
in Tàiyuán [Tàiyuán].
Initially, he entered the Cavalry Section of the Grand Chancellor’s [Dà Chéngxiàng] Residence [fǔ],
where he managed documents and accounts.
He was adept at paperwork and calculations,
and was highly recommended by his colleagues.
In the tenth year of Tiānbǎo [Tiānbǎo],
he concurrently served as Secretariat Drafter [Zhōngshū Shèrén].
When Sùzōng [Sùzōng] assisted in governance,
he was appointed Cavalry Adjutant [Qíbing Cānjūn] to the Grand Chancellor [Dà Chéngxiàng].
In the third year of Héqīng [Héqīng],
the Tujue [Tūjué] entered the border.
The two pastures of Dài [Dài] and Xīn [Xīn] were entirely composed of small horses,
totaling tens of thousands of steeds.
They were sheltering from the bandits in Bó Valley [Bógǔ] north of Mount Wǔtái [Wǔtáishān].
After the bandits retreated,
an imperial edict [chì] ordered Bái Jiàn [Jiàn] to go there for inspection and management.
Subsequently, a messenger was sent to Bái Jiàn [Jiàn]
to guide the horses to Dìngzhōu [Dìngzhōu] to be distributed to the common people for feeding and rearing.
Bái Jiàn [Jiàn] observed that the horses had long gone without food,
were thin and weak,
and feared that many would die if transported far.
Therefore, he violated the edict [chì] and acted expediently [yǐ biànyí cóngshì],
distributing them nearby to the military personnel.
When he reported this,
an imperial edict [chì] approved it.
As the military mounts suffered no losses,
Bái Jiàn [Jiàn] contributed greatly.
At the end of Wǔpíng [Wǔpíng],
he successively held the posts of Grand Master of Court [Tèjìn], Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng], and Director of the Central Secretariat [Zhōngshū Lìng].
Although Bái Jiàn [Jiàn] possessed no other great talents,
he was diligent in his public duties.
As the imperial enterprise was just beginning [wángyè shǐjī]
and military provisions [róngjì] were crucial,
Bái Jiàn [Jiàn] and Táng Yōng [Táng Yōng] both attained the positions of Minister [qīng] and Chancellor [xiàng] through managing military affairs and horses.
Jìnyáng [Jìnyáng]
was the auxiliary capital [xiàdū] of the state.
The Emperor visited annually,
issuing summonses, allocating duties [chāi kē],
and holding the commanderies and counties responsible.
The officials [liáozuǒ] of the regional administration [běn fān], down to the Governors and Magistrates [shǒuzǎi],
consulted, received instructions, and presented requests,
constantly rushing about with no leisure.
His various sons, though young,
all became Chief Secretaries [Zhǔbù] in commanderies and counties.
When the new ruler selected and appointed officials,
they were always the first to be summoned and retained.
When his sons married and daughters were given in marriage,
they all obtained spouses from prominent families [shèngliú].
The people of the time considered this the height of honor and favor.
He died in the seventh year of Wǔpíng.

Biographies Chapter Thirty-Three: Bào Xiǎn [Bào Xiǎn] Pí Jǐnghé [Pí Jǐnghé] Xiānyú Shìróng [Xiānyú Shìróng] Qílián Měng [Qílián Měng] Yuán Jǐng'ān [Yuán Jǐng'ān] Dúgū Yǒngyè [Dúgū Yǒngyè] Fù Fú [Fù Fú] Gāo Bǎoníng [Gāo Bǎoníng]
Bào Xiǎn [Bào Xiǎn],
courtesy name Sīzǔ [Sīzǔ],
was a man from Chìqiū [Chìqiū] in Wèijùn [Wèijùn].
His grandfather, Kuì [Kuì],
served as the Administrator of Lángyé [Lángyé Tàishǒu] and the Inspector of Shuòzhōu [Shuòzhōu Cìshǐ] under the Wèi [Wèi] dynasty.
Consequently, the family settled on the northern frontier.
His father, Dàn [Dàn],
was the Inspector of Wèizhōu [Wèizhōu Cìshǐ], Left Guard General [Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn],
and the Duke of Lè'ān [Lè'ān Gōng].
When Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] was young,
he saw a Buddhist monk [shā mén] who pointed at him and said:
"This young man has an excellent physiognomy;
when grown, he will surely become a distinguished general,
attaining the highest nobility among subjects."
As soon as he finished speaking, the monk vanished,
and no one knew where he had gone.
Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] had military experience from youth,
and was skilled in archery from horseback.
He once accompanied Emperor Xiàozhuāng [Xiàozhuāng Dì] of the Wèi [Wèi] dynasty on a hunt,
personally capturing seventy-three beasts in a single day.
In the second year of Xiàochāng [Xiàochāng],
he was appointed Superintendent of the Feathered Forest [Yǔlín Jiān].
In the first year of Zhōngxīng [Zhōngxīng],
he was appointed General Who Renders Awe [Xiāngwēi Jiāngjūn] and Chief Clerk [Zhǎngshǐ] of the Chariots and Cavalry Headquarters [Chējì Fǔ] in Jìnzhōu [Jìnzhōu].
Later, he followed Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] in raising the banner of righteousness at Xìndū [Xìndū],
and was granted the titles of General of the Central Bulwark [Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn], Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary [Sǎnqí Shìláng], Grand Commander of the Inner Camp [Zhàngnèi Dà Dūdū],
additionally awarded General Who Pacifies the East [Āndōng Jiāngjūn], Grand Master of Imperial Splendor with Silver and Blue [Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū],
and Founding Marquis of Túnliú County [Túnliú Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu].
In the second year of Tiānpíng [Tiānpíng],
he was appointed Administrator of Bóhǎi Commandery [Bóhǎi Jùnshǒu].
In the first year of Yuánxiàng [Yuánxiàng],
he was appointed Grand Judge of Yúnzhōu [Yúnzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng],
concurrently serving as General of the Martial Guard [Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn],
and additionally awarded General Who Suppresses the East [Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn].
In the second year,
he was appointed Inspector of Běixúzhōu [Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ]
and Grand Commander [Dà Dūdū] of that commandery.
He followed Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] in battling the Western forces at Mount Máng [Mángshān].
Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] ordered Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] to guard the Héquiáo [Héquiáo] garrison [zhèn]
and occupy Zhōngtán City [Zhōngtán Chéng].
In the second year of Wǔdìng [Wǔdìng],
he was appointed General Who Attacks the South [Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn] and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu [Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ].
When Hóu Jǐng [Hóu Jǐng] rebelled in Hénán [Hénán],
Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] was attacked by Hóu Jǐng [Jǐng].
Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] led about twenty cavalrymen from his entourage, breaking through the bandit camp,
escaping the difficulty and returning to the state.
At that time, Gāo Yuè [Gāo Yuè] and Mùróng Shàozōng [Mùróng Shàozōng] were campaigning against Hóu Jǐng [Jǐng].
Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] was immediately supplied with troops and horses,
and he followed Gāo Yuè [Yuè] and the others to defeat Hóu Jǐng [Jǐng] at Wōyáng [Wōyáng].
In the sixth year of Wǔdìng,
he was appointed Minister of the Grand Treasury [Tàifǔ Qīng].
He followed Shìzōng [Shìzōng] in suppressing Wáng Sīzhèng [Wáng Sīzhèng] at Yǐngchuān [Yǐngchuān],
and was granted the position of Inspector of Yǐngzhōu [Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ].
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to Inspector of Zhèngzhōu [Zhèngzhōu Cìshǐ].
In the eighth year,
he was additionally awarded General of Agile Cavalry [Piàojì Jiāngjūn],
elevated from Marquis [hóu] to Duke [gōng],
with a total stipend in his fief, including previous grants, of one thousand three hundred households.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo [Tiānbǎo],
he was additionally awarded Grand General of the Guards [Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn],
retaining his post as Inspector [Cìshǐ].
In the third year,
he joined the Prince of Qīnghé [Qīnghé], Gāo Yuè [Gāo Yuè], in attacking Lìyáng [Lìyáng],
and captured it.
He was accused of embezzlement,
relieved of his post in Zhèngzhōu [Zhèngzhōu],
and detained by the Grand Court of Justice [Dà Lǐ].
Before the judgment was finalized,
Héféi [Héféi] was besieged,
so he was dispatched with Bùhàn Sà [Bùhàn Sà] and Mùróng Yǎn [Mùróng Yǎn] to attack the Southern Liáng's [Liáng] Běixúzhōu [Běixúzhōu].
They captured the Inspector Wáng Qiáng [Wáng Qiáng].
He battled Yán Chāodá [Yán Chāodá], the Liáng [Liáng] Inspector of Qínzhōu [Qínzhōu], at Jīngchéng [Jīngchéng],
and defeated him.
In the fifth year,
he was granted the honorific title of Integrator of the Three Ducal Ministers [Yítóu Sānsī].
That same year,
he again joined Gāo Yuè [Gāo Yuè] in advancing south toward the Hàn River [Hànshuǐ],
attacking and taking Xīchǔzhōu [Xīchǔzhōu] from the Liáng [Liáng] dynasty,
capturing the Inspector Xǔ Fǎguāng [Xǔ Fǎguāng].
At that time, the Liáng [Liáng] generals Xiāo Xún [Xiāo Xún] and Hóu Tián [Hóu Tián] were besieging Mùróng Yǎn [Mùróng Yǎn] at Yǐngzhōu [Yǐngzhōu].
Bào Xiǎn [Xiǎn] was again made Grand Commander of the Naval Forces [Shuǐjūn Dà Dūdū],
and entered the Yangtze River [Jiāng] via Shèkǒu [Shèkǒu] to relieve the siege.
When the army returned,
he was additionally awarded Integrator of the Three Ducal Ministers with the Right to Establish an Administration [Kāifǔ Yítóu Sānsī],
and rewarded with five hundred bolts of silk.
In the tenth year,
he received revenues from Fànyáng Commandery [Fànyáng Jùn] in Yōuzhōu [Yōuzhōu].
In the first year of Gānmíng [Gānmíng],
he was appointed Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry [Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn].
In the first year of Huángjiàn [Huángjiàn],
his title was changed to Founding Duke of Lè'ān Commandery [Lè'ān Jùn Kāiguó Gōng].
In the second year,
he was appointed Inspector of Zhàozhōu [Zhàozhōu Cìshǐ].
In the first year of Héqīng [Héqīng],
he was transferred to Inspector of Luòzhōu [Luòzhōu Cìshǐ].
In the second year,
he was again appointed Inspector of Shuòzhōu [Shuòzhōu Cìshǐ],
and returned home upon completing his term.
In the first year of Tiāntǒng [Tiāntǒng],
he was additionally awarded Grand Master of Court [Tèjìn] and Grand General of Agile Cavalry [Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn],
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dìngyáng [Dìngyáng Wáng].
He died in the fourth year,
at the age of sixty-six.
Pí Jǐnghé [Pí Jǐnghé]
was a man from Xiàpī [Xiàpī] in Lángyé [Lángyé].
His father, Qìngbīn [Qìngbīn],
was the Adjutant for Military Affairs [Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Shì] in the administration established by the Prince of Huáinán [Huáinán Wáng] during the Wèi [Wèi] dynasty.
During the Zhèngguāng [Zhèngguāng] period,
while on a mission to Huáishuò [Huáishuò],
he encountered the turmoil of the age
and consequently settled his family in Shímén County [Shímén Xiàn] in Guǎngníng [Guǎngníng].
Jǐnghé was quick-witted and intelligent in his youth,
excelling at archery and horsemanship.
Initially, he served Gāozǔ as a trusted retainer,
later being appointed Deputy Military Governor of the Trusted Retainers (Qīn Xìn Fù Dū Dū).
In the second year of Wǔdìng (544 CE),
he participated in the campaign against the Bùluòjī.
Shìzōng suspected the enemy had an ambush,
and ordered Jǐnghé to lead five or six riders deep into a valley.
They encountered over a hundred bandits,
and immediately engaged in fierce combat.
Jǐnghé shot several dozen men;
none failed to fall upon being struck by an arrow.
Gāozǔ once ordered Jǐnghé to shoot a wild boar;
he secured it with a single arrow,
earning deep praise and admiration.
He was appointed Chief Military Governor of the Palace Guard (Kù Zhí Zhèng Dū Dū).
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo (550 CE),
he was granted the titles of Acting Commissioner (Jiǎ Jié) and Prefect of Tōngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Founding Viscount of Yǒngníng County.
Later, he followed in attacking the Kùmòxī,
and was promoted to Great Military Governor of the Left and Right (Zuǒ Yòu Dà Dū Dū).
He also followed in crossing the Yellow Dragon (Huánglóng),
campaigning against the Qìdān,
and pacifying the Jīhú.
Soon after, he followed in attacking the Rúruǒ leader Ānluóchén north of the Xíng Pass,
and subsequently followed in quelling the remaining Rúruǒ remnants.
Jǐnghé was quick and agile,
with military prowess,
and earned battle merits in every engagement.
In the tenth year (559 CE),
he received the stipend of Ānlè Commandery.
In the first year of Gānmíng (560 CE),
he was appointed General of the Martial Guard (Wǔ Wèi Jiāng Jūn),
concurrently serving as Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Jǐ Shì Huángmén Shìláng).
When Sùzōng became Chancellor,
Jǐnghé was provisionally assigned as Aide-de-Camp to the Grand Chancellor’s Office (Dà Chéngxiàng Fǔ Cóng Shì Zhōng Láng), retaining his original office.
In the first year of Dàníng (562 CE),
he was appointed Senior Administrator, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Grand General of the Martial Guard (Yí Tóng Sān Sī, Sàn Qí Cháng Shì, Wǔ Wèi Dà Jiāng Jūn).
Soon after, he was granted the rank of Grand Administrator (Kāi Fǔ).
In the second year (563 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Prefect of Liángzhōu.
In the third year (564 CE),
when the Turks besieged Jìnyáng,
Jǐnghé was ordered to hurry by post-horse to the capital
to oversee the rear guard and proceed to Bīngzhōu.
Before he arrived,
the bandits had already retreated.
He was subsequently appointed Grand General in Charge of the Palace Guard (Lǐng Zuǒ Yòu Dà Jiāng Jūn),
received the stipend of Qí Commandery,
and was additionally appointed Minister of War of Bīng Province (Bīng Shěng Wǔ Bīng Shàng Shū).
In the first year of Tiāntǒng (565 CE),
he was promoted to Minister of the Palace Hall (Diàn Zhōng Shàng Shū).
In the second year (566 CE),
he was appointed Palace Attendant (Shì Zhōng).
Jǐnghé, in addition to his military duties,
was also skilled in civil administration.
Furthermore, his nature was balanced and just,
hence he frequently received excellent appointments.
After diplomatic relations were established with Zhōu,
and officials traveled back and forth,
Jǐnghé was always ordered to receive them.
Whenever he competed in archery with the envoys,
he was always successful, hitting the target a hundred times out of a hundred,
and was highly respected.
During the Wǔpíng era (570–576 CE),
when many prisoners in the imperial prisons were supervised by Palace Eunuchs,
Jǐnghé was ordered to review the cases.
He upheld fairness according to principles,
and consequently, there was no undue injustice or oppression.
Later, he was appointed Special Promotion (Tè Jìn) and Central Leader of the Military (Zhōng Lǐng Jūn),
and enfeoffed as Founding Duke of Guǎnghàn Commandery.
He also followed Hú Lǜ Guāng in leading troops westward,
capturing the two cities of Yáo Xiāng and Báitíng,
and was separately enfeoffed as Founding Duke of Yǒngníng Commandery.
He was also appointed General Leader of the Military (Lǐng Jūn Jiāng Jūn).
He subsequently followed the army and captured Yíyáng City,
and was enfeoffed as Founding Duke of Kāifēng Commandery.
When the Prince of Lángxié assassinated Hé Shìkāi,
troops pointed towards the western gate of the palace,
causing panic inside and outside,
and no one knew what to do.
Jǐnghé requested the Later Ruler (Hòu Zhǔ) to exit through the Qiānqiū Gate to issue commands himself.
When the matter was settled,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs and Prefect of Zhàozhōu.
Soon after, he was promoted to Vice Director of the Right of the Henan Circuit Department of State Affairs and Prefect of Luòzhōu.
When the Chén general Wú Míngchè invaded Huáinán,
Jǐnghé was ordered to lead troops to resist him,
and was appointed Grand General Leader of the Military (Lǐng Jūn Dà Jiāng Jūn),
enfeoffed as Prince of Wénchéng Commandery,
and transferred his stipend to Gāoyáng Commandery.
When the army reached Zǔkǒu,
they encountered the local people Chén Xuān and others who were staging a rebellion.
Jǐnghé pacified them.
There was also Zhèng Zǐráo from Yángpíng,
who falsely relied on Buddhism,
holding vegetarian feasts.
He used very little rice and flour,
yet provided ample sustenance.
He secretly brought out cakes and cooked rice from an underground storage,
leading ignorant people to believe it was divine power,
and he gained followers between Wèi and Wèi.
He planned an insurrection,
but the plot was exposed,
and the raid failed to capture him.
He then secretly crossed the river,
gathered several thousand followers,
declared himself the Prince of Chánglè,
had already conquered Chéngshì County,
and also intended to attack the city of Xīyǎnzhōu.
Jǐnghé dispatched several hundred cavalry from Nányǎnzhōu to attack and defeat him,
beheading over two thousand people,
capturing Zǐráo alive,
and sending him to the capital to be boiled alive.
When Wú Míngchè besieged Shòuyáng,
an imperial decree ordered Jǐnghé and Hèbá Fú'ēn and others to go to the rescue.
Jǐnghé considered that Wèi Pòhú’s army had just suffered a defeat,
and was timid and dared not advance.
He halted his troops at the mouth of the Huái River.
Although imperial envoys frequently urged him,
he only then crossed the Huái River.
At that time, Shòuyáng had already fallen.
He hastily retreated north,
and military equipment and supplies
were largely lost.
The Chén general Xiāo Móhē led infantry and cavalry to intercept him at Cānglíng City north of the Huái River.
Jǐnghé managed to organize his formation and counter-attack,
and Móhē retreated.
At that time, many who resisted Wú Míngchè suffered defeats,
but only Jǐnghé returned with his entire army intact,
for which he received a reward.
He was appointed Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàng Shū Lìng),
separately enfeoffed as Founding Duke of Xīhé Commandery,
and granted two hundred thousand cash
and ten carts of wine and rice.
When the Chén people rumored that they were about to cross the Huái River,
Jǐnghé was ordered to station his troops at Xīyǎnzhōu
to manage the defensive arrangements.
He died of illness in the sixth year of Wǔpíng (575 CE),
at the age of fifty-five.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant, Commissioner with Authority (Shǐ Chí Jié), Area Commander-in-Chief of the six provinces of Dìng, Shuò, Yōu, Dìng, and Píng,
Grand Commandant (Tài Wèi Gōng), concurrently Overseer of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàng Shū Shì), and Prefect of Dìngzhōu.
His eldest son, Xìn,
was quick-witted and had a refined demeanor,
with some knowledge of literature.
At the end of Wǔpíng,
he held the titles Grand Administrator, Senior Administrator, and General of the Martial Guard,
and was praised for his insight and judgment
among the sons of meritorious and noble families.
He surrendered to the Zhōu army in Bīngzhōu,
and was appointed Supreme Grand Administrator and Grand Master of the Military Justice.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty (581–600 CE),
he died while serving as Prefect of Táozhōu.
His younger son, Sùdá,
was the Commandant of the Crown Prince's Residence at the end of Wǔpíng,
possessing literary talent and good conduct.
During the Kāihuáng era,
he served as Attendant Reporter (Tōng Shì Shè Rén).
He left office to mourn his mother.
After being reinstated,
when he was about to depart for the capital,
he cried so bitterly while taking leave of the spirit that he collapsed,
and was revived after a long time.
He was unable to eat
and died three days later.
Xiānyú Shìróng,
was a Yúyáng person.
His father, Bǎoyè,
was the Commander of the Huáishuò Garrison.
In the early Wǔpíng period (570–576),
he was posthumously granted Yítóng Sānsī (Attendant to the Three High Ministers), Cíbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Department of State Sacrifices), and Shuòzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Shuò Prefecture).
Shìróng was quick-witted and astute in his youth,
possessing talent and capability.
In the second year of Xīnghé (540),
he became the Vice Commander of Gāozǔ's personal retainers,
gradually advancing to Píngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West) and was granted the title of Earl of Shímén County.
Later, he frequently followed Xiǎnzǔ in campaigns against the Rúrú
and defeated the Jīhú.
He also followed Gāo Yuè to pacify Yǐngzhōu,
and was appointed Chíjǐe (Bearer of the Credentials) and Hézhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Hé Prefecture),
holding the office of Administrative Chief of Cháogē County.
Soon after, he became Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultative Counselor) in Sùzōng's chángxiàng (Chancellor's) residence.
During the Huángjiàn period (560–561),
he was appointed Yítóng Sānsī and Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Martial Guard).
In the second year of Tiāntǒng (566),
he was promoted to Jiā Kāifǔ (Added to Kāifǔ),
and was also appointed Zhèngzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Zhèng Prefecture).
During the Wǔpíng period (570–576),
for pacifying the rebels in Xìnzhōu,
he was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Leading Army),
and his administrative jurisdiction was transferred to Shàngdǎng Commandery.
He followed in the campaign to pacify Gāo Sīhǎo,
and was invested as the Prince of Yìyáng.
In the seventh year (576),
Hòuzhǔ (the Last Ruler) traveled to Jìnyáng,
ordering Shìróng, in his current capacity, to judge the affairs of the Shàngshū Yòupúyè (Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs),
acting as second-in-command to the Prince of Běipíng, Běigōng Liúhòu (Northern Palace Retained Official).
Soon after, an imperial edict ordered him and the Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Personnel Department), Yuán Yùxiū, to inspect and test the recommended candidates in the Department of State Affairs.
Because he rode his horse into the northern gate of the provincial office outside the Yúnlóng Gate,
the Department of Judicial Review impeached and dismissed him from office.
When Hòuzhǔ besieged Píngyáng,
Shìróng was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
When the Zhōu army was about to enter Yè,
he was appointed Lǐngjūn Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of the Leading Army) and Tàizǐ Tàifù (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince).
He resisted the fighting west of the city,
was defeated and captured,
and was killed by Zhōu Wǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Zhou).
Although Shìróng was a military man lacking literary arts,
due to the perils of the court and the disorder of governance,
he often secretly sighed about it.
Seeing the endless collection of taxes
and the excessive granting of gifts,
he spoke out in lamentation and regret.
His son, Zǐzhēn,
was granted the title Yítóng Sānsī at the end of the Wǔpíng period.
Qílián Měng,
courtesy name Wǔ'ér,
was a Dài person.
His ancestors bore the Jī surname.
At the end of the Six States period,
to avoid chaos, they fled beyond the frontier,
taking refuge in Mount Qílián.
They subsequently adopted the mountain's name as their surname.
Due to pronunciation errors among the northern people,
they were therefore called Qílián Shì.
His father, Yuánchéng,
was the Prefect of Yàn Commandery.
Měng was ambitious and spirited in his youth,
and became proficient in archery and horsemanship.
In the third year of Yǒng'ān (530),
Ěrzhū Róng summoned him to be a personal retainer.
When he reached Luòyáng,
and Róng was killed,
he immediately followed Ěrzhū Shìlóng to flee to Jiànzhōu,
and then followed Ěrzhū Zhào into Luò.
In the same year,
he again followed Zhào to campaign against Gědòulíng Bùfān,
and was appointed Dūdu (Commander).
In the first year of Pǔtài (531),
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians) and Zhōngsàn Dàfū (Grand Master of the Central Dispersed Office).
Měng's parents, brothers, and sisters were all in Shāndōng.
Ěrzhū Jīngkuàng wanted to defect to Gāozǔ
and said to Měng:
“The Prince (Ěrzhū Zhào) hears that your father and brothers are all in Shāndōng,
and constantly harbors mistrust.
If you do not flee,
he will certainly kill you tonight.
You must flee.”
Měng, considering that he had always been favored by Zhào's grace,
refused and did not follow.
Jīngkuàng said:
“I also want to leave now.
Will you follow me or not?”
Měng again did not follow.
Jīngkuàng then raised his spear and said:
“If you do not follow,
I will surely stab you.”
Měng then followed him.
Fifty or more *lǐ* (miles) away from the city,
he immediately turned his back on Jīngkuàng and returned to Ěrzhū.
When Zhào was defeated,
he then returned to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ asked:
“Ěrzhū Jīngkuàng was taking you to surrender to me.
Why did you turn back halfway?”
Měng then fully explained the principle of serving someone
and not having a second heart.
Gāozǔ said:
“Do not be afraid.
The method for serving people must be like this.”
Thereupon, he was appointed Dūdu.
When the Bùluòjī and others started a rebellion
at Mount Fùfǔ,
Měng was sent to suppress them,
and achieved a great victory.
He was specially rewarded and honored.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng (538),
he followed Gāozǔ toward Héyáng
and fought against Zhōu Wéndì (Emperor Wen of Zhou) at Mount Máng.
In the second year (539),
he was appointed Píngdōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the East) and Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
In the same year,
he was also transferred to Zhōngwàifǔ Zhàngnèi Dūdu (Commander of the Inner Tent in the Central and Outer Residences).
In recognition of his merit at Mount Máng,
he was invested as Founding Gentleman of Guǎngxīng County.
In the fifth year (542),
an envoy from Liáng came to propose marriage.
He claimed to possess martial arts
and sought out a northern man
to compete with him.
Shìzōng (Emperor Shìzōng) sent Měng to the residence to meet him.
Měng wore two quivers,
and rode and shot to the left and right.
They also competed in strength,
drawing strong bows.
The Liáng man drew two bows,
each requiring three *shí* (stones) of strength.
Měng then took four bows together,
stacked them and drew them,
exceeding the limit.
The Liáng man sighed and admired him.
In that year,
he was appointed Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
and separately enfeoffed as the Founding Viscounnt of Shíchéng County,
receiving a stipend from Píngkòu County in Sìzhōu.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (550),
he was appointed Dūdū and Governor of Dōngqínzhōu,
and separately enfeoffed as the Founding Baron of Fùchéng County in Jīngzhào Commandery, Yōngzhōu.
He followed Xiǎnzǔ in attacking the Qìdān,
and captured a great number of households.
He also followed Húlǜ Dūn on the northern campaign against the Rúrú.
Dūn ordered Měng to take a hundred horsemen and advance lightly and deeply to scout.
Upon returning to Báidào,
he met up with the army,
and consequently they gave chase,
and utterly defeated them.
He was rewarded with three hundred bolts of silk.
In the seventh year (556),
he was appointed Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
In the ninth year (558),
he was promoted to Wǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
In the beginning of Qiánmíng (560),
he was promoted to Chējì Dàjiāngjūn.
In the first year of Huángjiàn (560),
he was enfeoffed as the Founding Earl of Shíchéng Commandery,
and soon after was promoted to Jūn (Lord).
In the second year (561),
he was appointed to lead the Zuǒyòu Dàjiāngjūn,
and followed Sùzōng to attack the Xī rebels.
They achieved a great victory,
capturing two thousand horses
and thirty thousand cattle and sheep.
In the second year of Héqīng (563),
he was promoted to Kāifǔ.
When the Tujue invaded and pressed upon Jìnyáng,
an imperial edict ordered Měng to take three hundred horsemen to scout the distance of the enemy.
He traveled to fifteen *lǐ* north of the city,
where he encountered the enemy's vanguard.
As the enemy forces were numerous,
he gradually retreated and avoided them.
There was one fierce general among the bandits
who rushed out to fight.
Měng saw him from afar,
and immediately also put himself forward alone,
facing him.
In the space of a moment (literally: bowing and raising the head),
he stabbed the bandit, who fell from his horse,
and then immediately cut off his head.
In the third year (564),
he was separately enfeoffed as the Founding Jūn of Wǔ'ān County,
and promoted to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
In the first year of Tiāntǒng (565),
he was transferred to Yòuwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
He then received the imperial edict of Shìzǔ,
ordering him to be at the side of the heir apparent,
and to oversee the matters of internal and external military secrets.
In the third year (567),
he was appointed Zhōng Lǐngjūn.
In the fourth year (568),
he was promoted to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and separately enfeoffed as the Founding Jūn of Yìníng County.
In the fifth year (569),
he was appointed Píngshěng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
with all other positions remaining as before.
He was appointed Píngshěng Shàngshū Lìng and Lǐngjūn Dàjiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Shānyáng.
Since the death of Hé Shìkāi, Měng
gradually became involved in court politics.
Discussions, proposals, approvals, and rejections
were all submitted to him for consultation.
Zhào Yànshēn, knowing that Měng, among the military generals, strongly disliked corruption and flattery,
and whose comments were often worthy of adoption,
therefore brought him in to manage important state affairs.
After Zǔ Tǐng dismissed Yànshēn,
he considered Měng to be a member of Zhào's faction,
and thus appointed him Governor of Guāngzhōu.
He had already departed and reached Niúlán
when someone suddenly reported that Měng had also been privy to the affair on the day Hé Shìkāi was murdered.
Consequently, he was recalled and stopped.
Upon returning,
he was detained inside the palace,
and his family and assets were inventoried.
Soon after, he was released,
his princely title was stripped,
and he was only allowed to proceed to the prefecture with the rank of Kāifǔ.
While in office, he was lenient, benevolent, clean, and cautious,
and the officials and people praised him.
Ānàgōng, the Prince of Huáinán, had a previous relationship with Měng,
and always wanted to support him.
There was once an imperial edict summoning him to the capital,
seemingly intending to entrust him with responsibilities.
However, Hán Chángluán and others obstructed this,
and he was again appointed Governor of Jiāozhōu.
Soon after, he was summoned back
and ordered to defend Nányǎn.
When the Later Sovereign returned defeated from Píngyáng,
he was again summoned to Yè,
and appointed Dàjiāngjūn.
After Qí perished, he entered Zhōu,
and died soon after.
Yuán Jǐng'ān
was the fifth-generation descendant of Wèi Zhāochéng.
His great-grandfather, Qián,
was the Prince of Chénliú of Wèi.
His father, Yǒng,
served as Fèng Cháoqǐng in his youth.
Starting as Jìshè Jiāngjūn, he was recommended by Yuán Tiānmù to Ěrzhū Róng,
participated in the planning for Xiàozhuāng,
and was granted the title Duke of Dàijùn.
He was promoted to Jiāngjūn,
Tàizhōng Dàfū, and Left Administrator of the Xíngtái for Èrxià and Yōu Prefectures,
holding the staff (Chíjié) to recruit and incorporate more than four thousand surrendering households.
Róng also memorialized to enfeoff Yǒng as the Viscount of Cháonà County,
with an estate of three hundred households,
and as Governor of Nányōuzhōu, holding the staff,
with the acting rank of Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the beginning of Tiānpíng (534),
Gāozǔ made him Left Administrator of the Xíngtái,
and soon after appointed him Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
and then Governor of Běiyángzhōu.
During the Tiānbǎo period (550-559),
he was summoned and appointed Dàsīnóng Qīng,
transferred to Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū,
and his noble rank was lowered, according to regulations, to Baron of Gānxiāng.
In the second year of Dàníng (562),
he was transferred to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Jǐng'ān was profound, sharp, and capable of managing affairs.
In his youth, he excelled at horsemanship and archery,
and was good at serving others.
He began his career as a Staff Officer of the Standing Directorate (Zhǎngliú Cānjūn) in Ěrzhū Róng's Dàjiāngjūn office,
and was promoted to Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn.
He was then transferred to Staff Officer of the Standing Directorate in Róng's Dàchéngxiàng office.
When Gāozǔ pacified Luòyáng,
Lóu Zhāo, the Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn), recommended him to be appointed as the Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the Capital Region.
His father, Yǒng, memorialized to transfer the title Duke of Dàijùn to him.
He was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn
and Tàizhōng Dàfū.
He followed Emperor Wǔ to the west.
At the end of Tiānpíng (537),
when the great army campaigned west,
Jǐng'ān surrendered on the battlefield.
Gāozǔ praised him,
and immediately appointed him Dūdū.
During the Xīnghé period (539-544),
he was promoted to Commander-in-Chief of the Personal Guards (Qīnxìn Dūdū).
In the battle of Mángshān,
he fought bravely and performed meritorious service,
and was granted the title Baron of Dūxiāng, Xīhuá County,
while retaining the Duke of Dàijùn title.
When Shìzōng visited the court,
Jǐng'ān followed him and stayed in Yè.
At that time, Jiāngnán submitted and attached itself to Qí,
and tributes frequently arrived.
Jǐng'ān was skillful in rapid riding
and possessed refined demeanor.
Whenever the envoys from Liáng arrived,
he was ordered to engage in horsemanship and archery competitions with Húlǜ Guāng and Pí Jǐnghé against the guests.
Those who witnessed it praised their skill.
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he memorialized to reduce his imperial enfeoffment and distribute it to the generals and soldiers.
He was enfeoffed as the Founding Viscount of Shíbǎo County,
with an estate of three hundred households,
and promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
He was also appointed Governor of Tōngzhōu,
promoted to Zhènxī Jiāngjūn,
his viscount rank was promoted to earl,
and his estate increased to six hundred households in total,
with all other positions remaining as before.
In the beginning of Tiānbǎo (550),
he was promoted to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
separately enfeoffed as the Founding Earl of Xīngshì County,
held the office of Magistrate of Dìngxiāng County,
and was granted the surname Gāo.
In the third year (552),
he followed in the defeat of the Kùmò Xī at Dàichuān,
and was transferred to lead the Zuǒyòu Dàdūdū,
with all other official positions remaining as before.
In the fourth year (553),
he followed in the campaign against the Qìdān at Huánglóng,
and commanded the Administrator of Běipíng.
Afterward, he repeatedly followed the emperor and twice defeated the Rúrú,
was promoted to Wǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn,
and then transferred to lead the Zuǒyòu Dàjiāngjūn,
concurrently serving as Minister of War (Qībīng Shàngshū).
At that time, the Great Wall was newly constructed,
but the garrisons had not yet been established.
The Tujue were strong,
and there was concern that they might invade the borders.
Therefore, an imperial edict ordered Jǐng'ān and the various armies to patrol along the frontier for defense.
As the number of troops he commanded was large,
and since the soldiers under his command were wealthy,
bribery and commercial practices became common.
Xiǎnzǔ heard of this
and sent an envoy to investigate.
The illicit gains and corruption among all the accompanying people were rampant,
but Jǐng'ān was completely clean, having committed not the slightest offense.
The Emperor deeply praised and admired this,
and thus decreed that the relevant authorities award him five hundred bolts of stolen silk that had been amassed,
to honor his integrity.
He was then transferred to Dūguān Shàngshū.
He was given the rank Yítóng Sānsī.
He received the stipend of Gāopíng Jùn Gàn.
He was again appointed Yítóng Sānsī.
In the first year of Qiánmíng (560),
he was transferred to Qībīng Shàngshū.
He was given the rank Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn.
In the first year of Huángjiàn (560),
he also concurrently held the position of Shìzhōng,
traveled swiftly by post station to Yè,
to comfort and reward the various officials,
and inspect the local customs.
Sùzōng once held an archery banquet with his officials in the Western Park,
with over two hundred civil and military participants.
The target was set up more than 140 paces away from the hall.
Those who hit the center were rewarded with fine horses, gold, jade, silk brocade, and similar items.
One man shot the target animal head,
missing the nose by just over an inch.
Only Jǐng'ān had one arrow left unshot.
The Emperor ordered Jǐng'ān to shoot it.
Jǐng'ān slowly composed his demeanor,
grasped the bow and drew it fully,
hitting the animal’s nose precisely.
The Emperor sighed in praise and called it excellent,
specially granting him two horses,
and the jade, silk, and miscellaneous items were further increased beyond the usual standards.
In the first year of Dàníng (562),
he was granted Kāifǔ.
In the second year (563),
he was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and soon after transferred to Yòuwèi Dàjiàngjūn.
At the beginning of Tiāntǒng (565),
he managed the Affairs of Bīng Shěng Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
and soon was sent out to be Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the fourth year (568),
he was appointed Yùzhōu Dào Xíngtái Púyè and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the third year of Wǔpíng (572),
he was promoted and appointed Xíngtái Shàngshūlìng,
remaining Cìshǐ as before,
and enfeoffed as Lìyáng Jùnwáng.
When Jǐng'ān was in the frontier prefecture,
bordering other territories,
he pacified and harmonized the border areas,
so there was no mutual invasion or violence,
and the people and their property were secure.
Moreover, within his jurisdiction, there were many Mán tribesmen and few Huá people.
Jǐng'ān covered them with both authority and benevolence,
and they all achieved peace and stability.
By the end of Wǔpíng,
he had attracted and comforted tens of thousands of households of uncivilized Mán who submitted taxes and levies.
In the sixth year (575),
he was summoned and appointed Lǐngjūn Dàjiàngjūn.
Upon entering Zhōu,
holding the titles of Dàjiàngjūn and Dàyì Jùn Kāiguó Gōng, he led troops to suppress the Jīhú,
and died in battle.
His son, Rén,
was Yítóng Sānsī and Wǔwèi at the end of Wǔpíng,
became Pàoqí Jiāngjūn under the Suí dynasty,
and died while holding the post of Dānyáng Tàishǒu.
Earlier, Yǒng’s elder brother Zuò inherited the title of Chénliú Wáng.
When Zuò died,
his son Jǐnghào succeeded him.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
most members of the Yuán imperial clan who were close to the emperor were executed.
Distant relatives like Jǐng'ān and his associates deliberated on requesting to adopt the surname Gāo.
Jǐnghào said:
"How can we abandon our original clan
and follow another surname?
A great man would rather be shattered like jade
than remain whole like clay tile."
Jǐng'ān consequently reported these words to Xiǎnzǔ.
Consequently, Jǐnghào was arrested and executed,
and his family members were exiled to Péngchéng.
Because of this, Jǐng'ān alone was granted the surname Gāo.
All others were permitted to retain their original surname.
Yǒng’s younger brother was Zhǒng.
His son Yù, courtesy name Jǐngyù,
had a fine appearance and demeanor,
and possessed talent and capability.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
he was Yǔlín Jiān.
When Yuán Hào entered Luòyáng,
based on his merit in defending Hénèi,
he was granted the title Yǒng'ān Jūn.
Later, he became Púyáng Jùnshǒu.
Wèi Péngchéng Wáng Sháo recruited him as Kāifǔ Zīyì Cānjūn.
When Sháo was sent out to govern Dìngzhōu,
he petitioned for Yù to be Dìngzhōu Sīmǎ.
When Jǐng'ān reported Jǐnghào’s disrespectful comments,
he implicated Yù, suggesting his words corroborated the report.
Yù claimed, saying:
"At that time, I covered Jǐnghào’s mouth with my sleeve,
saying, 'Elder brother, do not speak rashly.'"
When Jǐnghào was questioned,
his statement matched Yù’s claim,
and Yù thus escaped punishment.
Several others who had heard the conversation,
were all exiled and banished to distant lands.
Yù died while serving as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Dúgū Yǒngyè,
courtesy name Shìjī,
originally had the surname Liú,
and was a native of Zhōngshān.
His mother remarried a man of the Dúgū clan.
Yǒngyè was orphaned in youth,
and followed his mother to be raised by the Dúgū family.
He consequently adopted their surname.
He resided among the soldiers.
He possessed talent and capability,
and was skilled in archery and horsemanship.
He was selected and promoted to Dìngzhōu Liùzhōu Dūdū,
and guarded Jìnyáng.
Someone recommended him as possessing insight and utility.
Shìzōng spoke with him and was pleased,
and rapidly appointed him Zhōngwài Fǔ Wàibīng Cānjūn.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo (550),
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and Yùzhōu Sīmǎ.
Yǒngyè understood documentation and accounting,
and was good at singing and dancing,
and was highly regarded by Xiǎnzǔ.
At the beginning of Qiánmíng (560),
he was sent out as Héyáng Xíngtái Yòuchéng,
then promoted to Luòzhōu Cìshǐ,
and then transferred to Zuǒchéng,
remaining Cìshǐ as before,
and granted Sànqí Chángshì.
Yíyáng was deep within enemy territory.
The Zhōu people built fortifications and garrisons at Hēijiàn to cut off the supply route.
Yǒngyè also constructed a garrison to resist them.
His border administration possessed great authority and trust.
He was promoted to Xíngtái Shàngshū.
In the third year of Héqīng (564),
the Zhōu people raided Luòzhōu.
Yǒngyè feared that the Cìshǐ Duàn Sīwén would be unable to hold out alone,
and rushed into Jīnyǒng to assist in the defense.
The Zhōu people constructed earthen mounds and tunnels,
attacking and fighting day and night.
After thirty days,
the main army arrived,
and the invaders consequently withdrew.
Yǒngyè had long been in Hénán.
He was skilled at attracting and pacifying people,
and those who submitted numbered in the tens of thousands.
He selected two hundred of them to be his personal guard.
Whenever they were the vanguard, they fought the many with the few,
and the Zhōu people feared them.
He was granted Yítóng Sānsī,
and his rewards were very generous.
His nature was frank and upright,
and he did not associate with the powerful.
Húlǜ Guāng requested two slave girls but did not get them.
Húlǜ Guāng consequently defamed him at court.
At the end of Héqīng (565),
he was summoned to serve as Tàipú Qīng,
and Qǐfú Guìhé replaced him.
Consequently, the western border became constricted and weak,
and the populace of the Hélǔo region became agitated.
In the third year of Wǔpíng (572),
Yǒngyè was dispatched to capture Húlǜ Fēngluò,
and then appointed Běidào Xíngtái Púyè and Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
The common people of Hélǔo
mostly longed for Yǒngyè,
and the court, seeing that the frontier was unstable,
appointed Yǒngyè as Héyáng Dào Xíngtái Púyè and Luòzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zhōu Wǔdì personally attacked Jīnyǒng.
Yǒngyè led troops out to resist him,
and asked:
"What high official is that,
and what action is he taking?"
The Zhōu people replied:
"The Supreme One has come himself.
Why does the host not come out to greet the guest?"
Yǒngyè said:
"The guest's travel was too sudden,
therefore I have not come out."
He then spent the entire night preparing two thousand horse troughs.
When the Zhōu people heard this,
they believed a large army was about to arrive,
and consequently lifted the siege and departed.
Yǒngyè was promoted to Kāifǔ,
and enfeoffed as Línchuān Wáng.
He possessed thirty thousand armored soldiers.
When he first heard of the defeat at Jìnzhōu,
he requested to send troops for a northern campaign.
The memorial was shelved and received no reply.
Yǒngyè was indignant.
When he later heard that Bīngzhōu had also fallen,
and was pressed by the Zhōu general Chángshān Gōng,
he then sent his son Xūdá to announce his surrender to Zhōu.
Zhōu Wǔdì appointed Yǒngyè Shàng Zhùguó.
At the end of Xuānzhèng (578),
he was sent out to be Xiāngzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
In the second year of Dàxiàng (580),
he was killed by the Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn Cuī Yànmù.
Fù Fú
was a man of Tàinán.
His father, Yuánxīng,
was Yítóng and the Cìshǐ of Běiwèizhōu.
Fú joined the military when young,
and gradually reached the positions of Kāifǔ and Yǒngqiáo Lǐngmín Dàdūdū due to his battle achievements.
