When the Zhōu Emperor previously attacked Héyīn,
Fú crossed the bridge by night,
and entered to defend the city of Zhōngtǎn.
When the southern city fell,
he was besieged for twenty days but did not yield,
until rescue troops arrived.
The Zhōu army returned.
Fú said to the Xíngtái, Qǐfú Guìhé:
“The bandits are already exhausted.
I wish to lead two thousand elite cavalry to pursue and attack them.
We can achieve victory.”
Guìhé did not allow it.
In the sixth year of Wǔpíng (575),
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Dōngyōngzhōu.
When the Zhōu troops approached,
Fú went out to fight
and repelled them.
When Zhōu conquered Jìnzhōu,
they captured the Xíngtái, Wèi Xiāngguì,
and used him to try to persuade Fú,
but Fú refused to comply.
The Later Ruler personally led a relief force to Jìnzhōu,
and appointed Fú as Xíngtái Yòupúshè.
When the Zhōu army came to raid,
Fú attacked and drove them away.
When Zhōu conquered Bīngzhōu,
they sent Wéi Xiàokuān and his son, Shìkuān, to persuade Fú, saying:
“Bīngzhōu has already been pacified,
so we specifically sent your son to report this.
You ought to surrender immediately.”
They offered him the title Shàng Dàjiāngjūn and the rank of Kāiguó Gōng of Wǔxiāng Jùn,
and immediately presented him with the letter of appointment,
along with two wine cups made of gold and horse teeth as tokens of sincerity.
Fú did not accept,
and said to Xiàokuān:
“A servant of the ruler must choose death rather than have second thoughts.
This son, as a subject, failed to exert utmost loyalty,
and as a son, failed to fulfill filial piety.
He is hated and resented by all.
I wish to immediately execute him
to issue orders to the world.”
The Zhōu Emperor returned from Yè and reached Jìnzhōu.
He sent Gāo Ānàhōng and over a hundred others to summon Fú from the Fén River.
Fú led his army out and met them across the water,
asking where the Supreme One was now located.
Ānàhōng said:
“He has already been captured
and taken through another route into the Pass (Guānzhōng).”
Fú cried greatly, looking up at the sky.
He led his troops into the city,
and in front of the hall, he faced north and wept loudly for a long time,
and then surrendered.
The Zhōu Emperor saw him and said:
“Why did you not surrender earlier?”
Fú wept and replied:
“For three generations, your subject has received food and clothing from the Qí family,
and been entrusted with such responsibility.
At the change of dynasty, I could not die for them,
and am ashamed to face Heaven and Earth.”
The Zhōu Emperor personally held his hand and said:
“A subject should be like this.
When I pacified the Qí state,
I only saw one man like you.”
Then he personally ate a lamb rib,
and bestowed the bone upon Fú,
saying:
“Bone is closer (related), flesh is distant.
This is why I pass it to you.”
He then separately invited him to eat with him,
and ordered him to stand guard overnight with Shì Bóyì.
He conferred upon him the title Shàng Yítóng,
and commanded him, saying:
“If I were to immediately grant you a high office,
I fear those who come to defect might become unsettled.
Make a good effort and serve well;
do not worry that you will not become wealthy and noble.”
He also asked what official position Fú had received for previously relieving Héyīn.
Fú said:
“I was granted one promotion,
appointed Tèjìn,
and Kāiguó Gōng of Yǒngchāng Jùn.”
The Zhōu Emperor said to the Later Ruler:
“Three years ago, I trained my troops,
resolute in my intention to capture Héyīn.
It was precisely because Fù Fú was capable of defending it
that the city could not be taken.
That is why I withdrew my army.
How meager was the reward and appointment you gave him at that time!”
He bestowed a golden wine goblet upon Fú.
Later, he was appointed Cìshǐ of Mínzhōu,
and soon died.
After the defeat of the Qí army at Jìnzhōu,
few generals and officers preserved their integrity completely.
Among those who sacrificed their lives to achieve benevolence
was the Yítóng Chìgān Gǒushēng,
who guarded Nányànzhōu.
When the Zhōu Emperor conquered Yè,
the amnesty decree arrived,
but Gǒushēng hanged himself and died.
There was also the eunuch Tián Jìngxuān, Kāifǔ and Zhōngshìzhōng,
whose original given name was Péng,
a Mán person.
At the age of fourteen or fifteen,
he was fond of reading.
After becoming a palace attendant (kūnsì),
he would seize every opportunity to anxiously inquire and seek instruction.
Every time he reached the Wénlín Guǎn,
he would be panting and sweating profusely.
Aside from asking about books,
he had no time for other conversation.
Whenever he read about the integrity and righteousness of the ancients,
he was invariably moved with deep emotion.
Yán Zhītuī valued his diligence in study
and greatly encouraged him.
Later, he became prominent.
When the Later Ruler fled to Qīngzhōu,
he sent Jìngxuān west
to observe and report on enemy movements.
He was captured by the Zhōu army.
When asked where the Qí Ruler was,
he lied, saying he had already gone.
He was beaten and flogged to force him to confess.
Every time a limb was broken,
his words and expression became more resolute,
and he finally died after his four limbs were severed.
There was also Léi Xiǎnhé.
After the defeat at Jìnzhōu,
he served as the Xíngtái Zuǒpúshè of Jiànzhōu Dào.
The Zhōu Emperor sent his son to persuade him,
but Xiǎnhé detained his son and refused to yield.
He surrendered only upon hearing the defeat of Yèchéng.
When the Later Ruler lost Bīngzhōu,
he sent the Kāifǔ Hēxī Yǒng'ān to urgently report the crisis to the Turkic Khagan Tābōlüè.
When he heard that Qí was annihilated,
Tābō placed Yǒng'ān under the care of the envoy from Tǔyùhùn.
Yǒng'ān spoke up defiantly:
“Since my homeland has been defeated,
how could Yǒng'ān regret this humble life?
I wish to hold my breath and kill myself,
but I fear the world will not know that Great Qí had subjects who died for their integrity.
I only request a knife
to demonstrate this to all near and far.”
Tābō praised his heroism and fortitude,
and gave him seventy horses before sending him back.
Gāo Bǎoníng
was a man from Dài,
but his origins are unknown.
At the end of Wǔpíng,
he was Cìshǐ of Yíngzhōu,
stationed at Huánglóng.
The barbarians and Chinese respected his authority and trustworthiness.
When the Zhōu army was about to reach Yè,
the Yōuzhōu Xíngtái Pān Zǐhuǎng levied troops from Huánglóng.
Bǎoníng led his fierce and elite troops, together with more than ten thousand cavalry of the Qìdān and Mòjié, to go and assist.
When they reached Běipíng,
they learned that Zǐhuǎng had already departed Jì,
and also heard that the capital Yè was undefended.
He then returned to his garrison.
The Zhōu Emperor sent an envoy to summon and placate him,
but he did not accept the imperial decree.
Fànyáng Wáng Shàoyì was among the Turks,
and he submitted a memorial urging Bǎoníng to claim the throne.
Fànyáng appointed Bǎoníng as Chéngxiàng.
When Lú Chāngqī occupied Fànyáng city and raised troops,
Bǎoníng led Shàoyì and gathered tens of thousands of barbarian and Chinese troops to rescue him.
When they reached Lùhé,
they learned that the Zhōu general Yǔwén Shénjǔ had already massacred Fànyáng.
Bǎoníng returned to occupy Huánglóng
and ultimately did not become a subject of Zhōu.
The Historian comments: Pí Jǐnghé and others, since the beginning of the hegemony,
registered their names in the military camps, overcoming difficulties and dangers,
until the final period of the dynasty.
They held high office and heavy responsibility,
and all maintained their original sincerity.
Each of them also met their time (or fortune).
Fù Fú and his group
all demonstrated loyalty and integrity.
If not for them, how could portraits and historical records be valuable?
Eulogy says: These various generals,
preserved their glorious names.
Without fault or forgetfulness,
they remained thus until old age.
The peers of Master Fù
encountered this adversity (unfavorable creation).
Unless fierce winds are met,
who knows the sturdy grass?
Chapter 34 of the Biographies: Yáng Fěi, Lú Qián, Cuī Jié, Lú Shúwǔ, Yáng Xiūzhī, Yuán Yùxiū
Yáng Fěi,
courtesy name Shūluán,
was a native of Yúyáng in Běipíng.
His father, Zǎo,
was the Grand Administrator of Jiàndé during the Wèi dynasty,
and was posthumously granted the title of Inspector of Yōuzhōu.
During the time of Xiàozhuāng,
Fěi achieved merit while supervising displaced people as the Area Commander of Western Yǎnzhōu,
and was granted the title Baron of Fāngchéng.
He successively served as Palace Censor,
concurrently Assistant Director of the Bureau of Judicial Affairs and Palace Administrator in the staff of Prince of Guǎngpíng,
and compiled the Record of Current Affairs.
During the Xīnghé period,
he was appointed Director of the Bureau of Works,
concurrently Palace Attendant Who Transmits Edicts,
and was sent on a mission to Liáng.
The Liáng Minister Yáng Kǎn,
a defector from Wèi,
was an old acquaintance of Fěi.
Kǎn wished to invite Fěi to his residence,
sending three letters,
but Fěi did not reply.
The Liáng people said:
"Yáng has been here for a long time;
your esteemed court has undergone changes and transitions.
Lǐ and Lú also went to his residence to meet him.
Why do you make difficulties, Sir?"
Fěi replied:
"Liǔ Xiàhuì could do so,
but I cannot."
The Lord of Liáng then personally addressed Fěi, saying:
"Yáng Kǎn deeply wishes to meet you.
Now the two nations are in harmony,
and the whole realm is one family.
How can we still talk about 'us' and 'them'?"
Fěi ultimately declined.
Upon returning from his mission,
he was appointed Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
When the Shíjì River overflowed
and the bridge was destroyed,
Fěi supervised its repair.
He also relocated the ferry crossing to Báimǎ,
built stone jetties in the middle of the river,
and constructed fortified gates on both banks.
This took several years to complete.
Lù Shìpèi, the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn, believing that the topography of the Lìyáng Pass and the river offered strategic advantages,
wished to utilize the mountains and valleys to establish a public park.
He sent Fěi a letter, saying:
"I shall consult the Great General to appoint you, Sir, as the master builder."
Fěi replied in a letter, refusing, saying:
"Currently, profound anxiety gives rise to sagacity;
the era meets with an auspicious calendar.
The former Grand Chancellor manifested his hegemonic achievements by Heaven's mandate,
re-establishing the Great Ultimate;
the Great General splendidly inherits the foundation laid by his predecessor,
and the succession of his accomplishments is greatly manifest.
The state's progress has just begun to stabilize,
but the people's labors have not yet ceased.
It is truly appropriate to lighten corvée and reduce taxes,
and diligently show concern for the suffering of the populace.
Does the *Shī* not say: 'The people are indeed weary;
they may finally achieve minor comfort.
Extend favor to this central realm,
to soothe the regions of the four quarters'?
The ancient emperors did indeed mark mountains and prune trees,
but this was not sufficient to fully express their intentions;
dismounting their carriages to hold banquets,
how could this exhaust their feelings?
These actions merely serve to waste the resources and wealth of Heaven and Earth,
and exploit the very marrow and brains of the living people.
Therefore, Confucius responded to Yè Gōng by emphasizing attracting people from afar,
and answered Āi Gōng by emphasizing governing the people.
Although the questions were the same,
the priorities were different.
Xiāngrú celebrated the grandeur of the Shànglín Park,
and Yáng Xióng lauded the rhetoric of the Feather Hunt.
Although they appended details like collapsing walls and filling chasms,
and interspersed descriptions of casting nets,
their words offered no benefit to moral principles,
and only served to illuminate their mistakes and offenses."
Soon after, he was transferred to Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo period,
he was appointed General Who Guards the South and Director of the Bureau of Civil Office in the Department of State Affairs.
He was dismissed due to a public matter.
After a long time,
he was appointed Commissioner of Waterways.
Xiǎnzǔ personally led the six armies
to repel the Tujue in the north,
and subsequently decreed that Fěi oversee the construction of the Great Wall.
After the construction was concluded,
he acted as Prefect of Nánqiáozhōu,
was promoted to Palace Attendant Who Transmits Edicts,
and Assistant Director of the Left of the Traveling Chancellery of the Shòuyáng Route.
He was transferred to Palace Attendant,
and granted the emoluments of Chénliú Commandery.
Not long after,
he was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu,
concurrently Assistant Director of the Left of the Traveling Chancellery of the Southeast Route.
In the first year of Qiánmíng,
he was summoned and appointed Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
then transferred to Grand General of the Guards,
concurrently Minister of the Bureau of Judicial Affairs,
acting Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
then moved to Minister of the Palace Hall,
and oversaw the affairs of Yíngzhōu while holding his current office.
He submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but an imperial edict graciously refused.
A short while later,
he was appointed Collaborator of the Three Highest Dignitaries,
and granted the emoluments of Guǎng'ā County.
He died in office.

He was posthumously granted Commissioner with Credentials, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Běiyù and Guāng Two Departments, Grand General of Cavalry, Collaborator of the Three Highest Dignitaries, Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, and Inspector of Běiyùzhōu,
with the posthumous name Jìngjiǎn.
His son, Shīxiào,
was a Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
Lú Qián,
was a native of Zhuō in Fànyáng.
His grandfather, Shàngzhī,
was the Inspector of Jìzhōu in the Wèi dynasty.
His father, Wénfú,
was a Palace Attendant Who Transmits Edicts.
Qián had a magnificent appearance,
was skilled in conversation,
and possessed the ambition of a grown man from a young age.
Hèbá Shèng, the Collaborator of the Highest Dignitaries, recruited him as Staff Supervisor of the General's Residence,
and he was later appointed Palace Censor.
Shìzōng promoted him to Libationer of the Western Gallery in the Grand General's staff,
and he was transferred to Army Advisor in the Central and Outer Headquarters.
He was capable and effective in strategic planning,
and was recognized by Shìzōng,
who said he could be greatly utilized in the end.
When Wáng Sīzhèng was captured at Yǐngchuān,
Shìzōng valued his talent and insight.
Qián once casually informed Shìzōng, saying:
"Sīzhèng failed to die for his loyalty;
what is there to value about him!"
Shìzōng said to his attendants:
"Having Lú Qián,
it is as if I have gained another Wáng Sīzhèng."
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo period,
he was appointed Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
but was dismissed for offending the emperor in a memorial.
He was soon appointed Director of the Bureau of Left Population,
but was prohibited from service, along with Wáng Sōngnián and Lǐ Shù,
for criticizing and commenting on the *Wèi Shū*.
It happened that Yuè, the Prince of Qīnghé, was about to rescue Jiānglíng,
and Qián was specially pardoned and made an Area Commander Aide under Yuè.
Upon returning,
he was transferred to Central Secretariat Attendant,
and soon promoted to Chief Attendant.
Zhèng Zǐmò, the Chief Attendant, presented a memorial stating that
when Qián followed the Prince of Qīnghé on the southern campaign,
the Prince of Qīnghé ordered Qián to persuade Hóu Tián, the Liáng general,
and Qián accepted large bribes,
but failed to report this upon return.
Xiǎnzǔ beat Qián one hundred strokes with a staff,
and subsequently cut off his beard,
demoting him to Administrator of Wèi Prefecture.
He was soon appointed Adjutant of Sīzhōu,
and then sent out as Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
and was known for his effective governance wherever he served.
When Sùzōng became Chancellor,
he appointed Qián as Assistant Director of the Left of the Traveling Chancellery of the Yángzhōu Route.
Previously, the Liáng general Wáng Lín had been defeated by the Chén forces,
and brought his lord, Xiāo Zhuāng, back to Shòuyáng.
The court appointed Lín as Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and instructed Qián to assist Lín in planning the southern campaign.
Many of Lín's old troops and retainers were in Yángzhōu,
which bordered the Chén invaders.
Qián harmonized the internal and external affairs,
and successfully brought peace to the border regions.
Wáng Fèngguó, the Chén Inspectors of Qín and Qiáo Two Departments,
and Zhōu Lìngzhēn, the Inspector of Hézhōu, invaded successively.
Qián repeatedly defeated and pacified them,
and was promoted for his achievements to Palace Attendant,
and granted the emoluments of Péngchéng Commandery.
He was transferred to Inspector of Hézhōu,
retaining his post as Assistant Director of the Left.
He was further appointed Minister of the Traveling Chancellery,
and soon granted Collaborator of the Three Highest Dignitaries.
Wáng Lín was eager to campaign south,
but Qián believed the time was not right.
Just then, Chén dispatched a letter to Shòuyáng,
requesting peaceful relations with the state.
Qián presented a memorial about this,
and further submitted a plea to temporarily cease military action.
The request was granted.
Because of this, a rift grew between him and Lín,
and they impeached each other in memorials.
Shìzǔ summoned Lín back to the capital,
and appointed Qián as Inspector of Yángzhōu,
concurrently leading as Minister of the Traveling Chancellery.
Lú Qián stayed in Huáinán for thirteen years,
managing all military and civilian affairs,
greatly establishing reputation and merit,
and was deeply feared by the people of Chén.
The Lord of Chén wrote a letter to his border generals saying:
“Lú Qián is still in Shòuyáng.
We hear when he is to return north.
If this captive does not die,
he will surely become a national threat.
You should prepare deeply for him.”
When Xiǎnzǔ first pacified Huáinán,
he granted ten years of special tax exemptions and relief.
After the period was fulfilled,
and reaching the Tiāntǒng and Wǔpíng eras,
levies and taxes became numerous and complicated.
Furthermore, Gāo Yuánhǎi held power,
banning fishing and hunting,
so households had nothing to sustain themselves with.
Regarding various merchants and foreigners who owed interest on government debts,
the eunuch Chén Déxìn allowed them to recklessly register claims against wealthy families in Huáinán,
ordering the prefectures and counties to levy and collect them.
Additionally, an edict was issued to send several thousand horses from the Tujue to the area governed by Yángzhōu,
ordering local magnates to buy them at high prices.
As soon as the money was collected,
another edict was issued to seize all horses between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and send them all to the government treasury.
Due to this, the common people were disturbed and agitated,
gritting their teeth and sighing in complaint.
Lú Qián pacified and comforted them in every situation,
while also employing timely strategies,
thus managing to maintain peace and stability.
In the third year of Wǔpíng,
he was summoned to serve as Minister of the Five Military Bureaus (Wǔbīng Shàngshū).
Because Lú Qián abstained from wine and meat,
and devoutly believed in the Buddhist faith,
the officials and people of Yángzhōu held a grand monastic assembly,
and spread incense and flowers along the road,
sending him off with tears flowing.
Lú Qián sighed and said:
“I just fear that I will return again soon.”
Not long after arriving in Yè,
the Chén general Wú Míngchè crossed the river and invaded,
and Lú Qián was again made Administration Commissioner (Xíngtái Shàngshū) for the Yángzhōu Circuit.
In the fifth year,
he was captured along with Wáng Lín and others.
He soon died in Jiànyè,
at the age of fifty-seven.
His family purchased his corpse and returned it for burial.

He was posthumously granted the titles Minister over the Masses (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúyè), and Governor of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
He had no sons,
so he adopted Yuánxiào, the son of his younger brother Shìsuì, as his heir.
Shìsuì,
courtesy name Zǐyān,
was appreciated by Cuī Áng when he was young.
Cuī Áng said:
“These brothers are sufficient to be considered outstanding among the younger generation,
my only regret is that neither of them studies books.”

He successively held the posts of Palace Censor (Shì Yùshǐ), Libationer to the Minister of Education (Sītú Jìjiǔ), Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Láng), Magistrate of Yè County (Yè Xiànlìng), Left and Right Deputies of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Yòuchéng), and Secretariat Director of the Bureau of Civil Office (Lìbù Lángzhōng).
He was posted out as Administrator of Zhōngshān (Zhōngshān Tàishǒu),
concurrently holding the position of Chief Clerk of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Chángshǐ).
He died after the fall of Qí.
Lú Qián’s cousin Huáirén,
courtesy name Zǐyǒu,
was the son of Dàojiāng, Administrator of the Minister of Education (Sītú Sīmǎ) during the Wèi dynasty.
Huáirén was well-read and possessed literary talent.
His disposition was calm and tranquil,
always having an air of detached ease.
He successively served as Recorder of the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Jìshì) and Administrator of Hóngnóng Commandery (Hóngnóng Jùnshǒu),
but did not take up the latter post.
He chose to reside in the area of Chénliú.
His collected poems, rhymed prose, inscriptions, and eulogies amounted to more than twenty thousand words.
He also compiled the *Zhōngbiǎo Shílù* in twenty volumes.
Huáirén had good conduct and integrity,
and was skilled at making friends.
He was deeply intimate with Wáng Yǎn of Lángxié and Lǐ Shòuzhī of Lǒngxī.
He once said to Wáng Yǎn:
“In the past, Tàiqiū (Chén Shí) was widely respected,
but Xǔ Shào knew of him yet ignored him.
Jīshēng (Jī Kāng) was naturally indolent,
and Zhōng Huì passed by him but was refused conversation.
I stand between these extremes,
avoiding their excesses.”
Wáng Yǎn agreed with him.
He died at the end of the Wǔpíng era.
Huáirén’s nephew Zhuāngzhī,
had a good reputation when young.
He successively held the posts of Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén), Vice Prefect of Dìngzhōu (Dìngzhōu Biéjià), and Administrator of Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng Tàishǒu).
During the Wǔpíng era, he was the Superintendent of Waterways (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě),
and died in office.
Huáirén’s cousin Chānghéng,
was the son of Dàoqián, Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè) during the Wèi dynasty.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era, he was a Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Láng).
He was composed and possessed talent and insight,
with a cultivated demeanor and bearing.
His appearance and deportment were admirable.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Wáng Xīn, Minister of the Department of State Affairs, was punished due to refined conversation,
but his younger brothers still upheld this tradition without abandoning it.
From then on,
this tradition greatly declined.
Chānghéng, along with Lǐ Ruò of Dùnqīu, Liú Tàimín of Péngchéng, Lù Yànshī of Hénán, Xīn Déyuán of Lǒngxī, and Wáng Xiū of Tàiyuán, were all considered refined scholars of the younger generation.
Chānghéng’s cousin Sīdào,
was the son of Dàoliàng, a recluse (chǔshì) during the Wèi dynasty.
His spirit was sharp and quick,
and he gained great fame for his talent and learning when young.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was a Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng),
and attended the court in the Wénlín Pavilion.
Sīdào’s cousins Zhèngdá, Zhèngsī, and Zhèngshān,
were the sons of Dàoyūe, Grand Master of Remonstrance (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū) during the Wèi dynasty.
Zhèngdá was a Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Láng).
Zhèngsī was Governor of Northern Xúzhōu (Běi Xúzhōu Cìshǐ), Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhànshì), and Minister over the Masses (Yítóng Sānsī).
Zhèngshān was Administrator of Yǒngchāng Commandery (Yǒngchāng Jùnshǒu).
Because their sister was the Empress,
the brothers were all granted high honors and special gifts during the Wǔpíng era.
Zhèngshān’s son Gōngshùn,
was recognized early for his literary talent.
During the Wǔpíng era, he was the Keeper of the Imperial Seal (Fúxǐ Láng),
and attended court in the Wénlín Pavilion.
He shared aspirations and was close friends with Cuī Jūnqià of Bólíng and Lǐ Shīshàng of Lǒngxī.
They followed the Emperor to Jìnyáng,
residing temporarily in a Buddhist monastery.
Court officials called them
“The Three Youths of Kāng Temple,”
and they were highly esteemed in public opinion.
Zhèngdá’s cousin Xīyù,
whose father was Dàoshū.
Dàoshū yielded his noble title to his eldest brother Dàojiāng,
and thus Xīyù inherited the title Count of Gù’ān (Gù’ān Bó).
He was unpretentious, maintained moral principles,
and possessed the demeanor of the ancients.
He was respected by his relatives and kin.
Lú Qián’s cousin Sùnzhī,
was the son of Yìxī, Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) during the Wèi dynasty.
He was pure, calm, and had few desires,
and died in the post of Recorder and Administrator of the Minister of Education (Sītú Jìshì Cānjūn).
Cuī Jié,
courtesy name Yànxuán,
was originally from Qīnghé.
His great-grandfather Kuàng,
crossed the river south,
and settled in the east of Qīngzhōu.
At that time, the Sòng clan established Jìzhōu south of the Yellow River,
setting up commanderies and counties.
He thus became a native of Dōngqīnghé Commandery.
As southern counties were reorganized and renamed,
he became a native of Nánpíngyuán Bèiqīu.
His family had been a great clan in the three Qí regions for generations.
His grandfather Língyán,
was Administrator of Chángguǎng (Chángguǎng Tàishǒu) under the Sòng.
His father Guāng,
was Grand Protector (Tàibǎo) under the Wèi.
Cuī Jié was pure, reserved, and had few desires in his youth,
enjoying study and possessing the family demeanor.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty,

starting from Administrator of the Minister over the Masses (Kāifǔ Xíng Cānjūn), he successively served as Secretariat Director of the Ritual Bureau (Shàngshū Yícáo Láng), Deputy Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng),
and compiled the Records of the Grand Historian (Qǐjū Zhù),
and Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
In the third year of Xīnghé,
he concurrently served as Regular Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
and was sent on a mission to Liáng.
In the early Tiānbǎo era,
because he advised on the abdication,
he was appointed Palace Attendant (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng),
granted the title Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ),
worked in the inner palace,
and oversaw confidential matters.
He was clean, frugal, diligent, and cautious,
and was greatly appreciated by Xiǎnzǔ.
He was appointed Governor of Southern Qīngzhōu (Nán Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ),
and achieved good administrative results during his tenure.
During the Huángjiàn era,
he was recalled to serve as Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān) and Great Arbiter of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Dàzhōngzhèng),
then transferred to Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Qīng),
and promoted to Minister of Budgetary Affairs for the Bǐng Province (Bǐng Shěng Dùzhī Shàngshū).
Soon after, he was appointed to the capital administration,
and shortly thereafter transferred to Minister of the Five Military Bureaus (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and supervised the National History.
While in the departments and bureaus,
he was praised for his simplicity and integrity.
When Shìzǔ was about to abdicate in favor of the Later Ruler,
he first consulted Cuī Jié.
Cuī Jié advised against it, believing it was improper,
and thus incurred the Emperor’s displeasure.
He was sent out to serve as Governor of Southern Yǎnzhōu (Nán Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
After returning from his post,
he was reappointed Minister of Budgetary Affairs (Dùzhī Shàngshū) and Minister over the Masses (Yítóng Sānsī),
and received the income from Wéndēng County.
He was soon appointed Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
granted the title Minister over the Masses (Kāifǔ),
attended court in the Wénlín Pavilion,
and supervised the compilation of the New Book.
He fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-six.
He was posthumously granted Governor of Qízhōu (Qízhōu Cìshǐ) and Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúyè),
with the posthumous name Wénzhēn.
Initially, Hé Shìkāi 賀士開 held sway at court.
He unscrupulously sought praise and favors.
The high officials, on account of this, often sought offices for their sons and younger brothers.
The scions of prominent families
mostly held metropolitan posts,
but Jí 劼’s two sons, Gǒng 拱 and Huī 撝, were both appointed to external positions.
Jí 劼’s younger brother, Kuòzhī 廓之, leisurely said to Jí 劼:
“Gǒng 拱 and Huī 撝 are fortunately not ordinary talents.
Why are they not in the provincial or governmental ministries, in positions of prominence,
but both sent out to distant prefectures,
which is a loss to our family’s standing?”
Jí 劼 said:
“Since establishing myself,
I have been ashamed to advance myself with a single word.
If I were to advance my sons now,
how would that be different from advancing myself?”
Ultimately, he sought nothing for them.
Those who heard this were all deeply moved with admiration.
Gǒng 拱,
during the Tiāntǒng 天統 era, served as Cángxiàng Zīyì Cānjūn 丞相諮議參軍 (Counselor to the Grand Chancellor) and Guǎnjìshì 管記室 (Recorder) to Rènchéng Wáng Xié 任城王湝.
Huī 撝
was Yángzhōu Lùshì Cānjūn 揚州錄事參軍 (Registrar to the Yangzhou Governor).
Kuòzhī 廓之 was profound and discerning, with a sense of measure,
and was acclaimed for his scholarship.
From Línshuǐ Lìng 臨水令 (Magistrate of Linshui), he became Lángyé Wáng Yǎn Dàsīmǎ Xīgé Jìjiǔ 琅邪王儼大司馬西閤祭酒 (Libationer of the Western Chamber for Grand Marshal Prince Langye Yǎn),
then was promoted to Lǐngjūn Gōngcáo Cānjūn 領軍功曹參軍 (Staff Officer for Military Merits in the Central Army).
He died during the Wǔpíng 武平 era.
Lú Shúwǔ 盧叔武,
〔一０〕a native of Zhuō 涿 in Fànyáng 范陽,
was the paternal cousin of Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Wénwěi 青州刺史文偉 (Governor of Qingzhou, Wénwěi).
His father, Guāngzōng 光宗,
had high aspirations.
Shúwǔ 叔武’s two elder brothers, Guān 觀 and Zhòngxuān 仲宣, both distinguished themselves in literature in Luòyáng 洛陽.
Shúwǔ 叔武 was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
magnanimous and chivalrous,
and fond of extraordinary strategies.
He admired Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮’s character.
He served Hèbá Shèng 賀拔勝 as Jīngzhōu Kāifǔ Chángshǐ 荊州開府長史 (Chief Clerk of the Kaifu for Jingzhou).
Shèng 賀拔勝 did not adopt his strategies,
abandoned the city, and fled to Liáng 梁.
Shúwǔ 叔武 returned to his home county,
built a house by the pond,
and lived a leisurely and content life.
Shìzōng 世宗 issued an imperial summons,
but he declined on grounds of illness and did not go.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo 天保 era, he was again summoned,
and, having no choice,
he arrived in Yè 鄴 in a coarse robe, riding in an exposed carriage.
Yáng Yīn 楊愔 visited him
and appointed him Sītú Zīyì 司徒諮議 (Counselor to the Minister of Education),
but he claimed illness and refused the post.
Upon Sùzōng 肅宗’s ascension to the throne,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子 (Central Private Secretary to the Crown Prince)
and awarded the title Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū 銀青光祿大夫 (Grand Master of Silver and Blue Light).
When asked about state affairs,
Shúwǔ 叔武 advocated for attacking Guānxī 關西 (the region west of the Hangu Pass).
He drew a map and expounded on military strategy, saying:
“When the number of people and enemy forces are equal, one must rely on wisdom and strategy.
When wisdom and strategy are equal, one must rely on strength and power.
〔一一〕Thus, the strong control the weak,
and the rich absorb the poor.
Now, the Great Qí 大齊, compared to Guānxī 關西,
differs in strength and weakness,
and is unequal in wealth and poverty.
Yet, with constant warfare,
we have not been able to conquer and annex them.
This is a failure to utilize our strength and wealth.
Light troops engaging in open-field battles,
where victory and defeat are uncertain,
is the method of the Hú 胡 (nomadic cavalry),
not a well-thought-out, far-sighted, and foolproof strategy.
It is advisable to establish a strong fortress in Píngyáng 平陽,
opposite their Púzhōu 蒲州,
with deep moats and high ramparts.
Transport provisions and amass weapons,
and build garrison cities connected to it.
If they close their passes and do not come out,
then we seize their territory east of the Yellow River.
Cháng’ān 長安 will be greatly distressed
and naturally perish in its distress.
If they send out troops,
unless they number over one hundred thousand,
they will not be our match.
The provisions they supply
will all come from within the pass.
Our soldiers will rotate,
with a fresh contingent each year.
Our grain and food supplies will be abundant,
and transport will be uninterrupted.
If they come seeking battle,
we will not engage them.
If they retreat,
we will immediately exploit their weakness.
From Cháng’ān 長安 westward,
the population is sparse and cities are distant.
Enemy troops moving back and forth
will indeed face difficulties.
If they hold out against us,
agricultural work will cease.
In no more than three years,
they will collapse on their own.”
The emperor deeply accepted his proposal.
He also wished to reside in Píngyáng 平陽 himself
to realize this strategy.
The emperor ordered Yuán Wényáo 元文遙 to deliberate with Shúwǔ 叔武
and compile a volume on the “Strategy for Pacifying the West.”
Shortly after, the emperor died,
and the matter was consequently shelved.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 ascended the throne,
Shúwǔ 叔武 was appointed Yítóng Sānsī 儀同三司 (Honorary Administrator of the Three Ducal Offices) and Dūguān Shàngshū 都官尚書 (Minister of Population).
He was sent out as Hézhōu Cìshǐ 合州刺史 (Governor of Hezhou).
During the Wǔpíng 武平 era,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì 太子詹事 (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince) and Yòuguānglù Dàfū 右光祿大夫 (Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness).
When Shúwǔ 叔武 was in his hometown, he had a thousand *shi* 石 of grain.
Every spring and summer,
he would let villagers who had no food take it themselves,
and in autumn,
allowed them to repay at their discretion,
without keeping any accounts.
Yet, year after year, he always received more than double back.
Once he became an honored official at court,
he considered himself old,
and had many sons,
so he built a large house,
saying:
“We will sing here,
and weep here.”
Wèi Shōu 魏收 once came to visit him,
inquiring about old affairs in Luòjīng 洛京,
but left without waiting for food,
saying:
“It is hard to cause you expense.”
Shúwǔ 叔武 detained him.
After a long while, food arrived,
but it was only millet gruel and mallow greens,
served in wooden bowls,
with a single slice of dried meat.
His accompanying servants
were also served food,
exactly the same.
When Qí 齊 fell,
he returned to Fànyáng 范陽.
During the chaos, the city fell,
and Shúwǔ 叔武 and his cousin Shìsuì 士遂 both died of cold and hunger.
Zhōu 周 general Yǔwén Shénjǔ 宇文神舉, recognizing his renown and virtue,
collected and buried them.
Shúwǔ 叔武’s clan grandson, Chénkè 臣客,
was the son of Zǐguī 子規,
Wèi Shàngshū Láng 魏尚書郎 (Secretary to the Imperial Secretariat of Wei) and Línglǜ Jùnshǒu 林慮郡守 (Prefect of Linlü Commandery).
Chénkè 臣客 had a very fine demeanor,
had high aspirations in his youth,
was elegant and disciplined,
and fond of Daoist teachings.
His elder sister was the consort of Rènchéng Wáng 任城王.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo 天保 era,
Rènchéng Wáng 任城王 recommended him to the imperial court,
and he was consequently promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人 (Attendant to the Crown Prince).
He was promoted to Sītú Jìshì 司徒記室 (Recorder for the Minister of Education),
but requested to return home to attend to his paternal grandmother, Lǐ 李.
Lǐ 李 urged him to serve,
and he reluctantly obeyed,
being appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人 and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子.
During the Wǔpíng 武平 era,
he concurrently served as Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 (Palace Attendant Consultant) and was sent on an embassy to Chén 陳.
Upon his return,
he died on the road.
He was posthumously granted the titles Zhèngzhōu Cìshǐ 鄭州刺史 (Governor of Zhengzhou) and Hónglú Qīng 鴻臚卿 (Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Receptions).
Yáng Xiūzhī 陽休之,
courtesy name Zǐliè 子烈,
was a native of Wúzhōng 無終 in Yòuběipíng 右北平.
His father, Gù 固,
was Wèi Luòyáng Lìng 魏洛陽令 (Magistrate of Luoyang in Wei) and posthumously granted Tàicháng Shǎoqīng 太常少卿 (Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
Xiūzhī 休之 was intelligent, keen, and had a dignified bearing.
In his youth, he diligently studied
and loved refined literature.
He gained fame in his early twenties
as a rising talent.
Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Cháng Jǐng 幽州刺史常景 and Wáng Yánnián 王延年 both summoned him to be Zhōuzhǔbù 州主簿 (Chief Clerk of the Prefecture).
During the Wèi Xiàochāng 魏孝昌 era,
Dù Luòzhōu 杜洛周 conquered Jìchéng 薊城.
Xiūzhī 休之, along with his clansmen and several thousand local families, fled south to Zhāngwǔ 章武,
then moved on to Qīngzhōu 青州.
At this time, Gé Róng 葛榮 was causing rebellion and chaos,
and many refugees from Héběi 河北 gathered in Qīngzhōu 青州.
Xiūzhī 休之 knew that a change was imminent,
so he asked his clan uncle Bóyàn 伯彥 and others, saying:
“The guest and host have different statuses,
and they are competing and insulting each other.
Disaster is about to break out.
In my humble opinion,
it is advisable to secretly return to the capital to avoid it.”
Most of them could not agree.
Xiūzhī 休之 tearfully took his leave.
Soon after, Xíng Gǎo 邢杲 rebelled,
and Bóyàn 伯彥 and others were all killed by the local populace.
〔一二〕Many perished at that time.
Dozens of the Yáng 陽 family died,
and only Xiūzhī 休之 and his brothers escaped.
When Emperor Zhuāngdì (莊帝) was enthroned,
he was appointed yuánwài sànqí shìláng (員外散騎侍郎) after doffing his coarse official robes.
Soon after, he was granted the additional duty of yùshǐ (御史) while retaining his original post.
He was promoted to gěishì zhōng (給事中) and tàiwèi jìshì cānjūn (太尉記室參軍),
and was granted the title of qīngchē jiāngjūn (輕車將軍).
Lǐ Shénjùn (李神儁), overseeing the "Diaries of Activity and Repose,"
memorialized that Xiūzhī (休之), along with Péi Bómào (裴伯茂) of Hédōng (河東), Lú Yuánmíng (盧元明) of Fànyáng (范陽), Xíng Zǐmíng (邢子明) of Héjiān (河間), and others, should be enlisted to compile and edit them.
At the end of the Yǒng'ān (永安) era,
Lǐ Hǎi (李海), the cìshǐ (刺史) of Luòzhōu (洛州), memorialized that he be appointed guānjūn chángshǐ (冠軍長史).
During the Pǔtài (普泰) period,
he concurrently held the post of tōngzhí sànqí shìláng (通直散騎侍郎),
was granted the title of zhènyuǎn jiāngjūn (鎮遠將軍),
and soon after became an assistant in the bureau of Zhǎngsūn Zhì (長孫稚), the tàibǎo (太保).
Soon, an imperial decree ordered him, along with Wèi Shōu (魏收), Lǐ Tóngguǐ (李同軌), and others, to compile the national history.
At the beginning of the Tàichāng (太昌) era,
he was appointed shàngshū cíwù lángzhōng (尚書祠部郎中),
and soon thereafter was promoted to zhēnglǔ jiāngjūn (征虜將軍) and zhōngsàn dàfū (中散大夫).
Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝) was sent out as the cìshǐ (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and memorialized for Xiūzhī (休之) to be appointed piàojì chángshǐ (驃騎長史).
When Shèng (勝) became xíngtái (行臺),
he again requested Xiūzhī (休之) to be appointed yòuchéng (右丞).
When Shèng (勝) was strategizing in Fán (樊) and Miǎn (沔),
he again requested Xiūzhī (休zhī) to be appointed nándào jūnsī (南道軍司).
Shortly thereafter, Emperor Wǔdì (武帝) of Wèi (魏) entered Guānzhōng (關),
and Shèng (勝) ordered Xiūzhī (休之) to present a memorial and proceed to Cháng'ān (長安) for an audience.
At that time, Gāozǔ (高祖) also memorialized that Xiūzhī (休之) be appointed tàicháng shǎoqīng (太常少卿).
Soon, due to Shèng (勝) fleeing south,
he followed him to Jiànyè (建業).
When Xiūzhī (休之) heard that Gāozǔ (高祖) had elevated Emperor Jìngdì (靜帝),
he informed Shèng (勝) and requested Emperor Wǔ (武) of Liáng (梁) to allow him to return.
In the second year of Tiānpíng (天平), he reached Yè (鄴),
and then, by Gāozǔ (高祖)'s order, proceeded to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
In the winter of that year,
he was appointed kāifǔ zhǔbù (開府主簿) to Shìzōng (世宗).
In the spring of the following year,
when Shìzōng (世宗) became dàxíngtái (大行臺),
he was again appointed xíngtái lángzhōng (行臺郎中).
In the fourth year,
Gāozǔ (高祖) visited Tiānchí (天池) in Fényáng (汾陽).
By the side of the pond, a stone was found,
on which there was a raised inscription,
its text reading:
"Six kings, Three Rivers."
Gāozǔ (高祖) alone in his tent asked him,
"What is the meaning of this inscription?"
He replied:
"'Six' (六) refers to the character for 'king' (王) with an extra stroke,
meaning the great king (大王) is destined to rule the world.
This is an auspicious omen for the great king (大王) to receive the mandate.
Since this stone was found in Tiānchí (天池),
it can be said that Heaven has destined the king (王);
its auspiciousness cannot be expressed in words."
Gāozǔ (高祖) then asked, "What is the meaning of 'Three Rivers'?"
Xiūzhī (休之) replied:
"The Hé (河), Luò (洛), and Yī (伊) are the Three Rivers,
also referred to as the Jīng (涇), Wèi (渭), and Luò (洛) as the Three Rivers.
The Hé (河), Luò (洛), and Yī (伊) refer to
Luòyáng (洛陽);
the Jīng (涇), Wèi (渭), and Luò (洛) refer to
the present Yōngzhōu (雍州).
If the great king (大王) receives the Mandate of Heaven,
he will eventually control Guānyòu (關右)."
Gāozǔ (高祖) said:
"People often say without cause that I wish to rebel.
Now hearing this,
it will cause even more controversy.
Be careful not to speak carelessly."
At the beginning of the Yuánxiàng (元象) era,
for his military achievements in Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he was enfeoffed as the founding count (kāiguó bó 郡國伯) of Xīntài County (新泰縣),
with an income of six hundred households.
He was appointed píngdōng jiāngjūn (平東將軍), tàizhōng dàfū (太中大夫), and shàngshū zuǒ mín lángzhōng (尚書左民郎中).
In the second year of Xīnghé (興和),
he concurrently held the post of tōngzhí sànqí chángshì (通直散騎常侍),
and accompanied Cuī Chángqiān (崔長謙) of Qīnghé (清河) as an envoy to Liáng (梁).
In the second year of Wǔdìng (武定),
he was appointed zhōngshū shìláng (中書侍郎).
At that time, a scholar playfully ridiculed Xiūzhī (休之), saying:
"There is a ram with horns entangled in a fence,
riding a dappled horse with a chain pattern,
traveling from Jìnyáng (晉陽) to Yè (鄴),
carrying a handful of letters."
Lú Fěi (盧斐), shàngshū zuǒchéng (尚書左丞), requested an audience with these documents,
and memorialized Gāozǔ (高祖) to prohibit such behavior.
However, he was pardoned and not punished.
In the fifth year,
he concurrently served as shàngshí diǎnyù (尚食典御).
In the seventh year,
he was appointed tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
promoted to gěishì huángmén shìláng (給事黃門侍郎),
and granted the titles of zhōngjūn jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) and Yōuzhōu dàzhōngzhèng (幽州大中正).
In the eighth year,
he concurrently served as shìzhōng (侍中),
and bearing credentials, went with imperial decrees sealed with a jade seal to Bīngzhōu (幷州),
to persuade Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) to accept the positions of xiàngguó (相國) and Qíwáng (齊王).
At this time,
Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) was about to receive the abdication from Wèi (魏).
He departed from Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and reached Píngyáng Commandery (平陽郡),
but as people's sentiments were not yet unified,
he returned to Bīngzhōu (幷州).
Fearing a leak,
he then blocked travelers.
Xiūzhī (休之) was naturally loose-tongued.
Upon his return from the mission,
he recounted the matter,
and everyone in Yè (鄴) knew about it.
Later, Gāo Dézhèng (高德政) heard about it and reported it,
and Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) was furious but did not act immediately.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
he was appointed sànqí chángshì (散騎常侍),
and compiled the "Diaries of Activity and Repose."
A short while later,
he was demoted to xiāojì jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍) for an error in an imperial decree,
this being cumulative with previous incidents.
Soon after, due to his participation in settling the rites and ceremonies during the abdication,
he was separately enfeoffed as the founding baron (kāiguó nán 開國男) of Shǐpíng County (始平縣),
and concurrently held the position of lǐngjūn sīmǎ (領軍司馬) with his original rank.
Later, he was appointed dūshuǐ shǐzhě (都水使者),
served as sīhú yuán (司徒掾) and zhōngshū shìláng (中書侍郎),
and soon after was appointed zhòngshān tàishǒu (中山太守).
When Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) passed away,
Xiūzhī (休之) was summoned to Jìnyáng (晉陽)
to oversee the funeral arrangements.
In the first year of Gānmíng (乾明),
he concurrently served as shìzhōng (侍中)
to inspect the capital and its environs.
He was then appointed dàhónglú qīng (大鴻臚卿),
and concurrently held zhōngshū shìláng (中書侍郎).
At the beginning of Huángjiàn (皇建),
with his original rank, he concurrently held dùzhī shàngshū (度支尚書),
was granted the title of piàojì dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍),
and concurrently served as Yōuzhōu dàzhōngzhèng (幽州大中正).
Sùzōng (肅宗) paid close attention to governance,
and frequently consulted Xiūzhī (休之) on administrative methods.
Xiūzhī (休之) responded that clear rewards and punishments,
careful appointment of officials,
prohibiting extravagance,
and caring for the people's suffering were the priorities of governance.
The Emperor greatly accepted his advice.
During the Dàníng (大寧) era,
he was appointed dūguān shàngshū (都官尚書),
and then transferred to qībīng (七兵) and cíwù (祠部).
In the third year of Héqīng (河清),
he was sent out as the cìshǐ (刺史) of Xīyǎnlüzhōu (西兗州).
At the beginning of Tiāntǒng (天統),
he was summoned back as guānglù qīng (光祿卿),
and supervised the national history.
While Xiūzhī (休之) served in Zhōngshān (中山) and governed Xīyǎnlü (西兗),
he implemented benevolent policies in both places,
and was cherished by the officials and people.
After leaving office,
the common people erected steles to praise his virtues.
Soon after, he was appointed lìbù shàngshū (吏部尚書),
received salary from Yángwǔ County (陽武縣),
was appointed yítóng sānsī (儀同三司),
and was also granted the title of kāifǔ (開府).
Xiūzhī (休之) was knowledgeable about historical precedents
and familiar with clans.
All those he selected and appointed
were invariably talented and suitable for their positions.
He was granted the title of jīnzǐ guānglù dàfū (金紫光祿大夫).
In the first year of Wǔpíng (武平),
he was appointed zhōngshū jiān (中書監),
and soon after concurrently held shàngshū yòupúyè (尚書右僕射) with his original rank.
In the second year,
he was granted the title of zuǒ guānglù dàfū (左光祿大夫),
and concurrently held zhōngshū jiān (中書監).
In the third year,
he was granted the title of tèjìn (特進).
In the fifth year,
he was officially appointed zhōngshū jiān (中書監),
with all other titles remaining as before.
Soon after, due to old age, he retired from office,
presenting a memorial to resign his position.
The Emperor graciously responded but did not permit it.
In the sixth year,
he was officially appointed shàngshū yòupúyè (尚書右僕射).
Not long after,
he again concurrently held zhōngshū jiān (中書監).
Cūi Xiūzhī’s fundamental disposition was straightforward and
praised by scholars and friends.
In his later years: when Zǔ Tǐng mentioned compiling the *Yùlǎn* (Imperial Review),
and the book was finished,
and he was given the title Tèjìn (Special Promotion),
as soon as Tǐng was dismissed,
[Xiūzhī] immediately spread word in the imperial court,
saying they had harbored a grudge previously.
When Dèng Chángyóng and Yán Zhītuī proposed establishing the Wénlín Guǎn (Hall of Literary Culture),
Zhītuī’s original intention was not to allow venerable elders or high officials to reside there,
but Xiūzhī immediately attached himself to the group,
and entered to serve as a dàizhào (Attendant in Waiting) along with young court visitors and participants in military affairs.
Furthermore, when Wèi Shōu supervised the history,
he established the annals for Gāozǔ,
taking the year he pacified the Four Hú tribes as the starting year of Qí Yuán.
Shōu was in Qízhōu,
and fearing that the historians might alter his intention,
he submitted a memorial discussing it.
During the Wǔpíng reign,
when Shōu returned to court,
an imperial decree ordered the assembly of court notables to discuss the matter.
Xiūzhī established the position that the reign of Tiānbǎo should be the dividing line.
While Wèi Shōu was alive,
the two proposals remained undecided.
After Shōu died,
[Xiūzhī] subsequently persuaded officials both inside and outside the court,
causing an imperial edict to be issued adopting his proposal.
Later, when he was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān (Director of the Imperial Secretariat),
he immediately said to people:
“I have already been Zhōngshū Jiān three times.
What good is this appointment?”
When Lónghuà returned to Yè,
the entire court saw many promotions and appointments,
and Xiūzhī was enfeoffed as Yànjùn Wáng (Prince of Yàn Commandery).
He also said to those close to him:
“I am not a slave;
why have I suddenly received this appointment?”
All these matters,
were deeply scorned by public opinion at the time.
Xiūzhī loved studying tirelessly,
and was broadly versed in the Classics and Histories.
Although his prose was not flowery or extravagant,
it was considered classical and correct.
After Xíng (Rǎo) and Wèi (Shōu) passed away,
he was highly regarded as a senior figure.
Although his position and prestige were high,
he treated others with an open mind,
and was loved and respected by the gentry.
When Zhōu Wǔ pacified Qí,

[Xiūzhī] was conscripted along with eighteen others—including Lìbù Shàngshū Yuán Yùxiū, Wèiwèi Qīng Lǐ Zǔqīn, Dùzhī Shàngshū Yuán Xiūbó, Dàlǐ Qīng Sīmǎ Yòuzhī, Sīnóng Qīng Cuī Dánú, Mìshū Jiān Yuán Wénzōng, Sǎnqí Chángshì concurrently Zhōngshū Shìláng Lǐ Ruò, Sǎnqí Chángshì concurrently Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng Lǐ Xiàozhēn, Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng Lú Sīdào, Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng Yán Zhītuī, Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì concurrently Zhōngshū Shìláng Lǐ Délín, Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén Lù Yì, Zhōngshū Shìláng Xuē Dàohéng, Zhōngshū Shèrén Gāo Xínggōng, Xīn Déyuán, Wáng Shào, and Lù Kāimíng—
and ordered to follow the emperor’s carriage to Cháng’ān.
In Lú Sīdào's writings,
he merely claimed that Xiūzhī, Xiàozhēn, and Sīdào were summoned together, which was a slanderous falsehood.
Soon thereafter, he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng (Duke-Appointed to Open a Residence with Ceremonial Privileges),
and successively held Nàyán Zhōng Dàfū (Grandee of the Center for Memorializing) and Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince).
Towards the end of Dàxiàng,
he was promoted to Shàng Kāifǔ,
and appointed as Hézhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Hézhōu).
In the second year of Kāihuáng of Suí,
he was dismissed from his post,
and died in Luòyáng,
at the age of seventy-four.
His collected literary works amounted to thirty volumes,
and his compiled *Yōuzhōu Rénwù Zhì* (Gazetteer of Figures from Yōuzhōu) also circulated in the world.
His son, Pìqiáng,
was Shàngshū Shuǐbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Ministry of Waterways) toward the end of Wǔpíng.
Pìqiáng was negligent and careless by nature,
and lacked literary talent.
Xiūzhī also arranged for him to enter the Wénlín Guǎn,
which was ridiculed and scorned by people at the time.
Yuán Yùxiū,
courtesy name Shūdé,
was a native of Yángxià, Chénjùn.
He was the son of Yuán Fān, the Wèi Zhōngshū Líng (Director of the Imperial Secretariat),
and was adopted as heir to his uncle Yuán Yuè.
At the age of seven, he suffered a bereavement.
His conduct and adherence to rites
were like those of an adult.
At the age of nine,
the commandery appointed him Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk).
He was profound and discerning by nature,
pure, quiet, and modest in desire,
and competed with no one.
He was greatly recognized and appreciated by Shàngshū Cuī Xiū.
During the Tàichāng reign of Wèi,
he received his first official post as Tàibǎo Kāifǔ Xīgé Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the West Gate of the Grand Protector's Establishment).
At age eighteen,
he served as Zhōngzhèng (Impartial Judge) for his native commandery.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Shàngshū Dùzhī Láng (Director in the Ministry of Revenue),
and subsequently held the posts of Wǔbīng Lángzhōng and Zuǒmín Lángzhōng.
Towards the end of Wǔdìng,
he became Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (Attendant in the Crown Prince's Household).
In the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (Official of the Crown Prince’s Household),
and served concurrently in his original capacity as Bólíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Bólíng).
After several years,
he achieved great reputation and success,
and was praised far and wide.
In the eighth year,
he concurrently served as Tàifǔ Shàoqīng (Vice Minister of the Grand Treasury),
and soon transitioned to Dàsīnóng Shàoqīng (Vice Minister of Agriculture),
and was then appointed Tàicháng Shàoqīng (Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
In the second year of Huángjiàn,
he left office due to mourning his mother,
but was soon ordered by imperial decree to resume his former post,
and was given the titles Guān Jūn and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the State).
He was appointed Lìbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Ministry of Personnel).
Not long after,
he was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk on the Left to the Minister of the Masses),
granted the title Piàoqí Dà Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry),
and concurrently served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Vice Director of the Imperial Censorate).
Sītú Lùshì Cānjūn Lú Sīdào privately borrowed 400,000 cash from the treasury to propose marriage to the daughter of Wáng Yì of Tàiyuán,
but the Wáng clan had already accepted the betrothal gifts from Lù Kǒngwén and confirmed the engagement.
Yùxiū was implicated because he was the chief subordinate
and also served as the nation's chief law enforcement official (Sī Xiàn),
yet knew of the matter and did not impeach [Lú Sīdào].
He was reprimanded and relieved of the Zhōngchéng post.
Soon after, he was transferred to Mìshū Jiān (Director of the Imperial Library).
During the Tiāntǒng reign,
an imperial edict ordered him and Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì to discuss and determine the Five Rites.
He was sent out to serve as Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xìnzhōu),
which was his native commandery;
people at the time considered this an honor.
His governance was pure and peaceful,
resulting in good order without overt effort.
From the chief officials downwards,
extending even to the widowers, widows, orphans, and young,
all gained his affection.
In the beginning of Wǔpíng,
Censors were sent out generally to visit various commanderies.
In the contiguous regions of Liáng, Zhèng, Yǎn, and Yù,
on all four sides of those commanderies,
there were impeachments and accusations.
Yet the Censors ultimately did not reach Xìnzhōu,
such was the extent of his recognized excellence.
When he concluded his term and returned to the capital,
the common people, both Buddhist and secular,
filled the roads to bid farewell.
Some brought wine and dried meat,
weeping and lingering,
competing to escort him far away.
Since it was high summer,
and fearing their exhaustion,
he often stopped his horse for them,
accepted a single cup of wine,
showed that he understood their feelings,
and thanked them before instructing them to return.
After returning to the capital,
over seven hundred people, including Zhèng Bōzōng of the commandery, requested that a stele be erected for him.
They collected several hundred bolts of silk and cloth,
and entrusted Zhōngshū Shìláng Lǐ Délín to compose the text commemorating his achievements and virtues.
The relevant government departments memorialized the request,
and an imperial decree approved it.
Soon thereafter, he was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū (Minister of the Ministry of Judicial Administration),
still holding the post of Zhōngzhèng for his native commandery.
He was then transferred to concurrently serve as Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) and Yítóng Sānsī (With the Privileges of the Three Dukes),
and soon assumed the Lìbù Shàngshū position officially.
Yùxiū was gentle and temperate in his youth.
Among the general
officials, he was the most disciplined and observant of rules.
As the son of a prominent family, he successively held positions in the purity and splendor (of the court).
At the time, many people highly valued
and respected him, predicting he would become a *fēngjiàn* (censor/high administrator).
During the days when he served in the Secretariats,
it happened that Zhào Yànshēn was the Director (*Lángzhōng*) of the Ministry of Waterways.
They were in the same office compound,
and thus became friends.
Later, Yànshēn was purged and removed from private duties (or, had his private means suspended).
Though his protégés were scattered like weeds,
Yùxiū still relied on their former affection,
visiting and inquiring about his well-being.
When Yànshēn was later employed (in office),
he was deeply grateful.
Although his own talent was undeniable,
this advancement was likely also due to Yùxiū's introduction and support.
After he became Minister (*Shàngshū*) of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*),
he himself considered that he obtained the position based on public reputation.
Initially, Fēng Zicóng had taken charge of selections as a Grand Marshal (*Púshè*).
Marriages (arranged through this influence) followed one after another.
Yùxiū often scorned and mocked him for this,
saying to others:
"Duke Fēng is busy arranging marriages,
and is busy every day."
When he himself resided in the Selection Office,
he could not avoid it either.
Contemporary opinion held that this was simply the nature of the position.
While in office, he was incorruptible and cautious.
Few at the time could compare.
During the Wèi and Qí eras,
most court directors (*táiláng*) could not avoid illicit dealings and accepting bribes.
Yùxiū served as Minister (*Shàngshū*) for ten years,
and never once accepted a gift, not even a measure of wine.
The Minister (*Shàngshū*) Xíng Shào had an old friendship with Yùxiū.
Whenever they joked in the department offices,
he always called Yùxiū "The Pure Director" (*Qīng Láng*).
In the beginning of the Dàníng era,
Yùxiū, as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Shàoqīng*), was dispatched on a tour of inspection.
He was also ordered to review the merits and faults of officials.
He passed through Yǎnzhōu.
At that time, Xíng Shào was the Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Yǎnzhōu.
After they parted,
[Xíng Shào] sent white silk fabric as a token of goodwill.
Yùxiū returned the silk and refused to accept it.
He wrote a letter to Xíng, saying:
"Having passed under your jurisdiction today,
it is a deviation from my usual practice.
'In the melon patch or under the plum tree,'
is what the ancients guarded against.
Excessive gossip is fearful;
it is like damming a river.
I hope to maintain this intention
so as not to incur heavy blame."
Xíng was also pleased and understood,
and replied in a letter:
"The gift of one day
was sent carelessly, without thinking.
This old man was heedless and did not consider this point.
I respectfully receive your instruction.
I have no objection.
My younger brother (you) was formerly a 'Pure Director' (*Qīng Láng*),
and today you have once again become a 'Pure Vice Minister' (*Qīng Qīng*)."
However, when he was in the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*),
it was a time when good governance was obstructed and moral principles were lost.
If he defied those in powerful positions,
he feared disaster would strike immediately.
Even though he upheld his personal integrity,
he still could not avoid the trouble of being petitioned and sought after.
When Qí fell, he entered Zhōu (service).
He was appointed Grand General of the Retainers (*Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn*) and Junior Grand Master of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù Xià Dàfū*).
Towards the end of the Dàxiàng era,
he was appointed Middle Grand Master (*Zhōng Dàfū*) in charge of the Clans of the Eastern Capital (*Dōngjīng Sīzōng*).
In the beginning of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
he was promoted to Grand General of the Retainers (*Shàng Yítóng*),
and transferred to Minister of Public Works (*Dūguān Shàngshū*) of the Eastern Capital (*Dōngjīng*).
When the Eastern Capital was abandoned,
he went to the Imperial Court.
He was again appointed Minister of Public Works (*Dūguān Shàngshū*).
In the second year (of Kāihuáng),
he was sent out to serve as Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Xióngzhōu.
He soon died,
at the age of seventy-two.
His son, Zhīlǐ,
was Registrar (*Cānjūnshì*) of the Grand General's Bureau (*Yítóng Kāifǔ*) towards the end of the Wǔpíng era.
During the middle of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí,
he was an Imperial Investigator (*Shì Yùshǐ*),
and successively held the posts of Vice Minister (*Shìláng*) of Revenue (*Mínbù*) and Vice Minister of Merit Review (*Kǎogōng*) in the Chancellery (*Shàngshū*).
In the beginning of the Dàyè era,
he died while serving as Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Zhōng Shèrén*).
The historian remarks: Cuī Yànxuán perpetuated virtue across generations,
and did not disgrace his ancestors.
Secretary Lú (Zhān) was fond of chivalry and strategic planning,
his ambitions were grand and far-reaching.
Grand Marshal Yáng held high rank and great prestige,
and he was an eminent leader of his time.
Minister Yuán (*Shàngshū*) possessed purity and wisdom,
and was employed based on his talent and ability.
He, along with Yáng Fěi and Lú Qián, were great assets to the court.
In the final years of the Qí dynasty,
power fell into the hands of flattering favorites.
It was fortunate that these gentlemen maintained proper morality and education.
Otherwise, the foundation would have been uprooted and the source blocked,
caps split and crowns destroyed—
how can one even describe it?
Eulogy says: These several gentlemen,
were calm regarding favor or disgrace;
neither harsh nor complacent,
they settled and stabilized the prevailing customs.
Biographies, Number 35: Lǐ Zhìlián, Fēng Shù, Xǔ Dūn, Yáng Liè, Yuán Biāo.
Lǐ Zhìlián
was a native of Gāoyì in Zhàojùn.
He was the younger brother of Yìshēn, the Prefect (*Cìshǐ*) of Qízhōu.
Zhìlián was young and had few desires.
When he was a child,
he never once asked his family members for anything.
His family members once purposely gave him gold and jewels,
but he ultimately refused to take them.
If forced to accept them,
he would immediately throw them on the ground.
The Regional Governor (*Zhōumù*), noting his youthful innocence and integrity (*lián*),
therefore named him Zhìlián (Young and Pure).
He was intelligent and fond of learning.
By the age of fifteen,
he had extensively studied the commentaries and phrases of the Five Classics.
During Gě Róng's rebellion,
his home commandery was in turmoil.
He fled the disaster and went to the capital.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
he first entered service as an Attendant at Court (*Fèng Cháoqǐng*).
In the beginning of the Pǔtài era,

he was appointed Registrar (*Jìshì*) of a Grand General's Bureau (*Kāifǔ*), General Soaring Dragon (*Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn*), and Deputy Administrator (*Lùshì Cānjūn*) of the Pacifying the South General's Headquarters (*Zhēngnán Fǔ*) in Guǎngzhōu.
He did not take up this post.
Soon after, he was transferred to Advisory Registrar (*Zīyì Cānjūnshì*) of a Grand General's Bureau (*Kāifǔ*) and General of the Vanguard (*Qián Jiāngjūn*).
During the Tiānpíng era,
Gāozǔ promoted him to Chief Clerk (*Chángshǐ*) of the Grand General's Bureau (*Kāifǔ*) of Tàizhōu and General Pacifying the North (*Píngběi Jiāngjūn*).
Zhìlián brought harmony among his officers and soldiers;
the military and the populace were pleased.
Gāozǔ frequently visited Hédōng.
[Gāozǔ] highly praised and admired him.
He was transferred to Chief Clerk (*Chángshǐ*) of Shìzōng's Cavalry General's Bureau (*Piàojì Fǔ*).
An imperial edict noted that Jìzhōu controlled the rivers and land access points,
and dealt with envoys from Liáng.
Therefore, a suitable person was especially needed.
Shìzōng recommended him,
and he was appointed Chief Clerk (*Chángshǐ*) of the Retainer General (*Yítóng*) in Jìzhōu.
He was then transferred to Chief Clerk (*Chángshǐ*) of Yíngzhōu.
When Gāozǔ traveled through Jìzhōu,
he collected the documents and registers from the six prefectures north of the Yellow River
to check and assess the increase or decrease in population.
Gāozǔ personally assigned the tasks,
often while on horseback.
He demanded the documents
and required them to be completed by a designated time (lit. 'pointing at the shadow').
The matters involved were numerous.
Zhìlián responded quickly and completed every task instantly,
meeting the deadlines ahead of schedule.
Everything he did perfectly accorded with the subtle intent [of Gāozǔ],
and became a standard example for all the prefectures.
Gāozǔ turned to Sīmǎ Zǐrú and said:
"Observing Zhìlián's management,
it is quite satisfying."
Consequently, he assembled several tens of thousands of civil and military officials,
and ordered Director Dù Bì to proclaim an edict of commendation.
He subsequently interrogated the Chief Clerks (*Chángshǐ*), Magistrates (*Shǒulìng*), and others from the various prefectures.
Everyone apologized for their faults,
but Zhìlián alone stepped forward and bowed in thanks for the favor.
All the observers praised and admired him.
On that day,
he was bestowed with beef and wine.
When Gāozǔ returned to Bīng (Jìnyáng),
he recounted this incident to Shìzōng.
Shìzōng was delighted and said to others:
"I know men well enough!"
When Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
he summoned [Zhìlián] to Jìnyáng,
and appointed him Registrar (*Yuàn*) of the Supreme Headquarters (*Bàfǔ*).
He said to Dù Bì:
"Bīngzhōu is the foundation of a sovereign.
We need a good Chief Clerk (*Chángshǐ*).
Each of you should recommend someone you know."
At that time, there were mutual recommendations,
but none were approved.
When the group had not yet answered,
Shìzōng then said to Chén Yuánkāng:
"I will tell you where the good Chief Clerk is:
Lǐ Zhìlián is the man."
He was consequently appointed Chief Clerk (*Chángshǐ*) of Bīngzhōu.
He often resided within Shìzōng's residence,
and, along with Xīn Shù of Lǒngxī and five others, was designated a 'Guest of the Residence' (*guǎn kè*),
and treated with the rites appropriate for honored guests.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo [reign period],
he was appointed General Pacifying the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Tài-yuán Commandery.
Xiǎnzǔ once summoned him for an audience,
asking him about methods of governance.
When the conversation touched upon the leniency or severity of administration and punishment,
the emperor favored detailed texts and harsh laws.
Zhìlián firmly maintained that this was incorrect,
and the emperor was displeased.
When speaking of Yáng Yīn,
he mistakenly referred to him as Gōng Yáng.
Due to his inappropriate answers,
he was dismissed and appointed Administrator of Jìyīn Commandery,
concurrently holding the post of Inspector of Xīyǎn Prefecture.
He was summoned to court and appointed Vice Minister of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Shàoqīng).
Soon after, he was transferred to be Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi Shàoqīng),
then promoted to Chief Clerk to the Grand Commander (Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ).
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he concurrently held the posts of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Envoy for Provincial Inspection (Shěngfāng Dàshǐ).
Upon his return from the mission,
many of the memorials he presented were accepted and utilized.
He was appointed Inspector of Hé Prefecture,
where he also had administrative success.
Before his term was complete,
he was made Acting Inspector of Huái Prefecture.
Returning to court,
he was granted the concurrent post of Minister Coachman (Tàipú Qīng).
He was then transferred to Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng Qīng) and Grand Arbiter of Zhào Prefecture.
In the first year of Tiāntǒng,
he was given the title General of Cavalry and Chariots (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn) and Minister of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Qīng).
The world praised him as fair and upright.
He served as Inspector of Nánqīng Prefecture.
Not long after,
he was summoned to serve as Minister of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū) in Bīng Province.
In the third month of the fifth year of Wǔpíng,
he died in Jìnyáng
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the titles Companion to the Three Excellencies (Yítóng Sānsī), Inspector of the two prefectures of Xìnyì, and Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
Fēng Shù,
courtesy name Jūnyì,
was a man of Tiáo in Bóhǎi.
His father, Guǐ,
was Minister of the Court of Judicial Review and Inspector of Jì Prefecture.
Shù possessed competence and ability.
At the age of eighteen, he became Adjutant of the Quartermaster Section in the Commandant-in-Chief Pacifying the East's office in Jì Prefecture.
When Gāo Dàomù became Surveillance Commissioner (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi),
he proposed Shù be made a Censor (Yùshǐ).
He was promoted to Secretary-Adjutant in the office of Qīnghé Wáng, the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ),
concurrently serving as Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Zhǔbù).
During the Tàichāng [reign period],
he was appointed Director of the Bureaus of the Three Excellencies in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Sāngōng Lángzhōng).
He was praised for his fairness and ability.
During the Tiānpíng [reign period],
he supplemented and curtailed old statutes to create the Línzhǐ Xīngé (New Regulations of the Linzhi Hall).
The rules and articles of these regulations,
were all revised and finalized by Shù.
When Lù Yànzǐ and Shěn Jǐng, Palace Attendants of Liáng, came to negotiate,
Shù was given the concurrent post of Court Gentleman for the Transmission of Edicts (Tōngzhí Láng) and sent as an envoy to Liáng.
Upon his return,
he was promoted to Palace Assistant to the General-in-Chief in Shìzōng's headquarters,
overseeing matters in the capital region.
In the fifth year of Wǔdìng,
he was appointed Administrator of Péngchéng and Supervisor of the Commandery.
He was then made Acting Inspector of Dōngxú Prefecture a second time.
In the seventh year of Wǔdìng,
he was appointed Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
In the eighth year,
he concurrently held the post of Attendant in the Imperial Secretariat (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
When Qí accepted the abdication,
he and Lǐ Jiǎng (and eight others) served as Grand Envoys,
touring the provinces and local customs,
inquiring about the people's hardships.
In the third year of Tiānbǎo,
he was appointed Administrator of Qīnghé.
He was promoted to Senior Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses,
managing affairs in the Eastern Capital,
and soon after, he was appointed Inspector of Hǎi Prefecture.
In the first year of Dàníng,
he was summoned and appointed Minister of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Qīng).
In the third year of Héqīng,

he was commanded, along with Director of the Department of State Affairs Zhào Yànshēn, Palace Assistant (Pūyè) Wèi Shōu, Minister Yáng Xiūzhī, Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ) Mǎ Jìngdé, and others, to deliberate and finalize the laws and statutes.
In the first year of Tiāntǒng,
he was promoted to Minister of Budget and Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū).
In the third year,
he was transferred to Minister of Military Affairs (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and given the title Companion to the Three Excellencies.
In the first year of Wǔpíng,
he was appointed Inspector of Nányǎn Prefecture.
After his term was complete, he returned to court,
and was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū).
He was also appointed Minister of the Palace (Diànzhōng Shàngshū).
Shù served as a judicial official for a long time.
He clearly understood the laws and statutes,
and his judgments and rulings were fair and just,
earning him high praise from the people of the time.
However, he amassed great wealth.
He never gave any gifts or handouts.
Even when close relatives or intimate friends were impoverished, ill, and seriously distressed,
he completely refused to help them.
Opinions among the court and the common people greatly despised him for this.
Although his outer appearance was proper and solemn, he did not avoid petitioning,
changing his behavior depending on whether he needed to evade or advance,
which often led to ridicule and shock.
His first wife was from the Sīmǎ clan of Hènnèi.
For one son,
he arranged marriage to the daughter of Lǐ Shìyuán of Lǒngxī,
paying a large dowry.
Yet, when the wedding ceremony was about to take place,
they still argued over outstanding obligations.
Suddenly, Shù took a devotional statue and swore an oath while hitting the statue in front of Shìyuán.
Shìyuán laughed and said:
"Fēng Gōng, how is it that you always have an emergency statue readily available
whenever you need to swear an oath?"
Another son married the daughter of Lú Zhuāng of Fànyáng.
Shù then went directly to the government office and complained, saying:
"When we sent the packing animal, they complained its leg was lame.
When we evaluated the fields, they said they were salty and barren.
They also complained that the bronze vessels were old and broken."
All these disputes arose from his stinginess,
often leading to confusion and conflict.
His son, Yuán,
was a Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince at the end of Wǔpíng.
Shù's younger brother, Xún,
courtesy name Jǐngwén.
He was a Supernumerary Gentleman (Yuánwài Láng) in Wèi.
During Wǔdìng, he was Judge-Advocate in the Office of the Duke of Yǒng'ān.
He was gradually promoted to Director of the Bureau of Construction (Qǐbù Lángzhōng) in the Department of State Affairs,
transferred to Director of the Bureaus of the Three Excellencies,
then left court to become Administrator of Dōngpíngyuán Commandery.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk of Dìng Prefecture,
then appointed Administrator of Héjiān Commandery.
He returned to court as Assistant (Zuǒ Chéng) in the Department of State Affairs,
and later served as Administrator of Jǐnán.
He died during the Kāihuáng [reign period] of Suí.
Xún had studied the classics and histories.
He maintained a simple and pure integrity.
In all his successive official posts, he demonstrated ability and competence.
His governance of the commanderies earned great renown and success,
and the people and officials respected and loved him.
Xǔ Dūn,
courtesy name Jìliáng,
was a man of Xīnchéng in Gāoyáng.
His father, Hù,
was Administrator of the two commanderies of Gāoyáng and Zhāngwǔ in Wèi.
Dūn possessed clear judgment and quick intelligence.
He was skilled in political affairs.
He served as Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses.
Because of his skill in making judgments,
he became well-known to the people of the time,
and was nicknamed the "Iron-Cutting Chief Clerk."
He was gradually promoted to Administrator of Yángpíng.
At that time, the capital moved to Yè.
Yángpíng thus became a commandery in the metropolitan region.
Military and state demands were constantly made,
and taxes and levies had no standard measure.
Moreover, requests came from powerful nobles and relatives,
demanding things day and night.
Dūn managed all this with integrity,
and neither the superiors nor the subordinates harbored resentment.
His governance was considered the best in the realm.
He received special commendation and distinction,
his portrait was displayed at the palace gate,
and an imperial edict was issued across the land.
He was promoted to Metropolitan Prefect of Wèi.
He left court to be appointed Inspector of Qí Prefecture,
and then transferred to Inspector of Liáng Prefecture.
His governance in both places was renowned.
He was promoted to Minister of Agriculture.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
and Wáng Sīzhèng entered and occupied Yǐngchéng,
the imperial army was dispatched to suppress them.
Dūn constantly supervised the transport of grain,
ensuring the army never ran out of supplies.
The plan to divert the Wěi River to flood the city
was Dūn’s strategy.
He was promoted to Minister of the Palace.
Dūn had a handsome beard and whiskers (xūrǎn),
which hung down to his belt.
In the Department of State Affairs, he was nicknamed "Duke Long-Beard."
Xiǎnzǔ once, during heavy drinking,
grabbed Dūn's beard and whiskers, praising their beauty,
then cut them off with a knife,
leaving only a handful.
Dūn was terrified,
and consequently never dared to let it grow long again.
The people of the time thus nicknamed him "Duke Even-Beard."
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Dūn concurrently served as Surveillance Commissioner (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and was made Inspector of Jiāo Prefecture.
Soon after, he was recalled to serve as Minister of Agriculture.
He was then promoted to Minister of Judicial Review,
and served a second time as Minister of Budget and Revenue.

He successively held the posts of Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàobǎo), Junior Mentor (Shàoshī), Grand Master of Remonstrance (Guānglù Dàfū), Companion to the Three Excellencies with the Right to Establish an Administration (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), Right Palace Assistant in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Pūyè), and Palace Grandee (Tèjìn).
He was granted the title Viscount of Wànnián County,
and held the stipend from Xiàpī Commandery.
Due to old age, he retired to his home,
and died three years later.
Dūn was pure and upright in his youth,
but later became unstable.
Following the style of the Qí Dynasty court,
the Great Impartial (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of the native prefecture was held by a capital official (Jīngguān).
Xíng Shào, from the same commandery, was Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
His virtue and reputation were very high.
Dūn competed with Shào for the Impartial position,
and consequently attached himself to Sòng Qīndào,
having Shào sent out as an Inspector (Cìshǐ).
The court heavily scorned him for this.
Although he had long been in officialdom
and held conspicuous and pure offices,
standing shoulder-to-shoulder with people like Xíng Shào, Wèi Shōu, Yáng Xiūzhī, Cuī Jié, and Xú Zhīcái,
those men sometimes discussed classics and histories,
sometimes chanted poetry and rhapsodies,
jesting with each other,
filling the hall with happy laughter.
Dūn did not understand witty conversation,
nor did he have scholarship.
He would either sit silently through the entire gathering,
or lean on a desk and sleep,
and was deeply looked down upon by the leading literati.
His son was Wénjì,
Director (Lángzhōng) of the Bureau of General Supply (Dùzhī) at the end of the Wǔpíng era.
Wénjì’s younger brother, Wénjīng,
was hardworking, upright, and elegant.
He committed no improper deeds,
nor spoke frivolous words.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
he was Palace Imperial Clerk (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ).
In the early Kāihuáng era of the Suí Dynasty, he was Imperial Clerk (Shìyùshǐ),
concurrently Palace Attendant and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sǎnjì Chángshì).
He served as Vice Envoy to Chén,
and Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Merit (Zhǔjué Shìláng).
He died while serving as Chief Administrator (Zhǎngshǐ) of Xiāngzhōu.
Dūn’s elder brother was Xùn,
courtesy name Zhòngràng.
He had administrative capability.
During the Qiánmíng era, he was Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Píngyuán.
He died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Xìnzhōu.
Xùn’s son, Wéngāo,
was a subordinate (Yuàn) of the Minister of Education (Sītú).
Yáng Liè,
courtesy name Xìnqīng,
was a native of Jùpíng in Tàishān.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Xiù, Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Qīng) of the Jìn Dynasty,
and the nephew of Zhǐ, Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Liángzhōu during the Wèi Dynasty.
His father, Língzhēn,
was Assistant to the Inspector (Biéjià) of Yǎnzhōu during the Wèi Dynasty.
Liè was bright and quick-witted in his youth,
self-cultivating and self-reliant,
possessing the demeanor of a grown man.
He loved reading,
was skilled at discussing principles (mínglǐ),
and was famous for his knowledge of Xuanxue (Mysterious Learning).
During the Xiàochāng era of the Wèi Dynasty,
Liè’s cousin Kǎn was an Administrator (Tàishǒu).
He occupied the commandery, raised troops, and rebelled externally.
Liè secretly learned of his plan,
