and, deeply fearing disaster for his family,
he rushed to Luòyáng with his cousin Dūn, Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Guǎngpíng, to report the rebellion.
The imperial court planned to bestow a generous reward,
but Liè told people:
“This is like cutting off a hand to save the whole body;
what is preserved is the greater part.
How could I rejoice in my cousin’s failure and turn it into my own profit?”
In the end, he accepted nothing.
When he reached manhood,
the prefecture appointed him Chief Secretary (Zhǔbù),
and concurrently Supervisor of Administration (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì).
The Inspector (Cìshǐ) valued his administrative ability,
and he became known for his competence.
He shed his commoner’s garb to become Mobilized Staff Officer (Xíng Cānjūn) to Xiányáng Wáng, the Grand Tutor (Tàishī),
and was promoted to Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng).
In the early Xiǎnzǔ era, he was appointed Companion with the Three Masters (Yítóng Sānsī),
establishing his own staff (kāifǔ).
He was also Staff Officer for the Bureau of Granaries (Cāngcáo Cānjūnshì).
In the early Tiānbǎo era,
he was awarded Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi) for the Crown Prince, and General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was transferred to Director (Lángzhōng) of the Bureau of Accounts (Bǐbù) within the Provincial Secretariat (Bìng Shěng).
He was appointed subordinate (Shǔ) to the Minister of Education (Sītú),
and frequently served as Director (Lángzhōng) in the Bureau of Sacrifices (Cíbù),
and the Bureaus of the Left and Right Populace (Zuǒ, Yòu Mín Lángzhōng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
Wherever he served, he was deemed competent.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yángpíng.
His administration gained a reputation for competence.
At that time,
there were repeated natural disasters and locust plagues.
The locusts did not enter the borders of Yángpíng,
and an imperial decree was issued praising him.
In the second year of Huángjiàn,
he was promoted to Lesser Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shàoqīng),
given the title General Who Leaps Like a Dragon (Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn), and Great Impartial (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Yǎnzhōu.
He was further promoted to General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn).
During the Tiāntǒng era,
he was appointed Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
concurrently serving as Lesser Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shàoqīng).
In the early Wǔpíng era,
he was appointed General of Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yìzhōu.
Soon after, due to old age and illness, he returned home.
He died during the Dàxiàng era of the Zhōu Dynasty.
Liè’s family followed traditional customs,
maintaining strict discipline within the household,
and was praised by the world.
No woman in the family ever remarried.
During the Tàihé era of the Wèi Dynasty,
a nunnery was established in Yǎnzhōu.
Widows in the family who had no sons all left home to become nuns,
and all maintained strict moral conduct.
During the Tiāntǒng era, Liè contended with Bì Yìyún, Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū), for the Great Impartial (Dà Zhōngzhèng) position of Yǎnzhōu.
Yìyún highly praised his lineage,
saying, “My family has been Inspector (Cìshǐ) of this prefecture for generations,
while your family served as former clerks of mine for generations.”
Liè replied:
“Since Bì Guǐ was executed,
your family has produced no notable figures.
Recent Inspectors (Cìshǐ)
are merely those gained back and forth on the frontiers;
what is there to boast about?
How can that compare to my ancestors, who were Governor (Yǐn) of Hénán during the Hàn Dynasty,
or Grand Tutor (Tàifù) during the Jìn Dynasty,
whose renown, virtue, and learning
have been praised for a hundred generations?
Moreover, our men are pure and our women are chaste,
which is sufficient for comparison;
besides that, there are many other things worthy of praise.”
This was a ridicule of Yìyún’s lack of moral discipline.
Zhǐ’s son, Shēn,
was Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng) during the Wèi Dynasty.
Shēn’s son, Sù,
was known for his scholarly aspirations,
and served as Libationer (Jìjiǔ) of the Eastern Office in the Grand General’s (Dà Jiāngjūn) residence during the Shìzōng era.
In the early Qiánmíng era,
he was Supervisor of Administration (Zhìzhōng) in Jìzhōu.
When the Prince of Zhàojùn served as Grand Inspector (Xúnshěng Dàshǐ),
Sù was dismissed for being slow and unfit for the job.
The court argued that Sù was innocent,
and he was soon reinstated.
In the early Tiāntǒng era,
he was promoted to Chief Administrator (Zhǎngshǐ) of Nányǎnzhōu.
During the Wǔpíng era,
he entered the Academy of Literature (Wénlín Guǎn) to compile books.
Soon after, he was sent out to be Administrator (Shǒu) of Wǔdé Commandery.
Liè’s younger brother, Xiū,
had talent and competence.
During the Dàníng era, he died while serving as Vice Minister of the Left (Zuǒ Chéng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
His son, Xuánzhèng,
was Assistant Director of the Palace Buildings (Jiàngzuò Chéng) at the end of the Wǔpíng era.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí Dynasty, he was Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Populace (Mínbù Shìláng).
He died while serving as Assistant Administrator (Zànzhì) of Lǒngxī Commandery.
Yuán Biāo,
courtesy name Wénzōng,
was a native of Lèdū in Xīpíng.
His father, Zǐgōng,
was Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng) during the Wèi Dynasty,
posthumously titled Gōng Wénxiàn.
Wénzōng was widely learned and astute,
and had a reputation in his youth.
During the Yǒng’ān era of Emperor Xiàozhuāng of the Wèi Dynasty,
based on his father’s merit, he was granted the title Count (Bó) of Línyǐng County,
and appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Supernumerary (Yuánwài Sǎnjì Chángshì).
In the fourth year of Tiānpíng,
he was Great Impartial (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Liángzhōu.
He left office due to mourning for his father.
In the early Wǔdìng era,
after the mourning period ended,
the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) summoned him to lead the Secretariat (Jìshì) of the Minister of Education (Sītú),
and granted him the title General Who Pacifies the East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn).
When Shìzōng oversaw the selection process,
purifying the Directors (Láng) of the Department of State Affairs (Tái),
Wénzōng was made Director (Lángzhōng) of the Bureau of Sacrifices (Cíbù) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
still leading the Secretariat (Jìshì).
He was transferred to Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
he was appointed Palace Administrative Assistant (Zhōngshèrén) to the Crown Prince.
In the early Qiánmíng era,
he was sent out to be Administrator (Shǒu) of Fànyáng Commandery.
In the second year of Huángjiàn,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
Wénzōng treated others with kindness and trust,
greatly achieving harmony along the border regions.
He was respected and admired by neighboring peoples,
and many who had been captured or plundered under the previous administration
were allowed to return.
At the beginning of Tiāntǒng,
he entered the court as Lìbù Lángzhōng,
and was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
supervising the selection of officials as before.
Soon after, he was made Sànqí Chángshì,
still overseeing the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) temporarily,
and was granted the title Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
When the Cìshǐ of Qínzhōu, Sòng Sōng, died,
the imperial court considered that the prefecture was situated on the frontier,
and because Wénzōng, when he governed Jīngzhōu,
had achieved considerable fame and merit,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Qínzhōu.
He traveled to the post via official conveyance
and was specially granted a rear honor guard band (gǔchuī).
Wénzōng governed as he had when he was in Jīngzhōu.
When Lǐ Xiàozhēn was sent as an envoy to Chén,
the ruler of Chén said to Xiàozhēn:
"If the Qí Cháo still sends Yuán Jīngzhōu to Guābù,
it can truly be said that our relations are harmonious and smooth."
Soon after, he was granted the rank Yítóng Sānsī.
In the second year of Wǔpíng,
he was summoned to lead the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Mìshū Jiān.
When the Chén general Wú Míngchè raided Huáinán,
Lìyáng and Guābù successively fell.
Zhào Yànshēn secretly consulted Wénzōng in the Secretariat for Imperial Daily Life (Qǐjū Shěng), saying:
"The Wú bandits are rampant
and have reached this point.
I have long hindered worthy men,
and my worry and fear are profound.
Given the present circumstances,
what plan should be pursued?
When you were formerly in Jīngzhōu,
you were extremely familiar with the situation between the Jiāng and Huái Rivers.
Now, how shall we defend against them?"
He replied:
"I am deeply indebted to the nation's great grace,
and have no way to repay it with service.
Since I have seen and heard certain things,
dare I not speak fully?
However, the court certainly will not entrust many elite troops to the various generals.
If the number is several thousand or fewer,
they will again be unable to contend against Wú and Chǔ forces,
and ordering a general to lead the army out
will instead make them bait for the enemy.
Wèi Pòhú's character
is known to Your Excellency (Wáng).
Since we cannot advance,
yet retreating is also not yet advisable,
defeat
is imminent.
If Wáng Lín can leave and return successfully,
the court and the populace will be devoted to him.
If, heaven forbid, there is a single mishap,
regret will be too late.
Based on today's strategy,
we cannot try this again and again.
The nation's treatment of Huáinán
is as misguided as firing an arrow into weeds.
If Wénzōng were to plan this,
it would be nothing more than solely entrusting Wáng Lín,
recruiting thirty or forty thousand men in Huáinán—
as their customs are similar,
he can gain their commitment unto death—
while simultaneously ordering the old generals north of the Huái River to hold their troops,
which would be sufficient for a firm defense.
Furthermore, it is clear
that Wáng Lín will not turn north to serve Tán Xù.
I secretly believe this is the best possible plan.
If we do not reveal our absolute sincerity toward Wáng Lín,
but instead dispatch other people to restrain him,
it will quickly result in disaster,
making the situation utterly untenable."
Yànshēn sighed, saying:
"Brother, this excellent strategy
is enough to secure victory a thousand *lǐ* away,
but after ten days of debate,
it has already not been followed.
With the state of affairs having reached this point,
how can one speak fully?"
Thereupon, they looked at each other and wept.
In the seventh year of Wǔpíng,
Zhōu Wǔ subdued Qí,
and Wénzōng, along with Yáng Xiūzhī, Yuán Yùxiū, and eighteen others, was commanded to enter the capital (of Zhōu),
where he was appointed Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn and Sīchéng Xià Dàfū.
At the beginning of Suí Kāihuáng,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Jǔzhōu.
Upon reaching the prefecture,
he fell ill and left office.
He died in the sixth year of Kāihuáng,
aged sixty-six.
Wénzōng rose through the court ranks as a son of a noble family.
His talent and knowledge were keen and comprehensive,
and he was recognized for his capability and organization.
However, he liked to visit the residences of the powerful and influential,
thus contemporary opinion held that he was skilled at flattery and association.
His son, Shī,
was fond of learning in his youth,
possessing clear discernment and understanding,
and was especially famous for his administrative abilities.
At the beginning of Héqīng,
he served as Sīkōng Cānjūnshì,
and subsequently held the posts of Shì Yùshǐ, Tàicháng Chéng, and Shàngshū Zuǒ Wàibīng Lángzhōng.
During Suí Kāihuáng, he was Shàngshū Bǐbù and Kǎogōng Shìláng.
At the beginning of Dàyè,
he died while serving as Dàlǐ Shàoqīng.
Wénzōng's younger brother, Wénjǔ,
also possessed talent and capability.
He served successively as Shàngshū Bǐbù and Èrqiān Shí Lángzhōng,
Zhǎngshǐ of Dìngzhōu,
concurrently holding the title of Grand Administrator (Jùnshǒu) of Zhōngshān Jùn.
He died while serving as Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ.
Wénzōng's cousin (son of his paternal uncle), Kǎi,
whose courtesy name was Nuóyán,
possessed dignity and capability,
and was skilled in *cǎo* (cursive) and *lì* (clerical) script.
He successively held the posts of Shàngshū Zuǒ Mínbù Lángzhōng,
Zhìshū Shì Yùshǐ, Grand Administrator of Chánglè and Zhōngshān Commandery, Jīngjī Zhǎngshǐ, Huángmén Láng, and acting Yítóng Sānsī.
When Qí was extinguished,
those nobles and renowned officials who entered the capital of Zhōu included: Dùzhī Shàngshū Yuán Xiūbó,
a descendant of Emperor Wèi Wénchéng Huángdì.
He was pure, simple, and had few desires,
and possessed clear knowledge of administrative principles.
In his youth, he successively held prominent positions:
Shàngshū Láng, Zhìshū Shì Yùshǐ,
Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ, Grand Administrator of several commanderies, and Cìshǐ of Guāngzhōu.
In all his posts, he achieved notable fame and merit.
When he served as Dùzhī (Minister of Revenue),
the government was mismanaged and the nation was weakened.
Reserves were exhausted,
and levies and labor services were numerous and increasing.
Xiūbó worried about the nation as if it were his own family,
showing compassion for the toil of the people,
and assisting in contemporary affairs.
He consulted with the Chancellor (Zǎixiàng),
diligently working morning and evening.
Together with Lù Shàngshū Táng Yōng, they adjusted and refined policies of acceptance and rejection,
yielding considerable benefit.
The Zhōu court appointed him Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn and Zàishī Dàfū.
Details of his conduct are lacking in the historical records,
therefore they are not included in the biography.
Late in the Qí dynasty, there were also Bīng Shěng Shàngshū Xīn Jì of Lǒngxī, and Sànqí Chángshì Pān Zǐyì of Chánglè, both known for their talent and capability.
Entering service in Zhōu and Suí,
their positions were consistently high and prominent.
Commentary says: Lǐ Zhìlián and others achieved fame and reputation
wherever they served due to their skill, ability, and capacity.
Fēng Shù accumulated wealth
and was damaged by his stinginess and narrow-mindedness.
Jì Liáng was hampered by superficial learning,
and Wénzōng was criticized for his skill in flattery and association.
However, the two worthies Yáng and Lǐ can be considered complete in their virtues.
How can a scholar and a gentleman not be cautious?
Eulogy says: These several worthies,
steadfast and firm in their duties,
were criticized during their lives,
but their names endure on silk and cloth after death.
Fēng, as well as Yuán (Wénzōng) and Xǔ (Jì Liáng),
ultimately brought ruin upon themselves.

Collected Biographies Thirty-Six: The Forest of Scholars (Rú Lín): Lǐ Xuàn, Diāo Róu, Féng Wěi, Zhāng Mǎinú, Liú Guǐsī, Bào Jìxiáng, Xíng Zhì, Liú Zhòu, Mǎ Jìngdé (son Yuánxī), Zhāng Jǐngrén, Quán Huì, Zhāng Sībó, Zhāng Diāosūn, Líng Huī, Shí Yào.
Bān Gù stated that
"the lineage of Confucian scholars
generally originated from the office of Sītú (Minister of Education),
assisting the ruler in harmonizing Yin and Yang,
and carrying out moral education."
The Sage illuminates the Way of Heaven,
and rectifies human relationships (lún).
Thus, the wise kings of antiquity followed this path.
Gāozǔ was born in the northern frontier
and grew up amidst military affairs.
Following the destruction and chaos of the Wèi Shì,
and during the cruel actions of Ěrzhū,
literature was thoroughly swept away,
ritual and music fled together,
the sound of singing and string instruments was nearly extinguished,
and the form of sacrificial vessels was about to vanish.
But when he took up the banner of righteousness,
sweeping clean the regions and districts,
thereby setting the relationship between ruler and minister right,
and equalizing the high and the low;
even when the sovereign fled afar
and the Nine Tripods (symbol of sovereignty) shifted covertly,
and the divine instruments of civil and military power
were settled under his gaze;
he still supported the establishment of the imperial clan
and stabilized the altars of the soil and grain (the state).
Was this not abiding in the realm of the teaching of names
and cultivating the spirit of benevolence and righteousness?
When the borders were troubled by many anxieties,
and war chariots were mobilized annually,
although there was no time for the system of schools (Xiángxù zhī Zhì),
the Way of the Scholarly (Rúyǎ zhī Dào) immediately took shape in their minds.
During the Tiānpíng reign of the Wèi [Dynasty],
Lú Jǐngyù of Fànyáng, along with his cousin Lǐ, started a rebellion in their home commandery.
Gāozǔ pardoned their crime,
placed them in the official guest house,
and utilized them to teach the Classics to the Duke of Tàiyuán and those below him.
When Jǐngyù died,
Lǐ Tóngguǐ of Zhàojùn was appointed to succeed him.
These two worthy men both received great favor and treatment,
being treated with exceptional courtesy (shūlǐ).
When Tóngguǐ passed away,
Zhāng Diāo of Zhōngshān, Lǐ Xuàn of Bóhǎi, Diāo Róu, and Shí Yào of Zhōngshān were subsequently summoned to serve as teachers and friends to the various princes.
In the courts of Tiānbǎo, Dàníng, and Wǔpíng,
famous Confucians were also introduced,
to instruct the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) and the various princes in classical studies (jīngshù).
However, from the very beginning of the foundation,
until the final generation,
only [the prince of] Jìnán, while in the Eastern Palace (Chǔgōng),
was naturally intelligent and perceptive;
he made considerable efforts to polish himself,
thereby achieving excellence.
The rest were mostly arrogant, indulgent, proud, and ruthless;
their actions constantly violated propriety (lǐdù),
and day by day, month by month,
nothing notable was heard of them.
Carving ice and sculpting decay,
they ultimately accomplished nothing.
This surely had a cause.
Indeed, imperial sons and royal grandsons,
were naturally inclined toward extravagance and license.
Moreover, since the sentiment for righteous instruction (Yìfāng zhī Qíng) was not earnest,
and the paths of depravity and evil were competitively opened,
if they did not possess innate wisdom,
or embody supreme intellect,
and internally indulged in the pleasure of music and beauty,
while externally pursuing the hobbies of dogs and horses,
how could they be earnestly diligent when at home,
and befriend the worthy when outside?
They merely had the resources of tutors and preceptors,
but ultimately lacked the reality of polishing and refinement (zhuómó).
When those below follow instruction,
it is like the wind bending the grass.
For this reason, among the families of hereditary nobility (Shìzhòu),
it was rare to hear of dedicated study.
If the class of high-ranking idle gentlemen (Guìyóu zhī Bèi)
were adorned with bright Classics (míng jīng),
they could be called the bamboo arrows of Jīshān,
further enhanced by fitting them with feathers (kuò yǔ).
Picking up the blue and purple [official robes] by merely bending down,
their success is absolutely predictable.
However, when the Qí [Dynasty] was in charge,
they sometimes neglected their duties.
The Masters (Shī), Tutors (Bǎo), Advisers (Yí), and Assistants (Chéng) were all rewarded veterans of merit;
the Academicians (Bóshì) of the National Academy (Guóxué) had only empty names.
Only in the one school of the Sons of the State (Guózǐ)
were there several dozen students.
If one desires officials to be upright and the state to be governed well,
how can that be achieved?
Among the noble descendants (zhòuzǐ) who entered officialdom by mastering the Classics were only Cuī Zifā of Bólíng and Sòng Yóuqīng of Guǎngpíng.
Outside of these, no others were seen.
Fortunately, the court regulations were lenient and simple,
and the net of governance was wide and sparse.
Idle hands and lazy loafers (yóu shǒu fú duò)
made up nine out of ten households.
Therefore, companions who carried the Classics (héng jīng) and received instruction,
were found everywhere in the villages and towns;
the crowds who carried satchels (fù jí) to follow official careers,
did not hesitate to travel a thousand *lǐ*.
They devoted themselves without slackness,
skillfully guiding without fatigue.
Entering the confines of the neighborhoods,
they begged for food to sustain themselves.
In the shade of the mulberry trees and catalpa groves (sāngzǐ),
their numbers often exceeded a thousand.
In the customs of Yān and Zhào,
this multitude was especially large.
The Qí system mandated: all commanderies should establish schools,
and appoint Academicians (Bóshì) and Assistants (Zhùjiào) to teach the Classics.
Students were all assigned through forced quotas to fill the positions,
and the literati class (shìliú) and wealthy families were exempt from this recruitment.
Since filling the quota was not what they desired,
they naturally did not concern themselves with the ancient texts (fénjí).
Moreover, they were often mobilized and employed by the officials of the provinces and commanderies.
Even if there was idleness or laziness,
it was not scrutinized or corrected.
All this was caused by the lack of preference from above.
All commanderies were permitted to recommend Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián) candidates.
Those Academicians, Assistants, and wandering scholars who were versed in the Classics
were selected and nominated for recommendation.
If they shot at the arrows (shè cè) for ten topics,
and passed eight or more,
they were allowed to enter service at the Ninth Rank (Jiǔ Pǐn Chūshēn).
Those who were exceptionally outstanding were also selected and promoted.
Generally, all these students of classical studies
mostly came from under the tutelage of Xú Zūnmíng, the great Confucian scholar of the late Wèi period.
The area north of the Yellow River (Héběi) lectured on the *Zhou Yi* (Changes) annotated by Zhèng Kāngchéng.
Zūnmíng transmitted it to Lú Jǐngyù and Cuī of Qīnghé.
Jǐngyù transmitted it to Quán Huì.
Quán Huì transmitted it to Guō Mào.
Quán Huì entered the capital early,
and Guō Mào taught under his tutelage.
Afterward, many who could speak on the *Yi* (Changes) came from Guō Mào's school.
In the area south of the Yellow River (Hénán) and between Qīng [Province] and Qí [Province],
Confucian scholars mostly lectured on the *Zhou Yi* annotated by Wáng Fǔsì,
but the masters providing instruction were few.
During the Qí period, Confucian scholars
rarely transmitted the study of the *Shàngshū* (Book of Documents).
Xú Zūnmíng was versed in both.
Zūnmíng received instruction from Wáng Zǒng of Túnliú,
and transmitted it to Lǐ Zhōurén of Fúyáng, Zhāng Wénjìng of Bóhǎi, Lǐ Xuàn, and Quán Huì.
They all used the annotation by Zhèng Kāngchéng,
and not the Old Text (Gǔwén).
The students in the lower villages (xiàlǐ)
generally did not see Kǒng's annotations.
At the end of the Wǔpíng reign,
Liú Guāngbó of Héjiān and Liú Shìyuán of Xìndū first obtained Fèi Hán's commentary (Yìshū),
and then paid attention to it.
The *Shī* (Odes), the *Lǐ* (Rites), and the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) were especially valued at that time,
and most students were versed in all of them.
The Three Rites (Sān Lǐ) all originated from Zūnmíng's school.
Xú transmitted the study to Lǐ Xuàn, Jǔ Jùn, Tián Yuánfèng, Féng Wěi, Jǐ Xiǎnjìng, Lǚ Huánglóng, and Xià Huáijìng.
Lǐ Xuàn further transmitted it to Diāo Róu, Zhāng Mǎinú, Bào Jìxiáng, Xíng Zhì, Liú Zhòu, and Xióng Ānshēng.
Ānshēng further transmitted it to Sūn Línghuī, Guō Zhòngjiān, and Dīng Shìdé.
Later students who could master the Rites Classics were mostly Ānshēng's disciples.
All students mastered the *Lǐ* of Xiǎo Dài (Xiao Dai Li),
but only twelve or thirteen percent were also versed in the *Zhōu Lǐ* and *Yí Lǐ*.
Those who mastered the *Máo Shī* (Mao Odes) mostly came from Liú Xiànzhī of Bólíng during the Wèi court.
Xiànzhī transmitted it to Lǐ Zhōurén.
Zhōurén transmitted it to Dǒng Língdù and Chéng Guīzé.
Guīzé transmitted it to Liú Jìnghé, Zhāng Sībó, and Liú Guǐ Sī.
Later, many who could speak on the *Shī* (Odes) came from the schools of the two Liú [scholars].
Among the various Confucian scholars in Héběi who could master the *Chūnqiū*,
they all favored the annotation by Fú Zǐshèn,
who also came from the school of Master Xú.
Zhāng Mǎinú, Mǎ Jìngdé, Xíng Zhì, Zhāng Sībó, Zhāng Diāo, Liú Zhòu, Bào Chángxuān, and Wáng Yuánzé all attained the subtleties of the Fú clan's teachings.
Furthermore, Wèi Jì, Chén Dá, and Pān Shūdù, although not directly transmitting from the Xú family school,
were also known for their comprehensive explanations.
There were also Yáo Wén'ān and Qín Dàojìng, who initially also studied the Fú clan's teachings,
but later also lectured on the annotation by Dù Yuánkǎi.
The Confucian scholars outside the Yellow River (Héwài) all devoted themselves to the Dù clan's teachings.
Regarding the two commentaries, *Gōngyáng* and *Gǔliáng*,
most Confucian scholars did not pay attention to them.
The *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) and the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety),
were thoroughly lectured on by all students.
Various scholars like Quán Huì, Lǐ Xuàn, Diāo Róu, Xióng Ānshēng, Liú Guǐ Sī, and Mǎ Jìngdé mostly compiled their own commentaries (Yìshū).
Although they were said to specialize in certain fields,
they were also generally familiar with the others.
The various students recorded in this preface,
some finished their careers during the Wèi court,
or their reputations and careers were not successful.
Even if they were able to become famous masters,
we lack information regarding their origins and the commanderies/states they hailed from.
We have merely preserved their names.
We have collectively selected those who were especially knowledgeable and prominent to be listed in the Biographies of the Confucians (Rúlín).
Xióng Ānshēng's name is in the History of the Zhōu [Dynasty],
Guāngbó and Shìyuán are recorded in the History of the Suí [Dynasty],
so they will not be redundantly recounted here.
Lǐ Xuàn,
courtesy name Bǎodǐng,
was a native of Nánpí, Bóhǎi.
At the age of nine, he entered school,
writing the *Jí Jiù Piān* (Quickly Completed Chapter).
In slightly over a month, he mastered it.
His family had always been poor and struggling;
he constantly engaged in farming during spring and summer,
and only attended school in winter.
At the age of sixteen,
he received instruction on the *Máo Shī* and the *Shàngshū* from Lǐ Zhōurén of Fúyáng,
on the *Lǐ Jì* (Record of Rites) from Liú Zǐměng of Zhāngwǔ,
on the *Zhōu Guān* (Officials of Zhou) and the *Yí Lǐ* (Book of Rites) from Fáng Qiú of Chángshān,
and on the *Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū* (Zuo Commentary) from Xiānyú Língfù of Yúyáng.
Xuàn felt that there was no one left in his region whom he could take as a teacher,
so he formed a group with Yáng Yuányì from his province, Zōng Huìzhèn of Héjiān, and others, and went to the great Confucian Xú Zūnmíng to receive instruction.
He resided under Master Xú for five years,
and was consistently named a superior student.
At the age of twenty-three,
he retired into seclusion,
discussing right and wrong,

and compiled and established commentaries (Yìshū) on the *Xiàojīng*, *Lúnyǔ*, *Máo Shī*, and the Three Rites, as well as the differences and similarities of the Three Commentaries (Sān Zhuàn), and the principles of the *Zhōu Yì*, totaling over thirty volumes.
He applied his mind with intense diligence;
for three winters, he never kept a pillow.
Whenever he was about to sleep,
he merely slept lightly (jiǎ mèi).
At the age of twenty-seven,
he returned home to support his two parents,
and consequently taught in his home region.
His students numbered several hundred.
Those who could speak on the Classics in the region of Yān and Zhào,
mostly came from his school.
When he was thirty-six,
he experienced his father's mourning period (dīng fù sàng).
After the mourning period concluded (fú què),
because his home village lacked literary records,
he came to the capital (Jīngshī) to travel and study,
reading books he had not yet seen.
The prefecture nominated him as an Outstanding Talent (Xiùcái),
and he was appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì).
During the Wǔdìng reign,
after Lǐ Tóngguǐ died,
Gāozǔ ordered Shìzōng, while in the capital, to skillfully select eminent scholars
to instruct his sons.
Shìzōng, judging Xuàn as suitable for the command,
summoned him to Jìnyáng.
At that time, Shí Yào of Zhōngshān, Yáng Xuàn of Běipíng, Wáng Xī of Běihǎi, Cuī Zhān of Qīnghé, Sòng Qīndào of Guǎngpíng, and the skilled calligrapher Hán Yì were all together in the Eastern Hall,
serving as teachers and friends to the various princes.
Xuàn believed that since the Sages (Shèng) were long departed,
many characters and texts were divergent and erroneous.
Moved by Kǒngzǐ’s (Confucius’s)
saying, “The essential thing
must be the rectification of names (zhèng míng),”
he sighed and developed the intent to revise and correct them.
During the leisure time of his lectures and teaching,
he proceeded to examine the Shuō Wén,
extending to the Cāng and Yǎ texts.
He deleted and corrected erroneous characters found in the commentaries of the Six Arts (Liù Yì) Classics,
naming the work Zì Biàn (Character Distinctions).
When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication (shòu chán),
Xuàn followed the imperial procession back to the capital.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo reign,

an imperial edict commanded Xuàn, along with the President of the Palace Affairs (Diànzhōng Shàngshū) Xíng Shào, Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Líng) Wèi Shōu, and others, to participate in discussions concerning Rites and Laws (lǐ lǜ).
He concurrently held the post of Erudite of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Bóshì).
At that time, an edict commanded Sòng Jǐngyè, Administrator of Běipíng, Qíguàn Huáiwén, Administrator of Xīhé, and others to draft the new calendar.

Gāo Lóngzhī, the Prince of Píngyuán and President of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū), ordered Xuàn, along with the Gentlemen-in-Attendance with Access to the Throne (Tōngzhí Chángshì) Fáng Yányòu and the Erudite of the Directorate of Education Diāo Róu, to examine its merits and defects.
Soon after, he was confirmed as the Erudite of the Directorate of Education.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèidì) was still in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
Xiǎnzǔ commanded Xuàn to enter and instruct him in the Classics,
treating him with great favor and courtesy.
A few years later,
he died of illness.
He was specially presented the posthumous title of Minor Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi Shàoqīng).
When his coffin was returned to his former commandery for burial,
the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) performed the rites of sacrifice and libation,
and also dispatched imperial envoys (wáng rén) to accompany the procession.
Scholars (Rúzhě) considered this an honor.
Yáng Yuányì
and Zōng Huìzhèn also both reached the official position of Erudite of the Directorate of Education.
Diāo Róu,
courtesy name Zǐwēn,
was a native of Bóhǎi.
His father, Zhěng,
was a Chariot and Cavalry General (Chējì Jiāngjūn) of the Wèi dynasty, posthumously presented the title Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Róu was fond of learning in his youth,
mastering the Classics and Histories,
and paying particular attention to Rites and Ceremony.
He had a strong memory,
and concerning both the internal and external relations of clans and lineages,
he was widely familiar with them.
Initially, he served as a Funeral Chanter (wǎn láng) for Shìzōng,
starting his career as Acting Staff Officer (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Ministry of Works (Sīkōng).
He lost his mother,
and his observance of the mourning rites was noted for its filial piety.
During the Yǒng'ān reign,
he was appointed General of Firm Center (Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn) and Commandant of Attendant Cavalry (Fèngchē Dūwèi),
and later granted the titles General Who Guards the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) and Grand Master of the Palace (Zhōngsàn Dàfū).
During the Yuánxiàng reign,
he traveled to Jìnyáng according to standard procedure.
Gāozǔ appointed him Perennial Staff Officer (Chángliú Cānjūn) in the establishment of the Duke of Yǒng'ān,
and also ordered him to instruct his sons.
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo reign,
he was appointed Erudite of the Directorate of Education and Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretary (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
Wèi Shōu compiled the History of Wèi (Wèi Shǐ),
and proposed that Róu and others share the task with him.
Róu’s temperament was rather stubborn and inflexible.
What he considered correct,
Shōu often resented and feared.
He also participated in the discussion of Statutes and Ordinances (lǜ lìng).
The deliberators at the time held that in establishing the five ranks of nobility and their enfeoffments,
if the successor had no principal son (dí zǐ),
the principal grandson (dí sūn) should be established.
If there was no principal grandson,
the principal son's younger brother should be established.
If there was no principal son's younger brother,
the principal grandson's younger brother should be established.
Róu believed that if there was no principal grandson,
the principal great-grandson should be established,
and the principal son’s younger brother should not be established.
The discussion stated: Róu argues, according to the Rites, succession (dì) is established by seniority.
Therefore, the eldest son is called the principal son.
If the principal son dies,
the principal son’s son is the principal grandson.
If he dies, the great-grandson (zēng) and great-great-grandson (xuán) follow the same rule.
In this case, the title of principal son
is fundamentally for transmitting the continuation (chuán zhòng).
Therefore, the Mourning Rites (Sāng Fú) state:
“A concubine’s son does not observe the three-year mourning for the eldest son,
because he does not succeed the grandfather and the deceased father (Nǐ).”
In the Lǐ Jì (Book of Rites),
concerning the mourning of Gōngyí Zhòngzǐ:
The Tán Gōng chapter says, “How could this be?
I have never heard of this before.
Why did Zhòngzǐ set aside his grandson and establish his son?”
Zǐfú Bó
zǐ said, “Zhòngzǐ was merely following the ancient way.
In the past, King Wén (Wénwáng) set aside Bó Yìkǎo and established King Wǔ Fā (Wǔwáng Fā).
Wēizǐ set aside his grandson Dùn and established his younger brother
Yǎn.
Zhòngzǐ was merely following the ancient way.”
Zhèng’s Commentary says:
“Bózǐ spoke guardedly out of respect for the kin;
establishing the son was wrong.
King Wén’s establishment of King
Wǔ
was an expedient measure (quán).
When Wēizǐ’s principal son died,
establishing his younger brother Yǎn
was the custom of Yīn (Yīnlǐ).”
“Zǐ Yóu inquired of Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said, ‘No,
establish the grandson.’”
The Commentary
says:
“This is based on the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ).”
Thus, under the custom of Shāng, if the principal son died,
his full younger brother (born of the same mother) was established.
Under the custom of Zhōu, if the principal son died,
the principal son's son was established as the principal grandson.
Therefore,
according to the interpretation of the Gōngyáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū Gōngyáng zhī Yì),
if the principal son dies having a grandson,
the Plain (zhì) family, valuing kinship (qīn qīn), establishes the younger brother first;
the Refined (wén) family, valuing status (zūn zūn), establishes the grandson first.
The Mourning Rites state:
“One who becomes the successor to the father
wears no mourning for his divorced mother (chū mǔ).”
The Xiǎo Jì (Minor Record) states:
“If the grandfather dies and then one succeeds the grandmother, one observes three years of mourning.”
The reason one wears no mourning for the divorced mother
is that the person in mourning does not perform the sacrifice.
The reason for the three years of mourning for the grandmother
is that the Great Lineage (Dà Zōng) transmits the continuation.
Now the proposal is that if the principal grandson dies, the full younger brother of the principal son should be established.
This full younger brother of the principal son would then be
the successor to the father.
The principal son’s full younger brother is fundamentally not the principal successor (chéng dí).
Because there is no principal successor,
he is permitted to succeed the father.
Then, according to reason, the principal grandson's younger brother
should also be permitted to succeed the father.
If this is the case, one who succeeds the grandfather after the father has died observes the most severe mourning (fú zhǎn).
Since he is already allowed to wear the severe mourning for the grandfather,
but not permitted to transmit the continuation,
this has not been heard of.
If we use the Shāng custom,
which values kinship,
then fundamentally, when the principal son dies, the principal grandson should not be established.
If we follow the Zhōu texts, which value status,
how can one properly set aside the grandson and establish the younger brother?
Whether
refined or plain,
I (yú) am confused by this usage.
The Xiǎo Jì further states:
“If the principal wife does not succeed her father-in-law, then the paternal aunt observes minor mourning (xiǎo gōng) for her.”
The commentary states:
“This means that if the husband is disabled by illness,
or for other reasons, or dies without a son and thus cannot assume the continuation (bù shòu zhòng).
Minor mourning
is the attire of a concubine’s wife.
In all cases where parents toward their son,
and parents-in-law toward their daughter-in-law,
are not going to transmit the continuation through the principal line,
or
where the person designated to transmit the continuation is not from the principal line,
the mourning worn for them is like that for an ordinary son or a concubine’s wife.”
The phrase "dies without a son"
refers to the extinction of the line without any male issue,
not merely the lack of a principal son.
If
he has a son,
how can it be said that there is no successor?
Although the husband may be disabled and childless,
the wife still holds the name of the principal spouse (dí).
Since the name of principal spouse exists,
whoever wishes to set aside her son,
what will become of the Rites
regarding this?
Rites suffer losses and gains
and change generation by generation.
If it is insisted that the principal lineage (zōng dí) may be altered,
then the severe mourning worn for a successor
should also be modified accordingly.
He died in the summer of the seventh year (of Tiānbǎo),
aged fifty-six.
Róu was not long in the History Office (Shǐ Guǎn),
but during the period when the compilation was nearing completion (lè chéng zhī jì),
he held biased opinions favoring his own faction.
In the History of Wèi, those related to him, both internally and externally, were praised excessively and beyond reality,
which brought him strong criticism from contemporary opinion.
Féng Wěi,
courtesy name Wěijié,
was a man from Ānxǐ in Zhōngshān.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
and his clothes and cap were very impressive;
those who saw him were immediately respectful and in awe.
When young, he studied under Lǐ Bǎodǐng.
Lǐ valued his intelligence and quickness,
and specifically intended to test him with questions.
He was able to understand and explain many things,
especially excelling in the Rites and Commentaries.
Later, he returned to his hometown
and remained behind closed doors for almost thirty years,
not concerning himself with production,
nor socializing with guests.
He concentrated his efforts and delved deeply into thought,
understanding everything.
When the Prince of Zhàojùn was stationed in Dìngzhōu,
he received him with rites,
sending three written summonses.
The county magistrate personally went to his door,
but he still declined, citing illness, and would not rise.
The Prince intended to order his carriage to personally invite him,
so the aides and clerks rushed back and forth to inform him.
The magistrate even personally straightened his cap and shoes for him,
and only then did he reluctantly emerge.
The Prince descended from the main hall to greet him,
stopped him from bowing and prostrating,
and they ascended the steps side by side.
He was accommodated in the guest house
and treated with great ceremony and respect.
The Prince intended to recommend him as an Outstanding Talent (*Xiùcaí*),
but he firmly refused the appointment.
After more than a year, he requested to return home.
The Prince knew that he did not wish to be constrained,
and so dispatched him with due rites,
giving him very generous gifts.
He accepted none of them,
only receiving seasonal clothing.
After he returned,
he ultimately avoided all social interaction.
The commandery administrator and county magistrate often personally came to his door.
During the seasons or festivals, they sometimes offered sheep and wine,
but he also refused to accept them.
He would not accept even a thread
of the tuition fees (*shù xiū*) from his students.
He ate by farming,
and clothed himself by silkworm rearing.
Eating from a basket and drinking from a gourd (*dān shí piáo yǐn*),
he never changed his joy,
and ultimately died of old age.
Zhāng Mǎinú
was a man from Píngyuán.
His knowledge of the Classics was extensive and profound,
and he had over a thousand students.
All the scholars highly esteemed him,
and his reputation was very great.
He successively held the posts of Grand Academy Erudite (*Tàixué Bóshì*) and Director of Studies Assistant (*Guózǐ Zhùjiào*).
He died during the Tiānbǎo period.
Liú Guǐsī
was a man from Bóhǎi.
He explained the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry) very precisely.
In his youth, he served Liú Jìnghé from the same commandery.
Jìnghé served Chéng Guīzé, also from the same commandery.
Therefore, many people in his hometown district studied the *Shī*.
Guǐsī
was appointed Grand Academy Erudite during the Tiāntǒng period.
Bāo Jìxiáng
was a man from Bóhǎi.
He was very clear on the Rites.
When listening to him separate the phrases and analyze the sentences,
the general meaning would naturally become clear.
He also thoroughly understood the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū*.
When young, he was the chief lecturer (*dū jiǎng*) for Lǐ Bǎodǐng.
Later, he also had his own body of students,
and was praised by the various scholars.
During the Tiāntǒng period,
he died while holding the post of Grand Academy Erudite.
His cousin, Chángxuān,
was proficient in both the Rites and the Commentaries.
Towards the end of the Wǔpíng period,
he served as an Aide to the Chancellor of the Prince of Rènchéng, Qiè.
He taught the sons of the noble families in the capital.
After the fall of Qí,
he returned to his hometown to lecture on the Classics,
and died at home.
Xíng Zhì,
courtesy name Shìjùn,
was a man from Mò in Héjiān.
When young, he loved learning,
and immersed himself deeply in the literary classics (*fén diǎn*).
He traveled and studied between Yān and Zhào,
and was proficient in the Three Rites and the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū*.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo period,
he was recommended by the commandery as Filial and Incorrupt (*Xiàolián*),
and was appointed Erudite of the Four Gates (*Sìmén Bóshì*).
He was promoted to Director of Studies Assistant,
and taught the Classics to the Crown Prince.
Zhì was upright, proper, pure, and sincere,
possessing the demeanor of a Ruist scholar.
When the steward presented food to the Crown Prince,
there was a vegetable called
“xiéhāo” (Crooked Mugwort).
Zhì ordered it removed,
saying:
“This vegetable has an improper name,
and is not suitable for Your Highness to eat.”
Xiǎnzǔ heard this and praised him,
bestowing upon him bedding and fine floss silk,
and appointing him Grand Academy Erudite.
In the beginning of the Huángjiàn period,
he was appointed Administrator of Qīnghé.
He had benevolent governance,
and the people and officials loved him.
Citing old age and illness, he requested retirement and returned home,
and died at home.
Liú Zhòu,
courtesy name Kǒngzhāo,
was a man from Fùchéng in Bóhǎi.
He was orphaned and poor when young,
but loved learning.
He carried his satchel to follow teachers,
dedicating himself to study tirelessly.
He was from the same hometown as the scholar Lǐ Bǎodǐng,
and they were very close and affectionate.
He received the Three Rites from him.
He also went to Mǎ Jìngdé to study the *Fúshì Chūnqiū*.
He understood the main principles of both.
Lamenting that his remote village lacked many ancient books,
he traveled with his staff to the capital.
Knowing that the family of Sòng Shìliáng, Assistant Minister of the Imperial Treasury (*Tàifǔ Shàoqīng*), had many books,
he went to his house.
Shìliáng received him.
He read indiscriminately,
day and night without rest.
In the early years of Héqīng,
he returned to Jìzhōu,
was recommended as an Outstanding Talent and went to the capital.
He failed the examination.
He then regretted not having studied prose composition,
and began to compile and construct rhetoric;
his language was very ancient and clumsy.
He composed one *fù* (rhapsody)
named
“Liùhé” (The Six Directions).
He considered it unparalleled,
and recited it constantly.
He then sighed, saying:
“Scholars toil but achieve little skill;
this is evident here.
I read Ruist books for more than twenty years and failed the policy examination.
I only began learning composition
and immediately achieved this level.”
He once presented this *fù* to Wèi Shōu.
Shōu said to others:
“Naming the *fù* ‘Liùhé’—
his foolishness is already extreme.
But upon seeing the *fù*,
it is even more foolish than its name.”
Zhòu also compiled three chapters of the *Gāocái Bù Yù Zhuàn* (Biographies of Highly Talented People Who Met With No Opportunity).
During the reigns of Huángjiàn and Dàníng,
he repeatedly submitted memorials.
His words were also critical and straightforward,
but mostly did not address the immediate needs of the world,
and were ultimately not adopted.
He considered himself extraordinarily knowledgeable and talented,
and enjoyed boasting greatly.
He often said:
“If my several dozen scrolls of books circulate in later generations,
I would not trade them for Duke Jǐng of Qí’s thousand four-horse carriages.”
However, his manner and bearing were slow and relaxed,
and his conduct was unconventional.
Because of this, he ultimately never advanced in office.
During the Tiāntǒng period,
he died at home,
at the age of fifty-two.
Mǎ Jìngdé
was a native of Héjiān.
When young, he loved Confucian studies.
Carrying his satchel, he followed the great scholar Xú Zūnmíng to study the Shī (Odes) and Lǐ (Rites).
He broadly understood the general principles but could not master them thoroughly.
Consequently, he paid attention to the Chūnqiū Zuǒ Shì (Spring and Autumn Annals with Zuǒ's Commentary),
pondering deeply and studying diligently.
He was tireless day and night,
and his interpretations were praised by all the scholars.
He taught between Yān and Zhào.
The students who followed him were numerous.
The Prince of Héjiān Commandery often sought him out in his place of teaching,
intending to nominate him as a Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt candidate),
but he firmly declined the offer.
Instead, he went to the prefecture to seek nomination as a Xiùcái (Flourishing Talent).
The standard procedure for nominating a Xiùcái was to select literati (writers).
The prefectural governor, considering him a pure Confucian scholar,
had no intention of recommending him.
Jìngdé requested a test of his strategy and policy.
The governor then questioned him regarding policy.
The five points he answered
all showed scholarly coherence and logic.
Consequently, the governor joyfully nominated and sent him to the capital.
Based on the Xiùcái policy questions,
he only ranked in the middle tier.
He then requested a test of his classical learning.
He was questioned on ten points, and he passed them all.
He was promoted and appointed as Assistant Instructor (Zhùjiào) in the Directorate of National Academy (Guózǐ).
He was later transferred to be Erudite (Bóshì) of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué).
At the beginning of the Tiāntǒng era,
he was appointed Erudite (Bóshì) of the Directorate of National Academy (Guózǐ).
When Shìzǔ (Emperor Wǔchéng) selected tutors for the Future Emperor (Hòuzhǔ),
Zhào Yànshēn recommended him,
and he entered service as an Imperial Lecturer (Shìjiǎng).
His wife dreamed that a fierce beast was approaching her.
Jìngdé ran, leaping over thickets of thorns,
while his wife lay prone on the ground, daring not to move.
Jìngdé interpreted this, saying:
"I will obtain a high official position.
Leaping over the thorns
signifies surpassing the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng).
You lying prone on the ground
means you will be a noble lady (Fūrén)."
Since the Future Emperor (Hòuzhǔ) was not fond of learning,
Jìngdé's lectures were sparsely scheduled.
He would occasionally enter to teach the Chūnqiū.
At the beginning of the Wǔpíng era,
still owing to the favor granted to tutors,
he was immediately promoted to Libationer (Jìjiǔ) of the Directorate of National Academy (Guózǐ),
with the added titles of Auxiliary Commissioner (Yídóng Sānsī) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
concurrently serving as the Great Controller (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Yíngzhōu.
He died shortly after.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Opener of the Palace (Kāifǔ), Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Yíng, Cāng, and Ān Prefectures, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yíngzhōu.
Later, the Imperial Amanuensis (Shìshū), Zhāng Jǐngrén, was enfeoffed as a prince (wáng).
Zhào Yànshēn remarked:
"How can the Imperial Amanuensis be enfeoffed as a prince,
while the Imperial Lecturer (Shìjiǎng) receives no noble title?"
Therefore, Jìngdé was also enfeoffed as Prince of Guǎnghàn Commandery.
His son, Yuánxī, inherited the title.
Yuánxī, courtesy name Chángmíng,
inherited his father's scholarly profession when young,
and was also skilled in literature.
Because of his father's position,
he was rapidly promoted from Secretary (Cānjūn) of the Collected Records Office in Qīngzhōu to Gentleman-Consultant (Tōngzhí Shìláng),
served as an Expectant Appointee (Dàizhào) in the Hall of Literary Studies (Wénlín Guǎn),
and was transferred to a regular post (Zhèng Yuán).
During the Wǔpíng era,
the Crown Prince was about to study the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety).
The relevant officials requested that teachers and companions be selected.
The Emperor said:
"Mǎ Yuánxī is the son of Our tutor.
His literary ability is not bad;
he may be ordered to instruct the boy."
Thereupon, he entered to instruct the Crown Prince in the Xiàojīng.
Confucian scholars honored his inheritance of the family reputation.
His nature was gentle and honest.
He gained considerable renown within the court,
and the Crown Prince also treated him with intimacy and respect.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Súi Dynasty,
he died while serving as Literary Aide (Wénxué) to the Prince of Qín.
Zhāng Jǐngrén
was a native of Jǐběi.
Orphaned young and poor,
he made a living by studying calligraphy.
He became skilled in the cǎo (cursive) and lì (clerical) scripts,
and was selected to fill a post as an Inner Scribe (Nèi Shūshēng).
He was equally famous as Yáo Yuánbiāo of Wèijùn, Hán Yì of Yǐngchuān, Yuán Mǎinú (of the same commandery), and Lǐ Chāo of Xíngyáng.
Shìzōng (Emperor Xiàozhāo) invited them all to be his retainers.
In the eighth year of Tiānbǎo,
he was ordered to teach calligraphy to Shào Dé, Prince of Tàiyuán,
and was appointed Secretary (Cānjūn) to the Opener of the Palace (Kāifǔ).
When the Future Emperor (Hòuzhǔ) was in the Eastern Palace (as Crown Prince),
Shìzǔ selected those skilled in calligraphy and of pure and careful character to serve as Imperial Amanuenses (Shìshū).
Jǐngrén was consequently brought in and promoted.
He was cautious, respectful, and prudent.
The Future Emperor loved him
and called him Bóshì (Erudite/Scholar).

He successively held the posts of Grand Master of the Crown Prince's Household (Tàizǐ Mén Dàfū), Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì), and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Jiànyì Dàfū).
When the Future Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Gentleman-Consultant Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
When the appointment was presented for approval,
the Emperor used his imperial brush to cross out
the character
"Tōng,"
so he became a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Chángshì).
Those around the Emperor, when speaking with him,
still referred to him as Bóshì.
The Hu barbarian Hé Hóngzhēn enjoyed favor with the Future Emperor.
Wishing to intermarry with court officials,
and seeing that Jǐngrén held a relatively high position among the inner officials,
he arranged for his elder brother's son to marry the daughter of Jǐngrén's second son, Zǐyú.
Because of this connection,
his favor and treatment grew daily.
Jǐngrén was often ill.
The Emperor frequently sent Xú Zhīfàn and others to treat him,
supplied him with medicines and rare delicacies.
Palace envoys sent to inquire about his illness
were constantly seen on the road.
After this,
an imperial edict commanded the relevant officials to deliver imperial meals to his residence.
He was promoted to Provisional Auxiliary Commissioner (Jiǎ Yídóng Sānsī) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū),
and granted the income of Shān County.
When the Imperial Carriage occasionally went on an excursion,
and stayed overnight on the road,
folding screens were always sent to him to block the wind and cold.
He was advanced in rank to Auxiliary Commissioner (Yídóng Sānsī).
Soon after, he was granted the title Opener of the Palace (Kāifǔ).
His position as Imperial Amanuensis (Shìshū) and other offices remained as before.
Whenever he needed to attend court in the morning,
he would stop and stay at the Eastern Palace.
When the Hall of Literary Studies (Wénlín Guǎn) was established,
the eunuch Dèng Chángyóng, anticipating the Emperor's wishes,
submitted a memorial requesting that Jǐngrén be put in charge of all matters of the Hall.
He was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the fourth year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiàn'ān.
After Hóngzhēn died,
Chángyóng still maintained their former friendship
and mutually covered up for each other,
preventing his fall from grace.
He was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and died of illness.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Governor (Cìshǐ) of the five prefectures including Qí and Jǐ, and Duke of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōng).
Jǐngrén originated from humble circumstances
and originally lacked insight or discernment,
yet suddenly became Opener of the Palace (Kāifǔ), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), and an enfeoffed Prince.
His wife's surname was Qí;
her family origin was unknown.
Her demeanor, bearing, voice, and speech
were vulgar and coarse in every respect.
Since she was appointed Princess Consort (Wáng Fēi) by imperial edict,
she was included in the ranks of those required to attend court audiences along with the various Imperial Princesses and Commandery Mistresses (Jùnjūn).
Those who saw her felt shame and awe.
His son, Zǐyú,
only vaguely followed his father's profession
and had no other skills.
Because of Hóngzhēn,
he was promoted and appointed Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
and later transferred to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
His eldest son, Zǐyù,
started his career as a Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng).
Jǐngrén's nature was originally humble and modest.
But when he relied on the influence of the Hu barbarian and the palace attendants (eunuchs),
thereby attaining high rank and prominence,
his ambitions and principles changed considerably,
and he gradually became arrogant.
Fine horses and light furs,
his retinue was numerous and extravagant.
High gates and spacious mansions
faced the main thoroughfare and street.
His sons did not reflect upon their origins
and regarded themselves as noble elite.
Since the time of Cāng Jié,
he was the only person
to attain promotion through the eight styles of calligraphy.
courtesy name Zhènglǐ,
was a native of Mò, Héjiān.
His aspirations were profound and refined,
and his actions always followed the rules of ritual.
When young, he received the *Yì* (Changes) according to the Zhèng school,
exploring the difficult and searching for the hidden,
profoundly grasping the subtle and the faint.
The *Shī* (Odes), *Shū* (Documents), and the Sān Lǐ (Three Rites)
were thoroughly comprehended in their meaning and phrasing.
He also clearly understood fēngjiǎo (wind angles/divination),
and expertly recognized xuánxiàng (celestial phenomena).
Early in the Wǔdìng reign of Wèi,
his home commandery recommended him as xiàolián,
and he ranked in the highest grade in the examination.
He was relieved of common duties and appointed Sìmén Bóshì (Erudite of the Four Gates).
The Púyè Cuī Xiān engaged him as a retainer,
holding him in great respect,
and ordered his heir Dánuó to treat him with the full etiquette due a teacher and tutor.
Huì thus became widely known.
Xiān wanted to recommend Huì, along with Mǎ Jìngdé and others, to be teachers for the various princes.
Huì's nature was tranquil and calm;
he did not admire glory or influence,
and was ashamed of serving as a tutor to the nobility (zuǒhuàn).
He firmly declined.
Xiān also understood his intention,
and subsequently stopped the recommendation.
Soon after, he received a warrant from the Shàngshū (Department of State Affairs) to be summoned as Zhùzuò (Compiler),
to compile the national history,
and to supervise the affairs of the Tàishǐ Jú (Bureau of the Grand Astrologer).
During the Huángjiàn reign,
he was promoted and given the added title of Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
while the rest of his appointments remained as before.
Although Huì's responsibilities were numerous,
his teaching duties were never neglected.
His nature was extremely scholarly and gentle,
seeming almost unable to speak,
but when facing an opportunity to respond to difficulty,
his replies were like an echo.
Every action necessarily relied on historical precedent,
and his words were never spoken in vain.
Because of this, he was highly regarded by the leaders of Confucianism (Rúzōng).
As for the sons of high-ranking officials and nobles who admired his virtue and righteousness,
some would come to his residence,
others would stay overnight at neighboring houses,
utilizing every spare moment day and night
to receive his instruction.
Huì happily explained the doctrines,
never becoming remiss.
Although he understood fēngjiǎo
and mastered xuánxiàng,
when it came to his private quarters,
he never spoke of them.
If students asked him about them,
he would ultimately say nothing.
He always said:
"This knowledge can be known but not spoken.
Gentlemen, you are all sons of the nobility,
and you will not advance through this path.
Why trouble yourselves by asking about it?"
Huì only had one son,
but he did not teach him these arts either.
Such was his caution and secrecy.
Once, he sent a family member on a distant journey,
who was long delayed in returning.
When the traveler returned,
and was about to reach the residence,
he encountered a cold snowfall
and stayed for rest at another house.
Huì was then in the lecture hall giving an explanation,
when suddenly a whirlwind abruptly occurred,
blowing snow into the door.
Huì then smiled and said:
"The traveler has arrived,
why did he stop midway?"
He immediately ordered an attendant to go to a certain place and search for him,
and it was indeed as he had said.
Whenever he performed divination for people,
his predictions, whether major or minor, were always accurate.
However, he only used the yáocí (line texts) and tuànxiàng (judgment symbols) to distinguish fortune and misfortune;
methods related to Yì divination
were never mentioned aloud.
Huì was originally born poor
and had no servants.
When he first took up the post of Zhùjiào (Assistant Instructor),
he rode a donkey up and down (to work).
Moreover, the locations of his duties were numerous,
and he constantly had to travel among them.
When he finished his meal and duties,
he did not return until late.
Once, he left the East Gate of the city at night;
the sounds of the bell and clepsydra had already ceased.
Huì was riding his donkey completely alone.
Suddenly, there were two figures:
one leading the donkey by the head,
one following behind.
They seemed to be assisting him,
but their movements were quick and ethereal,
unlike living people.
Gradually, they lost the road
and did not follow the original path.
Huì felt extremely strange about this in his heart,
so he recited the first section of the *Yì Jīng*.
Before one chapter was finished,
the two figures, one in front and one behind,
suddenly dispersed.
Huì did not even realize he had fallen off the donkey;
he became confused and dazed,
only regaining consciousness the next morning.
He then realized that the place where he had fallen off the donkey
was outside the outer wall (guōwài),
only a few *lǐ* away from home.
He had a son,
courtesy name Zǐxí,
who was intelligent, quick-witted, and diligent,
possessing the capacity of an adult from a young age.
Unfortunately, he died first.
Those attending the funeral were deeply grieved for him,
but Huì only wept once and stopped.
People at the time admired his acceptance of fate (dámìng).
In the Wǔpíng era,
while returning home from his office,
the horse he was riding unexpectedly collapsed on the road.
Consequently, he became unable to speak,
and violently died shortly thereafter,
at the age of seventy-six.
He composed one volume of commentary on the *Yì*,
which circulated in the world.
Throughout his life, Huì feared horses.
Due to the height of his position and reputation,
he was forced to ride them,
and indeed he ended his life this way.
Zhāng Sībó
was a native of Lèchéng, Héjiān.
He was skilled at explaining the *Zuǒshì Zhuàn* (Zuo Tradition),
ranking second only to Mǎ Jìngdé.
He compiled *Kānlì* (Examples of Editing and Publication) in ten volumes,
which circulated widely at the time.
He also studied the chapter and verse commentary of the Máoshī (Mao Odes),
and taught these two Classics to Qí'ān Wáng Kuò.
Early in the Wǔpíng era,
he became Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the Directorate of Education).
Zhāng Diāo
was a native of Běipíng, Zhōngshān.
His family background was poor and humble,
but he was resolute and possessed integrity,
and deeply loved ancient learning.
His energy and spirit surpassed others;
carrying his book-basket, he followed teachers,
traveling thousands of *lǐ* without finding it distant.
He thoroughly mastered the Five Classics,
and especially understood the Sān Zhuàn (Three Commentaries/Traditions).
The students who came from distant regions to study with him numbered in the hundreds,
and all scholars admired his forceful rhetoric.
Late in the Wèi dynasty,
he was summoned to the Bàfǔ (Hegemon's Residence) due to his expertise in the Classics.
Gāozǔ ordered him to lecture and read with his sons.
He began his career as Tiǎnkòu Jiāngjūn (General Who Eliminates Bandits),
and gradually transferred to Tàiwèi Zhǎngliú Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Grand Commandant) and Zhǔbù (Clerk) of Dìngzhōu.
He followed Shìzōng when he went to Bīngzhōu,
and was appointed Chángshān Fǔ Zhǎngliú Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Chángshān Residence).
During the Tiānbǎo reign,
he became Cānjūnshì (Staff Officer) in the residence of Yǒng'ān Wáng.
When Xiǎnzǔ died in Jìnyáng,
Zhāng Diāo was promoted and concurrently held the title of Cíbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Bureau of Sacrifices).
He managed the funeral affairs
and accompanied the coffin back to Yè.
Early in the Qiánmíng reign,
he was appointed Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was transferred to Píngyuán Tàishǒu (Administrator of Píngyuán),
but lost his official position due to corruption and bribery.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
based on past favors, he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (Gentleman-in-Attendance, Regular Mounted Escort).
Lángyé Wáng Yǎn sought an Erudite who specialized in Confucian learning.
The relevant authorities selected Diāo as the appropriate candidate,
and people at the time hailed him as the right man for the job.
Shortly after, he became Cìshǐ (Governor) of Jīngzhōu.
Not long afterward,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (Regular Mounted Attendant)
and lectured for Yǎn again.
It happened that the Emperor's Lecturer-in-Waiting, Mǎ Jìngdé, died,
so Diāo entered to teach the Classics.
The Emperor greatly valued him
and appointed him Shìdú (Attendant Reader).
He and Zhāng Jǐngrén were both treated with great respect,
entering the Huáguāng Diàn (Hall of Magnificent Light) together
to jointly read the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
He was granted the additional title of Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the Directorate of Education),
invested temporarily with Yítóng Sānsī (Ceremonial Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers),
and awaited imperial orders at the Wénlín Guǎn (Hall of the Forest of Literature).
*Hú* man Hé Hóngzhēn was greatly favored by the Sovereign,
and formed a marriage alliance with Zhāng Jǐngrén.
Diāo, because Jǐngrén belonged to the imperial clan,
attached himself to Hóngzhēn,
treating him with utmost respect,
and their affection and closeness grew daily.
In matters public and private,
Diāo always served as his guide.
At that time, Mù Típó and Hán Chángluán attended the imperial chambers alongside Hóngzhēn,
and knowing that Diāo was Hóngzhēn’s chief strategist,
they greatly resented and disliked him.
Hóngzhēn also memorialized that Diāo should supervise the National History (jiān guó shǐ).
Soon after, he was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
granted the title Kāifǔ,
and tasked with handling financial matters (dù zhī shì).
He was heavily relied upon
and his advice was frequently followed.
By special imperial decree, he was allowed to present memorials without having to hurry,
and was referred to as ‘Bóshì’ (Scholar).
Diāo, realizing he had risen from humble beginnings
to the position of a great minister,
applied himself diligently to public service,
possessing the virtue of selfless devotion.
Wishing to establish merit and efficacy
to repay the imperial grace,
he spoke openly in debate,
avoiding nothing.
Regarding non-essential expenses in the palace,
he greatly reduced them.
The dissolute hangers-on around the Emperor
were certainly restricted and disciplined.
He frequently criticized and attacked favored officials
and offered proposals for improvement within the court.
The Emperor also deeply relied on him,
and was preparing to entrust him with the affairs of government.
Diāo immediately took cleaning up the administration as his personal responsibility;
his spirit was extremely high.
He once said to Zhèng Zǐxìn in the court hall:
"When I entered the department just now,
I saw your worthy relative Táng Lìng issuing orders that were utterly pointless.
If it is a matter of preparing military accounts,
Diāo is not as good as Yōng.
But if it is a matter of assisting the ruler to achieve the level of Yáo or Shùn,
and placing myself in the position of Jì or Qiè,
then Yōng is not as good as me."
His arrogance and pretension were like this.
Chángluán and others feared that his interference in government would never cease,
and secretly plotted against him.
It so happened that Diāo and Palace Attendant Cuī Jìshū remonstrated with the Emperor against visiting Jìnyáng.
Chángluán used this opportunity to slander them,
and thus they were all executed.
As he faced execution,
the Emperor ordered Duàn Xiàoyán to question him.
Diāo replied, giving his statement:
"I, your subject, rose from the ranks of scholars;
I was mistakenly selected and promoted.
Having served several generations,
I have always received grace and favor.
My rank reached Kāifǔ and Shìzhōng,
and my honors and favors were abundant.
I constantly reflected upon the insignificant nature of my service
compared to the vastness of the mountains and seas (imperial favor).
Regarding the remonstrance made now,
I was truly the chief plotter.
Though my intention was good, my result was harmful,
and I cannot escape death.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty cherishes life and health,
and opens up your divine wisdom.
Frequently invite men like Jiǎ Yì
to discuss the methods of governance,
so that when you listen and observe,
nothing is concealed or blocked.
If this is achieved, then even on the day I die,
it will be as good as the years I lived."
He sobbed and shed tears,
bowing his head and submitting to execution.
None of the attendants and guards nearby failed to pity him and admire his bravery.
He was fifty-five years old at the time.
His son Déchōng and others were exiled to the northern frontier.
During the revolt of Nán'ān,
Déchōng and his younger brother Déjiē were both killed.
Déchōng was gentle, cautious, humble, and yielding.
He was skilled in human relations,
intelligent, quick-witted, and fond of learning,
having considerable knowledge of literature and history.
As the son of the Emperor's tutor,
he was early recognized and promoted.
He successively held the posts of Yúanwài Sǎnqí Shìláng and Clerk (yuàn) in the Grand Preceptor's (Tàishī) establishment.
He entered the court as Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
and waited for appointments according to regulations.
When his father was executed,
Déchōng was performing his duties in the palace courtyard,
and witnessed the injustice and cruelty with his own eyes.
He cried out, wept bitterly, and collapsed unconscious onto the ground.
After a long time, he revived.
Sūn Línghuī
was a man from Wǔqiáng, Chánglè.
Huìwèi, the great Confucian scholar of Wèi and Supervisor of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān),
was Línghuī’s paternal great-great-grandfather of the same lineage.
Línghuī was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and possessed great capacity.
One son of Huìwèi died young,
and many of his family's books remained there.
When Línghuī was seven years old,
he was already fond of learning.
He recited several thousand characters daily,
only studying the commentaries and memorials recorded by Huìwèi’s own hand,
and did not seek out teachers or friends.
He fully grasped the main principles of the Three Rites (Sān Lǐ) and the Three Commentaries (Sān Zhuàn).
However, when he questioned Bào Jìxiáng and Xióng Ānshēng regarding difficult points,
the explanations he offered
were no different from those of Xióng and Bào.
He was nominated as Xìucái by the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu.
He passed the imperial examination with high honors,
and was appointed Yúanwài Jiāngjūn.
Later, because of his deep understanding of Confucian scholarship,
he was promoted and appointed Scholar of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì).
He was transferred to Zhìzhōng of Běixúzhōu,
and then moved to be Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Tóng Jùn.
During the Tiāntǒng era,
an imperial decree ordered court officials to recommend someone suitable to be the tutor (shī) of the Prince of Nányáng, Chuò.
Wèi Jǐn, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), memorialized recommending him.
He was summoned to serve as Scholar of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Bóshì),
and taught the classics to the Prince of Nányáng.
Although the Prince (wáng) was not fond of literature,
he greatly respected Línghuī.
The Prince requested that Línghuī be appointed Consultant and Aide (Zīyì Cānjūn) in his establishment.
When Chuò was appointed Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dìngzhōu,
Línghuī followed him to the garrison.
Chuò's behavior was often reckless,
but Línghuī only worried silently and looked haggard;
he was unable to stop him with remonstrance.
Chuò wished to appoint his Secretary (guǎnjì), Mǎ Zǐjié, as Zīyì Cānjūn.
So, he memorialized requesting that Línghuī be transferred to the post of Royal Tutor (Wángshī),
and Zǐjié be made Zīyì.
The court held that Wángshī was a third-rank position,
and that the request was inappropriate.
The Last Emperor (Hòuzhǔ) wrote a reply below the memorial,
stating:
"Just appoint him,"
and then personally wrote a letter back to Nányáng,
approving everything as requested in the memorial.
Confucian scholars regarded this as a great honor.
When Chuò was appointed Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
Línghuī, as Royal Tutor, concurrently held the position of Grand General's Commandant (Dà Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ).
When Chuò was executed,
Línghuī was dismissed from office.
After Chuò died,
every seventh day and upon the completion of the hundredth day (of mourning),
Línghuī would invite monks to hold vegetarian feasts for Chuò,
chanting scriptures and performing rites.
He died a few years after the fall of Qí.
His son, Wànshòu,
was bright, perceptive, and astute,
widely reading various books.
He understood the core principles of both the Rites (Lǐ) and the Commentaries (Zhuàn),
possessed literary talent,
and was especially proficient in poetry.
At the end of Qí,
Yáng Xiūzhī appointed him as Acting Aide (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Kāifǔ establishment.
During the Suí Dynasty, he held the titles of Fèng Cháoqǐng, Literary Scholar to the Prince of Téng (Téng Wáng Wénxué), and Chief Administrator of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Zhǎngshǐ).
He died while serving as Director in the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sīzhí).
Mǎ Zǐjié
was originally from Fúfēng.
His family resided in the Liáng region for generations,
and entered Luò during the Tàihé period.
Both his father and grandfather held minor government posts.
Zǐjié had two brothers, making three of them,
all of whom were involved in literature.
When Yáng Xiūzhī governed Xīyǎn,
Zǐlián, Zǐshàng, and Zǐjié, along with other court scholars, each presented him with poems.
Yáng composed a single piece in response,
which included the line:
"The three Mǎ brothers all possess white eyebrows"
(referring to literary talent).
Zǐjié, who was Acting Aide (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Kāifǔ establishment, was promoted to Secretary (Guǎnjì) to the Prince of Nányáng.
He followed Chuò to Dìngzhōu.
Whenever Chuò went out hunting,
he would surely order Zǐjié to chase the prey on horseback.
Since Zǐjié was scholarly and slow-moving,
his clothes hung loose and his hat fell off.
Sometimes he cried out, sometimes he wept.
Chuò ordered his riders to drive Zǐjié along.
They would not stop until he fell off his horse,
and Chuò found this greatly amusing.
Because of this, Zǐjié gradually became closer to and more familiar with Chuò,
and thus he was requested to be appointed Zīyì.
Shí Yào,
whose courtesy name was Bái Yào,
was a native of Ānxǐ, Zhōngshān.
He also advanced through Confucian scholarship.
His tenure in office was exceedingly honest and frugal.
During the Wǔpíng reign, he served as the Administrator of Líyáng Commandery.
At that time, Hú Lǜ Wǔdū was appointed as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Wǔdū was the heir apparent of the Chancellor, the Prince of Xiányáng,
and the elder brother of the Empress.
His nature was extremely greedy and tyrannical.
He first passed through Wèi County
and ordered the County Magistrate and his subordinates to gather several thousand bolts of silk to present to him.
When he arrived at Líyáng,
he instructed his attendants to subtly influence Yào and the officials of the counties under the commandery’s jurisdiction.
Yào held one bolt of plain silk in his hand and said to Wǔdū:
“This is the produce of old Shí’s loom,
which I offer as a small token.
Anything beyond this must necessarily be sourced from the officials and the common people,
and regarding the property of the officials and the common people,
I dare not violate even a single strand.”
Wǔdū, knowing that Yào was honest, simple, and a pure Confucian scholar,
laughed and did not reprimand him.
He wrote the Shízǐ in ten chapters,
but the content was very shallow and commonplace.
He later died while serving as the Inspector of Qiáozhōu.
Records of his other actions are missing from the histories.
The Praise says: Since the Great Way was obscured,
the Doctrine of Names and Standards has been followed.
By means of this, the state is established;
by means of this, one establishes oneself.
The imperial plan combined with the hegemons,
and the Confucian style was not yet pure.
How is it that it did not decline?
Its propagation lies with men.
Biography 37: Literary Figures Zǔ Hóngxūn, Lǐ Guǎng, Fán Xùn, Liú Tì, Xún Shìxùn, Yán Zhītuī (Yuán Shì, Wéi Dàoxùn, Jiāng Gàn, Suī Yù, Zhū Cái, Xún Zhòngjǔ, Xiāo [Kòu Xīn], Gǔ Dàozǐ).
The profound image is made manifest
to observe the changes of the seasons;
this is Heavenly Pattern (Astronomy).
The sages and enlightened ones established their words
to transform and perfect the world;
this is Human Pattern (Culture/Literature).
To understand the essence of the visible and the invisible,
and to illuminate the nexus between Heaven and Man,
does this not lie in Literature?
Listening from afar to the three ancient eras,
encompassing the hundred generations,
in establishing rites and composing music,
in spreading virtue and elevating fame—
if one’s words are not refined,
how can one’s actions travel far?
The Master said:
“Since King Wén is dead,
does not the culture reside here?”
Though great sages followed in his steps,
a thousand years have swiftly passed.
During that time, the heroes and luminaries were exceptional
and too many to record.
They were all suitable for sheathing their brushes and putting away their tablets,
and not fit to speak of literature—
this is truly the difficulty of talent, is it not?
As for Yóu and Xià, who excelled in literary composition,
Yán Huí was almost saintly.
This is why Qū and Sòng followed in their dust,
and Qīng and Yún could not cease writing.
Consequently, literary talents and gifted scholars
surged like waves and gathered like clouds,
displaying the plumes of the phoenix and the egret,
releasing the patterned brilliance of the carved dragon.
People said they found the Dark Pearl in the Red River,
and commanded the running lightning on Kūn Hill,
opening the four illuminations upon the spring blossoms,
and completing the ten thousand treasures in the autumn harvest.
However, the origin of literature
is sentiment arising from within.
Man possesses the six emotions,
imbued with the excellence of the Five Constants;
emotions respond to the six energies,
conforming to the sequence of the four seasons.
Some possess imperial gifts and instantaneous understanding,
with abilities bestowed by Heaven,
who weave splendid patterns through innate knowledge,
and seek advice on virtue from those who realized it first.
They are like carved clouds that naturally form five colors,
or like the ceremonial phoenix that instinctively harmonizes the eight tones.
This is truly reaching enlightenment through spiritual inspiration,
and not achievable through mental exertion alone.
Even if one’s feelings and thoughts are stagnant,
and the crucial passages are blocked,
but one dedicates oneself tirelessly
and studies diligently,
pursues leading scholars,
associates with beneficial friends,
broadens one’s knowledge through vigorous study,
focuses one’s mind and abstains from distractions,
adorning pictures with color,
and carving and refining to achieve useful form—
in this way, learning allows one to know,
and is still sufficient to be considered worthy.
When one considers a rock to be a beast
and shoots at it, it pierces right through;
this is the utmost sincerity (concentration).
For years one dismembers oxen,
and the blade moves with a flash, gliding effortlessly;
this is the result of long practice.
If not for the chaos (Húndùn) that allows no carving,
or the monster (Qióngqí) that harbors unchangeable nature,
how could there be anyone who, with utmost concentration and long practice, fails to achieve success?
How excellent was Wèi Wén’s discourse when he wrote:
“Most people are not sufficiently resolute;
when poor and lowly, they are intimidated by hunger and cold;
when rich and noble, they drift into dissipation and pleasure.
Consequently, they busy themselves with present affairs,
and neglect the achievement of a thousand years.
