The sun and moon pass above,
while the physical form decays below.
Suddenly, one changes and vanishes along with the myriad things.
This is the great sorrow of a man of ambition.”
Shěn Xiūwén said:
“From Hàn to Wèi,
over four hundred years,
the literary talents and gifted scholars
caused the style of writing to change three times.”
However, since then,
the tracks and ruts have become even more numerous.
In the South during the late Liáng dynasty,
subtlety and complexity were greatly valued.
It began in the Crown Prince's palace
and became the norm among the common populace.
It mingled messy and impure sounds to form verse,
and thus, although sad, it was not elegant.
When the Wǔpíng era arrived,
government was in disarray and the age was afflicted.
Only in the beauty of refined thought
did the elegant Way still persist.
They trod the path of mild compliance to compose literature,
and faced great adversity yet were able to maintain rectitude.
Reflecting that the latter ages of both dynasties
both indulged in licentious sounds,
the Qí dynasty's change in customs
belonged to string and wind instruments,
whereas the Liáng period's change in elegance
was found in their poetry and prose.
Both resulted from changing customs,
and both were sounds of a doomed state.
Yet, while their responses to change were not dissimilar,
their emotional responses to things sometimes differed.
Why?
It was probably due to following the desires of the ruler above.
After Qí's hegemon plan was launched,
it broadly invited outstanding talents,
opening the four gates to admit them,
and encompassing the eight directions to gather them.
In Yèjīng,
they assembled like smoke and fog.

Xíng Zǐcái of Héjiān, Wèi Bóqǐ of Jùlù, Lú Yuánmíng of Fànyáng, Wèi Jìjǐng of Jùlù, Cuī Chángrú of Qīnghé, Xíng Zǐmíng of Héjiān, Zǔ Xiàozhēng of Fànyáng, Sūn Yànjǔ of Luò'ān, Dù Fǔxuán of Zhōngshān, and Yáng Zǐliè of Běipíng were all part of this group.
Furthermore, Zǔ Hóngxūn of Fànyáng was also counted among the literary figures.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐ Yīn, Lù Qióng, Cuī Zhān, and Lù Yuánguī were all in the Central Secretariat,
participating in managing imperial edicts and pronouncements.
Lǐ Guǎng, Fán Xùn, Lǐ Délín, Lú Xúnzǔ, and Lú Sīdào first became famous for their literary compositions.
During the Huángjiàn court,
Chángshì Wáng Xī alone held the distinction of excellence.
During the Qīnghé and Tiāntǒng periods,
Dù Táijīng, Liú Tì, and Wèi Qiān also participated in managing imperial decrees and commands.
From Yīn onwards,
those in the Secretariat only drafted edicts concerning composition and the appointment of officials;
most of the documents related to military and state affairs
were written by Wèi Shōu.
When it came to the Wǔpíng era,
Lǐ Ruò, Xún Shìxùn, Lǐ Délín, and Xuē Dàohéng served as Secretariat Gentlemen;
all military and state documents and major edicts
were penned by Délín, and Dàohéng and the others were not involved.
Although the Hòuzhǔ (Later Ruler) was lost in the company of low-lifes,
he was rather fond of recitation and poetry.
When he was young,
he once read poems and rhapsodies,
and asked people:
"Will anyone ever truly understand the meaning of this?"
When he grew up, he paid little attention to it.
Initially, because he wanted painted screens,

he commanded the Tōngzhí Láng (Gentleman-General) Lánlíng Xiāo Fàng and Jìnlíng Wáng Xiào Shì (Prince Xiào Shì of Jìnlíng) to compile poems, both those of ancient famous sages and heroes and those of recent light and glamorous style, to supply subjects for the paintings.
The Dì (Emperor) valued these increasingly.

Later, he further summoned Qízhōu Lùshì Cānjūn (Registrar and Staff Officer of Qí Prefecture) Xiāo Kè and Zhàozhōu Gōngcáo Cānjūn (Master of Merits Staff Officer of Zhào Prefecture) Yán Zhītuī to enter and jointly manage the compilation.
Still following the custom of the former ruling period,
they were called Guǎnkè (Hall Guests).
Fàng and Zhītuī intended to expand the scope of this work.
Furthermore, Zǔ Tǐng was assisting in government,
and highly valued Zhītuī.
He also entrusted Dèng Chángyóng to gradually persuade the Hòuzhǔ,
focusing his attention on literary matters.
In the third year [of the reign],
Zǔ Tǐng memorialized for the establishment of the Wénlín Guǎn (Hall of Literary Forest).
Thereupon, he again summoned and introduced literary scholars,
and they were called Dàizhào Wénlín Guǎn (Awaiting Edict in the Hall of Literary Forest).
Tǐng further memorialized for the compilation of the Yùlǎn (Imperial Overview).

An imperial edict commanded Tǐng, along with Tèjìn (Special Advance) Wèi Shōu, Tàizǐ Tàishī (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince) Xú Zhīcái, Zhōngshū Lìng (Prefect of the Central Secretariat) Cuī Jié, Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant) Zhāng Diāo, and Zhōngshū Jiān (Supervisor of the Central Secretariat) Yáng Xiūzhī, to supervise the compilation.

Tǐng and the others memorialized, requesting the recall of Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (Gentleman-General and Cavalry Attendant-in-Waiting) Wéi Dàoxùn, Lù Ài, Tàizǐ Shèrén (Attendant to the Crown Prince) Wáng Shào,

Wèiwèi Chéng (Assistant Minister of the Imperial Guard) Lǐ Xiàojī, Diànzhōng Shiyùshǐ (Palace Censor) Wèi Dàn, Zhōngsàn Dàfū (Grandee Remonstrant) Liú Zhòngwēi, Yuán Shì, Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the Directorate of Education) Zhū Cái, Fèngchē Dūwèi (Commandant of Carriage-Bearing) Suī Dàoxián,

Kǎogōng Lángzhōng (Director of Merit Rating) Cuī Zisū, Zuǒ Wàibīng Láng (Director of the Left Outer Armies) Xuē Dàohéng, along with the former Zhǔkè Lángzhōng (Director of Guests) Lú Sīdào, Sīkōng Dōnggé Jìjiǔ (Libationer in the Eastern Gallery of the Minister of Works) Cuī Dé,

Tàixué Bóshì (Erudite of the Imperial Academy) Zhūgě Hàn, Fèng Cháoqǐng (Attendant at Court) Zhèng Gōngchāo, Diànzhōng Shiyùshǐ (Palace Censor) Zhèng Zǐxìn, and others, to enter the Hall and compile books.
He also commanded Fàng, Kè, Zhītuī, and the others to join the writing roster.

Furthermore, he ordered Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant) Fēng Xiàoyǎn, former Lèlíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Lèlíng) Zhèng Yuánlǐ, Wèiwèi Shàoqīng (Vice Minister of the Imperial Guard) Dù Táiqīng, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (Gentleman-General and Cavalry Regular Attendant) Wáng Xùn, former Nányānzhōu Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of Nányān Prefecture) Yáng Sù,
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì Mǎ Yuánxī, along with the former Sāngōng Lángzhōng (Director in the Three Ducal Ministries) Liú Mín, Kāifǔ Xíng Cānjūn (Staff Officer Acting for an Open Residence) Lǐ Shīshàng,
and Wēn Jūnyōu to enter the Hall.
They were also instructed to compile books.

Furthermore, he commanded Tèjìn (Special Advance) Cuī Jìshū, former Rénzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Rén Prefecture) Liú Tì, Sànqí Chángshì Lǐ Xiàozhēn, and Zhōngshū Shìláng (Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Central Secretariat) Lǐ Délín to continuously enter and Dàizhào (Await Edict).
Soon after, an edict commanded all these people to recommend others they knew.

Then there were former Jìzhōu Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of Jì Prefecture) Lǐ Zhù, former Guǎngwǔ Tàishǒu (Administrator of Guǎngwǔ) Wèi Qiān, former Xīyǎnzhōu Sīmǎ (Controller of Xīyǎn Prefecture) Xiāo Gài, former Yōuzhōu Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of Yōu Prefecture) Lù Rénhuì, Zhèngzhōu Sīmǎ (Controller of Zhèng Prefecture) Jiāng Gàn, former Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (Gentleman-General and Cavalry Attendant-in-Waiting) Xīn Déyuán, Lù Kāimíng, Tōngzhí Láng (Gentleman-General) Fēng Xiàojiǎn, Tàiwèi Yuàn (Secretary to the Grand Marshal) Zhāng Déchōng, along with the former Yòumín Láng (Director of Right Commoners) Gāo Xínggōng, Sītú Hùcáo Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Ministry of Revenue for the Minister of the Masses) Gǔ Dàozi, former Sīkōng Gōngcáo Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Ministry of Merits for the Minister of Works) Liú Yǐ, Huòjiā Lìng (Magistrate of Huòjiā) Cuī Derú, Jǐshìzhōng (Attendant Consultant) Lǐ Yuǎnkǎi, Jìnzhōu Zhìzhōng (Administrator of the Capital Department of Jìn Prefecture) Yáng Shīxiào, Tàiwèi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Central Army for the Grand Marshal) Liú Rúxíng, Sīkōng Jìjiǔ (Libationer for the Minister of Works) Yáng Pìjiāng, Sīkōng Shìcáo Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Ministry of Personnel for the Minister of Works) Lú Gōngshùn, Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Central Army for the Minister of the Masses) Zhōu Zǐshēn, Kāifǔ Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Open Residence) Wáng Yǒubó, Cuī Jūnqià, and Wèi Shījiǎn, all entering the Hall to Dàizhào (Await Edict).
He also commanded the Yòu Púyè (Right Director of the Department of State Affairs) Duàn Xiàoyán to enter.
After the Yùlǎn was completed,
some of the people who had participated in the compilation were not retained to Dàizhào,
but were handed over to the relevant departments for reassignment.
Among all these people,
there were also thirteen or fourteen percent [of them] whose literary learning was superficial,
but who attached themselves to relatives and acquaintances,
and were recklessly recommended by each other.
Nevertheless,
the scribes who wielded brushes at that time
were almost all sought out.
Outside of this group, there were three or four people like Guǎngpíng Sòng Xiàowáng and Xìndū Liú Shànjīng,
discussing their talent and nature,
even the worthies who entered the Hall could not match them by thirteen or fourteen percent.
The Dàizhào Wénlín (Awaiting Edict in the Literary Forest)
was also a grand event of that era,
therefore their names are recorded here.
As for those from Xíng Zǐcái onwards,
some died while serving the Wèi Cháo (Wèi Dynasty)
and are already included in earlier histories;
others, whose fame and rank were already high,
have their own biographical accounts;
some are attached to their family histories;
and some have their names preserved in later records.
They are generally omitted here.
Now, we sequentially arrange Zǔ Hóngxūn and others in the section on Wényuàn (Garden of Literature).
Those outside of this group who are worth recording
are preserved at the end of this chapter.
Zǔ Hóngxūn
was a man from Fányáng, Zhuójùn.
His father, Shèn,
served the Wèi [dynasty], holding positions such as Yànmén and Xiányáng Tàishǒu (Administrator),
and was known for his administrative competence.
He died while serving as Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple).
He was posthumously granted the titles of Zhōngshū Jiān (Supervisor of the Central Secretariat) and Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōu Prefecture),
with the posthumous title Huì Hóu (Marquis Huì).
When Hóngxūn reached the age of twenty, he served alongside Lú Wénfú from the same commandery as a Zhōuzhǔbù (Chief Clerk of the Prefecture).
Púyè (Director) Línhuái Wáng Yù (Prince Yù of Línhuái) memorialized, recommending Hóngxūn for his literary talent,
suggesting he should be tested with an official position.
An edict appointed him Fèng Cháoqǐng (Attendant at Court).
People said to him:
"Línhuái recommended you,
and you immediately received an appointment.
Yet you never thanked him;
perhaps this is improper."
Hóngxūn replied:
"Recommending talent for the state
is Línhuái's duty.
Why should Zǔ Hóngxūn follow up and thank him?"
Yù heard this and was pleased, saying:
"I have found the right man."
When Gě Róng pressed south,
he was sent out as a Fánghé Biéjiàng (River Defense Separate General)
to guard Huátái.
At the beginning of the Yǒng'ān era,
Yuán Luó served as the Dōngdào Dàshǐ (Grand Envoy of the Eastern Circuit),
and appointed Fēng Lóngzhī, Xíng Shào, Lǐ Hún, Lǐ Xiàng, and Hóngxūn, all as Zǐshǐ (Sub-Envoys).
He was appointed Dōngjìběi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Eastern Jìběi),
but he requested resignation on the grounds of his father's old age and illness,
and ultimately did not take the post.
Later, Chéngyáng Wáng Huī (Prince Huī of Chéngyáng) memorialized, appointing Hóngxūn as Sītú Fǎcáo Cānjūnshì (Staff Officer of the Judicial Department for the Minister of the Masses).
He proceeded to Luò[yáng].
Huī said to him:
"I heard that Línhuái recommended you,
yet you never came to his gate.
Why have you come now?"
Hóngxūn replied:
"I have come now to take up my post,
not to offer thanks for kindness."
He was transferred to Tíngwèi Zhèng (Director in the Court of Judicial Review).
Later, he resigned his post and returned to his hometown.
His letter to Yáng Xiūzhī reads: "Elder Brother Yáng Shēng: Recently, because my family is poor and my parents are old,
I returned temporarily to my former commandery.
On the western border of the county,
there is Diāoshān (Carved Mountain).
The place is tranquil and distant,
the water
and rocks are clear and beautiful,
tall cliffs surround it on all sides,
and there are several *qǐng* of good farmland.
Our family previously had a rustic dwelling there,
but it was abandoned and ruined during the disorder.
Now, I am restarting construction.
I use rock to form the foundation,
relying on
the trees to raise the framework.
Moss grows to cover the eaves,
and springs flow around the steps.
The moon, pines, and windy grasses
gather like brocade around the courtyard;
the sunlight and clouds,
scattered like stars near the marsh.
Smoke flowing under the eaves
unfurls and rolls up with the ether of the clouds;
the peaches and plums in the garden
mingle lushly with the ailanthus and cypress.
Sometimes I hike across the stream by lifting my robes,
leaning on my staff to ascend the peak.
My heart drifts upward in solitude,
my body floats away as if departing,
and in the profound distance, I no longer know that I exist between Heaven and Earth.
After a long time like this,
I return to my dwelling.
I sit alone on a high rock,
pluck
the *qín* facing the water,
recite poetry alone in the mountain valley,
raise my wine cup to gaze at the moon,
listening to the sound of the wind to inspire thought,
hearing the cry of the crane to stir emotion.
I yearn for the carefree spirit of Zhuāngshēng,
and admire the pure expanse of Shàngzǐ.
My head is crowned with sedge,
my body clothed in coarse hemp.
I go out to sow millet and rice,
and return to serve my kind parents.
Walking slowly serves as a carriage;
having nothing to do is precious.
This is already contentment—
why must one engage with the dusty world?
Yet, since my life has been bound by the ropes and chains of fame and reputation,
I approach the fine carving tool of the skilled artisan.
I shake my pendant on the purple terrace,
and wave my sleeves below the vermillion steps.
I collect the scattered bamboo slips
from the metal cabinet,
and search for forgotten writings on Jade Mountain.
I exhaust my spirit on tombs and mounds,
and spend all my energy on the River and Han (the Milky Way).
When spreading eloquence, I aim for embroidered sash patterns;
when expressing opinions, they must contain fragrant
refinement.
This is self-aggrandizement,
and I take no pleasure in it.
Allow me to try to discuss this.
Now, where Kūnfēng (Kunlun Peak) accumulates jade,
the most lustrous pieces are destroyed first;
where Yáoshān (Jade Mountain) clusters cassia,
the most fragrant and lush are broken first.
Thus, in the Eastern Capital, there are officials who hang up their official hats,
and in the Southern Kingdoms, scholars are seen abandoning their ambitions.
How could this be because they despise fine silk and grain,
and prefer coarse vegetables and cloth?
It is simply because they wish to protect their seven-foot body
and live out their hundred years.
Now, your official
position is already high,
and your reputation and splendor have spread far.
Elephants perish because of their tusks;
fat is boiled away because it shines brightly.
Since you have read Lǎoshì's discourse on the Valley Spirit (Gǔshén),
you ought to embody the principle of contentment and ease exemplified by Liúhóu.
If
suddenly become pure and lofty,
unfastening pendants and discarding hairpins;
then, for me in these mountains,
a retreat can certainly be prepared.
To be able to link arms and enter the forest,
hang caps on drooping branches,
carry wine and climb peaks,
spread
mats on level ground,
speak of cherished aspirations,
discuss old friendships,
inquire about the methods of the elixir (Dān fǎ),
speak of profound texts (Xuán shū),
this is also happiness;
why must one seek wealth and high rank?
Depart, Yángzǐ!
Our paths diverge and our interests
differ.
To seek this meaning (Zhǐ) in the distance
is remote, like the Heavenly River (Tiānhàn).
Alas, it is finished!
The writing cannot fully express the meaning.
The envoy from Liáng is about to arrive.
Hóngxūn is commanded to receive the guest.
Gāozǔ was once summoned to Bìngzhōu,
where he composed the Record of Jìn Cí (Jìn Cí Jì).
Those who appreciate such matters enjoyed his writing.
His position reached that of Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Gāoyáng.
While in office, he was pure and simple.
His wife and children could not avoid cold and hunger.
The public opinion at the time held him in high regard.
He died in office at the beginning of Tiānbǎo.
Lǐ Guǎng,
courtesy name Hóngjī,
was a man from Fànyáng.
His ancestors migrated there from Liáodōng.
Guǎng was widely versed in numerous books,
possessing talent, deep thought, and literary renown.
In his youth, he was as famous as Lǐ Jiǎn of Zhàojùn,
and was second only to Xíng and Wèi.
However, he was hesitant in speech,
but quick in action.
When Yánmíng, the Prince of Ānfēng of the Wèi Dynasty, was garrisoned at Xúzhōu,
he appointed Guǎng as Chángliú Cānjūn.
He shed his common status and became Dàngnì Jiāngjūn.
Ěrzhū Zhòngyuǎn assigned him to be the Grand General’s Secretary (Dà Jiāngjūn Jìshì),
and he was subsequently promoted to Grand Master Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū).
Xīn Zuǎn, the Deputy of the Secretariat (Xíng Tái) in Jīngzhōu, nominated him to be a Xíng Tái Lángzhōng,
and soon after, he became the Recorder and Military Advisor (Lùshì Cānjūn) in the Chējì Fu.
The Commandant (Zhōngwèi) Cuī Xiān
carefully selected censors (Yùshǐ), all of whom were from established families (Shì Zhòu).
Guǎng alone, based on his talent and scholarship, served concurrently as Yùshǐ,
compiling the national history.
The memorials and writings from the Southern Office (Nántái)
largely utilized his words.
Yān, the Duke of Píngyáng,
recommended him as Zhōngwèi, and he was transferred to serve as Palace Assistant Censor (Shì Yùshǐ).
When Xiǎnzǔ
first succeeded to the imperial legacy, he commanded Guǎng to manage the secretariat (Zhǎng Shūjì).
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
the emperor intended to make him Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Láng),
but stopped when Guǎng became gravely ill.
Guǎng once wanted to attend the morning court early,
so he took a nap before dawn.
Suddenly, he woke up in shock,
and told his wife,
"I seemed to be sleeping just now,
when suddenly I saw a person emerge from inside my body,
saying: 'You have strained your mind too much;
this is more than your spirit can bear.
I must now bid you farewell and leave.'"
Consequently, he became distraught and unhappy.
A few days later, he fell ill,
and remained bedridden for years.
His assets were repeatedly depleted,
and he could not afford continuous medicine.
Guǎng was refined and possessed discernment;
his capacity and vision were grand and far-reaching.
He was candid and impartial,
loved by the scholarly class (Shì Liú).
They often supported and aided him year-round,
allowing him to sustain himself.
He eventually died of his illness.
He had previously recommended Bì Yìyún to Cuī Xiān.
After Guǎng died,
Yìyún collected ten scrolls of his writings and calligraphy,
entrusting Wèi Shōu to write a preface for them.
Zǐ Dào, a member of his clan, also possessed literary talent.
Fán Xùn,
courtesy name Xiàoqiān,
was a native of Běiyīshì in Hédōng.
His grandfather Yǎn,
and father Héng,
both held no official positions.
Héng was extremely filial by nature.
After his father died,
he carried earth to form the grave mound,
planting cypress trees across several tens of *mǔ*.
Morning and evening, he wailed in sorrow.
When Xùn was young and studying,
he was often given preferential treatment over his elder brother Zhòng.
Subsequently, he reproached himself, saying:
"Nominally being a younger brother,
yet alone receiving comfort and ease,
should I not
feel ashamed in my heart?" He wanted to apply himself equally to his work.
His mother, Lady Féng, said to him:
"Are you trying to be diligent in small matters?"
Xùn was moved by his mother's words,
and consequently devoted himself entirely to classical texts.
He wrote the four characters
"Seeing the worthy, think of matching them" (Jiàn Xián Sī Qí)
on the wall,
to encourage himself.
As his home prefecture fell into ruin,
he resided temporarily in Yèzhōng,
serving as a minor clerk (Xiǎoshǐ) in Línzhāng.
The County Magistrate (Xiàn Lìng) Péi Jiàn
administered his post with purity and diligence, which resulted in auspicious omens like white sparrows.
Xùn presented ten poems praising his pure virtue (Qīng Dé Sòng).
Jiàn greatly appreciated and esteemed him,
promoting him to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
and subsequently recommended him to the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè), Cuī Xiān.
He joined Lǐ Guǎng of Liáodōng and Fēng Xiàoyǎn of Bóhǎi as guests of Xiān.
Some people criticized him for being quiet and inactive, unable to conform to the times.
Xùn often admired the words of Dōngfāng Shuò:
submerging oneself (Lù Chén) in worldly affairs
and avoiding the world within the Jīnmǎ Gate,
is no different from being beneath the thatched hut in the deep mountains.
Consequently, he borrowed the persona of 'Master Lù Chén' [Lù Chén Gōngzǐ] as his host,
imitated the *Kè Nán* (Criticism by a Guest),
and composed the *Kè Huì* (Admonition to a Guest) to express his views.
Later, Cuī Xiān hosted a large gathering of guests.
Yuán Xù, the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) and Prince of Xiāngchéng, was also present.
They discussed appointing officials for the administration.
Xiān pointed to Xùn and said:
"This man is rich in learning and high in talent.
He would be an excellent Acting Military Advisor (Xíng Cānjūn)."
Xù looked at him and said:
"How can he achieve such a position?"
Xùn replied:
"Since my family has no hereditary rank,
I dare not accept this."
In the seventh year of Wǔdìng,
Shìzōng died.
Xiān was banished to the frontier,
and all his guests dispersed.
Xùn then traveled to Chénliú and resided there.
Liú Shāguǐ, the Inspector of Liángzhōu,
employed Xùn concurrently as Recorder and Military Advisor (Lùshì Cānjūn), and nominated him as a Cultivated Talent (Xiùcái).
The Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) examined the old statutes:
a lower prefecture could nominate a Xiùcái only once every three years.
Five years prior, Zhèng Zǔxiàn of Kāifēng had already been nominated.
It was calculated that this year was not yet the time for nomination.
Wáng Cōng, the concurrent Deputy Governor (Bié Jià), protested,
but the Right Vice Director (Yòu Chéng) Yáng Fěi could not refuse the nomination.
Gāo Lóngzhī, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), said:
"Although Xùn's talent and learning are outstanding,
serving next year is not far away."
Xùn eventually returned to his home prefecture.
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to serve concurrently as Chief Clerk (Zhǎng Shǐ),
and followed the army in the southern campaign.
When the army returned,
Shāguǐ was transferred to Yǐngchuān,
and again appointed Xùn concurrently as Chief Clerk of Yǐngzhōu.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
his home prefecture again nominated him as Xiùcái.
In the spring of the second year,
after gathering in the court hall and completing the policy examination (Duì Cè),
the Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Láng) Zhāng Zǐróng reported the result.
By the fifth month of the fourth year,
Xùn and Lǐ Zǐxuān, a Xiùcái from Dìngzhōu,
having failed to receive an appointment three years after the policy examination, were dismissed from consideration.
They submitted a petition requesting an appeal to be heard,
but the imperial decree gave no reply.
Liángzhōu once again submitted a memorial nominating Xùn as Xiùcái.
In the first month of the fifth year, an imperial edict was issued asking about the establishment of the Zhōng era name.
Xùn responded, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the rites of inspecting the Sacred Peaks (Xún Yuè)
are recorded in the Book of Yú (Yú Shū),
and the principle of examining the regions (Shěng Fāng)
is set forth in the Images of the Yì (Yì Xiàng).
The former emperors and previous kings
were not all of a single lineage;
those who sealed metal and engraved jade (conferring titles)
numbered more than a hundred million.
When Zhòngní (Confucius) observed Liángfǔ,
he could not fully identify them;
when Yíwú (Guǎn Zhòng) responded to Qí Huán,
few records remained.
However, the affairs of great virtue
must await the Grand
peace,
if it is not the right person,
it will further incur spiritual condemnation.
Qín Huáng was without the Way,
causing the calamities of rain and wind;
Hàn Wǔ was extravagant and licentious,
and suffered the harm of the Fèngchē.
When Wénshū received
the Mandate,
the fiery essence shone anew,
the four seas flowed peacefully,
and all under Heaven was harmonious.
Swords were granted to knights,
and horses pulled the drum chariots.
Thus, the writings of Zhāng Chún were employed,
and the doctrine of Bóyáng
was first followed.
Coming to the time of Wèi and Jìn,
although each had its ruler,
assessing virtue and assigning positions,
none could propose alternatives or dispute this.
Jiǎng Jì submitted statements before,
but merely defiled the paper and ink;
Yuán Zhǔn issued discussions
later,
but ultimately they were not implemented.
Generations passed through three dynasties,
years approaching ten cyclical years,
the time for establishing the sage,
this is a glorious gathering.
However, since the Water Virtue failed to contend,
Hángǔ was closed
off,
the Heavenly Horses ceased their songs,
and bundled reeds ceased being tribute.
Our Tài Zǔ received the auspicious sign of the Bǎojī,
grasped the writings of the Fènghuáng,
embodied a unified virtue to rectify the court,
bowed the tripartite realm to
serve the sovereign,
sweeping away these demonic bandits
was as easy as pouring water on snow.
But since Chāng has already received the Mandate,
to launch a punitive expedition now,
although Tài Bái (Venus) is high,
and the Central States ought to fight,
we put it outside
consideration,
hoping that they will reform themselves.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty, with the bearing of divine military prowess,
and innate strategy,
having horses abundant in Jìběi,
and generals superior to those of Shānxī,
the cool wind arrives,
the white dew
descends.
To ascend Tàiháng in the north,
and overlook Jiéshí in the east,
is just when you desire to swallow Bā Shǔ and sweep through Xiáo Hán,
to make Chángzhōu a park and Jiāng Hàn a pond.
Again, I fear that setting fire with the wind,
would cause the *zhī*
and the *ài* to burn together.
To restrain these Six Armies,
is not yet to employ the Nine Punishments.
Now, Zhōu Fā displayed the *yázhāng*,
and Hàn dispatched the bamboo envoys;
the meaning lies in aiding the people,
not in being known for loving war.
As for
the saying about "throwing at the rat but fearing the vessel,"
that is merely common talk;
and the words about using civil virtue to cherish distant lands,
how can they understand the path of expediency?
Now the fine sons of the Sāntái,
and excellent families of the Six Commanderies,
are accumulating strength and awaiting
the opportunity,
packing provisions and waiting for the decree.
It would be better to command the dragon chariot and don the tiger vest,
first gathering the people of Lǒngyòu,
swiftly turning like lightning and startling like thunder,
and then seizing the land of Jīngnán.
Formerly, when Qín attacked Cháng
píng,
the essence of Metal consumed Mǎo;
when Chǔ attacked Jùlù,
bent arrows flowed through the night.
How much more so should our divine might and spiritual power
not lack supportive aid?
We need only ensure that their common people, upon one glimpse of the Six Armies,
feel as
if they have seen King Zhōu,
or encountered Sīyīn.
After that, abolish their harsh laws,
grant them provisional laws,
mobilize the troops and return,
stopping the spear to constitute martiality (*wǔ*),
raising golden markers in Nánhǎi,
carving stone on Dōng
Shān,
recording the miraculous achievements of Heaven and Earth,
and spreading their fame throughout a thousand years.
If Má Er were not dead,
and Zǐyáng were still alive,
we would then wish to examine the diagrams of the Míngtáng,
and draft the ceremony of shooting
the Ox.
Comparing virtues and discussing merits,
we would feel much shame compared to those former ranks,
but when ascending Mount Tài and performing the *shàn* sacrifice,
your servant consequently has doubts.
When asked further about seeking talent and assessing officials,
Sùn replied: I have heard that carving beasts and painting dragons,
merely possess the appearance of wind and clouds;
golden boats and jade horses,
ultimately have no utility on water or land.
Riding out three times to honor the worthy
aims to gather practical utility,
while refusing to pull out a single hair,
what is the point of seeking him?
Therefore, Yáo treated the Recluse as a guest,
thereby maintaining the integrity of Jīshān;
when Zhōu moved the Shāng tripod,
they did not accept the words of Gūzhú.
But scholars
in retirement who steal fame,
although this has long been claimed;
court officials who usurp positions,
that is also truly abundant.
When Hàn appointed a chancellor,
there soon arose the calamity symbolized by bells and drums;
when Wèi employed the Sān Gōng,
it incurred
the laughter of Sūn Quán.
Thus, concerning those in the mountain forests versus those in the imperial court,
they must tolerate criticism and slander;
between comfortable retirement and serving the sovereign as a guest,
there is, conversely, a distinction of merit.
As for the idea that the time is not for jumping into the sea,
and yet saying one is ashamed to be a citizen of Qín;
and the situation differs from leaving the pass,
yet saying one is ashamed to follow Wèi’s chaos.
Although the stars violate the Emperor's Seat,
they do not change their lofty aspiration;
when the moon violates Shǎo Wēi,
they ultimately maintain their resolute will.
Since the time of Our Tài Yuè,
able to expand the grand enterprise,
from Yǔ to Shén Zōng,
Shùn reached Wén Zǔ.
Your Majesty received the bright Mandate of Heaven,
shining with the splendor of the sun and moon.
From
the time of entering the foot of the mountain,
one then reached Wén Zǔ.
Offices are established by emulating Heaven and Earth,
and duties are distributed by mirroring the stars.
The Hàn dynasty's Shénfèng,
is ashamed to be used for reckoning years;
the Wèi clan's Qīnglóng,
is ashamed
to be used to change the reign title.
Above, those who correspond to the constellations
are all extraordinary people;
below, those who model the mountains and rivers
are none other than remarkable scholars.
Therefore, in the painted halls and foremost pavilions,
the cultivation of virtue is renewed daily,
and the temple tripods,
songs, and bells
demonstrate royal achievements accumulating yearly.
By following the name and demanding reality,
selecting the multitude and promoting the capable,
the court is without dukes who smell of copper,
and the age has eliminated discussions of the Money God.
Formerly, Bǎi Lǐ was Prime Minister of Qín,
his name remains on the Sparrow Register;
Xiāo and Zhāng aided Pèi,
their surnames are in the River Scroll.
Today's dukes and ministers,
are likewise granted by Heaven;
governing in collaboration with them,
what desire is not fulfilled?
It is not necessary
to kowtow to the Tiān Shī,
to then hear the arts of horse-herding;
or to walk on one's knees upon the mountain,
to only then gain the Way of self-governance.
We need only ensure that the imperial virtue is excellent and bright,
and self-strengthening without cease,
studying documents in the first
watch of the night,
and receiving communications throughout the day.
Zhōu Chāng's discussion of Jié and Zhòu,
is happily accepted openly;
Liú Yì's comparison to Huán and Líng,
is ultimately tolerated broadly.
Highly confer royal peerages,
Only if these can be granted,
will the granaries and treasuries have nothing missed,
and fisheries and salt production be fully recorded.
Do not allow Huán Tán (who criticized the prognostications)
to have his office stop at Jùn Chéng;
nor Zhào Yī (who relied on his talent)
to end his career as Jì Yuàn.
Then the world will settle its heart,
and the visible and invisible worlds will recognize the affinity.
Suì Jīng will serve the Hàn,
Fēng Bó will pay homage to the Zhōu.
The True Man (Zhēnrén) departs and returns again,
the Tái Stars split open and gather back together.
The Shī praises the abundance of
capable men,
and the Yì describes the assembly of dragons.
Speaking from this perspective,
we can have no shame.
(The Emperor) further asked about the two teachings of Buddhism (Shì) and Daoism (Dào).
Xùn humbly replied: Your servant has heard that the Way of Heaven (Tiāndào) and innate nature and destiny (xìngmìng),
are what the Sages did not discuss,
because the principles are beyond seeking and understanding,
and difficult to define or name.
The discussions of Dàodé by Bó Yáng,
and the core meaning of Xiāoyáo
by Zhuāng Zhōu—
if one disregards the words and grasps the intent,
there is still something traceable.
As for the Jade Slips and Golden Writings,
the Divine Canons and Secret Records,
the wonders of the "Three Foot Nine Revolutions,"
and the marvels of "Scarlet Snow and Dark Frost,"
Huáinán achieving the Dào,
with dogs barking in the clouds;
Zǐ Qiáo attaining immortality,
with his sword flying in the sky—
these are all baseless statements,
tales of sea dates,
seeking them is like tying down the wind,
studying
them is like chasing a shadow.
Yet the Ruler of Yān, the Queen of Qí, the First Emperor of Qín, and the Emperors of Hàn,
trusted those magicians (Fāngshì),
hoping to encounter the truth (of immortality).
Xú Fú left and never returned,
Luán Dà went forth and gained
nothing.
They still believed that ascending to heaven and seeing inverted reflections
could be anticipated by clapping hands;
and that by sacrificing to ghosts and seeking spirits,
perhaps they might not die.
Although the Jiāng Bì stone disc was returned,
it still entered the tomb at Lí Shān;
although the Dragon Steed (Lóng Méi) had
arrived,
it ultimately went down into the Mào Líng grave mound.
Then we know that Liú Xiàng's belief in Hóng Bǎo
was a mistake that should be held accountable;
and Wáng Chōng's criticism of the Huáng Dì
comparing him to those who did not attain it.
Moreover, since recent
generations,
Buddhism has been greatly maintained,
scriptures copied from the Western Lands (Xītǔ),
and images painted in the Southern Palace (Nángōng).
The black ground of Kūn Chí
is taken to be the ashes of the world-ending conflagration (jiéshāo);
the nights of the Chūnqiū
are said to be the day
when the spirits descended.
The Dharma King (Fǎ Wáng) is completely free and unconstrained,
his transformations are endless,
placing worlds within a speck of dust,
and containing Xūmí (Mount Sumeru) within a grain of millet.
Generally, the principle is fundamentally void and non-existent,
demonstrated merely as skillful means (fāngbiàn).
Yet the followers of deception and extravagance,
recklessly seek to leave home (become monastics).
Yào Wáng burned his body,
Bō Lùn sprinkled his blood.
Assuming these are not true,
they ought still to subdue their desires.
How can there be those who change their form
and alter their appearance,
claiming to be different from ordinary people,
yet indulge their desires and release their emotions,
remaining just like common folk?
The remaining doctrines from the Dragon Palace (Lóng Gōng),
and the early teachings from Lù Yě (Deer Park)—
if these (indulgent practices) are tolerated,
the true spirit of the Dào will fall into decay.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty has received the Bright Mandate of Heaven,
subordinates yourself to benefit the people,
causing mountain sprites to manifest their efficacy,
and sea gods to lead their duties.
The stone swallows of Xiāng Zhōng
bathe in timely rain and fly in flocks;
the bronze bird on the platform
turns its scoop handle (biāo) when exposed to gentle wind.
Considering that the Zhōu capital was in Luò Yì,
but their governance was established in Hào Jīng;
the Hàn resided in Xián Yáng,
but their spirits returned to Fēng and Pèi.
In the lands of Fén and Jìn,
the imperial legacy is just beginning.
If you turn your attention to making imperial tours,
it will surely cause trouble for administration.
Nevertheless, you still condescend to grace the literary circles,
weighing and considering the Hundred Schools,
thinking of grasping jade at Yáo Chí,
and contemplating the search for pearls in
Chì Shuǐ.
I humbly believe that the Queen Mother (Wáng Mǔ) presenting the jade ring
was due to being moved by the virtue of Zhōu (Zhōu Dé);
and Heaven bestowing jade pendants
was truly a reward for the achievements of Yǔ (Yǔ Gōng).
The two Bān recorded history,
and the two Mǎ composed writings.
But they did not see the doctrines of the Three
Ages (Sān Shì),
nor did they hear the essence of the One Vehicle (Yī Chéng).
Imperial music and Royal rites,
still change and evolve over time;
the aberrant ways (zuǒdào) and monstrous people,
should naturally be winnowed out without question.
(The Emperor) further asked about the severity and leniency of punishments.
Xùn replied humbly: Your servant has heard that when a King establishes a state,
punishment serves to assist the rites (lǐ),
just as cold and heat support Yin and Yang,
and mountains and rivers connect Heaven and Earth.
However, since recent generations,
laws and statutes have gradually
proliferated,
the Qín seal script (Qín Zhuàn) is insufficient to record them all,
and the Chǔ bamboo slips cannot fully contain them.
Officials in charge, because of this,
open two doors (of judgment),
high or low depending on their minds,
warmth or cold determined by their will.
The Three Canons (Sān Diǎn) of the Zhōu Officials (Zhōu Guān),
are discarded as easily as blowing hair;
the Nine Chapters (Jiǔ Zhāng) of the Hàn laws,
are violated as easily as turning one's hand over.
Consequently, the prison air of Cháng Píng
only dissipated after receiving wine;
the Filial Woman of Dōng Hǎi
was only vindicated (by Heaven) through
a disaster.
Imperial edicts are hung on the wall,
containing goodness but nobody follows them;
when corrupt officials arrive at the gate,
there is nothing they demand that cannot be obtained.
This is all because the superiors have lost the Dào,
and the people do not perceive
virtue.
Yet those who deliberate stick to their confusion,
and do not seek the root cause.
Zhōng Yáo and Wáng Lǎng retrospectively resented Zhāng Cāng,
and Zǔ Nè and Méi Táo together blamed Emperor Wén (Wén Dì).
They then said that turning corpses upright
and reforming
relied on restoring corporal punishments;
and that achieving order and revitalizing the state
had nothing to do with the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ).
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty holds court at dawn,
concentrating on the arts of governance,
clarifying punishments to correct the various
marquises,
and extending benevolence to treat the common people as children.
The Yellow Banner and Purple Canopy (signs of rebellion)
have already disappeared from the Southeast (Dōngnán);
the White Horse and Plain Chariot (signs of surrender/virtue)
will soon descend upon Zhǐ Dào.
If you were to again employ harsh statutes and detailed writings (severe laws),
your servant genuinely
does not understand why.
Why is this?
Humans emulate Heaven and Earth,
and equally embody Yin and Yang.
When secure, they desire life;
when disturbed, they plan for death.
Therefore, the governance of a True King
prioritizes rites (lǐ) and music (yuè).
If there are
those who do not comply,
then the penal codes are employed.
Both leniency and severity must be used,
like presenting both water and fire.
There has never been a state that relied solely on Shāng [Yāng] or Hán [Fēi] and was able to last long.
In the past, when Qín returned Shì Huì,
the robbers of Jìn came
and submitted;
when Shùn promoted Gāo Táo,
inhumanity spontaneously kept its distance.
If only Shì Zhī and Dìng Guó could alternately serve as judicial officials,
and Gōng Suì and Wén Wēng successively act as Jùnshǒu (Commandery Governors),
examine the laws and regulations
edict
unites these statutes and regulations,
joyfully hearing the words of Jí Àn,
and weepingly cutting off the crimes of Zhāopíng.
Then the world will govern itself,
and the Great Way will operate publicly.
Suckling beasts will sheathe their fangs,
and fierce eagles will droop their wings.
The treasury
of the King of Chǔ will no longer need to be sealed,
and the unjustly imprisoned
in the Hàn jails will naturally receive justice.
Those from lands yet to submit
will follow the trend and desire civilization;
within the borders
that are marked out,
all will follow virtue and praise benevolence.
To be heralded as (the age of) Chéng
and Kāng, what difficulty is there?
(Someone) further asked about misfortune, fortune, and retribution,
and (Sùn) replied, "I have heard that although the Five Directions are easily distinguished,
(we) still rely on the South-pointing carriage;
although a hundred generations can be known,
one still needs to blow the pitch pipes (to verify the standard).
Moreover, the Way of Heaven is distant and secret,
and divine actions are hard to trace to their origin.
Without
spiritual communication,
who can fully comprehend them?
Floating on a raft until reaching the Milky Way (Héhàn),
one only sees the Cowherd (Qiānniú);
pretending to sleep and wandering in the Highest Mystery,
one merely encounters Zhái Quǎn.
The principles of creation and transformation
are silent and without transmission;
the coming of retribution
is certainly difficult to grasp and speak of rashly.
However, Qín Mù possessed the Way,
and Gōumáng bestowed longevity;
Guó Gōng possessed slight virtue,
and Rùshōu
sent down misfortune.
The Exalted and Luminous are above,
they surely have knowledge,
and it cannot be said that the spirits are obscure, dark, or unbelievable.
As for Zhòngní being distressed between Chén
and Cài,
and Mèng Kē being trapped in Qí
and Liáng,
this was due to not meeting their time;
how could it concern the ultimate principle of fate and destiny?
and Mǎ Qiān was subjected to subordinates.
To suffer execution
and incur disgrace, how can one blame others?
As
for those who harmonize the pitch pipes and are favored,
or those who row boats and gain imperial favor,
speaking from this perspective,
it is even less surprising.
The King of Zhōu caused pestles to float (a natural disaster),
thereby incurring Heaven's punishment;
Bái Qǐ executed those who surrendered,
acting according to his own
will.
Therefore, the mandate
of seven hundred years was still granted to the Jī clan;
the execution at Dù Yóu
still befell Wǔ'ān.
In the past, when Hàn officials presented their highest annual reports,
they did not exceed discussion of solar eclipses;
when Jìn tested their outstanding talents (*xiùcái*),
they were limited to the cold-fire phenomenon.
Former sages
and past scholars all regarded this subject as difficult.
Comparing the past to the present,
your servant finds it easy.
However, this common man from the remote fields,
having excessively received private grace,
having broken the cold pitch pipe three times,
and having twice strolled through the Jīnmǎ Gate,
the King's words
were illuminating and magnificent, his thoughts seemed divine,
and my impromptu
response was inadequate,
thus I bow profoundly in fear and trepidation."
The Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) ranked his performance,
judging Sùn to be the foremost of the time.
In the twelfth month,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, became Dà Xíngtái leading troops in a punitive expedition to the south,
and employed Sùn to follow the army.
The next year,
Emperor Xiǎnzǔ installed the Marquis of Zhēnyáng as the Lord of Liáng.
Yuè provisionally appointed Sùn as Dà Xíngtái Lángzhōng
and sent him south
to mediate peace with Xiāo Xiū and Hóu Tiàn.
Sùn traveled back and forth for five days,
obtaining a reply letter from Xiū and the others.
Yuè then concluded a covenant with Xiū on the riverbank.
When the main army returned to Yè,
Sùn was subsequently recommended by Dūguān Shàngshū Cuī Áng.
An imperial edict committed (the case) to the Shàngshū,
who evaluated him as pure, fair, diligent, and capable,
and sent him to the Lìbù.
In the seventh year,
an edict commanded the collating and standardizing of various books
for the use of the Crown Prince.

Sùn, along with eleven others—the *xiùcái* of Jìzhōu, Gāo Gānhé; the *xiùcái* of Yíngzhōu, Mǎ Jìngdé, Xǔ Sǎnchóu, and Hán Tóngbǎo; the *xiùcái* of Luòzhōu, Fù Huáidé; the *xiùcái* of Huáizhōu, Gǔ Dàozǐ; the *xiàolián* of Guǎngpíng Commandery, Lǐ Hànzǐ; the *xiàolián* of Bóhǎi Commandery, Bào Chángxuān; the *xiàolián* of Yángpíng Commandery, Jǐng Sūn; the former Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) of the Liángzhōu Prefecture, Wáng Jiǔyuán; and the former Water Section Aide (Shuǐcáo Cānjūn) of the Kāifǔ, Zhōu Zishēn—were all summoned by the Shàngshū to jointly edit and standardize the texts.
At that time, many books in the Imperial Archives (Mìfǔ)
contained errors. Sùn then proposed, saying:
"According to records, in the Hàn dynasty, Liú Xiàng, Colonel Who Guards Against the Environs (Zhōnglěi Xiàowèi), received an imperial command to collate books.
Whenever a book was finished,
he would memorialize
and typically state: 'The book of your servant Xiàng, the book of Colonel of Chángshuǐ Cān,
the books of the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ Gōng), the Erudites of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Bóshì),
and others, totaling a certain number of volumes, were compared and collated
before the final copy was made (*shāqīng*).
Now, the texts we are reviewing and collating
are intended for extremely important use,
originating from the Lántái
and to be housed in the Jiǎ Guǎn (Imperial Libraries).
Xiàng's past practices
are still preserved in the archives.
If we wish to proceed with editing and standardizing,
we must rely on many different editions.

The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng), Xíng Zǐcái; the Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàofù), Wèi Shōu; the Minister of the Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), Xīn Shù; the Vice Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Shàoqīng), Mù Zǐróng; the former Palace Gentleman (Huángmén Láng), Sīmǎ Zǐruì; and the late Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ), Lǐ Yèxīng—all possess extensive private collections.
I request that official letters be sent to borrow their editions for comparison and checking of errors and deficiencies."
Wèi Jǐn, Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān), forwarded the request to the Assembly of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Dūzuò).
In total, more than three thousand variant volumes were obtained.
Among the Five Classics and various histories,
scarcely any omissions or deficiencies remained.
In the eighth year,
an imperial edict commanded the Shàngshū
to conduct official selections for the Eastern and Western Secretariats. During the policy questions administered by the department in charge,
Sùn was ranked first of the time.
Yáng Yīn, Left Director of the Department of State Affairs (Zuǒ Púyè), appointed Sùn as an aide in his office.
Sùn declined, saying:
"My clan background is humble and poor,
and any official ranking (after vetting) will certainly not succeed.
I beg to be appointed to the supernumerary post of Cavalier Director (Yuánwài Sīmǎ Dū)."
Yīn said:
"High talent does not follow ordinary rules."
He specially memorialized and secured his appointment.
In the ninth
year, there was an edict promoting him directly to Supernumerary General (Yuánwài Jiāngjūn).
Afterwards, when Emperor Shìzǔ garrisoned Yè,
Sùn was summoned into the office of the Minister of Works (Sītú Fǔ) to manage the secretarial duties.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Sùn was transferred and appointed as Chief Clerk (Zhǔshū),
then promoted to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sǎnjì Shìláng).
At the beginning of the Tiāntǒng
reign period, he died of illness.
Liú Dì,
styled Zǐzhǎng,
was a native of Cóngtínglǐ in Péngchéng.
His grandfather, Fāng,
was the Grand Minister of the Court of Ceremonies (Tàicháng Qīng) for the Wèi.
His father, Huǐ,
was the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
Dì was sharp and clever in his youth.
He enjoyed falconry, hunting, riding, and archery,
taking pleasure in leisure activities,
loving socializing,
and being skilled in joking and teasing.
The commandery appointed him Master of Merit (Gōngcáo),
and the province ordered him to be Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
At the end of the Wèi period, he was summoned to the Supreme Headquarters (Bàfǔ),
and Shìzǔ made him Campaign Adjutant (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Office of the Open Palace of Yǒng'ān Gōng Jùn.
Dì, being far from his hometown
and weary of the journeying life,
steeled himself with indignation and effort,
dedicating his energy to reading.
Jìnyáng was a place where people gathered,
where officials from the Supreme Court (Bàcháo) converged,
and everyone was committed to feasting and assemblies.
While Dì was amidst the feasting and socializing,
books never left his hands.
Whenever he encountered a literary text he had not yet seen,
he would recite it all day long,
sometimes not returning home until dawn;
such was his love of learning.
He also paid close attention to literary expression
and was quite skilled in writing poetry.
Early in the Tiānbǎo era,
he served as the Magistrate (Xiànlìng) of Dìngtáo County.
He was dismissed due to an incident of impropriety,
and for over ten years, he could not receive an assignment.
In the Gānmíng year,
he served concurrently as Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Gate of the Palace (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì),
and was sent on an embassy to Xiāo Zhuāng, the Lord of Liáng.
Upon his return,
he concurrently served as Tri-Dukes Bureau Director (Sāngōng Lángzhōng).
In the first year of the Huángjiàn era,
he was appointed Stable Master of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
When Sùzōng died,
he followed Shìzǔ to Jìnyáng,
and was appointed Cavalier Attendant (Sànqí Shìláng),
concurrently serving as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies (Yícáo Lángzhōng).
After a long time,
he concurrently served as Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
Hé Shìkāi was favored and influential,
and Dì attached himself to him.
He was formally appointed Secretariat Attendant,
entering to manage confidential matters.
He concurrently served as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
and was sent as an envoy to the Lord of Chén.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng),
edited the National History,
and was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He was again appointed Acting Minister Director of the Agencies of the Third Rank (Jiǎ Yítóng Sānsī),
and served as Deputy Envoy to Zhōu.
The two states had just established relations,
and the ceremonial protocols were not yet settled.
Dì discussed and debated back and forth with the Zhōu court,
weighing both ancient and contemporary practices.
Most of the matters accorded with ritual propriety,
and his literary skill was also admirable,
earning him great fame.
After returning from the embassy,
he was appointed Minister Director of the Agencies of the Third Rank.
When Shìzǔ died,
he was sent out to be the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
When Zǔ Tǐng took control of the government,
Dì was transferred to be the Inspector of Rénzhōu (Rénzhōu Cìshǐ).
After Zǔ Tǐng was dismissed,
Dì was recalled,
appointed Attendant in the Hall of Literary Merit (Wénlín Guǎn),
re-appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and assigned to manage matters of the Palace Gate (Ménxià).
Not long after,
he was executed along with Cuī Jìshū and others,
at the age of forty-nine.
Initially, Dì and Tǐng respected each other for their literary talent
and established a bond like Lěi and Chén.
Furthermore, Dì arranged for his younger brother Jùn to marry Tǐng's daughter.
When Tǐng was about to dismiss Zhào Yànshēn and others,
he informed Dì beforehand,
and entrusted him with a secret memorial
to be submitted to the throne.
Yànshēn and others somehow learned of this
and lodged their defense first.
Consequently, Tǐng suspected that Dì had revealed his plans.
When Tǐng was subsequently dismissed,
Dì immediately sent his younger brother to divorce Tǐng's daughter.
Such was the lightness with which he initiated and severed relationships.
The poems, rhymed prose, and miscellaneous essays he composed totaled thirty scrolls.
His son, Yìmín,
was a Campaign Adjutant in the Office of the Open Palace.
Dì's younger brother, Chá,
was intelligent in his youth
and loved literature.
Between the Tiāntǒng and Wǔpíng eras,
he successively served as Attendant Censor of the Central Hall (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ),
concurrently Cavalier Attendant (Sànqí Shìláng),
welcoming and consoling the Chén envoy,
and Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yícáo Láng).
At the end of the Dàxiàng era of Zhōu,
he died while serving as Administrator of Lízhōu (Lízhōu Zhìzhōng).
His son, Xuándào,
possessed both talent and practical ability,
serving as a Cavalry Adjutant (Qíbīng Cānjūn) in Dìngzhōu.
Dì's cousin's son, Yǐ,
styled Jūnqīng.
His grandfather, Xīn,
was a Minister (Shàngshū) of Wèi,
killed by Gāozǔ.
Yǐ's father Jì, and Jì's younger brother [Wáng] Jùn, both fled south of the Yangtze River (Jiāngnán).
Yǐ was adopted.
During the Wǔdìng era, he returned north with [Wáng] Jùn.
[Wáng] Jùn was granted the title Viscount of Línyǐng (Línyǐng Zǐ),
and died during the Dàníng era while serving as Commander of the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Sīmǎ).
Yǐ loved literature,
was skilled in running script,
and had a very fine demeanor.
He successively served as Outer Military Adjutant (Wàibīng Cānjūn) in Yíngzhōu, Master of Merit in the Office of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōngcáo),
Attendant in the Hall of Literary Merit,
and was appointed Judge in the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Sīzhí).
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty, he was the Commander (Sīmǎ) of Fūzhōu,
where he died.
Xún Shìxùn,
was a native of Guǎngpíng.
He loved learning and possessed deep thought,
his writing was clear and elegant,
and was appreciated by those who understood him.
At the end of the Wǔdìng era,
he was recommended as a Cultivated Talent (Xiùcai) of Sīzhōu.
He was not appointed to office until the tenth year of Tiānbǎo.
During the Huángjiàn era,
Mǎ Jìngdé recommended him as a Chief Scribe (Zhǔshū).
During Shìzǔ's time,
he was transferred to be Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
His appearance was very ugly,
but he was employed because of his literary talent.
Once, he had a matter requiring a memorial to the throne.
It happened that Shìzǔ was in the inner court,
and the attendants transmitting the message could not recall Shìxùn's name,
so they referred to him as "the ugly Drafter."
Shìzǔ said:
"That must be Shìxùn."
They looked at the sealed cover, and indeed it was,
which caused all the palace staff to laugh happily.
When the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ) ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Secretariat Attendant,
and was deemed competent for the position.
He and Lǐ Ruò and others compiled the Diǎnyán (Canonical Words), which circulated in the world.
He died in the year the Qí state was extinguished.
Yán Zhītuī,
courtesy name Jiè,
was a man from Lángyé Línyí.
His ninth-generation ancestor, Hán,
followed Jìn Yuán (Emperor Yuán of Jìn) in crossing the river eastward,
holding offices that reached Shìzhōng, Yòu Guānglù, and Marquis of Xīpíng.
His father, Xié,
was the Cān Jūn (Adviser-in-Attendance) of the Zhèn Xī Fǔ (Pacifying the West Headquarters) under Yì (Prince of Xiāngdōng) of Liáng.
His family had traditionally excelled in the *Zhōu Guān* and *Zuǒ Shì* (Commentary),
and Zhītuī inherited the family legacy early.
At the age of twelve,
when Yì personally lectured on Zhuāng and Lǎo (Zhuāngzi and Lǎozǐ),
he immediately joined the disciples.
Empty talk was not to his liking,
so he returned to studying the Rites and Commentaries (*Lǐ* and *Zhuàn*).
He widely read all types of books,
mastering everything,
and his prose and sentiment were elegant and refined,
earning high praise from the Xī Fǔ (Western Headquarters).
Yì appointed him as the Zuǒ Cháng Shì of his state,
and additionally, Zhèn Xī Mò Cáo Cān Jūn (Adviser-in-Attendance for Records and Litigation in the Pacifying the West Headquarters).
He was fond of drinking alcohol,
often acting unrestrained,
and paid little attention to appearance or conduct.
Public opinion at the time therefore thought little of him.
Yì sent his heir, Fāngzhū, to garrison Yǐngzhōu,
and put Zhītuī in charge of the secretarial duties.
When Hóu Jǐng captured Yǐngzhōu,
he repeatedly tried to kill Zhītuī,
but thanks to Wáng Zé, the Lángzhōng of the Mobile Secretariat, he was spared.
He was captured and sent to Jiànyè.
When Jǐng was defeated,
he returned to Jiānglíng.
At that time, Yì had already established himself (as Emperor Yuán of Liáng),
and he appointed Zhītuī as Sǎn Qí Shì Láng,
managing memorials concerning personnel matters.
Later, (Jiānglíng) was defeated by the Zhōu army.
Grand General Lǐ Xiǎnqìng valued him highly,
recommending him to Hóngnóng,
where he was put in charge of the correspondence for Xiǎnqìng’s elder brother, Yángpíng Gōng Yuǎn.
When the Yellow River suddenly swelled,
he prepared a boat and fled with his wife and children.
Passing through the dangerous rapids of Dǐzhù,
people at the time praised his bravery and decisiveness.
Xiǎnzǔ (Emperor Wǔchéng of Northern Qí) saw him and was pleased,
immediately appointing him Fèng Cháoqǐng.
He was brought into the palace library (*nèi guǎn*),
attending the Emperor,
and was frequently shown favor.
At the end of Tiānbǎo (era),
he accompanied the Emperor to Tiānchí,
and was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Duàn Xiàoxìn, the Zhōngshū Láng (Secretary of the Central Secretariat), was ordered to bring the imperial edict out to show Zhītuī.
Zhītuī was drinking outside the camp.
When Xiàoxìn returned and reported the situation,
Xiǎnzǔ said,
"Hold it for now."
Consequently, the appointment was dropped.
At the end of Héqīng (era),
he was recommended to be Zhàozhōu Gōng Cáo Cān Jūn (Adviser-in-Attendance for Merit Evaluation in Zhàozhōu).
Soon after, he served as a commissioned scholar (*dài zhào*) in the Wénlín Guǎn,
and was appointed Sītú Lùshì Cān Jūn (Adviser-in-Attendance for Records in the Ministry of the Multitudes).
Zhītuī was intelligent and quick-witted,
widely knowledgeable and eloquent,
skilled in letter writing,
and fluent and clear in response.
He was highly valued by Zǔ Tǐng,
who instructed him to oversee the affairs of the Wénlín Guǎn
and countersign documents.
He was soon promoted to Tōng Zhí Sǎn Qí Cháng Shì,
and shortly thereafter took the concurrent post of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Whenever the Emperor required something,
he would order a eunuch messenger (*zhōng shǐ*) to transmit the command.
Zhītuī would receive and announce the instructions,
and everyone in the Guǎn (Wénlín Guǎn) received their orders and prohibitions from him.
The memorials submitted
all bore his seal and signature.
He presented them at the Jìnxián Gate,
and only left after receiving a reply.
He was also skilled in calligraphy and writing,
supervised the collation and transcription of texts,
and was diligent and quick in handling affairs,
earning the reputation of being highly competent.
The Emperor treated him with great kindness,
and his favor grew profound,
causing him to be envied by powerful officials and meritorious subjects,
who often wished to harm him.
When Cuī Jìshū and others were planning to submit a remonstrance,
Zhītuī feigned an urgent need and returned home,
thus avoiding signing the joint memorial.
When the remonstrating officials were summoned,
Zhītuī was also called in,
but upon checking, his name was not found,
and he was thus spared misfortune.
Soon after, he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
When the Zhōu army captured Jìnyáng,
the Emperor returned to Yè with a small escort of cavalry.
In his distress, he had no plan to follow.
Zhītuī, through the eunuch Shìzhōng Dèng Chángyóng, proposed the strategy of fleeing to Chén,
and furthermore urged the recruitment of over a thousand warriors from Wú (the South) to serve as personal guards,
taking the route through Qīng and Xú (provinces) to seek refuge in the state of Chén.
The Emperor largely accepted this plan
and informed the Chancellor Gāo Ānàgōng and others.
Ānàgōng did not wish to enter Chén,
and argued that the Wú warriors were untrustworthy
and should not be recruited.
He advised the Emperor to send valuables and heavy baggage toward Qīngzhōu,
and temporarily hold the lands of Sān Qí.
If those could not be secured,
they should then slowly sail south across the sea.
Although Zhītuī's plan was not followed,
he was nevertheless appointed Prefect of Píngyuán
and ordered to guard the ford on the Yellow River.
When Qí (Northern Qí) fell, he entered Zhōu (Northern Zhōu).
At the end of Dàxiàng (era), he became Yùshǐ Shàng Shì (Senior Officer in the Censorate).
During the Kāihuáng (era) of Suí,
the Crown Prince summoned him to be an Xuéshì (Scholar),
and treated him with great respect.
Soon after, he died of illness.
He authored thirty chapters of prose and compiled twenty chapters of *Jiā Xùn* (Family Instructions),
both circulating in the world.
He once composed the *Guān Wǒ Shēng Fù* (Rhapsody on Viewing My Life),
whose literary style was clear and profound.
Its words were: Looking up at the boundlessness of pure emptiness,
looking down at the vastness of deep mystery.
Having begotten the people and established teachings,
thus administrators divided the borders,
including Zhū Xià and excluding the Yí Dí,
praising the Five Thearchs and venerating the Three Kings.
The Great Way slept and the sun was obscured,

Alas for Zhào Wǔ who created evil,

The Máo Tóu
played with their golden cauldrons,

The Chán and Jiàn rivers turned into deserts,

Therefore, my King moved his destiny eastward,

south.

Eulogy: The Nine Schools and Hundred Masters
establish words and establish virtue.

Biographies Thirty-eight: Upright Officials: Zhāng Huáyuán, Sòng Shìliáng (younger brother Shìguǐ), Láng Jī, Mèng Yè, Cuī Bóqiān, Sū Qióng, Fáng Bào, Lù Qùbìng.
The former kings managed and governed the world,
ruling the common people.
Criminal law was used to prohibit their wickedness,
and ritual teachings were used to guard against their desires.
Therefore, offices were divided and officials appointed,
to jointly govern all under heaven.
The Book of Documents says:
"He who knows men is wise;
he who can appoint men to office and bring peace to the people is benevolent."
A wise and perceptive ruler
will certainly achieve clean and clear ministers.
A dim and chaotic court
often possesses greedy and cruel officials.
Gāozǔ restored order from chaos,
harboring benevolence (yǐn) in his heart.
Thus, the multitude of prefects and magistrates
were mostly capable and competent.
Yet, he also appointed generals who had achieved merit in battle
to govern the outer territories.
They did not understand the principles of governance,
and had no knowledge of administrative methods.
Not only were they ignorant of ancient sayings and past conduct,
but they even began by learning to rely on judicial decisions assigned to their departments.
They were insatiable in their accumulation of wealth,
and their depravity and cruelty never ceased.
Although some were upright (zhí shéng),
they ultimately never reformed.
Alas!
This was a great failing of the court.
After the Dàníng era,
both culture and refinement were lacking.
Offices were sold and judicial decisions bartered,
with collusion between superiors and inferiors.
Descending to the final years,
the defilement of goods and bribery intensified.
Among the upright officials of the Qí Dynasty,
such as Xīn Shù and others, there were not a few.
Many of them rose to prominence through official rank and title
and have separate biographies.
As for those like Fáng Zhònggàn and his group,
who were able to stand out prominently at the end of Wǔpíng,
they are all the more commendable.
Now, I have gathered and listed Zhāng Huáyuán and others here among the Upright Officials.
Zhāng Huáyuán,
courtesy name Guómǎn,
was a native of Dàijùn.
In his youth, he was intelligent and perceptive,
and possessed admirable capacity and bearing.
When Gāozǔ established the Grand General's (Piàojì) Headquarters,
he was brought in as Cānjūn (Staff Officer) of the Judicial Bureau.
He was promoted to Aide (Shǔ) in the Grand Chancellor's Headquarters,
and constantly attended the Grand Chancellor's side.
Following him at Xìndū,
he was deeply trusted and favored by Gāozǔ.
Whenever Gāozǔ issued commands to the three armies,
he invariably instructed Huáyuán to proclaim his wishes and intentions.
When Zhōu Wéndì first took control of Yōngzhōu,
Gāozǔ still wished to enlighten him regarding right versus rebellion,
so he sent Huáyuán to enter the Pass and persuade him.
Zhōu Wén secretly harbored the intention of detaining him.
He said to Huáyuán:
“If you can bend your noble path here,
we shall share wealth and honor together.
Otherwise, your life hangs upon this day.”
Huáyuán replied:
“The King of Bóhǎi was born in accordance with destiny,
surely permitted by Heaven.
Because you, Illustrious Sir, occupy the small territory west of the Pass,
and have cut yourself off,
he thus sent Huáyuán to convey his intent to you.
If you, Illustrious Sir, do not use this day to change your plans,
transforming disaster into fortune,
but instead wish to threaten me,
then death is all that awaits.”
Zhōu Wén admired his integrity and uprightness,
and therefore allowed him to return east.
Gāozǔ, believing Huáyuán had been gone long and had not returned,
frequently sighed with regret for him.
When he heard of his arrival,
joy showed in his expression.
Huáyuán was repeatedly promoted to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu.
The people felt moved and submitted to him,
and banditry gradually ceased.
The prefectural prison previously held over a thousand inmates.
Huáyuán decided their cases and released them all.
By the end of the year,
there were only a few dozen heavily convicted criminals remaining.
Huáyuán also sent them home to observe the New Year (Shēnhè),
and they returned to the prison according to the agreed date.
Previously, fierce beasts frequently caused havoc within the prefecture.
Since Huáyuán governed the prefecture,
suddenly, six *lùbó* appeared and devoured them.
Everyone believed this was due to the effect of his virtuous governance.
Later, he died while in office.
All the people of the prefecture, old and young, wailed and mourned him.
Sòng Shìliáng,
courtesy name Yuányǒu,
was a native of Guǎngpíng.
At the age of fifteen,
he already possessed courage and spirit.
He answered the call to join the army for the Northern Expedition,
and repeatedly achieved military merit.
Soon after, he became a Palace Attendant Censor (Diànzhōng Shì Yùshǐ),
and was sent to Héběi to register households (Kuòhù),
where he successfully registered a large number of undocumented and shiftless people.
Upon his return, seeing many bones beside the city walls of Jǐjùn,
he issued an official document to the prefectures and commanderies,
ordering all the remains to be collected and buried.
That night,
a sweet, soaking rain fell.
Upon returning,
Xiàozhuāng commended him, saying:
“I know that the number of adult males (dīng) you registered is double the original census.
If all officials applied themselves like this,
it would be like gaining another realm.”
He was sent out and appointed Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Qīnghé.
Shìliáng’s talents and knowledge were composed and brilliant,
and he was especially skilled in methods of governance.
He had not been in the commandery long
when his reputation was already very high.
To the southeast of the commandery lay Qǔtí.
A single clan, the Chénggōngs, lived there, taking advantage of its rugged terrain.
Many groups of bandits gathered there.
People had a saying about it:
“I would rather cross Dōngwú and Kuàijī
than pass through Chénggōng’s Qǔtí.”
Shìliáng implemented eight regulatory articles,
and the bandits fled to other territories.
The people subsequently sang a ballad:
“Though Qǔtí is dangerous, what good is it to bandits?
But when Sòng Gōng is here, they hide themselves.”
Later, during the Tiānbǎo era of Qí, there was a great amnesty.
Since the commandery already had not a single prisoner,
the many officials merely bowed to receive the edict.
Inside the prison, wild grain grew,
and peach trees and wormwood also grew profusely.
Daily, the yamen gate was empty and silent,
and there were no longer any litigants.
That winter,
Sweet Spring water (Lǐquán) emerged within the territory.
When his successor arrived,
the entire city came out to bid him farewell.
An old man named Dīng Jīngāng wept as he stepped forward,
and expressed his gratitude, saying:
“I am ninety years old
and remember thirty-five administrations.
You are not only skilled at governing,
but your integrity is also complete.
Now that we lose this worthy ruler,
how will the people cope?”
No one failed to cling to him, weeping.
He was appointed Administrator of Dōngjùn.
He died in office.
Shìliáng was diligent in his studies
and loved writing.
He authored the *Zìlüè* in five fascicles and the *Sòng Shì Biélù* in ten scrolls.
He and his younger brother Shìguǐ were both renowned for their filial piety and fraternity.
Shìguǐ,
was strict and orderly since childhood.
He loved law and regulations,
and gradually rose to become Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi Qīng).
People in Luòzhōu gathered together intending to rob the River Bridge.
Officials arrested and investigated them,
implicating the principal offenders and seventeen hundred associates.
When Cuī Xiān served as the Tíngwèi,
he considered the case to be treason (Fǎn),
and the case remained unresolved for several years.
When Shìguǐ became the Vice Minister (Shǎoqīng),
he ruled the affair to be robbery (Jié).
Consequently, the ringleaders were executed,
while all others implicated were released.
At that time, Sū Zhēnzhī, the Chief Justice of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Zhèng), was also famous for his balanced efficiency.
A saying circulated within the judicial court:
“It is Sū Zhēnzhī who resolves doubts and ambiguities;
it is Sòng Shìguǐ who examines the surface and sees the inner nature.”
People at the time considered them the “Two Excellencies of the Court.”
When prisoners from the Southern Bureau (Nántái) reached the Tíngwèi,
Shìguǐ often cleared them.
He was then transferred to act temporarily as Censor (Yùshǐ),
intending to investigate cases of abuse there.
The Commandant (Zhōngwèi), Bì Yìyún, refused to transfer the relevant documents.
The official transfers went back and forth without cessation.
Shìguǐ then submitted a memorial,
strongly denouncing Yìyún’s cruelty and arbitrary power.
Xiǎnzǔ summoned the two men for an audience,
and personally instructed Shìguǐ, saying:
“I know the Bureau (Tái) has long bullied the Court (Sì).
You are able to uphold justice and contend with them.
Just maintain this attitude,
and do not worry about failing to achieve wealth and honor.”
He instructed Yìyún, saying:
“What you have recently done truly deserves death,
but because your intention was aimed at hating evil,
I shall pardon you this once.”
He then turned and addressed the court officials:
“These two men are both my staunch and upright ministers.”
When Shìguǐ died from illness,
all the prisoners detained in the Tíngwèi and the Yùshǐ offices, hearing of Shìguǐ’s death,
all wept, saying:
“Now that Sòng Tíngwèi is dead,
how can we possibly live!”
Xiàowáng, Sòng Shìliáng’s cousin’s son,
was learned,
and also enjoyed composing literary works.
His appearance was short and ugly, but he enjoyed criticizing and evaluating others.
Contemporary opinion greatly disliked him.
He served as Registrar (Cānjūn) in Duàn Xiàoyán’s General’s Establishment (Kāifǔ),
and was later recommended to serve as Erudite (Wénxué) for the Prince of Běipíng.
When his request to enter the Wénlín Guǎn was unsuccessful,
he subsequently started slandering and criticizing the court officials.
He compiled the *Biélù* in twenty scrolls.
When Qí was pacified,
he changed its title to *Guāndōng Fēngsú Zhuàn*,
further expanding his observations and hearings,
compiling it into thirty scrolls, and submitting it.
His statements were often exaggerated and erroneous,
and the chapters were redundant and disorganized,
lacking the style of a scholarly work.
Láng Jī,
courtesy name Shìyè,
was a native of Zhōngshān.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
had a handsome beard,
had broad exposure to the classical texts (*Féndiǎn*),
and was especially proficient in official duties.
He started his career as an Attendant (Fèng Cháoqǐng),
and was repeatedly promoted to General Guarding the Frontier (Zhènjiāng) of Hǎixī.
Wú Míngchè of Liáng led his forces to attack and besiege Hǎixī.
Jī encouraged the soldiers and the populace,
and firmly held the city for over a hundred days.
Military provisions were nearly exhausted,
and weapons were also used up.
He even resorted to carving wood into arrows
and cutting paper for fletchings.
When the siege was lifted and he returned to court,
the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Púshè), Yáng Yīn, met him and commended him, saying:
“You were originally a civil official,
yet you demonstrated military strategy.
Carving wood and cutting paper
are both unprecedented methods.
How do the ingenuity of Bān and Mò
surpass your thinking?”
Later, he administered Yǐngchuān Jùn,
where cases had accumulated for years,
but within a few days,
all were analyzed and resolved.
When the official report came down,
it entirely approved Jī’s submissions.
Once the legal statutes were clarified,
litigation ceased and prisons emptied.
Officials and common people, far and near,
all celebrated together.
Jī’s nature was pure and cautious,
seeking nothing for himself.
He once told someone:
"In the place where one serves in office,
there is no need even to make a wooden pillow,
let alone something more important than this."
He only occasionally ordered books to be copied.
Pān Zǐyì once sent him a letter saying:
"Copying books while in office
is also a charming fault (fēngliú zuìguò)."
Jī replied in a letter:
"Observing one's faults and thereby knowing one's benevolence—
that is acceptable."
Later, he died in office.
When his coffin was being brought home,
people from near and far came to see him off,
all grasping the shafts of the carriage and weeping sorrowfully.
Mèng Yè,
courtesy name Jìngyè,
was a native of Ànguó, Jùlù.
His family was originally poor and humble.
When young, he served as a prefectural clerk.
His nature was honest and cautious.
When his colleagues stole official silk,
and offered him thirty bolts,
he refused to accept them.
When Shào, the Prince of Péngchéng of the Wèi dynasty, was appointed to Dìngzhōu,
Mèng Yè was appointed Diǎnqiān (Archive Keeper).
Liú Rénzhī, the Commandant, said to Yè:
"I am in charge outside,
and you reside within.
If we unite our efforts and work together,
perhaps we can succeed."
Soon after, Rénzhī was summoned to the capital to serve as Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Imperial Secretariat).
Before setting out, he reported to Shào, saying:
"Among Your Highness's entourage, the only person trustworthy is Mèng Yè.
I recommend giving him sole responsibility.
The rest are not reliable."
He also parted with Yè,
holding his hand and saying:
"Now that I am leaving the capital,
you will lose your support.
I fear that while you remain here,
you will not be able to protect yourself completely.
Only by being upright and straightforward,
I urge you to encourage yourself."
Yè possessed only one horse,
which died from emaciation.
Shào, knowing Yè's family was poor,
ordered the officials of the prefecture to eat the horse meat together,
intending thereby to compensate him handsomely.
Yè firmly declined, not daring to accept.
Shào then teased Yè, saying:
"You are trying to win a famous reputation (yāomíng rén)."
[Yè] replied:
"I, Yè, being humble and minor,
serve beneath your authority.
Since I cannot offer any benefit,
how can I bear to damage your reputation for integrity?"
Later, Gāozǔ wrote a letter to Shào, saying:
"The Diǎnqiān whose surname is Mèng is extremely dedicated;
why have you not kept him close by?"
Shào
was Gāozǔ’s son-in-law.
Rénzhī later became Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Before leaving, he spoke to Cuī Xiān of the Ministry of Personnel, saying:
"Among the gentlemen of your prefecture,
there is only Mèng Yè.
He should be selected and promoted.
Others are not trustworthy."
Cuī Xiān asked Yè:
"When you were previously in Dìngzhōu,
what administrative achievements did you have
that caused Liú Xīyǎn to admire and praise you so highly?"
[Yè] replied:
"I am by nature simple and honest.
I only know how to cultivate myself;
I have no other merits."
In the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era (550 CE),
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, was appointed Governor of Sīzhōu.
Hearing of Yè's reputation and conduct,
he summoned him again to serve as Fǎcáo (Judicial Official).
Yè was short and slight in appearance.
When he was granted an audience,
Yuè privately disdained his small stature,
smiling but saying nothing.
Later, having observed the decisions Yè made,
he said to Yè:
"The clarity of your judgments
can truly be said to surpass the usefulness suggested by your physical appearance."
Soon after, he was promoted to Governor of Dōngjùn.
He became renowned for his leniency and kindness.
That year,
wheat stalks grew five ears on one stem,
and others had three or four ears on one stem.
All the people of the commandery believed this was due to the influence of his governance.
He soon died of illness.
Cuī Bóqiān,
courtesy name Shìxùn,
was a native of Bólíng.
His father, Wényè,
was the Governor of Jùlù.
Bóqiān was orphaned and poor when young,
and excelled at caring for his mother.
Gāozǔ summoned him to Jìnyáng,
appointing him Gōngcáo (Merit Officer) in the Chancellor's residence.
He praised him, saying:
"Pure, upright, and dedicated to public service:
truly a good assistant."
He was promoted to Biéjià (Assistant Governor) of Yíngzhōu.
Shìzōng appointed him Sīmǎ (Commander) of the Capital Region,
commending him thus:
"You exhibited your abilities in the Yíng region,
where songs of peace have already become known.
The duties of the governorship are heavy,
and so this office is conferred upon you."
His cousin Xiān
held great favor and importance at the time.
Although Bóqiān and Xiān were colleagues, old friends, and former classmates,
unless there was a happy or sad occasion (like weddings or funerals),
Bóqiān never visited him to ask for favors.
Later, he was appointed Governor of Jìběi.
His kindness and trustworthiness became widespread.
He changed the whips used for punishment, making them of tanned leather,
unable to bear the sight of blood,
merely intending to inflict shame.
A certain court noble traveling through the commandery boundary,
asked the people how the Governor’s administration was.
[They] replied:
"The kindness and transformation brought by the Governor
are unheard of in ancient times."
Then they recited a song composed by the people: 'Governor Cuī,
skilled at governing,
changed the painful whip,
