spread his awesome virtue,
the people do not fight.' "
The visitor asked:
"Since you praise his kindness and transformation,
how can there still be awesomeness (wēi)?"
[They] said:
"The senior officials dread his awesomeness (wēi),
while the common people benefit from his kindness (huì)."
When he was summoned to Yè,
the common people cried and wailed, blocking the road.
Because his younger brother Ràng was in Guānzhōng,
he did not serve in an internal office again.
He was appointed Governor of Nánjùlù.
Regardless of whether matters were great or small,
he personally oversaw them.
If there were poor and weak people whose cases had not been addressed,
they all said:
"We have our own White-Bearded Duke (Báixū Gōng);
we have no worry that [the case] will not be decided."
Later, he became Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Imperial Household).
He died.
Sū Qióng,
courtesy name Zhēnzhī,
was a native of Wǔqiáng.
His father, Bèi,
served the Wèi court, rising to Wèiwèi Shàoqīng (Vice Minister of the Court of the Guard).
When Qióng was young, he accompanied his father near the border.
He once paid respects to Cáo Zhī, the Inspector of Dōngjīngzhōu.
Zhī jokingly asked him:
"Do you want an official post?"
[Qióng] replied:
"Offices are established to seek men;
men do not seek office."
Zhī was impressed by his reply
and appointed him Fǔ Zhǎngliú Cānjūn (Staff Officer and Commandant).
Wénxiāng, having received the title Yítóng Kāifǔ (Adviser to the State),
recruited him as Xíngyù Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Judicial Affairs),
constantly encouraging him in his duties.
There was once a case of highway robbery in Bìngzhōu.
The Zhǎngliú Cānjūn investigated the case,
and the suspected robbers had all been interrogated and confessed.
The families who lost property had identified the suspects,
but the stolen goods were not recovered.
Wénxiāng handed the case to Qióng, ordering him to conduct a thorough reinvestigation.
Qióng separately investigated and found the real culprits, Yuán Jǐngróng and over ten others,
and recovered the stolen property as evidence.
Wénxiāng laughed heartily
and said to those who had previously wrongly implicated the suspects:
"If you had not encountered my excellent Staff Officer,
you nearly caused people to be unjustly killed."
He was appointed Nán Qīnghé Tàishǒu.
That commandery had many bandits,
but when Qióng arrived,
the people and officials were reverent,
and villainy and banditry ceased.
If wicked people from neighboring territories
happened to pass through the borderlands,
none failed to be captured and sent away.
Wèi Shuāngchéng, a resident of Líng Xiàn, lost an ox.
He suspected his villager, Wèi Zǐbīn,
and sent him to the commandery.
After a thorough investigation,
Qióng knew Zǐbīn was not the thief,
and immediately released him.
Shuāngchéng complained, saying:
“The Fǔjūn let the thief go!
How can the common people recover their ox?”
Qióng ignored him,
but secretly went out to investigate privately,
and independently apprehended the actual thief.
From then on, livestock were not penned up;
many were left scattered freely,
saying:
“Just entrust them to the Fǔjūn.”
There was a wealthy notable from a neighboring commandery who deposited valuables within the borders [of Nán Qīnghé] to avoid bandits.
When robbers urgently pressed him,
he declared:
“My property has already been entrusted to Sū Gōng.”
The robbers then left.
In Píngyuán Jùn, there was a demonic bandit named Liú Hēigǒu,
who formed partnerships and gathered followers,
extending toward Cānghǎi.
The people under Qióng’s jurisdiction lived in connected villages,
but none were influenced or implicated by them.
Neighboring districts admired his virtue because of this.
More than a hundred former bandits in the commandery
were all employed as his attendants,
and whether it concerned human goodness or wickedness,
or a senior official offering someone a cup of wine,
he knew everything immediately.
Qióng was naturally pure and cautious,
and did not send out private correspondence.
The religious man Dàorén Dàoyán was the Jì Zhōu Shāmén Tǒng (Director of Monks),
with immense wealth and assets.
He had made many loans for interest in the commandery,
and customarily used the commandery and county officials to collect them.
When he sought an audience,
Qióng anticipated his intentions.
Whenever they met, Qióng would discuss and question him on profound principles,
and Dàoyán would respond with reverence.
Although Dàoyán came repeatedly regarding debts,
he had no means to open his mouth about them.
His disciples asked him why this was the case.
Dàoyán replied:
“Every time I see the Fǔjūn,
he immediately takes me up into the blue clouds,
how could I possibly discuss earthly matters?”
A commandery resident, Zhào Yǐng, had previously served as Lèlíng Tàishǒu,
and retired at the age of eighty.
In early fifth month,
he obtained a pair of fresh melons and personally brought them as a gift.
Yǐng presumed upon his old age,
and earnestly requested [Qióng] to accept them.
Qióng subsequently kept them for him,
and placed them on the beam in the administrative hall,
and never cut them open.
People then competitively offered new fruits,
but upon reaching the gate,
and knowing that Yǐng’s melons were still there,
they looked at each other and went away.
There were commoners, the brothers Yǐ Pǔmíng, who were disputing over land.
The dispute had lasted for years without resolution,
and each side brought in various supporters,
reaching up to a hundred people.
Qióng summoned the Pǔmíng brothers and admonished them before the crowd, saying:
“What is hard to obtain in this world are brothers;
what is easy to obtain is land.
Suppose you gain the land but lose the heart of your brother—what then?”
He then shed tears,
and everyone in the crowd wept and cried.
The Pǔmíng brothers kowtowed and begged to reconsider outside.
Though they had lived separately for ten years,
they subsequently returned to live together.
Every spring,
he would gather together the great Confucian scholars, such as Wèi Jìlóng
and Tián Yuánfèng, to lecture in the commandery school.
During the leisure time of the court clerks from handling documents,
he ordered them all to receive instruction.
People at the time referred to the clerk offices as “the students’ barracks.”
He prohibited excessive shrines,
and for marriage and funerals, he taught and commanded moderation and adherence to proper rites.
Furthermore, during the silkworm month, he would preemptively issue standard samples of cotton floss and silk fabric throughout his jurisdiction.
The order and method of military levies were all established with clear regulations.
As for corvée service,
the work was always completed ahead of schedule,
and the senior officials of the commanderies and counties rarely incurred the punishment of ten strokes for delay or error.
At that time, there was no Zhōu or commandery that did not send someone to his borders
to inquire about his administrative methods.
During the Tiānbǎo period,
the commandery suffered a great flood,
causing human suffering,
with over a thousand households running out of food.
Qióng universally gathered the households in his jurisdiction that possessed grain,
and personally borrowed grain from them to provide for the starving.
The Zhōu, calculating the households, levied taxes,
and also wanted to demand repayment for the borrowed grain.
The administration official told Qióng:
“Although you showed compassion for the starving,
I fear that this crime will implicate the Fǔjūn.”
Qióng said:
“If I alone incur guilt,
yet save a thousand households,
what cause is there for complaint?”
He then submitted a memorial explaining the situation,
and the investigating commissioner granted a full exemption,
and the households were saved.
When these people comforted their children,
they all said, “The Fǔjūn gave you life.”
He served in the commandery for six years,
and the populace cherished him,
and consequently, not a single person traveled to the Zhōu [to submit a complaint].
In the four reports sent before and after,
he was ranked as the most outstanding.
He was dismissed from office due to mourning.
When old friends gave him gifts,
he accepted none of them.
Soon after, he was reactivated as Sīzhí and Tíngwèi Zhèng.
Court officials lamented his demotion.
Shàngshū Xīn Shù said:
“Since he is both ‘straight’ (zhí) and ‘upright’ (zhèng) [referencing his titles],
the titles fix his substance.
There is no need to worry that he will not be promoted.”
When Qióng first served as Qīnghé Tàishǒu,
Péi Xiànbó was the Jì Zhōu Cìshǐ (Provincial Inspector of Jì Zhōu).
Péi was severe in his enforcement of the law,
while Qióng was benevolent in nurturing the people.
Fáng Yányòu served in Lèlíng Jùn,
and passed through the Zhōu capital.
Péi asked him about the public reputation.
Yòu replied:
“I only hear that the Tàishǒu is good,
and the Cìshǐ is bad.”
Péi said:
“He who earns popular acclaim is not perfectly impartial.”
Yòu replied:
“If that were the case,
then Huáng Bà and Gōng Suì would be your criminals.”
Later, an imperial edict was issued,
commanding each Zhōu to recommend officials who were pure and capable.
Because of his previous statement, Péi
was afraid of being trapped by Qióng.
Qióng reported Péi's wrongs and delays.
Those who discussed the matter praised Qióng’s impartiality.
Bì Yìyún served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor-in-Chief),
and governed his office with fierce harshness.
Judicial officials feared and avoided him,
and none dared to disobey.
Qióng’s investigations aimed strictly at fairness,
and those who had their grievances cleared were very numerous.
The case files of the judicial ministries and Censorate
began to be investigated by Qióng.
He was promoted to Sāngōng Lángzhōng.
In Zhào Zhōu, Qīnghé, and Nán Zhōng, there were people repeatedly accused of plotting rebellion.
Both before and after, these cases were handed over to Qióng for investigation.
Most of the cases were cleared of guilt.
Shàngshū Cuī Áng said to Qióng:
“If you want to establish achievements and reputation,
you should think of other principles.
If you repeatedly clear people accused of rebellion,
how lightly you hold your own life?”
Qióng replied sternly:
“Those I clear are innocent of false accusations;
I do not release rebels.”
Áng was greatly ashamed.
A saying circulated in the capital because of him:
“For decisive judgment without doubt, there is Sū Zhēnzhī.”
He was promoted to Zuǒchéng,
and managed the affairs of Xúzhōu.
In the Wǔjí Sì temple within the city of Xúzhōu, one hundred bronze statues were suddenly stolen.
The relevant officials investigated,
and based on neighborhood guards, night watches, and suspected trails,
dozens of people were arrested and imprisoned.
Qióng immediately released them.
The temple monks complained and resented that he did not pursue the thieves.
Qióng sent the monk away,
apologizing, saying:
"Just return to the temple for now;
when the statues are recovered, I will send them myself."
Ten days after that,
he covertly obtained the names of the thieves and the location of the loot,
and went directly to capture and ambush them.
All were verified and recovered.
The gang of thieves confessed,
and both clergy and laity praised and submitted to him.
The old system prohibited merchants and traders from crossing the Huái River without permission.
Huáinán suffered a lean year (famine).
He memorialized, requesting permission for them to buy grain from Huáiběi.
Later, the people of Huáiběi were starving,
and he again requested open purchase of grain from Huáinán.
Thus, merchants and traders were able to travel back and forth,
both sides mutually assisting each other,
and the benefits from water and land trade
extended to Hébĕi.
Later, he became Dàlǐ Qīng, and then Qí fell.
He served the Zhōu dynasty as the Administrator of Bólíng.
Fáng Bào,
courtesy name Zhònggàn,
was a native of Qīnghé.
His grandfather was Fǎshòu,
who has a biography in the *Wèi Shū*.
His father was Yìzōng.
Bào had an imposing physique
and a beautiful voice and demeanor.
He first served as Kāifǔ Cānjūn,
concurrently Xíngtái Lángzhōng,
following Mùróng Shàozōng.
Shàozōng claimed he was fated to die by water,
so he bathed inside his warship,
and also threw himself into the water,
hoping to ward off the disaster by preempting it.
Bào said:
"Destiny resides in Heaven;
how can human reasoning prolong or shorten it?
If your Lordship truly faces disaster,
I fear it cannot be averted by rituals.
If in reality there is none,
what need is there for rituals?"
Shàozōng laughed and said:
"I cannot escape common customs;
I am merely acting thus."
Not long after, Shàozōng drowned.
The contemporary opinion held that Bào knew the subtle signs.
He was promoted to Administrator of Lèlíng.
He governed with stable gravity,
showing compassion for the poor and weak.
Bào’s administrative courtyard was simple and quiet,
and the prisons were empty.
The prefectural seat bordered the sea,
and the water taste was mostly salty and bitter.
Bào ordered a well to be dug,
and sweet spring water was obtained.
People far and near believed this was due to his righteous governance.
After Bào resigned and returned home,
the water in the well became salty again.
When Qí was destroyed,
he returned to his home village to live in retirement.
He repeatedly declined official summons, citing illness.
He died at home.
Lù Qùbìng
was a native of Yángpíng.
His demeanor was easygoing and clear,
and his appearance was remarkable and unusual.
He first served as Kāifǔ Cānjūn.
An imperial edict required the use of scholars as county magistrates,
and Qùbìng was appointed Magistrate of Ráoyáng County, Dìngzhōu.
Qùbìng was adept and experienced in contemporary affairs,
and his character was rather stern and resolute,
so people dared not deceive him.
However, he was utterly incorruptible and impartial,
and was praised and respected by officials and commoners.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Chéng'ān.
Near the capital there were three counties: Yè, Línzhāng, and Chéng'ān.
Being close to the imperial court,
they were traditionally known as difficult to govern.
Furthermore, due to political chaos and difficult times,
the regulatory structure was not established,
and meritorious ministers and imperial relatives
made requests and intercessions in countless ways.
Qùbìng resolved matters properly
and firmly responded based on principle.
Those holding power and influence,
even humble servants and ordinary people, all respected his moral integrity,
yet it did not lead to resentment or hatred.
Since the capital moved to Yè,
among the governing techniques of the magistrates of the three counties,
Qùbìng alone was heralded as the best.
When Zhōu Wǔ stabilized Qí,
he valued his ability to govern.
He and Gōngsūn Jǐngmào, the Administrator of Jìyīn Commandery, were the only two not replaced,
and imperial edicts were issued in praise of them.
During the Dàyè period of the Suí dynasty,
he died while serving as Magistrate of Jìshì County.
Biographies, Chapter Thirty-Nine: Cruel Officials: Dǐ Zhēn, Sòng Yóudào, Lú Fěi, Bì Yìyún
The spiritual nature of humanity
is received differently by individuals.
There are distinctions between the firm and the yielding;
the slow and the urgent affect each other.
If one does not deeply investigate right and wrong,
there is no one who does not give free rein to their emotions and desires.
As for those who thoroughly observe the nature of water and fire [extremes],
and furthermore wear the leather and string [talismans of temperance], they are few indeed.
The harm caused by prison officials
has a long history.
Since the path of Wèi was unsuccessful,
the legal net became lax across the world.
Gāozǔ, correcting this leniency and laxity,
used considerable authority and strictness in governing things,
causing all officials, both inner and outer,
to be aware of the restrictions of the law.
Now we record Dǐ Zhēn and others to preserve the accounts of cruel officials,
as a warning, demonstration, encouragement, and motivation.
Dǐ Zhēn,
courtesy name Bǎo'ān,
was originally from Shàngqǔyáng, Zhōngshān.
He followed Gāozǔ in raising the standard of righteousness,
and was appointed Zhǎngshǐ.
His character was severe and violent,
and his demands were insatiable.
Later, he concurrently held the position of Shàngshū Yòu Púshè and Dà Xíngtái,
controlling all military affairs.
Zhēn governed his subordinates with cruelty,
and the hearts of the many soldiers became alienated.
He was eventually killed by the common people.
Later, he was posthumously granted the title of Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu.
Sòng Yóudào
was a native of Guǎngpíng;
his ancestors had moved there from Dūnhuáng.
His father, Jìyù,
served as Administrator of Bóhǎi.
Yóudào, upon reaching manhood, accompanied his father in the commandery.
When his father died,
officials and commoners offered gifts,
but he refused to accept a single thing.
He was known for his filial piety in serving his mother.
He lived separately from his uncle,
and his uncle was falsely accused of rebellion by a servant.
Yóudào lured the servant back,
cleared his uncle's name, and then killed the servant.
When Wèi's Prince Guǎngyáng, Shēn, conducted a northern campaign,
he requested Yóudào to serve as Kǎicáo.
When Shēn became Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu,
he again appointed Yóudào as his staff assistant.
Prince Guǎngyáng was killed by Gě Róng.
Yuán Huī falsely accused Yóudào of surrendering to the bandit,
and arrested his wife and children.
Yóudào pleaded his case and secured their release,
and together with the Prince Guǎngyáng's son, he escorted the body back for burial.
Lì Shàncháng, the Zhōngwèi, praised his spirit and integrity
and appointed him Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ.
A saying circulated within the Censorate:
"If you see bandits that can be suppressed, it is Sòng Yóudào."
When Xiàozhuāng ascended the throne,
Sòng Yóudào was appointed Zǔozhōngbīng Lángzhōng (Attendant Official of the Left Central Military Bureau).
He was reprimanded by the President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Prince Línhuái, Yuán Yù.
Yóudào then held his tablet, bowed deeply, and said:
"This humble official apologizes for the Prince's anger,
but does not apologize for the Prince's reasoning."
That same day, he went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial, stating:
"Yuán Fú, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, frequently submitted memorials saying: 'The false Liáng regime is extensively mobilizing officers and soldiers,
coming to seize Péngchéng.
I request an increase of two thousand Yǔlín (Imperial Guards).'
Since Fú is an important official of the Imperial Clan,
his request should be based on facts,
so I measured the request and reported granting him one thousand military officers.
Fú is now being relieved of his post.
Citing road obstructions as self-defense,
he subsequently absorbed eight hundred Yǔlín guards already stationed there,
excusing himself by saying: 'The border region is peaceful;
I request they be allowed to return home.'
Your servant is currently holding this bureau post,
and deeply knows this is unacceptable.
The President of the Department of State Affairs, Prince Línhuái, Yuán Yù, is Fú's nephew.
He sent the Secretariat Attendant Xiè Yuǎn to press me eight times within three days,
saying that the decision should be followed and the request granted.
Your servant dares not pander to subordinates and deceive superiors,
isolating the sagely wisdom.
However, when Fú was in office,
his requests for troops came one after another;
but as soon as he was relieved,
he immediately requested they be dismissed and sent back.
His actions, whether advancing or retreating, were for his own benefit;
he showed no concern for the state.
What he did was inappropriate,
and his offense falls under a minor charge.
Yù then summoned your servant to the main hall of the Department of State Affairs and said: 'You are just a minor official.
How can your concern for the state
be greater than mine?'
Abusive insults spilled from his mouth,
disregarding court decorum.
The Right Attendant Secretary (Yòu Púshè), your servant Hú Shìlóng, the Director of the Personnel Bureau (Lìbù Lángzhōng), your servant Xuē Shú, and more than a hundred others all heard and saw this.
Your servant truthfully offered plain words,
saying: 'When a loyal official serves the state,
the matter rests in their heart;
why should one distinguish between noble and humble?
Recently, when [Gāo Huān] entered Luò [yáng] from Běihǎi,
Your Highness was unable to dedicate yourself to dying in the crisis,
but instead cleansed the palace to welcome the tyrant.
Zhèng Xiānhù established a righteous cause in Guǎngzhōu,
yet Your Highness raised a banner and went to attack him.
You rush toward evil like flowing water,
but how quick you are to strike down the good!
Now that you have obtained the position leading all officials,
you attempt to use private interest to harm governance.'
Because of your servant's words,
Yù grew even angrier.
Since your servant is untalented,
and has offended a noble minister,
I request to be relieved of my Lángzhōng post."
The Emperor summoned Yóudào for an audience and commended and rewarded him.
Yù also submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your servant has been shamefully placed at the head of all officials,
yet I have allowed a single official to roll up his sleeves, raise his voice,
and speak abusively and aggressively.
I request to be relieved of the Shàngshū Lìng post."
The Emperor then issued an edict allowing Yóudào to resign from the Tái Láng (Department Official) post.
Later, he was appointed Zhōng Cóngshì in Sīzhōu.
At this time, he was preparing to return to Yè.
As heavy, continuous rain fell,
travelers were stuck at the Héqiáo bridge.
Yóudào constantly feasted and sang under his tent.
The travelers said:
"What kind of time is this to make such noises?
He is truly a great fool."
Yóudào replied:
"What time is *not* a time to make such noises?
You are also a great fool."
Later, Shénwǔ (Gāo Huān) came to court from Tàiyuán.
Seeing Yóudào, he said:
"Is this the Sòng Yóudào?
I have often heard his name,
but only today do I recognize his face."
He promoted Yóudào to Biéjià.
Later,
when Shénwǔ was in Sīzhōu,
he hosted a banquet for the court officials.
Raising his cup, he addressed Yóudào, saying:
"A great man is one who drinks the wine from Gāo Huān's hand.
Given your character,
you ought to drink this wine."
When he returned to Jìnyáng,
all the officials bade him farewell along the Zìmò road.
Shénwǔ grasped Yóudào's hand and said:
"I know very well that among the noble court officials there are those who hate and fear you.
Just focus on your work,
and harbor no fear or worry.
I shall ensure your rank becomes similar to theirs."
He then memorialized proposing Yóudào be appointed Zhōngwèi (Grand Commandant).
Wénxiāng (Gāo Chéng) strongly petitioned [against this],
so the Director of the Personnel Bureau, Cuī Xiān, was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi (Imperial Grand Commandant),
and Yóudào was made Shàngshū Zǔochéng (Vice President of the Left of the Department of State Affairs).
Wénxiāng said to Xiān and Yóudào:
"With one of you in the Nántái (Censorate)
and one of you in the Běishěng (Department of State Affairs),
the whole world shall be orderly and solemn."
When Yóudào entered the Department,
he impeached Grand Tutor (Tàishī) Prince Xiányáng, Yuán Tǎn; Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) Sūn Téng; Minister of Works (Sītú) Gāo Lóngzhī;

Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Hóu Jǐng; Director of Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū) Yuán Bì; and President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) Sīmǎ Zǐrú for receiving gold and silver from their offices.
He urgently demanded they repay the cost.
Although this did not amount to receiving bribes for specific tasks,
he ultimately did not shrink from powerful figures.
Furthermore, he memorialized overturning several hundred instances of errors committed by the Department of State Affairs,
and had powerful clerks in the department, such as Wáng Rú, whipped and expelled.
He was the first to revive the old custom
of establishing names for the gates of the Department of State Affairs,
to record the time of entry and exit.
Everyone from the President (Lìng) and Attendant Secretaries (Pú) downwards watched him sidelong.
When the Prince Ānpíng of Wèi died due to an offense,
the two Princes of Zhāngwǔ and all the princely consorts and grand consorts who were his close relatives were summoned and held to account.
The Director of the Capital Bureau (Dūguān Lángzhōng), Bì Yìyún, was in charge of this matter.
Some were imprisoned after Bì Yìyún memorialized their case,
while others were imprisoned without a memorial being submitted.
Yóudào ruled that the matter should be sent to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi) for sentencing,
but Gāo Lóngzhī disagreed.
Consequently, Gāo Lóngzhī falsely accused Yóudào of using harsh words to humiliate him,
and wrongfully interrogated numerous clerks to produce confirming evidence.
He then reported to the throne, along with the Left Attendant Secretary (Zǔo Púshè), Prince Xiāngchéng, Yuán Xù, and Department of State Official (Shàngshū) Zhèng Shùzǔ, saying:
"Adorning falsehoods to corrupt truth
is what state law must eliminate;
pandering to subordinates and deceiving superiors
is what benevolent rule cannot tolerate.
We respectfully note that the reputation of the Vice President of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, Sòng Yóudào, was originally lacking;
what meritorious deeds has he recorded?
During the beginning of the Yǒng'ān reign (Emperor Xiàozhuāng),
when court officials were scattered and absent,
during a shortage of capable personnel,
he improperly usurped the Tái Láng position.
With rash conduct and sycophantic words,
he gives free rein to his deceit and fraud.
He rarely recognizes proper principles,
and disregards standard texts and norms.
People despise his heart,
and the masses fear his mouth.
Having served outside in the provinces and inside the Department of State Affairs,
he has successively disgraced clean posts,
yet his increasing wickedness does not stop,
and he has no taboos whatsoever.
Praise and condemnation are decided by him,
and his hatred is governed by personal whim.
Recently, regarding the affair of Prince Ānpíng,
he gave vent to his narrow-mindedness,
using public office to settle private grudges,
and mutually denounced Bì Yìyún, the Lángzhōng, and himself.

Furthermore, Wèi Shúdào, the Director of the Left Outer Military Bureau, recorded in a document: 'The surrendered personnel Zǔo Zé and others within the bureau were sent by the capital region to the Department,
and an order was given to release them on bail.'
When the Great General (Dà Jiāngjūn, Gāo Huān) was in the Department,
he ruled 'Allowed.'
Yóudào angrily declared: 'What kind of government was the government of former days?
How dare they take this as a precedent!'
He further said: 'Relying on previous edicts and regulations—
what kind of edicts and regulations are these!'
When questioned regarding the facts of the matter,
Yóudào admitted everything.
According to the law: 'One who publicly defies an Imperial Envoy
shows no courtesy proper to a subject,
and shall die for high irreverence.'
Even one who defies an envoy is liable for death;
how much more so Yóudào, who uttered disloyal words,
committing the crime of disrespecting superiors!
He speaks of Yí [Qí] and Qí,
but harbors the intentions of Dào Zhí.
He cheats the public and sells the law,
accepting bribes and gifts.
His property increases with the importance of his post,
and his wealth accumulates alongside his rank.
Although his corruption has not yet been exposed,
his deceit is like this.
By citing this one corner,
the remainder of his deceit can be verified.
We now recommend, based on rites and law, sentencing Yóudào to death."
At that time, all court officials believed Yóudào would not escape [punishment].
But Wénxiāng, upon hearing of the words Yóudào had used to oppose Lóngzhī,
said to Yáng Zūnyàn:
"This truly is an outspoken, tough, and difficult person."
Zūnyàn replied:
"If we use the analogy of keeping a dog,
the reason we keep it is for its barking.
If we kill it now because it barks frequently,
I fear there will be no more barking dogs in the future."
An imperial edict committed him to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi).
Yóudào was found guilty and stripped of his rank.
Wénxiāng sent Yuán Jǐngkāng to tell him:
"You should hurry and follow me to Bìngzhōu,
otherwise,
others will scheme to kill you."
Yóudào followed him to Jìnyáng,
and was made the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù) in the Supreme Central Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái).
He was also appointed Administrator (Cóngyì) in the Establishment of the Duke of Tàiyuán.
When the Duke Píngyáng (Gāo Yáng) became Grand Commandant (Zhōngwèi),
Yóudào, still holding his Cóngyì post, was additionally appointed Shū Shìyùshǐ (Secretarial Palace Censor).
Soon after, he held his original post concurrently with that of Chief Clerk of the Left (Zǔo Zhǎngshǐ) in the Ministry of Works (Sītú).
When Wén Xiāng suspected the Palace Attendant Wēn Zǐshēng of knowing about Yuán Jǐn’s plot,
he imprisoned him and starved him.
He ate his worn-out jacket and died.
The corpse was abandoned by the roadside,
and Yóu Dào collected it and buried it.
Wén Xiāng said to him:
“Recently I wrote to the various nobles in the capital
discussing the court officials.
I mentioned that you tended toward factionalism
which would become a fault.
Now, you are truly a person who values old bonds, integrity, and righteousness;
this sentiment cannot be taken away.
I originally did not intend to kill Zǐshēng.
Why should you hesitate to bury him?
Those throughout the world who fear for you
do not understand my heart.”
Soon after, he was appointed Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi).
Dōnglái Wáng Dàoxí participated in selecting censors.
Someone submitted a petition after the deadline.
Dàoxí had a previous relationship with Yóu Dào,
so he ordered a clerk to accept it.
Wén Xiāng was furious.
He flogged Yóu Dào and issued a judgment stating:
“Yóu Dào is naturally aggressive and fierce.
He recklessly speaks of right and wrong,
finding flaws where there are none (lit. blowing upon fur to search for a stain),
criticizing and censuring people.
Previously, when he disputed angrily with the Gentleman Lán Jǐngyún,
he listed ten charges.
When investigation was carried out,
they proved to be fabrications.
Now, together with Dàoxí, he has insulted the court statutes.
As a law officer who commits crimes,
this is particularly difficult to pardon.
He should be handed over to the Department for punishment.”
Yóu Dào was imprisoned.
The jailer wished to remove his cangue,
but Yóu Dào refused and said:
“This was imposed by an official order;
it must not be arbitrarily removed.”
Wén Xiāng heard this and granted him a pardon.
Yóu Dào held firm to his aspirations and did not change.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo (550 CE),
Yóu Dào was made acting Minister of the Court of the Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng).
He then investigated the Court of the Imperial Grooms (Shǎofǔ), uncovering theft and embezzlement by officials
amounting to tens of millions.
The treacherous clerks instead falsely accused him in a memorial,
and he was thrown into prison.
Soon after he was released,
he did not return home,
but went directly to the prefectural office to handle affairs.
When he died,
he left instructions for a simple funeral,
no tombstone or marker to be erected,
and no posthumous title or honorific promotion to be sought.
He was posthumously granted the title of Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guāzhōu.
During the Wǔpíng era,
because his son Shìsù had long handled confidential affairs,
he was heavily promoted and granted the title of Grand Master of the Palace with Special Authorization (Yítóng Sānsī),
with the posthumous title Zhēnhuì.
Yóu Dào was rigid and upright,
hating evil like an enemy.
When he saw someone commit a crime,
he wanted to bring them all to the ultimate punishment.
When impeaching based on current facts,
he also loved to investigate hidden, private matters.
When questioning prisoners and investigating circumstances,
his floggings were severe and cruel.
When the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Lǐ Zǐzhēn, was corrupt and tyrannical in his province,
Yóu Dào prosecuted him.
Wén Xiāng considered that Zǐzhēn had participated in the initial righteous uprising
and intended to tolerate the offense.
Yóu Dào suspected Chén Yuánkāng was secretly assisting Lǐ Zǐzhēn,
and secretly memorialized, saying:
“Zǐzhēn and Yuánkāng are associates,
and I fear there might be special requests or instructions between them.”
Wén Xiāng grew angry,
assembled all the officials in the main hall of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Dūtáng),
and had Lǐ Zǐzhēn beaten to death.
Furthermore, the people of Yǎnzhōu erected a shrine for Yóu Dào while he was still alive,
inscribing the image with the words
“Lord of Loyalty and Purity” (Zhōngqīng Jūn).
Yóu Dào separately impeached five people, including Jí Níng, all sentenced to death,
and he showed delight upon their execution.
Court officials greatly scorned him for this.
However, he valued friendships
and upheld his promises.
Though strict and orderly in his successive offices,
he sometimes accepted large bribes,
distributing the money to relatives and friends who were destitute.
He arranged marriages for their orphaned or weak sons and daughters.
When attending a funeral, he was always deeply sorrowful
and personally participated in the rites.
As the Secretary (Gāngjì) of Sīzhōu, he clashed with the two princes, Chānglè and Xīhé, who were the prefects (Mù).
When the two princes died,
he subsequently provided for their families in every detail.
He met Lǐ Jiǎng of Dùnqiū only once
but immediately swore a bond of lifelong friendship.
Lǐ Jiǎng said:
“My years and rank are already high.
If I were to use you as my deputy (Zuǒshǐ),
merely having you face north toward me would be enough.”
Yóu Dào said:
“I cannot.”
Later, Lǐ Jiǎng became the Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn)
and invited Yóu Dào to be the Chief Judge (Zhōngzhèng).
Emissaries followed one after another,
carrying caps and robes to await his arrival.
They shook hands and joked happily.
When Yuán Hào entered Luòyáng,
Lǐ Jiǎng accepted his commission
and was dispatched as an envoy to Xúzhōu.
The Area Commander Yuán Fú, along with the city resident Zhào Shào, killed him with soldiers.
Yóu Dào argued for Lǐ Jiǎng’s vindication,
which was granted.
He also memorialized requesting a posthumous promotion for him,
transferring one rank from his own official assessment to add to it.
He also formed a bond with Liú Xīn
and entrusted Liú Xīn’s younger brother, Liú Cuì, with killing Zhào Shào in Xúzhōu.
Later, Liú Xīn was executed in Luòyáng.
Liú Cuì rebelled in Xúzhōu.
The imperial forces defeated him,
and Liú Cuì’s head was displayed in the marketplace of Yè.
Sūn Téng instructed a guest to inform the market official
that the head could only be collected after five million cash were paid.
Yóu Dào was then the Internal Aide (Zhōng Cóngshì) of Sīzhōu.
He ordered his family members to pretend to be Liú Cuì’s close relatives
and filed a complaint with the prefecture.
Based on the law, he ruled
“Granted”
and memorialized the decision.
The imperial decree arrived,
but the market official still refused permission.
Yóu Dào had the market official flogged
and ordered him to hand over the head quickly.
Sūn Téng was furious when he heard this.
At that time, Lǐ Jiǎng’s two sons, Gòu and Xùn, were poor.
Yóu Dào later instructed them to seek three wealthy men who had committed capital crimes
and ruled to pardon them,
thereby obtaining a total of one million five hundred thousand cash,
which he gave entirely to Gòu and Xùn.
His fiery and chivalrous nature was like this.
People at the time had a saying:
“Yóu Dào has a monkey face,
Lù Cāo has a tadpole shape;
perception is not related to appearance;
why say the ugly must be heartless?”
Gòu once used Yóu Dào’s gathering of guests
to play a trick on him, saying:
“Your cousin is outside the gate.
He is a fine-looking man;
you should welcome him yourself.”
He had the name announced as
“Cousin Yóu Shān.”
Yóu Dào went out to see,
and found a monkey dressed in a hat and robes.
Yóu Dào intended to sever ties with Gòu,
but Gòu apologized,
and Yóu Dào immediately forgave him as before.
After Yóu Dào died,
Gòu served as the Chief Administrator (Zhǎngshǐ) of Dìngzhōu.
Yóu Dào’s third son, Shìxùn, was the Mo Cáo official (responsible for records/penal affairs) and the Aide (Guǎnjì) to the Prince of Bólíng.
He colluded with the director (Diǎn Qiān) to falsely accuse Gòu in a memorial.
Gòu offered sacrifice to Yóu Dào while in confinement and pleaded his case.
Shìxùn was sleeping during the day and seemed to be dreaming;
he saw Yóu Dào angrily saying to him:
“Gòu and I shared kindness and righteousness;
how can you not know this?
Why conspire with petty men to entrap an honest and pure scholar!”
Shìxùn knelt in terror and said:
“I wouldn’t dare, I wouldn’t dare.”
He died ten days later.
Yóu Dào often instructed his sons Shìsù, Shìyuē, and Shìshèn, saying:
“I have been too rigid in enforcing the law,
frequently encountering difficulties and setbacks.
My nature is simply this way;
my sons and grandsons should not take me as a model.”
His sons respected their father’s words
and were gentle, moderate, and humble.
Shìsù was reserved and spoke little,
possessing talent and insight.
He gradually rose to become Palace Attendant in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
Zhào Yànshēn introduced him into the inner court (Nèi Shěng),
where he participated in managing confidential affairs.
He successively held the posts of Gentleman-Attendant of the Central Secretariat and Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng),
eventually being promoted to Grand Master of the Palace with Special Authorization (Yítóng Sānsī) and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
often retaining the position of Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng).
He held sensitive and crucial posts for nearly twenty years.
He was cautious, prudent, warm, and respectful,
and highly valued by Yànshēn.
Previously, when Zǔ Tǐng controlled the court administration,
he sent Yànshēn out to serve as Governor.
Tǐng proposed that Shìsù be made Prefect of Dōngjùn,
but the Gentleman-Attendant of the Central Secretariat Lǐ Délín advised Zǔ Tǐng to retain him.
Consequently, he was reassigned as Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng)
and jointly participated in confidential affairs.
Shìyuē was also a good man,
serving as Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng).
Lú Fěi,
courtesy name Zǐzhāng,
was a native of Zhuō, Fànyáng.
His father, Tóng,
was a dìanzhōng shàngshū in the Wèi dynasty.
Fěi was cruel by nature
and known for his forceful decisiveness.
Shìzōng appointed him xíngyù cānjūn in the prime minister's office,
and said to him:
“Kuángjiǎn,
Fěiránchéngzhāng,
is not a good name.”
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he was gradually promoted to shàngshū zuǒchéng,
and separately oversaw the capital's prison cases.
His cruelty and excess were beyond human sentiment.
Regardless of the size of the case,
he excessively tortured prisoners.
More than one died beneath the large club and chariot wheel.
Sometimes, in the extreme cold of winter,
prisoners were placed on ice and snow;
other times, in the intense heat of summer,
they were exposed to the sun.
The number of people unjustly implicated and killed,
both before and after, reached several hundred.
He also spied on officials for their faults,
and immediately reported them when found.
Court officials, upon seeing him,
all stepped back and held their breath,
calling him Lú Xiàoshì.
〔一０〕Later, Fěi was implicated in slandering the historian,
and he and Lǐ Shù both died from flogging in prison.
Bì Yìyún,
whose infant name was Ér.
In his youth, he was rough and roguish.
His family lived in the northern part of Yǎnzhōu.
He often robbed travelers,
and the people of the district suffered from it.
Later, he changed his ways and became an official,
and was successively promoted to shàngshū dūguān lángzhōng.
He was severe and cruel by nature,
and often got things done.
When Qí Wénxiāng became prime minister,
he considered Yìyún competent,
and ordered him to generally arrest false officials,
specializing in torture by chariot wheel.
He apprehended many.
However, this caused widespread resentment and slander.
He was once accused by a Sīzhōu clerk
of having embezzled and altered documents.
Wénxiāng, because Yìyún was investigating falsification
and people were resentful,
did not question him at all,
but instead arrested several clerks and executed them.
〔一一〕As a result, Yìyún dedicated himself to interrogations,
and his prestige grew daily.
When Wénxuān accepted the abdication,
he appointed Yìyún zhìshū shìyùshǐ.
He impeached without sparing meritorious relatives.
He was successively promoted to yùshǐ zhōngchéng,
and his discipline and impeachment became even stricter.
However, he was arrogant and unfair,
and was frequently subjected to resentment and accusations.
Previously, Zhái Sōng, the Tàishǒu of Jí Jùn, reported: Yìyún's paternal cousin, Sēngmíng, owed official debts.
Yìyún, while serving as the zhǎnglì of Jīngjī,
did not accept his jurisdiction
and set a strict deadline for collection,
thus holding a grudge.
He repeatedly sent yùshǐ to the commandery to investigate,
intending to impeach him.
He was also found guilty of privately harboring artisans,
having more than ten looms for weaving brocade at home,
and also making gold and silver artifacts.
He was then prohibited from these activities.
Soon after, he was released
and appointed sī tú zuǒ chángshǐ.
Sīmǎ Zǐruì, the shàngshū zuǒchéng, impeached Yìyún,
stating:
“In the fourth month of the first year of Tiānbǎo,
on the day of the funeral of Dòu Shì, the empress's maternal aunt's ancestor,
〔一二〕officials, both inside and outside the court, went to the residence to offer condolences.
Yìyún only sent an yùshǐ to submit his name,
and did not attend in person.
Moreover, Yìyún reported:
‘I am an impoverished orphan after my wife's death.
I later married Lǐ Shì'ān’s daughter.
Although Shì'ān himself has not completed his mourning period for his father,
his daughter, for her ancestor, has already reached the state of píngjí.
I humbly request to secretly welcome her,
not daring to prepare full rites.’
However, on the evening of Yìyún's wedding,
numerous provisions were arranged,
a day was set for the formal visit to the ancestral temple,
heralds cleared the road,
and a grand display of feathered insignia was present.
He also dispatched twenty Tái clerks,
demanding that they wear fresh clothes and attend behind the chariot.
This was merely a fraudulent attempt to get married,
deceiving the emperor.
Yìyún’s assets and residence are certainly befitting a wealthy family;
to suddenly claim to be an impoverished orphan
is also a deception.
If a law official is like this,
where can impartiality reside?
Furthermore, when the emperor visited Jìnyáng,
the Dūzuò ruled:
‘For presenting petitions of congratulations and greetings,
officials of the fourth rank and below, but above the fifth rank, should go to the Nándū署 to sign the petition one day in advance,
〔一三〕while those of the third rank and above should sign on the day itself.’
Yìyún, however, violated the rule.
On the day of signing the petition,
he asked for the petition to be brought to his home for him to sign in advance,
and then claimed a private taboo on the day itself and did not come.”
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to the Tíngwèi to sentence him,
but soon after, an imperial order exempted him from prosecution.
Zǐruì again impeached Yìyún on more than ten charges,
most of which were trivial.
The punishment was only a fine,
not dismissal.
Zǐruì’s cousin, Xiāonán, was the cìshǐ of Běi Yùzhōu.
Yìyún sent the yùshǐ Zhāng Zǐjiē to the province to gather rumors.
He first arrested Xiāonán’s diǎnqiān, house guests, and others.
Xiāonán became alarmed and afraid,
and subsequently rebelled and defected to Zhōu.
Public opinion at the time blamed Yìyún,
saying he was seeking revenge against Zǐruì.
The matter was also reported to the emperor.
Before this, Yìyún was always present at banquets and awards.
From then on, he was gradually excluded from gatherings,
and his reputation suffered greatly.
At the beginning of Qiánmíng,
Zǐruì was promoted to yùshǐ zhōngchéng.
Zhèng Zǐmò was being appointed to important positions.
Yìyún’s paternal aunt was Zǐmò’s paternal grandmother.
Thus, Yìyún was appointed dùzhī shàngshū,
and concurrently served as zuǒchéng.
After Zǐmò was executed,
Yìyún’s position as zuǒchéng was dissolved.
When Xiàozhāo went to Jìnyáng,
Gāo Yuánhǎi remained in Yè.
Yìyún deeply attached himself to Yuánhǎi.
Knowing that Yuánhǎi believed in Buddhism,
Yìyún often followed him to listen to lectures,
and because of this,
their intimacy reached every extent.
When Xiàozhāo was critically ill,
he entrusted the succession to Wǔchéng.
When Gāo Guīyàn arrived at the capital,
Wǔchéng was still hesitant.
Yuánhǎi sent an ox-cart to fetch Yìyún into the Northern Palace to participate in the deliberation.
He then, along with Yuánhǎi and others, urged Wǔchéng to ascend the throne.
He subsequently followed Wǔchéng to Jìnyáng
and participated in current political affairs.
Soon after, he was appointed Yǎnzhōu cìshǐ,
and was granted hòubù gǔchuī.
This was his native province.
He was proud and self-satisfied,
and hoped to be appointed to a high position.
He saw people presenting themselves
and preemptively promised to welcome them.
He also said that his departure would be temporary,
and he would not remain in the province for long.
He already had náochuī,
but when inspecting the departments during his travels,
he used both musical ensembles simultaneously.
He still wrote letters to Yuánhǎi,
discussing current affairs.
Yuánhǎi, when entering the palace,
accidentally dropped one.
Lǐ Xiàozhēn, the Jìshìzhōng, found it and reported it to the emperor.
Because of this, Yuánhǎi gradually fell out of favor,
and Xiàozhēn was consequently concurrently appointed zhōngshū shèrén.
Later, when Gāo Guīyàn rebelled,
Yìyún privately gathered men and horses in his province,
and also accumulated weapons and armor,
intending to defend himself.
He had no other intentions.
However, he was reported by someone.
When Guīyàn was captured,
Yìyún was further listed as his confederate who had acted arbitrarily.
Because of this, he was recalled.
Wǔchéng, however, remembered his past loyalty
and ultimately did not punish him,
appointing him concurrently as Qībīng Shàngshū.
Yǐyún’s nature was unrestrained and extravagant,
and he rather focused on dispensing favors.
His family had held the position of Cìshǐ of their home prefecture for generations,
and they were rich in wealth.
Many scholars who were in want
were aided and relieved [by him].
When he became noble,
he indulged his arrogance and extravagance.
The mansions he constructed were massive and imposing,
and they were completed in a short time.
His domestic life was sordid and promiscuous,
and his reputation spread throughout the court and countryside.
When he served as a Láng,
he had a furious argument with the Assistant Director of the Left, Sòng Yóudào, over official business.
Yóudào publicly insulted him, saying:
“The 'Poem of the Mighty Fox'
will be yours for a thousand years.”
Yǐyún said nothing in response.
However, he was fiercely brutal and cruel,
exceeding what human reason permits,
and this was especially true within his household.
His children, grandchildren, servants, and slaves
were constantly covered in wounds.
He had a bastard son named Shànzhāo,
whose nature was extremely malicious and stubborn.
He committed adultery with Yǐyún’s maidservant.
He was flogged countless times.
Yǐyún placed a cage-hood on him,
tied him to a tree in the courtyard,
and fed him grass and fodder.
He was released only after more than ten days.
One night,
Yǐyún was murdered by a bandit.
The weapon used was the dagger carried by Shànzhāo,
which was left in Yǐyún’s courtyard.
When Shànzhāo heard of the calamity, he ran and wept.
When the family members recovered the dagger,
Shànzhāo became terrified,
and immediately ran away,
taking refuge in the manor house of Píng'ēn.
The next day,
Shìzǔ ordered the Shèrén, Lán Zichàng, to go to the residence and conduct an investigation.
Before this,
Yǐyún had recently married a young secondary wife, Lady Lú of Fànyáng,
who was attractive.
Zichàng suspected that the murder was committed by Lú's paramour
and was about to subject her to torture.
Lú fully recounted Shànzhāo's deed.
Consequently, he was arrested and imprisoned in the Línzhāng jail,
and was to be executed.
Xíng Shào submitted a memorial, stating,
“This involves high treason,
and Yǐyún was also a court noble;
it should not be made public.”
So, he was executed in prison
and his body was dumped into the Zhāng River.
Biographies, Chapter 40: Imperial Relatives Zhào Měng, Lóu Ruì, Ěrzhū Wénchàng, Zhèng Zhònglǐ, Lǐ Zǔshēng, Yuán Mán, Hú Chángrén
Since the two Hàn dynasties,
there have been few cases where families of imperial relatives remained intact.
The details of their downfall
and the triggers of their rebellions
are fully described in previous histories.
Many families of the empresses and concubines of the Qí clan
managed to preserve themselves.
Only Hú Chángrén brought disaster upon himself through slanderous accusations,
and Húlǜ Guāng was executed due to his high territorial influence.
Neither was caused by the rise or decline of female influence at court.
Now, following the methods of the historians of previous dynasties,
we compile the biographies of the imperial relatives here.
Zhào Měng,
a native of Dínà in Tài'ān,
was the brother of the woman who became the second wife of Emperor Wénmù,
and she gave birth to Zhào Jùnwáng Chēn.
Měng’s nature was upright and straightforward,
and he possessed considerable ability and competence.
When Gāozǔ launched his uprising,
he was promoted to Cìshǐ of Nányíng Prefecture
and died there.
Lóu Ruì,
courtesy name Fórén,
was the nephew of Empress Wǔmíng.
His father, Zhuàng,
was the President of the Ministry of the South in the Wèi dynasty.
Ruì loved archery and horsemanship when young,
and had military capabilities.
He served as Gāozǔ’s Dūdū of the personal tent guards.
He followed [Gāozǔ] in defeating the Ěrzhū forces at Hánlíng,
and was successively promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng and Great General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn).
Ruì lacked true ability.
He gained wealth and favor only through being an imperial relative,
and he indulged his desires for wealth and women,
which caused him to be despised by contemporary opinion.
In the beginning of Huángjiàn era (560 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōng'ān.
When Gāo Guīyàn rebelled in Jì Prefecture,
an imperial decree ordered Ruì to go and suppress him.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Sītú Gōng (Minister of Education).
When Zhōu troops invaded the Eastern Pass,
Ruì led the army to reinforce the area,
and achieved merits in repeated battles,
capturing the Zhōu general Yáng Jí and others.
He was advanced to Great Commander (Dà Sīmǎ),
and was sent out to take overall command of a detachment of troops
and proceed to Xuánhù.
While Ruì was in the Yù region,
he remained there for over a hundred days,
infringing upon public and private property,
and acting exclusively outside the law.
He was removed from office for this transgression.
Soon after, he was granted the office of Grand Preceptor (Tàiwèi).
He died.
Ěrzhū Wénchàng
was Róng’s fourth son.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Chānglè.
His elder sister was Empress Xiàozhuāng of Wèi.
After the failure and destruction of the four Hú,
Gāozǔ took her in [as a concubine]
and treated her family very well.
Wénchàng was appointed Cìshǐ of Sì Prefecture due to this.
He was rich in wealth
and attracted numerous retainers and guests.
Relying on his noble lineage,
he pushed extravagance to the extreme.
He was deeply attached and intimate with the Chancellor’s Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ), Rèn Zhòu, the Chief Secretary (Zhǔbù), Lǐ Shìlín, the Commander (Dūdū), Zhèng Zhònglǐ, Fáng Zǐyuǎn, and others.
Outwardly, they showed themselves to be drinking companions,
but secretly plotted rebellion.
According to the old custom of the Wèi clan,
on the night of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, there was a game called "shooting the bamboo target."
Those who could hit the target
were immediately rewarded with silk cloth.
Rèn Zhòu ordered Zhònglǐ to hide a knife in his trousers,
and, taking advantage of Gāozǔ’s attendance to watch the game,
they planned to launch their attack secretly.
After the mission succeeded,
they intended to jointly elevate Wénchàng as their leader.
Xué Jìxiào, a family retainer of the Rèn clan, informed Gāozǔ.
Upon interrogation, they fully confessed.
Because of the favor shown to his sister,
only Wénchàng's immediate branch of the family was implicated.
His younger brother, Wénlüè,
succeeded to the title of Prince of Liáng Jùn
because his elder brother Wénluó had died without an heir.
Since Wénlüè should have been implicated
due to his elder brother Wénchàng’s affair,
Gāozǔ granted him special clemency.
Wénlüè was intelligent and exceptionally clever,
and skilled in many things.
Shìzōng once ordered Zhāng Yǒngxīng to play the Hú Pípá (lute) on horseback.
After playing more than ten pieces,
he tested Wénlüè by asking him to transcribe them.
Wénlüè managed to get eight of them correct.
Shìzōng joked with him, saying:
“Intelligent people often do not live long.
Prince of Liáng Jùn, you should be careful.”
Wénlüè replied:
“The length or shortness of my life
lies entirely with Your Excellency (Míng Gōng).”
Shìzōng said mournfully:
“This is not something to worry about.”
Initially, Gāozǔ left a posthumous instruction pardoning Wénlüè from ten death sentences.
Relying on this, he became even more arrogant
and frequently insulted and bullied others.
The Prince of Píngqín had a horse that could travel seven hundred *lǐ* a day.
Wénlüè wagered a beautiful maid against it,
gambled, and won it.
The next day,
Píngqín sent a request to buy it back.
Wénlüè killed both the horse and the maidservant,
and sent the maid’s head and the horse’s meat in two silver vessels to the Prince.
The Prince of Píngqín reported this to Wénxuān,
and [Wénlüè] was imprisoned in the Jīngjī jail.
Wénlüè played the Pípá,
blew the transverse flute (Héng Dí),
and composed songs.
When utterly exhausted, he would lie down and sing funeral dirges (wǎn'gē).
After staying there for several months,
he snatched the bow and arrows from the guards and shot at people, saying:
“If I don't do this,
the Son of Heaven will not remember me.”
The relevant authorities memorialized the incident,
and he was executed according to the law.
Wénlüè once sent a large amount of gold to Wèi Shōu
and asked him to write an excellent biography for his father.
Wèi Shōu’s assessment that Ěrzhū Róng was comparable to Wéi, Péng, Yī, and Huò
was likely due to this.
Zhèng Zhònglǐ
was a native of Kāifēng, Xíngyáng,
and the adopted son of Yán Shùzǐ, the Grand Messenger (Hónglú) of Wèi.
In his youth, he was rash and reckless,
possessing great physical strength.
Gāozǔ favored his elder sister,
and Zhònglǐ, as a relative, received intimacy
and was promoted to Commander of the Tent Guard (Zhàngnèi Dūdu).
He often bore Gāozǔ's bow and saber,
following him in and out.
Rèn Zhòu was fond of drinking and neglected public affairs.
Gāozǔ reprimanded him.
Zhòu was afraid
and plotted rebellion.
It was thanks to Wǔmíng Lóu Hòu pleading for him
that Zhònglǐ died
without his family being implicated.
Lǐ Zǔshēng
was a native of Píngjí, Zhàoguó,
and the eldest brother of Empress Lǐ of Xiǎnzǔ.
His father, Xīzōng,
was the Administrator of Shàngdǎng.
Zǔshēng had a handsome and graceful appearance,
with hands hanging past his knees.
He maintained good relations with his in-laws and was generous.
His literary skills were sufficient for self-expression.
He served up to the position of Regional Inspector of Qízhōu
and was killed by foot soldiers.
His younger brother was Zǔxūn.
When Xiǎnzǔ received the abdication,
Zǔxūn was appointed Secretary of the Palace Library (Bìshū Chéng).
When his daughter became the consort of the Prince of Jǐnán,
he was made Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng)
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Dānyáng.
When the Prince of Jǐnán was deposed,
he became the Regional Inspector of Guāngzhōu.
Zǔxūn was naturally greedy and arrogant,
and his wife, Madame Cuī, was also haughty and interfered in government,
which contemporary opinion scorned.
He was repeatedly accused of corruption
and dismissed from office.
He lacked talent or ability.
From youth to maturity,
his official positions were all due to inner favor,
and he had nothing worthy of praise.
He died.
Yuán Mán
was the adopted son of Yuán Jì, the Grand Preceptor (Tàishī) and Prince of Jiāngyáng of Wèi,
and the father of Empress Yuán of Sùzōng.
He successively held the post of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Guānglù Qīng).
In the tenth year of Tiānbǎo (559),
when the Yuán clan was largely executed,
Sùzōng bitterly pleaded for Mán.
Because of this, he was later pardoned
and granted the surname Bùliùgū.
Soon after, he fell ill and died.
Hú Chángrén,
courtesy name Xiàolóng,
was a native of Línjìng, Āndìng,
and the elder brother of Empress Wǔchéng.
His father, Yánzhī,
was the Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Lìng) of Wèi.
Chángrén successively rose to the positions of Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
When Shìzǔ died,
he participated in court politics
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǒngdōng.
The Left Censor Zōu Xiàoyù
and the Gentlemen Lù Rénkuì and Lú Yuànliàng closely associated with him.
Whenever Chángrén went to the chancellery (shěng),
Xiàoyù would certainly arrive alongside his carriage.
As the chancellery affairs were numerous,
and the files accumulated,
the clerks (lìshǐ) wishing to consult the chief administrator
numbered in the hundreds daily.
Xiàoyù would dismiss people for private talks,
and they followed each other even after court dismissal.
Rénkuì and Yuànliàng would also seize opportunities to visit,
causing public affairs to be suspended and delayed.
People at the time called them the Three Sycophants (Sān Nìng).
Chángrén indulged in private excursions and secret gatherings,
which they pursued everywhere.
Xiàoyù encouraged him to seek further advancement.
Hé Shìkāi deeply hated this
and therefore memorialized for Xiàoyù to be dismissed as the Administrator of Zhāngwǔ Commandery.
Yuànliàng and the others were also sent out.
Xiàoyù again advised Chángrén, saying:
“If Your Highness feigns illness and lies down,
Shìkāi will surely come.
You can then kill him.
Go and see the Empress Dowager.
You will lose your office for no more than a hundred days
and then replace him.”
Shìkāi learned of this plot
and transferred Xiàoyù to be the Administrator of Jiàndé Commandery in Běiyíngzhōu.
Later, Chángrén relied on his relatives
and became arrogant, reckless, and fearless.
Shìkāi was sent out as the Regional Inspector of Qízhōu.
Chángrén felt resentful
and plotted to have him assassinated.
When the matter was discovered,
he was granted death.
Soon after, the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) took Chángrén’s daughter as empress,
and Chángrén was heavily granted posthumous honors and titles.
Seven of Chángrén’s younger brothers and others were successively granted princely titles,
and his entire household became noble and flourishing.
His cousin (from his grandfather’s brother) was Chángcàn.
His father, Sēngjìng,
was the maternal uncle of Emperor Xiàojìng of Wèi
and reached the position of Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Chángcàn was quick-witted in his youth.
Due to being a maternal relative, he started his career as Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Zhōng)
and was promoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Yellow Gates (Huángmén Shìláng).
When the Later Ruler ascended the throne,
Chángcàn was ordered, along with the Yellow Gates attendant Féng Zǐcóng, to enter and exit the restricted palace,
exclusively handling memorials and reports.
When Shìzǔ died,

he participated in state affairs alongside Commander of the Guards (Lǐng Jūn) Lóu Dìngyuǎn, Recorder of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū) Zhào Yànshēn, Hé Shìkāi, Gāo Wényáo, Commander of the Guards Qílián Měng, Gāo Ānàgōng, and Assistant Director (Púshè) Táng Yōng.
People at the time called them the Eight Nobles (Bā Guì).
Subsequently,
Dìngyuǎn and Wényáo were both sent out.
Táng Yōng exclusively managed external military affairs.
Qílián Měng and Gāo Ānàgōng separately managed military responsibilities.
Chángcàn often remained at the side,
also proclaiming imperial edicts,
and followed the emperor to Jìnyáng.
The Later Ruler, having just ascended the throne,
was young in years,
and all general affairs were entrusted to Chángcàn.
Chángcàn wholeheartedly supported and assisted the emperor
and gained considerable renown.
He also served as Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng).
Chángrén desired in his heart to enter the sphere of crucial authority,
but the governing officials did not permit it.
Chángrén suspected Chángcàn was in collusion
and held deep resentment.
He then spoke to the Empress Dowager,
revealing Chángcàn's private misdeeds,
and requested he be sent out to a province.
The Later Ruler had no choice but to comply.
He was appointed Regional Inspector of Zhàozhōu.
When he took leave,
Chángcàn wept,
and the Later Ruler was also silent with sorrow.
Upon reaching the province,
he washed his hair and subsequently found his hands unable to lift.
He lost his voice
and died.

Chapter 41: Specialists and Technicians (Fāng Jì) Yóu Wú Dàoróng, Wáng Chūn, Xìndū Fāng, Sòng Jǐngyè, Xǔ Zūn, Wú Zūnshì, Zhào Fǔhé, Huángfǔ Yù, Xiè Fǎxuǎn, Wèi Níng, Qímǔ Huáiwén, Zhāng Zǐxìn, Mǎ Sì míng.
The *Book of Changes* (*Yì*) says: To determine the auspicious and inauspicious outcomes of the world,
and to accomplish the persistent efforts of the world,
nothing is better than the milfoil and the tortoise shell.
Thus, Heaven produced divine objects,
and the sages took them as models.
Moreover, Shénnóng and Tóng Jūn discussed the properties of medicinal herbs in the *Běncǎo* (Materia Medica),
and Huángdì and Qíbó explained the manifestations of diseases and methods of treatment.
All these were highly valued by the sages.
Therefore, Grand Historian (Tàishǐ Gōng) authored the biographies of the Tortoise Diviners and the Day Selectors (*Guī Cè*, *Rì Zhě*) and the biographies of Biǎn Què and Cāng Gōng,
all intending to broaden knowledge
and illuminate future generations.
Since the Qí clan established their hegemony,
they invited eminent talents;
anyone possessing a specialized skill
was fully enlisted.
We now record them together to complete the chapter on Specialists and Technicians.
Yóu Wú Dàoróng
was a person from Lángyé.
When young, he was fond of Daoist methods.
He sought together with his peers, entering Chángbái and Tàishān to live in seclusion,
where he thoroughly learned the Daoist techniques.
Subsequently, he traveled between Zōu and Lǔ,
studying Confucian pursuits.
A certain person from Jìnyáng
was a great master of magical arts.
Dàoróng sought him out,
but this man was working as a hired laborer for a family,
and no one recognized who he was.
Only after a long search did he find him out.
That man was thoroughly versed in Daoist talismans and holy water, incantations and prohibitions, calendrical calculations of Yin and Yang, astronomy, and medicinal properties.
Because Yóu Dàoróng was so dedicated,
he taught him everything.
This man said to Dàoróng:
“I was originally a Mountain Immortal,
but because I committed a minor offense,
I was demoted by the celestial officials.
Now my limit is reached, and I am about to return.
You should escort me to the Fénshuǐ.”
When they reached the river,
they found the water had suddenly risen greatly.
The bridge was broken,
and crossing by boat was difficult.
That man then performed the Pace of Yǔ at the water's edge,
threw a talisman into the water,
and the current immediately stopped.
After a moment, the water accumulated, piled up almost to the sky.
That man slowly crossed over the sand and stones.
Only Dàoróng saw it happen this way.
The onlookers all said that even though the water was so high,
this man was nevertheless able to float across.
They were all startled and amazed.
Dàoróng then returned to his home region,
secluding himself on Lángyé Shān.
He practiced abstention from grain
and ingested pine resin, Atractylodes, and Poria cocos,
seeking the secrets of longevity.
Soon after, he was summoned by Xiǎnzǔ to go to Jìnyáng.
When they reached Liáoyáng Shān,
a fierce beast appeared ten paces from the horse.
The men accompanying him were terrified and about to flee.
Dàoróng drew on the ground with his staff, creating a pit of fire.
The fierce beast immediately ran away.
Soon after, the state was overthrown.
Dàoróng defected to Zhōu.
He died early in the Suí dynasty.
There was also Zhāng Yuǎnyóu,
whom Xiǎnzǔ ordered to compound the Nine-Turn Golden Elixir with other alchemists.
When it was completed,
Xiǎnzǔ placed it in a jade casket,
saying:
“I am greedy for worldly pleasures
and cannot immediately fly up to heaven.
I will wait until I am about to die and then take it.”
Wáng Chūn
was a person from Hédōng.
When young, he was fond of *Yìjīng* divination
and was knowledgeable in wind omens (fēngjiǎo).
He traveled between Zhào and Wèi,
and could send talismans flying up to heaven.
When Gāozǔ rose up in Xìndū,
he invited him to be a retainer.
During the Battle of Hánlíng,
they were surrounded by enemies on all sides.
From the Yín hour until the Wǔ hour,
they clashed and separated three times.
Gāozǔ was about to retreat his forces,
but Chūn rode up to his horse and remonstrated, saying:
“By the Wèi hour,
we will certainly gain a great victory.”
He quickly tied up his son and presented him to the King as a hostage,
saying that if they did not win, he requested to be executed.
Shortly thereafter, the enemy was greatly defeated.
Subsequently, whenever he followed in military campaigns,
his predictions were often correct.
He reached the post of Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
and then died.
Xìndū Fāng
was a person from Héjiān.
When young, he mastered calculation methods
and was highly praised by his district.
He possessed ingenious thinking.
Whenever he studied intensely,
he forgot to sleep and eat,
sometimes even falling into pits and ditches.
He once said to people:
“The subtlety of calculation
— its mechanisms are ingenious and profound.
Whenever I immerse myself in deep thought,
I cannot hear the sound of thunder.”
His level of concentration was thus.
He petitioned Gāozǔ based on his technical skills and calculations and became a retainer,
later being appointed Cānjūn.
Zǔ Tǐng, the Storage Administrator under the Chancellor, said to Fāng:
“The technique of using pitch pipes to blow ash (lǜ guǎn chuī huī)
is extremely subtle.
It has been lost for a long time,
and my own thoughts cannot fathom it.
You should attempt to figure it out.”
Fāng subsequently paid attention to this.
After more than ten days,
he said:
“I have grasped it,
but it ultimately requires reed ash from Hénèi.”
Later, Hénèi reeds were obtained.
When he used the technique,
the ash that corresponded to the specific climatic node immediately flew out,
while the rest of the ash did not move.
However, the method was not valued by the people of the time
and was ultimately not implemented,
so this technique was subsequently lost again, it is said.
Fāng also compiled and arranged historical records of ingenious devices such as the armillary sphere (húntiān), seismograph (dì dòng), tilting vessel (yī qì), and water clock (lòu kè).
He also drew diagrams for all of them,
and named the work *Qìzhǔn* (Standard for Instruments).
He also authored the *Yuèshū* (Book of Music), the *Dùnjiǎ Jīng Sìshù* (The Four Arts of the Dùnjiǎ Classic), and the *Zhōubǐ Zōng*.
Fāng also privately compiled a calendar book,
named the *Língxiàn Lì* (Spiritual Constitution Calendar).
It calculated that months frequently alternated between long and short,
and that eclipses must happen on the new moon.
The evidence provided was very precise and clear.
He often said:
“Hé Chéngtiān also worked on this method,
but could not perfect it.
If the *Língxiàn* is completed,
there will surely be no further disagreement for a hundred generations.”
He died before the book was finished.
Sòng Jǐngyè
was a person from Guǎngzōng.
He understood the *Zhōu Yì*,
practiced the studies of Yin and Yang,
apocrypha, and prognostication,
and was also knowledgeable in calendrical computation.
Late in the Wèi dynasty,
he served as the Prefect of Běipíng.
When Xiǎnzǔ was serving as Chancellor
in Jìnyáng,
Jǐngyè submitted a memorial through Gāo Dézhèng, stating:
“The *Yì Jīlǎn Tú* (Prognosticative Chart of the *Yìjīng*) says: ‘The *Dǐng* hexagram,
the Fifth Month,
a sage rules.
Heaven grants long life.
In the water of the northeast,
a commoner becomes king.
Gāo obtains it.’
We respectfully submit that the 'water of the northeast' refers to the Bóhǎi Sea.
‘Gāo obtains it’
clearly means that the Gāo clan shall obtain the empire.”
This occurred at that time,
the fifth month of the eighth year of Wǔdìng of Wèi.
Gāo Dézhèng and Xú Zhīcái both urged Xiǎnzǔ to comply with Heaven’s will and accept the abdication.
He then traveled to Yè.
When he reached Píngchéng,
the great ministers blocked the plan,
and he was about to return.
Hèbá Rén and others also said:
“Jǐngyè has misled Your Highness.
He should be executed to apologize to the world.”
Xiǎnzǔ said:
“Jǐngyè is destined to be a teacher of emperors and kings.
How can I kill him?”
Upon returning to Bīng,
Xiǎnzǔ ordered Jǐngyè to perform divination.
He obtained *Qián* changing to *Dǐng*.
Jǐngyè said:
“*Qián* means the ruler,
which is Heaven.
The *Yìjīng* says: ‘Timely ride the six dragons to manage Heaven.’
*Dǐng*
is the hexagram for the fifth month.
It is fitting to take control of Heaven and receive the abdication during an auspicious time in mid-summer.”
Someone else said:
“According to the Yin-Yang texts,
one must not assume official office in the fifth month.
Anyone who violates this will die in that position.”
Jǐngyè said:
“This is actually greatly auspicious.
Since Your Highness will be the Son of Heaven,
there will be no date for stepping down.
How could he fail to die in that position?”
Xiǎnzǔ was greatly pleased.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he was granted the title of Sǎnqí Shìláng.
There was also Jīng Cìdé,
who possessed occult arts,
and predicted the success and failure of Ěrzhū Róng.
He also said that the state replacing Wèi would be Qí.
Gě Róng heard this,
and therefore styled himself King of Qí.
He treated Cìdé with extraordinary courtesy,
and asked him about matters concerning Heaven and man.
He replied:
“Qí ought to flourish,
and the Son of Heaven will emerge from Dōnghǎi.
Currently, Your Majesty occupies Bóhǎi,
which is the land of Qí.
Moreover, Tàibái (Venus) is aligning with the Moon.
It is advisable to deploy troops quickly;
delay will bring misfortune.”
Róng did not follow this advice.
Xǔ Zūn
was a native of Gāoyáng.
He was skilled in the Yì (Changes),
good at divination,
and also understood astronomy, weather prediction (fēngjiǎo), physiognomy (zhānxiàng), and fortune-telling (nìcì).
His predictions were like those of a spirit.
Gāozǔ invited him to be a retained scholar (guǎnkè).
He himself said that his destiny dictated neither great wealth and status
nor an unnatural death.
Therefore, he indulged his temperament, acting careless and unconventional,
often offending people,
but Gāozǔ always tolerated and accommodated him.
During the campaign at Mángyīn,
Zūn said to Lǐ Yèxīng:
“They are arranged in a Fire formation,
we are in a Wood formation.
Fire overcomes Wood,
we are certain to lose.”
It turned out exactly as he predicted.
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, appointed Zūn as Secretary in charge of field affairs (Tiáncáo Jìshì) in his administrative headquarters (kāifǔ).
When Yuè was enfeoffed as a Prince,
he informed Zūn.
Zūn said:
“Honeybees also make a king.”
Later, when Yuè was about to go and relieve Jiānglíng,
Zūn said:
“This journey will lead to misfortune later;
you ought to decline due to illness and not go.”
Yuè said:
“Circumstances dictate that I cannot avoid going.
I should proceed together with you.”
Zūn said:
“I prefer to accompany the living;
I do not wish to travel the same path as the dead.”
He returned.
Yuè arrived in the capital and shortly died.
Xiǎnzǔ’s immorality grew worse daily.
Zūn said to people:
“Bring many stalks for divination;
I shall divine when this madman is going to die.”
He then spread the divination stalks across his couch,
and declared loudly:
“He will not survive beyond the beginning of winter,
but I myself shall not see it.”
Xiǎnzǔ died in the tenth month,
and Zūn, indeed, died in the ninth month.
Wú Zūnshì,
courtesy name Jìxù,
was a native of Bóhǎi.
When young, he studied the Yì,
and entered the mountains to associate with reclusive Daoist priests.
Several years later,
he suddenly saw an old man who said to him:
“I grant you the Heart-Opening Talisman (Kāixīn Fú).”
Zūnshì knelt, received it, and swallowed it,
thereupon gaining mastery of divination and prognostication.
Later, he left the mountains and traveled to Jīngluò (the capital region),
becoming famous for his Yì divination.
When Wèi Wǔdì was about to ascend the throne,
he ordered Zūnshì to divine the matter.
The resulting hexagram was Míngyí changing to Bì, which yielded the reading:
“Initially ascending to heaven,
later entering the earth.”
The Emperor asked:
“What does this mean?”
Zūnshì replied:
“‘Initially ascending to heaven,’
means he will become the Son of Heaven.
‘Later entering the earth,’
means he will not last long.”
The outcome was ultimately as he said.
When Shìzǔ, acting as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), was guarding the capital,
he became suspicious of himself
and was filled with anxiety and dread.
He planned to raise troops.
Each night he prepared the divination stalks and ordered Zūnshì to divine.
Zūnshì said:
“You need not take action;
great felicitations will arrive naturally.”
Shortly afterward, the Prince of Zhàojùn, pursuant to the Empress Dowager’s order, recalled Shìzǔ via the imperial testament.
When he ascended the throne,
he appointed Zūnshì as Secretariat Recorder (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
but Zūnshì firmly declined, citing illness.
Zhào Fǔhé,
a native of Qīngdū.
When young, he was retained as a scholar (guǎnkè) due to his skill in the Yì and divination.
Gāozǔ died at Jìnyáng.
When the burial date was set,
Shìzōng wrote an edict ordering Xiǎnzǔ to personally divine and select the burial site north of the Zhāng Shuǐ (Zhāng River) plains, northwest of Yè.
Xiǎnzǔ and Wú Zūnshì chose the location.
Repeated divinations proved inauspicious.
They then went to another spot
and ordered Zūnshì to divine it.
The resulting hexagram was Gé (Revolution).
Zūnshì and several dozen others all said it was unusable.
Fǔhé, being young,
stood behind the crowd.
He stepped forward and said:
“The Gé hexagram is inauspicious for all ordinary people,
but for the royal family, using it is greatly auspicious.
The Judgment text (Tuàn cí) of Gé says: ‘Tāng and Wǔ changed the mandate (gémìng),
responding to Heaven and according with the people.’”
Xiǎnzǔ immediately mounted his chariot
and, looking back, said:
“Let this location be fixed immediately.”
This became the Yìpíng Líng.
There was a man whose father was ill.
This man went to the residence and privately asked someone he knew to divine.
The resulting hexagram was Tài (Peace).
The diviner said:
“This hexagram is highly auspicious;
the illness will heal.”
The man was delighted.
After the man left,
Hé said to the diviner:
“The Tài hexagram is Qián below and Kūn above (Heaven below, Earth above).
This means entering the earth (burial);
how can you call it auspicious?”
Indeed, news of the father’s death arrived shortly after.
During the Dàníng and Wǔpíng eras, Hé divined the births (gender and time) of children in the palace, often predicting correctly.
Consequently, he was appointed General Gentleman of the Palace (Tōngzhí Chángshì).
Huángfǔ Yù,
whose origins are unknown.
He was skilled at physiognomy,
and often traveled among the households of Princes and Marquises.
When Shìzōng returned victorious from Yǐngchuān,
Xiǎnzǔ followed behind.
Yù watched them freely from the roadside
and said to others:
“The Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) will not become the ruler;
it will certainly be the one sniveling by the north side of the road.”
After Xiǎnzǔ ascended the throne,
he decided to test Yù’s physiognomy skills.
He therefore covered Yù’s eyes with a silk scarf
and ordered him to touch various people one by one.
When he reached Xiǎnzǔ,
Yù said:
“This is the highest-ranking official.”
When he reached the Prince of Rènchéng,
he said:
“He will reach the position of Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).”
Regarding the two Princes of Chángshān and Chángguǎng,
he said they were both noble,
and secretly pinched each of them.
When he reached Shí Dòngtǒng,
he said:
“This is a clown.”
When he reached the palace chef (gōngshàn),
he said:
“He merely gets good food and drink.”
Yù once read the physiognomy of Gāo Guīyàn
and said:
“Your rank will be the highest among officials;
just do not rebel.”
Guīyàn said:
“Why would I rebel?”
Yù said:
“That is not the point.
You possess the bones of rebellion (fǎngǔ).”
Yù said to his wife:
“The one on the throne will not last beyond two years.”
His wife informed Secretariat Aide Hú Sīqìng,
and Qìng reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor angrily summoned him.
Whenever Yù looked in the mirror,
he said he would die by violence.
When he was summoned,
he said to his wife:
“I am leaving now and will not return.
If I can survive past noon,
I might possibly live.”
As soon as it reached high noon,
he was executed.
In the time of Shìzōng, there was a scholar from Wú,
who was completely blind but excellent at judging character by voice (sound physiognomy).
Shìzōng tested him repeatedly.
Hearing the voice of Liú Táozhī,
he said:
"He is bound to others,
yet he will achieve great wealth and status.
Many kings, marquises, generals, and ministers will die by his hand,
like a hawk or a hound used by a master."
Hearing the voice of Zhào Dàodé,
he said:
"He is also bound to others,
wealthy and dazzling,
but not equal to the former person."
Hearing the voice of Tàiyuán Gōng,
he said:
"He will become a ruler of men."
Hearing the voice of Shìzōng,
he did not react.
Cuī Xiān secretly pinched him,
whereupon he mistakenly said:
"He is also a ruler of the nation."
Shìzōng thought, "If my various servants are already destined for the highest status,
how much more so must I be!"
Xiè Fǎxuǎn,
was a native of Hénèi.
In his youth, he understood physiognomy,
and his judgments of people
always matched his predictions.
Hé Shìkāi often consulted him for physiognomy,
and Shìkāi appointed him as a Staff Officer (Cānjūn) of the Prefecture.
Wèi Níng,
was a native of Jùlù.
Because he was skilled at predicting fate and destiny (Lùmìng), he was summoned as a retained scholar (Guǎnkè).
Wǔchéng personally tested him,
and his predictions were all accurate.
Wǔchéng then used his own birth date and month, pretending it belonged to a different person, and asked Wèi Níng.
Níng said:
"Extremely wealthy and noble,
but this year he will enter the tomb."
Wǔchéng was startled and said:
"That is me!"
Níng changed his words and said:
"If it is an emperor or king, there is a different method [of interpretation]."
There was also Yáng Zishù,
who told people:
