"The popular rhyme says: 'Lú is sixteen,
Zhì is fourteen,
and the Ox-calf (Qiánzǐ) claps his head at thirty-two.'
Moreover, thirty-two (four times eight) is Heaven's great number,
the reign of the Supreme One (Tàishàng),
I fear, will not exceed this."
Soon after, Wǔchéng died,
aged thirty-two.
Qímǔ Huáiwén,
it is unknown from which commandery he hailed.
He served Gāozǔ with his knowledge of Daoist arts.
Early in the Wǔdìng era,
the imperial army fought with Zhōu Wén at Mángshān.
At that time, the flags and banners of the imperial army were all red,
and the western army's were all black.
Huáiwén spoke to Gāozǔ, saying:
"Red is the color of fire,
black is the color of water.
Water can extinguish fire,
thus it is not advisable to use red against black.
Earth overcomes water,
so they should be changed to yellow."
Gāozǔ therefore changed them to reddish-yellow (zhěhuáng),
which is what is called the Héyáng Banner.
He also manufactured the Sùtiě knife (steel left overnight).
His method involved forging fine raw iron repeatedly with soft bars,
and after several nights (sù), it would become rigid steel.
He used soft iron for the spine of the blade,
washed it in the urine of five sacrificial animals,
tempered it in the fat of five sacrificial animals,
and it could cut through over thirty layers of armor.
The Sùróutǐng (soft steel left overnight) now cast by the blacksmiths in Xiāngguó
is the remnant of this method.
The resulting knives are still very sharp,
but they cannot cut through thirty layers of armor.
Huáiwén said:
"Gānzǐchéng in the south of Guǎngpíng Jùn is where Gān Jiàng forged swords.
Its earth can be used to polish knives."
Huáiwén's official position reached Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Xìnzhōu.
There was also Sūn Zhèngyán,
who told people:
"In the Wǔdìng era, I was the Staff Officer of Guǎngzhōu.
I heard Cáo Pǔyǎn, a city resident, say: 'Of King Gāo's many sons,
Ābǎo will be the Son of Heaven.
When Gāo Dézhī succeeds him,
the dynasty will perish.'"
Ābǎo refers to Tiānbǎo.
Dézhī refers to Dèchāng.
The reign title at the time of the fall was Chéngguāng,
which means "to succeed/bear it" (Chéng zhī).
Zhāng Zǐxìn,
was a native of Hénèi.
His nature was pure and tranquil,
and he was quite involved in literature.
In his youth, he became known for his medical skills
and lived in seclusion on Báilù Shān.
When he occasionally traveled to the capital,
he was treated with great respect by Wèi Shōu, Cuī Jìshū, and others.
There are several poems dedicated to and exchanged with Zǐxìn.
Later, the Wèi dynasty summoned him as a Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
allowing him to return to the mountains when he wished,
so he was not constantly in Yè.
He was also skilled at Yì divination and wind omens (fēngjiǎo).
The Imperial Guard (Wǔwèi) Xī Yǒngluò was sitting opposite Zǐxìn.
A magpie was chirping in the courtyard tree,
fought, and fell to the ground.
Zǐxìn said:
"The magpie's omen is not good.
If, toward evening, a wind comes from the southwest,
passes over this tree,
and brushes the corner of the hall,
there will be trouble involving gossip and dispute (kǒushé shì).
Tonight, if someone calls for you,
you absolutely must not go.
Even if it is an imperial order (chì),
you must decline on the grounds of illness."
After Zǐxìn left,
a wind did come, exactly as he predicted.
That night,
Wáng Wǔ, the retainer of Lángyé Wáng, urgently summoned Yǒngluò,
claiming it was an imperial summons.
Yǒngluò wanted to get up and go,
but his wife strongly detained him,
claiming he had fallen from his horse and broken his waist.
The following morning, the disaster (nán) occurred.
Zǐxìn,
perished when the Qí dynasty fell.
Mǎ Sìming,
was a native of Hénèi.
In his youth, he understood medical techniques.
He was broadly knowledgeable in medical classics and prescriptions;
the Jiǎyǐ, Sùwèn, Míngtáng, and Běncǎo—there was none he did not recite completely.
When diagnosing people,
he could predict their life or death a year in advance.
Xíng Shào's son, Dàbǎo, contracted a cold-damage disease (shānghán).
Sìming diagnosed him,
taking his pulse.
He stepped back and told Yáng Yīn:
"Young Master Xíng's cold-damage illness will heal by itself without treatment,
but judging by his pulse, he will die within the year.
This realization came too late,
and cannot be cured."
Yáng Yīn and Xíng Shào were both attending a banquet in the inner palace.
Xiǎnzǔ said:
"Zǐcái's son,
I wish to grant him a nearby commandery appointment."
Yáng Yīn thought this boy was too young
to receive the seal of office (pōufú).
After the banquet concluded,
he reported:
"Mǎ Sìming states that Dàbǎo’s pulse is poor,
and he may die within a year.
If he goes out to a commandery,
medical care will be difficult to find."
Consequently, the matter was dropped.
Dàbǎo died before the year was out.
Yáng Lìng suffered from a swollen back (bèizhǒng).
Sìming applied refined stone (liànshí) to it, and he recovered immediately.
The method for making refined stone: Take coarse yellowish stone the size of a goose or duck egg,
heat it fiercely until it is red hot,
place it in strong vinegar,
whereupon it will crumble by itself.
Repeat the heating until the stone is completely crumbled.
Take the stone fragments and dry them in the sun,
then pound them and sift them through a sieve.
Mix it with vinegar and apply it to the swelling;
there was nothing it did not cure.
Later, he was promoted to Palace Assistant Remonstrant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
His acupuncture and moxibustion points
often differed from those in the Míngtáng classic.
Following the imperial carriage to Jìnyáng,
reaching the Liáoyáng Shān area,
in several places he saw notices,
stating that a certain family’s daughter was ill.
If anyone could cure her,
they would be rewarded with 100,000 cash.
Many famous doctors followed the notices and arrived,
but after inquiring about the symptoms,
they dared not attempt treatment.
Only Sì Míng treated her alone.
When asked about the cause of her illness,
she said she had once used her hand to hold an ear of wheat,
and immediately saw a red creature, two *cùn* long and snake-like,
enter her fingertip.
She then fell down in shock and terror,
and immediately felt her arm and hand ache and swell.
Gradually, half of her body also became swollen,
with unbearable pain,
groaning continuously day and night.
Sì Míng prescribed a formula and medicated soup for her to take.
By the time Sì Míng returned following the imperial carriage,
the girl had fully recovered.
Sì Míng,
died early in the Suí dynasty.
Biography Forty-two: Favorites (Ēn Xìng): Guō Xiù, Hé Shìkāi, Mù Típó, Gāo Ānàgōng, Hán Fèng, Hán Bǎoyè, and others.
How extreme were the favored courtiers at the end of the Qí [dynasty]!
It is likely something unseen since the invention of writing.
Their hearts were sharper than awls and knives,
yet they occupied the responsibilities of the high ministers (Tái Dǐng);
their knowledge was confused (unable to distinguish) beans and wheat,
yet they held the critical weight of governance (Jī Héng).
Castrated eunuchs mutilated by punishment, slave attendants (Cāngtóu Lú'ér), ugly Hú barbarians from the Western Regions, and musicians/performers (zá jì) from Qiūcí,
those enfeoffed as princes (Wáng) followed one after the other,
and those granted Kāifǔ status stood shoulder to shoulder.
They were not only court jesters restricted to personal service,
but they also frequently interfered with court politics.
The expense of their gifts and endowments
emptied the treasury;
the resources from weaving and spinning,
were about to be completely exhausted by plunder.
Even if the imperial mandate (guī dǐng zhī zuò)
had been divined to last forever,
encountering this decadence and darkness,
there was no reason why it should not perish.
That the Qí fortune was short-lived
was certainly appropriate.
Gāo Zǔ and Shì Zōng focused their energies on general governance,
and entrusted civil and military responsibilities
to many upright and capable ministers.
Only the petty man Guō Xiù
tarnished their luminous virtue.
After the fifth year of Tiānbǎo,
although [the emperor] lost his focus and acted wildly (wǎng niàn zuò kuáng),
the followers he favored merely rushed about assisting him,
being intimate with him both inside and outside the court,
but they were never allowed to hear about affairs of the imperial court.
After Dàníng,
the treacherous and corrupt gradually became numerous,
and the glorious undertaking and grand foundation
were consequently overthrown.
That the people were spared from becoming captives wearing hair unbound and folding their robes left-over-right,
was no small fortune.
We now compile these dangerous groups into the Biography of Treacherous Favorites (Nìng Xìng Zhuàn).
As for the cohort of eunuchs,
they were especially instrumental in the downfall of Qí.
Their scandalous reputations and filthy deeds
are endless and myriad.
Their specific deeds are omitted and not recorded here,
but their names are briefly retained,
and appended to the end of this biography.
The slaves of the imperial household and the Hú musicians/craftsmen,
who improperly attained high favor,
are also included here.
Guō Xiù,
was a man from Zhuō, Fànyáng.
He served Gāo Zǔ as the Right Assistant (Yòu Chéng) of the Mobile Secretariat (Xíng Tái).
His personal favor grew daily,
and he frequently received bribes and gifts.
When Xiù became ill,
Gāo Zǔ personally went to visit him
and asked him what office he desired.
He requested to be appointed Minister (Shàng Shū) of the Ministry of Arms (Qī Bīng).
He died before the appointment decree arrived.
Since his family had no adult sons or younger brothers,
Gāo Zǔ went personally to his residence,
and personally ordered officials to record the amount of his family's wealth, grain, and silk,
before leaving.
He commanded his son Xiàoyì to study alongside the Duke of Tàiyuán and those below him.
Previously, Xiù had been jealous of Yáng Yīn,
and had tricked and coerced him into fleeing.
After Xiù died,
Yīn returned.
Gāo Zǔ, recalling his anger at Xiù,
immediately banished Xiàoyì that very day,
and refused to associate with him for the rest of his life.
Hé Shìkāi,
courtesy name Yàntōng,
was a man from Línzhāng, Qīngdū.
His ancestors were Hú merchants from the Western Regions (Xīyù),
originally surnamed Sùhé.
His father, Ān,
was respectful, diligent, and good at serving others,
and gradually rose to become a Palace Writer (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
Emperor Xiàojìng of Wèi once held a discussion assembly with court officials late at night,
and commanded Ān to look at where the handle of the Dipper pointed.
Ān replied:
"This servant does not recognize the Northern Dipper (Běidǒu)."
When Gāo Zǔ heard this,
he considered him simple and honest.
Later he became the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yízhōu.
Shìkāi was clever and intelligent in his youth,
and was selected to be a student at the National University (Guózǐ Xuésheng).
His comprehension was quick and sharp,
and he was highly esteemed by his peers.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
Shì Zǔ was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chángguǎng (Chángguǎng Wáng),
and appointed Shìkāi as his Executive Advisor (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Princely Establishment (Fǔ).
Shì Zǔ naturally loved playing *wò shuò* (a board game),
and Shìkāi excelled at this game;
it was because of this that he was recommended for the post.
Furthermore, he was flattering, clever, and obsequious,
and could also play the Hú *pípá* (barbarian lute).
Because of this, their intimacy grew.
He once said to the Prince:
"Your Highness is not a celestial man;
you are the Celestial Emperor (Tiāndì)."
The Prince replied:
"You are not a mortal man;
you are a mortal deity (Shì Shén)."
Their profound mutual affection was like this.
Xiǎn Zǔ, knowing his frivolity,
did not allow the Prince to associate closely with base people.
He criticized their excessive jesting and familiarity,
and banished [Shìkāi] to Chángchéng.
Later he was appointed Staff Officer (Cānjūn) in the Ministry of Personnel (Shì Cáo) for the Capital Region (Jīngjī).
This was at the request of the Prince of Chángguǎng.
When Shì Zǔ ascended the throne,
he was successively appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and given the rank of Kāifǔ.
He experienced the bereavement of his mother, Madame Liú.
The Emperor heard this and was deeply distressed,
sending the General of the Imperial Guard (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn) Lǚ Fēn to his residence.
He was instructed to attend to Shìkāi day and night,
only returning after the mourning garments had been prepared.
That same day,
the Emperor also sent a calf-drawn carriage to escort Shìkāi into the palace.
When the Emperor saw him,
he personally grasped his hands,
and wept bitterly out of sorrow.
He consoled him for a long time,
and only then sent him back.
Moreover, his four younger brothers were all reinstated to their former offices.
The extent of his intimacy and favor was thus.
He was appointed Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè).
The Emperor had previously suffered from a respiratory illness,
which would flare up violently whenever he drank wine.
Shìkāi repeatedly remonstrated, but was not heeded.
Once, when the Emperor's respiratory illness flared up,
and he again desired to drink,
Shìkāi wept with choked sobs, unable to speak.
The Emperor said:
"Your action here is a remonstrance without words."
Consequently, he did not drink again.
His speech and demeanor
were extremely coarse and irreverent.
Day followed night [in their revelry],
and the rites between sovereign and minister were completely abandoned.
He even said to Shì Zǔ:
"All emperors and kings since ancient times
have entirely turned to ash.
How are Yáo, Shùn, Jié, and Zhòu ultimately different?
Your Majesty should, while young and vigorous,
indulge in pleasure as you wish,
and act without restraint.
One day of enjoyment is worth a thousand years.
Entrust state affairs to the great ministers;
why worry that they won't be managed?
There is no need to toil and exhaust yourself."
Shì Zǔ was greatly pleased.
In the twelfth month of that year,
Shì Zǔ fell ill in the Qiánshòu Diàn palace,
and Shìkāi entered to attend him with medicine.
Shì Zǔ claimed that Shìkāi possessed the talents of Yī [Yǐn] and Huò [Guāng],
and earnestly entrusted the future affairs [of the state] to him.
Just before dying,
he grasped Shìkāi’s hand and said:
"Do not fail me."
And then expired in Shìkāi’s hands.
The Hòuzhǔ, based on the trust given by the
Shìzǔ, relied deeply upon him.
Moreover, he had previously gained favor with
Hú Tàihòu, and thus became exceedingly intimate with her.
Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì, along with Lóu Dìngyuǎn and others, plotted to expel Shìkāi,
and gathered various nobles to form a strategy.
When Hú Tàihòu hosted the court nobles for a feast at the Qiándiàn,
Ruì personally presented Shìkāi's crimes and failures,
saying:
"Shìkāi was the late Emperor's favorite courtier,
a 'city fox, shrine rat' (a hidden menace),
who accepted bribes and goods,
defiling and disrupting the imperial chambers.
We, your subjects, morally cannot keep silent,
and dare to present this even risking death."
Hú Tàihòu said:
"When the late Emperor was alive,
why did you, the King and others, not speak?
Do you now wish to deceive this orphan and widow?
Just drink your wine,
and speak no more."
Ruì's words and demeanor grew increasingly severe.
Someone else said:
"If
Shìkāi is not expelled, the court and the land will not be settled."
Ruì and the others either threw their caps to the ground,
or stood up, shaking out their robes;
their speech was furious and aggressive,
stopping at nothing.
The next day,
Ruì and the others went together to the Yúnlóngmén,
ordering Wén Yáo to enter and memorialize the matter,
but Hú Tàihòu refused to listen.
Duàn Sháo called Hú Chángcàn to relay a message,
and Hú Tàihòu said:
"The Zǐgōng is still awaiting burial;
this matter is too great and hasty.
I wish the King and the others would reconsider."
Zhàojùn Wáng and the others then bowed and apologized,
and made no further comments.
Hú Tàihòu and the Hòuzhǔ summoned Shìkāi for an interview and questioned him.
Shìkāi said:
"Among the late Emperor's officials,
he treated me with the greatest weight.
Your Majesty has only just entered the period of mourning ([Liàng'ān]);
all the high officials harbor greedy ambitions.
If you expel me,
it will be precisely clipping Your Majesty's wings.
You should tell Ruì and the others: 'Let Shìkāi be appointed to a province,
wait until the burial rites are over,
and then send him away.'
Ruì and the others will believe I am truly leaving,
and will surely rejoice in their hearts."
The Hòuzhǔ and Hú Tàihòu agreed with this,
and informed Ruì and the others according to Shìkāi's suggestion,
appointing Shìkāi as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu.
When the imperial burial was completed,
Ruì and the others urged Shìkāi to depart.
Shìkāi loaded beautiful women, pearl screens, and various treasures, and went to Dìngyuǎn,
apologizing and saying:
"The various nobles wished to kill Shìkāi,
but I received the King's special grace in sparing my life
and appointing me as a regional governor (fāngbó).
Now that I am about to respectfully depart,
I humbly present two women and one pearl screen."
Dìngyuǎn was pleased,
and said to Shìkāi:
"Do you wish to return inside [the palace] or not?"
Shìkāi replied:
"Having been inside for a long time,
I was constantly uneasy.
Now that I have been allowed to leave,
it truly accords with my original intention.
I do not wish to return inside,
but only beg for the King's protection,
that I may long remain Governor of a large province.
As I depart far away today,
I wish to pay my respects and bid farewell to the two Majesties (Èrgōng)."
Dìngyuǎn consented.
Shìkāi was thus able to see Hú Tàihòu and the Hòuzhǔ,
and he offered advice, saying:
"The late Emperor suddenly ascended to the heavens;
I am ashamed that I could not die myself.
Observing the current state of the court nobles, they intend to make Your Majesty a puppet (Qiánmíng).
After I leave,
there will certainly be a great change.
How will I then face the late Emperor in the afterlife?"
Upon this, he wept bitterly.
The Emperor and Hú Tàihòu both cried,
and asked what course of action should be taken.
Shìkāi said:
"Since I have already been allowed back in,
what else is there to worry about?
Only a few lines of imperial edicts are required."
Thereupon, an edict was issued dispatching Dìngyuǎn as Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and accusing Zhàojùn Wáng Ruì of the crime of disloyalty (bùchén),
summoning him and killing him.
Shìkāi was reappointed as Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng) and Right Director of the Department of State Affairs (Yòu Púshè).
Dìngyuǎn returned the gifts Shìkāi had given,
and further bribed him with additional treasures.
In the first year of Wǔpíng (570),
he was enfeoffed as Huáiyáng Wáng,
and appointed as Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) and Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì),
his original official posts all being reinstated as before.
During the time of the Shìzǔ,
Shìzǔ ordered Shìkāi to play *wòshuò* (a board game) with Hú Tàihòu.
Furthermore, his entry and exit from the inner chambers had no set limits,
and he consequently engaged in illicit relations with Hú Tàihòu.
After the Shìzǔ died,
he became even more reckless.
Lángyé Wáng Yǎn hated him,

and plotted to execute him with Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn) Shèdí Fúlián, Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng) Féng Zǐcóng, Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ) Wáng Zǐyí, and Commander of the Imperial Guard (Wǔwèi) Gāo Shěluò, among others.
Fúlián mobilized the capital district soldiers,
stationing them outside the Shénwǔmén and Qiānqiūmén,
and secretly instructed them
not to allow Shìkāi to enter the palace hall.
On the morning of the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month of that year,
Shìkāi attended court early according to custom.
Fúlián stepped forward, took Shìkāi's hand, and said:
"There is a great piece of good news now."
Wáng Zǐyí immediately handed him a sealed box,
saying:
"There is an imperial edict ordering the King to proceed to the Grand Council (Tái)."
Soldiers were dispatched to guard and escort him,
and he was imprisoned in the office of the Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhìshū Shìyù Tīngshì).
Yǎn sent Commander (Dūdu) Féng Yǒngluò to execute him at the Grand Council.
He was forty-eight years old at the time,
and his household was registered and confiscated.
Later, Yǎn and the others were executed.
The Emperor grieved deeply,
not attending to affairs for several days,
and constantly recalling Shìkāi.
An edict was issued restoring his son Dàoshèng as Palace Attendant (Chángshì).
Furthermore, his younger brother Shìxiū was ordered to enter the Inner Secretariat (Nèishěng) to participate in handling confidential matters.

An edict posthumously granted Shìkāi the titles of Acting Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Ten Provinces (Shí Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), Left Chancellor (Zuǒ Chéngxiàng), and Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi), as before.
Shìkāi's natural disposition was common and vulgar;
he did not read books or commentaries.
In speaking and discoursing,
he relied solely on flattery for gain.
After the Héqīng and Tiāntǒng eras,
his power and authority grew increasingly strong.
Wealthy merchants and great traders filled his gate morning and evening.
Many court officials who lacked integrity attached themselves to him,
some even becoming his adopted sons,
ranking alongside common marketplace men as brothers.
There was also a certain gentleman
who once attended Shìkāi
when he fell ill.
The physician said:
"The King's typhoid is extremely severe,
and standard medicines will be ineffective.
You ought to take Huánglóng Tāng."
Shìkāi looked troubled.
This person said:
"This substance is very easy to take;
the King need not be suspicious.
Please allow me to taste it first for the King."
He finished it in one gulp.
Shìkāi was deeply moved by this loyalty,
and forced himself to take it.
Consequently, he sweated and recovered from his illness.
Such was the extent of his influence over the imperial court.
Even those who served him by unorthodox means (zuǒdào),
regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, were all promoted;
However, those who opposed him based on righteous principles,
he was also largely able to forgive (or spare) them.
When Shìkāi saw someone about to be subjected to punishment or execution,
he often worked to rescue them.
Once they were spared punishment,
he would immediately hint or instruct them,
demanding rare treasures from them,
calling these items 'life-ransoming goods.'
Although lives were saved,
it is said that none of it was done through upright means.
originally had the surname Luò.
He was a native of Hànyáng.
His father, Chāo,
was executed for plotting rebellion.
Típó’s mother, Lù Lìngxūan, had once been assigned to the imperial palace women's quarter (yètíng).
When the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) was in swaddling clothes,
she was ordered to raise him,
and was called his foster wet nurse (gān ā nǎi).
She thus became greatly cherished and loved by the Empress Hú (Hú Hòu).
Lìngxūan was crafty, cunning, and highly articulate,
using countless ways to curry favor.
Within the inner palace,
she alone dominated power and fortune.
Early in the Tiāntǒng era,
she presented Típó to serve the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ).
He was at the sovereign's side day and night,
and was greatly favored and intimately indulged.
Their playing and jesting were scandalous and obscene;
there was nothing they did not do.
His favor and treatment became exceedingly grand,
his offices and titles were beyond measure,
until he reached the position of Director of the Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū Shì),
and was invested as the Prince of Chéngyáng (Chéngyáng Wáng).
Lìngxūan also used flattery and seductive charm,
and Mù Zhāoyí adopted her as a mother.
It was for this reason that Típó changed his surname to Mù.
When Empress Mù (Mù Hòu) was established,
Lìngxūan was titled Grand Madam (Tàijī).
This was the title for the mother of the Empress in the Qí dynasty,
ranking as the First Grade (Dìyī Pǐn),
and her place in the ranks was above that of the Grand Princesses (Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ).
Since the Wǔpíng era,
the power of Lìngxūan and her son overshadowed both the court and the country.
All incompetent and mediocre officials trembled and held their breath before them.
Beyond this, their power to kill, grant life, seize, or bestow cannot be fully recounted.
When the army at Jìnzhōu was defeated,
and the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) returned to Yè,
Típó fled and surrendered to the Zhōu army.
Lù Lìngxūan committed suicide.
All her descendants, young and old, were executed in the marketplace,
and their household property was confiscated.
Gāo Ānàgōng
was a native of Shànwú.
His father, Shìguì,
had followed Emperor Gāozǔ when he raised his banner of righteousness.
Ānàgōng served as a warehouse administrator.
He followed in military campaigns and punitive expeditions,
and was promoted to General of the Guards (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn) for his meritorious service.
Gōng was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
he was eloquent, clever, and adept at serving others.
Whenever there was a banquet or archery practice,
he was greatly loved and valued by Emperor Shìzǔ.
Furthermore, he flattered and pleased Hé Shìkāi,
and they were particularly intimate and familiar.
Shìkāi often spoke on his behalf,
so he was increasingly favored and trusted.
When the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Left Vice-Director of the Department of State of the Bìng Province (Bìng Shěng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè),
invested as the Prince of Huáiyīn (Huáiyīn Wáng),
and further appointed Director of the Department of State of the Bìng Province (Bìng Shěng Shàngshū Lìng).
Gōng's talents and skills were mediocre,
he was not involved in literature or history.
His judgment and utility were especially inferior to Shìkāi's,
and his cunning and scheming ability also did not match Shìkāi.
Since he was favored by Emperor Shìzǔ,
he was often ordered to attend the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
This is why he was greatly cherished and favored.
After Shìkāi died,
the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) believed his judgment and demeanor were sufficient to succeed Shìkāi,
and thus granted him the position of prime minister.
In the fourth year of Wǔpíng (Wǔpíng Sī Nián),
he was ordered to serve as Director of the Affairs of the Department of State (Lù Shàngshū Shì),
and further managed all external military affairs and confidential matters of the inner court.
Yuán Shī, a Secretariat Department Director (Shàngshū Lángzhōng), once advised Gōng, saying:
"When the dragon appears,
we ought to perform the Yú sacrifice."
Gōng asked Shī:
"Where did the dragon appear?
What color was it?"
Shī replied:
"This is the appearance of the Dragon Constellation (Lóng Xīng),
requiring the Yú sacrifice;
it is not the appearance of a physical dragon."
Gōng exclaimed:
"You Hàn fellows are so determined to know the constellations!"
His dullness was exactly like this.
He was also made Right Chancellor (Yòu Chéngxiàng),
while his other posts remained as before.
When the Zhōu army pressed towards Píngyáng,
the Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) was hunting at Tiānchí.
Jìnzhōu frequently sent urgent reports.
From dawn until noon,
courier horses arrived three times.
Gōng said:
"His Majesty (Dàjiā) is currently enjoying himself;
why the rush to report this?"
In the evening,
another messenger arrived,
saying:
"Píngyáng city has already fallen,
and the bandits are now arriving."
Only then was the matter reported to the sovereign.
Early the next morning,
he immediately wanted to mobilize the troops,
but Empress Shūfēi requested one more round of hunting.
When the army departed for Jìnzhōu,
Gōng was ordered to lead the vanguard forward,
and also generally oversee all armies.
The Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) asked Gōng:
"Should we fight,
or should we not fight?"
Gōng replied:
"Do not fight;
instead, defend Gāoliáng Qiáo."
Ān Tǔgēn said:
"They are just a handful of bandits;
we should spear them immediately and throw them into the Fén Hé."
The Emperor's intention remained undecided.
The various inner attendants said:
"They are the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ),
and we are also the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
Since they were able to travel so far,
why should we defend and show weakness?"
The Emperor said:
"This saying is correct."
Thereupon, they gradually advanced.
Típó observed the battle.
When there were some soldiers retreating on the eastern flank,
Típó departed, saying:
"Run, Your Majesty (Dàjiā)!
Run, Your Majesty (Dàjiā)!"
The Emperor, with Shūfēi, fled towards Gāoliáng Guān.
Xī Cháng, a Commander (Kāifǔ), remonstrated, saying:
"Advancing partially and retreating partially
is the normal course of battle.
Currently, the troops are entirely intact,
and have not yet suffered defeat or injury.
Where can Your Majesty flee, abandoning this position?
The moment the Imperial Horse moves,
people's minds are startled and thrown into confusion.
You should quickly return and calm them."
Zhāng Chángshān, a General of the Guards (Wǔwèi), arrived from the rear,
and also said:
"The troops have already been recalled
and are very orderly.
The soldiers besieging the city have also not moved.
Your Supreme Highness (Zhìzūn) should return.
If you do not believe your servant's words,
I request to take an inner attendant to go and see."
The Emperor was about to follow this advice.
Típó pulled the Emperor's sleeve and said:
"These words are hard to trust."
The Emperor then rode north rapidly.
A soldier reported, claiming that Ānàgōng had sent him to recruit and lead in the Western Army,
and he was now deliberately reporting this.
The Later Ruler (Hòuzhǔ) ordered the Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng), Húlǜ Xiàoqīng, to investigate.
Xiàoqīng said:
"This man is speaking falsely."
Upon returning to Jìnzhōu,
a close confidant of Ānàgōng reported Gōng's plot to rebel.
This was also dismissed as false,
and the confidant was executed.
They then hastily returned to Yè.
The imperial guards and attendants had scattered and fled;
only Ānàgōng and a few dozen inner palace officials on horseback accompanied the Emperor.
After the Hòuzhǔ fled across Tàiháng,
Gāo Ānàgōng led several thousand men to surrender at Jìzhōu Pass,
and furthermore dispatched scouts.
Each report stated:
“The Zhōu army has not yet arrived,
and is currently assembling troops in Qīngzhōu;
there is no need to travel south yet.”
When the Zhōu general Yùchí Huǐng reached the pass,
Gōng immediately surrendered.
People at the time all said that Gōng had indicated
his wish to capture the Qí ruler alive and hand him over to Zhōu Wǔdì,
which is why he did not report the army’s arrival quickly,
leading to the Hòuzhǔ’s capture.
When Gōng arrived in Cháng'ān,
he was granted the title of Dà Jiàngjūn,
enfeoffed as a Gōng,
and made the Cìshǐ of Lóngzhōu.
He was executed.
In the beginning, during the Tiānbǎo era,
Xiǎnzǔ returned to Yè from Jìnyáng.
A drunken monk, Ātūshī, shouted loudly on the road,
calling Xiǎnzǔ by his full name and saying:
“Ānàguī will eventually destroy your state.”
At that time, Ānàguī, the ruler of the Rúrú, was powerful and prosperous north of the Great Wall.
Xiǎnzǔ was extremely wary of him,
which is why he launched punitive expeditions every year.
Later, those who caused the destruction of Qí were then attributed to Gāo Ānàgōng.
Although the character used is
“Gōng”
people of the time universally pronounced it with the sound of
“Guī”
This is truly
“the one who destroys Qín will be Hú (barbarian)” —
it was determined long ago in the darkness.
Hán Fèng,
courtesy name Chángluán,
was a native of Chānglí.
His father, Yǒngxīng,
was the Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
Fèng was intelligent and observant in his youth,
possessed great physical strength,
and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He was gradually promoted to Dūdū.
When the Hòuzhǔ resided in the Eastern Palace
and was young,
Shìzǔ selected twenty Dūdū to send to serve as his guard,
and Fèng was among them.
The Hòuzhǔ personally approached the group, took Fèng’s hand, and said:
“Dūdū, come look at the child.”
He was recognized because of this,
and was frequently called upon to play games together.
After the Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
Fèng was repeatedly promoted to Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn,
and was in overall charge of the inner court’s confidential affairs.
Zǔ Tǐng once discussed affairs with Fèng in front of the Hòuzhǔ.
Tǐng said to Fèng:
“There is no way to yield regarding strong bows and long spears,
but how can you contend with me
regarding military and state planning?”
Fèng replied:
“Everyone expresses their own views;
it is not dependent on whether one is superior in civil or military affairs.”
He was enfeoffed as the King of Chānglí Commandery.
His son, Bǎorén, married a princess.
In Jìnyáng, he was bestowed a mansion.
When the princess’s son, Chāng, reached his full month,
the Emperor visited Fèng’s residence,
and the banquet lasted the whole day.
All essential and secret affairs of the military and state
passed through his hands.
He, Gāo Ānàgōng, and Mù Típó jointly held central power,
and were called the “Three Nobles.”
They damaged the state and corrupted governance,
worsening day by day.
When Shòuyáng was captured,
Fèng and Mù Típó, upon hearing the news of defeat,
continued playing board games without stopping,
saying:
“It is someone else’s property;
let it go as it may.”
Later, the Emperor ordered him to build fortifications on the river bank at Líyáng,
saying:
“In an emergency, we can temporarily hold this place and become the son of the Guīcí state.
Life is fleeting and pitiful,
we should only seek pleasure.
Why should we worry?”
The ruler and minister responded to each other in this manner.
His younger brother, Wànsuì,
and his two sons, Bǎoxíng and Bǎoxìn, were all made Kāifǔ Yítóng.
Bǎoxìn married a princess,
and the Emperor again visited his residence.
All his relatives received official appointments and rewards.
Fèng’s mother, Xiānyú,
was the niece (daughter of a paternal aunt) of Duàn Xiàoyán’s mother.
Because of this connection, they became closely affiliated,
and Fèng recommended sending Xiàoyán to supervise the construction of the Jìnyáng Palace.
Chén Déxìn rode a relay post horse to inspect the work,
and saw that Xiàoyán was using imperial laborers and craftsmen to build his own residence.
He immediately told him:
“Púshè, the sovereign’s terrace and palace hall have not been completed.
How can you start building your own residence first?”
Fèng and Mù Típó also sent Xiàoyán to allocate laborers and craftsmen to build residences for themselves.
Déxìn returned and reported everything truthfully.
When the Emperor arrived in Jìnyáng,
Déxìn also reported that Fèng used imperial horses for others to ride.
The Emperor became enraged because of this,
and Fèng and Típó were both dismissed from their posts,
though their crimes were not publicly disclosed.
Their residences were subsequently demolished,
and the princess was divorced.
Fèng was then sent to the Bureau of Official Selection in Yè to act as a subordinate official.
When the Hòuzhǔ fled from Jìnyáng and returned,
Fèng was ordered to enter the palace,
and shortly thereafter an imperial edict restored his noble rank.
He followed the Hòuzhǔ across the Yellow River,
and upon reaching Qīngzhōu,
was captured by the Zhōu army along with him.
Among those holding power, Fèng
was particularly jealous of men of letters.
The cruel injustices suffered by Cuī Jìshū and others
were all Fèng’s doing.
Whenever court officials consulted him regarding affairs,
none dared to look up,
and he would frequently curse and scold them,
often reviling them, saying:
“These dog Han people are utterly intolerable;
they just need to be killed off.”
If he saw a military officer,
even one of the lowest ranks among personal retainers, he would tolerate them.
In the service of Suí,
his highest position was Cìshǐ of Lǒngzhōu.
Hán Bǎoyè, Lú Lèchā, and Qí Shào
were all former attendants of Gāozǔ.
They only served as eunuchs for domestic chores
and did not receive favor or grace.
Throughout the reigns of Tiānbǎo and Huángjiàn,
they never achieved great favor,
but gradually gained functional responsibilities.
Bǎoyè reached the position of Chángqiū Qīng,
and Lèchā and others were sometimes made Zhōng Chángshì.
During Shìzǔ’s time, there were individuals like Cáo Wénbiāo and Dèng Chángyóng,
who also reached the rank of Yítóng entitled to official salary.
However, only Chángyóng served as a participating chancellor during the Wǔpíng era
and interfered with court power.
Later, Bǎoyè, Lèchā, Qí Shào, and his son Zhēng were all enfeoffed as kings,
and were nothing more than oppressors.
During the reign of the Hòuzhǔ,
there were dozens of people including Chén Déxìn,
who all gave free rein to their treachery and flattery,
ruining governance and brutalizing the people—
something unprecedented in ancient and modern times.
Many were granted the title of Kāifǔ,
rarely stopping at Yítóng,
and some were also promoted to Guānglù Dàfū,
with gold seals and purple ribbons.
Many held the posts of Shìzhōng and Zhōng Chángshì;
there were dozens of people holding these two positions,
and they were all also enfeoffed as kings and Kāifǔ.
They passed in and out of the palace gates,
came and went in the imperial gardens,
attending constantly by the Emperor's side,
day and night.
They watched the Emperor’s expression
and competed in flattery,
making sure that every word they uttered and every action they took
met the deepest intentions [of the Emperor].
A single reward from a jest
often exceeded ten thousand coins,
and their accumulated wealth was mountainous,
their greed insatiable.
They even made a Persian dog an Yítóng and a Jùn Jūn,
sharing its official salary.
Outside the Shénshòu Gate, there was a place where court nobles rested,
which people at the time called the Jiěxiè Tīng (Hall for Taking Off Equipment).
When the eunuchs, who sometimes stayed inside for many days,
were temporarily released to rest,
their horses were led up to the steps of the Shénshòu Gate,
whereupon they mounted them,
galloping rapidly, competing with their whips,
in groups of several dozens.
The horse dust invariably billowed.
The court nobles, ranging from Táng, Zhào, Hán, and Luò, all silently listened and avoided them,
daring not to speak against them.
In Gāozǔ's time, there were dozens of male servants (cāngtóu) such as Chén Shāntí, Gài Fēnglè, and Liú Táozhī,
who were all quick and resourceful,
and received some imperial favor.
During the Tiānbǎo and Dàníng reigns,
they gradually became powerful and esteemed.
By the Wǔpíng era, they were all Kāifǔ and enfeoffed as kings.
Those who did not reach the rank of Kāifǔ by Wǔpíng were posthumously granted the title of king.
There were also Hé Hǎi 何海 and his son Hóng Zhēn 洪珍, both of whom were made princes.
〔一四〕They were especially close and important.
Hóng Zhēn 洪珍 abused his power,
selling justice and official posts.
There were also several dozen people like Shǐ Chǒu Duō 史醜多, including Hú Xiǎo'ér 胡小兒,
〔一五〕all of whom were skilled dancers and singers.
They too reached the ranks of Yítóng Kāifǔ 儀同開府 and were enfeoffed as princes.
The eunuchs, still busying themselves within the palace,
made themselves convenient at the emperor's side,
gradually becoming intimate and close,
until they reached high official positions.
The Cāngtóu 蒼頭, initially personal attendants,
were entrusted with deep secrets.
By the time of the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ 後主),
they were former retainers from previous reigns,
who, by virtue of their diligent service,
had illicitly obtained these positions.
As for people like Hú Xiǎo'ér 胡小兒, whose eyes and noses were deep and sinister,
and who were utterly useless,
their irrational favor,
and their pushing aside of court nobles,
were especially hated and despised by the educated elite.
Among those who attained high official positions through music were Shěn Guò'ér 沈過兒, who became Kāifǔ Yítóng 開府儀同,
and Wáng Chángtōng 王長通, who at fourteen or fifteen
was granted a *jiǎjié* 假節 and made Inspector of Tōngzhōu 通州.
At that time, there was also a Kāifǔ 開府 named Xuē Róngzōng 薛榮宗,
who often claimed he could summon ghosts.
When the Zhōu 周 army pressed closer,
he told the Later Lord (Hòuzhǔ 後主):
"Your servant has already dispatched Hú Lǜ Míngyuè 斛律明月 to lead a great army forward."
The Emperor believed him.
Passing an ancient tomb,
Róngzōng 榮宗 asked the Palace Secretary Yuán Xínggōng 元行恭 whose tomb it was.
Xínggōng 行恭 jokingly replied:
"It's Línzōng's 林宗 tomb."
He asked again who Línzōng 林宗 was,
and Xínggōng 行gōng said:
"Guō Yuánzhēn's 郭元貞 father."
Róngzōng 榮宗 then went forward and reported:
"Your servant just saw Guō Línzōng 郭林宗 emerge from the tomb,
wearing a large hat,
*jímò* 吉莫 boots,
and carrying a horse whip,
asking your servant, 'Has my Āzhēn 阿貞 come yet?'"
At that time, many charlatans were like this.
A eulogy states: The fate of peril and demise,
a court of confusion and disorder.
The way of petty people flourished,
the way of noble people waned.
